name: Trek to Yomi
detailed_description: As a vow to his dying Master, the young swordsman Hiroki is sworn to protect his town and the people he loves against all threats. Faced with tragedy and bound to duty, the lone samurai must voyage beyond life and death to confront himself and decide his path forward. Cinematic Presentation Breathtaking camera angles and striking visuals in the spirit of classic samurai film create a true cinematic experience in Trek to Yomi. Stylish Combat Engage vicious swordsmen and supernatural beings with a streamlined combat system based around the traditional weapons of the samurai. Mythic Storytelling Experience an enthralling story of Hiroki during his fall against the forces of evil and heroic return to make good on his failed promise to save the people he swore to protect. Thrilling Soundtrack The thrilling action and somber moments are set against a memorable score designed to feel authentic to the time and place of feudal Japan.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm recommending this game, but please be advised: The combat is GOD AWFUL Everything else in this game is top notch – the presentation, visuals, audio design, voice acting, all set a high bar, But when it comes to the actual combat, this game fails the rest of its highlights..Definitely check it out for its wonderful design, and then when you're done, think of how this game could have benefited immensely from a finely tuned combat system. It is the only thing that holds it back.

_childDocuments_.review: is a game that holds promise underneath many issues broken at its core. Unfortunately, as the game continues, these core problems suck away every last breath of the game and every ounce of patience.  is a delight with its audio and visuals, capturing the work of Akira Kurosawa with the dark edge of Kobayashi. The set pieces are also faithful to Japanese samurai films, especially in the first two chapters. The gameplay's pretty solid for the first hour and a half, even if the combat's depth is minimal and occasionally unresponsive. Unfortunately, these issues get overwhelmingly suffocating by Chapter 3 and especially Chapter 5 and beyond.The combat from the beginning is rather simplistic, but it's passable as an introduction to the game. It's stiff, but it leaves a lot of room for expanding on as the chapters progress. The biggest problem with  is that the combat rarely evolves in any beneficial way as the game continues. Sure, you get combos, but most of them aren't valuable and don't give you more of an edge than the starting attacks. Plus, killing several bandits in a row stops feeling rewarding as your combat doesn't get better with each kill. Combine all that with enemy types getting more annoying, including rangers and obnoxious boss fights, and  rapidly becomes a test of patience.The story isn't all that special, either. While the influence from Japanese films is a nice touch, it also doesn't forge its identity from them. Instead, it blends together with every samurai trope you've seen three times. While this isn't anywhere near as big of a deal as the gameplay, the story's predictability doesn't help keep the game going once the gameplay starts nosediving. It feels like the devs had a great idea for a short and sweet 2-hour game and got forced to extend it further. Unfortunately, all of its good graces fell apart by the end of Chapter 5, and it didn't recover by the end.It's also worth noting that  is surprisingly buggy. I had at least one minor softlock, and I had more than one instance where an upgrade would disappear after dying, and I couldn't recollect it. Not to mention a good chunk of dropped inputs and hit detection oddities. I've heard many other, much worse bugs happen to others. Feels like  wasn't given enough QA time before getting sent to the world. I'm sure they'll iron out some of the glitches and maybe improve the combat later down the line, but I don't expect revisiting  or recommending others to try it out even if they fix it.At the end of the day,  is a huge disappointment. I don't want to rag on the developers too much, as I can tell both they and Devolver Digital have the best intentions. Unfortunately, with clearly not enough QA testing and questionable design choices,  falls short of its goals. There are far worse games out there, and  playable at the very least. At the end of the day, though,  proves that gameplay matters the most.

_childDocuments_.review: I might have not recommended this game after my first playthrough, but completing the game at least once unlocks Kensei mode which changed my opinion completely.In Kensei mode, both you and all non-boss enemies are one-hit kills. I feel like this is the way the game was meant to be played and I had way more fun this way than during my initial "normal" playthrough.The combat becomes much more fast-paced and most of the combat issues people mention (and I also experienced the first time) are minimized because you don't get locked into long parrying matches or get boxed in while your health is chipped away. Once you get the timing right, you can slash your way through groups of enemies with pretty impressive finesse.I also feel this fits the old samurai film aesthetic much better, as it was usually one slice one kill, not hacking away until the other guy's health drops to zero. I'm not one for super-hard, punishing games, and yet I finished the entire game in Kensei mode with much less frustration and much more enjoyment than the supposedly easier "normal" mode.The game looks great, the audio is great, the atmosphere (especially in the later levels) is great. It's too bad that the more fitting and fun way of playing the game is locked behind a less polished preliminary run, but it was worth it for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this game in 2024, I encountered a bug in the last chapter where all my skills and upgrades were lost. This has been an issue for players since its launch in 2022 and is still not fixed, despite the devs claiming that it is fixed in patch 1.02. Very frustrating and unsatisfying, as it is now impossible to finish the game in the hard difficulty. The only way to get around this bug is to start the game all over, since you can't load a previous save.

_childDocuments_.review: About halfway through, but I feel I can safely review it and have seen most of what the game will offer.  The biggest complaint I see is the combat, and it's sorta true.  You absolutely cannot button mash in this game.  I was getting super frustrated with it playing like it was Devil May Cry, but something snapped in my brain.  It's a rhythm game, the combat is a rhythm game.  Your buttons and reactions are squishy and inconsistent if you don't anticipate the enemy.  Learn your enemies movements and skill set, and you will become undefeatable like a samurai.  After understanding the rhythm, the combat became easy and understandable and I was able to withstand bosses and multi enemies like a true samurai.  Besides the hard to understand combat, the game is amazing.  The presentation is absolutely incredible.  Still camera shots, the sound design, and the filters make this a visual treat during every second of gameplay.  If you're able to forgive a combat system that differs from the usual and give it a solid chance, this game is incredible and I recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: So the good first:I love the artstyle,unique and consistent troughout,coupled with the camera angle and the set-pieces it's an interactive movie...and this is where it splits apart.If it were an FMV/Interactive WS then it would easily be a 9/10,however we are talking about a hack-n-slash...of sorts.Gameplay: A bit off a mess,you have good combos yet you will rarely use more than 2 or 3,primarily stun + finisher to recover health.Enemy attacks are supposedly telegraphed but it's 50/50 if it will hit you or if yours will connect.Enemy variety is fine in terms of different attacks,I've seen some ppl have complaints about variety but I think its sufficient,the problem is rather the A.I. itself,fighting swordsmen and specters is balanced but Spearmen & Headbutters is just painful,forget comboing just create distance and shoot them (kind of strange for a Samurai game no ?  short balance sucks and those flashy moves aren't going to be used for 2 reasons,the first I've stated,so you might be thinking ok just play it on easy,however then enemies die in 1-3 hits making the combos yet again wasted.Movement is also clunky at times,or the enemy jumps 20 meters but just as you are about to  terms of gameplay I'd go with a 3/10 not enjoyable,which is a shame considering the theme.And while on the subject of wasted potential....Story: Cookie-cutter through and trough,the dubious voice acting doesn't help either.You have the typical oblivious goodie-two shoes protagonist,Sensei that dies instantly,Love interest that goes ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nowhere and well I can't even call him an antagonist but the main "bad guy" of the story who is just P O W E R & G R E E D,however his presence is never strong enough to warrant any attention.This is basically the main story,Sensei dies,Then your love dies and then you go to Hell/Heaven,yet Hell/Heaven decides on some cosmic irony to send you back to kill the big bad or there won't be any balance to the universe...like some guy who to our knowledge has plundered 3 villages is the next Armaggedon or smth.So yea main story 0/10.There are some moments after CH4 which as a player I enjoyed,its more of self-reflection and values on the part of the player which is hightened a lot by the visuals,now that part if that was the main story I would have considered this as a pretty good niche game,as it stands now it's a rough gem that is visually appealing and separates itself from most titles that go for hyper realism or just goofy trash.結論として: Artstyle & Visuals are worth the buy if it's on a very steep discount,if you are looking for combat or a good story you won't find it here.

_childDocuments_.review: I  wanted to love this game. The design, story, soundtrack all of those things excellent. So why the downvote? Because the  combat destroys this otherwise perfect game. Inputs are getting ignored a lot of the time. Or just getting read double. For example boss time you wanna dodge roll to his other side and then land an attack. What does your character do? Rolls twice and misses the chance to hit the boss. Or just swing an extra attack without you even hitting a single button. Or the best thing just ignoring any input for a few seconds before moving which obviously means that you get at least one hit from an enemy before you can do something.  Same goes for all the attacks which are purposely slow so that its "easier" to read or rather to parry. Those slowdowns in the attacks are messing the timings more up than they are supposed to help.If it would not have been for this awful combat system which sometimes works as you want and sometimes just does whatever the hell it wants, this game would have easily been a candidate for my personal game of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was one of the most disappointing games of my entire life!I remember it, being announced at E3 2021 and I was so damn hyped for this game and was hooked by the visuals and the Kurosawa like vibes that I pre-ordered it! But unfortunately that's everything the game had to offer. And nothing more, even if it pains me to say.The story is a complete Cliche of modern perception of Samurai warriors fighting off the Mongol like Invaders/bandits and there's no deeper level to it, other than fighting spirits and zombie like enemies I guess? There is a try or two, to show the struggles of this Ronin we're controlling but personally I couldn't really feel his struggle and journey to become a mature samurai (which wasn't actually the case). Because it felt just raw and shallow! And at some point we have a literal: "Love is the death of duty"! What I mean by that, is that there's no subtlety whatsoever and the story isn't really loyal to the traditional samurai ways as far as I can say and your "option of choices" make it clear that the games focus is based on ones desires rather than the hardship and the consequences of being loyal to your cause. But to be honest, one can't expect such a short game to put its hands on such a delicate matter. There are definitely AAA games that have covered that part. (Come on, you knew I was gonna name Ghost of Tsushima!)About the gameplay I can only say that the combat is just unbelievably repetitive and no matter how many "combos" you use, it's still the same thing throughout the whole game with you slashing through enemies like cheese. And the lack of enemy variety doesn't help that either. You are constantly fighting the same enemies, just in different forms. The visual design of the bosses were cool though. The fights themselves however not...To be fair though, comparing the story and the gameplay of this game to its visual design is a mistake and also not fair to this indie game, because the visuals are simply superb and to try to match them to the same level is a hell of a hard job to pull off...But all in all, I think I hyped this game up too much for myself and at the end was the victim of my own high expectations! There may very well be people, who would enjoy this game. Not me unfortunately. At its best a 4/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me a little to give this a thumbs down but I don't think that Trek to Yomi quite manages to be the game it wants to be.Visually, it's a treat. The game uses camera angles to great effect and the grainy, monochrome presentation is well implemented. I can only imagine that playing this on an OLED display would be next-level stuff. Level design, though simple, isn't bad either. Particularly when Hiroki reaches Yomi.The combat mechanics, however, feel unrefined if not plain inconsistent. For this reason, along with the placement of shrines (i.e. save locations), the game felt unbalanced. It swung between being too easy to too hard. Combat, of which there is a lot, soon got repetitive. On more than a few occasions progress began to feel like a grind; I was kind of relieved when the play-through was over.There's some magic sauce here. The sound design is tight and there are some cool sequences, but Trek to Yomi's successes just got swamped by the weak game-play. Maybe a re-imagining of the combat system through a patch is too much to ask for, but some tweaks to the inputs / controls would go some way to allowing its shinier bits to shine. I'll be keeping a close eye on the developers' future releases.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Maybe not, but it is fun nevertheless. Block an enemy attack - and strike. This is the essential gameplay element. In the style of classic samurai movies, we slice our way through hordes of enemies in artful black-and-white graphics. Somewhere in Japan, sometime in the age of the Samurai. We play the swordsman Hiroki, first as a boy, then as a young man. At the beginning, we are still training to become samurai and are training with our master when suddenly the village is attacked by a horde of brutal bandits who slaughter the inhabitants, burn down the houses and rob everything they can find. While our master goes to defend the village, we are supposed to stay behind in the training hall and wait for his return. Of course, we don't do that and run through the village to find our master. In the process, we use our katana to defeat bandits. Fortunately, we are already a reasonably good swordsman and can thus defeat most bandits quite quickly. To do this, we block their attacks and counterattack immediately afterwards, which is enough to kill an enemy instantly in most cases. The first few dozen enemies are not very resistant and have no chance against our sword skills. We already have the ability to perform a heavy attack, but it's not really necessary in the early stages. Also combos don't play a big role in the beginning, we learn most of them during the game anyway. The first chapter ends with us facing one of the bandit leaders. He is fair enough to offer us a direct fight - in which he defeats us, of course. We are saved only by the sudden appearance of our master, who continues the fight against the bandit leader, injures him severely, but is himself mortally wounded. We swear to him that we will protect the village and its people from all threats before he dies. From now on, we are the samurai in the town - and that's where the introduction ends.With the second chapter, the game really begins. We are no longer a boy, but a young man who is not a head shorter than most of his opponents. For opponents there are many. Again, bandits who have descended from the mountains suddenly attack the area. Not only our village, but also the neighboring villages. And again the resistance of the population is not very effective, and women, children, old men are massacred (or otherwise maltreated), while the able-bodied men either die in battle or are captured. So we set out to eliminate the bandit threat. We run through the countryside, coming to villages in flames, where most of the inhabitants have been slaughtered, while bandits are always in our way, which we have to eliminate in a duel. Often there is more than one enemy at the same time, and sometimes we are attacked by enemies from the front and from behind. Sometimes we can talk to residents, or help them in their time of need and rescue them or their families from unpleasant situations. Our weapon is the katana, a sharp sword that we also know how to wield skillfully. As the game progresses, we'll learn more and more new combos, because soon a simple hit won't be enough to kill every opponent instantly. Besides the sword, we can also hurt enemies with throwing stars, but they are rarely enough to kill an opponent. During sword fights we have to watch our stamina, otherwise we won't be able to hit hard or block effectively.The game is entirely in black and white, just like the samurai epics by the famous Japanese director Akira Kurosawa from the 50s and 60s. While the visual impression is always that of an isometric (2.5D) perspective, movement is often restricted to pure 2D - hence we, like our enemies, only move along a line. This makes sense in combat, of course, because it means we can't miss the enemy to the left or right. Outside of combat, however, we can often explore the environment in 2.5D, so we don't just move left or right, but also up or down in the frame. In doing so, our character is sometimes shown up close, and often from further away. The game is dubbed with extensive voice acting - but completely in Japanese. Well, at least everything is subtitled, of course. If you understand Japanese, you'll probably enjoy it, but I would have preferred a translation, because I don't have time to read the subtitles during the action sequences. A gamepad is strongly recommended, this is a classic hack 'n slay game, you don't play something like this with a mouse or keyboard. Even though the core gameplay element is the sword fights, we keep improving our character as the game progresses. We increase our health, our stamina and we learn new combos. This doesn't make it a classic role-playing game, but it adds simple role-playing elements that provide a bit of variety.We move from room to room, often just from right to left (or left to right) - though later on we keep coming to places where there are multiple exits in different directions, or where we can enter houses. So what starts out as just running along a path soon becomes a bit more complex and invites you to explore the environment. Often we find shurikens, new combos or collectibles a bit off the direct path. What starts out as an extremely simple hack 'n slay (block/strike) soon becomes a bit more challenging when enemies are no longer eliminated immediately after a hit, bandits attack from all sides, the environment hides secrets and we can talk to some of the inhabitants of the land.Classic hack 'n slay action game in the style of old Japanese samurai movies. Stylishly in black and white, we shred our way frame by frame through hordes of bitterly evil bandits who murder and rob everything and everyone. We don't have to think long about who is good or bad - every enemy is just plain evil.

_childDocuments_.review: Although Trek to Yomi DRIPS with atmosphere, theme, Kurosawa-esque aesthetic and LIMBO-esque gameplay, the combat itself (of which there is quite a bit) is absolute trash. In fact, the combat is so bad, it makes the game almost unbearable to play.The combat mechanics themselves are ~conceptually~ fine (definitely Dark Souls inspired - you have a weak attack, a strong attack, a couple simple combos, a block, a parry, and a roll) it falls apart due to the fact that your inputs are frequently are often ignored or badly delayed. The slow, untrustworthy, unreliable controls absolutely ruin this game. Timed your block perfectly? Too bad, you character didn't block. Wanted to slash? Nah, nothing happens... you just stood there, and now you're dead. That. Is. Not. Fun.If the developers fix their completely broken, absolutely miserable combat, this could be an absolute blast. But as Shigeru Miyamoto once said: "A delayed game is eventually good, but a rushed game is forever bad." Clearly, this game didn't get the time it needed to be good, and they may never get the chance to fix that mistake. As it stands, Trek to Yomi is an inspired game that is, unfortunately, absolutely miserable to play. They were so close, too. Such a shame.Sidenote for Ultrawide gamers: The game supports 21:9 but inexplicably does NOT support 32:9. Ultimate Unreal Unlocker can be used to temporarily fix 32:9 aspect ratios, but the game WILL lock up after a while if you do. So also keep that in mind when making your purchasing decision.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I liked this game more, the hard difficulty setting is just frustrating, unlike souls games, it doesn't feel rewarding.But the story and art style was good enough to keep me going.The story is really good, the art style is one of the best and most unique I have seen till now. the close up combat was looking so good, I wish the whole game was a little more zoomed in.I wish I had chosen a lower difficulty, that way I'd have enjoyed the story a lot more.The combat is just extremely basic, it just has 2 facets, Hit and Parry. There are like 3 enemy types whose moveset is very easy to understand and once you get a good combo, it's just parry and combo.When I was playing on the Bushido (medium) difficulty setting, I was enjoying it till the moment enemies armed with guns came in, it's very difficult to parry and if you get hit twice, you die. At one scene, I had to finish 4 enemies and 1 gun man and I couldn't just move over to the gunman, I had to finish the 4 enemies while parrying not only them but also the bullets, I somehow killed them and turns out the checkpoint is after 3 such scenarios, it not only got frustrating but also ridiculous considering that I had to fight off the same bunch of enemies with a different backdrop 3 times.I just couldn't get past them so I lowered the difficulty, then game got way too easy, no challenge but atleast I wasn't frustrated with the combat and could actually enjoy the story.The story was good enough to want me to finish the game but the frustrating combat made me want to just leave this game midway.But it was a good experience and feel like it was worth the time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: Great visuals, not so great combat. As another review here already mentioned there are several combos to unlock, but you'll really only ever use a handful of them. Pro tips: Forward + Y + X kills most unarmored enemies instantly. Backward + X + Y stuns most enemies immediately, giving you an opportunity for a finisher which gives you health. Hint for the final boss: just parry and follow up with Y,Y. Rinse and repeat. Buy this game at a discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi undoubtedly looks beautiful, but as a game it isn't particularly good; the controls lack precision and the fights quickly become repetitive. Sadly, I also don't think it uses its aesthetics to particularly good effect: as pastiche it feels somewhat hollow to me. It evokes the feel of classic samurai films more in stills than when you're actually playing it. Still, it's short enough that if you're *really* into the aesthetics you'll get a kick out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, it was alright! I started on "hard" difficulty, but around chapter 3 or 4 I switched to "normal". The enemies were just getting annoying, like, at moments you're just getting overwhelmed with enemies and I was losing interest in the combat. These enemies were more difficult than the boss fights. The story kept me going, I was interested in the story. It is a story of revenge, loss, and honor, to name a few- and you play as a samurai with a classic cinematic experience to it. It's a nice game! Just the combat was a bit meh.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a relatively short game, but it felt very long and repetitive.It is a very linear game, which is fine as long the story is good enough, but the story wasn’t good.I think what most people like about this game is the art and music, some might like the fighting style and the challenge, which was ok.My main reason for not recommending this game however is the lack of chapter selection.Oh, did you want to explore the 3 other endings, that are about 1 min long each? Then play the game all the way from the start! I can’t imagine how any developer thinks it is ever a good idea to not include chapter selections.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to love this game so much. I love Kurosawa films and love the aesthetic, however, the combat in this game is half baked at best. At worst, it doesn't function at all. There's this weird delay with all of your actions that never really goes away, keeping you from feeling like you're fully in control at any given time. On top of that, there are many moves that enemies do that do more than the normal amount of HP damage to you and the game makes no mention of this and there's no way to differentiate between a super damaging move and a regular one. If there is, please let me know because I would love to understand what was going on. I found the bosses extremely frustrating as well because half of them you're unable to counter, leaving your only recourse the TERRIBLE dodge roll which I really don't think has any i-frames. You have to dodge behind the bosses to attack them from the safe side, however realizing you can do this is done weirdly since dodge rolling into basic enemies rolls into them and not through them. So the game breaks its own rule with the bosses, leaving the cohesiveness of the game fractured. Countering enemies when you do fight them is A: strange because of the slowdown effect that the game decides to use sometimes which means you're stuck waiting for the ability to continue attacking, and B: irrelevant because every SINGLE basic enemy can be killed in like three attacks because of the stun mechanic in the game. There are a variety of combos and movements you can do in the game, yet the devs decided to completely invalidate the whole thing by adding in a basic 3 hit combo that insta-kills every enemy in the game (and also heals you). Baffling.The story and locales are pretty interesting, at least. I enjoyed the film filter and some of the camera shots, but there are some instances where the camera is so far away that you can barely see what's going on. All this being said. if you do decide to give this game a shot, do yourself a favor and switch the game to easy mode and pretend like there's no combat. Interestingly, I think that the mode you unlock once the game is over (enemies die in one hit and you die in one hit) might be a better way to play it in terms of pacing, however I don't think it would make up for the unresponsive feeling controls. Focusing on more of a rhythm and flow angle, your movement through a level without stopping, would have made for a better game. Unfortunately, it's definitely not this one.P.S. The final boss is dumb and takes too long.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely pains me to not recommend this game, which I had looked forward to a long time & pre-ordered, but outside of the incredible art style it has very little going for it.-Controls are absurdly janky-Character often faces the other way despite not pressing the reverse option-Balancing on both normal and hard difficulties is awful (coming from a seasoned gamer)            -Hard difficulty completely invalidates what it feels like to use a Katana-Platforming is awkward-Dialogue is solid, but often overlapped, and crying is extremely loud-Checkpoints are either extremely close together or way too far apart-Combat itself can be extremely tedious due to questionable block windows and sword strike timings-Story is generic-Skills fill relatively useless outside of standard combat-Finishers are impossible to perform as it is insanely tough to tell when an enemy is stunned-It is absurdly easy for enemies to stunlock your characterUpdate 5/7/22After beating the game I would not change any of my complaints. In terms of positives, the graphical design is incredible, some of the combos feel good to pull off, and the music is top notch. If you are a patient gamer, I'd recommend trying it once it's on sale or if you have GamePass. The individuals criticizing this review are clearly Devolver fanboys or just braindead.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed playing this game, even though it got a lot of bad reviews when it first came out. I was patient and waited for the right moment to get it, and I'm glad I did.The graphics in the game are absolutely stunning, and they make the whole experience a visual treat. There's a lot of combat in the game, especially the boss fights, which are super challenging and intense. The music and sound effects are really well done and add to the whole experience. When I played, it felt like I was in a black and white Japanese movie. But, there were times when there were just so many enemies on screen, and it got a bit overwhelming and discouraging.It's important to mention that the gameplay and combat have gotten some criticism, but it seems like they were intentionally designed to be tough. If you're up for a challenge, you can still have fun with this game. One thing I liked was that there are plenty of checkpoints, which is a big plus. I can't make a final judgment about the game yet because I've only played up to Chapter 3, and I needed a break to collect my thoughts. I'll update my review once I finish the remaining four chapters.Also, I watched a review by a guy named Jack Baldinho (I hope I spelled that right), and he said the game gets more enjoyable as you play further. That made me reconsider not getting the game at all. I do hope I won't start dreaming about it, though – I tend to dream about the games I play at night. So, let's hope that if I do dream about it, I'll be a skilled samurai in my dreams.The game's level design is like a work of art, inspired by cinematic shots, and each frame feels like a carefully crafted theater set. I'm definitely looking forward to going back to this unique gaming experience. Ultimately, whether you should get the game or not is up to you. It's been a while since it came out, but I still think it's worth considering, despite the initial negative reviews. It's a playable and enjoyable game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are finding the combat to be a bit boring, I recommend CHANGING THE GAME'S DIFFICULTY TO HARD (you don't need to restart the whole campaign to do so). The game becomes a lot less forgiving, and once they start to introduce new enemy types, you have to recognize what is the best sequence and defense options against them, or else you will likely lose.I love the fixed camera angles. It reminds me a lot of Fear Effect rather than RE, with the scenario sometimes obstructing your view. Positioning yourself properly in combat, or interacting with the scenario to clear the view is important, so you can properly react to the enemies's attacks.Exploration is rewarded with items, collectibles and new moves, which can help you against the enemies you will eventually face and keeps the combat interesting, giving you new things to try.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version:An art gallery that comes bundled with one of the worst combat systems I've had an experience with.I don't recommend unless you want this game for the sake of visuals. 2/10 for combat.10/10 for visuals.Add in some form of NG+ at least or level select option, for the love of god.Overall a 4/10 game that's worth of looking at but not buying, even if I don't regret the money I chose to spend on it.Free-form version aka "I rant about whatever gripe I have in no particular order so it's going to be long" version.It's finally out. I've been waiting for the game, and I can't help but feel disappointed.Visuals - The game lulls you in with the artstyle, and let me be clear, every minute of this game is screenshot-worthy. I think this game holds a record on how many screenshots I took in a game. It looks gorgeous, and I saw at least one review that called it eye-straining, but I personally never found my eyes to be tired from looking at the game. Now, the visuals are where pros of this game end, because even though I didn't expect side-scrolling Ghost of Tsushima in terms of combat fidelity, I didn't even get a good game in it's own right when it comes to fighting enemies.Combat - It's cool when you're fighting just average bandits, but falls apart as soon as archers show up, or let's be fair, any other enemy variety for this matter. You have some pretty basic combos at your disposal, and at times combat can be split directionally because enemies surround you, plus you do get new moves via collectables and story progression. But worry not, you have a lottery roll with no i-frames, which sometimes CAN actually make you dodge an enemy attack. I love it when sometimes you get hit by an arrow which logically you roll under, but hitbox says otherwise. Don't even get me started on spearmen. It would be fine if only you'd know how the damn parry operates. When your timing is right, it enters this weird slow motion as to add to the cinematic flair, but the question is WHEN EXACTLY timing would be right? Sometimes you block way before an enemy even swings a sword and it parries the attack. Other times an enemy just skips a frame because you didn't block 3 years prior to enemy attempting to swing at you, so now you're getting undeservedly dusted. You cannot block projectiles nor dodge them, by the way. So it's always nice to see when your solution to a projectile enemy is to dash towards them, prioritizing targets, only to get a scripted kick which knocks you back, because you entered their hitbox range and they get a free projectile in because you just can't recover in time to do anything about it. And it's by design, so it's supposed to be fair. Solution? Strike before entering a projectile enemy hitbox so they enter their pain state/stagger. Sometimes you can get unlucky even by doing that, but most of the time it works. Sometimes there's also enemies with spears. You'd think that blocking and closing in occasionally would work, right? Wrong. You spam block so that you can parry every attack that spearman dishes out and kill them. You'll thank me later. Actually spamming block is viable tactic against almost every enemy in the game, because the game doesn't know any better, so it'll just begrudgingly snap you towards the attacking enemy at times, which is just an addition towards how bad the combat system is in this game. Boss fights - an actual JOKE. Laughably bad. You can beat final boss by spamming block and "parrying".Replay value - none. It has a system of choices, and there's 3 paths from what I've seen in total. Got the worst ending personally, and I'm not replaying this game. Those 5 hours are more than likely will be what I'll spend in total with this game. Which is fine, I didn't expect a long game, but I did expect some basic options like level selection or NG+ maybe, where you keep every collectable health points and stamina from your initial playthrough. But no, once you beat the game, no level selection, no NG+ option. Just a new difficulty. I played the game through on "Bushido" or "Normal", and at times I hated this game for how stupid some of the combat arenas were. So I'm not even going to pretend like I'm that one guy who wants a challenge. I just want a fair game to begin with. And in this game, new game means your collectables reset.Collectables - are in name only. When really those are upgrades. They're absolutely essential to your playthrough, and the game "encourages" you to look for the upgrades. You upgrade your health points and stamina meter in that manner. There are actual lore collectables, and I love that it's all about Japanese deities. As for upgrades, you can miss them by design, because often you will find yourself at a crossroads with two ways. Left and right. If you're lucky, one of the directions will end up having an upgrade. If not, you trigger a story event that will either bar you from backtracking (like rolling down the hill which you can't get back up on), or just end the level overall. Awesome, love it. If you will not look for upgrades, you're absolutely screwed even on Normal. Didn't find all of them because of cutscene or level end? Too bad, can't come back, there is no level select, as previously mentioned, so you can only deal with it.Wanna replay to see other endings/choose other options to see how narrative shifts? Play through the game again with having to look for collectables yet again. No thanks.Conclusion - I have utmost respect for indie devs looking to bring their creation to fruition. It's a real shame that this game is brought down by design. Artistically it's impeccable, and I think I'd rather get a story-driven walking simulator with these visuals rather than the fill-in abomination called "combat". Overall, unfortunately I can't recommend this game, and the issue isn't a price, it's mostly combat, honestly. I'd like to see this game being supported just for the sake of having a better sequel where maybe devs will collect feedback and iron out the issues of the first game. But supporting a subpar game isn't justifiable in itself just for the sake of "maybe" having some other iteration that would be better. If you like the aesthetic as much as I did, then I can't blame you. Nor would that be a really bad/regrettable investment. But in it's current state, I can't in good faith recommend it, so I'll mirror the sentiment from the start of this "review".Great game to look at, bad game to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to keep this review short.I was incredibly excited for this game when it was announced but after beating the game I felt nothing but disappointment. It's a big shame as the game is visually stunning, has incredible scenery and amazing camera angles.  The music made me incredibly nostalgic for Kurosawa's movies too. But visuals alone can't carry a game. The reason I cannot recommend this game is because the gameplay is some of the most boring I've ever played! it gets incredibly repetitive, especially on harder difficulties where fights are just sluggish and you repeat fighting the same enemies over and over. After the first two acts of the game, I'd seen the entire gameplay loop and it was dull to essentially just repeat the exact same combat over and over but with a different backdrop. _childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi is a unique experience that won't please everybody. The art style, imitating the works of early samurai movies with distinctive black-and-white colours, is a sight to behold and possibly the hook to catch everyone's attention. I personally enjoyed this design decision very much, albeit I have to admit that, in later parts of the game, it led to a couple of minor confusing moments. Enemy design is nice, but throughout the game, there is not much variety in them. However, this fits the plot and helps to better identify their strengths and weaknesses.The gameplay involves 2D hack-and-slash combat with both melee and ranged weapons like bows and explosives. The term "easy to learn yet hard to master" could be applied here, but, in general, fighting battles tends to become very easy and, unfortunately, somewhat repetitive towards the end. At some point, I would have been happy to completely avoid combat and instead take in the beautiful scenery and plot. Still, correctly parrying attacks and dealing out finishers feels satisfying.The story is intertwined with Japanese culture and beliefs about the afterlife. It feels predictable and cliché, but then again, it mirrors the old-school cinema feeling so well that I still found myself pretty much invested. Trek to Yomi gives players very minor options for story branching, but there are a couple of different endings. These won't necessarily reflect the choices you made earlier in the game, so it did feel somewhat pointless to offer them anyway.The voice acting was incredible, as was the sound design, which gave me some moments to rest and breathe in the mood of depression and bleakness you felt in feudal Japan, on your "Trek to Yomi". Combat wasn't bad ─ it just felt a bit too tedious. Maybe fewer, more capable enemies would have helped to make it feel more engaging. Overall, it is a game that plays with heavy atmosphere rather than catchy gameplay. It is an unforgettable, short experience that stops short of overstaying its welcome but offers something I haven't seen in many other games lately: a clear vision.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like Trek to Yomi, but this is underwhelming. The art style is wonderful, the story is nice, and the atmosphere, especially in the last half of the game, is very chilling. But where Trek to Yomi falls flat is in the gameplay. The combat controls are quite clunky, and there's not enough variety in the combat to experiment with. It's just light attack, heavy attack and block, with a couple of ranged attacks. That's it. That becomes boring after so long. Even though you unlock certain moves as you progress through the game, it's still boring in encounters, because the waves of enemies you face become increasingly annoying as you continue. Trek to Yomi is a very good idea. If the gameplay was better, if it was more fun to play, this could've been a very good game. It's very unlikely I'll be revisiting this game anytime in the future. A pity.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: This is an edited review, since all the gripes; myself and many others have expressed, have been dutifully adjusted by the devs. I was a bit critical of the combat, but now that the adjustments have been made, combat is now FUN and rewarding to the patient and focused. Difficulties seem noticeably balanced. Well done!The visuals and music are wonderful, and the fine attention to detail is gripping. One example that comes to mind is a particular setpiece in which you're running through a marauded village, and the camera is behind the silhouettes of onlookers in the second story of a building. It's as if you're one of the onlookers in the room. All these elements; big and small, weave what I'd consider a unique and creative experience that's worthy of the Kurosawa legacy. I don't particularly prefer the film grain option, but I definitely appreciate it. I praise the immersion of this game. The story is simple and digestible, nothing that left any sour tastes in my mouth. Although I've discovered there's multiple endings, so replay value exists beyond things like an extra mode (insta death for player/enemies), which is nice for me because I suffer from post-credit syndrome; no further plot incentive (or it's a sandbox game like GTA.) Voice acting, directing, and ESPECIALLY the music scoring are prime, again lending to the immersion and charm.Collectibles are a simple yet appreciated touch. They at-times provide backstory tidbits, but most are artifacts that provide brief summaries of Japanese myths and deities. Interesting if you're unfamiliar to Japanese mythology, but very cool if you are. Sidepath exploration is a major theme, and I love it. There's always a reward for doing so, even if it's uncommonly superficial. I feel like I'm being rewarded and acknowledged for stopping to smell the roses. Ammo, capacity, collectibles; all part of the unassuming or "wrong way" path. You may even find some very handy surprises at times. They also make the environments naturally more immersive since they bar any monotony of a completely side-scrolling experience.Infact, many setpieces have you moving Hiroki up, down, and all-around to get to the next objective. 2-D side-scrolling seamlessly transitions into isometric angles in exploration, while combat is always side-scroll. I suppose pre-release footage didn't emphasize this approach, so to see the game have a fair bit of multi-directional traversal is a nice surprise.So there you have it. A game that had a bumpy launch, but now fully lives up to its vision. If you're into Kurosawa, or just samurai, this is a must-have game.

_childDocuments_.review: Buy this on a sale.Around 5 hours of content. 3 paths to choose from.The thing which makes this game is the art,environment, audio and japanese voice acting. Top notch.Combat - Absolutely horrible. Delay in movement, enemies do weird things by randomly  going in and out of combat mid-fight so your hits intended for the enemies miss and you get hit instead, A weird predictive/slow-mo dependant parry system drives combat which is absolutely terrible.Fantastic story based game, atrocious combat. Buy on sale would be my suggestion.

_childDocuments_.review: Some style, almost no substance. Attempts to capture the feel of classic samurai films with a monochromatic style but a short and dull story and combat that starts awkward and bland and gets worse makes it hard to recommend. Combat lacks a visceral feel as even some of the weakest enemies can just ignore and attack through your hits, all getting worse halfway through the game when you start to fight undead and spirits. Combos and parries don't respond well, and parries don't really time like they do in normal video games while also being much easier to do than in most games that have them. Dull collectible hunting, a lot of useless lore items but you can also miss health and stamina increasing items as well as some combos of which there are already few of. All but the most basic enemies will likely have you just using a light, light, heavy combo to stun them to allow for an instant kill finisher that will also regenerate some of your health, these finishers tend to be the only hits that have weight and good looking contact to them but there aren't that many and you will see the same ones even among different styles of enemies. The larger bosses from the later chapters seem to barely function in this style of game and can even just be beaten through sheer brute force on the normal difficulty.Going from more free explorations to the fights that lock you to only moving left and right once enemies attack leads to some odd moments as enemies can get in each others way and you find you can't quite hit some targets that haven't fully entered the locked plane of movement when other enemies or the environment is in the way. You have to manually turn around with a button press to fight enemies on both sides of you but you quickly get the ability to block from other direction and attacks that can attack behind you and turn you around, that combined with most enemies being in front of you anyway tends to make being surrounded a fairly pointless feature. When it is always easy to just charge the ones in front with a stunning attack anyway I never found much use for all the backwards spin and attack combos you can do, some even coming near the very end of the game when they no longer matter at all. You unlock three ranged weapons that can get you some easy kills while you have ammo for them but none feel particularly satisfying to use. There are some nice visual moments often involving a way an encounter is framed or the background or by the use of fire and water effects but just as often an odd camera angle or the brightness of a certain area can make it difficult to make out enemy attacks.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: I won this game through SteamGifts.As a vow to his dying Sensei, the young samurai Hiroki is sworn to protect his town and the people he loves against all threats. Faced with tragedy and bound to duty, the lone samurai must voyage beyond life and death to confront himself and decide his path forward.The story was compelling and interesting, with beautiful monochromatic artstyle and frustrating combat, the game offers a pretty okay-ish experience. I really did want to enjoy it more honestly, but the combat and the fact that there was multiple endings that didn't really differ in any other way other than ONE choice right at the end of chapter 6 and the ending scene with the final boss, it was an experience I wished I could have gone through faster. I managed to play through the game once on ronin difficulty while getting the no hit boss achievements, and a second run with the kensei difficulty. I save scummed for one of the endings to avoid the need to run through the game again, since I didn't really see a need for it. My favorite ending was probably the love route, and it really was heartwarming at the end.I honestly think people who can manage through the combat will really enjoy the game, but I don't think it's worth almost 20€, so if you do decide to get it, get it at a big sale for sure or a bundle. That being said, I do think it's worth a recommendation from me anyway.

Unfortunately, the combat system is frustrating and inaccurate at times. Purchase the game if you're interested in the aesthetic/atmosphere, not as a fighter.Sidenote: played entirely on Steam Deck. Works great at 1080p on an external monitor as well.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of Akira Kurosawa's films, the game is a *must* play. If you've not seen Kurosawa's films, you should really go and do that, just because it's a generally good idea, and then maybe come back here and play Trek to Yomi. Kurosawa's movies are basically the inspiration for almost all cinema since...well, after he made them. Star Wars? Yeah, that's Kurosawa's 1958 film "The Hidden Fortress". The Magnificent Seven? That's literally just a western remake of Kurosawa’s "Seven Samurai". Last Man Standing is just a remake of "Yojimbo" (but not even remotely as good). Etc. If you like movies but you don't know Kurosawa's work, you really don't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like movies. So go fix that problem first. Then come back and play this. It is visually striking. Gameplay wise, it's a side-scrolling strategic melee sword-fighter, and this aspect of the game is fine, I guess. Decently fun. Great finisher animations, but there's only like 10 enemy types, and you learn their attack patterns pretty fast. Anyway, I'd say it's worth at least $10-$20. So buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is almost great. Cool visuals, interesting camera angles for fight scenes, a story. But the input reading for the controls is beyond awful, to the point of making this game unplayable. The parry and attack animations have obvious visual lag to them. The counterattack simply does not work on controller, and will work maybe 25% of the time with a keyboard. The  "change direction" button does not work on command on keyboard or controller. You have to press the key/button 3-4 times for the character to change direction, and by then it is too late.I'd love to comment on more about the game since I think I was a decent way through it, but honestly in this condition it is unplayable. I bought this on sale and am disappointed i paid for it at all. Another example of Steam needing a better refund policy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a great atmosphere, interesting story, good voice acting, cinematic camera angles and obviously a lot of love put into the presentation. Unfortunately that's where the good things end. Sadly the animations are subpar and the combat feels laggy and basic. You learn more moves and combos as you progress but to be honest, you don't need any of those special moves to win fights. The AI is pretty one note and brain dead. Press X, X, Y and you're pretty much done with fights. This is a real shame because this game has a lot of potential with its presentation. Hopefully the dev makes a sequel and improve on the combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi is an Akira Kurosawa movie in game form. While it offers striking visuals, cinematic camera angles, and a generic samurai story, it fails to deliver a decent gameplay and there is only one reason for that: clunky combat system. You will tremble at your first dive into the game since you'll find yourself trying to figure out how to avoid getting stun-locked by enemies. However, if you manage to figure out how to stun enemies and execute them, you'll end up cheesing it for the whole game because there is no other reliable way to stay alive unless you're very good at parrying. Of course, repeating this over and over again will give you the feeling that combat is repetitive and I'll tell you what: you're correct! Although you will unlock many different moves and ranged weapons as you progress further, you won't be using them since most of them are technically useless. The game itself is not that difficult and it takes about 4-5 hours to complete. Apart from regular difficulty modes, there is a one called "Kensei" which unlocks after beating it once on any difficulty and everyone dies in one hit except bosses when game is set to it. It's quite fun and for me, it was the only way to make combat more diverse for I was not worried about getting stun-locked. Story is your generic samurai story. It feels like straight out of an Akira Kurosawa movie as I've mentioned in the beginning of my review. There's a group of bandits, they raid and terrorize villages for supply but things get a bit personal with our protagonist Hiroki. Depending on your choices, he goes down to a path of duty, rage, or love. I liked the fact that the story, even some dialogue change depending on your choice. There's also a hidden ending and I'd say it's the most impactful one. You can also discover Hiroki's past and many other additional information about the lore thanks to collectibles scattered around the game. I'd like to conclude my review by saying that despite its janky combat, I enjoyed it a lot due to its atmosphere and excellent voice acting. I think it's a game worth playing if you enjoyed movies by Akira Kurosawa. Oh, before I forget, English dub is horrible and it kills the whole atmosphere so, I'd avoid it if I were you.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played much of this game to speculate anything (I'm at chapter 4 as I'm writing this review) and I can already tell that it's a great frigging game!Trek To Yomi puts you in the shoes of Hiroki, a young proficient Samurai, who is looking for Aiko, the love of his life, after she gets kidnapped in a raid on his village. The bosses are mostly Ronin armored individuals tied directly to the raid, and as he slays them, the hero will uncover more about why the raid came to be until he is slain and sent to the Feudal underworld, Yomi, where he gains new powers that will help him avenge the deaths of his loved ones at the cost of his own soul; a deal he would rapidly agree to.Trek To Yomi is really an amazing game; although short in nature (like any other platformer), its artstyle oozes Nostalgia as you play in literal Black and White Feudal Japan. Hiroki also gains a few skills along the way, such as rolling and some really useful combos that end up in decapitation, and let me tell you... It's satisfying as all hell to relieve the heads of your malignant enemies from their shoulders in one swift fell swoop. While you can't actually jump and the platforming is really bad in this game, it's the swordplay that catches the eye... and in Ronin Mode, it gets more realistic than ever! You die in one hit, and your enemies as well as bosses get the same treatment... Just like in a real sword fight, the first to penetrate your ribcage with a sword is the victor.Trek to Yomi gets a solid , I can see myself playing it forever... and in a way it reminds me a lot of Dark Souls... Really don't know why, it just does lol
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: In Trek to Yomi, you play Hiroki, a young orphan studying to become a Samurai and embodying the values taught in Bushido from your Sensei. Your path won’t be easy to follow. Bandits attacked the village and killed your master, and it now falls on you to protect your town.Trek to Yomi is a game that comes with an atmosphere and ambience. Whether it is its story, soundtrack, or artistic design, you can’t help but feel like the leading actor of an old movie. This almost cinematographic experience and cutscenes don’t take anything away from the game.On the contrary, it made it stand out and tied it all up together.In terms of gameplay, you will get to decide Hiroki’s path and how he will handle the adversity and challenges. Primarily by slashing his enemies with this Katana while using various combos. You will learn new combos that are more flashy but not quite as effective throughout your journey. Either unresponsive or too complex, they aren’t offering anything that mashing up two buttons can’t do. The mechanics and patterns are pretty simple and easy to read, reinforcing the idea that Trek to Yomi isn’t Sekiro, a rogue-like SIFU and neither was it supposed to be.I particularly enjoyed exploring the world of Trek to Yomi; there are quite a few collectables to gather to better understand Japanese folklore and more lore from the story directly.Sadly, the game is relatively short but offers a lot of replayability. There are different endings, and after finishing your first run, the Kensei mode unlocks, where everything will die in 1-hit. This game mode adds a lot of challenge to a game that lacks difficulty. Maybe we would expect this game to get progressively more difficult because of our gaming habits, but this isn’t the case. Very few fights were challenging, but every single one was satisfying.Finally, Trek to Yomi is a good game that will offer you an experience, more than a challenge. While short, it is reasonably priced and accessible to everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot believe people were complaining about the combat in this game. At first I didn't buy it because of all the bad reviews. I am so glad I decided to get it anyways later on down the road, and oh man what I would have missed. This game is a masterpiece. I absolutely love it. The combat can get repetitive, but just about when you master your new moves you get a new set that is helpful. Very, very enjoyable game. The atmosphere is astounding. Don't listen to the haters. If you're interested in it, grab it. Nothing like it honestly.

_childDocuments_.review: This game's focus is on the cinematic style & narrative of this game. In that regard, this game succeeded in making a game that is as cinematic you can get, while still having plenty of gameplay action. However, the gameplay does take a backseat to the cinematic style. As such, you can see why this game has so many negative reviews. People thought they were buying Sifu, but instead got this Akira Kurosawa inspired game. I really loved the cinematic look & feel of this game. I don't think people are giving this game enough credit for how simply unique it is. Many scenes are just absolutely breath-taking. The visual shots make you feel like you're inside an old black & white kung fu movie at the theater. The musical soundtrack is also very good. There's not another game like it at all. The best comparison I can make is that it is closer to Inside or Limbo. However, the gameplay is more punishing for sure. It took me about 7 hours to complete the game on normal difficulty. I died a lot. My problem with the gameplay is that it just wasn't as dynamic or as fun as it could have been. A lot of combos are simply never used. A lot of sections of the game are simply framed badly for gameplay. I felt like this game at times was a test of my eyesight. It was difficult to see the enemy attacks because they were so tiny. A line of enemies come at you from both sides and you end up facing the wrong way. Enemies will shoot you or there's even one enemy that tires you when you wound him and you'll end up getting backstabbed by a different enemy while you can't do anything.I enjoyed the ride though. I thought the story was good, even though it was a lot more supernatural than I was thinking it would be. The Japanese voice-acting is excellent. My one gripe with the narrative is that it seems that the choices you are presented with are meaningless. I think this game would have been better with just one true ending and the player not being asked to make any choice ... like in cinema.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Ambience is perfectly well rendered, that is a great tribute to Akira Kurosawa.The camera angle can make the game difficult but on most places, Trek to Yomi is pretty beautiful and immersive.People will complain because of the lack of colors, but it's part of the game. Don't forget the original experience.Trek to Yomi visuals and sound are flawless.But there is one thing that bring the game down : the fighting. This latter is a large part of Trek to Yomi gameplay and unfortunately, they are clunky, really imprecise and unresponsive.To be honest, I was pleased with Trek to Yomi but fighting mechanics make the game not so good. And the game is really short : around 5 hours to complete.If you enjoyed Sekiro and/or Ghost Of Tsushima you might like Trek to Yomi.I don't recommend at full price or wait for a patch that will rework combat encounters.Or play in EASY in order to skip combats and focus on story.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: I have watched way too many black and white samurai movies for my own good, so you could say I was a bit excited for this one.Trek to Yomi absolutely bleeds style, with authentic, detailed environments, perfectly placed camera angles, and the studio went so far as to even have the voice actors deliver their lines in the same manner as an older Japanese samurai movie. If you thought the black and white filter in Ghosts of Tsushima was something - this is like an entirely different level and I am absolutely here for it.Even disregarding that authenticity, the game itself still looks great. The models look good, the use of lighting is expertly done, and I really liked all the weather effects in particular. It’s just good-looking all around and the atmospheric sound design only adds to this.The combat, at least on the surface, looks simple, but once you start playing, you quickly find that the handful of base moves you start with combo into a variety of different strings. Upward slashes, downward, thrusting attacks, heavy attacks - the full slate can then be made into something like down, down, heavy for a stun or back light, light, light for a spin attack string that does massive damage to enemies behind you.You are constantly unlocking new combos as you play and the game does a good job presenting them at a consistent pace to give you something to look forward to. Granted, if I am being honest, the basic strings worked well enough for me way into the experience that I oftentimes had to actively force myself to use some of the fancier stuff.There are also ranged attacks courtesy of a few ranged weapons, such as the bow and arrow. The ammo for these are limited and must be found hidden away in the environment, but they are great options when you have an annoying ranged enemy farther away and are another nice addition to some already solid combat.Overall though, the combat works. It feels great to play, looks great in action, and has intuitive enough controls that you get this nice sense of fluidity from it. It took me maybe twenty minutes and I was completely into it, slashing down enemies, parrying, and rolling around with ease. The parry is very forgiving, so that’s definitely something I would recommend using.Trek to Yomi is not a long game. It took me just under four hours to clear and if you shave away all of my deaths that settles to just under three hours. That doesn’t make it a bad game though - the studio intentionally crafted an experience to be authentic to the samurai movies of old and pacing was a part of that.However, this is also one of my main complaints. Not that it is too short, but that the pacing itself becomes a bit rocky towards the end. You get some really solid first few levels and then the last couple it felt like they kinda lost their way. You get environments that aren’t as cool and repetitive enemy encounters that have you fighting like five or six at a time just to get to the next little segment which will have you repeat this. A lot of the game was like this, but the balance was WAY better early on with the exploration, the enemy encounters, the story bits.Otherwise, the length is fine. If anything, the story lacks the depth for anything longer than it already is. Not to bash the story by the way, it’s fine for what it is, but it can be boiled down to a simple revenge story at its core that also happens to touch on more personal elements like morality and honor. So nothing too crazy there, but also not boring - I think the studio did a decent job maintaining a good story-gameplay balance even if I can’t say that this is a story I’ll remember after maybe a week.There is not a whole lot of exploration and the game itself is mostly linear outside of different story endings you get based on certain key dialogue decisions (there are only a few of these). However, to make a different decision, you have to literally play through the entire game again - there’s no chapter select despite the experience being divided into distinct chapters.I will say though that the difficulty unlocked after clearing the game once is cool. It’s called Kensei and it basically makes everything one-hit kill, including yourself. Doesn’t apply to bosses unfortunately, but a cool hardcore take that honestly would have been fun to have from the start.I ran the game at 1440p, 144fps on my RTX 3080 Ti and didn’t have any technical issues outside of one instance where I fell off the map and had to reload to a checkpoint not even ten seconds prior. Controls are great on a controller (although not rebindable) and are also fine on keyboard and mouse (which are rebindable). Granted, I still recommend controller.Trek to Yomi is about as authentic as they come. The lighting, the camera angles, the graininess - the aesthetic is all there and is matched with some equally nice combat that has a surprising amount of depth to it. It may falter later on with its pacing and lackluster enemy variety, but it’s an experience well had and I am definitely satisfied as someone that watches a ton of the movies for which this is based on. Even if you’re not into the movies though - it’s good enough on its own to warrant a look.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this. The combo and parry timing windows are all over the place and needlessly hard to pull off at the weirdest times. It's just very inconsistent. Some enemy attack animations come out of nowhere feel impossible to parry, while others have the enemy seem to sit to and wait for you to parry. One of the simple combos is just x, x, y and yet I swear to god it fails half the time I try to execute it. I managed to cheese a boss with just thrust attacks and only figured it out because i got fed up with the fight and started mashing buttons.The story, tone and artistic design is all very nice. It's got the great energy and style of many Devolver games, it reminds me of My Friend Pedro, or maybe Katana Zero. Run through level killing all the guys in increasingly difficult encounters. But the combat needs a LOT more polish. This game needs a few more months in the oven.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is visually stunning, one of the most realistic and beautiful games I have probably ever played. _childDocuments_.review: Another one of those tragic "I really want to like this one, but..." situations.For a four hour game, it surprisingly wears out its welcome. Past the mid-point, you (spoilers) go to Yomi, which I surmise to be some kind of Hell or unpleasant afterlife. Before the plot kicks in again and has you actually go on your 'spiritual journey', you are just trudging through droves and droves of spirit forms of enemies old and new, and... it gets a bit samey.You learn new moves, but the enemy rarely gives you proper breathing space to really give them a try. Eventually you learn a move that guarantees a stun (the one where you do a back light slash then heavy) which you can follow up with a Finisher which always regenerates some health, and... seriously, none of the other moves size up.The only time it doesn't work is against spear/halberd/trident/whatever enemies, which throughout the game remain unpleasant to fight. They really don't let you get in close, back away when you do, so... just block them. Let that pacing grind to a halt whenever you meet one. It's fine, the game barely knows what pacing is anyway.You ask me, this game could've been a two-hour experience, but that probably would've made it susceptible to steam refunds. So they drag out sections with largely uninteresting combat, especially after the mid-point. If I'm constantly saying in my head "Get on with it!" then that's a sign.The filter is a cute idea until you're a few hours in and you have to squint to spot secrets, as they tend to flash white. Sadly, fire and anything lit up flashes white too, so it's mainly a practice in frustration.Yojimbo and Sanjuro are great movies (seriously, check them out, reader), but that's also all they are: movies. It's okay if the black and white makes you miss a small thing in a movie, a good director makes sure you get the important stuff.In Trek to Yomi however, chasing secrets is almost an essential part of the game, because half of them are collectibles, and the other half are stat upgrades like stamina and health boosts. So here I am, in a rush to defend my village, but I gotta make sure I go divert from my path into some alleyway so I can get an extra dot of health which, you bet, is almost essential to survive some of the more annoying enemies/bosses!You know what's also a good movie? Schindler's List, which made great use of Black and White as well, but kept fire and (story important) red still in colour, making for a great contrast that was also eye catching. Trek to Yomi could've really used something like this, but that probably would've required a more complex filter than "Oh just slap black and white on it, it'll be fine". 13 Assassins is in colour, doesn't hold any punches on gore, and rocks just as well. It didn't need a filter to set itself apart.Speaking of which, 13 Assassins is rather gruesome, much like this game tries to be. Meanwhile Yojimbo and Sanjuro, while having violent deaths, are a bit more 'fun' and tongue-in-cheek at times. So which direction is this game trying to reference, anyway?Story/character wise... It's inoffensive and unsurprising. Cookie cutter stuff, with no surprises to be found. If a game has stellar and outstanding combat, that would've been fine. For this though? It needed to be better. It needed more, but it straight up is just... samurai trainee kid has traumatic past, grows up grizzled samurai that fails to protect his village from an attack, dies, has a spiritual journey and then gets revenge on the big baddie who's pretty much responsible for the entire lot. Oh yeah, and the love interest, there's that angle of forgettable tragedy too. Oh well.I really don't want to be reductive about this, but I expected more, and I'm kind of frustrated that "expecting more" is starting to become a running theme whenever I play a more recent game published by Devolver. This could've done with more polishing.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended, yes, but understand what you're getting into: it's not much of a swordplay game, much of a platformer, or much of anything, really, from a gaming perspective. In terms of gameplay, it's an ultra-lightweight, paper-thin parry-slash adventure that even a crappy gamer like myself can finish with ease. (Ok, so it took me about 11 hours - twice the time most of y'all spent with it. Sue me). There are signs throughout that the developer wasn't interested in providing a meaningful action challenge. Save points (which fully replenish health!) pop up after every 3 or 4 encounters - your hand, in short, is being held.So what's the appeal? The game is crafted as an experience: it's atmospheric, cinematic, and visually beautiful. No, there isn't much story to grab onto, but in the 5 (or 11) hours it takes you to zip through, you'll marvel at being plopped into a 1960s samurai/horror film reel, complete with an excellent voice cast of Japanese talent channeling Toshiro Mifune. If you're a stickler for sharp action platforming or credible sword combat in games, pass on this one... but if you're looking for a quick fix that's a helluva lot easier than Sekiro and wonderfully dependent on Japanese cinema history, give it a whirl.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really pretty, which is probably the only good thing about the game. I wanted to like the game but half way through it I was wishing it was over.The combat boiled down to spamming the fastest stun move and doing an execution on everything except for 1 enemy and bosses. I am not sure if its just hard mode but every boss can 1-3 shot you. A few of the bosses you can block and parry some of them are simply roll behind the boss and heavy attack. Riposte/counter attack does not make sense, heal for 1 when it works or do a stun combo execution and heal for 3. The AI either stand still unresponsive or attacks every time you do. Checkpoints are placed badly, this can be too far apart, too close, or being able to get a checkpoint for a side area with no enemies after you get the further checkpoint and no way to correct checkpoint. I do not understand when wheel matching puzzles have a hidden rock with the solution, you can simply change the last one 4 times and get it. The controls can be jank, on the last boss some times I would roll behind him turn around then get turned around when I do my stand still heavys. Portions of the game give you control of your character at weird times. There are a few choices of the game, they might matter and change the last fight but there is no shot I will play and find out. Ranged weapons are awful but it is a samurai game, why are you using them.

_childDocuments_.review: For such a short game, it felt very reptitive. Using pretty much the same enemies for a majority of the game, using the same level three times, reusing a boss, and the game was extremely easily once you found the simple exploit of "two light attacks, guard, two light attacks" with the occasional heavy. The last boss on Normal Difficulty had two phases, both taking about three hits to kill him. The voice acting was really good, as well as the music too, but the story was extremely boring and generic. The art style is cool for a few minutes, but it really doesn't do anything super interesting with it except for a few screens, and definitely not enough for what it was going for. I'd skip this unless you can get it super cheap on sale.
