_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi looks great, plays ok-ish, and is mostly lukewarm. The story could be summarized in essentially two sentences. You’re a student turned warrior after your master dies, making you the new protector from enemies who would do you, your village, and your love interest harm. Lo and behold your village gets attacked, your love interest is killed, and you must decide to stay with her in death or continue to live after defeating your old enemy who destroyed your village. Even that sounds more in-depth than the game is. What the game actually entails is being under constant attack from pillagers and evil spirits as you side-scroll run across an almost 2.5D environment. It’s not bad, it’s just not something they do anything interesting with. If you’ve seen any samurai movie you know this game almost exactly.I like the way it maintains a pseudo side-scrolling status, where you can sometimes go towards or away from the camera depending on the section. It goes back and forth from 2D movement and 3D movement so fluidly that you don’t even really notice it as you play. Some more environmental puzzles taking advantage of this would have been welcome. Regarding the aesthetics, It goes without saying you should keep the black-and-white film grain on. If you’re playing this game there’s really no reason to turn it off. For the sake of the creator's intent as well as really completing the picture of old samurai flicks. The art design of the game is undoubtedly its strongest point, and it’s quite well done. That withstanding I could have done with a lot less dawdling in Yomi, the death dimension. That dragged on far too long that even the creepy imagery couldn’t compensate.The fighting is sadly mediocre, and probably the weakest part of the game. I’ll give credit where credits due, they have quite a few combos for so few inputs. It’s just not very engaging, especially seeing as it’s the lone source of interaction. The parry system is also really finicky, sometimes it feels generous and other times it feels demanding. As a general rule you should parry a good bit before their attack actually lands, otherwise they’ll just keep hitting past you, draining your health startlingly quick. All in all, Trek to Yomi is a fine time, but like many indie games before and since, it’s missing that secret ingredient of creative pizzazz.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics and style are amazing (some wonky facial animations aside), it nails what it is going for on that front. But, the combat, which is most of the game, is just not there. I did not have issues with lack of responsiveness that some people did, but it is just that the game does not reward you for playing with its tools, and in fact feels like it is punishing you if you do.Except for a small number of enemies you have two options to kill them:- A long battle where you are parrying, striking, managing spacing and dealing with the fact that there may be a guy behind you that you also need to pay attention to. You may need to hit this guy a dozen times depending on the combo you are using, and there's a decent chance you will take a hit in there.- OR, XXY and stun him and finish him. During your finisher you are immune to damage, and in fact heal a bit when you do it.You get the finisher very early, it is your primary means of getting HP back, and it works on 95% of the enemies you face in the game. The ones it doesn't, you just need to heavy attack a couple times and they die, or they are bosses and you need to do other combos and actually have a duel. Not doing a finisher is far slower (which lets enemies with ranged attacks shoot you to death since you cant get to them through their buddy), and don't heal you, so why would you want to do them? And it isn't like most games where you open an enemy up to a finisher after doing damage, no the first hit you land could be that final hit in the stun combo and they are now instant-killable. I just do not get why that was the design.

_childDocuments_.review: If there is something we must understand, a creator or artist can drink water from other to get inspired. Expression is the way to reveal a comprehension by presenting one or more perspectives. This is the case of the game: a trek to the «underworld». Or at least that's how, the Westerners, we comprehend it. Living the game through Hiroki's journey, reminds me the story of Dante Alighieri or Virgil but told as a film by Akira Kurosawa, Hiroshi Inagaki or post-war Japanese filmmakers. Among other artistic influences are integrated as a muse that give birth to an imaginative game.As a prologue, this story begins when Hiroki was young. During his instruction, he was interjected when a messenger came to his mentor Sanjuro, since their village is being attacked by bandits. The young samurai stayed with his master's daughter, Aiko, but they opt to assist him. They leave the dojo and go to the gates of the city. The lad crosses paths decimated by thugs. Soon he finds his leader, the fearsome Kaguro, and both decide to face each other. The little experience of the young man makes him lose; about to perish under the enemy's katana, Sanjuro faces him to death. However, both die; but in his deathbed, Hiroki swears to protect the city and Aiko. The years elapse, the city hears the arrival of the bandits commanded by a warlord. Moved by glory, a tragedy is transformed, through which Hiroki's adventure begins.There are two important features that grabbed my attention: its narrative and art. On the one hand, the story is based on the form of a tragedy (periplous). The way of telling —so as not to provide spoilers— is performed through the hero's journey that goes from the world of the living to Yomi. It relates in a circle that depending on the final decision of the player can lead to a denouement. That same trek has a greater potency in the gameplay, since it’s a journey of learning and teaching. As sensei Sanjuro says: teaching is learning. The script is well elaborated, through which the development of the character is seen as also its argument is simple and clear. The voices are tremendous: they have life force that can be heartbreaking, tragic and pitiful at times. The game is quite emotional, drama of which is intriguing. It gives an air of watching a film with strong and poignant scenes.On the other hand, its artistic part is beautifully impressive. It's superb, well worked, especially if you enjoy classic Japanese movies. The level design is based on the cinematic shots and, at the same time, each frame is a theatrical set. To that’s added the grayscale, black and white, the noise in the image, good illumination  management, to provide that effect of old film. All of that’s appreciated along with the gameplay. The succession is consistent with the narrative, while the sequence with the gameplay. Every scene tells or happens something. Although the combat animation is sometimes not pretty, it's good to appreciate the flow of the narrative from the visual side. The game is like interacting inside a movie, it offers an enjoyment to the eye.Also its soundtrack is marvelous, composed by Cody Matthew Johnson and Yoko Honda. It presents a theme similar to the plot, the descent into Yomi, the redemption and the verdict of the samurai. From beauty to horror in the course of loss of balance, for which it’s revealed through mellifluous and sweet melodies that are transformed in the journey to the underworld into disconsolate and corrupt tunes. They’re pieces of traditional Japanese music, although it’s combined with ambient sounds within the game, which makes it pleasant at all times. It expresses an adequate soundscape that emphasizes the scenes of the story. The gameplay is tied to the narrative. First, the way of playing is guided through the pedagogical way, namely, the hero's path in which each step something is learned. The game is primarily melee combat. On my journey, after training with Sanjuro, I learned the basic moves. Every time I progress in the story, I acquire new movements that will allow, to put it in a way, «improve» my character in combat. Also in the course I can find three types of enhancements: health, physical resistance (stamina) and equipment improvement (thrownable such as arrows, bo-shuriken and Ozutsu). In the inventory I can perceive: the movement guide (skills, a good idea to practice), collectibles (artefacts), and a journal where little by little narrates the story as well as what to do.Secondly, the game's camera is side-scrolling, with which it emphasizes fights and cinematic shots. It should be noted that there’re two game modes: combat and exploration. From the combat, I sometimes fought with enemies along the way, while at the end of each level there is a boss. You won’t be able to proceed until you defeat them. From the exploration, I only recommend you open your eyes wide before progressing. Because nearby are hidden paths, trails or doors where you can find upgrades, collectibles and some hazard environment that will let you to use them against the enemy. Those objects usually shine to locate them. The games are saved in the sanctuaries located along the way, as well as it regenerates health and stamina.The game is quite simple and the movements are learned as you go along. Also something I really enjoyed are the collectibles. They tell you a little about Japanese mythology, which turns out to be enriching. As they also talk about Hiroki's past, thus allowing an understanding of the plot. The game isn’t difficult, as sometimes the AI of the enemies is a bit clumsy. I enjoyed the story more than the gameplay as there are always new things being revealed. But if you like gameplay, you can appreciate various combat combinations.This is the second samurai-themed game that I've liked, of course after . The story is remarkable, it can capture the player as long as it’s immersed in the plot and not looking for action. The development of the plot becomes gradual, the sceneries and the character take a turn that rethinks the theme. The scenography are usually the similar, but always with a different atmosphere, thus managing to give a new perspective. Nevertheless, despite the exploration and a possibility of contemplation in some scenarios, the game is short. The game continues to receive improvements in order to remove some bothering bugs. Although I didn’t detect them, except for the AI. You can either consider the difficulty or, as I did, enjoy an inspired story told in the Kurosawa style. The game is re-playable, although the choices of certain actions do not fully affect the game, because in any mode the ending is selectable based on our consideration in the last part of the story. But it’s worth playing it: inasmuch as it’s equivalent to interacting an excellent medium length film. Perhaps, in the future, there will be more artworks of this type. _childDocuments_.review: Consider this review as neutral.So, I do remember when the game was announced to us and was waiting to see what could it be. Everyone waited for a "Kurosawa" game, and we were not wrong, but as always there is a but. The visuals are great, and the characters look pretty nice considering that 99% of the game you will not see faces. (Except the face of MC as a kid... His face is a bit…weird)Audio is very good. Big respect to the voice actors that had to represent screams of pain because those really felt as they were tortured in real life (Or were they…?) The story of itself is not about revenge. Many people played the game from 20 to 50 mins and think that it is about revenge, but it is not. It's more about redemption and facing the inner demons because of the guilt that the MC feels and is responsible for the decisions.Now comes the ButsAi is stupid. They wait till you fight with one and come one by one to fight you. You will only fail if you will make a mistake, and that is hard to do.Combat is the weakest part of this game. I played it only with one combo Up-Light-Light-Heavy = Win and Heavies on bosses. Don't get me wrong the animations look good, and the finishers are bloody as hell, and it does feel like you are watching a Kurosawa movie but the way how the combat works is making it painful as hell.I am not sure, but there are 3 ending in total. I only lasted for 1 and don't think that will play it again. The game doesn't fit the role of a "Replayable game" and only requires one ending.Buy it if you want, but beware that the combat is not the best here unless they will fix or tweak it

_childDocuments_.review: After hating the game at launch, I hoped that the patches would make it better. While some may say its too easy and boring, the bigger issue cannot be fixed by upping the difficulty (I tried). It is just fundamentally broken; the animations are poor and unresponsive and the awful ai makes for terrible combat. I see some recommending it just based on the games other features but honestly, outside of the cinematic style, I find it very mediocre. The story and soundtrack did not stand out to me at all. Overall, I would just stay clear of this game and recommend that you watch a Kurosawa movie instead.

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10I ONLY RECOMMEND ON SALE!!!SALE!SALE!Trek to Yomi is a game that tries to emulate the style and aesthetics of classic samurai movies, but fails to deliver a satisfying gameplay experience. The game is set in feudal Japan, where the protagonist, a young swordsman named Hiroki, vows to protect his village from invaders. The game features a side-scrolling perspective, black-and-white graphics, and a minimalist soundtrack.However, the game suffers from a lack of depth and variety in its combat system, which is the core of the gameplay. The combat is simplistic and repetitive, requiring only a few button presses to execute attacks and parries. The enemies are predictable and easy to defeat, posing little challenge or threat. The game also lacks any customization or progression options for the player, making the combat feel stale and boring.Many reviewers and players have criticized the game for its mediocre combat, saying that it is not fun or engaging and there are parts where i Coincide. Some have even compared it to a glorified walking simulator, where the player just moves from one cutscene to another. The game does not offer any incentive or reward for mastering the combat, nor does it provide any alternative gameplay modes only difficulties (which are annoying as S$$T btw). The game is also very short, lasting only about 5hrs.Trek to Yomi may appeal to fans of samurai movies who appreciate its artistic direction and narrative, but it does not offer much else for gamers who are looking for a thrilling and immersive combat experience. The game is a disappointing attempt at recreating a genre that deserves better treatment and respect.

_childDocuments_.review: A disappointing experience that fails to live up to its potential, despite the few redeeming qualities it has. The game has a decent story, great aesthetic, good voice acting, and a fantastically handled camera which provides beautiful camera angles when exploring the 2.5D side scroller. however, these positives are overshadowed by a myriad of flaws.The game's combat system is the biggest offender by creating a frustrating and unsatisfying experience. Parrying feels clunky and without weight, enemies feel unfair as they always seem to be faster than the player, input to action response feels slow, certain enemies do not stagger when you attack them with a blade, and telegraphing is handled poorly with enemies either over telegraphing or under telegraphing attacks. This is disappointing considering the heavy emphasis placed on combat throughout the game.I personally dealt with technical issues such as crashes due to alt+tabing but I could be in the minority.The black and white post-processing, while visually appealing, can sometimes hinder visibility, making certain in game elements difficult to see.Overall, while Trek To Yomi may have its redeeming qualities such as its narrative and visual style (camera angles during exploration), the gameplay issues ultimately lead to a disappointing experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Like many other reviewers here, I wanted to like this game. Look, if you want a pretty, quick, and easy story to interact with: go for it. Dig too deep and it gets ugly though. I played this on Hard mode right off the rip because I like melee/sword combat games (Sekiro, Hollow Knight, Elden Ring, you get the idea) and I figured this little guy's probably short, so lets make it last a bit. Probably a mistake... For me. Look, these are my thoughts on the game, so it's ok if you didn't feel the same way.Graphics: First Glance: Purty. No denying it. They went for a particular look and they got it.Closer look: Don't. Reused enemy skins and types, bland faces... anything effects that happen because of gameplay (like, ohhh, I don't know... Blood splatters) look lazily implemented and just disappear. It's a lot like the OG Resident evil games, where the pre-rendered stuff got all the love but little to no effort went into anything else. Sadly, even the neatest looking boss of the game was lazily animated (some of his attacks look like they just rotated him and added effects without bothering to actually animate his body for it).Gameplay:First glance: I've heard the game can be beaten in about 3 hours. I'm guessing enemy health is lower and all the combos you learn are neat for that short run throughCloser Look: The combat is broken. On hard mode I got : Unresponsive or ignored commands, inconsistent movement, ignored attacks, randomly swapped where I was facing at times, inconsistent combo timings, seemingly random hit-boxes, cheese-heavy enemies (looking at you Archers, Gun users, Spear wielders), and randomized damage from enemies (One boss attack dealt me a couple of points of damage one time and then the next time it wipes out 12 with no difference in distance/blocking, etc), and also Bugs. Probably more noticeable on higher difficulties, but I've been teleported back in front of an enemy after rolling past him just so I can get hit by their attack.  You may have seen a few people mention cheesing the same attack (Up then light attack, light attack, Strong), and who can blame em? A majority of the time the longer combos are interrupted by stronger enemies halfway through because they don't react to anything but that final blow if at all. The executions look cool the first couple of times, but you start to realize there was a missed opportunity for some cooler, more cinematic ends to the bad guys. Let 'em fall down from heavy damage in a slump, lose a limb, or simply have that initial fatal swipe lob off their head (why bother running the guy through after Every time?). There's not enough variety, and what IS there isn't worth bothering with because it might just get you killed instead. In the end, I can't recommend this to anyone who loves video games for the gameplay. For the price point, it's a neat experience and you probably won't regret buying it on sale if you just want to casually run through it. If you want a challenge and loads of cool content, the bar has been set too high by other games from small developers for this to be worth your time. I'm really bummed out by how far this missed the mark and all the missed opportunities. Uninstalled after enfuriating, cheap, ubalanced boss battles and one of 3 different endings that I felt was lackluster. I don't want to bother with two more playthroughs, even on easy. Ya Broke my heart Trek To Yomi....

_childDocuments_.review: Conclusion: Worth it for people who appreciate atmosphere, presentation, and story as much as they do combat in a video game. We beat the game on Ronin difficulty with 5.5 hours gameplay from start to finish. This was played as part of review on a live stream with the game at no cost to me.It was atmospheric, great sound design, excellent voice acting, immersive, cinematic, unique use of camera angles, has some interesting and accessible collectibles items with Japanese folklore included. Combat was not a mechanical barrier to  progress the story and kept me interested with what it had to offer as well as how enemies scaled with progress. Checkpoints are fair. Should be beatable by anyone on the easiest difficulty.Combat is repetitive, I would place it on the same scale as a side-scroller beat 'em up where you learn new moves as you progress. You learn from a handful of 20 moves over time and eventually choose the few that work best for you. There are times that you must adapt to bosses in ways that the game didn't prepare you for otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi is what I would describe as an "interactive painting"-Each scene from this game is like a painting or a clip from an old vintage Japanese film. The camera angle, the use of excellent lighting and props placement make each scene aesthetically pleasing and screenshot worthy, from beginning to end. If you're looking for a game about 4-5 hours long, with beautiful art style, different renditions of both the real and supernatural worlds, and abundant opportunities for screenshots, this game is for you.-However, this game takes a pretty sharp turn when it comes to gameplay. Trek to Yomi is a very linear game. There is really no big area to explore, except small hidden rooms scattered throughout the game, no metroidvania or meaningful progression element to boost replayability. It's just a 5-hour cinematic experience and really nothing else. The story follows a young samurai named Hiroki through his journey to slay the bandit leader, Kagerou. Overcoming his weaknesses and reflecting upon himself in Yomi, the land of the dead according to Japanese belief, Hiroki can choose which principle to rely on, which will result in 3 different endings, with 1 additional secret ending.-The biggest drag that pulls this game down is its janky combat. The use of both your movement inputs and attack combo strings disrupts the flow of combat, and becomes an issue in boss fights and enemies that require you to move or strike at an opportune time. In addition that this game consist mostly of combat against groups of enemies of various types, Trek to Yomi can be a chore to go through once the novelty of its art style wears off.

_childDocuments_.review: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME UNTIL A PATCH!I'm the type of person who says graphics don't matter, but Trek to Yomi blew me away by the stellar environments and beautiful attention to detail like no other game before it. The art direction is fantastic, and the entirely black and white palette bathes it in life like no color could. Reminiscent of the Kabuki films of early Showa Era Japan, Trek to Yomi follows a young samurai preventing a war after his master's death.This game however I do not recommend. The combat - like many other people say - is not only quite unresponsive, but even tiresome and repetitive. It is apparent to me that Flying Wild Hog did not conduct proper and disconnected quality assurance. This issue may have been caused by Devolver Digital pushing for a release date, or by a lack of funding. It's been about one week of disconnected play testing, and they should immediately see to fixing this glaring issue.You can bypass many issues with easy mode, but at what point does it stop being a computer game and become a reel of film you roll by pressing 'W'? I cannot recommend this game on graphics alone. In its stead I would end up recommend what inspired this game, film. If you want a cool samurai game, I personally recommend Fromsofware's Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. I hear Nioh 2 is good, but have yet to try it; I was not too keen on the first one.Thanks for reading, and here's to hoping FWH fixes the issues with combat very soon!

_childDocuments_.review: This game sells itself on the visuals and cinematics but what shows great in trailers does not really translate to combat. You unlock new combos as you progress but they're really not needed because none of them feel any better or worse than you what you start with. Every encounter feels the same. Enemies are very predictable and don't seem to think. All you do is stand there, wait for them to start to swing their weapon, parry, and counter attack. Every enemy is the same except some just have more health.The game certainly looks really cool but after an hour or so, I just don't have any desire to continue. All you do is run through a linear line, face some enemies, deal with the exact same fight as all the others you've had, then run down another linear path to the next cutscene. The combat is just too repetitive to want to continue and everything else isn't engaging enough to muscle through it.

_childDocuments_.review: Visuals:Trek to Yomi does a great job of using fixed camera angles and monochrome to evoke a cinematic experience. The animations are smooth & dynamic: time slows when you successfully parry an attack, the blood spray hitting the floor and the bodies going limp and falling off the side of a bridge are all wonderful additions. The cut-scenes actually feel like they could've been taken from a classic samurai movie.Environments are gorgeous and the game gives you plenty of moments to stand still and take in the view: of course, it's up to you if you'd rather run ahead to the next fight.I found myself taking screenshots every time I loaded up the game and I'll be using them as desktop backgrounds for a while.Sound:The sound effects are impressive— swords clash, steel cuts through flesh and trees fall with a deep and crisp audio which adds to immersion.The soundtrack is beautiful and, in some parts, hauntingly so. Every environment has a fitting piece of audio, whether that be a suspenseful build up, eerie ambience or even near-silence.The voice acting (Japanese, I haven't played with English audio) is incredible. Wails of agony, arrogant boasts and death groans are all a real treat for the ears.Gameplay:The mechanics seem simple at first but you learn more attacks and combos as you progress— and new ways of using them. New enemies appear semi-regularly through the game, challenging you to switch up your combat and experiment with new techniques. If you are willing to put yourself in harm's way for the sake of cool points, you can create some stunning blade-dancing choreography. The combat can take a little getting used to, it's not entirely intuitive and occasionally you still get hit even though you could've sworn you were blocking or parrying correctly. I'd say it's one of the better side-scrolling combat systems I've played, though. The "everyone dies in one hit" mode is an extra challenge for those who want to feel intensity and danger in every encounter.I'm not the young gamer I used to be. Both my reflexes and patience aren't as good as they once were. Despite that, Trek to Yomi's combat system was both supportive and rewarding once I'd put in a little practice.For the price I paid (£15) and the amount of time I've enjoyed getting 100% completion (20 hours) I would say it's well worth it. It's not a groundbreaking experience but it is meaningful and beautiful, you can feel the passion behind it and it's not unnecessarily long or complicated.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is not as epic and memorable as I was anticipating, but generally it was an enjoyable and thoughtful journey, especially as this kind of setting is not that common in games and the exploration and interpretation of Japanese folk lore here is interesting.I do not like nitpicking things in reviews, because I find myself too often when looking into reviews to overfocus on the negatives too much, which this game sure has, but overall I think this game is a Trek worth taking.I have abstained from looking up any reviews or opinions until I finished the game – I chose an old approach from my childhood, where if a game looked interesting, I just went for it – and I am glad I did. I was surprised when I saw the reviews that they were generally mixed, as I was expecting for them to be at least mostly positive here on Steam.One thing to mention of what I read is that people had responsiveness issues with controls – I have not experienced any of that myself playing with mouse and keyboard.

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this game for it's visuals alone. The cinematography in this game is a masterpiece. Really enjoying every frame.Edit: Here's my full take on Trek:This game scratches an itch that a lot of games can't reach right now. It's not a game I have to put long sessions into, however, in my short sessions, it is very highly engaging. I'm not as skilled a gamer as many out there, but I found the combat to be just challenging enough that it was fun to learn but didn't distract me from the story. I think there is a lot to say about how you can interpret the moral of the story as well.Trek does a lot in 5-6 hours that many games fail to do even after 50 - 100 hours of game-play. It doesn't feel like any sacrifices were made to achieve this length, nor does it feel like there was any unnecessary filler content. I know I don't represent a majority of the gaming community out there, but I consider Trek to be a fine work of art in the gaming world and I wish there were more similar games(in length and immersion) that were as visually appealing as this.

_childDocuments_.review: A stylish game with very little substance. The combat is clumsy -- mostly serviceable but certainly not engaging or satisfying. _childDocuments_.review: Controls lack precision and combat is very inconsistent, but it's alright because outside boss fights you can cheese almost all of it with a simple stun combo + finisher that replenishes your health. Devs were aware of the jankiness, because enemies will politely wait to duel you one by one even when they have you surrounded. Combine that with a fixed camera angle on a 2-D plane where characters can get obscured with objects in the foreground and you simultaneously have a very easy and very frustrating experience where rare deaths can feel unfair. One more pet-peeve of mine is that game doesn't let you practice combos outside of combat, because  your character will draw his sword only when he plans to use it. True to the samurai trope I guess, but a very poor gameplay choice. It also doesn't include chapter select feature so you'll have to replay the whole game to pick up collectibles you missed.Story is uninspired and formulaic and I felt very detached from the character(s). With all that said the only leg to stand on game has, is it's graphics and monochrome presentation evocative of old Kurosawa movies. While nice, it's sadly not enough to justify full price. Buy at a deep discount.

_childDocuments_.review: The combat is simple and predictable and not complicated or random like most games.I also think this game deserves some credit for trying to be intuitive with the different sense of cinematicI've seen a lot of people say the fighting is very scuffed and obnoxious, I think they're just on hot air because they don't understand how the game works, so they blame it on the game.People are dumb and dont use their brain sometimes, they just don't want to admit it.But I guess everyone starts somewhere. To enjoy this game you need to master its base mechanics, that means recognizing attack patterns and timings to outplay your enemies. Learning the game is part of the fun and theres simply no fun in games if you just breeze through them without stubbing your toes first.Now I believe that the intended difficulty for this game is Ronin (hard), as it's generally the hardest difficulty available, Kensei mode is hard to a certain extent but in the end you can just 1 hit your normal enemies which isn't inherently fun  gameplay (besides you'd have to beat the game first to unlock it lol)Ratings:🎚️ Difficulty🔲 My cat could play it☑️ Easy🔲 Normal🔲 Significant struggle🔲 Darksouls🗺️ Graphics🔲 Bad☑️ Normal🔲 Beautiful🔲 Amazing🔲 You forget what reality is📚 Story🔲 No story☑️ Lousy☑️ It's there for people who care🔲 Well written🔲 It could replace my life⌛️ Length🔲 Short (-1h)☑️ Average (2-5h)☑️ Long (+10h)🔲Very long (+25h)🔲 To infinity and beyond🎶 Music🔲 No music🔲 Not fitting☑️ It makes sense🔲 Would listen outside the game🔲 Deserves an award🕹️ Gameplay🔲 Watch grass grow🔲 Hard to enjoy☑️ Gets repetitive after a while🔲 A good moment🔲 You'll have a blast⚙️ Grinding☑️ No grind🔲Average grinding🔲Necessary to progress🔲You schedule your whole day around this game🔲At this point hire someone else to play for you🔁 Replayability🔲 A one-time experience🔲 NG+☑️ Multiple endings☑️ For achievements/speedruns only🔲 Infinitely replayable🐛 Bugs🔲 No bugs whatsoever☑️ Minor bugs🔲 Can get annoying🔲 Impacts the game badly🔲 The game itself is a big terrarium for bugs🖥️ System Requirements🔲 Check if you can you run paint☑️ Low-end pc☑️ Decent pc🔲 High-end pc🔲 Ask nasa if they have a spare computer💰 Price🔲 Free☑️ Perfect Price☑️ Could be cheaper🔲 Overpriced🎯 Expectations🔲 This game is a scam🔲 Fast food ad vs reality☑️ Looks similar to the steam page🔲 Better than expected🔲 MasterpieceYou should almost never attack first, let your opponent go first so that you can focus on countering them. Attacking first wastes stamina incase they block, and yourself wont be able to block in time midswing.You are taught how to parry in the tutorial stage, simply a timed block when the opponent raises their sword above their head as they are about to strike.Parrying attacks are risky but will provide value in the earlier chapters. As these counterattacks will deal additional damage, stun the opponent for a tiny bit, and heal you of 1 hit point.Preemptive blocks are decent and a good defensive habit if you're not good at parrying, although heavy attacks will put you in hit stun while blocking. If they're charging up a heavy attack you need to quickly unblock and block again so that you have a chance to parry.Regular enemies have different types.The ones with headbands are fast and aggressive, so watch out for that. In most cases they will go for a quick 2-hit attack, but if they see you blocking they can also hit you with a heavy attack first.These are one of the only enemies who will actively try to dodge your attacks, especially your heavy attacks because of its slowness and high commit.Usually the best strategy is to preemptively block for their first attacks and then stun combo them. But if you think you're faster just try parry them and then combo right after, if you do you're pretty wicked.Strawhat enemies I believe are the only normal enemy that will sometimes try to block your attacks. But its fairly easy to deal with. Since stunning combos work through blocks and ignores it completely.. Armored enemies are tricky, but don't be fooled, they don't have a lot of health, just armor. You need to break through their defenses by stunning them and killing them with a finisher attack. Unless you plan on hitting them 15 times before they go down, thats also a strategy, just not a very good one...Armored enemies will always try to hit you with a heavy attack first, making it easy to parry if you time it right, but if you fail you will take a lot of damage.Spear wielder's weakness is a well timed parry that puts them in recoil, then follow with a combo and finisher. (The chapter 2 boss will often try to kick you, if you see they try to do that, block and roll away, as they will try to slam their spear on you after. This is why you always need to make sure you have space behind you during this bossfight.)Zombies do not care about hit-stun (getting their attacks canceled), combos will be hard to pull off and needs to be done preemptively. For the armored zombies I suggest Heavy>Heavy>Parry>Counterattack (after 2 heavies they will try to quickly counterattack you, so you just have to quickly parry it.)You can unlock a Heavy Stunning combo hidden in this chapter if you explore a bit.The input is Backward>Heavy, making you take a step back and give the enemy a good whack that immediately stuns them. It's going to make all future chapters a breeze.For teleportation ghosts I don't really have a good solution, just make use of different combos you unlock or find.For archers & canons, I would dodge roll right as they shoot and then slice them up in close range, you can also interrupt their ranged attack with a bo-shuriken.Parry>Light>Light>Heavy>Finisher combo is your best friend for regular enemies; they can effectively be killed in potentially 3 hits, just make sure to use the finisher button as this will also heal you by a good amount. (Keep in mind that you can only unlock this combo by progressing past the river in chapter 2).So before this point I would suggest using the Light>Heavy option. So for context, if a Light Attack is 1 damage. Heavy attack is about 2.5 Light attacks in damage, and a parrying attack is about 1.5 Light attack damage. Normal enemies theoretically dies after 3.5 light attacks. Enemies will inevitably die after 4 uninterrupted Light Attacks or 2 uninterrupted Heavy Attacks.2 Heavy attacks is about your highest damage output during boss fights, you should almost never use light attacks due to its low damage.At the start or end of each boss, to increase your damage output, you can always try to use all of your ammunition to chip away a good amount of health without needing to risk yourself in close combat.

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi is not just a game, but a cinematic experience that pays tribute Akiro Kurosawa. And it does that in an amazing fashion! You will like (or even love) this game, if you like cinematic adventures like Balckthorne, Oddworl: Abe's Exoddus or eastern themed games like Ghost of Tsushima, Ninja Gaiden or Sifu.+A strong story that not only delivers tropes you might look for, when eyeing this gem, but that takes you by surprise when you least expect it – without being over the top or cheesy! And that is a huge accomplishement for a genre that tends to be predictable.+Another plus is the replayability: there seem to be different endings you can achieve.+A great score that doesn't get in the way and just underlines what is happening, making things more believable; also, the Japanese voice acting is marvelous (you will have to play with subtitles, though, if you want to know what's going on storywise)+It's just incredible how colourful a world, that is black and white, can be. I'm serious: The dark tone not only feeds the atmosphere, but works so well with the visuals. Kudos to the developers!-you will only like the story, if you are willing to engage in an old-school style of chanbara or martial arts film. And that might not be everybody's cup o' tea.-there is one core point of the game, that made me feel miserable and almost made me quit: the combat!I understand that mastering a katana is hard work. But in a game, that is supposed to be immersive and wants you to play a fluent story, a quite complicated combo-heavy combat machanic just doesn't feel right. Not only does the game not let you practice said combos, but they are not actually intuitive either. But mayba I'm just bad, I dunno …-strongly tied to that point is the timing of the parry. I couldn't figure it out until the very end of the game. And that is bad on the double, because the combat system relies so heavily on that very same parry. You will be frustrated a lot because of that. for gamers for fans of good (and also bad) chanbaraTrek to Yomi is great game, that manages to be great, although it has a giant flaw with its combat: The frustration you will feel – and believe me: You will! – might be the reason, you will just stop playing. But then you will miss out on one of the best told stories in video game history, insane moments of a journey straight to he**, and a unique experience no other game can deliver.

_childDocuments_.review: Throwing my review into the mix mainly because i don't really agree with the combat issues people seem to have with this game.We all know what makes the game great so i'm not going to bother regurgitating points that others have made, it looks good sounds good and the stories pretty memorable IMOPeople have issues with the combat which i don't completely agree with. I made sure to beat the game on ronin difficulty and i think i get the combat of this game. Combat in this game is simple with few strings of combos which can feel limiting, i say theres only a few but theres actually plenty but most of them are very situational and i didn't use them often throughout my playthrough. The combat is fast and flashy a single enemy won't last more than a few seconds but neither will you. The game is asking that you master the combat and I think that its really fair (for the most part) I never felt that the combat was "repetitive" even has I was approaching the end of the game and if someone does feel like thats the case the game isn't long enough for it to really hinder the experience. The execution finishers were always satisfying to pull of and the game rewarded me for being a badass and clearing foes with these stylish finishes. I think the combat was really solid but I do have a few gripesI only had a few issues with combat on my first play through. It would have been nice to have a few more parry animations for attacks that didn't come from the top but this is more of a nit pick and doesn't affect the gameplay. Some of the middle bosses used large sweeping attacks which some i found could be blocked whilst over went straight through, it would have been nice to a something to distinguish between an attack that can be properly blocked or one that must be rolled thorugh (If i did miss that this is a thing that ignore this point and im just stupid) However my least favourite thing about the combat is that the roll felt really inconsistent especially with the bigger enemies in the game.To summarise I think the combat can be improved but i don't think its so bad that you shouldn't buy the game I actually think the combat is really solid and i really enjoyed it.So buy the game. I think you either click with the combat or not I just wanted to say my opinion because I dont think the combat is that bad unlike most other people who played the game. You'll know if the combat clicks with you before the 2 hours is up and get your refund if it isn't your taste.

_childDocuments_.review: Practically everything of not has already been said about the uninspired story, flat characters and atrocius combat system.First however, praise be to the art direction in this one: Visual design is unique, the usage of light and shadow well executed, the backgrounds well becoming to the occasion. The environments are far more varied than expected.The decision to have voice acting be done in japanese is quite fitting indeed.Some criticized the useless nature of collectibles bar upgrades or ammunition. Besides, had they affected gameplay, the sometimes confusing layout of the environment would have made finding all of them quite the hassle.So far a few of my impressions.Sadly I do not believe that I will be finishing this one soon. Not only does the story wholly fail to excite, the unremarkable characters leave no impression either. Worst offender however is everything surrounding the actual gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: Beautiful visuals with an interesting story (if you manage to finish it). Notes and optional collectibles are done in a cool way giving detailed historical descriptions. A plethora of combat options that keep encounters from being as linear as they could be (you will hate yourself if you don't figure out and abuse the most busted ones). This is where the positives end: The difficulty spike is insane in the mid to late game and comes out of nowhere. The ranged combat is god awful which blows considering you need to use it if you want to stand a chance in a lot of fights. If you play on any difficulty higher than easy then the bosses are super unfun to face as they will bombard you with undodgeable aoe attacks and stunlock you into oblivion so you have to abuse ranged spam to come out on top which just promotes boring gameplay. The saving system is a cool idea and I think it works fine for the most part, the exception being their spacing in some levels is egregiously bad.I was able to make it to the final boss on the games version of the hard difficulty, but was unfortunately forced to lower the difficulty after fighting the boss for a half hour cause even though I got close multiple times I didn't feel like spending an extra hour or two dealing with a boss that can basically two shot you with maximum upgrades. My last two negative points are end of game factors: There are 3 different endings but there is no chapter select and with how much of a sanity investment beating it once was, there is absolutely 0 chance anyone is playing the entire game again just to change the final cutscene. Lastly, after you complete game there is no way to access your journal/collectibles menu and I doubt I need to explain why that is dumb (especially in a game where you can collect everything).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for August 2023, this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before September 5th, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A beautiful cinematic samurai game. Trek to Yomi’s cutscenes are gorgeous.  The level of detail on most characters’ faces is beautiful, and the scenery and backgrounds are gorgeous celebrations of the artform.  Battles are visceral, with your blade killing most enemies in two or three strikes, and the story is very good. The game evokes a sense of old Japanese Samurai movies, especially those of Akira Kurosawa.  All of this makes me kind of ignore the game’s flaws. But honestly, Trek to Yomi’s combat is a bit shallow, and I’ve heard it never really gets the depth it deserves.  While the backgrounds are lush, all combat is done on a 2d plane.  The exploration is quite weak with almost no value to finding collectibles, and sometimes it’s hard to know where to go because of the gorgeous art.  It’s also only a 5-hour title. Pick this up if you're enchanted with what you’re seeing on screen.  I am, and I’ve played this before and still just love the look and feel of the game.  The story is good, and the combat is sufficient, but if you want a deeper and more robust combat experience that’s not this.  Still, I think this is a satisfying experience. _childDocuments_.review: Saw the trailer for this game a few months ago and figured, "If Devolver is backing it I should grab it." After just finishing Elden Ring and feeling like playing something more casual. To be honest, I assumed this game would be much more simple but I was entirely wrong. There are combos, extra weapons, descriptions for whats happening, and collectibles. All of which are pretty interesting. The combat itself is pretty deep, you could use one move set the entire time and probably get away with it. But I can see that in harder difficulties picking combos and watching your stamina are huge. Not to mention this game is beautiful, I played it with the filters on as it starts normally, only finding out later you can turn some of them off. Which really probably would have helped in some sections. Personally, I bought this around $17, and I got about 5 hours as I write this. It could be longer, it could have an endless mode, and it could have a dojo as to practice moves. This game has extreme replay value, I can also see speedrunners playing this on all sorts of difficulty for years to come. I think for the money though, there maybe should have been more. _childDocuments_.review: If I could give this game a mediocre score, I would. But between thumbs up or down, unfortunately, I have to go with down on this one.Trek to Yomi is a side-scrolling, cinematic action game, with a style that copies old Japanese samurai movies. The aesthetic alone is the games primary appeal and is by far the best aspect of the game. It looks damn COOL and is unique among a sea of indie side-scrolling games. It's completely in black and white, which is both a pro and a con (more on that later). The game is not completely a side scroller, as half of the time you can move in a 3-D space, but from certain cinematic camera view points; then it transitions to 2-D for the combat, then back to 3-D, etc. It oozes atmosphere and the sole reason I completed it to the end.So what sucks about it? The combat. The game asks precision from the player, but the input is so hit-and-miss I found myself baffled at the inconsistency. Sometimes an enemy will hit you and it takes only a few blocks of health. Other times it will be the same enemy, with the same move, and it will take off significantly more. Same with your attacks. Sometimes an enemy will take 2-3 hits and he goes down. Other times up to 10 or more, even though it's the same exact moves and button presses. Parrying is also a mixed bag. Sometimes you'll get a huge open window to parry, and other times none at all. I'd sometimes do combos really consistently and that's when the game was fun, only to be suddenly met with frustration as the combos suddenly stopped working. I was using the same combo, with the same timing, on the same controller (Xbox controller btw), and it just didn't connect a lot of the times. The combat is extremely inconsistent, and also highly repetitive.Combine the combat frustrations with the black-and-white aesthetic, and sometimes enemies are straight up hard to see, including what kind of attack they were using. It caused some cheap hits and deaths, and I found myself more frustrated than having fun. Luckily, the game is really forgiving. There are plenty of save spots and if you die, you start right away from the last save/checkpoint.The story is decent as well, and the game offers 3 different endings depending on what choice you make 3/4ths of the way through the game.I really wanted to love this game. I was hoping it would be something like a 2-D Ghost of Tsushima. If I were rating it on it's graphics and aesthetic alone, I'd highly recommend it, but since the gameplay kind of sucks, I just can't. It's a really short game, and I found myself wanting to just finish it, and that's not really a good sign of a good game. It needed some more time in the oven to tweak it's combat and controls, and offer a bit more variety.

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi would be a much better game if it made any attempt to include modern features instead of being unapologetically outdated. It's true that the visuals are absolutely stunning - evocative of Kurosawa movies and complete with the film splotches (constantly) that anyone who watches old films from before the 60s will recognize. Unfortunately, this is also one of the games major downfalls as the parry system relies entirely on seeing sword glints at the right time. The film splotches are frequently mistakable for item pickups, and the distant,  wide lense camera shots often make it needlessly difficult to see what you or enemies are doing.The soundtrack is also incredible, appropriate for a samurai era Japanese piece with lots of  flute and drums. You're better off just buying the soundtrack separately and ignoring the game because no matter what the price is, it's not worth the hassle.The gameplay, however,  is absolutely nervewracking, inconsistent and frustrating. Yomi's combat system is simply broken. That doesn't mean it doesn't work, but it's a repetitive chore to not die on higher difficulties and on easy it's too easy. It's like no one even playtested it at all. From the beginning - the tutorial - it is obvious the parry system does not work the way the tutorial implies and the game makes no attempt to explain it or identify if you are doing it wrong because you can pass the tutorial without parrying correctly.  The tutorial shows a little visual aid when you are supposed to parry, but this doesn't always happen in the game or it isn't always visible. Some enemies can attack at 9 times the speed Hiroki can which leads to an age old problem where enemies can literally hit you while your sword is in their chest, in addition to spamming 9 move combos that drain your stamina and there's nothing you can do about it - you're framelocked into an animation.  You don't learn block-breaking attacks until chapter 5 out of a 7 chapter game, either, and even when you do it's nearly impossible to use them because you're constantly being attacked.When you do parry, the game doesn't have a reliable or explained "perfect parry" system. A perfect parry will knock an enemy offguard, but there's no way to guarantee it happens.  However you parry, you can counter-attack but its often ineffective. There are two  stun combos, too, that allows you to use the finisher, but the stun combo can't be used effectively many times because you're constantly being attacked. More often than not enemies end up stunned when you aren't trying to and by that time it's impossible to capitalize on the stun to  use a finisher because your sword is already swinging from a combo. You will learn a finishing move early on that can heal you when enemies are stunned, but like the armor-ignoring combo, it is also borderline to execute the finishing move while being attacked simultaneously by 5 enemies or more. On the opposite end of the spectrum, once you master how to cheese the stun combo, the game becomes so stunningly easy that it's barely fun. Many enemies have ranged attacks and even ranged melee, which also means you need to be right in their face to avoid being shot or stabbed with a spear. Conveniently putting you right in the middle of an uninterruptible spam combo of the enemy doing five attacks in less than a second. What makes all of this even worse is that if you just play the game through the first time on Kabuki difficulty instead of normal, you can learn how the game is MEANT to play and then you won't have issues ever again. Compounding that are the stuns and finisher moves. The game is misleading about the combat - once you unlock stun and finisher, they are the ONLY move you should ever do and the combat is simply ridiculous without using them. Stun moves ALWAYS stagger an enemy if they follow through and on top of that, using a finisher restores health. It is the only way to actually play the game. Again, that's something you can only learn after playing through it multiple times.And then you will stop using finishers because there are only 3 finisher animations and it gets boring. Trek to Yomi uses an increasingly incompetent checkpoint save system where checkpoint shrines are spread throughout levels. The vast majority of them are crammed up against each other, some of them back to back serving only to save your progress, then you will have to do a huge stretch of a level with 30 enemies between you and a savepoint which provides desperately needed healing. When achievement hunting, this combined with the lack of a chapter select means if you miss any of the 150+ collectibles or skills needed for the achievements, you have to replay the game at least up until the items you missed. It's worth noting that the game is SIGNIFICANTLY easier on Kabuki difficulty, and all the game mechanics work fine on easy. That's not acceptable though for a game with 3 other difficulty settings.I wanted to like this game but after playing through 10 or so times it's just average. It gets better and easier on repeat playthroughs - which you have to do to get all the achievements because there are 4 different endings - but to anyone playing this, I highly recommend playing on easy the first time to learn the combat system. Once you learn the animations and what enemies will spawn when, it gets much easier.At least I can positively say it's a consistent experience across PC, Xbox and PS5 if that counts for anything.I'd like to give one thumbs up and one thumb down but that's still not a thing for some reason.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Art direction is amazing, and the game-play is fun. And if you are a Kurosawa fan, then this is going to be a delight for you. The combat is actually excellent, and provides you with simple move sets that can be combined into successive blows. It is deep if you want it to be, but you can also just parry hit, parry hit if you have no interest in actually learning the intricacies. Enemy types require different combo stratagems if you want to slay with flare, and so far the combat overall feels perfect for the stage it is set upon. I am playing the game on the Hard difficulty so this may have upped my appreciation of the combat over other reviews. Too many save points for the hard difficulty, but 2.5 hours in and I am still enjoying the ride.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is good.The overall visual design, the camera angles, everything.I started playing on Ronin difficulty (equivalent of hard mode) and I was getting stomped early on. I really hated the combat until about ~1-2 hours in when I started decapitating people left and right. Trek to Yomi does a solid job at trying to keep the combat fresh by adding new combos and abilities, but in all combat doesn't change too much throughout the course of the game. The enemy types are limited and would begin to feel boring and repetitive if not for the really well designed encounters and scenery. The story is also deep. Like, really deep. I found myself on multiple occasions taking a step back and grappling with the intense feelings and guilt that the protagonist goes through throughout the story. There is much less of an obvious character arc but once you understand what things mean, it's like a punch to the gut.I also found this to be a really refreshing experience coming off of games like Elden Ring. While 3rd person open world isn't a bad thing, this 2.5D samurai adventure reallyyyy hit the spot. Overall, I really think that this game has a lot to offer for those samurai/classic Japanese cinema aficionados out there. Combat is good, presentation is amazing, and story hits hard.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Breathtaking visual and sound design makes this game a symphony for the eyeballs, but the story is boring and cannot engage even with such a nice premise, the characters are uninteresting, and I absolutely despised the combat which is a shame considering how much of it needs to be done, the bosses are shockingly easy especially the final boss, some normal enemy encounters were much harder than any boss
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Visual style of this game is breathtaking. With the UEVR mod, playing Trek to Yomi was like being on set of a Kurosawa production. I was totally blown away by the beauty and composition of almost every scene, combined with the ambient world sounds, soundtrack and japanese voiceacting, Trek to Yomi is a love testament to chanbara movies of old, and this filled my heart with childlike joy and warmth. Wow, more of this!!!!!Gameplay mechanics are a bit on the easy side, but works ok. I would love to have full 3d freedom and more advanced sword play but all in all this is an experience like none other.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Steam Deck ReviewGame looks great on the OLED although needed the gamma increased for comfortable viewing as it's a very dark game. Sometimes the different scenes are very zoomed out or the wide screen effect makes it a bit hard to spot collectibles and consumables, but this is infrequent. Generally though it works well out of the box if not 100% suited. I do recommend turning down the power usage though in the SD game settings as this game drains battery for no good reason. Controls are great.The game story runs about 6-7 hours so perfect for a handheld, and it mostly keeps you engaged throughout. Combat does get a bit repetitive around 4-5 hours in, but the visuals kept me hooked throughout. If you like combat that's about timing parries, counters, and lining up combos this game will likely scratch that itch for you. I would recommend it generally to anyone who is interested in the theme, art style, or style of combat if you can get it at a good price.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Never in my life have I had such a promising game be ruined in such a way by god awful gameplay/controls. The gameplay itself is actually promising if the controls did not randomly decide to kill you. When I press R to turn my character around I do not need the game to decide for me that I actually wanted to turn my back to the Chapter 5 boss again. Any and all difficulty in this game is artificial due to the controls just not working. Save your money, this game is not good for anyones blood pressure.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Stunning Visuals completed with dream-like medieval Japanese vibe, kinda reminds me of PS2 era adventure action games like Onimusha, although puzzle / explorations are pretty weak in this game. _childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time fan of Samurai flicks I was quite excited for this game, the visual style is very well done, and the presentation is good too. That being said, the game is an absolute chore to play, and I had no enjoyment playing it. The combat is clunky and boring. I had entered this game expected a good story with average combat, more of an experience then a game, and while that holds mostly true, the gameplay heavily hampers the experience to the point of ruining the game. I would not recommend this game for anything over ten dollars personally, and would highly advise waiting for a steep sale before getting the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: The GOOD:I really liked the aesthetics of the game, the atmosphere, and the story, though a bit simple.The VERY BAD:The combat is horrible. It feels clunky, non consistent and non responsive. For instance, you may wanna change the direction you're facing to fight a flanking enemy, guess what, sometimes it just doesn't work and you get hit. Sometimes you strike at an enemy, and you see the blade going through him, but no, it won't register as a hit. Don't get me started with the enemy AI, which has no rule. They may hit you once and retreat, and may keep hitting you for five, no sense of stamina. And a lot of other issues with the AI.Keep in mind that I'm someone who tolerates a bit the gameplay aspect if the story and the atmosphere was the main thing. But here, since most of the time you're engaging in combat, those issues will trouble you a lot. I was bothered to the point where I've switched from hard to easy in the 4 chapter just to finish the story. It really a shame to give this game a thumbs down, when considering the effort went to the art design and the cinematography, but this ain't a movie.I'm looking forward for a second game where they polish, "re-engineer", their gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: A fun sidescroller, but a short game. ~15hrs to 100%. The visuals and music are outstanding and evoke the feeling of older samurai films. There are multuple endings but may not be worth a replay for some. It does get quite repetitive in the later chapters and you can't skip the tutorial/intro. I just wanted the game to end at points in later chapters, especially on repeat playthroughs. However, I would highly recommend Trek to Yomi on sale. The combat is enjoyable, stylish, and it is satisfying to pull off chains of combos. I only rolled to dodge projectiles. You can parry every attack but jumping attacks that some bosses do and block most. If you are familiar with fighting games(like mortal kombat stuff), it will be an easy adjustment. Understanding what combos to use, when to use them, TIMING of button inputs and stick movement, and not to button mash is key. You can easily stagger bosses if you chain combos right. Beat last boss on Kensei with only a couple parries and not using any utilities. Instead of timing like X,X,Y. Delay a heavy atk input like X,X--YMy first playthrough was on normal difficulty then my second was on Kensei (one hit mode for you and all enemies except for bosses) that was about a 5hr run for each playthrough. I did not find it too difficult. Kensei is fun, but I think it lessens the game. Since it is one hit, it defeats the purpose of combos and executions when facing common enemies. For me, I try to go into fights thinking how I can make this encounter look like movie, especially with the amazing backgrounds, rather than dispatching enemies with one hit.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: 8 hours in and I still haven't beaten the game. The first game i ever played where I only walk from scene to scene. This is art and a love letter to Akira Kurosawa. The fact that it goes from Yojimbo to Silent Hill makes it even more of a unique take on the classic Samurai film. I don't mean to call out people who want to just have a scenic sprint, but you are missing the beauty. Each scene is crafted into a picturesque black and white painting. *This game is meant to be played on the hardest difficulty as well. I can't imagine normal mode, but I know it would smear this Cuthlian horror's intended dread. 10/10 Highly recommend if you enjoy the classic Samurai tales, and know a bit of creepy pasta level Japanese Mythos.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: The black-and-white samurai film aesthetic is nice, even if a bit derivative, and is further aided by the choice to have fixed camera angles as the cinematography and framing provided remain well executed throughout. It never really outstays its welcome and the simplistic exploration and combat on offer here work in its favour, some annoying difficulty bumps aside. The only major drawback I have with this is how formulaic its story is, as it draws from samurai films of old in the worst way possible by recycling plenty of predictable tropes. A very solid 3/5 game otherwise.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Recommend that game.  It feels like an old samurai film.  It is slightly buggy and doesn't have some features that would be helpful.  Biggest thing it should have is a chapter select.  Once you complete the game you cannot go back to parts you would maybe enjoy.  On the second way through I made sure that I made a copy of the game save so I didn't have to deal with doing the game a third time just to see the ending.  Again I would recommend it but it should have had some people thinking about the user experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful example of great concept but bad execution. A nice chanbara inspired game with a cinematic quality on a 2D combat field sounds great but it requires that you're able to see what you're doing, especially when combat is centered around parries. The unfortunate reality of this game is that it is extremely hard to see what is happening to you on screen in combat even with every single effect turned off. You are relegated to the smallest portion of the screen which, while feeling cinematic, detracts from the experience by obscuring critical information. This is on top of performance issues that seem to not change based on which graphics settings. From the lowest to the highest sometimes your parry just doesn't come out if your stamina is full. Not to mention that occasionally the game just kind of lags for no discernible reason making an enemies attack invisible or your attack miss. I wanted to like this game but these issues aren't something you can look past because of how heavily it negatively impacts the main point of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Great game for those who love Japanese culture and samurai movies, like . _childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi became one of my absolute favorite games within the first hour. It is old feudal Japan at its most beautiful interpretation. Amazing atmosphere, voice acting, soundtrack and gameplay. It can be a hard game if you are not careful, but you usually only take hits, or die, if you are rushing in to defeat your enemies. take your time and master the blade. This is a game I will revisit many many times. I can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: I really had a problem whether to give this game a positive or negative review. I have chosen positive because the game is beautiful, the camera movement does a great job at creating a stunning cinematic experience. This is somehow similar to Journey in my opinion. I really enjoyed slowly walking through the locations to admire them. But that is all in terms of positives. The story is not bad but nothing special. Since the views and scenery are the greatest asset of the game, I really regret not playing it on the easiest difficulty. Because combat is TERRIBLE. Reach and hitboxes are ambiguous. Animations are badly timed. The character is sluggish in responses. Out of more than a dozen combos 3 or 4 are actually useful. Stamina is just an annoying limit which only purpose is to grant enemies some free hits from time to time. Dodges are inconsistent in their behaviour and hard to time appropriately. Not to mention that enemies are boring, range weapons are more of a gimmick than a useful tool, and the whole combat is hardly rewarding. Additionally controls on an Xbox controller are the most non-intuitive ones I have ever seen and they cannot be changed. Hence my hesitation whether positive or negative review. The game is mostly about combat after all, and combat is awful and frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Great story, great gameplay, gorgeous visuals. Trek to Yomi is like playing your way through a classic samurai movie and of course it's amazing. Very easy to pick up with a simple but visually appealing combat system based on parries and combos. Story is just like something out of one of the aforementioned classic samurai movies with all the revenge/redemption/honor/duty themes you love and expect from the genre and is very well paced across 7 chapters that can be completed in 3-5 hours. Trek to Yomi does not disappoint on any level, do yourself the favor and check this one out for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey there!I just finished Trek to Yomi and I can say for certain that it's not  what I expected "style and story over gamplay"  which is not a bad thing by any means ......it's actually  GREAT !   Let's start with ......."STORY"The game narrates the story of a Samurai struggle and arduous journey to decide his fate . without any spoilers here I would say the story is fantastic , backed  by  superb voice acting and player choice ( different endings  story) . _childDocuments_.review: I thought this game was pretty cool for the first hour and a half. However, the combat quickly starts to feel INCREDIBLY stiff and the enemies get very boring. Combos are borderline useless because the only way you'll get to use any full combo is if you miss the first hit or two, since all the enemies die in like two hits or sometimes even one (this is on normal). I understand why the admittedly satisfying stun-executions are so rare to get, because if you actively try to do multiple in a row you will find that there's only 3 or 4 animation. I wish they played more on that execution gimmick and the dueling aspect of this game because the way they handled it is just really boring. This is an example of a game that is all flair, no substance. The environments are gorgeous and the black and white aesthetic is pretty neat, but after an hour and a half I really felt like I was just watching a bunch of tech demo style environments instead of playing a game. It's a real shame because I love this time period and really wish there was a good samurai game until Ghost of Tsushima hopefully comes to PC. I don't know if such a game exists on PC, but if there is let me know in the comments lol.

_childDocuments_.review: First, I hate combat part in this game It should be better than this, It's too easy to find a way to fight a boss I suppose that should more complex.But I love The Visual and Art Direction, Yes I'm Kurosawa's Film Fan,I'm so glad to see Kurosawa's style on gameUnfortunately, This game not good as game playBut OK I recommended this game if you need to see amazing visual and sound.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't review a lot of games but either I'm in a very lucky minority or the combat issues with this game are incredibly overblown. I played through the game on the hardest available difficulty using a Switch Pro controller so take that into consideration.With the exception of rolling, I didn't feel any delay on my actions. If present, it was small enough to the point where I couldn't notice. Combat felt very limited until about 4 stages in. A majority of new combos are acquired by defeating specific enemies, some mandatory and some not, so it's possible to miss out on some of them. I think the most important ones are on the main path however. Complaints about combos being only 2 hit are just plain wrong. As mentioned before, combat feels very limited in the initial stages, but later extends into a variety of 3 hit combos, and a single 4 and 5 hit combo (from the ones I've found. Not sure if I have them all). By experimenting with these you'll find that a lot of the stronger combos can be chained with smaller ones afterward. My personal favorite being Forward-Strong, Light + Down-Light, Up-Light, Down-Light, which took out most basic enemies and could be spammed in boss fights, most notably the final boss. Trek to Yomi doesn't have the best combat ever, but it's good. Good enough for me to say that I consider the story to be it's lowest point.Style and camera angles are where this game truly shines. I probably don't have anything to say that hasn't been said already so I'll keep it short.  The camerawork and lighting is spectacular, and the use of the foreground and background to visually spice up combat scenes, alert you of upcoming enemies, or to convey the haunting atmosphere of Yomi were very well executed. I'd say these are the main reasons for playing the game, but if you want a decent challenge, try it out on the harder difficulty.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Just a short preview of a review for the ones insecure whether to buy or not.I've played 3 hours on Hard/Ronin and had great fun. Meaning A-/B+ fun.Most crucial point: In my opinion the combat system is not bad. It feels like a pure "sword-’em-up-souls-like". You have to react precisely, move dynamically, you have to be careful with your stamina and you have to think of a strategy at challenging sections - at least if your muscle memory is not yet developed enough. At moments where you're stuck, you can feel the depth of the system, piece by piece, it is not remarkably complex, but a lot more satisfying than your typical indie brawler. Learn the specific patterns of the enemies, learn to parry precisely, find yourself to be successful with a seemingly useless combo thoughtfully executed at a specific situation, throw your sparse shuriken in just the right moment – to me this is fun, I don’t know about anybody else.However, I guess if you play on lower difficulty levels, the experience won’t be the same. Therefore I’d recommend to:1. Put the hype aside2. Set it on hard3. Enjoy the bloody black and white carnage
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: is a fine cinematic action game for one evening. Visual style, music, and voice acting are pretty solid while gameplay is a bit clunky. I mean, it's okay for a half-price 4 hour long game, but I still see no reason for dozens of combos and stuff you're learning throughout the walkthrough when you'll probably use one of them for the entire game 'cause there is no reason to do otherwise. Maybe on high difficulties where enemies and bosses are most likely more deadly you'll be forced to rotate your fighting style depending on the enemy type, but on the standart difficulty there's no reason to do so. It's also great to have multiple ranged options, like kunai, bow, and arquebus, but I found a bow the only useful thing in some occasions, and all the ranged weapons completely useless for the most part of the game.  So yeah, gameplay gets old pretty quickly since there are no enemy variety and combat is mostly mashing same 3 buttons all the time, but I still believe that visuals and art style could carry this game at least for one playthrough, which is worth it. Storywise, it is a dramatic tale about love, duty, and vengeance, which is simple but serves pretty well to propel a player to move on. There're also multiple endings (three, I believe) which depends, as far as I can tell, on multiple dialogue choices you have to make throughout the story, which does not affect gameplay, only some cutscenes.Overall,  is worth your time and money at least to appreciate the effort of the devs to place you into  movie, which they handled pretty good.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I just beat this game in a single sitting which is very uncommon as someone with a busy schedule. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to enjoy Trek to Yomi more than I did.  There is so much to like about it.  The aesthetic is amazing, it really feels like you are in an old timey samurai film.  The game has the feel of a film, I like how it controls the camera for you, and takes dramatic and/or cinematic angles.  The problem is the action.  It is too one note.  Incredibly sadly, as much as I love the bold choice of black and white with film grain, it may have contributed to the feeling of sameness in each level.  I did not finish Trek to Yomi, I thought maybe I would enjoy it more on Steam Deck, but it did not reinvigorate me.  I did not finish Trek to Yomi, but I think I am done with it, hence the review for the unfinished game.  Perhaps there is something more interesting, and I just didn't make it, maybe one day I will go back and see, but it looks doubtful at this point.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Visual presentation and music is great, but gosh is the combat awful, repetitive, and floaty. It's like inputs have a frickin 10 seconds delay.
