_childDocuments_.review: I think everyone agrees that the presentation of Trek To Yomi is outstanding. That is not the issue, and in my opinion, is enough for a recommendation with an asterisk. If you ever wanted to feel what it is like to be in a film, to participate in the scene and not just be a witness, than Trek To Yomi achieved it and then some. However, the complaints about combat has some validity even though they are exaggerated. In my opinion  The combat actually has flow, it has rhythm and it has motion. There was thought and a system. The problem is that it is very unpolished, which I will explain with further detail below. That's not saying the unfavorable reviews are wrong. In fact, they're not entirely wrong, just not very accurate. Not everyone is going to like this game. As for myself, I like it. I believe Flying Wild Hogs has shown tremendous potential here and as a game on balance, Trek To Yomi has more good than bad. Soft recommendation, 7/10. Describing Trek To Yomi is pretty would be doing the game a great injustice. Flying Wild Hog really wanted to make a game out of a Kurosawa film and they nailed it. They nailed so well that if you're a fan of Akira Kurosawa, you're going to love this game. Love it. I can't overstate what the feeling is like to play a Kurosawa film. It is the same feeling as people playing Kingdom Hearts, or those old school Disney games like Aladdin, Castle Of Illusion and Duck Tales. Each of these elements, the sound design, the graphics, the script and the amazing cinematography marries so well with each other to create a seamless and (almost) flawless immersion. The  story is not original but I’ve always held that, you don’t need to have an original story; you just need to tell a story well.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Story is not bad although following standard recipe which I found a little boring at times, but the combat system is just meh.Enemies instantly recover from attacks be it thrown or sword, but you get staggered quite a bit despite being the "samurai master" going against bandits who can barely wield a weapon. This especially goes for armored unites who you stab with your sword for example, and can then just instantly swing back at you. It's just bad design, not "git gud" So it just makes it very static where you have to be sure you get first strike unless they start always jumping back from every attack you make.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game with an amazingly well captured Kurosawa-style look and feel.Unfortunately that's where the the good really ends. It's combat is more or less a one-button parry affair with the world's longest parry window that it's almost impossible to screw it up. Meaning you can more or less one shot every enemy in the game.After two hours of playing there was no sign anything was changing or getting more interesting gameplay wise so I refunded it. A shame as I had been looking forward to this since it was first shown. I'll maybe pick it up in a sale when it's $5 or less but the price it's asking vs how much there is to actually play? Not worth.4/10
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I wanted to recommend this game at first I really can't. The story is okay and the visuals are stunning, sometimes you feel like in a 60s samurai film... However, 80% of the game is combat and the combat system is really bad.Playing it on hard is more frustrating that it should be. There's no challenge, only frustration. The combos, inputs and movements are really clunky. The game doesn't register hits really well when you're facing two enemies or there's a difference in heigh, like fighting against someone on top on a hill (being a 2D game this is really bad).Sometimes you get trapped or bugged, specially after a fall, and some achievements doesn't properly register. Everything could be explained as "low budget indie game" but when you focus so much on the combat system and the whole experience is feeling like "The clumsy Samurai" something is off... Sometimes your combos are perfectly timed, sometimes they don't... but you're pressing the buttons the same way. Sometimes the enemy needs one hit to die, sometimes four, sometimes the boss does nothing, sometimes does a 5 hit unblockable combo... Everything feels random, you can die by two hits on hard and you end up passing stages because of luck, because your moves are so glitchy that you simply never know.Easy and normal is too easy, Kensei is fun (everyone dies by one hit, including you) and hard is just a mess.Play it for the visuals and move on, at least the game is short.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful visuals and presentation let down by some truly dull gameplay. The combat system is too basic.  It feels sluggish and unresponsive.  There is a parry mechanic that allows you to skip most of the combat system by trivializing it to essentially one hit kills.  There's practically no enemy variety.  Once you dial in how to parry against the two or three incoming attacks you'll ever see, that's all the combat becomes.  There's other skills and even ranged attacks that I don't see why you'd bother using.  Beyond that the gameplay involves just moving in one direction killing the same enemies over and over again with an occasional annoying boss fight.It supports 21:9 great in gameplay, cutscenes, and menus.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: This game is for sure stylish, but both the story, and the gameplay share one fatal flaw. This game looks great, sounds great, but it's TEDIOUS. The combat ain't it chief. It's sluggish, irritating, often gets weird interactions with the Block/Parry mechanic, and completely devolves into using whatever Stun move you have, into the Finisher button. It's like Sifu, except even more simplistic, and lame.It sucks, because I'm a sucker for Samurai games, but until we get like... a new Way of the Samurai, I guess we're just gonna have to suffer with mediocre games like this and Ghost of Tsushima.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Very confused about the other reviews because not only did I not have issues with the combat, I thought it was smooth, fluid, and rewarding. There are a myriad of combos and move-sets that you gain as the story progresses. The complaints about only two or three combos are from people who have simply not progressed past the second chapter. The complaints about ranged enemies are also a head scratcher because you also have ranged weapons. Countering bowmen and gunmen often come down to closing the gap and staggering them with quick attacks. Stunning combos and finishers is the way to dispatch of many foes as quickly as possible. Simply get better at the game or lower the difficulty if the combat is too hard, but don't let these reviews stop you from enjoying one of the best releases of this year.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: The word cinematic in thrown around a lot in games, but well this game has taken it to another level. I am a fan of old Japanese cinema and they have nailed the visuals, the music, the environment, and the story. All phenomenal. For that experience this game should be definitely played. I cheated and saw the 4 endings on YouTube and the definitely the resolution to the story is great. The negative is the combat, I wish the creators also paid more attention to the gameplay as the cinematic experience and this would be touted a masterpiece, it is just too repetetive and unresponsive. But I think the game should be experienced alone on the basis of the visual journey. Just phenomenal.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: It feels very much like those old samurai movies, at least, until the supernatural stuff happens and the VFX there doesn't at all feel like practical/film effects they could have done in the 1940s.But, the combat is very simplistic and repetitive, game would have left a better impression if it was an hour or so shorter.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to recommend this one. The artstyle is stunning (the visuals are reminiscent of old samurai movies, the black and white color palette is a good choice for this setting), the Japanese VA sounds great, the music is fitting, the atmosphere is on point, the combat is very satisfying and requires some skill, the story is decent and the "plot twist" halfway through the game is nice.The main problem is that the game feels drawn out, you kinda feel like it's going to end any moment, only for it to keep going for a couple more hours. There's little enemy variation, you can't avoid fights and are forced to fight the same enemies over and over again. The boss fights (and to some extent even normal enemies) feel cheap at times, as they don't really seem to have the same limitations as the player and can keep on attacking (it's also a bit annoying how easily you can get stunned/locked in a combo). The exploration is limited, there aren't all that many secrets to be found. There isn't an incentive to replay the game, maybe only if you are interested in seeing the different endings (I got the bad ending, and online I've seen the good ending, so there are at least 2 endings, depending on what choices you make throughout the game).Overall, I kinda enjoyed my time with Trek to Yomi. I would have preferred for it to be shorter and maybe focus less on fighting hordes of samey enemies. The aforementioned issues do subtract from the enjoyment, making the game a hard sell.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like Trek to Yomi. It has such good visualization, good audio, a mediocre story that is heavily reminiscent of old samurai movies that tugs right at the nostalgia. The game play itself is simple, and because of that, the problems with the combat ruin what could have been a cult classic of a game. With an input of only five or so buttons the imprecision of the combat combos, counters, defenses, and ranged weapons makes the game frustrating and not in a fun roguelite way. Additionally the game offers little desire to replay to see the different paths because the combat is repetitive and frustrating through one play through, I'm not doing it two more times or going back for the collectibles. tl;dr Beautiful game ruined with subpar and repetitive combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Video Review: Steam Curator: Trek to Yomi is quick, repetitive, and pretty fun to watch. Extraordinary lighting and camera direction fulfill this game's well-marketed promise to deliver breathtaking, cinematic visuals in the spirit of classic samurai films. But beneath this brutal side-scroller's lovely monochromatic kimono lurks an unsightly birthmark or three.  STORY - Plot (3/5) | Characters (2/5) | Dialogue (4/5)As stories go, Trek to Yomi is well-paced if predictable. It tells the tale of Hiroki, a solemn samurai who vows at a young age to defend his town from all threats. Not ten minutes later, a grown-up Hiroki returns from a mission gone wrong to find his town a smoldering ruin (which probably explains all the one-star reviews he’s getting). Our sad samurai then battles his way through hell, literally, to reclaim what was lost, and along the way gains clarity as to his role in this wicked world. If you think that summary was too surface-level, try playing the game, which does remarkably little to flesh out its one-dimensional characters. That is unless you count some easy to miss collectibles, at least two of which contain developments vital to the plot that, inconceivably, didn’t make it into the plot. Luckily, it's not all bad, as the game’s Japanese voice acting is very well-done, and not like steak well-done, you know—that's, that’s overdone. I’m talking a tasty medium here. Still, grounded voice acting, alone, isn’t enough for me to recommend Trek to Yomi’s story, so let’s move on to its gameplay and content. GAMEPLAY - Combat (3/5) | Non-Combat (2/5) | U.I. (3/5) | Playability (3/5) & CONTENT - World (4/5) | Objectives (3/5) | Bosses (3/5) Puzzles (2/5) | Value (3/5)If 10% of Trek to Yomi is gawking at its at times haunting and always beautiful environmental set pieces, the other 90% is kicking down doors and killing everything in sight. Too bad ALL you’ll see is the same handful of standard enemies. You know the ones I’m talking about—you’ve got the unarmored trash that goes down no questions asked, the armored units that put up a fight, and some of the most overpowered ranged enemies. Good thing the game gives you ranged weapons of your own, some of which make it hilariously easy to cheese those tough-talking bandits. Other than that, the game's actual swordplay is nothing special and feels a bit stiff—there are a few interesting combos, though.As for playability, my time with Trek to Yomi was bug-free and boasted snappy load times, but inconsistent difficulty spikes and input lag lead to some frustrating deaths, after which you’ll respawn at the last bonfire I mean shrine you lit I mean closed. Be sure to check those obscured side alleys, lest you miss one. The game’s brisk five-hour playtime is broken up by a handful of decent boss fights, some of whom feature interesting move sets that will take you a few attempts to get down. You’ll have no such trouble with Trek to Yomi’s puzzles, however, as these symbol-matching respites are so simple as to feel insulting. Still, despite this and the game’s disappointing dearth of non-combat activities, Trek to Yomi delivers so unique a stylistic experience as to make its modest price tag probably worth it. STYLE - Art (5/5) | Music (3/5) | Sound (4/5)Indeed, Trek to Yomi is a visual feast unlike anything I can remember playing, and I feel comfortable recommending it to folks on the "Art" micrometric alone. Meanwhile, the game’s subtle soundtrack adds authentic atmosphere to its historic, feudal setting, though the music lacks melody and struggles to stand out from all the screaming and crying and crying and screaming. Man, this game is dark... and white. *Ba dum tish*CONCLUSIONIn conclusion, Trek to Yomi is an easy game to like and a hard one to love. Still, I think it’s worth it if only to see something you haven’t seen before. After averaging up our micrometrics, Trek to Yomi earns a decidedly average MEGA score of 3.07/5. Thank you so much for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: I did not have fun playing this game.The entire thing felt artificially long and combat was always frustrating, and because of this the story's pacing, and my investment in it, was completely destroyed.Difficulty wasn't an increase in the complexity of the enemies, but rather simply an increase in enemy numbers, both with how many are thrown at me between checkpoints and how much HP and Damage they have. Even when they introduced enemies with special abilities, they were quickly spammed to the point where they just became a slog to get through.Ranged enemies felt unfair for the entire game, as you can only dodge their shots which requires the stamina you need to conserve to parry enemies, turning every fight one is in into a mad dash to try and kill them as soon as possible, cutting your health in half (if not less!) before you can properly engage the rest of the fight.Environments look pretty, yes, but with how things keep dragging they feel repetitive even within the level they're introduced in, and sometimes the attempts to have objects appear in the foreground can actively get in the way of your fighting.Exploration is also quite frustrating. Whenever I'd face a possible branching path I'd have to pause and figure out which way is the way forwards, and which is the side path, because you ALWAYS want to take the side path. Not only is it safer, and you don't get anything from killing enemies anway, but those side paths can be the only place to find your much needed health or stamina upgrades. Or, more importantly, those side paths can lead to your actual checkpoints which for some reason aren't directly on your main path.I luckily didn't encounter any bugs that ruined my game, but if there were any that happened to me, I missed them amongst the number of intended game mechanics that were frustrating me instead.As for the story, it might have been interesting if I could bear to pay attention to the small spurts of it between long stretches of repetitive gameplay. As it was, it simply exists, and that's all I can say about it.3/10, quality over quantity next time please.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: To start, I don't like writing bad reviews, people spent time and money working on this game, and clearly tried to make something compelling and beautiful, it just didn't work out.For all its flaws I can say this: this game is pretty, it looks great and the art direction is amazing,  I just can't recommend it based on this alone.The problem is the gameplay. It really, really sucks. Its a deflect based sword game that's a weird mix of being too easy and too hard, most enemies can be killed by the same 3 -hit combo, and the ones that can't do so much damage you'll likely be dead before you can get to them, and because of a serious lack of enemy types I never enjoyed any of the encounters this game has to offer. This gameplay is also nowhere near refined enough, half the time that 3-hit combo i was talking about never comes out. Serious refinement is needed before this game becomes anywhere near fun to play, and that refining is likely never going to happen.This game also has the definition of shoe-horned in puzzles and mechanics, really unnecessary, and completely ruins what little flow this game has, especially in the latter half.Finally, the final boss is awful. Ridiculous damage, health, phases and attacks, creating a boss that just doesn't fit with this games combat mechanics. It got me so worked up that I could barely concentrate on the ending and made me immediately come write this review.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: ***First off, this is a Samurai game for Samurai movie lovers, if you haven't seen the movies then you won't understand how much of an achievement this game is. Watch these movies before playing (Sanjuro, Seven Samurai, Musashi, Zatoichi or Sword of doom) Story: Spot on for 1960s samurai movies with a lot of Japanese mythology.Visuals: Truly incredible work with lighting, Depth of field and perspective.Sound: Very good sound effects.Music: Perfectly sets the tone, more traditional than samurai film but excellent, makes you want to just stop and listen.Gameplay: Typical samurai game mechanics, cut at the right time or die. Loads of hidden paths and secrets. Summary: This game accomplished exactly what it set out to do, make you feel like you are in a 1960s samurai movie and is only costs $20, go for it, you will be happy you did.My opinion: This is a true work of art. Everything from the story, sound, music, cinematography to the visual effects. Combat is very spot on for samurai games, reminds me of Kengo and Way of the Samurai on PS2. In my opinion this is probably the best 2.5D game ever made. It is a perfect tribute to the Samurai movie genre. There are so many moments in the game where you just have to stop and take in the view its insane.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals and audio for the game are fantastic. If you are a fan of Kurasawa, Hideo Gosha and other directors of older samurai movies you will greatly enjoy the aesthetics of this game. The game is heavily influenced by these directors and their movies and it shows as you progress. The movie like camera angles in the game are generally great throughout the entire game. But, there are times that these angles and visuals can get distracting for the combat. The combat is not amazing but its not the worst I have seen. There are different combo's you unlock as you progress so it does open up to more diversity. On the harder difficulties you will tend to use stuns and finishers more often which can get repetitive. Overall I would recommend the game for the visuals alone if you enjoy watching the movies this game drew inspiration from.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first ever bad review. I was very excited for this game when I saw trailers for it. Smooth combat, amazing visuals, this looked like a movie! Yeah the visuals are the only good part about it. The combat is maybe some of the worst I have ever played. Every fight feels like the video of two robots with swords that are programmed to fight each other. The combos are basically useless since you can literally use one combo throughout the game and be just fine. I bought this game and I'm hoping my refund goes through. If they end up fixing it, great. I'll play it on my Xbox on Gamepass. But there is no way I'm ever spending money on this again.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun and visually stunning. I'm a tad disappointed that the writers felt the need to branch into the supernatural- I was really looking forward to having a samurai game that just kinda avoided that whole cliche- It feels like its so rare to just get an honest game about Samurai in feudal japan that isn't a warriors game or some anime chibi adventure. Either way, worth the price for sure but combat can get repetitive and by the end of the game I was 100% ready for it to be over- So it doesn't really leave you wanting more, but also doesn't overstay it's welcome. Edit: Having finished the game on normal difficulty- I'm not completely upset with my purchase. I Stand by the fact that the Supernatural portion of the game is boring, cliche and all together way too long, and that's a shame because the parts that take place in the actual "real" world feel great and I wish there was more of that because that is what is sorely lacking from most Feudal era japan games that have been released lately. My recommendation is that you get a month of Game pass, and play it on there to your hearts content for a month- you will save 10 bucks and ultimately be able to do everything you could ever want to do in the game. Also the puzzles may as well have just not been in the game at all- that's all i have to say on that front. In light of how long, boring and repetitive the Yomi portion of the game turned out to be after posting my review the first time. I'm changing my score from a 6.5/10 to a 5.5/10 and have chosen to NOT recommend this game at it's current price point- Ultimately the game is entertaining but the mainstay of the game plays with themes that have been absolutely done to death by other, better games- and the gameplay itself (while novel in the beginning) becomes incredibly tedious after the first 20 or so fights. 5.5/10 - Get it on sale or on Game pass.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: All Style, little substance. While the Kurosawa influences are expertly recreated and honored, as a game it has very little going for it. All enemies are easily defeated by a single combo (which you will be repeating endlessly since it can get you health back) while bosses are un-fun to fight given the vagueness of what is and isn't rollable/punishable/deflectable etc. The levels are beautiful to look at in whole, but you will be doing little sightseeing since you'll be scouring the screen for tiny flashes to find collectibles and ammo; if I didn't care about picking stuff up I would have appreciated the beautiful art style much more. TLDR: Short, beautiful game with shallow mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, the gameplay here is rather lackluster, but I the visuals and story-telling presentation more than make up for it. If you're on the fence with this one, I would suggest definitely picking it up on a sale! It's a short enough game that any of the  wanting elements of the game won't have enough time to wear you down.If you'd like to check out my full thoughts then please watch my review here:

_childDocuments_.review: Faced a game-ending bug that hasn't somehow been fixed nearly 2 years after launch.Really disappointed with this game. After trudging through the combat (which isn't too bad), and it's really interesting story, I cannot even finish the game because of the bug.At chapter 6 after you make it to the end of Yomi, I had the choice to choose which type of ending to go with. After making the choice and returning to the world, i realized I have none of the skills and weapons I had in Yomi. (Basically 80% of the weapons and skills) Checked all over the net and it seems it is a common problem.This has made the game unplayable because even my health can barely manage with the late game enemies. (Who have their late-game weapons)Just really sad that I cannot even finish this game, because the art direction and story is genuinely interesting.But I cannot recommend this game to anyone if there's a bug this big that's still happening with no fix.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Plays like a 2D hack-and-slash, feels like a Kurosawa film. Gameplay is simple but honed, giving you the tools to flow through enemies without holding your hand. Normal mode is much easier than anticipated, but with two higher difficulties and multiple endings, mastery through replaying is achievable and reasonable. Story and aesthetics are definitely the biggest draw. Once the more supernatural elements begin to show, the visuals go from good looking to outstanding. Leaning on the Kurosawa cinematography style with fixed camera angles helps to make for some outstanding backdrops and set pieces.Worth the $20, but if you really can't justify dropping that much for a 5-6 hour game, then waiting for a sale is a valid option.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: This game is Fantastic! An absolute piece of art. The Japanese film aesthetic is spot on. The camera angles, details to depth perception, the soundtrack, etc... I LOVE this. It has its own artistic character that sets it apart from other games. Do not let any negative reviews cause you to hesitate to experience this gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: At first i wanted to leave a positive review, obviously the art/graphics and camera angles are really great, very well crafted. But let's be honest here, the game is an hollow shell, a beautiful one for sure, but it's simply empty or i should say filled with an insufferable gameplay and a very forgettable and boring story.

I was super excited about this game because of the ascetics and story but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is it not fun to play. _childDocuments_.review: Interesting story, well paced, dynamic boss fight's and great sound design. Picked it up through steam sale and couldn't put it down. would recommend the final difficulty, learning to go through the entire game and boss fights hit less is an amazing feeling once you learn the patterns and pull it off. i'd give it a 10/10 except for one achievement for the hidden ending had to restart the game four times just to retry that section due to no chapter select and it did make me rage. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I just completed the game. Surprisingly, it was fun adventure, with unusual visual approach and atmospheric story. Don't listen to people who says about "terrible controls". Through each stage of the game you unlock more moves, which make combat a bit more interesting during playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great, it really does a great job of making you feel like you're in a Kurosawa film.The combat is a bit janky, but nowhere near as bad as others are saying. Controls can be a bit unresponsive and the combat is definitely a bit undercooked, but that hasn't ruined the experience for me so far. _childDocuments_.review: Cinematically beautiful, engaging gameplay, a typical Samurai story of love and vengeance. Combos need to be very precise and it takes practice, but once mastered, almost nothing can touch you. I really recommend this game for those who loves samurai and swords with a little bit of horror and supernatural.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game,It's artstyle is unique and briliant, it feels like feudal japan, plays like feudal japan and have everything to make you feel it to.It's story is simple yet entertaining and intrging and it has choices that changes your playthrough.Gameplay is good, by going through story and exploring you get access to more combos evolving your playstyle from black, left fast, right slow to combs that you can use freely and feel good. Enemies are also mainly well made, I said mainly, because there's one enemy in which, if you fail you can't recover and last boss has an attack which is very hard to block and deals much dmg.Overall 9.5/10 would love to have chapter selection after finishing the game so I can collect collectibles which I missed without replaying all of the game. Difficulty settings are well balanced, I played on hardest and had fun while having a challange. I've never been stuck, but if you don't want to be on edge most of the time normal difficulty or easy are also aviable.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: The game is beautiful, both the graphics and story.The artwork is to die for. I love the scene and the background the game is set it. It really makes the game feel like a movie but it also pulls you in and makes you a part of it.The combat can be difficult at times but only when facing like 6 enemies at once then it's difficult but other than that I feel like as long as you can memorize some combos you'll be fine. It's a great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Controls:           While a lot of people are saying that the controls are bad or unresponsive I played this with a controller and I feel like that is how the game is meant to be played. I found that the only time that the game would not track my inputs were when I was entering them too fast or spamming them and, I found that they had to be entered as they were executed by the character this may be a work around that I unintentionally found or it is by design however, I think after a while you get used to it.Gameplay:        The gameplay can get repetitive at times as it is a 3D side scroller with some elements of freedom in areas where there is no combat to be had this is usually where they put ammo ability pick ups and collectibles. The bosses are good and get progressively harder as the game goes and it becomes more souls like where you have to identify their move and attack patterns and they will change as you progress through the fight. As you progress through the game you will receive many new attack abilities and you will find that there are only a few that you will use, typically  the ones that stun so that you can do a finisher and regain some health which leads to deaths happening because you really messed up a fight or you encounter a new enemy type that you don't know how to fight. Otherwise, you should have full health through the most of the game. The AI will only attack one enemy at a time with the exception of ranged enemies who will attack you while you fight the melee characters. However, with the melee enemies they will try to avoid you and back away from you when you try to attack or approach while another one is engaged with you in combat. Now that doesn't mean that they will attack with only one until that enemy is dead because they will switch who is engaging you from time to time and that one that was fighting you will go from attacking to defending and avoiding you. Story:        The story is pretty good but and it can be a story based on your choices. It can be a game about revenge, love, or honor and duty it progresses at a good pace I feel like it can also be a story about perseverance as well.Presentation:         The presentation is great and honestly ti's probably the best thing about this game. It is in black and white with and overlaying film grain (which can be turned off, I advise against it) that makes it feel like you're watching an old samurai movie and it's great however, I find that the subtitles are a bit strange so I changed the game to have all the characters speak English. This allowed the voice actors to deliver their lines in a more fluid and organic way as to make more sense grammatically than the subtitles do. However, they keep the same theme and meaning that the subtitles show that they are trying to convey and only venture slightly from them only when it would make more sense or sound more fluid said another way than the way it's spelled out in the subtitles while keeping the same overall meaning.Conclusion:        I feel that this game is definitely worth the price it is asking for and I think that this game is definitely worth your time and money. I do recommend using a controller for this game as I feel that is how it was meant to be played.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of films like Sanjuro, Sword of Doom, Hara-kiri and Samurai Rebellion, then Trek to Yomi is for you. BUT if you are not a fan of these films and are just hoping for a cool looking action game to muck around with, then you mileage will greatly vary and you're not going to appreciate what this game is trying to do.Trek To Yomi is a love letter to Samurai Cinema. Not just Akira Kurosawa films, but the whole Black and White Samurai movie genre. The devs have absolutely nailed the look of these films; from the framing, to the way it uses light bloom and depth of field. Even the combat, has that classic look and feel. It's all so visually stunning and I find myself pressing F12 for screen shots every other scene. The sword play can be a little messy and unforgiving at first, but once you get the hang of parrying and decide on a few favorite combos, it becomes a lot of fun. I per-purchased the game with a 10% discount and it is worth every penny to me for the artistic value alone.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly stylistic, and reminiscent of yesteryear's noir samurai films. The story is interesting, a tale of revenge and redemption interwoven with Japanese mythology and bits of history from the feudal Japanese time period.  The combat was great in some places, but super janky in others. I found it playable but honestly dropped the difficulty down a notch at the last boss as he felt a bit overtuned on the higher difficulty. With a little more polish, I think this game would've been a certified hood classic. It felt like I was playing a spiritual successor to Onimusha: Warlords, another great game in this genre by Capcom. In summation, the cinematography and art direction felt like the game's strongest asset and I could take or leave the combat. If you catch this game on sale, I'd highly recommend checking it out, but if you really need to scratch that samurai itch, $20 isn't too bad to take a chance on for entertainment these days.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game, it's a movie. In fact, it's such a compelling movie that I'd rather just watch it than play it.This game mimics a style of film that you might expect from an Akira Kurosawa film. It's a great thing to mimic, because this game looks really good. Like, this game looks fantastic. However, judged on the merits of a game, is one of the worst games I've ever played.This game is 99% a beat-em-up, and it's the worst beat-em-up I've ever played. Buttons feel unresponsive, combos don't work, your actions feel sluggish and you can literally hammer buttons during a combo and they won't work (I'm aware that you're not supposed to hammer the buttons).I would describe this game as having awful timing. In combat, everything requires timing that only the game seems to know how you're supposed to match. Regardless of what your character is actually doing, if you timed your original combo incorrectly, the move won't work. The game has its own timing, and you must respect it.On the cinematic side of things, the problem is the exact opposite; the pacing feels awful because it's trying to give you a collectible hunt while at the same time trying to make you feel like there's urgency in the events happening on screen. You as a player want to explore, but the game as a movie wants you to press on and not explore.As a result, every second of playing this game was pulling teeth; I want to enjoy this experience like a film, but I can't because the game was actually painful for me to play.Do yourself a favor and wait for someone to record a playthrough of this game that makes the game look like a movie; I'd argue that's what the developer wants you to do, anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: Was absolutely over-hyped for this game, and it's delivered on every front.Masterclass in camera work. Dripping with Akira Kurosawa flavor. Some interesting enemy behaviors, but not until you're a fair bit into the story.Update after finishing the game:Alright. Not quite 11/11. But nearly! Bit of jank in the controls keeps it from being flawless. But hot damn. What an experience. Very easy to recommend for anyone brought in on the theme or visual style.

_childDocuments_.review: First off this is more a neutral review, the gameplay is average and completely playable but for me it was such a disappointment! I really love the setting, and the atmosphere & style of this game are exceptional, but it's really let down by the combat and save system. The combat is just not very fun....button presses are unresponsive, inconsistent, and ignored half the time, which turns all the fun you were having into frustration. The game seems to be going for a 2D Sekiro souls-like combat system, but lacks the precision & polish to pull it off, and it just becomes annoying replaying sections over and over because the game is not consistent reading inputs. It's get me wrong, it's not unplayable, or even hard, it just kills the enjoyment when you're punished because the game didn't read your input or just decided not to block or parry and you take a hit. I feel like the game would flow better if the it saved at every new screen or allowed you to quick-save that way the player doesn't have to waste their time running around, climbing a ladder, talking to a NPC, going down a path just go get back to a fight. Anyway I really hope the devs patch or update this game, it's got so much going for it to leave it like this is a real shame. Let's all hope they tighten up the combat a bit, and make this something awesome!** 5/23/2022 After Patch 1.01 Still the same, I did tests in multiple areas (trying to sprint and different attacks) I noticed when using the controller it is either lagging, or not registering button presses like 30% of the time. When I switched to KB+M I had zero issues, so I don't know if it's a controller reading issue or what, but I would suggest playing with KB+M it's a little weird at first, but it's working much better for me and the keys can be re-mapped thankfully.

_childDocuments_.review: First off... can we please stop with the Kurosawa talk? It's cringy as hell already. Sure, it has samurais and it's black and white. WOW IT'S LITERALLY HIS MOVIES RIGHT? No, it isn't. The story and style of it has close to nothing in common with his movies, and what it tries to emulate of him is superficial at best. This is like making a random movie where because the characters dress in suits and speak in italian accents everyone say it's literally the Godfather.Anyway, while i enjoyed my time with this game, as i do in fact enjoy samurai stories, i have to warn you that it is not some deep, engaging indie action game, at all. It's in fact full style over subtance. Think of Ryse: Son of Rome, but as an indie samurai game. I enjoyed that game, and enjoyed this one too. It works, and it's cheap and short enough not to overstay it's welcome, so i was satisfied with what i paid for.What i like most about this game was how beautifully crafted the scenarions were and the nice camera work that makes them stand out. Kinda made me miss those oldschool static camera games. The black and white filter and some decent music really added to their atmosphere too.The gameplay here is serviceable. Works fine (most of the time), and it has a nice fluidity to the animations, but yeah, it's shallow. The only tip i can give you is to abuse the stun attack on spongy enemies so you can kill them quickly and replenish some health, and don't bother saving the secondary weapons, as you get plenty of them.So, if you're ok with a short and simplistic fun game with a lot of style, i say go for it. If you're in doubt wait for a sale. Still, it was an enjoyable little game, and i hope the devs can flesh it out more for their upcoming games.

_childDocuments_.review: I WANT to recommend this game but just can't. Aesthetically I love it. I love the IDEA. It feels like being in a 1950's samurai flick but a few things stop me from giving it the thumbs up. The biggest being:COMBATLike most 3D samurai games its NOT FUN or rewarding in the leastIt seems to be a genre issue as MOST 3D samurai games in the past have always had this issue. Developers struggle to give a rewarding game in which you feel the "hero's journey" and "wise sages" arm you with increasingly more skill and weapons that you use to your "quest for fire" and in the case of samurai/kung fu/westerns avenge your family/master and beat the BIG BAD.This game does not even give you the basic concept of growing. You START OFF as a kid who appears to have very little training. IMMEDIATELY start killing grown men and then age up instantly with VERY little increase in skill. On the fly you gain new skill with NO instruction in ways that anyone who has ever swung a stick would have. I just randomly decide to swing the sword an extra time now because I killed X people?Enemies are BORING and require you to have the patience to just trudge through them. You have NO significant skill superiority in these types of games. Simply tapping the block button or WAITING on an enemy to swing so you can swing or later charge and swing to stun and then swing again to kill IS NOT FUN. This is at its worst when one of your enemies has armor. Its block to swing swing to block to swing swing to block to swing swing to block to swing swing for most of the game I've played so farOther enemies go from swing when they are 2-3 body lengths away and HOPE it hits them before they hit you to run at them and power swing to stun them to THEN have to hit them again to kill them....The enemies surround you in the laziest way and although there is a turn button and a few skills that deal with enemies attacking you from the rear its never really done in a way that pushes you or requires you to use it. They never really TIME it to challenge you and your space use like a real sword fight. It just kinda happens predictably at intervals and you see it is going to happen before it does.I REALLY should be cutting through smaller enemies gaining power and speed and being challenged by sub and stage bosses which require me to develop timing and space control like a FIGHTER It needs to pick a lane, either im mindlessly slashing through enemies and interacting with a story or I'm developing some timing/space based skill. Instead these developers use this slow methodical boring stuff to add artificial difficulty and HOURS to the game to dictate that they have given you your money's worth in a $/hour ratio. Its LAZY!!!! The "skill" is having the patience or a mindset where this is actually fun and you can do it for however many hours it takes to get through the storyIt wouldn't be half as bad if I attacked faster OR I AND my enemies attacked faster. I'm supposed to be a SAMURAI. It only takes a look at the source material (samurai movies) or youtube videos of Kendo or fencing to see how explosive people who practice swords areIts to slow and clunky to be objectively entertaining for the length of a game I want to play.Objectively it needs either more speed on the swings or it needs a more interactive sword technique

_childDocuments_.review: This game is more than just pretty visuals, although it's not like in lacks those, with Mizoguchi style camera movements and intentional use of lighting so that you are rarely unaware of what you need to know, despite the dark environments. The biggest complaint I see is people saying the combat is bad. I do not understand this. I chose the hardest difficulty available for the first playthrough, so there was definitely a slight learning curve, but once I got used to it, with good timing, I was able to kill the enemies quickly without taking damage. But then the game introduced armored enemies, and I had to adapt to those, and find the patterns needed to take out those guys efficiently, then archers, then spearmen, and more that I won't get into so I avoid spoilers. With each enemy added to the combat loop the player has to adapt, but ultimately, if they are skilled and persistent, they can learn how to overcome the enemies without taking damage. I see no flaws in this system.

_childDocuments_.review: Cinematic, immersive beat'em up. Everything in this game serves its specific mood, from the most breathtaking landsacpe, to the smallest line of dialogue. Japanese dubbing does great job, and so atypical camera angles, which work for gameplay better than expected. Simple exploration supports story (best worldbuilding colletcibles I've seen so far, thanks to their description being narrated by the main character) and simple, yet fun combat. Fighting animations are visibly influenced by kenjutsu, and I liked them far more than those from Ghost of Tsushima. The cherry on top is the fact, that normal and halfsword (!) thrusts penetrate armor, while cuts don't. Using specific techniques for armored enemies is rewarded. I finished the game four times, each time on different difficulty levels, gaining different achievements and choosing different ending. There are four endings, very well implemented - those change your experience in terms of roleplaying and storytelling, but don't interfere with the core of the game. Trek to Yomi is one of few games that I squeezed 100% from.

_childDocuments_.review: Because I assumed that the problems I was having with Trek To Yomi were unique to the game pass version, given that the quality of games may differ based on the platform. While this is generally the case, Trek to Yomi is the lone exception due to its shared issues throughout both platforms.To date, Trek To Yomi has been the most frustrating time I have spent with a game I wanted to like. Storywise, it holds up rather well. The environment is ruined by an annoying HUD that constantly displays data you should already know. Any potential for immersion is shattered when a huge black panel with white text presents the most worthless information.Unfortunately, the fighting system leaves much to be desired since it relies less on ability and expertise and more on luck and frequently inaccurate input feedback. Nonetheless, I chose something other than this game for its gameplay, as I did not anticipate being impressed by its battle systems. Nonetheless, it is regrettable that combat is insufficient by any criterion to be considered desirable.The voice acting is adequate but could be more exceptional. It almost squeaked through with a passing grade. Aside from the terrible HUD, the stutter counter between scenes is the most irritating feature. A cut scene's stuttering on the climax has never made me so angry. It completely negates any meaning that the scenario attempts to convey.The game's performance is by no means poor. Still, terrible micro stutters during the transition from gameplay to cutscene destroy crucial story-defining moments.Overall, the game's plot and scripting are well-done. However, it occasionally detracts from the plot that you feed on-screen material that serves no purpose. If the game followed the same premise as INSIDE, where players learn at their own pace, it would be highly recommended. The situation is different from Trek to Yomi, though. The tale of Trek to Yomi is relayed to players through conversation, and the game makes every effort to facilitate their progress.In addition, this game has checkpoints for storing your progress but not a manual save feature; in 2022, manually save is not yet a typical feature since heaven forbid you to have real-life obligations and need to exit the game.The game has issues, and many of them cannot be overlooked. Having a clunky, MMO-style HUD in a single-player story game is a major turnoff. I can only suggest this game if you share my inability to see past its shortcomings, but if you are more tolerant than I am, you could like it.It is a 6/10 game overall. I was looking for a game that focused on linear storytelling while incorporating other game-style components. Still, whoever designed the HUD hopes someone takes a piss in your coffee.

Well, for the first few hours, it's a fun experience. But, spoilers ahead then you get to Yomi and things get real weird. Cool! Except it drags on. And then you have another chapter. And it drags on. And then you have another chapter. And it just drags on. All the while combat encounters start getting incredibly samey.If the Yomi part of the game were compressed into one longer chapter where you get all the weirdness of the last three chapters condensed, it would be fine. But once the novelty wears off and you just squint at the screen to find any white-flashing collectibles in a black-and-white game between longer and ever more tedious fights... it starts being just meh.Especially once you get certain attacks that quickly stun the enemies, allowing you to execute them regardless of their health while also regenerating your health, you just stop trying to use any of the other skills, which is a shame. Oh, and then you get to fight a boss at the end of chapter six which tests all you learned so far - sadly this strategy does not work on him.Now, I played Sekiro and I loved the combat in that. This sadly does not compare. Parrying sometimes feels like it straightup does not work, same goes for rolls. That really sucks, especially when enemies can kinda stunlock you into taking three or four hits. I didn't want to try and get negate any of that damage anyway.All in all this game shows some real promise, doesn't deliver and then sadly overstays its' welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like Trek to Yomi so much and was hyped for the release. In some ways, I love what the devs were able to create, but fundamental aspects seemed to be overlooked/undercooked and ruin the experience.Trek to Yomi's artsyle and visual presentation is awesome and sets the atmosphere beautifully. Where Trek to Yomi fails is in combat. In a Samurai game one would assume the combat mechanics would be focus #1 for the devs, but that doesn't seem to be the case here. Janky, unresponsive, delayed controls make playing unenjoyable. Combine that with glitches and terrible hitboxes make Trek to Yomi close to unplayable. As well as being messy (to put it nicely), the combat in general is monotonous and makes progressing through the game a slog. I'm on the final stretch and plan on completing Trek to Yomi, but that will most certainly come with frustration and disappointment. Unfortunately, I cannot recommend in the current. If the devs fix the combat and the game goes on sale, I could recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible love letter to classic samurai cinema with its most obvious inspirations drawing from Akira Kurosawa's films.GRAPHICS:To my tastes, visually this game is an absolute stunner.  Much like the films this game is trying to replicate the dev's ability to paint with light is nothing short of amazing.  I understand that a game should probably be judged on its own merits without requiring additional information or historical context but I can't stress how great a visual achievement this game is having watched and studied many of the movies that this game was inspried by. Clearly the devs have done their own film studies as their ability to marry together things like light exposure, camera lens choices, composition, and movement make it look as good as any celebrated film from that time period.  In certain ways, they also emulated real world set design for their environment builds.  Sometimes the screen would be exploding with detail with nothing left unchecked from grand vistas right down to individual cracked and crooked tiles while in other instances the use of minimal and basic shapes combined with the right lighting creates eerily beautiful scenes where your mind fills in all the details naturally. From a technical perspective there are one or two animation transitions that are a bit janky but I'm being picky as it never really drew me out of the game.GAMEPLAY:I did a single playthrough on what I understood to be "normal" mode which is one step above "focus on story rather than combat".  I've played hack'n'slashers in the past and to my taste this was a pretty balanced setting.  Easy enough that you can allow yourself to fight one or two enemies with style and flair but difficult enough that you won't be able to get through a larger group of enemies by button mashing. If you're not paying too much attention to your timing or position on screen then you're probably going to wind up dead.  Having said that, the save points scattered throughout the journey were pretty evenly distributed which was nice.  For the longer and more difficult stretches I died maybe half a dozen times at most and the loading times for checkpoints are so fast that you can hop right back in with the knowledge of what you need to do to correct your mistakes staying pretty fresh.The fight/counter system was decent enough but nothing to write home about.  In terms of the abilities of your character they definitely took a more realistic route-- a handful of strikes and combos will get you through the game.  Some techniques are granted naturally as you progress while others (some of which are pretty powerful) can be learned by exploring some less obvious areas of the levels and finding technique "scrolls". While were talking about exploration, you can also find "collectibles" that don't change anything gameplay-wise but do add interesting historical, cultural, and spiritual context to things which I'm into.  I think I had somewhere in the ballpark of 9-10 techniques by the end of the game but I probably used only about half of them with any regularity.  Different enemies require different approaches which largely come down to timing and distance. When fighting a group the challenge comes from prioritizing the order in which to take them out (even if the methods to do so are not wildly different from enemy to enemy).  You have secondary weapons at your disposal with limited ammo as the focus is generally on sword play.  They include a bow for long range hits, a musket that can penetrate multiple enemies but is very slow to reload, and small blades that can briefly stun weaker attackers.  I generally saved the bow/musket until I got to spots where I was being overwhelmed/killed by larger groups.  Again, checkpoints are so frequent that I didn't mind taking a second to reload and change strategies.The TLDR here is don't go in expecting God of War levels of depth and the system will serve you fine.SOUND:The sound effects are all well crafted and the score/soundtrack is INCREDIBLE.  All the sound design perfectly connects to the films that the game is trying to emulate right down to the hisses, clicks, and pops.  I played the game in Japanese with English subs and I couldn't imagine doing it any other way.  I am not a native Japanese speaker but it all sounded as good/appropriate as any movie I've watched.CONCLUSION:For the 7 hours I put in to this it was more than worth my time and money.  Narratively, there are three paths that you can take to the end which carry themes of LOVE, DUTY, and REVENGE. Considering that I can probably cut my playtime in half the second time through since I won't just be staring at all the level design like an idiot, I'll probably go back and choose at least one if not both to see how it plays out.TLDR:Considering the overall length of the game, If you love old samurai films you will 100% be able to forgive any  mild hiccups in the game mechanics as we have a near perfect homage on our hands.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't write game reviews but Trek to Yomi must be one of the most gorgeous games I have ever seen. The developers quite clearly made a lot of effort in capturing the spirit of old japanese samurai movies like seven samurai, yojimbo, sanjuro and other akira kurosawa masterpieces. This starts with the type of film grain, the subtle shifts in brightness levels and even the camera angles. If you like Metroidvania style games, are looking for something unique and pleasing, and are a fan of traditional Japanese culture, and just want a really fun game that gets your blood pumping, please do yourself a favor and pick this one up - you won't be sorry. Since this is a samurai game, I was expecting fluid controls. I wanted to slice and dice my enemies with flashy combos. Trek To Yomi doesn't have that. Clunky controls and input delays ruin the whole game. Out of 5 buttons I press, the game only registers 1. Just trying to turn around while fighting against 2 enemies is a f*cking nightmare. Don't even get me started on performing those long combos. IM-F*CKING-POSSIBLE. The whole combat is so basic and shallow that I just used the same combo entire game and finished it without a problem. You can perform finishers on stunned enemies but after a while seeing the same animation over and over again really becomes boring. A wide variety of killing animations would be nice. Overall, this game is just presentation and nothing else. Calling this game's gameplay boring is an understatement. The fighting scenes should have made me feel like a cool samurai, instead it was a chore to kill a single enemy and turn around. Trek To Yomi is a huge letdown

_childDocuments_.review: Path to Yomi is fairly YummyIts good.  Its not the best, and is not game of the year - but I really liked it.Mix up of beat-em up , meets samurai-swordsman, 2d(ish) platforming.Many OTHER people HAVE SAID the art style is good and the combat is boring and underdeveloped:I found the art style to be alright, it was good, and there were some areas that did suck you in.  However, there is not a very large variation of (colour)palettes from looks, most areas are dark -particularly after a certain point.  I can see there is a strong theme of death there, and I'm sure that palette shows that, but I would have liked it if it varied.  The Evil Within achieves this better.I mention this as looking at dark images for a long time can become depressing and un inspired.The story itself, along with that was quite serious as these wandering ronin stories tend to be (where their masters were slain - not that they were dismissed).The war theme that went with that was relentless and always appeared hopeless, surrounded by wailing and delirious, lost people: it was, like the art style, quite dark and certainly wanted to highlight the hopelessness of war.The problem was with the levels in-between the check points and various events, was that they dragged on quite a bit - although I think that was like that so that you may learn the combat and experiment with the kills that you learn.The combat was alright, given I played shadow Warrior 1 , and like that stuff, even on the slightly watered down Shadow Warrior 2, I enjoyed combat alot actually and though could not remember most of the moves, as they were all mostly similar from first conceptions, could see how some moves were able to counter others, such as up and down light attacks were very fast, they could be countered by thrusts or heavy strikes.The telegraphing was quite fast, so I'm sure it is a gamble sometimes.  Though once you knew the skins  of the various enemy types, you would understand some would use fast strike, whilst other heavy attacks : meaning some moves were better vs certain assailants  Others have said it was boring, and vs the ai sometimes, 60% of the enemy was effortless, but some could be challenging , particularly if you experimented or did not know what attacks to use.It's worth noting that this is the sort of game you dont pick up and play, at least at the harder difficulty where it shines.  Some of the bosses are tough and you may continue dying until you get something right/get lucky.  Much like combo games similar to  Bayonetta, the longer you play, the more settled you get into the combos and understand what is required ; which is why there is plenty of replay-ablity to be had , you just need to commit to it.Im sure I could play this through again, namely for the combat, but I'm unsure if I would choose to.  A pretty decent game though in all though.

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi : By Triple F"Trek to Yomi" by Flying Wild Hog is a cinematic action-adventure that draws inspiration from classic Japanese samurai cinema, notably the films of Akira Kurosawa. Set in feudal Japan, the game tells the story of Hiroki, a young samurai on a path of vengeance and duty, as he battles to protect his village and uphold his mentor’s teachings. With its striking black-and-white aesthetic, traditional Japanese motifs, and minimalistic combat, "Trek to Yomi" strives to capture the spirit of a samurai epic, presenting a world both hauntingly beautiful and brutal.The standout feature of "Trek to Yomi" is its visual presentation, which perfectly replicates the look of classic black-and-white samurai films. The game’s attention to detail is remarkable: every scene is designed with dramatic lighting, sharp contrasts, and a depth of field that emphasizes the starkness of Hiroki’s journey. The use of fixed camera angles not only reinforces the cinematic quality but also lends a sense of scale and drama to each setting, whether it’s a misty forest, a devastated village, or a quiet, moonlit temple. This dedication to period-authentic visuals immerses players in the experience, making every scene feel like a carefully composed frame from a classic film.Narratively, "Trek to Yomi" follows a simple yet effective path, focusing on Hiroki’s journey to fulfill his duty and honor his fallen master. The story explores themes of revenge, sacrifice, and honor, presenting Hiroki with choices that carry moral weight and reflect his inner conflict. The dialogue, delivered in Japanese with English subtitles, adds authenticity, and the characters are written to reflect traditional archetypes of the genre like loyal warriors, treacherous foes, and innocent villagers. Although the story may feel predictable to fans of samurai cinema, it is executed with sincerity, allowing players to connect with Hiroki’s journey even if they’re familiar with the genre’s tropes.Combat in "Trek to Yomi" is deliberately minimalistic, placing emphasis on timing, precision, and quick reflexes rather than flashy combos. Players use a limited set of moves like slashes, thrusts, blocks, and parries to defeat enemies in side-scrolling battles that require focus and discipline. Mastery of blocking and counterattacking is crucial, as button-mashing will quickly lead to failure. While the combat system is simple, it forces players to adopt a measured, almost meditative approach to each encounter, echoing the discipline of a real samurai. However, this simplicity can feel repetitive in later stages, as the limited move set doesn’t expand significantly, and players may find themselves yearning for more variety as the game progresses.Level design in "Trek to Yomi" is linear, guiding players through beautifully crafted environments that showcase the diversity of feudal Japan’s landscapes and architecture. Exploration is often rewarded with collectibles and brief detours that offer glimpses into Hiroki’s world, adding a layer of immersion. The game balances exploration and combat with puzzle elements, allowing players to interact with objects to solve simple environmental puzzles. While the puzzles aren’t particularly challenging, they provide a break from the combat and add a sense of place to each location. These carefully constructed environments, combined with fixed camera angles, create a feeling of immersion as players move through bamboo forests, ancient shrines, and fiery battlefields.The sound design and music in "Trek to Yomi" further enhance its atmospheric qualities. The game’s audio captures the quiet tension of samurai films, with ambient sounds of wind, footsteps, and distant battle cries creating a foreboding atmosphere. The sound of steel clashing is crisp and impactful, lending weight to each sword strike and parry. Traditional Japanese instruments like taiko drums and shakuhachi flutes underscore tense moments, enhancing the cinematic tone. The soundtrack is composed with restraint, allowing silence and ambient sounds to create tension in quieter moments. This careful use of sound and music complements the game’s visual and narrative style, drawing players deeper into Hiroki’s journey.One potential drawback of "Trek to Yomi" is its reliance on cinematic presentation over gameplay depth. While the game’s artistic choices and atmospheric design are commendable, the gameplay itself may feel limited for those looking for complex mechanics or deep progression systems. Combat, while disciplined and well-suited to the game’s tone, can grow repetitive, and the linear level design offers limited replayability. Additionally, the game’s runtime is relatively short, which, while appropriate for its story-driven approach, may feel brief for players seeking a longer, more involved experience.On the whole, "Trek to Yomi" is a visually arresting tribute to samurai cinema that captures the tone and spirit of classic films while delivering an engaging, if simple, gameplay experience. It excels in creating an atmospheric journey that immerses players in feudal Japan’s world of honor, duty, and sacrifice. While the game’s minimalist combat and linear progression may not appeal to everyone, its commitment to cinematic storytelling and aesthetic make it a memorable experience for fans of the genre. For those drawn to samurai epics and atmospheric, story-driven games, "Trek to Yomi" offers a uniquely crafted homage to a timeless tradition.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a worthwhile play. Well considered, very stable, ultimately beautiful, and with simple but unbelievably engaging and challenging gameplay that will satisfy both casual and tryhard gamers. As the game gets more difficult, the combat becomes more thrilling, and the boss fights share similarities with soulslike games. The checkpoints are just forgiving enough that it doesn't feel mean-spirited, but the encounters are challenging enough that it makes you grit your teeth and go in for more.The main gameplay difference between this and other similar games is the lack of skill progression. You unlock 3 ranged weapons throughout the game, but in the end your strongest moves are always your light attack (X), heavy attack (Y) and parry (LB). The base effects of these moves never changes, and so the game forces you to learn timing and combos to get through tougher and tougher opponents.This is probably the only second-person game I've ever played. Combat scenes are done in a 2-dimensional Street Fighter sort of experience, but in between encounters is a unique 2nd-person view that allows the developers to create all sorts of dramatic and interesting scenes. I find this cool and interesting.Overall a beautiful game. You will only get your money's worth if you're game to take on higher difficulties, though. Wait for a sale if you're unsure is my advice.

_childDocuments_.review: Masterclass in visuals- one of the most immersive games I've ever played. Trek to Yomi is pretty much a love letter to classic Japanese Samurai films. The cinematography, color scheme, audio- it's all top notch.This is much more of an audio/visual experience rather than a video game and hence, the gameplay itself is quite basic. The game is very linear-combat is pretty basic and not very fun, which was quite disappointing; puzzles are almost non-existent and even more basic. The length is alright for it's type, around 6 hrs.I definitely enjoyed Trek to Yomi, however it's quite flawed. It's meant as a single course experience. There's not even any chapter select option or ng+ which makes getting all the collectibles and upgrades quite a hassle. I recommend this game but make sure you know what you're getting into, have low expectations in terms of combat and enjoy the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to the Stuttering City.• Enemies seemingly don't run out of stamina and their heavy attacks are faster than even your light attacks. Input reading that would make the most blatant input reading Elden Ring bosses blush. Hyperarmor out of nowhere, while the player gets to enjoy getting stunlocked galore.-- Cheap as all that may feel, it didn't bother me as much as the combat just feeling plain boring, there's clunk and a lack of precision to every player action and the control scheme can be fairly annoying.• The black & white filter, I do understand its intent but the aesthetic just doesn't do anything for me, gets dull really fast and I consider it a huge detriment to what could've been interesting art direction. I'm not sure if I missed a setting but the option to turn it off would've nice.• I was about to check off the game until the bait & switch happened. Everything from that point onwards feels and looks infinitely more interesting than the starting chapters.• "Environmental puzzles", those that can kill you are incredibly frustrating and ruin first-time "no shrine" runs.• ROUGH performance. Stutters that can get as bad as 2 second freezes are real with this game which is kinda nutty cause it is a sidescroller most of the time, you wouldn't expect the dubious performance from a game like this.All in all, if it weren't for the "environmental" crap I would've rated this 3/5, just for everything that came after the "bait & switch". As it stands with the frustrating puzzles and everything else added on top (mostly the awful performance), this is a 2/5 and definitely not Recommended, a "Mixed" at most.

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi is not what I expected. I assumed I was rather going to hate it, or just find it as a okay game.But actually it's pretty good, the story takes you somewhere I didn't expect it to take it.The gameplay is much better than other side scrolling sword fighting games I've tried. Very simple and easy to learn which I appreciate. The soundtrack is perfect for the setting and tone of the story. I love a good soundtrack for a game not only for how good it sounds, but how good it blends into the game's setting and tone of a scene. The story itself is not bad at all, without spoiling it for anyone it goes into a more supernatural and afterlife type of way in the story. Which I didn't mind at all, however I do wish it didn't go so far into it. The boss fights were confusing at first, which I assume is every game in history, but after one or two tries you understand the boss pretty quick.I was focused more on the revenge part of the story, I found it much more interesting and loved the good old Samurai times in Japan. I just love those settings. Which is probably what drove me into buying this pretty cool game. I wouldn't say it's Amazing! But it's pretty great to play!I wish we got more detail into the duty of being a Samurai, I think we got the least with that path compared to the other two as it's only mentioned two or three times before you're character starts persisting about keeping his duty in line.Overall, I think Trek to Yomi is a Great Samurai game. And if you're a fan of sword dualing and Japanese settings, I recommend this game.

The 1st escort mission the girl not only poor pathing, but she also just floats a lot of the time.Audio is ok though, but thats not enough for me to spend anymore time with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi is a visually stunning samurai action-adventure game that transports players to the Edo period of Japan. The game's striking black-and-white aesthetic, inspired by classic samurai films, creates a cinematic atmosphere that sets it apart from other titles in the genre. While I found that the gameplay may feel repetitive at times, with a limited variety of enemies and environments, the combat system is fast, satisfying and challenging. This is fundamentally a game about timing attacks and parries-a skill that takes time to learn here.  The style leans to simplistic, but there is more to this title than the sum of its parts.The game's narrative, while not earth-shattering, is well-paced and told in an engaging reveal, with surprising moments of emotional depth.I recommend this as a short but interesting title that is just different enough to be well worth your time, but most definitely on a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- The visuals in Trek to Yomi are one of its standout features. The game uses a unique art style that blends 2D hand-drawn graphics with 3D environments, resulting in a stunning and atmospheric world that feels both authentic and otherworldly.- The attention to detail in the game's art direction is impressive, with intricate character designs, beautiful landscapes, and hauntingly beautiful set pieces. - Also It's inspiration from Kurosawa's films adds depth and richness to the game's world-building and storytelling.Cons:- While the combat system is satisfying and challenging, it can become repetitive over time, particularly during longer battles. - Although it offers some collectibles and skills to unlock,there are a few incentives to replay the game once it has been completed.- The game's difficulty also can be uneven at times, with some sections feeling too easy and others feeling excessively difficult.Overall, Trek to Yomi is a visually stunning and engaging game that captures the spirit of feudal Japan and samurai culture. While it has some flaws, it's still a worthwhile experience for fans of the genre, especially those who appreciate atmospheric visuals and compelling storytelling.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: -Beautiful game. -Audio is wonderfully integrated.-Combat is easy to understand.-There is some level of progression.-No customization.-Difficulty is Challenging if you want it to be.-Short game. First playthrough took 10 hours on 2nd hardest difficulty.-$20 USD for 10 hours is not a bad purchase imo.-Not a revolutionary groundbreaking story. It's a tale old as time.I can recommend this game to friends, especially if it was on sale, for a good time. If you choose not to immerse yourself, you can still very enjoy the well polished combat.I don't know if I will remember this game years from now, but I think there is a good chance I might.

_childDocuments_.review: Although my playtime shows 4.4 hours, it feels like it was far longer. I was glad it was over by the time it ended, and I don't see myself replaying this for the other two endings. This game has a very simple combat system that feels sort of clunky with how many moves and combos you get. All you'll ever need is the anti-armor combo and one "power" combo of your choice to deal more damage quickly. Aside from that you'll also have three different ranged attacks at your disposal consisting of throwing knives, arrows, and a handheld cannon. The bow and arrow are the best mix between stopping power and speed.The main draw here is the story and its visuals, as you can see if you check out the screenshots I'll be uploading. I played it entirely in ultrawide, and I think the game greatly benefits from this aspect ratio. The entire game is in a black and white 1950's style, complete with film grain and distortions every now and then. It draws very heavily from Japanese creation mythology (as if that wasn't obvious from the game's title) and will probably put a smile on many a history weeb's face. I was very impressed with the presentation in the opening chapter, which was the main reason I kept playing even after finding the combat less than satisfying. Once you actually enter Yomi is when the game's environments get really interesting and varied. There are collectibles strewn throughout the entire game that add a little flavor text for those who want that, as well as the protagonist's own journal entries that summarize the events and his thoughts. As stated before, there are three endings, but I doubt I will come back to try and get them any time soon, if ever. This is a great game for an afternoon. I won't spoil anything, but it's hard to get really attached to any of the characters. There are four difficulties, with the highest being a no-hit run where everything dies in one strike except bosses, which also has several achievements tied to getting through those without being hit.tl;dr, it's a short enough romp through medieval Japan drawing inspirations from its creation myth, fully voiced and with excellent presentation with many different environments that suffers from a slightly clunky combat system that is saturated with moves you'll probably never use. I may sound negative here, but I do highly recommend it. One last thing: DO NOT look at the dumb ass trading cards, as they'll spoil what little attachment you may have for the characters.

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi is me wanting to kill myself when I'm playing this game to be in the land of the dead. The game has janky controls that made all combats more of a nuisance than a challenge. Almost every encounter can be spam with one or two moves. Everyone fought like they have diarrhea, making this game truly a feudal experience. Every background NPC will moan and whine and cry non stop, making you want to just run and find loot and collectible as fast as possible and get out of the area to kill more people. Because at least when the enemy in this game dies, they stay quiet.To give the game credit, the art and style of this game is their strongest point along with average story contain in a small playtime land this game in an only when it's on sale category. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Great experience with beautiful art and a solid narrative. The game play is repetitive. It's a great game (about five hours for me) that I loved playing but will likely never play again.This is a great gaming experience; however, it's not a great "game".  The reason is fairly straightforward: The art direction is absolutely stunning with a story that is well portrayed - both through dialogue and setting (At times, it is as if I am watching scenes lifted from an Akira Kurosawa film.); however, the game play itself is fairly rudimentary and repetitive. With that said, I loved it and it was well worth the few dollars I spent on it. Likely, I'll never play it again; however, I don't think I'll ever forget the experience.
