_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: The game is beautiful artistically and just amazingly cinematic. I don't know what people are talking about regarding the combat, because it is amazing. However, I do understand if people think it's a little rough or bland at first, because you attain all the combos as you progress. But damn does it feel good when I got some of the more cool combos and got good at the combat. By first playing the Ronin difficulty, the enemies were a little tankier, therefore, I was able to use the entirety of combos and weave them together against multiple enemies. So, perhaps enemies being weaker on the normal and normal difficulties made the combat feel a little weird, I'm not sure about that because I haven't tried those yet. At the end of the day my opinion is subjective, but at the same time, people might just not like the combat because they suck. I, too, sucked at first, then I got a handle on it, and it was amazing. Personally, value was worth price. Minimal replayability, only with difficulties, but reasonable and perfect for price.  Simple and sweet, nothing really new but not bad. Extra interesting if you are into Japanese folklore.The visuals and cinematic angles/shots are this game's signature. If you are a fan of classic the black and white samurai type films, this game does it best. If you aren't into that type of vibe, then you probably wouldn't even be playing this game.The sound design is great, I didn't notice anything bad with it and it matched really well with the visuals and gameplay. The music was great too, nothing to complain about, super fitting. I'm talking about "gameplay" and "combat" separately for my sake of grading. The gameplay outside of combat is simple exploration when in-between fights, kind of like Limbo (visually and functionally too). What makes this simple "walking" aspect of the game so nice is the visuals and shots that are following you and transition as you go. It's truly awesome if you are a fan of that kind of cinematography. Another aspect of the gameplay design is the function of lighting. The devs have done a really great job highlighting where to go and highlighting explorable paths/things by making it seamlessly glow a little brighter in  the frame. It's done well and not over the top. There are also important pickups that provide maximum health/stamina buffs and ammo for projectiles. The other kind of pickups are called collectibles that just provide random information about folklore. All these pickups are made aware to the player by the classic "shine" method, and are placed in spots that are usually either off to the side of shrines and main paths, or down other paths that could be missed.  Figuring out the proper spacing and timing of attacks and when to attack are the key.     Kind of spoiler aspect about the final boss:The combat seems to be the most criticized aspect of the game, which worried me when I started playing, but ultimately surprised me when I found the combat to actually be quite amazing. Sure, I can understand if people are say the beginning could be a little rough because you obtain more of the combos as you progress. For me, as I obtained a couple of the nicer combos after about 30-40 minutes in, the combat started falling into place and feeling really good. Every new combo I picked up during progression only made the combat better and better, by about 3 hours in, not only did I have a good amount of the combos, I started to get better at the combat, which is where it started to shine. How long it takes for people to get a good grip on the combat varies by person, but when I got it, I loved it. The critiques that I have are minuscule, and that is with hit-boxes on some of the strikes from the bosses. It's not really bad, but starts to become noticeable the more you grind a boss and really learn their every move on Ronin difficulty like it's a Dark Souls boss. Remember, spacing and timing are key.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: it is a very neat game with a  great art style looking like an old samurai flick, it has a forced perspective to just fully embrace the samurai flick vibe, but besides the art style the game play it self is also pretty good it is a bit simple but it shakes up the game play enough for it to stay fun true out the entire game, in short the game is cool
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a love letter to the period cinema of feudal Japan (if you couldn't tell already). Movies like Yojimbo, Hara Kiri, The Tale of Zatiochi - all masterpieces - are massive influences to this game.  The music, cinematography, animations, weather scenes, sound effects, the blending of nature and industry, art, man... I could go on and on.  The game is just a visual and auditory feast.  Coming from a  fan of this genre and period of cinema, the game is an absolute treasure.Buuuut, the combat sucks ass. It's repetitive, and there's more complexity in your average mobile game.  That said, the game is absolutely worth it.  I think the trailer, with it's flawless animation and fluidity managed to hide just how mediocre the combat actually is.  I'm highly recommending this game, simply for what it is - a visual masterpiece that allows you to interact and control the main character in a stunning motion picture based in feudal Japan.  The plot is simple and engaging.  The acting is solid.  Cinematography is 10/10.  And the soundtrack is phenomenal.   8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Combat takes some getting used to, but once you get it... it's SOLID. Simple, fast, visceral. There's some jank here and there, but dear lord, do the visusals of this game carry you through it all. It's a beautiful story that sweeps you off your feet and gets ya plowing through it straight to the end. A short game that I beat in 4 hours, but absolutely worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: This is a loving ode to bygone samurai cinema epics, and it is done with an attention to detail and direction that is commendable.  If you find yourself wanting to experience that, then it is well worth it.  However, it is also a side-scrolling combat game, and in that regard, it can be frustrating.Trek To Yomi tells an age-old story of a samurai protecting his village and following his vows, albeit with a deep supernatural viewpoint.  When not in combat, you are exploring enclosed areas and are encouraged to look for hidden pathways or rooms that might have secrets or alternate routes.  Sometimes you'll find extra save points, health or stamina bonuses, or flavor artifacts to enhance the story.  A friend called the camera angles in these zones 'Resident Evil-esque', and I think that fits.  They are specifically crafted to give a cinematic feel to it, and it works very well.When in combat, you are essentially on a 2D plane, going back and forth and fighting enemies.  The issue is that combat can take a while to correctly grasp, and then it is a question of whether it's rewarding to be aggressive or just sit and wait for a counter opportunity.  As you learn more combos, it does become more flowing and easier, but there are only a few times where it seems to shine or 'work' in such an otherwise epic story and presentation...and that's a frustrating flaw.I do recommend this if you want to see a fantastic experience told in a cinematic, gorgeous style, and I don't think the combat really takes away from that too much.  It doesn't elevate it any further, however, so do keep that in mind.  I think this ended up being exactly what I expected and thought it would be, so I am recommending it on my own preferences, but I can see how the lack of a 'worthy' combat system can hold this back from being a really great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. I got hyped about it with the trailer at E3 in 2021, and have waited patiently for it ever since. And at first, I was honestly on board. The world theyve built is eerily beautiful, and the way you interact with this Japanese Noir-world is amazing. But that is where my praise stops. The combat is boring, bad, has weird lapses in inputs where it just doesnt recognize them, etc. You get taught a lot of combos, which are mostly unnecessary, because most of the fights, you really dont need to get creative. Parry-Heavy-Heavy-roll backwards, rinse repeat for a lot of it. The story is not creative either. Young samurai's sensei dies at the hands of THE VILLAIN, but with his dying breath, he asks you to protect his daughter and the village. The story continues to be predictable from here other than a few plot twists, some of which are interesting, but mostly its meh. I wanted to like this game. I gave it every chance. But it just wouldn't let me. 4/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: it looks like old Kurasawa movies, there's a character named after the hero from Yojimbo, and the plot, while original, seems to channel some of Kurasawa's darker movies. Gameplay starts almost too simplistic but the combat gets much deeper over time. I loved this. Gonna play it through a bunch more.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome short story! Personally liking PVE, i enjoyed this very much*SPOILERS AHEAD IF YOU ARE WISHING TO PLAY AND EXPERIENCE YOURSELF*I wish we were fighting actual enemies and not just ghosts, they had  random things that drew away from the samurai era aspect of the game. BUT i get what the developers were going for! Overall I give it a 7.5/10 for story telling and the combat!
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: If there's something to be learned here, it's that you can't compromise on the gameplay for aesthetics. I'm sure you've seen so many reviews saying that the combat is really really clunky. It's true. I've only learned the basic three hit combo timings near the end of the story. That being said, the visuals in this game is extremely cool. The environment and ambience enhances the story very well. On top of that, the audio complements the experience. The story is very similar to the Izanagi folklore, and you will see references of that in the game.I would recommend to buy this on sale. This game is a really nice experience.8.1/10
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Ehhh it's not that easy to recommend, even though the videos make it look like a sure hit.The gameplay videos make the game seem more "responsive" than it actually is even though that's not the kind of thing you would remark since the graphical style is so unique and masterfully done.So yeah, the game's art is absolutely crazy, be it environments, music or voice, the issue is the gameplay. I don't really know how to describe it except by saying that the fighting gameplay lacks some "oomph", it's not super responsive and that interesting, even though visually it looks awesome.And that's pretty weird, right? Any other game with the same "meh" gameplay would have been discarded instantly by the consumers but the art literally carries the games to a "Good" status.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Super refreshing to get a samurai game that’s down to earth & a mostly accurate representation of feudal Japan on PC (haven’t been able to play ghost of Tsushima yet). No flashy moves, or powers, or any of that crap. And to top it off it feels like a Kurosawa film! I’ll admit I’m not one to play games like these so I can’t speak on behalf of the mechanics but I’m a nerd for this niche subject.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, I bought the game and beat it in the same day, but I must say this is one of the most cinematially awesome games I have ever played. It's like you're playing a samurai movie. Overall, the game goes very quickly and the combat is repetetive, but not boring. I would definitely reccomend playing this game, maybe not at full price though.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic short game, combat can get a little repetitive but its a short enough game where it doesnt matter all that much. I loved the story, visuals were amazing, sound design also amazing. It got frustrating at parts with multiple enemies at once but thats mostly due to my lack of skill lol i highly recommend if you want a short game as a break from longer games like elden ring.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: This game has such a unique atmosphere that i can't even write down because you can only experience it.The story itself isn't too shabby but it is also really short and you could complete it in a very short time.The fighting system however is poor and i think that there should be some improvements made because i see a lot of potential in it(By poor i mean that there aren't many combos which is available but i like the conception that you have to collect them yourself found scattered around the game).Overall this game is great and everyone should try it if they like old-school japaneese fighting games.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: I've been eyeing this game ever since it was first teased, and now that I've gotten a chance to play it I can say it masterfully delivered.First, I'll talk about what I don't really like: I played on Ronin (Hard) mode, and the overall clunkiness of the combat system made it super frustrating to play. The game offers a lot of combos you can use in combat, but realistically you'll probably only use about maybe 3-5 of these. Even then, inputting the combos can be a bit inconsistent at times and can get you killed more often than not. The parry mechanic is also very clunky. I'm a huge fan of parry mechanics in video games, but this game's just isn't it. You'll either accidentally parry even though it's very early, or you'll apparently miss it even if you got it down. It's not about waiting at the last moment for the enemy's attack, but rather waiting for a certain timing in the enemy's attack which is only half of what parrying actually is.I have other complaints about the combat system like the AI, but I think I've talk enough of what I dislike about the game. Especially since I'm recommending it.Now let's talk about what I love about this game.The You'll notice right away that everything is black and white to mimic an Akira Kurosawa movie. The game does an excellent job of making you accept that it is in that color scheme to the point where you forget it is in black and white. Despite being a side-scroller kind of game, the level design and environment feels so dynamic and dimensional, and the camera angles only help to highlight that. The This is a very short game, taking me about 8 hours to complete it even after all the retries I had to do because of dying a lot in Ronin mode. However, I think that's a good thing; sure the pacing of the story felt rushed, but any longer and I think it would've dragged out too much even. The short moments allow you to really appreciate the beautiful scenery that the game has laid out in front of you.I've still got a lot to say about why I enjoy this game, but I can't quite put it into words. In any case, I'm giving this game a Definitely buy for the experience and aesthetic alone.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Just wow. Like playing through a Kurosawa film. One of the most visually striking and atmospheric games I've ever experienced. The gripes from others about the combat being basic are understandable, but in no way did they detract from my experience at all. My only nitpick is that the last projectile weapon you get feels a bit too clunky and the animation takes too long. That being said, the emphasis is very much on the sword combat. I can't stress enough how unreal the presentation is in Trek to Yomi. It's truly remarkable. Can't speak for the other difficulties, but Ronin felt like a solid challenge and I'll be sure to attempt the highest difficulty unlocked after first play-through.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Decent all around, the combat was good the story was good, the small exploration was good what really made it great was the sound design and how well it capturs akira kurosawa samurai film directing style. overall I'd give it like a 7/10 the multiple endings none of them felt like a canonical good ending and I was able to beat it in under 4 hours and thats with like 30 mins away from the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: It's a great visual treat, but the combat gets repetitive and the story isn't a masterpiece.First, the upsides--It's a great love-letter to Kurosawa and jidai-geki classic films. The visual style and environmental design is fantastic. The gameplay manages to do a pretty good mock-up of a lone samurai hacking through gangs of mooks without breaking a sweat. When you become proficient in the combat, you will flow through groups of enemies like a wave crashing onto the shore.The downsides--It gets a bit repetitive. When you know how to fight you'll smash through encounters. Then you'll do it again. and again. and again... and again... It's pretty trivial to stun-lock enemies and instantly use a finisher on them. None of the regular enemies present any real challenge. It's not a long game, but around act 4 (60% or so) it'll start to get a bit boring.-= Spoiler Section =-The story is pretty meh-okay. Your characters motivations are forgettable, as are the rest of the cast of characters. I only remember Sanjuro because... well... Kurosawa films. It just turns into a 'you lose against the bad guy because you're conflicted' you get presented with some choices that don't seem to affect much. Then you beat up the final boss and get your special ending cutscene depending on which option you picked.Most of the actual quality comes from the 'Trek to Yomi' itself. The environments and visuals are great, and it's very clear that it was the focus. You will get such a variety of 'underworld' locales. I honestly spent a good deal of time just looking around at the scenery. The story, the protagonist's imbalance, and the NPC's all take a back-seat. Even having just beat it, I could easily sum it up as "Your master dies, you swear 3 different oaths, you pick one to keep at the end for a cutscene."-= Spoiler Section =-
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Great short game. The combat can get a bit repetitive, but that doesn't seem like what this game wanted to be. The combat is a bit rough if you don't pay attention to what you're doing, for example hitting forward + attack launches you into a slow jab attack. It really shines in its storytelling. I liken it to Hellblade, where the combat is there, but you're mostly focused on the story as it evolves. 4.4 hours to beat, I had a lot of fun, worth it to me for the experience and the story. YMMV
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game has a simple but tight control system that rewards precise inputs; mashing buttons will render you a flailing mess. The fighting is satisfying, albeit a bit repetitive after the first 2 hours. It rewards going off the beaten path and has a slew of informational collectibles to grab. There are a handful of melee and ranged enemies that can all be woefully dispatched the same way if you're quick enough. The bosses were... a pain to put it simply. Blocking is a major part of the game, but large attacks pierce through blocks as if you weren't blocking at all (Though this may be because I was playing on the hardest difficulty on my first playthrough). Not particularly a problem if you can read the moves and dodge accordingly. The last boss was a ♥♥♥♥♥ and a half to beat. The amplified damage coupled with the amount of health I had at the time, getting hit a measly 3 times put me down. Other than some gripes here and there, I had a fun experience hacking and slashing in this samurai game.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful  graphics but there are several times in the game where the character refuses to attack, just stands there are gets hit and killed, nothing wrong with the controller but the game just won't respond Really disappointing as I was really looking forward to playing this, but it is not playable the way it isEven after the recent update, I tried to play this again, can't even get past the tutorial, it says parry and counter strike, but when you do just that the game doesn't consider you did so won't let you proceedSUCH A SHAME, this game is so beautiful yet so very, very flawed in the game design as to be unplayable, the people who screwed this up should be ashamed of themselves forever
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: I will make this simple at its price its excellent. The visual style is great. The game play is good. There is complaining about parry....the controls ARE responsive not sluggish as a few have stated. The parry has a very small window to counter attack have to be fast. The parry works all day long with no effort really good timing button press. My one complaint is the collectibles they can be missed until you memorize path as you can't go back depending where you are my solution was to just not go to far into branching areas. Game is fun visuals are great. Its atmospheric. Plenty of branching paths some not so obvious...take your time look everywhere. Having a blast with it. I recommend Trek to Yomi
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Experiencing game breaking bugs at the final boss fight making the game unbeatable. No response from the devs so far. Some jank is fine but game breaking jank is not. I have changed my rating to not recommended. Read my first impressions review below. Score updated to reflect current view.Edit 2: My game is still bugged, empty room where the final boss should be, after installing the 1.01 patch. Uninstalled for now and may come back to it for a fresh playthrough down the road if things are fixed. Will updated my review at that time.Trek to Yomi is an absolutely gorgeous game visually and audibly from the 2.5 hours I have played so far. Combat is fun if a little tricky to get the hang of at first. Gameplay itself is very linear with the occasional branching path for crush the enemy shenanigans. The linear aspect of the game fits well with the Akira Kurosawa style camera and direction. Story is minimal at this point but serviceable as an old Samurai flick.Be forewarned I've experienced a ton of jank. T pose characters during scenes, enemies dying and just standing around, the spearman in the village KOing me whilst the dialogue is still going on and controls are frozen, getting stuck in the kicking the door down animation, the cloth physics on some clothes stretching across the screen for a split second.... Some issues required a reload but I was able to button mash my way out of a few bugs. Nothing majorly game breaking or that detracted from the experience too much and I'm sure things will be ironed out a bit over the coming weeks. On the plus side i'm playing this on Epic settings on a fairly run of the mill laptop.Positives:Beautiful VisualsGreat sound directionFun combatRuns on potatoNegatives:Minimal story maybe?JankExtra Jank just in caseIf you like old school Samurai movies and methodical combat I would highly recommend this Trek to Yomi.SCORE 5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Visuals are great and the environments tied to them are well crafted and wonderfully done. This is tied together by great atmosphere and weather effects. However, the combat that is supposed to be simple and seamless is clunky and already repetitive. I cannot say much about the story, because I am not that far in because of Tunic, so I'll get back to you on that. Solid 3 out of 5.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Oh wow, what a gorgeous looking game. It really is beautiful. The voice acting is fantastic. The fact that it is all voiced in Japanese makes the game feel that much more immersive into the world of the samurai.The game play is ok. It can get a tad repetitive as there isn’t too much strategy in in the combat unfortunately. Timing of your blocks and strikes is essential. I am hoping the combat evolves as the game progresses or develops. So far however, it’s a great game and Im really enjoying it.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi presents its world through the lens of classic Japanese cinema, reinforcing its thematic exploration of self-reflection and overcoming failure with masterful presentation and design to form a captivating experience. Combat presents a satisfying learning curve that rewards carefully studying your opponents and mastering the moves in your arsenal, and while overall it can falter at times due to uneven pacing, it's well worth undertaking the trek yourself.Full review at
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a quick Samurai Action filled with exciting levels, designs, and powerful diolagues; Look no further! Trek to Yomi is an actual proper cinematic experience. It is beautifully created and organically put together that almost feel real while exploring the entire maps. You'll find hidden entrances and upgrades in home out in the blue that just need their doors kicked down and more. The monochrome color perfectly suits the game and has been specifically designed for it. The OSTs and SFX perfectly give the game the essence it needs. The overall combat mechanic is easy and fun, however it dosent gets any deeper or harder, instead the enemies become more armoured and annoying. However, its still quite easy so you don't have to sweat it. The story might throw you off or may become quite predictable but it is there and it ain't bad either. Overall, a great 6 hours (Average) experience on normal difficulty, and definitely a MUST PLAY.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing you notice about this game is the fantastic presentation. The use of framing and lighting and mise-en-scene, along with other details such as the focus changing between the background and foreground depending on where your character is, gives the game a visual style where 'cinematic' is actually an accurate description and not just a corporate buzzword. Combine that with the visual style that evokes classic samurai movies (including neat little touches like how the film reel appears to 'skip' to show you that you've reached an important checkpoint) and you have a game that looks like an authentic and meticulous homage to a particular era in cinema.But of course, I judge games on their gameplay first and everything else second... and fortunately, Trek To Yomi has the gameplay to match the presentation. The combat system is intuitive and satisfying, requiring skill and thought while also being it's own thing instead of just copying Souls-likes. There are also different difficulty levels in case you need to make the combat harder or easier.This is one of my favourite indie games of 2022 so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Trek to Yomi

_childDocuments_.review: Trek to Yomi is an ultra-stylised cinematic action-adventure that follows an enthralling story of Hiroki during his fall against the forces of evil. Experience his heroic return to make good on his failed promise to save the people he swore to protect. As a vow to his dying Master, the young swordsman Hiroki is sworn to protect his town and the people he loves against all threats.  Faced with tragedy and bound to duty, the lone samurai must voyage beyond life and death to confront himself and decide his path forward.

name: Kao the Kangaroo
detailed_description: CHECK OUT OUR GAME! JOIN OUR DISCORD! About the Game ANNIVERSARY EDITION A year after the world premiere of the newest adventures of Kao the Kangaroo Anniversary Edition is now Available! It only happens once a year and it is worth celebrating! Kao the Kangaroo: Anniversary Edition is now available and includes: Kao the Kangaroo - full game - embark on a journey with the cutest Kangaroo and face the Eternal Warrior Bend the Roo'les - the newest DLC with the new campaign and 5 additional levels - defeat the Crab King! Oh! Well DLC - 5 playable Eternal cells to conquer and 5 spooky skins to unlock Exclusive Art Book - with the most beautiful locations, most interesting characters and elements you can find in the game Epic Soundtrack - immersive music to the game composed by talented Partyk Scelina Enjoy the ultimate platforming experience! __________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ ABOUT GAME 🥊 THE GAME 🥊 Kao The Kangaroo is a 3D platformer from veterans of the genre Tate Multimedia, featuring a plucky, cheeky but a cutie, Kao The Kangaroo (Hey, just like in the title!) on a quest to uncover the truth around the disappearance of his father. 🥊 THE JOURNEY 🥊 During his journey, Kao will explore a wide variety of beautifully detailed environments, each harboring secrets to uncover. At every turn, Kao faces new challenges. He’ll have to use all his skills while learning some new ones...not all of them being natural to the world he lives in! As they say, it’s the journey that makes us, not the destination. 🥊 THE CONTENT 🥊 Being inspired by the heyday of 3D platformers, as well as building on Kao’s 21-year legacy, Kao The Kangaroo is packed with plenty of jumping, thumping, puzzle-solving, and collecting. A whole new amazing adventure with all the charm you’d expect from not just the genre, but Kao himself! 🥊 THE CAST 🥊 Kao’s beautiful and bright world is filled with a host of colorful characters just waiting for you to meet them... in some cases (try to) defeat them! From wise mentors and inquisitive inventors to big old bullies, the cast of Kao The Kangaroo is as memorable as it is expansive! 🥊 THE FIGHT 🥊 While on his journey Kao will have to overcome many foes. Quick and nimble strikers, slow and lumbering brutes, and everything in between. Kao will have to use all the lessons he’s learned to defeat those who stand before him… 🥊 THE GLOVES 🥊 The mysterious, mesmerizing, long-buried, gloves Kao has on his paws are oozing with power yet to be fully unleashed. They’ll be a key tool in Kao’s journey, helping to ward off foes and traverse the world. Will the secrets of their power ever be fully understood? Kao looks to find out. 🥊 THE WORLD 🥊 Explore a diverse range of Unique and beautiful interactive worlds filled with fresh challenges, enemies, puzzles, and secrets! Jump, climb, dive and ride your way through highly detailed environments as Kao progresses on his journey! 🥊 THE MISTERY 🥊 Lurking behind Kao’s plane of existence lays a whole other world filled with mystery, uncontrollable power, and chaos...the Eternal World. A link between the two worlds exists, melding together. Its secrets are in Kao’s hands, giving him new powers...but at what cost? 🥊 KAO IS BACK 🥊

_childDocuments_.review: Join Kao on his biggest adventure yet! This time the brave kangaroo has to find his missing sister and solve the mystery of what happened to his long-gone father. He will need to travel the world and confront the famous fighting masters, who are influenced by the mysterious, dark power. On the course of his journey, Kao will learn under the guidance of his master - Walt, how to become not only an awesome fighter but also a clever one who uses his head as much as his fists.

name: GRAVEN
detailed_description: A faithful priest of the Orthogonal order–exiled unto death for a crime in defense of another–you live again in a small boat, adrift in a swamp. A stranger ferries you to solid ground and bestows upon you a cryptic warning, along with a mysterious staff and book. Go forth, pious priest, alleviate suffering, uncover deceptions, and smash the eldritch perversions encroaching upon reality itself. Perhaps you will even earn your peace. A marriage between modern development tools and techniques with a stark late 90s aesthetic brings the first person action-adventure GRAVEN to life! Featuring character designs by Chuck Jones (Duke Nukem 3d, Half-Life) and the voice talent of Stephan Weyte (Blood, Fire Emblem, Dusk) in a dark yet distinct medieval fantasy experience. Solve puzzles and scour lore to uncover the motives of the foul heretical sects behind the plagues and seasons undermining the land. Spread fires, charge machinery, reveal hidden paths, and freeze rivers to walk across. Discover new weapons and upgrade them at blacksmiths and alchemists to customize your capability. Expand your horizons by returning to old stomping grounds with new abilities and seeing how far down the chasms go and what powers they hide. Slay over twenty distinct enemies and three bosses in an ever broadening world across multiple biomes. Band together with up to 7 friends in hectic cooperative play. Walk the parallel path, lest you stumble into the recesses of the world and reality becomes only a bitter plaything.

short_description: Action, mystery, and a chance for redemption await you in the gritty first-person action-adventure GRAVEN. Explore a dark fantasy world as a wrongly convicted man of faith. Battle the horrors of humanity, the wilds, and beyond using armaments, magic, and the environment.

_childDocuments_.review: First let me just say that as you scroll through the reviews, you'll note a lot from 2021 and early 2022 slagging the game because it's supposedly "dead" with no updates. There was, in fact, a major update in Spring 2022 and development of the game is ongoing. Will any of those "lol dead game" people ever come back and edit their reviews (especially the ones who specifically said they would if there was ever an update)? Not likely. All of that to say, you should disregard all of those old reviews that just say "game is dead/abandoned." So with that out of the way, let's talk about the actual merits of Graven. I really wanted to like the game. I was (and still am) totally smitten with the late 90's "3Dfx-esque" (or maybe "PS1core") aesthetic. The level design is pretty good. The glimpses of story shown in the part of the game that's done so far are intriguing and hit just the right vibe. The game right now is buggy. I am not talking about minor bugs here, I am talking about serious, quest-breaking bugs. This is more frustrating than it should be because of some design decisions made, but I am not going to torch the game just for that because this is an early access release and some bugs are to be expected.Let's talk about those design decisions, because they're what actually stops me from recommending the game right now. Combat is not good. Most of the weapons are not satisfying to use and killing any but the most basic enemies is a tedious exercise in circle-strafing and whittling down their too-abundant health. In general it seems like Graven can't figure out whether it wants to be like Heretic and Hexen (in which case combat this clunky is a deal-breaker) or be an immersive sim more along the lines of Thief (which gave players far more options for avoiding direct combat than Graven does). The player has magic, two different elemental types of it right now even, but spells are little more than cantrips used for things like little environmental puzzles. Magic is not a meaningful combat tool against any but the most basic enemies. This seems to have been a deliberate design decision meant to force a grittier, more challenging experience but for most people it will just be disappointing. Worst of all is the save system. The game uses checkpoint saves. In a game with Graven's heritage, not being able to just make manual saves is inexplicable. Because the checkpoints are based on your location, it's entirely possible to hit a checkpoint in the middle of a fight, die, and respawn immediately with the same enemies mauling you so you just die over and over. Worse still, saves and respawns between game sessions (as in quitting the game and coming back to play more later) are based on the hub location of whatever part of the world you're currently in, typically meaning a long slog through the wilds (through respawned enemies) to get back to where you were if you don't have time to finish a whole quest and go back to the hub in one sitting.Bugs I can forgive. Design decisions that are at best strange and at worst wrong-headedly anti-fun I cannot, and Graven is far enough along in development now that I can't see major stuff like this changing. Because of this I cannot recommend Graven and while I will continue to check in on its development I don't anticipate ever being able to recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: GRAVEN

_childDocuments_.review: After three years in early access and now with this 1.0 release, this game is still unfinished. It's very obvious that at some point, Graven was envisioned as some sort of RPG or perhaps immersive sim, but the devs just didn't manage to go through with their original plan. Areas are sprawling with nothing in them, in the same way a coloring book's shapes are unfilled. Assets are constantly re-reused in a placeholder kind of way. Enemies respawn in a nonsensical way. Puzzle logic is not coded properly, so on and so forth. It's a real shame, because I think this could've been something truly great, But not being able to do anything right is quite characteristic of Slipgate Ironworks and 3D Realms.Edit - As an added question, why does this game have co-op? Maybe the resources meant to address all of the shortcomings above went into co-op. Whoever made that decision is something else.
_childDocuments_.name: GRAVEN

_childDocuments_.review: Normally ı refrain myself from giving negative comments, ı know game development is a extremely hard job and most of the time developers do their best. But after giving two years to graven, and despite its charming art and atmosphere that captivated me in the first place, ı have to warn people to not to do the same mistake ı did and fall for graven's unique look and feel, now the game is going out of early access with all those issues.I seriously can't believe some of the design choices in this game, that even though community cries that they do not work, that developers stick to and do not change. There are TONS of issues with graven, most of them other comments point out, like coin penalty on death and most weapons feeling useless. What ı want to especially point out is the check point system.It feels like someone designed the levels without thinking where the player will save, then some else came and put force save points on map without playing any part of that level. The game saves right next to an enemy mob or boss, so if you die you will spawn RIGHT NEXT TO the enemy with half your health and without ammo so it res-kills you until you feel like you are being bullied by the devs. just right now, ı spawned right on top of the same acid pool that killed me, only to die again 1 seconds later. I mean what the hell is this?  Not to mention you lose half your money everytime you die, the money you need to buy upgrades so you can progress in game. Overall the game design of graven feels like a sick joke and ı have to warn the reader to definitely do avoid falling for it's charm.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start by saying Graven is a very short game right now. It only took me about 4 hours to finish all available content so take that into consideration when you spend your 25 dollars. I had a blast playing it and there are a lot of great things going on though. It seems like the devs are hard at work though so Graven should be worth every penny soon.Pros- Enemy VarietyThere were quite a few different enemies considering the length of the game right now. I loved opening a door or moving into a new area and fighting something I havent seen before. They all have different move sets and require different approaches to take them down. Some need a swift kick in the chest or an explosive shotgun blast from a distance. Im looking forward to what new enemies will be added in the future.- Map DesignProbably my favorite aspect of the game right now. I loved running through areas looking for secrets and finding interesting architecture. The backtracking didnt take so much time that it felt repetitive and I loved those "AHA I know where I am" moments when I opened a shortcut back to an are I was in previously.- AmbienceMan the ambience is on point. The sound effects and music are great and really amp up the feeling of being in a filthy plague ridden hell hole full of monsters ready to rip you apart. Fog in just the right places and the green sky really put an emphasis on the fact that everyone is screwed and the world (or maybe just this part of it) is suspended in a time right on the brink of destruction.-Movement SpeedI love love love the movement speed. In videos showing previous gameplay the movement speed wasnt nearly as fast and for how large the maps are turning it up was the right move. It really gives it the feeling of playing Hexen or Quake.Cons- Enemy AIThey dumb, like real dumb. They dont track well, some of them will leap right past you wile youre standing still. Other enemies just walk up to you and let you move around behind them without doing anything about it. Right now none of the enemies have any difficulty at all. In numbers they can be dangerous but individually every enemy is very easy.- LaddersGetting onto a ladder from the bottom isnt an issue at all, its fine. Getting on ladders from the top needs work. Most of the time I would just skip getting onto a ladder and just jump down to where I was going and take the damage. The one time it really got under my skin though was the really big ladder in the last area. The first couple tries it was as if there were an invisible wall stopping me and the third attempt I made I fell down. I moved into the ladder while falling and couldnt grab on and fell to my death. After that when I made my way back the ladder worked fine and I was able to get down ok. The consistency of getting on ladders from the top needs work.- Short StoryRight now there are only 4 quests to complete. I really hope the devs have a clear vision of what story Graven is telling because right now it isnt telling very much at all.- Lack of  EquipmentOn the steam page and on youtube you can find videos of gameplay which show  equipable rings. Right now those are not implemented and im not sure why. Could be balancing issues or their purpose isnt being served because other elements arent implemented right now. Either way its a bit disappointing to see those things in trailers and previous gameplay and not be able to use them.Edit - Lightning has been added after the previous patch. It works well however the flying enemies just float in place when stunned instead of falling out of the sky and the range is pretty short. You need to be directly underneath to hit them. Turning the range up slightly would make knocking them out of the sky feel a lot better.Mixed- CombatHitting enemies feels good and there are a decent amount of weapons at your disposal. In Alpha Beta Gamer's video there was a flail that isnt in the game at the moment so I would like to see that come back at some point. Most of the issues with combat lie in the enemy AI. Right now you can just spam left click with your sword and avoid most damage with some side steps. When you encounter a group of shielded enemies you can just spam them with explosive fletchant rounds since they cost so little to use. Although combat feels good it certainly needs some balancing.Edit - Hazards have been added in the form of Swamp Gas that can be ignited with the fire spell and you can now kick enemies into the Cheval De Frise. The kicking is an excellent addition, it both looks and feels great. The swamp gas is very situational. In the Lice Slough you can use it pretty effectively but in other areas trying to bait enemies into it doesnt work well. Maybe after more levels are added to the game the devs will find better ways to implement that feature.- MapThe map is good and bad. Although filling it out as you make your way through the game works well  It would be really nice to have markers for secrets that have already been found too.Edit - Map markers have been implemented and make using the map easier but there are quite a few different markers and no legend. Some markers are easy to understand and serve their purpose perfectly but others dont make much sense at a glance.Overall I loved what I played even though it needs improvement. I hope the devs have solid plans for whats to come. Theres a really solid foundation here and as more updates come out Ill be sure to come back and update my review.BTW the voice actor for the opening video sequence was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh Graven, dear Graven. Dear devs who worked on Graven. Dear customer who wants to know if Graven is worth the purchase.I hate to leave a negative review, particularly right upon release, and since I am only 3+ hours into the first hub.But...This game needs work.I do want to make anyone reading this aware that these are EARLY GAME THOUGHTS, and some critiques of the game overall, from what I have experienced THUS FAR.Let's just say, in the spirit of Graven itself, the devs have some serious peat to shovel until this game can properly shine.There are some serious design decisions, or lack thereof, that I take issue with. Until there is substantial tweaking done, or else I subject myself to figuring out just how to progress, I cannot recommend it.Firstly, the ill-begotten checkpoint system. Yes, everyone has been complaining about it, but for good reason. Quicksaves are a no here, I get that. But why must I be subjected to running all the way back to where I was to begin with before having exited the game previously? It makes it hard for me to want to come back.Secondly, the map. Or, actually, the blatant absence of one. I usually don't have too much of an issue navigating complex levels, but this is more of an issue of being unsure of where I am even going. It is so, so obvious to me that this is a clear oversight. Either the devs had completely memorized the maps, or just totally forgot to implement them, but this only makes the checkpoint situation worse, and navigation all-the-more confusing. When I read in my 'Journal' to go "there", wherever, say, the "Clotted Alcoves" may be, I feel more like turning the game off than exploring.This finally brings me to my third major issue. The level design as a whole. As I mentioned before, having come to the "Clotted Alcoves", sans the help of a map, I have been asked in my 'Journal', to find the Totems used by Cultists in the area, so as to complete a puzzle. But there seem to be hints at the foot of the puzzle. And I scour the entirety of the "Clotted Alcoves" two or three times wondering just where I am being pointed to. This is without even mentioning that there are plenty (and I mean PLENTY) of inaccessible areas that seem to warrant returning with items/abilities I do not yet have. Now,  this would be fine, if I only could find the trail of breadcrumbs to progress through the area I AM allowed in. I get the sense that the sprawling ruins are "Fromsoft-esque", but it is hard to find any answers as to how to proceed. It just feels as though the level designer did not get feedback. Who knows, maybe all my answers can be found at the shops. Maybe I screwed up.Overall, I would say the experience of playing Graven is akin to finding yourself in a strange new-world, only no one tells you to "follow the yellow brick road", or even what direction the "City of Oz" is in. I just feel directionless.Similarly, I am none-too sure about the stamina system. It is a literal thorn in my side, and once old-man John Graven runs outta juice, prepare to hear him wheezing for a minute or two, particularly if you are doing literally anything other than standing still. Even your jump is weaker, so you have to wait if you are platforming at all.The crouch is... deceptive. It barely registers as having lowered your body, and yet you can make smaller gaps than you may first realize. This is so odd that I am certain it isn't intended to be this... poor at conveying its use.Its still EARLY GAME for me, so take the combat critique with a grain of salt. Spells are really not all that exciting for combat-use, and the kick is fairly ineffective. Combat is fine overall so far, melee combat could be a little more satisfying/deep. The cuff arrow is not very inspiring to use. I believe an FPS can have a great starting weapon, just look at games like Ion Fury (a 3DR joint) and Incision. Great pistols, and as a starting weapon with a similar purpose, it just feels... ineffective.I HATE the bat things who spew acid. That's it concerning enemies this early into things. I do have legitimate critiques concerning them, however. I dislike how far off they tend to be when they begin attacking, probably to incentivize the purchase of the scope (which I have yet to find). I also don't like how HUGE their acid pools become after a few seconds. See the Scrags from Quake for a similar enemy, who isn't a war criminal. What a role model.I have been horrifically negative so far, so here are some POSITIVES:Nothing about this game tells me its a bad game, only that it needs some adjusting and a few changes. This isn't a broken, bad, or waste of a game. In fact, I absolutely LOVE what is going on here, in Graven. Levels are atmospheric, exploration is compelling, art/music is extremely top-notch, Stefan Weyte is killer. But this game just needs some polish.Here is to 3DRealms, hoping they can pull a classic gem out of the rough. I'm so happy for them that its out. Given all the layoffs and development time, I seriously hope they can improve Graven. It could go far, if pulled off correctly.In that spirit, as this game continues to get the love and attention it deserves, keep an eye on it, and soon (I hope) I can recommend that you BUY THIS GAME. Until then... probably don't buy it. Unless its on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an identity crisis. It wants to be many things, and as a result, implements design choices that conflict with each other, such as:-having to complete jumping puzzles/mixed combat and platforming sections while having a limited stamina bar, which just feels clumsy-being a medieval fantasy game where the melee combat sucks and the spells are utility-only, meaning that the only worthwhile combat option is using the equivalent of standard FPS guns-using a Dark Souls-style respawn system, but without the retrieval mechanic that incentivises that kind of playI really want to like Graven, as I've been waiting for a spiritual successor to Heretic/Hexen, but the core gameplay just feels weak. I first played the demo and got it in early access as I had faith that certain issues would be ironed out, but it's just not FUN. The design is littered with choices that just feel ANTI FUN. It feels like the devs are clinging so hard to certain ideas that they will never change them despite negative feedback from players. Examples of this include the aforementioned non-combat spells (which are so very rarely useful for any utility purposes that i question their overall inclusion), as well as the respawn/save system that requires you to traipse all the way back from the hub area every time you start up, which just feels like a waste of time.Following on RE the earlier point about the combat - it really does suck. The monster AI is dumb, the hit connection from melee monsters is wonky, and the difficulty wildly varies between encounters. The first ranged weapon, the cuff crossbow, feels so wimpy. The shotgun bow is pretty solid, and the peat burner is very fun to use (I especially love the slight delay before the projectile explodes, which can be fun for setting traps). The lighting spell can be used to stun monsters, but by the time you have switched to another weapon to inflict damage, the monster is no longer stunned, which is fundamentally pointless. A minor point, but the writing is pretty terrible. The flavour text found in diaries/letters thoughout the maps is mostly overwritten, flowery purple prose, provides barely any context. The quests are designed in a way that feels vague and I generally don't feel any investment in the plot. This would be fine if the game was fun, but it is not.There are some positives: I like the environmental design, and I've always got time for a first-person Metroidvania map. The attempt to capture the colourful yet depressing style of Heretic and Hexen is mostly successful. Stephen Weyte rocks and should voice a character in every game.Overall, I can't think of who this game would appeal to. It doesn't have the satisfying masochism of a Souls game, it doesn't have the blistering pace of a boomer shooter, and it doesn't have the freedom or creativity of an immersive sim. Unless this changes significantly before the 1.0 release, I would avoid playing it. I'm sad to say it is just another one of 3D Realms' recent misfires

_childDocuments_.review: So I've had my eye on Graven for a while now. While reviews used to be mixed for a while, they recently turned more positive, prompting me to give it a go.It's a game that feels like it should work but it doesn't quite. Visually, it's all there. Movement feels responsive, the environments are detailed and interactive. Level design works all in all. But there are some baffling design choices that hold back Graven's potential. Let's start with the combat. The good part is, that ranged weapons work as expected and feel reasonably enjoyable to use. The baffling ♥♥♥♥-up is that ammo is survival horror-levels of rare. In an action shooter game. Especially early on, you only get a peashooter crossbow and a melee option and that's all you have for a good long while. The peashooter can clear maybe half a room before it runs out, melee takes up to 6 hits to kill the basic starter enemy and is risky because you have no defense. You only option is to tediously circlestrafe enemies, whacking them endlessly. Groups are just chores at this point. This is the basic experience for a long time. You might think more weapons bring fun and momentum into the combat but they are also chronically short on ammo.Because pickups are rare and early enemies rarely drop ammo, you have to go for smashing pots and crates. Those are everywhere but can take several hits to crack open and are not a guaranteed ammo source. So you pretty much have to smash everything you see, grinding your momentum to a halt EVERY SINGLE ROOM. And even then, you barely have enough to run out halfway during the next encounter anyway, even if you make every shot count.And the most frustrating thing is, in the rare moments when you are well equipped and allow yourself to just navigate the levels, ignoring pots and crates, it kinda sorta works. Until you inevitably run dry again.Now there are some alternative tactics like magic and kicks. They just don't work. Magic deals minimal damage and is more of a stun/trap activation tool. But stunning implies you can do something other than being out of ammo when enemies are stunned and setting explosives on fire has such a low range that you risk taking explosive damage every time, kiting enemies behind you precisely all the while.The kick is a joke. There are spike traps but enemies get stuck on each other when kicked. Seeing how often you deal with groups, this renders it useless in most scenarios. Even then it is unreliable. Sometimes it flat out doesn't register or activate. Enemies have a lunge that is unaffected by the kick and triggers as you approach kicking range. So instead of dishing out a kick, you have to gamble on eating an unblockable heavy attack every time. It it infuriating. Now I get that there are upgrade options down the line but I'm four stages into the game now and the blacksmith is locked even though I've been collecting resources all along the way, the hordes get bigger, the enemies tankier and I've yet to have any experience other then constant, nerve grinding tedium.I don't get it. It's not hard to fix. It doesn't take a redesign. Just adjust a few values.But then there is the weird progression and save system. Basically there are no saves, just checkpoints. But for some godawful reason, checkpoints don't save on quitting. You just start again in the hub. Granted, you don't lose all progress but what the ♥♥♥♥? How could this possibly enrich the experience? It just means more tedious backtracking. Dying also just moves you to a checkpoint, resetting nothing. Enemies are still around, right back to attacking your ass at 30 health, trapping you in some endless checkpoint cycle until you cheese them to death. Death has absolutely NO consequence in this game. Why even avoid death? Checkpoints are placed fairly regularly so death is never even a problem whatsoever.So all in all, you have a game that is endlessly tedious to play, provides neither challenge nor reward and has some added annoyance on top. And that all within a framework that is frustratingly close to coming together. You'd have to ♥♥♥♥ this up on purpose.

_childDocuments_.review: Graven is a modern take on classic shooter gameplay with huge, complex, sprawling levels and occasional puzzles. I found it very enjoyable, but the complete lack of updates (or even communication) for the past several months is worrying.Inspired by HeXen, Graven takes place in a medieval fantasy world where magic exists. You play as a priest who is originally opposed to magic, but finds himself in situations where he has to use it. You have been exiled to a land that's been overrun by zombie-like citizens and other undead as the result of a plague, and you'll have to fight these enemies in order to prove your worth to the citizens of your new home.There isn't a lot of story in the game, it mainly serves as a backdrop for the action. But what is there, through occasional notes as well as very rare conversations with questgivers, creates an intriguing mix of ominous events and mystery. I cannot tell if the story is planned to receive more attention as development goes on, or if the focus will remain on the gameplay - either would be fine in my opinion. Currently the tasks are very mundane (like "fix the blockage in the sewers"), but I expect it to become more epic when the later stages get added.Graven provides classic shooter gameplay: You explore huge, complex levels and fight the enemies that either exist already, or get spawned in response to your actions. Currently there are only 5 different enemy types in the game (6 if you count the stationary, magic-missile-shooting totems), but you can already see that they have been designed competently and with an eye for variety.Movement is fast and combat is visceral. Enemies hit fairly hard, but have short cooldown periods after attacking. Reading their patterns and finding the correct timing for your movement and attacks is essential. The levels are littered with containers that can be smashed to reveal health vials, mana, or ammunition, which appear plentiful at first, but are (usually) finite, so if you burn through your resources quickly, you might eventually run out. As in many classic shooters, you'll have to use all your weapons in order to manage your ammo levels. However, _contrary_ to classic shooters, the levels are interconnected and you can move between them without enemies respawning or drops vanishing, so you can always backtrack to areas where you may still have access to resources that you've exhausted on your current map.Currently there are 2 melee weapons, 3 ranged weapons, and 2 spells in the game. Some weapons have a secondary attack. As most game elements, they are nicely done and provide decent variety already, but the game obviously needs more content in this department as well.Death is very forgiving - you get teleported back to your last "respawn point", but you keep all of your items, and enemies don't respawn. I'm not sure if this will stay that way though, it might just be a temporary compensation for the poor save system (see below). But as it stands, you cannot get stuck even if you completely run out of resources - as long as you can kill at least one enemy before dying yourself, you can whittle any opposing force down.Apart from the fighting, Graven also provides several puzzles, which I appreciated a lot. Most of them are inventory-based: you simply need to find and apply an item (e.g. a key), which will be shown as a silhouette at the place where you need to use it. There's also an environmental puzzle where you need to rotate parts of a pillar correctly after finding clues elsewhere. I found the puzzles mostly well-integrated into the story and pretty logical and easy, though the pillar puzzle does seem to throw some people off. I don't think they'll give any trouble to players who at least occasionally play games with puzzles, though.Due to the large, sprawling levels, you'll also spend some time exploring. This usually gets rewarded with some drops, and there are also a couple of secrets to find, which is nice. The game does not hold your hand (e.g. there is no quest marker guiding you to the next objective), but you do get clues in your journal, which were helpful when I didn't know where to go next. (There is one particularly hard-to-find door that only comes with a very vague hint when you pick up its key, but as a player who tends to look at any nook and cranny anyways, I didn't have problems finding it, it just took a while.)The graphics are reminiscent of classic shooters, and therefore mostly low-res, but look pretty good overall. The art direction managed to use retro aesthetics in a way that feels appreciably nostalgic to old players like me, but shouldn't be off-putting for people used to a more modern presentation. Some of the textures look very crude though, especially those depicting text.Sound effects and music are competently done. The game does include a bit of voice acting, but due to a combination of the accent and some odd mixing, I didn't like it very much.Graven felt quite polished for an Early Access title. The options menu offers several quality settings for AA, shadows, post-processing, etc., but doesn't go further into details. A gamma slider, an FOV slider, and a frame limiter are provided as well, Four separate volume sliders allow you to fine-tune your audio experience. Keys are fully rebindable (an important functionality that sadly, many developers neglect).At this point, the game does not offer accessibility options for visually impaired players. Colorblind filters are probably not necessary since nothing is color-coded, but would of course still be nice to have. The game's font (used for notes, the journal, and subtitles alike) looks rather squiggly, which fits the fantasy setting, but can be hard to read, an option to switch to a clearer font (and perhaps increase the size) would be useful. Deaf players may have trouble with the combat as there is no visual indication as to where an attack is coming from.Graven's current save system is very crude: the game saves your inventory, and which quests you have completed - everything else resets. This is a _massive_ step backwards the classic shooters that Graven was inspired by, in those you could usually save manually at any time and place. In Graven, if you have to leave your PC mid-mission, you have to fight all the enemies again, find all items again, and solve all puzzles again. I hope that this is just a temporary issue though - it's certainly something I'd expect the developers to spend more time on later, but it's understandable if their focus lies elsewhere at this stage of development.Here comes the huge caveat: The game has not seen any updates for several months, and there has been no communication from the developers either. Allegedly they are active on Discord, but since I'm not active there, I really can't tell if the game even _is_ still in active development.As enjoyable as the game is even in its current state, it's obviously unfinished (the story does not lead anywhere, it literally ends with the note "This Early Access version ends here."), and it clearly needs more content. According to the devs, the game is supposed to have 3 hub areas with half a dozen connected areas for each. If the developers can deliver that amount of content (while keeping the current level of quality), then this game gets a strong recommendation from me. But in its current stage, the game only has one hub and 3 other areas, i.e. only about 20% of the planned content. And if it stays that way, then the price tag is _way_ too high.Graven looks like it might become a great game if it ever gets finished. I found it very enjoyable already. But the current price only makes sense if development continues, which (sadly) seems unclear at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't even know where to begin...Lets first set aside the facts that this is pretty much a paid demo right now with very little content, and that 3D Realms clearly have some sort of project ADHD, as they still have not finished a single episode of Wrath now nearly 2 years on from its EA release. We wouldn't want any of these facts to color our opinion of the game. With that out of the way....This game is not fun. You should not play this game.Why? As it stands, this game just has absolutely no idea what it wants to be, because it clearly doesn't have a game designer working on it. There is a person who wanted to write, using the parlance in the game: "Lore" , for the little fantasy world they've dreamed up in their head. They dug deep into a thesaurus for this one, pulling out winners like "the brine muskeg" and "the lice slough". Anyways, beyond the poor writing, there really is a horribly confused gameplay loop at hand. Part of it is probably the fact that this is an Early Access title, but its very clear otherwise that there is no prevailing vision for the game.Of , idk, 3 and a half hours it took me to complete this game, probably 2.5 of those were spent smashing barrels. The rest of the time consisted of fighting extremely dull AI that could barely navigate to the player properly, let alone land an attack. When you do get in a fight, you just circle strafe and mash left click. Hitting enemies is unsatisfying and unresponsive. Really like, hitting the hundreds of barrels strewn about is more satisfying. There is absolutely no mechanical subtlety or depth to the combat whatsoever. Enemy types are completely bland and don't change the combat landscape at all. Weapons, while seemingly creative at first glance, serve absolutely no functional difference from each other, and there is practically no real reason to switch weapons. And even if you do decide to, you will never run out of ammo. The reason? well lets move on to the level design.The "level design" , and it is a reach to call it that, is really amateurish. They seem to be crafted by people who have an idea that levels can be more that straight hallways, and maybe researched games like "dark souls" and others similar. But they just have to idea how to make any of it work in an interesting manner. Most of the world is straight paths connected by dull arenas, and the occasional opportunity to open up a shortcut that you will never use because theres no gameplay purpose for them to even be there. The levels are FILLED TO THE BRIM with boxes and barrels to smash. Just absolute loads. I think the designer maybe didn't realize that when they added a currency to the game, and made breakables randomly spawn that currency, players will want to smash the things to get the items. This results in nearly ALL of your time being spent smashing trash cluttered about every possible corner. Now you have players flush with cash, and completely full on ammo and health. You then offer the player the chance to buy nearly every weapon early, so that the gravity of the designed moments to receive a new tool is totally destroyed. Add to this the complete and total lack of of rising or falling action of any kind, and you just get a grating high pitched whine of level design for 3 hours. There are a small handful of """puzzles""" mixed in. They are toddler level at best, and poorly thought out at worst. Really, not much to talk about here, they exist to slow the player down pretty much.That leaves the small things graven does okay. The art is pretty nice for the most part, although there are issues with pixel density across assets. It seems like there were troubles communicating style rules across different artists, but I'm sure that will be cleaned up by full launch. Other than that, the audio is pretty alright, not much to complain about here. Anyways, this is really just a terribly underwhelming package from 3DR, who by now I have pretty much zero faith in, as nearly every product they launch is either heavily flawed or a borderline early access scam. I don't know who has fallen asleep at the wheel over there, but this isnt the company I knew 30 years ago.edit: for those about to comment about how "3DR is just the publisher idiot!" please do some research, or try reading the comments section.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings on this one. Last time I played, the game felt a little barren and raw still, but I will play again with the recent content update and see how I feel. Nonetheless I give this game a recommend. Why?The developers are talented, the game looks INCREDIBLE, and the environments never stop wowing me with their chunky glory. The gameplay right now is serviceable but not amazing. Combat feels jank as **** sometimes, there's checkpoint issues, and generally I thought the spell system was a bit disappointing since it only was for scripted puzzle segments and not also fighting. You're gonna give me a sweet fire spell but I can't kill enemies with it? No, hitting them with your stick is far more effective. I don't wanna sound like entitled prick gamer here, but that kinda sucks in my book.But I still recommend this game because I have faith that the devs are gonna make something really cool out of this impressive framework. Slipgate Ironworks might've bit off a bit more than they could chew trying to develop like 16 different games under the revived 3D Realms, and it's not like they have millions of dollars and thousands of staff to throw at all these projects. So I will be patient. If that shaky recommendation gives you pause, I don't blame you, wait on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is NOT a boomer shooter, alot of people were expecting a Heretic or Hexen clone but it's not even remotely close to either of those games. It's more of an action/adventure game with a Dark Souls-like hub world that branches out as you progress through the game. You'll be revisiting old areas with new upgrades and spells to uncover more loot and items.Yes it's pretty janky and development for the last half of the game was clearly rushed but what's here is enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted this game to be good. It's as close to a proper modern Hexen 2 as it gets. Sadly, in the current state playing it feels like a chore, not entertainment. Combat is slow and tedious, with very limited variety of very basic and extremely tanky enemies. Most of the pickups are hidden in destructible items like barrels, crates and corpse piles that also have way too much health, so you find yourself repeatedly whaling on furniture to get needed health, ammo and gold. I think I spent roughly half of my entire playtime doing exactly that.Maps are very good looking, but feel very empty. They are vast and form a continuous world, but that doesn't work in the game's favor. You can unlock shortcuts after exploring new areas, but still there's a ton of legwork through mostly void spaces, with not very engaging enemy encounters placed too far between.Weapons are not very effective and don't feel particularly fun to use, and magic is literally a bad joke in the current state. You have whole two spells, one sets stuff gently on fire, almost with no animations of flame effects, the other electrifies them for a second, but both are next to useless apart from one or two instances where you need to electrify a door button. There are some upgrades available, but through my entire gameplay I never could afford even one of them, despite hunting for secrets with gold, etc.What's worse, there's no manual saving and autosave system doesn't exactly work, every time you close the game, you're back in the city and gotta walk to where you were last and your inventory is shuffled. What's more, all enemies respawn, while ammo and health items don't - and that's perhaps the only sliver of difficulty you face in this game, as otherwise it's pretty trivial.It really pains me to see so much potential and all the work of some talented people blatantly wasted due to bad design decisions. This game needs a complete overhaul before it will be worth recommending. Sadly, updates are very rare and don't address the main problems, just adding a bit more of the same flawed gameplay.
