_childDocuments_.review: So, where to begin with Graven... The best way to shorten my review for this game is to say that I experienced a form of... Potential-filled tedium. Let me get in depth for a second.First of all, let me start with what I think is good about the game:- It's a retro FPS RPG, not unlike Hexen or Heretic II. Hell, it even feels like it's trying to be some form of spiritual Hexen/Heretic III sometimes. The artstyle compliments this beautifully. Most models are highly detailed yet maintain that grainy, dirty, 90's game engine look. The theme and tone of the game however are what carried me through. From filthy swamp to plague-ridden city, it never loses the dark tones while, at the same time, managing to portray some different locations. All in all, I consider this a win.- Enemy Variety: There's a few different enemies so far in the game. I will get into their balance in a second, but for now let's talk about their looks and variety. All of the enemies are easily distinguishable. From shambling plague peasants to hunched, mace-wielding cultist looking guys, it is easy to tell enemies apart from a distance. This is what made the old shooters so great (or bad). You look at an enemy and after your first battle, you know exactly what the enemies are going to do.- Sound design: Although I have to admit that this game has a bit of an invisible sound track, I didn't find it grating and I think that this is a very important thing in retro games. When I say invisible, I mean it didn't stand out to me like the happy electro tunes of ROTT's Suck This, or DOOM's heavy metal E1M1. It blended perfectly into the soundscape. Weapons and enemies sound fantasy enough to be alright and once again nothing stood out to me as particularly terrible.Now onto the things that cause me to put this game aside until a few major updates have happened:- Combat: Let's just put it this way... Combat doesn't always feel like the right thing to do. In a retro fps rpg. At first you start with a beating stick that does abyssmal amounts of damage to enemies. If you don't quit this EA release purely because of that you find a sword that, luckily, makes the melee combat bearable, even a little fun. But then there's the ranged weapons. Ammo is, at the best of times, scarce. Especially for the 2 weapons you'll find easily: the game's grenade launcher and shotgun. Add onto that that there seems to be some odd form of RNG damage calculator (enemies sometimes die in a single bodyshot from the "shotgun" or sometimes take 2-3.) and you are gonna find yourself circle strafing your enemies with the sword...- Enemy balance: and that leads me to the next point. The enemy AI is absolutely braindead. Zombies and swamp frog things will lunge at you even if that means impaling themselves on the spiky barricades. The masked cultists will run after you while you circle strafe them to death. The spitting bats sit still in the sky waiting for a while before they spit on you or move. All the enemies are rather stupid when it comes to tactics. The game counters this by having them do rather high damage (there is no difficulty selector I know off and even if there is, what I played would be the default). Add to this that you have next to no ammo after a few fights and you've got yourself a winner combo.- Confused design: This one might be on me personally, but I feel like this game has some confused design choices. You have a spellbook you cannot unequip from your hotbar and the cover of the game shows your character wielding a magic staff and the spellbook. Well... The spells are for solving puzzles. Both the flamethrower and shock spell do either abyssmal, if any at all, damage to enemies. That being said,  mana is everywhere. There are more mana drops than ammo drops in the game, I'd dare say. Combine that with my previous point about the weapons having low ammo caps and few ammo drops and this game feels more like a puzzle game than an RPG. Buuuuutttt... There aren't many puzzles in the EA that require the use of spells, at least not if you don't go out of your way to hunt for secrets.- Inventory management: We all played Resident Evil or Silent Hill at some point. I think most of us loved those games too. Well, Graven has adopted their sort of inventory management grid system. Weapons take up a certain number of slots in the inventory. Then it has a hotbar similar to MMORPG's. Nothing wrong with that right? Well here's the catch: weapons take up the same amount of slots on the hotbar as they do in the inventory. The sword I have mentioned takes up 2 slots. The shotgun takes up 3. Two of the slots are taken up by the staff and spellbook, both of which you cant unequip cause they are needed for the few puzzles the game has. In reality, you have 2 weapon slots and the sword as of now.- Early access scam?: This game is nowhere near ready to be sold. The three areas it has can be run through relatively quickly if you're any good at this sort of game. Weapon variety is limited. There are animation bugs and balance changes that need urgent changing in one way or the other, as well as the game figuring out what it wants to be: FPS RPG, or puzzler action adventure. Right now it's neither and it certainly isn't worth the 24 or so bucks they are charging for it.Yet... I pity this game. The potential it has, the setting, what little story it has are amazing! There is so much ways this can go, so much interesting things that could happen. The places that could be explored, the enemies players could face.Do I recommend this game? Not right now. It has way too much issues to be sold at all. If anything, you're currently paying for a beta. But if you're interested in the game at all, I would advise you to keep some cash aside and keep an eye on updates. If the devs gather their senses, this game might have a future.Edit:Now that we finally have some more content, this game is not worth it. Puzzles and quest guidance are beyond obtuse, they are sometimes borderline impossible to figure out. The game skimps on resources but has no issues respawning enemies ad nauseam. The new map is absolutely huge, beyond reasonable. It is simply not fun to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been looking at Graven for a very long time, and last day I bought it.Reading on Steam, my only source of information up until purchase, alot of people gave the impression that development had stopped, that it was a mindless beat zombies with a stick game and lack of depth/content in general.I have to say, they are all wrong. Graven is, a couple hours in, the best fantasy FPS (early access) title i have played!The atmosphere, graphic, sound's, weapons and enemies are all well done, and so far the map design and missions has been intuitive and easy to follow.By the time you wish you could parry with your trusty stick, you'll find a sword with the ability to parry. The magic i have found so far have a reason to be there other then tickle the enemies, and as far as i understood from Discord lurking, it will be even better in the full releaseExploring is a treat and i go out of my way to try and find it all. Every now and then, you even loop around that way, like the famous 3'rd person action-RPG that everyone like's.. From Discord i also learned that they are working hard (TM) on the final release, and i doubt we will see that many update's to the early access until then,since they said there will be Alot of changes to core mechanics and .. well .. everything!So when it launches, you'll have to start a new game. _childDocuments_.review: Graven feels like it was made by someone who played a handful of first-person games, and then decided to borrow a bunch of ideas from them to make their own game, but failed to understand what made those ideas work.For instance, I would guess that one of the designers played Bioshock at one point. It probably led them to discover a mechanic where you can zap a pool of water with a lightning spell, which affects any enemy who happens to be standing in that water. So, this designer figured that it's a great idea that will work great in their own game about spell-casting wizard dude. The only problem is, they didn't consider that in order for this mechanic to be fun and serve as a viable tactic in combat, the electrified water would actually have to do some damage or perhaps stun the enemy for more than half a second. You know, something more effective that would maybe give you enough time to switch to a sword for a quick stun attack. If you remember the "one-two punch" from Bioshock, rest assured, the designers of Graven did not.And this is just one example (out of many) to illustrate what's wrong with this game. It's full of cool ideas, and it has potential as this atmospheric fantasy immersive sim. but almost everything about it feels half-baked or poorly thought out. I had to stop playing it after few hours and I'm not even sure if I'm gonna go back to it, because I kept walking in circles around the first few areas with no idea where to head next, and it gave me a headache.

_childDocuments_.review: Thanks 3D Realms for pushing out yet another game that feels unfinished and has serious problems!I really want to love GRAVEN. The first hour of the game I found really enjoyable. The world and atmosphere is perfect! The world is big and has lots of detail, filled with puzzles and secrets. The slower pace movement makes you plan out your combat more carefully. I like this change of pace cause not everything needs to be a fast pace boomer shooter!Then GRAVEN just throws that out the window and forces you to fight brain dead enemies that are more suited for boomer shooters. I also found most of these weapons just don't feel that powerful, especially the magic feels super weak. The fire spell at the beginning of the game is a joke. It does basically zero damage. It's sole purpose is to solve puzzles. The wrist crossbow has such piss poor hit feedback and horrible accuracy I can't tell if I hit enemies most of the time. The "scope" upgrade for it is useless cause the scope is dirty so you can barely see. At least the melee weapons are decent, just remember there is a STAMINA bar, and it takes a long time for it to refill. It's not bad early in the game, but once you start fighting big mobs of enemies or even the fast moving enemies, you'll be out of stamina way too often.The checkpoint system is abysmal! The placement for some of these checkpoints are the worst! Nothing like dying, the have the game re-spawn you at the checkpoint with half of your health and what ever ammo you had when you died, that's right beside the enemy that just killed you, and kills you again! Oh and dying makes you lose half of your money, which you need to get upgrades and gear. I've only just made it past where the original Demo ended, and I'm already lost on where I'm supposed to go. GRAVEN is horrible for giving the player any sort of visual hints on where you are supposed to go. I spent 40 mins wandering around trying to figure out where I'm supposed to go. It sounds like the game gets even worse for this in the later areas. You know what would be an easy way to help? Maybe if they added f***ing SIGNS that tell you what is what or what direction something is in!! Do you know how many times I've gone to a sign hoping that it would tell me something, but upon going up to it and pressing interact it does NOTHING?! Do you know what building is the Library? I didn't even know what building that was until I picked up the key that said it was for the Library! There was ZERO information in the world indicating that this one locked door was the Library. GRAVEN also doesn't have any form of map! GRAVEN also has a really bad habit of having the text "Something has moved" and I'll be looking around trying to figure out what actually opened, but most of the time having no idea what actually did. It sounds like people are having issues of the game soft-locking them cause the map or something bugs out. GRAVEN doesn't know what it wants to be, and has some big issues, and that makes it so hard to recommend. Just remember this game has been in Development for 4 years, and the Devs have taken little to no feedback from the community. I really hope they give GRAVEN a couple patches to make it better. If anything make the combat better, and I'll deal with everything else. 3D Realms is on a good track record of delivering disappointment.Oh, and the dog petting animation is broken. It worked fine in the Demo before.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: No more polished, no more thought-through, absolutely embarrassing. I implore you: do not purchase.Not worth your time or money in its current state: a 4 hour beta-demo with questionable design decisions and technical problems. Presently, the game lacks coherent direction: is it an immersive sim or a straight-up fantasy first-person slasher/shooter? It's failing at both possible descriptions with trivially easy combat, worthless magic (solely intended for non-combat use and acting as little more than a Use button replacer), and non-puzzles save for one (a certain pillar puzzle which, while simple, would be tediously difficult to solve without locating easily missed lore notes).The atmosphere, aesthetics, and music are terrific however, and I'll be happy to update this review as the game progresses. _childDocuments_.review: Graven needs serious work. It's not good. The story is nonsense. You might even say there is no story at all. Every act eventually ends with a boss that you kill, then nothing happens, a voiceover tells you "whew you sure killed that guy, but...," then you spawn in the next act. The game literally ends, after a terrible final boss, with a voiced-over cutscene saying that the reward for the priest is in "doing". Credits roll. There is no story to end because no story was ever told. Not posting spoilers, but come on developers REALLY WITH THAT ENDING? The final boss is never introduced, never given a motive, never shown to actually do anything throughout the game, and then he's gone and nothing happens. Okay, so the story is bad, but how about the combat? This is a classic shooter and if anything the combat should be energetic, challenging enough to keep your attention, full of gibs & gore, and fun. Graven has the gibs. That's it. I adore so much of the modern boomer shooter/classic indie fps genre like Dusk, Blood, Ultrakill, Boltgun, Turbo Overkill, HROT... You name it and I've played it. This game has the worst combat by far out of any of them. Three reasons: 1) Graven has the dumbest AI I've seen in a FPS in decades; 2) Graven also has terrible weapons in terms of design, feedback, and sound; and 3) Graven has a minuscule stamina meter which slows you to a crawl if you sprint or jump too much. Please, for the love of everything Developers, ditch the stamina meter completely. AI first: enemies will legit just stop moving randomly. Maybe 1 out of every 5 enemies will bug out in one way or another and stop doing anything. Stop firing, stop moving, turn back and run away for no reason, or get stuck on geometry. It's insane how this was not addressed to an acceptable level since this game was revealed as a "spiritual successor to Hexen 2" on September 5th, 2020. By Act 3 I just stopped shooting enemies unless they were in my way and blocking my ability to progress down a tight corridor. There was no point - the AI was too stupid to ever hit me even if I walked through hordes of melee-attacking enemies. Enemies would literally charge at me, swing, and miss by the time I walked - not sprinted - out of their range. This would cause enemies to either reset and try to charge again, or more commonly they would just bug out and stop moving because they charged already so the AI would break.Unlike most classic shooters with a bar 0-9 with weapons at your disposal, Graven limits you to 3-5 weapons on your bar that you can swap out. Developers: ditch this and put everything on 0-9. The inventory serves no purpose. First thing first: melee weapons are worthless. Absolutely worthless. They can make enemies ragdoll and explode into gibs, sure, but they are not worth your time because their damage is bad, swing animations are so slow, and getting into melee range of enemies is a waste. The game also showers you with ammo, but sometimes you run out and need to switch mid-combat. Okay, let's open the inventory. Hey devs, do you know that the inventory doesn't show ammo totals? You have to guess what weapons have ammo. Last thing. Some of the weapons, I swear, do not have sound effects. Or if they do they are so unbelievably quiet that you can't hear them over the sound of your own footsteps. The crystal staff is a good example of this. Let's see. Game has 3 act "final bosses." I beat the first boss without getting hit as it slowly trudged around until its AI broke. Second boss killed me several times since it had an arena-wide grab attack that one-shot me. Then its AI broke and I killed it. Third boss killed me about 7 times. But here's the thing: when you die to a boss, the boss does not heal. You just spawn outside the arena, walk in, and resume shooting. There is zero challenge; it's just an unfun slog. The final boss is different - you spawn inside the arena and often times INSIDE THE BOSS while it is firing at you as you spawn in. Died a few times to that.The game has practically no music. Entire areas are just dead silent. Occasionally you will hear the whispers of music, as if someone two houses down put on a random string quartet for 8 seconds. Then you'll strain to turn up your speakers and stand in a place away from random sfx and listen, but they music has already died down as the music track is now done. The music could be 500% louder. Boss arenas are entirely devoid of music. The most common sound you will hear, incessantly, is the CAW CAW CAW of the ravens as they blare in your ear whenever you pass a checkpoint. Please, please fix the audio in this game. I want to hear music. The level design is abysmal. I had to watch four different no-commentary youtube paythroughs at 1.5 speed to figure out several BS sections where the game gives you no indication of where to go or what to do. The funny thing is that I could see each youtuber at various points struggling with the same thing I was, tab out to a guide they found, and then come back and point to the way to go. It's not uncommon for the game to randomly unlock a door that you passed by 10 minutes ago with zero indication that the door is now unlocked. "Hope you like backtracking constantly to pad out the play time," says Graven. This game took me 12 hours and 7 hours of it was just figuring out where the hell to go. Maybe one in 10 journal entries or updates will give you a vague clue. Sometimes you'll see a text overlay that says "You hear a metal door open somewhere above you." Obviously the developers understood that people were getting lost and needed help, so A for effort. F for execution - give me more hints on where to go.The only pro I can think of is that the game can be beautiful at times. Kudos to the environmental art team.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are expecting a Hexen boomer shooter, this isn’t it. That aside this is a pretty cool game.It’s a slower paced, more engaging game mentally, mix of FPS, RPG, and Metroidvania. You will explore, find weapons and upgrade them, use spells to solve light puzzles and open paths in a pretty satisfying loop of gameplay. Shooting is meaty, melee is fun, and the spells serve utility and function as opposed to being the center gameplay. Spells can be used in combat, but more like Bioshock where say a lightning spell will activate machinery as well as stun enemies or electrify water and environmentals to do damage thus rewarding clever use of your surroundings.Big thumbs up! Grats on 1.0!

_childDocuments_.review: Needs a ton of work. Has the trappings of an immersive sim type of fps but is heavily flawed so far. Really hope the upcoming content patches give the game a more solid identity and define the mechanics better.* Save system is actually checkpoints, which would be fine if ending a session didn't mean you lost all progress on an unfinished quest and it puts you back at the hub. If your game crashes or you have to bail after spending half an hour of making progress tough luck. For a game where quests are full of massive fights and sprawling maps this is ridiculous. * Inventory is fine in theory with a grid system requiring management depending on how large an item is.  However they make it also apply to your quick select bar. Two slots are permanently taken by your default staff and spellbook. You have to choose whether it's worth it being able to use healing potions and have a pair of empty quick select slots or to not pack potions and be able to use your grenade launcher/useful melee/shotgun.* Weird mix of old school fps and fps rpg. With a game like System Shock 2 supplies are relatively abundant but proper management of those supplies and balancing equipment vs ammo/consumables in your inventory.  In most retro style FPS you don't manage an inventory and can carry all your weapons and gear up to a hard limit for each ammo/consumable. This game does both. You have to both manage your inventory for equipment and deal with hard limits on ammo/consumables regardless of inventory space.  30 rounds for your pistol equivalent would be a stack that takes up a space of your inventory in SS2, instead that's your absolute hard limit for that ammo type.  If you get in a fight in a massive arena with enemies that take 3-8 shots each that's all your ammo gone with barely an impact. A retro style FPS would give you a way higher hard limit on ammo and not limit weapon selection so you can enter a fight equipped. An FPS RPG would let you use your inventory to define your playstyle and favour certain supplies/ammo appropriately. * World's feels empty. Massive sprawling maps with lots to explore; but currently there's nothing worth doing so in giant chunks. Gold doesn't have a use at time of writing there's no point looking for it.  Ammo/Consumables have a tiny hard limit so you fill up quick and burn out of it even quicker. In other immersive sims they'd use supplies, currency or lore as an incentive exploration but there's not really any of that here.

_childDocuments_.review: Right now, I just can't recommend this.  It's just is one of those games that feels like it should be more fun than it is.  The 'save' game system artificially pads the playtime because you are forced to play through re-populated areas to get back to where you were before, which gets to be a real slog.  This game BADLY needs one of two things.  Either 1. A save system that saves where you actually are in the game, and doesn't put you back in Cruxworth every time you come back or 2.  A teleport system that allows you to move easily through the game world. There are regular content updates, which I applaud, but good luck finding out where the new areas are due to the confusing layout of the map.  I appreciate the developers wanting to do something different with the inventory system, but honestly, this is another design decision that doesn't make the game more fun.  Instead of just cycling through the weapons you have (like in pretty much every other game of this type), you have to move them in and out of inventory spots to be able to use some of them. Frustrating.I absolutely love the game world, graphics, and the mood, but, boy, this game needs to up the 'fun' factor a little bit.Nothing would make me happier than to change my review after the full release, if some of these things are addressed.  A lot of effort has gone into Graven, but as far as buying this as an Early Access title, I really can't recommended it at this time.

_childDocuments_.review: Graven and the Incredible Technicolor Identity Disorder, Starring Slipgate Ironworks!Does Graven want to be Blood? Diablo? Gauntlet? A dungeon crawler? A boomer shooter? An RPG? I don't know, and neither does Slipgate. If you make a game without a map, you better have strong signposting and memorable areas that are not nightmare labyrinths. If you want to make a decent game of any kind, enemies shouldn't damage you before their telegraphs or slide all over the place or attack you after dying.They sure want you to bust open crates all the time, but make it extra tedious in that they don't burst in a single blow even with the fully upgraded staff. Which I got in the first two hours, because it only has two shop upgrades apparently. Achievements are also broken, by drinking three of the healing potion I got the drink every type of potion achievement, and by finding one shrine I got the find every shrine achievement. The enemies are also terribly designed outside of their outright glitchiness.Really, there's not too much to say here that hasn't been said a hundred times before. I can only assume they rushed this out to rush the Ion Fury sequel out, which sounds like it also isn't good. If for some baffling reason you do buy this game, just play it on a lower difficulty. It's not balanced at all and you still end up taking a lot of damage, even with armor.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, am i disappointed. The trailer makes this look like a boomer shooter of the likes of heretic/hexen: i.e fun spells, awesome weapons relentless enemies, ammo supply up the wazoo,.This game is none of it at the moment. You start off with a melee stick and you will be relying on it for most of the early access playthrough. The spell that you initially get only sets fire to explosives it serves no other purpose AFAIK. You can but projectile weapons and a sword  from the blacksmith. But there is very little ammo throughout the game, and  your ammo capacity is very low. So just expect to be hitting your enemies with your stick/sword most of the time. The enemies are a joke. You just circle strafe around them and you will never get hit. The enemies are very uninspired and repetitive. The level design is horrible. The devs tried to make the levels detailed by having multiple winding  paths. But most of the paths dont yield you anything. I was going around the city backstreets trying to find something interesting...there is nothing.  Just locked doors and crates and barrels.....endless crates and barrels. You get no incentive or reward for exploration. The good: great looking assets. The best way to sum up the experience is Imagine if  someone with little experience/bad taste in game design was given a competent game engine and good assets....the end product would look good in screenshot and short sequence videos, but it will ultimately be a boring and uninspired game.  I had some high expectations for this game.  the devs need to really sit down and rethink this game. To be fair, its early access, but its better to lay it on them thick right now so they can release a good final product.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't tell you how much I loved the demo of Graven. But man, what the hell happened to the early access? The GUI is different from the screenshots, it's missing most of the features and mechanics that would make it interesting. The early access has one area further than the free demo did, but is missing weapons. If you don't complete a zone in one play session, you have to restart the zone completely. Your hotbar resets every time you reload the game. The fire spell does barely anything, and its the only spell you get (even though the demo had a chain lighting spell that interacted with the environment). As far as I've made it, there's no rings either, and the flail is missing. To top it all off, the boss was removed too. I'm sitting here scratching my head thinking "How was this ready for an early access release? And why did I buy it?"I've played enough that I can't refund it at this point. So hopefully they'll fix all of this--but given the apparent reputation this developer and publisher have (supposedly they're the same company?), I expect that this will have just been wasted money. Shame, because the story and gameplay (while melee was lacking) felt good. I was really looking forward to this.Edit: So, they've added content so that the content is around parity with the demo. There's a little more in the EA release, but not much more. I still can't recommend it as we haven't seen more than one or two patches since it launched. Edit 2: So, it's November 2021. If you take a look at the Recent Events & Announcements, you'll find you can still see the first update for the game was on September 16 2021. If you check the Roadmap, however, you'll notice something. The first content update doesn't include any of the features listed as coming in Summer of 2021. September 22 was the last day of summer. I can safely tell you, that we haven't seen a single update since September; more just teases of "new updates" on occasion. By now, nearly into Winter 2021, we are not only missing content update 1 as per the roadmap, but also update 2, and the idea that we'd get update 3 this year is laughable. There's no way Graven is releasing for summer 2022. I'm not sure it's going to release at all at this rate.Edit 3: Around 9 days after my last edit, they released a revised roadmap. It looks far more achievable, though has no dates (specific or even estimated) so that makes it pretty easy. A lot of the content that was on the  is no longer there. You'll also notice that the original roadmap stated a Q1 2022 release, though the first two content updates for Graven are now slated as "potentially early next year." Which means we may make it through the whole of the first quarter without  of the first two updates we were promised last summer. Graven is a joke of an early access game, and you need only look at games such as , ,  and  to see what early access done right should look like.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll give this a positive rating, but I have a few reservations about the game. It's a rough gem riddled with questionable design choices, poor execution and mimicking the wrong parts of the games that inspired it. I'd recommend this game only if you REALLY liked Hexen and Heretic otherwise it's probable this game's flaws will be too much for you to enhoy it - hell, I WANTED so badly to love this game and more than once I thought about just quitting!Well, if you're still here, let me say I think at least part of the harsh criticism this game got has to deal with too much expectations. If Blood got its Cultic, Hexen doesn't have an heir of the same caliber. The game starts so strong: the aesthetic, the sounds, the writing, the voice acting... everything looks so promising! It doesn't take long for Graven's flaws to dampen its brilliance though.For starters, no map. Hexen and Herectic were mazes, but they had the decency of giving you a map. It's weird because Graven HAD a map in EA, but lost it, apparently because development was affected by time/money constraints. A simple compass would've helped a lot if a map wasn't possible.Then you have no save system (quick save/load or manual saves). If you quit your session you start at the hub area. Good luck finding where you left off with no map! Be prepared for a good amount of backtracking. This games wastes so much of the player's time with this and figuring out what the hell I'm supposed to do and where. It kills the pacing and is frustrating. This is less of a problem in Acts 2 and 3, because they're much shorter and smaller in map size/side quests. Those acts flow much better and keep the momentum (mostly), but at the cost of simpler interconnected maps and less content. Probably because of the troubled development as well.I could go on, but I'll just say that despite all this, Graven had charm enough to make me put up with its flaws until the conclusion. I have no doubt it's a much better game in a second playthrough, but I doubt most will finish the first. It's one of those games that are hard to recommend, but that can be great for a particular kind of gamer.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, with the last patch being a month and a half ago and reportedly over 50% of Slipgate being fired, entire history of scarce early access patches and how many reworks this game needs, I think it's now safe to say - there is not going to be saving GRAVEN, while Slipgate - just like CDPR cements its reputation as "marketing first, game and development second" studio. There was potential here - people really want games like Dark Messiah or Elderborn - heavy on visceral, first person combat, with exploration and occasional puzzles. This is not it. This is a misguided first-person Metroidvania with a melee combat that can at best compete with Morrowind with its player feedback. Where spells - as one of the other Steam reviews stated - are support only, yet again lacking any feedback and are mostly reserved for low, over-time damage or puzzles, and where the only thing that does any kind of damage are literal equivalents to first-person shooter weapons. Combine that with absurd, out of place stamina system and save system that doesn't store information which mob enemies you have killed and you have an extremely tedious game, where you run through massive maps, filled with brain-dead enemies, having barely any plot to give you a motivation and not even having any atmosphere - it's not fun! Freakin' Underworld Ascendent is more fun than this.

_childDocuments_.review: I hated leaving negative reviews, especially for games from small teams. I wanted to love Graven so much--it is deeply nostalgic, ticks all my boxes for 'fantasy game that brings me back to childhood and fulfills a sense of wonderment that modern games lack for me.' But despite being on the cusp of greatness, being so close to a Hexen-Gothic-hybrid--my absolute dream game--it felt as if Graven wanted to punish me for wanting to love it. I won't get into every issue, as so many have been covered in other reviews. I will simply say this: after stubbornly working through all of the game's faults to experience the rough gem hidden within, Graven punished me one last and final time for wanting to love it by softlocking in act 3, a softlock devs have been aware of for many, many months and have claimed (but failed) to fix. After completing the first major quest of act 3--which due to the poorly explained mechanics, rushed and nonsensical map design and lack of navigation aids took about 4 hours of my time--the mandatory encounter fails to trigger. So despite my journal and game progress saying a barrier has been removed to allow me into town to progress the story, I am fully locked out and thus unable to actually play the game any further. That's it: bricked. And the claimed fix by the dev--spawning you into the city anyways if the encounter fails to trigger--is non-existent. I simply load in outside the encounter trigger and nothing happens. I even tried to brute force it by reloading back in a dozen times, from various locations, force quitting, main menu quitting, as well as fresh installs 3 times. I put in far more effort than deserved from a game that does not respect the time of its players. As of now, it pains me to say that Graven deserves its abysmal rating. And after 3 months with no updates and a massive softlock barring many players from actually completing the game, I can't say I remain hopeful that Graven will become the thing I would so much love it to be. It's a true shame.

_childDocuments_.review: PSA: You now drop some gold where you last died so it's harder to reach the health penalty and saving up for the shops.Graven is a title barely anyone will get to experience, nevermind finish to completion on any difficulty, ignoring hotfixes. At the time of writing roughly less than 14% of players completed one of the earliest quests, which is to go in a sewer, blow up 2 piles of bodies, and enter a new part of town since the route is blocked. 0.5% roughly have killed the last boss if I'm not misreading (on any difficulty). Graven is heavily inspired by Metroidvanias and Hexen, with hub based levels that are interconnected by shortcuts and items that aid you in destroying and overcoming obstacles, these are to be achieved by exploration or puzzle solving with clues only appearing in your journal at vague intervals or other NPCs. You are invited to scour most nooks and crannies of each map, particularly in Act 1, which is boggy,  visibility is at its lowest in the whole game (there are landmarks but boggy bog bottom can get samey), and you are also at your weakest, with low gold to replenish your ammo and boost your damage, as it is hard to go back into town frequently. I played Act 1 before any hotfixes, so there were a couple of times where I had to run past a mini Serious Sam horde while micromanaging my stamina hoping to reach the next hamfisted save/check point, since the game for some reason does not trust you to save yourself, with the possibility of making a horde of enemies spawn camp you, despite also it having quite large immersive sim roots (immersive sims are not just when you stack barrels and do perilous platforming you absolute buffoons, it's also when there are simulation systems at work like being able to freeze water or at your own leisure, choose your own path, to your detriment or otherwise, for completion). Act 2 and 3 by comparison to Act 1 are very streamlined, almost hard to get lost, and the player gets showered with resources, but again, this sentiment might have been felt due to a hotfix, but alas the hotfix was late, looking at the discussion threads on Steam, this was long overdue, and it makes no sense even on the hardest difficulty which I managed to complete the game on. The bosses are quite standard fps fair but also a mixed bag, but Bog Man (my moniker for Graven's dubbed Priest(?)) has a hard time traversing without a specific potion or stamina upgrade, so you will die to a boss multiple times with its hp bar being withered by you already. Graven is at its best when the absolutely gorgeous art (please someone be inspired by the act 1 halloween-y bog please please please) is allowed to be taken in and the player is left to their own devices to figure out how to go forward, but the game adds respawning enemies so that the maps don't feel too l i m i n a l. It's a title I ultimately enjoy and could see it be so much better with the questionable design choices mentioned early and fixing out the obvious, like Unreal Engine 4 performance bugs, softlocks in corners, falling through the map, enemy physics, you know, the usual that some might be thrown/turned off by if they're not seasoned jank enjoyers. Graven is not for the faint of jank. Speaking of jank, Graven is also a comedy game when it comes to its mostly (?) optional puzzles. Act 1 has a sliding puzzle, this is fine, I'll ignore the fact that finding clues for it is a bit annoying or needing to pull paint out for some theory crafting on a puzzle and interpreting it, no, what steals the show, adds the cherry on top if you will, is that it seems there's a common bug or at worst, INTENDED mechanic of a ghost hunting you down which doesn't stay dead (!) while you are trying to solve a riddle. The punchline is delivered when this same sliding puzzle is advertised on the Steam store page under the screenshot section. Players will go: "ah, an FPS game with puzzles, how nouveau! haven't played a thinking man's fps game in a long time", little do they know that they need to play ring around the Rosie while fiddling with a sliding puzzle and possibly needing to pull out a dictionary to figure out what a trowel is.I rate Graven a "I'm glad to have experienced this" out of 10, because there will not be a title like this for a LONG time, it screams Metroid&Castlevania, Thief, Tomb Raider, Dark Messiah of Might and Magic, Hexen, BioShock, Deus Ex, System Shock, Prey 2017 and it comes so close most of the time, but it can definitely feel like you're being tested on your patience as opposed to skill and intelligence.

_childDocuments_.review: This could be a promising game. Sadly I can't really judge it, because I'm not able to see all that much from the game thanks due to the saddest excuse of saving feature I ever encountered.It works the following way: If you complete a quest (which can take you several hours at this very early point in the game) the game svaes this progress. If you quit before this point, or die, or your PC crashes etc. you can reload from the hub world (if you die you can choose a respawn point) and everything will be reset. So you have to do everything again, ioncluding travelling back to the area where you quit and along the way fight each and every monster again, do every puzzle again etc. This makes the game unplayable if you're on a tight time schedule.The devs mentioned on release day, that this "save system" (I just have to put this in quotes, it does not deserve that name) is on purpose due to the (not yet implemented) coop feature. Sadly, thje devs since then retreted to only answer selected threads, in the forums, so no new info on this. In the worst case it's a sign of incompetence on the technical side of things, or in the best case just lazyness. Either way it's a major red flag and I can not recommend the game at this point.Edit: If all this is no issue for you: Be advised, that even the current "save system" is bugged...

_childDocuments_.review: I just played through the Early Access game. Here's my personal feedback. Keeping it high level with just my thoughts. It's an interesting looking game marred by rather kind of lacklustre gameplay and challenge (where is the enemy AI, why are combatants just walking in single file at me, getting stuck in corners, hardly attacking?). The Early Access game takes you through a Dark Souls like castle and village and you eventually wind your way back to the hub (blacksmith, and quest giver) and into a Library area with an NPC telling you there is no more to the game at this time. I spent more time breaking pots and barrels than in combat. All this time I wanted to be flinging fireballs and dodging challenging enemies through fun combat loops. For a game with a spellbook, I spent 90% of my time using the sword and bolt caster weapon for the flying combatants. Where is the magic?I really wanted to like this, I loved playing Heretic and Hexen as a kid (I am 35) and I am a sucker for these 'boomer shooter' (slasher in this case) creations. I was drawn to using magic in the trailer and it was seldom used except for a couple of puzzles and not for combat. Maybe I'll check back in the Fall to see what's new but I wasn't really impressed with what I played. The sound, art, music, graphics are fine for what it is, the rest needs work.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately I cannot recommend Graven at this stage. It's painfully evident, that 3D Realms wanted to "finish" this project as soon as possible to avoid layoffs or even closure from Embracer Group. Its unfinished and unpolished, even after THREE years of early access. This game wanted to be an FPS / RPG hybrid with metroidvana and immersive sim elements, but became "just" a shooter with a lot of missed potential.Pros:+ Very nice graphics+ Great atmosphere+ Great music+ It has that Hexen vibe thats going forCons:- . I mean, really? The levels are HUGE and confusing, and you couldn't even include a simple minimap?- . Annoying and unnecessary. Most of the time I listen to my character panting, because he is out of stamina, I cannot even jump or run away from enemies. I just wait for like 20 seconds to recharge it. Waste of time.- . No manual saves, only checkpoints, but even after I reach a checkpoint, leave and resume the game, I still have to walk for like 5 minutes to the point where I stopped playing. Combine this with the huge levels and the dumb stamina system, and guess if it's a fun time or not.- . From animations not playing to softlocks, physics glitches and inventory wipes there are plenty of them.- . You cannot sell items (so for example you cannot sell the useless swamp potions after Act 1), cannot use items from there, and cannot bind items to keys. So you just swap weapons on the fly, which pauses the game anyway, so what's the point? I really hate that I can only equip 2 weapons at most too, because they reserve a lot of inventory space.- . They are mostly the same, some kind of crossbow. Some weapons are great, but some are just useless or redundant. I mostly used the "shotgun", the "rocket launcher" and the ballista.- . You don't have much spells, and they are so underpowered, that you are better off using any other weapon. They mostly used in puzzles, which is a huge missed opportunity in my opinion. You can upgrade them, but it's expensive, and the point you acquire these upgrades you have much better alternatives to dispose your enemies.- . Another useless thing is the staff upgrades. I only used the green gem, because it illuminates your surroundings. The others are just a waste. Speaking of melee...-  (at least after Act 1). The enemies hit HARD, have a lot of hitpoints, and using your melee weapons consumes stamina. So what will you do, risk your life with some crap melee weapon, or just shoot them in the face with a crossbow which you have more than enough ammo for?- . Some enemies are just bullet sponges, but no threats to you, some enemies are so fast that you cannot even run away from them, some enemies two-shot you from far away... The game needs quite a lot of balancing of the weapons, enemies and spells.The more you play the game, the more unfinished it will feel. Act 1 is like 7-8 hours of gameplay, has quite a few sidequests, NPCs, puzzles and secrets. It's pretty good, and feels polished. Act 2 is around half the length of Act 1, and has much less stuff in it, but overall not bad. Act 3 is a travesty though. It's the shortest act by far, and the level is a confusing mess without any flow, reason or interesting things to do, packed with empty rooms and placeholder items.Maybe the developers will patch out most of the issues with the game, but after 3 years of early access I'm not very optimistic.

_childDocuments_.review: Really love all the new immersive sim games of the recent yearsDishonored is the spiritual successor of Thief, Prey of System Shock and I guess you could say that Graven revived HexenWhile it has a similar art style and (much less confusing) key hunting, it's much more than just a Hexen revivalI really enjoyed the combat, reminded me of Dark Messiah a lot since they both move you into using the environment, there is a kick function, and are a bunch of damage dealing spike barricades. Your starting weapon is bad but useable, so it naturally leads you into using the environment more instead of forcing it down your throat. I also like that every time a weapon is introduced the next encounter is there to perfectly demonstrate your new capabilities. The short sword for example is faster and deals more damage and makes it easier to take on a group of enemies, so instead of luring them into a chokepoint it's now much better to strife around and dodge enemy attacks.The maps are all connected and fun to explore, good design even tho I feel the spells are underused.My only negative is how the game handles saves and checkpoints, so if you want to quit mid quest you will lose all your progress on that quest but you will keep all the items, so it's just pointless and also the map will still contain the weapon/map/spell pickups you already got. I like how the checkpoints work, so you don't lose your gold for example that you collected between checkpoints, but I dislike how missions are handled as also a form of meta-checkpoint (?) Honestly the game should just save your progress on the last checkpoint instead globally on when you started a mission/quest, the only reason why that might not work is if you get somehow stuck on a checkpoint

_childDocuments_.review: No way.I was waiting for years for GRAVEN to hit 1.0, having previously completed Act1.The game had great potential, what could go wrong? Well, something did.Playing it now, it's a significantly worse experience than in Early Access.Just random annoyances in the 2-3 hours I've played it:- Physics are a wonky mess. I got pushed away by VFX of a broken wooden table, or saw gold coins loot flying off.- Rat behavior makes no sense. Neither do rats that run on water surface.- Combat behavior is inconsistent. Collisions are weird, zombies randomly can either go slow, or leap in ways and distances their animation does not predict or telegraph.- Picking up gold, another core moment of this game, is terrible. You have to walk exactly on it to pick up, because it's 2024 so who needs bigger collision box or loot vacuum, right?- I think there was a map originally? Now it's gone. No plausible justification for this one, other than (guess) the devs did not want to make minimaps for 2/3 Acts. Boo!- Gold does not get picked up sometimes, despite it disappearing and the sound of pickup playing. Either that, or the UI messages for pickup don't work correctly.- The water slowdown effect is ridiculous sometimes. A ~15% of regular speed in a half-meter water poodle? Are you joking, who came up with that?- The 2/5 difficulty has barely any mobs. At this point, should have reduced their stats, rather than quantity.- The crossbow scope is broken. It comes with a thick white dust that makes seeing anything through it barely possible. This makes no sense, and is either a bug that shows how bad the QA process is, or another 'feature" decision showing incompetence.And I've barely started playing.But if you see me racking up more hours, know that it's not because I play to enjoy.I'm just taking screenshots, because the OG artist team have done a great job with setting the mood!TL;DR: Whoever is handling the game right now, managed to make the experience worse than it was.In its current state, I cannot in good faith recommend this game to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Having already purchased Ion Fury and Wrath, I've been excited to play this one as well, and it hasn't disappointed so far.The same modern retro feel exists in this engine and the added '3dfx graphics' option was a really nice bonus. It really did make me feel like I was back in the golden days of gaming with a huge nostalgic kick that felt sublime. Both Wrath and Ion Fury left me wanting to play the game as a port to original retro hardware and I did think that was a testiment to how well they made those games like the original engines. However, this game does it so well, with the 3dfx graphics and a few things turned down I felt at home, as I would on real retro hardware. Nice.The game itself runs pretty good on my 1050ti card at 1080p with everything on ultra, 3dfx mode included, as well as the lower 720p res with everything set to low. Haven't noticed any slow downs or FPS dips so far.The story intro is a little basic to get started with, but does a better job than most of the original retro titles of the time. Something I'm thankful for as I wouldn't be reading the manual for the story and lore on the way home now. There are lots of little snippets of the world laid about that you can read, I think I would have liked more of them to open the world up a little more, but it is what it is and I probably did enjoy smashing everything in sight a little too much... but I don't think that'll hold my interest in the game long term... and unfortunately it seems that's where the majority of the mana and health comes from, along with a lot of the coins (I don't know what the guy on the boat was talking about when he said he didn't want my coin *shrug*).Combat so far, is of it's age and kind of basic. The mobs perform the same attacks so once you work them out you can take them down pretty quickly. The zombie guys are near silent most of the time so they kind of just creep up on you.Sound is great, seems to work extremely really with Dolby Atmos with headphones on Windows 10. I don't know if the game was designed to make use of it, but it makes a huge difference to the game if it's enabled.Very happy with early access so far, looking forward to the full game.

_childDocuments_.review: Last game in the Humble Bundle Boomer Shooter bundle. It kinda sucks. It's not really a boomer shooter. It's an immersive sim that wants to be a boomer shooter. I got most of the way through Act 1 until I got to the mansion in the Bog. I had no clue where to go or what to do and wandered around the mansion for 20 minutes when I had done the same thing in the library earlier. Weapons and enemies are fine. Combat plays well enough. Level design is kinda crappy. Levels are sprawling and maze-like with the expectation that players utilize things like crouch jumping or dropping in from places you shouldn't normally be able to get to. Or... god forbid... stack boxes up until you can get over the obstacle. Like the solutions to puzzles and obstacles feel like they are unintentional and that the game just isn't designed well. If it is intended for you to come up with these backwards ass solutions, like jumping off a tower and ending up with 10 HP left when you land from the fall damage to get a gear, it's not fun. I played the demo for this game several years back when all that was available was first zone that ended with lighting the tower fire and THAT area is actually well designed. It flows well, has a good number of interesting secrets, and doesn't overstay its welcome. It's once you get past that into the library sequence that it starts to suck. I normally love games that give you a problem and then a bunch of tools and say "Go figure it out!" because it allows for creativity and critical problem solving. Thinking about it more I realize why this is different. You have no tools. You have stacking boxes. You have manipulating level geometry and getting out of bounds. You have abusing the save and quit feature to teleport back to town. It doesn't feel intentional that you can do these things. It feels like the devs expect you to break their game but don't give you anything to facilitate that. I don't want to have to stack boxes for 10-15 minutes just so I can climb over a wall that seemingly has no other path in. If the game had leaned in fully to the immersive sim aspect and made it an actual immersive sim with tools or abilities to aid in level traversal and make the levels designed around that, that would work. Also, if the game had leaned fully into the boomer shooter aspect and made the levels around the boomer shooter combat and level layouts that facilitate that sort of combat that also would've worked. You can definitely make this kind of a game work where it is mashup of different genres but you have to make sure you don't leave out the hallmarks of what makes those genres good.This is the last game in the Humble Bundle Best of Boomer Shooters bundle that I cared about. This makes that bundle 2 out of 6 good games and 4 out of 6 not great games. Not exactly great numbers. Oh well.

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure if this review should be more for the devs, or for potential buyers...let's say, for buyers, I just don't recommend Graven. I really wanted to love it. But as it is now, it's not worth 25 bucks. The environments do look quite good, and the opening minutes are pretty compelling (with some quite competent voice acting, kudos there), but the gameplay is...mostly jank. The enemy animations don't look quite right, enemies often path around randomly, looking confused, getting stuck on doors, the spells are ineffective, (not what you want in a successor to Hexen...), etc.Now, I think this has potential, but as of yet (early 2023, as a reminder), that isn't realised. The combat simply doesn't click, and the puzzles were simplistic enough that they're probably not even worth the bother of implementing them (seriously, Skyrim-tier pillar puzzles are a waste of dev resources. Just don't do it.)The difficulty feels off. I started on the highest difficulty, because I like to have a hard time, and it just was nowhere near challenging enough. The first hour or two are mostly just kiting with a staff, which...well, in Hexen, there was something like that, but it was just one very short intro level...Speaking of, Hexen's difficulty was no slouch. It was filled with death traps, many of which were fairly cheap, but I still remember them. I certainly remember its enemy roster, too. In my view, Graven hasn't quite taken the right stuff from its intended inspiration. Another very important thing that is lacking : impact. A good shooter needs to feel good, first. Sound design is one part of that, but weapon effects also count, as do enemy reactions, and gore, too, if that's the kind of game you're making. Graven isn't there yet. Firing a bolt that flies silently into an enemy, that doesn't flinch and just ragdolls unnaturally when it dies, just doesn't cut it. Seems like a detail, but it's presentation, and presentation is like half of a good FPS. Nothing can quite describe the disappointment of receiving a spell that promises to be really cool, only for it to be far less effective than a piece of sculpted wood.  Just yesterday I finished the early access version of Wrath : Aeon of Ruin, and it's a comparison worth making. The level design just works, with purposeful enemy placement, on top of their designs being very memorable and really quite cool. Plague zombies, contextless skeletons and ninja cultists won't a great game make, especially not when placed seemingly randomöy within a level design that is fairly ordinary at best.

_childDocuments_.review: The look and setting of Graven is great but sadly everything else about the game disappoints. It is styled as a medieval immersive sim but plays much more like a retro FPS and plays like a poor one at that. The gun (or rather sword-feel) feel lacks impact, the overall sound design is very lackluster and enemy variety functions more in levels of frustration than challenge and creativity. What put me over the edge of writing a bad review for the game was not the fact that development is progressing at an incredibly slow pace or that the updates to the game thus far has added very little compared to similar titles with the same business model, such as games like Blood West, but it is rather the wasted potential of the look and setting of the game as a whole. Graven sits itself in the now very saturated "boomer-shooter" or retro-FPS camp with it's classical graphics and approach to health, ammo and mana, but it fails to do anything remotely new or interesting despite being one of the few games of it's kind that takes place in a medieval fantasy setting. One should think that this setting would lend to a greater focus on melee combat but the actual sword/staff fighting in the game is incredibly ineffective, boring and beyond repetitive. Instead the game relies largely on the use of ranged weapons such as different variations of crossbows and the odd brick-firing invention that equally lack punch and become just as repetitive as you're forced to circle strafe your fast but dumb foes while you pelt them with an assortment of bolts, marbles and masonry, praying to god that you do not run out of shots and are forced once again to the confines of melee combat. A lot could be done with a fantasy setting, such as magic which is also a feature of the game, although it's functionality seems reserved for puzzles within the game world rather than combat and the game refuses to take a page out of games such as Bioshock where Plasmids could function effectively for both or even better, offer a different playstyle for players who prefer solving combat encounters with clever elemental combinations rather than simple brute force.TLDR: Any game released at the pace of Graven would find little succes on the other side of it's release window, but Graven is fundamentally impared by it's boring design, lack of vision and poor game-feel, making me seriously doubt if it will ever be worth the wait (or it's significant price tag compared to what you're getting).

_childDocuments_.review: At this point only a proof of potential and little else. The combat is not very fun and the exploration is more tedious than it has any right to be for multiple reasons. It takes a lot of bad aspects from classic Hexen II without feeling as good and tight to play.Usually I rate Early Access based on a simple prospect: “if there was more of the game (levels, enemies, weapons etc.) but the gameplay and mechanics stay the same – would I recommend it?”For Graven the answer is a definite NO.I’ll be keeping an eye on the development of this title with a reasonable amount of hope that it will eventually get good, but for now I don’t recommend buying this game at it’s current state in early access.Here are problems I believe need to be addressed:A lot of people complain about it, but few go into detail. At first I thought that it’s an exaggeration, but that changed about 1 hour in. Here are few things that I found (and remembered).First few enemies are lunging at you from mid-short range. If you are standing on a set of stairs above them, then they are unable to attack you because their lunge only lunches them forward with no ability to travel the stairs towards you.Some enemies will have serious trouble walking on some surfaces. They will move at less than quarter speed, seemingly being blocked by the floor itself – maybe they spawn inside the geometry to a degree? First time I’ve seen it was next to the first melee weapon during the lighthouse quest.Some later enemies are completely unable to approach or attack you unless you are standing right in front of them. They seem to throw their attacks in random directions sometimes.The AI in these games is supposed to be simple. See player → move to and attack player. Somehow this game has trouble achieving that.You will be doing a lot of running around large environments in search for something you’ve missed in order to progress. That’s also a thing in Hexen 2, but it’s not really a good thing to copy from that game. I can enjoy some switch or key hunting, but this game seems to be just badly paced.There’s a lot of breakable objects like barrels, that may contain items inside. While containers with HP items inside of them are slightly highlighted, you will still need to break a ton of pots and whatnot in search for ammo. This takes time in an already pretty slow-paced game.You also have to mostly rely on simplistic melee combat with enemies taking many hits to kill and providing nothing in terms of actual challenge. Note – killing player in just few hits isn’t challenge. Making player have to come up with strategies for encounters is challenge. Strafing around enemies and hitting LMB for 10 seconds is not challenge, it’s tedium.In melee you will be strafing around enemies and flailing at them until they die. Some enemies will enter a pain-state once hit and then you can stop strafing. There is no other strategy to melee combat and it’s as boring as it sounds. I mean this is supposed to be an action game, while combat is less deep than in Skyrim (and Skyrim’s melee depth is already pathetic). Apparently there is a kick (news post from devs talks about it), but I’ve never used it and I don’t feel like this would fix the problems. If we want to focus on melee then we need much more than ability to push enemies into environmental hazards. Devs should look to Dark Messiah for inspiration, maybe?That would be fine, I guess, if ranged weapons were fun, feel good and have plentiful ammo, but they aren’t much better. Most weapons don’t have a nice feedback and you will lack ammo unless you search through breakable containers all the time, which takes us back to the tedium. Note that developers (and some players) seem to think there’s too much ammo around (judging from a news post), so I guess they want players to rely even more on the unfun melee?I’ve found 2 melee (including the starting stick) weapons and 3 ranged ones + 1 spell that’s not meant for combat. Out of all these weapons the only one I liked was the most powerful ranged weapon that acts as the game’s grenade launcher. All other ones either take too much time to kill things or just don’t look or sound very good.I have not finished the demo. During my 110 minutes of play I got to the last stretch (I think), but failed to find the way to progress through one of the final, magically locked gates. Look for a different review if you want a full summary of entire content. I won’t be playing this any more due to refund policy.There’s a long road ahead for this game. I won’t rate it at this point, since there’s so little of actual game that rating it would be pointless. I simply recommend staying away perhaps until later in development. I will attempt to refund this for now and keep an eye for release and updates.I really hope devs will be able to turn this around into something good, because there’s clear effort and love put into it.

_childDocuments_.review: I backed this in early access thinking it'd be a straight up new Hexen. I played and re-played, and it is only through familiarity did I think it a nearly positive experience. The negative vote is influenced, sure, but did I look back and think "I had fun with that"?Not particularly.Some terrible design faux pas.- Some very long treks to reach map points, and too much backtracking- A dire checkpoint+respawn system- Whoever signed off the inclusion of a stamina system needs a kick- Most of the weapons are lacklustre, with ammo drops forcing you to swap to things you hadn't bothered upgrading, and having to swap them into "use" slots- The game dumps you into the next episode after a boss fight without warning - I wanted to finish exploring unlocked areas and quests...The rest are picky, and lack of a map I could live with. The only other real frustration was spending an hour finding the skull key in episode 3 to unlock the crystal. Priest's last ritesGiven the way the ride in was designed, I was half expecting the ferryman to turn up at the end, half-life gman style - to take you to the next episode, or twist that you were actually responsible for it all. Maybe :)Other than that though it is graphically consistent, and wasn't hard, especially after the initial episode (clearly had the most work) the others were actually fairly straightforward to navigate.Should you buy this? If you really want a hexen game, then find a gzdoom modded game instead. If you've run out of things and it is cheap, then maybe :D

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like Graven.The technology is good, the maps are O.K., the enemies might have too many HP, but the save system sucks the fun out of it.Save checkpoints are used, which can be far from the action.You can’t save more than your current point of progress, so you can’t go back a few minutes and try something different.Loading a saved game resets you to the central hub and respawns the baddies, without replenishing ammunition.The game appears balanced for one long session, reloading many save games results in a slog of clubbing baddies and respawning to get back to your point of progress.You have to double your time breaking everything to recover ammo, mana and gold.The big boss at the end takes all your ammunition and some luck, bosses should not make you want to quit the game and feel cheated.

_childDocuments_.review: Given the actual stage of development, I wouldn't recommend to buy this game. It is not about bugs, as I was lucky enough not to find them, but rather the game mechanics which, right now, are just broken:1. Enemies AI is inexistent: the poorly designed creatures will try recklessly to jump on you, ending slaughtered by your absurd amount of weapons. Stupidly enough, you can simply outsmart them by strafing left or right and beating the living crap out of anyone. So what's even the point with fighting them? Furthermore, to give this indecency a balance, programmers made the damage of mobs disproportionate, in order to give enemies the slightest semblance of threat.2. Items and drops: I spent almost 2 hours of the adventure destroying a multitude of crates and barrels that continuously drop mana / health potions, always ending up with mana and life at the maximum. It's quite obvious that just this mechanic destroys the challenge of the game.3. Blacksmith: why am I given the chance to buy weapons that I'll find FOR FREE a few steps ahead from this feller? Why not give the blacksmith some resemblence of profundity by providing him with quests that will unlock special items? Furthermore, due to the afore mentioned continous drops of gold from barrels/crates, in the very first encounter with this feller, you'll be already able to buy the sword, which is absurdly overpowered.4. The spells: Jesus Christ. Why on Earth would someone use spells JUST to solve puzzles? Wow, I used firebolts to destroy webs, that's FUN! Have you ever played Dark Messiah of Might and Magic? Why not give the player an offensive tool that he/she may combine with physical weapons in a creative and personal way?Let me answer that: the developers forbid this chance as they KNOW that using spells this way will just destroy the weak game mechanics, with players killing entire HORDES with a simple spell. Again: JESUS!5. Models and environment: there's nothing bad about the overall aesthetic mood of this work. Dark and fantasy-looking as we, lazy nerdy fattyasses, love. I'm not a developer and I can barely imagine how hard must be to work on models and maps, but during my adventure I felt like the overall implant lacks any sort of artistic inspiration. At the current point of the adventure, the PNGs and monster models are quite anonymous (especially that flying d@#k with wings). The maps feel uninspired and quite empty, but since this is a EA I'm confident that the devs will make the environment more interesting.I don't mean to be harsh on the developers or the game itself, as it has some potential and I was sincerely thrilled and hyped by its release. I still believe in this project and I want this review to be a food of thought to think about the chance to reconsider/change some development choices. From my point of view, this games has some REALLY BAD FLAWS on its own CONCEPT, which, I think, is the worst for a videogame beyond graphic issues, bugs etc.Since it is an EARLY ACCESS I still want to give it the benefit of the doubt and I am aware that the developers are actively working hard to solve the various problems reported by users. By now, the atmosphere looks great and you can tell the effort the developers spent in recreating a plausible old style fps. In the future, who knows, it could be a decent game, but at the moment it looks like a '98 fps, and a bad one, produced by a studio of desperate prisoners locked up in a Soviet bunker. We're talking about 3D realms, what the heck, I expect a lot more from this team.

_childDocuments_.review: GRAVEN, This is one of those times like you see in most reviews where they wish there was something in-between a thumbs up and thumbs down. This game does alot right but sadly, at the same time, alot wrong. I sadly didn't get to finish the game due to one really annoying factor currently that is a ridiculous way it handles it's backtracking when you reload a save game. Off rip with this system, there really needs to be added some sort of fast travel so I can easily get back on track with where I was, or actual save locations. As it stands every time you save and close the game you will ALWAYS end up back at Cruxworth, (the main city hub). Normally this wouldn't bother me too much, but with how little the in game map tells you (This map needs some kind of system to split up/show individual layers of maps. Yes I get this genre is about exploring and remembering areas, but currently it just lays it all ontop of one another and can get VERY confusing.) and the main factor that made me quit this game, it's a slog. Now to the most annoying point, and honestly all of this could be overlooked, and I will come back to play it again and change my review assuming this one factor gets changed. Having to re-clear areas I've already cleared 5 times prior. The game currently handles mob respawns in one of the most idiotic ways I've seen a game in this genre do, and I can't help but think it's an oversight. Right now when you reload a saved state everything in the world is how you left it, mob drops, doors that are opened, all that. Cool, I like this, I can use my memory of remembering where I left drops so that I can save gold for upgrades instead of ammo and such. This falls flat right out the door however once you realize the mobs respawn as well. The reason this doesn't work well and can almost brick your save if you don't finish this game in 1-2 play sessions is because you'll eventually just run out of ammo/gold due to you having to constantly be re-clearing old areas. Combine this with the respawning always at Cruxworth on a save load, and the way the in-game map is currently, it doesn't equal fun in a game like this. The reason too why I feel like this is an oversight is due to how they respawn as well. In these games you always end up opening doors/pathways from the opposite end you entered on to allow easy backtracking, (this game does that well). But the catch is the enemies wont respawn if you go through the area "backwards". Example: 1st time through the graveyard enemies spawn like normal, I open all gates, save and reload. On reload I can freely go through the graveyard, as if I'm going back through the way's I've opened, but if I at all end up on the "normal path" I would of taken the first time through, they all start to respawn practically infront of you. You're even able to test this by going through the areas backwards, and just listening. As you turn around corners you can literally hear the mobs spawning. As it sits, I love the art, the music, just the vibe and aesthetic of it all. The combat is fine, it does what it needs to do, the animations are great, the mobs are cool, and the weapons are super appealing coupled with the graphics/art style the game goes for. I would of given this game a full on thumbs up but as it stands until the whole mob respawning is addressed, I just can't. Unless you're able to finish this game in 1-2 sittings or pick it up on a decent sale ($10 or so) I would wait. The game gets decent updates so I'm hoping I'm able to revisit and finish this game soon and change my review.

_childDocuments_.review: I had Graven on my wishlist for years now. I thought the game looked cool. And tried to be optimistic about mixed reviews because most of them were just complaining about long early access and low content updates frequency. I was waiting for a full release to give this game a shot myself.Unfortunately, it didn't live up to any expectations. Even the lowest ones. Yes, it does look cool - the art style is awesome, the atmosphere is great and it's interesting to explore around.Everything's good in the sound and music department as well. No complaints there.Where the game does fall short is the gameplay.It is a prime example of "where the f*ck do I go?" And I'm not usually the one to complain about that sort of things. I'm fairly good at orienting in 3d spaces and game environments. However, Graven doesn't even tell you which way is the progress.There's no map, no indicators. Nothing in the dialogues or a diary/quest log. The level design doesn't lead the player either. I spent almost an hour just running around trying to find a door that opened somewhere randomly after I lit the lighthouse. I came back to the main hub, checked all the other exits - everything's closed. I went to the quest giver - he wasn't there. After a bit I found him at a completely different location. He gave me an item... that didn't make any diference and doesn't help with progression in any way, and didn't tell me where I should go next.After some more running around, I resorted to stacking barrels to make a pyramid so I could try and get over some wall to see if maybe I can progress somehow that way. Nope.In the end, after I returned to the hub once more... one of the exits, that was previously closed when I checked the last time, and was waaaaaaaaaaaaay outside of the view and in the furthest possible direction from the quest giver - was now open.What made it worse is that the game re-spawned all the enemies and barricades and other stuff that I cleared the day before. So I had to do it all over again just to find one random door that opened somewhere on the map.The combat is alright. However... for some reason there's a stamina "system". And by "system" I mean that it doesn't do anything except getting in the way of player playing the game. It has no bearing on gameplay whatsoever. It just prevents you from sprinting and jumping "too much" for no reason. And it takes 20 seconds to regenerate!The game itself is unpolished and sometimes buggy. It has an identity crysis and doesn't know what it wants to be. Why is there an inventory? Why can I only have couple weapons bound on my hotbar if I can just pause the game whenever I please and swap weapons anyway? Why is there an aforementioned stamina?There is a cool title screen where the main character is about to strike monsters with lightning from his staff and magic book. But in the game spells are all but useless in combat. And I really REALLY tried to make them work. Yes, I can sometimes explode gas clouds with fire spell... But that's pretty much the only useful thing I could get from spells during the fight. They barely do any damage and chew through mana quickly.Every single encounter is just "strafe and hit with stick" or "backpedal and shoot". The "mighty foot" doesn't do anything. The damage sucks and it doesn't even push enemies away properly. Just shoves them back a little. Even less than a default attack with a staff.Graven also doesn't respect player's time. There's no manual saves. There are scummy "gotcha!" death traps that punish you by respawning on checkpoint and taking away your gold. And no, you can't get it back like in dark souls. Sometimes I was wondering "can I jump there?" But I wasn't goint to check becuse I can't just save and see if there's a secret or an instant death. The game repeats multiple times - when starting a new game and in the guide/journal - that "this is a DIFFICULT game!" That's not an excuse. I've played a lot of difficult games and rarely felt the way as I did here.In short, Graven is a very cool looking game with an identity crysis and boring gameplay. Disappointing.
