_childDocuments_.review: After playing through the early access twice, and exploring every inch I could find here are some thoughts as of 5/27/2021 + Linear level design that opens up on itself, what I mean by this is something similar to Dark Souls, where you reach a point far enough in the game after progress you find new routes that can unlock to bring you back to other areas and make navigating and exploring a much more enjoyable experience than running back and forth for a half hour. Almost every area connects to each other the further you get in the game, and it really makes looking for secrets enjoyable. They did such a FANTASTIC job with this that I was actually surprised, not too many games doing that nowadays they tend to usually stick to open designs or linear designs and never inbetween. Secrets play a big part in this, because there are secrets that you can clearly see but are not intended to get to until later in the game, The game being very vertical helps in this to make it feel so much freeing. I love it.+ Sound design. Music and Ambience. I found myself getting actually pretty immersed with the sound pumped up, there are a few moments where some tracks cut in that just.. felt so appropriate for the world itself. I know that should be obvious, but some games just do not nail it. Graven does.+ Artstyle. Graven does this insane thing where it wants to be a game of my childhood and it nails exactly how I thought those games looked at the time. Not realistic, but stylized and just so clean, but yknow with 20x the resolution. For what is shown in the EA, I'm pretty confident the rest of the game will be equally as gorgeous.+ Progression... sorta. It felt pretty nice paced, but I had bought all the weapons before I even found them in the world, off the blacksmith. However seeing the intended paths to pick up the weapons and where you're supposed to use them, the game is well paced in that regard.+ Atmosphere. It really does feel like you're in a bad place that doesn't want you there after they took over. The game just nails what I think they were trying to convey.+ Weapons. Weapons could improve with some balancing, but I like the feel of them at the moment. The staff becomes more of a tool on top of being an early game weapon, while the sword is really great for actually pumping out damage, and breaking barrels. The crossbow has this nice kick feel to it and is great at obliterating skeletons when they put their shields down. It's also great to alt fire and push explosive rounds into enemies and watching them run into their friends and die while harming those closest to them. The Wrist bow is really great for explosive barrels with enemies near them, and great for the flying enemies. I also used it to kill totems. Kicking can be used to kick enemies off of things, and with todays update can be used + Immersive sim qualities and world building. Don't get me wrong, this game is not Deus Ex and I don't think they're trying to become that. But there are little things, like lighting torches, or using props from the environment to assist you, though the props are mostly for puzzles at the moment, I did also find a few spots I could skip sections of levels by stacking objects. Interacting with NPCs and finding random notes scattered throughout that really benefits the world building, in my opinion. I'm really curious to see how this world unfolds.+ Magic as a tool. I know some people were expecting to be able to use magic (currently only fire) as another weapon, but that is not what this game is doing. Fire is a tool, you can use it to clear dead bodies or crates or even light explosive barrels on fire and run away. Using it to get through spiderwebs rather than walking real slow was another perk. Again, you can use it to give you some lighting (though it seems bugged in certain areas) in dark areas. A dev in discord even said fire is planned to be able to break skeleton shields in the future, which I love. Overall do not expect to go into this game to use magic as a weapon currently, it is meant to be used as a tool in the world.+ Easter eggs and secrets. There are a few, if you know where to look of course. Every game needs secrets! This games secrets so far are both rewarding to find, and even more rewarding to loot.--------------- Combat loop. It is mostly just a hack and slash except a handful of moments. HOWEVER it's important to stress this is the earliest level in the game (in EA) and of course there aren't going to be any real real big bads right off the bat. It is important to note that there are sections of the game (about 2 parts atm) where you're fighting in large open spaces against hordes of monsters where there's like 20 dudes trying to kill you and it starts to become really enjoyable, then it's over. Quickswapping weapons to explode some skeletons clumped together or a monster leaping at you followed by slicing some zombie up to not get overwhelmed felt really good. I do think in a game like this it's okay to not have that many big arenas like doom, but that is just where I had the most fun when it came to combat. The rest of the time I just simply spammed left click with a sword (or early on, the staff). It could be more enjoyable, but it is not a dealbreaker for me. It might be for you.- Saving and Quitting mid-quest. I'm unsure if this is intended or not, but even if you are like 99% of the way through a quest and you have checked off several steps for it, if you close the game or it crashes for some reason (have had 0 crashes btw), your progress is fully reset back to 0 when you hit continue game. Checkpoint saves are only relevant when you're ingame, the second it closes you lose them all and it boots you back to town and you now have to go through all those steps again. It just felt bad when I had a bug to where I had to restart cause I'm a dumbass that got stuck by being in places I shouldn't be, and I lost all that progress.- AI. It's pretty mediocre and only offers a threat when it's a horde of enemies. If you're just taking out 1 or 2 at a time you'd pretty much have to be afk for them to kill you. It's hard to tell if this matters for the rest of the game since it's basically just the first chapter, and in most oldschool games the first chapter enemies aren't really threats either. It could improve, but it might be improved with newer enemies + newer combos fighting together too. I guess we'll have to see.- Visual clarity on the map. I know this is a weird one probably and she be a personal complaint rather than a general complaint, but there are bits of the map where they really start to overlap each other with no way to discern what exact parts you're at, mostly when it comes to verticality. Perhaps some sort of fade for things that aren't on your current level? Then again it does add to the grittiness of the map being handdrawn rather than a UI component in a videogame.--------------Overall closing thoughts. Is the game worth 25$ in it's current state? That depends. Do you want to support the devs that seemingly have a very promising game on their hands? If you do then I'd say go for it. You will get about 3 hours out of the Early Access build at the moment on your first run, 2 if you're not really exploring. I'm happy with the money I spent personally.My gripes for this type of game are honestly minor compared to the overall gameplay experience I got. I see nothing but potential in the future of this game and I'm looking forward to it being finished whenever that may be. I can't wait to see the upgrades, and the rest of the magic to interact with this world.One thing I'm massively hoping for in the future is a level editor, this game just seems like the PERFECT type of game to make maps for, for the years to come.

_childDocuments_.review: Important note: "Fulqrum (Publishing) is owned by China."I am really bored out of mind mind so this will be a bit shorter than usual. 6 hour long game (campaign+quest+secrets=I had most of my weapons upgraded to purple etc.). +1 hour on top of that wasted trying figure out the obscure puzzles and find workarounds for game breaking bugs - yes 1.0 release with game breaking bugs. _childDocuments_.review: I initially played around 30 minutes of the game, as a blind unbiased look at the game, and really enjoyed it. I played an earlier build, and there were some issues with sound, but they have been addressed in the latest build.I jumped back on it today, and spent just over 5 hours on it, and I am still really enjoying it. I am still in the first act.I like that there is very little hand holding. Too many games basically hand out what to do. At this stage, I am ok that there is not a map. Not sure if it will become an issue for the other acts. We shall see. I love the art style too. Very cool.I find the combat quite satisfying, especially the shotgun style weapon. The enemies are fun, and varied enough to challenge you, but not overwhelm. The controls are super smooth, and bopping the enemies in the face with the staff, and one hitting them, never gets old. Overall it's a great game, but will not suit everyone. I am an older gamer, and this really hits me in the reminiscence! I think it is a little pricey, but that may be unfair for me to say as a) I got a review copy for free, and b) with me only playing 5 hours and still being in the first act, have I even given it a chance. I'd happily pay £14.99 for this game.With regards to the reviews, it's a shame that this is mixed, as many of the reviews I have seen appear to want things that other games have. I like that this is different from the usual dross that's out there at the moment.I will be continuing to playing this one for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, right now Early Access so this review is based upon the recent content update.I quite like the game,the atmosphere is good, nice graphics style, music decent and the gameplay thus far fast paced and enjoyable.Additionally i generally like the level desgin, although the swamp later can get a bit disorienting.Now now the cons i see at this point...Gameplay is a little bit too simple bordering on repetitive, which is not bad if you want to have just a bit of popcorn cinemaesque entertainment.Some enemies are a bit buggy, mainly the poison spitting birds seem to have problems with flying and wayfinding.Last but not least the story......yeah......well.......is neglectable but honestly who plays the game for the story....The small lore bits in documents are nice though.I give the current state of the game a 7/10, its a short but enjoyable ride in reminisence of the likes of hexen.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game since its inspired by some of my favourite classics such as Heretic and Hexen. Unfortunately, after four or so hours of game play, i can confirm my disappointment in that it is pure tedium, bland, and quite uninspiring. Enemies are hit-sponges making weapon choices largely pointless, and the bugs still present in the game are beyond irritating. For instance, I can save and quit in one area (that's the only save option, by the way), and end up back in another upon reload meaning that I have to fight through hordes of damage soaking enemies again.Because most areas look very similar navigation is a nightmare, especially so without a map system. The labyrinthian layout and appearance can make frustration a core part of the gaming experience.Being charitable for a second, not my forte you understand, the potential for this to be a decent game is present. The quests are generally decent, I like the semi-RPG system for inventory and "levelling" when you find an Orthagonal Shrine, destructables everywhere will keep diehard crate smashers more than happy, and the enemy types are varied if unbalanced. It's a shame that none of it really meshes.My recommendation? Wait until they've fixed the bugs at least and only then if you want to kill a few hours.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted and tried to like this game, but now after almost 20 hours of playing I give up.In the first 15 mins of gameplay I thought that the game had cool graphics and atmosphere, but then I got to melee combat for the first time and was wondering why do the enemies teleport or disappear. Playing more I learned that enemies just attack thru your game character, disappear behind you and continue attacking you. Sometimes without making any sound. What a stupid idea to have enemies going thru your in-game character like he doesn't exist at all in the game world. At first this isn't such a huge issue, but just wait until you get to Act 2 and get killed in one or two hits (when full armor/HP) without getting a single sound effect.And talking about Act 2. Holy crap this act has some of the cheapest enemies in videogame history that can kill you in a single hit. Especially those bald guys shooting fireballs that sometimes lock on you and lock on you - even behind corners. You see an enemy shooting at you, strafe behind a wall for cover and suddenly just drop dead to a homing magic missile. Even those blue ice guys' projectiles follow your movement even when you're strafing, but I think they don't even shoot homing projectiles.And here in Act 2 the "not getting any sfx from attacking enemies" and "enemies going thru your character" just made me quit the game since Act 2 is full of enemies that just charge you and you drop dead. Game going mute was already a problem in some parts of Act 1 and it seems that there were a few rooms/caves where every sound just stopped working - excluding my character's attack sfx.And no map in a FPS that sometimes require a lot of backtracking? Really?!Apparently there was a map at some point, but it got broke and developer couldn't fix it so they just removed it completely. I think wasted like 5 hours in Act 1 since I couldn't find THAT ONE way in a hedge maze to progress the game and ended up just running around searching for a hidden passage or a breakable wall.Now it's time to uninstall this unfinished "game" and never play it again.I wasted 20 hours and in the end I think I DID NOT HAVE FUN with it.Graven - good riddance...

_childDocuments_.review: This is where labels get us into trouble.  There are a lot of old FPS titles that didn't necessarily go down the Doom/Duke/Quake route of shoot/kill/repeat.  A boomer-shooter is more of the essence of these games from the past.  Unfortunately "Graven" has the tag, but it's not a boomer-shooter in my mind.  It's a retro-inspired fps-rpg hybrid as it was back in the day.  Two games come to my mind playing this:  Strife, and Hexen 2.  Do yourself a favor and play both of those games.  You'll appreciate what's been done with "Graven".

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this twice and loved every minute of it. I just wish there was more. Now I seem to have fully understand that the spells are not weapons, but you can use them to help with some attacks like if an enemy is by a red barrel. So far I seem to understand where to go and not once did I feel lost in the game. I love the world of Graven, it kinda reminds me of Dark Souls universe. This is a fun immersive sim game so if you love that type of game then you will enjoy this. I highly recommend and after typing this review I think I might play for a third time.Update: I have played 16 hours of this early access demo. The game isn't finished and there is only like 3 missions, but it's extremely fun. Yes this does have it's boomer shooter roots like all of 3D Realms games, but it's still a immersive sim game. So you can have the best of both worlds. Again I didn't have trouble figuring out the puzzles. Now some were tricky but when you finally figure it out, it just feels amazing. Again with the fire spell I also didn't have trouble figuring that out. No, it's not a weapon, but you can still use it in fights and use your items around you like a red barrel, which if it was to catch on fire it would blow up. Please don't change the fire spell. Now I do agree the turtle key could confuse some players. It didn't me, because I like to explore areas before I even should and I found the door for it. Before I even knew where the key was. I just love exploring this game and it's becoming like my favorite game of this year and it's not even finished. I highly recommend this game and I'm excited to see what's next for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but it is utterly GARBAGE in many aspects. Let's outline:1. No map. No map whatsoever. It HAD a map before 1.0, but was removed for petty excuses. And the game gets really mazey fast.2. The spells, introduced early, use too much mana for what? Puzzles and convenience of igniting junk from a safe distance, are a less reliable source of damage than your walking stick. And by "less" I mean to say that punching (if it was an option) would STILL be stronger than spells.3. The enemies have two damage levels: tickle tickle, and goodbye health. And VERY early on you come at a an everlasting respawn point of the later ones that mobs you faster than you can react. And you get no way to damage a group of them other than igniting gas clouds, which are few and are GONE for a while after you burn them.4. AWFUL flying enemies ALSO very early on, and that leaves a lingering pool of PAIN from their long range sniping spit.5. No save options, it boots you ALL the way back to town, making it so you HAVE to do long sessions. They haven't learned from more games using autosave and quicksaves as time went on.6. Checkpoints are barely useful, since SOMEHOW a checkpoint can just choose to NOT work on random, resulting in you, guess what, WINDING UP BACK IN TOWN!The game was better in Early Access... But rather than improve from it, they made it worse. If I knew it would come out this bad, I'd have refunded it way back then, back when it was good, so I'd have never to see it devolve.

_childDocuments_.review: I wrote a negative review after hour of play, but I felt it wasnt fair, so I played more. Now I have over 9 hours, I ended act 1 so I can review it again. Sadly after getting a bunch of fresh quests with no direction, and having to backtrack the same areas for 15th time I just lost desire to play and cant give it positive score.There is a good game hidden somewhere there, but its unfinished and dragged down by so many strange design decisions and bugs it baffles me.PROS:- Atmosphere is great- Hitting zombies with enhanced staff to make them fly is cool, and exploding enemies are always funCONS:- no map (its not game breaking, you can play without map, but quest descriptions are so vague (no quest markers either) that you dont know where to go and what to do most of the time, which is very annoying and tiresome)- no save system (after quitting you start at hub and have to backtrack, which wastes your time)- identity crisis (game wants to be exploration game with riddles like Hexen2, but also fast arena shooter like new Doom, and it has elements from souls/metroidvanias like respawning enemies, losing currency on death, tools that open areas- this mix while awesome on paper doesnt work here very well)- total lack of balance, some enemies are spongy and/or very fast for how bad your weapons are, and how slow and clunky you are, also game throws more and more of them, by the end of chapter 1 there are so many high tier enemies in already visited areas its really hard to kill them all. Game doesnt give you required tools- you are slow and ammo is scarce and it ends fast (and its on normal difficulty). Its better just to run past enemies than fight- game feels clunky- tons of bugs- like floating items, items from chests spawning on terrain, sometimes impossible to get- to jump higher you have to crouch mid air- im a boomer so i get it, but why is it present in this game? its 2024, not 1997- annoying restrictions- like stamina (in fast paced shooter? with a lot of backtracking required), or inventory (if I have 2 main weapons, arm crossbow, staff, spell book and health potion, I cant use mana potion [even from menu], because I dont have space on my belt, so I have to drag it from inventory to belt and then use- WTF, its pure nonsense and waste of time)- overall game feels quite messy with its lack of focus and direction, and really unfinished, with hints of scrapped ideas everywhere (rpg sheet). I heard act 2 is much smaller than act 1 (like half of it), and act 3 is barebones. I suspect they put 1.0 version on it because they dont want to spend more resources on it. So lets say its finished and move along.Some of these flaws can be fixed by patches I guess, some unfortunately either cant be fixed or require months of hard work. My prediction- its not gonna happen.I cant recommend this game. Better play something else, something finished and fun.I wanted to love Graven, but I dont even like it.I dont even start about 3DR situation. They are extremely untrustworthy, with many projects started, that probably will never be finished, or be 'finished' in sorry state like Graven here. I put them and Slipgate on my black list.They taught me well to not buy any Early Access games ever again.

_childDocuments_.review: I originally reviewed the EA release of this game and tore into it pretty badly. Now I'm here to tear into again.Graven: A Horribly Mediocre Experience.TL;DR: This game is a bug filled mess that will force you to slog from one end of the map to another looking for keys so you can progress the game, only to find another locked door with more keys to find. It needs to be put back in the over for a few more months and then maybe, just maybe, it'll be a good game. If it had decent level design, it could be completed in less than two hours. The two new areas they added only add more than an hour of game time because of how convoluted everything becomes. The snow area could have been completed in less than an hour if my journal had updated me with anything more than "I'll have to find another way inside." The desert is equally stupid and ill-designed, with a section that had me running around like "What am I even supposed to do?" This works for games like Gloomwood, where you know you're on the right track when you enter a new area, but entering a new area in this game means nothing since more then 3/4s of the time, you'll be looking for keys. I'm convinced anyone who says this game is "fun" and "worth playing" hasn't even made it out of the first area, given the second area and third areas give you an achievement that less than 1% of the people who own this game currently have. So, maybe a couple HUNDRED people have made it to the second and third areas. With even fewer probably suffering through to beat the game.One of my original complaints was that the map sucked and didn't really do much to show you where you were in relation to major landmarks around the world. So, instead of working on the map, they completely removed it and added in a section that explains that running and jumping sap your stamina. Really intelligent. I'm glad this game sat in EA for 3 years and they have to tell us that running and jumping will use stamina. It's not like there's a icon that slowly degrades when you run, jump, or attack. The magic didn't even get touched outside of the addition of one new spell, which is basically useless and I forgot I even had it after I got out of the snow area, which is the only place it will be even remotely useful. Stupid, right? I suppose it could be useful in combat, but there's such a delay when you're changing weapons/spells in combat that it probably will get you killed. The enemy variety is lacking. You'll face the same exact enemies in the first area and the last, while the second area had a few new additions that are extremely fast and will just bum rush you until you die. And then you'll respawn right next to where you died, and they'll do it again. The weapons are still the only real way to go, since they're the only ones that make any difference in combat, but the addition of another melee weapon when you'll only ever trade damage in melee combat is a horrible design choice. If you do end up wanting to suffer through this game, just upgrade your wrist crossbow and flechette and you'll be fine. It's not worth wasting the gold on upgrades when you'll need it for healing potions. The boss design is fine, I guess. They're all bullet sponges with attacks that do a stupid amount of damage to make them seem more "challenging." For instance, you'll find armor, go into a boss fight, take one hit and your armor and a chunk of your health is gone. It's just a really shoddy gimmick to add any level of "challenge" to this game outside of constantly getting lost in these massive areas with very little direction to go. The ONLY redeeming quality for this game is the fact that some of the areas look really nice. I could probably overlook the vast majority of my grievances against this game if it had one thing:More paths that lead you to your objective instead of forcing you along one where you'll be running around for hours looking for keys.Like, it's not outside of the realm of possibility. Look at Gloomwood (since so many people want to call Graven a good immersive sim), very rarely are you ever forced onto one path. When you are, you usually get to do something cool, or there's a nice setpiece for you to witness. Sure, there's only one objective, but you have so many ways to get to that objective.  Graven just forces you along a single path to pad out the run time since most people who are good at these kinds of games could probably beat it with enough time to refund it and doesn't really offer anything along that one specified path except the end of the area. My only hope for this game is that they continue to work on it. Maybe someday it'll be a game I could come back to and actually want to play all the way through, but with how it feels now, it's not worth the slog or the $25. I'm sure for that price, you can pick up 2 games similar to Graven that'll fill the void more than this game can in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like immersive sims? Ok, well this is not quite there.Do you like oldschool boomershooters? This ain’t quite there either.So what is this? A very confused mess of ideas that is often as brilliant as it is busted. As if the initial version of Quake (the RPG design) started to go toward the FPS it became, but stopped in the middle.Welcome to Graven; a game where you are likely not going to be sure if you like it or hate it.Graven is one of the most lopsided games I’ve playing in a long while. For every good element there is a bad one, for every interesting system the game introduces there will be a moment later where you think “Wait! Why did they introduce this? It does nothing!” and there will be many, many moments where you will get annoyed at something because it seems useless only for you to find out later that it is was really badly explained and is actually really useful. If you are willing to stick with it, there is quite a cool game under the mess, but is sort of misses the mark by a small amount.If one was to describe Graven it would be a sort of imsim light, but not quite. This is due to there being a whole raft of somewhat half-way house RPG bits that never seem to fully commit. Examples of this would be the character inventory screen or the customisable item keys. On one hand this indicates a level of complexity the game is striving for, but for one it seems impossible to actually fill the inventory, meaning there is a grid system that, at best, will get half full. The item hotbar as well has the weird choice of weapons and items taking up more slots. A weaker weapon will typically take up one slot, a melee weapon or more mid range weapon take up two slots and then the majority of the main weapons taking up three slots. This makes it seem like you have to plan things out, picking and choosing the best balance, but in reality to change the weapon loadout all you need to do is open your inventory, pausing the game, and swap them about. This just makes the game a little tedious rather than deep.This stands in stark contrast to how the moment to moment play goes. Generally, it feels like a standard FPS game but with magic and medieval weapons as opposed to firearms. For the most part the weapons are fun to use, and once you start to upgrade them they get REALLY fun to use. In truth this is less an imsim and more Hexen with a fake level of complexity laid atop of it. This is where it sort of makes me think of how Quake was once going to be an RPG but pivoted to an FPS when it was clear things were not working out. Graven feels like at some point they pivoted to FPS but never fully committed, leaving a bunch of weird RPG bits floating around.One thing the game does not communicate well, but absolutely shines with, is the way weapons and spells upgrade. Initially a lot of the spells and weapons are somewhat flimsy, so much so it appears the spells are just for puzzle solving and breaking items (and I have to say, smashing items in this game is REALLY satisfying). However once you upgrade them they become insanely powerful to the point where they frequently replace your weapons. Initially the fire spell tickled zombies and eventually burned skelletons. Fully upgraded it torched almost every enemy, caused them to run around in panic and set others on fire when they touched them and turned burning enemies into living bombs. In short, upgraded spells rule! Simlarly the weapons go from things like a shotgun crossbow (though almost all the weapons are crossbows) from having a basic shot, to penetrating shots that use mana for damage boosts and an alt fire that shoots exploding barbs. All the things a battlepriest would need!Oh! You play a priest! I guess I should address the story as that is somewhat key in psudo-imsims. The story starts with you being accused of murder, killing another priest who sacrificed your daughter to a demon whom a cult was trying to raise. Now you are out to combat that cult and find out what happened to the world. Well, sort of. The intro lays out the story beats up to the point where you wake up on a boat and then things get somewhat murky. There is a journal in game where the priest narrates what is happening, but even then it is not exactly clear what is happening exactly. You clear out a plague in a swamp town, then you purge a cult from a frozen realm, then you fight through a desert city to finally destroy the demon people are worshiping. At least I think that is what is happening. The ongoing narrative is very moment to moment and there is no clear overarching goal: You go places and do things. This lack of coherence comes to a head in the final act where it seems the game ends with sequel baiting, hinting at further adventures for the priest, but never fully confronting what actually happened on the journey, making the whole thing seem like it was unravelling as the game went on.The game unravelling as it goes on is a theme it seems. The deeper you get into Graven, the more it feels like it got to a set point before the team were given a deadline and they just wrapped things up. Each of the three hub worlds not only seems smaller than the one that came prior, but also seems more unfinished. The first hub has numerous quests and side quests, many secrets that make it worth your time to backtrack through as you unlock items and the whole chapter feels deeply interconnected. This shrinks a great deal with the second hub, with far fewer quests to do and only really two dungeon areas to explore. This continues with the third chapter having a rather sprawling and open-ended city level that largely brings the interconnected nature of the first hub, but it feels very half baked and only has a couple of quests. The differences between the first and final town areas highlight this the most, where the first world has almost all NPCs react to you with some dialogue while the final town has 3 NPCs that say things and all other folks simply face you silently. It is a shame as it is clear there was great ambition for each of these areas. Even with the weird flaws regarding the half-way-house imsim elements, if all three chapters had the quality of the first this would be a highly advisable game, but it does not and by the mid point of chapter 3 it is clear that things are starting to unravel.To finish off there is the elephant in the room with Graven: the save system. Graven has a really odd, almost PS1 level of saving: while in play you hit checkpoints every so often which respawns you at them on death, taking a small portion of your gold as punishment. This would seemingly be ok if it were not for the fact the game spawns you back in the town every time you boot up the game. This means if you are deep in a dungeon and need to stop playing for whatever reason, it is back to town with you once you load the game again. Mix this with the game having no map or fast travel system and you have one hell of a frustrating concoction. For this reason alone you have to be cautious about if you do or do not want to buy into Graven. If you are a person who cannot dedicate to long, hour plus sessions, avoid Graven.To cap this off there are numerous bugs with the saves. Frequently the game would lose items in the world, or doors that were previously open will suddenly become locked again. When this happens items, keys and switches seem to retain their used status and thus the way forward is blocked, frequently locking you out of some quests and, in some nasty cases, softlocking your save game and preventing you from finishing it. In this regard, even if you can overlook the other issues, you should avoid Graven for now.To conclude, Graven is a frustrating experience. It has so many great elements that few other titles can provide, but it also has a boat load of half-baked design flaws stacked atop of clear budget and time constraints topped off with a lot of game breaking bugs. Maybe great one day, but not yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Graven is a game that wears a lot of hats; some better than others but none quite as comfortably as its aesthetic and its tone. This first person metroidvania with boomer shooter combat wears its 2000’s PC-game look well, and the dour atmosphere is so thick you can eat it with a spoon. The first quest is to trim down the body pile in the sewers just a little bit so the water can start flowing again, and this plague afflicted world doesn’t get any more joyous from there.At times, the path forward can be unclear a little more than I think was intended, but Graven’s beautifully ugly world and its punchy combat make for a satisfying play.I’ve spent 16 hours over the past few days with the 1.0 build of Graven, and I haven’t rolled credits. Based on the games advertised world count I’m probably like ~60% of the way through.I’m sharing this with you both as a transparent reviewer acknowledgement (we’re deviating from my usual beat-the-game then review-the-game format), but also because it ties into one of this games key themes: Graven is one obtuse bastard, so much so that it warns you upon file creation that you’re gonna spend a lot of time trying to figure stuff out.One sequence towards the end of its second of three acts did me in and I’m going to be waiting for some community guide material before wrapping a bow on this instead of beating my head against it for another 8 hours. If you don’t plan on utilizing similar texts yourself just be prepared for what you’re getting into.For those who grew up on a diet of Heretic and especially Hexen this should come as no surprise. These Graven forebears are more than just fantasy reskins of Doom, they’re also arcane in ways beyond their grimoires—and Graven embraces that.Structurally the game is more like three small scale metroidvanias rather than one big one, where your usual power unlocking and key acquiring exploration happens within discrete acts. Each has a central hub for quests and vendors and then juts out in all directions with hostile exploration zones  like spokes on a wheel.You’ll be navigating these areas with no compass and no markers, and for the most part this aids the games tone. Fumbling around in every direction bolsters the helplessness the games world exudes, and also gives you time to really soak in every sequence. There’s also plenty of secret rooms and extras you stumble into when seeking out the main path forward that are rewarding consolation prizes when the thread you followed wasn’t the right one.Where it goes a stretch too far is when the one lifeline it does give you, auto-written journal entries, are vague to the point of uselessness. Trying to read notes outside of real-time is awkward because there’s no visual accompaniment.You’ll read a note that says “ah yes this room should let me get up to the balcony” or something, but that may have been an entry from an hour ago and you have no idea what room it’s actually referring to.I chuckled when another entry told me to go to “the bog.” What do you mean the bog, singular? I’ve been in nothing but bogs for hours; the entire first act is a swamp.These worlds are fun to explore and I largely believe the right balance of guidance and obscurity is found, but the few times you find yourself hopelessly stuck are usually because you don’t even know what you’re looking for, let alone where it is.The other hat Graven wears is fast paced combat. You have a high move speed, especially when sprinting, that you can use to weave in and out of enemy fire. All of your foes use either traveling projectiles or high windup melee swings. Outside of a few specific bosses, this lets you outplay most encounters with clean movement fundies. Different spells pull from different mana pools which demands you switch things up and balance ammo and mana counts. It feels great; spells and effects are punchy and aided by some great animation work. You magically flick through pages of your tome to access different techniques, and one weapon is literally just unleashing the crackling energy of a spellbook on your foes.It really nails the fantasy of escalating power. Part of that is because you spend a lot of time with your dinky wizard equivalent of a pea shooter. You have to ember before you can inferno, which in a gameplay sense will demand you commit boss drops and lots of gold towards the most important spell upgrades.This progression slots very neatly into the kind of stuff you were already doing: the steep currency requirements give extra value to all the gold you find in the secret rooms littered everywhere which is a particularly nice touch.It’s a very satisfying game to peel your way through, with the combat and exploration feeding rewards back into each other with higher power levels and more shortcuts unlocked. Where Graven is lacking, even in its 1.0 build, are a few minor but consistent technical issues and some general traversal awkwardness. I can’t remember the last time I had a bone to pick with a games’ autosave and checkpointing systems, and that might be one of the few areas where Graven is throwbacking in the wrong ways.Every time you quit the game and return to it, you get transported back to the town hub, which ensures that each booting of the game is coupled with an unceremonious trek to where you left off, if you even remember. This is despite the fact that there are obvious in universe checkpoint markers, they’re only there for respawning and not what ‘checkpoints’ mean in most other video games. On top of being annoying, especially if you’re playing in small bursts, it also turns ‘going to the main menu’ into a really clumsy but really powerful ‘town portal spell’ that the game otherwise does not have. It’s a really effective way to avoid death and nullify the gold penalty that death was supposed to be distributing, and it’s hard to unsee the main menu as a tool in your arsenal even though it shouldn’t be.And for all of his horizontal speed, our protagonist’s general agility is low. Obstacles that visually read as easy to clear seldom are, at best requiring a running start you didn’t think you needed and at worst catching you in small patches of terrain and ditches you can’t escape. Ladders aren’t his strong suit either, with clunky entry and exit into the climbing state that doesn’t flow with the game’s otherwise fast movement.I also had a recurring drowning issue where half the time I died by drowning, I would respawn retaining the drowning debuff and instantly die again unless I restarted.Graven can be an awkward game to play at times, but none of its vices are so overpowering that they take away from its strengths. It’s a beautiful world with an incredible tone, fun combat, and a slow enough exploration pace that allows you to soak in its atmosphere.I’m motivated to get back to it after the internet reveals what I’m doing wrong on this damn floor puzzle. Once I shook off the embarrassment of getting filtered I could accept Graven's capacity TO filter as a strength. This is not a game you wade through, it’s a game that makes you fight for every inch of progress.Graven has its flaws, but it’s a satisfying experience regardless. It may deal in magic, but you could never accuse it of not sticking to its guns.

_childDocuments_.review: V1.0 update.... had this since EA...TLDR: Still not recommended, unless you want something to burn time.Gameplay is just as buggy and anemic as the early release was, this time just with more levels and stuff. Lot of others mention the dumb waypoint system/lack of saving where you left off - have to travel from the VERY beginning, enemies respawning, textures and world objects popping in, like its missing some LOD settings... objects floating mid air like they werent quite placed in the world properly (such as wall lights). Hitting a stack of barrels magically makes all of them bounce around like a bunch of balloons (especially the giant barrels), kind of like an early physics game that hasnt gotten it worked out yet... and you need to hit all of them for the loot to survive. Loading screens suck, and are glitchy depending on where the transition is from one level to the next, even if they are a few seconds.Notes on missions very general and basic, which is fine, i dont want another waypoint game so finding your own path is trail and error, lots of circling around (complete with random enemy respawns as you go... Maps are pretty big, and LOTS of secrets everywhere.Its not a fast pace game, doesnt need to be, but there is no FEEL when moving around and shooting/fighting, just feels floaty and... anemic. Enemies feel like sponges, no feedback on hits.Overall its just a bigger early access release, and if it were still EA, i wouldn't like it, but would have forgiven it. There is a distinct lack of refinement here. Maybe there will be future updates.... but somehow i think the core mechanic is what it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Graven is a GEM of a game. It definitely deserves a positive overall review. At the time of this review it still has yet to get above mixed. Do not be persuaded by negative reviews.I began playing Graven on the day of its full release. It was buggy and crash-prone, but the developers sorted that stuff out quickly. Now it runs very well.Graven is for players who appreciate games from the 90s, and for those who want to play a brand new game built with a retro game engine, that retains the same aesthetic, feel, difficulty, nostalgia and pace from what they remember — but modernized.Playing a game with fat pixels and low polygons again is so refreshing! Graven is a lovely game to admire. After awhile I barely notice the look... because it seems SO RIGHT. Fog effects, well produced music and sound effects, lighting, etc definitely makes it a modern title. It's a delightful gaming experience that is way overdue.Combat is awesome, and takes skill to be good at it. Finding keys, and the doors for them is tough. Finding something overlooked is tougher. Keeping enough coin in your purse to buy weapon upgrades is even more challenging.Game maps are expertly crafted. In my opinion, one of the best mechanics of Graven is starting at the same exact point in a chapter every time you start playing. This game saves everything EXCEPT your location. This is a feature, and makes Graven quite unique.My Review: Overwhelmingly Positive

_childDocuments_.review: It is a modernized Hexen with RPG elements and a story.If you have not observed until now, let me tell you that many modern 3D games relies on flat terrains to create their worlds.PROS:- has verticality into the maps- BSP like walls and buildings that enable non repetitive layouts- maps are interconnected in non obvious ways trough doors and passage ways- every single house of this world is unique, precisely made to suit the alley corner or maybe the upper part of the level- the world feels like a living painting and not like a IKEA filled dorm room- impressive texture design that enhances that painting feel- image contrast and colors are perfect to conjure a peril mood in a fantasy universe for the player- this game is cheap!The cons of this game are less relevant than the pros and I think for me even if the cons remains into the game it would not make it less of a marvel.CONS:- save system is not flexible, it saves on predefined points and this is a rather small annoyance- too many barrels / crates to break to get consumable loot that distracts me from analyzing the world these details they do make sense into the scene but their loot appeal makes the combat and the rest of the scene to be ignored- more hints of where to go next that are not very obvious would be needed- low resolution textures that would could have easily increased without any perception penalty from the low mesh polycount

_childDocuments_.review: Really wanted to like this game, but its just not quite there. The art style is really nice, but the combat animations feel weightless and clunky. I feel its greatest issue, however, is the exploration. It rapidly becomes frustrating. I also experienced a crash during my playtime, so make of that what you will.What kills the exploration for me is the complete lack of direction given to the player. Don't get me wrong, I am 100% down with not having quest markers and the like, but only when the game is designed to work well without them. This game is not. There are hundreds of doors but no indicator as to which ones you can interact with. The maps are a convoluted maze of empty back alleys with seemingly no purpose, and pretty much everything is destructible. You will quickly realize that the game expects you to smash every barrel and try every door in order to move forward. The exploration simply isn't fun.I think the game could certainly be made much better with future updates, but at the moment I do not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: FULL RELEASE (AGAIN):So it seems that the developers released a patch that fixed the gold on death issue. They (I think) tried to fix the enemies on fire FX but it still looks awful. The performance hit I got from lighting 5 enemies on fire as well is tremendous. Like less than a quarter of the frames for a bit while they were on screen. Awesome that there was a patch that fast on the gold on death issue but just makes it super frustrating when this game was released in Early Access, one or two content patches added to the game after a year or so, then silence for more than a year and the full game drops. This wouldn't have been an issue if the developer actually used Early Access like they said they would.After trying it out again, there's two MAJOR issues, AI are dumb as bricks and AI also float. I'm not going to bother picking this game back up again with those two issues and probably avoid this developer in the future. FULL RELEASE:I was definitely surprised that this early access game with only like, one or two patches throughout the entire lifespan would just drop a full release. Same kind of nigglings in the early access still remain from my original look at the game. Not making me have great confidence in the product so far. The fire doesn't "warp metal" anymore. The "ultrawide fix slider" seems to make your camera fish-eyed. - Upon death, you lose all the gold you are carrying and respawn with as far as I know, no way to get the gold back. I'm all for playing through your mistakes but currently this is far too punishing. - The hitbox on spells and melee are not very clear. If you are hitting an enemy with a melee or fire spell, there is no sign of actual impact. - Not sure if you can throw picked up items but not being able to is pretty bad- There's some weird ghosting or something when you light an enemy on fire. It looks incredibly awful. This game was released to Early Access but instead of doing a proper Early Access, the developer made it more of just a preorder period. I doubt Early Access reviews made many changes to the full release nor could they with the lack of actual updates before stealth dropping the release date and release. This isn't how you are supposed to do Early Access.EARLY ACCESS REVIEW: I've been looking forward for this for a while so I might be biased when being one of those people that say "it's good for an early access game".I've gone down to the sewers and I'm actually lost which brings me to discuss the issues with the game so far:There is a severe lack of just, information given to the player. - One example is the mouse sensitivity option. There is "infinite" granularity but for some reason, the developer only coded the sensitivity number indicator to be integers. - You can't (I don't believe) see what a spell does after you pick it up. I swore to go the fire spell said it could "warp metal" among other things but it doesn't seem to affect anything metal that I fire blast.- I'm overall just confused on what to do in the sewer level. I think I'm only supposed to be lighting the blue one but there is no indicator anywhere to signify that you did somethingThe "ultrawide fix slider" doesn't scale the UI, it basically just lowers the FOV, separately from the actual FOV slider that is already implemented in the game. Seems very silly.- The save & quit functionality, while saves and quits your character progress, doesn't seem to save the monsters nor your location. Very annoying if you clear an area out to start exploring but then need to get off without making any progressIf those are fixed, I will have less of a problem with the game. A MAJOR problem though is the slow development cycle of this game. This game didn't really get a single content update from release on steam to 2022, when they slated the game to be out. Yeah, a lot of projects don't meet that deadline anyways but not a single update is rough.

You get out of the boat and that's it, that's all the context you need. Now go out there and start killing all the evil ♥♥♥♥ that is tormenting the people of this place, and to my surprise the character is a killing machine. In short: IA is dumb, then the game gives you tons of resources all the time like if you were a casual baby,  the one that annoyed me the most is that you will always have health potions and you will never use them because the enemies and environment drops you health everywhere and there you are just storing more and more health potions in your inventory, never using them.This game should have rpg stats, use a souls/blood currency for it ala soulsborne and make the gold currency to have a limit because makes no sense the amount of money we can have and for no purpose.The game hasn't alt paths, they are hub shortcuts, not alt paths, and this game is not an immersive sim as people say.Just make it more like Dark Souls and boom, replay value. _childDocuments_.review: Not for the price currently asked.The core design is broken. In other words, it has potential but the basis it stands on isnt solid enough.They have to invest tons of work on that basis first.The basic broken parts are for example enemy AI or combat in general.Too easy, the enemies cant do anything really, their AI is useless, the hitdetection not working well as hits on the player arent connecting.Another borken basic part is the magic.You get a fire spell, its only use is to light torches and barrles, what?Dont get me wrong. I think its cool to use spells to solve puzzles.But use them  for that?Nah.Sorry, but i am running around fighting Zuuuhhhhmbies with a fire spell that doesnt do anything?I never ran out of Mana and personally a fire spell should be a great way to cleanse the world of the filth.And to be honest, there are multiple ways to balance that stuff to get the best of both worlds.Since that magic uses mana, using it for combat could drain more, using it for puzzles could be free or drain only a bit.Furthermore, it would be nice if i was allowed to define my own path.If i deem magic as the way to go about combat, let me go that path.Give me upgrades for it, allow me to make spells stronger, allow me to use them to melt their faces.And then i accept when they roll my face over the floor once my mana is drained and im crap at using melee or crossbows.However, magic is also a broken part because it doesnt show any feedback.I see an explosive barrel, yeah i know its a videogame trope, and want to light it up with my firespell so it blows up the people next to it.First off, theres no range indicator. I cant tell how close i have to go, but in this case i couldnt light the barrel until i was standing literally right infront of it.Second problem is, even aiming at it with your crosshair, it often doesnt work.You use your spell, nothing happens.The first area is relatively small, its content light, theres barely any sidequest to be found although there could be tons (and should be). The map is somehow linear but branching so confusingly that you easily miss the main path, key items or other stuff.Thats just a few examples of rather bad things about it, but there are more. More issues, more missing stuff that you ask yourself why it isnt there after half an hour playing.Which has me scratching my head. When so many notice a lacking feature after half an hour playing, why dont the developers? Tunnelvision?Early Access is for giving feedback, but not on absolute details.For example not being able to pick up coins with "E" and thus not being able to collect them because they are at a space you cant reach (you have to run over coins to collect them), is just such a mundane thing they overlooked that it feels crazy.Those are basics a developer has to notice earlier.The style.Voice acting in the introduction. The story itself, while a bit stereotypical, is edgy enough to be fun.It certainly has a great look and appeal. The vocieacting is insanely good. Just sparringly used and as it seems only for the introduction.Thats ok, but then it doesnt carry long enough as a pro point.So presentation is top, gameplay is flop, content isnt there.I dont need tons of levels. What im looking for is replayability.Replayability comes from different things.Personally at first i would like to see a Permadeath Mode and Difficulty Settings.Which means, giving me the option to set it up high and when i die its Game Over.Second, a New Game+ Mode.I reached the end? Ok then loop me back to the start, ramp up the difficulty a lot but i keep my stuff.This motivates me to play much longer, even that one area we currently have.Another way of replayability is some sort of system that allows me different playstyles and embracing them.If i want to be the edge-lord of crossbows, let me. Give me upgrades that increase my pouch size so i can carry more ammo, give ranged weapons more damage, accuracy, let me buy special ammo types for it.If i want to use Magic as a caster, let me do that. Let me use it as a weapon if i want and give me upgrades to embrace it.And finally if i want to combine magic with physical combat, melee or ranged, so i set my sword on fire or load my bolts with electricity, let me do that.Sure, all of those playstyles have their pros and cons, but thats fine. This motivates me to replay a game like this 3-4 times with different ways to build my character.I wished those things were there and maybe they will be (although i doubt that).I refunded the game on Steam (i paid 17€) and would have left it that way until i felt its price is more on par with what it offers.Not just in terms of content, but also thought and awareness.However, i rebought it on Epic for 8€ and feel like thats low enough to test new builds and play with what is there.See this review as a warning of "its by far not ready yet and the price asked is too high for what it currently offers".Because any Early Access Game should be fine enough the moment you buy it, so you dont feel any regrets if it doesnt reach its destination.If Graven doesnt reach its destination for the 8€ i paid, thats ok. To me.For 17€ however, its too much trust they ask for.I played 3 hours total and am through the early access version.Theres also nothing else to do at that point. Its not open world, going back to previous sections holds nothing of interest for you, there are no sidequests to speak of, no higher difficulty or new game+.Nothing. If you want Steam and you are ok with a higher price, then you can get an additional discount if you own the other games in the Bundle with Wrath.Since i own both other games in that bundle, i got an additional 1,86€ off from the purchase.Whenever you can on Steam, consider a Bundle purchase, which is cheaper and applies all current discounts.

_childDocuments_.review: Game suffers from a severe lack of polish. Picking up coins and runes are tedious because you have to walk directly over them. Combat is janky because generic enemies will jump from slow telegraphed swing to 3 yard 2 frame startup lunge attack that chunks you. The upgrade button in the blacksmith screen isn't even all the way on my monitor. There is an on screen notification if you are underwater but I saw no indication of how long before you start drowning. Falling certain heights also uses stamina too for some reason? There are a lot of little things that add up to show just how rough this game is around the edges. Game is carried by a strong visual style and the dog you can pet.  Speaking of which I will now explain how to get dog% while still being able to refund: 1. off spawn grab one of the red barrels you see while on the dock carry it to the boarded door up the steps and smash the boards off to open. With the barrel run downstairs and open the gate door and grab the fire spell.2. Once you get into the slough jump onto a ridge at the top of a flight of stairs with a floor sconce on it. turn right onto the waterway and place the barrel and light it at the foot of the corpse pile (the spot is indicated) be careful as 3 zombies will arise near the pile. make sure they do not hit the barrel. 3. Once the bomb is lit, run back towards the gate and turn right you will see the lever you need to open the gate behind a fence. Run along the ridge on the left side of the staircase down and jump over the fence. Once you get the lever, run around the corner back up the stairs on your right (since the skeletons from the entrance will be chasing you I find it safer to run all the way up and jump down in front of the bomb storage gate). place and pull the lever. Once the gate starts opening you can crouch under and grab barrel 2. 4, once barrel 2 is in your possession run down the stairs on your left (the right side facing corpse pile 1). While not necessary you can drink the bog pot you can grab to make running through the water faster. run dead ahead through a gate and up the stairs till you meet a lone zombie in front of a gate with a lever. 5. Drop the barrel away from the zombie to keep it from his grasp circle around and hit the lever. grab your barrel 2 and bank left through the door place and light in the indicated spot. Once you get the quest complete notification double back the way you came all the way back to the door you broke through at step 1.6. On exit, turn around and run all the way up the stairs to the main gate. talk with the guard on the right and inform him of your precognition and task completion. The gate will open once you close out of his rambling. run inside and dodge the tax collector. we aren't here for him. 7. home stretch. Run past the left side of the statue at the far back of the courtyard there is a porch to the left of the blacksmith's forge. on that porch is our grand prize. One pet for one certified good boy. Congrats you have beat Graven dog%. My first and sloppy run of Dog% was a whopping 2:17. If you're only here for the dog you may refund or you may continue your play though. Though I suggest saving your money until the devs polish this game into something worth your time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: Graven on Steam beckons players into a richly atmospheric medieval fantasy world where the stakes are as high as the priest's quest for redemption is deep. Merging the nostalgic charm of '90s gaming with sleek modern visuals, this game offers a unique blend that appeals to both retro aficionados and contemporary players alike.Pros:- Retro-Modern Fusion: The game brilliantly combines the essence of classic '90s gaming aesthetics with modern graphics, creating an environment that feels both familiar and fresh.- Challenging Puzzles: Puzzles in Graven are thoughtfully integrated, encouraging exploration and rewarding problem-solving skills, adding depth to the gaming experience.- Engaging Combat System: The combat is robust and varied, combining magic and melee in a way that keeps each encounter intriguing and dynamic.Cons:-Clunky Keyboard Controls: The game's controls can feel somewhat awkward when played with a keyboard, often making a controller the preferable choice for smoother gameplay.- Limited Enemy Variety: Despite a strong start, the diversity of adversaries may not keep up throughout the game, which can lead to a somewhat monotonous combat experience as the game progresses.- Occasional Pacing Issues: Some players might find the pacing inconsistent, with some areas of the game moving slowly, which might affect engagement during longer play sessions.Graven carves out a niche that nostalgically nods to the past while firmly planting its feet in the present. If you're drawn to the shadows of dungeons where spells and swords clash, this game will likely capture your heart—or at least enchant your gaming hours. Overall rating: 4 out of 5 spell books.

_childDocuments_.review: I have deleted my last review for Graven because I felt like it was negative just to be negative and I would like to have something a little more constructive. I will start with some of the positives of Graven before I get to some of the negatives for me.Positives -Unlike other people, I have been really enjoying the layout of the levels and the way they have a pretty good MetroidVania feel to them by connecting back around and offering you some shortcuts. Each of the levels have been very distinct, are fun to look in every nook and cranny for secrets, and each area having different enemies for you to fight keeps you wanting more.The variety of weapons all handle very well and I would say they are varied enough to keep them feeling different.Graven doesn't hold the players hand and you need to pickup on the context clues from your journal to finish up quests as you go instead of the game pointing you in the direction you should be going. A real call back to old school gaming. Sometimes I find it to be a headache but not with Graven.Negatives -Not having a map in a MetroidVania style game feels like a big no no. Most of my time spent in game has been me walking around trying to figure out what to do or what opened after I pulled that level. I think this is probably my actual biggest complaint with Graven.Enemy balancing just seems all over the place. Most of my deaths feel very cheap and unfair. While the weapons all handle well, combat doesn't feel all that fun. Just keep them at bay and fire away. Enemies don't seem to need any form of special strategy to be dealt with. Dropping gold upon death can be okay at times because you have the chance to reclaim it after respawning, but when it falls off the map or you end up dying a few times in a row can leave a deep hole in your pocket that really ends up holding you back.When you finish up a stage, it's on to the next one and locks you out from going back to finish up that level so make sure you did all the things you wanted to do before moving on.No. Fast. Travel. I sear that 40% of my in game time has been spent backtracking to pick up my gold I dropped, figuring out where I need to go next, or just to do some more exploring to be safe. Having some form of Fast Travel would have really helped keep the gameplay experience a little more fun.The game has crashed on me a few times. Now, it wouldn't be too big of a deal for me if 1) there was a fast travel system in place or 2) didn't spawn you back in town every time you load your game up.The more time I spend with graven, the more I am coming around to it but the negatives really do hold it back from really being a game I love. I think there will be a lot of people who will get a lot of enjoyment out of it but I think there are more who should just pass on it or maybe give it a try on a deep sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Graven is an enjoyable and occasionally challenging fantasy game with light RPG elements. The development team took some clear influence from the likes of Heretic/Hexen and Half-Life but it doesn't feel like they learned any lessons from the failings of those games - Puzzles in Graven may not be as senselessly confusing as those found in Hexen, but some of them are very obtuse in execution although that may be partly a result of the massive buggyness of the game in its current state. Another point where Graven seems to miss the mark is in its level design, the game is split into three chapters with three different maps. The first chapter feels like it got the most development time and, somewhat ironically, feels the messiest - to my eye it looked like they made a ton of middle of development changes to player progression but didn't fully go through and change the level design to compensate. The second chapter felt the most well thought out but lacked content and felt like it could have been a bit longer. The final chapter felt pretty sloppy, the first half of it was fine if a bit confusing in regards to level design but the second half felt like they wanted to make a big open-ended area and weren't quite sure how to tailor combat encounters for that environment.There are 3 types of weapons/attacks in Graven:Melee - which is largely a liability as most enemies will absolutely demolish you if you let them get closeMagic - which is mostly consists of spells that are just useful for shoehorned puzzles that don't add a ton to the game. There are some mechanical nuances to the magic in the game but the usefulness is VERY situational. There are a couple weapons that use magic for ammunition and, while they aren't terrible, they really don't feel useful enough to justify taking up limited equip space.Projectile - 4/5 of the projectile weapons feel pretty good to use and are what I used primarily. Ammunition isn't particularly scarce as long as you make sure to swap between them periodically. The shotgun equivalent in particular is a standout in my book and it carried me through 75% of the game.I would recommend Graven as I did genuinely have fun with it, but the game in its current state is a buggy and unpolished mess and really doesn't feel ready for full release.

_childDocuments_.review: Graven is an okay first person action adventure. It's mostly a spiritual successor to Hexen 2, with similar combat balance and slightly more sensible puzzles. It's a good time when it works, assuming you know what you're getting into. It's not better than Hexen 2, so I recommend starting with the classic, just so you don't get burned. My lukewarm opinion of this game mostly boils down to lackluster quality on release. The game is extremely unpolished in many ways. To the point where months after release, the main way to get past a quest in chapter 3 is to glitch the spawn points. The game uses a checkpoint system comparable to dark souls, except its implementation makes the game bug out with certain quests. Also, you get kicked to the hub after closing the game for some reason. You kinda lose progress, but monsters don't always respawn, so sometimes you just have to run back for a few minutes.Aside from the technical issues, most weapons don't feel good to use. They're balanced okay, they deal almost the same damage based on boss health bars. However, the animations and sound are lacking. Chapter 1 can be discouraging as you'll be relying on a dinky little staff for a long time.Another big issue is the story. It's unfinished and haphazard. You play as a priest who was sentenced to death for killing some cultists. For some reason, you don't wake up in heaven or hell, but on a boat going to a backwater town dealing with a plague. Magic now flows through you as well. You remember the town had a library, so you decide to depart towards it to seek clues about your situation. You have to fight the plague along the way.This sounds like a fine hook for a story. Until the game forgets about it and starts going into places at random. The game never again acknowledges that you should be dead or shouldn't be a spell caster. You use the library to help solve the plague. Then chapter 2 starts with the protagonist deciding to visit some guy. You have to play through the chapter to figure out that he's some inventor the protagonist knew, as if the game couldn't establish that before randomly sending you off. Very much nothing comes out of the second chapter, either. By the end of the game, nothing is addressed, whatsoever explained. You just find some evil to get rid of. It's like listening to the story told by an Alzheimer patient. Then why do I still recommend the game? Well, at least on sale I do if you like exploration. This is a low-energy shooter about running around in first person, seeking little secrets and pathways, and solving simple puzzles. The first chapter also has some good music and atmosphere, though don't get used to it. If you know what Hexen 2 is, and you liked it, buy it. If you don't, it's most likely not for you. Don't confuse it for a retro shooter. It's not Hexen 1.It's a bit of a proof that Early Access games don't improve, they just get more content. Devs rarely have time to go back to polish and refine the fundamental features of their releases

_childDocuments_.review: this game appeals to me, but for the same reason that it looks like many reviewers dislike it:- this is NOT a boomershooter or anything close to itit seems to take inspiration from Heretic and Hexen, but that seems to go only as far as aesthetics and story elements.If you took Unreal and Deus Ex, added in some modern game design, you'd get closer to what Graven is.here's my bulletpoint list to what i'm most interested in and what differentiates Graven from, say Heretic.- it's pace is slower, more deliberate. You need to conserve stamina.- there is plenty of backtracking and your adventures center around hub areas, as some of the maps are pretty interconnected.- enemies require different damage types to land crits, or to even just do normal damage.- magic spells are not weapons, but utility that can be used with the environment to hinder the enemy.- weapons and spells can be upgraded and you can't fit them all into your belt assigned hotkeys.Things that cause me most grief about Graven (not necessarily bad things)- many enemies interact and play together in pretty nasty combinations- i'm teased about treasure spots and secrets so many times, but they are progression capped- enemies can deal colossal damage if you're not wearing armor. even early enemies can tear you apart quick, if you get cocky.all in all, it's a cool game with some mildly infuriating aspects.

_childDocuments_.review: its a shame graven has a low score, because this game is wicked fun. i love immersive sims, and this is a pretty dang solid one. i really dig the art style, its a mix of retro and 3d that they nail. 3d realms devs have been really good at this type of art direction, similar to how well New Blood is doing in the art department. you can pick up objects, spread fires, electrocute gears to operate mechanisms, electrocute enemies/water to stun enemies and whack them in the head. hitting weak points on enemies does increased damage which i like, meaning aiming for the head with melee weapons is essential. it usually 1-2 shots standard enemies. ive only played a limited amount of the game, but the game has a decent amount of secrets, some of which to access kind of give me a metroidvania-like vibe, since you do receive power-ups or upgrades that you can then use to unlock areas/secrets from previous regions. everything is also interconnected with shortcuts it seems, which i just discovered in my playthrough today! i didnt expect that. the game apparently has 4 regions in early access, and i just reached the second. the first region is a pretty good size, and theres still things there i havent done secrets wise, like a breakable wall i think i can now break down (wont spoil how). i think if youre interesed in graven, the game is cheap enough for you to at least give it a shot. i think the game is good, and when it is finished this January its gonna add tons of new content which im really excited for. 2 additional hub locations, over 10 new weapons, 9 enemies, new bosses...thats really all this game needs at this point. so if you really cant wait, i think its worth checking out right now. about 8-10 hours of content is in the game right now, and thats definitely going to increase at launch. im looking forward to continuing my playthrough and im waiting very patiently for release!

_childDocuments_.review: When it comes to EA games I can only rate what's there in front of me not promises of what's to come. And what is here I can't deny is substantial and enjoyable even if there's little transparency as to what comes next.Graven sits somewhere between Hexen and Dark Souls. The levels are large and sprawling with multiple shortcuts you unlock. Quitting the game respawns monsters with all treasure and shortcuts being persistent. Death takes away a chunk of gold, unfairly sizable at first but by the library level gold drops pretty quickly outpace the punishment of death.At 7 hours in and no end to sight I can say wholeheartedly I don't regret the $18 spent on the bundle. It does reek of that distinct Eurojank feel that classifies several other games I love, most of them by Arkane. Movement is snappy and the weapons feel great in particular a grapeshot-shotgun that can be upgraded to fire exploding rounds. The magic system is odd, giving you a literal flamethrower that does no effective damage and eventually a shock attack that briefly stuns enemies long enough to get maybe one whack in. They can later be upgraded to a point where they become viable attack options but to start you with these expensive and useless functions is a head-scratcher. The player is a wizard-priest, why does the game deny us cool magic for a large chunk of its playtime? Unfortunately melee combat leaves a little to be desired especially when dealing with enemies that instantly track you. The short sword has a parry function that bafflingly only seems to work some of the time: I can't tell if it's a random chance or you have to physically deflect an opponent's attack with your blade model, in either case the game offers no opportunity to practice and sheds no light on how it functions.Where Graven really succeeds is in the level design. Secrets are telegraphed well, the circuitous design creates moments of tension where you're just praying for the next shortcut to zip back to town before you lose a big pot of gold, and enemies are placed in clever ways that keep you looking around every corner.Even if Graven is never finished I feel like I got a complete game's worth of investment out of it. If the idea of an abandoned EA game is a turnoff look elsewhere but if you want a real good Souls-like as an FPS experience this has it all and doesn't overstay its welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: Graven is a difficult game to talk about, mostly because much of it still isn't finished yet. It's a slightly janky immersive sim/shooter/melee combat/rpg thing, and as such this game is doing a lot of very interesting things, and is also very ambitious. The question is has that ambition succeeded. So far, kind of? Like a lot of this game works, and it works well. The combat is on the whole fun and dynamic despite being a bit janky sometimes, and feeling maybe not quite done yet. The environments are gorgeous and in general the game looks great, even if some sections of it feel a little repetitive visually. The game doesn't have much story from what I've played of it so far (I've done most of the early access at this point, I think there's just the one area I haven't gone through yet) but what story there is is actually pretty interesting when the game gives it to you. More than anything what holds this game back is the fact that it still needs a lot more content and some fine tuning in addition to that, mostly to the combat and to a lesser extent the AI, which is pretty dumb at the moment, in a way that feels not the most fun to play against sometimes (some enemies are better than others, the zombie hordes for example work great). Also there are just some really strange design decisions here. Like saving works super weird for some reason, you can't actually save your progress for a quest until you've completed the main quest in question (this might work differently for sidequests, not sure) which is just kind of a baffling decision, like why not just let the player save normally? If you want to prevent save scumming couldn't there be more traditional save points? This and a few other things do stand out as issues in game (the fire spell isn't super useful beyond basic utility and very occasional uses in combat, the story could really stand to be expanded on and I would really like to see more dialogue from npcs, the checkpoint system is weirdly implemented, etc,) Despite all this I do recommend the game overall but not at full price currently, get it on sale. Reason being is despite all it's flaws a lot of the game really does work and there's massive potential for it down the road. So yeah, I'd say to at least keep an eye on it, because if this game does end up realizing it's potential, it'll be spectacular.
