_childDocuments_.review: In my initial Early Access review of Graven I had mixed feelings on it but was overall leaning toward positive as the game had a lot of potential, but I had reasons to expect that the game would never actually get finished at the time. Now that it has, I wish it hadn't.Graven is a game of squandered potential that ends up being, at best, mediocre. It is trying to be a sort-of spiritual successor to games like Hexen but with a slower pace and elements of an immersive sim, but it is deeply flawed with massive and confusing levels with lots of backtracking, combat that doesn't feel good with underwhelming weapons and overpowered enemies, magic that is absolutely useless in combat, and numerous bugs including ones that can soft lock you and block crucial progression. I still stand by saying Act 1 can be an overall solid experience assuming you don't hit any game breaking bugs but the rest of the game is rushed and unfinished.Graven is not a bad game, but it is not a good game either. If it is on a deep enough sale, give it a shot if it looks interesting  to you but honestly it is a safe skip.

_childDocuments_.review: alright so here we go on GRAVEN. I personally love myself a boomer shooter and this game hits that on the mark. I got this game when it first hit early access and that was 3 years ago....the publisher of this game 3D Realms seems to be known for creating some pure gems of games but also just forgetting about others and graven seems to be one of those that have been left on the back burner for a bit considering we only have 3 levels to explore (now these are good level for the majority of the part with plenty of secrets and fun combat flow) and a couple of side quests to mess with after you complete whats here in early access. Graven seems to be trying to capture the spirit at least of some of the older fantasy shooters aka hexen, heretic, etc. and even though it does do this well it also brought some distasteful things with it so I will confront these first along with other issues i have run into. Cons-1. THE MAP AND DIRECTION OF OBJECTIVE: So in this game it revolves around going through levels and filling out your map as you go through them will reopening doors and passages to loop back through to make travel easier but theirs a issue. After the first "level" the maps have almost no indicators on the quest locations and you will end up just rerunning though areas just trying to figure out where to go and along with there being no legend to speak of (to be fair some of the symbols that you do get early on are self explanatory AKA a light house is a light house but like others are a bit off for example 2 squiggly buildings apparently mean that the library is that way and took me a bit to pick up on) plus the map only covers the main floor level meaning theirs no upper or lower map so if you get lost on a building or in the basement sections have fun looping around everywhere tell by dumb luck or a you tube video (if you can even find one since not a lot of people play this game) that you found the right way. now this wouldn't have even been such a issue if the the journal actually told you where to go all the time instead of just feeding me a paragraph of lore and my surroundings and 1 to 2 sentences about what to do if you even get lucky and it tells you where you need to go. for example pretty early on you will get told through the journal on a quest that your have to deal with some towers to deal with the binding thats got some doors locked down and nothing else, you have to just run around not know what these towers even look like and hoping you destroy all of them and waiting to get a new journal log. This may be some peoples cup of tea but i think that with just some more clear and concise journal entrees and a bit more detail to them along with the map actually having markers past the first level it would have made the experience more enjoyable and a lot less tedious and annoying.2. KINDA BUGGY AT TIMES: So the majority of the time i played GRAVEN the game play was smooth as butter running on my 3060 on ultra setting but the game did crash once because i threw a explosive barrel at a pile of corpse but also sometimes items will just bug out with audio or glitch into you and get stuck along with just explode your ears with the classic gmod clatter sound of stuff knocking into each other. Along with at the library a certain door and switch wouldn't work so i had to reload the game 4 times to get past it (keep in mind that once you reload the game it will load you at the center hub AKA town so you will have to go through everything on the level again to get back to were you where at which can kill the fun pretty quickly and normal enemies hurt and will pursue you so most of the time you will have to deal with them making it more time consuming). also when you reload in i have noticed that shortcuts you have opened will just reclose and you have to go back through them to reopen them. KEEP IN MIND that this is a early access game so this stuff will happen but i hope this stuff gets fixed before launch.3. WEAPONS/COMBAT: So basically the 5 main weapons you will be using is the staff, spell book (which is more or less utility even upgraded), crossbow shotgun, wrist crossbow (AKA cuff shot) which is amazing after being upgraded and agrueably the best weapon in the game with cost of resources and damage outpute, and peat launcher which is basically a sticky bomb launcher. the game does also give you a new spell book but it just cost so many resources most of the time wont be being used and the short sword which does the same damage as the staff but is just worse than it because it has a parry tagged to it that you still end up taking damage even if you parry them and the staff has a push away thats just far more useful and will just one shot normal enemies with a bonk to the head. the ballista just takes up so much space on your bar that it makes me not want to slot it compared to all my other options I have which are also already upgraded. I wish they would have made magic have more of a impact in combat then just making it feel like a utility item. for example I mainly used fire for burning boxes to quicken getting resupplied and used electricity mainly whenever it was required since the cuff shot gets a upgrade that makes it shoot arcane bolts that uses the blue mana and i didn't see a point stunning a enemy for like 1 second compared to melting them with a few bolts for less mana. i like the concept but if your gonna have magic you might as well have it have some form of actual combat use....besides setting skeletons on fire and zapping puddles. Also in a game like this the stamina system feels really off and just makes running through levels to only have to wait 10 seconds to get your stamina back to full feel bad but also makes melee combat feel rough since it uses the same source when you would normally want to be combining those 2 to make a melee build feel fun and viable instead of just shotgunning anything that gets close.PROS: Now for all that have said there is a reason i recommend it. this game has a amazing soundtrack, aesthetic, and mood. The lighting and audio are amazing and really help to add to the atmosphere and the combat is fun along with the amount that there is to explore in this game will keep you busy for at least a solid 3 day weekend binge or more depending if you got some friends to tag along with (yes there is multiplayer but i haven't tried it at all so i don't know how good it is) or just want a atmospheric dark fantasy game to play in your free time. If you got the spare cash and aren't worried about when it will be finished I would definitely say to give GRAVEN a shot and i do feel that you will be happily surprised.

_childDocuments_.review: This is wonderful. I've played through the entirety of what the game has to offer in terms of its narrative so far. I have not explored the game 100% in its current state, i believe i have missed plenty of things, judging by ammo for weapons i do not yet posses. Either way this was a blast.The atmosphere. It's amazing, the soundscape is breathtaking. I was using my headphones and i heard a roll of thunder, and got freaked out, thinking "is it thunder outside" for a moment before realizing that it happened in game. Quake but in fantasy-style is amazing it really gives it the needed grit and disgusting-ness to really show you how things are messed up, really get you into the mood. The sound, the looks, the gameplay. The gameplay. I grew up on quake arena and unreal tournament 2004 so i feel right at home. It has that fast paced, precision feel to it, but you're not guns blazing wrecking everything, it's more akin to resident evil where you have to watch your supplies. Now there is definitely some jank that needs to be touched upon, like the ai getting stuck on something and staring at you, which can have its own charm and with the tougher enemies, i was actually glad when something like that happened, but it definitely took away from the danger, so i hope that will be fixed. Now i don't know if the devs are reading the reviews, but if you're a buyer, i suggest skipping this part, as this is a more spoiler territory underneath, but for anyone wondering if they should buy the game right now, i would definitely give it a go, it's not crazy pricey, and even what it has to offer will give you plenty of content to have fun around. Right now i'd say the game is in the "we've got act 1 ready" territory. Some bugs. There is some oddness with the enemy placement and spawning. One quirk this game has is that the enemies don't respawn, not until you restart the whole game. Regardless if that will be kept or not, or if it's even a good design philosophy, there has been some unique issues with it. Sometimes i go into an area where i know a bunch of enemies spawn... but they are not there, then i return through that area and suddenly they are there. A lot of the times what happened to me, was going through a place with bunch of dead bodies and some of the dead bodies slided into their place (these bodies were actually alive waiting to get a drop in) like they were some Tony Hawk pro-deader, it was funny, but it both reveals which bodies are the problem and also breaks the immersion.Stuck in geometry. This didn't happen a lot of the times, it happened like once or twice. One time i remember swimming somewhere and getting myself wedged somewhere and unable to get out, drowning and having to respawn. Second time was when a BBEG gave me a whack sending me flying across the arena and getting me stuck somewhere, but luckily that didn't last for long. And later, in the black building, there's an early section where you can jump up on toppled-over bookcase to get some stuff, but the geometry doesn't allow for that, i had to stack some boxes and barrels to get there instead. I wish the blacksmith and alchemist will get more stuff to buy. I think the alchemist should be able to sell you mana. You run out of that stuff quickly if you use your two spells for anything other than cleaning cobwebs and turning on the radio with your zapper fingers. So being able to just fill up your mana, as you're gearing up to get out there would be highly appreciated. But it also brings me to another issue i had is the lack of usability for the two spells (i didn't get the chance to try out the scroll much). I get that they are supposed to be used for puzzles, but except for turning on few gates with the zap or cleaning up pesky cobwebs, they are quite underwhelming when it comes to combat. Maybe they are better when upgraded, but i haven't got to that, in the current version it's just too pricey and i found it unneccessary to upgrade either of them. Blacksmith should also be able to sell you armour. I was hoping that when i brought him his notes, he would be able to make armour for me, even if it would be the lowest tier. The one use top tier armour was nice, and i could see what i could get, but in the end it didn't last me very long when i was on my way to get the Tax Collector his stuff. And the armour, even the lowest tier is a life saver, so having a better access to it, would be appreciated. I think those are all my thoughts. I just recently ended my playthrough, i'm hoping to hear more, cause this game is just tickling all the right spots that i always wanted out of a game like this. I'm really excited for the future of this game. I didn't try the multiplayer, there is noone playing, which is a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATED 5/27/22:Well, it took me two months, but I got around to sinking my teeth into the "new" GRAVEN. To ground this review, I just entered the big ol' hedge maze of the Cruxfirth Archives.My original complaints concerned the moment-to-moment gameplay not having enough variety, particularly the spells lacking flexibility (which can be attributed to their original intent as utility and puzzle-solvers). It felt like a game pushed out way too early to live up to "immersive sim" expectations.With the March content, tweaks, and fixes, I am happy to say GRAVEN feels leagues more worth the $25 point of entry. My favorite changes concern combat, as damage-type weaknesses and a critical hit system tying into it make every weapon feel equally important. It could be my imagination, but it also feels enemy aggression and damage are heightened and mistakes cost more than they used to (likely related to the AI changes).The environmental changes are a close second. I don't have much to say in that respect, except thank ♥♥♥♥, you moved the pillar clues to the turtle key pedestal. The blacksmith has useful upgrades and, paired with the new alchemist, the options are finally opening up as I wanted from the start.This game already had A+ environmental and sound design, a strong aesthetic, and all of the trimmings, so bringing gameplay options up to parity was the best step forward.The review ends there with a "Buy It" out of 10. I only have two complaints, medium and small-sized, otherwise:Medium: Those spell upgrades are BONKERS expensive. I have to assume I get fat stacks in the Archives because I was only getting 2k-3k a run through the first several areas.Small: Explosive barrels and boxes! Please, oh please, can they *not* blow up after I throw them? There are fantastic opportunities for area control and combo potential if I could throw them and they stay intact. Weapons and fire should pop them all the same, yours and your enemies'. I just want more excuses to use the fire spell, man.

_childDocuments_.review: Graven is a beautiful game that continues the fantasy fps legacy of titles like Hexen and Heretic.  The early access version contains a couple of hours of early game content, so if you are really worried about playtime, it may be better to wait, but if you are a retro fps fan, I think it's worth purchasing now to support the devs and get an early look.The atmosphere and graphics are top-notch.  The dev team has created an amazing art style that blends the old and new, and I can't think of anything else like it.  The gameplay is mostly engaging with a small variety of spells and weapons to play with at this stage.  I was hoping for more interactivity in the vein of Dark Messiah of M&M, but right now the action is more traditional and straightforward.  Hopefully more features will be implemented (a kick, more physics based attacks, wider use of the elemental spells etc.) but even if the final version doesn't change substantially, the combat is still enjoyable in it's own right.  Where the game truly shines is in the large interconnected level design.  The levels are enormous and satisfying to explore, filled with atmospheric settings and multiple areas that loop back in on themselves. I can't think of any games in the last few years of retro fps resurgence that even come close to the quality and complexity of Graven's levels, and I'd say this is the number one reason to buy the game at this point.  There are small annoyances that people have complained about in other reviews, but most of these should be easily fixable in the future early access builds.  If the game looks of interest to you, I'd recommend buying it now and supporting the hard work of the dev team.

_childDocuments_.review: Many people are talking about how they dislike a lot of changes to the game upon release but i would like to say: if you just play the game you'll find it fun. it reminds me of the old action adventure games from back in the day but a lot smoother and more open worldy One of the smaller issues is how the game has all these "secret" areas that require you to use certain items to get through only for most of them to bring you back to areas that you've already been. I feel that these secret areas should hold something akin to a secret boss or a special item or weapon, or even just a stash of ammo, items, health, etc. that being said though, the game is at an early release and you can get to the end of the story at about 1-2 hours currently (though obvious expansions will come considering how far the progress actually is in game.) my biggest issue atm with the game is how the inventory system works. i understand what they were trying to do with the hotbar, but frankly i think it's just detrimental and prevents you from being immersed in the world. to explain: the hotbar system has boxes for 1-0 to represent the numbers on your keyboard. small items such as your staff, the magic book, and potions only take one slot. larger items such as a sword takes 2 slots, and certain weapons can take up to 3 slots. this means that to carry all these things so you can use them, you have to pause the game by going into your inventory, switch out a weapon with another weapon in your inventory so you can actually use it, unpause and equip that weapon and then you can use it. it just seems so counter intuitive when you talk immersion. I know they drew inspiration from turok so i'd like to reccomend that they consider using the scrolling weapons list from turok or the weapon wheel from Turok: seeds of evil or something, as it'll allow people to try out new ways to play and will help with immersion since you can switch weapons on the fly with this system, allowing you to use more interesting combinations. as for switching magic: holding F with a magic selection wheel would be better than pressing F to scroll through magics. making it quick and intuitive would allow players more customizability to come up with some interesting combinations to getting the job done. either way these were just my suggestions that could help with the game, but in the end of the day: i do reccomend this game, and i think it's a lot of fun! I personally cannot wait to see what the creator has in store for us

_childDocuments_.review: So the art style and atmosphere are perfect. And this definitely has a kernel of something good. However, it's not quite blossomed yet. I do think the devs are onto making a great game but a few tweaks could really set them down a path for excellence. Yes I definitely recommend this game but I also want to offer any ideas to help improve the experience. These are my critiques so far:I absolutely hate that I cannot save my progress mid-quest. If you quit the game mid-quest you will have to start it from scratch. That's very ANTI-FUN. They already have a spawn checkpoint when you die while playing BUT it does not save progress. I think this needs to be reworked ASAP.My next critique is that combat is rather boring. This could be due to it being early game and my weapons have not been upgraded BUT the enemies are almost silent when in combat. They hardly make grunts of pain or aggression. Their animation and behavior is very jank. I would recommend the devs look at the game 'Blood' (1997) which I'm sure they are familiar. In Blood, you can FEEL the impact your weapons are having on enemies. I also feel like the range of melee weapons is a tad too short. I often swing at an enemy point blank and no hit is registered.The enemies are also missing that X factor. They need something that makes you think 'wow'Whether that's glowing eyes, haunting SFX, more decomposition... ect. I don't know what the right answer is but I know they need work.I hope this is not an issue with weapons too. Obviously its hard to judge the early-weapons but I hope to be 'wowed' by later weapons. I would recommend Amid Evil. I do find it annoying that I have to cycle past my staff after getting the sword. The staff is useless after get the sword. So unless you can upgrade the staff later in the game I would recommend being able to sell or drop it. OR combine it with the spellbook and have the staff shoot the projectilesAnother issue I had was the low ammo capacity. The wrist bolt continuously runs out of ammo and I found myself breaking out of the 'fun-zone' to BACKTRACK and collect ammo. It's a weak weapon so why does it need such low ammo capacity?Switching weapons is very slow. Especially opening the book for spells.The map is way too vague and empty of labels/landmarks. Making it an absolute CHORE to navigate and route with it. I found myself not using it at all.The HUD could be slightly bigger and more unique. Again where is the X factor? Impress us! You obviously have phenomenal art team, why are they playing so safe?I didn't even realize stamina was a thing. I thought running was glitched in the game. Eventually I noticed the bubble on the HUD.Don't get me wrong, I do really like what I've seen so far. Especially the art, level design, music, and atmosphere. I would just like to ask the team, "What are you going to do to stand strong among the giants of games like Blood, Heretic, Hexen, Dusk, Amid Evil, Wrath, ect?

_childDocuments_.review: Growing up on classics like Doom, Quake, Heretix, Hexen, and countless other similar titles, it was easy to fall in love with the retro-FPS wave that hit us in the past few years. Due to that I am always looking forward to the next one, hoping that it will rekindle the same memories and feelings the best do, and Graven is no exception. It is focused on exploration rather than combat, and it's maze-like levels actually require time to be fully discovered. I like the currently available repertoire of weapons - although the sword is very much OP - but what I absolutely adore is its world: Graven is much more focused on building its own universe rather than thinking only in levels, and the engine used is perfectly capable of that purpose, thanks to the colour palette, the character models, and the overall atmosphere. I can't wait for further content to be released!
_childDocuments_.name: GRAVEN

_childDocuments_.review: Well...TL:DR - Keep an eye on this game for the full release, it's got a ways to go.More of a proof of concept than full, or even, early access title. Everyone is hyped about this because of a potential Heretic/Hexen vibe, but it's more of a "ye old shooty-slashy" FPS vibe with a smidge of magic splashed in. I REALLY like the aesthetic this puts out, but it's purely conceptual at the moment. Battle is currently flat, boring, and easy, magic has only a utility use which is kind of a bummer when hoping for a Heretic/Hexen type game (though wouldn't be too bad if it had heavy puzzle solving or utility uses), certain amount of glitches to work out (saving the game doesn't save progress or inventory properly, trying to jump out of water can sometimes trick the game into thinking you're falling and you hit the bottom of a lake with fall damage and die, walking over fallen enemies makes your player view go NUTS), expansive exploration areas with little to do, kick is WAY overpowered and you can basically bully enemies with a kick/sword assault, boxes and barrels out the ASS, way too much ammo/mana regen, and some areas to explore and a little unintuitive. Overall: Great idea, too early to enjoy fully unfortunately. Looks great, feels worse. Give it time though.

_childDocuments_.review: Personally this is already very enjoyable to me in the state it's currently in. It seems a lot of the people haven't really grasped the concept of Early Access, but as someone who has been testing the earlier builds I can at least assure you this game is being very actively developed, and a lot has changed over the last months.As the game stands thus far there is a lot already in, but in both a technical as well as a content sense it really is what it says on the tin: Early Access. So far there's the foundation the game is being built upon, with the limited amount of quests, weapons and enemy behaviour currently available (there is more done but that is not in this build - yet) but the game already does a good job of conveying the style of gameplay and type of quests and story they're aiming for - if you're expecting a mindless boomer shooter it's not that at all, this has much more adventure elements. One of the things the story will convey is that you play as a fallen priest, who by chance has to start using magic despite this being against his beliefs. So would you expect him to wield an array of spells right from the start? This game is all about the development and progression you as the protagonist will make throughout this murky, filthy world.There are definitely issues with the game in its current form. Enemy AI, animations and behaviour are far from complete, fair amounts of tweaking and balancing are continuously needed along the way and the current save system is not working  very well. But with the rate the game is being worked on and the promising foundation it has I gave high hopes this game is going to earn its place amongst the gems we've seen rise from the retro shooter community.

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely don't understand all the negative reviews and comments. It's an EA game and it's by no means complete. Currently it offers about 3-4 hours of gameplay and that's not great for the asking price BUT!The developers are active and seem very enthusiastic and eager to improve the game. Furthermore, the existing base is incredibly solid and will be an incredible game once more content is added. The foundation is there, now they need to expand it.The weapons and effects are great. The sound design is awesome and the level design is old school in a great way. Think Heretic/Hexen or maybe Dark Souls 1. It loops around, it's both horizontal and vertical. You spend a lot of time unlocking shortcuts and finding intricate details that ultimately lead to a more direct path to your next objective.The art style is also great and really feels thematic and atmospheric. I personally enjoyed my time a lot. The ambient sounds also go a long way in selling the setting.As for complaints - it's short. That's it. That's my only complaint. I want more. I personally didn't encounter any bugs besides on invisible barier that spawned in the first section but it's not the only path so I got around it. Overall, for an EA game - it's among the best considering what kind of drivel people buy *cough* Fifa 21 *cough*

_childDocuments_.review: I completed the early access content which is limited for now but gives you a good idea of what they're aiming for. If you played Heretic, Hexen or Hexen2 back then you'll feel right at home with Graven. The potions and life flasks are even the same as in those games! The combat is very similar too so don't expect something like Doom Eternal or recent shooters. Also while there is magic in the game, the only spell there is for now serves more as a tool than a weapon.The exploration is exactly like old games meaning you explore the maps killing enemies and looking for keys or puzzles that will open your path. The world is dripping with a dark ambience and begs to be explored to find secrets. Everything is seperated by regions and there's a check point system when you enter each region saving your progress in case you die. The checkpoints work even if you've previously been there cause there is backtracking. The sounds in the game are all what you would expect for a game like this and pretty nice. The music is quite pleasant and not overly present. I hope they'll release the soundtrack eventually.The save system will displease some people since you can't save anywhere like most games of this type. They instead went with the checkpoint system I mentioned above and a save and quit option which saves your quests data, inventory and will bring you back to town when you load your game. Personally I don't mind it at all. It prevents save scumming and force you to keep going and play more cautiously.I've read that a lot of players thought the sprint was useless but I actually liked it. It made backtracking faster and escaping easier when you are surrounded.This is in early access so like I wrote earlier content is limited for now. It took me 5 hours to reach what seems like the end for now but I enjoyed every second of it. Remember you're paying for everything that is now and what will be added later. If you can't deal with that then you should wait for the official release.Here's some things I think should be looked at:1 - The Blacksmith shouldn't sell the weapons you'll find later. Sure it's cool to get the sword earlier but paying for something you'll find minutes later is not cool. He could sell ammo and potions though which would be useful.2 - Sometimes when you run into the corpse of an enemy the camera will shift like there was a collision problem. Makes you think you're getting hit and this gets annoying.3 - I don't really see the point of having 2 types of crossbows as weapons. Maybe make The hand crossbow stronger and change the big one for a canon or something else. Might just be me nitpicking though. Well that's it for now so if like me you enjoyed Heretic, the Hexen games and were still waiting for Hexen 3 then I really recommend Graven.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so much potential, but falls flat. Great atmosphere, great retro look, but like the games of the 90s I'm constantly getting stuck. It is a problem of level design ultimately that makes this game so damn frustrating. I played this before early access and loved the retro feel and bought it on the first day of launch, but the lack of saves and the poor level design makes this hard to recommend. Gameplay is pretty good, fast and slick like 90s games, but most enemies are easily defeated by circle strafing. Checkpoints only restore on death? I'm not sure as I've not died. However, when you quit you restore from town and the entire level is reset. Keys are not saved. Hours of progress are reset. This wouldn't be acceptable in the 90s and it sucks now. Furthermore, locked doors do not appear on the map so when you find a key you do not know where to go. This was a feature of Doom!! What the hell?  You cannot see what keys you've picked up and often don't know where to go when you pick up the key. I've searched for an hour to find a door and only to unlock it an find nothing that allows progression. It tries to have a Dark Souls style level design and I love Dark Souls with paths that loop back on themselves, but the levels in DS are much more playable and intuitive. Optimization seems poor. My PC's fans run hardest when I pause the game when I open the menu. Running over enemies causes a weird drop in frame rate that is hard to describe, but it happens a lot and is annoying. Seems strange that my modern PC would struggle with a low poly, low res texture game.I kind of want a refund but I want this game to do well. FIX THIS GAME!!!!UPDATE 6/9/21===So I'm happy to report that they're still working on this and things are very different from the last time I played. HOWEVER, most of the changes are crap. They've made this game harder, but not in a good way. Strafing still defeats them without too much difficulty.  Enemies now spawn randomly behind you, skeletons are tougher, you face more enemies at once. I am now dying even tho I know the map pretty well at this point (because I've been replaying it over and over and not because it's fun, but because I've been stuck). I don't mind dying because the game was too easy before, but now I feel like I'm dying because I'm running out of resources. When you respawn, there seems to be less or less difficult enemies but you start with 30 health. You also carry less healing potion, an item I rarely used before this patch.  **Difficulty has been increased but drops have not.** Skeletons are tougher, great. You can burn their shields, great. You're going to run out of mana so you won't get to use your spells, crap. You won't pick up enough health between fights so you're constantly dying, crap. Journal entries are not enough to get you through puzzles and navigating the map. The critical path is still not obvious. You can now see where the keys are used on the map, which was badly needed.. so that's cool but not enough. As of right now, go play Hexen and hope that this game get's its ♥♥♥♥ together in the meantime. I'll try again in a few weeks.

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is in Early Access, IN MY OPINION, its one of the few which is actually VERY solidly built. And its old school "quake" like aesthetics are pleasing to the eyes. Additionally, ammo isn't as rare as some of the negative star reviewers are saying, and combat is easy to mid level. To me this is a comfortable mid ground. The story while simplistic works very well for the setting within GRAVEN, and is a testament to Slipgate, 3D Realms, and 1C Entertainment, and their previous games that are also coming out under similair engine designs.All in all Graven is a great seemingly "immersive sim" like game, with satisfying combat, a design that harkens back to the early to mid 90's, but with a touch of modern gameplay design and mechanics throughout. And a sound design that I simply fall in LOVE with, the eerie ambience, the enemy cues, and the music, just ties this game together SO WELL!

_childDocuments_.review: Graven is a love letter to all who played old FPS games and immersive sims. _childDocuments_.review: Graven, baby! Now that's a game that brings back memories. It's like a nostalgic trip to the good old days of Hexen and Heretic, when first-person fantasy shooters ruled the realm. I used to play those games like a man possessed, and let me tell you, Graven keeps that spirit alive.The gameplay is like a shot of pure adrenaline straight to the heart. The dark and atmospheric world sucks you in, and the enemies come at you with a vengeance. It's a battle of magic, weapons, and pure badassery. You'll be slinging spells, swinging weapons, and leaving a trail of destruction in your wake.The level design is top-notch, just like Duke Nukem demands. From ancient castles to eerie dungeons, Graven takes you on a journey through twisted landscapes that'll make your head spin faster than a demonic whirlwind. And let's not forget the puzzles. They'll test your brainpower, making you feel like a true warrior-philosopher.If you loved Hexen and Heretic, you're gonna eat Graven up like a pack of ravenous aliens. It's a game that pays homage to the classics while adding its own dark twist. The developers nailed it, and they deserve a round of applause.So grab your staff, load up on mana, and get ready to unleash hell in Graven. It's time to show those dark forces who's the real boss. Duke Nukem approves, and when Duke approves, you know it's gonna be a hell of a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: I had been following this game for a while, I enjoy the aesthetic (I hate that term) of these retro games and have always been a fan of the Sword & Sorcery genre. That being said, Graven seemed like the perfect marriage of those things. At the time of this writing, I have finished the EA portion of the game and have no complaints!Key Features:Breakables!- You can smash most scenery in this game, barrels, crates, wheel barrels- its a nice way to get some cash or other power ups (ammo)Magic- In this game, while you do get access to spells such as flame, they are used primarily for exploration and puzzle solving. You won't get far setting enemies on fire, but you can access some new areas by torching the spider webs.Gear- As this is EA, the gear system is a bit immature. You have a staff- which you upgrade with stones, a spell book, and the option to find or buy a sword, a small wrist-mounted crossbow and a stone hurler (its a shotgun). Also, spoiler alert, you get to find a Peat Burner, which acts as a sort of grenade launcher. Otherwise there isn't much to the EA gear selection. I would LOVE to see some more melee weapons like the swords and halberds strewn around the maps, and maybe some option for protection as well.Game Play- Surprisingly fresh. Its your usual, FPS-brought-back-from-the-past with great attention to detail both in the level art and design. The controls are responsive and both exploration and combat are rewarding. I enjoyed how there is the option to unlock multiple paths throughout the different sections of the game, and by the end of the EA portion I could navigate from one end of the world to the other through a series of unlocked passages and secret byways. The story is a bit loose, but the Devs are working on it, so I won't judge. As it is, its a fun 6 hours of running around killing monsters, brought me back to the old Hexen 2 days!

_childDocuments_.review: The low-poly action-adventure game I didn't know I wanted!I bought this on a whim and went in pretty blind. The game play and flow is very fun and engaging, and I found myself chomping at the bit at work the next day waiting to play more. The level-design lends itself well to the early 2000s art style, immersing you in the world and rewarding exploration. The game is certainly difficult early on, requiring careful movements.I can definitely see the rough edges that are talked about. The Blacksmith is useless; after you meet him for the first time you may splurge and buy the cuff arrows, only to roughly 3 minutes later getting one for free with barely a chance to test it. This immediately discouraged me from making big purchases down the road, though the blacksmith's inventory never updated anyway. This in turn means gold is useless beyond buying potions, which you never need to. There is also little use for red magic, and no use for blue. I can sense a power-creep for weapons toward the end of the current build, and hope the devs continue to reward plain skill as a your main power "upgrade" more than plain firepower. That being said, all the weapons are very fun, and I hope a more powerful melee weapon with a different feel than a sword is added! It seems like there may be about 4 hours of content currently, and none of the snowy sections yet. But honestly? I bought it on the day of the EARLY ACCESS release. I knew what I was getting into, I knew that it was unfinished, but I had fun anyway. To me, it was $22 well spent, and I look forward to the complete game!

_childDocuments_.review: I only just started playing (Im surprised, since I only found out about GRAVEN about a week ago), and it blew my mind. Alot of Heretic/Hexen spiritual successors ended up being very poor in my opinion, but this one stands out much more than any to come before it. The aesthetic, sounds, and art design are so well mastered as to make you actually think you're playing Hexen 3. The only faults I have of the game so far are that its a little too easy; with too many health pickups and not enough enemies (in Hexen you'd be swamped by 10+ at a time. I've yet to see more than 6 even very weak enemies that pose any threat), and a slower pace of game. You spend alot of it smashing boxes to get loot since your melee weapons swing very slowly compared to the older titles which can get tedious. It makes up for this in having a fast movement speed to keep things feeling like the old Hexen.

_childDocuments_.review: While the game looks awesome and feels great, right now I can't recommend it. But, before I go further, I want to say that this is a great premise and visually striking. That being said:I closed the game after my brief first-play before work to find my 'Continue' puts me on a game dev tile and after the inevitable leap to my death, I respawn with zero items. That was okay, I figured I could just start a new game and keep going. Nope. After finally getting the first quest done, I talk to the blacksmith just to have my game crash. Surely, I won't suffer the same fate as before? Reloading the game and one 'Continue' later and I'm back on my super cool and exclusive dev tile. _childDocuments_.review: OK, so just went through the game — here're some of my thoughts. Total playthough time for the first EA build is about 2 hours, although I could see you spending 3 if you decide to explore and look around.The Good:* The graphics are stellar, bridging chunky textures and models with modern lighting effects in a non-forced way.* The gameplay loop is pretty good, and very Hexen-y with melee combat and puzzles giving way into one another.* The weapons are solid. The shotgun/grenade launcher is definitely the star, but the sword and cuff arrow are very satisfying to use too. The Meh:* The enemies are dumb as bricks. They are supposed to be zombies, undead, and hulking swamp beasts — so that works — but they are still dumb. Having stronger\faster\smarter "sergeants" (think pinkies/ogres) among them would improve the combat a lot — right now you can win each battle by circle-strafing and hitting them until they die.* The level design is pretty good but the areas are not distinct at all. The Bad:* The blacksmith is pointless. He sells weapons that can be found on the ground in later levels, and really breaks the balance. Don't buy anything right now and you'll have a better time with the game.* Too many pointless boxes and barrels. At first you want to break everything but once again — don't, and you'll have a much better time. If the devs like the boxes so much, they should make like Dark Souls and have all of them be empty.* Pointless secrets. 500 gold sounds nice, until you realise that the only way to spend it is pick up a weapon early — and you don't want to pick it up early and mess up the balance of the game.Overall, it's a promising game but it's missing a lot right now. I had a lot of fun with this build still, but there are downsides that must be addressed. Hopefully they will be, because the foundations are extremely solid.

_childDocuments_.review: Enormous potential, but it's got that early access feel, so be forewarned. The game opens with promising atmosphere and a great soundtrack. After a short intro, you're cut loose into a beautiful, but grim world that's at the mercy of a mysterious plague. The character models, and graphics in general, have a very familiar Quake Engine feel, while simultaneously possessing its own unique style. Overall, I love the presentation, and can't wait to explore more of the world and its lore.The combat and weapons are fun, but it can be a bit janky at times. Zombies will lunge quickly at you, regardless of the terrain, and you will stare with amazement as they quite often fly over you as if lighter than air. The "shotgun" crossbow is awesome, but when it gibs an enemy, more often than not, the model will simply disappear, with no viscera to mark your gruesome kill. How disappointing. Another quick pet peeve; the maps are quite large and labyrinthine, and you're given very scant info in your journal. I spent more time than I would like navigating paths already trod upon in my efforts to figure out where to go next. Not a major issue, as exploration is part of the fun, but perhaps if the map system could provide more detail about landmarks, locked doors, etc, that might make it less tiresome. I'm looking forward to seeing how this develops, as I think it could be a mighty fine boomer shooter/caster.

_childDocuments_.review: Graven is a tonne of fun, and if it hasn't convinced you so through it's marketing already, it'll certainly surprise you with how enjoyable it is!I first came across Graven through the Realms Deep Retro FPS Livestream, amongst other titles that I was incredibly excited for such as Viscerafest and Prodeus: Now admittedly, Graven (at the time) actually really didn't grab my attention that much, when compared to what else was on show that I was previously familiar with.However, since I had just finished what's available with Viscerafest as of it's Early Access release and seeing that Graven had literally just gotten a surprise release - I decided to pick it up - Ignoring my previous impressions and giving it a go - As it turns out, I was extremely pleasantly surprised!The best way I can describe it is as if Hexen got it's well deserved evolution, akin to DOOM's evolution to 2016. Overall, really promising - I look forward to what comes next in it's Early Access evolution.

_childDocuments_.review: Game shows a lot of promise. _childDocuments_.review: This game brings me back to a world were developers actually cared about the content they put out. GRAVEN is amazing, and beautifully crafted. I have played so many different games throughout 2021 and none of them seem to pull me right in.but GRAVEN...Oh man, I fell in love with the combat, world, story telling, graphics, just about everything there is. _childDocuments_.review: So one of the big things in this to remember at the moment is in EA, so I can put that to the side for a moment.  Having played so far in two hours there are some minor hiccups I've come across such as a load delay when a respawn point is passed or loading a new area.  Nothing critical in the rapid running around I have done so far.  The textures do feel a bit lacking at times on some of the monsters at the moment, but I feel there is a bit more polish that will be added still.The game gives you very little instruction on what to do at first, just kinda figure it out.  This is a bit reminiscent of the old days of Hexen and Heretic where you just gotta proceed through.  The world is dark and interesting as it seems like this pulls a lot of ideas from Heretic 2 with the idea of the plague.  I'm going to continue playing it and watch as more is added in through till full release.  But I'm enjoying it so far as it gives you the ability to get completely lost at times and figure out what exactly you are looking for.  This game does not do much hand holding (like burning body piles is never told something you can do or how you have to jump to burn body piles in water.)  So I can appreciate that aspect as I'm being more observant of the surroundings rather than looking at a marker on the map as to where I gotta go.One thing I would like to see improved specifically would be a slightly improved highlighting/notification of people you can talk to rather than smash my face into every person, looking for the slight highlight that they can be spoken to.I recommend it if you are a fan of old school Doom, Hexen, Duke Nukem 3D, or even Heretic.  But if graphics and super detail is your MO on judging a game, this definitely is not for you as this has the early 2000's design elements to give it a classic feel.  Its fun and can get hectic when swarms come at you and you only have your smashing stick.

name: Card Shark
detailed_description: 'Our adversaries tonight? An unscrupulous group of scoundrels and rogues, rumoured to possess an unlimited fund between them. If we stick to the strategies you’ve learnt, this will be a walkover.' - Comte de Saint-Germain Card Shark is an adventure game full of cunning, intrigue, and delectable deceit. Enter a world where you’ll need to play your opponents better than you play your cards. LEARN AND MASTER NEW TRICKS Cheat your way to the top of 18th-century French society. Master deceptions using card marking, false shuffles, deck switching, false deals, and more! Use your ill-gotten gains to buy your way into the closed world of high-stakes tables. UNCOVER A CONSPIRACY ... as you climb from local card parlors to the King's table. A word of advice: Don't get caught. Your fellow gamblers do not take kindly to cheats… TRAVEL THROUGH 18TH CENTURY FRANCE Discover small towns, remote mansions, and luxurious lounges imagined by Nerial team (Reigns) game creator Arnaud De Bock (Pikuniku). Immerse yourself in the ornate visual artwork of Nicolai Troshinsky. Have your every move accompanied by an original score from Andrea Boccadoro as interpreted by an orchestra.

_childDocuments_.review: Card Shark is kind of special for me. I got sick then saw it randomly recommended for me on steam, so I checked it out. Immediately I was hooked. A game about cheating at cards? Sign me up! I soon found out that the game was not at all what I expected, and I thought I might refund it. But I noticed that I was over two hours, so I thought: "Eh, I'm sick off work, and I already paid for it, might as well keep playing." Soon enough, I was hooked again. You know a game is good when it fails to meet your expectations and you still love it immensely. While the input registry is still a bit rough on mouse and keyboard, it is absolutely worth picking up.Card Shark is a story based card cheating game that will quickly and heavily test your memory, dexterity, and quick thinking skills. As you progress, you will be provided with increasingly more complex and precise slight of hand tricks which will be then tested in your next mission.I am in awe of the immense work the devs put into the gradual increase in difficulty. Each mission consists of a learning period, where you learn the ins and outs of a new trick that you will use to cheat, then you may practice the trick to your liking. After that is the test, where you perform the trick on your victims, going quickly and subtly to avoid their suspicion. This slow buildup of difficulty works perfectly into the story. As you get richer, the consequences of being caught rise, and the increasing difficulty puts that stress into reality. At almost all times you feel as if you are just barely keeping it together, getting away by the skin of your teeth.Card Shark's gameplay is of a rare breed. It is not only mechanically satisfying, requiring legitimate skill, but also ties into the emotions that the game wants to evoke, thus connecting the player to the protagonist, and also adding a slight bit of extra challenge. In a game based on precise, quick movements, nothing is scarier than stress giving you a shaky hand.I really didn't see Card Shark being a new favorite of mine. It seemed to me like a cool game with a really good art style and interesting gameplay. I never expected a full story with recurring characters, a finely tuned gameplay journey, and mechanics that simultaneously stand on their own and support the story's drama. But I guess it befits a game about slight of hand to keep a few cards up it's sleeve.Card Shark appeared in my life and stole my heart, specifically my Ace. I fully recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't bad. But also isn't something I can universally recommend.For full disclosure, I've finished 1 playthrough of this game. I wanted to try to go back to other areas to try other choices in certain situations such as (Major spoilers) , but the amount of time it took to get through dialogue and gameplay I'd already seen and thus didn't care for was too high.Ultimately, of the results of those choices I have seen in other places, it is absolutely not worth your time to replay the game for the minor differences that they provide.Anyway, the reason this game is hard for me to recommend is because the fundamental strength of this game is immersive storytelling that is more enjoyable in a casual setting, but the gameplay is often extremely punishing, binary and downright unintuitive.When you get the "cheats" to work, it really does feel like something special, as you're absorbed in the world, learning tricks from a master cheater and constantly adding to your "toolbox" of things you can do to get money or information out of people. The first 2 hours of this game genuinely are really really fun and if you're the type of person who doesn't need to finish every game in their library, then maybe this game is for you.But enough with the praise, there is a major issue for the rest of the game, the way the game handles failure states.Early on in the game, if you mess up, it might set you back a small amount by increasing the suspicion of a given "enemy", or making you lose money, which is a fair enough  punishment. But the game struggles to scale this properly into the mid and late game sections.At the 3 or 4 hour mark, you'll be doing tricks that require multiple finicky steps to pull off perfectly. Whether it be selecting cards in the right time, in the right order, or reaction time tests. Failing even one of these small steps, of which there are often 10 or more in a single round will, more often than not, instantly make the player unable to win the round. This could be implemented in a sane way, but instead the player is forced to play out the entire round anyway, meaning that if you mess up a single input by, for example, accidentally clicking for slightly too long, you now have to finish a full "trick" which can involve multiple steps knowing it will all be for naught.Now, this may sound bad enough on it's own but it gets even worse. Because players don't instantly see the "you lose" screen when they fail, they may (like I did) assume that it is possible to either correct one's mistakes using later on parts of the trick, or that they may still have a chance of winning the round, but it is lowered.As soon as players find out that this isn't the case, the gameplay goes from being incredible to absolutely average. You could literally give one player 5 face cards and another 5 low cards and the game will still lose you the round because it isn't coded to actually count the cards and instead is just a veil for a warioware-like minigame(I get that tracking an entire deck of cards is not something thats easy enough to just plonk into a game, but there could have at least been small instances put in place to cover specific situations, or more could have been done on the gameplay side to reduce the number of occasions players are put in this position in the first place).This means that trying to actually be smart and engage with what you assume would be the game's systems or to put it another way, trying to actually be a  will result in failure. Now, you may think that all of this is something you can potentially sweep under the rug and I think I could agree if the game wasn't constantly asking you to improvise in certain situations. So you might have to figure out what you're supposed to do without a specific tutorial. This in a vacuum is great game design, but allowing players to improvise sometimes and not allowing it at other points with quite literally no indication of when this is going to be the case makes for an extremely frustrating game experience.I take no shame in saying that I save-scummed my way through the last 2 hours of the game. There's no way I was going to sit there replaying sections of cutscenes over and over and over due to a single missclick or missed timing window. Even then, each loss was no longer met with an "oh no I got caught this is scary", but an "oh for ♥♥♥♥♥ sake now I have to slam my head against this for another 10 minutes before I can advance the story".I won't comment too much on the "after death" games because I actually liked the concept, although the execution felt a bit off, as I feel like permadeath in a narrative driven game with simple but punishing skillchecks is one of the worst combinations ever. I'll note that I didn't play on the "permadeath" mode, but the fact that the game can opt to kill you forever over a couple of bad clicks really isn't something I want to see in more games going forward.You might think it creates tense moments when you're going "ooh I hope I don't get caught doing this", but in reality what's more likely is that you'll be doing a trick, go "oops, I pressed one time too many in that step, guess I'm just dead".Is there a market for highly punishing games? Yes. Definitely. Absolutely. I love heavily punishing games. But the difference is that these games are often designed around the player dying a lot. Card Shark is not. It is not a game that is fun to play on your 3rd or 4th ot 5th or 18th death. Nothing is re-contextualised. You don't feel like you're learning. The punishment for death is boredom.It doesn't help that this games struggles a lot with clarity. Not in the visual department, where the game is arguably stunning, but in gameplay. For example, the second visit to the manor No time for thinking "oh wait, this isn't such a good idea". No time for discussion. No option to reconsider what you're doing. Just "you interacted with x choice out of two that just happened to be there and if you're doing what most players do aka interacting with everything, you have a 50/50 shot at death. This is like if at the start of pokemon red and blue, you walked into oaks lab and he had 3 pokeballs with pokemon to pick between, you walk up to the closest one, press A on it to see what it is and then oak immediately gives it to you with no option to look at it, consider your options and exchange it. Bear in mind he hasn't even told you anything about the balls. You just inspected one to see what was going on and now you're stuck with charmander. Don't want it? Too bad.I didn't want to get caught by something like this again, meaning I spent ages and ages agonising over small decisions that didn't matter or carefully considering what I interacted with. This wasn't fun. You'd think with all I wrote that I think the game is terrible. I don't. There is clearly a lot of effort in this game and the parts where it shines are very good indeed. As I said, I really enjoyed the first 2 hours and also probably the last 10 minutes. The midgame and most of the lategame is a gigantic drag, though. Reduce punishment, increase clarity and this game becomes good. 5/10. Not bad.

_childDocuments_.review: I wished we could practice the tricks on an arcade style mode since it was very hard remembering all of them. This can be frustrating at times. A single mistake can make you repeat a whole rather slow paced level that follows the same exact steps each time. This is especially true in some instances when an unexpected thing happens and you are clearly expected to rely on knowledge from previous tricks that perhaps you haven't executed in hours. The couple of times I got it right it felt awesome, but most of the times I couldn't remember the steps and felt dumb and frustrated. That being said, I do believe the mechanic is truly unique and deserves to be experienced. I saw people finishing this in less than 4 hours. It took me about 11. I guess I'm dumber and need way more rounds of practice before each round. I read some reviews complaining about the practice sessions. As I said previously, I wish I could practice more. Practicing makes it more immersive since you just know that in order to pull off this tricks, a real card shark needs to practice a lot. But that's just me. Ah, the art style and music are pretty good too, but that's kinda obvious, isn't it? It honestly left me wanting more 18th century themed games. It's a setting that is pretty exploited in other types of media, but certainly not gaming.

_childDocuments_.review: has drawn many comparisons, at least as far as I've seen, to , and I think it's a comparison with a lot of merit to it in some way: cheating at card games is done in a multitude of ways, and there are a lot of techniques you get taught throughout the course of the game, such as various ways of shuffling, dealing, how to mark a card for yourself, or how to signal valuable information to another player. One way of conceptualising these is as a set of independent mini-games, requiring specific inputs to succeed; you are taught a technique and given as long as you like to practice it, before stepping into 17th Century France to attempt to pull it off for real, with the additional pressure of real people and their scrutinous gaze. The difference here is that you will use one technique for one "level", repeating the technique the requisite three times in order to successfully strip your mark of as much gold (or, I suppose it would be livre?) as you possibly can while avoiding detection. It's tempting to suggest that there should have been a  more variety in these techniques - really, each one you learn and catalog is a combination of smaller techniques, and I think there could be *some* room for expression and creative combination to make your own full techniques - but the method presented helps to keep you on your toes as you pivot from strategy to strategy while trying to generate funds.I will readily admit that I found the intersection of narrative and gameplay absolutely gripping; to briefly get you up to speed on the narrative premise, you play a peasant boy from a small village who is swept up by the Comte de Saint-Germain into the French aristocracy, whereupon you and your new partner intend to lie, cheat and steal your way to both financial and political success. Along the way you meet various significant historical figures, and become enveloped in plots and intrigue. The story plays out in little snippets of dialogue in between rounds of the popular card game of the era, the specifics of which are completely abstracted away from you, the player, to much benefit. Playing Solitaire with Voltaire would be frightfully boring; taking all of his copper, on the other hand? Exhilarating.Presentation is really the keyword for , which feels very appropriate given that it's all about cheating at cards; it's all well and good knowing and understanding various forms of cheating cards, but you need to know how to do it discretely, use distraction, subterfuge, seize the smallest windows of opportunity to give yourself the upper hand and, if you're feeling especially confident, your opponent the lower hand. Something I really like about  is the double impact of both the lovely painterly aesthetic, evoking baroque paintings - of the very era in which we find our protagonist - and the visual presentation resembling a stage play with you in the audience for it all; often times a character will enter another room, which will then be transitioned as a parallel to the former, which looks superb and really evokes the idea of a stage play. It's even backed with a beautifully composed soundtrack; one highlight is the piece which , a suitably think-y tune that matches the atmosphere of preparing for a night of deception in high society.It's a really nice combination of all the various aesthetic choices which combine with the gameplay to make a really compelling experience altogether; there's a moment early in the game where a fatal accident results in the Comte profiting financially, which is presented by the UI akin to as if you had just won at the card game you had been playing moments earlier; might have just been a convenient way of signifying you had earned money, but there's something I really liked about this way of presenting the information, like everything was nothing more than a game to Comte, and so you must too embrace that mindset. There's an even greater example of this sort of narrative design, that I really don't want to spoil, so I'll just tell you: Death is not the end.I played  over the course of four nights, stopping for the night each time I reached the end of a chapter - it's funny to think of each break like an intermission - and was thoroughly engrossed the entire time. You won't learn much about French history, despite the presence of real historical figures, but you might learn a thing or two about cheating at cards, even if its just knowing you'd be terrible at it, like me.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game about playing cards. It's about performing complicated tricks which combine observation, memorisation and dexterity. I've seen someone compare these tricks to QTEs; and while I can see the similarity, I'd say they're more like executing combos in a fighting game. Timing, muscle memory, strategy.But is it any good? Well. The tricks are fun to execute, even if I'm getting an ungodly amount of performance anxiety. They are also all real - and while you're obviously not handling an actual deck, you really need to think and act like a cheat. Like a deceiver.Because, my friend, this is a story about deception. It's about deceiving, about being deceived, and about being deceived about being deceived. Who knows, this review might be a deception as well.You're playing a mute orphan who for one reason or another finds himself on a run with the legendary Comte de Saint Germain - an absolutely fascinating real world figure who remains baffling to this day. The Comte is running from someone as well; as such, you travel France, robbing bored nobles of their money by beating them at cards.But a plot like this is never what it seems. A game is afoot, the players shrouded in shadow, and you're but a pawn in their grand schemes. The Comte is very nonchalant about not telling you anything about himself. Your other allies also find ways to surprise you, sometimes in a benevolent way, sometimes... not. As for you? You get to plant fake evidence on your opponents, fight fencing duels, crossdress (to cheat, of course), turn brigands against each other (by cheating), and perhaps even face Death himself at the table - and cheat there as well. You also get to bust a cap in a mutha's... leg, I believe?So that probably sounds pretty ridiculous. Would you believe me if I said that it'a all true? Oh, you shouldn't. In some circumstances, trust is a liability. That's why I invite you to take a look yourself and determine how much of my words are hogwash.

_childDocuments_.review: I intended on waiting until I'd finished this game before reviewing it, but I decided I'd rather throw my recommendation in the ring early in the hopes that someone else might pick it up, then re-do my review once I've finished.In Card Shark, you join a band of travelling ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in 1700's France, swindling folks from town to town alongside your mentor as you make your way towards the main story's goal. That's the long-and-short of what you'll be doing for the majority of the game, and it's a fun and rewarding loop.To me, Card Shark is a wonderful expression of some of the unique strengths video games have as a medium for engaged storytelling. Without going into too much detail, the gameplay is unlike any other game I've played, but is nonetheless quite simple, game-ifying cheating at table games in a tense yet fun way.The game intuitively builds the player's repertoire of skills as the game progresses, and marries your adventure beautifully with a gorgeous painted art style. The story and dialogue  is often funny or gripping, and always charming.I dived straight into the game on the perma-death difficulty, which I .This might seem like common sense, but I figured as long as things were always kept fair and consistent, it wouldn't be an issue. Unfortunately, this is where my minor gripes (so far) come into play. I estimate I made it roughly 1/3 through the game on my first playthrough before being unfairly knocked off. See, alongside the main story towns where you learn new tricks and rake in the French peasantry's hard-earned cash, there are also permanent locations you can revisit at your leisure, making money by using a selection of the tricks you've learned so far. I went to one such location after unlocking a bunch of new story levels, and was prompted to choose between 3 tricks the game hadn't taught me yet. I managed to bumble my way through to the second round, assuming it must've been some kind of glitch, before I was yet again forced to pick between 3 tricks I'd never seen, and was summarily stabbed after failing at it spectacularly.I have to assume this is an issue related to the fact that I'd unlocked more learning opportunities and hadn't completed them yet, but this bled into my second gripe; there is little to no accommodation for an experienced player starting a second save. I'm not sure if there's any kind of NG+, but starting a new game after already seeing the first two hours or so, there's absolutely no way to skip the lengthy story introduction of your character leaving their old life behind to join the caravan, and being slowly dragged line-by-line through the incredibly basic starting tricks once again.Ultimately I did bring these problems upon myself by jumping straight into perma-death, but I nonetheless hope there may be some kind of changes made in these areas to make them a little less painful.Right, I'm off to keep playing my second Con Artist save file.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this game absolutely gets a positive review, but there are many frustrations that some players may want to consider before buying.First of all, the positives. The overall concept of the game is great - playing with the idea of QTEs & making them into rhythms & patterns for cheating at cards is ingenious & a lot of fun. The art style, characters & overall story of the game are very compelling & enjoyable to experience. The unique concept, art style, music & general atmosphere absolutely save the game from some of its more disappointing issues.Now the criticisms; which aren't enough to merit a negative review at all, but definitely something that should be discussed.Firstly, the game's pacing feels somewhat off a lot of the time. You learn a trick, use it once, then move on to a new trick, use that once etc. etc. so you never really get GOOD at any of them. You just kind of fumble your way through each one hoping that you don't mess up badly enough to get murdered. There's a place you can go as many times as you like, where you get to pick from a selection of 3 gambits each hand, but again because you only get to use one & a random 3 of the 28 you know are shown each time, you never really get familiar with any of them. To my knowledge, there's also nowhere outside of the initial tutorial for each trick that you can practice it, so if you put the game down for a bit & come back - good luck remembering. It also feels very strange to be learning so many new tricks when the old ones haven't exactly failed you. Sometimes this is explained due to constraints of player numbers, or being recognised, but the characters in this game seem to have never heard "if it ain't broke, don't fix it". Learning specific tricks for specific situations, then picking your gambit based on the scenario before you would maybe have encouraged memorisation & becoming more of a master of techniques.Next issue is the lack of tutorialisation of several sequences. I spent 20 minutes trying to figure out how to perform a counterattack during a sword fight, because it doesn't tell you, until I eventually looked it up. At another point you're told to inspect a deck and see what's wrong with it, while the suspicion meter is filling up. If you do discover what's wrong, you then also need to counteract it, which is something you've never had to do before & which you're not helped with at all. The answer isn't all that difficult to figure out, but it is time consuming. By the time I figured out both what was wrong with the deck & fixed it, the meter was so high I couldn't physically perform the next part of the trick & got murdered. Going back knowing exactly what to do, going as fast as I could, the bar still went from 0 to about 70% full in the time it takes.You're requested to use a game pad for this game, to which I happily obliged, however there are some absolutely horrible pattern matching sequences where the left stick has to follow a series of movements, the slightest deviation from which will cause you to fail. There is nowhere near enough wiggle room here, as if you don't keep the stick absolutely rammed as far as it can go in the required direction at all times, it'll just fail you.Finally, I'm currently on what I assume to be the last mission, & quite frankly it is a chore. Any fun you may have been having with these tricks & gambits up until now vanishes in an instant. You're taught the most complex strategy yet, as well as a backup strategy - as mentioned earlier, for no apparently reason, because why wouldn't your older ones work? Any single mistake in this section results in your death & a 2 minute rapid-clicking through dialogue options session to get back to the gameplay. I'm on attempt 12, so have had to spend 24 minutes just getting through the cutscenes again. Not only that, but there is a section guaranteed to fill up at least half your suspicion bar almost instantly, so as far as I can tell you have to not only be perfect at every step, but also move at LIGHTNING speed, because there are at least 3 other sections, all of which have to fit within the remaining 30-50% of your bar. It just feels unnecessarily punishing, even for a final 'boss'.EDIT: Having now finished the game, I also feel like the entire side plot of the Cascarots was entirely unnecessary - just a quick "thanks for the money" makes me wonder what the point of donating at all was, in a gameplay sense. The game itself also ends very abruptly, where a bit more of a conclusion could have been nice. I especially would've liked the chance to redo the final sequence a few different ways, rather than having to look it up on youtube.As lengthy as my criticisms are, they're only like that because of the extremely high regard in which I hold the game & its developers for having made such a fun & interesting experience - I'm only this detailed & critical BECAUSE of how good everything else is. I very much hope we'll see a Card Shark 2 & I look forward to seeing what the developers learn from & improve on in the next instalment!
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: The trailers and promo led me to think that Card Shark is a point-and-click adventure game with a cool twist.Well, it's not. It's more like a narrative-focused QTE minigame/memory game collection. The art is amazing, especially animations. The backgrounds are nice, the music is pretty nice, too.The humor lands, too, especially due art style.What isn't nice is the actual gameplay loop -- rather than make you think, take your time and feel clever, game forces you to memorize a QTE sequence and perform it, like a stressed magician. But there's decent game design behind it, with difficulty you can change on the fly and "skip this dumb crap to enjoy further story" pop-up if you get really stuck.The really poor aspect of game design is the pace. The game teaches you a complex card trick. It's nice. But rather than letting you get good at it and use it to advance, it just forgets all about it next scene and teaches you next one. So, instead of being a "card shark", you feel more like a QTE monkey on sped-up training. And that is the worst aspect of this game. It's like developers didn't really understand why people play point-and-click adventure(-likes) and thought that time limits and rapid pace of player teaching is necessary (, people play those games to chill and relax, not sleight-of-hand like they're on amphetamine).So what I really see is an extremely cool idea with quite wasted execution, but the price feels fair and there's fun to be had. So, recommended. It's surely a fresh breeze on gaming landscape and something you couldn't really expect.
