_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: As an enjoyer of indie games with unique premises/mechanics, I really loved this game.I was worried going into it that my lack of cards knowledge would be an impediment, but the tutorials were well done but the slow beginning and the repetition made it a way smoother experience. It made me feel really big brain when I got to the end of the game. However, I struggled a lot trying to understand the technique near the end of the game. It felt really good throughout the game when they would test your comprehension, but the comprehension check at the end was a bit rough.The writing was wacky in a good way -- a kind of "twist on twist on twist" sorta story! The music and art really sold the overall atmosphere. It was just a really solid game and if you're on the fence of getting it, you should definitely get it.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I would say this is indeed a good game I have enjoyed a lot (roughly 6 hours for first round). It focus on cheating, a topic which is rarely touched or found in other games. The mechanism is interesting, and sometimes there are unexpected accidents that require your improvisations. This kind of excitement is pretty unique.Also, the music is great and the story line is quite reasonable, which I always appreciate.There are some minor issues though, especially on the controller. Hope they will fix the input problems in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game expecting pretty art and a nice soundtrack -- I never expected to learn so much about card cheating! I love the gameplay loop of practicing new tricks until you feel comfortable with it, and then doing it with higher stakes. The gameplay isn't particularly involved, but it is more than "press X to cheat." And the game is made such that sometimes my palms start sweating as I realize I have to flip through the deck again while the timer ticks down -- even though it's all pretty "easy." Definitely exceeded my expectations, from the simple but enjoyable writing, the period setting, the beautiful art, the "cinematography" of the card scenes, the thoughtful historical gameplay conceit, the simplified but just-involved-enough card cheating mini-games. I find myself thinking about the game when I'm not playing it. If the premise is interesting, and you don't mind slower-paced games, you'll probably like this one! FYI, definitely don't play on the hardest difficulty for your first playthrough (permadeath). I tried this, thinking maybe the game had roguelike elements and not many ways to die. Nope! You die a lot, and then just have to redo the story you've already done. (If anything, I think they should lock this difficulty for first playthroughs.)
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: This was a game like no other, there is no other game of its genre. Having played what Kojima would describe as the first and only "card-shark-type", I highly recommend. It it like a visual novel if visual novels were worth playing. It is a game that is entirely QTEs, in the best possible sense. It is difficult to imagine more humble origins than those of the genius now cooking at Gusteau's, who is, in this critic's opinion, nothing less than the finest chef in France. I will be returning to Gusteau's soon, hungry for more.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Quaint game about cheating at cards in 18th century europe with nice hand drawn art. Card tricks are a mix of memorization and timed events, though there are usually some on screen prompts to help you out. One thing that bugged me is that the "suspicion" meter increases a lot in some cases and not as much at others, and it's not always obvious when or why you need to hurry through a specific part. Then if you fail badly enough to get a game over there are some long-ish unskippable sequences you need to go through to get back to where you were before. Other than that I enjoyed it.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: This game took me out of my comfort zone by making me think, a lot. This wouldn't be a complement if it were a puzzle game, but I wouldn't call it a puzzle game at all. It's a test of memory and pattern recognition, both things that I think I'm terrible at. Nonetheless I am having SO MUCH fun AND the story is actually quite good so far. I struggle to find any meaningful improvements to suggest as it would only be a matter of opinion (for example I would prefer some swaps to background music during scenes like duels).Super well done, great visuals, cool music, engaging.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Normally, if I review something I wait until I have beaten the game, but in an attempt to get this game more attention: I am posting a review early.  Five hours in I have to tell you: this is one of the most unique gaming experiences I have ever had.The art is superb, the writing witty, and the characters lovable.  Whereas most games use quick-time events (QTEs) as artificial game lengtheners, in this game QTEs are the very core of what you are playing.  However, they have an added depth that make for a very engaging gameplay mechanic that I think will inspire more games like it that are yet to come.  Some QTEs are simple, some are intricate, and some are legitimately complicated and I still don't think I understand; but the story compels me to keep playing.Get this game, it is well worth the $20 full price, but if you see it on sale then it is 100% a must-buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool game play, but it really just made me want to play poker.  For a game that bases itself on the deceit of the card game, it felt a little insincere to base the success of ones game purely on cheats.  A true card shark also knows how to actually play cards.  There is no card playing here, it is merely tricks, which is this games biggest strength and it's greatest weakness.  It was such a pleasure to play, and learning each new trick was incredibly engaging, but it left me wanting.  I wanted to actually play cards.  No win felt truly earned.  The betting seems to have little to nothing to do with the actual game play.I would maybe forgive all of this if the plot of the game wasn't so convoluted.  It very much plays like an old french aristocracies drama, which i get is the point, but it's outdated and very "Soap Opera."Although this is a highly critical review, I thoroughly enjoyed this game. It's incredibly rare that you get to experience new and unique game play.  This game was a pure joy! ...even though it was maddening at times.  I would like to see the developers take this game a step further and give the player a little more agency.  I could see this becoming a really cool card/gambling rouge like game, rather than an adventure game with a unique mechanic.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: It's a wonderful game, I played the demo and knew that I would be finishing the game within the day. It doesn't have a huge amount of play time, but it's still worth the money. The gameplay is mostly QTE so if you're not into that, then you might not like this game. The art is great, and the story is very good as well. I was thoroughly impressed with this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: From what little I've played of the game so far, I've been enjoying it. I'll discuss some non-gameplay aspects of the game before going to the actual gameplay itself. The stylized displays gives me a papercraft feeling with wonderfully vibrant colors that slots right into the feeling of the world. The colors pop and everything gives a warm feeling. The music was advertised as a live music performance and it is wonderfully done. The orchestra's work adds a mystique to many of the scenes, The Magican's Theme comes to mind. The character writing is fantastic as well. The Comte is snarky in a way that you'd feel he is being polite to you, the mute has a level of personality despite being unable to verbally communicate. Other characters that you meet in the story speak in ways that ooze personality and frames them in the exact archetype that they were designed to be.The gameplay, while difficult, is equally rewarding. It may just be me, but I can't help grin whenever I can finally figure out whatever cheat that you are using feels good. Sometimes the explanations can be a bit confusing, but that is the nature of a trick. You can't really watch to figure it out, and having the additional steps explained by the characters feels good. It's a very brain-y game, and it can be confusing at times. I've seen people say that the game isn't for them and they are frustrated by it, which I can understand, but there is a difficulty slider. The game starts you on the intended difficulty, but you can go up one to have a harder story in which death is a legitimate concern. You can also go down a step and have more forgiving experience. Overall, I would recommend the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Short, charming game about performing real-life card tricks to cheat your way for money and information.Sound design and visuals are satisfying and never get old. Story holds well until the ending which felt rushed for the sake of adding an ending to the game, which felt like a bummer with all the ploys and details leading to the final act.I used mouse controls and while sometimes iffy for the occasional card trick, it was never a big enough deal to affect my gameplay.If worried about the game being too short for its price or replay value, I definitely recommend going for achievements. The game has a surprising amount of interactions you might not have known even existed on your first playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant game with fantastic artwork and perfectly suited background music. The game challenges you to use your brain in a new way I've never experienced before. The story-line flows coherently from place to place and is expertly told throughout the game. I would rate this 9.5/10.My only concern is the dealing animation speed on some mini-games (The shinier one especially) is a bit tedious, especially when you have to redo a stage a few times.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Card Shark is easily a standout title this year. The gameplay loop is based on learning how to cheat at cards in a controlled environment (which is needed for some of the later tricks) before moving to an environment where you need to put your skills to the test to progress the story. Conveniently enough, the favourite pastime of France in the 1700s is a good ol’ game of cards, so even with the increasingly escalating stakes, it always comes back to cards. The mechanics are a combination of shuffling through cards and QTEs. While this seems basic, the elements of these tricks evolve over time to the point you’re picking specific cards out of the deck and having to place them in exact spots (I could never wrap my head around the transparent stack!), and the QTE inputs are similar enough each time that you never feel ambushed by them. On top of this, your opponents are slowly growing suspicious of your actions during the course of the game, represented by a bar at the bottom. If you take too long and the bar reaches the end, you’ll find yourself in the slammer for the night, reflecting on where it all went wrong. The most surprising element of Card Shark is the twists and turns the story takes throughout its roughly 8-hour campaign that kept me engaged from the start and eagerly had me wanting to figure out an incredibly complex trick just so I could progress to the next story beat. The game has a tremendous sense of humour about it, with a collection of outlandish characters - Death even shows up if you end up dead, giving you a chance to return to the living through - you guessed: a game of cards (spoiler: he’s not very good cards). There’s no doubt the element of frustration exists within Card Shark: the tutorials are not the most engaging and are not always well explained; the games/levels can be quite slow-paced, meaning failing and redoing them can turn into a chore, though the developer, Nerial does shift the dialogue to reflect you showing up for the same card game considering you were arrested for cheating previously. With this said, when you do pull off a complex trick and swindle your opponent out of their money, oh mon Dieu does it feel satisfying. Card Shark is a game that excels in spite of its flaws and is an essential title to play for its originality in 2022.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Use actual slight-of-hand techniques to cheat at cards, and rob everyone blind while discovering the secrets of the French upper-crust in 18th century.  Better think fast and keep track of all those cards, because if you screw up or your marks get too suspicious, you can lose more than just your coin.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: This game is downright stressful to the uninitiated. You'll learn to think in an interesting way to solve the timed puzzles this game throws at you while also slowly but surely feeding you pieces of an overarching mystery. You'll meet a fascinating cast of characters in this charming little card game, accompanied by a beautiful art style and wonderful music. In the end, it all comes down to the hands of fate, and whether or not you can twist it in your favor.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I've never been a huge fan of puzzle games, but once in a blue moon, there's one that gets my attention, and this one is easily one of the best I've played. The idea is unique and one of a kind, and the mechanics, while simple on their own, make for a challenging and intense experience. I've been more terrified of getting caught cheating cards in this game more than dying in many others. The story is simple and tasteful. While it may not be TellTale or Naughty Dog levels of storytelling, it was still very much fun to go through, and the twists and turns did actively shock me! If you want a fun game for a very good price, I couldn't recommend any other game! Go show these developers some love!
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Always on the look out for original gems from the indie scene. And this is a title that sure fills that gap as a historically story driven puzzle game.Very nice hand drawn arts style accompanies some suitable classical music that slides right into the late 1700's setting. The story that fits into that setting is a mix of twists and intrigue that revolves around King Louis XV of France. Because of the unravelling mysterious nature of the story, including the players choice, it kept me very engaged from start to finish. Where this title stands out is the game-play. It might come across as a card playing sim of sorts, but really only focuses on the cheating aspect. All the cheating strategies come with their own set of gimmicky controls, which makes this more of a puzzle game than a card game. As the game does hold your hand by thoroughly guiding you through each strategy, your memory is tested more so than dexterity. It all blends really well with the overall story and atmosphere, making for a pretty solid experience.You're going to have a hard time finding another game like this one. Might not be for everyone. But for those that are after a heavily story driven puzzle experience, you'll find it is well worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game SO MUCH MORE than I did.The idea is great, the design and atmosphere is great. The mechanics themselves are fiddly as ♥♥♥♥ and when something goes wrong, as it inevitably does, the game is not forgiving in the least. You'll make a tiny mistake -- or maybe you won't, you'll do everything right as far as you can tell, and the input just flakes out, or the suspicion mechanic goes nuts, or some other random thing happens -- and you'll spend the next five minutes tediously playing through the rest of an already doomed scenario, and then if you're lucky you'll just have lost a lot of money but still be able to continue, and if you're unlucky you'll be broke or in jail so get ready for even *more* tedious clicking and iffy mechanics, just to get back to where you were before the first tiny mistake. I won't refund it out of respect to Nerial and DD, and maybe they'll make some changes to reduce the fiddliness and I'll try it again. But if you pick it up, bring a lot of patience for twitchy unforgiving mechanics and punishing tedium. There's probably a great game in here somewhere, if you can get past the mechanics to find it.

_childDocuments_.review: DO NOT PLAY THIS WITH A MOUSE. The deck stacking interface is beyond terrible for a mouse and will routinely give you cards you didn't even pick. _childDocuments_.review: While it can be a little overwhelming with the sheer volume of dense card-trick information the game drops on you, the feeling of pulling it off in practice is incredible- every successful execution gives the vibe of a barely-pulled-off heist. Plus, it's just a beautiful game visually, what an incredibly charming art style!The game also does its alternate endings really well. There’s not too much variation but still a lot of little instances that make you feel like your choices mattered, leaving the player with the feeling that they got an ending reflective of their choices, but not feeling pressured to replay the game (with choices they aren’t invested in) just to see the other slightly-different endings.

_childDocuments_.review: Card Shark is a delightful little game about learning to cheat at cards, and do magic like the greats. Well... okay, not magic, per se. It's all about learning sleight of hand, and little con games. The crazy part is, I genuinely have no idea what game we're actually playing when we deal the cards out. I think that's kind of neat, since it could translate to any card game really. The actual game being played at the table doesn't really matter. Admittedly, I'm very early in the game. At time of writing, I'm only 1 hour in, but I wholeheartedly plan to keep playing all the way through. Card Shark is insanely charming, and I recommend giving it a look-see. To really blow your socks off... how about a magic trick?

_childDocuments_.review: A visually striking game with a compelling narrative and entirely novel game concept. If you have any interest whatsoever in playing as a cunning scammer, wheeling and dealing cards to make your fortune this game is definitely worth a look. There are a few things I struggled with personally that you might also, and one critique. Please do not take the length of my criticisms as indicative of degree of sentiment. For reasons that may become clearer, its much easier to convey what frustrates me about playing this game than it is to convey what enchants me about it.As you progress through the game, you will learn new techniques (i.e. scams) to run from mentor. These have very evocative names, and flashcard-like UI elements to remind you of what they entail. Often on your way to a job your mentor will say "ok this time we will run X scam, do you remember how to do that scam?", which in practice means you can review the steps of said scam as many times as you like, whether its new, or you simply forgot how to do it or what he's talking about. Each scam is comprised of multiple mini-games, usually requiring precise timing or movement. These mini-games are often times variations of one another to the extent that if you have poor working memory you might forget whether its the one where you "move the glass and wipe the table down in a specific direction to indicate what card that dude has", or "position your hand on the glass to indicate face card and then wipe for suit". Even as I type this I'm forgetting, for one or both, or perhaps it's another mini-game also has you indicate the amount of the suit in question.There is a help page meant to remind you of what to do, but in my experience its insufficient to convey the steps beyond what you can recall based on image association. In practice this meant I avoided at all costs any scam that I was remotely confused about, as often as I could.Sometimes, while learning a new mechanical element in the game, some word choices or UI elements will be ambiguous. One example is at some point in the game, an NPC will teach you to fight. In Simon-says fashion, you will have to mirror his attacks back at him in order to defend. He will then instruct you to strike back. The screen will show you three vertically arrayed buttons/keys to press, with a timer on each. I have no idea what the timer on them means. The attack sequence will go something like this HIGH > MID > LOW > LOW > (In Red Text) HIGHHe then says attack me during the opening, so I press the buttons corresponding to HIGH, MID, LOW, LOW, HIGH, just like he said. He then says something like "YOU HAVE TO ATTACK WHEN YOU CAN". I have no idea what I did wrong. I'm stuck in a loop again.Through your cardsharpery you will earn coins that will clink satisfyingly. You can bring these to an NPC and elect to donate any amount of, and any money that you keep can be used as largesse from which to ante in future scams. In practice gold affords you better chance of having to restart a scenario, thus avoiding repeated dialogue. At one point, largely resulting from Critique #1, I got stuck in a loop where I couldn't remember the steps of any scams necessary to escape poverty so I could move, something like Broke > Run Repeatable Small Scam Designed for Player to Get Enough Gold for Bigger Scam > Try to Run Bigger Scam at Location Designed for Player to Get Enough Gold to Move on with Story > Crap I don't remember any of these scams I'm being asked to choose from > YOU'RE A CHEAT AHHHHARHAHGUHG > BrokeIf I hadn't donated gold perhaps I wouldn't have had to do the activities in question that got me stuck.I would have liked an interesting choice for the gold instead, like finer clothes that give more time before your mark flips out on you and accuses you of cheating, or more forgiving time windows for quicktime events. Then again, the game doesn't market itself as an RPG, so perhaps that's not a fair ask on my part. But then why have me choose how much gold to keep? It's certainly not a resource allocation game either, but in practice that's essentially what's happening: it's a limited scope version of Kings of Dragon Pass; limited in that you have one resource, and you may spend it on a story element, or use it as a protective element to avoid a time/effort penalty of minigames that don't progress the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Card Shark is worth the money.TL:DRCard Shark is a game about cheating at cards, you never actually use them.I consider myself rather knowledgeable at Texas Hold 'em and many other poker games.My knowledge means nothing in this game. Because you aren't playing cards, you're cheating at them.more specifically, you're cheating for your friend.Card Shark has a beautiful art style, animation style, charming characters all well written, 28 different card tactics that can all be applied to real life and is an incredibly stressful game on the normal difficulty alone.It's top tier in every regard except endgame.No spoilers, but this is a game where the journey is the payoff, not the destination.Enjoy your time and enjoy cheating at cards, fail on purpose once or twice and see interesting alternatives to the game.It's rather great through and through. But only THROUGH and THROUGH, once you're done, you'll enjoy the parts you actually played instead of where you ended.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Spoiler free review. Try Card Shark. You will like it if you are patient.After struggling to like this until just before the end of the game, I surrendered.The game is hard, and most of the time, it felt needlessly so. The designers must've recognised this, as they included a "Skip" option for when you fail an encounter JUST ONCE which allows to progress the story. The main problem with the game's mechanics is as follows. You learn "tricks" every time a new encounter is unlocked. Initially, the tricks seem like an opportunity to skew the probabilities to win an encounter in your favour. In reality, it quickly becomes clear that they are simply sequences of actions that you need to perform perfectly in order to win each round of an encounter. A single card missdealt and you will 100% lose the round. Lose two rounds in an encounter and you will likely lose the encounter. There is no chance or probability in the win logic, and you do not need to actually follow the game, you just need to do what the trick consists in.I was really keen on this game, so I started with the best intentions. I listened through all the explanations in details, trying to make sense of how these tricks actually correspond to the real deal in a deck, which really helps understanding and memorizing them. Logic understanding and memorization are key to this game. Reflexes only amount to a very small part.However, each encounter introduces new tricks, and they keep piling up. While this helps keeping the gameplay varied, and in most encounters you are required to only remember the last learned trick (or the last few), at some point you collect over a dozen of them. This is where I started having trouble remembering the older ones. The game is happy to provide refreshers, but overall it started feeling like a chore. When the game clicked, and I performed a successful set of tricks in a particularly story-rich encounter, Card Shark felt really good. However, I also started to be annoyed at every new encounter, being forced to understand and memorize new stuff. I do not know what I was expecting, really. Not introducing a large number of tricks probably would have meant too much repetition, and the game would have had to be much shorter. The designers brilliantly introduce also non-card related mechanics towards mid game, which help keep the game fresh, and they really are a great fit in the game itself, both narratively and mechanically.It was towards mid-game that I started losing some encounters a bit more frequently. Without giving spoilers, this is where I got to see the how Card Shark deals with _game over_. I will only say that I found it really brilliant, with one exception: there's the possibility of perma-death, or other time-wasting punishes for your failure. While I initially appreciated the originality, this also kind of killed the mood for me, because I stopped to feel free to experiment and I realized I just had to do everything perfectly. I just wished that I could fail some of the mechanics while getting others right, maybe balancing a less successful round via observation, initiative, or just chance.Additionally, some encounters started to include brilliantly narrated and interesting "surprise" mechanics, which however were terribly difficult to get right without losing the encounter at least once, or even multiple times. I also got really involved by the story, which I found really engaging and well-narrated, and I didn't want to spend so much time rehearsing. These factors led me to lower the game's difficulty – which I don't think had a strong-enough impact – using hints, and save-scum, from there to the end.All things that frustrated me, but kept me playing.Here's where I dropped it. Towards the end, one of the (presumably) last encounters forced feed me a very complex trick, probably some sort of grand finale mechanic. I would've been happy to not understand _fully_ the mechanic and go for the odds in the last encounter: risky, but that's what my character would've done. "Worst case scenario, I will fail the encounter and then take advantage of the skip option". But no: the game mandates that you learn the trick, and that you repeat it to your teacher, before you can even attempt to play it in an actual encounter. The trick was really complex, and despite trying to follow the instruction to the letter, I kept failing the tutorial. I persisted for three repeated sessions, each of about a dozen tries, even going back to review and memorize previous tricks that appeared in this sequence. I still failed, it was over my level. This was it for me.Despite this, games like Card Shark remain something I want to see more of. The curated art style, the choice of music, the sounds, the characters, the plot, the atmosphere, and even the game's mechanics really are interesting. I guess that the mechanics probably needed more balance for me, and finding a way to be a bit more lenient, or driven by not only memorization, but also some other factor. I also get that designing an original game like this is incredibly difficult, and I do recommend everyone to give it a try. Perhaps you will be more patient than me.

_childDocuments_.review: I am going to be updating my review, but leaving the entire original below the update, so if you want to see what was first, scroll down a bit.This game has very good art style, animation, gameplay, and the story is good. The devs seem to be on top of most bugs that they have gotten reports on. My only complaint, and this is the same as in my original, is that the devs DID NOT email me back after 5 ish days, but instead responded to my steam review. If I hadn't have thought of reviewing this game, I would not have even gotten word from the devs about this bug that I had that was patched, but the part of the bug I had a problem with wasn't in the patch notes, so I wasn't aware of the fact that the bug I encountered that broke the game was patched. The reason why this is a problem is that this is their official email on their website, and that is, what I and most people I'm sure would think, is the most direct line of communication publicly available. Again, if I didn't hop in the game after I didn't see my bug patched in the notes, and didn't write a review, I would have just gotten a refund and forgot about this game, because if you are familiar with steam's refund policy, I can't have over however many hours and have owned the game more than however long, so I was making sure I got my moneys worth one way or the other.In case anyone goes through the original review and says my bug was definitely in the patch notes, let me rephrase what the bug was, and the was in the patch notes. I ran out of money after the barn went away. Then, I went to the camp to see the Magician because I'm like hey, I've given him 2100 livres, I'm sure he can give me the min bet for the next farm. My bug that I knew shouldn't have happened was that the Magician did not give me 40 coins, but instead only let me check the state of the fund, where I SAW that I had given him 2100 coins. The patch said that I was able to go back to camp. When I saw that in the notes I sent another email saying hey, this bug wasn't in your patch notes, I will be getting a refund soon. Then, I just decided to show my friend hey this bug wrecked me, and, like the patch notes said, I was able to go back to camp. I was like, "ok now watch this, I gave him so much and he won't give me anything." And of course I got my 40 back. TL:DR Great game, but if you need to contact the devs for anything, write a negative steam review cause they pay more attention to that than they're own emails.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------(ORIGINAL REVIEW)I want to start this review off by saying that I really did enjoy this game.That is, I enjoyed it all the way up until I got soft locked pouring wine for my mentor. After a frustrating few minutes of google searching, I went and gambled away all my money, just to realize that the way of making money just up and disappeared, and that was the only way to get money. If you have played or seen this game be played, you may already realize what is going to happen from here.The way that travel works in this game is that the game gives you as many locations as you can go to, and will only let you click on the location if you have the minimum bet. Well, as there is no longer a way for me to get money, I can't get the minimum bet, so my job has just went from professional cheat to professional cartography checker.This game has amazing gameplay systems, good animation and art style, and good story. But after playing the game for 6 hours, and making about 75% progress and then just getting cucked by this hard lock, some may say that asking the developers may be the next logical step.This would be if the developers ever checked their emails.I have emailed them 2-3 days ago, and as I am writing this on a Friday, I can't actually afford my 20 dollars that I want back for them to respond. Basically, only buy this game if you are very confident you won't get frustrated at the sometimes game breaking bugs or just holes in the system, and you are fine with restarting when you were pretty close to beating the game and your game just won't let you progress anymore.

_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10It's closer to a visual novel than a card game. It's quite the novel though; buried in this lore heavy backdrop of 18th century France is gameplay scattered to test your reflexes, timing, and memorization of tasks. You learn to apply real card tricks so that you and your mentor can swindle folks and uncover the answers to a bigger mystery.It's a game that asks for your full attention; it's very easy to find yourself distracted by the unique story (and wonderful soundtrack) as you try to rehearse each new skill.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: The art and music are fantastic in a charming game that was one of the more mechanically intricate ones I've played in a while. The amount of memorization involved with all the different techniques will make your head hurt at times, but the story the game tells along the way, is worth the pain.Oh, and this played really well with controller.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game with plenty interesting mechanics and mini games. The main story is also entertaining! _childDocuments_.review: Card shark is one of the most visually and mechanically interesting games i have played in recent memory. You will find yourself learning all sorts of ways to cheat at cards, manipulating stacks and hiding cards in your sleeve, in order to further your goal of helping the people of paris(?). Every table a nail biting exercise in precision and speed as you work quickly enough to not arise suspicion, while squeezing as much money as possible out of your victims. The gameplay loop makes for an addictive circle of learning, and applying, with the stakes for messing up being quite high. The game is at its absolute best when you are utilizing a strategy at a table, only for some new variable to be thrown into the mix, meaning you have to adjust your strategy on the fly, or risk being caught. These moments are frantic and intense, with a great sense of relief and pride washing over me after successfully navigating them. Of course there has to be a reason to learn how to cheat at cards, and a reason there is. The story is told through the various meetings with different characters, all providing more information into some mysterious story that would allow you more power, potentially even getting you a spot on the royal court... Its a game of information, and cards are how you bargain. In my experience the wide cast of characters got a little confusing at times with long, old french names making people hard to remember, although the artwork helped much in that sense. The relationships between characters might not always be clear as well. While the game provides a "journal" that your character fills out throughout the game, it does nothing more than recap your last journey. It is a nice help, but not always enough. overall a fantastic way to spend a few hours, if a little repetitive at times. but if you dont mind a bit of indie game roughness this is a super unique experience. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Oh so much fun. I spent about 9 hours playing the game (I tend to go slow, so you might finish in 5-7 hours instead) I guess you can call it a mix between QTEs and memory games but the way its staged really makes the experience. The art and aesthetic is fantastic. It really does make me feel like I'm in 18-19th century France. I will say that the game can be hard. Each card game requires near perfection (and speed) if you want to win. There was an easier mode I didn't try, but I do not think It means you not longer need to do things near perfect.  In game, you need to keep tract of cards without anyone noticing and once you lose the card to the pile, there's no way to find it again. Which honestly does make perfect sense. There were only a few times I questioned the logic (How does only keeping track of the opponent's main suit a guaranteed win?). But it's certainly not immersive breaking or spoils the fun in anyway.And for all of you with poor short term memory, have a pencil and paper in hand. You'll wanna write some cards down.Won't say anything about the story, but I really love the way it handled death and the protagonist's gimmick.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent little game! Very unusual and fresh in both premise and its execution. What I especially like about it is that it all makes perfect sense: sleight of hand in cards does consist of individual tricks that one has to master, and it is very natural to represent the tricks as minigames based on memory and reaction. Even further, I'm not an expert but all tricks look very plausible, I'd be surprised if they were inaccurate. The story is also quite well written, the setting of XVIII century France is cool and underused in games, the art style is nice and matches the setting. Importantly, the game as a whole does not overstay its welcome: it could easily drag for another five hours but the authors decided to call it quits just in time. A very pleasant 4-5 hours that I heartily recommend to everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Holy crap, what an amazing, underrated gem of a game! I have never played anything like Card Shark before. I've yet to even finish the game, but I feel so passionately about it that I couldn't help but go ahead and write a review, which is already something I scarcely do.I immediately fell in love with the colorful cast of characters and the dramas they are caught up in. The player character in particular has captured my heart, despite communicating only through his facial expressions, though i've always had a soft spot for silent protagonists.But the gameplay!! It's so unique, and so much fun. Every strategy feels so elegantly designed and plays the same, and remarkably, despite usually building off the same  techniques, they never feel repetitive at all! The satisfaction when you finally get it down perfect and are ready to try it out for real is unbeatable.Reviews are not my strong suit (wait... _childDocuments_.review: Card Shark is a game that’s hard to put into a particular genre, beyond just “this is so clearly an indie game.” Certainly it has a variety of elements, such as a rich and compelling narrative, and fun characters, but its core gameplay is unlike anything I’ve played before. The heart of the game is learning and perfecting sleight of hand tricks so the player - a mute orphan travelling with a ne’er-do-well count - can rig card games as they travel throughout pre-Revolutionary France. To be clear, when I say “perfecting sleight of hand tricks,” I don’t mean deciding which trick the character will perform. No, the player themselves must learn the trick, practice it, and pull it off perfectly in the moment, all while a timer ticks down the time until the ruse is discovered. It requires being able to memorise and repeat a perfect pattern of motion. I played as much of the game as I could before I couldn’t get past the mechanics. That I played as long as I did, I think, stands as a testament to the power of this game’s story, art, and overall feel. It is a beautiful game with excellent art and music, and a story that kept pulling me forward. I wanted to see where it went, dive into the intrigue, and watch the pieces of schemes fall into place. I enjoyed the story of the Comte claiming a mute orphan as his son on their merry adventures through France. It was lovely.But I am terrible at the mechanics of this game.I did not finish Card Shark, though I wish I had. It is beautiful and fun, though if you cannot master the art of sleight of hand and stealth, it will be impossible to complete. In a sense, though, that feels in line with the story itself. If these two characters can’t master their own card tricks, they fail and die in the chaos of France. It feels appropriate that I couldn’t finish, since I couldn’t master what I needed to survive.Card Shark sets out to tell a story of deception and card games in pre-Revolutionary France. It does an excellent job, though would likely be enjoyed more by someone who bothers to go get a controller.

One can easily tell from any given still image that it comes from Card Shark.  Every frame a painting, especially apt considering it is set during the Enlightenment period in France,

_childDocuments_.review: Every character in this game is more complicated than I expected. It reveals a magnificent journey, showcasing how corrupt France was at that time and ends up in a rather peaceful inn which reminds me of its very beginning. Apparently, I love it, no matter its impressive characters or eye-opening cheating skills. A con artist is the best magician who conjures miracles like a real artist. Thanks to the comte, I would like to stay far away from casinos for good owing to his cunning tricks... (In this regard, he is really a good instructor, isn't he?)
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Card Shark has surprisingly a lot of depth to it for a game of this type. You play as a mute French boy traveling the country using a variety of cheating techniques to win games of cards against your opponents. Learning how to do the first few tricks is easy, but after the 10th or so technique this becomes challenging, as the game makes you recollect older tricks later in the game. The game has a great story and great gameplay alike, as well as a unique art style and plenty of classical music to get the player immersed in its world. Another gem from publisher Devolver.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: According to the trailer, "It is NOT a card game" but I wish it was a card game. I got Card Shark in a bundle with other Devolver games I actually wanted to play. There is a lot of dialogue in Card Shark and I didn't think it was very interesting. It is a major pet peeve of mine when a game offers you dialogue choices but they are not meaningful and always lead to the same outcome. Why bother? I knew within 10 seconds I wasn't interested in the story. The music and game design are nice, but this is a phone game at heart and I don't personally enjoy these kinds of locked down linear experiences. I would rather read a book for the same effect, and more depth. I think that the art and music of Card Shark work well together, although neither are my personal taste.  Some people will enjoy it, but it's not for me.

I still managed to finish it despite struggeling hard but that should tell you about how forgiving it can be.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything from the dialogue to the art, the music, and the animation oozes with charm, and the aesthetic is absolutely perfect. The game is a decently challenging, but in a very fun way; doing your best to adapt to situations or not ♥♥♥♥ up a trick in the tense moments, occasionally dodging death by inches really gets your blood pumping, and Card Shark makes you work for it too. The story is equally good, keeping your ass glued to the seat for the full 6-10 hrs you'll be binging this for. Absolutely worth the purchase.For your first time, I'd recommend playing on the Gambler difficulty (Normal), but if you want to feel the pressure of not having second chances then by all means go for the Con Artist difficulty first. _childDocuments_.review: This game is so fun! It's one of the more rewarding games I've played in a while, and one of the few games I've played where it really takes all of my attention and focus. _childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's great in a way of story, visuals and sounds, but I gameplay part is a bit bland, mostly consisting of QTEs and remembering sequences, in rare cases giving you freedom to handle in own way. Sometimes it just doesn't make sense how using one or another tactic gave you enough advantage to win.If you're looking for some chill card experience feel free to grab it.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: An unexpectedly fun time!The Story of this game is told really well and is pretty enjoyable to watch unravel and learn all the ins and outs. The characters are also really fun to be around with each of their motives and personality traits that make them stand out from one another. The Settings that you venture through are really beautiful and show the many sides of France back in the 18th century. Many of the locations are extravagant and adds to the feeling of these games being high stakes. Visually, its beautiful. Performance was really solid without there being any bugs or glitches through my playtime. The Art Direction is really nice to look at and it really fits the era that this game is going for. Sound and Audio are perfect with the soundtrack being these harmonic symphonies and the audio perfectly matching things such as the cards and the coins in this game. In terms of gameplay, its a fun bunch of mini games done in a really cool way. There isn't much to it from it being a bunch of mini games but it teaches you different cheat techniques and can be pretty challenging if you don't know what you're doing, but its a really fun time and very satisfying when you successfully pull off a manoeuvre. Overall, Card Shark is a really fun and interesting experience that will put your cheating skills to the test
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Card Shark is a game where placing the right cards in the right hands is all that matters, it will teach how to manipulate cards and you have to be quick and precise enough to not be noticed.The interesting things being that it actually teaches you how to perform real tricks in a way that'll make you understand how they work in real life, leaving you able to master these tricks yourself.Early, the game teaches you more techniques and as you progress, it mixes them up to show you how they can interact together while adding an occasional new trick, the story features a few trick scenarios where everything doesn't happen the way it was meant to and you have to change your way of cheating on the spot.The story is interesting and is supported by great art depicting the locations visited.Card shark is one of a kind and I would easily recommend it if you are interested in card tricks, its setting or simply want to try something different.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic, well paced story with all sorts of surprises, packed to the brim with so many sleight of hand tricks and stacking techniques, you're always learning something new without being overwhelmed.  Teaches you bit by bit, but adds complexities and twists just interesting enough to keep you on your toes.  Highly recommend playing with a controller for the extra little input touches the game provides.  Love the art, sound, and music choices.  One of the best games I've played in years!

_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Card Shark is a wonderful, story-driven game about scamming people.This game makes you feel like a total mastermind as you learn just about every way to cheat at a simple game of cards. You use your tricks and the wit of your partner across the countryside to get rich, and investigate a mysterious scandal about the king of France.+ Fun and challenging gameplay+ Mysterious and fun storytelling+ Great visual and audio design- Very linear, low replayability- The amount of money you gain affects little to nothing besides gambling buy-ins. (It's more of a health bar than a resource. You can also donate your money to charity, but as far as I can tell doing so doesn't do anything)
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: I always enjoy seeing developers improve their craft. You can see how it's the same devs as Reigns, but that it's increased in scope and competency in every imaginable way. The story of this game is fun, the characters are intriguing, and they really get a lot of mileage out of building on certain mechanics. This game's presentation is top notch, and it makes the transition between gameplay and cutscene feel seamless.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Played on a  with a gamepad at standard difficulty around 10 hours.I have never been so invested in playing a set of mini-games as a core mechanic.  What I really like is that the tricks (or set of mini-games) are non-trivial and requires concentration, counting backwards and so much practice to perform fast and consistently. The context of cheating adds narrative stakes as well as incentive to perform well as cheating  is risky. It is just so rewarding to learn a difficult trick, understanding it then performing it well which I think is the main appeal.For some minor points, the story is okay which provides an overarching mystery and motivation. I really appreciate the visual aesthetic as it is soothing and relaxing for long play sessions. Although it did make it harder to determine a spade from a club and heart and diamond at a glance, but I believe this is appropriate in context. Music is also okay and in context. I do have a peeve with the protagonist being mute.  Seeing the protagonist get better at writing and drawing in the journal is endearing; however, I wonder why the protagonist does not use the same talents to communicate with the other characters like carrying a notebook. Although, I like how being mute is incorporated in the story and tricks.Another peeve are the player choices which tend to have the same result but not create meaningful reactions. In this case, I would simply prefer not to have these choices, but I do see they are harmless for this game. Strangely, the game does offer some semblance of meaningful choice via gameplay like in the last game. That would have been better overall and I believe is a missed opportunity specially for replayability.Some other criticism or suggestions:Nonetheless, an unique game that I can strongly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting premise and great execution.How luck takes part when the trick isn't done accordingly and the lack of details related to partners actions on card customization plans appear as glimpses to a still good puzzle/strategy game; all of its beauty is rightfully disposed on the store page description.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't enjoyed a game as much as I enjoyed this one for quite some time.The art and soundtrack is fantastic and the story is well done and interesting.Characters are likable and there is a lot of fun moments and interactions. The gameplay is unique, in a good way. It is simple but at the same time engaging and feels tense when it needs to.Even if the gameplay can be a bit repetitive or simple, the game is just long enough for the charm to never really wear off.I can't do anything but recommend this game to anyone who thinks it sounds interesting and there is a demo for it, a rarity these days.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Love the story, art style, and music. Game play can get pretty challenging later in the game as tricks start to stack on top of other tricks, but game has lots of hints and ways to help you out. If you are worried about it just being QTE's, it's not that. QTEs would just require you to press buttons at the correct time. This requires you to remember things you have seen or done previously, and make quick (albeit simple) calculations to ensure you make the right choice.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: I usually try to respect developers' intentions for the difficulty setting of a game, and play on whatever is recommended, but this game is SO MUCH more enjoyable when you put it on the easiest difficulty and turn on hints...because it is still very challenging even at the lowest difficulty! I love a game with a very specific setting, a unique art style, and funky mechanics, so this checks a ton of boxes for me (and may be an all-time favorite).
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Put simply, this game is a work of art. The ambiance of 17th-century French aristocracy, the art style, the simple mechanics and fluid storyline all work together to create a story-driven game inspired by historical events to keep one enthralled for hours at a time. The card cheating techniques shown in this game are real, and can be learned IRL by experts and laymen alike. The story itself has all the intrigue and mystery of any swashbuckling tale of the place and period, and as one who enjoyed Dumas' "The Three Musketeers," the only gripe I have is that I wish there were more content.The developers also put out videos on youtube explaining the techniques in this game in detail, which is just fantastic. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend this game if you're fond of memory games/puzzles! I thought the difficulty level was perfect-- practicing some tricks enough to get them right took just long enough to be supremely satisfying, without taking long enough to start getting frustrating. The characters and plot were a lot of fun, and overall it captured the exact vibe and cool gameplay that I was looking forward to after seeing the trailer. Also, the art and music are both wonderful!
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: When I first saw this game, I didn't think anything of it, but then I learned that the game was about cheating in card games and I fell in love with that idea, plus it was published by devolver digital so it's a win win.Surprising amount of depth to the cheating tricks and the way it's implemented with the controller actually feels like you're pulling a sick trick, I really enjoyed the different ways to use the controller for the tricks, it's clear the developer put all the effort and thought into this obviously since it's the main core of the game, but it's still impressive what was accomplished.I really love the art style and it's setting, it really fits with the whole cheating at card games story, and the animations where super charming, specifically the hand animations, as an animator I really enjoy looking at the way the characters move and fiddle with the cards.The story was also very good, full of twists and turns, I kinda screwed the ending but thankfully the game has replay value on the choices you can take thoughout the story, so I'm probably gonna play it again!I'd deffinetly recommend this game, I think it's a 8/10 for me, maybe a 9
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing story and unique gameplay!Reading some other reviews, I agree that a controller is HIGHLY recommended, and I wish you could load save files instead of starting the game over once you finish, but those cons are nothing compared to how great of an experience this game was. The story has great twists that keep you hooked, the levels keep a balance of old cheats and new tricks to make sure the game doesn't feel repetitive, all while the music and art make this game beautiful. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Played this game on the Steam Deck and it ran flawlessly. Really unique game with an interesting premise. I give the developers credit for creativity.The entire game is centered around learning different techniques to cheat at cards. The techniques start off fairly simple and progressively get more and more complicated.The art style was great and the story keeps you engaged.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: A fun collection of Warioware or Cooking Mama esc microgames that surround themselves with a fun and interesting story. The ambiance set forth in the game is really well done, from the music to the art style, the feel of the game works incredibly well. Unfortunately it is a little hindered by one or two late game tutorials being overly wordy and ending up confusing, and controls on kbm being fickle to sometimes feeling nonfunctional. Might be something you might want to dodge if you're not willing to put up with some frustrations along the way on kbm, but likely completely avoidable with a gamepad.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game! The narrative was engaging enough, and the visual style is just great.The gameplay seems like it shouldn't be much fun - it teaches you quicktime events, and then you perform them. Where's the fun in that?But actually because they teach you real sleight of hand, and because they're quite complex, it's genuinely fun. You feel like you're learning how to actually be a card shark, and that you're rewarded for paying attention and understanding the mechanics.Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Great, innovative concept. Art is amazing, on the level of Pentiment. One complaint is that there are lots of scams and playing this over multiple days, you tend to forget some mechanics. There are descriptions of each scam you can reread, but it would be nice if the mechanics were explained there too.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting game with a unique art style and wonderful accompanying soundtrack. The story was extremely compelling and I was hooked. Gameplay is essentially a bunch of quick time events prompted or unprompted (being a card shuffle you need to execute). There was a balanced learning curve although some instructions and tutorials were not comprehensive. This is a game you probably want to finish in one sitting if not you would probably forget the tricks. I had the most fun near the end game where the tricks were no longer being spoonfed to you and you had to figure it out for yourself. Unfortunately, this game has little replay value. When you die in this game, you can cheat death and retry...as expected of a narrative game. But during the last round, I wanted to see the different endings so I just let myself get caught with the intention to die, thinking I will get another try (as the game teaches you). Nope. Permadeath, your save is gone, start from the beginning. More story than game.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent story-driven experience. Like some of the best historical fiction, Card Shark starts with fictional characters and layers in familiar historical faces as feels appropriate. It's obviously well-researched and well-executed, but it's also unafraid to be anachronistic when the situation calls for it. The plot itself is an awesomely paced mystery with just the right amount of twists. I was kicking myself by the end of the game because a lot of them are basically in plain sight.The gameplay is, essentially, a collection of QTEs. Under the tutelage of the Comte de Saint-Germain, you infiltrate high society by traveling to gambling dens and executing a new scheme in every location. You're allowed time to rehearse each con's details, but with the caveat that you have to remember and execute them quickly enough to avoid suspicion once you're actually at the gambling table. Sometimes complicating factors are thrown in mid-scheme, and you have to adjust plans on the fly. It's a simple loop, but it never overstays its welcome (owing to the great writing).If you like Barry Lyndon, cheating, cross-dressing, and/or QTEs, you'll like Card Shark. Highly recommended, this is one of my top games of 2022.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting concept/innovative gameplay.The whole game revolves around learning these card tricks (which become more complex as the game goes on) and gambling on your ability to repeat these tricks during the cons.There isn't really any other gameplay apart from that, but that basic premise combined with the game's story and style make it an enjoyable time. It's not the type of game i'd recommend to everyone, but if you're interested in the theme I can say this definitely delivers.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: The Steam description really does not do this game justice, as the gameplay boils down to performing quick time events to cheat at cards. The story is by no means a masterpiece, but the dialogue was interesting enough to keep me invested during my playthrough. Overall, Card Shark was an enjoyable experience that I'd recommend whenever it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is simply a few swiping and clicking motions, with lots of reading in between. The story is a little captivating, but the ending is unsatisfying.Why do I recommend this? If you're even the slightest bit interested in card mechanics or even history (there are countless references for you to find), you will be entertained by this game. But what makes it is both the art and the soundtrack. They are both flawless. The art is simplistic, purposely older-styled, with glowy lighting effects that are eye candy. The music, even if you don't like classical, completes each scene and makes this game something special.All in all, definitely try this one if the topic or setting interests you. Even if not--you still probably won't be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Exceptionally elegant game, simple implementation that gives rise to a very good experienceThe Artstyle and music is also beautiful, and fully immerses you into the worldIt introduces you to the world of cheating in card games and games in general, by requiring you to engage in it as a series of minigames, all strongly integrated inside a meaningful story you want to see the unfoldA true Gem that is worth experiencing
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a fun game with an interesting story, but the gameplay does become bloated after a while. There were multiple times where I was arrested because the game wanted me to participate in a mechanic that I was not exposed to before needing to use it. Despite this, the game does still feel nice to play, especially on controller, and the story has interesting story beats and twists that keep the player engaged, and a very intuitive progression system with the number of tricks left to learn before the conclusion.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really unique and beautiful. The art style is outstanding and everything in the world feels super immersive to the theme they went for. The gameplay is pretty fun, especially at the beginning when you are learning how it all works. It keeps a good pace of new skills to keep it from getting too hard or too boring, however near the end it gets VERY fast. The story, the skills and the character progressive goes from 0 to 100 super fast and then the game is over. It feels like there was almost a cut for time. The game is pretty short, I finished it in one day, but I still thought it was enjoyable and worth it. SOME OF THE ACHIEVEMENTS ARE BUGGED AND UNATTAINABLE...which really sucks when you spend a while playthrough trying to get them and then get *nothing*...Its not game of the year, but its a really unique game that I have never seen before and probably won't see again. Beautiful art, fun for what it is. Definitely worth a play.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark

_childDocuments_.review: A really unique game, full of great music, history, and card tricks. The last chapter ramps up the difficulty significantly. I failed it several times while not failing many other times before it.One minor issue that I had - I left for vacation while near the end of this game. I came back to it and forgot some of the moves. There is a guide to help you, but I would recommend playing this short game in a sitting or two.
_childDocuments_.name: Card Shark
