_childDocuments_.review: Suppose that you were sitting down at this table. The napkins are in front of you, which napkin would you take? The one on your ‘left’? Or the one on your ‘right’? The one on your left side? Or the one on your right side? Usually you would take the one on your left side. That is ‘correct’ too. But in a larger sense on society, that is wrong. Perhaps I could even substitute ‘society’ with the ‘Universe’. The correct answer is that ‘It is determined by the one who takes his or her own napkin first.’  If the first one takes the napkin to their right, then there’s no choice but for others to also take the ‘right’ napkin. The same goes for the left. Everyone else will take the napkin to their left, because they have no other option. This is ‘society’... Who are the ones that determine the price of land first? There must have been someone who determined the value of money, first. The size of the rails on a train track? The magnitude of electricity? Laws and Regulations? Who was the first to determine these things? Did we all do it, because this is a Republic? Or was it Arbitrary? NO! The one who took the napkin first determined all of these things! The rules of this world are determined by that same principle of ‘right or left?’! In a Society like this table, a state of equilibrium, once one makes the first move, everyone must follow! In every era, this World has been operating by this napkin principle. And the one who ‘takes the napkin first’ must be someone who is respected by all. It’s not that anyone can fulfill this role... Those that are despotic or unworthy will be scorned. And those are the ‘losers’. In the case of this table, the ‘eldest’ or the ‘Master of the party’ will take the napkin first... Because everyone ‘respects’ those individuals.

_childDocuments_.review: JoJo's All-Star Battle R is a clear improvement of the PS3 original, adding a few new characters (mostly ones we've seen in Eyes of Heaven before), making changes to every character and polishing up the experience.Every piece of voicework has been redone, not only for characters that previously didn't have established anime voices, but also for characters that have had the same voice actors before and it's a treat. While there are certainly a handful of lines that fall flat with the new voice acting, such as Funny Valentine's iconic "Dojyaaa~~n!", most voice lines are brutally better compared to the PS3 original, which is most notable with the line delivery for Jotaro, whose performance in the original always felt really off to me. By far my favorite aspect about the new voice acting is that Joseph's "Your next line" skill now features the voice actor actually imitating the voices of other characters. Additionally textures and models were edited where applicable to make characters and stands more closely resemble the anime adaptation, while still retaining design aspects that are closer to the original manga.The new assists mechanic helps the game feel fresh, the new method for unlocking cosmetics is far better compared to the original version and the new All Star-Battle mode feels like a great replacement for the original game's lacking story mode, with the non-canon fights being a treat to see for fans of the series.There are quite a few strange decisions that were made though. For example, a lot of graphical elements and designs weren't updated to match the anime adaptation, which leads to a strange mismatch of styles. Characters will use their anime designs during battle and then will use cut-ins with their designs from the original version of the game. Most strange is Jotaro 4, who uses his first outfit out of the 3 he had during the events of DiU, with none of the other outfits being unlockable, even though the third outfit was already used in Eyes of Heaven. Yet the game's cut-ins and other UI elements will still depict him wearing the outfit used in EoH. Stages have not had their designs updated, nor has the Ripple, so while the anime adaptation will show the Ripple as yellow/orange, ASBR continues to use blue instead.To everyone's surprise (somehow), this licensed Anime game doesn't have good netcode. I honestly don't believe anyone should be surprised or shocked by this, considering this is the kind of game I buy because I like JoJo's and not because I want to play the next big fighting game and get on some online leaderboards, but seeing as not everyone is the same person as me, it is definitely worth noting for those who do care about playing online and/or competitively.buy if you like funni jojoe, otherwise its still a fun game but i'd recommend Heritage For the Future over it any day if you're moreso just interested in playing a fighting game

_childDocuments_.review: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: All-Star Battle Royale (ASBR) is a fighting game that brilliantly captures the essence and excitement of Hirohiko Araki's beloved manga and anime series. As a die-hard JoJo fan, I can confidently say that this game is a must-have for any enthusiast of the Joestar bloodline and their extraordinary Stands.First and foremost, ASBR is a visual marvel. The character models are stunningly faithful to Araki's iconic art style, bringing the vibrant and eccentric world of JoJo to life. Each character is painstakingly detailed, showcasing their unique abilities, fashion choices, and signature poses. The attention to detail extends to the stages as well, which are brimming with references and easter eggs that will delight fans.The gameplay mechanics in ASBR are a joy to master. The Stand system, which allows characters to summon their supernatural partners, adds a layer of complexity and strategy to the battles. The variety of moves, combos, and special attacks perfectly capture the over-the-top nature of the series. Pulling off flashy and devastating attacks with your favorite characters feels incredibly satisfying and true to the source material.The roster of playable characters in ASBR is extensive and diverse, featuring fan-favorites from various story arcs. Whether you prefer the stoic Jotaro Kujo, the flamboyant Dio Brando, or the unpredictable Josuke Higashikata, there's a character to suit every playstyle and preference. Each fighter feels distinct, with their own set of abilities and Stand powers, ensuring that every battle is a fresh and thrilling experience.The attention to detail in recreating iconic moments from the JoJo series is commendable. From the dramatic poses to the intense battle quotes, ASBR captures the spirit and personality of the characters with utmost care. The game's story mode faithfully follows key story arcs, allowing players to relive their favorite moments and unravel the enigmatic Joestar legacy.Multiplayer in ASBR is an absolute blast. Whether you're engaging in local versus matches with friends or testing your skills online, the competitive nature of the game shines through. The online matchmaking is smooth and offers a chance to pit your skills against players from around the world, adding a layer of excitement and unpredictability to the experience.Finally, the game's soundtrack deserves a special mention. ASBR features an array of catchy tunes that perfectly complement the high-energy battles and dramatic moments. From the iconic "Stand Proud" to the menacing "Dio's World," the music immerses you in the JoJo universe and elevates the overall experience.In conclusion, JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: All-Star Battle Royale is a must-play for any JoJo fan and fighting game enthusiast. With its stunning visuals, engaging gameplay mechanics, diverse character roster, and faithful representation of the series, ASBR stands tall as a love letter to the Joestar lineage. Prepare to unleash your Stand's true potential and engage in epic battles that will leave you craving for more. JoJo fans, rejoice! The ultimate showdown awaits.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game, but only if you're a big JoJo fan who loves fighting games or wants to get into them. While the core fighting gameplay is extremely fun, unique, and satisfying in a way few other fighting games are, modern FGs are ultimately made worthwhile by their online, which this game struggles with. Though I think some people overstate how bad the netcode really is, but it's certainly not good. I can get stable matches with comfortable connections most of the time, but when it's bad, it's BAD. Even if rollback isn't possible for this game like the devs have stated, I'm skeptical they even tried making any improvements to the online mode, considering it's unchanged from the original. No lobbies or spectator mode, no rematching in Ranked, no penalty for disconnects/ragequits, no way to filter opponents by connection, and sometimes the game just won't put you into a match or disconnects during the loading screen. All these issues make the lack of rollback sting more, and aren't things we should still be dealing with in a fighting game. The singleplayer modes are mostly just fun distractions that all boil down to CPU battles with some unique character interactions. The ability to customize your characters' taunts, quotes, and victory poses is nice, and the game has a lot of additional costumes for characters that all reference the series. Though, I have to wonder why none of the Eyes of Heaven original costumes were ported over for vanilla ASB characters who got new costumes in that game. The roster is huge, but the lack of part 8 characters also stands out and was personally very disappointing. Pretty great game if you're a JoJo fan, and I'm sure general fighting game fans can also get something out of it, but the online holds it back from being a truly great fighting game everyone will keep coming back to. Hopefully CC2 makes some improvements in the future, but I'm not holding my breath.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely fun for JoJo fans, but for someone looking for a deep and complex fighting game, this one likely isn't for you. It's main appeal is the aesthetics, and it does that very well, but it's kind of shallow when it comes to actual gameplay.I play a lot of Tekken, so going from that to this game, the movement feels very stiff, and the movesets just feel so limited. I do appreciate the special attack variations, but the use for each move and it's variants feels so specific, as if they are only meant to be used for one particular thing. In my opinion, this limits creativity, an issue that I feel is quite common in this game.As previously stated, however, it is fun for someone who is playing it more for the JoJo aspect rather than for the technical aspect. I appreciate how faithfully all the characters were portrayed, and how not everything is just a basic damaging super, such as Diavolo's moveset being more evasion and counter-based rather than just offense.I only do not recommend this game because I enjoy the more mechanical side of a fighting game, which i have to say I'm a little disappointed with. However, if you don't care about that, you may find enjoyment here.

If you are looking for a fun time to fight with your favourite JoJo characters against each other (even in Online mode with friends (if you have any)) then this is a reccomendation.But if you are a fan of fighting games and are looking for a mechanically complex one to master, maby look at Tekken, Street fighter, Guilty Gear etc... they will have more Options then this game has and in my opinion are more interesting to play.

The rules of this world are determined by that same principle of ‘right or left?’! In a Society like this table, a state of equilibrium, once one makes the first move, everyone must follow! _childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, the online is not what you hope for when it comes to a modern fighter; however, JJBA ASBR is one of the best fighting games I've had the luxury of playing as of recent. The cool factor of the JoJo IP is great, and the gameplay is definitely good at low levels for some easy fun. I believe this games shines when you decide to delve in a little bit into its combo system. Being able to cancel from modes to extend combos allows players to get the most out of characters' movesets. The combos aren't incredibly excessive in varied inputs if you choose, but you can really see the growth and achievement that comes with the game. Every character manages to hold distinction in their playstyle which is a large achievement on a roster of this magnitude. Another point that is important to get across is that this is not your standard anime arena fighter. Not Storm 4 (Naruto), not Hinokami Chronicles (DS), and not A Hero Nobody Knows (OPM) which I view as a good thing. This 2.5D fighter style that is championed by games like Tekken does a great job expressing the value of the game's neutral, while giving some characters wacky ways to engage that is common in the anime fighter scene. Whether you are from Guilty Gear or Street Fighter alike, this game is an interesting step outside of your comfort zone that I hope you are likely to enjoy. Definitely a labor of love that I hope will receive more support as time marches on.

_childDocuments_.review: Do NOT buy this game. That is my sincere review.I have bought this game three times - I imported the original JP PS3 release, I bought the localised PS3 release and I have now bought this version.Although they have added new characters and assists to this game mode, it feels more empty than the PS3 releases. They removed any sort of progression and replaced it with a "medals" system that allows you to unlock outfits but means you just have to grind fights all day without mixing it up in any way.The previous story mode has been replaced with ASB mode, which is essentially story mode without the story. The gameplay is the same - secret missions give you unlocks - but it feels artificial. Even more so since most of them you can't use assists, one of the new features added. I will say the new characters are good, Speedwagon, Diego etc all play well and feel natural. But this doesn't make up for the lack of any other improvements.The biggest problem right now is online play. It's truly awful. Games are all laggy with no rollback, the characters are massively unbalanced and 70% of the time queuing for a match will end with "Session lost" or "Session is full" (none of this has changed since the PS3 release!). The games you do get in to will be janky because of the aforementioned issues which means that maybe 1/10 matches where you end up with someone on the same continent of you will be playable. Even then, there are a number of bugs such as infinite combos that make it a truly unfun experience (and these are _actually_ infinites, not just combo-breaking).The game has ranked matching that you are forced to play to unlock certain content, such as outfits. This appears to have no region or rank match-making (or if it does is too lax) and suffers exactly the same issues. The worst issue, however, is that "easy-beat" combos are enabled by default, and there is no way to disable it for your opponent. This means that you can get in to a match with players who just have to hit one button to do a full combo, and with broken characters this will end up with you losing half your HP in one chance. If your assist is on cooldown you have no recourse.Do not buy this game. Wait until a) it is patched to fix the above issues and b) it is 75% off. Ignore all the meme reviews like "is this a JoJo reference?!" and consider it seriously - You will _not_ enjoy playing the game in it's current state.

Online matches can be smooth sometimes but are often just a little bit off, or just outright unplayable.In addition, some new characters like Jotaro 4 and the aforementioned Diego just feel like afterthoughts, having limited tools and a scattered arsenal.It's important to note that this game is pretty much a love letter to JoJo and Araki's work at large, so you'll need to be familiar with the series to truly appreciate what it has to offer.Nevertheless, despite all I've just said, this game could become something great and honestly the singleplayer is a fun enough time killer to enjoy it. _childDocuments_.review: TO ANYONE HAVING TROUBLE WITH THIS GAME FREEZING OR CRASHING: make sure it is running from your graphics card and not integrated graphics. A significant number of games from this particular time, even re-releases, often still have the problem of not automatically using your GPU. This leads to freezing and crashes, and it's hard to find anyone else who has this problem and talks about it. You can go into your control panel for the graphics card and set up a rule for the specific game or application.This is a good, solid game, and much improved from the original release. I got this game when it was originally released for PS3, and I imported it. It was a little stiff, but it was still a good, solid fighter and a fun enough game for me to even get online -- which was often remarkable for even working, since I was usually connecting to Japanese servers -- and play extensively to unlock various costumes and looks for the characters.I'm so glad to see it on PC, and really looking fantastic. It is visually gorgeous and very true to the feeling of the series. It looks like the art from the comics, which I think is a very good choice for the game. Games that are stylized age better, in my opinion, and this remastering effort allowed them to make the visuals just burst forth even more beautifully. It's significantly a better game than it was, in pretty much every way I've seen so far.It plays well, you can change the difficulty levels on things and it actually has an effect (which is a big thing for me), it has a more accessible mode that you can optionally turn on or off, and it has a lot of other features that make it more engaging to newcomers and people who don't play a lot of fighting games. However, anyone who wants a challenge can get one, and there's a lot to do in the All-Star Battle Mode. I will say that sometimes, the CPU seems to cheat, and that can be really frustrating. This happens mostly with higher-level difficulty battles, but these are also where you're supposed to unlock certain parts of the game, which I don't like. If you are going to have unlockables, don't make it so that most people will never even be able to enjoy them. That's not giving me what I paid for.One of the best parts of the game is its customization. You can put the characters in a variety of costumes, you can get them to use specific taunts and victory lines, and you can choose from a range of poses too. There's so much that you can do to make this your own personal Jojo adventure, and that is something I especially love about it. Too often anymore, fighting games aren't that customizable, and there isn't a great feeling of personal distinction in most. I like that this game showcases its ability for uniqueness.Overall, it's a great game for any Jojo fan, and it is one of the more solidly enjoyable anime/manga-based fighters out there. Just be sure you get it running on your graphics card, because it can give you a frustrating time if you're not. Once you get started with this game, you're not going to want to put it down. It's so easy to lose track of time and lose yourself in the weird, interesting characters and bizarre, surreal landscapes, the bold fashions, and the soundtrack.It's also got hilarious tongue-in-cheek bits like Funny Valentine saying "Filthy acts, done at a reasonable price." They knew what they were doing. And Joseph shouting "OH MY GOD!" Of course.Get it, on sale or otherwise, depending on how much you like Jojo.

_childDocuments_.review: Jojo's Bizarre Adventure All Star Battle R is a fine game (even if the title is a bit lengthy to write out). I enjoy the combo system and really do enjoy learning how to optimize a few characters. Some of the roster does feel a bit samey but that's understandable due to the pure size of the roster. There's even a fair bit of content to play single player which is always appreciated.Now then, you might be wondering why I would not recommend it then. It's because it genuinely has some of the worst online I have ever played with. Mind you, my internet isn't bad, I can play a wide majority of other games with little to no lag at all, but that's just not the case with this game. Sometimes you will get matches with good connection and you can actually have fun. But other times you'll be disconnected before the match even starts, be disconnected mid match, or face input delay so bad that you might as well be guessing what the opponent might do at all times. It is borderline unplayable online. There is stuff to do offline yes, but this is a fighting game, you are going to want to fight other people online and if the netcode isn't up to par then it could take a lot of enjoyment out of the game. I want to love this game, I really do. It's a pretty nice Jojo fighting game with a fair bit of customization and a fun fight system. But due to the fact that you'll wanna be playing this game online with friends, I would not recommend it. Hopefully they fix the online issues, and hell, add rollback netcode. Cause if the online doesn't get better, then this game will be dead within the month.If you really want this game and have irl friends to play it with though, pick it up on Xbox or PlayStation instead, I can't imagine playing this on only one computer monitor would be fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This is pretty much everything I wanted out of a JoJo's Bizarre Adventure game. The only things missing are an actual story mode and a functioning online matchmaking system. I managed to play for almost 50 hours in my quest to get the 100% completion. It's a fun game. There's an incredible variety of characters to pick, all with different color palettes and costumes to choose from. They have some of the most iconic costumes... from Josuke's red sweater look from Volume 42 to Dio's shadowy-faced shirtless appearance. There are even some costumes solely created for this specific game, although they're essentially just base versions with special patterns on them. All Star mode is essentially the 'story' mode and all it offers are a set amount of battles. There are 'secret' (they're quite visible and have no unlock conditions) stages where, for example, Jonathan (Part 1) faces off against Giorno (Part 5) and so on. It adds a nice touch to the game and basically goes down the same way it did in Eyes of Heaven with just a few words traded between characters that never meet each other in the mainline canon. Online matchmaking is just as garbage as everyone says it is. You'll likely be queued for anywhere from 5 to 15 minutes to find a game in Ranked. Once you finally get in, the game is so outrageously choppy that it's a miracle Bandai's servers are even intact. If you start destroying your opponent, they will quite literally disconnect and, for whatever strange reason, the match won't register and you do nothing but waste time. I honestly do not know why they have an achievement for ranking up and one for playing 100 battles... The game really makes you feel like Father Pucci witnessing a miracle when you finally get a game that ends properly. I don't think I'll ever see a match go down at the proper framerate without the horrendous lag Bandai imposes upon us. There are challenge modes as well. There is a Tournament Mode, 8 battle Challenge, and an Endless Mode. These all give some nice supplementary gold for Gallery purchases and can be boosted by the Harvest effect (random, I think?) for even more gold gains. The Gallery feature is quite nice, it's about what you'd expect for a fighting game. You can get 3D models to view, check out concept art, final 2D renders, listen to some of the music, play different voice lines, etc. Wish they would have included scans of the manga volume covers and some of the other art, but oh well. If you are a huge fan of JJBA and want to play as some of your favorite characters, pick the game up! Just be wary of the abysmal online matchmaking. The demo's pretty cool too and gives you a good idea of how the game plays. There's only 1 stage and 5 characters or something like that, so there's not a lot to see otherwise there.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is fun and has some interesting new modes you can do with the new characters they added. Not the biggest fan of the new assist system, but it did add some more depth that allowed for more options in the game.Although, if you want to play this game online you are in for a rough experience. Rollback netcode should have been the number one priority for this game coming out considering how much it enhances players experience and it gives them more freedom to do things in matches without suffering the restraints of having their inputs eaten by latency issues. Even doing simple things like combos links is a pain on online due to how barebones the delay netcode is.I can't recommend this game in good conscience. Delay netcode is the one thing slowly killing this game and I hope the community puts more effort into bringing those issues forward to Bandai Namco. As both a Jojo fan and Fighting game player this game deserves way more love than it has. There's still a batch of content coming out for DLC, but that won't matter if the online enviroment for this game is poor.

_childDocuments_.review: Suppose that you were sitting down at this table. The napkins are in front of you, which napkin would you take? The one on your ‘left’? Or the one on your ‘right’? The one on your left side? Or the one on your right side? Usually you would take the one on your left side. That is ‘correct’ too. But in a larger sense on society, that is wrong. Perhaps I could even substitute ‘society’ with the ‘Universe’. The correct answer is that ‘It is determined by the one who takes his or her own napkin first.’ …Yes? If the first one takes the napkin to their right, then there’s no choice but for others to also take the ‘right’ napkin. The same goes for the left. Everyone else will take the napkin to their left, because they have no other option. This is ‘society’… Who are the ones that determine the price of land first? There must have been someone who determined the value of money, first. The size of the rails on a train track? The magnitude of electricity? Laws and Regulations? Who was the first to determine these things? Did we all do it, because this is a Republic? Or was it Arbitrary? NO! The one who took the napkin first determined all of these things! The rules of this world are determined by that same principle of ‘right or left?’! In a Society like this table, a state of equilibrium, once one makes the first move, everyone must follow! In every era, this World has been operating by this napkin principle. And the one who ‘takes the napkin first’ must be someone who is respected by all. It’s not that anyone can fulfill this role… Those that are despotic or unworthy will be scorned. And those are the ‘losers’. In the case of this table, the ‘eldest’ or the ‘Master of the party’ will take the napkin first… Because everyone ‘respects’ those individuals.

_childDocuments_.review: Dio Brando (Japanese: ディオ・ブランドー, Hepburn: Dio Burandō) is a fictional character and the main antagonist of the Japanese manga series JoJo's Bizarre Adventure written and illustrated by Hirohiko Araki. He is featured primarily as the main antagonist of the series' first part, Phantom Blood, appearing in the debut chapter "Dio the Invader" (侵略者ディオ, Shinryakusha Dio), published in Weekly Shōnen Jump in 1987.[1] He later returns as the main antagonist of the series' third part, Stardust Crusaders. Now solely known as DIO (ＤＩＯディオ), he is a powerful vampire and user of the time-stopping Stand named The World.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite my negative mark on this review, I will keep playing this game, however, apart from the fact it's a fighter with JJBA content which isn't common (and does have some interesting mechanics), a nice graphic style that aged just fine  and a banger of a soundtrack, I'd like to use this review as a warning for whoever is looking for a nice online fighting experience, don't get this game if that's one of your main reasons.Apart from the well known fact it lacks good netcode (delay based), the game itself isn't very smart on other online aspects either: players can get a penalty in their  "disconnected mid-match" stat count simply because the game failed to connect properly, and whoever rage quits steals the opponent's win from counting, since the game cannot recognize it as one.I hate being the person who has to say it, but it's not sci-fi to at least try to bring some quality (or literal fixes) to a messy online experience, especially in 2022. It still feels like (despite its marketing) the direction is the same as the original title, a love letter to the series, especially to Japanese fans, best played local with your friends.

I think the most amount of fun you can have from this game mostly stem from local play with some friends, because there is no delay and you can just have fun. Although there are some workarounds for a better online experience if you are looking for it.

_childDocuments_.review:
All JOJOs Unite! Fight for Your Destiny!

Jonathan Joestar, Jotaro Kujo, DIO, Jolyne Cujoh, and other characters from JoJo's Bizarre Adventure gather across multiple generations! With 50 playable characters from all arcs, you can experience popular battles from each story, and see characters from different universes interact for the first time!

This title is based on the All Star Battle fighting system that was released in 2012. The game design of JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: All Star Battle R reinvigorates the experience with adjustments to the fighting tempo and the addition of hit stops and jump dashes.

With new audio recordings from the Part 6 anime voice actors, the full atmosphere of the animated series is realized. Both fans who have played the original All Star Battle and newcomers will be able to enjoy the experience.

name: Cloud Gardens
detailed_description: Coming Soon About the Game Harness the power of nature to overgrow lo-fi scenes of urban decay and manufactured landscapes. Create small plant-covered dioramas of brutalism and beauty by planting seeds, repurposing hundreds of discarded objects and creating unique structures for nature to reclaim. Dive into a relaxing sandbox mode with no goals, or take on a multi-chapter “campaign” where the task is to strike a balance between the natural and the manufactured. Adding objects will encourage lush vegetation to grow, but each object must be covered in foliage in order to proceed. Cloud Gardens hovers somewhere in between a sandbox toy and a game with challenges. Partly a gardening simulator, partly a dystopian landscape builder, and partly a puzzle game that is both satisfying and without frustration. It is a relaxing experience that takes you from one scene to the next while encouraging creativity and coming up with your own solutions. This is a chill game where the primary goal is to delight in your own creativity. Players can download looping videos of their completed dioramas and share them with other gardeners from across the internet, and our Discord server has a lively community of gardeners. Solve organic puzzles in a serene 3D space. Create to your heart’s content in creative mode. Unlock an enormous catalogue of objects and plantlife. Share your creations. Featuring generative soundscapes by Amos Roddy, composer of Kingdom.

name: Twin Breaker: A Sacred Symbols Adventure
detailed_description: Twin Breaker: A Sacred Symbols Adventure is a story-driven brick breaking game molded in the style of ‘80s arcade classics like Arkanoid and Breakout, but with a plot, characters, and meaning! In the early 2300s, Earth is still recovering from a decades-long World War that engulfed most of the planet, except for an isolationist United States that used its power and prestige not to fight, but to reach for the stars. But when NASA’s generation ships disappear in interstellar space, only two pilots are capable of figuring out why. Featuring 40 stages, four boss fights, New Game+, multiple extra features, plenty of story and dialogue, collectibles, a rocking soundtrack, and a fun achievement system, Twin Breaker is an ode to both the past and the future. Twin Breaker's story is written by long-time media personality and podcast host Colin Moriarty. Features: 40 exciting story levels New Game+ 7 unique game modes Loads of power ups Challenging boss fights Story written by Colin Moriarty

In the early 2300s, Earth is still recovering from a decades-long World War that engulfed most of the planet, except for an isolationist United States that used its power and prestige not to fight, but to reach for the stars. But when NASA’s generation ships disappear in interstellar space, only two pilots are capable of figuring out why. Featuring 40 stages, four boss fights, New Game+, multiple extra features, plenty of story and dialogue, collectibles, a rocking soundtrack, and a fun achievement system, Twin Breaker is an ode to both the past and the future. Twin Breaker's story is written by long-time media personality and podcast host Colin Moriarty. name: INDIKA
detailed_description: FEATURES: Play a TPP adventure game that combines an imaginative story with a dark sense of humor Join a young nun Indika on her journey of self-discovery Meet the devil himself as Indika’s unlikely travel companion Explore the hidden depths of Indika’s soul while tackling unique puzzle elements Travel through surreal landscapes of Russia seen in a distorted mirror Uncover Indika's troubled past in the form of 2D pixel art mini-games MEET A NOT-SO-ORDINARY NUN INDIKA is a third-person, story-driven game set in a strange world where religious visions clash with harsh reality. It tells the story of a young nun who sets off on a journey of self-discovery with the most unusual, horn-headed companion by her side. On the outside, Indika seems to be a typical nun attempting to adjust to a difficult and monotonous monastery life. Humble and innocent in her appearance, do not be deceived as this young girl has also made a highly unlikely acquaintance—as she speaks with the devil himself. Indika’s unusual connection with the Evil One leads her on an errand beyond the safe walls of the monastery. The world she discovers can only be described as a wild combination of comedy and tragedy straight out of the novels by Dostoyevski and Bulhakov. ENJOY AN INDIE GAME WHERE EVERYTHING GOES The subjects of religion and authority are prevalent throughout Indika’s journey and she’ll be faced with many questions along the way. Guide her to find the answers one by one before she can finish her life-defining odyssey. Odd Meter is a small, independent studio formerly based in Moscow and now operating out of Kazakhstan . Its members put aesthetics at the forefront and aren’t afraid to tread the fine line of ethical norms. Their game is a great testament to that, as INDIKA constitutes an open challenge to the industry's established approach to creating video games.

_childDocuments_.review: First off if your interest in this game is based solely on the bizarre AI-inspired art of cackling nuns laughing at our earnest protagonist, you're going to be in for a bad time here.  It's something weird that doesn't really go anywhere and the same could be said for everything else 'weird' in this game.   The fact it CTD a half dozen times with a less than generous checkpoint system didn't help either.  The first hour shows a lot of promise but I'm still not sure if the game comes through on the themes it was trying to sell or perhaps I'm just not smart enough to grasp them even if it did.  The 3 hours or so runtime is a very slow burn that leads to a final 10 minutes of 'wat' to wrap things up, which certainly compliments the entire theme of .  That theme is never going to make for a thick ending but it still seemed a bit hurried all the same.  I really liked this game but I'm not entirely sure why.  The first 1/3 of the game is surreal in the best possible way and then the rest of it just feels like it's trying write a check that it no longer has the energy to cash.

_childDocuments_.review: Indika squanders the opportunity to convey a deeply personal story of the spiritual awakening of the titular nun. The hitherto under explored yet intriguing setting of an atmospheric convent and an impending road trip (which no doubt is supposed to represent the protagonist's transformative journey) devolves into navigating banal semi-urban environments and solving simple but insipid puzzles. The verbal jousts between the principal characters are sometimes interesting but mostly cliched. The game also introduces a backstory in the form of pixelated retro mini-game segments. While charming, this design choice seems jarring and at odds with the mood of the rest of the game. In summary, Indika is largely a walking simulator, built on a good story premise but let down by poor execution, which is mercifully short.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - It's unique, interesting, needs polishing, but the plot does just enough to keep you wrapped in. (and plz add more checkpoints)Long:Jesus Christ, I have no idea how I feel about this game. Some moments I feel blessed by the Holy Spirit that a refreshing, cool rush of water has beseech'd my life and there are moments where I question whether God has any course for me other than my own sin and frustration.Cutscenes look great yet running the game on ultra, 120fps, 2k and it still kinda looks like it could be ran on a Xbox 360 Slim due to the sharpness of the taa/fxaa/whatever they use on the edges of all objects. The well water portion in the beginning was almost unbearable to get through, at some points the pacing seems slow enough to piss off a donkey yet the plot grabs you at just the right time to rope you back in. The mixed game design of realism and classic indie homage is really unique and I can appreciate it, the last game I enjoyed that was akin to this factor was Nier: Automata; although they took it to another level. Ultimately, for an indie game from and indie dev in an indie genre, they've done a good job. There is some polishing needed with movement getting clunky, major clipping, texture rendering, etc. Sometimes the game looks great, sometimes it looks horrible, even with tweaking settings. I look forward to more titles from this developer.EDIT: Forgot to add, the one NEGATIVE thing about this game: the lack of checkpoints on a level. I've had to restart a few areas due to getting off/back on and there not being any checkpoints in the beginning (although some times I quit towards the end of a level unknowingly and have to start over) and it's the WORST when you have to go to the menu to change the voice language and also have to start the level over again. I like to switch between the eng/rus dialogue at times.

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA is an effective criticism of the (Orthodox) Christian doctrine that highlights its failures to help one integrate their shadow (or "inner devil"). The protagonist's active rejection of her "inner evils" as part of her core personality results in the manifestation of an autonomous "devil" that haunts her throughout her journey, often serving as her unexpected ally.The gameplay mainly consists of walking through a bleak environment and completing simple puzzles that don't require much thought. However, there are a few puzzles that use a "prayer mechanic" where the world is physically altered by "the devil" and the only way to restore the world back to normal is by praying. These puzzles require you to go from point A to point B and you cannot do so without navigating through both the altered and normal world. I wish more puzzles used similar mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: its tough for me to recommend this game for $20. theres not much to it, i fully completed the game and all achievements in just under 4 hours and the gameplay itself is nothing more than a few puzzles. the story itself is an interesting an odd look into faith based psychosis. a lot of the themes it touches on are things i think about in avenues of my own life and in that regard, its excellent. the graphics are incredible and apart from a few stuttering issues here and there i thoroughly enjoyed the playtime. all that being said, if youre like me and appreciate a weird game for what it is, i think its just worth the money. if youre asking yourself what is the point of this game, well thats exactly it. its weird and its cool and if youre okay with spending $20 for a 4 hour experience rather than a fun game; i think youll enjoy Indika.

_childDocuments_.review: A Russian realist short story steeped in Eastern Orthodox Christianity and told with ironic distance and a flair for religious parable.The physics of the nun's habit were a total delight, as well, her veil might have been as much a protagonist as she was. My assessment may not carry much weight since I don't play many high-level AAA games these days, but this was the best rendition of clothing I've seen in a video game yet. And it makes perfect sense that this is the case: you can't render religious habits poorly, especially in a Russian game about a nun who encompasses within herself most of humanity.LATER EDIT: It's interesting to compare it to  to see how the different religious worldviews translate into game design: the central concept in  is suffering. The presence of the Catholic in the world is based on that, so suffering is central and omnipresent in that game, almost to the point of parody, but not quite, the game knows very well where to stop to avoid getting there. But everything evokes anguish and misery in  you have all those faces contorted in agony, all those hideous, malformed bodies twisted with pain. Everywhere you look you see it, suffering is material in that game, almost like a second set of paints the artist is using to render those horrible tableaux of agony. The Orthodox worldview, on the other hand, is based on insignificance. Man is just an ant in God’s incomprehensible design. That's why everything is so big in the game, the buildings, the animals, the canned fish... (there's a hint of parody here as well) This is the essence of that surreal world in  it's meant to dwarf you, to make you feel small, show you how insignificant and worthless you are. Your actions are meaningless as well: you can fight all you want, nothing you do will ever amount to anything, you're just collecting points that don't have any meaning, because God can save you or doom you on a whim, there is no divine plan, no grand design that will carry you to salvation. Not in the game, at least. shows that you can redeem yourself through suffering, in  suffering is useless because, if you are insignificant, why would your suffering mean anything in that world? You're not even allowed to suffer  because suffering is indecent and only deludes you, it doesn't bring you anywhere closer to the truth.

_childDocuments_.review: An arthouse walking simulator about good and evil, faith and doubt. _childDocuments_.review: Man. What a fantastic, weird little game.The closest thing I can relate this to is oddly enough Alan Wake 2, I don't want to spoil in this review what you might encounter but Indika is just so tonally dissonant but in a *controlled* way that it gave me the same feeling the impromptu yacht rock concert did in Alan Wake 2 where it was "This shouldn't be happening but I'm so glad it is". Indika is f*cking weird as hell, it strays from pretty much every single gaming convention I can think of from the way it opens to the story it tells to the way that it tells that story and beyond. I would just like to say that I feel like... proud? Lets call it proud. I feel proud of the dev team for taking such massive chances and knocking it out of the park and I have to applaud 11bit Studios for being unafraid of publishing the weird^tmI am very much looking forward to The Alters (also 11bit) later this year, because frankly I like weird games and that just seems to be what they want to publish. The moment to moment gameplay of Indika isn't anything to write home about but the fact that this costs 25 dollars and is capable of this level of presentation and graphical fidelity is absurd. I mean seriously, 2024 is the year of the indie but good god, they're (AAA studios) already dead.The voice acting, the facial animations, the visuals, all of it is just packaged together in this phenomenally oddball game with such an oddball story that will both make you squirm and hide behind your eyes at a few points but you can't help peeking out past your fingers. What a ride. I knew more or less from the demo I was going to love this and it did pretty much every single thing I didn't expect and then some. It was subverting my expectations without being annoying about it and it was overall, just absurdly fun to experience. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game!The environment is eye candy the whole way through, and feels very dream-like. Many buildings are absurdly massive in scale, or sinking lopsided into the earth. You can be in the coldest, grimiest place and still find little shrines to pray at. There's good exploration to be had, and it's usually pretty obvious which way will take you forward and which will lead you to the optional collectibles. Each area also has a bench to find, which will treat you to a handful of screenshot-worthy vistas.The puzzles can be pretty unique. Deceptively simple, but fun to get to the "A-ha!" moment all the same. There is a lot of pushing boxes and climbing ledges like in other narrative puzzle adventures, but even those sections usually feel different from each other by tone or by a giant, weird thing to look at while you do it. The pixelated minigame sections act as nice breathers after heavy moments in the story. Pacing is great in both story and gameplay, and I never felt like I was doing something too samey for too long.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a ton of promise, but it often fails to deliver. While the voice acting, graphics and cut scenes are all very well done, those high points are undercut with uninspired and uninteresting gameplay. There are two puzzles that I thought were quite interesting and fitting for the style of game, but the majority are too simple and tedious. And for the parts where you need to run away or ride the motor bike, the movement is incredibly clunky. It feels like these parts were afterthoughts, being shoehorned into the game. They weren't fun to play and felt disjointed with the connecting cut scenes. The redeeming qualities are the philosophical discussions between the main character and the narrator, and the devilish humor sprinkled throughout. I was able to complete the game in just 4 hours from start to finish without rushing through it. The game is missing the depth and polish. 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: 8/10Story:Indika places you in an alternate and sometimes very bizarre timeline in 19th century Russia as young nun full of guilt and self-doubt, on a journey that questions general faith and morality, with a healthy mix of dark humor and riveting storytelling. Surface level, this game seems very strange and all over the place. However, as you begin to read between the lines and look at everything more critically, there is actually a very compelling and thought-provoking narrative about organized religion, trauma, and personal spirituality as an individual.Visuals: Being developed in Unreal Engine 5, the visuals are absolutely gorgeous. While Indika is obviously not the most saturated/colorful game out there and can look somewhat bland in certain areas, the graphics absolutely stand on their own, and I personally think the overall colorless and cold vibe adds to the themes of the story perfectly subtly. Although, this statement gets flipped on its head during the short, but very bright and story-rich pixel levels that detail Indika's life prior to becoming a nun. Through lighthearted and nostalgic visuals, the dark underlying story serves as a perfect contrast. Music/Sound Design:The music in Indika is satisfactory. Throughout the main story, I consistently felt that the music was fitting and adequately composed across each level, but there was never a moment where I found myself genuinely "WOW'd" while listening. In my opinion, the best way to describe the music would be, "good, not great."I would argue that the general sound design is slightly above the soundtrack in regard to quality. The most obvious example of this is the crunch of snow as you walk/run around, but even the sound of collecting coins, the pixel art levels, water splashing, etc. all sound very satisfying to hear.Gameplay: The gameplay of Indika starts off slowly with walking simulator vibes, but pretty quickly jumps into the compelling narrative with support from other gameplay like puzzles, chase sequences, and other pretty simple minigames. I 100% believe that this is the games weakest feature. It's easy to write off the average gameplay as being average just because of the game being a linear, narrative-focused experience, and while I will usually defend this point, I do believe that the gameplay needed more time in the oven or at the very least more interactivity. Even with the variety of different gameplay styles, the physical progression felt pretty uninteresting. As uninteresting as most of the gameplay may have been though, no sequence overstays its welcome or becomes a chore to complete. The price point can definitely be a point of contention in regard to the gameplay. Regardless of how good or how bad both the narrative and the gameplay may be, this is a very short game. I saw a few claims that Indika can be beaten in 5-6 hours, but I personally finished the game in around 3.5 hours and 100% it in 7, and I am by no means a speedrunner. You should definitely take this into consideration when contemplating purchasing. World:The linear narrative being told in Indika doesn't allow for much large-scale world building, but this definitely is in the games favor. Each level has a commonly very obvious "correct" path, but still allows for some minor exploration within certain intimate yet detailed locations. I also feel that the way the story is told allows for the game to present vastly different environments between each of the levels without them feeling jarring or immersion-breaking. I feel like each map was appropriately sized for the scale of the experience.TL;DR:Indika is a very compelling, but short narrative focused game with an especially intriguing story, world design, and audio. In contrast, the gameplay while varied, is not very engaging or overtly entertaining, and is a rather short experience overall. Despite both the story not being the longest tale to come out this year and the gameplay being generally underwhelming, I think the story is absolutely one worth playing through. The pros do outweigh the cons. As for the price point, that's for everyone to individually decide, but I feel content with my purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great and really evocative. I think it does a lot to push games into more of a film medium, using the tech we have today and a sharp eye for cinematography to deliver a uniquely uncanny experience. Yet, I just wish they pushed it further. Without spoilers, the story just ends. It's one of those stories where I think it's asking the audience to think about the concepts discussed - the false reality of religion, the promises that it's mythology can never keep - but I was just looking for that last gut punch. Anyway, I hope these developers get a second chance at a game like this. The strange confluence of ideas comes together really well when connected to the primary themes, and I would want to experience something else like this game where the concept gets expanded upon even further.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a narrative game that forces you to challenge your own perceptions, not just those of the titular character, but also those of you the player. I'm going to have to keep it vague to avoid spoilers, but this is clearly a narrative-first title and that is what you should expect - gamedesign suited to telling that narrative - and for what it's worth I think the game succeeds here. The team have made the right design choices for the story they are trying to tell.As for visuals, they are stark - but this is by design and the things you see become more and more warped as you progress. I did not expect to see lake-fish the size of humpback whales strung up by their tails, for example. Overall I would recommend it if you like narrative games and especially if you're interested in a bit of history as it's quite interesting to see this take on religion and dogma in 19th century Russia.

_childDocuments_.review: "INDIKA" immerses players in a hauntingly beautiful world where spirituality and surrealism intertwine, offering a unique narrative-driven experience. Developed as a third-person adventure, the game unveils a tale centered around Indika, a young nun grappling with the clash between her religious upbringing and the unsettling visions that plague her.The narrative unfolds against the backdrop of a mysterious and sometimes foreboding environment, where the line between divine revelation and haunting hallucination blurs. This juxtaposition sets the stage for a journey of self-discovery that challenges Indika's perceptions of faith, reality, and her own identity.At its core, "INDIKA" shines in its storytelling. The protagonist's unlikely companion, a horn-headed figure presumed to be the devil, adds layers of intrigue and moral complexity to the narrative. Their relationship evolves as they navigate through a world where every encounter and decision carries weighty consequences.Visually, the game captivates with its atmospheric design and art direction, effectively conveying the eerie ambiance of its setting. From serene monastery interiors to ethereal dreamscapes and unsettling visions, each environment is crafted to evoke emotions ranging from awe to apprehension.The soundtrack of "INDIKA" deserves special mention for its ability to enhance the game's emotional resonance. Composed to underscore moments of introspection, revelation, and uncertainty, the music reinforces the game's thematic depth.Overall, "INDIKA" distinguishes itself as a thought-provoking journey into the psyche of its protagonist, exploring themes of faith, temptation, and the blurred boundaries between good and evil. Its compelling narrative, coupled with atmospheric visuals and a haunting soundtrack, makes it a standout experience for players seeking a deeper, introspective gaming adventure.For those intrigued by storytelling that challenges conventions and explores moral ambiguity, "INDIKA" offers a memorable and evocative journey worth embarking upon.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Is it a criticism of the Catholic religion?  Maybe.  If it is it still VERY respectful of the faith.  The game is art, there's no other real way to explain it. _childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: My spoil free summary is, imagine a Russian novelist flirting with Suda 51.While by and large a walking simulator, Indika has some decent and clever puzzles, some mini games, and some downright creative settings. My personal favorite puzzles were the ones where Indika has to use the unique aspects of a hallucination, such as her frustrations shattering the world, and her penitence repairing it, or a portal-esque Escher room with seeingly shifting gravity. The retro memory bits do eventually pay off, but until they do it really does feel like a gimmick. Thankfully, it really does pay off in the end.While there is a dark humor to Indika's surreal setting, the focus is largely on deconstructing choices, decisions, and the nature of free will. I found myself impressed on more than one occasion with the conversations and counterpoints continuing past the points they usually end at with other "philosophical wank" games. Furthermore, our growing understanding of Indika and her travel companion organically feed into that topic, and we gain fascinating perspective into how circumstance, expectations, and environment can manipulate choices to such a degree that the very concept of "sin" itself can, and perhaps must, be questioned. And then a nun uses a forklift to arrange giant cans of fish and solve a climbing puzzle.Gamification and video game tropes are used as metaphors in a number of ways, underscoring a surprisingly deep study of what makes people choose the things that they choose. There's a running gag throughout the game involving "points" - despite a point-based "level-up" system being present, complete with there being a point tally in the upper-left of the screen at all times, the game tells you flat-out that the points are meaningless. And yet, you get rewarded with points every time you find religious objects or perform a contextual act of worship. This does pay off in the finale, in a way that left me quite shook.On that matter - the ending is very nihilistic and interpretive. I personally found the ending quite powerful and haunting, to the point where I'm gonna be replaying Indika with a whole new perspective (and that's saying something, as the only other walking simulator I have ever replayed was What Remains Of Edith Finch), but I have also heard there are many people disappointed with and even mad at what they consider a "non-ending". This is gonna be a "your mileage may vary" situation.CW/TW stuff: There's two scenes depicting SA that don't show anything, but the implications are still very disturbing. There's one particularly poignant but nonetheless disturbing scene involving a dead animal. There's also some very brief and heavily obscured nudity; a setting in the options lets you censor it. And, of course, the general horrors of war, disease, and that generally gross early 20th Century Eastern European aesthetic.I can now say I've played a game about a piano-climbing nun that has some poignant things to say about the human condition.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, solid visuals, audio. Quite a lot of interesting puzzles. Not too difficult, predominantly logical. I played the game in Russian, but the English voice acting is good (what I heard of it). In this, however, intent is largely ignored, which somewhat undermines the material. Nevertheless, this is a thought-provoking game with adult themes aimed at a mature minded audience. It's on the short side, but I'd easily recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you aren't put off by a short game, then I can absolutely recommend this - it didn't overstay its welcome, but I can understand people waiting for a sale. _childDocuments_.review: In today's landscape of safe releases and unoriginal ideas, Odd Meter and 11Bit partnered to develop and publish a risky and original story. I highly enjoyed it, and wish more of this type of experiences to be created, therefore I advise anyone who likes interactive stories with engaging topics to give it a try, especially since it's not a 20h+ experience. It's the price of a movie ticket, for an extended-cut edition interactive story.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a special game. The narrative is crafted with a quiet, deliberate confidence. The developers trust you to experience this challenging story without compromise. It won't be for everyone, but I think this game is worth the full price.The game is short, strange, and sad. It took me about 4 hours to complete, and that playtime punched far above its weight. The game is set in pseudo-19th-century Russia, steeped in industrial rot, religious zealotry, and Slavic nihilism. The environment you pass through tells its own story, and you are rewarded with flashing glimpses of world-building if you take the time to explore your surroundings.The gameplay is there to serve the story and is quite slow at times. It's weird in obvious ways and ways that only become apparent if you pay attention to what your character is doing/seeing. If you choose to give it, this game rewards your close attention with a passive narrative that adds to the already compelling story.This is a sincere and sad story. Indika is a great protagonist and she's easy to invest in. The writing is deliberate and restrained, there's no self-indulgence or cheap tricks. Gaps are left in the story in ways that give your imagination the rewarding task of contemplating the histories, relationships, homes, and agonies of characters you'll know for only a few hours.These developers trust you to take this story without the comforting rails of a typical game's narrative. It's a nice change of pace and makes this short game feel far larger than it is.One of the main reasons why I liked this game so much is because of how it ended. Light Spoiler:

_childDocuments_.review: Althought short, it is a lovely narrative experience. Hopefully the studio makes more similar games in the future because this story telling was really, really well done.  The voice actor of narrator (english dub) did a phenomenal job.

_childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY:An excellent skeleton with too little meat. Feels like "Inside", but not reaching the same heights.THE GOOD:The setting is amazing. I include several things here:- 18th century Russia feels totally engrossing for me.- The Christian/monastic background is intriguing.- A doubting nun and a prisoner with an epiphany are fertile ground for good drama and conflict.- The tone is very unique in how it blends the real with the surreal, meta-level and outright absurd.Moreover, the graphics are quite impressive, most voice actors are great (especially Indika and devil) and at times the direction is wonderful.THE BAD:The game just doesn't do much with what it has in hands. Much of the time is spent simply walking up stairs or along corridors in silence, "solving" banale puzzles. That COULD be fine and totally worked in "Inside", but here it kinda falls flat for a number of reasons imo.Inside knew that the environments ARE the game and, hence, have to do all the heavy-lifting. In Indika, they start out very inspired and the graphics are always pretty, but I found that they got quite samy very quickly. The surroundings do not build to much and have no huge dramatic curve - just highlights here and there. So my wide-eyed wonder from the beginning slowly and gradually disengaged as I played and just occasionally got sprinkled with curiosity.Also, Inside is explicitly a silent game from the get-go and commits to that, which is not true for Indika. The game opens big topics in the conversations between the two protagonists, but then goes barely anywhere with them. They are simply too shallow and bland, so that I neither feel value on an intellectually-philosophical level, nor am I emotionally engaged due to the deeply personal ramifications for the characters. This feels like some huge wasted potential and confused me through my playing, as I kept waiting for that Chekhov-gun being fired, which then barely was.The story just feels very odd, as there is so little of it. Some collectibles hint at that some themes intertextually link to bible passages and saint stories. If so, then I mostly missed that and I'd guess so will 90+% of players. What I did get from the actual plot, character motivations, archs etc. was quite minimal, shallow, confusing and unsatisfying.The MEH:Huge kudos to the devs for making such an impressive looking game. Some visual problems, however, came up through my playthrough. This includes water looking a bit off, lots of stuttering and some pop-in. This was not a huge issue for me, but it did hammer at my suspension of disbelieve a bit and dragged me out of that wonderful illusion.I understand that the puzzles aren't really the main-content in a game like this and mostly serve as some downtime between intense story beats (and, lets be honest, padding). I like it, that the devs decided to make the puzzles rather too simple than to hard, but they dangerously dip their feet into flat out boring time-wasting in this process. I wonder whether something like the vignettes in "What Remains of Edith Finch" would have worked?Lastly, the game was short with my playthrough clocking in around 4 hours. That seems a bit little for a €20 game (on sale), but for story games I could live with that. My problem here is that the story just about goes nowhere in this time. About 10-20 minutes before the end, I said to myself: "Oh finally it really gets going!", and then the game simply stopped, what felt like, half-sentence.Ultimately, I find the game quite frustrating: I'm totally fine with aspects of story, setting, dialogues and gameplay being lackluster. But something has to pick up the slack and be the game's nucleus --- like, what you remember your playthrough and the experience for. Unfortunately, Indika does not really commit on that front and maybe ends up spreading itself too thin. The environments mostly appear to position itself as the main focus, but imo does not do enough to really carry the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a game for everyone. Just like an indie film, this game is more of a narrative art form than a game. It is definitely linear, with easy puzzles but at the same time it makes you think about its themes: faith, self-doubt and trust. Well written, descent voice acting and poignant storytelling.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA is a cinematic puzzle platformer, that'll take you on a journey of self discovery, You follow a nun who hears an antagonistic voice in her head as she grapples with morality.The game has a little of everything when it comes to gameplay so it's hard to put it into a box. It's truly a gem in terms of cinematography and storytelling. It'll leave you contemplating what you just played. I will say, if you're expecting horror you'll be dissapointed as the only horrors here are that of the human condition. On that note, the game delves into serious topics which may be much for some.It'll take you around 4hrs to complete give or take and the achievements are easy to complete if you're into that!
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I'm pretty shocked that Indika isn't getting talked about more. While short, it crams in such a high amount of varied gameplay into an original and breathtaking world in order to tell a unique story. Absolutely a game you should go into as blind as possible. Fans of Firewatch, It Takes Two and arthouse cinema will get an absolute kick out of this.There is a technical issue with the game not having the option to pre-compile shaders currently, resulting in stutters during the start of gameplay. However, the devs have said they are working on a patch to fix this.EDIT: A patch has been released with pre-shader compilation. Haven't tested this myself but should hopefully fix the stutters and general performance issues during the beginning of the game :)

_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Let me get something out of the way first:This game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gorgeous. With its genuinely impressive graphics and unique Slavic-Diesel Punk design, there's so much to enjoy here visually.Gameplay wise, its not much more than a walking simulator with some moments of pixelated mini-games that feel a bit out of place even though they are fun.Indika tells an interesting story about a young nun's struggles with the line between faithful and sinful and does so with grace, showing how world events and fickle humanity can influence faith in its favor or disregard it completely. I believe the devs did a good enough job handling this subject matter, but cut themselves off too soon, by making this game as short as it is. Imagine trying to explain a point to someone, and midway through you get tired of explaining and just stop. That's what this felt like.I WAS super impressed with the narrative until that abrupt ending kind of killed it for me. Overall, a stunning adventure with really unique level design with a (could have been perfect) plot marred by The Order: 1886 syndrome. 8/10 - Hope there's a part two, cause these devs have extreme potential.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The game's premise is interesting - you play as a nun, Indika, who is tormented by the Devil, who has suffered a life of trauma and abuse. The nuns at her convent despise her because of her outbursts caused by the Devil's torments, and send her away with a letter.The game itself is very much just there to push the narrative along - the actual elements of a game are pretty sparse.As the game gets going, you continually hear dialogue between Indika and the Devil. However, Indika's understanding of faith is limited, and her own faith is waivering at best. At this point, the game is interesting. The game lost my interest toward the end when the exposition from the Devil became greater, and you realise that the game's message is not terribly deep, but communicates arguments almost identical to a Nietzschean "beyond good and evil" discussion.At this point I was pretty disappointed, because I thought the game would have more to say than that. Especially given that it is Russian, and Dostoyevsky is in many ways a thorough refutation of Nietzsche, not to mention others in the Russian intellectual tradition that counter him.But really, that was it. The game had many a dialogue about how the analyses of sin (as the Devil frames it) makes no sense, and the climax of the game reveals that  MEH.To pull off a game like this that deals with theology and morality and is entirely exposition-driven, the writing and theological grounding of the author needs to be a lot better to be able to say something on this topic that wasn't already said.Disappointment.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA was a great experience from start to finish. The game's narrative explores themes of religion, faith, and reality with depth and philosophical insight. Its mesmerizing, almost black-and-white landscapes and vibrant pixel-art flashbacks breathe life into Indika's past, enhancing the impact of the storytelling. The blend of third-person exploration and 2D platforming keeps the gameplay fresh and engaging. Despite its relatively short runtime of about five hours, INDIKA's impact is long-lasting. The story resonated long after the game ended and left me pondering the profound questions it raised about life and belief.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is one of those games that sees itself as art. If you like titles like this you should definitely give it a try. I would like to highlight the general story of the game and how stylistically it works with jumps in time. It's really unique.If I had to pick something negative it would probably be the mechanics of the game. The execution of the puzzles and platforming passages is very good but also very random. There were some  unique mechanics that are discarded as the game progresses but remain very unexplored. I would have liked more of them. But despite that I'm very happy with the game and can highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: A unique game that approaches topics I've never seen another game do before. More for those who appreciate the cinematic elements in video games rather than pure game play. There are fun platforming, puzzle and arcade elements but the atmosphere and linear story telling intertwined are the special parts of this title. I finished the game in about 5 hours so its not a long experience but at the current price point I think it is reasonable. If you like subversive, strange and twisted titles - that don't necessarily have complicated game play mechanics - then you'd probably like this one.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika has one of the most intriguing settings/worlds I've seen in a long time, I'm in two minds whether or not I would've liked to see more of it explained or maybe it's a case of stories better left untold.Maybe this game would have benefited from being a tad longer just to flesh out more of it's themes, and it wouldn't of hurt to see more of the world and people living in it but it's short length feels deliberate so that it never lingers on something too long letting it become comfortable. But what is here is great, I didn't know what I was in for before playing and I think that really helped my experience with it tbh.This game is deceptively funny too, the tonal range is really quite good.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing game. I only wish I'd given myself more time - I ran through pretty much in one long session.  It felt like a really poignant film or novel, moving through different tones with good pacing, and delivering great storytelling.  Characters and dialogue felt substantial, with some great dark humour along with legitimately tragic parts.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: My oh my! This game had so much potential, but It's still a strong 9/10! Please make an Indika 2, a continuation of the story! But please take these points in consideration!Let's begin with the negative thoughts first.The game ran incredibly slow at the beginning, I had to turn down the graphic quality to the lowest and shut off some functions such as motion blur and v-syn in order to make it run smooth enough to be able to even play it, this needs to be fixed!Secondly, colorful happy pixel art has nothing to do in a beautiful and atmospheric game such as this! This implies even to the point system symbols,fonts and in general. It gave a rather unprofessional and un-serious impression! The memories could have been made in the style of the game itself but in black and white or in movie sequences. it would have had fit nicer.Third point is more of a personal taste, but why did the story end so abruptly???? The story is so engaging and the game is so nice and makes you root for the characters and the environment and the total vibe but after becoming engaged and invested in the story and seeing the characters' journey through so much hardship Also I didn't quite like the fishing factory, I was hoping to see more of the story play out in the monastic environment. A taste oriented thought is that there could have been puzzles involving the bible passages/verses in the game, that would have been cool!Now to the positive thoughts:What a lovely game! I really like the idea of walking between monasteries and doing small things, the winter time, hard and harsh living environment and the elements of faith that keeps up the hope and keeps the demons away. It was such a joy to play this game! As a believer I would love a good nun/monk simulator game with visually accurate monasteries, the way of living, prayers, passages from the bible, artifacts, icons, masses, small quests and mystical experiences! That would be so lovely! I got some of that in this game and it was really nice!I really liked the character development, the sound design, the voice acting and the music, the visual environments despite the slow graphics, there could have been some more details but it was all good. The story was very nice and engaging beside the abrupt ending.
