_childDocuments_.review: After my initial INDIKA playthrough, a friend asked me how it was. I went along with something like “Yeah, it’s great, might be one of my favourite games this year.” It was indeed great, but with all the other stuff on the horizon, it was safe to say the crown had been reserved for something else. That's how long it took me to realize I was so wrong. This tiny little thing right here is actually one of my favourite games ever.Sure, a solid chunk of that time was spent on virtual photography. INDIKA's world is bizarrely fascinating, and looking for fancy angles, fiddling with shaders and rendering that hi-res bokeh never comes cheap. That's to be expected, nothing new.And yet, in between the usual VP business, I found myself... still paying attention? Returning to the most memorable levels not just for pretty sights, but to listen back to dialogues, see the characters interacting with each other, reread item descriptions — and, well, be in the general flow of the game once more. Now  new.So new for someone who rarely replays games, in fact, that I decided to stop for a moment and figure out what's going on.Full disclosure: I lost a close family member earlier this year. Without going into much detail, it hit me harder than a million trucks, and sure enough got me into existential paralysis. Got me thinking about... I don't know, life? The unfairness of it all, the meaningless struggles, the abstract concepts carefully placed along your entire way to make it viable on some kind of an objective scale. It made me feel lost and, more than anything, filled me with an unexplainable mix of regret and guilt.Enter INDIKA. "Hey," it said. "Wanna talk about it and kinda have fun together maybe?"And talk about it we did.In something that only resembles a fever dream after watching way too much obscure Russian cinema, no stone was left unturned. Trading questions both direct and implicit, we debated about societal norms, about how religion is not inherently bad, but how its (or any similar) escapism fantasy gets all the more tempting when that very guilt is weighing you down. Give in to it, and you’re going down a never-ending spiral of delusions in hopes for magical salvation, only to stray even farther away from the actual things that matter. Things that give purpose to your existence, should you overcome your regrets and offer yourself a choice to live and grow as an individual, sins and all.There was barely anything groundbreaking in the conversation we had, as the game really did stick more to asking than answering, but it gave the thoughts that bothered me a distinct shape, and in part it helped me come to peace with them. All the while coming up with the most insane comedy skits I've seen in a while.Here's another important thing. INDIKA's story is dark, depressingly so at times, but in its delivery, there's one key implication: no matter how messed up things get, there's always a perspective that makes them a tad brighter and manageable. It's a very Monty Python point of view that I always admired and did my best to adopt — but failed to when it mattered the most. Albeit way more melancholic in nature, the poor nun’s misadventures presented in colourful pixel art and dozens of hilarious gameplay segments served as the perfect reminder. Life’s a laugh, death’s a joke, best you can do is be yourself and give the audience a grin on your way out of this unfair, absurd play.Tying that kind of message to any cultural or historical context feels wrong. It’s an all-invited dialogue about ethical boundaries, coping mechanisms, and experiences that shape us — every single one of us — as human beings. The rest is inconsequential.Certainly, my interpretation may be far off the conventional one, but isn’t that what makes good art? Being able to look at someone else’s work through the prism of your life and, ultimately, make a piece of art your own? In that sense, INDIKA is definitely my game now. A game about a couple of broken people that steered my grief in the right direction, from internal discord towards acceptance.Yes, acceptance is probably the right word. The feeling that’s been slowly eating at me isn’t gone. Doubt it will ever be. But now, with the right questions asked, I think I’m able to start transforming what was once a destructive force into something new. To create. To just keep going.To the entire dev team: thank you for making this game. This review is a trainwreck of a love letter written almost in one go, and it’s exactly the way I want it to be as an expression of just how much your work resonated with me. Know that for at least one person out there, INDIKA made a difference — and it truly is second to nun.

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a game which I definitely want to review, but still do not know if I should give a thumbs up or thumbs down. Although it is a thumbs down review, I encourage you to try out the game yourself to make up your own mind.Because in my view, Indika makes a lot of things good - but in the end, ruins it's own potential.The potential comes from it's visual style and unique setting. I spent a lot of time gazing at various details: house interiors, books, icons, advertisement leaflets. They are all historically accurate in style - and disturbing in substance. Like the first book you encounter tells how a mundane hydraulic machine should be operated differently during Orhodox holidays. Another detail - the size of many things in this world makes you feel small and insignificant, and this fits very well in the game design. Great visuals, music, voice acting.The problem is that the game doesn't want to explore its own unique setting. The characters pretend that it is the same old Russia and keep ignoring the unique aspects - like the animals which are all enormously huge in this world. Level design-wise there are just too many boring caves and empty industrial corridors which are the same in every setting.2D pixel graphics and 3D realistic graphics clash in a good way, but you expect some explanation later in the game - which you never receive. This unique stylistic feature is not supported by the narrative or gameplay.But here is the most important part. Indika makes a courageous and daring attempt to pass a serious anti-religious message via the media of a video game, and this is a demanding task. This brings this game to comparison not with other video games - but with other forms of art, including books, theatrical plays and movies. After you look at Indika's message in this broader context - the message becomes old and dull.Although the monologues are very well written and voiced, the subject is always the same: "Religion is a form of oppression, and the idea of God's grand design of human life is a big fat lie". We have heard this statement a lot of times: from classic literature to death metal albums, and here in Indika it is just the same. Indika is ironic and cynical about lots of things: 4th walls, XPs and levels in video games, orthodox church, russian fools and drunkards. This is the cynicism of a rebellious teenager, full of hatred and without any answers to "And how should we do instead?" question.

The minigames are not skipable, and if you avoid certain game types because you do not like them or (in my case) suck at them, it's possible you may not be able to progress the game.In my particular case, I do not do well with precision platformers due to my age and ability, and typically avoid them. Because of this, I cannot progress past the fish dryer minigame and am essentially stuck. This occurs approximately 3 hours into the game, which is well outside of the refund window.Again, this review is more of an informative review of the minigame aspect, and not a knock against the game. It seems to be a well made game with an interesting story. If you have no problems with multiple minigame types, then give it a try. Thanks.

_childDocuments_.review: Indika started out very strong but lost its lustre towards the end of the game.  The setting and visual presentation is top notch.  I was taken in by the gorgeous environments.  Whats even more impressive, in my opinion, is the sound design and ‘music’.  It is absolutely superb.  The sound effects add to the immersion in a massive way and the music is clowny, circusy, 8 bit nonsense which makes you feel the confusion in the protagonists head at certain intervals during the lead characters journey.  The game does a very good job of making you feel what the character is feeling, outlining her confusion and past trauma.  Very well done.  My only problem here was the pacing, especially in terms of the late game puzzles which bring the narrative to a screeching halt.  I believe this would have been a better experience as a walking simulator.  Its almost as if the puzzles were thrown in simply in order to make this title a ‘game’.  I didn’t feel like the game needed these puzzles.  Now that I've completed my first run-through, I am excited to play through the game again, this time knowing the solution to the puzzles so that I can carry that immersive story telling all the way until the end in one fail swoop.Recommended, but not as good as I was hoping for.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Hope betrays you. Is there meaning behind ritual beyond the self imposed? Does mankind need be pulled apart by the struggle of good and evil?Indika is a girl troubled by her past and outcast by her fellow nuns who does her best to uphold expectations, but is set upon a journey to question all that around her. This is not a game for everyone, even those already interested in the genre may find it abrasive. The intro sequence sets up a pretty good filter right off the bat with slow walking and a 10 minute bucket filling sequence. This is a walking simulator, though I hesitate to use a word with such a stigma attached to it, there are some light puzzles and interaction but largely you are here for the audio/visual experience and the story. Which are great, the graphics are impressive and some spaces elicit a P.T. level of unnerving realism. The artstyle feels very authentic and tactile despite being an alternate world with steampunk machines and some fantastical elements. Characters are well animated and well voiced, I played it with Russian voices and english subs which is probably best to do. The story and presentation is refreshingly adult, this easily could have nosedived into juvenile edginess or turned it into a cheap horror game or something but instead feels like a good art film which I rarely see in games. Which isn't to say its "just a movie" while the gameplay is light it does pay off well in the end how it uses the points mechanic. Hellblade would probably be the closest comparison to be made, just without the combat. Also reminded me a bit of the in-between level parts of Echo, there is a similar dynamic here between the 2 main characters as they philosophize between areas.Its a short game, clocking in around 5 hours if you go at a normal pace and take in the sights. I guess I could say I would like to see more of the world and it could have been a bit longer. But these days I would much rather take a lean game with no extra padding over the bloated 60+ hour AAA games we get these days. I think it was worth the price but I'm a bit biased as I have a thing for nuns, and eastern European settings. This is also a really strong outing for a dev who has only previously made a VR game and I look forward to their future works. That's all I can really say about this without ruining the story, as that is the core part of the game. If the setting and premise interest you and you aren't put off by a bit of walking sim gameplay I highly recommend it. And if you are interested in another piece of media about nuns and questioning faith, albeit a lot less weird in presentation, check out the 1947 film Black Narcissus

_childDocuments_.review: - If you're anything like me, you were drawn to Indika by the trailer's weird juxtaposition of the arcadey HUD, devilish narration, and acid jazz overlaying a frigid Eastern European winter setting. Not the most coherent flavor pairings, but it was exactly that odd combination of sights and sounds that really piqued my interest- And thankfully, none of that is false advertising. Although the snowy rural setting dominates the visuals, there's still plenty of anachronistic music and retro gaming tropes to be found- Perhaps it's the predominance of snow, the troubled female protagonist, or maybe even just the graphics themselves, but Indika's slushy forest paths reminded me of A Plague Tale: Innocence and Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice- The 8-bit visuals aren't merely limited to the HUD. You'll also be tossed into full-on NES-evoking flashbacks occasionally. In contrast to all the neutral tones of the main game, these usually feature a bright, cheery palette that frankly offers a welcome change of pace for the eyes- The settings really do deserve some praise. Indika's hallucinations (more on that in a bit) often manifest within the world's design, usually in the form of unnaturally large objects. This interaction creates some very trippy scenery and some of the most visually engaging locations in the game- The electronic soundtrack leans heavily into the video game motif courtesy of the heavy use of chiptunes and sound effects. The tracks cover a full gamut of emotions, but nearly all of them feature chaotic, driving, irregular breakcore tempos- The voice acting is excellent. While the main characters (Indika, Ilya, and the Devil) are all well voiced, I think the real star of the show was Silas Carson, the voice of The Dark Lord himself. He's insidious, sinister, and—above all—convincing- Indika's plot kicks off by putting you in the shoes of Indika, a troubled nun confined to a Russian cloister. Unfortunately for this bride of Christ, she's been experiencing a crisis of faith. In addition to seeing strange hallucinations (little dancing men, giant goats, some sort of hell dimension, etc.), she also hears the voice of the Devil constantly undermining her every thought and action- After a tutorial and a particularly embarrassing communion experience that angers her mother superior and horrifies her fellow sisters, she's sent to deliver a letter to a priest. The action of the game begins as you set out to do this- I'll avoid spoilers, but suffice it to say, things don't go as she planned. Not long after her journey begins, Indika encounters a maimed soldier named Ilya. After offering some palliative care, the two of them set off to find a mysterious religious artifact called the Kudets. People from far and wide have been traveling to experience the object's mystical healing properties, and both Ilya and Indika become convinced that it's the only way that the two of them will heal their minds and bodies- As I mentioned above, you'll occasionally be thrown into an 8-bit flashback. These serve as the primary backstory drivers throughout the game. Like all the other subplots in Indika's somber tale, her story is not a happy one- Now for the elephant in the room. Are Indika's hallucinations symptoms of underlying schizophrenia? Counter to what a lot of the armchair psychologist reviews are saying, I think the answer to that question is immaterial. The narrative focuses on Indika's relationship with what's written in a singular book, and it isn't the DSM-5- To focus solely on diagnosing Indika is tantamount to overlooking the philosophical journey that underpins the physical one. It simply doesn't matter with respect to the story's themes or message. Indika is trying to salvage her faith despite the fact that the cruelty of the church reflects the cruelty of the world around her. Even if God does exist, he's turned away from Indika's Russia- I've been a little surprised to see some reviews and posts calling the ending ambiguous or unclear. I think it's pretty evident in its message: Indika has overcome her delusions, including her religious trepidation. I won't spoil how, of course, but the symbolism is fairly straightforward- Indika presents as a walking simulator (contrary to the launch trailer's assertions) with heavy puzzle elements. This isn't much like What Remains of Edith Finch, however. It's a continuous story instead of being chopped up into little vignettes- While not all of the puzzles in Indika are great, some really do stand out, particularly those that are couched in Indika's physics engine. Whether it's a platform getting stuck just long enough to jump over an icy river or using your weight to shift a crumbling building around to reposition objects inside, some of the puzzles were fairly unique- Other platforming puzzles are notably less inspiring. At some point, you really do get sick of mantling up edges, pulling levers, inserting objects into other objects, and riding elevators- As you guide Indika along her journey, you'll sometimes stumble upon prompts to pick up religious relics (altarpieces, paintings, rosaries, etc.), light votive candles, or offer a quick prayer. Doing so will earn you points, which are part of a meaningless level up system. Like the TV show "Who's Line Is It Anyway?", everything's made up and the points don't matter. As you probably already guessed, this mechanic emphasizes the game's message regarding the futility of faith- In addition to the visual variety the flashbacks offer, they also switch up the gameplay a bit. I appreciated being able to take a quick 5-minute break to race around on a motorbike from an isometric perspective a la Micro Machines or to rhythmically time jumps in a little 2D platforming sequence- Although I was a single achievement shy of 100%ing the game, I don't think I'll be back for a replay. That missing achievement in particular involves a platforming challenge in a fish factory that's saddled with some pretty awful camera work. Trying to dodge giant fish that you can't really see is a recipe for frustration- Narratively, I was somewhat annoyed by the overly dramatic depiction of someone losing their faith. In practice, it's so much more mundane than that. The hallucinations and level-up system add some spice to Indika, but I couldn't help but feel that the hallucinations and mock level-up system were a lot of song and dance for something that can happen without really noticing- Still, the story does have some merit. The character dynamic between Ilya and Indika was especially interesting, particularly Indika's effect on Ilya's faith as the plot wears on- Similarly, the puzzles featured some noteworthy high points. The physics-based ones were really clever, but one can only navigate mazes of ledges and elevators so many times before it becomes disengaging- Aside from a single crash, the game played mostly fine on the Steam Deck. I noticed that the handheld had some trouble loading textures on the various religious relic collectibles I found, and some took several seconds to load properly. Probably wouldn't have been an issue on my laptop. Overall, Indika is a flawed but unique experience. There's more than a few flashes of brilliance contained within. Unfortunately, those moments of innovative puzzle design and intensely thoughtful ruminations on faith are fleeting and few. Knowing that, is it worth your time? If the content seems up your alley, I'd say so, but if your interest in the story is more casual, you're not missing anything revolutionary

_childDocuments_.review: is a short psychological story-driven game, and it features one of the most thought-provoking storylines I've played in years. Without a shred of doubt, it is one of my favorite games of this year. The video below perfectly encapsulates the game in my opinion. ✔️ An original storyline will stick with you for days.✔️ For an indie game, the voice-acting, lip-sync, and facial expressions are of AAA quality.✔️ Realistic visuals and a top-notch atmosphere that immerses players in the game’s world.✔️ The gameplay blends multiple genres, offering a unique and engaging experience.✔️ An intriguing soundtrack enhances the overall experience.❌ None that I can think of You play as Indika, a devout nun in 19th-century Russia, released from her convent to deliver an important letter. As she progresses through her journey, she grapples with hallucinations, mind-bending illusions, and inner dialogues with the devil.The narrative delves into serious philosophical themes such as religion, faith, temptation, and mental illness. The inner conversations with the devil are also thought-provoking as it forces Indika to question her faith and religion as a whole. Throughout your journey you will meet different and memorable characters, including Ilya, a prison escapee with a broken rotting arm who will be some sort of a traveling companion.Throughout the game, a point system tracks religious actions, such as praying and collecting religious items, allowing players to level up through a skill tree. What is the skill tree about? The game doesn’t explain it, but it adds depth to the gameplay. However, the game's loading screen humorously reminds players that collecting points may ultimately be useless.All in all, it took me 3-4 hours to finish the game and it was the perfect length with excellent pacing, the final 30 minutes climax was the game’s high point and the ending will leave a mark on you.It is mainly a 1st person game but it sometimes transitions into a platformer, walking simulator, driving simulator, and much more that I’d rather not spoil. The game features unique and challenging puzzles alongside linear exploration. While much of the gameplay involves walking from one place to another, the variety of experiences and artstyle keeps it engaging.The visuals are excellent, reminiscent of a AAA title, with life-like face models and how detailed the world is. The game takes place in 19th century Russia, so the buildings, environment, and atmosphere authentically reflect the time period. Kudos to the game’s cinematography, as the cutscenes feel like you are watching an Oscar-nominated movie. The game also transitions to 8-bit graphics during flashbacks to Indika's past every now and then, which adds more depth to the story.The game worked wonderfully at ultra settings, 120fps and 1800p resolution. No issues to report.The soundtrack is interesting. There is no church choir music, as it only features 8-bit retro ambient music and they are played even during serious moments, which surprisingly complements the atmosphere and contributes to the overall immersion of the game. Also I like the fact that the songs are named after books of the Bible. I can’t emphasize enough how unique  is; it has everything that I was looking for including a thought-provoking and original storyline, mind-bending environments, and realistic visuals. The game's exploration of the mentioned themes makes it a truly unforgettable experience which leaves a lasting impact long after the credits roll.

_childDocuments_.review: Be me.Orthodox Christian.Confession, Communion, Easter, Christmas (on January 7, ‘cause unlike Pope Gregory XIII, we’ve actually adjusted our date like the chads we are) – the usual batch of prosphoroi.Howbeit, an instinctual victim of peckishness for various manner of puckishness. Less verbosely – love transgression. Guilty.A tombstone-toothed sh⁠it-eating grin plastered across my face all throughout the beginning of the game in sweet anticipation of an absurd sacrilegious rayok.The velvety purring of Shifrin-voiced Devil, the accuracy of Orthodox paraphernalia, the problematics of the Church as an enclosed 98% gender segregated corporation, the titanic imposing white stone masses of the Novgorod school of architecture (at least, I think it’s Novgorod, I’m not sure), the way the permanently uptight protagonist drops her eyes, crosses her hands, bites her nails, moves both gracefully and tensely (how can anyone not like the neurotic messed-up creature?), the stone, the wood, the mud, the snow, the garments.And the possession segments... The possession segments are a bleeding documentary. If you know – you know.And then…The game starts taking itself seriously.Like its gorgeous setting, ’s treatment of religious issues has time-travelled to us straight from the end of the XIX century. Any nuance (re)introduced into the European understanding of faith in the past 100 years – absent. Like its marvelously crafted setting beautifully mutating under the gigantomaniac influence of -esque aesthetic continuum that has permeated serious fantasy art for at least the last decade, ’s ideas of faith mutate under the ultraviolet sun of French existentialism. In that – maturing from religious worldview into the freedom of Self entails suffering, it’s not an optimistic process.All right. Hold it right there. I’ve seen the trailers. I’ve seen all the cool action camera angles, all the ostentatiously weird imagery, all the varied modern music. Where is all of that? Worry not, it’s all there – wholesale. Except – it’s not the main theme. It’s not even an ever present undercurrent. The absurd just pops up in beautiful little fountains strategically positioned throughout the game. Meanwhile the main course is good old-fashioned серьёзные щщи. Turns out, rhetorically the Devil in you (and consequently the game itself, as the Devil is the game’s unreflected mouthpiece) does not even reach levels of Nietzsche or even flipping Sade, he just goes for the most blatant truisms of logic and humanism.Authority is always abused.Miracles don’t exist.People hate what they don’t understand.Religion takes away your agency.We have to accept the dark side of our nature.But of course, not to the point of harming others – except in self-defence, because the game never presents you with conflict situations other than self-defense. Like I said – not even Sade.So, at the end of the day the absurd in  serves not to ravel in universal meaninglessness, but to highlight the meaninglessness of some things and meaningfulness of others. Such as friendship, love, reason and beauty.Well then. Pardon me, but in that case it’s just not the true, the pure, the noble kind of absurd.It’s the dramaturgic, the instrumental, the tamed, the castrated kind.It becomes an aesthetic tool, a seasoning of sorts. And being such, transform the fabric of reality (which was the sole purpose of the absurd ever since its birth as an aesthetic) it does not. It cannot. For, once compromised, the absurd evaporates from the piece for good – however many times it is invoked again.Not what promotional material has led me to believe...By the time the ending comes – the absurd is no longer there in any way, and all that remains is its corpse animated by the necromancy of the truly fantastic scene direction. And the ending is unironically the best thing  has. It’s masterfully built-up towards. It’s quiet. It’s silent. It’s mature.It gets completely spoilt to the player in the very first loading screen when they tell you that arcadey faith points you accumulate throughout the game serve no purpose. Which is why I’m not putting it under a spoiler either.The game hurries so much to establish its main theme that it undermines its core strength for which the absurd was sacrificed – dramaturgy.This reminds me of an encounter I had on my tourist trip to the Pskovo-Pechersky monastery (yes, a tourist trip, and no, not a pilgrimage – I’m not  deep into Orthodox gameplay). A fourty-ish years old mother and a fourteen-ish year old son on a tour around the monastery. Both well-built, sufficiently decently dressed, clearly cityfolk. The mother displays indecent levels of reverence. The boy is the epitome of disdain.‘Look, these are all saints…’ (Like, if you’re saying it in such a solemn whisper, would you care to elaborate, madam? What saints, lived when, preached where, achieved martyrdom how?)The epitome of disdain turns its chiseled chin.‘Mom. It’s all ерунда.’ (Mind you, ерунда, and not фигня or something harsher – he’s still trying not to offend his mom too much).Let’s pretend this boy finds himself talented, gets good education, acquires good taste, runs with the art crowd. That’s how I envision  being made. Through the many layers of quality work a before-suppressed cry from the bottom of the heart – as if sick to death with the parent’s demonstrative obsequiousness – rises and compromises the entire structure.Sigh… The thing is – I love resolute atheist art. I love the movie . Not the 2016 Scorsese’s deus-ex-machina remake version (although it’s a beautiful film, I guess). I mean the Japanese faithful-to-the-source-material 1971 version . There’s a great 1973 film  starring Martin Sheen before he was propelled to the heights of his career by Coppola. I’ve never seen a less accusative and simultaneously more brutal rendition of crisis of faith - with no resolution. Hell, I firmly believe that the best piece of cinema of all time is  (2013) – I watched it like five or six times – I dare you to suffer through it once. And that’s just one medium off the top of my head. The thing is – all those works address the same simple issues, because in the end it’s the simple issues that stand most firmly against faith, but the way said issues are addressed in them is so much more profound, so much more immediate, so much less conceived. And they keep you guessing. They make you feel hope that maybe – just maybe in this films’ universe God exists and He will manifest Himself somehow - which makes the inevitable resolution all the more powerful. Meanwhile here –  “The points serve no purpose”, right away.  I’m only saying this because I had high hopes for this game. And the direction is occasionally so brilliant that it can’t keep me mad. Only sad.In the end,  is still an original, one-of-a-kind experience and a great game. Look, it’s right there – sitting in the  section of my Steam library – cozily sandwiched between  and .But it’s so, so much less than it could have been…PSOn the bright side, I can pray to Karl Marx in this game. I don’t get points for that, but I surely give them. A cool reference to Тихий Дон. PPSIf you want some Orthodox lore, allow me to present to you a post-punk-opera-in-a-form-of-historical-treatise  by protoiereus Georges (Georgy) Florovsky. It’ll allow you to appreciate,  things actually have been. And where to.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most beautiful game I've ever played. The world they built is probably inspired by 1900's - 1930's Russia, with distorted inhumane-scale proportions suggesting industrialisation for great abundance while the common folk however lives in deep poverty and great superstition.It has a quality of writing I've only seen in art-house movies. The acting is phenomenal, there were moments when I forgot I'm watching a game cut-scene rendered in a game engine. The characters, their interactions and their development are written with so much care. They will make you feel their hardships and disenfranchisement with their cruel reality, without unnecessary fanfares and drama (of which trap story-driven games usually fall into so easily).The game is about two characters coming to terms with their own beliefs and superstitions while the society and their organised religion they live in repeatedly wipes the floor with them. The game goes into truely dark and horrible places with them (rape or untreated frostbite, just to mention two and not spoil too much), but the traumas these characters go through, the way how that's told, are handled with utmost respect.The more I think about this story the more I can see how nicely it's woven together. There's this phrase of an old Hungarian comedian that "You can have a 2 hour speech, which is dissolved 5 minutes, OR you can have a 5 minutes speech but the weight of it will be 2 hours". The same translates to this game very well. The four hours duration of this story carries its weight for months, while I've played epic 40-60 hours story campaigns which I forgot immediately after finishing them,

_childDocuments_.review: If I have to use one word to descrive INDIKA i'd say it's .Too many times the videogame's industry, from it's highest representatives, has submerged us with souless empty titles. Often promising revolutionary experiences, but delivering safe and shallow , with the only purpose to keep us entertained for as long as they possibly can, seducing us with beautiful graphics, gameplay fit as a perfectly crafted pair of gloves, and an endless list of unnecessary little chores to justify its usually substantial price tag.Then there's INDIKA. With roughly 4 hours of never repeating the same puzzles, surprising with unexpected story sequences, philosofical dilemmas married to silly absurdies, all paired with an impressive care for details, witty dialogues and visionary artistic direction.When you finish this game, you feel like you just went through something unique, that you can barely put two words together to describe it. And before long you find youself starting a new game, because you want to experience it all over again. Like its the only thing capable of quenching a terrible thirst, which has dried out the palate for so long.

_childDocuments_.review: A very weird experience. I watched the demo and instantly got this game as my most antecipated release of the year. I am definitely not disappointed, it was very close to what I was expecting, an unique story driven game with mild puzzle segments. What this game does very well is the atmosphere. It's not a frightening game, it's not funny either, it's an odd unsettling inbetween, and I find it fascinating. You can't predict what the characters will do, or where the story is going, even as a completely linear game. There are key themes and religious takes all over the place, but the ambience is so intense that the writing is hindered by the marvelous landscapes, cities and environments. The sound mixing is a bit raw at times but overall it's good too. The very light puzzles and platforms are greatly executed, they do not interfere with the immersion and add a few fun segments.I loved the main character development and I honestly liked the pixel art parts, they are a bit random at start but they contribute greatly for the game's uniqueness. I enjoyed how the protagonist is literally just a usual nun with so many internal conflicts, like a normal human being. Her companion has good writing and development too, he's tied to religion but with different beliefs, and he felt like a true helper character sometimes, leading the way and sharing his own stories, not just an useless burden of plot/gameplay device.I'm not the biggest fan of the ending segment, it is interesting but it felt very rushed - I'm still trying to understand what they really meant by that. It's like the game ends in half/three quarters of the actual story, there's no big conclusion sadly. This does not make the game unenjoyable, but the short length also hurts a bit here, I wanted more. I also experienced some small glitches and stutters, the optimization feels just okay.I'm not sure I recommend full price, it's not exactly cheap, a 20%~30% sale feels like the perfect price for the experience, it's still a bit expensive for a 3.5h~4h game but INDIKA has exceptional qualities that you hardly find in most projects.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Really unique experience, highly recommended to anyone interested in themes of faith, religion, morality, guilt, obedience, or maybe a glimpse into orthodox Christianity. It has a bleak and quite depressing atmosphere at times but the visuals are honestly breathtaking, especially the outdoor levels look almost photo-realistic. The story is short but never boring and the characters are pretty easy to empathize with also I found the ending to be quite moving. The game-play consists of navigating a series of levels by solving environmental puzzles with a few short 2D pixel art platforming levels sprinkled throughout. What this isn't though is a horror game, good thing too since I almost didn't buy it mistakenly thinking it's a third person horror. All in all if you're looking for a short game with an original setting and interesting story I would say Indika is very much recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the type of game where I chose to support the developers in spite of the game's flaws. _childDocuments_.review: On the surface, Indika is a third person adventure game in which you play a nun who hears the devil’s voice and is exiled from the monastery with the silly task of delivering a note to another monastery. Deep inside, Indika is an authorial drama that investigates society through religion and authoritarianism. The humanity depicted in Indika seems indifferent and constantly rooted in her convictions. Whether this is a social criticism related to current events, there is little room for any personal interpretation of Indika’s spiritual journey because it is quite self-explanatory after some thinking.Set in an alternative version of Russia at the end of 19th century, the game will let you live Indika’s journey through surreal landscapes and environmental puzzles to be solved. It actually feels more like a movie than a game, with obvious pros and cons. The story is narrated through multiple camera shots, even from some disturbing perspectives, but always with a brilliant artistic direction and a focus on Indika’s interior metamorphosis. There is a Narrator who constantly reveals and questions Indika’s inner thoughts and desires, but he can also communicate with her because he is the Devil himself. Their dialogues are a big part of the story, as Indika walks through multiple scenarios, sometimes alone, but most of the time in the company of another key character. While the writing is generally great, I was expecting the Devil to play a bigger role in the game. He is a recurrent presence, but he’s more a narrator than a tempting and malevolent figure. He has the power to change the surrounding environment in a more infernal version that blocks Indika’s path, so she must pray to return in the real world and understand how to reach the other side by swapping between both dimensions. Unfortunately, this type of puzzle-event only happened a couple of times and probably could have been better executed. Another thing that negatively affected the whole journey for me was the ending, which felt abrupt and kinda rushed. I enjoyed the moment just before the ending, which represented some sort of climax, but not the last seconds of it with the credits rolling.  For me, when Indika tries to be more a game than a cinematographic experience, that’s when it fails. It seems like the developers thought really hard on how to make the game more than just a walking sim, adding some playful sections in-between the story cutscenes. These sections often require solving environmental puzzles in order to continue. Most of them are quite easy, but some can be a bit confusing because you can’t immediately figure out where you are supposed to go or what items can be used. They don’t provide any sort of satisfaction the way usual puzzle-solving does. Additionally, you can also find hidden collectibles such as religious items and you can light candles in front of the paintings of Jesus Christ and… Karl Marx. These actions reward you with points, but the game immediately makes it clear that they are pointless. You also have a skill tree, but it’s useless and doesn’t affect anything other than your time. This creates a fun, but weird, contrast with the serious and dark tone of the story, which is further enhanced by the 16-bit music and some flashbacks that are narrated through cute 2D-pixel graphics (featuring a younger Indika). It’s like the developers’ intention was to mock these common elements (skill trees, points, attributes) and gamification in general, which makes me think they were somehow forced to add these and make the game more “playful” (also more sellable), at least on the surface. There are also some “chase” sequences that feel forced and don’t play very well because Indika’s movements are generally rough, with poor animations that are very noticeable when climbing or falling.Graphically speaking, the game looks really beautiful and photo-realistic. I particularly appreciate Indika’s facial expressions, which are rather impressive. The performance on PC could be better though, as there are frame drops here and there depending on the scenario, but the pre-release version I played didn’t have any sort of patch so hopefully things will be better on release date or the days after. I had one particular issue with the prologue, during which the game was using 94% of my CPU power for apparently no reason, but after this part it went back to normal usage for the rest of the game.Indika is a short and linear experience that is definitely worth trying if you enjoy walking sims with some puzzle solving and brilliant cinematographic storytelling. It is intriguing, bizarre, but also obsessed with showing itself more as an arthouse movie than an actual videogame. Despite the flaws, I can’t say I got bored while “playing” Indika and that’s probably because I became fascinated by the storytelling more than anything else. It took me 7 hours to complete the game, while spending some time looking for collectibles (even if they are meaningless), so it can probably be completed in 5 or 6 hours for those only following the main path.

_childDocuments_.review: A tightly packed narrative adventure game that, despite its small scope and obviously limited budget, is wildly ambitious and 10 times more creative per cubic meter of content than anything I've played recently. The concept alone is exciting: smashing together gritty but magical realist Russian religious drama and anachronistic pixel art and videogame elements, but the developers managed to execute on this vision with a deft creative hand that lasts throughout its admittedly brief runtime. Unlike other games in the genre, INDIKA actually does things with the camera: places in surprising places and uses jarring lens effects to create a consistently engaging image. An early scene has a GoPro-ass shot of Indika (the protagonist, not the game) as she whirls around her convent in a daze. It's jarring and ridiculous and not at all the kind of camera work you'd expect in a period piece, but it totally works.And while I said "obviously limited budget" I think that may be too harsh. It is a beautiful game and not just in its style. The pixels are all there—the environments look like tech demos sculpted with expensive volumetric light (so expensive that it suffers from what I assume is the same shader compilation hitches that many modern games seem to have) and littered with dense polygonous models. Where seams show are in the tense moments that needed a bit more crunch from the audio department or the intimate moments where the virtual bodies could've articulated a bit better. It's an unfortunate edge to an otherwise immaculate production.I wish I had more to say about the story, but I think it's enough to say that it's a quality drama about love, faith, and the lack thereof. I don't think you'll be nearly as surprised about where the characters will go emotionally and psychologically as you will with any other part of the game, but it's still a compelling story well told. I just wish I'd read more 19th-ish century Russian literature to engage more with its critiques of Russian society and religious institutions. I bailed out of the Brothers Karamazov about 200 pages in, but to this game's credit, I'm genuinely considering coming back to it. Great game. Buy it. Support art that tries cool things (and, in this case, overwhelmingly succeeds).
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: It's like a 3A quality game but keeps its unique and weird vibe. The narrative and performance is unforgettable and touching.The pixel part and the level system is so harmonious and deep, out of my expectation.The only thing I question is, are all these puzzles necessary? Although these puzzles and levels are well-designed. But I cannot get most of their connections with the narration. And they break the flow of my walking through.Overall, it is a great game
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The ending was immensely disappointing as it felt like the midway point for indika's story. It ended so abruptly and suddenly just around the time where I felt like her story of accepting herself and coping with her past would have started but nope all of the investment that you have for her is just shot in the head for a bloody open ended ending. My biggest gripe with the ending is that you maximize the player's investment into the character and I was so deeply interested in what else was going to happen to her and how her story would end but then it just cuts to credits and I feel like an idiot for being invested in her as a character and as a story. The developers did an overall amazing job with a lot of the content but I would strongly recommend them to not go for open endings because 9 out of 10 times it leaves a bad taste in ones mouth and the story feels incomplete. I really hope for their next game they pick a different approach because i legit love 99% of the game except for the ending. the ending left such a sour taste in my mouth that it pretty much ruined most of the game for me.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I fundamentally disagree with every theme this game presents. If like me, you can find your own meaning in the logical, good for you. Though, Unlike this game, I fully believe that logical nihilism is infinity more pitiable than those who find meaning in the illogical. But the game caused me to think about what it was trying to say for at least a few hours after finishing the game's 4hr run time, even If I decided that I thought it was wrong. Plus, it is one of the few 3D games I've played that I would describe as having actual cinematography (I wont go into specific "shots" here as they would both be spoiler filled, and I would end up sounding like Ricky Fitts from American Beauty). The game cares about something, and it wants you to think about that thing. That simple fact makes more worthy of your time than most things that are released.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I did expect a little bit more puzzle wise after playing the demo, and it seems  a llittle bit repetitive towards the end  (except for the great ending) but it's still a very memorable experience which could had also been a movie. You can clearly feel the budget contraints with this one . I still recommend it, even if not playing it then at least watching a walkthrough on yt
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Despite an abrupt ending that kept me wanting more closure, INDIKA’s journey, with its different varieties of gameplay, gorgeous if drearily realistic environments while exploring and playful retro pixel art for the mini-game flashbacks, captivated me from beginning to the credit roll. It’s a story of right and wrong, and realizing that doing what’s expected of you through the doctrine of religion doesn’t safeguard you from evil. It raises the question of whether you should resort to turning “evil” yourself then, and whether all acts can even be categorized that way to begin with when looking at basic needs and survival. Are morals universal or merely a human construct? Is religion an absolute truth or a manipulative tool? While I was expecting quite a controversial game, I was happy to find it isn’t all that in-your-face. It certainly offers food for thought if you like to philosophize, or you can simply play the game, experience the (sometimes disturbing) five-hour story and ignore all the symbolism. I for one will be praying that the developers make more games like this!
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: PROS- English voice acting- Unique characters- World puzzles that take a different approach on what you normally see- Awesome graphics showing dark, evil, dirty place in our mindsCONS- too short4h is just not enough to tell the entire story and have a playful time solving puzzles and exploring that dirty world. _childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The intensity of the story and beauty in every painstaking effort to detail that the developers put forth in creating this game makes for a reflective journey through an imaginary world where choices seem very real. Pros:- Beautiful journey through a landscape of which every inch is worth exploring, even when there's not an item to be found.- Captivating characters, Indika espeically, whose development throughout the story keeps you wondering what's next.- Sudden twists in gameplay (no spoilers here, but they're equally as jarring as they are inventive making it easy to never get bored).Cons:- Only wish the game was much longerHope that Odd Meter sees how this amazing world they've created deserves more, whether through a sequel or additional games that happen to take place in the same universe with different characters.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game. I really like cinematic story games, but this just did not do it for me. _childDocuments_.review: Let me say first of all that this game is an experience and if you decide to buy it you most likely wont be bored. now that aside, there's just things i cant ignore about this game that made me choose a negative review (which i don't think i ever given to a video game). the reason i'm doing this is because i think this game is special and i hope that maybe the publishers could fix some things and maybe add a dlc.Now, there's the obvious frame drops and to maximize this game graphic potential you need to have a pretty decent graphics card (3060Ti and above, and even with 3060Ti you'll have fps drops). but as people mentioned the gameplay is a bit lacking. it wasn't a BIG DEAL for me personally because if there's good narrative, sound and art design i can enjoy the game. and the sections the game where you play 8-bit gameplay is rather fun.the thing that off put me the most about the game is 1. the awkward kind of uncanny/unnatural dialogue scenes. it was really bizarre and not in a good way, most of the time it just killed the immersiveness of the game.and 2. the ending. i wont go in detail about it to avoid spoilers but it felt like a lot of things were left untouched. overall pretty disappointing ending. Fps dropscon 2. lacking gameplaycon 3. awkward dialogue con 4. not so great ending.TO SUMMARIZE, this game is fun and worth the play but not at that price for just a little under 4 hours of play. it has obvious flaws yet the concept is an interesting one so i think if you either get a deal on it or think you really want to experience this game then buy it regardless of the flaws. just be aware that its not the perfect short game it looks in the trailers.i hope the team behind this game see more reviews like this and try to fix the game by adding more content and maybe a dlc with a better ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous game. Essentially this "walking simulator" but with great narrative all the way from start to the end,some interactive puzzles with environment. _childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: When it comes to the actual gameplay, don't expect much more than a "walking simulator" for most of your playthrough. Indika's strength's lie in its truly bizarre and unique presentation. You'll play as a young nun (who no one seems to tolerate very well at her convent) tasked with delivering a letter to another church a few hours away, She seems to be tormented by a very cheeky and devilish voice inside her head that constantly fills her with self-doubt. Is it her conscience, or is she possessed by an actual demon? The game portrays nature and buildings and other objects as being much bigger than they'd be in real life. I thought this was an interesting way to show the lead character's fears about the world outside her convent. Shortly into her journey, she falls in with an escaped convict, and from here on to the end, Indika will constantly be struggling with her true desires, and what she feels her religious faith expects of her.i won't spoil anything, but Indika has a handful of flashbacks where we learn her backstory. These flashbacks are portrayed as retro 8-bit games, and it always brought out a chuckle when they popped up. Other surreal moments will weave in and out of the gameplay, and they were always really interesting, and ranged from funny, to downright creepy.As I said, the actual gameplay isn't terribly interesting. The game feels much more like a visual interactive novel. My recommendation would be to watch the trailers, and I think you'll figure out pretty quickly if this will be up your alley. I would definitely recommend this to someone who wants to see something truly off-the-wall.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, very atmospheric and well worth getting into if you like a "show don't tell" style of world-building. The story felt engaging and was elevated by its world. It's very "arthouse" if that's your jam. Some minor glitches that required a reload happened, such as getting stuck on some level geometry, but happened only rarely. Puzzles weren't difficult, but that's not a negative to me.On the whole I'd recommend this game. It felt worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet. Uses religion as a setting to play with morals through simplistic gameplay. There aren't many puzzles in the game, but what they have is varied and just tough enough to warrant some out-of-the-box thinking. If you're not interested in something like this, you'll know just by looking at it.That said, if you're the least bit curious about what this game has to offer, I'd say jump in. Something like this can stick with you for a while if you approach it with open arms. I had a few laughs, got creeped out, had some truly visceral reactions to certain story beats... Not many games can have you asking why the game couldn't have been a show or a movie, only for the game to remind you why shortly after.Recommended for a specific type of person.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Whenever I speak about games as an art form, this is the kind of game I am refering to. Indika belongs to a genre most know as "Walking Simulator". I, for one, really don't like this title as it diminishes exactly what this game is: an experience. I prefer to call games like this "Sights and Sounds" games.Indika is the breath of fresh air I needed in my life. Absolutely wild from start to finish. Dark where it needed to be and hilarious everywhere else. I was absolutely floored by the visuals, specifically the lighting and the production design. Holy hell that level design. Some of the most interesting and memorable set pieces in any videogame. And I can't forget to talk about framing, my God the camera placement in this game was immaculate. I am a massive sucker for a beautiful shot and this game was littered with them. The puzzles weren't the most innovative thing in the world, although a few of the mechanics were, but at no point did they overstay their welcome and they always felt well placed with the world they inhabited. The sound design was grounded yet ethereal and always very spooky and fun. The entire vibe of this game cannot really be described, it just needs to be experienced.I cannot sing the praises of this game enough. Indika is, from start to finish, an interactive artistic experience the likes of which I haven't seen before. I have a good feeling I won't see another game quite like this one.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: What in the Unholy Christ did I just play?? I was not expecting any of this if I'm being brutally honest. Not only is this game beautiful (AAA standards)... but the voice acting is some of the best I've ever heard in a game (the "voice' is on point and was a huge talking point for most of the time I played this game). The story is a beautifully woven tale... that will make you feel so many different levels of emotion that you'll leave this game thinking you've just watched a full length (hollywood-esq) movie... and when the game ends you won't want it to be over. This is one of those rare gems that definitely needs more exposure than it's been getting. Maybe with the Helldivers II mishap that happened earlier this month... that will help a game like this (a genuine experience) gain some exposure in the GOTY talk. Because that's the caliber of game you've been given here. Games are fun yes... without a doubt... but when a game can make you have an experience... that's on a whole different level. If I had to akin this game to something similar in comparison... I would say that if you played and enjoyed the Plague Tale games... you're going to absolutely love this game. Seriously... if you pass on this game... the only thing you're doing is robbing yourself of a very intricate woven story that won't leave you for a long time. You're going to think about this game in the future... whether you believe me now or not... it'll come back to you...
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Odd Meter have done a fantastic job in raising the bar of walking story based games. They have taken the linear and firstly delineated it through the use of camera, narrative and the quirk of the protagonists clear mental illness. From a technical point of the view the game is gorgeous, the environments feel stunning detailed and the lighting is a masterclass on what UE5 can bring to the table. Games of this nature should be encouraging you to stop and look, to take in the environment and allow it to add the necessary dimension to the story and INDIKA does just that. If you are a fan of the walking story genre this game will not disappoint!

_childDocuments_.review: It is both fresh and insipid, gameplay is great when there is some to have, walking is half of the game, which I don't complain about, but its length is shorter that you would expect and takes to long to get too little story, execution could improve a lot, there are interesting mechanics that are exploited once or twice and no more, the ending is fine, even if it's rushed, it needed more content or levels. _childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a sucker for games that integrate their mechanics with their story to make you empathize with a character in a deeper way than any movie could.The juxtaposition of pixel art and realistic graphics clangs at first, but starts making sense as you learn more about Indika's past and how it led her to become a nun. Equating dogmatic adherence to religious menial tasks to video game tropes like leveling up and collecting points felt truly inspired. All along her journey, both Indika and "the devil" question the value of treating life like a video game by keeping score.The worst thing I can say is that the ending felt deflating and abrupt, but in retrospect it is perfectly in line with what Indika is trying to communicate. There is no final boss to defeat or ultimate power to obtain, life just goes on.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This game won't be everyone's cup of tea, but the niche audience that it's meant to cater to will appreciate it for what it is. At core, it is a 'walking simulator' that is brilliantly odd and weird at its presentation. It tells its story in a way that doesn't insult the players intelligence by feeling the need to constantly clarify everything, but rather leaves a lot of it up to interpretation. It's rather short at just about 4-6 hours, but I'd say that's a good thing as it doesn't drag out the story longer than it should be. If you find yourself interested in trying it, picking it up at a discount might be the way to go. Personally, I enjoyed it and don't regret getting it at full price, but at the same time, I am not sure I would buy it at that having experienced it.

_childDocuments_.review: Indika, Mother of All Scaffolding and Civil Engineering.I'm surprised she didn't twist an ankle with all that ice. Indika should definitely work with Sam Bridges and forget about all this nun nonsense.This game exudes personality and charisma. It doesn't always entertain, but as a micro-experience it delivers. _childDocuments_.review: Profoundly great. This game made me extremely happy, there is a sense that everything from game mechanics, to visual design and sound was done by the people who knew very well how to amplify the metaphors, concepts and narrative how to carve the awe inspiring experience and direct the player, playing Indika is like seeing an extremely skillful chef cooking their famous dish or a musician play their opus grande - a pure magic is born under their fingers. _childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I give this a reluctant thumbs up, because though I definitely enjoyed the game overall for its narrative and unique style and interesting characters and slightly challenging, but not frustrating puzzle gameplay, there is a massive caveat to it all. The game is very very short. TOO short if you ask me. Yes, I do understand that this is from an indie dev company and I can definitely respect how time consuming and arduous it is to make a game period, let alone one when you're a small team, but still I can't deny that the lacking playtime of this game just bothered me quite a bit. What was even more bothersome though was that the actual ending of the game itself felt extremely anticlimactic for me and completely caught me off guard when the credits started to suddenly roll. I was expecting it was just going to be the turning point for the third act, but instead...nope, the end. That's it. Very disappointed by that. Still, like I said it is an overall worthwhile experience and its always good to support indie game devs who make true works of video game art instead of just generic AAA slop, so I say give it a buy overall. Just be prepared to not get much bang for your buck out of this one.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA was a surreal adventure into the mind of a deeply disturbed nun. I found the entire game end-to-end to be a unique and fun twist on platform puzzler gameplay styles, complete with fun mini games as well. What I think I enjoyed the most was the story and how the game presented itself. From the outstanding voice acting to the amazing soundtrack, this game really managed to be a vibe. Without spoiling anything,I highly recommend anybody who is a fan of surreal psychological horror story games to give INDIKA a try.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: A Catholic nun in Russia, possibly suffering from serious mental illness, experiences a crisis of fait. It's a solid set up for some philosophical pontification on the nature of free will, the coercive nature of a relationship with an all powerful creator, and so on. I came in worried that Indika would just be a "religion bad and so are people who do it" type game, and maybe it is a bit, but the approach here is quite thoughtful. I ran through may of the same lines of reasoning in breaking with my Southern Baptist upbringing many many years ago, so I found a lot to relate with here.Outside of the philosophy, Indika is a delightfully weird and psychedelic trip. The game is mostly played as a surprisingly  high fidelity 3D walking simulator/puzzler, with flashback sequences in gorgeous 2D pixel art. Sequences are frequently bizarre and almost illogical, following Indika's mental state. As the game progresses, sense of scale goes right out the window. The soundtrack is impactful and playful, expertly highlighting the bizarre situations Indika finds herself in.That said, the game isn't without some significant demerits. Cutscenes frequently have jarringly choppy transitions that are disorienting to the point of taking me out of the moment. Some of the sections lean a bit too much into making a point about the drudgery of Indika's life and feel frustratingly like busy work. Thematically appropriate, but not really enjoyable. Most frustratingly, the save system is based on checkpoints, which aren't communicated to the player. This resulted in me having to replay a significant chunk of the game early on, before it got its hooks in me. If I hadn't already heard good things about the game, I may have refunded at that point. While I generally love games with short run time, I think Indika could have used a bit more time to breathe and flesh out its themes. What's there is completely solid and tells a full story, but there was a lot to dig into, and some of the bigger topics felt like they could have used more limelight. I also wouldn't have minded a few more of the "split reality" sequences. I only mention this because Indika had the potential to be an all time favorite for me, but falls a bit short with some frustrating jankiness and being a bit over-short. Still, it's easily one of the best, most thoughtful, and most unique games released this year.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare to see a game that makes such clever use of it's form. It's like... Fairy-tale realism meets Hellblade meets dadaism meets Stanley Parable.My head cannon: as the credits role she empties the cash register, steals a bike and rides off into sunset. The script and direction are on another level.As a game, it's a puzzle adventure with elements of platforming and timing based segments. Ballance wise, it's pretty accessible to non-gamers, but may still be frustrating in places. In any case, it's much better in this regard than 90% of similar games out there.Narrative wise, it's a very modern, yet distinctively niche (in games world, that is, but be it a movie, I'd say almost the same) masterpiece and a ginormous breath of fresh air. It, in my humble opinion, shows what russia was, is, and will be until the, hopefully inevitable, collapse of russian federation. It's also a discrete spit in the face of the modern Western far-right and their "traditional values", imho. The "surface" story about a confused young lady is very good too.[played it in russian]

_childDocuments_.review: I was really between good or bad. If this would be 1 to 10 rating like on other platforms, I would give it 5.What is good about this game:-Art design is just amazing and fits perfectly into the story-Game has a very good performance on average hardware-In some cases mechanics are quite tricky, but in-spite of this, I haven't seen any bugs. _childDocuments_.review: Indika is a brief, weird but altogether engaging game about a nun having a crisis of faith while she travels across an almost post-apocalyptic winter landscape. There's a lot of philosophical and rhetorical exploration into concepts like faith and morality so if you enjoy that kind of thing, you'll likely dig this game.Gameplay-wise, Indika could best be described as an adventure game because there's a lot of dialogue (though you don't get to choose what to say) and puzzles. The puzzles are relatively simple but still involved enough to be interesting. There is a unique mechanic where you can alter the environment by either praying or listening to your inner doubts, though this is sadly underutilized. There is also a surprising amount of platforming. I found the exploratory 3D platforming to be enjoyable enough, though there are segments that involve 2D precision platforming and I found those to be pretty annoying because the controls aren't tight enough for that style of gameplay. Luckily, these segments are few and far between so they don't bog down the experience too much.The narrative is the main reason why you'll be playing Indika and it mostly delivers on that front. Dialogue and voice acting are well done, the characters are memorable and I was intrigued to find out where the story was going. I also just wanted to see more of the weird world the developers crafted. The ending is likely going to be divisive but I thought it worked given the game's themes. At ~4 hours long (if you're thorough), this is a short experience but there's plenty of variety in what you see and do. The game also pokes fun at some popular gaming tropes so there's a bit of humor as well.All-in-all, if you enjoy story-driven games with unique settings and premises, Indika is an easy recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: My journey with this game was so off-kilter, and that is fitting for this game. This game first entered my peripheral due to the controversy it caused. Interest piqued, I looked further into it and stumbled onto the trailer for this game which was a bizarre, A24-esque, eccentric teaser for what was to come -- and I still stand by the opinion that the trailer for this game is one of the best trailers for a game I have seen in a long time if not possibly ever. After watching the trailer which in itself is like the advertisement of a movie, I had no expectations for the game but I knew I had to play it. So, I did. What I found in this game really surpassed every expectation I had somehow, even though I had none to begin with. It is unlike anything else I have ever played. It mixes sometimes painfully mundane tasks with incredibly fantastical scenery, making you live out the boring, day-to-day routine Indika lives through which in essence humbles us as the player while setting up the story. We quickly find out that Indika is a troubled woman, haunted by an 'evil' presence that we come to find out through the story is the devil, which causes her to have outbursts and be shunned by the other nuns of the convent. It unfolds throughout the rest of the story and is well worth it. The story of this game was beautifully handled in my opinion. It gracefully approaches serious topics such as , questioning of faith, man vs God conflicts, war, ostracism, murder, bullying, and even at times gender. These topics are not there for shock value. They are thoughtfully explored, never did I leave any of these occurrences thinking they were there to wax poetic or outrage us as the player. Many times during the game it felt as though Indika was actually an old friend I was on a walk with when I was listening to her contemplate about the ethics of religion and moreover God himself, saying things that friends and I have said to each other when these topics have occurred. To the people who say that this game philosophically brings 'nothing new' to the table with its themes especially in the theology department, my answer would be that it isn't trying to. It is touching on topics that many people struggle with especially growing up in or around the omnipresence of religion ( or Christianity specifically ). Indika fills the role of the  which in or out of the context or religion, most of us in some sense or another understand the feeling of being the outcast oddball. The story of this game is one that you can tell the writers of the show not only enjoyed writing but also felt connected to. The gameplay of the game is fun and fresh. The puzzles are unique and there are also novel platforming aspects to multiple parts of the game. Because there are so many different aspects to the game you really don't know what is coming next. The puzzles aren't extremely hard but they are very unusual at times, which I enjoyed. The strangeness of some of the puzzles makes you stop and think about what to do but not so hard as to become frustrating. I love the pixelated parts of the game especially, finding them to be very fun usually arcade style gameplay. I thoroughly enjoyed even the walking around parts of the game, including finding and reading the religious artifacts. Visually this game is stunning. It is set against the drab, gray backdrop of the convent and later the Russian landscape. The snow is beautifully bleak. The game spices up so much of the scenery by its use of the fantastic. So much of the game takes place in settings that mimic Indika's mental state. You find yourself in a fishery surrounded by building sized fish, buildings where furniture has turned all upside down, broken and distorted episodes playing out that only prayer can fix, and more. The pixel artwork in the game is also beautiful. Despite much of the game taking place in the dreary snow, I never got bored of it. This game has easily entered my top 20 games of all time, and that is after just one playthrough. I am eager to play it again. The dialogue at times sent chills down my spine, brought tears to my eyes, made me think about my own relationship with religion and my own mortality. There's nothing more I can ask from a story narratively than that. It is a lovingly crafted indie game that posed more questions philosophically than many AAA games will ever try to. It is a haunting, surreal psychological-horror with themes I think many people, myself included, will understand and relate to. The acting, both for voice and body, I thought were really well done, especially for an indie game. I , without a doubt recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a tragedy. I can tell that there was thought put into its visuals, camerawork, narrative, and themes. But I just don’t find any of it appealing in the slightest. It’s easy to cynically criticize institutions and societal behavior, but that alone is not enough to be compelling. And unfortunately, that’s really all I got out of this game.Perhaps I was mislead by what I read about this game before buying it, but I was expecting it to be a surreal horror puzzle game. In reality, the game is just one of those things. From a gameplay perspective, the most interesting sections were the parts where world bathes itself in red and rips itself apart while the devil narrates Indika’s doubts and despairs, and you have to chant a prayer to bring the world back together and navigate through it. This is a really effective use of gameplay as a narrative tool, and it only happens twice in the entire game. The rest of the “puzzles” are the most basic “put the cube block through the square hole” type of gameplay, with absolutely no thought behind it beyond the visual setpiece. The only “horror” outside of some very uncomfortable, yet mature, depictions of sexual assault was the section where you had to run away from a giant monster of a dog as seen in the trailer. But I don’t know how you could possibly feel any tension with how slow it chases you down in the actual game. The only part I feel this game nailed was its surreal world. From the moment you start your journey, the world feels like travelling through a dream. Upside down destroyed houses, an infinitely huge fish factory harvesting fish the size of buildings, and a church city with impossibly huge bells all look incredible, and the fact that none of the characters acknowledge it makes it all unnerving.From what everyone else says about this game, the story should be the best part about it. Indika has a lot to say about faith, or so it would seem. The long philosophical arguments between Indika and the devil inside her end up being no deeper than baby’s first atheist arguments. The game has a point system where you earn points and level up by finding religious iconography, and it outright tells you multiple times that they are completely meaningless.  Some of my favorite media is about as unsubtle as this, but there is at least a more interesting concept underneath that is being toyed with.This game made me think, just not in the way I imagine the developers wanted me to. Instead of pondering the nature of faith and the struggle between free will and determinism, I was thinking “would I recommend this game?” It’s certainly made with intent and others clearly feel differently about its narrative than I do, which is why I want to recommend it so that you can draw your own conclusions. But I found this game to be incredibly shallow and not worth the time and money I spent on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ludonarrative Disonance: The gameIt's a weirdly immersive story with some great dialogues (both in writing and acting) and really good cinematography. And it constantly breaks that immersion with 16-bit SFX, pixel-art dream sequences and a leveling system that seems pointless. Even the loading screen tips mention that the points and levels have no purpose. Which is not entirely true as it just is used to represent something else than advancement in game mechanics.It's a very purposefully confusing, messy game. And it kinda works. It draws you in and forces you to ask yourself "but what does it mean?"After finishing the game, I'm fairly sure that it will stay in my mind for a while. I don't know if I'd be so intrigued if it was more straightforward and consistent.The only 'objective' negative i can think of is length of the game. I was slacking and I clocked just 4 hours when the credits started rolling. The ending isn't particularly "satisfying" but i don't think it's meant to be.If you like exploring what video games can be as an art form and how games can represent certain ideas - It's a really interesting title.However, it may be a good idea to wait for a slight discount.

_childDocuments_.review: One of a kind game that takes risks, punches you in the stomach, tickles your brain, and then saps your heart.It's hard to describe this game because it does not fit in any one individual genre.  There are oppressive elements of monumentality that make you feel small and there are events that make you feel helpless. The game touches upon insecurity, religion, free will, or rather lack thereof, determinism, the duplicity of sanctimony, the contradictions of piety, sexual repression, abuse, heartbreak, and other heavy topics. Throughout the game you'll be collecting "points". - What are those points?- Well, how many "points" does one have to score in life to get to heaven? - Is there a number, even? - Do you lose "points" every time you do a bad deed?- Do you gain "points" every time you do a good deed?- What if that good deed ultimately leads to greater harm? Do you lose points for that?- Do you lose "points" every time you have a bad thought? - Can you even stop yourself from having bad thoughts? - Do you gain "points" every time you light a candle to a fictional or historical figure?- How does one good deed outweigh another bad deed, if it does so at all? - What if you "let" yourself be raped even though you swore an oath of abstinence? - What if you did it to escape greater harm? - Do you lose points for that in the eyes of god? - If your actions indirectly made someone else doubt their faith, do you lose points for that?- If you are religious, do you feel insecure and rejected if another religious person claims to be speaking to god?- If so, why wouldn't you be happy for them instead? - Perhaps, you'd rather think that they are deluded. Surely, god would have chosen you over them.- And what if your actions resulted in someone's death? Didn't you just increase their chance of going to heaven since they have no more chance to sin? - If people actually truly believed in heaven, wouldn't it make sense to kill all newborns before they got a chance to sin? The game masterfully shows the absurdity of faith and these arcane decrees by tackling some of these questions that would not even have to be asked or answered if people did not delude themselves in the first place.
