_childDocuments_.review: That's the best way to describe the experience of INDIKA.It's a "not for everyone" type game. Either you'll love it or you'll hate it.Personally, I loved it. It's not something I'll probably ever return to, but it's the type of media I instead will enjoy to remember. I feel it's best suited for a one-time experience, since it is essentially a "story first, gameplay after" type game.If that makes sense.Essentially, it's a postmodern experience about faith, free will, good and evil. It doesn't inherently discuss or delve into or about any directly religious themes, but instead uses its characters to create an unique perspective in regards to religious faith; and how that skews their view on deeper topics.It gives you an opportunity for you to ponder by yourself afterwards.I quite enjoyed the dynamic between the do-gooder underdog nun and her struggles with the taunting but not ill-meant philosophical devil within.The game will surprise you, it will intentionally annoy you, and I enjoyed every bit of it.There are sections where you're basically suddenly playing a whole other game. It presents you a cool idea, and then never or barely ever brings it up again. I thought that was really cool, kept me engaged and excited to see what's next.Though, is most of the time a ''-type TLOU game.

_childDocuments_.review: The moment I saw the trailer for this game, I knew it was going to be amazing. It was very artistic from the get-go, and I loved everything from the color composition, to the over exaggeration of animal's sizes, juxtaposing the frailty of Indika, and the environment that overpowers her control. The transition from the 16-bit atmosphere to realism in the beginning of the game was so good, I had to start over to experience it again, as I was in complete shock in how it was cleverly portrayed. I did not expect anything while playing the game, its deliverance in beauty did not give me room to assume what could happen or why Indika acts or feels the way she is (SPOILER). Every detail of this game was well thought out, and it keeps you guessing throughout the journey of you patiently roaming around the pale snowy fields begging you to find an answer, a way of finding a solution, but you are left on your own, unguided but with perseverance, a motif of the reality of having faith in god. The game was not shy to express humor, and it can be scary if it chooses to be. I could notice that this game took inspiration from motion picture films such as "A Christmas Carol, 2009" and "Polar Express, 2004", which arguably share a freaky element of realism that barely touches the boundary of fiction. While this game definitely not just tickled my senses, I do pray (pun intended) that the game could have multiple endings. I know that this art piece is trying to tell us something specific, but I would like to have an ending that reflects how we choose to have faith, and I think this game would have had so much potential with that aspect. Additionally, nothing could go wrong for a way longer segment which sheds light on her possible return to the nunnery. Put it simply, this game is too good to end, and would love to see more of it, if possible. To the game developers, please make more games like this, we need them!

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I’ll give it this: INDIKA—a linear puzzle horror adventure game set in a surreal 19th century reimagining of dieselpunk Russia—is not only the strangest  I’ve ever played, but arguably the strangest  I’ve ever digested, regardless of medium. And, frankly, I’m still digesting it while reading this script, long after the credits rolled.   Play as the titular “anti-heroine,” Indika—a troubled nun with a troubled past and an unenviable present due in large part to the fact that all of her covenant sisters openly despise her. Why? Well, Indika’s chronic acts of blasphemous clumsiness sure as hell don’t help, and the game’s opening sequence is really just a long montage of you screwing up and getting punished with menial task after task. But it isn’t her fault! For poor Indika isn’t just uncoordinated, she’s possessed by the devil. And when Lucifer isn’t busy tormenting her with the strangest hallucinations you’ve ever seen, he’s busy filling her head with philosophical and existential doubt. Now imagine lugging all of this emotional baggage halfway across Siberia when Indika is tasked with hand-delivering a mysterious letter to a faraway priest. The ensuing journey makes the game’s oppressive prologue seem downright jubilant by comparison, as the world outside the walls of Indika’s covenant is a bleak, Kafkaesque nightmare full of bizarre industries, werewolf dogs, and escaped prisoners, one of whom becomes Indika’s reluctant one-armed traveling companion. There’s not much more I can say about INDIKA without dipping into spoiler-territory, so instead I’ll just say that the game’s story elements kept me consistently intrigued if a little offput. It’s not the easiest story to stomach as it grapples with some pretty challenging themes, but so did Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice, and I’m still thinking about that game years later.  While INDIKA is first and foremost a linear story adventure, it does sport a number of inventive puzzles along the way. The game makes poetic use of Indika’s internal turmoil, occasionally giving you the ability to rip the world in two, in doing so opening up otherwise inaccessible passageways. Other puzzles ask Indika to manipulate giant objects via diesel machines, something she shows a natural proclivity for given her upbringing in a 16-bit bike shop. You heard that right—when Indika isn’t busy running from photorealistic monstrosities in the present tense, she’s probably daydreaming about quirky jumping puzzles from her 2D past. During these or when completing real-world objectives, Indika will collect intentionally meaningless nun points she can use to level up her ability to collect even more meaningless nun points.  Like I said, it’s a crazy little game that equal parts delights in and is horrified by the absurdity of existence itself. And, while stiff movement controls hold INDIKA far back from gameplay greatness, the game’s super friendly checkpoint system means you’ll never get the chance to grow truly frustrated, even as that massive fish knocks you into the smoker for the tenth time.  As for Style, INDIKA is drenched in a desolate, dread-inducing atmosphere: blankets of white snow and the washed-out grays of mostly abandoned Russian architecture are only occasionally punctuated by the flicker of fire and Indika’s emerald-green eyes. These settings are further unsettled by harsh ambient sound design, but the whole vibe is often undermined by a silly retro 8-bit soundtrack that seems to exist solely for the sake of clashing with everything on screen. Hey, I get it—it’s an uncompromising art house game with a particular vision, but that doesn’t mean I have to like all of it.  In conclusion, INDIKA kept me confused, depressed, horrified, and most importantly engaged for the duration of its six-hour runtime. While its story and gameplay elements both fall short of spectacular, it’s certainly the most interesting game I’ve played all year, and I can recommend it to the strong-willed for that reason alone. I’m giving INDIKA an aggregate MEGA score of 3.46/5 (full scoring breakdown, from “Plot” to “Sound,” available in video form) and am happy to answer any questions you have about the game or my review.  Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA was not what ive expected it was so much more.To be honest from only one trailer i thought i get a religious nun-horror game but this was definetly not that.The dialogues between Indika and the Devil and Indika and Ilya are something that can really stay with you and make you think. The change between the past and the present is really clever with the pixel games, and I liked those games a lot (but they were too short though). Maybe two things that i would say against this game:As for the gameplay there is not really much to do. If you want to make a puzzle game then make those puzzles if not hard but harder to solve. Because there are no hints I mostly overcomplicated them, then, when I realized what to do, I got really dissapointed how easy to solve them. Make them more challenging please.The game itself is just too short. The story is great but I liked the atmosphere that much I wanted to spend more time with this whole thing. To sum it up INDIKA was amazing but I needed more of everything.

_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Overall interesting and somewhat unique experience, but feels like the story, which is one of the main reasons you play such game - was somehow cut or just rushed in the end, when it gets the most interesting, so it's just leaving you with "wait, that's all?". I got used that you only see like 10-20% of the game in the trailers, but here it feels like you could see over half of it.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Some of the best writing I've seen in a game in a while. Many of the ideas and arguments throughout the game may at their face seem trite, such as do animals have souls, or what is good without evil, the characters add interesting points that are simultaneously within their character and twist the the original argument in a new way. The game contrasts it's bleak and realistic, yet beautiful world with it's surreal and absurd elements, that without giving anything away, run the gamut from hilarious to unnerving. It is unapologetic about these aspects, feeling no need to justify them, and it is better for it. For Indika, theses are simply things she lives with. I feel like this game came out of nowhere, with little fanfare, and really deserves your time.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA is an extremely short game, that being said, the way the game portrays it's story is amazing. it is genuinely a cinematic masterpiece and it's not often that games will be able to convey such a message in such little time with such little said. I wish there was more to the game, or a DLC, or an after game, because the game play and characters are beautiful.I saw a review comparing it to a movie and in all honesty, that's what it is. This doesn't take away from the game play nor does it  make it any less of a game. I hope they one day expand on this because the way it ends is sad and unfulfilling in the most logical way, the way it ends is the way it should've ended. An absolutely beautiful game.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I just beat Indika and I must say that it has me stuck in thought... on one hand it's a less than 4 hour game that moves at a very slow meditative pace with not a lot of gameplay bar walking and what moments of "gameplay" there are isn't particularly amazing, some puzzles are neat but never particularly complex and in all honesty I can see this game boring a lot of people... You need to know that going in because on the other hand this is some weird art-house stuff that can be engrossing, unnerving, and genuinely very funny at points, it goes for weird but in that weird is a really genuinely interesting story about faith and perspective that hooked me to the point where I unintentionally beat it in a single sitting unaware of how much time had passed.But it has to be said that it is a story that works through allegory and imagery and is very much one that's going to make you read into it yourself which, for some will probably have it feeling anti-climactic as an experience but I honestly really appreciated it; because through all the oddness it felt honest and, as I sit here in silence writing this review I already know I'm going to be thinking about this for a good while.What helps it immensely is a phenomenal sense of cinematic direction; some of the angles and moments the game holds onto are just brilliant and I'll say that, if you happen to be a cinematographer or someone who really appreciates cinematography, I think some moments in this are going to have you smiling. Add to that a really surprising soundtrack that absolutely shouldn't work and because of it strangely works perfectly and you got a game that is going to be pretty divisive  but, personally, I found myself distinctly won over by it.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I imagine that the experience of this game must be analogous to what it felt like seeing a great painting or sculpture back in the Renaissance. A piece of art that, while also appealing to your every definition of aesthetic beauty, manages to bend its own medium and allow for the contemplation of profound matters such as faith, morals, love, or sacrifice.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This game was ART!!! Played from start to finish in one setting. As someone that grew up figuring out how to come to terms with my sexuality and the balance of having a relationship with god, it hit hard. The whole point system of "i did this so im closer to heaven" was something I thought in my own head growing up. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Although short, I really enjoyed Indika. Knowing how short it is now (2-4 hours) I wish I had waited for it to go on sale a little cheaper. It's an excellently crafted game and I really enjoyed the story and puzzles, but it feels more like a demo or a vertical slice. The puzzles that are here though are a few of the more creative ones I've seen in a game in a while! If it looks interesting to you I'd say go for it, but take the time into consideration.For those who like achievement hunting, they are pretty straightforward to get and there is a level selector. It was a nice bit of bonus content to go back and 100% this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Very impressed with the production and the creativity and SKILL  of the narration.  It isn't about any particular shocking twists, but the story was told kept me engaged. I typically do not like religion horror like this - namely, with nuns as the main character - but this one surprised me! It wasn't "one of those" and I guess is now an exceptions to me. Everything was very well done. The flashbacks being pixelated along with the "gamey" stuff like the rings was smart. The change of POV when it mattered is 10/10. _childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika has a captivating, weird story that never loses momentum. Dark visuals perfectly match the narrative, creating an immersive and unsettling atmosphere. While the focus is on the story, new mechanics and puzzles are cleverly introduced, keeping things fresh without repetition. The varied minigames provide the backstory, hilariously throwing me back to classic games with their clunky controls.If you crave deep gameplay systems, Indika might be a short experience. However, its focus on a concise narrative ensures no wasted time. The ending leaves room for an intriguing continuation, which hopefully comes to fruition :>.I'd add a few more save points to make it easier to come back later and avoid repeating parts of the story.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. If you like Firewatch, you'll probably like this too. Honestly feels like a black mirror episode, except religion instead of technology. It's only about 5 hours long but definitely worth it in my opinion. The story is very intricate and well thought out and plays on a lot of complex themes and ideas like morals and free will. If anything, though, this is not a bad game, nor is it bad on purpose. It's main goal is to tell a story and it does it very well. The ending is a little unsatisfying, but very fitting. I'll let you figure it out for yourself, but for me it's very clear what they were going for. If you've played, then one word sums up the adventure: futility.

_childDocuments_.review: much stranger than i expected (a good thing), though that strangeness tapers off and starts to feel less purposeful in the middle. some times the screen just cuts to black and loads back in on a puzzle area that doesn't feel like it connects much with the story as it is.having said that, the Whistler is amazing and i love themthe game's facial animations aren't on the fidelity level of Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice, but Indika gives some incredible microexpressions that sell the character a lot.The last few minutes of this game are in first person, and it was gorgeous to the point where i wish the entire game had been in first person.finally, this felt more like a book than a movie, which is a compliment. the only real arc is the character, and events that happen feel more like the randomness of life rather than anything like destiny, which is, i suppose, appropriate for the game's themes.Indika shows you some deeply dark scenes, some that will stick with you, and yet treats all of them (except one) as very matter-of-fact. not so much violence, but the lingering and very upsetting after-effects of violence. an impaled, dying man on morphine coughing blood and slowly getting consumed by the icy water while a man plays an instrument for him as his last wish.ultimately, i don't think the video gamey and (extremely gorgeous) pixel art aspects quite achieved what the devs wanted them to. past the fact that, even in this alternate period piece, indika would have no way of knowing what pac man is, it doesn't quite evoke the nostalgia/gameifying of a person's life save for certain rare moments, and breaks the flow of the game without a thematic justification. many prestige-drama-games like last of us and god of war have these little extra objects to collect on the side that give you a small amount of resources or a new upgrade. indika can light candles at altars and pray to them, which gives you points towards a deliberately boring skill tree. this, again, is something indika wouldn't reasonably experience like pretty much all the rest of her hallucinations and visions. this makes it feel like that is there just for the player, which i don't think fits at all - they should have stuck with those incredible early hallucinations (which i know from second-hand experience are very accurate to people who experience being on the schizophrenia spectrum - goofy or horrifying kind of blends together into something you're forced to interpret as real). TLDR: the coin collecting xp bar nonsense never quite ties into the game in a way that feels natural. i feel like it would have been a stronger choice to ditch the pixel art and instead commit completely to the alt-history the rest of the game usually evokes quite well.i wish the loading screens had made the game feel a bit more seamless, and some parts felt like they were stapled together last minute, but it's a memorable, astoundingly cynical B-tier slavic gem that will probably stay with you.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This is a shockingly good adventure/puzzle/walking sim.  It's extremely linear.  It has themes of nihilism, religious trauma, and belief.  I can't say a lot without spoiling.  But you basically have the devil in your ear most of the game telling you very helpful things and causing you to interrogate your faith. The setting is in late 1800s Russia, with photo-realism and then beautiful surrealism. Gameplay is puzzles; 3d  3rd person platforming and environmental manipulation, and a few timed events. One part where you're being chased by something.  And 2d pixel art platforming, and basically a level of pac-man at one point.  And then FPV at the end.The plot isn't really important. But the character moments and intrusive thoughts made me feel a lot of things.I think this game is a really interesting character exploration.There is a points system in the game, that the game tells you are useless, they are useless, and then get turned around to be profound in the last minute of the game.It took me 4hrs.  Maybe if you're good at puzzles you can drop that down to 3hrs.TW: delusions, disassociation, SA (alluded to, not on camera).
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Good graphics, some puzzles not too hard though.   Some platforming sections, although plenty of checkpoints and not that often.Liked how they played with perspective and surrealistic take on the different levels.I clocked in just under 5 hours, sure some could get closer to 3 or 4 hours.   Paid $18 for it, was interesting.   Bugs wise it run fine, aside from UE5 stuttering when transitioning to new areas.  Controls felt fine and worked.VA was good and seemed to fit well with the couple different characters featured in it.If the price seems a bit high, I suggest waiting 6 months to 1 year, by then I sure it have been on 50% or greater sale.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I really like to think of Indika in the same realm as Limbo/Insiders.Yeah, there are puzzles in there, but this is so much more. It goes to such strange places to tell a story and ignores everything that has been there before, standing by itself, uncontested.This is ArtThe puzzles are annoying though, not gonna lie

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little game, overpromised in the trailer (I was expecting to get a slap in the face)... _childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I only played to about half way as I didn't know the game was full of jumping puzzles and such like, which is not my thing.  However, an extremely powerful story and 'rethink' of certain concepts.  I grew up in a very much Christian society.  I saw how the paranoia, fear of the devil in every corner and suspicion of almost every action, created monsters out of people.  Who was this fictitious character of Satan anyway?  Simply a being that wanted us to eat from the tree of knowledge and be 'educated', where the white bearded man who had his own child nailed to a plank, championed ignorance.  The wisdom of this young character Indika, considering her fundamental background beliefs, was very interesting to watch.  Very thought provoking game.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Great atmosphere and cinematography, good writing. These could be the properties of a great movie. But for a video game, these alone do not cut it. I see other reviews comparing this game to Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice, which feels like a slap in the face to Hellblade. These two games only share superficial similiarities and are in no way in the same league in terms of novelty, creativity, gameplay and storytelling.There is not much you actually DO in this game as a player. You follow a linear path, sometimes interacting with unimportant items you find in your path with a press of a button. The puzzles, if you can even call them that, require zero thought or effort. Most of the story is presented to you in the least interesting way possible, which is listening to two characters talk while walking (With the exception of the flashback scenarios, all of them unique and pretty creative, but those only constitute a fraction of your playtime).There is absolutely no substance here, it feels like addig some sort of gameplay was just a sorry afterthought by the developers.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there were more to it because the story abruptly ends just as quickly as it began.  I would still recommend it but some of the ending (unskippable walking, drawn out cutscenes, etc.) makes more sense now if you look at it as the developers stretching the playtime to avoid the 2 hour refund window for Steam.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderOne of the most interesting, deep and peculiar indies I've played in a long timeIndies have had a tendency to repeat themselves these days but this one, without presenting new mechanics, gets you with its weird and profound atmosphere, its simple but very intersteting and well-crafted puzzles, and its mashing up of several styles in term of music, graphics, or visual direction.The only two faults I found was its length, normal for an indie like this but there is many mechanics I would hae liked to explore moreAnd unfortunately the very abrupt and disppointing ending, especially for all of the philosophy and surrealism of the game, there definitely could have been a more transcendental fate to this unique character.It's the mix of this nun solving heavy mechanical puzzle while having theological discussion in her head that gives it its glow, it's wonderfully whimsical, profound and weird at the same time. Oh and it's stunningAbsolutely recommended if you want fresh art direction and game design, as well as a unique tone and style
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: A strange, historical narrative game taking place in a bizarre, alternate version of 19th century Russia that presents its dramatic story with a healthy dose of absurd comedy, developer Odd Meter’s odd little project is something that I can only describe as a genuine breath of fresh air. 8-bit music, hilariously Monty Python-esque scenes and a macabre tale that dives head-first into questions of faith? That... is quite the gaming cocktail, but it’s exactly what INDIKA conjures up for its audience. And yet, I wish it pushed the envelope a bit more. I wish it went crazier and crazier instead of settling into the all-too-familiar mold of a narrative walking simulator in its second half. There are flashes of brilliance here and there, but I was hoping the game would get bolder and more unorthodox in its style and tone as it went along; it’s still a memorable experience, mind you, just one with lots of unmined potential. Put another way, it's got an intriguing premise and a strong beginning, but it loses a bit of steam towards the end.There’s nothing about it that’s particularly bad: the puzzles are fine, the tragicomic tone is entertaining and the visuals are pure eye candy, but the game ends before it has a chance to fully capitalize on its ideas. That said, I can still more or less recommend it, but maybe temper your expectations a little before diving in.For more honest indie game reviews, check out our Curator page:
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: A horror game that let's you relax and enjoy exploring as there's no jumpscares or need to shoot demons and zombies. It's more like an immersive game where you guide Indika through her religious journey, as she questions her faith. As a casual gamer who doesn't like adrenaline-pumping games and only wants pure storytelling, puzzle-solving, and exploring the place, this game is top-tier. I hope there are more "horror" games like this. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a very tasty appetizer that will leave you hungry for more. Indika can roughly be completed in a 4-5 hour session that's all about the ride more so than the destination.I hope this team can create more entries in this series or create something different with the same flavor.This game very much reminded me of American McGee's Alice: Return to Madness...another game that more about the ingredients than the actual meal. Not that that's a bad thing. I really enjoyed Indika.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Biggest surprise of the year so far.Not sure if awesome is the right word, but this game sort of is awesome. The story is creative and not easy to digest. A lot of surreal stuff is happening and some scenes will stick to your mind for quite a while.But if you're not sure this is something for you, try not to watch too many videos about it. This thing is worth your time and money.This game is a piece of art.

_childDocuments_.review: Not much of a game in a more narrow sense but more of an experience. And what an experience it its! Great aesthetics, an atmosphere constantly shifting between eerie and strangely peaceful and existentialist themes, dialogues and ideas throughout. Beautifully existentialist ending. Like a novella by Gogol or Dostoyevsky with a dash of Sartre, smashing!
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible. It's interactive art and thoughtful storytelling rarely found in any medium, let alone "video games" if that's what you want to call this. Beautifully animated, performed and designed. Fantastic sound design and music. This is what I want from any experience in life: something surprising and celebratory of what it means to be alive. Great puzzle design and pacing too. Love it top to bottom. Also, rarely have a felt the level of empathy and compassion for a protagonist like I feel for Indika. These developers and actors are amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: I have no idea what the hell was going on, beyond a young girl who was a nun who thought she was a worse person than she was, her probably imagined devil, and the soldier she meets along the way who she talks to about faith while also navigating a fish packing plant and occasionally hallucinating in old NES graphics. _childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a wonderfully bizarre game with heart and soul.  It has light and heavy moments, and makes you think about life, religion and humanity.  The puzzles and platforming were fun and well paced throughout the game.  The mix of 3d and 2d, while at first odd, is a great fit and allows a great mix of gameplay and storytelling.Overall I recommend Indika and hope the developer continues with games like this in the future.(Edited after finishing the game)
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I say this sort of thing a lot, but this truly is one of the weirdest games I've ever played. It's only like 4 hours long but it's story and imagery are going to stick with me for a long time. _childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: You need to play this game for yourself in order to judge it. Do not listen to others reviews. Depending on your state of mind and how you perceive things in life, that's what you will enjoy the most when it comes to this. Rich dialogue, very intriguing. I enjoyed it a lot more than I thought I would. I haven't enjoyed a game like I did this one in years! However, the ending was a bit short for me, quality and the amount of time it takes to finish the game. I must say though, I wish there was more. The only reason I didn't enjoy the ending is because I enjoyed the game as a whole so much that I wanted to see more of it. Indike 2? HOPEFULLY!
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I really wanted to like this one. Me giving this a thumbs down doesn't mean you shouldn't buy it, as I don't actually regret my purchase.The game is essentially a walking sim with a few puzzles. It leans heavily on its narrative and metaphores, which I like to see, however the actual game part of it is not good. I can't shake the feeling that if the dev just went all in on walking sim and just skipped gameplay it would have turned out much better.First of all, don't get tricked with installing this on anything other than an SSD or you will have to sit through some very painful loading screens. Secondly, the puzzles are a slog. You generally get the solution in your head quite fast but executing them is such a chore, because everything in the game (from indika to the puzzle pieces) just moves s-o-o-o s-l-o-o-o-w. The game is trying to have a philosophical debate between good and evil and the relativistic nature of it all, but you get yanked out of it to play with some legos (I'm only slightly exaggerating).In the end, . Yes, I know that's the point and exactly what the author intended. I'm not criticizing the artistic vision, I'm criticizing the execution. This game is art, and art should be allowed to convey negative emotion, but most forms of art are very upfront about what you're going to get and don't demand too much effort and time investment.This is a great piece of art, and if you care only about that, then you should get it. But it insists on trying to be a game as well, so I have to judge it how I would judge any other game.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. Unfortunately, the playable time is roughly 3 hours if you play straight through. For $25, I expect to be able to play at least 2 to 3 times that for a story based game to be worth it. There's a really good story to be told here, but this isn't it. It just scratches the surface of the issues addressed (God, mental illness, the problem of evil, faith, and more). The puzzles are okay (some of them, like the fish, are just kind of annoying), but there's very few of them. I reluctantly don't recommend because of the gap between the actual game and its potential.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is interesting — the ending was a bit of a letdown, but the game has a lot of potential it never fully leans into. I was expecting more things to discover in regards to the religion Indika was at crossroads with, and perhaps a better take on what seems to be mental illness. Overall, good game but leaves much to desire.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece! This is a very original idea - combining a religious plot with arcade elements! And the music has these references, it is unusual, brilliant. _childDocuments_.review: Indika is essentially an interactive movie. It's about the length of one, with a good amount of cutscenes. But I think it's a particularly good interactive movie. The art direction is really stellar and I really like the dialogue and voice work (in both main languages). The story is great, dealing with an almost fairy tale-like journey through an alternate history Russia where animals are over-sized and steam power is all the rage. But the most interesting parts of the story deal with how the protagonist and her friends grapple with the nature of "right" and "wrong", and how that relates to the Christian faith that dominates the land. I did respect how the game delves fearlessly into religious themes during the narrative and the philosophizing that our protagonist, Indika, is so fond of. There are some puzzles and some light gameplay segments, but the main focus is obviously the visual style and the narrative. So if you're looking for a interactive story in the purest sense, I'd recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA is a 3.5-hour-long narrative game. If the asking price is too much wait for a higher discount. I managed to snag the game with 17% off as I already had part of the bundle it came with. Now, for the game itself, I'll start with the positives.+Incredible visuals in cutscenes. I often found myself smiling with the way they presented the shots, truly original and interesting takes in video game cinematic.   +- The story in many parts was intriguing yet, they were mostly eye-candy that lacked depth.  For example, the story takes place in a very surreal version of Eastern Europe with bizarre architecture and enormous buildings that defy logic and physics. They also have machines that are highly steampunk-inspired. These aren't necessarily bad they just feel empty as no character ever attempts to explain or hint at why or how this exists. The game mainly focuses on the psyche of INDIKA, the nun, who clearly is losing her damn mind, yet, within my 3.3-hour long journey with her I don't feel like I know her, or that I GOT TO know her. The game doesn't feel unfinished, but it is lacking in story. By that I mean near the 2-hour mark I felt as if I had missed 10 levels and I was already seeing the finishing line. That feeling didn't feel like the devs rushed the game but it felt as if the devs just plucked those levels out of the game and forcefully connected other levels. It's hard to explain. +Interesting visual storytelling, I can't talk about this because it will spoil a huge section of the game. And now for the cons-Dialogue: The game attempts to critique or dissect faith and religion not by dumping philosophy on the player but by forcing INDIKA to experience things that are supposed to make her question things. Yet it mainly fails at that. It could have worked if the game was better paced or better written, but it doesn't seem to even try to take a stance on the "debate" it creates. INDIKA never tries to fully protect her religion, nor does the game ever attempt to kill it. Again I feel it fails at this because of its short run time and lack of events. Even the ending feels lacking in tone and message because we are thrown to it with insane speed that it ruins any impact it wants to achieve. -Lacking in meaningful gameplay: Now, this is a walking sim, yet the good walking sims know that interactions and player agency are a top priority. This game lacks in all departments of gameplay. You do simple puzzles that are somewhat connected in theme and story and pick pointless items or light random candles. The game even says the points and levels you gain are pointless. Yes, it does connect to the theme and message of the game. Yet, in my opinion, it does it poorly. If the game wanted us to have the feeling of empty interactions it could have implemented it better to the narrative with dialogue and story events. Yet it doesn't and it seems like someone forced the devs to add it.  - Too short: 3.3 hours for $25 is quite a heavy price, especially when there isn't a game. I would argue this is a movie more than a game. It does attempt to be like one with how it is presented. I did enjoy the start of the game, I have to make that clear, but due to the extremely fast pace of the story and lack of events I can't recommend this game to anyone. Not for $25. Narratives in walking sims are arguably the most important aspect of the game as it is known by genre walking sims are supposed to be lacking gameplay features. But if the narrative is bad it has nothing to fall on. INDIKA attempted to create a game that forces dialogue and debate with religion and other themes of belief. I believe it failed at doing so. The message the game presents at the end doesn't have a buildup and most dialogue sections don't hint or dance around it. And many events of the game are just thrown in the face of the player without ever settling.  2/5 I would recommend watching it on YouTube.

_childDocuments_.review: Poignant title. Powerful imagery. Great visual impact. Recommended for those who not only want to play but also to reflect
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Bleak, sad, a tad hamfisted in some parts, but ultimately an honest (If artistic) look at the deconstruction of one's faith in the face of reality. As a once avid believer now turned atheist, I found pieces of myself in Indika's story and struggles, even if our faith backgrounds weren't the same. It's ending was particularly poignant.    As far as the 'game' portion goes: It's linear, it's very pretty, the puzzles and platforming are simple, and it doesn't overstay its welcome. It's obviously short, and I don't really have a reason to play again - But since I value games by experience and not longevity, I consider my money and time very well spent.  Very well done and recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: this game is something different for once!! the graphics look great, the mix with the pixel style is really nice, the voice actors are great and you never really know what will happen next. my favorite thing tho..... were the camera angles in cutscenes or when you can sit down. It just helps to get this eery feeling across very well. But I wouldn't say this is a horror game, more like a surreal beautiful experience.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I'm recommending because the game is undeniably a true work of art on a whole number of levels. Like many others have said, I wish there were many more games like this, that dared to be this original and meaningful. I do have a complaint, however, if the developers happen to read this: the control mechanics on the mini-games are, in this player's opinion, atrocious. You can barely get the character pointed in the right direction(thinking in particular of the bicycle mini-game). I admire the concept of it all, especially in a game like this where the mini-games provide an unexpected contrast of sorts. But if you could tighten up the controls somehow or even, as I've seen some suggest, add an option to skip the mini-games altogether(?), that would be much welcomed. Apart from that, congrats on a masterpiece of a game.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: A24 movie in video game format is an apt description. It's a surreal world with an entertaining enough story that is on the shorter side. I generally prefer shorter narrative-based games so that's a plus for me. Gameplay consists of light puzzles while the story unfolds, interspersed with pixel platformer segments that divulge Indika's backstory. Graphics are interesting -- they are both bad and good at the same time, if that makes any sense?? I played in 2160p with DLAA on and it often looked like it was actually running in 1080p, however, some elements and scenes are very detailed in a very beautiful way. You can tell a lot of work went into Indika's habit's cloth physics.All in all it was a story that kept me engaged for the 4 hours it took to finish. I enjoyed it.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This was a very good, albeit also very depressing game, which I suppose is to be expected with it being set in Russia. Indika is a deeply philosophical, surrealist game that criticises the oppressive shackles that religion can be, how blind faith can ruin your life, and how hopeless the situation for a woman in 1800's Russia really was. Indika was controlled and tossed aside by men all her life, and convinced that she was possessed by the devil because she's not a perfect human being. She feels lust, pride, envy, wrath, all these human emotions that the clergy has convinced her are the work of the devil, and something she must suppress at all cost.The gameplay was decent, although it was fairly short. I liked the puzzles, they were challenging, but not frustratingly so.My biggest criticism of this game is the performance. The first part of the game set in the monastery, and the part set in the paint factory, have such terrible performance issues that I was getting around 14 fps on average through them. This game does have good graphics, but they don't look any more demanding than some of the other games I've played, yet the impact on my fps was much worse. Weirdly, turning the graphics down actually did nothing. Luckily the rest of the game is better when it comes to performance, but having these issues in the very first chapter of the game is a bad thing, as it leaves a bad first impression, and I wouldn't be surprised if someone just got a refund after seeing the fps on that chapter, thinking the rest of the game would be as laggy.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. What a game. Did not expected so many parts in it. Every few seconds there was another mechanic, another detail where i just paused and said ''What the...''. A positive surprise for sure. Beautiful yet sick details here and there. I recommend it if you have a few hours to spare - and a few more hours after that to think about the story, which is dark but also so meaningful. Combined with this cinematic world.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: + The game has a lot of cool camera work. Lots of scenes filmed from angles that a movie could never properly make work and they all look great. Contributes nicely to the surrealness which permeates the entire game.+ The pray mechanic which reverts the environment from its altered hellish state is nice and severely underutilised. It should have been a core mechanic and used for other types of gameplay as well.- Instead, the puzzles are all various degrees of tedious. Nothing tricky about the solutions, but all tedious to solve.+ The religion level-up mechanic is nicely integrated, intentionally jarring and completely pointless, a good example of narrative and gameplay mechanics working beautifully together in a way you wouldn't expect.+ Art direction is beautiful and the surreal elements (giant dogs and architecture, etc.) combine really well with the depressing Russian turn-of-the-XIXth century setting.+ Strong writing across the board with sharp dialogue for the two main characters, Indika and Ilya. The ending is grim, depressing and bleak and I understand that it fits the game's inspirations of Russian literature, but there is a scene close to the end that is tough to come to terms with for me. * I played with Russian voices and English subtitles and I thought the voice acting was great personally, despite not speaking the language. Indika's English voice is very different from her Russian one, so different that it kind of alters her portrayal in my opinion.- The pixel-art mini-games were certainly visually impressive, but they didn't really do anything special mechanics-wise, maybe apart from the rhythm-based Frogger one.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: It's like if Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote the scenario. The visual style is astonishing, the voice actors are truly the masters. I'm not a good player in terms of reaction, so I had to ask my partner to play the retro-style arcade parts for me. Some parts of the gameplay were quite complicated for me, so I looked up into playthrough like in half of the cases after some attempts of solving them myself, because I wanted the follow the story more than to spend a lot of time on the puzzles. Anyway, a masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika throws a lot of cool things at the wall, but too little of it sticks, creating a mess of elements which work in a proof-of-concept but fail in a full game. While the narrative and storytelling are capable of moments of intrigue and even greatness, the game as a whole is a thematic skeleton where nothing substantial ever came to be. It succeeded in pulling me in, but didn’t do a great job of keeping me there. That said, there were enough exceptional elements that I am eager to see what Odd Meter/11-bit studios do next.Full Review:
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a game that sees itself as an A24 flick. Normally, this would lead straight to an eye roll, but i feel like the theme, settings and art directions are interesting enough to earn the player attention at least for an evening. It certainly never overstays its welcome, with a lenght of just under 4 hours it can be confortably finished in a day, letting the atmosphere work its magic onto you without getting stale. If anything, and i can’t believe i’m writing this, after playing the first level and subsequentially finishing the game i caught myself wishing for a more boring experience. The first level is a masterpiece in game design, providing a really well crafted critique of authority and religion through mission objectives while also getting meta on the role of the player and gaming itself. Its a shame that as soon as we step foot outside of the convent, Indika starts to fall bit by bit inside the boundaries of its own genre. Having said this, it always remains comfortably inside the treshold for considering this title as one of the most interesting games of later years.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This game really throws you off from the start.makes you question about some interesting ideas that your probably never thought about before.As mentioned by other reviews, it a narrative-focus game with hardly any gameplay but its there to fill the gaps.its a one-time experience but overall made me engaged through the story.will recommenced it for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: Title: A Thought-Provoking Journey Through Faith and RealityINDIKA is a captivating third-person adventure that intertwines religious motifs with a whimsical yet poignant narrative. Set in a peculiar world where divine visions clash with the harshness of existence, the game follows the journey of a young nun named Indika, accompanied by an unlikely companion—the devil himself.One of the game's standout features in my opinion is its charming 2D-pixel art mini-games, which added depth and immersion to the storytelling experience of the game. These segments offer a refreshing break from the main narrative while still contributing to the game's thematic exploration. also the music during those parts is the best.The narrative delves into thought-provoking themes of religion, authority, and self-discovery, inviting players to ponder existential questions alongside Indika while having the devil speak to us. However, while the story is engaging and the character development compelling, the ending may leave some players perplexed, lacking clarity and closure in my opinion.One of the highlights of INDIKA is the stellar voice acting, particularly the portrayal of the devil, which adds an extra layer of intrigue and charisma to the game play.In summary, INDIKA offers a unique and thought-provoking gaming experience, blending captivating storytelling with thematic depth. While the ending may leave some questions unanswered, the journey itself is an unforgettable exploration of faith, reality, and the human condition as we know it.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: A truly unique and dark narrative experience akin to experimental arthouse cinema with impeccable art direction, craftsmanship, and performances. A wild ride through unsettling environments of sublime beauty, this indie gem confronts you with thought-provoking dialogue and predicaments on faith - whether it be towards an entity, an institution, an object, to another being, or to oneself - and the tragedy of a desperate yearning for belonging (in spite of which I felt hope in the end). Highly recommend the Artbook and Soundtrack - can't get enough of the bold yet purposeful creative choices of dissonance.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a problems with it. The perspective of the person who made the game is too clear and it seems like its made from someone disillusioned by religion or a hard atheist, that is not a problem on itself, the problem is when it gets in the way of the game's potential. I like how the game is written in some places but the fact that all the religious people in the game are evil and how it paints religion as a just bad and pointless thing. The other side of it is bringing people together and people following saints not blindly but for their example of living out of temptation and being good. There is a part of the game where there is an artifact that has the last supper painted on it, if you analyze it it literally says “how corny”. I am not a religious person. I consider myself agnostic or believe there is something out there but the games message sometimes feels like is saying “In this moment, I am euphoric, Not because of any phony god’s blessing. But because I am enlightened by my intelligence”  I get that the game tries to give the message against "blind fate" but also it does not go out of it's way to show how good religion can be for people when something is "divine" and how people can come together and be good. The game is made to have nothing to counter argument the game's point of view.   While I loved the game. The more I think about it the more I get to the conclusion that the only theme is "religion is a big lie and church is evil" while I agree organized faith can be dangerous and many times is, this game compares itself to Dostoevsky's novels. Dostoevsky was a faithful Orthodox when he wrote he presented different stances and made you get to your own conclusion. That was one of the best things about Dostoevsky, you can see that he massively struggles with his faith, and explores challenges to his faith through his characters. Here it seems that there is only one stance all throughout. While I agree that Art should not only focus on showing all sides I feel this game really needed it. Once the first questioning of religion happens in the game you already have heard almost all of what the game has to say.       I think the writers are quite competent but their limited open mindedness played against them here. Not opening the discussion further than what they believe results in a game that wants to touch deep themes but isn't open to many deep ideas and becomes the other side of the coin of what they are "against". What we get in the end is a game that thinks itself of as deep but is not open to the conversation of different perspectives and doesn't say anything unique to the argument or different that has not been said a thousand times in art before. When we make art about a point, it is extremely important to add different perspectives, otherwise the final product ends up being "self-referential" or an "echo-chamber" and has nothing deep or of value to add to a subject, unfortunately I think this is what is happening here in most parts of the game.Still there are many good things here.I hope we get INDIKA 2 either way with the concepts fleshed out more and longer runtime. Good game.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I have played allot of games in the last 10 years that seem to have deliberate game stoppers in them at some point. This is horrible design. It's not fun reloading and reloading due to a flawed area in hopes of delaying progress for the player. Challenges are OK but to the point of giving up due to game design is not. This makes for a poor game that is deleted and placed on a back burner just because of one area. Games are meant to be fun and having to reload repeatedly misses that mark. However, I did manage to get through the game finally. There were parts I really enjoyed and the slow pace was different from allot horror games and I actually liked that for a change. The story was interesting and makes you think about your own life. That is if you have a conscious. I still recommend a play through.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start by making it clear that I think if this game looks interesting to you, you should pay the price of admission and install it immediately. But, also. I have 3.4 hours in this game and I'm done. I can't imaging re-installing it any time soon as there's very little in the way of replay-ability. I also did not at all rush thru this game, I took my time admiring the beautiful surroundings, puzzling over the challenges and sticking my nose into every detail and corner. I think you could finish in 2 hours if you don't care so much for hunting down secrets or sitting on benches to appreciate the architecture. This isn't worth it to a lot of people, I get it, you can play a £5 game that'll entertain you for the same amount of time. So I want to put the warning out that this experience is short. But by god does it pack a punch. This is a top 5 of 2024 for me, I know it. This game is written so fantastically that the talented voice cast feel REAL. The surroundings will leave you astounded at giant fish and snow soaked ramshackle houses. The pixel art games are genuinely fun reprieves with electronic music that never feels out of place as it fades into the realistic scenes of the world beyond them. Philosophy, driving sections, giant frogs, DEDICATED PRAYER BUTTON. This game has it all!

_childDocuments_.review: Faith or Delusion - The GameA good compliment to stories like The Pillars of the Earth, though this time from a more Orthodox perspective with emphasis on the marginalization of individuals with mental disorders. I can't shake the feeling that some of the imagery is lost on me- (possible allusions to other media I'm unfamiliar with that are themselves making reference to Jonah and Moby-♥♥♥♥) But this is a really good work worth some in-deph analysisThe juxtaposition of different videogame styles to represent the past and present is also a very nice touch.The ending of the story is open ended, leaving it up to the player to imagine what comes next, and I really respect that in a title like this.Well worth the ~4 hr playtime, would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a very weird and wonderful experience. I like the strange mix of modern graphics with it's 8 bit music and I thought it all blended well. However, I wasn't a fan of the timing based 2D platforming, even though I dig the art style. Like others have said in the discussions, the mini games could do with a skip button because I can see how some people would struggle and discontinue playing. In some ways I wish they'd taken these out and just made the game longer. I really enjoyed the other puzzles and exploring the houses which are full to the brim with detail. Indika is like no other game I've played before and it's really refreshing to see something this unique and creative in a time where a lot of indie devs are all following the same trends. It's a bold move which has pulled off quite well.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: 'I don't know. I don't know what "bad" means. Nor what "dishonest" or "unfair" means. I don't even know what am I... what am I truly, let alone know other things.' It was heard.To that, I said, as Indika said: It's natural. You know in your heart and feel what's honest and what isn't.'Only we can sin. Only we can talk to Him, and only He can choose who to talk to among us. Only we enter his Kingdom. And only we have seen the imaginary pictures of those burning, slowly, over, and over. But we never saw the imaginary images of those blessed to attain a ticket to the Heavens eternal, cured, blessed, and forgiven. Why?' it was asked.'When everything is subjective, almost nothing is anymore. Good doesn't matter because without Bad we can't measure it, see it, or even acknowledge its existence. Is it fair that a tree has 1000 leaves and another has 1000... and 1? Is it fair that we suffer? Why couldn't He have made us perfect from the get-go? In His vast starry sky, we matter not.' it was told. To that, I say: We are what matters most, for we have the capacity to not only see and reason about the starry sky in ways no other beings can, but we also go beyond to ask about our relation to it. Seeing the snow on the ground is one thing, but asking where it comes from and why it comes even in the first place is what we, humans, do.And that is but one drop, in an ocean of proof, of why we matter most.'Evil and Good are the same, for they can't exist without one another. Cold and heat, dark and light. Everything has its opposite, thus rendering everything as we know it what it cannot be without its opposite pole.'To that, I say: Such grasping of things is one tied to the context of life as we know it, and our knowledge of it is limited, short-sighted, and crippled, for if it wasn't, we wouldn't be needing to ask those questions in the first place.Heal... live. We try to justify everything as long as we feel content with what we did. As long as we are the 'good' guys. Ironically enough, we try to veil good and evil as subjective things half the time, furthermore coping and trying to muddle it all till nothing is clear anymore. At which point no judgment is valid, no punishment is warranted and no sin should be repented. Funny enough, then no 'good' deed is rewarded either. It's really something how this everything is relative outlook is a snake that bits its tail.'Is true and sincere kindness real? Does a dog have a soul?  Is there such a thing as a choice? and when I do choose something, am I not predisposed to do it? What does it all mean?' it was pondered. To that, I say: We are the masters of it all, He wouldn't have wanted it for us to be any other way.An incredible mini-showcase of Russian literature. It's strong, it's sad and bleak.I'm naive because after I finished it I said to myself I wish I had power over this story to make it end differently, start differently. but then what's the point? It's so strong and moving because we feel so hopeless to do anything about it. So helpless that in fact, we cannot even control our emotions and thoughts when perceiving those events. That weakness, is our greatest strength, for it is what sets us apart, and makes us grow and strive.

_childDocuments_.review: I would have given this a sideways-thumb.- I finished the game in 5 hours.- The story is nice and immersive. The praised 'dark humor' is something I was looking forward to, but I don't think the writer meant for it to be funny. It's mostly things an ambivalent trickster demon would whisper to his victim.- The puzzles are very easy - which is good, so you don't get stuck but you do have to overcome a challenge. But it would have been nice if the difficulty level increased a bit while the story progresses. The developers could have used the specific puzzle-mechanics more often, which would make the player feel like they come to understand the world a bit more, although it gets more challenging. (for example: the 'portal' room)- The different styles of game, another thing often mentioned in reviews of this game, is what disappointed me most. Basically there's the real world (TPP) and the memory world (isometric pixel style) and that's it. For the most part you play the game in the real world and only for 4 or 5 little mini-games you are transported to the memory world. The developers could have played with this a whole lot more, although there's the risk it could become a game about gaming and that's not what it's about.- Everything looks beautiful.- I look forward to the next game this studio makes.3,5/5

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA is FineI play a lot of puzzle, story-rich indie games with really dark themes and I feel like if you want a really interesting story and an enjoyable gameplay experience that tackles difficult themes, play Little Misfortune instead.If you care about how pretty a game is and want to have good atmosphere and are ok with really tedious puzzles, a story that's not unique nor very interesting that sort of kind of edges around dark themes while waxing poetic about the meaning of religion and of life, then this game is perfect for you.If any of the above sounds like it's not worth $22, like I felt at the end of this game, then wait for a sale.Some positives: one of the few games to use magical surrealism, which I feel like is missing in the game industry, but I find to be fun to experience. There's also a great sense of humor throughout this game and absurdity. It's also very atmospheric and pretty, but that's about it.  INDIKA isn't a Bad game, but it's not a Great game, and to be honest I don't really understand the hype. I am totally fine with a dark story, no payoff at the end of a game and puzzles, but it felt like every aspect of this game was beating me over the head with the theme: life is unfair, nothing really matters, and religion is stupid. It also took me about 5h to play in total and a lot of that felt like padding.EDIT: I've been thinking about this game a lot since I played it initially, which I think makes it fair to say that the game was a bit more impactful than on first glance.However, I still stand by my initial review, I think the game was just TOO long for what it was and I think if I were to review it as an *experience* vs. a *game* I'd have found it to be enjoyable. But given that, I do think that the game plays on a lot of metaphors, which were effective overall. If it was about half of the length I think I would've loved it, but as it is, it's a bit long, a bit ham-fisted with the "meta" and tried to do too much without enough convincing. Still definitely recommend waiting for a sale!

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA, or How I Learned to Abandon Faith and Hate Myself.Okay, that's a bit reductive, but the spirit (pun intended) is there. INDIKA tells a story of personal worth, and identity, and challenging both while constrained by society, our relationships, God, faith, gender norms, civilisation versus nature, and everything in between, and namely the price we pay, or don't pay, in pursuit of confronting the Self. Or if we do play a price, does it have any value if the economy doesn't exist? And is there meaning to be found in absence?I think the less said about INDIKA, the better. Where it fumbles most is in keeping itself mechanically engaging. Expect a lot of walk-and-talk and small handful of rudimentary puzzle solving, with cheeky gimmicks wrapped in for good measure. On one hand, elegant simplicity works best when a production is constrained by budget and size, and I think Odd Meter have done the best they could with what they've got. That sounds dismissive, but it's not supposed to be. To its credit, puzzles rarely outstay they're welcome. Each is used sparingly rather than repeated. But it does lead to a game that is mechanically minimalist in its engagement, and quite rudimentary, versus simple-but-inventive. If that makes sense. You've 'played' this stuff before.But where INDIKA excels is in its quirky, self aware presentation and prose. It's unexpectedly funny amidst the drab, dire premise, and at no compromise to meaningfulness and brevity where needed most. It's narratively not what I expected, and I mean that as a compliment. I think there's a deliberate, conscious method of prose being used here to inflict absurdity and surrealism as a diversion from the raw truth of the narrative and what's really beating at its heart. It's conscious of you, the player. It's conscious of being a video game. And it's conscious of how to use these facets as a strength deliver it's story.It's the ending that really brings it all together, one that seems sudden, as if it's missing something. But when you realise, well, that's the point, the brevity is felt and the strength of everything leading up to that moment is felt at its most profound. There's some really clever stuff leading up to and nailing the climax, and I think the devs should celebrate that achievement.Very excited for whatever comes next from Odd Meter. Thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10Really weird but entertaining experience, sadly really short also. It's beautiful, dark, but also humorous and light-hearted sometimes. Most of the game is a fun theological/philosophical discussion. Both Indika and the Devil provide some compelling arguments. Indika is also interesting as a character. I definitely didn't expect the abrupt ending though, kinda wish it was a bit longer. Overall can recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing setting, presentation, voice acting and general 'vibe'. The story won't be for everyone, but even then some of the bizarre things that happen, and the way they are presented, are worth experiencing anyway. _childDocuments_.review: If you've ever laughed about the "Press F to pay respects" meme, which juxtaposes reverence with absurd gamey elements, that's exactly the kind of humor you should expect from this game.Indika is a short walking sim with many brilliant, haunting, and absurd set pieces. _childDocuments_.review: I bought this game thinking the trailer for the game was cool and I wasn't expecting much out of it.I was really shocked to find out how good this game is. The puzzles were maybe too much but the visuals and the story is stunning. The story was deep but the ending was kinda unexpected for me at least. The mechanics of praying was fun. I wish we could see more indie games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a fantastic experience. It offers an interesting and funny story, world, and characters with a sprinkle of the surreal. The cinematic journey is sprinkled with a few not-very-difficult puzzles. Enough to keep you engaged and give breaks from the cinematic story. If you are looking for something different I would highly recommend this title.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a 3rd person story driven game about a nun who goes on a quest to deliver an important letter and starts to question her faith, while trying to deal with the voice in her head.This is a story only game with no enemies and some 2-D puzzles that range from very easy to somewhat annoying. There are some light puzzles as well during the main story that are not difficult to figure out, such as pulling switches, and finding a missing object.The voice acting in this game is 10/10 from all involved, it really made the journey worth playing as the game has serious and comical parts.I had no idea what this game was about nor did I know of its development, but I purchased it anyways as it looked like something I would enjoy, and it did not disappoint.This is not a game where it throws Christianity in your face and shoves religion and god down your throat. It’s actually quite the opposite, and makes the protagonists question everything she has ever known.Awesome game when you just want to chill and enjoy a story.I briefly tested on steam deck and it played very well getting 40-50 fps on the wide open areas.8.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Many reviews name the 4 hours you need to finish the game as the biggest drawback. While this is true for a game, Indika is more of an interactive movie. And 4 hours is a good length for an art house movie.The feeling you get is rather the same as when you read a good book, less of gaming experience. One can obviously see Dostoevsky and Bulgakow here, for me it was closer to "Chapayev and Void".Approach this game as a novel and you will not be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly narrative driven walking simulator, but it's probably the best one yet. Atmosphere, worldbuilding, and even gameplay are all tightly bound around the protagonist's inner struggle, and I still find myself turning over and analyzing bits and pieces of the story. I often feel most stories are better expressed in movies or books, but I was surprised at how cleverly the videogame mechanics actually supported the narrative.There's a little bit of jank here and there. Some odd cuts and sticky movement. If you're looking for fun game mechanics, you will hate this game. If you like Dostoevsky or good stories, you'll love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This is a rather simple game which you play for the story. The graphics are quite impressive. I played the game with the VO in Russian, the voice acting was stellar and made me laugh a good few times. In that regard I can't comment on the English VO. However as I had the subtitles in English I can confirm the translation was about as good as can be. I'm mentioning this as not all games get a good translation/VO to languages other than the one they were "made" for. I wouldn't pay full price for this game as its rather short (I finished it in about 5hrs). But if its on sale & you like story games & your pc can run it at maxed out graphics I would definitely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I’ll never not recommend an experience so bold, ambitious, and straight up bizarre. One that needs to be played to be believed.On that level, I had a great time. Totally appreciated what it’s going for and was constantly surprised by the turns it takes. As a gameplay experience it didn’t fully connect with me. Its sporadic puzzles are so simple at times that they feel more like small annoyances than meaningful interactions, but there are plenty of other interactions that do feel meaningful, so I’m not yet sure where I’d draw the line there. I’m kind of left believing that it would work better as a straight up “walking sim”, without some of these mildly annoying puzzles sprinkled about.I do wish I connected with some of the themes a bit better. I’m sure that some of the lines hit deeper if one has something of a connection or more knowledge about Christianity than I do. I didn’t grow up religious, so I’m sure that some stuff flew over my head or didn’t land as hard as it did for other people. Still, I’m sure revisiting it later on will make certain moments land as intended. Enough worked for me to truly make it a memorable time that I hope others give a chance.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly expected more.the game starts off very strong, hints at interesting subplot such as the relationship between the two main characters, but some don't go anywhere while others are resolved abruptly.i'm still recommending it because of the balls it takes to make a game like that, so far away from mainstream. the risk is huge, and the output product is good, but yeah. expected more in terms of story, of twists, and of content too. barely past 3 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The fast answer, is this game worth the price, No. Did I enjoy this game, Not until the very end when the ball starts rolling it just ends.So as the game starts your greeted by nice visuals, and a short cinematic, which leads you into the explorable zone, everything looks nice, and then you're met with the first mission of retrieving and delivering a basket of potatoes, rapidly followed by another boring mission of walking back and forth from a well with a bucket of water to fill a barrel, this takes about 7-10 minutes, give or take. Upon completion you're rewarded with points to buy something from a skill tree, What do the points do beyond giving you a perk that gets you more points? Nothing. Even the loading screens with give you a hint that says "Don't waste time collecting points, they're pointless"...So, why put that feature in the game if it serves No purpose other than to waste time?There are scenes in the game that are dragged on for so long, for instance there's a moment after solving a puzzle where a cut-scene will play, and shows a man, presumably the devil, whistling, and this goes on for a few minutes, before it takes you to the next section of the game. Doesn't add anything to the game, just a long winded cut-scene that just didn't need to be added.This game is tagged as "Horror" does that meant the game is scary? No, not in the slightest, it's just because it deals with subjects like the devil, and because having something like the devil in the game allows them to use that tag, because it loosely falls under that umbrella. Make no mistake there is nothing scary about this game, it's a walking simulator with puzzle solving, that's it.At some point in the game something happens to a character that you did, to which they hate you for it and leave you, telling you to "Get away from me" or "Leave me alone", and then literally 5 minutes later they forgive you, and decide "Hey, what you did, it's fine". Everyone in the game feels incompetent, apart from the Nun you play as who is apparently an expert in every field.The one thing that really irritated me, was with some situations that are supposed to be "Intense" they play music straight from an NES or something, so there's 1 chase sequence in the game, it's not scary so don't worry, but you're really pulled out of it, by some old school 8-bit music, this happens several times through the game.Flash backs to your past are also played back in an NES style, why? Dunno.The game sadly just isn't what I thought it would be, you have this beautiful looking world, with a mediocre story, characters that are impossible to like, and gameplay that's just "Walk, do puzzle, walk, do puzzle, cut-scene, walk, do puzzle" to me that gameplay isn't satisfying, it's boring.Also the game is set in Russia, but everyone apart from 1 guy is English, now i'm English too, so it's wouldn't be as much of an issue, but when you got someone with a name like Svetlov talking like "You awite mate? Yeah not bad Geezer!" it's just real disconnect.So finally, would I recommend this game? No.But as always I'll say read some legitimate positive reviews  of what people liked and disliked, and then form your own opinion on if this game with worth your time and money. And should you find that it is worth your time and money, please wait for a discount, the asking price is too much for what it is, get it when it's about £10, £15 at the absolute most.

_childDocuments_.review: The demo last year left me very impressed and while the final game is still intruiging it ultimately didn't live up to my own expectations. It's good, better than most walking simulators even but not great. There's some annoying sequences where you're not sure what to do or otherwise poor signposting that can be frustrating when you just want to get to the next story bit. However with a direction this striking and unique you can't help but to be completely absorbed from start to finish. There's some remarkable scenes in  from both technical and cinematographic standpoints and the writing manages to go places few games have gone before. I just wish there was a bit more  to it; a rare instance where I wouldn't have minded a few more hours of playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a masterpiece, and possibly one of my favorite games ever.This game masterfully juxtaposes the figure of a nun of seclusion with that of an inmate on the run. Both of them casted out from the institutes that enclosed them, find themselves in a converging road. During the quest to find a religious artifact that is being displayed in a cathedral for people to worship and pray to it for miracles, both characters will engage in philosophical debate about god, faith and humanity. Indika speaks also to a voice in her head, which presents itself as the devil, and puts religion into question in the most absurd and delightfully dark ways (is opening secret correspondence bad? yes? as bad as killing a man? how many letters would you have to open for it to be equal to murder? say you open 20,000 stolen letters, would that be as bad as killing someone then?). Indika's vision of the world and her engagement with this voice begins to distort reality and the way you interact with it as the rules of space and time are broken and bent to transverse the puzzles.This all takes place in an absurdist and surreal alternative version of 19th-century Russia where factories pack whale sized fish in man sized cans for a never to be seen rich upper class, and rewards you for exploring and collecting items with points that as the game keeps telling you don't bother with them, they don't mean anything. Although you can use them to level up things like grief, shame and regret! Which don't do anything. Oh and the sound track is incredible, just a pleasure to hear.Would recommend even at full price, 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Well made, acted, and pretty funny in places. However the mystery being presented as to what's actually going and what the real story being told here is ends up not really feeling worth it. The actual story here is a lot flatter and more basic than I would have liked; game has one thing it explores and that's it. That can certainly be fine but in this case I feel like if this is the only thing this game's going for a lot of the rest of it just feels kinda pointless and like a big wasted opportunity. Given this fact and the price I wouldn't recommend it.
