_childDocuments_.review: Tonally, this title makes some bold choices, but those didn't all gel for me, nor did I feel that they were explored in a particularly engaging way (and no, that's not throwing shade at the water bucket chore scene which, on the contrary, has coherent and purposeful immersive facets in service of the game's table setting). Ultimately, it's unlike anything I've ever played before. I don't know if I'll ever be interested in playing it again though, and at the listed price of $25USD, it's a hard sell.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Well, after having just finished the game, what the hell am I thinking?Disappointed to say the least. I'd put Indika in a YES+NO recommendation since there are parts of the game that are interesting and original but other times, it is just annoying with lame puzzles padding. The story is messed up and seems inspired from Russian novels set in an alternate reality. I didn't like much the story to be honest. The gameplay also was not fun. The "retro-minigames" were becoming annoying too. They only have a meaningful way to tell INDIKA's backstory, in a different fashion.The redeeming factors of INDIKA are the visuals, voice acting, music, dark humour with the Devil and the game's religious theme. Someone mentioned this game could be one hell (pun intended) of a A24 movie and I really agree there. INDIKA could be a great f-cked up movie but as a game, it was just too average.The game supports Ultrawide screen very good and offers a good assortments of visual options. I didn't experienced any bugs, game glitches or crashes.

_childDocuments_.review: Completed Indika Review:6/10TL:DR: Overall I am gonna give it a positive review because I feel like from a narrative standpoint it achieved what it was supposed to, I was just disappointed in the gameplay and felt like it could have done more.Pros:- Dark creepy atmosphere throughout the entire game, I loved the aesthetic so much, it complimented the story and felt pretty tense at parts- Really good story, the entire game is extremely philosophical like all the time, questioning a lot and making you think about a lot of stuff, the ending was depressing but it was EXTREMELY relatable for me so I really liked it.- Voice acting was pretty good and I liked all the dialogue, its abit jarring though how its set in Russia but everyone is British.- Details, theres a lot of details in the story that I liked that were well done, e.g. Indika prays so hard to avoid the voice in her head that it casues her hand to bleed from clutching the rosary beads too hard.- AMAZING CINEMATOGRAPHY Cons:- (Biggest Con) THE GAMEPLAY: I at extremely disappointed with the gameplay, it was advertised as this really cooky, wacky game very similar to Madness Returns and it was NOTHING like that, im not sure why they marketed the game this way, the worst part of all, the coolest part of this game, AKA the time in the demo when she was praying and it changed the environment ONLY HAPPENED TWICE IN THE ENTIRE GAME, I dont understand why they didnt use this more often, it was a sick as hell concept that they literally barely ever used at all.Essentially the entire game is pretty much a walking/running simulator as you listen to the characters discuss religion in a philosophical way, occasionally you will have a puzzle that you need to solve to continue on to the next area and it would sometimes transition into 2D gameplay as like a minigame which for the most part was kinda pointless, it was just to add context/flavour to the story.- The marketing, they advertised this as a game that did a lot of genres as one but in reality it doesnt, like e.g. They said that it had RPG elements to it with the point system and levelling up however like 20m into the game, the game tells you that the points are essentially useless and dont bother to collect them or focus on them too hard, I was annoyed at this but in the end the points ended up being a metaphor in the story which was pretty clever but still slightly annoying.- Playtime: The game is 4-5 hours long, I feel like they could have gone much longer with the story and gameplay.- FPS, the game at parts is really badly optimised and there are major FPS drops, normally id just wait in the area abit and it would fix itself but it was pretty annoying this only happened like 20% of the time though.Overall I am gonna give it a positive review because I feel like from a narrative standpoint it achieved what it was supposed to, I was just disappointed in the gameplay and felt like it could have done more.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this game the same month it dropped after loving the demo. Playing as a nun? Already hooked.☛ Deeply PhilosophicalThe game nails the idea that faith is personal and diverse. I loved the contrast between Ilya and Indika's endings – it really drives home the different views on faith, free will, and doubt. The writing felt authentic, especially how Indika, as a woman, weighs her choices. There are some scenes where we can see nuns and priests as humans first, not saints, they can also be vile and have prejudices. It's so important to remember that under every robe of various faith lies real emotions and flaws, everyone is capable of making mistakes. ☛Visual StorytellingThe pixel art for flashbacks is genius – like foggy old memories. Then, in the present day, the hyper-detailed art adds atmosphere. I also loved how environments outside the cathedral feel oversized, reflecting Indika’s shrinking sense of self.☛Quirky Sound DesignThe frog-beat puzzle? Genius! It’s a unique moment where the solution is subtly hinted through rhythm. The frogs’ croaks naturally align to a beat, and when you catch it, you realize it’s the key to solving the pond puzzle. It’s such a creative way to engage players, blending sound design with gameplay mechanics like this. I also liked other scores, it sounds really unique and quirky!I also respect the devs for tackling such a sensitive religious setting. Some might be offended, others might skip it altogether, but it reminds me why critical thinking is so important in society. It’s an experience worth having.I do wish the story was longer, with more of Ilya's arc, and that choices had real weight. Still, this is one of the most unique indie game I’ve played. ★ 8/10 ★

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a glimmer in a muddled sea of creatively bankrupt products that the video game industry is currently offering to it's customers. It's an unpredictable game, presented in a fresh and inventive way.  People will complain about the price of this title and call it expensive for a "movie game", but you should probably ask those same people how much they've spent on loot boxes and skins. I spent over 6 hours and completed it in it's entirety. People are spending a lot more than $20 to go to the movies and only spend a fraction of that time being as engaged as this game will have you. I do wish it was longer, and as hard as it is to squeeze a dime out of me for games these days, I still  don't feel like I have been shortchanged in the slightest. If the price seems like too much for the average playtime, then wait for it to go on sale, but I think the price to value of this game outweighs your typical AAA title, and these developers deserve it more.I believe that games like this, and folks like this, are what we should be funding.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet. May be very much your cup of tea if the AA boom of more art-house fare like Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice and Plague Tale: Innocence/Requiem have scratched a particular itch. The performances here are largely excellent, especially from Isabella Inchbald who plays the titular protagonist. Mechanically, it's about as pared back as the aforementioned games, but Odd Meter find ways to surprise with gorgeous interstitial segments that feed us Indika's backstory. Overall, excellent. The 19th century Russian hellscape that the devs conjure is a joy to soak in and, along with maybe Kojima and Machinegames, Odd Meter justifies the slavish attention to cinematic tricks with genuinely interesting cinematography and a clear understanding of composition.Definitely worth the asking price IMO.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's one of the best narrative experiences of the year...Update after 100% completion:Well, it was really impressive. I'm pretty sure it's not going to be a blockbuster in any way. Not a game for everyone either (I can't recommend this game to anyone - there's a chance you'll be totally disappointed). No Spoilers:Indika is the short story that can make you think about your life, not about religion itself (and not just the Russian Orthodox one, no). About the choices you make. About the people you keep around you... That's Indika.It's not Russophobic or anti-Russian. I am convinced that if every game studio loved their country as much as Odd Meter loves Russia, the world (well, Steam and other gaming platforms) would be a better place.Thank you guys. Hope to see more projects made by you soon.

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a game that I loved. The story weaves together some commonsense religious "philosophy", life in Russia at the turn of the XX century, good story with several twists, top notch voice acting (Indika is played superbly), and great environmental puzzles. Even more, the game is done in about 4 hours, so you can finish it in an afternoon. The artistic style is very suitable for the themes of the game, and the graphics is, frankly, great for an indie game. What's even better is that the game is explicitly surrealistic: the tech shown in "Indika" is not physically impossible but fantastical for the setting; characters are talking in a very modern way, and I mean not just the language but also the reasoning style and some minor well-placed anachronisms that are just enough to make you wonder. And man, I loved the retro levels! (you'll know what I mean when you play)Overall, great game, highly recommended! There is a caveat, though - I'm talking about the Russian version of the game. I didn't try the English version but I'm pretty sure the voice acting wouldn't be as great there. But most importantly, the plot and the main themes of the game would probably not be familiar to foreigners, at least not familiar enough to enjoy the game as fully as you're supposed to. If your brain doesn't immediately give you a wide range of associations when it hears "Russian orthodox monastery", you may be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Beautfiful and original game, based on exploration (some would call it a walking sim, but it's way more than that).Atmosphere is really great, with great voice acting (kudos to "the devil").I'got it for free (from AWA) so I'm not complaining about the fact that it is short - but it is for the price. But it's also an indie game, so they are probably not sitting on gold and that explains the price.Puzzles are not too hard, but I would have loved to have more of them.There is only one big flaw : I don't expect action parts based on quick reflexes when I play a puzzle / exploration games. There are in Indika a few times that can be difficult depending on your skills. While the devs put a lot of checkpoint in this case to ease the thing, I didn't see any 'skip' option, that may be game breaking for some people. Personally, I struggled a bit but went through it.Anyway, I really enjoyed my time in the skin of Indika and warmly recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: On the modern gaming landscape, Indika is like a breath of fresh air. Not many games have dared to explore the subject of religion at all, especially not in a rather unsafe and provocative way. And I am using these words in the most positive sense because we are talking about the experience that makes you think and feel here. An experience that is emotionally strong (if not brutal) and that keeps you engaged all the way through until the end.The world of Indika feels very real and twisted at the same time. We find ourselves in the steampunk-infused and disproportioned setting of late XIX century Russia. The late-March spring is dark, depressing and it creates the perfect setting for the story to unfold. And it is also looks stunning for the most part. The childhood stories of Indika are told through some bright and colorful 8-bit style minigames, greatly contrasting the bleak world of the game. These minigames are also quite challenging, adding up to the feeling that you are actually playing and not just walking around.As far as the gameplay goes, aside from the minigames, Indika is mostly a walking-simulator type of game. There are some puzzles to figure out, some platforming, some driving, some chase scenes. While none of them are particularly complex, together they create a well-balanced (and well-paced) gameplay experience, especially given the fact that the game is only a few hours long.Last but not least, the Russian voice acting in the game is really great. I strongly recommend switching the voice to Russian (and leaving the subtitles in your language on) - this will definitely enhance the experience.To sum things up, Indika is a perfect indie-game and a must-play for those of us willing to broaden our perspective on videogames as the form of the art.

_childDocuments_.review: You like European "Art" movies? You like bizarre Russian stories where nothing seems to matter, and nothing makes sense? _childDocuments_.review: In the realm of gaming, there are titles that firmly grab your attention, others that leave you indifferent, and then there are those that hover somewhere in the middle, like this one. At first glance, it held a tantalizing promise, particularly with the captivating presence of the devilish narrator whispering in the protagonist's head. The premise was ripe with potential, offering a journey into the depths of the human psyche, but alas, it falls short of delivering on its initial allure.The game ambitiously flirts with a plethora of themes, ranging from morality and existentialism to the blurred lines between reality and illusion. Yet, as the story unfolds, it becomes increasingly apparent that these themes are explored merely at surface level, never fully delving into their complexities or providing satisfying resolutions. Instead of tying up loose ends, the conclusion leaves players grappling with more questions than answers, leaving a lingering sense of dissatisfaction.Despite its shortcomings, it's hard to deny the appeal of the game's concept. One can discern a clear sense of direction and purpose at the outset, but as the narrative progresses, it becomes muddled and convoluted. It's almost as if the creator lost themselves amidst the intricate web of their own creation, unable to navigate through the maze of ideas and concepts they had set out to explore.In the end, while the game may not live up to its full potential, there's still something intriguing about its flawed execution. It serves as a reminder of the delicate balance between ambition and execution in the world of game development, where even the most promising ideas can falter if not handled with care and precision.Game time is about 3 hours (up to 6 if you want to get all the achievements).

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting story, captivating atmosphere, great voice acting, walking simulator with easy puzzles; however an useless point/leveling system and a "stupid" open ending (which IS the point of the story). _childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a surreal story-driven game that made me feel a mix of emotions I have never experienced in a game before.You play as Indika, a nun whose convent looks down upon and shuns. It's evident there's something not quite right about her, which his portrayed by a voice in her head that antagonizes her throughout her journey.Everything in the game is done deliberately to really make you feel on edge, through the uneasy dialogue, strange happenings, and some of the most unusual and interesting camera angles I've seen in gaming. The game even has strange video game theming woven into it, via its UI, and level up system, further pushing forward the feeling of being out-of-place. As for the gameplay. For the most part, you explore desolate locations, talk to companions, and solve simple puzzles. That's because the game at its core is a narrative-centric one, and everything else is a means of delivering Indika's unusual story, of which I found very intriguing, and incredibly uniquely portrayed.The gameplay isn't its strongest suite, but that's okay, because it's a ride unlike any others. Indika's most compelling selling point by far is the fact that its story-telling devices are so fresh and original. I really haven't experienced something like this before. I would regularly be laughing, disturbed and intrigued all in one scene.And if that sounds like something compelling to you, I'd recommend picking up the game!It's a short experience, but definitely something very unique!
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The cutscenes are pure arthouse film, great direction and always visually interesting. The environment is extremely atmospheric. The pixel art and retro gaming moments are integrated seamlessly. The music is moody and discordant and sometimes even something like a steam engine in game is making music in a subtle way. The game isn't horror, but it's frequently unsettling, and then sometimes comedic. The whole time it has felt like a singular vision

_childDocuments_.review: Indika: A Sureal, witty and genre defining narrative experience.--------------------------------------------------------------------------🎮 Gameplay: ( 6.95 / 10 ) Indika takes the "walking simulator" genre and gives it a jolt of existential caffeine. The gameplay still follows the basics of a walking simulator but Indika adds a depth of layer with its switches to 2d and its occasional minigames and puzzles. This method gives players a minibreak from constantly walking, which I would say is rather refreshing. The puzzles are not hard, but challenging enough to make the player not lose focus, while the minigames often are timing based. What they did right here, is having the right balance of difficulty, not make anything seem tedious. 📘 Story: ( 8.9 / 10 ) The story is a philosophical deep dive wrapped in layers of humor, sarcasm, and some good old-fashioned trolling. It's like a therapy session with a snarky therapist who sometimes questions your choices and makes you laugh at the absurdity of it all. Themes of religion, self-worth, and reflection over what’s good and bad are explored with a unique twist, making you ponder your existence while trying to decipher the surreal world you are currently bound to. The characters are both unique and well crafted, it does not give you the sense of like heroes or generalized characters, they seem both surreal and real, in some sense they are comical. But If you were in their shoes, in this time period, the reflection of how they act is, funny, sad and in a sense real to the situation they are currently in. 🌆 Worldbuilding: ( 8.9 / 10 ) The world of Indika is a surrealist's dream (or nightmare). Imagine walking through a Salvador Dalí painting while having a conversation with Douglas Adams. The game uses proportions to its advantage by making smaller objects much larger, giving the world a sense of surrealism while still having familiar elements in the right proportion. They also take geometry to the extreme, and have things at really sharp angles, extreme heights, or really big and broad objects. Indika really nails the fact that they have created their own surreal world, even though it’s based in a realistic timeline. The way sound, visuals and characters are portrayed, helps this game create a really unique world that further help establish its own true identity, amidst a dozen other titles that fail to do the same.📺 Visuals: ( 8.1 / 10 ) Visually, Indika does pretty good, it could be compared to the game “the invincible” but it falls a little bit short. The art style is bold and unconventional, it does a good job at complementing the game's twisted atmosphere. The graphical design melds together elements of dreamlike fantasy and gruff reality, creating a visual experience that keeps you engaged. The attention to detail could be improved. The same thing could be said about facial animations and expressions in general. Even though this game has 80% of its game in 3d, implementing a certain percentage of 2d, elevates the game overall feel, and the visuals are overall pretty good. 🎧 Sound: ( 10 /10 ) What makes this game truly shine, is for me the sound design. The aim is to throw you off your normal rhythm for this kind of game, it seems almost trollish, which creates an unique and interesting atmosphere. The sound effects sounds nice, crackling wood, wind, sudden chimes and different elements that you don’t expect also helps you be emerged in the game. Now the best part of the game: The narration. The narrator’s voice is compelling; he is great at putting pressure on different tones to different words, which helps immensely with immersion. The narrator keeps mocking you through the play through with witty remarks and sarcastic comments, but also gives you a change of pace with philosophical questions that make you reflect. It is easy to focus on his words, rather than thinking about the fact that you are playing a walking simulator. Which is what story driven games should be doing. In a sense it reminds me of Hellblade: Senuas sacrifice, only better. --------------------------------------------------------------------------🏆 Overall Score: ( 8.6 / 10 ) Indika is a refreshing take on the walking simulator genre. It deftly combines surrealism, humor, and philosophical reflections to create a game that is both thought-provoking and entertaining. The game has a really unique feel compared to other walking simulators, with its twisted vibe and cleverly thought out distinct aura. While it may not be for everyone, those who appreciate a good dose of sarcasm, witty humor, and genre defining narration, will definitely enjoy this gem of a title. --------------------------------------------------------------------------📖 Notes and tips- The game is pretty short, playtime is around 2 and a half to 3 and a half hours, so even though this a gem, the price is pretty steep compared to the content you get.- I also found the audio to be somewhat off balance, and would recommend players to set the environmental volume to 75, while keeping the other values at 100.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, I mean I finished the whole thing in a single setting when I only meant to check how well it ran to play later today (oops!). That being said the trailers on the store page REALLY give the wrong idea of the game. Although to be fair I have no idea how you market a weird little experience like this. It did leave me feeling the world in the trailers was way more "wacky" than the actual world in the game.The ending works but at the same time due to the weird obtuse nature of the game all the way through and the way the ending intends to let you draw your own conclusions I ended up thinking it was some kind of fake-out or something, but nope. When the credits play it really is over.I really enjoy how the game uses its criticism of religious faith in a way which it then throws back in the players face on a meta level through the game its self.ALL THIS BEING SAID the game is very short, and although I have no issues with this, if you have limited funds and want your purchase to keep you busy for a while this isn't the game for you. _childDocuments_.review: ⭐⭐⭐⭐☆Indika is a captivating indie game that deserves a solid 4 out of 5 stars. The graphics are impressive, bringing the game's unique, slightly psychedelic art direction to life. The story is decent, and the well-written dialogues add depth to the narrative, making for an engaging experience.The themes explored in the dialogues are intriguing, adding layers of meaning to the gameplay. However, the ending feels a bit rushed, and I would have liked to see more development of the characters towards the conclusion. Despite this, Indika offers a good overall experience.The game is relatively short, taking about 3.5 to 4 hours to complete, with easy puzzles that are accessible to most players. For those aiming to achieve 100% completion, it might take around 4.5 to 6 hours. Indika is a memorable journey that combines strong visuals, interesting themes, and enjoyable gameplay into a neat package.

_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a little short and left me wanting a little more from the ending, but I have to absolutely applaud the effort. This is a truly unique game that is a work of art. If you like narrative driven games like "Firewatch," you'll love this one. It by no means has the same kind of charm, haha (it's meant to be bleak), but it has the same kind of emotional depth and atmosphere. In fact, it has more gameplay than "Firewatch"! There's actually real puzzles to solve! And platforming! To name a few.If you like narrative driven games, enjoy unique experiences and a little bit of the absurd, I highly recommend this game! If there's one thing I might fault it for it's that the religious, spiritual, and philosophical conundrums are a little surface level, though they would be easy to grasp for someone not familiar with the ideas of religion and morality portrayed in the game. If you want a game with deeper philosophy and is more puzzle driven, I recommend "The Talos Principle."
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a work of art. I strongly recommend it but keep in mind it's not ...normal. Overall, it's dark, extremely creative and hard to classify. Sometimes it's like a horror game but you don't go around trying to find bullets and shooting things. Other times it's an exploration based "walking simulator" with surprisingly fun environmental puzzles. I'm personally not a huge fan of puzzle games, however these are orchestrated really well for the most part (minus some fairly minor technical issues from time to time). The exploration and puzzle solving are broken up by profound dialogue, an A+ surreal story and refreshing mini-games. I just finished it and wow. It's good.

_childDocuments_.review: "It's truly an outstanding game. A nun who talks with demon, and a bandit who talks with the God. The story and its narrative are brilliantly crafted and portrayed. It's been a long time since a game with such a beautiful, unique, and human-like plot has come out. Whether it's the moment when Indika succumbs to his own instincts and the devil takes over his thoughts, or when the world shifts to a different dimension, or the puzzles in the level designs, everything was truly perfect. The 2D pixel sections that support the story, showcasing both Indika's past and his present experiences, added a unique atmosphere, and they were also wonderfully executed. Truly magnificent."-Do not collect points. It is pointless.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: If big AAA games are like hollywood blockbusters, this game would be more like some soviet-era art film: There isn't much going on in terms of action, it's more of a surreal contemplative experience with symbolism, beautiful visuals, interesting cinematography and meandering sequences with a clear focus on the characters themselves and their discussions about philosophy, religion and fundamental questions. And then it ends quite abruptly with a lot of things open to interpretation. For some this will sound boring, for others it'll immediately pique their curiosity. If you fall into the latter category, you will probably thoroughly enjoy the game.The puzzles are relatively simple and the game is quite short. It can be completed in under 4 hours with no real replayability but I think it's ok for that kind of game. It doesn't overstay its welcome and you don't want artificial padding especially in a game with an artistic vision that is so precise. I'm looking forward to the next games from those devs and hope we see more and more daring experiments like this in the indie scene.

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILER REVIEWIndika is about our heroine's self discovery, when she causes the death of her romantic interest she goes insane, the devil appears in her head and she joins the convent to get closer to god in order the cast the devil off her head. You start off in the convent where everybody literally hates you for... reasons? Reasons I guess being annoying and loud during religious ceremonies? At the very beginning we see one of these moments where Indika freaks out bc she is insane and she sees something? I thought this was a horror game or at least it featured horror elements since it is tagged as such and our heroine seems to be possessed by the devil but there is not one scary bit. After she freaks out you start carrying out mundane tasks and there is this voice always implying the contradictory nature of religion but you don't really understand that this is the voice of the devil in Indika's head bc honestly the voice actor sounds more like a narrator and Indika never really interacts with it at the start. Later we see a glimpse of her visions. During a ceremony one of the nuns' mini form comes out of her mouth dancing and jumping around very weirdly to a weird ass song almost resembling early 2010s goofy tf2 animations, and she freaks out (neither scary nor weird). There is also a scene later in the game, where we see a closeup of a whispering nun, again resembling tf2 animations, was that supposed to weird out the player or something.. cause its not weird, scary nor eerie. It feels out of place and insignificant because it is, it has no value in the narrative yall put that in the game just because you thought it would increase the weirdness value of the game, it is meaningless stupid and annoying like that stupid mini nun. Weird doesn't equal absurd. After all the unnecessary drama Indika is given a delivery task. On her way to delivering a letter she encounters a person who is on his way to "The Kudets" travelling miracle workers promising to heal any ailment. Upon hearing this the heroine joins him hoping this what might finally get rid of the voice in her head. Up until this point you don't really know where the story is going so it feels like a very long prologue to a very short game and it leaves a bad impression.  A lot of people seems to agree that this is a weird game (it is also marketed and listed as such) if you consider that to be the same as being out of place and nonsensical sure this is a "weird" game but I suggest yall to watch more movies. To me it feels like they were trying too hard to break convention (mixing pixel sections and ui to a 3d game and a soundtrack that doesn't match the setting, their understandment of breaking convention lacks nuance and feels shallow). Fish factory to me was the only weird part of the game and thats mostly bc of those huge fish and empty vast spaces we see through out the big level. They should've relied more on their level design to make the game weird bc the game is actually fun, plays smooth and the atmosphere is great. The part you would expect to see nuance are parts where our two main characters have deep talks about free will and morality and these dialogues are actually well written and they are deep and nuanced but only to our religious characters. For it to be nuanced for the player you would have to be 10 years old or something grown up in a religious environment bc to non believers these are all too obvious. There is not much to say other than it being too much on the nose. Yes religion is stupid and if you debate over free will, morality and determinism through the lens of religion and god, it contradicts, doesn't make sense. What annoyed me the most was the dialogue between Indika and the devil at the end where the devil tries to use semantics to argue and like omggg stfu that part was so meaningless I dont even know what the reason was bc at the end non of the things the devil said actually contributed to Indika's eventual disbelief to god, it was bc the kudets didn't work and she said ♥♥♥♥ it there was no need for the empty philosophy between the devil and Indika. Dialogues between Indika and Ilya actually meant something to the characters and to the player bc they were talking about the human condition it is actually relatable bc it is something each person does. The characters and dialogues are written well but the execution of the devil was so poorly bc it never really feels like the devil but rather like intrusive thoughts, the only image of the devil you get is at the end and thats quite literally the image as they modeled it lol. Its a good self discovery story but the whole idea behind the title being weird and unconventional ruined it for me, especially after seeing that 11 facts trailer, a weird title doesn't need to be marketed as such to be seen weird it should inherently be so

_childDocuments_.review: beatification any% speedrun is a russian game where you play as nun that talks to the devil. Her name is shockingly Indika.It's as shocking as this russian game being ostensibly russian. Very eastern european, ear to ear grin full of misery.  It's arthouse movie in game form.Indika is also a very political game - per director's own words - it's commentary on the Eastern Orthodox Church and political situation in Russia. How the Orthodox Church takes advantage of people to further agenda of the powers that be - the earthly, not the heavenly. There is no specific genre or neat box you can put Indika into - it tries a lot of different things. It's mostly 3rd person perspective game where you have to solve various puzzles to progress. But it is also a 2D platformer. And a 2D racing game. And some other genres. While game doesn't necessarily stand out in any specific way in any of those - it stands out in how it combines all of those creatively, to deliver a very humane, but also tragicomic story. While a lot of commentary on religion feels like something you have seen before if you ever showed any interest or discussed atheism, it's put well into writing that feels very energetic and flows well.  The story is best experienced by yourself and by going in as blind as possible. It doesn't overstay its welcome, clocking around 4 hours for me. Understandably, the hamfisted messaging might not resonate with everyone, but it's worth experiencing.Visually the game is beautiful and nigh photorealistic in many cases. Game uses that photorealism very well with its bizarre art-direction, where you have lifelike looking bizarre architecture, machines and monstrosities. It's a very fun contrast that helps set the sombre, but also tongue-in-cheek mood and atmosphere.Aurally, it's also very well done. The music complements the game well, though there isn't much that stands out by itself. Voice acting performances are well acted - both in english and russian. Together with immersive sound effects they really manage to sell you on atmosphere of a place, no matter how bizarre it may look. That crunch when walking on snow is really damn good.While definitely ambitious, it's clear the game was made by small team. Modern technologies such as Unreal Engine 5 helped them punch way above their weight. But the smaller team and budget is still visible in the occasional jank.And since the game looks so photorealistic, it can be sometimes difficult to tell what to interact with. This leads some puzzles not feeling very intuitive - but nothing that should put you off  the game.Overall, I really liked Indika. And I liked it because it was a huge swing to try to express something and try something new. It definitely wasn't a miss and I am not sure entirely how far the ball flew in the end  - but the swing itself was beautiful.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought it today, played it through in one session, about 5 hrs.Developers created a playbale introspective movie, with lovely introduction and ending credits that go beyond technical necessities and proove this work to be art. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. It looks gorgeous and the story is gripping, but the gameplay caused me frustration through the entire experience. I understand that there are elements that are intentionally frustrating, but after some of the endlessly similar looking climbing puzzles about figuring out the correct position of some elevator or machine, I just wanted to close out the game and do something else for a while. And the worst part is, whenever I did this, I needed to redo entire sections, because the game does not allow you to save, and only saves at infrequent checkpoints. For me personally, the worst part is that in the puzzles where you can fail, the time until the game lets you try again is way too long. I understand that this kind of game does not put as much focus on interesting gameplay, but in this title, to me, a lot of the puzzles and the overall interaction with the gameword just feels unpolished. It is often not clear how high Irina can vault, and the over-the-shoulder perspective makes it even harder go get a feel for how she can move through the world. I want to finish the game, and I hope the ending will be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a great little game. It felt original and it felt fresh. Funny too! The game does have a trigger warning and you can also turn nudity off, so the reviews complaining about it are kind of unjust in my opinion cause its not 'hidden' in any way. Also, literally nothing is graphically shown as it goes into a philosophical conversation with the devil as its 'happening' which is a much better way of including something potentially triggering than, say, the way games like BG3 showed it imo (very graphically). I played the demo a few months ago and have been looking forward to it's release, and I really love the juxtaposition it does of this realistic scenery and pixel graphics with arcade gameplay. It's such a stunningly made game and I'm honestly surprised it didn't brick my laptop- I even played it on the highest settings too!Gameplay: Good (mostly standard puzzles, but some are really visually interesting; such as, literally tearing the world apart)Graphics: Great (god that snow shader is to die for)Music: Great (It's unsettling and that's its aim, loved it)Story: Very GoodPC Requirements: Mid (I have a 3+ year old laptop that played it fine but I also use it for development)Game Time: 3 - 4 hrs. There is a level selection, so if you want to 100% the game, you can just replay the relevant level too- which *chef's kiss*.Overall: 8.5/10I appreciate a good, short, well packaged game. It's more of an experience and it definitely delivers on that. Its for certainty, an art piece as well as a game. I'm really looking forward to this Studio's future releases!

_childDocuments_.review: The good- Lovely visuals with detailed graphics and nice weather effects. Especially with these fish eye lenses sometimes it look so realistic. Its world is cold and unwelcoming and manages to immerse you right from the beginning.- Great direction. It has nice cut scenes, awesome close ups scenes and clever use of various lenses to enhance each situation. It's very cinemetic.- Indika is an amazing character with strong personality, inner thoughts, backstory and cute sense of humor. Her kind, optimistic nature comes in contrast to the gloomy world and the harsh situation she's been into. There are a few interesting secondary characters too.- It's well written. Indika's inner thoughts, narration, dialogues. Everything feels genuine, has something interesting to tell and will never bore you.- Great voice acting performances that feel absolutely convincing and fit each role. Narrator's creepy voice is also a perfect fit.- Simple, yet good audio design with environmental sounds that create a convincing, pretty realistic atmosphere.- Nice music. It doesn't get overused, instead it enters only when necessary letting environmental sound design and dialogues do their job.- Cool, smooth animations and interactions. Indika's clothes are waving realistically with her movement. Facial expressions are great and full of emotions.- Parts with the pixel graphics, mini platform games as well as the point system are all nice additions. A clever way to show past events and describe a girl's playful mind.The bad- The story is decent with some interesting events and thoughtful dialogues, yet it loses its balance soon. Surreal elements are rushed and don't manage to elevate the atmosphere or transfer you to Indika's esoteric world. Parts of dialogues and actual gameplay are too distinctive each other which makes the game to feel fragmented. After the first hour it gets transformed into a light action adventure forcing you to climb on rooftops and operate gigantic cranes. It feels more like filler content that doesn't communicate organically with the story. Some situations look a little bit ridiculous. I expected a much more esoteric, cryptic experience.- Gameplay is shallow without fresh ideas. The few puzzles are too simplistic with worn, uninteresting mechanics like moving boxes to climb on higher levels. Ideas like praying, that transforms the world around you, had much more potential, but it is used only two or three times.

_childDocuments_.review: Using the irrelevance of my review to the game's approval rating as an excuse for sharing a negative impression. I don't particularly like giving small developers or artists in general "grief," but this just bored me to tears enough that only an attempt at articulating my disinterest will satisfy the forfeited hours and $19.99.I think the acceptance of video games as art (they are) too often lies in their ability to present themselves as "cinematic" or "mature," qualities which INDIKA immediately exudes. It has a stark setting and premise unlike those seen in the majority of mainstream releases, and bases itself on topics of religion and guilt almost equally uncommon in video games.Sure, nice. Where INDIKA caught my eye was in the flashes of eclectic 2D segments, or the mocking tone of some of the marketing material. Maybe this grim and serious game wasn't as dry as it appeared? And to its credit, I think the most interesting parts of the game are the 2D interludes, flashing back to Indika's past to peel away layers of what makes her tick, and the opening scenes of monotony where you're asked to labor over getting water from a well. When the game uses its gaminess to prove a point is when it succeeds. But the truth is, beyond that, things peter out. The story takes on layers of ambiguity and surrealism that I've seen compared to Wojciech Has or Bela Tarr films, but whereas films like Werckmeister Harmonies or Lars von Trier's Europa exude a foreboding atmosphere through the devices of their medium (long takes, dramatic lighting, etc) INDIKA continues to play as a droll, I hate the label, "walking simulator."Really makes you appreciate how Kojima and his team made Death Stranding so engaging, or how fun it is to just roll around in Katamari Damacy.The point that I think INDIKA and a lot of art games miss is that the act of playing, manipulating the game, is what should be zeroed in on in terms of eliciting a response from the player. Crackdown is as much a work of art for how jumping 50 feet in the air feels as Journey is for how it effortlessly and mysteriously connects you with strangers. The feedback of a DOOM shotgun is as poetic a manipulation of code, visual, and sonic feedback as Hemingway's description of a bullfight's harsh light and dusty arena. I don't really care for Hemingway, so the point is moot if you don't buy into it.As a jaunt through an imaginary world, INDIKA is perhaps worth the investment. "Investment," being a cruel way of deciding whether to engage with a work of art, but maybe true. Clearly the game has taken off, and I wish it and similar visions and commitments to expression nothing but success. I guess the alternative means of bringing something like this to life through animation or a live-action production would simply be unfeasible. Would love to see StudioCanal greenlight a couple hundred million to make sets like the locations in INDIKA.Yeah right!I watched The Devil and Daniel Webster a few days before impulsively buying this, so I was just sort of in the mood for a little Faustian stuff I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: Very few games have made me want more.  Doubly so for how short of a game Indika was.  I'm sad I don't get to see more of the story, or see how the character(s) handle how the game ends.A very well put critic on religion and beliefs.  The game is just as long as it needs to be for the message it's trying to send, and probably wouldn't be quite the same if it was much longer.  Says what it wants, drops the mic, and exits stage left.I would've been fine if they removed some of the puzzles and just put more dialogue, but then I could see people complaining that "iT sHoUlD bE a MoViE iNsTeAd".  And to be honest, it would probably end up being a walking simulator (albeit a beautiful one with an interesting world).It's a shame it's so short.  I would've loved to explore the world this takes place in more, and see more of the characters in it.  There are so many little details to look at and investigate, I think the world by itself makes me wish this was a longer game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are interested in a game that has a message about free will, the dangers of defying other people's expectations of you, and the nature of personal faith, Indika will suit that interest. The impressive bit is that it accomplishes all of that without making you feel like you're hanging out with that one atheist dude that took a theology course just to argue with people better. On top of the message of the game, the radical use of "in camera" effects created quite a few images that will stick with me for a long time. I hope that future game devs take note and use these techniques in the future (assuming there are any devs in the world left after the next few rounds of layoffs.)

_childDocuments_.review: honest review.  {Spoilers}It was a cool theme and good idea. The story was none existent really. I got halfway through the game to come across the credits. The game ended without anything actually happening. Cutscenes made no sense. A character dropped something down the stairs, Indika goes to crab it. Suddenly the character who dropped it is at the bottom of the stairs having apparently fallen down without being shown happening. I assume its a story of regret. In the flashback scenes, Indika sleeps with a guy who stole something of her fathers for some reason. The guy suddenly wants to run away with her because Indika is going to be forced to marry someone else. He wants to steal from, her farther yet again... She says she doesn't want to do that to her own farther. He takes the key to the shop and steals anyway. The farther corners the guy. Indika says she doesn't know him because imo she did this because if she said she did know him, her farther would assume they're working together to steal from him. Which isnt the case. He for some reason is irritated at Indika for not telling her farther they knew each other. Indika's farther shoots him. I understand she would feel regret not knowing that her farther would shoot him but none of its her fault. She stole nothing. The rest of the game was supposed to be about Indika delivering a letter. She s meets a guy she randomly follows. Then she is sorta kidnapped by him. Then she stays with him again. Indika reads the letter. Idk what it said, but I'm assuming the person who wrote it expected her to read it because suddenly she couldn't go home again. Then Indika and the guy go to a church. The guy thinks god attach his arm to his body. You get this artefact. It squirts lots of points out. Then the game ends. Bad ending.I did like that Indika's reflection is the devil mirroring her demons.  But the story was pretty none existent. Audio lines kinda felt out of place at times. I was hoping just before the credits came. That there would be a solid goal for the game and that if that was the case then it may have been better. I'm not necessarily annoyed by how short this game is. 3 or so plus hours is acceptable for me if the their is an actual story and goal. It felt like too many interesting ideas together. The story being the last though out thing and so rushed. Its a somewhat interesting experience with the detail of the world. But I do not think its enough to enjoy the experience as a whole. _childDocuments_.review: Only barely scratched the surface on this one, but I can already tell it's a very interesting and unique game. This will not be for people who are looking for a "typical" game, rather for people interested in a unique story/narrative based game: you play as a russian nun in an alternate XIX universe after all... Are you ready to go on a simple journey that touches on all the religious stuff?It's 3D and 3rd person and mostly involves the traversal and puzzle elements, whilst having dialogue and narration infusing the negative space with thought provoking mostly religious stuff. You see, Indika is a "troubled (no spoilers here...)" nun and the game absolutely lets you live that. And also the game has some "gamified" elements which makes it weird and clashing with the other stuff, but strangely it works and it gets more intriguing because of that? Definitely intriguing.The graphics are quite good for a seemingly AA game: quite good lighting in particular and no major issues other than some AA jank with animations - this is not a AAAA polished game, but totally nice looking, not that demanding on your system (btw nice settings menu), and bug free at launch (omg, that's a miracle right there on this day and age).In particular, I'm struck with the simply "standing" animations for the main character: she looks down and fidgets with her hands and fingernails and rosemary in a very expressive way. They capture that very well for a kind of an AA game, and the visual character design and also voice acting performance supports that all the way. Again, for an AA type game, I'm impressed with the result of bringing the character to life.I'm so glad stuff like this is still possible: unique games that go shoulder to shoulder with the usual commercial stuff. Even if the polish isn't quite to the same AAA-console level, the originality alone brings life to the player.

_childDocuments_.review: After watching the trailers and playing the demo I was genuinely excited for this game. It seemed so unique and unhinged.Then I purchased the game and I was disappointed. I know the devs probably poured their heart and soul in this but it feels rushed. Like the hell puzzle sequences where you alternate between hell and normal by praying are the most beautiful scenes but there's very few of them, and one of them was already given away in the demo.The most amazing chase sequence is with the dog and that's it, you never get another intense moment or even an enemy to evade except for that one.There was a lot of promise in how Indika explained how the technology worked in the paint factory but again, you never get any more technical explanations of things after that.Basically all the best things were in the demo.The skill tree in the demo made it look like it was going to be a thing but that too is a fake-out. You never get to allocate skill points to anything. The devs tell you that the points mean nothing and they are not kidding, the points mean nothing.The ending is the most anti-climactic ending ever, with nothing really being resolved, nothing really making any sense, and nothing really happening, no big final boss battle, no big adrenaline rush. And the 2D platformer parts were cute bit completely unnecessary, very out-of-touch with the cold bleak world of the 3D world, almost like its a different story. And the story they tell does not make much sense either.So I'm sorry but I really wanted to love this game and honestly I commend the devs for trying to do something new and coming up with such an amazingly well crafted universe but in my eyes they failed to deliver on their promise and this was a letdown for me.

_childDocuments_.review: A really good narrative puzzle game from a small indie studio. Of course the topic and the protagonist is what will get your attention, but also seeing Orthodox Christianity in a game is something new for me. There are plenty of games that add Catholic Christianity topics either for narrative purposes or for world building.You can think of this game similar to Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice, only with puzzles and no combat and with a different topic. If you liked that one, you will like this one. The graphics and visuals are very well done, the characters look really good and their facial expressions stand out in every scene.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally a game with an honest secular world view. I loved the game both for asking some of the most clarifying philosophical questions, and giving the true answers, without concern for those still holding to folklore as fact. It is kind of brutal about it though. Still, i could see this game leading to more rational people in the world. on top of all that, the art design and surrealist world are incredibly realized. best graphics since Alan wake 2.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: definitely is one of the weirdest games I've ever played.Blending a retro aesthetic through its flashbacks and music with some pretty realistic visuals and an interestingly short assortment of cut scenes. This is unlike, well, almost anything I've played before.First half hour of  will be spending on completing on some, seemingly irrelevant tasks. Though that is definitely intentional by devs. All those tasks serves one purpose: To creating an engaging gameplay loop. To put player in the shoes of Indika as she questions the point of not only these tasks, but her entire faith. To create a sense of contrast between her monotonous life in the monastery and puzzles and exciting sequences found outside of the walls. I do enjoy those puzzles, even though I'm not a puzzle game lover. Genuinely engaging and inventive brain teasers.This odd position between the honest but boring life of a nun and the sinful but exciting gameplay found in the wider world is exemplified by the voice inside of Indika's head--the devil. She's intensely flawed, but profoundly relatable, what some might describe as the perfect depiction of a sinner.The narrative I experienced in  had me engaged, deep in thoughts and above all else disturbed. These are the feelings that stuck with me long after I reached the credits.The visual of the game is very impressive. Just to remember that this is from a indie dev. The level of detail in every unique environment  and interior is absolutely mind-blowing. And I'm not sure what exactly they're using for lighting, but it looks really good.In summary,  is an incredibly unique experience that isn't afraid to ask some big questions, with it's interesting and varied visual presentation along with some inventive and engaging puzzles. It's an outstanding display of what Indie dev can offer to this media.

_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Initially this seemed like a game right up my alley. Odd, surrealistic visuals set in a unique and obscure setting mixed with slow-paced gameplay that really lets you enjoy them sights? Well, you've got all that in this game and then some. The soundtrack was also just as great and inventive as the graphics.Based on all of that I guess I was expecting more from the story rather than just kinda feeling hollow and falling into that typical "religion bad, mkay" trap that is so common in this scene. Feels like even the "score system" had more to say than the actual story yet managed to do it without a single line of dialogue.Ultimately Indika is a fairly short (~5h) and light puzzle game about what is "good" and what is not with some questionable platforming sections that probably account for most of that playtime. Depending on how you feel about the story, your mileage vary and you may end up enjoying it, but for me it didn't hit the mark.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that's best enjoyed alongside friends, and you need to have the kinds of friends who are good at sitting through movies and talking about the movie as they're watching it - this game is also rough with how it ends and is very much an art piece, but it's weirdly enough an art piece I needed.This is also the kind of art piece that is very much built to be viewed through a lived lens - and by that I mean this is one of those stories that is meant to resonate with a specific kind of person... Or people who know that kind of person. From my own personal interpretation, this story is heartrending and beautiful but I don't know if it'll resonate with others without them having lived it alongside me, or me telling them.If I tell you then, too, dear reader, then your experience will be poisoned in a similar to that which the Devil talks to Indika in this game... If you can stomach a vague ending and a short game with pretty decent puzzles, a very beautiful storyon the nature of where Spirit and Mind meet that will not answer the questions it leaves you with, just pick it up for yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Great and weird game. Sadly a little short. It is one of the most unique games I've ever played. Loved the atmosphere, the story, the world, the puzzle variety and the weird mixture between realism and pixel art. My only complaint I feel like the game ends quite abruptly. I wish it was 2 times longer.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This game is somewhat reminiscent of Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice. No, there is no Scandinavian mythology, battles or strange symbols everywhere around the world. But as well as Hellblade, Indika focuses on a young girl with mental problems who travels through gloomy landscapes in search of salvation for her and her companion souls. And even the voice in the head of the main character is also there. The gameplay is in similiar way based on walking through semi-open locations and solving puzzles. The world of the game is saturated with the Orthodox religion and totally deserves to be called the land of the dead. I don’t know if the creators of Indika were inspired by the game of Ninja Theory, but in any way they created an original, unique style thing. The game is very short and takes a few hours to go through, but at the same time the plot narrative is very intense, there is little superfluous in there. It feels mostly like a kind of game-like theatrical performance.I recommend Indika to people who like offbeat independent story-oriented games that are unlike anything else, as well as deep and paradoxical reflections on human, God, conscience, passion and fate.Other players may like puzzles and pixel mini-games that are integrated into the gameplay pretty cool, and the gloomy beauty of alternative Russia of the late 19th century, carefully recreated in detail and surprising with its surrealism. In addition, you will find here very smart constructed dialogues full of irony and philosophical issues. Indika is a powerful anti-religious statement warning of the dangers of blind faith, which demands its followers undoubted obedience, humility and passive acceptence of everything that they face in their lifes. These dangers concern not only Orthodoxy, but also any other form of authoritarian suppression of the will of large masses of people.Finally, the work of game designers is just remarkable: the graphics and animations in the game are great for a such small indie project and sometimes it looks as good as in AAA games.At some scenes the game can be violent and naturalistic, so I would not recommend it to children and teenagers.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is unlike any other game I've played before. The storyline is dark, twisted and depressing at times, but weirdly philosophical. The graphics are stunning. The music and ambience really keep you focused.It's got some very interesting puzzles, most with no "help" as to what to do, but you eventually manage to work out what is needed on your own if you take a minute to look.Some of the games are done in a way so completely opposite to how you play majority of the game, but the realisation is no less gut wrenching.Not 100% sure about the ending, but overall I'd give it a solid 8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Short and sweet. Puzzles are solid enough (maybe 2 or 3 that got my head scratching), and although it may be a bit of a "walking simulator", the pacing is just right and with the given short length of the game,; you'll most likely blaze through it. The game's story is very personal, and Indika was a well-written character to lead it. The vision is weird but not too artsy where it gets lost in it, and instead pulls off a very charming vibe (at least to me personally).Definitely recommend if you're looking for a weird 3-4 hour weird tale about a nun having a heartfelt faith crisis.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Picture this.... it's like scooping up a shovel full of imagination and diving straight into your mind! Indika follows this awesome young nun who's totally shaking up her boring surroundings. It's like strolling through an art gallery in third-person, with her deep thoughts jamming in the background. _childDocuments_.review: I can't fully explain how I feel about this game, but it is, without a doubt, incredible. The change of environment depending on the character's situation is excellent. The puzzles are fun and very well designed. I highly recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: I’ll be up front: you’re not going to play another game like INDIKA this year.  Sure there will be other third person adventure games largely rooted in story-related set pieces and light puzzle mechanics to break the walking simulator aspects that will pop up on your catered game store page of choice, but they’re not going to be like INDIKA.  Set in the outskirts of Russia in the 19th century, you play as Indika, a monastery nun outcast by her compatriots for past indications we learn later in the game, and also her wild instances around others based on her internal struggle with a voice inside her head, the voice of the Devil.  Indika is given a letter to provide to another church leader that calls her to traverse across towns but is sent on an unexpected adventure draped in self-discovery and sobering questions regarding the morality of religion and the balance of free will and heavenly expectations.INDIKA starts with an over-the-shoulder perspective going through daily chores, done almost as a penalty than a necessity, giving the player a front row seat in the uselessness and unnecessary nature of the tasks.  Taking a basket of potatoes from one part of the village to another with no thanks, having to walk back and forth several meters to fill a barrel with water from a well, using each keystroke to begrudgingly turn the crank, only to finish the task with an elder dumping it all out.  No respect given, but respect is expected to be earned.Past experiences where Indika has inadvertently put herself in this scenario are peppered in this slowly-paced intro, highlighting some real off-beat, slightly confusing, but chuckle-inducing cutscenes where you get a front row view of what Indika is having to deal with while maintaining her stoic status.  The pixelated, 16-bit flashback scenes and UI are pleasant to look at although initially a little confusing on a design scale as the game’s more realistic presentation everywhere else doesn’t allude to these whimsical diatribes.  Is this Indika’s representation of a more fantastical world before being succumbed to the lowly drudges of an emotionless standard?Indika can perform godly tasks, such as lighting lamps draped with images of Christ and praying for the recently deceased, giving Indika “points.”  These points are used to “level up” with skills such as Guilt and Repentance.  It’s a tongue-in-cheek way to show that people will use the continuous need of doing things for their religion to internally level up and feel like they’re reaching a higher point in their beliefs: but the game will flat out tell you they’re worth nothing.  Karl Marx will agree as well.Once she is given the letter to present to another church leader, the world opens up to a blustery winter landscape and our adventure truly begins.  Indika is soon attached to Ilya, a prison escapee who is looking for divine intervention to repair his frostbitten, mangled arm.  Ilya takes Indika hostage and forces her to escape with him while she pilots a steam-powered bicycle in what has to be the funniest chase sequence I’ve seen in years.  Monty Python aficionados would be proud at the ridiculousness and pure comedy of this moment and gets you in a great set of laughs in between the bleakness of the surrounding travel.Because going forward, INDIKA puts the realizations and hypocrisies of specific parts of religious happenings to light and in turn, putting Indika in a state of teetering belief and splitting guilt.  Fighting the other side of her arguments literally splits her psyche in two, retreating to muttered prayers to temporarily fix her tempted ways.  INDIKA uses this mental anguish to introduce small puzzles while your internal Devil birades your attempts to ground yourself.  It’s a very cool mechanic that sadly isn’t used often, but is remembered fondly when it did show up.INDIKA spends most of its time outside of cutscenes and plot advancing to break the tension with smaller puzzles.  Puzzles range from building puzzles, to navigation, to…uh, maneuvering past a massive dog-wolf being looking to make you a human chew toy?  None of the puzzles are too hard but are satisfying enough to finish and are a nice break in the walking simulator path the game takes when not putting the square peg in front of the circle slot.  It’s worth noting that INDIKA’s use of camera and perceived angles, especially as truths are slotted in front of Indika and the world before her is started to be seen in a different light in the third act are some of the smartest I’ve witnessed in a long time.  The use of different perspectives on a point of view level left my mouth agape as it defined what it meant without even saying a word.The story clocks in at a tight 3-4 hours but never feels like it overstays its welcome.  Though there really isn’t much in terms of replayability, you don’t really need it for this: it’s telling its story and you’re here to indulge.  I did run into some minor slowdown in the more popular areas that really did not enjoy motion blur, even on turned-down graphical settings.  I was really jazzed to play INDIKA in its natural Russian language, but text used within the world is not subtitled nor is the small talk from other characters, so I moved back to English to avoid missing anything, which the English voice actors did a damn fine job in and of itself, so I have no complaints other than missing out on some wanted authenticity.INDIKA is a weird game to score because it is, like said above, nothing like you’ve played before.  It’s proudly weird but grounded in its reasons to be, laugh-out-loud funny and despairingly somber on the flip of a coin, and just long enough to get its deeply rooted point simultaneously into your heart and your brain.  Odd Meter and 11bit studios embrace a topic often left alone, but the glory of Video Games are that you can take concepts as silly, in-depth, depressing, enlightening, eye-opening, soul-crushing as the ones provided in INDIKA and with enough heart and tenacity to do so, you can create a near masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: When I stumbled upon this game, I had pretty high expectations, but also feared that the game would only use the whole Christian setting in a superficial way.I have no experience with the actual practice and rituals of Orthodox churches. But I grew up with Catholic and Orthodox Christians in Germany and the extreme behaviors and values shown in INIDKA match up well with those of many.INDIKA did not disappoint me and at no point did I feel that there were unnecessary horror elements "just to make the game look scary". The emotional journey was just too realistic and relatable for me.I recommend this game to people who have had to deal with fundamental feelings of guilt. In my opinion, there is a need for a human, empathetic perspective on morality these days; this game provides such a perspective. Thanks!

_childDocuments_.review: As @marindavys on Twitter pointed out, this game is littered with AI-generated posters and assets, which frequently took me out of an already dismal and uninspired experience. It's just boring - the gameplay is dreadful, the narrative is rote, the visuals are 'UE4'. What else is there to say? Any developer using text-to-image software right now should be completely open (from the outset) about their use of those programs, as (from a consumer standpoint) I feel cheated of my time and money, being that this is an artistically compromised experience that poses itself as 'sophisticated' in regards to its visuals and level design.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful, mature storytelling with realistic voice acting (I played it in Russian with English subtitles). It's short enough that I would revisit it just for the story like a long A24 road trip movie. I would recommend it to non-gamers like I would Gone Home or Edith Finch HOWEVER a couple mechanical aspects felt too demanding (for example, the high sensitivity when balancing across a beam or the low FOV in the fish tower), but the checkpoints are very generous. At 40 GB it has high production quality for what is essentially a walking simulator.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I became interested in INDIKA from the trailer.  At first, it seemed like a strong, very "autur"-esque story of a young nun in tzarist russia. And in a way, that's how the game starts. But the zany-ness is quickly replaced by often times boring puzzles and 8-bit-style flashbacks which show the characters past, which are amusing but ultimately tonally both deaf as well as flow-breaking in their nature. That, combined with the fact that INDIKA is one of these very personal games, I cannot really recommend it. Sure, it does somewhat explore the difficulties and mental struggles the protagonist has to go through, but the abrasive and often times trite nature make it very difficult to care.So, sadly, I cannot recommend this, which is painful because you can constantly see how much would be behind this premise. How the entire look, the feeling of utter russian despair that so strongly pervades their industrial-era literature can be felt, but ultimately falls flat on its face.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: At its core, Indika is a serious game with a few quirky, humorous moments. You play as a distressed nun who, among other things, must travel from place to place in order to deliver a letter—but along the way, her true priorities become apparent. Platforming, challenging but manageable environmental puzzles, and an insightful narrative are all part of the package.Here is the full walkthrough
