_childDocuments_.review: Similar to a work by Kafka, INDIKA presents a dark, nihilistic world. The game deals with themes such as oppression, power and religion, leaving the player with a feeling of emptiness and hopelessness. But it does so with a beautiful art style and great voice acting. A refreshing experience and further proof that really good games come from small studios with fresh ideas and a willingness to take risks. I don't mind that it's quite short, I like it.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Mindbending absurdity meets with absorbing theme and atmosphere, avant-garde music merges with grotesque architecture... Indika is probably the game that is closest to being a piece of art. And the best part is, its not hiding behind those. It still has some high quality and high variety puzzles, mini games and interesting tempo switches with a fantastic narrative that made me relize i missed playing bizzare games like this a lot. A nun is waking up to the real world and struggling with her existential / religious crisis? Yeah take my money i am in. Indika has a really interesting story to follow because of well written carachters and superb cinematographic camera angles. Voice acting is top notch as well. Dark ambiance and odd things popping here and there gives you chills and a little bit thriller game vibes as well which i also liked a lot.Maybe not the best execution in terms of gameplay but still good enough. Also a little bit short which might make some people sad but i don’t mind it because this type of experiences needs to be intense and terse.I absolutely recommend this playing without getting interrupted, grab the drink of your choice and dive into it. You will beat it around 4-6 hours. Also you have absolutely no other alternative if you wanna experience something like this and looks like you will never have an alternative unless Oddmeter decides to make another one which i hope they do. Please make it even more weird.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: + English audio is very well done and it was a pleasure to listen to the 'devil'+ cool persisting snow tracks- 4h play time (slow playthrough with 'wall-licking' took around 3h, but I spent some time in menu and tried to re-do some achievements)- bugs, bugs and bugs (got stuck in a crate and died; got stuck in a crane and died; got stuck in a wall and died; horrific shaking of the character; got stuck in a fish and died; floating objects like mechanisms; got stuck on a barrel and died; characters clip through walls; devil character clips through ceiling; clothes look weird underwater and clip as well; character says going up when actually going down)- unskippable minigames (1990 was over 30 years ago, we seriously don't need to play 2D crap from back then again to progress the story)- shallow undelivered story (demo promised so much... and it turned out to be nearly 1/4 of the game)- only 2 scenes of praying (where whole screen shatters etc)- nearly no character exploration (you don't care about them)- it's a walking/riding simulator with a few basic riddles [not horror, not dark; the tags are off]- looped shouting 'f*** you and f*** you too' in the city scene when operating the crane was seriously driving me mad (supposed to be a meme?)- how could the convent be so bad if you had only 1 thing to do (again, I didn't feel/care for the character at all)Forgot the rest, as I hope to forget this title.EDIT1:I read an interesting review by  in Russian, which I translated and pasted below. Indika endured, endured and told us everythingBut the author of the game turned out to be not so simple. First they announce a game about a nun and the Orthodox Church. They do an interview, calling him “Orthodox Game Dev”. Afterwards, on the official YouTube channel of the game and on Twitter they talk about what kind of Russians are martyrs and thralls. As a result, they make a game that essentially criticizes and ridicules religion as such. This is simply brilliant.What would you like to say specifically about the game? There is a feeling that the game was simply abandoned halfway through. The demo version, which was given to try at the festival, was the most polished part of the game. The dialogues there are more or less normal. A dog that added dynamism to the game. Just so you know, there was a dog in the demo. She appears there and dies. AND THIS IS, if I may say so, THE ONLY OPPONENT IN THE WHOLE GAME. The rest of the game is a walking simulator and simple puzzles. There is well pumping that simply does not give anything. Why was this even added? It’s just an element of wasting time, given that the points menu itself is forced to open when you gain the required number of points. The plot itself is complete crap. Very interesting premise aaaaand............... nothing. 2D inserts that were made to apparently save money. Many people praise the production, but by the end it just breaks down and nothing is clear at all. It's a pity. When I started playing, I was very interested. Yes, the game has some flaws in its design and gameplay, but it had its own, soulful feel. Some kind of creative. But in the end it all goes nowhere and you sit, watch the credits and don’t understand what to think about all this. I don’t want to give the game a negative review, but you can’t give a good one either. We didn't make it. There wasn’t enough money, or at some point they just didn’t care about the project. It shows potential. But what is. Thanks to Dmitry Svetlov for spending his invaluable time to tell who is who in Russia, but he could have spent a little more of his time on the game and finished it.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The greatest Nun adventure I've ever played in a video game.  I think I can safely say that.  Graphics are nice but the art style and the world building is beautiful.  The contrast in the tone of the music and gameplay is superbly done when the game wants to accent it's psychological style.  Story was tragic yet thought-provoking.  This is a gem.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting game, the settings are amazing and the atmosphere is great. The puzzle elements feel well integrated into the world rather than being a side thing you must just do to get to the next place. I like the psychological and religious bits, i think they give everyone something to think about, not just those who are religious (as i am not really)
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: An universe where Nietzsche decided to hang out with Monty Python for a round of beers, and they set out to create a game together.This game is a short cinematic experience with the sporadic puzzle sequence and even some 2D sections, concentrating bits and pieces of Russian culture of the '800s. The philosophy of INDIKA revolves around concepts of free will, acceptance of one's dark thoughts, all through the prism of a nun that is rapidly starting to question her belief.It also critiques its typical problems - the unanswerable questions, chasms between faith, organised religion, the church as an institution and guilt (this time Orthodox flavoured, to be different). If the themes feel too heavy-handed, I'd advise you not to play the game.The second half starts to lose steam towards the end, with the humour drying up and the ending being definitely abrupt. Still a worthwhile experience.To summarise, a brief and linear indie / arthouse game with little to no replay value. Know what to expect.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The "opening" screen of this game wants you to click on 15 moving dots. I can see if you are young this would not be a problem however older people do not have the hand eye co ordination to do this. It took me 2 hours on 2 different days to finally do this. "That started the game."  After an hour of play it did a similar thing again. After another few hours that was the end for me. I really liked this game but there was just no way of doing all these silly little side games.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: There are some things to like about this game, but it gets bogged down with tedious puzzles and lengthy philosophical conversations. The voice acting and setting are great, and some of the 8-bit sections are well done. The visual aesthetic is nice to look at. It's a very short game and doesn't quite justify the $25 price tag. I can see certain people enjoying this game but I feel slightly more negative about it than positive. Also it crashed literally 10 times during my playthrough. Maybe in a patch it will have become fixed, but that was very annoying. I have to give it props for being unique, but I just can't recommend this for the average gamer. 6/10
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I desperately wanted to like this game, I really did. Unfortunately INDIKA fell short of pretty much everything I hoped it'd be. The game(?) is short, about 4 hours long, those 4 hours consist of walking, puzzles, and minigames, none of which are enjoyable. Most of the reviews here are positive, stating that the game is "weird" or "absurd", which it absolutely is, but that just isn't enough to make this game interesting. The heart is clearly there, but the execution just doesn't land for me. A real shame.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best indie games I've played. Not necessarily a good game, but in my opinion a near-perfect, uncompromising and brave experience.It is DEFINITELY not a game for everyone. But if you're looking for unique and strange thing, you'll be delighted. If you're not, you'd better let it go.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a strange and beautiful experience. It's a walking simulator that knows what it is. It presents the story in an excentric way and it works. The puzzles are great, because they are hard enough to make you think for a bit but easy enough to not make you wanna rage quit. Indika herself has a lot of layers that could have been more explored or shown, but she's still a great main character. The philosophical discussions the game provides stand between mainstream and profound and are somewhat esential to it's plot. All in all, it's a solid 4,5 out of 5. PS.: The ending scene is awesome, it's cinematic, intense and deep all at once, good job odd meter.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: If A24 movies were games I suspect they'd look a lot like this: it's a bit like A Plague Tale except instead of fighting rats and knights the antagonist is creeping doubt about God. The Devil chatters away in your ear like a Bulgakov character while God remains silent and absent. If that sounds like your idea of a good time you'll enjoy the bleak environments and philosophical debate, and it's very pretty in a desolate kind of way that you might appreciate. If you prefer your enemies to be a bit more killable and your outcomes a bit more concrete and hopeful then maybe look elsewhere - the short duration, ambiguity, and lack of action sequences will probably turn you off. For me the writing and acting were brilliant, as were the surreal puzzling and odd sense of proportion and scale - if the God of Indika is indeed real, you get the sense that He is vast and inscrutable and that to Him you are very small and unimportant. Fans of Spinoza, Schopenhauer, existentialist navel-gazing and depressing Russian classics will lap this up. Plus, there's a bit of nun nudity - we're only human after all.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA is...a weird game. "Game" is even a weird term for it. It's a walking simulator mixed with a few interactive mini-games, mixed with what I will loosely define as "puzzles" despite them having a set solution that only takes a few moments to solve. With all of this being said, I...I don't know. I enjoyed it? I came away from the game thinking, "Well, that was it, huh?" Despite that actually being "it," I will still give this a thumbs-up, because what it does do well it does EXTREMELY well. It's hardly the first "is belief enough or is the act of believing what causes disbelief" chicken or the egg argument, and the open-ended "is it, is it not" style of storytelling certainly isn't for everyone, but I do think that the theme of the game is one that is still worth exploring.My true recommendation of the game is to watch someone else play it and decide for yourself if it's worth the time invested. It's a weird one.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The setup of a nun who has the devil speaking to her is not one I was expecting in a game, and after playing it, that's only part of the experience. It feels like it's trying to mimick Tarkovsky and other russian movie makers and becomes this surreal lynchian walking simulator that turns into a philisofical essay. There where some anoying puzzles moments (but I feel that was part of the point) they where not overly long so it's not that much of an issue. "It's not for everyone" is not really good critique and doesn't say much, but in this case it's warranted because I can absolutely see people hating it if they come in thinking this will just be a regular 3D puzzle platformer. If a surreal walking simulator where you discuss theology, choice, personal freedom and agency with some dark humor interspersed and only some minor gameplay puzzles feels like it's something you enjoy, go for it.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This was a gem to play.  I didn't know what to expect going into it, although saw something on YouTube that made me want to get it when it was on sale.  The only complaint is that it was over too soon.  The puzzles and switch between pix-elated and gorgeous graphics I thought worked well.  There are some deeper meanings going on here with good and evil, and why your reflection is the devil.  I didn't really follow that or I guess pay much attention to it, I am not at all religious.  But the narrative and story was interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The experience Indika offers will not be for everyone, but if you’re a fan of narrative-driven games, you ought to at least give it a try. The game tells a cerebral, character driven story that explores the nature of faith within the modern world of industrial excess and human caprice. Some will find it dull or nonsensical because it doesn’t speak to questions that interest them, but rest assured there is no pretence here. Though cryptic, this is a very sincere story told with a lot of love on a limited budget, and for those who can vibe with it, it will deliver.The vaguely magical realist, soft-steampunk world oozes bleak and understated majesty, and the puzzles, although simple, always manage a clever solution, rewarding lateral thinking while remaining accessible. I played in the original Russian with English subtitles and found the performances compelling.Technically, the game ran flawlessly at max settings, without so much as a texture glitch as far as I noticed. Indika might just be my game of the year at this point, and its Tarkovsky-esque vibes offer a nice salve from the eminently digestible, melodramatic, “primary colors” storytelling of your God of Wars and Last of Uses for those who want it.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA is a short game, which is nice, because it isn't any longer than it needs to be.I think it is an experience everyone should go through and reflect on it.The Audio Design was one of the technical things I loved the most about this game, very well made. The steam machines were extremely loud and, in a way, terrifying.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Like in a modern action adventure game when you're kinda between actioning and adventuring, so, walking and the characters are talking to each other instead of having cutscenes, but cool like that for the whole game, with mood and scenery and ideas and other shoes to walk around in for a little bit. I liked it. It looks cool, feels cool like an indy film or good short story. With retro type gameplay interspersed throughout as story flashbacks. Well done.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The game surprised me on different aspects: On the one hand, Indika, the protagonist, was different from what I expected. On the other hand, the world was incredibly atmospheric. Walking or driving through landscapes, making your way and solving small environment puzzles best describes the game world. It is dark, cold, full of little mysteries and almost enchanted places. Industrialisation meets faith. Fears meet principles and philosophies. A successful title that can keep you busy for 4.5 hours if you look left and right. A lovely Sunday game that focuses primarily on the story.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: A walking simulator meets a 16-bit arcade game meets a discussion on the nature of faith meets a puzzler. Puzzles are very basic but it feels like they are providing some insight in how this alternative early-cen Eastern Europe with light steampunk sprinklings work.The setting absolutely oozes ambience, and despite the slow tempo I feel the urge to replay it again very soon after finishing it just to see if there is stuff I missed or if some scenes hit harder the other time around.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: At first, I expected this to be a horror game. After playing a bit, I thought the game would be a cynical, surreal and dark comedy. The voice of the devil reminded me of the sarcastic narrator from "Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes" and together with the weird atmosphere and various gameplay mechanics (like retro game segments and a motorbike chase sequence), I was excited to dive into a crazy fever dream. Unfortunately, my excitement vanished while playing the game further. The puzzles are extremely simple, a certain chase sequence in a mill is complete trial & error, the weird humor from the beginning of the game is mostly gone later on and the industrial environments feel pretty boring. I'm also not quite sure why this game is labelled as "Horror".I don't want to say that "INDIKA" is a bad game per se, it has it's charms and delivers some interesting messages - but be sure, what to expect when you buy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting story driven game that depicts the struggle of a nun and her relationship to religion. While the story takes place in late 19th / early 20th century Russia, the reality gets mixed with surrealism, that adds to the psychological elements of the story. The visuals, soundtrack and story are really great. and the puzzles are well integrated into the flow of the story telling. Would highly recommend to those of you interested in a narrative driven game on the topic of religion and philosophy, and perhaps fans of Russian literature such as Master and Margarita.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is a quaint yet peculiar gem of a game that I thoroughly enjoyed. Its brief duration belies a rich tapestry of narrative depth and emotional resonance. With its quirky storytelling and a setting that cleverly blends the supernatural with the psychological, Indika offers a unique adventure that leaves a lasting impression. It's a small game with big ambitions and even bigger heart. Highly recommended for those who appreciate a story that dares to be different.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Story is intresting, the game give some valid pov and doesen't go for cliche stuffGameplay is mediocre with poor puzzles most timesGraphics for a indie game are very descent. Sadly game doesen't have a detailed graphics settings and shaders compile when you enter a new chapter so its a little bit annoyed. Game runs pretty well thoI defenetly recomend this game in a fair price of course. I beilieve when its drop to half price its very good dealAlso game has easy achievments. In total of six hours was enough for me to unlock all the achievments. Game has level selection after finish. Every level when you know the puzzles are fairly small
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the story of this game, the characters are very interesting as they develop despite learning very little about them and the gameplay levels are jarring and confusing but the dialogue ties the themes together very well. It has very strong russian themes of symbolism with heavy ecclesiastical emphasis. the game is very short and doesn't have much replay value but it feels like watching an epic film in length as you're often not interacting with the environment as much as you are appreciating the atmosphere and the dialogue.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: The game: Indika is challenging and upsetting in its style of expression, and therefore not for everyone, I know some people for whom the game would be too intense. At the same time, the game demands a lot from you, both emotionally and intellectually. It's about existential questions, interspersed with some very bizarre scenes and surprisingly hilarious parts. I think the game would only be disturbing without this element of humour, but the developers have found a good mix. For me it's a very special game, almost like a film or a crazy trip. Technically and in terms of gameplay, there are honestly a few weaknesses and the running time, also in terms of the story, is simply too short. But it's definitely a unique experience that I wouldn't want to miss and it looks pretty good.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, amazing experience. I am always looking for games that are able to give me a unique experience that no other piece of media can, and Indika hit that desire right on the head for me. First, beautiful game, obviously, all around in terms of set design, audio, voice acting, story, face rigging, everything was great. The music also was masterfully designed for each scene to suck you in and amp up your emotions. It also hit just the perfect amount of werid absurdism to keep me saying “what the ♥♥♥♥ is that” but without detaching too far from reality. The reasons to buy this game are for the atmosphere and the story. Not much of a reason to replay it other than to get achievements (unless your a perv and want to play through the end of the fish factory level again.) The main complaint I’ve heard about the game is that there isn’t a ton of “options” (although that is one of the intentional themes within the game’s story), and it isn’t long enough. IMO, the production level is similar to that of a large budget movie, and it’s twice the length of a box office film, but less than the cost of 2 movie tickets, so it’s 100% worth it in my opinion. The best way to play it is to just sit down and get through it in one sitting, allowing yourself to get really invested and in the story and atmosphere. Certainly may be a bit too abstract for some people, but I think if you watch the trailers you’ll know if this type of genre is interesting to you.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: A strange but deeply interesting game. At its core it remains a story focused walking simulator with some simple puzzles and a few mini games.Thematically the game is deeply interesting, imagine a short story written by dostoyevsky, but co-authored by the writers of monty python. The game never veers too deeply into absurdist comedy or russian tragedy but remains a deeply strange game all throughout. Everything from the UI to the story to the world around you tie into that.I would say i wish it was a bit longer, there's little to no replayability (unless you want to achievement hunt, which amounts to collecting a few collectibles and dying X times during certain challenges). At 3.6 hours i enjoyed the game, and i do recommend it with the caveat that you should look up a playthrough of the demo (which is sadly no longer available). Specifically the demo not the main game, as the first chapter is intentionally boring for ludonarrative reasons. I likely would not have given this game a second glance if i hadn't played the demo before it came out.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Not much of a game honestly, especially at this price point. INDIKA is barely 4 hours long, has 0 replay value and its gameplay is very unengaging. You could just watch it as a movie on youtube and get pretty much the same experience.Its all about the story and characters and both are pretty interesting and thought provoking. Unfortunately that doesn't justify the pricetag for me. Game is over in a flash and none of the gameplay is worth experiencing, its puzzles are bit of a filler that would be considered a minigame in other games.If you are into walking sims with strong emphasis on the story, you will probably enjoy it, but get it only on a discount.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is truly a bizarre little indie game. I use the generic term because it's not easy to pin this game down to a specific genre. You could argue it's a walking simulator, and in terms of gameplay, you'd be pretty close. While there are occasional puzzles that become more challenging as the game progresses, most of the time, you're simply walking and travelling through the game world.But what a world it is! The alternate-history setting is absolutely remarkable. It's surreal, strange, and often depressing—at times, it feels like the graphics are limited to only black and white—but it's also intriguing and full of mysteries. There are always small stories waiting to be discovered.The true standout, however, is Indika's story. Not because it's particularly thrilling, but because it's so candidly approachable. Events just happen. They may not be pleasant, but Indika has to live with them. She can't influence the world as she wishes; it's the other way around. While empowerment is a typical theme in most video games, Indika leaves you with a sense of "depowerment," so to speak. More importantly, she has to live with herself and the demon in her head. This combination is, on the one hand, almost humorous, but on the other hand, it's psychologically complex and thought-provoking. The game leaves you with much to ponder.Time and again, the game shows that it doesn't really matter what Indika decides—the major developments of the story are out of her control. This is reflected in small details, like literal paths that seem to diverge but always converge again. Or, to give another example, no matter how many collectibles Indika gathers or how much she levels up, in the end, it doesn't matter at all. You filled the buckets? It doesn't matter; they get thrown over anyway. You crossed the pond without falling in? It doesn't matter; you get pushed in anyway. This may sound like bad game design at first, but I find it rather ingenious. Just like Indika, sometimes you're not able to turn something for the better. And you have to live with that.The same goes for her faith, which gradually crumbles under the harsh reality she faces. That's quite hard for her. Not because there's suddenly no God, but because there's no longer a devil on whom she can project all her morally questionable thoughts and actions. How refreshing!The entire concept of this tension is unique in a game like this. And for that reason alone, it was worth it for me—even though, and this might be my biggest "criticism," Indika only offers about 4 to 6 hours of gameplay. At the same time, I feel like there could have been (even more) depth to Indika's personality. I guess that's also an issue related to the little time you spend playing her. At a price of around 20 euros, this might seem too short for some, but for me, it was time and money well spent.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: It starts off very well, with a story that seems to have a horror twist and interesting mechanics... but unfortunately, after the first hour, nothing happens. The ending is really uninspired, it feels like they ran out of ideas after the second hour of gameplay. Such a pity. So much wasted potential.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika is very much like a good european festival cinema. It has an IDEA, literary roots and interesting implementation. It reminded me Syberia game series in style and Seventh Seal in represented thoughts.I'm Russian, I live there. For me, it's maybe one of the first games that really shows Russia from a Russian perspective. Grotesque, gargantuan, surreal, megalomaniac, insecure, different Russia from different reality but oddly familiar. And even like this it is strangely attractive. It's like Jules Verne meets Lower Depths :)I consider myself as non-believer, or maybe I've been living in this constant crisis of faith for a couple of years. So the game touches deeply something inside me. Maybe for somebody it's just an odd walking simulator, but I can relate to Indika as a game and as a character.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: A bit more expensive than a movie ticket. Slightly longer than Lars Von Trier film (the perfect length, and actually would have fitted well into Lars Von Trier's filmography). Beautiful audiovisual and cinematography. Extremely unconventional and exquisitely memorable.I cannot ask for a better way to spend money on videogames.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: What if A24 made a video game?As I played this game, I couldn't help but think of films like The Green Knight and Poor Things. The surreal aesthetics, unconventional use of focal lenses and angles, retro gaming interludes, and quirky soundtrack all come together to tell an incredible, deeply personal story of struggle. It’s a unique experience that feels like a cinematic journey you’d expect from A24. I truly hope more games in the future take such bold risks, and I’m excited to see what Odd Meter has in store next.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not quite done yet but I had to come in and say how incredible this game is. It's almost Death Strandingesk. It's very heady, deep with a lot of meaning, doesn't use violence to be fun, and is very surreal. While DS basically required you to be in a very particular kind of mood to enjoy it, because of its gameplay, Indika is just plain fun. It does it through classic arcade mechanics , puzzles, and lite-platforming. The arcade segments are so well done and look incredible. I hope a lot of people give this unconventional game a chance. It's a good time and is really impactful; it discusses a lot of complicated parts of being human in a grounded relatable way. It manages to do this without being a downer by using humor and with the surreal dream like elements. They just change the tone and make the serious subject matter digestible. I hadn't heard of Odd Meter but I hope this sells well for them. It's would be well deserved and I really wanna see what this team does next.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: For a game, this is such a unique story concept and reminds more of work by Tarkovsky and Parajanov than anything in the game sphere. Although I'm not religious at all, I was fascinated how my cultural heritage kicked in when deciding what action to take for some of the puzzles and the choices were not immediate even when it was quite clear what path to take. There's of course an uncanny valley feel to the characters look, but it actually doesn't take away from the game at all and, I find myself caring for the main protagonist the same way I would if this had been a book or real live action. The length of the game is pretty perfect and I feel something much longer or too open world would start to lose direction and purpose. I'm hoping for a follow-up though! Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most unique narrative adventures I've ever played. I love everything about it so far. music, art style, gameplay... it's all superb in my opinion and something you might not often notice that is excellent in this game is the directing. camera positions, acting, voice acting... it's all excellent.A must in my opinion for lovers of story driven adventures games.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Indika, destined to become known as "The Nun Game" is delightfully weird and likely to garner quite extreme reactions within gamers, who will either love it or hate it. Even those who hate it will have to admit that it dares to do something different though.Many people seem to be billing it as a horror game but it's not, although it does delve into some quite dark themes that may rattle people, and the atmosphere throughout the game remains pervasively oppressive despite some twisted humour here and there.It is narrative driven and is primarily a blend of walking simulator with puzzles broken up by short levels of pixel-art platforming. Some of these can be quite challenging (I'm not very good at platforming) and the Drying Fish level may take some people quite a few attempts.If you enjoyed or appreciated games like the first Hellblade then you'll probably find that you enjoy this too.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Something really incredible happens pretty early on. And more really dope stuff probably happens. But uh. I couldn't be bothered to get through the laborious puzzles to see even a short title like this all the way through. A me problem more than a game problem? Likely.If this game is for you. It's going to be all the way for you. If it's not... it really isn't.Will I ever finish INDIKA? Probably not. But I'll be first in line for Odd Meter's next game.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: This was a'ight. I don't really see room for replayability, but the ride was interesting while it lasted. I really enjoyed the presentation and the visuals, too. However I think the story could've continued, but ending where it did, I think it still turned out well. At the end, I felt sort of how I did when I played The Order 1886. I was ready for more, but there just wasn't anything left..Still, not a bad game.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute woeful story that is incredibly disinterested and fails to take any meaningful direction. Some of the most simple gameplay mechanics used in modern times which leave you bored as hell, do not buy this trash. 4 hrs or walking and cutscene simulator, had to literally force myself to finish it, paid $36 AUD for waste time and money.DONT BUY THIS GAME
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Hell yeah I recommend it!Not going to spend time here getting into the story or atmosphere because if you’re reading Steam reviews you probably have an idea if it interests you. I will say I loved the story, even the end which a lot of reviews haven’t been big on. But maybe that's just because I lean towards absurdism.Being so narrative-heavy it shouldn’t be a surprise the game play doesn’t exactly shine here. Nothing broken, but it is just walking around a bit and than doing some puzzles. The puzzles were enjoyable but nothing revolutionary here. Not too challenging but still engaging for the most part. Much of the “difficulty” for them stemming from a combination of awkward controlling vehicles/mechanisms and a camera that seems to work against you at times. Quick note: I played this a few days after release, and had some issues with bugs. Hopefully a little love and attention will help with that.Short game. But worth it if you think the story and it's themes are something you want to dive into.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for INDIKA's release since it's announcement trailer and I think I came in with wrong, or big misconceptions of what the game actually is or tries to portray. It's not a 'fun' experience, and all my feelings of wanting something greater.. this game is more a sobering, grounding experience than a game.Profundities aside, it's a walking sim with a few puzzles sprinkled inside. The artstyle and graphics are truly fantastic, the Russian voice-over is great, the story is I believe very per-basis experience; I didn't love it but I appreciated it. The themes presented aren't by any means unique but the way the story plays out is rare to see in the video game format. The all around writing is really good.It's hard to talk about anything relating to the story without really spoiling the experience INDIKA wants you to have.Biggest criticisms would be that the sound mixing for some of the voice acting was really off, Indika's dialogue would be really loud and others half her volume. A few of the times, Indika or her companion would remark about something but I don't understand why they would when nothing in the environment would cause them to remark about said thing. Some level transition to the next  awkwardly without really making much sense.I think the game is a bit too short, but I'm on the fence about this way of thinking.There's some jank here but it's all around a short experience, maybe about 3~ish hours if you rush. All in all, I'd recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Astounding and possibly shocking. And not without flaws.The experience as a whole is artsy and compelling. The rendered world pulls you through striking scenes of Slavic winter, destroyed towns, and impossible factories dripping with dream-like surrealism and nostalgia. These are interspersed with fully contemporary "comments", as well as unsettling and even very traumatic moments. No gore, but be warned: one scene towards the end can be very upsetting.Gameplay is serviceable but sometimes annoying. The puzzles are simple but nice. The chase scenes and platforming are not nice at all. Very annoying is an opaque save system. If you quit the game you might be thrown back earlier than you had hoped. At least it's possible to skip cut scenes when that happens.So, does it all really work as a whole piece? It didn't really for me. I appreciated the creativity and execution, but I didn't find the anything real at the destination. It was a journey that was ultimately more curious than satisfying.That said, it was a memorable journey, and I do recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Some thoughts right after finishing it (4h on the clock while taking my time to explore and read most things; currently going back for achievements)It is admittedly much more of a movie than a game, has puzzles but easily fits into the walking simulator label for most other parts. Its discussion of religion, fate, purpose, etc is poignant but at the same time I can't ever imagine a religious person avowing this game simply because of how dead set Indika is during most conversations; there are parts where she entertains the opposing idea or admits her own view isn't a monolith or the full picture, but the game is still fundamentally built upon a basis of questioning this invisible power structure and its control not only over Indika, but also over Ilya. And to be honest, considering Indika's background and everything that's happened to her, I find it difficult to see the journey going any different way as she still is, fundamentally, an outcast.This is what Playstation fanboys delude themselves into thinking their games are both thematically, in writing and cinematography-wise lol10/10, one of the best narrative driven games I've played in a long time
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: Frankly a little disappointingly light in terms of story and character writing. I assumed I was going in for something unabashedly surreal and disturbing, but those elements mostly manifested within the first few hours and disappeared completely before emerging slightly in the final moments. I wondered why there wasn't more interfacing with Indika's "demonic" visions, why I couldn't get a stronger grasp on her agency and inner conflict as a self-doubting "sinner", when most of her "bad" acts were either out of her control or obviously normal human impulses. Perhaps it was a mis-management of my own expectations, but if you're looking for something particularly dark or complex you won't really find it here. My positives is that it's a pretty game, with good audio mixing, and the puzzle elements were never frustrating.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review: INDIKA is a great, short, really crazy game. It has a rather dark philosophical/theological angle and gets more surreal the further one gets in the game. The ending is somewhat abrupt but i liked it and was fitting and i think more effective this way.The puzzles are mostly easy but a few got me scratching my head for some time. I really liked the prayer scenes but it could have been used more.Its definitely unique and making a game like this is certainly a risky endeavour
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

_childDocuments_.review:
INDIKA is a third-person, story-driven game set in a strange world where religious visions clash with harsh reality. It tells the story of a young nun who sets off on a journey of self-discovery with the most unusual, horn-headed companion by her side.

On the outside, Indika seems to be a typical nun attempting to adjust to a difficult and monotonous monastery life. Humble and innocent in her appearance, do not be deceived as this young girl has also made a highly unlikely acquaintance - as she speaks with the devil himself.

Indika's unusual connection with the Evil One leads her on an errand beyond the safe walls of the monastery. The world she discovers can only be described as a wild combination of comedy and tragedy straight out of the novels by Dostoyevski and Bulhakov.
_childDocuments_.name: INDIKA

name: Dark Deity
detailed_description: Terrazael. A world torn apart by oathbreakers, warmongers, and wielders of forbidden arcane secrets. A world on its last strand of hope brought to its knees by a Calamity centuries ago that tore down its mighty civilizations. Petty kings rule in place of grand emperors of old that wage fruitless, ill-advised wars picking over ancient ruins like glorified scavengers. Lead a team of four students in the Brookstead Military Academy, who are shut down on the mysterious orders of King Varic. The ruler of the Kingdom of Delia is preparing to break a millennium-old treaty and Brookstead students make for fine cannon fodder... However, these four soldiers are destined for more than just acting as unwilling meat for another grinder. They may not know it yet, but they will make their mark on history. Lead soldiers into the fray across a world torn apart by endless war and magical cataclysms. Fight through hand-crafted, turn-based combat scenarios spread out across 28 chapters, as rookies become veterans. Test your tactical mettle. Maneuver, attack, break through, and - maybe - turn the tide of the war. Engineer the rise of legends, from a pile of raw conscripts to a band of mythical heroes. Carefully nurture your squad to ensure survival through long bouts to make a difference in a seemingly hopeless world. Assemble the squad from 30 playable characters, with their own background, personality, and motivations, then train them and pick from 54 distinct classes, with their own iconic attacks and skills. Outfit each team with hundreds of weapons and spells, from simple blades and missiles to ancient, eldritch artifacts that produce world-ending magic. Defeat doesn’t mean permadeath, but there is a price to pay: Every time a warrior falls, it means a grave wound, a stat penalty, and weakening your squad. Hope is a rare commodity in a world ruined by Calamity, good thing these heroes are filled to the brim. Defy the fates and make a difference as the head of this unlikely band of heroes. Watch characters bond together on the battlefield and their relationships evolve through 400 individual conversations. Remember: Any hero can make a difference - if they live long enough.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a decent experience overall, but keep your expectations in check. It truly does mirror a more old school Fire Emblem feel, but the story and characters do feel rushed if I'm honest. This doesn't mean that there isn't a good heart behind it and the story does have some fun moments, but there is a lot of jumping between plotlines and new characters get added almost every map. The bonds between characters do give them some more depth and the interactions themselves are pretty fun, though keep in mind that you will not get the same level of attachment as for example Fire Emblem or Disgaea or something like that. Mostly due to the fact that you're restricted only to the story maps, which you cannot replay.This makes it so that experience points are a precious commodity, in theory. I personally haven't really been trying it, but it is pretty easy to farm experience from enemies that do zero damage. As such you only have the story to go on and that blitzes through characters and plotlines as said before. You also do not get the ability to grow/cultivate romances or the likes between characters. I have to say that the game kind of suffers from the lack of a real main character or at least a tighter focus on the four kids said/implied to be the the main characters.The gameplay is fun, though don't expect any grandmaster level strategies to be necessary. It sounds like I've given this game a lot of negative commentary, but that is just because there is a lot of potential here, potential I know these developers can fulfill. I would recommend this game but personally I'd wait for it go on discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I could talk all day about what I liked about this game and what not, but instead ill summarize it here.Tl;dr stellar: pixelart, combat animations, class designs good: supports usually, most of the characters, music, general gameplay most of the time, class system, line voice actingbad: story, minor bugs and glitches, some map designs, some parts of balancingDark Deity is basically an indie Fire Emblem game. I takes familier turn based strategy elements we all know and love and does some innovation on the formula. Its strongest selling point are the gorgeous battle animations and pixelarts. Its artstyle is boasts incredibly charm and personality, I intentionally never skipped animations mid combat because they were so satisfying to look at over and over again, perfectly complimented by the sound design. Music will win no flashy awards, but it succeeded in creating atmosphere and some of the tunes will probably stay in my head for a little whileMap Design was 50/50. A lot of maps had a very interesting and varied premise to them. And I found myself asking "Hmm, how am I going to solve this problem" a lot. Objectives were varied and usually involed secondary problems or created tension and upped stakes with bonus rewards or by other means. But unfortunatly there are maps that are just straight up enemy slogs with no thought whatsoever, especially in the later part of the game which is a shame. The game created strategic depth with its take on the weapon triangle, armor and weapon class interactions. Takes one or two maps getting used to, but looking up info on how matchups play out is easily accessible mid battle. Its a constant problem solving and matching up your units against enemy units, especially because you frequently split your group into two or three smaller groups to efficiently play the map or complete objectives.Characters were overall decent. Sometimes hits, sometimes miss but they did a decent job of making them interesting and I did care a lot  for a decent chunk of the 30 cast members by the end of the game. Nothing groundbreaking, but most had meaningful character development by the end. But you really need to unlock a lot of supports to have any idea of whats going on. More on that in the next part.And the main gimmick of the protagonist being a born leader keeping everyone together wasnt really shown unfortunatly. Characters just constantly said that its the case, even though he did little. My biggest issue with the game is its story. Massive exposition problem at the start in both directions of the spectrum. Imo way too over ambitious world design that was exclusively communicated via supports. Which is not bad in itself, however since the characters live in that world they know what they talk about and you have to piece everything together for yourself, while being bombarded with a bazillion names with very little context clues on if that name is a person, a city, a state, a county, a continent or even something completly different.The story is mostly bland, gives little reason to care about it and knowing so little about the world you play in also doesnt help. Its just a means to keeping a cast of diverse characters together so they can have their talks. Rushed, non impactful, unfortunatly forgettable.Other issues are somewhat unintuitiv UI Design, however I personally had little problem with that due to being a seasoned gamer. Minor bugs and little glitches happened from time to time, but it was definitly not making the game unplayable. Balancing games like this is always hard and I think they didnt get it right, maybe due too lack of experience. Growth rates are way too high, the added mastery stat just makes things messy because you cant easily judge how much damage enemies will actually deal to you. But on the plus side that meant that nearly none of my characters was ever irrelevant. One of the most irritating things about balance was a so called map percentage modifier on accuracy. Neat system in theory to globally tinker with accuracy on certain maps like dark forests etc however one map just overtuned that to the max (Im sure that has to be by mistake) and made some enemies at the beginning nearly unhittable.THe class system was really well done. I have seen a lot of criticism that the sky high growth rates make every character feel samey, however I disagree with that because the classes in combination with armor and weaponn types gave every unit a unique spin and role in a battle. And if I look through my units at the final map every one of them feels different. THere are good support options, a variety of damage types and classes with gimmicks that were fun to play around, for example the drifter/outcast line.Also criticism I saw was the character permadeath being replaced with a permanent stat loss was a bad thing. But I disagree, it not only makes the games more inclusive it also creates interesting choices. Permadeath on its own is a pretty outdated mechanic on its own imo, unless it creates interesting choices the player can make after a mistake. As an example I made a blunder and lost one of my mages late into a map. The game checks for the type of damage that killed the unit and creates a narrative around it. She was killed via slashing damage and therefore lost a thumb, permanently decreasing her dexterity. Seems insignificant at first, however I chose to not reset on that death and finish the map because It took me a while to get there and I got very good level ups. Afterwards my mage was still around and capable of fighting, however the lost dex meant I had accuracy issues against more speedy units, therefore affecting the number of targets she can efficiently dispatch. This led me into reclasing her into more of a support role and class. Situations like these happened a few more times and while my unit didnt die, they also got permanently scarred and couldnt fill roles they could before. A speedy dodgy swordsman permanently loosing 3 speed really hurts his potential. I personally really like that system, even though its not perfect and also falls victim to the stat inflationI agree that this game has issues and would need more polish, aswell as an underwhelming story. However the gameplay core is solid and I absolutely fell in love with the artstyle. I would recommend giving it a go if you are into turn based strategy. I spent a total of 30 hours into a single playthrough on this game (mostly offline and not displayed) and I enjoyed it. Not a hall of fame game, but definitly worth a try

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Deity is a strategy RPG in a similar vein to Fire Emblem or Shining Force, but is a bit too rough around the edges for me to recommend. There are bugs in everything from targeting units, movement, threat area, character sprites, and even the sound effects that play during text. It really feels like this game needed a bit more time in the oven. The story is a bit on the generic side. Two warring kingdoms with a faction that operates in shadow with plans to dominate the world through the Aspects. Our hero MC must ally with members of the opposing kingdom in order to foil the plots of the true evil, potentially coming to blows with his former allies and friends still loyal to the crown. It's alright, but there are a few plot points that are brought up once but appear abandoned (). Artwork is decent, and gives off visual novel vibes (detailed, static backgrounds and character bodies, with some changes in character face depending on the emotion). There is a bond system as well that doesn't have any impact on the gameplay, which is interesting if you want more lore. Artwork seems anime inspired, with some characters (typically one-off or background) being a bit closer to the style than others.Combat-wise, it is a more confusing Fire Emblem. Weapon damage, instead of working in some sort of rock-paper-scissors, now depends somewhat on armor that has certain strengths or weaknesses against certain attacks. For example, arcane has -5% damage to cloaks, -10% to leather, +15% to chain, and +35% to plate. Each character's weapon and armor is dependent on the class. This is in addition to the stat spread for a particular unit, so you can run into a situation where even though the advantage icon favor's your opponent, you can still end up victorious (e.g. the anti-magic knight/inquisitor classes against some type of caster). The issue is that this data isn't readily apparent on the battle screen. There is only a single arrow denoting effectiveness (i.e. slightly and super effective read the same way). There is a reference in combat (at the bottom of the tutorials section; tutorials is located right above end turn), but this isn't explained in the tutorial mission.In addition, I have an issue with the character progression. Like the earlier Fire Emblem games, there is a limited amount of EXP to go around (there is no free battle). The game auto-deploys your strongest units each combat, and with 2-3 characters being introduced about every other chapter for about half of the game, you will feel pressure to bench your units that are lagging behind. There was some justification in Fire Emblem due to the permadeath system (i.e. you would need replacement units for any miscalculations you make during a mission), but here it is replaced with a wound system. In this system, a character loses 10% in a stat (determined by damage type) on death instead of outright dying. This system exists even on the lowest difficulty. Of course, every stat isn't important to a class, but if the unit went down at a low level or earlier in the act, they miss out on the EXP in addition to taking a hit to their stats, which risks making them unviable even without permadeath. I don't know, I feel like this should have been an option to toggle off, at least on easy mode.The game also grants the most EXP to units that experience combat or get the enemy kills most often. This means that your support units end up being a lower level on average even if they use their support skill each turn (which is de facto required to do if you don't want them lagging even further behind). There also appears to be a level cap for each map or character class, above which every action will net a single EXP point vs the normal 15-20 for most actions. Of course, you don't know that you have hit this cap until you have performed the action, which ends up taking a portion of the map experience away from your other units if this resulted in a kill. This leads into a feedback loop where the units you have fed EXP (intentionally or otherwise) end up being required to take down enemies because your other units are too far behind. Finally, the inventory system is way too clunky to be usable (at least on controller). Unit stats and inventory management are on separate screens, and stat upgrades and Aspects (equippable boosts) can only be used or equipped from the Unit screen. If you, by some unfortunate circumstance, have an item you want to use in the Convoy (party storage), you must first go to the trade screen, scroll and select your unit, select someone you want to trade with (even if you aren't trading), select convoy, and then find your item you want to withdraw. If this was a stat upgrade, you must then go to the Unit screen, scroll again to your unit, toggle to the stat window, and then scroll down to the bottom of that window where your items are. If you have more than 4 stat boosts you want to use on a particular unit (assuming you don't have an equipped Aspect on the character or healing items), you will have to do this again.A lot of this would be alright (i.e. design systems that I may not like, but function within the game), but there are too many bugs/issues for me to recommend this game in good conscience. Here is a list of some I have experienced (on version 1.58).

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to like about this game, no doubt! The writing is solid, the gameplay is good enough if you love FE. The characters are likeable, however there are WAY too many of them. I wish it wasn't the case because I enjoy the game overall and really want to love it, but the game is quite flawed. There's a few design decisions that have me very confused. I stopped caring about my character progression because every chapter I'm handed 3 other new characters that are 5 levels higher than my current beloved and trained up units. The balance there is way off and it takes you out of the experience. The shop/item system is shallow which makes the after chapter camp prep feel not very engaging. Unit's speed stats are always so low you almost never attack twice it seems unless you upgrade the lowest wt weapon on every character (which also stops you from getting double attacked by the enemy in most cases.) I don't regret buying or playing the game, but I'm left feeling pretty luke-warm and would only recommend it to die hard FE fans.

_childDocuments_.review: In my life I have played all the Fire Emblem games and dozens of other SRPGs and I can't understand why this game has so many bad reviews. There are so many chapters! (it took me 30 hours to beat the game!). I also appreciated some small changes from the classic FE gameplay, for example the x2 critical damage (x3 is way too much!).What I disliked is that each character has 4 preset weapons that cannot be changed (often you will only use the one that you have upgraded) and characters with little defense are easily oneshotted by random critical hits (there is no possibility to reduce the % of critical hits, so each enemy has a big/small chance to do one).In general, a good FE-like and a solid srpg.

_childDocuments_.review: I gave this game a solid chance, but I don't think I'm going to finish it.To preface, I'm a huge fan of grid based tactical RPGs. It's probably my favourite genre, but a lot of the mechanics in this game rubbed me the wrong way.  While I'm not opposed to the idea, the amount of stats your character loses when they fall in battle is crippling. At any point in time if an archer or something gets a lucky crit on any of your softer units they can lose 10% or more of a random stat, . This point is exasperated heavily by the other mechanics of the game, and I'll come back to this a lot. I understand the devs not implementing this to avoid save scumming to cheese the rng, but some fights can take 30 minutes to an hour to complete. You can be going hard in a battle, doing very well, and then all of a sudden the game decides it wants to crit on a 5% crit chance/20% hit rate attack and one shot your thief, causing them to lose 9 of their 60 hp permanently and you need to decide if you want to do the last hour all over again, or live with the fact that your favourite character is crippled for the rest of the game. Also, you know, if you have a life and can't dedicate the time for 1 battle you just have to get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ I guess lol. The game throws a lot of characters at you. Like, a lot. And you can't use them all, so naturally, some start to fall behind. Can't bring them into battle to train up, because they'll likely die and lose stats. So your "party" is filled with a lot of dead weight later on in the game. Also, you only get a limited amount of money, so investing in the characters you get early is always a risk because you might be handed a character that either does their job better, or they fall behind due to not getting a lot of kills (Looking at you, priest). If there was some way to train between battles, losing stats from death might not sting as much since you could just go into a mock battle and get a few levels to compensate. There is a rock paper scissors armor/weapon system, but a lot of it is kind of overly complicated and mostly irrelevant. I went through most of the game with a party where a couple units were completely overpowered and were able to one-shot mostly everything they came across and the other 10 members of my team hitting like wet noodles or falling over as soon as something came into melee range. The game awards more exp to those to get the finishing blow, so it causes the problem of the stronger damage dealers get more and more experience while your weaker units fall farther and farther behind.For my two cents, the game would be better if it got rid of the stat loss and took away the battle forecast to compensate.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd only suggest this depending on what you're looking for out of the game, I feel like the battle system needs a fair bit of polish but it is very enjoyable so far. I was kind of looking to play an FE like game, so it was great for me. So far I haven't used much more than power and finesse weapons, the other two types go kind of neglected. I really do find myself sticking the same handful of characters though, not really much incentive to mix up a team much and sadly half of them end up benched despite me wanting to use all the characters. I would like to view supports again once unlocked, though not sure if it exists already and i just haven't unlocked it maybe?The character designs are nice for the most part, though some are a bit noisy looking Vesta and Iris in particular for me. Faust is perfect though. The artbook is nice, the sketches are very lively - though I feel some dropped designs are better (but that's just a personal thought). The battle sprite animations are nice. Visually, this game is great.I think everyone's compared it to the FE franchise, but I can see the things it is trying to do differently. I think it just lacks the polish, which is fair, it's an indie title from a new developer.  I hope more supports happen, I find it weird that Faust mentions Maren in one set of dialogue but doesn't have a support with her.I look forward to more.

It also has plenty of its own mechanics that have a bit of a learning curve but there's so much depth to its customization that I'm already thinking about future playthroughs.You might've seen seen other reviewers critiquing bugs and quality of life like weird quirks with the UI which is true, right now. _childDocuments_.review: I had some crashes the day after release, but I haven't had a single one since. This has been a very fun and refreshing experience with a nice balance of challenge and difficulty. For fans of fire emblem or other turn based strategy games this is likely a good pick up. While similar to Fire Emblem in nature, it has enough differences and quirks to differentiate it from it's older brother. The graphics aren't particularly flashy but they have a fun look that is more reminiscent of older GBA fire emblem. It can be a bit challenging at times but the death system is far more forgiving in this game as instead of permadeath you are simply penalized by losing stats. I've enjoyed it a lot so far and look forward to the challenges of the higher difficulty, 4.5/5
