_childDocuments_.review: I played it on "Hero" difficulty (normal); it was still pretty easy, so if you're generally familiar with turn-based strategy you might want to go straight to hard mode. Hard to imagine how much easier easy mode could possibly be.There were a few weird bugs where occasionally a unit wouldn't render to its new location, then interacting with it would become difficult, and (I think related) sometimes a menu would get stuck. I was always able to eventually get sufficiently out of the weird state, but usually with one or two units doing something that isn't what I wanted, so if the level *wasn't* easy the bugs could have been pretty frustrating.Healing items seemed a bit pointless - healing units are free to use, healing items are expensive and not really any better. If you could use them without it consuming a turn then they'd make maybe sense for the few slightly difficult boss battles, but since they consume a turn of the unit to be healed, you're better off using a healing unit's turn to heal the combat unit, and the combat unit's turn to keep the combat progressing.The stats are also a bit weird and unbalanced, in that speed seems like it's by far the most important stat - if your speed exceeds an opponent's by five your damage is doubled, if it's five less *their* damage is doubled, *and* speed contributes to your ability to dodge. That means 10 speed in the right place is approximately equivalent to more than 25 power/magic (whichever determines the unit's damage) *and* more than 10 dexterity *and* more than 25 defense/magic-defense (whichever the incoming damage is).Though it doesn't increase your accuracy, so some dex is still useful.But all that's okay, it's nice to have things you can figure out to your advantage. A side-effect of this is, since "true speed" is actually the one that does all that, it's also generally better to upgrade the "balance" weapon rather than the "power" weapon, because the weight doesn't go up as much, and weapon weight decreases "true speed".Overall, I enjoyed the game, and would recommend if you like turn-based strategy (though IMO it's not as fun as some of the ancients like Lords of Chaos, Laser Squad and Rebel Star 2; nobody makes them that way any more except for "I Am Not A Monster", which I would recommend more.)

_childDocuments_.review: I am a long time fan of strategy games and Fire Emblem in particular. Of the games I've played, Dark Deity would not rank highly among them. That said, it's a decent game with a lot going for it, but it also has a lot going against it. It's strong points would be its character art and unit customization through classes and aspects, while its weak points would be its story and map design. If you're a fan of Fire Emblem and are craving a new Fire Emblem experience, I would pick it up, otherwise I might not.The parts that I liked about the game were the non-sprite artwork, the different character classes, the aspect system, and some of the characters. The character portraits, cutscene images, dialogue background, character health bars, and pretty much everything that isn't pixel art is fantastic. It has a great unified style and consistent quality. Most of the sprite work is also quite good, I was impressed by many of the attack animations(though others were underwhelming) and the map sprites. The different classes and aspects allowed for a lot of playing around and customization. Every unit ends up with 5 skills by their final promotion and it's fun to try to engineer synergy between a unit's personal skill, the classes they get to pick from, and the aspects that you have available. Most of the characters are likeable and their interactions through the bond system were interesting enough.As for things that I didn't like as much about the game, number 1 would be map design. There are multiple maps in this game that are literally just blank, no terrain, no walls, just a big field with enemies on it. There was maybe one map that I would describe as "good". Most, if not all, maps have a lot of empty space and there is a lot of traversing. Practically every map is unnecessarily large. There is no terrain in this game, which removes an aspect of positioning which is often important in these types of games. I was also not a fan of teleport/go tiles that take you to different parts of the map. Most maps devolved into baiting the next 4 enemies in, defeating them, spending a turn to move towards the next 4 etc. etc. which made the gameplay mostly uninteresting. I played on the 'hard' difficulty and the game was pretty easy throughout, barring a few difficulty spike chapters.The story is pretty terrible, but it is in the spirit of Fire Emblem so that is pretty par for the course. Things just sort of happen, and the characters meander from place to place on a whim, rarely having a long term goal or explored plan. The events that set up the beginning of the story are presented as a mystery, yet are never elaborated on. Most of the things that happen in this game happen for next to no reason, at least none that is explained in the game. The final villain has maybe 4 chapters that he speaks in. The pacing and what is elaborated on and what isn't is all over the place, such that emotional moments feel ridiculous at how suddenly  and without reason they happen. The story does do some things well, there is a decent amount of world building and a good variety of characters make consistent story contributions. I have some issues with some of the sprite work. My biggest issue is with the map tilesets. They aren't very aesthetically pleasing, especially when compared to the stellar quality of the art in other aspects of the game. The tilesets are for the most part very plain, with sort of low contrast and muddy colors. Many of the late game maps bring in a whole bunch of grid lines in white that are kind of hard on the eyes. The magic effects on the maps like the portals on the first undead map just look kinda amateur. Another issue I have is that the female variants of the attack animations seem to be very obviously quick adaptations of the male animations. The female characters in this game are very slender, but the attack animations have the same bulky/shapeless proportions as the male ones, and so there is a bit of disconnect between the character art and the sprite art. I realize that it is an indie game and that commissioning twice as many animations would cost a lot, but it bothered me. There are also a lot of animations that have weird proportions, especially arms. The arms of all bow classes seem to have very variable length, extending to nearly the whole height of the character at times. Priest is another class that has really long arms. For the most part, the attack animations are quite good, but the quality is not high across the board.There are also a lot of just odd design decisions or balance things going on in this game. There are a lot of things that just seem like missed quality of life improvements, like moving items around in the pre-chapter inventory is kind of annoying. There is no way to equip or use items from the inventory screen that I know of, so you have to switch to the unit screen if you want to use a statbooster or equip an aspect. There also doesn't appear to be a button that cycles through your available units, like L/R in Fire Emblem, which is especially annoying when the maps are large and encourage splitting up your forces. It would also be nice to be able to switch between buying weapon tokens and upgrading weapons quicker.The advanced stats in this game are confusing. In Fire Emblem, if you have hit of 130 and your enemy has avoid of 60, you have a 70% hit rate. In this game if you have 70 accuracy and the enemy has 60 dodge, you have like a 50% hit rate. How do 70 and 60 combine to give you 50?  I don't know and couldn't find it in the game anywhere. It makes it hard to judge how well someone is going to dodge all the attacks from incoming enemies.It is also not explained how exactly a character's stats combine to form their advanced stats. As far as balance, speed is, like in Fire Emblem, the most broken stat in the game, providing one of the most powerful offensive advantages and the most powerful defensive advantage. Most of the enemies in the game are easy, and then occasionally they hit you with some speedster that your whole team struggles to get over 50% hit rate on and doubles everyone. Very few units have respectable defensive bulk, so dodge tanks or life-drain units will become your tanks. There is also no way to fight crit chance, so once the enemies start getting weapons with crits you'll start getting hit by random criticals all over the place. The weapon system is kind of strange, each unit has 4 weapons that each specialize in a different thing, either damage, crit, accuracy, or a mix. In the end most of my units ended up with 1 weapon that they favored and then a high hit weapon to fall back on when the enemy speedsters show up. I never really figured out the armor/mastery/penetration mechanics, other than that green arrow means go. It might provide some interesting depth, but at least in hard mode it didn't need to be understood or planned around that deeply.For the most part I liked the characters. Monroe is my favorite because he is a god tier unit and I like his attitude and bond conversations. The only character I really dislike is Faust, he seems like someone's weird quirky self insert character who is pretty disconnected from the rest of the story. I was disappointed that there were no ending cards for the characters like in Fire Emblem.At present, there are still a lot of bugs in the game. It has been steadily improved since the game came out, but they are still there.I had some fun playing it, but a lot of the maps are just kind of boring slogs and the story is a poor motivator to see it through. If you are really craving a new Fire Emblem-like experience, buy it and play it, but if you haven't already exhausted the existing (modern) Fire Emblem titles you might want to play those instead. If there were challenge maps where you could quickly build up a character and play around with all the different classes, that would probably be a lot of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big Fire Emblem fan I was excited when I saw the kickstarter.And though the game is not bad, I also wouldn't call it great.From a visual and an audio standpoint, it scratches the FE itch.The mechanics however feel klunky and awkward. A few major points in the game feel like it wasn't tested enough.1) CharactersThere are a ton of those. Like I am at chapter 10 and I got almost 20 characters. Fire Emblem also has those but you get time to get to know them. To bond with them.Here it feels rushed. Every chapter at least 1 character joins and while I was invested in the first few characters, I lost interest soon. There are jsut too many characters, too quickly and they just get dumped on you.I remember with FE:TH that you also got allcharacters at once and yet they all got some interaction with one another that felt more natural. The bonding doesn't happen only between chapters but also during cutscenes or side quests.While in Dark Deity, the only bonding is at intriduction of a chjarater or in the bonding section which feels like a chore to read through.2) CombatI am no stranger to the random shenanigans that FE had so I cannot complain there. It feels ever so rewarding when you get a crit or hit a 30% hit. Although it does feel like the rolls are skewed at times. When a rogue with 30% crit chance only crits once the entire fight, it feels kinda off.What does irk me is the weapon system. Every character gets 4 weapons. You get one focused on damage, one on accuracy, one on crit and one more balanced. But they all get it. And when they change classes, so do the weapons which isn't always an upgrade and frankly you don't notice it until you use the character. It doesn't feel as strategic or satisfying as FE does it when you use the right weapon for the right fight.There also is no rock/paper/scissor mechanic as FE has. Instead it is all percentage changes but even those I don't really feel. Just send your units forward and take the enemy down really. I miss a strategic element of sending the right unit forward.3) StoryFE stories always have had a generic RPG feeling and that is ok as long as it is given well. But here it feels rushed. I am in chapter 10 and I went through multiple bigger scenarios. and it goes too fast. I don't get time to feel anything that is going on. In the academy I don't get time to get to know the first few heroes. When the war happens, I don't get time to know what it is all about or who'se side I am on. And now I have to save the world from a threat I know nothing about done by guys I know nothing about. It is just "a feeling" the characters have which just feels like plot railroading.Fights that should feel grand just feel the same like all the others. Fighting undead is the same as bandits or soldiers. Fighting a great spirit feels like fighting the regular army.CONCLUSIONThe game isn't bad but I raised the bar perhaps too high for a small company.tl;drDecent soundtrack, good chraphics with a hint of nostalgia.But the core of the game feels lackluster and should an attempt be made at another one, I hope they change the mechanics and slow down on thedumping of story and characters.

_childDocuments_.review: It a game with a lot of potential. The main appeal for me was the number of classes. Unfortunately the characters are on a set path where they get a promotion at 10 and 30 which gives them passives depending on their starting class. So it limited creativity and they are locked in when you select them. I can easily see someone getting softlocked if they made really bad choices. For me I ended up having a overpowered character that soloed many chapters. the way exp and death in this game works is very frustrating. They act like positive feedbaack loop where characters that live and kill a lot of the enemies will get more exp and become stronger. While the opposite happens for death where the ones that die will permanently lose stats making them less less viable. This lead to many situation where one or two characters would do the mission while the rest died. by the end of the game it limits your character choices. They just throw new characters at the player which most likely are at a higher level than other characters. There is no way for low level characters to catch up. You can try bring them into the missions but most likely they will die in one hit.Another problem is the lack of abilities. All units have 2 main abilities besides items, attack and the other is class dependent. Most of them are bad or just not worth it. Heal is the only useful one. most units end up feeling the same. you end up have to cheese the game with op characters or memorize units and their strengths and weaknesses then meticulously manage them. tl;dr the game doesn't have that many options for units. Just use the strongest units.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I would only recommend this to people that love Turn-based tactical RPG's. Dark Deity is still enjoyable because  it is a cheap clone of Fire Emblem but it's a bad game without any optimization for the time and very little identity. I would buy this is if it were 5-10 dollars but at 25 dollars it's not worth it.Pros: - Great Battle Animations- Large variety of charactersCons:- Terrible, hokey writing in between battles that seems to only exist as a vessel until the next battle. The story is uninspired and boring.Tutorial - There is no tutorial at the beginning of the game or explanation of, really, anything related to combat. There are attack types, elements, etc. but you will only know which counters another through experimenting and seeing what happens. There are times when it appears that an attack counters an enemy only for it to do zero damage - makes sense. :)- Characters - You receive so many characters through-out the game that are (almost) always higher level than your starting characters. After every battle multiple random people will be introduced with some flimsy backstory and be integrated into your team (sometimes without choice). As a result, you pretty much swap out your original characters for whatever new characters the game provides to you or you waste time attempting to grind your older characters rather than replace them - neither of these options are ideal. - Classes/Weapons - At first I was interested in the class structure but it's overall pretty bland. There aren't any weapons in this game which could have worked but the system in place leaves something to be desired. At any point you can pretty much choose any attack type and it will be about the same as the others.- Combat - The combat is very water downed compared to Fire Emblem and other Turn-based tactical RPG's - every attack is either melee or ranged (one extra space) - there is very little overlap on characters providing more options for combat or down-sides that are present in other games. I want trade-offs - Do I use AoE magic on these two enemies and also nuke one of my own? There is a severe lack of decision-making in the combat that ultimately results in every character basically running it down together.- Difficulty - The game is really, really easy compared to other games in Turn-based tactical RPG market. Characters barely die, weapon/type advantages are negligent, and even if someone does die the consequences are loses some random stat point. The battles that have 'objectives' are so easy that you don't need to divert resources or attention you can just play normally and the task will complete itself without worry.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who is a huge fire emblem fan over the past few years I would recommend Dark Deity to you and here's why.Dark Deity impressively was made on Game Maker Studio 2 and as someone who has used it before it isn't the easiest to work with so seeing someone make a fire emblem style game with Game Maker kinda blew my mind even though i'm still kind of new to this. I really like the character designs, whilst some are the basic main character protagonist design you get there are some characters that really stand out and had me invested into the story and interested to learn more about them as a character and how they interact with other character's! Some of my favourite character design wise being Maeve, Corvan, Sloane and Helena! Even though look wise, those characters gravitates me towards them more than other characters that didn't stop me from enjoying some really fun supports between characters that pair well with each other such as Cia and Garrick there's something about those two I really like and ended up using them a lot through my play through because they were both quite powerful. I also really liked all of Monroe's supports it really showed how two different or similar characters are portrayed and Monroe really underlines the difference as someone who grew up with almost everything at his hands, to someone like Cia where life has not been so kind to her but then again you find Cia's supports really interesting and I fell in love with her character as a whole she is a great unit and a great character even if she wasn't on my top character list to begin with. As they say don't judge a book by it's cover because you'll fall in love with some great characters that have been written so well. I could go on and on about each character honestly some more than others but I definitely feel a sense of attachment to some like Benji or even the crazy Faust! Support's aside some characters you like won't be the best units on the map to fight enemies that character for me that was Elias.This was when I originally played so there has been an update or so since but he wasn't the best kept getting murked all over the place, so sometimes when you want to get that support it can be frustrating when they keep dying all the time but then again that might just be on me, but some characters just won't be it and that's fine sometimes I would just shield them with my ultimate hench strong characters to build that support game.When it comes to the combat it definitely has that fire element to it which I love sometimes the story can take a dip and really make me loose interest and the only thing I have to look forward to is the combat but it does give you a decent challenge and I really did enjoy it although I did come across a bug or two along the way and surely some people may have gotten more or less than me but I'll give them the benefit of the doubt because it's game maker. One glitch I came across honestly wasn't too bad for me atleast i would get that level up token just so many times because usually when you interact with the chest it's one and done but it just kept going and going and I just got a bunch of level 1 tokens am i complaining no? Was that meant to happen? probably not! : ) As I mentioned before the story plot isn't the strongest and can feel like a basic plot at times and can be predicted quite easily but I was here more for the gameplay which is rare most times  but then again I like fire emblem games so who am I to complain about plot? In all seriousness don't go into this game thinking it be the best story go more for it's gameplay elements cause it's just so fun honestly.Not got a single complaint on the art style and animation so beautiful and welldone just wow what can I say?  Really good and got me inspired to draw again after taking some time off!Overall this game is pretty good it has it's negatives but it also has it's positives! _childDocuments_.review: This game has so much potential, I can't help but want to play it. I am on chapter 4 at the time of this posting. I unfortunately cannot recommend this game to people, as I do not believe anyone outside of "fans" of this style of game would enjoy it.I began a new game and explored difficulty settings. This is a nice touch that can add loads of replayability and I commend the team for inserting this option. I roll on Hero mode, as it was listed as the way the game was meant to be played.I am given way too much information (regarding lore and world building) much too quickly for me to care about it. I don't know any of these names or have things to tie them to, but I resisted the urge to skip ahead. I am immediately after thrown into a mock-battle as the "training" mission, but the game does not tell you how to play (despite the controls being quite simple, if a little odd). I notice right off the bat that the map is long and the enemy vastly outnumbers me. I welcome the challenge.I cleave through the enemies no problem, they can't land any hits and when they do, it is single digit damage. This is bad design as it extends the amount of time per level without adding any difficulty. But, this is the first level and I am sure things will develop.I move ahead in the campaign and get some new party members. Some are powerful and others are quite weak (one "veteran" soldier in particular was very underwhelming). This carries over into the next three levels where my starting characters can wipe an entire level, and my new comers can barely survive somehow. This is concerning especially when considering stat values (there are many). A thief character has an insane amount of strength, killing all kinds of foes with ease. My "veteran" soldier can't scratch anything with her assortment of spears. I'm getting a thought that the Adepts aren't bound for melee, but my other adept seems quite capable in battle, so that doesn't hold up either. This is showing poor design by having some party members with inflated stats and other members under performing all across the board.Playing on Hero mode, "the way the game was meant to be played", I am very concerned about the development of later stages.Then there are the weapon types...I am totally lost on this and barely understand it as a "power/precision/critical hit" type of function. Though all party members have access to a full array of weapons right off the bat. The game would be much more interesting if units STARTED with certain weapons, and were given the ability to find/collect/buy more as they become more powerful. Some weapon types seem better than others in what resembles a rock/paper/scissors format. This also seems to accent that some classes are better suited to fighting certain enemy types than others, but I can not confirm as I see nothing in the game speaking on such.The spritework is absolutely beautiful, though I would love to see some things expanded on. The animations are smooth and some attacks look amazing. I love the spells in particular. The animation highlights are cut down by the moments where a unit just walks backwards to their starting position, as opposed to others doing a backflip or a leap or a spinning shuffle back to their side of the battle screen. Also, having a unit attack twice with a two-hit animation (when you get two attacks in a retaliation animation, for example) would be a really cool and unique addition, compared to a leaping slash, leaping back, leaping slash, then leaping back again.The characters are well drawn, and I love some of the loading screens. Overall I am not a fan of the art style as I find it lacking (depth?). The artist(s?) was not afraid to hold back on some characters breasts, and all the characters seem to have that similar slim/toned fantasy style to them. I haven't met everyone in the game yet, but I'd welcome a character of any kind that broke this barrier. This doesn't mean the art is bad, I think it is quite well done. The style of each character (so far) is too similar for me personally.There doesn't seem to be much to do in between battles. I have a couple of conversations through a bonding menu and just load into the next fight. Some of the cutscenes in the game (more like dialog sequences) aren't well done. The "bandit ambush" where every sprite popped in at once was a low point for me. A short sequence of some sprites moving in and closing in around you would have made that so much better.I touched on this earlier, but the sheer number of enemies is really just an annoyance instead of a challenge. Having fewer, more powerful enemies on smaller maps can create a greater sense of battle and accomplishment than mowing down mob after mob without using brain power. Again, I am only in chapter 4 so this may change, but I do not believe it to be the case. I do understand there are difficulty modifiers to make the enemies more difficult, but please note that I am playing on Hero difficulty..."the way the game was meant to be played".Newcomers to the genre will not be satisfied with this game. This game is very appealing to people familiar with Fire Emblem, Tactics Ogre, Shining Force, etc. I will not refund this game as much as I want to, because after this review the game deserves to be completed. I REALLY do have high hopes for the developers as they do REALLY seem to be onto something, and I am EAGER to try any games they create in the future. This game just falls flat in the meantime. Perhaps it is simply a taste of just how good a game they can truly create.**EDIT**After an additional 16 hours, my initial concerns proved to be warranted. The maps did not get better. The battles are too large. The units vary greatly in strength and usability. I actually feel penalized for bringing the maximum number of units as the game is significantly easier using the powerhouses it bestows upon you. Gold is a finite resource and I spent it all on weapon tokens, should I have used my finite resource to make weaker units slightly more bearable with stat-boosting items? Currency in this style of game is an important resource, though feels half-baked.The class system is not as deep as one might think. The combinations are nice and I do like that you aren't locked in a tree and are able to pick an alternate class if you so choose.The story became less and less interesting as I progressed, and I feel no interest or connection to any of the characters. The bond menu has become a chore due to this.The only way I can recommend this game is in an attempt to support the devs, as I do think they could make something greater than this.

_childDocuments_.review: Having backed it when it was a kickstarter up-and-coming, I was exposed to the amount of work the team actually put through and, in comparison, how polished it is right now. I feel.. obliged to actually write (my first!) a review at this point.A love letter to an older FE iterations made in a similar fashion. Having played it, there are several tropes that followed through, and although I know it is not intentional, there are several QoL upgrades that is -at least at the time of writing- sorely missed.-There are a grand arc and it felt nice that our band of do-gooders wasn't a hero of the past or a seamed-in saviour of some sort.  Your significance grew as you recruit (or being recruited) more people and parties. -However, the game have a huge cast and haven't been able to artfully nuance most character's personality or flesh out the backstory into it. It feels rushed and loose because the game keep handing you a new characters that 'out-relevant' the last ones.- It is a well made epic SRPG. There are class balance issues with Rogues, Mages, and Tanks and it can be game breaking if you want it to be.  - Definitely have the feel of an older FE game in it and , at this point, have successfully shown me the stuffs from the more modern iteration that become more of a necessity than it is an addition.- Promoting seems.. very much rushed, you cannot consult another screens and plan as you don't know how the cast is going to shift in the coming chapter and which character will work better in what role.- One thing I never realized have changed for me is the availability of maps to farm. It followed the old school FE trope that EXP is just a valuable resource, much like Gold, and you need to prioritise. My issue with it is that I have now turned into an equal level player, it felt extremely hard keeping the whole cast on roughly the same level, when, at some level, you need to rely on some character's strength and it completely unbalance the EXP distribution.- Controller interface seems.. off sometimes.- Do not expect any hand-holding. There are literally zero tutorial. i totally understand how this can put an entry barrier for newer playersI have never played games for the way it looks. Character art is well drawn and the map looks OK. Unlikely to win any awards on this front, but not one to found lacking.- VA is fair. I can't find any solid comparison on steam for the similar genre, but this is a welcomed addition to the old-school vibe they are after.- Music is OK. Much like the graphics, I find it serviceable.- Would I recommend it to everyone? No, there are elements of it that can be asphyxiating to anyone not seasoned in the genre, even at the lowest difficulty.- For anyone that find the genre appealing, I would ask you to at least try and see if this scratch your itch.- For a group of people with limited experience, this is a very well made product, there are raw edges, but very palatable. I am really looking forward if these guys will come up with something else in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I was drawn to this game because it looked a lot like the classic  games that I love, and I haven't been able to find anything on PC that scratches that itch, and I know Nintendo won't be bringing any of their games to Steam. These types of games are all about gameplay, and the gameplay was pretty solid. In  when you lose a unit in combat, instead of dying permanently, your unit will have a randomized stat decrease- at first I thought this was really interesting, but eventually I realized that it actually just punishes you for losing. A player who is struggling to get through the campaign and keeps losing units, will realize their units keep getting weaker, making the campaign even harder. This isn't a big deal on the lower difficulties, if anything, it forces you to try out different characters and classes when certain units become weaker and less useful. However, on deity mode, it can make some of the game's only good units completely worthless and force you to retry the chapter or restart your save. Another gripe I had was the difficulty settings. I did my first playthrough on the medium difficulty, I believe it's called Hero. It was strange because there are moments where the enemies are programmed not to approach you, yet you can't get into range to attack them in one movement, so it forces you to take damage. This was fixed in Deity mode, which I tried out for my second playthrough, but only made it about halfway through the game before calling it quits as it is very challenging and your troops are quickly stormed by enemies on nearly every level.On the bright side,  is a really enjoyable casual playthough and has great strategy gameplay that keeps the player motivated. It has a very nice class system, and I enjoyed the elements it took from the best  games- such as the bonding through combat and friendship ranks from . Additionally, the story is a nice length, although not the most interesting, as I eventually found myself skipping through dialogue in order to fight more enemies. Ultimately its an enjoyable experience for fans of the genre or any nostalgia-seekers, but don't expect to be blown away.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: They added the suspend feature, so I'm flipping my recommendation.I would love to recommend this game, the art is good, the gameplay and maps are really fun, the story is decent. But the lack of a suspend  feature kills my ability to play this game. Right now, when you start a map, you have to finish it before you are able to save again. This makes it a game that you need to sit down and play for 30-60 minutes at a time to advance to the next chapter.  If you can get by without a suspend feature, go ahead and give this game a shot, otherwise, I would wait and see if the devs add that feature to the game.Outside of that, this is a unique take on the fire emblem formula with a campaign that feels very much like a pen and paper rpg campaign, and seems intentionally written to have an "And this also happens" style of plot which is a nice touch . The writing and characters are good enough, the designs for the pixel art units is good and the character portraits range from great to ok, the unit advancement is fun and has some unique paths (although it feels like some paths are not amazing for certain characters). Leveling is great but typically randomized stats tend to cause you to have some advancements that are stellar, and other's that are painful, but it leads to unique runs, so you can have some variance in how a character might look in multiple campaigns. Despite my minor annoyances and the lack of a suspend feature, this game is really fun. I really like how this game feels like the GBA era Fire Emblem games. I feel like the tactical decisions are crunchy. There is a nice variety of character advancement as well. The game also still contains the bits where you get your favorites killed trying to get them to advance a simple conversation, which is appropriate for this genre, but it's much simpler to make your units bond since they now have a decent range for bonding. I like that there isn't a weapon durability system in this game, the weapon system could've been explained better, but you pick it up fairly easily (Cycling through weapons with arrow keys is strange, but not a deal breaker).The UI needs some work, the controls aren't re-bindable and are very finicky. Combine this with the lengthy map times and the lack of a suspend feature and suddenly you're restarting a map you've been playing for 30 minutes because instead of attacking an enemy you double click and open a door instead. Other issues such as moving my hands back and forth from the keyboard to the mouse become grating during some of the sequences, but otherwise don't are a minor nuissance. Check it out if you are ok with not having a suspend feature, otherwise I would wait until it's added.

_childDocuments_.review: I see a lot of reviews comparing this game to fire emblem, which ive actually not played any of. But i did play a lot Shining Force 1&2. Coming from that, i absolutely loved it.  With that in mind, things i like is that all your units are unique heroes rather than generic soldiers, giving them personality and (admittedly light) interactions outside of combat. I do miss the light RPG and exploration elements from SF; with this game just being mission, dialogue, shop/upgrading, next mission. I really enjoy the pixel sprites getting visual upgrades as you promote them and the promotion trees feel rather varied; you can have 2 characters that started in the same class playing completely different by the time theyve both been fully promoted.  I do wish there were some completely unique characters like SF that instead blended classes. but i dont think thats a fair critique, there are (iircc) 5 characters for each starting class (with 5 different classes) and 3 different choices for each  each promotion within each class. which is already a fair amount of variety for a 14 person team. Theres a mechanic for characters bonding while fighting together which unlocks additional dialogue during mission pre-prep, which is neat, but has doesnt have any mechanical effect, which i dont know is objectively bad or good thing, but i personally feel is a missed opportunity.  Overall, gets a solid recommend from me. Especially for anybody coming from Shining Force and looking for something to fill that void.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, so this game is... okay. It's in situations like these where I wish I could leave a "sideways thumb" instead of just thumbs up or down.Pros: Gameplay is pretty goodWeapons system is innovative and uniqueClass upgrade system is alrightCons: No borderless full screen optionNo option for anything above 1920x1080 in a standard aspect ratioLoooots of loading screens (this game should not need to load that much, if at all tbh) Story is mediocreCharacters are absolutely dumped on you. I have no idea who most of my characters are or where they came from and I'm only on chapter 6. Level design ranges from ok to awful. If you absolutely adore Fire Emblem style gameplay and just can't get enough of it, then I would absolutely recommend this game for you. If you like Fire Emblem, then I'd keep an eye on this and see what updates are made. There seem to be a few minor bugs here and there but nothing game breaking as well. Dev has already released two patches in just a couple days, so that's a good sign for sure. A few examples of poor design decisions:1) Enemies in a locked room. I put my healer next to the wall assuming she's safe. Enemy attacks over wall, out of locked room and kills her? 2) One of the chapters puts you in a large, wide open arena. You basically have to hide in a corner and wait for the enemies to come to you or else you are 100% guaranteed to lose characters. Having a massive swarm of enemies surrounding you at the start with no way out just isn't fun level design imo. 3) Every character has 4 weapons that need to be upgraded. I have 12 characters at the point where I'm at. There's no way that I can reasonably upgrade all their weapons for the different scenarios where they're good with the resources allotted. I guess you can min max and make some characters OP like I'm trying, but even then it's just... not interesting to do. All in all, I would give this game a solid 6/10. Decent gameplay (except when bad levels), novel weapon system, just a few things that make me go "????" and a mediocre story that doesn't make up for what it's lacking.

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Deity was very obviously made by big fans of classic Fire Emblem games. I can easily imagine the developers thinking about all the things they loved and some of the things they didn't from the series when making Dark Deity. Anyone that knows Fire Emblem will understand when I say Dark Deity functions essentially the same. Though I must emphasize that this is classic FE we are talking about here, stuff you might have played on your Game Boy back in the day.Lets see if I can avoid saying Fire Emblem every other line and talk specifically about Dark Deity. The character artwork is well done and looks good. You got all types of characters from your beautiful ladies to your scruffy villainous looking guys. The in battle sprites and animations are amazing, likely the best part of Dark Deity. The voice acting is limited to things like level up expressions and critical hit one liners, but its decent enough.Perhaps I should talk about what is NOT like classic Fire Emblem instead of what is. Probably the biggest change is the weapon system. Durability is not a thing in Dark Deity. Say so long to not using that super powered weapon because you are afraid of it  breaking. You will also never have to fill character's inventory slots with weapons. Making for plenty of space for healing items. The way weapons work is that every character has access to 4 different weapon trees that change based on your class. The power tree, the crit tree, the accuracy tree and the balanced tree. You can swap through these weapons at any time just like you could in FE. Each tree can be upgraded with upgrade tokens that you either buy at the shop or get from enemies. Something I would like to draw attention to before I completely move on. For magic users not only do they have 4 different spells available based on class but the spell ANIMATION actually evolves and changes as you upgrade it to new tiers. That's some good quality stuff right there.There is a lot of class variety in Dark Deity. 6 base classes that start at lvl 1. Each of those classes have a set of 4 intermediate class that start at lvl 10 and then there are 4 more advanced classes for each base class that start at lvl 30. This leads to a lot more options then simply having your cavalier always become a paladin. Something im sure the developers must have struggled with is whether or not to have perma-death. Classic FE was always perma-death and it became a staple of the series. Though any more modern players might perfer a more casual approach. I think Dark Deity does a decent job at a compromise. There is no perma-death, BUT, that doesn't mean that is no penalties. If a character is defeated not only will they be unavailable for the rest of the stage but they also get a permanent stat reduction. A character might get -2 strength or magic, forever. So you still don't want your units to die. I was actually surprised at the variety of stages in the game. Each one feels very different from the last one. To avoid spoilers I won't name specifics, but stage variety is great. No game is perfect and this one isn't either, there is one major problem I have with Dark Deity. While the overarching plot is fine most of the specific character motivations and backstories are either paper thin or non-existent. An example being that we rescue someone from prison and then they join our party. Why did they join us? I have no idea. The game is full of characters sort of popping out of nowhere declaring that they are now joining you and you are like "ok thats cool" and that's all there is too it. It really feels odd when you got people who stow away on your ship and then suddenly appear in a conversation and  both you as the player and the other characters ask "Who are you?" and they guy just said "Oh im here to join you." and then that's all the info you get. The bond system can be just as bad. Some conversations feel like they assume you know a character's backstory. You will have this conversation happening where the two of them are talking about some kind of important event in the characters past but you as the player have no idea what that event is. You sort of just have to figure it out with context clues, it can lead to some confusing conversations. At the end of the day I do recommend Dark Deity, the gameplay is absolutely top quality for anyone who loves these kind of games. If you can get past the weirdness with character motivations and backstories then Im sure you will have a great time with Dark Deity.

_childDocuments_.review: I write this review in sadness. I thought this game was a fresh take on the SRPG genre with a lot of potential. I wanted it to be good, hell I put over 100 hours into this. Due to the "balance" of the game, many characters also had to be banned. Apart from the balancing issues, there are tons of glitches, bugs, and random errors that occur for many people, many of which are game crashing. Things get worse, the developers have not done well to keep the community updated. This last patch they included a new installer which only created more game crashing bugs, and provided no update indicating this change, or why it was done .The last update we did get was an update to the artwork, because apparently that was the most important change needed :|  The soundtrack which I paid for isn't even done correctly, with volumes being different, and some songs starting in the middle and not having the entire track present. This game at $25 dollars is genuinely scummy due to the state of the game. I use to recommend this game on sale, but even $15 dollars is pushing too much for the current state of the game. I am sad to say that I cannot earnestly recommend this game until there are some serious changes to the game and the way the developers interact with the community.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay loop is good, the Steam Deck controls are a bit janky, and the story is so-so. Given all that, I've enjoyed the time with the game. If you've played Fire Emblem, the gameplay is very similar to classic Fire Emblem games. Your unit attacks another unit, there are rock-paper-scissors styles strengths and weaknesses against other types/weapons. Though each character has four weapon types based upon their class that have slightly different properties. You can take other actions when it makes sense (heal, command actions on the battle field, swap characters around, lock enemies in places, etc). Instead of character death, it seems you might lose a stat. Reasonable trade-off between character being gone and no real impact, though not sure I love it. Between fights is basically just a camp/menu where you can upgrade weapons, view party members talking to each other, and save. I used the Steam Deck to play, though I imagine the controller input is the same for all devices. Navigating menus can be tricky, I would often over navigate even when using the d-pad. The on screen button help only appears approx 2/3rds of the time, and there were a few areas I could never figure out how to navigate without using the touch screen. None of this is a deal breaker, but it sure feels like controller input was tacked on and not something from the start. Mostly it wasn't a big deal, a couple times it did end up causing some real pain though, so do be careful. The story however lacks much that really pulled me in. It started alright, but the motivations of different players in the story were totally lost and they seemed inconsistent, mostly just driving the plot forward. I struggled to really care about the story, just looking for the next fight. Overall, I don't regret my time with this game but I do say it's not a super polished, brilliant experience. If Fire Emblem style tactical games are your thing though? Absolutely.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game of its type.  More characters than you need, so if you do not care for the comic lunk-head, you can just stop using him. Another may be average at everything but frequently double hit.  Characters have two tiers of level up with 4 choices each without locking you into a tree.  Before you commit to an attack you can see the expected outcomes- so even if you do not note the relationships between types of weapons, you can see if your choice is dirty.   There is a relationships dynamic with much reading and there were actually  a few good one-liners hidden in the expected 'do your best' type of chit chat.

_childDocuments_.review: While I'll probably play more (at the 1.2 hour mark, mission 3)... I'm not going to recommend this game.The mechanics are there, the art for characters is nice, though the main battle screen is really low quality pixel art.. There is a separate battle screen when two characters engage which has better pixel art, but if they're going to do that anyways, why not just animate the main battle screen that way? The artist has to do 2 separate animations per character when they could just do one. Three if you count the anime-esq character portraits as well...That said, the story is bland and characters appear to be locked with no customization or load out changes. Camp screens offer upgrades but the game is designed to allow you to win. That makes it too easy. I'm assuming missions can be replayed if you lose since you can save after every mission, so that makes the game low stakes as well. Tactics battles are done well, but there's no explanation of things, no tutorial. You basically figure it out since it's mostly intuitive, but knowing that you can just reload each mission and that each character you have is designed to overpower enemies, this game doesn't really have a challenge. Which makes me wonder why I try to attempt battles at all. And with the story being bland and uninteresting, there's no real reason to play for the story either.I think if they allowed customization of teams adding in the ability to hire different characters and such this would be a much better game. As it stands now, this game is a linear story with no way to lose and it's not really fun. 4.8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to just go right out and say I didn't buy this game for a fair while because the negative reviews scared me but honestly, I don't get what the problem is. I'm going to address some of the things I saw a lot of in reviews that turned me off buying the game intially:Polish:Yes this game could benefit from a little more polish here and there but that's basically par for the course for an indie developer and there's nothing game breaking only the occasional minor annoyance.Story: I really don't understand the problem people have with the story, It's not an original epic but the characters are so fun and interesting to see interact with each other that it honestly never felt uninteresting.Level up system:I thought this system was cool.Rather than choosing where to put your ability points for your characters, you go a little more akin to the Pokemon route where you can't exactly control the stats at individual levels, but depending on the character and how you build them, they will balance out to where you want them to be eventually.I wouldn't necessarily recommend this game to everyone but if you love ttrpgs, I believe you'll have a lot of fun and be challenged by this impressive Indie game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for PC alternative to Fire Emblem, then Dark Deity won't be a good choice. It's not complete crap, but it's far from being a good sRPG. I can't recommend it, especially not for the full price.Your standard story about saving the world. Nothing special, nothing actively awful. Just boring.The characters are also far from great. There are simply too many of them (30!) and not enough time to properly introduce them/expand them. Besides conversations between characters, while you're using Bond mechanic, there's literally no other way to know them better. No side quests, a lack of "screen time" in the main quest, and almost zero banter while in combat. Faust is the worst offender - Poor man's Fire Emblem, but without any semblance of balance. Unless you're playing on the easiest difficulty, you'll be always outmatched by the enemies. They are always higher level than you, and they don't have the same artificial problems as you (constant misses). It may not be unplayable (okay, the level where you're fighting your copies is in unplayable territory), but it's annoying after a few hours.The lack of side quests to level up your characters totally kills the idea of using your whole roster. There's no reason to experiment or switch characters. Just stick to your main roster, unless you have enough chapters left to catch up.I didn't like the weapons mechanic. It's basically a money sink that you need to invest into if you don't want to be useless in later chapters. It doesn't add anything entertaining - just constant swapping of weapons in combat mode to deal more dmg/miss less.Don't get me wrong. When everything works as it should, you can feel a dab of the spirit of Fire Emblem. Unfortunately, these moments are rare.The visuals are divided into two halves - ugly combat and pretty everything else. To be fair, that's a common issue with games of this type, but in the case of Dark Deity, it was especially jarring. The story is mainly told on nice backgrounds with well-designed characters' sprites. Then we have fights with RPGMaker-like graphics. The gap in quality is simply too damn big.There's not much to tell about audio. Characters are only partially voiced (sometimes they will say a word or two), and music is forgettable.There's an extremely high amount of bugs and glitches in Dark Deity. From simple bugs, like characters unable to move, to exploits with chests. The controls, camera, and UI are not much better. I had a lot of annoying problems with selecting attacks and items, characters that didn't want to go where I wanted them to go, UI elements that were hard to interact with at times, annoying camera work at the start of each fight.I could go on like this endlessly. There are simply too many problems that were never fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a love letter to Fire Emblem, but not a direct clone as some would have you believe. Overall, a fantastic game. For those of you into Fire Emblem but wanting to know what's changed, let me go through some key things I've noticed.1) The weapon system is changed. Each character's weapon can be swapped between 4 different weapons, each with its own focus; strength, accuracy, crit, and weight/speed. Gone is durability, you don't have to worry about each weapon only having a set number of uses. Tokens are acquired during missions which are spent to upgrade your weapons, with higher level tokens required for higher level weapons.2) The class system has a few hallmarks, such as advancing at level 10 and level 30, but the classes themselves are rather varied and each have their own strengths and specialties that makes changing class a really interesting question. I personally didn't feel as locked into certain class change paths as I do for Fire Emblem games.3) Gone are the level grinding missions of modern Fire Emblem. Just, poof, vamooshed, gone. We back to a bit of the hardcore now, yo.4) There are no skills like Vantage, Desperation, etc, that were the core part of Fire Emblem games. Instead, each character has their own personal traits with further traits being added on depending on what class you choose that help push characters towards certain roles. Some of your healers will trend towards battle popes, basically, becoming heavy cavalry and dishing out hammer blows as well as heals. Even the mages can feel substantially different, instead of just being different element variations of the same basic attack.Overall, I recommend the game for anyone who was left feeling unsatisfied after recent Fire Emblem entries like Three Houses or Fates. It might feel like a placebo, but even methadone can scratch that itch, you know?

_childDocuments_.review: At it's heart, this is a love letter to Fire Emblem, made by a team that was trying to fix some of the rough spots that commonly come up when analyzing Fire Emblem.  What you end up with is an enjoyable experience for Fire Emblem fans.  However, it seems to assume you already understand how this game works, even though it has some notable differences from Fire Emblem.  On top of that, there are still numerous minor bugs and glitches that distract from the fun chapter goals.  I recommend it, because it isn't a bad game, and I did enjoy it, just be aware of what you will get out of it - a fun but complex battle system and unique maps and goals on each chapter.  Despite my playtime (idle computer time), I took about 40 hours for a playthrough while reading all of the story and figuring out the game mechanics, and about 15-20 hours on a second playthrough skipping a lot of the dialog.Pros: - Unique chapter goals for each map, keeps things feeling different- Fun new classes, with a wide variety of combinations you can pick (some offering crazy synergy)- Unique out of Combat skills (heal, push, chain, disarm, phase) are all helpful in different settings- There are few irredeemable characters suffering from their stat growth, so for the most part you can pick favorites and be ok- Right from the beginning you can change the difficulty and various randomized stats for both your units and the enemies.  This allows you to set your preferred challenge level very easily.  - The game is not overly challenging at default settings, so even without completely understanding mechanics, the penalty for losing a unit is low and it remains approachable.  For a challenge, you can raise enemy stat rates by up to 200% of their norm, if you need it easier, you can raise your units stat rates instead.Cons:- The story is meh and doesn't make a whole lot of sense at times.  It feels like there were cool ideas for maps that needed the story to do some gymnastics to make the map make sense.- Balancing is an issue, and some of it is caused by the weapon/armor effectiveness mechanics (that are not explained well to the player) and some skills being way better than others (ahem...dragoon)- Skills and weapons do not always increase when leveling up.  As a player, this feels like a development sin. I don't like investing in a unit and have them worse off because of it.  Dodge and Hit % are impacted by your character's level, and weapons that you level up increase in weight, causing your unit to be slower.

_childDocuments_.review: If its on sale, youre a fan of fire emblem style games, and you want a cheap pick up to scratch the turn based grid tactics itch, then sure, get it. OTHERWISE, no, pass.The game is buggy, has more of a random difficulty spike than difficulty curve, is missing some key fundamental components, terrible UI with consumables, and the story is scatterbrained at best.BUGS:In combat, you have a combat table that tells you outcomes and battle stats of selected actions before you take said action, which is good. But the moment you have any character that has multi hit, the table and the numbers displayed in the combat, almost never match. Example, you have a unit that hits twice in its combat (not 2 separate attacks, but 2 hits in a single attack). The table will say you do 15 damage. But in the animation, and the damage numbers that pop up, each swing will do like 8 or 9... which is 16-18 damage... not 15. If you're ever in a situation where you have to take risk and play a move that would have you close to low hp... you essentially cant rely on anything and you have to just kinda guess.Each map is a grid, composed of multiple squares, layered upon a background image that makes up the map. This is fine, but its done so poorly it creates 2 problems ive never seen before. The first problem is that what is and isnt considered a passable grid square, wont always be accurately reflected on a slope. So you can end up in situation where you position your guys on the squares at the top of a ramp, to like block to path, only to find out that the next square in that line, which is sitting on a cliff face based on the image, is also a passable square, and the enemy will run right passed you cause you didnt think to try and put a character on the cliff face... this seems like just bad implementation of a grid layout.The second issue is something ive never seen before. You would think that a grid square is a single whole unit of measurement, because... thats what a grid square is. But for some reason, it isnt. They act like they have a decimal or something attached to their values. As a result, you find random squares that you can put your character into, but then in order to interact with them, you have to click on the empty square next to them. This becomes a huge problem if that empty square is off the edge of the map, cause you cant interact with it. You can cast support spells on the unit, you cant phase them out of it, they just become soft locked into that square, cause the grid square they are actually on is calculated to be somewhere where their model isnt.Difficulty Spike and missing key component:Up to chapter 10, its fine. But around Chapter 9 or so you start getting missions where you cant take all the members of your party, and so, the members you leave behind dont gain any experience. Then suddenly out of no where Chapter 11 theres this MASSIVE difficulty spike.  Every enemy is suddenly level 18+, runs in packs, and swarms targets. In most games like this, this would be annoying, but not an issue. Just go to the map, travel to the "insert grindable location here", and grind. But in this game, you cant do that at all. There are no grindable locations, theres no grindable mechanic, theres not even a real overworld map. Theres NOTHING you can do. If you dont power farm levels in combat on specific characters, it almost becomes a soft lock, because theres just no way to gain the levels and stats you need to win.Every character has 4 "weapons/attacks". Each weapon focuses on a different fundamental, with those being raw dmg, crit chance, accuracy, and defensive/multi-hit. You need tokens, which you can get for killing some random enemies but for the most part you buy them between missions from the shop, to level these weapons up. BUT, since theres no way to grind gold, you cant buy whatever you need, whenever you need it... so you cant max these out. You have to decide to either focus on specific weapons fro specific characters and pray you dont get in a situation where those weapons on those characters screws you, OR... your whole party ends up kinda meh... and everything is way more difficult.The UI:The UI almost seems like it was made for a mobile game. Everythings done with the mouse left click, and thats it. Theres no sorting inventory based on any feature, you have to double click items to use them rather than confirming to use them, and theres no click and drag or anything. You cant move multiple items and you cant sort inventory.Scatterbrained story:Soft Spoiler warningWhats sad is the story has all the parts to be really intriguing and really interesting. But it skips massive chunks for no apparent reason. You'll complete a mission, and then they'll talk about the next thing they need to do, and then suddenly you're in the next mission, and you have no idea wtf is going on. They dont do a good job setting the world up, so you dont really have any vested interest in the different kingdoms, or who's fighting who, or where the country borders are... it feels like theres a massive world wide inside joke, and you're not in on it, so you dont understand whats going on.They try to make up for this by having side stories told through the "bond" system, but the side stories either reference events in the past tense that havent happened yet, or never happen. You're just sitting there like "wait... what do you mean just like last time? what was last time?"Chapter 11 is a great example. In Chapter 11, two armies are supposed to be fighting each other. Theres a weird mage on the other side of the battle field casting some giant world ending spell. You're job is to get to he mage to stop him. But for some dumb reason, the two armies dont fight each other. Despite being in the middle of a war, theyre all just codded to be "bad guy", so the two armies merge together as allies. Are they gonna help you try and stop the psycho world ending mage? NOPE, they are gonna team up just to try to kill you. Like "hold up lads, I know we're at war, but what do you say we call a truce, to kill that small group of people that just rolled up, who dont belong to either nation, sound good? Oh the big ole world ending mage? IDK what you're talking about"OK, fine, so you fight both armies at the same time, which is where the game starts throwing over leveled swarms of units at you. And after you fight your way through, you get to the mage. Your brother shows up, and you decide to team up with him to fight the mage. Do you get battle him? no... is there some crazy story of the fight? no... Do they do as mush as have the character models smack into each other with sound effects? NO... Theres literally just a flash, and it goes to a dialouge screen, where the mage wins, decides to leave, you got your ass kicked, and your brothers moments from bleeding to death.... No explanation at all. Just "oh no.... we suck again..."It gets even worse...So during dialogue screens, the characters all have their own voice acted one liners. I actually thought this was kinda cool right up til this event. The scene is supposed to be super sad and dire. Your brothers dying, theres nothing you can do, youre panicking... A sad moment... but the characters one liners are all single recordings, and whatever emotions they are recorded with are the tones they have. The healer for example is this upbeat but shy girl, and theres a scene where you beg the healer to help, but she cant cause of the type of wound he has, and the whole thing as a scene goes to ♥♥♥♥ cause her perky upbeat voice line plays, when shes trying to say "theres nothing I can do".... Like... why do you sound excited?The last thing I noticed that was kinda meh was the music. The same soft pirate accordion music plays during every bond dialogue plays during every dialogue, regardless of emotion or tone of the dialogue.

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Deity is a very solid Fire Emblem-like game that moves into its own directions and does its own thing. It will be immediately recognizable if you have played a more modern Fire Emblem game, and it will be sufficiently different to not only offer something that feels pleasantly and refreshingly different, but offer some things that the FE series can itself crib from. The weapon system is a pretty amazing facet of this gem, something I expect to see other games and series take notice of. The devil is in the details with this one. You can clearly see where the development team put their creative effort and what they focused on, and see what they chose to skirt by on. It shows a forward-thinking kind of intelligence that more teams want, and more than those need. The As and the Cs are clearly visible on the report card, here. And, those details matter; there are several little things that Dark Deity needs polished to feel truly amazing to play.It needs some of that polish in the quality of life department. I would love to have the ability to access a load game function at the menus between battles. Heck, I would enjoy being able to quit the game from that menu. I want both, but would take either, because I have neither as the game is.When you're playing with a controller, the game feels like it's better optimized for mouse and keyboard. When you're using mouse and keyboard, it feels like you would be better served plugging in a controller. Interacting with the game's systems is just that touch too unintuitive that makes me wonder whether I am missing something. But, it feels like the same clunk whether I am zero or three drinks into a night of strategeryness. And, I keep asking myself why I can't seem to load a tooltip that tells me what an enemy's item does. Is a Raw Egg good? Do I want that? Gotta break a few omelettes to find a raw one, I guess.As it stands, this is a great game to play. Or, "merely great", if you like. There is a roughness to the edges that makes it a chore to handle Dark Deity sometimes. The overall experience is worth having if what you want is a strategy role-playing game that pushes its writing, character artwork, combat animations, and combat systems forward over its map art and controls. But, I will take these (generally) competently designed battle maps over ones that are gorgeous to look at. Still, I immensely appreciate the use of color. One map in particular uses a lot of color, and poorly, but the use of color is generally fantastic. Dark Deity is vibrant.There are better games for getting someone into this style of gameplay, but you could certainly do worse. You could start your friend on SRPGs via Thracia 776. Can't think of a better way to torch a relationship, except maybe stealing their dog. If you have never tried a game of this style before and want to see what it's like, spend the twenty-five smackers or get it on sale. Dark Deity will not do you wrong.It does not always put its best foot forward, or follow up with the correct next step in the dance. But, Dark Deity does know the right moves and gets them down to the dance floor much more often than not. It knows the routine and gets you there while touching on some of the fantasy tropes that you would expect, yet without it feeling procedural or inevitable. Recommended, with some caveats, and very highly recommended to fans of games in the Fire Emblem style.Please clap.

_childDocuments_.review: Like you'll see in every one elses review and can probably tell just by looking this game is a Fire Emblem clone. More specifically the older entries in the series. I dont say that as a knock on it, I love Fire Emblem and its similarity is why I bought it. There are some things done right here and if I could give a neutral or mixed rating I would. Lets talk about where it lacks however. The character art is great but the sprite work is terrible. The character sprites will barely if at all look anything like the character art, and sometimes the enemy will be female on the map and have a male sprite in game. The animations are being oddly held in high regard by this community which confuses me because they are acceptable at best. I think its just a buzzword kind of thing to say the animation is smooth or whatever. The animations are fine but could be alot better is my point. The game does offer a good amount of customization options for play throughs, essentially allowing you to control or randomize elements like item drops and even what order you recruit characters in. I played the game on the default Deity setting which I guess would be hard mode. I would be lying if I said the game had good balance. One chapter in particular has a character named Benji show up and placed in the center of the map where he will be immediately killed with no way for the player to intervene. This isnt part of the story or anything but rather just a result of the stat inflated enemies on hard mode vs this character you just got. The tutorial literally doesnt exist and nothing ever explains any of this games systems to you including its weapon system and it more complex, convoluted and objectively worse than Fire Emblems weapon triangle. All in all its not a terrible attempt at a FE clone however it would be downright dishonest to say its on the same level as Fire Emblem. It doesnt look, or play as good and it keeps alot of the antiquated systems that Intelligent Systems has long since changed because lets be honest...they arent very good. This is a 5/10 game. Its worth a play for hardcore fans of older FE's, maybe worth a play for turn based strategy game fans and should be an easy pass for everyone else. Priced fairly but is it worth your time? _childDocuments_.review: Edit: After going through the game I decided to change my review. I still stand by most of the issues I had, but it was an enjoyable experience in the end.As a "Fire Emblem" clone, it does its job. It does enough things differently while maintaining that FE feel to make the game interesting. The classes feel nice, its great to see growth rates, and the weapon/armor system, while a bit bloated, provides a different combat feel than standard FE games.However, that being said, this game is horribly unrefined. There's a lot of things we often take for granted that isn't present or just done very sloppily. For example, the button layout is all over the place. I tried using keyboard and mouse at first, but it was so bad I was forced to use a controller and even then there were a lot of issues. Things like the button prompts sometimes appearing as keyboard bindings or sometimes I lose some controller functionality if I move my mouse.And then there's the menus. Oh god, navigating the different UI elements was a nightmare because most of them have different control schemes. The Options menu was the most normal, you can navigate the different options using D-pad or LTS, A button is confirm and B is cancel. However, some in-game UI you can't use LTS and must rely on D-pad. And then there are others that have the Back Button as the confirm button. Why the Back button!? There are other examples, but what I'm saying is that it's so eclectic that every time I enter a different menu I have to spend a few seconds to remember how to navigate it.There's also a bunch of UX and game feel issue, but I'm going to give them a pass on those since they are a small studio and I'm sure others have already mention those already. As for gameplay, I haven't gotten far enough to provide a comprehensive review, but base on the power scaling I've seen so far, I feel that there might be some noticeable issue later down the line.TLDR; fun game so far, but in its current state it feels like a Proof of Concept rather than a finished, polished product

_childDocuments_.review: Switched my review from positive to negative, but I didn't hate the game. I just... don't care about it and it's hard for me to feel and want to feel even more invested. I wish there was a neutral option for recommendation because that's what I'd pick.I don't know how much I'll remember of the game when I finish it (if I finish it, although I'm trying to chip away at it slowly), but while it's not the best of it's genre out there it's sufficient if you're looking for a FE-style game. The story is luke warm and isn't intriguing enough for me to have ever wanted to play multiple chapters in a single sitting and instead do one chapter per play session. There are some interesting characters, but not the most intuitive of mechanics so it can take some trial and error to figure out what you're doing. For instance, the sub-classes (red, blue, green, yellow fighting styles -- blanking on the name) and tier tokens I figured out as I went along, but unless it was explained early on and I quickly forgot I'm not sure it was ever made clear what I was supposed to do with it.Although a solid game overall, but kind of clunky in terms of controls especially. ESC exits out of menus, sure, but once you hit it enough to enter the general menu "resume, options, etc." pressing ESC doesn't close that menu and instead you have to manually hit "resume." It's a small thing that may only annoy me, however. Turning off combat animations causes there to be a pause between selecting the attack command and the result to be implemented which can give the impression of the game lagging or freezing for a few seconds. It's faster to leave combat animations on despite how it can be a bit tiresome to sit through. I wish turning combat animations off did the same thing as Fire Emblem where the sprites would briefly attack, but it'd all be over much quicker than sitting through the animations. I also wish you could change combat animation to either be completely on, off, your turn only, like FE as well. All this makes battles feel like they can drag on.EDIT: So apparently if you hit "Enter" it skips animations without the pause between actions, which I only found out by accidentally tapping it during a battle phase. The UI feels very clunky and definitely needed polishing.Loading screens can take a surprisingly long time as well. Not several minutes long, but still longer than you'd think it'd be. I've also experienced some lag in-game and dropped frames despite it not being a game that's demanding on my computer at all. I also found critical animations cause lag too sometimes.I wish there was some way to either remove the permanent debuffs on characters that takes place if they fall in battle, but I understand it was the devs way to try and change things up since they wanted to remove permadeath to save people from restarting chapters when characters die. However, the permanent debuffs can lead to the same thing anyway as the stronger characters get the more severe the debuffs get if they become incapacitated. There's also a difficulty spike such as between chapters 3 and 4 if your units aren't around 5-8, which most of mine weren't (most around 4-6), which makes splitting up your units into teams rather risky and may be safer to take up more turns but keep them together instead.The art itself is good and I like that the characters are voiced. I can't speak much to the music as I haven't listened to it extensively and usually listen to something else while playing, but from what I've heard it's fine.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - it's not worth it. Looks tempting, but do yourself a favor and move on.Although it looks promising, the game is pretty deceptive in it's mediocrity. The problem is that those additions come with little to no tutorial or even a half-way decent explanation. Sure, there are tutorial textboxes, but they are pretty light on details, so it's ultimately more frustrating than helpful.The music is pretty bad. It always feels out of place. And even when it tries to set the right mood, it just feels...sad.The user interface is frustrating and unhelpful.And good god, the story is just awful. Some of the laziest and uninspired writing I've seen in a long while. Also, the game's equivalent of the Fire Emblem "support conversation system" is their Bonds system. Here's the kicker - the Bond system is a waste of time and is utterly useless. I tried to set things up like I would in Fire Emblem, pairing people off, thinking that the Bonds would provide some minor in-game benefit. They. Do. Not. It's utterly useless.
