_childDocuments_.review: I’ve apparently found myself on a tactical RPG trend considering the last few games I’ve been playing. Disgaea 6 ate up too many hour of my life (and continues to do so as Disgaeas tend to do), and now I’m powering through Dark Deity and reliving the old days of the genre. The differences between the two are as staggering as one might imagine and while the former streamlines and modernizes, the latter embraces its old school roots and charges full speed ahead.Our story begins as many stories do with those in power having a dispute and pulling those below their station in to do their dirty work. The four heroes that make up the starting party are cadets of varying ages from a particularly prestigious military academy. Thanks to the king’s ambitions and lack of respect for tradition, all of the stuents are drafted for service immediately, no matter what their age.The twists and turns that follow are interesting enough and keep the story moving forward even if there isn’t much that will make Dark Deity’s tale stand out in your memory in the years to come. It’s a linear story without any side scenarios to improve your party so you’ll need to make the most of the experience and loot in each chapter. Maybe it’s the recent grinding of Disgaea that’s still cooking in my mind, but I would have liked to see more opportunities to level my characters. You’re bombarded with new recruits along the way but there’s nowhere near enough experience to keep them all viable and the most effective strategy is to focus on a smaller group.Dark Deity’s significant number of characters is paired with a healthy number of classes that are available to them. Leveling and experience complications aside, the sheer quantity allows you to spread them out over your impressive roster. Always a classaholic myself, I loved seeing so many options and only wished that I’d actually been able to use them all from start to finish. I would’ve liked to see larger battles that let me take all of the characters in as opposed to the increasing number of heroes that became professional bench warmers.Each class tree comes with its base class and it splits into four second tier and four third tier classes. Though each tier provides improvements over a similarly themed class of the previous tier, the transition from second to third isn’t a linear one. A character who is upgrading to the top tier has access to the same classes as any other character of the same class tree would. This can make for some interesting leveling paths that mix up the attribute design of a character.A pleasant surprise in the class system that I enjoyed was the weapons mechanic. Each class has four different weapons available to them at all times that can be swapped on their turn to suit your strategy. Though there’s some variation on the overall focus between classes, they’re broken up into four focuses: raw damage, critical chance, accuracy, and speed. Two characters of the same profession can play quite differently as upgrading these weapons will help them hone in on which enemies they excel against.The nostalgia flows strongly through Dark Deity, but it’s both its gift and its curse. Though it hits on the classic aspects of the genre effectively, you’ll recognize some issues that tend to have been hammered out of more recent releases. Though there were a number of minor issues, the most blatant offendors for me were the lack of in-battle saves and the subpar menu navigation.Combat tends to take some time to muscle through and saves only being available between scenarios often lead to me being frustrated that I had to play a full hour plus or not at all. I’d really like to see this changed; even if Dark Deity wants a more hardcore, ironman feel to it, I’d prefer they went the single autosave route instead.Controls are an issue that you get used to but it isn’t as smooth as I’d like to see in a title that involves a lot of menu navigation. They seem to march to the beat of their own drum and even a few hours in I was still struggling to move through them effectively without having to work around it. Though these controls don’t ruin the experience, they make navigating just restrictive enough that it’s likely to become a pet peeve along the way.A final point of note that some may find lacking but other may not be particularly bothered by is the lack of voice acting. You’ll have grunts and repeated phrases that add some character to your party, though you’ll want to bring your reading glasses to this one. There’s plenty of chatting before and after each scenario and there’s a healthy amount of character relationship conversations that will pop up between each scenario reminiscent of the Fire Emblem series. I spend a lot of time playing older RPGs so this wasn’t a big deal to me, but it’s one that you want to be prepared for if you’d rather listen than read.Dark Deity is a respectable entry in the tactical RPG genre that skillfully pays homage to the classics without innovating in many ways itself. Some elements that were retired from TRPGs for good reason see a return, such as a limited window for saving, but overall it’s a title that you should check out if you miss releases like Shining Force or the old school Fire Emblems. If you go into it expecting some flavorful jank, there is a solid title here and one that I’d love to see improved upon with a sequel.But please, Sword & Axe, let us use all of our characters next time!

_childDocuments_.review: When I first bought this game, it infuriated me so much that I almost refunded it. I ended up finishing it but I found the whole experience... mediocre. It scratches that SRPG itch if you're having a bad case of it, but it won't make you full. If you're not a big fan of SRPG, I wouldn't even touch the game. I'll discuss the game's flaws below so you can see if you can live with them or not:1/ Story: The story is not terrible per se. There are some decent world building and political plotlines in there. What the game sorely lacks is good pacing. Sometimes, the game speeds through plot points like crazy. Case in point is the death of an important character that serves as motivation for the party. The death happens in like 5 seconds from the point that the character shows up. I ends up being bemused rather than touched by the whole scene. Dark Deity is a game that never learns the art of showing the story and not telling it. The prime example is Irving, the MC of the game. Irving somehow becomes the leader of your band of fighters despite the fact that your group consists of several seasoned commanders, important nobles, and legendary warriors. It was never explained how Irving, a fresh recruit, becomes the leader of this group other than that the story needs him to be the main man. Realistically, he's not even in the top 10 of leaders among your playable characters.2/ Dialogue writing: Whoever writes the dialogue for Dark Deity has to be the most passive-aggressive person. Characters never fail to offer a smart or cynical retort to even the most mundane statement. Seriously a common conversation in this game goes like this. A: "How's the weather?" B: "Oh oh do I look like a weatherman to you? Right, let me just look up and check out the sky for you... Yeah it looks like it's raining douchebags over here!" It's a miracle how this group can even travel together with how antagonistic everyone is, let alone win a war together.3/ Gameplay: The game takes a relatively safe approach to copying FEs. This is about as faithful a FE clone as it can get, with only a few additional features and ideas. Some ideas are nice. I particularly like the grave wound system as a middle ground to permadeath. However, most other ideas fall flat. The game tries to expand on FE's weapon triangle system but went too far. There are dozens of weapon types, each with varying degree of effectiveness against different armors. The simplicity of FE's system allows the focus to be on your strategy. In Dark Deity, being effective is less about your strategy and more about meticulously making sure you have the right weapon and the right armor. The only other strategic option that the game offers is the use of Aspects, which essentially add a passive ability to the character. Most of these Aspects are just adding a percentage to some stats though. Only a few represents interesting trade-offs. By the time your characters get their third promotion, the organization part of the game becomes boring. There is nothing else to customize or to upgrade. In later chapters, I spent almost no time between chapters because there are nothing else to improve upon.4/ Saturation of characters: This is the most avoidable flaw that the game has. For whatever reason, this game throw characters at you like crazy. Up until the mid-point of the game, you get 2-3 characters every chapter. And it's not as if the game needs all these character to tell its story. The narrative uses only 10 or so characters. Some characters barely speak at all throughout the game. It feels comical how more than half of playable characters might as well be faceless generic mobs. This creates a gap between the story and the gameplay. Some important characters in the story never showed up in the gameplay. Some absolutely dominant characters in the gameplay never says anything in the story.5/ Bugs: The game still has a lot of bugs. Some skill descriptions are just wrong. Sometimes when you move the characters on the map, weird stuffs happen like the character would move on top of an enemy instead of attacking. There are times that I cannot move a character at all or attack an enemy. None of the bugs are game breaking but they are common enough to be annoying.Overall, while I did play through the game, it felt to me like I was just passing time rather than doing something enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with the Good:The promotion system is interesting, which lets you get some very neat skill combinations. The procgen mode to give it replay value.The neutral:The story line is a pretty bog standard fire emblem plot. If you like that, great. If you don't, the story won't really hold you. The spritework is alright. The music is pretty hit or miss. The bad:The game balance is all the ♥♥♥♥ over the place. The attempt at tactical depth with damage and armor types was an attempt, but I think it's pretty godawful in practice. The fact that weapons are just part of your class removes a great deal of tactical depth that Fire Emblem has. For example: A lance wielding class only has melee options - There is no ranged option, as there are in Fire emblem. The only classes that break this mold are at the very end of the promotion tree, and get hybrid damage types, and become melee/spellcaster types. This actually ends up removing a lot of tactical depth. The support conversations and bonds don't seem to actually have any game effect as they would in Fire Emblem. The conversations themselves are fairly insipid, but occasionally interesting. The weapon upgrade system was an attempt - but the problem here is that you've got 4 flavors of weapon on each char, and often the upgrades are not entirely upgrades. The weapon will for example do more damage at the expense of weight, which may make a weapon that previously struck twice slow the character down instead. Often upgrades add some accuracy or crit, and many times there is little difference between weapons. You are choosing between 4% higher accuracy on one vs. 4% higher crit on another. Extremely underwhelming. The game is buggy as hell. I had a few crashes, and many instances where enemies (or my own) units would become untargetable. During a chapter an enemy cav unit became untargetable after their turn, thereby allowing them access to my backline, and letting them down one of my healers. Sometimes characters would show pending a support conversation, but there was no convo available in their options. Tons of damage display issues. ex. Attack in the tactical overview says it will do 28 damage. The actual attack animation shows 30 (but the enemy took 28) - Tons of stuff like that. I also personally found the voice acting pointless and in many cases obnoxious. Ultimately, this game is very rough around the edges. It does scratch the fire emblem itch, but it's honestly not very good. I would not recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: IF YOU ARE A FIRE EMBLEM FAN READ ON, IF NOT YOU CAN SKIP OR WAIT FOR SALE.Forgot to add, The controller support is really weird, maybe its cause I plugged in a controller during the first map but I have had to use both my mouse and keyboard and controller. And on promotion screens, I cant accept the promotion unless I have my controller plugged in.After about 2.5 hours in, (I'm on Chapter 5) I can say that this game is.... okay. I will update this review as I play. The story is pretty much just basic Fire Emblem stuff so far, bandits etc. But the characters appear rather charming.The game is not fully voice acted as I was led to believe, The characters are like awakening where they go ah and oh in cutscenes and have battle quotes. The gameplay is where i have most of my criticisms:The map design is basic not super interesting or any side objectives to get you to take risks for rewards. One map told me that the faster i did the map the more gold i got but I took my time to recruit the 2 characters on the map instead. The Grave Wound system, their substitution for perma-death is underwhelming. I lost a point of strength on one character and a point of luck on another, and with how high the growth rates feel, It seems like you will be able to make up those losses pretty easily. Class Progression: This one they should have nailed. They class choices should be really cool and interesting, You promote at level 10 and 30 with 4 class choices at each promotion. The class skills you get are different enough for varied playstyle. For example, one class increased your crit everytime you healed by 6% and stacked up to 4 times until you attacked next. Where another class gained strength the more the magic the opponent had. The problem, Is that lifesteal trivializes the game and the other skills you get are based on chance, which isnt something you can reliably plan a strategy around. (similar to how movement stars in FE5 can screw you over,) one of these abilities not activating can ruin what was a good strategy.The Armor/Weapon and Advantage system: These systems really seem like they were put here so that they could have something to differentiate them from Fire Emblem.There is literally no explanation of this mechanic unless you inspect your character and even with that its still confusing me. Every class has a damage type and an armor type. Certain damage types do better against certain armors. At least thats what it seems like should happen. I cant really tell if im getting an advantage or not. It not clear cut at all like the weapon triangle in FE is.Every class has 4 weapon that it is equipped with that you can upgrade. Now i understand what this should be. One of the weapons has more might than the others, one weighs less than others, one has more crit than others, and one is more accurate than others. So far I havent really found a reason to use the crit weapon, The few times i have i have not gotten a crit. Even though it says I have a 15-25% crit chance. And as for rangers, just stick with War Bow as it has so far outclassed everything else in the class.The 4 weapon system seems interesting enough, but i cant help but think a more traditional system could have worked better with weapon forging etc. Or maybe instead of 4 you have 1 weapon and choose what to add to it when you upgrade it.Now if you've made it this far into the review I want to say first and foremost, I have enjoyed the little time i have spent with this game. Kudos to the devs for trying to add something different even if it feels like some of those changes turn out to not be as good as they seem. Unfortunately I would only recommend this game to hardcore Fire Emblem fans not just anyone. And only if you can get it on sale for less than 20 bucks.Good first attempt for these devs though.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd critically say this game is awesome. Really great at capturing the army of individuals feeling that Fire Emblem fans will love. the classes are really cool and I enjoy navigating the armor/weapon type system. and the amount of character dialog is honestly gargantuan, but very nicely written and technically optional to read. Definitely much harder than any Fire Emblem game which is great, but I feel the punishment employed for poor play is too good at ruining a save file. When a character dies in a level, one of their stats is lowered based on how they died. I lose maybe one unit every other chapter, but with the rate that the enemies scale from chapter to chapter, even one death can potentially put that unit behind for the rest of the game unless you spend a whole lot of money to rectify the stat loss. and this is slightly solved by very often receiving new units, but they simply don't scale with the enemies in the chapters they are introduced in, because none of their weapons are ever upgraded, and the enemies are usually more upgraded than your units. Because of that it can feel like a constant game of catchup instead of actually developing characters over a long period of time. In certain chapters it feels like the task of babysitting the new recruits is actually a liability because the funding you receive in game is largely dependent on how fast you clear a level, but if you play it safe so none of your units get their stats lowered, you don't have quite enough money to make their weapons useful. and I said I enjoyed the armor/weapon system and truly i do, but past a certain point in the campaign the balancing seems to fall apart with magic being extremely polarizing even if you use the correct armor and weapon against enemy mages. this works in your favor as well of course, but there are so many instances where im surrounding an enemy trickster mage that just -cannot- be hit effectively even by my glaive(v good accuracy weapon) user. if you're still reading you should know that this is still a good review. I love all the ideas going on with this game (except stat loss, id honestly rather permadeath) and think their worst faults can be fixed with some balance revisiting, but if you want a brutal character driven strategy game with lots of classic FE vibes definitely try out this game.

_childDocuments_.review: *Disclaimer*If this game is trying to be a spiritual successor to Fire Emblem, its on the right track. It takes the bones and structure of what made Fire Emblem unique and while paying homage and respect, finds new and interesting ways to stand on its own. While some of the artistic choices can seem dated, the nostalgic feel of the old school Fire Emblem games from the GBA era is translated well. It looks gorgeous, and I can tell the artist(s) were very meticulous with their work. I cant say the same for the sprite work, however. For a maiden game, Its forgivable, but its not great. Still, because the animations look like care was taken with them being made, I enjoy watching the combat animations. Which leads to what needs improvement with the Sound: Its horribly balanced. Sound Balancing is a major part to making sure things sound like they are in equilibrium. I had to spend about 25 minutes fooling around with my sound settings because the levels on the various sounds, music, and voice lines were not balanced well.(Fixed and Added in a recent patch)The biggest drawbacks are the User Experience/User Interface.(Added in a patch: There are now tutorials in the game menu when you click on empty tiles. Not ideal, but they exist and explain things adequately enough)And when information IS presented to you, sometimes its presented to you awkwardly. Prime example: The Promotion Screen. (Promotion screens were adjusted and edited in a patch to make it easier to see all the pertinent info before classing up. New units have their growths AND base stats determined by which class you pick upon acquiring them in the story)Other issues that highlight the problem of the UI being bad at conveying information is:How Money is Earned Chapter to Chapter. You'd never know it unless you caught the text box in chapter 4 or 5 saying that clear speed influences how much gold you earn on a clear. Killing enemies earns gold too. But how is the gold gain calculated. What is the rate? Are there bonuses to how you kill enemies? Penalties? Do you get more gold for killing higher leveled enemies? Less for lower leveled? Bond. The Bond system is not explained. Like, I enjoy seeing the characters interact with each other, and while your opinions on each character and how they are written and characterized can be highly subjective, what isn't subjective is how little the bond system tells you. What is it even there for? Is it just flavor? Am I correct to assume its supposed to add combat bonuses for units in close proximity? If I'm correct, why wont it tell me what those bonuses are and how to use them? Why is there never any sort of indication that this system matters?The weapon system. Do the weapon types have clear uses and designations? Are they effective vs certain armor types? Is it just a flavor thing? Do characters have hidden specialties? What does that Letter mean on a unit when I'm fighting an enemy? How does the game handle character deaths/defeat? I know now, through an eventuality, but the game never outright tells me how it handles death and defeat. You have to find out that when a character is defeated, they sustain a wound of sort that issues a permanent penalty to a stat that seems to be random, but might be linked to the damage type you sustained upon defeat. How do you keep track of these penalties? Can you clear them? All in All. For an indie dev team (only 6 people from what I could tell) and their first game, this is a good start. But it needs some work.

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Deity is an interesting game. Playing it I often thought about Sea of Stars. It's obviously a passion project by developers who love Fire Emblem as much as you, like Sea of Stars is to Chrono Trigger. Is it Fire Emblem quality? No, but what an insane standard to hold it to. To be fair, it's not Sea of Stars quality either, but I can't help but be impressed by what a small team and a kickstarter campaign has done here.What I like about Dark Deity I like a lot. The class-promotion system is super cool, allowing players to freely hybridize between 4 level 10 and 4 level 30 classes. This creates a depth of customization that bolsters replay value significantly. Replaying on Hard with knowledge about this system I was rewarded greatly compared to my first playthrough on Normal where I was figuring it out as I went. Each class stage offers not only different skills but also stat growth patterns, which lends different approaches to different characters who all have unique skills and stat distributions of their own. There aren't really any "bad" units, and weaker units can be supplemented with adequate game knowledge turning them into destroyers. My off-meta units on my second playthrough were stronger than my meta units on my first.On the topic of units, at first glance I thought the social "Bond" system in this game was going to be tedious. Between levels it might offer up to 10 unique dialogues between 30 units all with unique stories. At first I found these dialogues a bit cliche, but as they advance from stage 1/3 to 3/3 they become more interesting, specific, and nuanced as the characters develop relationships with each-other. By the end of the game I found myself cherishing my bond dialogues and lamenting levels where I had maxed them all out between my team of 14. This drove me to choose a completely different team on my second play-through to learn about the characters I had benched on my first, another testament to the game's replayability. I love games with hefty character rosters, and Dark Deity features a colourful cast some of whom I know I will think about in the future. The story writing mirrors the writing of the bond system; at first, it seems pedestrian, but it grows from typical beginnings to an interesting conclusion that I didn't predict with some really cool boss designs along the way.The most common gripe I've seen with this game is the gameplay. I will make no illusions about the negative elements: It's kind of buggy and the game lacks polish in general. I'd personally have changed some of the UI controls like target selection and input confirmation (special commands take the place of the attack button leading to some extremely frustrating misclicks). If this is a dealbreaker for you then I understand, but I believe in giving grace to indie developers—Dark Deity is still more polished than some AAA games and I know that here it's not for lack of care. The learning curve is artificially inflated because the tutorialization is insubstantial. If you play this game you should know that there is a battlesave feature, which itself is buggy but can be used to savescum bugs. The lack of terrain tiles makes gameplay a matter of choke point control and matchup knowledge. This is exacerbated by the matchup chart being very hard to get a handle on, with the game offering differing interactions between 3 types of armour, 4 types of magic damage, 4 styles of weapon or spell, and 5 physical types of physical damage, and on difficulties below hard these differences don't feel significant or worth knowing (damage variance of -10%-40%). I myself choose to view this as a positive—let us not punish indie developers for being overly ambitious in experimenting with a classic formula. In fact, for all its flaws I think that Dark Deity shines in its innovations on the Fire Emblem formula.The overly ambitious matchup chart may seem daunting, but once one learns how it works it rewards proper team building. I think this is a meaningful departure from the Fire Emblem approach, which is robust in its simplicity. I’ve never been one to condemn games for using similar mechanics and systems to others. This is a meaningful difference between videogames and other media. One would not decry Salem’s Lot as a Dracula clone, for a quick example, and yet a game like Dark Deity is written of as a Fire Emblem clone, life sims like Sun Haven are written off as Stardew Valley clones, platformer metroidvanias are called Hollow Knight clones and is that not itself a Castlevania clone? All of these games including Dark Deity are engaging with the form of games they’re in the tradition of, and I for one hold that it’s more interesting to see how they expand on and experiment with that established form and one’s expectations thereof. The best example from Dark Deity is its boss fights. In Rekka no Ken the most mechanically advanced boss is one who you can only counterattack safely. Dark Deity offers raid style bosses that use AoE attacks, apply effects outside of regular combat, require specific engagement with units other than themselves, and generally require a different style of play from ordinary levels;I found this experimentation on the Fire Emblem form extremely impressive and engaging. Beyond this are smaller QoL changes that I appreciate: tradable items that customize unit stats and effects when equipped, no weapon degradation, and perhaps controversially no permadeath. I’m a player who resets Fire Emblem levels when a unit dies—I want to bring everyone with me! Dark Deity’s injury system lets players weigh a permanent stat loss against the time they’ve spent in the level. This choice is not insignificant, and while I have eaten a late stat loss I found myself resetting more often than not. You might hate this system, but I love it!	Dark Deity can be a Fire Emblem clone if that’s all one chooses to see in it, but I think it’s much more. It’s fun, the world is beautiful, the characters are memorable both in their visual design and writing, the story is good and is affected by every one of its 30 unique characters, and it expands meaningfully upon the Fire Emblem formula. I’m not going to sugar coat the bugs; they can be extremely frustrating. After one Windows related crash upon stage clear I switched to playing exclusively on Steam Deck and had a great experience for the rest of my time with the game. I quite enjoyed and recommend Dark Deity to fans of Fire Emblem. That said, if your interest is piqued but the flaws seem too insurmountable, know that Dark Deity 2 is set to release in 2024 and the devs have engaged with player feedback and seem to have created a game that expands even more radically on its original formula; beyond QoL improvements they claim to have added terrain tiles, players will have access to more radical tools that affect the battle outside of traditional combat, and the costume design for female characters seems a bit more realistic too. One can never truly recommend a game before it releases, but my time with Dark Deity has guaranteed that I will purchase Dark Deity 2, and I think that’s as strong a recommendation as I can give for both.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a GBA Fire Emblem style game, and you only have a PC, this is the game for you.The storyline starts off a little bit basic, and some of the maps can be a bit frustrating... there are little bugs here and there, usually involving the game "losing track" of where one of your units is supposed to be on the map, sometimes placing them "underneath" an adjacent allied unit on the map, meaning you have to move the ally in order to move the glitched unit.But when your troops start reaching level 30 and getting their second promotions... damn, are they powerful! It's satisfying to see a character, such as Cia, Bianca, Vesta or Wren, holding the line against a horde of enemies.It also has memorable, frustrating moments, such as Samara as an Inquisitor holding a narrow corridor against two enemies -- a melee and a caster -- and a friend backing her up with healing. 50% chance to hit the melee enemy, yet she misses 12 times in a row, somehow giving the entire party enough turns to run completely around the building to back-attack the caster. I was literally saying, "You can do it this time Samara... WHUMP!" *she whiffs* "Dammit!"I'm very near the end of the game, and in spite of all the frustrating bits, I can't wait for the next playthrough. Well done, Sword & Axe!Just, for the love of God, PLEASE add a "Save & Quit" feature to the game! Or at least, to the next game! Having to dedicate 1-3 hours of uninterrupted time to completing a stage makes it very difficult to commit to playing the game -- for instance, I can't play it on my lunch at work, as I only have one hour available and would have to Alt-F4 the game, losing all of my progress.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good: The gameplay is essentially what you'd expect from a Fire Emblem "clone", the class system is very reminiscent of Trials of Mana (AKA Seiken Densetsu 3), and the Aspects (think Relics/Artifacts) add some interesting possibilities into builds. I was particularly pleased with Bianca taking Reverie and Windrunner as her Classes, and pairing it with an Aspect that drained her Magic Stat (a useless stat with this specific Class progression) to boost her defensive capabilities. The Mediocre: The writing is amateur, at best. So many chapters are either, "we're seeking a macguffin" or "we need to meet with someone's heretofore unmentioned contact." Many characters join up for weak or even no reasons (looking at you, Faust!), and the amount of characters leads to the majority of them getting very little development. The Bad: Buckle up, sports fans; this is gonna be a rant.    The game is buggy as all get-out. I had numerous stat boosters simply vanish into thin air during the last 10 chapters instead of being sent to Storage as I was told they were. There were numerous instances of characters (friend and foe alike) being simply impossible to target on certain tiles. The main character's physical appearance changed after a plot event in Chapter 8 or so, but then reverted right back for the next 10 chapters before righting itself.    There is simply not enough Gold or Experience Points to make use of the majority of the bloated cast, and this issue is compounded if you use the Classes that can equip two different weapon types, such as Dragon Knight. Weapon Upgrade Tokens are essential, but you scarcely get more than a small handful of Tier 3 and 4 Token drops throughout the game; you're gonna have to buy quite a few of them, ESPECIALLY if you decide that you want to use many of the characters who arrive later into the game (for reference: the game has 28 Chapters, and new units stop trickling in around Chapter 18). You see, every single unit, regardless of whether they join in Chapter 1 or 18, come with basic unimproved weaponry. You cannot refund upgrades, nor can units trade weapons even if they use the same weapon types; if you bench an old unit for a new one, then any Weapon Tokens you used on them are just plain wasted.   The map design is largely dull, and this is largely the result of there being no defensive or detrimental terrain effects. No forests for Defense and Dodge boosts, no sand that slows mounted units but not mages and flying units, or even any difference between flying unit movement and infantry movement; in almost every single map, a tile is just a tile. It's frankly boring to have every map feel so "samey", particularly in the maps that run on the larger side. The one major exception is a map that has you fighting as you flee upriver, with all units suffering massive movement penalties, making it a quite literal slog through the mud. I backed this game because I love Fire Emblem. It brings me no pleasure to say that this is a far cry from Fire Emblem in terms of map design, plot, and economy balancing. Do yourself a favor, and just replay your favorite older Fire Emblem game that you haven't touched in a while. If you've never played a Fire Emblem, then look into them instead of looking any longer at this disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I begin, I want to say this at the top - despite the issues this game has at the time of writing, I had a lot of fun playing it and would recommend it to anyone who is looking for a strategy RPG in the vein of Fire Emblem. I was first introduced to this game only a few weeks before release, and the clearly GBA era-inspired look of the sprites alone was enough to sell me on it. I've always had a soft spot for this style, so seeing a new game emulating it was exciting! And fortunately, I was not disappointed even once throughout my entire time playing the game - I would consider the sprites to be one of the game's highlights. Especially once you begin promoting characters into their second tier classes! The Reverie class's hammer throw and then magically calling it back to their hand, the Trickster's slick three thrown knives animation... Not to mention the spells! Each and every spell has a unique basic and crit animation, each of which are simply stunning. As someone who thinks this style of painstakingly-crafted sprites just can't be beat, I have to give credit to the Dark Deity team for nailing it.On the other hand, other areas probably could have used a little more polish - namely, the maps. For the most part, the looks of the various maps range from "pretty nice" to "serviceable", but there are a few spots that have problems. Certain key elements are confusing (such as in the case of one very early-game map, where color-coordinated teleportation tiles are presented to you, with several being nearly-identical shades of red-orange), or look like they may have been rough drafts that needed just a  extra polish. On the whole, though, this is a minor nitpick, as most of the maps in the game are actually rather interesting and varied!In fact, I think this is another one of the game's strong suits. If you're a fan of Fire Emblem and found yourself getting bored when the game presents yet another "rout the enemy" map, Dark Deity has you covered. Even in the very earliest hours of the game, you're presented with a shocking variety of objectives and styles of maps. Admittedly, some of these would work better with explanations for how the game expects you to interact with them. And on that note...This game could use even  tutorials. I recall a very early chapter where I was sitting there, confused about what the glowing blue tiles in certain parts of the map were about. Fortunately, it didn't take too long for me to grasp that these were "interaction" tiles; moving a unit onto them and selecting the tile-specific action allows your unit to do something specific at that tile, such as opening a treasure chest or moving between rooms. On that second point, it would be very helpful if the game let you know that you'd regain your movement when interacting with one of these tiles that transports you elsewhere, instead of leaving you to figure it out by doing - this is a genre about making tactical decisions, where imperfect information can leave your limited units on the field vulnerable, or removed from the field for the remainder of the chapter.Now, if you're familiar with Fire Emblem, what I just said might have caught your intention - yes, if your units fall in battle, they do not die. However, there is still a penalty for your units falling in the form of Wounds - permanent stat debuffs. When a unit goes down, you'll receive a message informing you which stat was lowered and by how much. It is possible to essentially reverse these debuffs, if you've found or saved up the gold to buy a matching stat booster! Between chapters, you'll be dropped off at what is essentially a base camp menu, from which you can review your list of units (sorted from highest level or lowest in a scroll menu), manage their inventories, upgrade their weapons, purchase items from the shop, and view Bond conversations - as well as save and advance to the next map. Bonds are similar to Supports in Fire Emblem; they are built up by having two characters on the map, taking actions near each other, and then you can witness a conversation between them. However, there's more beyond just racking up Bond points to see the next conversation; some seem to have story-based gating, resulting in Bond conversations that have more to do with what is going on with the story's events, rather than being utterly disconnected. That isn't to say that every Bond conversation is going to be plot-relevant or -adjacent, however; there were a few that had little to do with any of the story beats, such as a particularly memorable one wherein one character attempts to explain the concept of microtransactions to another.While the character writing may not be winning any awards, I did enjoy the members of the cast I got to know... Which, actually, was a surprising number. Since none of your units can ever permanently die, Dark Deity actually has the entire cast appearing in scenes long after they are first introduced, letting them all feel like they're present throughout the story even if you aren't actively using them in battle. Admittedly, some are utilized less than others; the number of scenes certain characters took part in scenes  their introductions could be counted on one hand.As for the gameplay... With all of the ways I can compare this game to Fire Emblem, it makes me appreciate the things it does differently - such as with the classes. The horse-mounted Dragoon, for instance, has a Skill which gives it a critical hit boost for every tile it moves, while the Duelist class has a Skill that grants them a very nice boost to several of their in-battle statistics so long as there are no allies adjacent to them. Once your characters reach level 10, they have 4 possible promotions available to them based on their base class, and then another 4 possible promotions at level 30. Each promoted class has 2 associated Skills you obtain by entering that class; by level 30, a character will have a full list of 5 Skills (including 1 personal Skill), resulting in a good variety of "builds" you can try out between playthroughs even on a single character.The Damage Type and Armor Type systems are interesting, at least at first glance. Rather than having a system where, say, someone who wields a sword has an innate advantage against someone wielding an axe, Dark Deity has 9 Damage Types and 4 Armor Types; each Damage Type has an interaction with each of the Armor Types. In theory, this is a very cool system, but in practice, I found that it was confusing, especially when it became difficult or outright impossible to tell what Armor Type a given enemy would have just by looking at them. Even by the end, I couldn't tell you the  of the Damage and Armor Type matchups. While it is a cool take on a matchup system, but I feel this is one area the developers could stand to improve upon if they were to make another game in this style.There are some things that I did not touch on in this review, such as the customizable parameters when you start a new game (which include things like changing the order in which characters are recruited); I do not feel qualified to talk about them simply due to my utter lack of experience with them, but I am very much excited to check them out in the future. They seem to add more than a fair bit of replay value to the game, similar to what you may see from some Fire Emblem ROM hacks. At the end of the day, despite some of its shortcomings, I can tell you this - if you read through the entirety of this review, I absolutely recommend this game to you. It may be a little rough in spots right now, but with the way the developers are currently putting out patches to fix things up, smooth out some rough patches, and add some community-requested quality of life, I fully expect this game to be in an even better state by the time I can come back for future playthroughs.

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this game up for a little over 5 USD, and I think it was possibly worth it at that price. It's a pretty creative, well-written visual novel with interesting characters and supports that develop them nicely that is unfortunately plagued by menus with glitching cursors, typos or misleading/wrong skill descriptions, opaque game mechanics, very slow cursor movement during battle, painfully boring 1v1 animations, and the list goes on and on. Sometimes I think it's a miracle the game even runs. it's basically Fire Emblem if Fire Emblem was made by teens on a tight budget. There's some creativity in the class and weapon systems, but everything is so poorly implemented and hard to navigate it falls apart into a frustrating mess. My biggest issue? Your characters' performance scales inversely with level, meaning that as you gain experience, you actually get weaker.In short, this is a decent story with pretty good characters that takes place in a remarkably interesting world, and somebody somewhere put time and effort into putting it together. Then someone else was responsible for the coding and technical work to bring it to life, and that person failed miserably. The whole experience is pleasant at times but deeply flawed overall, and I reluctantly recommended it until playing a little more, then just settled on a thumbs down. Pick it up on sale or if you want some laughs on stream, but 25 USD is way too much for a game that makes it this difficult to sell a crab cake.There is a second game in the works or possibly out now. I will be avoiding future games by this developer though, since clearly nothing gets actually tested before release or updated after.

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Deity is a grid-based TRPG heavily inspired by classic GBA-era Fire Emblem. If you liked those games and are wondering whether this game is worth your money, the short answer is: yes. The core gameplay loop of "opening cutscene > fight > closing cutscene > camp activities" is faithfully recreated and will scratch the same itch. The long answer is: in some ways it's worse, in some ways it's better, and in some ways it's just different.The worse: - The main story moves *VERY* quickly. Every single chapter has a major plot point or twist, and you'll likely just disengage from the story altogether because you're never given time or reason to care about any of it. This problem extends to the character roster as well, with one or two units being added every chapter while only a handful are given time to establish roles in the story.- The map tilesets could use some more love. They're functional but barren.- The weapon triangle is replaced by a more complicated system with different armor types being less or more effective at blocking different damage types. This system itself is fine, but it's not effectively communicated by character sprites and you're going to spend a lot of time mousing over units to figure out who should be attacking what.The better:- Options! There's multiple difficulties, gold and EXP scaling, and even a built-in randomizer. - The character writing is superb. The "bonds" eschew tropey anime dialogue in favor of thoughtful conversations that might genuinely occur between people of different professions, nationalities, and social strata, and you'll look forward to every one of them.The different:- No weapon durability. Instead, each class has four weapons which focus on power, accuracy, speed, or crit chance. You can switch between weapons at will and upgrade them between maps.- No permadeath. Instead, characters take a small but permanent stat loss upon losing all HP.- The aforementioned armor and damage types. These are determined by class and cannot be changed except upon being promoted to a new class.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: Basic premise/StoryFrom developer studio, Sword and Axe LLC and directed by Chip Moore Dark Deity is an srpg indie Kickstarter project. Finally released on June 15, 2021. The game is a love letter to Fire Emblem. You play as a group of young cadets who recently graduated from Brookstead Military Academy. On the continent of Eltan, these four young friends will brave through battles the likes they have never thought possible upon graduating.Unique GameplayOne of the most fascinating aspects of the gameplay in Dark Deity is the inclusion of the grave wounds system. Whenever a unit loses all of its health points a random stat will be permanently lessened. While this may seem like a harsh penalty for some. I welcome the change rather than a permadeath mechanic if any of my units lost their health. Thereby forcing me to reset the map again to not lose out on the potential experience and a chance to increase bonds with my troops. It's a great way to encourage players from resetting and taking the loss well in hand. Making players move forward accepting the consequences of their actions.The gameplay formula revolves around fighting on small to medium maps while completing the main objective. Each map has different objectives for the party to tackle with different environments as they trek across the continent of Etlan and beyond. Before and after battles a visual novel segment would take place where characters talk with one another before transitioning into a break phase. These break phases allow the player to upgrade their units weaponry, buy items in the shop and my personal favorite is viewing ‘bonds’ between each unit. Doesn’t take too long either, on average I probably spent less than a minute reading or more for each bonding rank. They’re well-worth seeing and flesh out the characters even more than what my characters undergo during maps. Final thoughts/RuminationsLet’s start with the not so good stuff first:I want to say I encountered at least 7+ crashes in my playthrough and the same number for errors when loading my save files. While this didn’t hamper my experience a great deal, it should be noted for newcomers. I tested the game out on my decent pc specs and one on high spec pc. And it seems like these instances occurred more on my decent pc specs with my high spec pc barely having any crashes. However, it should be noted I primarily played on my decent pc. So these results may vary depending on your pc specifications. Despite my decent pc being well over the pc system requirements. Map graphics - About half or more maps contain generic texture map palettes. This is mitigated somewhat by new map objectives and mechanics I didn’t expect. This makes me think most of the budget went to the animations of the units and voice acting. Sadly the Kickstarter doesn’t show how much the budget was split so I’m left wondering how much went into the map artist category. Still, it’s not the absolute worst map textures I've ever seen. The game more than makes up for these qualities with good map objectives and design mechanics. Such as defeat the enemy leader, escape to the other side of the map, kill a certain number of enemies, survive for ‘X amount of turns, defeat certain types of enemies to prevent a key objective from falling, and some more I won’t spoil for newcomers. Still texture quality aside, some maps do look decent, just wish a bit more varied textures for the map environments could’ve been fleshed out more.Music - The soundtrack re-uses several combat themes throughout the game. Not a major issue in the beginning. However, it can be kinda boring listening to the same old battle track again. And a different one in the following map. By the time the final map rolled around, I was so glad there was an exclusive final map theme instead of the several music tracks I've heard re-used throughout the game. Still, it’s not bad by any means. The game could’ve benefitted with more battle tracks used. And overall the majority of the whole soundtrack is at the very least pleasant to listen to.Now time for some strengths the game does well:+On the grave wound system instead of the usual permadeath mechanic seen in Fire Emblem games. I think it's great. I didn’t have to reset the game so many times because my unit died. More often than not I did so to not lose out on the experience and chance to increase bonds with my party members. Once I maxed out my bonds for my units I no longer needed to reset. Making my overall experience fun, enjoyable, and overall less stress-inducing. Having to redo the same maps for several hours just because one unit died is not fun IMO. Here it’s okay to have my units become wounded. And thereby, increasing my gratification of finishing a map with my units intact. Sure I lose out on some stats. But if rng is with me I only lose out on stats I don’t care about hah! +Map objectives and design mechanics are pretty good. Didn’t get bored throughout the whole campaign. There is a great number of conversations before battles start and after in a visual novel type design I enjoy seeing. +Characters - Pretty fleshed out if you see the “bonds,” section. Think of it like support conversations fire emblem characters have. But these only occur between chapters in a more transitional part of the game where you can upgrade your unit's weapons, buy food, upgrade items, and stat boosters. Ranging from C to B to A. Each character has more than a handful and some reach more than 8+ bonds they have with other characters. The only caveat is that a unit needs to be at least 3 or fewer spaces away from the other unit to activate bond progress during map segments. Wasn’t tedious at all to do so. Since I could have multiple units next to one another and have them proc to the next bond rank. By endgame, all my characters had maxed A rank bonds. Except when newer characters were recruited.+The story is great. Loved seeing how my characters go from graduates from the academy straight into war. And the events that follow. While I wasn’t hooked in the beginning. The slow approach kept me interested, especially the mid-late game which was very satisfying to a degree that I respect a lot. The developers took the template of what makes Fire Emblem great and enhanced mechanics that could be better for it.+The new gameplay mechanics like 8 different promotions for a single unit is awesome. Each character has a unique skill is super cool to differentiate from other characters. With the elimination of permadeath and weapon durability, I think we're good substitutes IMO to induce more fun gameplay and reduce the amount of resetting for every map. Total Times Beaten: 1Score: 8/10 Date Finished: 7/12/21Date Reviewed: 7/12/21

_childDocuments_.review: Really good game, but read more to avoid some frustration...Several things in battle aren't obvious (and not super well explained as far as I can tell).Right click on the ground.  From there, you can see:The objective.   if there's a timer or damage to what you're protecting, it also shows turns left or health left.The tutorials, which explain a LOT.Little squares of a different color (blue, red, it varies.) are special.  Some are doors, some are chests, some are points where the enemy can damage the thing you're protecting, etc.Hover over a tile, and it may explain more about it.Select your units:  Units are arranged highest level to lowest level.  If you have more people in your roster than you can deploy in this fight, you can click on a unit to deselect/select it.  Map prep: you can see enemy types and starting positions.  You also see your deployed units and starting spots.  You can't change the starting spots, BUT you can click any two of your units to swap starting spots, repeatedly.Put the cursor on a unit and hit shift to see detailed info about them, including enemy units, including their drops.  This is also how you switch weapons for a character that has not taken a turn this round yet.  Every character has 4 weapon types.  One focuses on power, one on crit chance, one on accuracy, and the last is balanced.Weapon weight: Reduces true speed.  When two characters fight, their true speed is compared.  If one is 2x as fast, that character gets to (try to) hit twice!  Probably some of this is explained in the game somewhere, and I just missed it.  And some IS obvious, at least to you.  But playing a tactics game with this info from the beginning is going to be a lot more fun, so this is what I missed at first.And this game is fun.  The battle board sprites are pixels, but the combat animations and dialog pictures are nicer.  There's a good story (I'm on chapter 17 so far) with some character development.  Best ever?  Maybe not, but I'm interested and want to keep my team alive.   A variety of maps with hazards, variety of objectives and map types, variety of units and some cool rock-paper-scissors mechanics going on.   (The game makes it easy to see -hover on your unit, and green up arrows show enemies vulnerable to your unit's attack.  Hover on an enemy, and see who of your people to protect from that enemy.)  You can save in camp and save before the battle and have 8 save slots.  If a unit is KO in battle, they take a small but permanent penalty.  If you lose a battle, it's reload from the save of your choice.  I'm a bit concerned I might build badly and reach an unwinnable battle (no repeats, no random encounters), but there are 2 difficulties and some customization options for stats,  xp and gold.  All in all, the normal price is TOTALLY worth it for hours and hours of fun tactics and a little strategy of what weapon type to upgrade for whom.

_childDocuments_.review: My absolute biggest complaint about this game is that it was not labelled an early access title. Realistically, that's what it is. If you go into this game treating it as such, then it's damn good. The core gameplay loop is fun, the classes are fun to experiment with, the animations are cool, the characters are interesting, and the music is fine enough. The developer is consistently putting out patches with bug fixes and fine tuning. The game has a ton of replayability too, which is absolutely fantastic for an early access game. However, this game is not described as early access. This game is being sold as though it is complete and finished. It isn't. I have experienced many minor graphical, audio, and gameplay hiccups. I know that others have experienced far worse, so I'll just consider myself lucky. I'm giving the publishing team the benefit of the doubt here. They're new, and I'll defer to Hanlon's razor that the general lack of QA and common bugginess are due to inexperience, and not greed or a lack of caring. I like the game thus far. I've had tons of fun. I think the team behind Dark Deity really care and want this game to be great, just like me and the many other people who backed the game on kickstarter. I think that people who are willing to treat this game as early access, as somewhat of a work in progress, will find a ton to enjoy here. But anyone who's looking for a complete experience with all the polish and ironing out you should rightfully expect from a title being sold as finished needs to wait. Unfortunately, you're not getting that here yet. However, I implore you to wait for the developers to fulfill their vision, as I have the utmost confidence that when this game is actually finished, it will be something truly special.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game for FE purists, its challenging, with enough innovations over the core system so that it feels fresh and not just like added maps to an existing game. There are some hiccups of course, music doesn't reach the levels of a main line FE game, and the some of the map textures leave a bit to be desired. But the sprite animations are all wonderful, and the balance feels mostly well implemented. Some quality of life fixes would help, but from what the dev has said, those are coming. Highly recommend to any FE fan, and to any fans of the genre in general, it scratches the exact itch I've been looking for.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: Its an OK game. For the price I would recommend this if you are missing Fire emblem games and dont want to replay them. The combat gets very easy during late game (played normal mode). Dodge mechanics is a bit obnoxious with enemies having high dodge mid game making it frustrating. If you get stats screwed then the game wont be fun because of this. The maps can get quite repetitive. Although I completed the game in 24 hours, it felt like like was dragging a lot towards the end. The story isnt that good. There is no coherence and the motivations of any of the character that join the party, even the main cast is not well thought out. If feels like a bunch of artists wanted to do a fire emblem like game and phoned in the story. The character portrait are quite good.The weapon system is quite unique in this game. There arent any tips or tutorials to help you selecting which branch to go so it can be confusing but towards late game I felt this weapon system just made the game more bland.Essentially, if you want to scratch the FE itch then get this when its on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Fire Emblem for PC- Different takes on dead penalty, if a character died their stat will be negated (compared to permadead in some early FE titles) - Every character can use multiple weapon with different attribute, maybe affecting the Rock Paper Scissor mechanic but in the end you will only use one type- Some role have extra skill set (thief class can make enemy skip one turn, spear class can make enemy lock enemy movement in one turn), but kinda useless except in certain situationCons:- Story is kinda meh- No romance (not really a factor)- Enemy has no actual level scaling, it's more like level jump- No training mode (if your character dead a lot or rarely chosen, good luck fighting enemy 2x or 10+ of your level)- Not clear rock paper scissor mechanic, but if you play for 1-2 hours you know which class is better against which (heavy looking knight will lose again magic, but somehow flying magic dragon is lose against knight not archer)Honestly, I would buy a sequel as long as there is a new training mode in the sequel

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a bad game. it runs fine, the art looks good, and the story is interesting enough, but the Lack of alternate story paths, extra missions, and side content really kills the Replayability. _childDocuments_.review: I went into this game with absolutely no expectations. I was surprised to see that this game is actually pretty good. I was happy to see that this game doesn't just rip off other tactics rpgs. It does it's own thing. Sure, it takes some things from the Fire Emblem games, there's no way to hide that. Yet, it's originality still shines through. It has a class system with branching paths to encourage replayability. It's story is surprisingly deep and nuanced, dealing with depression, death and the loss of ones purpose in life. All in all, good game, would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, but there were just a few too many issues for me to recommend this.Obviously, it's not fair to compare Dark Deity to Fire Emblem directly, given that Fire Emblem has a much more expansive pool of resources, but I will be using my experience with FE to frame my review of Dark Deity since the devs have expressed that Dark Deity was inspired by Fire Emblem.Let's start with some positives because Dark Deity does definitely have some good things going for it.- The art and character designs are really nice, and the overall aesthetic of the game is great!- Dark Deity's version of the skill reposition works at different ranges and diagonally, which I thought was a neat upgrade.- The class change system is simple but interesting.- If you're coming as an FE fan, there's plenty of content that pays tribute to Fire Emblem, including their battle quotes, quotes when you select a unit on the map, etc.Unfortunately, there were quite a few drawbacks to the game too. A few that have bothered me the most include:- My biggest problem was that there were tons of small bugs that, when aggregated, really take away from the experience. The math gets messed up pretty frequently, which is a big problem for a strategy game like this one.- Many of the map designs are quite bland.- AI issues. I've run into several instances where enemies just don't attack me even when I'm in range.Dark Deity's not a bad game, but it needs a lot of work. If you're looking for something to fill that Fire Emblem-shaped hole in your heart, there are lots of fan-made games out there available for free or less expensive than Dark Deity which I feel have done a better job. If you're just looking for a strategy RPG, I can't recommend Dark Deity at full price either, but I could see this being up some people's alleys.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Deity is very faithful to the GBA Fire Emblem titles. I enjoyed the game, but the bugs it has were far too frustrating for me to recommend it. I've had units with their sprites on a completely different tile. I've had units rubber band back to the spot they were at the previous turn. I was able to push one of my characters off the map. Units would bug out and be completely unusable for a turn. I had to restart a couple maps because I wasn't able to get out of a menu.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good little turn-based tactics game. While not the best out there, it is solidly done.The mechanics are fairly standard for a turn-based tactics game, with a wide range of unit archetypes, grouped into warriors, rogues, mages, another type of mages, and healers. The battles are mostly decently challenging (though one is broken so the enemy doesn't attack, making it rather easy) without being too punishing (I played on Hero).There is a friendship system, which could have been better. Characters level up their friendship by doing something when they stand next to each other. But with 30 characters and only 14 slots per battle, many characters will never get even one act next to one of their designated buddies, let alone the three needed to complete the friendship. This aspect of the game would have benefited a lot from cutting down the number of characters—maybe even by half.This would have also helped with making the plot a bit more focussed. Often it seemed to drift a bit, which was needed to justify the inclusion of so many peripheral party members. In the long end “cutscenes”, some characters weren't even mentioned! Why include them in the game if they aren't important enough for us to know what they did after the last battle? Again, the solution is to drastically cut the number of party members.Otherwise the plot is an enjoyable if standard fantasy romp. It is often a bit cringe-worthy in its earnest liberal progressivism (particularly it's attitude of revolutionaries-are-always-the-goodies) but I understand that the developer was a young man, so it's understandable. It hits the required notes and there are some genuinely moving moments and semi-surprising twists.Overall an enjoyable game that is worth picking up if you're an established fan of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: The combat system suffers from some serious usability issues that take the fun out of combats, one of the largest parts of tactics RPGs. For example, your characters may have ranged attacks, but there is nothing that tells you the range. Neither textual, nor visually. All you can do is move first, then check if the attack buttons lights up, and if it doesn't you have to cancel your movement and try again with a different tile.If you're looking for something like Final Fantasy Tactics or Disgaea, you might be disappointed by the combat system.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Deity is a great tactical RPG, similar to Fire Emblem, but a little less depth. The characters were all fun and there is a good variety of archetypes and classes. I think my biggest complaint is that there is SO many characters that all of my favorite ones became very underleveled very quickly, forcing me to either use weak characters, or drop the ones I liked to make room for the newer, higher leveled units. Otherwise, i think this was a great game with lots of gameplay value for its low cost.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: I am loving this game so far. As you might have noticed this game takes a lot of inspiration from the Fire Emblem games, however they put their own spin on it. The Grave Wounds in place of perma-death is a great choice for the game. I am one that restarts chapter if characters die in FE, however, I don't feel the pressure to restart every time someone dies. Also, if you are looking for an FE-like game I would highly recommend this game, especially if you didn't like the social aspect of the newer games.

_childDocuments_.review: Was worried by the reviews but ended up liking it. Bought it from the Tactician's bundle for peanuts probably not worth full price. Took me 15.5 hours to beat from my save but 21 total with reloading from deaths on normal.The game's balance feels off. Some classes are way better than others and most of the subclasses felt pointless. I put almost all my units down the same upgrade path and they were gods without messing with aspects. Dodge everything and kill everything in one attack. Used 3 rangers, 1 rogue, 2 clerics, 2 warriors, 3 mages and 3 adepts. Thought the adepts weren't that great after midgame and 1 or 2 would have been better. Most enemies just stand there until you get close then get auto countered leading to their death.Caius (Strider/Blade Dancer) Maeve (Strider/Blade Dancer) Sophia (Archer/Sniper)Cia (Duelist/Gladiator)Alexa (Dragoon/Dragon Knight)Monroe (Arcanist/Wizard)Were all complete killing machines.Bianca (Gale/Windrunner) - Was great for the majority but damage fell off near the endIrving (Barbarian/Champion) - Garbage level 10-30 then could 1 shot everythingThe story is completely skipable and so are the character bonds. They don't effect gameplay and I didn't care about any of them.It's good not great and felt like a Fire Emblem lite. Gives way to many characters and you'll be struggling to pick which to drop. Most are irrelevant toward the plot.

_childDocuments_.review: Unless you're looking for a Fire-Emblem-esque experience to turn off your brain to, I would not recommend getting this game.  It takes the base gameplay formula of Fire Emblem (or tactical rpgs like X-COM in general), adds a couple of interesting flavors, and then completely botches the rest; the story is a barely coherent mess that tries to be interesting and flamboyant but instead falls on its face, the characters are only as interesting as the archetype they shamelessly copy and paste (haha can't have a Fire Emblem clone without Commedia dell arte), and the class/character balance is atrocious (the game incentivizes dropping older units in favor of newer units that usually have better bases and equal or better growths).  That isn't to say the game can't be fun at times, but the poorly organized story and horribly bland characters make it hard to stick with the game if you're looking for more than just a way to scratch your TRPG itch.  If you do want the game, buy it on sale, and prepare yourself for Fire Emblem 16.5: Editing Begone.

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of fun! The story isn't that great tbh, I kind of just skim it. But I do really like the different subclasses and matchups that are in this game; there's a lot of customization such as choosing whether you want a cleric to go even more down the healing skill tree or they can be a kind of battlemage, or you can choose if you want your adept character to stay with weapons or change to magic. Even though this game isn't as fleshed out as a Fire Emblem-type game, it's a lot of fun and I love how each map is different and each enemy group makes you think tactically.Only major complaints are like I said: the story. Nothing about it really stands out to me. Some of the characters are funny or interesting but most are just kind of "meh." Another complaint is that for the most part bugs are pretty few but the ones I did encounter either forced me to restart a chapter, essentially losing all my combat progress, or I would be forced to choose the "Wait" option in combat because I wouldn't be able to hit an enemy for some random reason.Anyway, super fun game if you like strategy. I've played it for 10 hours so far since I bought it yesterday.

_childDocuments_.review: Fire Emblem-esque game that scratches that FE itch. The animations are amazing and I really like the "weapon triangle" replacement. It is much more in depth which I appreciate. The class uniqueness was also something that I really enjoyed with each character having 4 T1 classes and 4 T2 classes to choose from. They're not balanced perfectly, but that is the case in every game.The characters and world building I think were ok, I just wished that the writers delved more into the reasons the bad guys did what they did. Other then that I don't really have many complaints. For $20 this was a steal!8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a super fun game to fill the void of SRPG's right now, but it feels a little unpolished and still needs a lot of work. Just for the creative innovations on genre staples, the game is worth playing. Hopefully the support will allow the creators to continue in game development and make more polished works in the future. Sorry for the long review, but I really, really enjoyed the unique aspects and want to help make it better!In terms of what those unpolished items are, my biggest complaints are as follows.Clunky UI: weird mix between mouse and keyboard controls doesn't feel very intuitive. I'm used to playing SRPG's on a controller/emulator, and would love the option to use just keyboard controls. The issues I've run into besides just the uncomfortable feel is that sometimes clicking a button that's on top of an ally or enemy can mess up the controls. (click chain from menu, but thinks I want to attack because it registers as clicking directly on the enemy, etc.). Also, if you move toward the bottom of the screen, the wait command can be pushed off the bottom and can't be clicked. You have to cancel the move, readjust the camera zoom and then do it again to have the wait button be visible. Explanation: There is an extremely cool weapon upgrade mechanic and armor mechanic, but the game doesn't explain them very well. The armor mechanic mixed with mastery stat mixed with skills makes it really weird to try and predict battles. I still don't know how the mastery stat actually affects damage or anything else and if it scales with your advantage against armor types. Also, I still don't know what causes the E to S grade that comes up in fights or how much that affects battles. The tutorial fight could really benefit from having an introduction to "hey if your sword unit attacks this armor type vs this armor type, here's why the outcomes are so different."Promotion: The screen is really good-looking, but the Promote button doesn't look like a button or light up when you mouse over or anything, so I spent a good amount of time just double-clicking the class option to try and solidify my choice before just randomly pressing the promote and figuring it out. Also, it would be nice to toggle between potentials (growths) and current stats, just useful always, but especially so for characters you get and instantly promote, and I have no idea what their bases were which would affect if I want them offense/defense or whatever. Positives: The weapon system, promotion branches, stat loss by death, and overall flow of the gameplay is really fun, but I would enjoy it more if the game had more polish. Still definitely recommend this game, but probably after a few updates so that you can enjoy the experience more on your first time through.Thanks and well done to the creative team though! Awesome for a first game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not recommending this game. This is not a game for everyone. I had a lot of fun, though, so let me extrapolate.I find reviews that tell me what was wrong with a game far more helpful in making a purchasing decision than telling me what was right, so let's get down to business.The story is jarringly bad. Tons of tonal shifts, extremely inconsistent, super reminiscent of Fire Emblem games, but just *not* fluid, cohesive, or generous with exposition. It starts off as a generic Fire Emblem 'war between kingdoms' story, but then with no explanation, no foreshadowing, and what feels like must be an attempt to force the story into a direction, you're fighting a necromancer with an army of undead. It's just not paced, written, or portrayed well at all. You'll sort of understand what's going on, but there's not really anything that makes you care. It's like reading a history book for school; you're doing it because you want to pass the class, not because you particularly want to or enjoy it.Now, let's get on to the other writing problems; the characters and dialogue. Characters in Fire Emblem are already monochromatic, one-dimensional, quirky archetypes of fantasy tropes, and that's fine, because there's so many that you're bound to find the tropes you love best to make your army. If Fire Emblem characters are the diet soda of characterization, Dark Deity's are the sparkling waters. There's barely enough flavor to sate you, but the fizziness of growth rates and a build coming to a head is enough to keep you drinking until you finish the glass. You don't particularly love it, but it's better than water, I guess. I found myself loving characters for what they could do on the battlefield, not because of any writing or characterization they were given in dialogues or cut scenes. I couldn't even tell you the background of my favorite character, and I just finished the game yesterday.A lot of folks complain about balance issues; I played this game on Deity, blind, for my first run, and with a background in Fire Emblem, the only problem I ran into was a difficulty spike in Chapter 18, where suddenly every character, even my most accurate, using accuracy weapons vs. the types they were strong against, couldn't get above a 65% chance to hit. This tapered off dramatically within two chapters, but this map's design was awful. It took me about 2 hours to get through simply because everyone kept missing. A constant chain of "heal, miss, end turn, get attacked" rinse and repeat. This was not the norm of the game, and I am thankful for that; the rest of the maps were a lot of fun, and I had a great time making walls, sending in bait, and swarming enemies, as one is wont to do in Fire Emblem-likes. With the exception of the Chapter 18 difficulty spike time-waster, and maybe a couple other straight-forward ones, the game was tuned well and played smooth. I don't think there's much to actually complain about there. I don't feel like the balance was off, and the core gameplay was solid. Once in awhile my character would glitch into a different square without the icon moving, which would make healing them awkward, but once you realize how the bug works, it isn't game-breaking or map-restart hindering, just a little annoying.The art would be great if the women weren't so jarringly objectified. Vesta's a tank. I don't want a skin window where her cleavage is. She's wearing full-plate. Full-plate is worthless if it isn't *full* plate, y'know? ? ? With the exception of those quirks, which are not exclusive to Vesta, the art is good.At the end of the day, you play this game because you love ripping open level-up packages to see which of your characters are going to be mythic heroes, and which ones are condemned to pleb status by the RNG gods. You can choose to go all in on what characters are good it, or risk it all in hedged classes. Classic Fire Emblem. You'll have that one character who defied the odds and turned out an invincible and integral member of your team, and the other one who, based on growth rates, should have been S-Tier but ended up benched. That's it. That's the core thrill of Fire Emblem, and Dark Deity provides.Play this game if you love Fire Emblem gameplay; the game is very bare-bones in delivering any kind of meaningful attachment to story or characters through dialogue and plot. That's the niche this game fills.
