_childDocuments_.review: Sweet game - nice homage to old school fire emblems. I have a couple of pros/cons I'll run through. Overall, I enjoyed this game a lot and think it was worth the $25. Game is about 30 hours for a first playthrough.1. AWESOME class leveling system. Each of the characters will be sorted into a base class template, like rogue, warrior, cleric, mage, etc, and will promote into two of eight classes of your choice. Despite there being 20/40 different classes mid/late game, they all feel unique and have specialized roles and traits. A big part of advancement is mixing which two classes you want each unit to take. This experimentation gives a great deal of replayability as a tactical RPG. The classes lead into point 2 -2. The battle art was very satisfying to me, especially later in the game. Battle animations for each class are unique and feel very "fire emblem 7" to me. The upgraded magic was especially satisfying to use.3. Story was done as well as I expected it to be. It is hard to tell a fleshed out story in this "VN light" format, with a couple dozen lines of dialogue between a couple dozen chapters. That said, I think the devs did a great job managing the format, and they put hella effort into the bond dialogues. Each of the characters has a fleshed out subplot with 10 other characters that develops slowly over the course of the game as the characters battle alongside each other. I loved checking the bonds between chapters. If you are a player that doesn't care, the bonds are entirely skippable and don't affect gameplay (no 3-houses dating giving stat buffs here).4. The level design was very big brain. I was very, very impressed by some of the levels and the strategies they encouraged me to try. As a con, some of the levels were too big brain.  . Not every level was cool and unique, there were still plenty of "go to point A and kill everything". But as a fire emblem, this was a step above what I'm used to seeing.5. No weapon durability!!!! Each character has four weapons with infinite durability that you will keep and upgrade for the whole game. One of each weapon tree - power/crit/accuracy/balance. It was a little tough to learn the pro/con of each tree at the beginning of the game, but it scales really well into the late game and balancing a character's weak points. Also as I said earlier, the upgraded spells were awesome across the board.1. Maybe this isn't a con for some players, but for me I disliked the large cast size. Your party balloons chapter by chapter for the entire midgame, and you end up with many more units than you can play. With no permadeath, a lot of units just won't be used.2. No permadeath isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it felt a little inauthentic to me.3. I'm sure each of the characters has a viable niche and set of upgrades. With con #1 though, it is very hard to continue using a character that has "missed" after they have fallen off. Some of your characters will "hit", and you keep using them. I was not able to figure out how to make several of the characters useful. This probably isn't a real con, it's probably just me. Take it as you will. On the flip side, some of the characters just seem like they will always "hit" and be good on any/several of their upgrade routes. 4. Difficulty curve - the game started out challenging but became easy in the mid/lategame as my units outscaled the enemy growth. This was true even on the higher difficulties.5. I did occasionally see bugs. Occasionally a cavalry unit wouldn't be able to move, or a unit would stack on the same tile as another unit. I got all the bugs to go away by exiting to main menu and loading the battlesave, which reloads the start of your current player turn. Annoying, but not gamebreaking.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I had a great time with this game and certainly had my money's worth, the countless issues I encountered makes me question the many issues plaguing the game. The gameplay itself kept me engaged, but the many other aspects of this game were too frustrating for me to recommend to other people who were looking for a solid Fire Emblem-like title.I'll go over a list of things I thought were great, terrible, and some personal grievances of mine.  -Dark Deity's Class system is fantastic. Being able to re-class all new units gives you a great amount of control over team building, and no need for Master Seals. You can promote during a battle seamlessly. Also, the sheer variety of build paths and available classes are the best part of this game. (Please add re-classing!)In addition, classes having unique actions, such as Heal, Push, Phase, are great ways to make the game more interesting, offer more EXP gains, and give all units solid utility outside of combat. The Cleric class is also great. No longer are they just relegated to Heal bot. I just love what Dark Deity has done to diversify the healing class. -All the VAs did a great job on this game. -Battle Save system. I have no idea how it actually functions, but it saved me hours of headache. It's basically a back-up save file from your latest battles. -Animations are actually quite stellar in this game. I do wish they went a bit more crazy with the animations, especially since they are trying to emulate the style of the GBA-era Fire emblem. -The power scaling in this game feels amazing. I'd say that this game's power levels rival that of FE: Three Houses, but it feels more consistent. It feels great to be strong in this game.  -The Battle forecast system is somehow a step down from even some of the oldest FE titles. You have to switch a target, then press confirm to update the battle forecast. Also, with the abundance of abilities in this game, damage calcs are not always entirely accurate. -The Danger Area is unreliable at times, and is also a downgrade from many FE titles. Upon selecting a unit, the danger area disappears, and also, the danger area does not account for movement-reducing terrain. -Terrible Audio Balancing. There are some things in this game that are so unnecessarily loud, such as the Aegis and Dragon Knight classes. Other things are quiet in comparison, such as the Level Up, Player / Enemy Phase themes, which ALSO overlap with the map music. Why? -No Map battle animations. Older FE Games, when turning off the battle animations, you can watch the map sprites battle instead but in this game, all battles are skipped as they happen. Kinda nerve-wracking to be honest. -Inventory management was clunky, cumbersome, and just tedious to use. -Lack of options, such as Smart Cursor (Why does the game start in the top left?) and disabling battle music.-Controller seems to bug out a lot when tabbing in and out of the game. -The UI. This is probably the worst part of this game, and I haven't seen other games follow this game's horrible UI functionality. To note, there is no option selection memory. Even if you have a save file, when booting up the game, your cursor will always be on New Game, not Load Game. Then, for whatever reason, if you load a new game, it will default on "No". Selecting "No" will then select the next save file in your list. I've never seen a game do this before, because of this (partially my fault), I had accidentally saved over one of my files. This would have never happened if not for how weird the UI functions in this game. It is standard for many games to put you on "Load Save File" when booting up a game once you've made your save file. Then, allowing you to select your save file and have it automatically hover over "Yes." The fact that this system works this way is mind-boggling.The game will not remember the units you use for the next battle. It will always select the highest level units for map prepping. Problem is, you're always being bombarded with new and high level units, so you have to constantly de-select the new units, and re-select your favorites. There's also no indication that you're selecting a unit to swap on the Map Prep screen. In addition, the cursor moves too slowly on this screen. There needs to be cursor acceleration when you're moving in one direction. The process of positioning units becomes extremely tedious, especially with maps where your party is split. And lastly, this game needs a confirmation screen. Please just ask me if I'm sure I want to start a battle, go back to the main menu or anything. This is standard for a reason. Because of clowns like me.  -Not a fan of the designs of some of the classes. Some of them are kinda ugly or out of place. There's the Drifter who is a cowboy in a game that's basically a JRPG.The Firelord just looks like Endeavor from MHA.And overall, the class designs don't quite resemble what the character portraits wear, which I think is a shame. They're either plain or strange looking. (Blaze / Surge IMO)-The story felt lackluster and uninteresting to me. For most of it, it feels like our protagonists are at a theme park, being lead around from place to place to accomplish their mission. -No "tink/ting" sound when doing no damage? :(-No critical hit sound. Surely, Dark Deity could have tried to emulate FE's iconic critical hit sound, but they didn't even try. Wasted potential.-Battle sprites are really bulky, even for the guys. I feel like everyone is a bit too wide looking, and it's especially unfortunate for female characters who share sprites with male characters. -Music is kinda meh, save for a select few map themes. Also the music in this game is way too compressed for its own good. Certainly wasn't having a good time listening to crunchy audio the whole way through. -This game could use Mila's Timewheel. Obviously have it be weak in comparison to SoV or TH, but I think it would be a great addition to this game just to correct a few mistakes.  Ultimately, I did have a great good time playing the game itself, but the numerous UI issues and lack of attention to detail makes this feel like such an inferior game to the FE series, even compared to the GBA series. Three Houses came out in 2019, and this game came out in 2021. It's a shame for DD to be lacking so many features or having such a buggy UI. The devs can clearly make a fun game, but it's prudent that they make sure this game feels AS GOOD if not better than modern FE to play. I'm trying to fight enemies, not the game itself. Here's hoping DD2 is a significant step-up from this game. And last note, Orangutan Arms Sniper is the best.Edit: Took parts of my initial statement and fixed some harsh language. Game dev is hard, but I was miffed when I had lost my save file due to the game's UI. I also personally found it cynical to copy IS's summer unit obsession, but not its many control schemes and features. Idk. There are not many FE-adjacent games on PC, so it's important to nail the market here.

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Deity is a decent game, clearly inspired by Fire Emblem and, perhaps to an extent, Shining Force.  It's not a ripoff of either series.  Its battle system is much more complicated than FE's simple weapon triangles and there are more decisions to be made about your characters.  That seems to have drawn the ire of some people getting this game, expecting more of the same Fire Emblem they're used to.+ You can tell a lot of love went into this game.  Like or hate the system, anyone should clearly recognize that.+ Tons of maps and solid turn-based combat.  Like many FE types, it's pretty easy to succeed once you know the system.+ Campaign customization!  Wow, I've never seen so many customization options: shuffling order of recruitment, altering stat growth and initial stats, fixing enemy weapon types, randomizing reward items.  This alone makes for a ton of replay value.+ Most maps allow for 14 units to be used, which is a big plus for me.  These types of games work poorly when it's only possible to field a small number of characters.+ Plenty of text for those who place high value on the visual novel portion.  There's a ton of dialog between individual characters that can be unlocked by having them fight together.+ Dev's humor hits me spot on.  The weapon and class descriptions are occasionally hilarious.  *There's no better way to protect your magic user than to stick them in a tin can!*+ A lot of stages contain some pretty good background piano music.+ I liked the Aspect system, but creativity is required to get the most out of some of them.= Completionist nightmare.  Gold is a limited resource.  Getting every weapon for every character leveled isn't possible, even if I jacked gold to the maximum and sold every stat-up item found.  I knew that going in and had units specialize in one weapon.  = No repeating missions or side missions.  I had to pick and choose which party members got the EXP, being unwilling to farm/exploit, thus using the entire crew was counterproductive.  You know, similar to older Fire Emblem titles.  It's not a bad thing in my estimation, but your mileage may vary.= Fixed Crit.  In FE, crit% was altered by the Luck stat, both in giving and receiving critical hits.  DD uses Luck for giving  crits and not for crit defense.  An enemy with a high crit must be dealt with carefully, and enemies with medium to low crit still have a significant chance of knocking out a weak character.*** Let me say to those who hate this high crit and consider it detrimental to allowing for good tactics - Change Luck to 0 and make all enemy weapons red or green.***- Still early in it's release, there are bugs.  They're documented in the forum.  I have every confidence that they'll be addressed in time.  Nothing game breaking for me.- Menus are extremely awkward.  Trading items is a hassle.  Items can be traded between any two units who have not acted regardless of distance.  Odd design decision.  In the Inventory menu, being unable to compare the effect of equipping different aspects without going back to the Unit menu leads to a lot of shuffling back and forth.  Also, to see the effect of a weapon upgrade on a character's stat sheet, I had to click a different weapon then re-equip the upgraded one.- The story was long, but honestly, it wasn't immersive for me.  My standards are set pretty high, though.  I found this to be too predictable and lacking plot twists.  Admittedly, the story works.  It is good they kept a core group having most of the lines.  Getting background on other characters requires unlocking the conversations.- Most people aren't going to care but I hate that every female had huge chest art.  Standard for anime, I know.  Blasted anime. - Here's my obligatory, age-old complaint against the "all of my characters go, then all-y'all go" speed system.  Yeah, I know, it's how we roll in FE.  Doesn't make it right, though. It's more than worth your time and dime as long as you aren't expecting an exact clone of Fire Emblem.  A quick comparison to Vestaria Saga - the combat in Dark Deity had more variables (which I liked) and I had more choice over which characters I could use, but the story wasn't quite as good.

_childDocuments_.review: A very solid Tactics RPG for fans of Fire Emblem and other similar games. With some unique growth systems that allow the player to meaningfully decide exactly how they want to grow their units, it leans a bit more RPG than tactics game, but isn't lacking in the latter category for those who enjoy tactical gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: So bought this game because it did remind me of Fire Emblem. To be honest I have no regrets buying this game. I enjoyed playing the heck out of it and it's story line that has so many unique characters building upon it. Now to make this as clear as I possibly can this is not the same as Fire Emblem by no means! It took the base idea and made it into it's own idea creating the game that it is. Which I am ok with honestly.As I said there are a lot of unique characters that you will come to love and enjoy. While working on there bonds and improving combat skills you will still need to upgrade their items from time to time. Down side to the game is that it is time consuming and that you do need to build up a team of unique warriors, healers and casters to best fit the fights your in. it's not hard but not as simple as it sounds either. mainly because the way the class system is set up is very unique where you have to choose what your willing to gain and what your willing to lose.over all it's a solid game and has unique banter amongst the party members after a mission is done. So in he end I do recommend this if your willing to put in the time for a actual strategy based game similar to Fire Emblem.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played better FE clones made with SRPG Studio on DLsite than this absolute trash.The 'innovation' of eliminating weapon with durability and give all characters 4 different weapons with unlimited durability and trade off from the start is interesting, but it's a bad choice when you also have weapon upgrade system. Because this means you either rely on one crutch weapon type, or you need to waste 4 times the resources to fully empower one character.What's worse, this game commits the cardinal sin of not respect player's time. The loading screen everytime a scene transition kills any momentum or patience I have to keep playing the game. Which makes me question why the dev team didn't just use SRPG Studio to make this game since SRPG Studio even had arguably the better visual fidelity than this 8+ bit graphic stretched to massive size.Ultimately, what sealed the deal for me in the end is the lack of battle map save function. Just why isn't there a battle save (and if it's there, it's too hidden in the menu)? I'm going to assume it's to stop the save scum at level up to get maximum growth for the hardcore FE players (which to some, IS the fun of playing Fire Emblem to get max growth character for self-imposed challenges of using bad characters). But it simply means the player waste a lot of time if they have to turn the game off mid battle and have to replay both the intro scene, and half of the battle.It would be fine if this is a $15-10 budget title. But at $30, you can find better (and slightly cheaper) alternative if you are willing to comb through DLsite.

_childDocuments_.review: Listen I'm hungry for games like Fire Emblem on PC, so just for that reason, I really don't feel like hitting the thumbs down button, but this isn't a Fire Emblem game. I discovered this is more like a puzzle game. You have units, you have enemies and depending on which enemy you decide to attack (by standing on them with your cursor), there appear green and red arrows on all your units. Green arrows indicating you should attack this target with that particular unit and Red arrows indicating to avoid any kind of engagement with this target with that repective unit since it really isn't favorable to you. How that exactly works, I haven't a clue. Sadly it shouldn't be like this.Also when you engage combat you have a choice of attacking with 1 of your 4 weapons. 1 Is overall medium in everything, 1 is designed to hit (raise your hit chance), another is designed to crit, and the last one is designed for dealing extra damage. You might ignore this in the beginning, but as you noticed your units start missing a lot, you are forced to pay attention to something rather stupid. Like I said, this is a puzzle game, not a strategic game where you pick certain classes equipped with certain weapons, keeping them close to some friendly units for better synergy, forming frontlines and putting archers in the back together with healers. NO NO this is a puzzle game where you walse through hordes of enemies by attacking your enemies with the right units and leaving these units 1 out of range of the harmfull enemies meanwhile 2 keeping them in range to be attacked by enemies that can't do much against them. The story is weak enough to not really engage you into playing this puzzle game further. I didn't want to continue playing it, so I started playing something else, promising myself I'll finish this one later, BUT... I had so much fun with Sniper Elite 4, I now seriously doubt I'll play this one again. Because 1 I don't like puzzle games and 2 I was not having fun. So I'm sorry but my inner Roman emperor says nay.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played this game for a while now, I enjoyed it for the most part. It is a solid game with suprisngly good unit customization. While you can play with any character without much difficulty, you can also up the difficulty and have a couple other options if you like min-maxing your characters. Also, theres no permadeath in this game so you can experiment a bit more and take risks without savescumming.Many people have experienced crashing, I have yet to experience any myself but it seems to be an issue with some people. Another issue many reviews pointed out was the lack of battlesaves. However, there is in fact a battlesave in the loading screen at the bottom right. I guess people just couldn't find it or didn't really look for it.The one detail that really annoys me is the load times, they are pretty absurd sometimes.I do recommend this game for fans of the old fire emblem games and some newcomers looking to get a forgiving glimpse of what it was like.

_childDocuments_.review: this game does have a couple glitches but overall I found this to be a very enjoyable experience, especially with the battle save system helping to patch up the occasional glitch or crash. The story itself isn't anything too out of the ordinary, with the direction being somewhat predictable from the start, however one thing this game does that say fire emblem doesn't, is having characters that aren't a part of the main cast having a level of importance in cut scenes outside of their recruitment chapter. For example at a point later in the game, your army will use a river to flank the enemy, as a result of one of the units you get much earlier in the game being familiar with the area. The characters themselves can be hit or miss, but with mostly a positive hit rate, at least for me. For example some characters like Sloane having a decent amount of interesting backstory explored in her supports, with some of the more immediately known aspects of her character having plot relevance long after her recruit time. If you're a fan of simpler characters, there are also some bangers, like Benji being an absolute moron but in an endearing way, or Fenton being very pleasant, and a much more positive character than I expected him to be. As for the gameplay, it's very similar to fire emblem as anyone interested in this game has likely heard, with a few changes such as the lack of weapon durability, instead opting for each class to come with a set of 4 weapons for a unit to swap between, consisting of hard hitting, high crit, high accuracy, and balanced. Another change being that rather than having a weapon triangle, advantages and disadvantages are instead determined by a unit's attack type, versus their foe's armor type, while I personally never found myself able to memorize the match-ups and know them ahead of time, the game does have a little arrow indicator on each foe to indicate whether the unit selected has advantage or disadvantage, which I found myself making heavy use of. The overall difficulty of the game, I personally found to be pretty similar to that of fire emblem (I'll stop making comparisons I swear), and on a similar level of fun if not sometimes more than that of fire emblem. If there's one problem I had with the gameplay it would be the occasional dips in map design, for the most part it is really good, providing a good balance of fields of space and choke points, however you do have occasional bland uninspired map design, and of course the infamous chapter 15 field of nothingness. If there's one aspect of the game I have no problem with whatsoever it would be the visuals. The portraits are really well drawn, and the backgrounds and spritework are simply stunning, my personal favorite being those of the windrunner class. Overall I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys tactical rpgs such as fire emblem, or advance wars, so long as you can withstand the occasional glitch or two. I personally loved my time with this game and can't wait for its sequel to drop. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: It does attempt to do alot that games like Fire Emblem do on a more simplified scale. But the things it does, it does quite well. Class Development: The classes and class development are at least interesting and make me feel like my choices mean something. For example, on the typical "rogue" unit, I could choose one of 4 paths: maybe I want a more bursty 'assassin' type with high first-turn damage, or maybe I want a tankier unit who's better in 1v1 without allies, or maybe I maybe I want to give him some ranged options, or maybe I want a unit who rides a horse and has increased movement speed and pillages (has increased chance to find items) but whose stats are so-so. And this is just one tier; there are multiple tiers. Maps:I also found the maps and scenarios to be unique, especially the more you progress (the dam scenario was new set-up I have not seen very often in games), and not every scenario is as simple as "kill all the bad guys" which was nice.  Even a typical "rescue the prisoners" level ended up being much tougher than I expected.Game balance:Even on standard difficulty, the game can be a nice challenge, which again was a nice change to games that I can usually steam-roll through on all but nightmare difficulty. Several levels had me die at least once because units far away don't always just sit there and wait for you to engage them--vs similar games where if you aren't in 'threat range' they're just pawns on a chess board. Social Game:This is the one aspect I thought was lacking. There is really no VA, and I even found a minor glitch on the social screen at one point (it kept saying I had a new social interaction between two heroes, but there wasn't one). The social part does give combat boons eventually more like older DS versions of Fire Emblem than the complexity of FE:TH, so it's important to do, but I found myself just clicking through. Overall it's a very well done game, if not super original.  TLDR; Pro's: -Well-balanced difficulty, good challenge-Unique maps and scenario design (Looking at you, water dam level)-Interesting class progression with meaningful decisions (don't worry you can recruit enough to experience them all, I think?? so don't sweat it too much. If not, just play the game again, it really is that fun!)-Personally a fan of the retro graphics-Gameplay is actually fun and requires some actual strategy (imagine that)Con's-Social system is rudimentary, but passable. -Story is a little on the cliche', but again not bad. Don't write this game off as "another Fire Emblem clone." This game does the genre justice. If you're looking for a dating sim, go elsewhere, but if you want a fun tactical romp that will push your strategical mind. This game is it.Definitely a buy for lovers of the genre and for newcomers alike.

_childDocuments_.review: The main problem with Dark Deity is that it is too linear, lacking some major stuff usually present in [somewhat] similar games such as Final Fantasy Tactics, Tactics Ogre or Fell Seal. (I can't talk about Fire Emblem, as I have never played it.)It lacks a global map to move on, optional levels, unlockable characters, items to grind or farm for, choices.  of that is present in the game -- you have  freedom, nothing to  to go after. You are railroaded from start to finish. There isn't even a New Game+ mode, which is sad because I actually wanted to play it a second time, this time knowing what I was doing so that I could put a perfect party together. This game would have been  better with all, or at least some, of these things.Dark Deity is also a bit flawed both in design and execution. Some of the game is too RNG-based (character attribute growth, surviving critical hits on later levels) and there are some ugly, although not game-breaking, bugs in it, most notably and frequent the one that leads a character  to be where you see them, after moving (then you have to click on an empty spot, as if your guy was there).There is also the "Bonds" mechanic in the game, which handles the relationship between your characters. And it is . I finished the game on the highest difficulty without ever even looking at it, because I had read multiple times beforehand that it served no purpose (it only reveals alternative dialogues).The game's visuals and animations are good, except for the actual levels. These look like crap, as you can see on the screenshots up there. And there is too much talking between missions as well. After 2/3 of the game or so I just stopped caring and skipped over the remaining of the story.You can only equip  item on each character, besides consumables (only healing and attribute-increasing ones that cost a lot). The "one items" can make a huge difference, but you also get them in bundles, at two fixed points in the game -- there are no more to be found, you don't get any from enemies, from side-quests (since there are none in the game) or anything. They are just given to you for free, twice, and those are  the items you'll get to see in the game.OK, so... that's a lot of bad stuff, and it  be enough to ruin the game. But I still had a good time with it, and even wanted to play more, with a different set of characters/classes, to see how that would go. The best thing about Dark Deity, for me, was the theorycrafting. I had to spend some 2 or 3 hours deciding how to build my guys. ... I had to use a guide for basic information, because the game does not provide it -- you'll only receive vital information, such as attribute-growth and weapon type of classes once you unlock them (by reaching level 10 and 30) and, by then, if you messed something up, there's no going back. You'll have to start the game over from scratch. So, if you are going to play this,  check a guide beforehand to know how you are supposed to build your characters. I'm not saying you should  the guide, copying it; I'm saying you  the information they provide.In Dark Deity, you'll take 14 heroes (less, at first) to one fight after another. There's virtually nothing to do in between, other than to equip them (with  item) or upgrade their weapons (each character has 4 types of weapons, and should favor 1).The combat mainly consists in throwing the right guys against the right enemies. Magic and crushing weapons are good against plate armor, piercing damage is good against chain mail and... leather armor (I think) you need to throw high-accuracy guys against their dodgers, high Defense/Fortitude/Dodge ones in front of your squishy dudes, and so on.If you pair up one of your heroes against the wrong enemy, he's screwed. It can lead to you doing 0 damage and/or being killed in a single hit. So, this is a major thing.If/when one of your characters die, they'll permanently lose a random number from some random attribute. These can be recovered by purchasing and consuming certain items available on the store (store items are the same from the beginning of the game until the end, BTW), but they cost 5k gold each, which is a lot. In the whole game you make something like 200k, and most of that you'll spend upgrading your weapons (upgrading one from the 3rd to the 4th and last tier costs 6k).And... and... there isn't much else to say. That's basically the  game.Planning how to build your party, before you even start playing, is actually were most of the fun lies. Then you just stick to your plan and see if it works out as you expected, hopefully well enough to let you win the game (which is not so hard, if you get most things right).Each character gets to pick one class at lvl 10 and another one at lvl 30. Each class comes with two passive skills, they keep those skills from the lvl 10 class when switching to the lvl 30 one, and you can mix-up any 2 classes of the 4 available on each of those two tiers. So, you  have some room to decide  to build each of your characters.Each character also has a certain  of gaining a point on each individual attribute when levelling up, and each class has its own as well. This, along with the passive skills mentioned above and the damage/weapon types mentioned earlier are the things you have to take into account when deciding how to build your characters.Dark Deity actually  more than it . But I actually enjoyed the whole 36 hours it took me to finish it.The combat, though very basic (one move, one action, no active skills), works just fine strategically, given positioning and how you must match your heroes against the enemy's.Character-growth, though simple, automatic and random, still gives a decent margin for tailoring up your party to your wishes because you have to choose  will be of each class, and how many Clerics, Adepts, Warriors, etc. you'll want in your definitive party. It does require you to put some serious thought into it.All things combined, I recommend you buy this on sale.  I'd actually buy the DLC because, again, I'd like to try a different set of characters but, apparently, it only adds some useless character portraits and 7 new missions, which are played independently, one at a time, apart from the main game. WTF is the point of that? Seriously, there's something wrong with these developers. A lot of things are lacking in Dark Deity, some of it is weird, there are a few bugs that really shouldn't be there on/after release, the DLC makes as much sense as the "Customize New Game" options (), they use the DLC sprites on the  game's Store Banner, which is just wrong  gives away a bad impression (a couple of kids in swimsuits? This must be a damn silly game).Their "idea guy" should probably be fired.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game, and I had an overall enjoyable experience.The Good:- The combat / upgrade classes / overall tactics in the game are fun.- A lot of people seemed to not like the extensive dialogues between characters as you progress, but I liked it because it made the character development feel more personable and engaging.  Not every story needs to be a 1-Dimensional march to save the world with no context between the characters.The Bad:- In the last 1/3 of the game, I encountered some technical issues on the maps with characters glitching out on terrain when using the Push and Phase abilities.  Sometimes when you put characters in corners or edges of the map, they'll randomly become unusable for some rounds, or the rest of the match.  When this happens, all you can do is move what characters you can move, and "End Turn" without using the others.  There's a few instances where characters got frozen, and I couldn't end the round, so I had to restart the map about a half-dozen times.- The weapon upgrade "4 Tier System" seems interesting at first, but unless you put all your money into tokens and put all the tokens in the "Red Power Option", your characters don't do enough damage fast enough to progress consistently.- There isn't any way to grind maps to power level your characters if you get stuck in progression by making bad upgrade decisions in the beginning.- Money is very hard to come by, so if you find any "Bonus Stat Items" from enemy drops or chests in a map, you MUST sell them if you want enough money in game to upgrade your weapons to max per character.- By end game, all of my characters were equally leveled between Lv 36-38, and half of them were 1 upgrade short of maxing weapon upgrades.  As new characters rapidly get introduced, you could just "Stick with the highest Max Level Characters", and the game doesn't punish you for this.  Unfortunately, this design decision invalidates the need to use half the characters if you just want to plow through the game and not care.Overall Rating:  7/10- If you can get this game on sale like I did for under $10, it's a good value.  At full price, not so much unless you want to replay the same game to high difficult settings.If you like Old-School Fire Emblem Shining force games like this, there's 2 other games on steam I'd also recommend:- Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga- Langrisser 1 & 2 Collection

_childDocuments_.review: While I initially recommended this game due to my impressions being positive, after playing a far larger chunk of the game, I was, unfortunately, prompted to revise my opinion. Dark Deity very much misses the mark of what makes games such as Fire Emblem great. It is affected by some fundamental flaws that are difficult to reconcile with a well-designed and balanced game. Suffice it to say, it's not going to dethrone Fire Emblem anytime soon.The story of Dark Deity revolves around a young man who is forcibly recruited from his military academy, and soon is forced(?) to turn against his former nation which has taken a turn towards evil. It starts on a small scale, but then becomes a far-reaching JRPG tale about saving the world.While passable, not much more can be said than that. The story is meandering at the best of times, so when it attempts to elicit emotion, things are much too sudden for that to actually happen. While an attempt was made to add in a large amount of lore, the lore that does exist is rather cliched with your standard elves, dwarves and other typical western fantasy tropes. It doesn't attempt to differentiate its universe with unique aspects.The supports aren't very engaging either, and the character writing is mediocre compared to almost any Fire Emblem.The game has a surface level resemblance to Fire Emblem but features a system where you have a selection of several weapons, all upgradeable, to exploit enemy weaknesses. Theoretically you can have different units specialize in different strengths and weaknesses.Sadly, the game is poorly balanced. There are too many characters you encounter over the course of the game, and every time one joins your party, you are almost always better off switching to them immediately and dumping your previous party members.See, while I made a valiant effort to use some of the starting party members and level them up over the course of the game through all promotion trees, the fact of the matter is that the new people who join your party will just be straight up BETTER.One particularly telling moment was when a mage joined my party. She had roughly the same stats as one of my earlier mages, but her defense was a full 20 levels higher. This is particularly striking because level ups are not actually random in this game, so there's no way in hell that old character could hope to match those stats. I'd have to be crazy if I did not switch characters and permanently ditch the older mage.In the Fire Emblem games I usually go with what characters are my favorite, but this game is relatively on rails and forces you to use the characters it wants you to use. It's strange that the cast of characters is so massive because there is not any permadeath, so you don't even have to risk losing units. If you really wanted players not to be able to lock themselves out of progress, just give promotions some minimum stats.The game's maps are also poorly designed, with spaces that are way too wide and open, allowing enemies to gank you without mercy. Perishing is not a permanent punishment, but the game feels unfair at the best of times, and its poor balance causes some units to feel totally useless as their 0 damage attacks clink off enemy armor where they were doing significant damage just last map.My favorite map was one where everyone had to join forces to fight a dragon with a tremendous health pool and AOE attacks. It felt like an epic boss but it came out of nowhere and ultimately had zero story relevance, which sadly is par for the course.There are also still perlexing bugs, like buttons double tapping and the map cursor going all the way to the top left for no apparent reason. The UI is clunky and hardly works half the time. The game was released in a half baked state even despite all the patches.While decent, especially with the UI and character art, which is quite detailed (if generic), corners were clearly cut for some of the maps. The tiles in some of them look more like "my first indie game" than a professional product. I mean, technically it is, but given that the rest of the game is decently polished, that stands out all the more. One particular map of note is the one with numerous similar colored portals that I can only imagine is hell for colorblind people.The animations are cool, but don't depict the characters' outfits properly. One can only imagine it could be tweaked better if they cut the amount of characters in half, while not harming the gameplay in the slightest.If "generic, mediocre but does its job" could be applied to the story, it could also be applied to the music. While some of the tracks are okay, it was not memorable enough to make me go back and want to listen to the soundtrack. It is standard Western fantasy fare and lacks the catchy tunes of many JRPGs, including recent Fire Emblem games.While I have beaten Dark Deity, knowing what I know now, I would not have purchased it to begin with. Most GBA romhacks of Fire Emblem will likely be better, simply by virtue of having game balance that functions. Perhaps in the future a sequel may improve on these issues, but I'd be giving it far more scrutiny after playing the previous game.

_childDocuments_.review: While I can very well recommend this game at the end of the day, there are some small nitpicks I have that make it edge dangerously close to a game I could not recommend.PROS:Gorgeous art. Stellar job on animations, locales, various effects, and all other sprites.Combat. All the things you liked from Fire Emblem, now at your fingertips.Interface. The interface allows you to hover stats, showing what they do, and the percentage chance of having them upgrade during a level up (I believe that's what it is), making building into different classes not only easier to think about, but more rewarding to think about, rather than simply "click man with big sword haha".Classes. The classes all feel distinct, and give their own flavors. Some, I see as unnecessary, given that other roles can fill their shoes better, where other roles are overly necessary, and must be protected. This helps you feel big brain when you position nicely.Bugs. Rather, lack of them. A couple of reviews said the game was laggy, or that the animations were bugged, or that the game would crash on them. I have not encountered a single crash, or game-breaking error. Only a couple of annoyances that are easily looked past.CONS:Interface. While it is nice to hover and see stats, a lot of times you can't hover the interface and see what the stats do, notably during promotions. I'd love to be able to tell what the stats do so I can figure out what I want to prioritise during rank-ups. As well, in weapon upgrading, it doesn't show what weapon you currently have equipped, which I think would be a nice touch, since I frequently forget and have to go back into the menus to find out again. As well, the interface sometimes glitches with unit positions, forcing you to misorder your actions to allow you to use that one glitched character.Story. While it seems a well-thought out story, it isn't engaging. You start with a party of 4 characters, but within about 3 levels your party size has doubled. You aren't given enough time to learn about the characters inside of the story, and that makes the story largely skippable, which is sad.Characters. The characters all seem to be disposable. I can count on one hand the amount of party members that are actually important to the story. The rest are sorta there.Bonds. They've got this system that works off of god-knows-what metric, that allows your characters to build relationships with each other over the course of the game. However, some characters that should have bonds with each other already, like a brother and sister, two years apart, have no bond, and must start from scratch like the rest of the cast. This is also the only character-specific dialogue you'll get, so if you like a certain character, you'd better pray you get their bonds.Voicing. The game advertises "voiced" characters, but you'd be hard pressed to hear a full voice line outside of a level up. It's similar to free time in Danganronpa, where the character will say "Lay off! I've got my own problems to worry about." but the voice line will play only "Geez!". I was expecting each sentence to be read, and I was disappointed. It would have helped the impact of the story, and maybe made me more attached to the characters, but that's probably just me. What they DID put in is disappointing.Shopping and items. Items are worthless. Period. You have a healing item that heals 30 HP? Your healer can do that for free. Stat boost items are more useful, but they cost WAY too much. I found myself selling all my healing items in bulk, because why would I deploy a healer if they weren't needed? Weapon upgrade tokens have taken 100% of my funding, and even those are too expensive, since keeping my whole party up to snuff is emptying my wallet before I can even think of getting stat boosts.Inequality. Not all units are created equal. Bow users are remarkably ass, whereas thieves are absolutely overpowered beyond belief. There are certain units that should never be picked, regardless of whether or not your team already has one of each of the other ones.A couple of other small gripes, like being able to shoot through walls or past supposed height differences, unclear unit highlighting, etc.Overall, I'd give it a 7/10, where 1 is "I couldn't be paid to play it", 5 is "I'd play it for free", and 10 is "I would buy it twice". Get it on sale, don't expect a $60 dollar game for the ~$20 you pay for it, and you'll have a fun time. Not worth full price in my opinion, but seeing as the game just had an update, I have no doubt it will evolve, and I'm darn well looking forwards to what it could be in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros--Gameplay feels good-Character art is great, very 90s vibes but toned down to feel cleaner (and the shoulder pads are smaller)-Soundtrack is charming if not mind blowing-If you are jonesing for Fire Emblem, this will fill the itch a bit-This game is clearly built by someone who loves Fire Emblem, because it has the things people who have played FE 500 times between launches wish mainline games had (a randomizer, as well as a lot of other tuning options)Cons--The game doesn't explain most things. If you haven't played Fire Emblem, or don't like surprises, you might find that frustrating. Hero difficulty is not so hard that you feel deeply punished if you just pick what looks cool, although you might find yourself restarting more. -Sound Transitions can feel awkward-Loading screens come too often, and although they are quick they break up the action in a weird way-There are some bugs and UI issues that make the game feel unpolishedTo the developers credit they have already released a patch addressing some day 1 bugs and issues, and seem very connected to the community. The game is great for $25, and if you like this kind of game I highly suggest it. if you don't, you might want to wet your feet with the more polished Fire Emblem series, but if you like that you should comeback for this anyways.

_childDocuments_.review: Played on Steam Deck.Fire Emblem perfected. Dark Deity is rooted the classic GBA style and mechanical foundation but has found a surprising number of tweaks and QoL improvements that elevate the game even higher than its inspiration! TLDR: this game is great and any classic Fire Emblem fan will love it!The controls and UI out of the box are perfect, any action I want to take or info that I need to see is intuitive and only a click or two away. This is ideal when comparing units or examining promotion options because the ability to see stat growth percentages is right there so you always can make a plan for which units to invest in. There are a bit too many unit options though, but better more than not enough especially because the death mechanic is lenient to let you keep your units if they fall in battle, but they get a permanent debuff in the form of a battlescar which is a very intersting mechanic that achieves increased player engagement while also fostering emergent gameplay experiences. From the start the slight differences to FE are apparent, with all units having a secondary ability to use as an alternate to directly attacking, such as healers having the Heal ability instead of using a healing rod, but the movement ones are the most interesting with some being able to reposition an ally relative to themselves which can set up some very impactful movement opportunities. When attacking there is no more weapon choices but instead four attack styles with tradeoffs such as high damage but low accuracy, or low damage medium accuracy high crit if you need to gamble on a killshot. These attack styles can be individually upgraded per unit too, for a specialization into that style which leads to less all around flexibility but higher success in their particular use case. With the removal of weapons, there is no more weapon durability to manage, and that includes taking space in your pockets! Previously having to manage weapons + consumables + valuables did get a bit tedious, but now valuables are taken into a shared inventory so the only item management is consumables which further streamlines the whole gameplay to let the player focus on the tactics! Valuables such as promotion crests are also gone, and units automatically promote at levels 10 and 30, so no more worrying about waiting to promote until 20 to squeeze out the more minmax stat points and working around level caps, just level up and keep on fighting! The promotions feel like they determine the identity of a unit instead of just being a stat boost. Each unit starts with a passive skill and each promotion gets two more, so determining the role of the character by their promotion and combination of skills feels like such a satisfying decision. The skills are really cool and interesting too not just "+10 dex" or whatever; when promoting my first unit, a simple cleric that I was using for healing, I had to read the descriptions for a bit too long to figure out I was actually being given choices between essentially antimage, tanky healer, ranged healer, and lifesteal attacker! That's just the first promotion for one class, so when the avaible units are all specialized and the knowledge of each tool is practiced any combat is very satisfying and gets to the heart of what a tactics title is all about. This can get a bit overwhelming depending on how much optimization is desired, but it is not mandatory and can actually lead to a bit more challenge in a mission if the micromanaging feels like too much. The outcome is a great feeling of achievement when the effort into planning pays off in an clean victory, or the rush of clutching the final turn of a mission without having spend the hours of prep on units; success isn't locked behind a certain playstyle but just depends on which systems the player wants to utilize. Can't wait for Dark Deity 2!!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that very much falls into the vein of Fire Emblem. So much so that it can be considered a fan response to the series and its mechanics. If you want a TL;DR review, skip to the bottom. At the time of writing this review I have completed the story on Hero mode while playing on version 1.07.Mechanics: 7/10This game introduces a somewhat original equipment system. While each unit still has 4 inventory slots for accessories/consumables, weapons are fixed. Each class has 4 weapons, which are balanced towards power, crit rate, accuracy, and speed. They all seem to have the same range, so if your unit normally has a range of 1, it will stay that way until a class change. Weapons can be upgraded permanently, which is nice. What's not so nice is that as a player you can only see what weapon stats will improve in the next upgrade level. This makes it hard to evaluate whether or not it will be worth it to upgrade a weapon in the long run. Weapons are also non-transferable between units, meaning that any resources spent on upgrades are wasted if you don't intend to use that unit long-term. Furthermore, these weapons may change significantly when a unit promotes to a new class. What might have been a good choice in weapon upgrade may no longer be the case in a new class.Another notable departure from Fire Emblem is weapon/armor matchups. Rather than a weapon triangle, each unit has both an attack type and an armor type. Different armors have varying levels of resistance against each attack type. While it is possible to see whether or not an attacking unit has an advantage at a glance, it ISN'T possible to see how much of an advantage a unit has. This is further confounded by a new character stat, called mastery.  I really like a more granular system for matchups in theory, but right now some improvements need to be made in visualizing that granularity.Classic and Casual modes have been condensed into a new single mechanic, in which a unit that "dies" gets a permanent debuff to a random stat. This allows the player to fodderize some lower tier units if they want without much real consequence. This is very refreshing on the whole.Run difficulty can now be customized on a very granular level. Growth rates, base stats, recruitment order, etc can all be controlled when selecting your difficulty for a new game. Most of the mods used by challenge runners on classic FE titles can be found here. This can be really fun to play with, but it also cheapens the achievement of say, beating diety mode when you can start with massively buffed units.Map Design/Balance: 6.5/10I want to start positive here: the diversity of map objectives on the whole is great. Plenty of boss maps, defend maps, arrive maps, and yes, rout maps. The tile work also looks pretty great overall. Unfortunately, in many instances these objectives form a false diversity. Most of these maps turn into rout maps in spirit, where in order to get to your objective you still have to kill a vast majority of enemy units. Many of them also feel too large, to such a degree where competent mounted units really push ahead of the rest. One thing in particular that irked me is that in many indoor maps, going through a door RESETS the units movement range, allowing them to traverse double or even triple their normal range. This really helps the rich get richer in terms of movement, and needs a rebalance. This is not to say that these maps aren't fun. They just are let down a bit in terms of letting each unit shine. My opinion on this may change after trying diety mode.There is no stat in the game that gives a unit crit avoid. On one level, I love this. No longer can we just assume that enemies will hit us with nice an neat damage numbers. On another, it doesn't really seem like this is something we can control for as players. It leaves me with the impression that on a truly high difficulty, I would at times live purely by the mercy of RNG, which doesn't sit right.Classes in general do feel a bit fresher than Fire Emblem, but many of them still fall into the typical tropes and traps of the series. Mounted units are just a little too good. A good dagger user can turn into a dodge tank crit machine. Armor units still pretty much suck (because the maps are too good with too few defensive choke points). One meaningful improvement is that clerics are on average CHONKY in comparison to fire emblem healers. Now you don't need to just heal spam them until they get enough bulk to hold their own. They can break skulls from the start.UI/UX: 4/10This bit really bums me out. Unless I'm missing something, there is no option to remap controls. Not for keyb+mouse or controller. Controller icons also seem to be locked for xbox. Mouse controls are a little unintuitive, you can either click a unit and a destination or click and hold until you select the destination. This made me make a few accidental inputs that were frustrating. The on screen guides for what input does what are decent, but it would be nice to have a full controls page, even if we can't remap. There is no UI in the game for comparing units. As a player, I want to be able to directly compare my rogues on one screen. I don't want to constantly flit between their stats to see the differences. This also applies for ally vs enemy units. I won't really have any good idea of how a matchup will go until I look at a combat forecast unless I individually select each unit to pull up a stat menu, write these stats down, and then do a number crunch. Plot/Supports: 7/10Keep in mind that I'm rating this in comparison to a normal FE game. FE games normally have weak plots. This game is basically on par there. Dialogue can feel pretty damn stiff, and while in general each character has some dimension to them, you wouldn't know that from the main story-line. The de facto MC has a pretty bad case of the Mary Sue, and the main antagonist doesn't do much better. The antagonist is pretty majorly undeveloped by the end of the game. In general, the bad guys are lacking any fleshed out motivation other than getting moar power.Support dialogue does a bit better overall. There's a lot of support dialogue, so there's definitely ups and downs in terms of believable conversations. The good stuff properly endears the players to the characters, and reveals a little bit more about how they behave outside being a foil to the MC/their own relationship to the main plot.Voice Acting: English Dub Anime/10If you like English dub voices in a typical anime, you'll be fine with this. If those voice types tend to grate on your ears, consider muting them in the EQ. This is a game made in English to start, so I would have preferred a more naturalistic approach to character voices. "Cool" character types tend to come off a bit more believable than "cute" or "energetic" ones, but even the tough folks can come off a bit wooden. The actors themselves did a pretty good job on the whole.Music: 3/10I don't know that I can grade this fairly. Multiple times while playing, it felt like multiple tracks or loops where playing that didn't really coordinate with each other. I'm not sure if this is an issue with implementation or composition, but the end user experience wasn't really enjoyable for me, so I muted them after chapter 4. That means I could have missed some great tracks, but what I experienced had some pretty glaring issues.Holistic Rating Compared To Fire Emblem: 7.5/10This game introduces some interesting elaborations/responses to tradition Fire Emblem mechanics. It might be better served by integrating techniques from other successful srpgs. Mechanics like flanking, elevation, death saves, or FF tactics style "rules" would all be welcome here. The voice acting is fine, impressive even for a project of this scale. Music and plot is a bit of a letdown, but the world building is alright. Controls also need polish. Buy it if you like GBA era FE.

_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: While I can't completely recommend the game in it's current state, I still had a lot of fun playing it, and there's a fair chance you'd still enjoy it as well. I implore possible buyers or the devs to read this comment in full instead of just looking at my yes or no rating.My biggest complaint with the game is a general lack of explanation regarding system mechanics. I played on both the easiest and hardest difficulty, so it's not an issue of being unavailable on higher difficulties, there's just no explanation. The "tips" option also tends to be unhelpful, as it only gives surface level knowledge that you can already view by simply hovering over the stat in the stat screen. For instance, the mastery skill tells me that it makes a unit better able to utilize the advantage system, but I don't even know what the advantage system is or what it does!I'm not sure how true speed is calculated through weapon weight - does strength play a part in it? I don't know, the game doesn't say. The same is true for hit, crit, and avoid - I'm not sure.This is a big issue when the game has a bunch of mechanics to it that are pretty important to play - the fact that the player doesn't know how to use them leads to a lot of guesswork and just hoping things work out. This wouldn't be that hard of a fix to make - simply add a glossary with more terms defined and explained or expand the tips option to be more helpful to the player. The greatest fix would be to add a tutorial option that asks the players if they want a concept explained, but even that wouldn't be necessary if there was just more clarity on the part of the game to speak to the player.Onto more minor complaints.- When pressing a key to skip one enemy's battle animation on enemy phase, it skips the entirety of enemy phase. That should only happen if you press the enter key during enemy phase while units are moving and not while they are in combat.- When I turn battle animations off, the map music is still interrupted when combat happens. This is a more minor issue, but if I wanted to hear the battle music instead of the map music, I would have animations turned off.- Sometimes the battle forecast blocks my units if they are pressed up against a wall and I have to blindly click to confirm attacks or change targets.At the end of the day, I did enjoy the chapters I played through, even though I was lacking a great deal of information about system mechanics. The devs very clearly have put a lot of heart into the game, and it is very fun to play. If they can do something as simple as explain more to the player up front, I will have no issue being able to wholeheartedly recommend this game to possible buyers.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: Massively overpriced.This game is a decent homage to the much more refined Fire Emblem series from where it draws its inspiration, but the fact of the matter is it has far too many bugs and glitches for the $25 price tag. Far too often, units completely glitch out when you move them onto certain map tiles, even if you haven't locked them into place. You have to be especially careful near any type of wall or ladder type terrain, even if you're just temporarily scouting out the location. I don't know what else to say except that this is unacceptable for this type of game. You can be over an hour into a mission, move a unit somewhere to scope its attack against an enemy, only to find that the unit is locked into that tile. Or that the unit is treated as unavailable for the rest of the map. Or any number of issues that demonstrate this game is simply not a finished product. I would hold off on purchasing until the many, many bugs and glitches have been fixed, or the price tag drops to something closer to $10.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: As launch day experiences go, this has absolutely been a positive one. Dark Deity scratches that GBA-era TRPG itch that always makes me happy. A big draw for me has been the voice cast, as that was how I learned about the game to begin with, and their performances do not disappoint. The whole experience has been a delight.That isn't to say the game has no flaws. There are some noticeable typos which made it into the first release, although mainly in menus and areas where players are less likely to see them. The game takes a while to properly explain some mechanics, and treats several aspects as if they should be self-explanatory when they might confuse new players. In that sense, it might not be the best introduction to the genre, but for those familiar with the TRPG play style it is sure to delight.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy Strategy RPGs then you owe it to yourself to play this game as this is the best SRPG to come out since Three Houses. It is innovative in many areas but you will recognize all of the things that make this genre so good in Dark Deity, if you take anything away from this review let it be this bit. More in-depth critique follow below.Dark Deity is a Tactical RPG that simultaneously draws from other staples of the genre such as Fire Emblem but manages to carve a unique niche for itself at the same time, this is not merely a rip-off of conventional design choices but a game that while rough in some areas is clearly a labor of passion. It is very rare for me to get hooked on a game the way I did with Dark Deity but I found myself playing it nonstop for twenty hours and only pausing to eat and sleep.The game might have been made with a low budget but everything that went into it is refined, the portraits look stunning, the music is nice and the writing is remarkable with each character being given a distinct personality that cleverly avoids the stereotypes that has plagued games like this for decades.Its storyline is not a grand opera by any means, sticking true to genre conventions on the whole about reclaiming a lost homeland but although this might be considered a cliche to some it is remarkably well-executed due to excellent writing overall. Unlike Fire Emblem there is no Permadeath here, with death instead permanently lowering one of the dying units stats by a small percentage and this is fortunate because Dark Deity is different enough from its predecessors that it has a fairly steep learning curve in the beginning, which is exacerbated by the fact that it has no formal tutorial to explain its new ideas which is one of the few legititmate issues the game has from a design perspective, but it is an issue the Devs are looking to correct.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a couple things I have to say so far. Overall I think the game is very good so far, and I will continue to enjoy the game. This is constructive criticism, I'm not bashing the game.First thing that jumped out at me was the exp screen. It jumps from the battle screen back to the map incredibly suddenly, and its quite jarring. I would recommend adding a transition effect in between the exp gauge and returning to the map, even a brief pause after the exp is finished counting would do the trick, just to make it easier on the eyes.The other thing was the beginning chapter. To be frank, It feels incredibly rushed. there is barely even an introduction for the main 4 or what they are doing before you are thrust in. the map and enemy placement is so basic its insulting (It gets much better in the later chapters from whats I've seen) but this first level feels like its babying you. and then it jumps to the main plot. this in all in the span of 20 minutes. I wish we could have gotten more out of this first chapter. More character Dialogue, More interesting design, a little bit more down the earth talking in between the characters before the inciting event. This is supposed to be what hooks your players and draws them into the story, but its criminally easy on the standard difficulty, and it feels like its just there to get me to the main story as quick as possible, and it really doesn't do much to catch my interest.

_childDocuments_.review: it's buggy, the writing is generally embarrassing, and it does a terrible job of explaining just about everything that makes it interesting and unique - but if you're willing to engage it on its own terms, dark deity has a surprisingly meaty core that isn't afraid to slaughter the sacred cows of fire emblem, and which allows for quite a decent amount of strategic expression. get it on sale, maybe, but if you play fire emblem for the gameplay and want something different but adjacent, it's a pretty healthy meal.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this could have been a great game -- like one of the old Fire Emblem games, which I love. And, to be frank, it doesn't suck completely. There are things that I enjoyed, but in the same vein, there are just so many tedious things that after a while, I couldn't bring myself to play the game, especially when there are much better tactical games available. The good things:- The game looks nice, very classy look; I personally liked the artwork. - The first battles were fun. Very Fire Emblem.The bad things:- There is no tutorial. None. You have to infer the meaning of things from your Fire Emblem knowledge.- The story is so thin and generic that I fell asleep after three sets of dialogues. Oh c'mon, it can't be that hard to write a story that is half-decent and has not already been used by every second tactical game. - I personally found none of the characters really likeable. Most of them are heavily stereotyped and I am personally past the point where I enjoyed when nearly every second girl looks the same with their tight body armor, the heavily pronounced breasts and the same generic face. If that's your aesthetic: sure, go for it. It wasn't mine. I would have loved to have some variety, because after a while, those girls really all look the same. - I encountered two major and a few tedious bugs in my 6 hours. I had to restart two maps and I didn't really like this. - Speaking of restarting: There are a few quality-of-life improvements missing. I'd have loved to have a restart button for example.- There is no variety in the gameplay loop; there is also not much of a gameplay loop, really. It always consists of fighting, buying things in the shop, listening to bonding dialogues, upgrading and then going back to fighting again. That's just not enough after a while.TL;DR: The story already bored me after 20 minutes. I played for the combat for the remaining 5 1/2 hours, but the bugs killed my joy. I will probably wait for the next Fire Emblem (or the next indie title with some improvements).

_childDocuments_.review: Like many others have said, if Steam allowed for a mixed review, this game would receive one from me. As it is, I am going to err on the side of caution for other prospective buyers. I've reached the late stages of the game now but I'm throwing in the towel, not because the game is too difficult (it's pretty reasonable on medium difficulty for someone familiar with this style of game), but rather I have run out of patience with the relentless average-ness of the levels, the classes, the story and the pacing. Too often the maps are funnels that don't allow for interesting tactical choices. I can put up with having to cut loose a character I enjoy because they were outclassed by a new recruit and I can skip through the story if it's getting too pedestrian but the gameplay has never been particularly fun or engaging and I've given up hoping it will improve.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly think people are being a bit harsh, considering this is their first game. It is by no means perfect and it has some obvious flaws. Controls are a little unwieldy, the story is nothing to write home about (but you play fire emblem, you never cared *that* much about a super compelling story) and the characters are certainly a bit flat. The UI could be better in a lot of places. Turning off combat animations (you see em 20 times and don't need to waste the time anymore) is a pain, because then you don't see damage dealt/taken at all.Edit: The devs have been working hard to pump out bug fixes since release and pushed out a patch that enables saving mid battle quick as they could. Clearly they are dedicated to fixing issues with the game. And are very open to suggestions in their discord as well.But as far as fire emblem clones go, it is still the best I've played on PC. It scratches that itch. You hit level 10 and you have 4 class options for each base class and an advanced class for each of those, which is a breath of fresh air for me after three houses generic class tree. Unit growths are completely visible from their unit screen and not hidden. Maps are pretty good in design so far, only one has had a unique mechanic so far (I am on chapter 10/28, so still plenty of maps to see). As far as I can tell the game does not have permadeath, but instead units lose stats on "dying", so if someone goes down they lose 1-2 of any random stat. Edit: Units do die after receiving too many wounds, personally unsure how many it takes thoughIn terms of weapons/magic/healing, it's all unlimited use. You upgrade weapons/magic between maps with tokens, which you get from enemies and you can buy them in the shop. You do have to make unit choices here, as you can't reasonably keep everyone on par in upgrades, there is no gold farming and higher tier tokens just can't be bought for everybody. Personally I really like this system, it's a nice way to do weapons I think. Speaking of weapons, everybody has 4. One for raw attack power, one for crit and less power, one for accuracy and less power/crit and one that seemingly applies a small amount of each. They each have different weights as well which effect your speed for doubling.Unit and class skills are mostly if not entirely passive, things like doing more damage to full health enemies, applying 20% of your magic to your speed, stuff like that. Classes are pretty unique and fun, regardless of if they are "good" or not. We all know this matters little in the end as your army becomes unstoppable in these games anyways.Difficulty is on par for a fire emblem clone. Currently playing on the "medium" difficulty and I've had a few units go down, there are definitely spikes where enemies start to get their weapon upgrades and such, usually the first map is a pain when they just have their newest upgrades put in but you kinda adjust your play accordingly after.I suppose this was more of a rambling run down of the game than a "I like it and you should too" review. But I'm not a professional reviewer. Anyways, my consensus is if you like fire emblem, give it a try. Maybe it's too crusty for you or maybe you just don't like it, that's fine, live your best life. But I am genuinely excited to see a fire emblem clone get it right and hit a nice landing for once.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard game to review. I'd give it a 6/10. If you like turn-based tactics or strategy RPGs a la Fire Emblem, this is that. The gameplay is flawed, but overall very fun.The biggest reason why I can't recommend the game right now, though, are the many, many, MANY bugs. There's a lot of them. They are being worked on at a truly impressive rate through nearly daily patches, but currently the frequent bugs tip this over to not recommended from me. Maybe once they're ironed out I'll be able to change this review, but for right now I'd hold off, even if this is the kind of game for you. Come back in a month or two and see how it's shaping up.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this is a fantastic game and you should invest in it if you're a TRPG/Fire Emblem fan. It plays much like an older Fire Emblem with some modern twists. The little additions and tweaks are really nice for the most part, and the game offers a lot of freedom and tools to engage the chapters with. One particularly nice touch is you get control over every character's promotions, even ones who qualify before they join you. The game is tough without being too punishing and the chapters have almost all felt satisfying. I think the biggest and best addition comes in the form of items that can drastically change characters or combat rules. You get a vast array of them and they open up new and powerful alternative strategies. The only cons I would be aware of is that being a new game from a new group, it lacks a lot of the QoL stuff more modern Fire Emblems have. It is basically story, combat chapters, base management/supports. I like some of the fluff from other games, but I think this is a refreshing balance and something that could be expanded upon. The only other major annoyance for me involved new party members. Upon getting one that qualifies for promotion, you are immediately asked to choose their promotion. This is great, but you're asked to make the choice with only seeing the character maybe once, little idea of their stats, and almost no idea of their personality. Not a major issue, but I have some characters I regretted promoting after learning more about them or seeing who joined my army next.
