_childDocuments_.review: OK so this is my first review of a game on steam so here we go.As someone who is a huge fan of fire emblem, I appreciate what this game has to offer. I am only 6 chapters in so far (at time of making this) but it has many interesting aspects to itThe Good:I like the art style. The characters are well drawn and the backgrounds are nice to look at. The sprite work is very well done as the characters move fluidly and their battle animations are cool (especially when you land a critical). The weapon system took a while to get the hang of but wasn't troublesome. Unlike In fire emblem where a unit can hold whatever type of weapon the want so long as they can wield them (examples being critical edges, ridersbanes and brave weapons), Each character has four weapon types. These types focus on power, accuracy, critical chance or a balance of all three, making you want to upgrade the type that would be most effective for that specific unit. The classes diversity is wonderfully varied and I like the voice acting as well.Nitpicks:Personally the music is the weakest aspect to me. It's not bad, it's ok but there aren't any that are memorable to me at least compared to other RPG's I've played ( of course adding in Fire Emblem). I think they should add a feature where you can see the supports you've already unlocked.The Bad:As simple as some of the games mechanics are, the game doesn't tell you what they are because it has no proper tutorial. I feel like this can be a huge improvement especially for players who are new to this type of genre. It is especially needed because, without help from one of the forums here on steam, I would have no idea how the weapon and armor type systems work. All you get are green and red arrows telling you what units will be effective on whom but that isn't much of a consolation. It could also give some clarity on how the perma-death system works and I'm not a fan of that here either. Once a unit dies they can't be used for the rest of the chapter, which is fine but now get stuck with a stat debuff for the rest of the game. You can use said unit again after the map is cleared but if they die too many times you won't be able to use them again. I'm also not a fan of how boring the main cast is in terms of story. Don't get me wrong, when you initiate support conversations the characters are fun to watch, It's just that the characters don't show much of their personality in story cutscenes, which hurts the main four that we play as in the game. The player is just expected to accept the fact that their friends when we haven't been shown that.Final Thoughts:Overall I think that Dark Deity is a good game, It just has some issues that, if fixed can make it way better. I encourage people to check it out if you're a fan of Fire Emblem (Sorry for using it as a constant point of comparison) and if you don't like it, that's fine. I wish the developers the best of luck on this project.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: Brings me back to Fire Emblem: Sacred Stones, in the best way possible.Rather than a weapon triangle, Dark Deity has 4(?) different armor types, leather, chain, plate, and cloth/robes. Different weapon types (slash, pierce, fire, shock, etc.) are more or less powerful against certain armor types. Bonds/friendships are prevalent, yielding some interesting conversations. Unit upgrade paths seem more in depth than the fire emblem games I'm used to, with the ability to prestige a character to one of four intermediate classes quite early into the game, and another possible class upgrade after that. The fact that there is no weapon durability like in many similar games is a nice quality of life touch--instead, each character has four weapons. Cosmetically identical, each weapon instead confers a specific upgradable bonus: damage, crit chance, accuracy, or balance. These features combined produce a satisfying result with tactical depth and likable characters

_childDocuments_.review: Tentative recommend. If you like Fire Emblem, that's more or less what this is.The class upgrades are nice, in that each base class has 4 options to upgrade to, and then can upgrade again later to 4 other classes, letting you mix and match some abilities. Obviously some synergize better than others, but my only qualm about it is that some mid classes have no direct upgrade available into the 3rd tier. They're all generally better than second tier classes, but occasionally it's a small disappointment.The weapon upgrade system does away with any durability, and all characters have 4 weapons they have on-hand at all times. One for Damage, one for Crit, one for Accuracy, and one that's Balanced. You can spend money/items to permanently upgrade these items to be "better", and always available to you, even if you change classes into a class that uses a different set of weapons.However, since this game uses a similar speed/double attack system as Fire Emblem does, the major drawback to upgrading weapons comes when the weight of weapons increases at certain tiers. Some of these weight jumps are very large, and very often you'll have wished you hadn't upgraded to the next tier, since you can't double some enemy anymore you would have been able to before. You'll often times find yourself using upgraded weapons, for the simple reason that they're lighter and will grant that x2 attack that's enough to finish off an enemy. This may be intentional, but it's rather annoying that investing into a weapon can render the weapon very much niche and you start to use it less and less, even though it's your 'best' weapon.The whole upgrade system is a bit lacking in imagination. You can purchase weapon upgrades and stat upgrades with money. Therefore money directly translates into character power. Character power that can only be invested into one character, when literally every chapter throws a new character (or two) at you, none of which have any upgrades innately. It also forces you to use them in those chapters, which later in the game can really be a hinderance since you're forced to use characters you have no investment in.The characters themselves are fairly simple. Mostly Tropes and one notes, but with so many joining your group, they all start to blend together into a stew of "I can't care about all these people anymore". The main character has a pretty big problem when for the first half of the game I wasn't entirely sure if he was the main character. He was just some schmuck following orders. Then at some point everyone in the growing gaggle of anime tropes declared "YOU'RE THE BESTEST LEADER EVER LLOYD", and pledge their undying fealty to him. So I guess after that he can talk to god now, or whatever.Spoilers for the 'story':The story is also rather frenetic and uninteresting. One moment there's a wizard over there that you need to stop for... some reason? Then you need to apparently murder your way through your countrymen to get to him, then when you reach him, the screen turns white, some people the characters (but not you) care about are dead, and it happens so fast I was extremely sure I completely missed something. But, turns out I didn't, it just has things happen extremely fast sometimes, and extremely slow others.End spoilersThe later part of the game starts to also feel a bit lazy in level design. There's a particular map where it's an enormous open area, with zero map features, and just a swarm of enemies pouring in. The goal is to just break through them, which is plenty possible, but I have a hard time calling it 'fun'.It's okay as a budget title, the game makers obviously have a passion for Fire Emblem as a whole, but they haven't quite gotten down all of the details of how to turn the formula into a well-rounded experience fans are used to from the classic SRPG series.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: It's $25. If you were looking at this game because you simply liked fire emblem gameplay, and don't really care about a strong story, then I would definitely recommend this game. However, if you like fire emblem (or similar games) more for its story, characters, and writing, I would look elsewhere. That's not to say the writing or other aspects outside of gameplay are bad, but I feel most people would be disappointed if they wanted the story of this game to be the same quality of fire emblem. I'm someone who really values both equally in games, and if you are too, I'd recommend reading further to get specifics and see if this game is for you.Pros:+Good core gameplay loop+Great artwork and presentation+Many different classes and skills+Clever map design+Controller support+Well thought out UI+Good mix-up of map objectives+Voice acting is great +No apparent glitches (my personal experience)+Cool battle animations and critical animations+Great character visual designsCons:-Mediocre story-Bonding system isn't fleshed out and rarely adds more characterization to units-Too many characters that it's hard to care about all of them-Map tile-sets aren't as vibrant as the unit sprites, and it makes units seem out of place-The tutorial should be hands on rather than a text menu-Needs more of the voice acting than what was used (Not full VA cutscenes, but the VAs helped add character)Gameplay is what has carried me through this game so far. Every choice I make in positioning characters is really important. I'm playing on the second highest difficulty, and the challenge seems well balanced. Unit deaths are significant, but not permanent, they simply get lowered stats. I think this was a choice so all characters could still participate in the story without being "dead", but I think it's an interesting twist to gameplay that's more forgiving. Maybe the developers could include a permadeath mode in the game. I think the spritework is well done, and the animations telegraph clearly what each unit is doing. Voice acting is great, and I really wish more of it was used throughout the game. I like the unique classes and warriors you get.The maps are also really fun, and force you to think carefully of how to maneuver around in. There's a map with portals that you really have to think who goes in what portal, beforehand. Another map where it's like you're playing a horde survival game, and you have to fend off enemies for eight turns. Not all maps are brain-busting puzzles, but there's was obvious care put into map creation. The 4 weapon type systems is unique and an interesting idea, but the fact that I can quickly swap between all four on the fly takes any thinking on my part out of it. I just compare all for modes when I'm about to attack and choose the best one. Similarly, the green and red arrows that indicate advantages and disadvantages really simplify my thinking in who I have to use in an attack. However, I think the arrows are necessary simply because the armor weapon advantage system that replaces the weapon triangle is never thoroughly explained, so if I didn't have those arrows I wouldn't really have an idea of how to take advantage of the proper units. Of course all of this can be learned through a little experimentation.The story of this game really adopts the approach of throwing the audience/reader into the world without much setup. There's many little hints of cultures, organizations, and nations that suggest a larger world, but they are often noted once and never again. Sometimes it makes me feel like there was a bigger world/story written that was cut. I feel this game needed to adopt a simpler straight-forward story, simply because there are so many characters, that it often gets convoluted. Later-on it's harder to pick up what bits that the characters are talking about are actually relevant. Characterization is also a big problem in this game. Fire emblem doesn't always need a solid over-arching plot, but it definitely needs multiple strong characters to fill its units rosters. During the story, everyone seems to be on the same page the entire time. There's no interesting conflict between characters, when there probably should be. There's just no character development that is engaging in the story cut scenes (with one or two exceptions). The bonds system should alleviate that problem, but it doesn't. I feel the bonds system doesn't need to be as impactful on gameplay/story as the 3DS fire emblem games, but as is, it seems a purposeless addition. There's no effect on gameplay outside of 1 item. There's characters that are jerks to each other, there's little meaningful resolution. There is little to no romance, which is fine, but you still miss out on more character growth and the dating-sim mini-game. There's also, again, too many characters to the point where I want to skip bonds so that I can get rid of the exclamation point notification. Recommendations:*Maybe limit classes to only have access to 2-3 weapon types. Or take out the well-rounded weapon type. (EX: An archer has finesse, accuracy)*Have a quick access diagram of advantages and disadvantages between weapon and armor types so players can strategize appropriately, and also so the game doesn't have to tell the player which units are good against which through the use of those green/red arrows. I'd even take out a few weapon/armor types to simplify it if need be.*Thoroughly establish the initial cast of characters, and give them clear character boons, flaws, and misc. traits.*Streamline the story, without having random bits of worldbuilding (if they're of no consequence to the plot)*Make bonding significant by having fewer conversations, but have those be more impactful.*Really develop the characters that matter to the story. Not every character needs deep development, but the MCs do imo.

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this make me wish there was a Neutral rating, because I don't dislike the game, I just have a hard time recommending it.Dark Deity is a turn-based strategy game taking heavy inspiration from the old GBA-era Fire Emblem games. You control an army of fighters from 6 different class trees and mow your way through enemies, undead, and elemental spirits alike to foil the machinations of some sorcerer I dunno I'm halfway through the game and I have no idea what's actually going on yet. Also, those "undead" and "elemental spirits" I mentioned are all just more of the character classes.The story bounces from plot point to plot point, picking up elements and then abandoning them three chapters later. You encounter what passes for the main character's father 12-ish chapters in and I guess we're supposed to be touched by this reunion with someone whom the MC admits he doesn't even know. Who then immediately sends us out to "prove our worth" by finding some nebulous MacGuffin with no explanation as to what it is, why we're doing it, or how it will help.Class variety is somewhat anemic. There are 6 base classes, each of which have 4 advanced classes. It sounds like a fair bit, until you realize certain classes are just straight up better than others. Same with certain units. Irving, the aforementioned not-quite-but-basically-MC, completely breaks the game as a Dragoon>Dragon Knight. The Rogue line of classes are all pretty bad, honestly, with the exception of Cia if you make her a Duelist>Gladiator. But Cia's case is unique among Rogues because she's recruited early in the game and doesn't suffer from the game's broken stat scaling of units who join later. Any rogues who join after Cia suffer from remarkably low damage output unless you choose another specific upgrade path.The damage formula is needlessly complicated, as well. This is the one area where they should have simply copied FE's base damage formula (unit Atk/Mag + weapon power - enemy Def/Res). The addition of %-based modifiers creates instances where HUGE variances are possible. Against one enemy, a unit might deal hundreds of points of damage with a single crit, and then almost nothing against the next.The battle animations are extremely smooth and detailed, especially the magic spells. The bond scenes are enjoyable and really do a good job of showing off their characters. Overall, it has very solid elements of a great strategy game. But it's just not put together very well. I haven't even mentioned the frequent crashes when enemies attack certain ally units. For $25 and the dev's first game, it's not too bad, but as a fan of the games it's trying to copy, I can't really recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game overall, really reminds me of Fire Emblem, the GBA ones in particular, though it does have enough differences to have its own identity. So for a bit of context I have played all the american releases of FE and the fan translation of 6 and I rate them as such Path of radiance, FE7, Sacred Stones, Radiant Dawn, Awakening, FE6, Fates, Echoes, and finally 3 houses ( I just cant get into it the school and all the changes like no weapon triangle etc just feels wrong)So if you really liked the GBA FE games and probably the tellius ones as well I think you'd enjoy this. The gameplay is solid its turn based strategy on a grid there is a weapon and armor system so certain weapon types are more effective against certain armor types and it is a graded type system f to s of having an advantage its a little more complicated the FE weapon triangle though it seems less punishing. All the characters have base % growths which are then modified by their class upon promotion there are 2 promotions and 3 options at each and you can mix them up you dont have to go to the next one in that line. Maps are pretty good with a few objective types none of them made me wish it was over sooner, none were amazing either though. The late game bosses are a standout as well theres a few with different gimmicks and huge hp pools. Decent length campaign 28 chapters 3 difficulties and theres options to alter or randomize growths stats of your units and enemies and party recruitment order. There is a autosave in battles at the beginning of every turn so you can quit and resume.Writing wise its pretty good a kind of standard fantasy type story but I liked it well enough and want to know more about the lands and groups. The characters are pretty good IMO as well none of them felt completely one note after reading a majority of the bonds, and some I really liked and was very interested to learn more about in their conversations.Art is almost all around excellent the pixel graphics are nice and the anime style character models look great (except for vesta I have no problem with skimpy designs but hers is just silly). Combat animations are really good for the most part (I think assassin is kind of silly) especially the spells every spell has its own animation that does make it disappointing that theres only the one for each physical unit and sometimes the crits are just the base animation with a aura around their weapon its also kind of disappointing theres no follow through for 2 attacks in a row its just the base attack twice.Sound is fine no strong feelings either way.Controls with m&k are a little janky, not awful I did play most of it this way but a controller is better.Overall I really enjoyed it and think its worth it even at full price.My thoughts on the DLC Its ok it adds some extra battles with a dialog scene before and after expanding on the world and story some and including two after the main story some let you play with NPCs from the base game(with no voiced dialog btw) which is cool but theres only 8 of them and they go fairly quick with your auto leveled to 40+ characters (it took me about 2 hours to do them all). Then theres the "beach mode" puts all the playable characters into swimsuits which I think is just shrug some are good some bad some silly it sucks you can only switch it on or off no individual toggles. I dont think it was a bad deal I did really enjoy the epilogue defense map I just had hoped for more gameplay in it.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall enjoyable experience, in short if you want a game like Fire Emblem, play Fire Emblem as this is not a substitute despite sharing some base mechanics. (This was feedback done after 2 playthroughs on Hero mode)Pros- Nice overall visuals, especially for unit attacks. No lack of scantily clad female units if that is your thing.- Big Maps and a generally big unit cap is my preference, was nice to have that to differentiate from other games in the genre. - No need to worry about weapon durability! I was never a fan of this in other Strategy games, instead you simply focus on upgrading your weapons which provided different bonuses from higher damage, increased critical hits, accuracy or the all rounder.- Decent variety in missions and environments, from boss fights to rescue missions it felt like it was good at keeping the player on their toes without becoming  stale.- Plenty of options to build your characters the way you want, with the obvious caveat that some classes simply a better pick.- Instead of traditional supports, we have bonds. Bonds are separate and have no impact on unit usefulness, meaning you won't require extra grinding and add a bit of extra flavour/backstory which helps flesh out the story and characters. - After your first game clear you can make custom runs! I really love this idea as it makes the game feel fresh and helped to reduce some of the frustrations in game, things like buffing the amount of gold gained, buffed stats or increased enemy variety. - Item buffs felt well balanced since you were only allowed one. This made it so I could even out my characters weaknesses or change my tanks into mighty glaciers, felt pretty well thought out in general and would love to see this in more games. - Many viable healers, extra points for those who can also deal out good damage! Found a dedicated healer or a few hybrids worked surprisingly well.Cons- Frequent bugs were rather off putting considering how long this game has already been around for, leading to crashes/unusual things to occur such as unselectable characters or other strange interactions.- Sound design was hit or miss, some attacks were great while others felt like a whimper (also the rare bug which removed sound altogether). Also some musical variety in mission would have been very helpful, almost had to turn it off after my second run just from hearing the same theme over and over.- Tactical movement felt shallow. Something as simple as adding more environmental effects to encourage map interaction would go a long way.- Late game missions/map variety become quite stale. More specifically enemy types which sometimes had better stats than all but my strongest characters, making for a frustrating experience despite a reasonable difficulty curve or simply too many reinforcements encouraging save scumming or mass turtling.Pick the game up on sale if you found this helpful, hope they will continue to work on this game/add some map making tools.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, now that I've finished the game I can finally get my thoughts down. Warning, I will be referencing Fire Emblem. A lot. TL;DR for people scrolling, this game is most similar gameplay/map design-wise to Fire Emblem Fates Conquest, with some escape maps, some gimmick maps, and many route/defeat the boss maps. The class system is very customizable, with many combos and synergies with personal skills and varying play styles. If you like Fire Emblem, or want to get into it, this is a decent starting point with 3 difficulty options.Now for the meat of the review. I want to start off by saying a lot of the negative reviews for this game are somewhat confusing to me. I see complaints on there being no tutorial, but I think you need to be using 20% brain capacity to not understand what is going on, even as a new player, but especially as someone who has played even the first 5 maps of any FE game. I have also seen complaints of there being too many units thrown at you, and there being some difficulty choosing who to use, but you can see all character's base stats, growth rates, personal skills, and full customization of their promotions, even when they join at a level that they should already be promoted. This should not be something that anyone is losing hair over, it is the easiest time I have ever had deciding when to use a new unit, and bench others. One last complaint I have seen and will talk about is about the "encouraged use" of the bond system. There are no gameplay benefits of the bond system in this game, it is not forced upon the player AT ALL, unlike in other FE games where they provide the player better hit/dodge rates or damage. These complaints, as far as I'm concerned hold no water.There are definitely a few criticisms I have for the game, but widely I would consider this to be an above average Fire Emblem game if it had come out in that series. The story is serviceable, it's not great, but it's not bad either. I played the entire game on patch 1.0.7, and there were a few bugs, but none so bad that I would dwell on it, and the devs have been pumping out patches since launch, so I wouldn't lose sleep over it. The spritework is great, if you like the GBA Fire Emblem style, you will love this game's sprites. I live by the rule of cool, and I can tell you that the classes and class system are cool. The customization, the gameplay variance, the synergies you can make are all so cool, and I will definitely be experimenting in a future playthrough. The weapon system is a new take that I personally enjoyed, each character has 4 weapons (with no durability) that specializes in damage, crit, accuracy, or speed, and trade off different stats, and throughout the game you get tokens from killing enemies, or by buying them, and these tokens are used to upgrade your weapons. Also something that is nice, especially for those who have played Binding Blade, the main character isn't force deployed :) Irving has good growths, but mine got RNG screwed, so he got benched and he was never needed in gameplay thank god. You can also skip attacking animations, and fast forward enemy phase if that just isn't for you. Bond conversations are locked behind story beats, which really lets a character develop, unlike in Fire Emblem games (like Bernadetta learning to be confident, then in the next conversation with another character is fainting at the sight of them). This really let me get attached to some characters, or grow to like them a lot without the whiplash of trying to figure out if that was real development. Sloane's relationship with Monroe and Sophia, and Cia's with Bianca stand out to me.I don't think I need to go on any more. You should know if you would like this game by watching a few minutes of gameplay, or reading a few reviews, and if negative reviews are complicating things, just try to keep what I said in mind. This is an 8/10 Fire Emblem game, and if you're on the fence, wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game completely blind, hoping it would fill my need for Fire emblem content. To say the least, it did. I am now half way through the game, so some of this may be incomplete. The gameplay is very similar to the GBA era fire emblem games, with modern twists and a few changes. Lets start with the good.The gameplay is Fire Emblem. It is almost identical in combat, stats, etc. What makes this game different are the promotions. Each class feels unique and fun, providing different stat growths and skills to suit how you want to play and how the unit's stats are. Speaking of stats, the growths in this game are very high, so you will probably get many stats every level up, making it very satisfying seeing your units grow 5 or 6 stats per level up.The characters and art are both great. Each character feels unique, and their designs are memorable, except for a certain pair of green haired women. The comic-relief-y characters are funny, like best boy Benji, and the cool characters are... likable. The animations are all fun to watch, especially once you have promoted a few of your units. The story is basically any JRPG, an unlikely group of heroes band together to save the world or something. There is a small twist early on that makes it unique, and this game needs unique things. The story is nothing special, but its not terrible. Now it is time for the bad. First things first, you will notice the lack of any sort of tutorial for any of the functions that are unique to this game, be it class abilities (Phase, disarm, haste, etc), or the weapon system, so you will have to figure it out yourself. If you are new to this genre or have just never played a Fire Emblem game, and even if you have, you will get confused at one point or another. The interface in this game is not good. In between chapters, the menus are a mess. Managing items, bonds, upgrading weapons are all clunky. Items feel like an afterthought, since most are just some form of healing. There are stat-boosters to patch up your units' weaknesses, but they are both expensive and extremely rare. The unique items are Aspects, and they are fun and unique as each do something different, but are also very rare. The difficulty in this game feels nice, as even on normal mode, I do feel challenged to make the right decisions so as to not lose my units. Even without permadeath, losing one or two stats is enough of a deterrent. Enemies feel like they are getting stronger right along side you. The reason this is a negative, however, is because of the way maps are layed out. The map designs in this game are bad. They are just terrible. It feels like every enemy unit was placed in just the right spot and in the right amount to where you can't turtle, but you can't rush because you will probably be overwhelmed either way. The first couple maps are okay, but as the game progresses it gets worse and worse. All that and I haven't mentioned a single bug, which this game has plenty. I did not want to talk about this too much, since they have been updating constantly trying to patch them, but it cannot be ignored. Most are minor things, but when one of my units becomes a statue so I can't control it, therefore being unable to end my turn without doing it manually, and am able to move other units onto the same tile, it gets very frustrating. Overall, I cannot recommend the current game to anyone that has not played Fire Emblem, and even then I would warn them. That being said, I am going to finish the game, so take that how you will.

Despite its blatant inspirations, I believe this game will be a positive experience for most players.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall its an enjoyable tactics game. The classes look cool, and being able to develop units the way you want is nice. Like all of these games some units seem to excel no matter what and some get left behind. A big cast of characters may bring some replayability as well as trying units different ways. I liked the look of the game and the splash art for the characters are well done if you like that kind of thing.Music is average with a few tracks above average. Story is basically non-existant, which is also something this type of game often falls into. These games could use some real choice on what to do for added character development. Every character in this is forgettable as is the world. Theres a bond's system where two character talk back and forth (very little voice in this game, its text, which is fine) but unless you care about them you can just ignore it, which is what i quickly ended up doing. Some of the characters are very annoying which made me not use them.The game got surprisingly glitchy for me near the end. Units sharing the same square, characters attacking more than they should, 100% counters that dont go off. Saw a few bosses have more hp than their max. Happened enough chapters over enough days that its clearly part of the game and I didn't just get unlucky.So some bad, but more good than bad. It's got replayability and different difficulty modes if your looking for more challenge, but i'd say the game is about a 16-20 hour game from start to finish, which is fair for the price. The sequel is due out this year (2024) and there was enough here to justify buying the next one for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: For the first few hours it seemed interesting but then it went downhill. I thought the first few maps were basic because it was early game but it turned out that the rest of the maps would be similarly (and in some cases more so) simple. It didn't take long until I felt as though engaging with the battles was unimportant and that just throwing my stronger units out without any thought became an acceptable strategy.The combat mechanics are simple which is fine, but games like this and Fire Emblem require solid map design to make the game interesting. Unfortunately, Dark Deity's maps are really under-designed. For example, not much is done to counter turtling and side objectives largely don't exist. Side objectives would be hard to implement anyway since automatically recruited party members and the streamlined weapon system means that there isn't much to reward you with for pursuing them. Maps really needed to have some sort of events occurring on them; see Vestaria Saga for an example. I don't think a lot of these issues can just be patched out, unless the developers re-do large portions of the game.Gameplay aside, I liked the spritework for characters though the maps themselves were oddly much lesser quality compared to them. The character portraits looked great though some might say that they look weird alongside the pixel art; I personally don't care too much about that. Music was okay; a track or two stood out to me. I didn't care for the plot.I know that game development is challenging, especially as an indie team, so it's not fun to say that I don't recommend it; however, sugarcoating it helps no one. I'm still curious about future games from these developers to see if their next project learns from this one. Good luck!
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Deity

_childDocuments_.review: For SRPG and Fire Emblem fans, after my first clear, I would recommend Dark Deity, but more for the gameplay than the story.Pros: Nice combat system, viable cast of characters, weapon and class customization allows you to fit teams to your playstyle, cool GBA style animations.Cons: Story feels kind of disjointed with weird pacing and a plot that really doesn't explain itself well. Some classes are weak or can really fit poorly for a character without any real chance to rectify it.For an indie studio in its first offering, it's a pretty solid game. What it lacks in writing and flashy effects, though, it makes up for in just solid SRPG gameplay. For people who are used to Fire Emblem, this will feel familiar and scratch that itch. The core is solid here and if they went on to develop a sequel or other similar SRPGs in the future, I think they could make something pretty special.

detailed_description: Under grim moonlight, the fierce clayborne warrior Grey Irma battles, driven by a lonesome purpose: Find the Sculptor, and unravel the mystery of her existence. Push the limits of your combat skills, and master new abilities to progress through an unforgiving nonlinear 2D world. Face off against the relentless darkness that seeks to destroy you. In Moonscars, every death is a lesson learnt—and as you overcome each challenge, new truths will be revealed. Before you rise, you first must fall. Mold yourself into a master warrior through a cycle of trial and triumph. Explore the shadows and secrets concealed in the moonlight of a painterly nonlinear 2D realm marred by desperation and despair. Sharpen your skills and reflexes in challenging, action-packed combat. Slash and parry with your sword, wield unique special weapons, and command powerful Witchery. Unearth a strange, dark fantasy tale filled with twists and intricate worldbuilding. Seek the truth of your creation and be rewarded. Bear witness to tales and memories of betrayal, suffering, and revenge as Grey Irma and her fellow beings of flesh and clay seek truth and purpose.

_childDocuments_.review: It blows my mind that a skeleton crew dev team churned out this outstanding game. I could ramble forever about Moonscars, but I'll breakdown what I really liked about this and list where I feel the game has opportunities for improvement:- The art style, overall theme, and gameplay mechanics are clearly influenced by titles like Blasphemous, Salt & Sanctuary, Bloodborne, and any of the Dark Souls games. I love all of these titles, so I felt right at home as soon as I jumped into gameplay.- The combat is simple yet addicting, and accompanied by a hell of a Witchery skill tree. You can get by without relying or investing much into it, but it will make things much easier for you unless you want the added challenge.- Special weapons granted to the player are frequently changed up. Even if the same special weapon is offered to a user as it was previously, it won't always grant the same bonus as it did before. I can see some people not being a fan of this, but I personally like the idea of having to adapt to different combat styles.- The user interface is very intuitive and accompanied by brief tutorial prompts both in-game and through pop-ups with easy to understand instructions. While I didn't need to rely on these instructions, this is a very nice thing to have for users who do. - Punishing mechanics are included for death, such as lost currency, your health/ichor bonus being nullified until your special weapon is replaced, and enemies becoming stronger, which is the "Ravenous Moon" phase. This is reversible at the expense of a special type of currency or after killing a boss, but on the flipside, not reversing this results in better drops. If you're like me, you'll probably intentionally let death happen just to crank up the difficulty and rewards. It also affects any active quests you might have, allowing them to progress for better or worse. Who knows! You'll have to find out. ;)- Most of the bosses are a lot fun, especially the endgame boss. I was only a little underwhelmed by one of them, but I didn't see it as a concern. This can always be improved after release anyway.*UPDATE 10/1/22: Did another playthrough of this game post release and the underwhelming boss fight in question was vastly improved and a lot of fun this time around. Nicely done!- Accessibility could use a little more work by adding custom binds for controllers (keyboard users are fine here). To be fair, I'm only speaking for other players; I personally didn't have any issues with the predetermined controller binds and thought they were perfect, but I understand that other players have their preferences. In the meantime, I believe you can *kind of* work around this using Steam's controller configuration tool, so don't let the lack of this feature dissuade you from trying the game. I'm sure this will be addressed sometime after release.- The story comes off as cryptic and hard to follow. At the same time, this may not be a bad thing as it invites the community to make their own interpretations to connect the dots and allow for interesting discussions, so my opinion on this may change over time.- This might not be a popular opinion, but I think the game overall seems to lean a little on the easy side, even with punishing mechanics in place. That isn't to say I blazed through the game as if it was devoid of challenges. I'm only saying this because it didn't take much time to predict how all enemies function, and I was able to complete the game multiple times while sticking exclusively to melee combat without the use of items and *very* little use of Witchery. The game is still fun and challenging, but maybe don't expect it to be as hard as other masochistic games you've played.- Related to the above point, despite the sizable Witchery skill tree and various items included in the game, I didn't feel like there was much reason to use them unless I absolutely had to, like using Witchery to open certain walls or attacking enemies that have high defense against every other attack. This also might be related to my point above about difficulty, so take this more as an FYI rather than criticism.- Subsequent playthroughs of the game felt short once I had the whole game mapped out in my head, especially with the absence of a New Game+ mode. I understand that such a small dev team can't be expected to create large scale games, so I don't really hold this against them. I'm just hungry for more content, but that's what post-release support is for. Maybe we'll see additional content and/or a New Game+ mode!I've had a lot of fun late night gaming with Moonscars, and even after completing the game in its entirety more than once there's something about the charm of this game that keeps me coming back for more. The dev team really knocked it out of the park and I'm hoping they'll be creating additional content. I refuse to believe this is where they'll leave it at.I was fortunate to receive this game for free and have access before release, but I can say with my chest that I would have zero regrets spending $20 on this. So, I'll be hooking up some friends with Moonscars instead. I strongly recommend this game, especially if you own a Steam Deck; it plays VERY well on that platform and is a must have for your on-the-go gaming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: To anyone skeptical of this game, read the patch notes, they did a lot to make the game feel more intuitive. Also I haven't experienced a single glitch in my entire time playing so far.Adjusting to Moonscars' zippy and frantic combat took a minute, it's a big shift in gear from similar titles. A lot of encounters can be stressful in a way that's fun as you have to juggle two or three different enemies' attack patterns to avoid getting dying within a few seconds. Just be patient and keep at it. Take a break if you need to. There are maybe twenty unique enemies at most, but that's all this game really needs for its length. It's taken me eleven hours to get to the end, but I could see myself doing a second run and cutting that time down by at least four hours.What this game does so well is it gives you some great incentives for fighting enemies at all, which is the Spite System. Basically for every couple of enemies you kill, you pause and select one of three perks such as increased healing percentage, or the chance of a critical hit, or reduced cost for using ichor (magic). Also you need to engage with enemies because every hit gains you back ichor, which means you can manage groups better and heal more often. You're a glass cannon in this game and it's all high-risk, high-reward. And that's in addition to being able to upgrade magic spells used and also pay a gland at the mirror checkpoints to get more ichor with each hit from enemies or have them drop more bone powder (money). I read some reviews saying that glands were almost non-existent, and a few are definitely hidden, but I never felt short of them at any point. Looking back I wish I had spent more of them. Also fast travel between the mirrors is immediately available, so any chance you may need to backtrack makes things a breeze. Other than items, there's no real secrets in terms of weapons or areas, just a few quests. This game's very meat and potatoes.Movement in this game is quick but intuitive. There aren't any movement upgrades other than one, but that's okay because it's all you really need. Also a tip for players - to go farther in the air, dash, then slash. The timing is extremely tight but you can make it work in the Earth Bowels to get an upgrade early. And if you can survive the brutal enemy onslaught.The game's art direction is serviceable, but I feel like with its impressionist inspiration that it could have gone further, a little more color to differentiate the biomes. The story makes it clear that this is a dark and depressing world, sure, but even The Last Faith, another game like this with a muted palette, had more color. The Depths would have been a good place to put in some autumn foliage. The Apex could have had a golden or orange glow from catching all that sunlight. Just a little something to make the areas pop more.So yeah, Moonscars is a tough but rewarding experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't mind the negative reviews; if you are into metroidvanias, you should enjoy it.Yes, the game has some minor issues I see people complaining about in their reviews: there are "parry-me" telegraphs which are a bit confusing, most of the time, like for lunging enemies; you are better off just timing when the attack arrives on you. However, I recommend that you rely more on dash-dodging, except for some heavy-armored slow enemies, because they are more predictable, and the high damage output of the counter-attack saves you a lot of time while draining their larger health bar.There is a roguelite mechanic, too, with stacking boosts, which unlock after you defeat a certain number of monsters, and goes away when you die. As you stack buffs, it triggers a mode where the Moon gets angry at you (yes), and enemies are harder to kill. Problem is: it won't go back if you die. You must spend "glands" in a ritual to make it easier again, or you defeat a boss in this mode. I think those mechanics could be optional, but they don't ruin the experience, because they do not raise the dificulty that much: you just meet more of the "angry" variety of enemies on your way.Special attacks could be more devastating, because they are hard to hit and too risky to cast: the nice animations come with a somewhat long priming till the part when it really deals damage. Magic is okay, though, but costly enough to remind you that the main character is primarily a sword-maiden.That said, it is challenging, the visuals are very nice, the story is compelling, and none of the said "defects" was trouble enough to get in the way of the fun (which is what matters, after all, right?), and I am having a very nice time playing. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: A visually impressive action-focused platformer marred by several design decisions that are as inexplicable as they are terrible.  Not just "You died, so now you have to pay to go back to your regular difficulty" which you can read about on the forums, but also:* inconsistent / poor signalling of what can be parried and when (the timing is generous IF you ignore the thing the game tells you to pay attention to), * spells that would be cool if you could cast more than one every third enemy (and if healing didn't take your "fresh" mana first even though there's a mechanic to allow you spend it on spells and then use it to heal), * windup for spells and special attacks that cost you more in vulnerability than they give in status effects or damage, * combat that leans far too hard on a simple just-frame parry (seriously, 90% of the damage you'll do throughout the game is going to come from this), * forced switching of your special weapon and penalties for having one you prefer, * checkpoints just far enough away from boss fights to annoy,...it's a death by a thousand self-inflicted cuts.

_childDocuments_.review: Sorry, devs, I just can't recommend Moonscars.Let me start with the positive stuff, first. The game is very pretty, in a gloomy souls-like kinda way. That won't surprise anyone who's on the page right now, because the trailer does a fantastic job of showing that off. Secondly, the music is good! It does a fantastic job of reinforcing the atmosphere that the visuals present. I especially love the various boss fight themes. Thirdly, the animations on things are fantastic. Just... yeah, I like them a lot!Seriously, kudos for presentation.The problem, though, is that this game is frustrating to play. When you start moving around and swinging your sword, it feels great! You think, yeah, this is gonna be a good time! But then the infinite annoyances start to pop up.Why can I not slash up or down? Why does every witchery use your entire freaking  sorry ICHOR supply? And why does it take 234523 sword strikes to refill the damn thing? Why is the parry window shorter than the halflife of a virtual particle? Why can attacks damage stuff behind the attacker, but parries can't parry behind the parry-er? Why bother giving me health increases when I still die in like two attacks anyway? Why do witchery upgrades make the witcheries cost soooo much? Why can I buy an upgrade that makes the witchery too expensive for me to even cast, thus making it ENTIRELY UNUSABLE until I find an upgrade to my Ichor????The list goes on and on, dear reader, but I'll cut it there and address something that really damns it, in my eyes.Here it is: Everything in Moonscars is a negative feedback loop. Take damage? Better heal, which uses up your Ichor. Ichor is required for using witcheries (spells), so every time you heal, you lose access to your most damaging abilities (especially since, as I said above, most witcheries take HUGE portions of the ichor bar). Use some ichor on witcheries? The thing fills up so slowly you won't be casting one again for a long time, and doesn't fill up at all unless you hit enemies or, occasionally, certain walls.Moonscars expects perfection from you, and will harshly punish ANYTHING less than 100% perfection. That might sound like standard souls-like fare to you, but it isn't. Sure, Dark/Demon's Souls reduced your health when you died, and you could easily get stunlocked if you weren't careful, and other stuff like that. But imagine if casting Dark Souls' sorceries required your estus! Imagine if whenever you died, all the enemies got several times more difficult to kill (read: get extremely spongey). Imagine if half the enemies in the final area were mostly immune to anything but your estus-eating special attacks!!Please do not mistake me here: I am not unhappy that the game is hard. I am unhappy that even when my reflexes and parry timing and dodging improved, the tiniest mistake would begin a horrible downward spiral as my resources vanished and all the enemies got tougher.After all that, I could probably have pulled through for an interesting story. But the story suffers from the same issues as the main game: intriguing ideas, good basic material, flawed and frustrating execution. Irma's voice/tone is all over the place, everyone speaks in ridiculous circles like they're desperate to hide things from us, the players. And it's not like other souls games, with sparse, cryptic dialogue. Some of these conversations go on for lines and lines and I cannot tell wtf they're on about. Words are given incredible significance ("cleft," for instance), but very little is done to actually describe what the significant word means. There are a ton of language errors, too. Honestly, it feels like a bad translation. I hope that's what it is, and that the writing is better in whatever the original language is.Regardless, I couldn't really get into the story either.So yeah, can't recommend. Sorry again.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been browsing a lot trying to find a metroidvania in the style of Blasphemous, and Moonscars is the closest you'll get!(seriously, we need more pixel art metroidvanias in the vein of Blasphemous and Moonscars!)It's quite impressive how Black Mermaid came out of nowhere and dropped this amazing game.Snappy combat, fluid animations, beautiful scenery, lovely ambiance tracks, challenging encounters, enjoyable progression, a dark story and plenty of powers, charms and abilities to play with. Keyboard & mouse support is also great which plays a big role in offering an enjoyable experience to the player.The only setbacks I'd say are some of the writing style choices alongside the length of the game being on the shorter side and some abilities being way more useful than others. The game also happens to stutter a bit after launch, but this doesn't last long and the devs are probably already working on an update for that.All in all, I'd say this game is an absolute must if you've liked Blasphemous and are looking for something similar.Thank you for this gem, Black Mermaid, I hope to see more from you in the future :)⬛	grind⬜	missables⬛	highly difficult⬜	multiple playthroughs⬜	guide recommended⬛	players needed⬛	online play

_childDocuments_.review: Eeeh, I'm having a hard time recommending this one. Don't get me wrong, there's a ton to like here, but if you're not interested in a lot of detail; The game's fun, the story is poorly told and the game doesn't really reinvent itself past the first hour. If the first hour interests you and you can live with that, go right ahead.The game looks gorgeous and the animation and art style is phenomenal. Combat and animation is so impactful and satisfying. It is easily the game's greatest point. The art and the combat together just makes it feel GOOD to fight.The story...doesn't grip me. It feels like there's a good story in there, but it's so poorly told through obscure nonsense-language and overdone mystery that you have absolutely zero chance of putting any of it together. I assume that if you ever get to the end, you might get some form of explanation, but I am just done with the story. I stopped caring 4-5 hours in because the game just wastes my time with every NPC. One of the worst offenders was Wanda. Everyone tells you "GO TO WANDA! SHE HELP!" and you get there and she just vomits pointless dialogue at you about how her realm is so peaceful and you go: "ok? And?"That's about the point where I decided that if the game is going to waste my time with its story, I'm not going to bother. Rather quickly after that I found that while the combat *is* great, it doesn't reinvent itself. The pseudo-roguelike elements of switching up your build all the time also gets tiresome after a while. I feel like if the game was 8 hours long, tops, it would've worked. But it just drags on and on and on with the same core gameplay loop and it gets old. For as great as the combat and gameplay is, it really does get old.I love the art style, combat is great, bosses are overall SUPER cool. I had a lot of fun with this, but after eight hours I have no desire to finish it. The story is just far too poorly told for me to give the slightest about any of the story or the characters. It's just "artsy obtuseness" because "Dark Souls", I guess. Look, Dark Souls had great gameplay. What Dark Souls *didn't* have was good storytelling. Stop copying that!In summary: Great combat and mechanics, fun for about 6 hours romp. Forget the story.Addendum:After another couple of hours I have some more thoughts to add. The combat doesn't really get better. If anything, the combat gets difficult enough that the design of the game starts showing its flaws. The controls aren't precise enough to be truly satisfying. Too often you get animation locked for too long, causing a death when it could've been prevented with just tighter controls and less reliance on "I am now stuck in this animation for six business days".The new weapons added in the patch are kinda meh. Especially the Guantlet is just pure, solidified garbage. It pulls enemies to you and then punches them away. Neat for gaining space, but what they don't tell you is that it has no stun or even an interrupt. If an enemy starts doing a combo while you use the gauntlet, you *will* pull them into your face as they swing and it doesn't get interrupted by the gauntlet pull. You are essentially giving the enemy free hits on your face.The story doesn't get any better. It's very clumbsily told and relies and insane amount on pure nonsense mysterybabble. The events are completely impossible to follow, even after the ending, because it's told in such a gibberish way. This game tries really hard to be Dark Souls and fails miserably in the storytelling department.Once you bone out the details of the story, it is very much an average grade "plot twist" kind of story with zero interesting twists. You really don't care in the slightest for the story by the time you get to the end.The game also suffers a lot from backtracking syndrome. You spend a lot of time running headless around, not knowing what to do or replaying the same sections over and over because the mirrors are 20 billions miles apart.As for the Wanda event: Turns out, you're supposed to kill her. Nothing in the scene indicates that. She's a friendly person and there appears to be no animosity between the characters whatsoever, but apparently, you're supposed to kill her. Uh..ok then. The twists at the end make me laugh because they were blindingly obvious and filled with tropes.My original verdict stands: If you want a fun combat romp for a couple of hours, sure, get this. Otherwise: don't bother. It's an average, or even slightly below average, metroidvania. Great art style, great atmosphere, good combat that unfortunately doesn't quite hold up for the entire game and a story that is obtuse, filled with snooty NPCs that tell you nothing and a protagonist that is really, really hard to connect with. The story is, by far, this game's weakest part. The rest is great, good or passable. The story is ... not.Art style: 9/10Audio: 8/10Music: Forgettable/10Combat Mechanics: 8/10Game mechanics: 7/10Story: 2/10

_childDocuments_.review: Moonscars was a flavorful metroidvania, which let its aesthetics overtake some more critical components. While I enjoyed my 7ish hour playthrough of the game, some detailed notes below for those who are on the fence and have a few minutes to spare.  Grim and beautiful, a visual treat. The game's art direction is reminiscent of impressionist water colour, with a heavy use of red, white, and black. What I really appreciated is that this art direction bled (literally lmao) into the story beats of the game. From the first five minutes, you can tell if the art direction will please, or leave you feeling ambivalent. A highlight for me was the swirling shadows of the mirrors which serve as bonfires / ways to return to the workshop (hub). There is a lot to enjoy in terms of weird fiction in Moonscars; and this fiction translates well into the mechanics of the game, most notably the way in which ichor, doppelgangers, the melding machine, and the mirrors function. The first few hours of the game feel very disorienting as you come to terms with what the game's core loop will be, which mirrors the mental state of the protagonist. While the writing itself sometimes drops the ball with how heavy-handed it is, the implementation of those ideas into game mechanics felt very fun to experience. Combat in Moonscars is deceptively complex, given how simple it can appear at first. You alternate between fast and heavy attacks with a single weapon (a longsword), and eventually unlock a secondary special weapon. These are varied, and each apply a unique debuff. I suggest trying out a few of them to see which you prefer before committing. Note that it is always possible, from a mirror, to reset your special weapon with an in-game item (gland). Apart from weapons, customisation for combat comes from three slots for talismans (which grant various buffs to the character), and from 'witchery', spells which rely on ichor (a rage resource accumulated in combat). Ichor was, in my opinion, the best variation this game provided on other games in the genre. As it served as the resource for both healing and for casting witchery, it's implementation rewarded aggressive gameplay which either relied heavily on self-healing, or on proactive use of spells.The spells themselves were varied, and could all be obtained by about the mid-point of the game. This allowed me to experiment with them early, but to finesse a build before getting to the final act of the game, which I found rewarding.  No surprises given the art direction / graphical conceits, but the game ran smooth as butter for me. Since this is a sticking point for some players, I thought I'd mention it in passing. This was a real mixed bag, which I'll lump together. There weren't too many enemy types to speak of, and fewer still which felt fun to fight against. I feel like the developers relied a little too much on a game mechanic which gave enemies three variations on difficulty. As an example, you have your normal little quarter-back guy who damages you with a tackle, and he can appear as (normal) -> (enraged) -> (gilded). The last of these categories, gilded, was reserved primarily for the last third of the game and was particularly vulnerable to witchery. I can appreciate the amount of work that went into some of these enemies (my favorite being the necromancer, adorned in candles, that could heal its allies, but also summon some mid-fight), but the over-reliance on scaling for the same enemy designs left me a little underwhelmed. As for bosses, I'd mention that there are very few (about five in my run). The first of these is particularly underwhelming, so I'd caution against thinking that 'it' represents the sum of the boss experiences in the game. While I did find the bosses easy on the whole, the second-act bosses in the depths  were my favourite. The former of the two limited the space of your fight for the first time, while the second introduced a mechanic which drew out the fight, forcing you to rely on learning it's (admittedly quite simple) attack pattern. Rewarding on the whole.I think the game's story, and the writing in general of Moonscars, could have used a heavier edit. It sometimes read like a first draft which, while often engaging, sometimes spiralled into overly self-indulgent monologues. I happen to be a sucker for the moody themes of self-loathing and sentience, but the writing often felt lost while trying to convey a mood rather than a cohesive story. This is a shame because, as noted above re: Eldritch elements, the disorienting aspect of the writing felt purposeful at first, but quickly became overdone and lost any sort of impact. There are only so many times a protagonist can come to realisations about the world, and contradict themselves in the process, before it starts to feel a little lazy (i.e., if everything is a plot-twist, nothing is). Personal high-points for me were Etalag (a semi-helpful guiding spirit), and the moon priestess, whose sound cues and banter with the protagonist were particularly well crafted.Going hand in hand with the above were some wild fluctuations in the tone of the writing. While most of the writing was committed to reading like american gothic fiction, some encounters were broken by some strange word choices which could have used revision. One example being a noble character claiming to be the . The incongruity often felt unintentional, but unfortunately took you out of the fiction crafted by the devs. I think it was all the more frustrating when it happened given how visually consistent Moonscars was. Some later text revisions could address the above.  Look listen. I understand that the map's design was probably limited by the art style and graphical conceits by the developers, but a little more information would have gone a long way. I enjoy getting lost in these types of games, and part of my enjoyment of metroidvania's is searching for hidden rooms and trying to make a mental map which is more helpful than what the game provides. However, there is a lack of polish which could have been addressed by the developers in this case, even if they intended for the player to make good mental notes. One example being that the walls in the game are not all represented the same way in the map, which can lead to confusion as you attempt to find the next zone to explore. Like with the editing of the script of the game, Moonscars would have benefited from a few more months of QA. Two separate bosses soft-locked during my play-through, which was unfortunate. Given the lack of difficulty the bosses pose, it never felt like a big ask to do them again when it happened, but I can see players who struggle to kill them really being frustrated by these locks. While I enjoyed being able to place markers for later exploration, the tool bugged on several occasions, making it impossible to add or remove markers until I restarted the game. These are all elements which could be addressed in later patches, and I think the importance you'll give to it comes down to how much you rely on information being communicated to you through a map. ----

_childDocuments_.review: Outside of three or so bugs that disrupted some gameplay moments, the game itself is incredibly solid. There is just enough uniqueness to Moonscars that it doesn't scream "I'm a clone" of X or Y, etc.The pros:-The art is just incredible. I mean really - wow. So gorgeous and pretty dang varied.-The combat feels great - although it does not quite match Kratos' axe or The Penitent One's sword from Blasphemous, Grey Irma's sword feels great to swing and the hits feel responsive.-Outside of a few seconds after loading in, I had 0 performance issues.-Bosses/enemies are creatively designed.-There is a good amount of enemy variety for a game that takes 10 or so hours to beat.-The concept for the story is unquestionably creative.-Something about the game is addicting and makes you want to keep playing.The cons:-The map needs markers. Badly. It can be very difficult to tell what has been left unexplored.-Some bosses do a little too much damage. Other than that, for experienced gamers this game does not trend on the difficult side.-There were a handful of bugs that prevented me from accessing certain areas.-Navigation issues left me backtracking more than I'd like.-The special moves felt too slow to use in combat with practicality.-The parry, although satisfying, felt too risky to use in challenging combat scenarios over the dash.-Aspects of the story are incredibly cryptic, and certain lines of dialogue appear out of place, particularly in Moonscars' unquestionably dark world.For its current price, Moonscars is worth it and a must-buy, especially if you are waiting for big releases in the second half of October. I can easily see myself doing another playthrough of the game in the future.8.2/10

_childDocuments_.review: It really pains me to not recommend this game. Moonscars has everything that can win me over easily: a great artstyle and atmosphere, satisfying combat, and a quite interesting story. Yet, the game tries to do a lot of things and excel at none. Most of the mechanics in game are either not well-developed or not fully evolve to their potentials.It`s really rare, especially metroidvania, for a game to let you have a rather "functional" character early. I am talking ten to twenty minutes into the game. Our protagonist can wall jump from the start which is quite a traversal skill in metroidvania genre. The game then immediately introduces Witchery to not only aid you in battles, but it also is a tool for you open up some hidden path. Usually abilities like these are unlocked after about 1 to 2 hours into the game, but Moonscars does it quite differently. This design simply elevates the first level of the game. It is fun to playthrough, and it coincides with a lot of the tutorials to make learn the mechanics easy and fun.→Boss fights are interesting.→The artstyle is terrific.→I think the overall story is quite interesting.→: Albeit basic, Moonscars does follow the principle of metroidvania decently to say the least. Plus Super Dash is fun to use and great way to traverse the level faster.→:Other aspects of metroidvania is lacking. I am not against short metroidvania, but you have to really make the experience exciting to offset that opinion. With only two kinds of ability-gating(One great, the other is just a key in other format), it's hard to justify the satisfaction of going back and finding new things. Also the map is not inter-connected, at least not in a good way.→: I like the Witchery and Special Attacks. They have good animations and are great tools to make combat encounters interesting. Witchery can be swapped freely, and Special Attack  is associated with one of the mechanics of the game I quite like.→: The issue of the two is the fact that they are not well-developed. The upgrade system does not specify how you've upgraded them, just a roman numeral of 1, 2, and 3 after the name of the skill. I wish the game can do more than just pump up the damage number and actually give variants to individual skill upgrades.→: I adore this feature and wonder why there aren`t many games doing this kind of hybrid feature. Basically the longer you can go without dying, the stronger you can be. This feature creates a simple yet strong dynamic -- do you want to go straight through obstacles, or do you want to go do a little farming and come back slightly stronger?→: I think the game is way too conservative about the upgrades you can get, and too little, too. Surely it`s hard to argue with +10% crit chance and -10% Witchery cost, but I still wish to see more direct buff or some situational buff that can be fun to play around.→: Arena-style fight is inherently fun and challenging. It`s a good way to test your skills how to fight against multiple enemies at once and how to deal with special enemies in a group.→: Yet when you have to deal with the same kinds of fight four more times in a row, the experience soon becomes tedious. Late-to-end game is full of these fights, which easily make me think that these parts of level design are hastily and poorly done.中文小簡評→美術氣氛都很到位的類銀河系惡魔城。→開場主角就擁有一定的技能，能讓開頭玩得盡興。→王戰很有趣。→故事我覺得滿有趣的。→許多類銀河系惡魔城該有的特色沒有好好發揮。→技能升級只有傷害提高而已，沒有任何衍生變化。→偽Rouglite升級機制很有想法，可惜選項過於稀少，簡單保守。→後期關卡用太多鬥競場型戰鬥，感覺草草了事。

_childDocuments_.review: Moonscars is a Metroidvania with heavy souls-like elements developed by Black Mermaid (3 developpers). You'll take control of Grey Irma, a warrior made of clay and bones, who must track down her maker, named the Sculptor. -A memorable MV/souls-like experience. Nothing "new" to the genre except maybe the "Ravenous Moon".-The plots and characters develop quite a bit throughout the game. Rich in dialogue.-Graphics won't please everyone but I absolutely loved it. Wish there was more animations.-Sounds and musics are on point. Always felt like it was the perfect vibe for the game.-It was definitely on the harder side of things. The average players will struggle.-Except for a few exceptions, it was linear. You won't get lost.-The game length is about 8-15 hours id say.-There's a few steam's achievements and the game is fun enough that you might want to repeat it.-Despite the game being on the shorter side, $20 for a gem like this is totally worth it.-Controls were ok and on the slower side of things. 'Sluggish' but suited the theme of the game.-Combat Mechanics was complex for the genre. Dodge, dash, parries, spells, attack combos etc...Satisfying-There wasn't "a lot" of different enemies. That being said, they were all different and unique.-Handful of bosses but they were challenging and had a wide range of attacks. Some had a second phase.-There was a luxurious amount of save points and fast travel throughout, making navigation a breeze.-Handful of Biomes and they were not that distinct from each others.-Not to much exploration to do, by playing the story line you'll see everything you need to see.-There was quite a lot of collectibles considering the game being relatively short.-A few secret passages here and there but nothing to pull your hair.-There was no puzzle solving that I witnessed.-Platforming wise it was generic. Anybody can do it.-A good variety of rpg elements, skill upgrades, equipment, different weapons...*Overall, I had an absolute blast playing this game. You can't power through the game or smash buttons. The ravenous moon add a great difficulty challenge but is optional. The only "icks" I have that I can recall is that there was nowhere to see your completion %. A preference thing. Also, I thought it was silly to sell all these items when you organically find them in your playthrough...Heavy on the souls-like portion in every aspects, I enjoyed it but it won't please to everyone. I wish the game was 2-3 time longer with a bit more exploration/back tracking to do.-Also, there's a cat in the game, so play it.My Ranked list of Metroidvanias Played at the time of this Review :Aeterna NoctisSuper MetroidCastle Vania : Symphony of the NightBlasphemous 1Hollow KnightProntyEnder LilliesMoonscarAxiom Verge

_childDocuments_.review: Moonscars seems to try to create a compelling but mysterious world, like many of its apparent inspirations, while also trying to introduce some unique mechanics. Unfortunately, neither aspect seems to land quite right. Probably responsible for piquing a lot of people's interest in the game. Similar in style to Blasphemous, but gets somewhat monotonous. Told in bits and pieces, often in awkward terms and phrasing; I'm sure some of this is for style, but a lot of the awkwardness is doubtlessly from the translation.In games like these, you sometimes don't see a character for a huge stretch of the game, only to find them again and have a development revealed to you by as little as a few lines of text or environmental clues, yet they can still be quite compelling. Ultimately, I can't say Moonscars really managed to make me feel this for its characters - not even the protagonist. You have a sword, you swing it 3 times to combo. You can parry most enemy attacks to get a damaging counter in, or you can always dodge them and the others that you can't parry.The game will give you three special attacks to pick from at certain intervals: you can take one of them. Generally speaking, you will have only one special attack. Unfortunately, they're all very slow, so not as worth using as they might otherwise appear.You also have magic. Some enemies need to be hit with magic once to take any damage, and are awkward to hit without certain spells, so I'd recommend getting a few different ones. For some reason, you can only equip 2 spells at once, though you can pause to swap them out freely. It's just slightly cumbersome to have to go into the menu to do this. Some of the magic summons minions to fight for you, while others are AoE blasts or projectiles. You can walljump or dash in the air.  Lacking some variety; there aren't a huge number of enemies, and the game uses doppelganger "minibosses" for unlocking fast travel points. (Doppelgangers share your moveset, but aren't incredibly smart about using any of it.) The environments aren't incredibly varied either. Moonscars has a few systems that relate to you dying.  ashes(/"souls"/money) you collect are dropped on death, and can be reclaimed by returning to where you died. Ashes are used to buy a few items, or to unlock new magic.  Dying too much will turn the moon red, which increases enemy strength, but also causes them to drop more ashes. You can use rare consumables to turn the moon back to normal.  "spite" level-ups grant bonuses to stats, but are lost on death. If you die to a boss, you have to grind a little if you want to fight it in peak condition again, essentially. Other similar games do it better. I'd wait for a sale or give it a pass.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a husk of a good game here but it's really held back by some really unpolished aspects and utterly bizarre mechanics.In general, there's a very flimsy attempt with all the games UX elements like the menus, the HUD, etc, but it also just feels like a very unfinished gaming experience. The beginning exposition both in narrative and onboarding feels cobbled together. A lot of games combine show and tell elements with their onboarding, whereas Moonscars either just drops a really vague hint text box item, or just leaves a really important item like health upgrades in the middle of a nothing area with zero fanfare. It's like it knows to include all these core formulas but has no idea that you actually have to provide some kind of meaningful interactive exposition to them.The combat is pretty fine, but all the other elements of gameplay and mechanics make no sense. The magic system feels utterly pointless as you rarely ever have the opportunity to use it. The method of MP regeneration is really dumb, and it's tied to your heals too. It's like they wanted to take the risk/reward aspect of Bloodborne by having to hit enemies to regen health, while also making it the same mechanic to use your magic. Utterly daft, especially when you realize the entire skill tree is Witchery based, and the game has the temerity to tell you that certain enemies require witchery to be defeated, when you can literally use a spell every 30 seconds. Stupid.Same applies to the special weapons. You get them, but then they disappear, but you can obtain them again? There's also this really weird bonus system that resets after every death/warp. Some kinda roguelite insertion when it's really not applicable. Beyond the meaningless Witchery skill tree there's little character progression beyond upgrades you find in the wild.The moon system requiring an item to revert? These same items are used elsewhere for other purchases.Just some really, really whack game design choices across the board

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot imagine a game that hates its players more than this one. I just can't recommend Moonscars.I respect most of what it's doing; the combat is clean, the animations are crisp, sound effects crunchy, atmosphere is impeccable. Cycling between tough mobs to afford rituals/upgrades and setting the moon back to normal, cool idea.The secondary weapons randomized as you explore lets you mix and match, plus there's always the option to reroll at the mirror if you do some farming.Spite levels granting you some bonuses as you rack up kill chains.The bad: frequently traps you in rooms that strip freedom of movement and verticality, the boss rooms especially, where you're expected to keep track of three different attacks at once, and you're surrounded on all sides by (not always) insta-death spikes. The walk-backs to the bosses are TERRIBLE (2nd boss not so much, 3rd one is THE WORST I'VE EVER SEEN), often taking you on circuitous routes, especially since you frequently need to offer resources so that you don't make it to the boss room with 1 hp and a dream.Speaking of bosses, losing your Spite levels is also a crusher. I want to keep trying at the boss so that I can learn it, I don't want to be forced between choosing bashing my head at it without any upgrades and farming for 30 minutes so I can go back and attempt it with upgrades that I may lose because I didn't even get to see phase 2 last time.Since you don't have actual stats, it's impossible to know how much hp and mana you have, so you can farm for two hours to get the upgrade for the spell you want to use and then find out that you can't use the spell AT ALL because the upgraded versions overwrite the lower level ones, so now you just have to deal with it until you can unlock a new area and find your next upgrade.Overall: an interesting experiment with the Dark Souls+Metroidvania formula with great movement and a crisp fighting system that is ruined by the developers' hatred of the player, as they routinely lock the player in a deathbox.
