_childDocuments_.review: Bottom line first.  is an excellent Metroidvania that has just about everything you want from the genre:As Metroidvanias go, it is most similar in style to . I would even say that I enjoy the combat and the story more in . There are sidequests but they do not change the ending. I suspect the developers are planning future content because one region is signposted but never visited. Do keep in mind that  and even  received more than one humongous, content-adding patch in the years after their release, and I expect at least one similar content update for .  I turned over every rock in  over about 30 hours and loved every minute of it. confesses an unseen entity in the trailer. You, the player, are Grey Irma, a fierce warrior and servant of your divine creator, Zoran the Sculptor. The world has been destroyed by claybournes, maddened clay warriors animated with ichor. Your mission--broadly speaking--is to retrieve what Zoran requires  from your former allies so that he can set the world right.The story is compelling and the characters and lore are interesting. The English script needs grammar, spelling, and style revisions but hey, so does this review. The developers are from Eastern Europe, including Ukraine, so that's just another reason to buy. What immediately makes  different from other Metroidvanias is that you start the game with some abilities that other games in the genre make you find later. You can climb walls, wall-jump, and ground-pound right away. This is an interesting choice that pays off because you get to explore the majestic ruins around you at the start of the game. There are still some ability keys you need to obtain from bosses to fully explore areas and find new areas. Your starting combat abilities are more limited, but not for long, and what you do have is lethal fun.Combat is a very polished highlight of this game.You carry a longsword and can parry any attack that has a red visual indicator. If you succeed, Irma will deliver a devastating, fluid counter attack that will make the screen shake and your enemy explode into red mist (if the blow is fatal). Parrying is an essential combat skill later in the game as it is the one of the only ways to break enemy defenses. It feels insanely good to pull off. You can also dodge through most attacks. The ground-pound move mentioned before is not actually used for traversal, but for stunning smaller enemies from above.When you activate and return to most save points (dark mirrors), you will you need to dispatch a rogue doppelganger. Doing this gives you a choice between three heavy weapons (i.e. a claymore, a great hammer, a spear, spinning chains, etc.) These weapons are a little slower than your main attack but can come with buffs like higher max health, higher max mana (ichor), various enemy debuffs and damage-over-time.Instead of leveling up, you can put your points (bone dust) into learning new spells. You can hold two different spells on you at once and they are easy to execute. Spells are the other other way to break some enemy defenses. You can even summon a doppelganger to fight beside you. There is a charm system that very nicely compliments different play styles and weapon choices. You can hold 3 charms at once.When you die, the state of the world will change to "Moon Hunger", where all enemies (including bosses) are more aggressive but drop more consumables and currency. The difference is very noticeable. Some bosses are almost impossible to beat during Moon Hunger. Even regular enemies become variants that are much tougher to put down. I required about 30 consecutive attempts to beat one boss. The good news is that all the bosses are visually and mechanically distinct. They are a lot of fun to lose to over and over again, but if you want an easier time, you can pay the toll to restore the moon to its default state.

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid game with lots of exploration, secrets to find and challenging combat/bosses. It doesn't hold your hand and punishes you from dying by making the game harder (this can be counteracted rather easily by a plentiful resource you get). Definitely hooked and will see it through to the end.EDIT after finishing the game:I really enjoyed my 8/9 hrs on the game. Loved the magic/healing balance as it made my decisions to use magic even riskier. You can use magic and then heal, but you can't heal and use magic without refilling the bar first.The game doesn't have a leveling system, all your permanent power ups come from exploration. But you can "grind" temporary upgrades to make an area easier to explore, you do lose these upon finding the next saving point or dying so you can't be overpowered going from area to are (or you can, at a greater risk).Lastly, as long as you explore enough no boss will have a respawn point too far from them and there are *plenty* of shortcuts that lead back to the respawn point, so if you're having to backtrack a lot, exploring different areas for that shortcut first benefits a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only a couple hours in, and I could say I'm pretty confident it will end well for me. It is pretty challenging for me (7/10 in difficulty for me, and I compare this difficulty as equal as Elden Ring on my first run)Do note, I'm not exactly a fan of the metroidvania genre, but this one seems to get it right. It's soulslike elements & skill tier-ing's, though nothing new or ground breaking, seems to be structured well enough. Not too simple, not too complicated. Enemy variants are pretty good for me at this point. Confident I'll be encountering more as I go further. Additionally, a unique mechanic where death is both punishing and rewarding you, is very approachable. It's like a Hard and Normal mode hybrid depending on whether you choose to 'remove' the Hard part. I'll leave the details out to avoid further spoiling this. *Sorry if I already did*What is also appreciated is the art style and story. Would love to see more in-game character voice on the narrative but at least the 'reading' is not overbearing.No bugs or glitches throughout my 4 hours and like I've said, I have a good feeling about this while I patiently try to finish this game. And for it's price... man, give it a go. it's almost a steal.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: 3 hours in and here is what I can say so far:: The gameplay in my opinion is considered quite ruthless especially with the moon hunger every so often (or all the time if you keep dying). You can see a bit of blasphemous in the game as you continue along the story however currently the story is still unclear. Overall I love the challenge this brings and I will continue to play this game twice over!: The fighting aspect of the game seems really well done I have had no specific issues with the melee combat, nor the special abilities. However I will say the witchery skills are hardly used aside from breaking walls and getting the cheeky kills on the enemies you'd rather no deal with for the n'th time.: Much like Blasphemous the UI is heavily styled by the games world / setting. Which in itself is exactly what a UI, especially in games should embody. They did a very excellent job in making the player and myself feel immersed in the menus. Another thing to add is the lack of menus. This is actually a good thing in terms of UI. The smaller the footprint the less frustration the player has getting to the task at hand. My ONLY caveat is that the interaction with the dark mirror can be annoying, mainly because of the way the options / list works. To scroll through the options and then loose sight of the indicator can get confusing.: The most trouble I've had with this game is the platforming mechanic. Not only have I not died to spikes on countless whims because I couldn't land on the platform, it seems the player can hardly ever clip on the platform let alone make it within a simple jump. Instead of jumping on the platforms you'll find you clip to them instead and pray to god you don't miss the corner.: Ive seen a ton of reviews stating the lack thereof of accessibility within the players controls, and I definitely agree that they should have at least implemented keybinding changes to make the game enjoyable to different types of players. Because this feature was left out a good share of there would-be players are left sitting in the dark.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: It can run at super high frame rate.  If you have a 240hz monitor, it can do that.  Graphics are beautiful.  All the little animations and effects are fantastic!  Combat is good and clean and pure.  Movement is good.  Feels really nimble.  Difficulty varies depending on how you play but it's definitely not easy.  Bosses are great, good number of attacks and randomization.  The Spite system is an interesting take on the souls genre and can make you pretty OP, until you die.  As a modern metroidvania its got some neat stuff with a classic gameplay feel.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: I like the game so far, but im having some issues with the fact that i invested into a spell all the way through tier 3 and now i can't cast it because i don't have enough ichor. THAT'S REALLY BAD GUYS!! Serious?? I mean, im not gonna give a bad review just because of that, but that was really annoying and im still salty about it because i can't reset my spell tree. but besides that, this game its everything i love: beautiful pixel art, dark atmosphere and tight fast combat with parry. I'll give a 8/10 for now. once i finished the game i might change something in the review, but so far im having a blast.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: just the early impressions are well enough for me to recommend this game to anyone who enjoys metroidvania's. Big map, lots of secrets, unique visuals, awesome soundtrack. Top to bottom i'm really having a harder time finding anything to critique about the game beyond a few minimal bugs. granted i'm totally only 6 hours in, it has been an absolute blast.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: Game is fun! Gives me big blasphemous vibes which is a good thing. I will say that the game is very challenging so be ready to die a lot. Overall though, the game feels rewarding when you finally overcome some of the challenges the game offers. If you are into games like blasphemous and are up for a challenge then I would pick it up.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: 3 hours in, so far so good. The combat is delicious and brutal. Upgrade mechanics are fresh if not necessarily innovative. The story is vague but has me questioning my own existence (that's a good thing!). The gloomy gothic graphics are oh so much pixely goodness, and the soundtrack fits perfectly. This game is getting compared to Blasphemous a lot - I didn't like that game because getting good didn't feel like I was getting skilled, just that I died a bunch and learned the game's dumb tricks. Moonscars' combat is much more satisfying - there is one main weapon and a few secondary weapons that are simple to use but require mastering their use for each enemy. My one complaint would be that although there is large spell tree to learn, the spells are mostly useless due to their heavy mana cost and the fact that you need that mana for healing. Hoping this changes as I get more upgrades.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: Having been a fan of dark souls 3 and elden ring, I could see the inspiration beautifully glowing through.It's an amazing amalgamation of these amtospheres brought into the world of platformers a.k.a. metroidvania. I must say, it has been a blast so far and I'm intrigued to keep going!Personally:Music: 10/10Fun factor: Through the roof.Story: Intriguing and unique.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: Very conflicting gameWhile the style and art is incredible, the whole game feels almost exactly the same.The sounds are good but the general background music is bland.Combat is fun, but enemies become unfun to fight.There are alot of secret walls and treasures, but they are always just XP or non unique items.There is a risk and reward difficulty where you get more xp, but that xp is only used to buy a few charms and to unlock spells.Spells are cool, but most of them are pretty meh, and take alot of resources.The list just keeps going on like this, for every good and interesting choice, there is a counterpart that tears it down. Its not a bad game at all, but its also not a good game. I will give a thumbs up since i do lean slightly more towards a positive feeling. But its a close 50/50.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fast, brutal, fair, unfair, mildly infuriating, story is captivating and the visuals are stunning. I’m in love. After playing Blasphemous, I ran through a drought of Metroidvania’s in a dark beautiful setting. I’m not a fan of bubble gum type characters and visuals. Moonscars has arrived and takes its place proudly beside my love for Blasphemous. Congratulations to the dev team for a knockout game!
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: It's kinda what I expected going in, although the trailers showed more promise. But I will keep playing and see how it feels further down the line.Straight off the bat I must say the animations are very well done, smoothly animated, and the combat is what I had hoped for - quick and intuitive instead of the typical soulslike slow paced that feels like a chess battle. Don't get me wrong, slow is perfect, but in 2D games I like the approach of Dead Cells, which the devs seemed to have been inspired when developing this.The visual style seems to be something I haven't seen before in a 2d game - upon the first glance it has similarities to Blasphemous, but once you start playing you will notice that they did it in their own way, kinda reminds me of oil paintings mixed with pixel art?!? It's a matter of personal preference, I guess. This might not be for everoyne.Probably the worst part were the weird dialogues and confusing story, but I hope that with more hours that I put in, it will become clear what's going on as I will assemble new pieces of the lore puzzle.Overall, it's an enjoyable experience, with the core gamplay being the strongest aspect of it. 7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so insane so far. Very well balanced, story and lore is super intriguing so far, and the exploration is exciting, even if pretty straight foward. A Soulslike world, with systems similar to Hades and Hollow Knight, while making you feel like you're playing a Castlevania game again. Well crafted all around, even with my limited time in game.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonscars

_childDocuments_.review: Push the limits of your combat skills, and master new abilities to progress through an unforgiving nonlinear 2D world. Face off against the relentless darkness that seeks to destroy you. In Moonscars, every death is a lesson learnt—and as you overcome each challenge, new truths will be revealed.

name: Ghosts 'n Goblins Resurrection
detailed_description: Watch as this nostalgic yet completely reimagined storybook world unravels before your very eyes. Taking cues from both Ghosts 'n Goblins and Ghouls 'n Ghosts and giving birth to something entirely new, Resurrection is a title worthy of its name. Don't be fooled—this picturesque storybook world, while gorgeous, is a love-letter to the original titles and maintains the same punishing gameplay that fans have come to expect. So go on and test your mettle, for the gauntlet has been thrown! Story A long time ago... In a far off land our tale begins, its beauty matched by none. The knight, Arthur, and the princess there, bathed in midday sun. ...but suddenly something's amiss, the town is up in flames, a cloud of darkness does emerge, the palace it does claim. The shadow then extends its reach, to the Umbral Tree divine. Its color fades, its vigor drained by powers most malign. And with this chaos wrought, the Demon Lord plays his vile hand. While Arthur's back is turned, the princess he kidnaps as planned. In haste does Arthur don his armor, to save his maiden fair. To the Demon Realm he does depart, so demons best beware. Gameplay Just like its predecessors, Ghosts 'n Goblins Resurrection makes use of simple controls that anyone can enjoy. Use them to your advantage as you fight your way through weird and spooky stages filled with unique enemies in this enchanting world brought to life with modern technology and game design philosophy! Ghosts 'n Goblins is, well, hard. Its unyielding difficulty has been a defining characteristic of the series, and Resurrection pays respect to that legacy. You'll die, and you'll die again, but you'll dust yourself off and get better with every attempt as you learn more about your foes and further craft your strategy. You'll struggle, but you'll also bask in glory once you do eventually emerge victorious. That is Ghosts 'n Goblins. In Resurrection, Arthur can obtain 8 types of weapons, each with its own unique characteristics. Fell your foes with old favorites such as the Lance and the Dagger, shoot shockwaves with the Hammer to launch enemies, or send a Spiked Ball crashing along the ground to bowl them over instead! Use these—and more—to your advantage as you form your plan to progress through the Demon Realm! In addition to his large arsenal of weapons, Arthur can also learn a magnitude of magic and skills. Use Thunderstorm to unleash a hailstorm of bolts in four directions, or learn Kitted Out to increase Arthur's inventory space and carry more weapons. With tons more available, be sure to make room for magic and skills in your strategy! Make full use of Arthur's weapons, magic, and skills as you brave the ordeals of the Demon Realm to bring the princess home safely. Muster every ounce of grit you possess; you're going to need it! On top of single player mode, which focuses on the fun of hunkering down and overcoming challenges alone, Arthur can be aided in his quest by support characters, the Three Wise Guys. This gameplay style makes for an intense two player co-op experience—a first for the series. Connect two controllers to play with a friend, side by side. Note: Local co-op only. Online play is not supported. Experience the sweaty palms and white-knuckles that come with single player mode, or share the fun with your friends in a party game-like co-op experience!

This gameplay style makes for an intense two player co-op experience—a first for the series. Connect two controllers to play with a friend, side by side. Note: Local co-op only. Online play is not supported. Experience the sweaty palms and white-knuckles that come with single player mode, or share the fun with your friends in a party game-like co-op experience!
short_description: Watch as this nostalgic yet completely reimagined storybook world unravels before your very eyes. Taking cues from both Ghosts 'n Goblins and Ghouls 'n Ghosts and giving birth to something entirely new, Resurrection is a title worthy of its name.

_childDocuments_.review: I only ever had the C64 version of Ghosts N' Goblins and it was super tough, frantic fun. I remember getting to the final castle, but I don't believe I ever beat the "final" boss. So, 30 odd years later, my reactions are not what they were but I can't help but play on the so-called "Legendary" difficulty, which is just the difficulty of the old games.If you happen to be unfamiliar with Ghosts N' Goblins and Ghouls N' Ghosts, it is a fast-paced side scrolling platformer with a slow moving character who has only 2 hit points as standard, and a small selection of weapons to defend yourself. Only one weapon at a time, no double jump, no upgrades (beyond a golden armour that adds 1 hit point over standard), lots of randomly attacking and constantly spawning enemies, no patterns to learn or phases to remember, no mid-way checkpoints, and to top it off, you need to play the game through twice to get the true ending.This remake changes some of that, though, which is great for old and new players alike (again, none of us are getting any younger).Difficulty levels now change how many hit points King Arthur has, being represented on how his armour breaks down. On Legendary it is a one hit and you're in your tighty-whiteys, on the lower levels you lose your plate armour in sections, affording yourself more hits.Lower difficulties also adds checkpoints mid-level, nice for those whose reactions may have either not gotten to 100% yet, or the days of 100% are behind them. Just allows you to draw a breath now and again.This version also gives you unlimited lives, and allows you to keep your current weapon between deaths, features that were not so back in the old days. I have zero issues with this, nice changes for modern home gaming, but a "Classic Rules" option would be a nice addition.An unexpected delight was that both sets of levels from both "Ghouls" and "Goblins" are present, in lovely modern cartoony art style which fits perfectly with the game. It looks pretty much like how I imagined the SNES versions to look through some super tuned nostalgia goggles. Very smooth and nice art and animation that is respectable to the originals. Awesome use of the engine that was originally created for Resident Evil 7.Totally different from the old GNGs is a "Magic" skill tree. Collect magical fireflies throughout your adventure to unlock spells to help you combat the legions of the undead. A nice unique spin which is ultimately optional. Again, I like it, no real problems. If you don't want the magics simply don't slot them. The issue  come if some of the "new" enemy placements or bosses require use of such abilities, or have a weakness to certain magics "Megaman" style. Only time will tell on that.Honestly, I would give this title a 10/10, and I  give 10/10s. This is exactly how I pictured a modern take on both Ghouls N' Ghosts and Ghosts N' Goblins. Additions and quality of life changes that are respectable to the originals, no major gameplay changes such as sprinting or double jumping or multiple paths or super weapons, just you, a King, a lance, some sexy underwear, and lots of undead.Lots and lots of undead.Fantastic, challenging, nostalgic fun. And I am truthful when I say this; don't feel bad if you have to play on lower difficulties. These games were considered super challenging in a time when games were almost masochistic in their difficulty. Just get out there, have fun, and wear your pants with pride.Edit: Some spelling and formatting.

_childDocuments_.review: So I've spent some years boxing during my youth and I can tell you that playing this game is like sparring one of the nasty old dudes who hang around gyms and used to be national champions in 1983: They will see each and every move of yours coming from a mile away and they will punish you every time. They will treat you way rougher than any modern coach would and in spite of all their experience they won't be above making fun of you and humiliating you. Accepting this, you can still have a great time sparring these dudes. You WILL learn and become a bit fiercer for it. The most important thing is a CALM MIND. You need to remind yourself that it's about the long run. Sooner or later you'll figure out their dirty tricks, you'll learn how to avoid and counter and you'll show them why the 80s are OVER.That's how you need to approach GHOSTS AND GOBLINS: RESSURECTION. You won't win this game at the first try. Maybe you never will, maybe you're punching above your weight. But so what? If you play this for what it is - a goofy video game about a knight wearing hearty undies - without taking it's trollish nature too seriously, you'll sooner or later start to GET it. It's not about winning, it's about trading punches, insults and grins. It's about one more round, one more round. If you approach it like this, with a calm-mind and no expectations except trying to learn how to deal with that particular dirty trick next, you WILL progress. And if you progress, just like in boxing, you'll get to experience all kinds of crazy adventures (zombies! fire foxes! dragons! devils! GHOSTS AND GOBLINS!!!) and you'll be glad to have endured and persevered.

_childDocuments_.review: A simple premise, from a much, simpler time: A demonic horde torched your kingdom to rubble and kidnapped your daughter, and you, King Arthur, are on a mission to... wait, did you see the stages? There's nothing left, really. Everyone is dead, and those who aren't are undead, and everything is destroyed... so you're on a mission to... kill Lucifer and dig two graves? Ok, that one's a bit darker than I remember.With all the great nostalgia gaming going on in the late years (Wonderboy, Streets of Rage, Alex Kydd, etc.), it's surprising Capcom didn't bring back this delightful piece of torment back sooner. Just as with Wonderboy and Alex Kydd, it looks exactly the way it should ever had, neither better nor worse, and the music is as charming and nostalgia-charged as ever.The gameplay, though, it's both its greater asset and worst liability. "Souls"? "Rogue-like"? THIS is the game that started it all. Ghosts n Goblins is not about 1337 skillz, it's not about pattern recognition, or even about muscle memory... it's about LUCK, luck and perseverance. The game is outright unfair, cheap shots are the house's specialty, and you'll die, and you'll die, and you'll die, over and over and over until neither heaven or hell want you... and a window of opportunity opens that takes you to the next save point, then rinse-repeat. Granted, the lowered difficulties make it a bit more accessible, but only so much. This game is clearly not for everyone, but if you're into "souls" game, you owe it to yourself to experience the roots of the genre.If you're a Gen-Xer, then you owe it to yourself to re-experience it, and then ask yourself "why did I put up with this again?" I finished the game, and enjoyed the ride, but probably don't have what it takes to get the true ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this are rare...very rare! The programming of the AI enemies, the placements of spawns and the projectile pathing is God like in it's execution. The level of precision that has gone into ensuring you will die as often as possible is breath taking!! The presentation is clean and tight, no fat...it's exactly what it needed to be...simple and to the point. The art direction is superb and everything is animated really, really well. The basics feel great...jumping and attacking all feel great and it really isn't a chore to rerun the same segment 100 times trying to achieve progress.I've only just started my Legendary playthrough (hardest setting - recommended if you grew up in the 80's!) and have already taken over 2 hours to get to the first checkpoint on the first level so...very, very challenging but an absolute joy to play due to masterful programming.Dev's around the world should look and learn at Ghosts and Goblins. Games do not need to be weighed down with features and 4K graphics with ray tracing to become loved and wanted. This game understands the laws of gaming and respects them with every frame. A masterpiece in my opinion...9/10 - I will return to update this review once I've completed it...(UPDATE: 20+ hours in and I've only completed 3 worlds - Legend difficulty is pure evil man!)

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:If you're a huge fan of Ghosts 'n Goblins and Ghouls 'n Ghosts that were originally released on NES and Mega Drive/Sega Genesis, I recommend playing Ghosts 'n Goblins: Resurrection! It's very fun classic 2D Side-Scrolling Action Game. But nevertheless, game is supposed to be hard but hard in a good way. Cons:-Game doesn't support ultrawide aspect ratio 21:9 and 32;9 which I had to set back to 2560 x 1440P Resolution.-It is $30 USD but if you run into budget issue, you can always wait until Steam goes on sale. -Game was challenging but very rewarding once you get used to it. -Utilizing RE EngineThoughts:You will need a Gamepad Controller to play this game which is strongly recommended! Also, you can adjust metronome to alter game speed after completing the game. Yes, the game was capped at 60fps which is normal due to framerate tied to physics engine. _childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed the absurdity of the old games, especially the original, then you're in for the same painful but ultimately rewarding experience when you play this one. It's hard, very hard, but at the same time, it's aware of this, and the sooner you accept it, the more fun it will be. This isn't the type of game where you can expect progression every single time you sit down and pick up the controller. On the contrary, you'll find yourself dying many times, over and over again. While some might complain about "poor game design," "cheapness," and a "lack of fairness," I think they're missing the point. Games don't, by their very nature, promise fairness. What they do implicitly promise the player is that they are beatable. Is this game unbeatable? Absolutely not, and as soon as you progress after many futile attempts, you'll feel a great deal of satisfaction that's sometimes missing from more modern games. It's just going to take a great deal of patience.The game compensates for it's absurd difficulty by allowing you to continue where you left off (provided you cleared a check point) at any time, and since you have an unlimited number of lives, gone are the days where you have to repeat an entire level just because you made one mistake. What really adds to the difficulty (and feelings of unfairness) is that enemies can attack from off-screen and you're more or less at the mercy of a RNG when it comes to spawning (sometimes enemies simultaneously spawning on your location and the only area available to move out of the way). Yes, that makes this game unfair, but when the RNG gods grant you divine favor, you feel like you rose up, alone and against all odds, to be the chosen one that dons that lousy, rickety suit of armor and saves the flippin' world. So sit back and be prepared to spend countless areas revisiting the same area over and over again in the hopes that the stars align and you finally progress. Very few will progress via their own devices; for most of us mere mortals, it will be because the game simply decided to show us mercy.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghosts 'n Goblins Resurrection is a classic, white-knuckle, action platformer where memorization, twitch gameplay, and a healthy dose of luck are a necessary recipe for success. Despite popular opinion, Resurrection is not nearly as difficult as the arcade original... not by a long shot. In fact, I would say that this game is most similar to Ultimate Ghosts 'n Goblins for PSP. The developers here have given players an abundance of pain reducers in the form of check points, multiple hit health system, multiple weapon slots, and a bunch of magic options that really help you customize the way in which you play.Graphically, Capcom has opted for a storybook-esque look throughout the entire game. This is rather subjective, but I personally really like the look of the game... it reminds me of those incredibly detailed pop-up books from my childhood. (And a welcome relief after the last game's pseudo 3D models...)Overall, I really appreciate what Capcom has done with this game. It is brutally difficult, yet fair. It becomes increasingly rewarding the more you play - especially when you realize how much Resurrection has to offer in terms of content. If you are looking for old-school challenge with a dash of modern upgrades, this is your game. As a life-long GnG fan, I heartily recommend Ghosts 'n Goblins Resurrection. However, I still recommend it for new gamers (who have a bit of patience) as well!

_childDocuments_.review: I really didn't want to give this a bad review, I have fond memories of the original entries, I tried for hours to like this one, but this version is just tragically inferior to its predecessors, being maddeningly tedious, and difficult in a way the originals never were. The game play is made up of a mix of platforming, infinitely spawning enemies, and pre built "gotcha" traps that will most likely kill you instantly in you didn't know about them before hand, and a lot of the time will even if you do. Your characters hit box, options for manoeuvrability, and your projectiles are extremely limited by the geometry of the stages, while enemies are not, leading to situations were a limitation of movement, enemy spawn, and enemy projectile will all convalesce at the same time causing a unwinnable situation and death completely outside of your control. And sadly this is a core part of Ghosts 'n Goblins Resurrection difficulty.This double jump has been excluded from this version, making combat less reactionary and dynamic and more of a waiting game or memorisation exercise. It's less about "reacting" to the threats and challenges presented and more about knowing the perfect place to stand at the perfect time to avoid the screen trap and following death situations mentioned previously.It also just feels generally unfinished when it comes to enemy spawn rates, weapons, and magic options.Sadly not the definitive Ghosts 'n Goblins I was hoping for.

_childDocuments_.review: I do not recommend that you buy this game unless you already know you like the game.  Don't misunderstand - I don't think this is a bad game.  In contrast, this is an excellent remake, with plenty of new content.  It's super pretty while still maintaining the sprite-driven feel of the original.  Do not let the leagues of positive reviews fool you though - this game hates you, and will do everything short of cheating to make sure you fail.  Unlike other game series known for their difficulty, this game is not fair.  You will break controllers if you don't know what you're getting into.  So, I repeat, unless you are CERTAIN that you like this game, DO NOT BUY IT.Now that that warning is out of the way, this game is an improvement over the original in many ways, but at the end of the day it's still the same fundamental experience.  Capcom has added 3 new difficulty modes to the game.  Legendary is equivalent to how the original game was, in that if you take one hit, you lose your armor, and if you take another hit, you die.  At Knight difficulty, you can take 2 hits before losing your armor, and 2 before dying.  Squire difficulty is Knight difficulty but with about half of the enemies.  Page difficulty is Squire difficulty, but you automatically respawn at the location you died at, no checkpoints required.  None of this is explained in the difficulty menu, however, and Capcom chose to use the opportunity of selecting difficulty to almost taunt players for not playing at Legendary.  Even for a game whose difficulty is the point, there's very little excuse for not explaining what difficulty levels mean.Another big Quality of Life improvement is the inclusion of extra checkpoints.  Each level is divided into two areas, but within those areas are multiple spawn points.  The game gives you infinite continues - as long as you're willing to keep pushing back into the fray, you can keep trying.  These QoL improvements are not an unvarnished good, however.  For players who enjoy the difficulty of the original, you may find yourself feeling patronized by the game.  If you find yourself struggling on an area and respawn several times, you will see a "Lower Difficulty and respawn" option begin to appear on the continue menu.  This isn't great, because if you want the accomplishment of beating it at your chosen difficulty it feels like the game is insulting you, and if you actually do want to lower the difficulty, you have to die about 10 times before the game will give you the option.  They should have simply put this option permanently on the continue menu.There are two new weapons added to the game, but just as with the original all of them are absolute trash except for the lance and knife.  New weapons are a relatively common drop from either chests or the pots that random enemies carry, and all it takes to pick them up is to touch them, which is breathtakingly easy to do by accident if you are surrounded by enemies and fighting a desperate battle for survival.  Since you have 3:1 odds of the weapon being trash, this is almost certain to kill you, and can make you need to give up and restart a level just to go back to having the lance.Another thing faithfully copied from the original is the platforming controls - they're awful.  Arthur runs painfully slowly.  Jumping is faster, but once you're in the air you have zero control over the character, so if you are still when you start jumping, you can't move after getting into the air.  This makes dodging projectiles and platforming painful, rather than fun.  Again, this is accurate to the original game, but if you are used to modern games Arthur will feel awful to control.The addition of some sort of progression through Umbral Bees is a nice one.  Using these collectibles unlocks various magic spells for Arthur, and these can be very powerful.  Further, it also unlocks passive abilities, such as tripling the damage of your first attack after losing all your armor, or unlocking a second and third weapon slot.  Once you've unlocked the extra weapon slots, any weapon you pick up will replace your inactive weapon.  This is a real game changer - once you no longer need to worry about accidentally losing one of the only two decent weapons in the game, you can be a lot bolder about how you play.All in all, this is a very faithful remake of the original game, warts and all.  If that's what you want, then this is 100% a good buy for you!  But if you aren't sure, and decide to buy the game anyway, I'd recommend starting a timer when you start the game up.  You'll want to make sure you don't accidentally spend too many hours dying to get a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghosts 'n Goblins is back and it's harder than ever!  Having played four games in this series I was convinced that I was more-than-ready to tackle its hardest difficulty (Legend) for my first playthrough, oh how wrong I was.  Ghosts 'n Goblins Resurrection (GnGR) is best described as a remake+.  It borrows heavily from the gameplay, enemies, levels, music, and more from the first two games but also contains new content that fits in with what the original games established.  GnGR features four returning stages that are significantly longer and play completely differently as well as three brand new stages.   In each stage you're tasked with running and ""gunning"" your way to each checkpoint and boss.  Arthur is limited to a single jump with a fixed jump arc and it’s up to the player to use its high vertical height and ability to stay mobile while attacking with caution and speed.  GnGR features two types of checkpoints, Progress Pennon's and Banners of Rebirth.  Progress Pennons are available on all difficulties (Legend, Knight, Squire, and Page from hardest to easiest) while Banners are additional checkpoints exclusive to lower difficulties.  You'll find on Legend that Progress Pennons are incredibly far from one-another with some stages only giving you two checkpoints for an entire level!  Health and checkpoint scarcity requires the player to treat their trek carefully, there are no pushovers in this game and everything can and will take away your precious armor / life at a moment’s notice if you don't treat it as such.  Enemies in GnGR are ruthless, numerous, and even have a fair bit of personality.  It's hard to spend even 10 seconds in the game without being constantly swarmed by enemies and successfully fending off a horde with no scratches to your armor feels incredibly satisfying, doubly so for the illusive Red Arremers.  The sound design coupled with each enemy's animations give them a playfully evil design and animalistic tone.While the game's challenge is brutal and largely fair it does unfortunately have moments where you'll take unavoidable damage.  Certain bosses have no telegraphing on their quick attacks and you'll oftentimes find yourself unable to avoid taking damage if you need to jump to avoid an enemy while another spawns mid-jump.  It's uncommon for the most part but the further you travel the more prevalent this will become.  The player can also find hidden chests, bees, and demon orbs throughout the game.  The harder the difficulty the less you'll feel inclined to search for these since you're much more fragile, have more enemies to impede you, and have much more of a consequence after dying.  To reiterate, I played on Legend since I've finished the previous games but STRONGLY recommend trying Knight difficulty or lower depending on your skill level if you’d like to go for 100% completion.  Legend feels best suited for repeat playthroughs after you become familiar and confident with tackling the game's difficulty.  Excluding Page (easiest setting) difficulty as a whole is completely optional and regardless of choice you’ll be able to unlock any achievement and complete the true ending.  NOTE: If you’re interested in completing the true ending make sure to NOT play the final level’s shadow variant until you have found all demon orbs, otherwise you’ll be required to finish each stage a third time. The game's visuals have been met with a fair amount of controversy since the initial reveal with its motion-tweening animations which seeks to evoke a puppet-like storybook style.  It looked a lot better in motion with a controller in my hands and I’ve heard similar feelings from other players that were initially put off by it.  It was fun to re-experience the many familiar enemies and bosses from the series in a new style and I enjoyed the expressive animations of Arthur as well as the many goblins and ghosts throughout. The soundtrack largely consists of familiar tunes from the original games, some arrangements of the classic Ghosts ‘n Goblins theme, and brand new music which is equally as good.  Zone 3 and 4 have new stages and new music to accompany them with both evoking the established feeling the series is known for.  The perilous and sinister demeanors these exude complimented with memorable melodies not only captures the theme of each stage and their challenge but also never manages to never get old, even with hundreds of attempts.  While nearly all of them amount to short loops and play throughout the stage (most of which feature stark change at their midway points) they fit GnGR’s iterative gameplay loop and locales surprisingly well.Overall the game is incredibly faithful to a fault, it's appeal is aimed towards existing fans of the series (like myself) and gives newcomers a great representation on what Ghosts 'n Goblins games are and how they play.  However, in its Resurrection, GnGR has retained many of the design choices that were cemented since the beginning.  Some like the fixed jump arc and slow base movement speed is mostly down to personal preference while the aforementioned unavoidable damage feels egregiously dampening on enjoyment due to the game's increased emphasis on randomization over previous entries where it was less prevalent.  Irregardless there's plenty of enjoyment to be had with each successive stage clear and plenty of replay value with shadow stages feeling unique from their "normal" counterparts.  Beware for this is Ghosts ‘n Goblins!

_childDocuments_.review: The best way I can describe playing this game is like going on a date with someone who thinks embracing and acknowledging their toxic personality traits instead of changing or fixing them somehow makes it cute and quirky~Difficult games are fine, i've had no issues with many before but there's a difference between being difficult and fair versus being cheap and throwing impossible scenarios at you that you cannot win then trying to say that's "difficulty". Those are not the same thing, and this game goes so hard on being as cheap as possible that the entire thing is flawed and contradicts itself just to make you lose, seemingly because "we're Ghosts n Goblins, it's different if we do it!". (Just read the store description lol). No, you're still just cheap. It doesn't somehow make it better because that's what you're known for. There is no improving in this game like you can with other difficult games, because the way its designed doesn't let you. The developers seemingly didn't want you to be able to just memorize each stage layout and enemy spawn areas, so in an attempt to have their cake and eat it too they put in infinitely spawning random enemies that you cannot account for. So trying to study/learn from anything is pointless as it might be different the next time. Meaning that whether you win any stage or not is going to be almost purely up to what RNG you get instead of skill/improvement, which makes the concept of dying hundreds of times in each stage laughable. Your success is not up to you, but whatever the stage decides. Enemies will spawn right where you're about to land, right where you are jumping to, just to get some quick hits in when every hit counts. Arthur's movement is stiff and sluggish, he cannot stop his jump so once you do it you're stuck with it, charging your abilities takes forever to use a single one when it would actually be useful. Platforming does not feel good either and you can only hit in 4 directions so in some instances all you can do is just die. Every aspect of it is designed to try to be as annoying as possible, and not "this is hard" annoying, but "there was literally nothing I could do" annoying.Half the weapons are useless, you might as well stick with the knives/lance combo. I was in a boss room once where I COULD NOT DAMAGE THE BOSS because of the weapon I had. Speaking of bosses, readability on their attacks? Nah, just hope you're in the right spot I guess. (Shout out to the last stage btw, which throws most of the previous bosses in it!)To the games credit, they do give you difficulty options and abilities you can unlock to try to make it easier but that isn't enough to overcome its inherently flawed design. Even the little things seem purposely made to try to make you lose progress. You're going to die hundreds of times in each stage so you'll obviously want to retry as quickly as possible. But the respawn screen defaults specifically to an option from a much further point in the stage, sometimes even the very start, instead of the last checkpoint you reached. It's like they know people are going to be spamming it and want you to hit the wrong one without thinking and lose progress, I had to restart an entire level twice because of it. I beat the entire main game and I never once felt like it was because I managed to adjust to the game or improve, only that the RNG was in my favor. So if the developers truly wanted this to be as insufferable and miserable to experience, true to "what Ghosts n Goblins is" then congratulations they nailed it, but don't be surprised when some people don't think that's fun. The only enjoyment I had in this entire thing was finishing it and knowing and I never have to think about it again.

_childDocuments_.review: is a ruthlessly unforgiving action platformer that demands memorization, fast reflexes, determination, and yes, even a bit of luck to succeed. It's an update to the hard-as-nails Ghosts 'n' Goblins franchise, keeping and even  the punishing game play that is core to the series, while adding a few new elements to flesh things out for a modern audience. A game this brutal almost certainly won't have mass appeal, but for those dedicated souls who are compelled to return to a challenge again and again, fighting for progress as the game laughs in your face, well, Ghosts 'n' Goblins: Resurrection might be just the thing you're looking for. If you play this game, you will be expected to:- Replay areas repeatedly as you learn the level layouts, static enemy spawns, and item locations- React quickly to the seemingly random enemy spawns that threaten to overwhelm you (after lots of play, I don't think they're quite as random as they first seem)- Develop tactics for dealing with extra-tough segments, often involving unlockable magic spells- Search for and collect lots of hidden pick-ups- Put up with runs that occasionally screw you over with really bad enemy spawns- Put up with a menu that can accidentally erase some of your progress if you're not careful- Die, a lotNow, that may sound rough, and it really really is, but the developers  give you the tools to win, even for less experienced players. Unlike the older games, you can now save your progress, even at mid-level checkpoints. There are no more lives or continues, you can simply replay the levels as often as you want. The ability to work on a full run over multiple play sessions makes it much more likely that you'll be able to finish the game, assuming you're determined enough to stick with it.There are four difficulty settings to choose from, with the hardest of them (Legendary) being a real test of your mastery and patience. I recommend you skip Legendary mode at first, and come back after you learn the game in one of the lower difficulty settings - they give you extra hits and more checkpoints, with the easiest of them eliminating checkpoints altogether, instead respawning you right where you died (even mid-boss fight!). The easiest setting probably isn't the most satisfying way to play, but for someone new to the genre, it's a good way to prepare for the harder difficulties.There's also a good selection of unlockable magic spells that add some strategy and experimentation to the game play, giving you new ways to approach tough spots. Thoughtful use of these powers can turn nightmare sections of game play into something a bit more manageable (semi-nightmarish?). To unlock them you need pick-ups found in the levels, many times hidden, usually tricky or dangerous to grab, but always worth the effort - there are some fun and handy abilities to unlock.So it's true, this game is really tough, even to the point of feeling unfair at times. But with unlimited lives, the option to lower the difficulty if you're struggling, and the unlockable spells and powers at your disposal, Resurrection's intimidating challenge becomes a bit more approachable.Difficulty aside, the overall quality of the game is good, befitting a budget release from a large studio. The controls are precise and responsive, although Arthur, your character, does feel a little sluggish until you get used to it. The art is detailed, colorful, and has lots of personality. The paper doll animation put me off at first, but it's grown on me over time - at least it fits with the game's premise that we are watching the action unfold on a scroll. The music features great renditions of classic Ghosts 'n' Goblins tunes, sounding modern while still capturing the spirit of the originals. Very nice. There's also a good amount of content here - new challenges open up after your first victory, there are lots of collectibles and unlockables, and a good ending to work towards if you want to truly conquer the game. All in all, it's a pretty great package for the price.If there's one major gripe I have with the game, it's the menu. Specifically, the menu that pops up after you die, which is going to be happening a . The way it's set up leads to a bunch of unnecessary button presses over the course of hundreds of deaths, and even worse, the possibility that you accidentally erase your mid-level checkpoint and go back to the beginning of the level instead. Trust me, if you just lost your hard-won checkpoint after hours of death and failure, you are NOT going to be happy about that. It only happened to me twice in over 50 hours of play, but man I really wish they had come up with something else here. It's just poorly thought out.But hey, aside from that one major blemish, I'd say that overall, Ghosts 'n' Goblins: Resurrection is a great game. There's a good amount of content to justify the price, the presentation is nice, and it's designed with care for lots of challenging game play. Easy to recommend, for the right kind of gamer of course. Thank you Capcom for making this, and for making it stand up to the legacy of the Ghosts 'n' Goblins franchise. I can only hope we get another one!

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, let me express my admiration for the game's impressive visuals, great design, music and solid mechanics. However, it's clear that GnG (Ghosts 'n Goblins) games have always been synonymous with challenging difficulty. While I managed to walk through the relatively easier Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts on the SNES on 'normal', the difficulty in this particular installment feels excessively high. I initially began playing on 'Legend' difficulty, which seems to be the intended (pre-selected) mode, and after nearly four hours, I'm still unable to reach the first boss.The difficulty is made worse by the fact that just remembering things doesn't help much, because enemies can show up randomly in tricky places. It's really frustrating when enemies suddenly appear right on top of you while you're in mid-air, just to send you straight to death. This was always part of GnG games, but it's even more extreme here. Sometimes, there can be up to 10 flying enemies on the screen, with at least three of them shooting things at you.I changed the game to an easier setting, but it doesn't feel quite right to play a GnG game where I can survive more than two hits. I would have liked a version that stays true to the original but has a bit fewer enemies, with probaby a normal mode with the option to make it harder. It's disheartening to see the standard difficulty level set to 'Legend,' making you feel inadequate unless you end up in baby-mode - aka instant respawn - just to maintain a slight feeling of progress. Certainly, I acknowledge that this is not meant to be a walk in the park, and especially that I'm not among the elite GnG players who can flawlessly navigate the game, pulling off 0-hit runs. However, it feels like this game is aiming at joystick-virtuosos rather than the average player. Without a doubt, this game is inaccessible for players like me unless the difficulty is adjusted to a point where I start to feel completely unworthy.I also understand that in today's gaming landscape, there's an increasing niche for hardcore players who thrive on challenges that are inhumanly difficult. Those who claim that this game isn't hard likely fall within this elusive category.I initially gave it a thumbs up due to its graphics and gameplay, but upon thorough reflection, I had to revert the decision. While it is true that I can potentially advance in the game, it does barely feel like a true accomplishment. It's more like one lucky outcome after doing the same thing over and over again for an exorbitant and unproductive amount of time. It's not exactly fun, but rather feels like enduring some sort of random torture.The repetition inherent in many old-school arcade-games becomes enjoyable when it aids in learning patterns and gaining a feeling of mastery. Nevertheless, when enemies display inconsistent behavior—e.g. attacking at times but not in others—it creates an impression that success is attainable purely through sheer luck after endless attempts. This isn't the kind of gaming experience I'm looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: -Endearing visuals-infinite lives and a better checkpoint system-upward attack -Arthur is a real G-Enemy spawn rate and spawn randomness-No double jump-Magic changes feel like an afterthought meant to bandaid the game design-60fps cap-Probably more bullet points I’m forgetting (see below for more thoughts)I’m a stupid tryhard. I’m that person who preaches the merits of challenging games to friends. Cave Shmups are fun! You just have to learn the patterns! Souls games are fun! They’re supposed to be hard! You just have to keep at it until you find a weapon that fits your playstyle! No seriously! Super Ghouls and Ghosts is a masterclass in game design!You know what all of those games have that this game doesn’t? I’m gonna get raked, and I don’t even care. I’ve beaten every G&G game dozens of times (including NES, which is widely considered “unfair”) They all have their issues…. Some of those issues are shared in Resurrection. Resurrection however, does nothing to mitigate them. Being forced to constantly overcommit to a decision because of a jump that isn’t granular enough (do you like to short hop? Tough!) isn’t fun.  Do you think you can get used to that jump? Too bad, because:Enemies that spawn directly where you’re going to land, aren’t fun. This isn’t a git gud moment. Git Gud is my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mantra, friendo. You’re literally going to experience a time, probably hundreds, where after you’ve committed to a jump, an enemy will spawn in your landing zone at just the right time to hit you before you can actually recover. (Super G&G remedied this with the double jump, which was more than a way to reach out of sight areas....it was a way to renegotiate a decision you made while navigating a level...and it was intended to fix the exact issue it's needed for here). The spawn rates in Super and Resurrection are nearly identical, and the only reason it  in Super was that double jump.Did you like the Magic system in Super? It was fun right? It gave you a reason to find that certain weapon you liked the magic attack for the most, and spam it into oblivion… Guess what? They separated the magic from the weapons, so now you can pair anything any way you’d like! Should be fun, but it’s not , because you are going to have to grind Bees to unlock abilities in the magic tree, only to find out that spells are mostly useless. I abused Flame Wall for the entirety of the time I played The Graveyard, and enemies spawn too frequently to make any real use of it. At best if gives you a tiny bit of breathing room to make jump decisions, at worst it will get you killed because it’s still tied to your basic attack button (ie you charge your basic weapon attack to use your magic attack). Why even separate the two conceptually if you aren’t going to change them functionally? I can almost understand this change... It keeps everyone from spamming Dagger Super to get i-frames against boss attacks.... but you don't give us tools to deal with the sheer amount of enemies you throw at us in return.I have a  of Super under my belt. That game has been in my Top 10 Games of All Time list for 25 years. Resurrection is probably the biggest gaming disappointment I’ll face in 2021.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough game to recommend, but if you know what you're getting yourself into it can be very enjoyable. It's very hard, and often feels not "fair" - enemies spawn on top of you, platforms and branches plunge you into instant-death pits, enemies shoot through walls that block your projectiles, new hazards appear without warning and generally sometimes it feels like the game is trolling you with how the levels are designed. Restart from the checkpoint and try again. The old G&G games weren't THIS hard, but here you have unlimited continues. Your movements also feel sluggish, especially considering what the game expects you to pull off in some sections, it takes time to get used to. Still, the game also takes skill and persistence and you get unlimited continues, so if you don't mind trying over and over again, beating a challenging section can be very satisfying. After a while levels and bosses that seemed super difficult on first try can be beaten without losing a life.The game also looks gorgeous, though you probably won't have much time to admire it during gameplay because you're too busy trying not to die.

_childDocuments_.review: A game for the Souls-like era of gaming. Ghosts 'n Goblins Resurrection is a simple to understand but brutally hard platformer deriving its difficulty from hamstringing the player at every turn: Arthur is slow, cannot change direction in mid-jump and dies after very few hits, depending on the selected difficulty. Most weapons are highly situational (get the knife!), enemy AI responds to the player’s position and movement, and they respawn at seemingly random intervals and/or locations which prevents beating levels by simply learning their layouts and enemy placement. Trying to clear sections from seemingly safe positions will usually be punished in some way, forcing players to always be on the move.Unlike the series’ older arcade-style games, this instalment comes with unlimited continues, allowing a return to all previous checkpoints without having to completely retry levels - unless players want to because they have maneuvered themselves into a disadvantageous situation. The game should be approached like an action-puzzle game. The main goal is to understand the situations, where to advance best and how to react to enemy movement. The levels are successions of short, complex sections and are meant to be explored by dying a lot and trying to learn from previous execution mistakes. Reload times are short and allow for a quick breath before tackling the latest level section again. Ghosts ‘n Goblins Resurrection requires a LOT of patience and the reward for succeeding is success itself as there are no lavish cinematics or intricate world-building and lore to be found. It is a bare bones arcade experience, but with great nostalgic music and charming 2D graphics reminiscent of storybook illustrations and a paper cut-out animation aesthetic. With the right mindset Ghosts ‘n Goblins Resurrection is not an exercise in frustration but a trial-and-error challenge in which every inch of progress feels earned!

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to chime in on how Resurrection compares to other games in the GNG series, and also Cuphead, because I've seen criticisms of this game, some justified and some not.1 and 2 are incorrect. This may be a platformer, but you're supposed to learn each level step-by-step like it's a rhythm game song or a hard boss fight. You shouldn't expect to get through a section on your first try, and this game demands patience. That goes hand-in-hand with the jump system; you're supposed to learn how to use the jump judiciously and plan around it. The levels are specifically designed for Arthur's jump trajectory. Besides, jumping in real life is fixed too.3 is a real issue though. The weapons you get at the pick-up spots are randomized, and it's not fun nor realistic that you'd have to replace your weapon just because you touched another weapon. Cuphead does it best by not having weapon pickups during the levels at all, so a run of a level start-to-finish with a particular loadout is never compromised. I agree that some of the weapons are worse than they should be:-The crossbow/arrow is slower and has a terrible ground trajectory where one of the two arrows just shoots into the floor (useful if you're shooting off a cliff, but 50% utility in every other situation on the ground, and lob weapons exist); those are straight up nerfs from Super GNG's arrow.-The hammer is slow, hits hard as a melee, and has a minor projectile, but the projectile only comes out if Arthur is midair or aiming up, and most enemies die to one knife hit.Both of these weapons are good in certain situations and would be good as support weapons, but , so your progress could just slow to a crawl if you get stuck with the hammer early on. However, once you have the additional slot, these become much more useful because you can throw out an attack with one and then immediately switch to a proper weapon like the knife to get good coverage; weapon switching is snappy.I have my own points of unfairness that I haven't seen in reviews: 1. The hitbox on the guillotines make no sense with perspective. 2. You can't aim up while you are at the foot of a ladder because Arthur would just start climbing the ladder, and then he's vulnerable to the enemy you were trying to hit. This has been a problem in every GNG with upward aiming, and there's no excuse for it. You should be able to hold a button to be stationary while aiming in any direction, like in Cuphead.I could see why people would find the game more fun with double-jumping, but (like the fixed-jump arcs) having only single-jumps is fine because the levels are specifically designed for it, just as Super GNG has levels designed for double-jumping. Original GNG and 2 don't have double-jumping either.No. It looks great. The new storybook/painterly visual style fits GNG very well, and the artists made the most of it. For example, the plant enemies expand and contract when they attack and move around. The grass blows with the wind, and sometimes there are subtle fog effects between different layers. I found it weird that supposed longtime fans of GNG complained about the animation, since the GNG pixel art games aren't better animated than Resurrection is- not like Capcom's top 2D visual stuff like Darkstalkers and 3rd Strike.This is wrong, and also a stupid idea. I'm pretty sure Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts is the only game in the series with finite continues. The actual original GNG is an arcade game, so you'd get more continues just by paying quarters, and the NES version says "Game Over" when you die enough, but you still get the option to continue at the same level.That's the default option on Squire mode, and it's apparently a deliberate design choice so that players who prefer the old school style on higher difficulties don't hit that by mistake, so I don't think that's necessarily a flaw, but the developers should have made the continue menu more functional and uniform for everyone, so I agree that a problem exists.The upgrade system is cool, but there is a balancing issue that makes progression less fun than it should be. The first few upgrades are attacks that are outclassed by the knife because the knife is faster, has almost no startup, has similar trajectory, can kill most enemies in one hit, and is able to hit the red arremer. The devs should have made the weapon slot unlocks come first.As I'm writing this, I don't have much time logged into the Steam version, but I played the game a lot on Switch, and I made sure to check the Steam version's performance and configs; everything is good. The RE Engine continues to be a miracle across different hardware.On Switch, I completed the game on Legend and collected all the Umbral Bees. Just a few things to add:1. While the crossbow in its base form is a bit underpowered, the golden armor version is easily one of the best weapons in the game, and definitely a huge improvement over the golden armor crossbow in Super GNG.2. The game is designed around the fact that you have access to spells at all times (and sometimes you pretty much have to make use of the startup invincibility), so definitely work spells into your play. Emboulden (even at level 1) is a lot more useful when you factor in the startup invincibility and the additional hitbox it has when the boulder is being formed. 3. The game absolutely has some unfair moments, but for the most part, you really just have to learn to use your resources effectively (though getting access to those resources is a lot to ask upfront). Keep in mind that you can reallocate Umbral Bees to build by the situation.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghosts 'n Goblins Resurrection is Nintendo hard. As a kid, I relied on the Konomi code and passwords to beat games. I was never particularly talented. Here, I can't beat the first stage on Legendary. Am I stupid for insisting on the hardest difficulty? I just might be. But, I haven't experienced failure like this since high school algebra, and it's refreshing. Trying again when you die is a near instantaneous affair, and I always feel like I almost had it. If you grew up with an old Nintendo in the 80s, this is worth your attention. If you're a curmudgeonly hipster who stopped evolving in the 90s, it's an auto-buy. Two thumbs up.EDIT: So, last night, my four year old says, "Daddy, I like your computer", to which I said, "Let's make that true". We tried some other games, but nothing clicked because he's got no videogame coordination. I started a game of this for him on Page mode, and he's hooked. Ended up playing till almost midnight. While I've not seen even the first boss because I've constrained myself to Legendary, he's midway through stage two. Granted, he's getting there WW1 style - sacrificing a thousand lives to progress one inch, but he's progressing nonetheless. When it was time to quit, rest assured he needed proof that he could pick up at the same spot tonight. Maybe other people's little folks would like it the same? The Page difficulty seems like it was made just for that. Four thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: 1.) Arthur runs slowly, but the whole game is paced around it. Keep calm and hold right. Otherwise, the spawning  overtake you.2.) The spawns are always the same, but you have to keep moving to see the patterns. I will admit, many of them are overwhelming on Legend.3.) Only two GnG games had double jump. I get it, but does every platformer have to have it? If we could jump twice, some platforms would probably be farther apart and the enemy projectiles might move faster. Not bad, just different. I suspect that single jumps result in fewer considerations during level design.4.) On Legend, the "Retry Area" option is the default and it takes me back to my most recent checkpoint (the blue "Progress Pennons"). It turns out that "Banners of Rebirth" are not in the Legend, or Page difficulties. They're red and I guess you place them where you want. That being said, all checkpoints are saved to the map and the game warns you before overwriting a banner.5.) There are traditional animated sprites in this game, but they're not used exclusively. Flash animations  to use some of these techniques because they're much faster to process and take up substantially less texture memory. In my opinion, this game looks literally fantastic.For me, this game easily lives up to its predecessors. The new asymmetrical local coop is a nice touch. Prior to this installment, the arcade and genesis versions of Ghouls 'n Ghosts were my favorite GnG's.They've implemented numerous features that help reduce the overall challenge, for a more general audience, while staying true to the original design's core mechanics and difficultly. There are multiple paths, checkpoints, checkpoints right before bosses, weapon boxes before bosses, a flexible magic system, and you can temporarily lower your difficultly.Btw: If you like this game, I recommend you check out Volgarr the Viking. It's got a 1cc path.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played the old releases of Ghost and Goblins/Ghouls and Ghosts, then you know what you are in for.  If not, this is the side scroller that inspired Dark Souls type difficulty.  You will play the game over and over, death after death until you have polished your play down to a mirror shine and become unstoppable.  Having started the game on "normal", forgoing hard and legendary until I learn the level design, I can say the game is easily beatable.  It took me about 3 to 3.5 hours to beat the game since it provides you with limitless lives from each check point.  Does this mean the game is easy?  Hell no!  I was dying upward of 25 times in each level until I learned how to beat it.  This is a nice sweet ride down memory lane.  Tons of new level designs and ideas, plus lots of old favorites have been poured into this game.  As for the game itself, you get to pick between two starting levels for the first two levels.  The top levels have a distinct Ghost and Goblins feel and design.  The bottom maps have a Ghouls and Ghosts feel and design.  After that the fork in the road converge and you play out the rest of the game.  I do miss the armor levels (green to gold) that were in the SNES (Super Ghouls and Ghosts) since it was fun to get the powered weapons and the magic from the armor sets.  It is still in the game, only it comes with the gold armor which will upgrade the weapons being used and the magic tree (literally a tree with magic nodes) is separately upgraded and usable despite the armor (or lack there of) in game at anytime.  Now the price....  if you are a fan of the series, you probably already bought it.  If not, then watch some Twitch of the game and you will know if it is for you.  Personally, this was a blast from the past and a game I know will be coming back to enough times to validate the cost.****EDIT****After beating the main game you unlock shadow versions of the levels which have more enemies, darker/fog covered sections and torches that trigger events if they are extinguished!  You will find that these levels will reward you with more secret chests and a large number of wisps, which can be redeemed to unlock the high tier magic skills.  This will change the way you play the game and adds a ton of extra playability.  <3 Lots of love for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: For players that define fun as an experience that allows them to roam, explore and progress at your own pace, this game doesn't fit that description. For players that will immediately turn down the difficulty, you'll find fun here, but you'll be missing most of the highs this game has available. There are definitely lows, when you realize that enemy spawns and patterns are 50/50 situations most of the time, but as you practice and get better that matters less and the real joy to be found is mastering every situation thrown your way. Dark Souls fans, Arcade fans, NES fans and all that aren't afraid of a challenge, this game is for you. Pay the price of purchase, then sit and have a time. It's one of the most rewarding games I've ever played and though I could progress a lot farther, I keep going back to the first level, polishing and mastering the game play. It's simply awesome.

_childDocuments_.review: GRADE A: Its a fun retelling of the Ghosts 'n Goblins story in a beautiful pop up book art style that i simply love. It is still hard! But thats not a bug, its a feature that is a core part of the franchise. Ghosts 'n Goblins Resurrection basically retells the classic Ghosts 'n Goblins story but through the lens a a Pop-up Fairy tale book. You're Sir Arthur, a knight who spends way more time in his boxers than his armor, battling a menagerie of monsters through Gothic graveyards and ruined churches. Your paramour has been abducted and your going to save them. You start off with a quiver of infinite javelins that you can sling like missiles, and a suit of armor that falls apart each time your hit until your left wearing only your boxers. And you quest this way, running and jumping from left to right, throwing javelins and searching for power-ups. Until you reach a Boss that you have to beat to finish the level.  In addition to the beautiful art style and the classic game play there are some fresh additions to the formula. Things like multiple branching pathways that you can replay and a new magic system, which lets you shield yourself or turn enemies into frogs or shoot bolts of lightning out across the screen. But it does keep a good balance between staying faithful to the series trademark difficulty while still drawing you in to the world of this pop-up  story book  fairy-tale. Its not easy and its not revolutionary but its is Ghosts and Goblins and like Contra or Mega Man, its not something that's broken so there's nothing that requires much change or needs to be fixed. It takes familiar characters, nostalgic enemies and iconic locations from previous games in the series and uses them to tell the classic story in a new way. And the whole thing is rendered in a beautiful fun new way. And i think its worth your time and money to play and support.

_childDocuments_.review: I was offered some cookies if I reached the true ending of this game in legend mode (the most difficult one), and I did. On legend mode, this game isn't borderline unfair or almost impossible, it *is* unfair and impossible. The number of enemies, projectiles, and random pits that you have to keep track of at any given moment is obscene and the scant number of checkpoints makes overcoming each of the game's obstacles a brutal challenge. However, the game is very upfront about this. The series is infamous for its difficulty and the game says "you will die" upon selecting legend difficulty, so you know what you're getting yourself into. At the end of the day, I had fun with this game because I went into it expecting it to be unfair and wanting to overcome that. So, if you're looking for a ghoulish challenge that will drive you to the brink of insanity, you can't do much better than this. If you're looking for a fun platformer to chill out with, look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good, of the three versions you can get of the game it might be the worse though, simply because they added some upgrades that are a bit of a mixed bag; some of them are good, a lot of them are useless. Then there are some platforming sections later on that can get a bit annoying, they're not many, but they are enough that they can really grind your gears.Real problem is the fact that the game devs decided to add difficulty options, which is good, but they punish you if you play on the easiest one, by locking you out of the "true ending" of the game, it's not that big a deal, you can still play through the game and finish it just fine, but it's annoying when devs do this, either let me play on my chosen difficulty setting, or not have difficulty settings at all if you're going to punish me for how I like to play my games.The art style is nice though, I was a pretty  big fan of it from the start, in motion it can look quite crazy, but it shouldn't be as much of a demanding game as it is, it's unbelievable how those system requirements straight up lie to you; if you try to play this game on a laptop with anything other than 8gb of ram -at least-, you won't be able to even get past the menu, half the times.So yeah, good game, but not without its flaws. Play the other trough emulators if you get the chance, "Capcom Arcade Stadium" has both the original NES one and the SNES one with an added invicibility cheat code -that you have to purchase-, ♥♥♥♥ me. But it also has a rewind feature, which is pretty cool; in my opinion the original games are a masterclass in game design, they're fantastic in their presentation and gameplay.The music is also great in all of them, so there's that.
