_childDocuments_.review: I'm not one who usually writes reviews for things. I'd only write a review if I either really liked something, or was very let down. And hooooo boy...Let me get this straight: If you played the original Drawn To Life games for DS, you're going to be heavily disappointed in this. I grew up playing the two main series DS games. They hold memories dearer to me than one could imagine. In fact, I likely wouldn't be who I am today without them. Let me start off with the good things; The drawing system is significantly better than ALL the games that came before it, though it doesn't blow them out of the water. We'll get back to that later...The pixel art is pretty good too. Although I don't think the music is very "Drawn to Life"-y, there's a couple of really good tracks in here. Especially the lo-fi ones. The character dialogue is good.And this... is about all the good I can say.The entire game feels like it was built on an engine for some kind of budget mobile phone game with Drawn To Life stuff tacked on top of it. The main DRAW (get it?) of the title barely gets used at all, if so it's just as a fun little side activity. Graphics glitch out quite a few times during cutscenes and gameplay.The gameplay isn't terrible, for the most part. Like many have said before me, it's a puzzle-platformer instead of a pure platformer this time around. It COULD have been executed well, but it's just so buggy. The collision detection is iffy a lot of the time. The levels aren't poorly designed, actually. But the main story levels ramp up in difficulty very quickly, which can make it frustrating to play for long periods of time. The side levels seem hard at first, but once you get a certain power-up they become pitifully easy.Remember what I said about pixel art? In the overworld it's good, but in the levels it gets kinda weird. The level terrain is all pixel art... but the backgrounds are 2D illustrations that look like paintings and the enemies / level assets look like they were ripped out of some kind of Scribblenauts bootleg. All the art styles clash with each other, and it's really jarring. About the only enemy that looks like it belongs in the game are the Baki (and maybe that trumpet guy). The story. Hoooooo, the story. THIS is actually what inspired me to write this review.It starts off a bit weak, with Mari summoning the player character for seemingly no reason. Some shady guy with a hood (not Samuel) has given Mari a macguffin book that exists solely as an explanation for gameplay. No mention of the book of life being torn up in the prequel at all... some shenanigans happen in the village and then you're introduced to the human world. The story is a lot stronger throughout the rest of the game, UNTIL the ending. It doesn't go out with a bang, it doesn't even go out with a "wumpf". After what seems like just another story level, the game just... ENDS. just like that. There's lots of clues about a possible sequel, but I honestly don't even think it's going to happen. The game just suddenly ends with a very vague cliffhanger ending that leaves questions to be answered. Where did the book come from? WHY is Mike the only one who can see darkness / go to the raposa world? and most importantly, WHO WAS THE SHADY HOOD GUY? Hell, there's an an entire section of the Rapo village dedicated to the Galactic Jungle, and yet there's a grand total of 1 person who lives there. And I think I know why.I'm convinced this game was rushed HEAVILY. The overall lack of polish, bugs and weird ending just don't seem like something you would see in a game that had actual time and thought put into it.  If there really WILL be a sequel, like the ending suggests, I'm not going to buy it. There's a sour taste left in my mouth by this game that I don't think I'll be able to get rid of. If you're looking to scratch a Drawn-To-Life themed itch, just go and buy the Spongebob spin-off. It's more of a DTL game than this one is.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m late to reviewing this, but I was pretty darn disappointed in the game. I have a lot of nostalgia around the original 2 DS games, so I was very excited to series revived after a decade. What I got wasn’t what I expected at all. It’s nice to see the series return along with the characters, but it’s held back by a lot. Notably, the change in gameplay genre was a very poor decision. It’s very alienating to the people who were excited for this series to come back when the games we loved just weren’t in this style. The old games were an explorative action-adventure platformer type of game where you had a number of weapons and a variety of gear or alternate forms which you used and drew yourself.  This game is a lot less adventurous and much more racking your brain. Not that the previous games lacked puzzles, but this game is ONLY that. Past games also had really cool boss battles which are completely absent in this game. Furthermore, drawing as a staple was absolutely reduced in this game and in some areas regressed from the original entries. In DtL1 & TNC, you drew a lot of things that appear in levels, draw your own weapons, draw far more town things than you do in Two Realms, and you can edit these drawings later in Town Hall. Please, make the next more like DtL1 and DtL TNC from a gameplay standpoint, and then use it as a foundation to build something new from. Remember, the series is called “Drawn to Life.” Two Realms really should have featured more drawing

_childDocuments_.review: ===============CONCLUSION FIRST:Overall, Two Realms isn't a bad game on it's own! It's very cheap and a great puzzle platformer. As it's own game it holds up very well! But returning fans may find themselves disappointed, Two Realms was unable to accomplish the greater aspects of the first two Drawn To Life titles. The genre change may be jarring for some, not everyone likes puzzle games.This is not a triumphant return to the series but a calculated attempt to make a solid game with a clearly limited budget.The creative director has explicitly stated Two Realms is designed to revive the series and set up the world for ADDITIONAL sequels. They did not have the time nor money to make a  third title, so they're using Two Realms to fund for a much better 4th instalment that can match expectations fans have been waiting 11 years for.That being said it's a , which if you ask me; Justifies any shortcomings I have with the game. Well worth it.I'm quite enjoying Two Realms and would greatly encourage anyone interested in the series to try it out to see how they feel! But it's perfectly acceptable to be disappointed... Hopefully this game can fund future titles! ================First I will clarify:Two Realms was made by most of the original team for Drawn to Life. Same Writer.Same Creative Director.Same Pixel Artist.Same Musician.This is a good game! But there are some clear gripes about it...Let's talk about gameplay.Where previously Drawn to Life was an . Two Realms goes the complete opposite with a PUZZLE PLATFORMER.It's certainly getting harder as time goes by, and for the genre it's actually really really good!The character feels responsive and surprisingly doesn't feel as floaty as trailers might imply.It has a unique gameplay loop where you place level objects and enemies to the stage (like mario maker), then have to play through it. It's a very cool and requires you to think differently about stages, "Do I put an enemy here to jump for extra height? Or will this just make the stage harder? How can I use this spring to launch myself in the direction of the goal? How do I make a stage that knocks this bomb into the breakable blocks?"It's really unique and enjoyable gameplay that (while simple) is far more polished and refined than earlier Drawn to Life titles.That being said it is a sharp genre change... Not everyone's a fan of puzzle games and that's totally justified. It gets difficult too.Oh by the way... There's no drawing. At all.I KNOW RIGHT?The only drawing takes place during story events, you don't draw level gimmicks like platforms or swords... Just your character and other trinkets around the raposa village.I can see why they made this decision, so the gameplay part of the game isn't interrupted every 5 seconds to force you to draw something (Which was a huge issue with the earlier titles). But DRAWING is the point of the series, they could have gone the route of The Next Chapter and simply added presets for every available drawing so you don't HAVE to draw if you don't want to. A very strange and very disappointing loss... Perhaps they didn't have the resources for it.There's plenty of charm. Can confirm there were several chortles.It feels great to see all the characters again.Also Mike has a personality now.The story touches on some surprisingly heavy themes, which was great to see tackled. Honestly kind of heart warming.Wouldn't be Drawn to Life without some existentialism.Good twists too.BUT it's not as large scale as The Next Chapter or even the original Drawn to Life. Which I suppose could sum up this entire game. Good polish for this small title, but doesn't reach as far as the original games.A lot of bugs and a few oversights currently, a patch or two could easily fix this though.You earn stars for every level depending on how many points you get, and some stages have these bullet bill cannon guys that infinitely shoot out rockets.You can jump on the rockets for 100 points and they don't stop coming, they always give 100 points.That's a pretty huge oversight lol.======Conclusion at the beginning!

_childDocuments_.review: At risk of beating a dead horse, I'm going to throw my two cents out there.This is, simply put, not a Drawn to Life game and I'm very bothered by the fact that this is actually a main part of what's now a trilogy.I went into this expecting to love it like I loved the other two games, with all the possible customizations included. In my current experience with the game, however, that aspect has been put on the back burner.I see this as an issue if only because of the fact that the creative aspect of Drawn to Life and The Next Chapter were what MADE the games! The entire point was having you draw stuff into the world and, in logical addition, color it in.Here you just... basically play a Mario game. Which is fine on its own, but as the third installment of the series proper is a letdown.Let me sort my points out a bit better. Possible spoilers.Story - Opens up instsntly from where we left off...kinda. Takes a surprising amount of time to exposit before we're able to play. We get given THAT book, and then it just kinda tapers off til the villain randomly shows up? After that I checked out because it just failed to hook me at all. The "not all darkness is some outside evil force" concept seems cool, with people just being really cruel til you fix their mind. But it feels half baked given it's happening because of the outside force.Gameplay - Like I said, it's a Mario game. Albeit, 2.5D Mario, which means it's at least accessable. But it isn't a Drawn to Life game. The most creative you get inside of actual gameplay is some levels that are like fill in the blank forms of Mario Maker levels. All the enemies are just toys that exist in some mental toybox. And no, that's not a joke, they're literally called toys. Bakis are just durable goombas, those weird... armadillos? Basically koopas. It's just a standard platformer really.In addition, the day-night cycle feels a little forced, especially for a mechanic that stops you in your tracks every couple minutes to be like "Hey it's changing to day now." Cycle should either be MUCH longer, not exist at all, or just..not pause gameplay for a pointless popup.Overall, this game feels like it was supposed to be something else entirely, and then they slapped Drawn to Life on the cover. Probably better off emulating the first games, or finding a copy of them on Amazon or something.

_childDocuments_.review: im admitting defeat - this likely isnt an unbiased review. so, these are just my thoughts directed toward anyone who's considering buying this game. sincerely, someone who likes dtl too much <3tr is a game that requires a lot of patience no matter why you pick it up. pick it up for the story, nostalgia, love for the franchise in general, maybe just for a puzzle game? yeah. the game itself isnt as buggy on steam as its other counterparts cross-platform. i mean i'd say i encountered no bugs except for some iffy physics. lag-wise, i had no issues except for the last level in font of darkness.okay story-wise! for the average dtl fan, i think its worth having an open mind. this narrative does put a lot of focus on belleview and mike, but i find it and its story to be reminiscent of rapoville. its a very charming town just like rapoville is/was in tr/dtl1. although the plot's substance is in belleview, rapoville does get a little bit of spotlight. maybe not enough for casual fans though. the view we see into mike's town thats plagued with shadow is awesome to me. themes of divorce, death, survivor's guilt, and inner demons are present here. mmm yumy i love it so much. you might be disappointed with the rapoville side of things, but again, keep an open mind!im a bit biased seeing as ive always loved mike, but he's an interesting  protagonist to follow throughout the game. although i have strong thoughts about his conclusion that dont fit here/are spoilers, he's not flat like he was in dtl1/tnc wii+ds LOLsomething i find hard to understand is our villain aldark. genuinely his motives seem all over the place, and he has the air of a cartoon villain (in the bad way). its difficult to describe him. thankfully he doesnt impact much till later in the game with aly.the overworld experience is a bit odd, with it clearly being built for mobile. the slightly-incomplete air to the assets can be ignored but to me its harder and harder to the more i play this game. but dont get me wrong though - this is a beautiful game. i love the isometry and pixels here, and the ui is cute if not a bit plain. ♥♥♥♥ like the toys and stickers are so stinking cute!!! and the levels themselves look cool to me, save for the occasional odd tiling. its not a stellar puzzle-platformer by any means. the physics/toy ai are slightly unreliable at best and the levels themselves can be easily cheesed if you're clever. occasionally, things such as chain reactions dont work due to the weird physics/ai - this risks frustration. to anyone else, it tends to be a frustrating experience due to the above. now, ive played tr multiple times so i know my way around the levels and its quirks, ergo i can embrace the scuffed experience and make some fun out of it. this isnt possible for everyone though.also, there really isnt enough drawing in this game. its all optional save for the hero and a watch for mike (which isnt visible in the overworld). this paired with just an 'okay' drawing engine makes for a meh drawing experience. my only complaint abt the engine is that the color picker doesnt change accordingly whenever you eyedrop a color. as an artist this was so painful LMFAOkeep in mind that i dont think theres any way to change keybinds and such. maybe im blind idk. so if you have a limitation, keep that in mind. my left pinky is currently broken so i had a really hard time with throwing and stunning.also keep in mind that there's no way to replay story levels unless you nuke your save and start again. in that vein, there's an okay amount of postgame content if you dont mind the optional imagination battles. keep an open mind with these too, trying out combos is very fun imo! there's other stuff like music and development and ♥♥♥♥ that i will likely not touch on. because im lazy .i love this game so much! i always cautiously reccommend this game to dtl fans for the above reasons, so im reflecting that with a thumbs up here. be patient, give this game a try! ask the community for help if you get stuck or have issues, we'll love to help out. also ask us about what we know about the development of this game before being *too* harsh. there's a lot of context to keep in mind before deciding this game is the scum of the earth LOLwhatever DC does next (dtl or not), im there for them. (also circi sweep)

_childDocuments_.review: It breaks my heart to say this is such a wasted opportunity to revive an obscure franchise. After being dormant for 11 years I assumed that this franchise was dead, and I wish it would have stayed that way. Basically what Drawn to Life was known for was being able to draw your own elements to the game such as your own hero, platforms, and weapons. This game tried the Mario Maker approach to level design, which you would think that this game would lent itself to so many creative possibilities to create. Sadly all the level elements are predetermined. How did they screw this up?!  It's not a broken game by any means and it does pay tribute to past games by continuing where the story left off, but it does leave alot to be desired. Playing Two Realms makes me wish the other two games were available on steam because I would rather be playing those games.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is my first ever review, so apologies if I sound rude, snooty or whatever.I've played the first two drawn to life games recently and darn well had a good time! Imagine my shock and happiness when a few days later a NEW DtL game was announced! I understood 5th Cell and Jeremiah Slaczka wasn't on board for this game, but I was still expecting a pretty nice time!After 10 or so hours and clearing story mode, is this game better than the first two games? Personally, I don't think so. Distant 3rd place for this title. Game's only about 9 bucks after taxes (at least where I live) so I'm not expecting some uber excellent polished indie game like Shovel/Hollow Knight or maybe Shantae. It's not BAD it's..."eh?" The main reason I'm a bit sour is the levels. More of the level design which I'll explain later below.The first two Drawn to Life games were more Adventure/Action Platformers with a pretty sweet and concise story that manages to get you really attached to the world of Raposa. This story and dialogue leaves more to be desired in a "needs more meat on the bones" way. It's kinda disappointing that we don't get more lines of chat from the characters we really like after an 11 year absence. This is also a more of a PUZZLE GAME of sorts mixed with DtL platforming, which eeeeeh, not really a fan of. Especially when a chunk of said puzzles are you on a time limit waiting around for an enemy or enemies to cycle back so you can advance.I don't mind the hub worlds and how they're different. The graphics in them (not in the levels themselves) are pretty snazzy. I loved walking around the worlds, looking at locations from past games recreated in beautiful 2020 pixel art. The pixel artists did an excellent job as for as i'm concerned. If you are one of said artists reading this review: WELL DONE!This soundtrack is snappy! I can tell a heck of love was put into it! Even when I was frustrated with some levels the tunes were keeping me from groaning out loud. I'll have to pick up the soundtrack ASAP! Again, if you are said composer or composers: WELL DONE!Maybe I absolutely suck at Mario Maker type games, but some of these levels I spent upwards of an hour on. And I mean these levels you get stuck on are AGGRAVATING. TRIAL AND ERROR is the name of the game, too. There's too many resets for my liking and I think I only got through some because of cheesing said hitboxes. I don't agree with the hit detection having to be on the very top of an enemy's head instead of the upper sides or their foreheads.One thing that the previous games had was an introduction or explanation of enemies. Y'know, so you can figure out how to deal with them and experiment around. Then, in later levels they'd be back with a new and more difficult twist on them. There was....variation! Something this game lacks if I'm honest. It's Mario Maker but without that high quality platforming feeling. The "unf" that made the platforming in the previous two games is gone. Look at footage of 1 and 2 and this game and you'll know exactly what i'm talking about. Ya can't even run in the hubworlds anymore as it's replaced by something questionable in my mind.And holy heck do you barely draw throughout this game! I mean, I'm not knocking off points since I absolutely suck at drawing and therefore use the templates (much thanks for including them!), but if you're expecting using your skills and having what you made appear in the levels.....you're outta luck. The stuff you do get to draw is cosmetic and only appears in the hub worlds. Of course you did this in the first two games, but you also drew a ton of stuff in the levels themselves.RIP Shooter, RIP Slasher and RIP Slinger. You're only using the ground pound and spin attack this time around. That's about all I have to say. Leaves a lot to be desired gameplay wise. I still say pick it up because I'd like a 4th game with more fleshed out ideas they had here. This review has a "thumbs up" but it's more of a "mixed, halfway thumbs!"P.S. I AM VERY HAPPY at something that happens endgame. I won't spoil it, but..."YA FINALLY DID IT!"
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly disappointing. The DS games were fun platformers that had lots of charm and polish. This is a rushed mobile game. The UI has plenty of mistakes, such as the header fonts getting cut off at the top, a pixel brush having bilinear filtering, or a mouse cursor in a tutorial video. The music is bland and forgettable, unlike the amazing record scratch filled compositions of the DS games. The gameplay took a considerable change, going from a 2D sidescroller to a single screen puzzle platformer. The movement is janky and not fun to control. There are plenty of bugs around as well. The achievement triggers are incredibly broken, with me getting an endgame achievement after beating one of the first levels in the game. This is a real disappointment, if you really want to buy it, get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: It's like a cheaply made Mario Maker wearing a DTL branded Mask. The ONLY reason this game has ANY sales is because of the Drawn To Life "comeback"It's talk to 3 npcs and now do 3 puzzles that consist of getting past enemies in 1 room to get to the door, on repeat. That's it. That is the ENTIRE game.Get to the door by placing enemies. Talk to NPC.It's just as soulless as Drew's lifeless replacement.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I bought this game on Switch originally, but wanted to get it on here to support the franchise so my hours will look weird.I absolutely LOVED the original Drawn to Life games. The original game's story broke my heart when I was a pre-teen. I didn't expect the heavy religious parallels and dark themes, but I lived for them. Mari and Jowee were lovable characters and their relationship really showed me the borderline of Friendship and Love at an age that was appropriate, as well as how different people react to trauma and many different ways they cope.The Next Chapter absolutely knocked it out of the park. The revelation at the end of the game, and the major moral dilemma that faces the villagers and the sacrifice they have to make is such a massive philosophical debacle. I understood Wilfre's motives. I felt sorry for him.  I was devastated when Jowee was betrayed by the person he thought he could trust, and witnessing the strain it put on them.Now, onto Two Realms.Two Realms is a return to the series 11 years later. Massive Nostalgia play. Well it worked, because I bought it twice.Story wise, it's a continuation that has a weird place, especially given how final TNC seemed to be. They leave it much more open ended, which has me excited for more games in the future and I appreciate that.Two realms gameplay is a divergence from the Adventure-Platformer level design of the previous games, and instead serves as a series of Puzzle-Platformers. It's a weird change; I'd have preferred the original level design formula. The levels are a decent variety of skill levels of puzzles at least for me, and I appreciate that, and there's a certain level of replayability in trying to get higher scores and better rewards.The drawing (A massive part of the franchise) is very good on Steam. Mouse and Keyboard art is significantly easier than on the Switch version. It does feel slightly toned down from the NDS titles, which is understandable from the aspect of them trying to expand the variety of devices the game can be played on. However, in a game called Drawn to Life... there should be a bigger focus on art.The art-style and music is fantastic. Very true to form, while also being toned up for higher resolution devices.All in all, scattered thoughts aside... I do recommend it. I recommend the first games far more; and I strongly hope there's a more accurate return to roots in the future... but I liked the story, and the gameplay was pretty fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of Drawn to Life, this game isn't for you. And if you're not a fan of the series, this game is also not for you. Drawn to Life: Two Realms is a far cry from the series' roots, and worse than that is just boring.The fun platforming levels are replaced with what are essentially unpolished micro games that are either dirt easy or nails tough with no real natural progression. On top of that, you have to place items and enemies in each level, which could've been done well, but wasn't and just makes the levels more confusing and longer to complete. The levels specifically are riddled with glitches/bugs, and I had the game crash on me many times along with being soft locked in levels far too often, creating a very frustrating experience especially after finally making progress in the harder levels.The integrations of drawings into the levels and worlds are replaced with bland pixel art that you really only get to do a handful of times throughout the game, when creating your character and to make a few decorative objects around the world. When I say "bland pixel art", I'm not talking about the pixel art used throughout the game. While I prefer the hand drawn aesthetic of the previous games, the pixel art in Two Realms is really good. Drawing the pixel art yourself, though, (the few times you actually get to) IS bland. Unless you're good with pixel art, chances are it's going to just feel more lifeless than a free form drawing would, which oozes character even if you aren't good at drawing. Furthermore, the game is called DRAWN to Life. Drawing is a core and crucial element to the series, and what largely sets it apart from other games. Lastly, the story. This is what mattered the most to me, as I love the story of The Next Chapter, and was excited to see what happened next. Unfortunately, Two Realms' story is mediocre at best, and overall forgettable. It features a generic, nothing villain who isn't menacing at all, and it was hard to actually make attachments with the characters throughout the two worlds. I was overall disinterested in the game after the first few hours, and the rest of the game was a genuine slog- which is made even worse as it took me almost TWELVE HOURS to beat the game's main story.TLDR; unpolished, glitchy, meh story, frustrating and tedious gameplay, untrue to the series
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: I heard that they were coming out with a new game and went ballistic. Drawn to Life was a game I played for hours as a kid and I loved so so much. Booting up this game I wanted to cry because I missed this ip so much. It's quite a bit different from the old games, but that's not a bad thing! I hope this means we'll get more!Note: If we do get more, please, please, bring back some of the old mechanics from the first games. I'm not much of a puzzle platformer person and I enjoyed a lot of the older mechanics more as well as drawing our platforms.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, so here's the deal, from someone who just recently went back and played the first two games in preparation for this!Is this the same as the action/adventure platformer that made up the first two games? No. It's a puzzle platformer and therefore has a lot of different mechanics. The drawing ability is a bit decreased, likely because we're out of the years of the DS and 3DS. HOWEVER, I think that's just fine. The game was a lot of fun and often brought a smile to my face. I really enjoyed it and sometimes didn't want to stop playing, as you can probably tell by my playtime. Some of the levels were a bit tough, but I usually managed to figure them out with time. That's not to say that they couldn't have used some variety, however.  I would have really liked if there was a few more type's of puzzles, and maybe if, in future games, they could mix some of the adventure platformer in. However, I'm someone who very much enjoys puzzles so I'm alright either way.I really liked seeing the characters that I knew and loved from my childhood, and catching up with them and seeing new characters was a lot of fun! On the note of characters, the villain was wonderful and genuinely scary at times, and I found him extremely interesting. I do wish there was more of him because of this, however.Though the story might seem a bit lighter then other games, it focuses on people going through loss, grief, guilt and mourning loved ones. At it's core, it has a lot of heart. This means that, much like the previous games, the characters and story are still the very heart of the game and genuinely what I found most interesting.The music is also still wonderfully composed and very good at getting emotion across, as it's always been.However, one thing is I would have loved an option for pronouns!That being said, it's a good game. I very much enjoyed it!
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: If I could give an "okay" review on this, I would.I found out that the game was released yesterday, much to my nostalgic love of the first two DS games and decided to give it a shot streaming it to some friends on Discord. A few hours playing in, I noticed that there...were some inconsistencies.I do want to state initially that I LOVE the art style of the game. It has kept the original charm of the games and it was even a refresher to see bits of the original levels in The Next Chapter dotted around Rapoville. The music is absolutely amazing as well.However...The game almost plays nothing like the originals. If you were expecting linear platforming with epic bosses and weapons you get to draw like in the original two games, spoiler: there are none. The gameplay is comprised of three-staged "areas", no bosses and completely optional extra drawing segments, unlike the first two DS games where whatever you drew actually had an impact to gameplay like the guns and wings. The story was also emotionally lackluster, really surprising especially since The Next Chapter had me absolutely balling in tears. This doesn't feel like Drawn to Life. Even the character creation's elements got downgraded; I distinctly remember being able to change the length of your characters' limbs for extra drawing room in The Next Chapter, so why is it gone here?I will still play through to the ending because I love this franchise dearly and it has made an impact on my childhood, but you're better off buying the original 2 DS games on eBay or emulating it. The gameplay and story on those two are way better. I am genuinely upset the third entry in this amazing franchise was not like how it used to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely disapointed with this oneHaven't played further then an hour in but it seems that the game has a really dull loop of "Find character, enter level, clear level either with ease or utter frustration" and then you move on to the next oneThe good;-The art is still really good, dunno if they brought back the same artist from the previous games but its similar-The music's pretty good, it's pretty nice to listen to and I really like the OST, from the little bit i've heard-Character creation tool is actually pretty good, you can draw just like the previous games but you also unlock "stickers" to get new customization options for your character (like a tail, boots, etc.)The bad;-The levels are boring as hell, instead of proper levels like the last Drawn To Life games, its all shorter levels, which would be fine if they'd be interesting but they really aren't--Also the levels do this weird thing where you have to place enemies in a specific way or else you cant progress which... at that point... why even give us the illusion that what we do matters? Just build it yourselves-As I mentioned at the beginning of the review, there's a loop and a very dull one, it's not very hard to pick up on and it's not very fun-The story, from the little bit I've seen, is boring and can be easily summarized with "Characters grumpy, use book, now they're happy again", might come back and change my review once i delve deeper into the game but it doesn't seem to be going any deeper then that-You literally don't even draw anything outside your character... Again, might not have progressed very far into the game but to give an example, within the first hour of Drawn To Life 1, you'd have been able to not only draw your hero but also a melee weapon and even the town's torch. This game STILL doesn't seem to have a hint of letting you draw ANYTHING by the time it took something the original which is just... weird since the game is called DRAWN to life.

_childDocuments_.review: This game suffers a lot from being connected to a franchise it is too different from. The puzzles are over-thought, weakly explained and generally slow and same-y. The story however is barely there, what exists is a reprint of the older titles with less character or charm. If I had to pick specific issues to fix, the multi-level puzzles are annoying, poorly laid out and don't make as much sense as the prior titles. If, per mind you entered (plot spoiler) you had one level of varying difficulty enemies instead of "Heres 4 puzzles, goodluck!". Also, and this is a real turn off, you HAVE to use the mouse. You can E on the keyboard through dialogue but not to start levels, I dislike having to click top right every level (and every restart). As for the plot fixes, that's debatable down to taste but I preferred travelling through the raposa lands than one, poorly town and its very surface level raposa counterpart. SAD!

_childDocuments_.review: Drawn to Life. Where do I start with this series. What could've easily been a series of games produced to push a touchscreen drawing gimmick became much more due to the story, soundtrack, and how few games have utilized such a design element.But that's the old. How does Two Realms stand up?In one word? Poorly.If you have any experience with the main Drawn to Life series you'd expect quite a few things, and unfortunately few of those things are especially strong in Two Realms.Lets go through this one by one.   -For starters, Two Realms moves the gameplay focus significantly pushing it squarely to puzzle platforming which means it lacks bosses, combat, and exploration.    -The story is a huge step down from the surprisingly dark and mature story present in The Next Chapter. Not once did I feel any tension or threat from the foes in this game, nor did I ever worry for the well-being of these characters.   -The art has always been a strong point of Drawn to Life, so Two Realms has got to do well in this area... right? Well, it's good but in large open areas you'll notice they got a tad lazy and just used solid colours or gradients without a hint of pixel art detail and on some of the characters you really notice how asymmetrical the pixel art is.   -The most disappointing aspect of Two Realms is it's occasional opportunities to draw. In this game you can only draw 14-ish things, and aside from your player character every single one is a town element.   -Lastly the soundtrack. While it lacks the same instruments as the DS soundtracks and it also lacks an especially standout piece (like Real life or Light of my Life) it's overall quality is incredibly high and it fits quite well with the levels and gameplay.For the price? Two Realms is quite worthwhile. As a Drawn to Life continuation? Two Realms feels like a cash grab. I never expected to see a Drawn to Life game that feels so... lifeless. I'd probably recommend it more to people that lack any experience or interest in the series as it's a decent little puzzle platformer, but taken as what it is and what it's come after? I cannot recommend buying this game unless you absolutely have to experience this piece of the Drawn to Life story first hand.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Game is worth if you want to revisit the world, Music and art holds up, gameplay is puzzle-platformer segments instead of adventure-platformer levels, story(I'm still progressing), buy to support the series and possible future titles.Honestly, I am just stoked that they decided to continue this series. It's nice seeing the DTL world again and the music and art still one of the best aspects of the series. I will admit the gameplay is not all there, it takes a Mario maker puzzle style approach with its levels, which I don't mind too much but I hope they go back to the old design adventure like levels in the next installment. The story although not as intense as the previous games still is nice to go through experiencing the world again (Though I believe I'm really not that far in at the time of writing this).Basically, I view this game a nice stroll through the world and characters of Drawn to life, and for that reason I would say it was worth my purchase. I would also recommend you purchase the game if you simply care about the franchise as it is showing to the developers that there is still in fact a fan-base in the DTL series which could further on provide a similar game like the previous installments.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: I used to play the original DTL games for hours on end. This game? It feels like a joke. A slap in the face. There is no adventure, no action, no drawing in levels, no nothing. The release of DTL 3 was a pleasant surprise, tainted by its underwhelming, mobile-game style gameplay and modernized UI.  In short:DTL 2 made me cry with how rich the story was, and the beautiful art and soundtracks to go with it.DTL 3 makes me cry because of how much of a travesty it is.However, I will press onward and complete the game, no matter how it pains me to do so. I will update my review when I reach the end.(update: I couldn't bring myself to play this disappointment again, I'm sorry.)
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: Drawn to Life: Two Realms has a very good foundation, but it seems like 505 pushed the game to a specific release date before it was actually ready to ship. This game was developed by many from the original team and its evident that a lot of love went into *most* parts of the game, but it just doesn't click together as well as the team wanted it to.If you're a Drawn to Life fan in any sense, pick this game up, not because its a good continuation, but because the support for the series will help green light future Drawn to Life games, which I'm 100% positive will be a TRUE return to form.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely a mixed bag, it continues a franchise i was SUPER excited about, but its watered down by a bunch of issues, it's character creator is less advanced than its previous entry for the ds, its hard to draw especially without a pixelgrid to reference, when you colorpick a color, the color wheel does not change to that color as well, and there is a noticeable lack of v sync, leading to a lot of screen tearing. I just hope these get patched.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: For a drawn to life game, the story is bland, the adventure aspect is missing, the only thing you actually draw is your character, and every level is so trivially small and easy you can beat them in a matter of seconds. This makes much of the game a chore to complete as opposed to a challenge, and instead of being rewarded with progression after most of them, all you get is a sticker you'll never use. I was, and still am a massive fan of the original two games because of the connection formed with those characters and that world as a whole, and it breaks my heart to say that this game is a major let down to any fan of the series up until this point. I admittedly haven't finished the story, so maybe there's some big twist i just haven't gotten too, but the long I played waiting for this tutorial to finish so I could get to the real game, the more it sunk in that this shallow imitation is all that this game has to offer. The potential story almost writes itself, they could have gone with something along the lines of "as Mike wakes up after the accident, the world of the Raposa begins to fade and its your job to save it", but as far as i can tell, there is no threat or danger, and the whole game is just wandering around the hub doing favors for people. Everything in the game sadly doesnt rise up to the bar set by the previous two entries, so if youre a fan of the previous two, just let the story end there and youll be just fine.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: Drawn to life was the first ever game i ever played and i loved it. I could not think of any other game with such creativity and charm. I loved the sequel just as much. While the games aren't nearly as good as i remember them to be they are absolute must plays for any platformer fan. So how is this game? Insultingly bad. I have played a lot of bad games in my time but this doesn't feel like a game that was made by incompetent developers. There is moments where the passion of the developers shine through such as the pixel art. This game was clearly on a low budget and rushed out. Also doesn't help with the fact i stayed up to midnight to play this... On my birthday.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who grew up with the original Drawn to Life being my favourite childhood game, this one hurts. I was so excited to see it come back from the dead, with an all-new play style and on modern consoles no less, but the product we've gotten feels mediocre at best. It feels and looks like a vaguely DTL-themed app game by the giant UI, very short levels that vary between incredibly easy and skyrocketing hard, and how while there are recognisable characters the 'Drawn' in Drawn to Life is nearly entirely missing. You draw your hero and a few props for Rapoville as far as I can tell, but that's it - as opposed to the sun, the eternal flame, the snow gun, the platforms, and so many more from the originals. Travel in the overworld is slow, and the speed-up fruit dotted around instead of, say, a sprint button cements that (and again makes me think this was an app first by needing no buttons.)I'm honestly just sad that I played a little too long to refund this, hoping that it would get better, overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING: Spoilers. DO NOT KEEP READING UNLESS YOU ARE OKAY WITH SPOILERS.Initially, the game has an overall interesting premise, and mostly good music, but has the absolute most dissatisfying third act out of any video game I've ever played. In many ways, the game ends in a way that kinda reads like it doesn't even know it reached the end, not just of the series (if this is in fact the final entry) but even just its own individual story. By all means, put this game's soundtrack in your music playlists (unless you're putting together some epic boss music playlist, in which case void this part of my review), but don't stay for anything else. I hate to have to say this of a game in a series I've loved for almost as long as I've been playing video games, but I'd be a liar to defend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It just isn't all that interesting, and I wanted to experience it for myself despite the bad reviews, but the levels are so different from previous entries. I loved the exploration of the previous games, and despite most people not enjoying the second so much, I still liked it. _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed my time playing this game. It has its flaws and I can understand the complaints other people have about this game, but my overall experience was fine. There are a few important points people who played the first two games should know about since Two Realms is very difference from the previous installments of Drawn to Life.The gameplay is very different compared to the first two games. If you remember the sections of Drawn to Life: The Next Chapter's levels where you draw lines to act as platforms to reach an exit, this game's entire focus is on challenges like that. Instead of drawing the platforms you use to cross the level, you utilize various "Toy" enemies to cross gaps, unlock doors and complete objectives. Everything, even the boss fights, are these puzzle levels, making the game a lot less action-oriented than its predecessors. Some stages are pre-built while others allow you to choose where and in which directions the Toys move in, giving you some freedom in figuring out how to solve certain stages. It was fun seeing how all the various Toys interacted with one another and coming up with creative ways to solve the levels. There were moments where the levels got frustrating when I was trying to collect every coin in every level, since that requires much more precise Toy placement and usage to achieve than just blowing through the level and reaching the exit. Other than that, I liked the gameplay and didn't mind how different it was from the original games.I liked the storyline stages but the optional battles where you have to collect points to achieve three stars seemed a little strangely designed to me. The vast majority of the optional levels are beatable regardless of the kinds of Toys you chose to complete it with, meaning the only goal was to use Toys to collect as many points as you can in the time allotted to you. On top of this, the optional levels give you a random assortment of Toys and make you spend coins to manually choose which Toys you want to use, meaning there was an incentive to exit and re-enter puzzles over and over until you got the Toys you wanted. In my experience, I ended up refreshing the optional levels over and over again until I got the same two toys I knew gave a ton of points when they interacted with each other, meaning the way I solved the optional levels had nothing to do with the Toys I used. I only wish more of the optional levels had challenges that required you to figure out the proper Toys to use to complete it since it was boring using the same exact set up every level in a situation where I had access to every Toy in the game to solve it.Most of the things you draw as the Creator, other than your Hero, don't show up in the actual levels themselves like your drawings had in the previous two games. There are things like the buttons and crates inside the levels I thought could have been drawn by the player but instead the only drawings you do are for objects in the hub world, kind of like the drawings you do in the first game when you return a new page to the village. I personally didn't mind this, but like the drastic change in gameplay I can see why some people who played the previous games wouldn't like this.  I liked the story of the game. It has the same goofy interactions with side-characters and gut-wrenching, emotional moments I had fallen in love with in the previous games. If you enjoyed the story of the first two Drawn to Life games I am confident you will like at least some aspects of the story in this game. My only complaint is how poorly explained the return of the Raposa universe was after the ending of the second game. We see the Raposa and their realm disappear at the end of the second game and it isn't explained how they came back or if everything they had believed about their world in the second game was wrong. I didn't like this because discarding the idea that Mike waking up would destroy the Raposa realm undermines all the difficult and awful choices Mari and Wilfre had made believing they were doing what was best for their realm. The story of Two Realms was good on its own, but it's set up on the principle that the Raposa realm never disappeared, which didn't sit right with me. Overall, I am happy I made the choice to buy this game. Seeing a third game existed prompted me to replay the first two games and I am satisfied with the way Two Realms has continued one of my favorite game series from my childhood. Despite its flaws I still really love this game and I would recommend you give it a shot if you love the first two games as much as I do.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who adored the previous Drawn to Life titles, I was initially mixed on Two Realms. This is going to be a lengthy review, but I hope it helps anyone who also loved this series as a kid.First of all, before you comment on my time played, I beat this game on the Switch a couple days ago and decided to see how it played on PC... thus the short two hours. They play very similar, but performance and controls on PC feel better.Alright, onto the game itself. First, the cons.The first noticeable change is... definitely the gameplay. Instead of it being an action platformer where you draw your hero, draw your weapons, and draw items to help you with your adventures, Two Realms is more of a puzzle platformer with minimal drawing involved. You still draw your hero and other minor items in the Raposa World, but the scope of how much you actually draw is minimized.The lack of drawing was disappointing. I think I'm a bit more forgiving than most people with this, though. Seeing as the original Drawn to Life entries were optimized to play on the Nintendo DS, right down to its touch screen gimmick, I never really expected the same experience with Two Realms - a game not only developed for the Switch, but for PC and different mobile devices as well. So, I do understand the change to a certain extent.As for the levels, I personally found them frustrating. I did not like them. But, it's important to note I have never been a fan of puzzle games. The puzzles in Two Realms are clever, but not impossible, and I am sure puzzle fans will have a lot of fun figuring them out.This is honestly where my major issues end. I have always prioritized story, characters, music, and art over gameplay, so that is important to note with my final rating.Now, for the pros.Despite issues with gameplay and minor glitches, Drawn to Life: Two Realms feels like it was made with great respect for the plot of its predecessors. When I first found out there would be a new Drawn to Life game after 11 years, I assumed the worst. I assumed this would be a cheap cash grab with a team of developers who would toss the previous entries' stories and characters out the window. Considering how it's been 11 years, and considering the shocking, definite ending of The Next Chapter, I honestly assumed Two Realms would be a soulless reboot of the whole series.Well, I was wrong.Two Realms continues right off of The Next Chapter's ending, and does not shy away from the consequences such an event had on the characters. Two Realms' story definitely has a smaller scope... this seems to be a common complaint, but it is one I disagree with. I feel like the smaller scope fits what it was trying to address: a more personal story focusing on Mike coping with the accident. A large, dramatic tale with high stakes and awesome adventure would have felt inappropriate, in my opinion.Two Realms, in typical Drawn to Life fashion, leaves a LOT vague and can act as either a closing point for the series or a brand new start. Regardless of interpretation, characters and important plot points are left relatively intact and treated with a surprising amount of respect.As for the art and music, they're both wonderful. The original artist and composer are back, and they do a fantastic job. I know some people are not fond of the music, but just because it's different doesn't mean it's bad. I feel like it's down to personal preference, though.My final thoughts...?At first I was mixed, but the more I thought about Two Realms and everything the developers had working against them, I have definitely come to appreciate it a lot more.Drawn to Life was a niche, gimmick game made specifically for the Nintendo DS in 2007. The series' last entry came out 11 years ago and ended on a shocking twist. It was never as popular as Scribblenauts, and it wasn't too well known, even in its prime. THQ went bankrupt, Drawn to Life was sold to 505 Games, and it seemed like it was the end.But, "[it was] not The End".... For Drawn to Life to come back as it did is amazing. This thing had everything going against it: a gimmick game for an outdated handheld device with a VERY niche fandom. Developers interested in continuing the series had proposals shot down all throughout the 2010s. I'm not surprised Two Realms had a smaller budget and was forced to play on mobile - it was a risk and acted as an interest gauge for bigger and better entries.Ultimately, Two Realms was a small, enjoyable experience that rekindled my love for the series. It is not the same as older entries, and the gameplay felt a little disappointing, but considering the circumstances of its release, I came to appreciate it. It isn't perfect, but I had a lot of fun with it. Old fans should approach this game with an open mind. The game is different, and has a smaller budget, but is not bad by any means.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game and I will keep playing it however this is just not a worthy sequel. I really enjoyed the original 2 DS games, I even enjoyed the Wii and Spongebob spinoff titles. But this just ain't it. The story is meh and a big let down compared to the original 2 games, but that is not my biggest complaint. The worst thing about this game is that it isn't even Drawn to Life. Drawn to Life is an adventure platformer with a story and some unique mechanics involving drawing, this game just throws all of that away. This game is essentially a Mario Maker like puzzle platformer game with levels that take literal seconds to beat, the levels also don't feel connected and just a lazy filler for the story. You need to collect stars to progress by helping random characters and completing a few of these levels, again this all just seems like unnecessary filler. It's nice you can see all the characters of the old game again but that is about the only nice thing to it. The characters themselves feel kinda lifeless in this game and the story just feels rushed. The only reason I play this game is so I can be in the world of Drawn to Life again. I will update my review if any of this changes as I complete the game but I just can't recommend this game. Go play the original Drawn to Life and Drawn to Life: the next chapter instead.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fine. It absolutely is a departure in gameplay from the previous two games, going from an action platformer to a puzzle platformer, but I still had fun throughout. Levels are much more bite size, but there are a lot more levels than the previous games, so this can either be a plus or negative depending on what you prefer.  All the characters act how you would expect, I just wish they had more interactions with the player and each other. The game is good on its own merits, but labeling it as a direct follow up gameplay wise would be misleading.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first heard that there was going to be a new addition to this series, I was overjoyed. I was also ready to see how such a big span of time would change factors such as story development, character and level design, and the overall style of the game.Focusing solely on the story, I was bored during most of the cutscenes. I am also under the impression there were two characters who added nothing to the game: the hooded figure and Aldark. Yes, Aldark, the main villain. If this character were removed, I do not think much would change within the game. Maybe the introduction of a new villain would have been out of budget or not worth the effort, but the Shadow really do not need Aldark to be their driving force. There were also some story elements that I got a little lost in or did not find clear enough. There were also callbacks to the previous games which do not align with the story already established. It honestly feels like the developers forgot the story they originally created.Focusing on everything else, I was impressed. I am absolutely in love with the soundtrack! All of the songs featured were great and I love listening to the soundtrack outside of the game. I also adore the polished style of the Raposa village as well as the Human realm. This is definitely nitpicky, but there is one female character who seems to have an unfinished design. Her name is Ms. Esow and her character sprite appears differently from the rest. Additionally, there are not many opportunities for the Creator to draw. This was puzzling, as it is such a big feature of the other games. In total, there are about 10 creations in this game. The only other issue style-wise is the occasional visual glitch, which I know are getting ironed out. As a big fan of puzzles and platformers, I enjoyed playing through these levels. There was a good balance between levels used to teach new mechanics and levels that were genuinely challenging. I do not have many complaints gameplay wise, other than some items such as not being able to customize your own controls. To expand on this, some actions share a keybind, such as the spin-attack and throwing enemies. Another example is the ground-pound ability and dropping held items. It would be nice to separate these actions. Another questionable aspect is the difficulty of some imagination battles. It seems you can do everything right, but still only finish the level with half a star. The appeal of these battles are the sticker rewards. For those stickers that I just couldn't live without, I found ways to grind points in order to meet the point threshold without completing the level as intended. When I heard negative stories from other players, I wanted to give this game a chance to redeem itself and not listen to the overwhelmingly negative opinions of my peers. Upon finishing the game, I was disappointed. However, I would still recommend this game to anyone looking to play. While it is not as fun as its predecessors, Two Realms is still an enjoyable game that looks and sounds great. It was so nice being able to revisit characters as well as meet some new ones. :)

_childDocuments_.review: having 100% Drawn to life 3 all aside from 1 level thats glitched; I can sadly say that this isnt a "drawn to life" game. This is a glorified puzzle game which slaps the name "Drawn To Life" onto it; hoping fans will think this is a squeal we all wanted.This game has no sense of story, direction or even genre. This game doesnt know what it is or what it wants to be. What made the previous titles so rich was the deep compelling characters whose issues people could relate to. The title Itself "drawn to life" is barely applied in this game, you draw your main character and thats literally it. _childDocuments_.review: I really, really want to like this game; a revival of one of my favourite series should be something I like. But I can't; it doesn't continue a lot of what the older games are known for, and the thing it tries to be instead doesn't really work the best either.For the first point, it continues the story, yes. It has a similar artstyle, many returning characters, similar feeling if different music. But it doesn't really feel like the older ones. But that's largely it, from what I've seen; the gameplay is drasticly overhauled into being a puzzle game when the others are all platforming adventures. Even with most of them having one hub, you were clearly exploring different worlds, while here you go into peoples minds. And the actual drawing element? While in earlier games it was a big thing, here the hero and some misc. items are all you draw, and the tools are better in some ways (unlimited colours) and worse in others (no scrolling while zoomed in). That said, I don't mind the retroactive addition of a new villain too much, since the alternative would be a new setting altogether.As for how well it works for what it is, it's not entirely bad; it's fairly respectable as a puzzle platformer. But I still don't feel satisfied playing it; challenges vary a bit too wildly in difficulty in my experience, and there's no sense of a climatic stages when villains appear. The concept of going into imaginations feels somewhat wasted, as the environments feel relatively generic still. There's no incentive to do particularly well on mandatory stages. Overworld navigation is a bit too slow, and having items on the map to speed up is strange. Oh, and in my playtime I found a layering issue with the schoolhouse's lit windows at night where the hero is below them if you stand by the wall, and at one point seemingly arbitarily stopped earning bonuses on the side levels; this was fixed by restarting the game, but given those bonuses are essential to getting even two star rankings the bug should not be there at all. (Unfortunately I cannot reproduce the bug, being unsure what the trigger for it is.)I will be honest, if not for things like the bugs I found I'd likely either not review this (Steam really needs a neutral review option) or leave a positive one; I don't like the change in direction but can respect it. But as is I don't think it makes good use of the older material and that it's not quite there for what it wants to be either, which prevents me from being able to recommend it as of this writing.

_childDocuments_.review: There are some small bugs here and there, but nothing that has had a genuine impact on my experience. I think the decision to switch from long form levels to groups of platforming puzzles is interesting, and I've mostly enjoyed figuring out solutions to the puzzles presented to me. I think the only actual criticism, albeit subjective, is in regards to the soundtrack. David J. Franco is an excellent composer and it's nice to hear what he could do with Drawn to Life's melodies and motifs using modern hardware and musical nuances, but I feel it lacks a certain charm the old DS midis had. It's somewhat surreal hearing a Drawn to Life OST without those iconic record scratches.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played Drawn to life ever since I was a little kid. Seeing that they made a sequel that follows after the 2nd game, which I thought ended the whole series, makes me feel REALLY nice. I missed this series a lot, and bein' given an opportunity to work with new concepts I've made in the decade since has been really nice! One of the few respites of 2020. Now of course, I can tell this was made at a much lower budget (Fortunately, the price point mirrors this and they aren't tryin'a haggle) so I'll be gentle about the bad aspects. If you enjoyed the first two games and wanted more content, then this will be right up your alley! Note that the gameplay isn't like the first two though, as this one is a puzzle platformer, and some elements of creation the first game had has been discarded (with some new elements taking up the space they left, fortunately. We've got a color box for coloring now! Like, actually selecting hue, etc.!) The story and character dialogue is also a lot smaller in scale to mirror the budget. That's alright in my own opinion, since the gameplay is fun and engaging. I do got a good feeling that, provided this game succeeds, we may see a more true to form sequel to Drawn to Life, but honestly? 2020's been a mess, and I'm just happy to have a new game from one of my favorite game series.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick disclaimer / TLDR: I only really recommend this game to people that enjoyed the original two games, like me, since I'm pretty sure that's the audience the developers were making this game for. The story and characters were my biggest sources of enjoyment from this game, but that's only because I played the previous games growing up, and I don't think newcomers will really be able to follow along or get the same level of appreciation that I did out of it.In terms of actual gameplay, I'm honestly pretty mixed on Two Realms. This game is more focused on small puzzle-oriented rooms rather than the action-adventure obstacle course levels of the previous games. You don't ever get access to any additional weapons or gadgets as you progress, and there are no boss battles during climactic story moments. Drawing is also very underutilized, which was weird to see, since it was the main gimmick of the previous games and is what the series was named after in the first place. With that being said, the puzzle levels did grow on me the more I played it, and they do get legitimately interesting and challenging later on in the game; it was just somewhat strange to see such a large departure from what the previous games offered.Some smaller complaints that I had were that the physics felt somewhat cheap and clunky, and were reminiscent of old Flash browser games. I did eventually get more used to the physics the more I played, but there were still moments where it was frustrating to deal with. Without getting into spoilers, the game also drops hints that there will eventually be more to come in the future, but the future of this series has always been notoriously uncertain (this is the first game in 11 years btw). The developers themselves have basically flat out said that the future of this series depends on the sales performance of this game, which leaves me feeling uneasy since the gameplay is so controversial among fans.With all those concerns being laid out, I'd still say that I enjoyed this game overall. As I said earlier, the gameplay did eventually warm up on me and I began to have more fun with the puzzles, even if I did miss the action-adventure style of the previous games. The artstyle and music are as good as they've always been, and I enjoyed getting to see this world and cast of characters again, and hope to see more in the future. Going off the developers' earlier comments, they seem to be interested in remastering the older games and creating a bigger-scaled sequel to this game, which I would personally love to see. If you have fond memories of the DS games, you really can't go wrong with this game for only $10, and I'd say go ahead and show your support for the developers. For anyone else, I would say wait and see if they make remasters of the original games first, and see how those turn out.[Edit] Source for the interview with the founder of Digital Continue regarding the future of the series:

_childDocuments_.review: Despite this games budget clearly being how much the devs could find behind their couches, the devs clearly made the most of it, and as a result the game is alright. Now, this is a game that downright REQUIRES knowledge of the prior games in the franchise, so play the first 2 before playing this, or reading this review, or ever looking at the games store page frankly, because it's all relevant to the story of the franchise.In other words...SPOILERS FOR THE Original 2 GAMES PAST THIS POINT.Story: 68/100The game takes place after the 2nd game, instead of the Raposa world being erased after Mike awakes from the coma, it is implied that as long as Mike remembers the existence of the Raposa, even subconsciously, the world remains intact. This, while being the only natural way for a sequel to the 2nd game to play out, is quite jarring and it leaves many challenges for the writers to overcome, most of these challenges, the writers either ignored or solved in a fairly understandable way. However it leaves the parts of the story up to the player's discretion, which again, is necessary for the story to function as a sequel.Overall, while the story is fairly unremarkable opposed to the original 2 games, it still has many of the same character interactions and story beats that made the first 2 games so great. The main Villain however, is unremarkable, and their overall plan is nowhere near as ingenious or oddly sympathetic to Wilfre's grand plan to preserve the Raposa world. Oh, and of course, the fact that the Raposa world remains after Mikes awakening also undermines Wilfre's goal in the original 2 games entirely, which is disappointing, yet again, necessary for this game's story to function in a linear fashion.Gameplay: 61/100This game's core Puzzle-Platforming gameplay seems to be the most controversial aspect of this game, but i for one enjoyed it. The core gameplay revolves around simple action platforming, like the first 2 games, or more prominently, a bizarre blend of Mario Maker and early 2D platformers. In each puzzle level, you have a set number of 'toys' which are either simple contraptions like springs or trampolines, or enemies. Yep, enemies, you are required to place all toys before starting a level, but enemies play an interesting role in puzzles, half the time they are a threat, but they always have a use. It amusingly fits in with the series theme of necessary evils i suppose!Although as basic enemies, they can be killed, and once an enemy is killed, it ain't coming back. This causes problems when an enemy at the start of the level ends up being crucial later on. Luckily, the levels themselves are fairly short, that does not mean they won't take a while however, you will most likely die a fair few times, but not to the enemies themselves, but not understanding the solution to the puzzles. Oh, and there are no bosses, so don't wait for them, its dissapointing, but they would not fit in with the gameplay well.Also worth noting, is that despite the simple gameplay, this game is buggy as all hell, its strange, but given the likely minuscule budget, the game's engine was bound to be janky and strange.There is also a few side quests which have their own gamemode called Imagination Battles, and honestly? A cool idea, but poorly executed. These levels revolve around comboing your 'toys' in unique ways to score points, however, the provided toys are randomized every time you start the level, meaning it is best to just reset the level most of the time to get a better selection of toys to combo. It's a shame that this gamemode is lacking too, as a total of 27 stars are required to finish the game, so you will need to play quite a few.Difficulty wise... some of these puzzles require quite a bit of thinking, and can be fairly challenging and complex, but others are quite tedious.Music: 74/100While i don't have much to say on the game's music, almost everything i DO have to say is positive, the game's soundtrack takes sound motifs from throughout the series and implements them in tracks in a satisfying yet still unique way. And the original tracks that dont borrow from previous tracks in the series are still quite remarkable! From the synth based Galactic Jungle tracks, to the lo-fi inspired Raposa village tracks, this games soundtrack adds to the experience a fair amount.Art: 21/100Unfortunately, this games art took the biggest hit opposed to the first 2 games... At its best, the pixel art is still about average, but very underwhelming when compared to the first 2 games, and at its worst... The UI and Menus are truly awful. They do not match the games pixelart style at all, and look as cheap as a shovelware games UI. This already compromised art style is bogged down further by the over-abundance of pixelart games already available.So to summarize this games art style... Gone are the days of lively rustic buildings with animated spritework, beautiful hand drawn backgrounds, and high framerate character animations. Because this game's art style is one of the greatest problems with the game.Also worth noting, the already habitual drawing mechanics of the first 2 games is even less significant in this installment.Summary:In comparison to the original games, Drawn to Life: Two Realms sits in a strange spot. While all aspects were done better by the original games, Drawn to Life: Two Realms still manages to be a decent instalment, that feels closer to a passion project than a new instalment or a reboot. The game is just as humble in price and length too, retailing at $14.50 AUD. and boasting a fair 10 hours of game time.Story wise, the game fulfills a sort of 'good ending' to the franchise, with its canonicity left somewhat ambiguous. And the game in some regards adds to the overall legacy of the series, even if ultimately the game lacks the overall impact of the originals. I can tell that this game was made with lots of heart from the devs, even if it may not seem like it at first.Overall Rating: 61/100

_childDocuments_.review: A slightly different and smaller game than the originals on the DS, however the low price makes up for this.What really matters to me more, however, is the fact that this is a direct continuation of the original games - it's not a reboot. Despite the fact that the last game released 11 years ago, the original team wanted to return to the original world and characters, and continue this story. You won't see many games be made with that level of love and dedication, especially ones with a small fanbase. If you played the DS games, the main menu music will bring you a wave of nostalgia that hasn't been rivalled by anything else I've seen or played recently. This really helps elevate Two Realms in my eyes - and i'm sure fans would appreciate this too.If this game can help revive the franchise and result in bigger sequels, I'd be over the moon. I'm extremely grateful this game exists.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a Drawn to Life game. If you enjoyed the gameplay of the original game and the next chapter (either version, Wii or DS), you will not enjoy this game. The gameplay is made up of short little levels that largely require you to use enemies as platforms. This makes restarting the level an inevitability unless you can do it perfectly first try, since you can accidentally kill enemies you need to cross gaps or gain height. Some levels make you place the enemies yourself to get to the level end, and it leaves you at an impasse sometimes- are you failing the level because you put things in the wrong place, or are you failing the level because you're just messing up an input. The tragic thing is this couldn't even be recommended to people who have never played Drawn to Life because the story is inherently based off of the ending of the Next Chapter. If you haven't played a Drawn to Life game before, then you have no clue what's going on and if you HAVE played drawn to life you're yelling at the screen saying "when will I be able to draw?!?!"Finding out THQ went bankrupt and this was made by an entirely different company and was also put on ios and android made everything about this make so much more sense, honestly. It's sad, because using a computer mouse to draw would be at the very least better than the wii, and probably equal or greater to drawing on a DS depending on your general skill. I even busted out my drawing tablet for this on my first time trying to play, only to be presented with the utter lack of things to actually draw.  Save your time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: I recently saw that 505 Games had made a third Drawn to Life, and I flipped. How had I not seen this game advertised??? The first two games (Drawn to Life and Drawn to Life: The Next Chapter) were essential to my childhood, and still to this day hold a special place in my heart. The story, the creativity in the different aspects of the game enticed me, but not this game. I watched a play-through of Drawn to Life: Two Realms and was mildly disappointed by what I saw, but I decided to get the game anyway to experience it for myself. It in itself is not a bad game, but it functions completely differently with a different art style than the original two games, wearing the name as a title for a different game instead of being an actual sequel. _childDocuments_.review: In terms of a "Drawn to Life" franchise game with "Drawn to Life" game mechanics, this is poorly done. The original platforming levels, creating your own equipment, and objects have been mostly-- if not entirely-- watered down to a minimum. Do NOT spend your money on this game if you came looking for that aspect of your childhood.The pixel art and music on the other hand is glorious. The stylization is a tad different on the overworld from the original game, but not in a bad way, it adds more detail than ever before to expressions, and looks adorable. The music was catchy in the little platformer-puzzle-minigame-things, and the lietmotif of "Ooo Wilfre!" took me back to my tween years.Overall it wasn't a bad experience for me, but only after I stopped looking for the first two games in it. Drawn to Life: Two Realms brought back some great memories, and at the end of it all, I'm glad I got to see Jowee tie the knot.See y'all in another decade.(Wapo Song slowly kicks in as screen fades to black-- roll credits)

_childDocuments_.review: These are my first impressions from an hour or so in.I adore this game. I think, despite its at first off-putting visuals, it's the spiritual successor to the original Drawn to Life. The original Drawn to Life level design was a unique blend of very simple, relaxing drawing segments with surprisingly methodical platformer elements that usually ended in an easy, cute vehicle level to cap things off. The player was notably rarely able to interact too much with the level, except for the Draw your Platforms mechanic in The Next Chapter. Drawn to Life Two Realms is not a puzzle game, the level design is deceptively simple and forthright. Platforming however is surprisingly complex, a balance of player interaction and mastery of mechanics. You have time to think about what you're going to do while you're doing it. The result are these yummy bite sized levels, with a nice challenge at the end where YOU'RE thinking about where to place enemies and how you'll need to interact with them. Conclusion: Don't be fooled by the cover! This is an excellent pickup to dip your toes in from time to time!
