_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game as I loved all the DS titles, but what attracted me to the series was being able to draw things and bring them to life in the game. With that gone, aside from the creation of the hero, which is the only part that still felt like a Drawn to Life title, it loses a lot of what made the games what they were to me. If I had known drawing the hero was all I was going to get to do I probably wouldn't have bought it even at the $5 that I got it for. When I first looked at the screenshots, it didn't look like the type of platforming game I would enjoy so I held off purchasing it until it was on sale for a good price. I had been hoping I would be wrong and I would find this as enjoyable as the other games, but the Mario Maker style puzzle platforming just doesn't work for me. It just isn't my kind of game. It makes me glad I still have the old titles and wish those would come to Steam. I get that it's harder to draw things on PC, but the games were never about how good of an artist the player was, it was just one of those games like Scribblenauts that inspired a bit of creativity which made them stand out from other games, while this one doesn't feel like anything special to me in any way.

_childDocuments_.review: Drawn to life is my favourite series. Not even joking. Before this game was announced, I was getting pretty sad and nostalgic over the fact that the series didn't have any foreseeable future at the time. Now, this game exists.I'm gonna be honest, it's quite a departure from the reasons i love the original series on DS (and a lil bit of the wii game). The iconic soundfonts and music were ditched for a slightly more generic feel, there's less overworld interactivity, weird, out-of-place mechanics, and SIGNIFICANTLY less drawing on the user's behalf.Do I think this game's bad?well, no, not really.Despite the weird new format, it's honestly not that bad, and some platforming challenges are genuinely kinda clever and require forethought. And at the very least, i can still draw my hero, even if the little additions from the next chapter on ds aren't here (tho i feel like there's a story reason for that, so i guess it's not the end of the world) and... it's still drawn to life. The art's still great, the sense of creativity is still there, there's plenty of great nods and references to past games, and on it's own it's still a decent game.I don't wanna give this game a negative review primarily because i really want this series to come back. This game gives me hope, and if a good enough review score can help make that happen, then take my positive feedback.

_childDocuments_.review: Two Realms is a very welcome addition to the Drawn to Life universe. (I played mainly on the Switch; I have about 30 hours and beat the game on that version.) It follows the theme of the previous two DS games by sounding on the surface to perhaps be a “basic,” or “gimmick” game, but then strongly impacting the player with deep emotion and feeling. The plot is a faithful sequel to the DS games. The pixel art style and the soundtrack are fantastic. The gameplay of the “levels mode” differs from the DS games. But by different I don’t mean bad- to each their own on how much they enjoyed the new format. Two Realms levels are puzzle-platform style. I don’t normally play puzzle games, so it was significantly harder for me to beat this than the first two games. Though I do prefer the original style, I did end up enjoying the puzzles!I recommend paying close attention to subtle dialogue and insinuations, and considering various interpretations of game events, to have the best experience with the plot. I absolutely loved it.Also, I strongly recommend playing the first Drawn to Life and Drawn to Life: The Next Chapter before playing Two Realms. The most impact and understanding come from beating the games in order.Overall, I greatly enjoyed Two Realms. Its release has made me fall in love with the Drawn to Life series again.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: "Drawn to Life: Two Realms" is the sequel to "Drawn to Life" and "Drawn to Life: The Next Chapter". The series hits new gaming territory coming to PC, smartphones, and returning to another of Nintendo's Consoles the Swtich. I will be focusing on the PC version. "Two Realms" could be considered a soft reboot of the series. The previous game left a conclusive ending to the series, but it was rather bleak. This game makes the second games ending not as dark, but not taking away from the consequences of it. Establishing this game as a soft reboot is fitting, but perhaps not the best thing for the series with changes resulting primarily within the game play mechanics. These mechanics shifting to puzzle platforming. I have no problems with the Drawn to Life series becoming a puzzle plat former. Games of this variety have been fun. Unfortunately, the game is not primarily fun. As I have stated I have spent 20 hours within this game, 4 of which were dedicated to one single level. Levels are called imagination battles, and are supposed to represent characters inner emotions. We, the Hero, are supposed to help the individual with their emotions via these Platform Puzzles. There should be difficulties, in any good puzzle game, this enables problem solving. However, level design contradicts the rating of this game, E ( for Everyone). When an adult has extreme difficulties overcoming a level, how is a child supposed to try and solve it? The story levels struck dread into me. I merely wished to continue the story, but these levels would just take up so much time. I had to quit at one point because one of the levels didn't spawn my character into it. I called it a night after that point. I think with adjusting this could become a new style for the game, but one thing needs to be re-implemented, drawingDrawing things into the game is a staple of the series. In fact you are drawing things to "life", but there is no drawing within any of the levels, which is a huge change from the previous games. You can draw a variety of things in Rapoville, but most drawings ,you create are static they do not move. There are only two things that actually move within the game. The Hero, which is the main character you play as, and Mile's Friend. That is only two lively drawings in a game called Drawn to Life. The mechanics, and staples of the franchise may have changed, but the story is a continuation from the previous installments. The story for "Two Realms" is fine. Yes, only fine, which is hard to say for myself. The story is not bad, but it could have been better. I won't spoil anything, but the main theme of the game is forgiveness. Taking our hatred, and forgiving those that had previously harmed us. This is the primary story for Mike, the human character, and is also paralleled by what appears to be a completely off screen side story for Raposa, Mari. I believe if these story lines were given more depth, and explanation; the game play would be more rewarding. The individual Mike is angry with doesn't have a full in-game explanation for why Mike is angry. We are told that he is the cause of the problem, but whether or not the blame is justified is never explained, especially when the ending of the previous game seems to have the same individual not causing bad situation. This was probably the part I had the most issues with, but there are some ways the game could be improved. Improve the Levels they are too difficult, adjust it for proper demographic. Improve the Story. The story is fine, but as stated it could have been better. For future reference give your story more time to breathe, and have better explanations for events like the Character ???, The Book of imagination, the plot of forgiveness, and so many others. Implement more drawing/ more lively drawings. The game is called drawn to life. I may be beating a this topic over the head to much, but its a staple, that should be kept. My overall ratting would be 6/10. I don't reccomend this game due to shere difficutly, but if your up for a challenge go for it. In terms of it being a sequel, its underwhelming, but is still a welcomed addition in my collection. ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this game is visually excellent, and has great soundtracks. If you are a fan of both platformer and puzzle, give it a try.However, if not, and you are just buying this game because of memories of previous games, I do not recommend this game. This game is a lot different from the previous games, and it won't meet your expectations.Pros(+) - Can draw your own character : This is the identity of this game. The drawing tool isn't that great, but it doesn't really matter. - Cute characters and nice backgrounds : These are my favorite parts of this game. Maybe you will like them too. - Great soundtracks that go well with the game. - Simple puzzle platformer : You can enjoy this game casually.Cons(-) - Boring level designs : Throughout the game, you will play similar types of puzzles over and over again. - Bad controls : At first, controls are very stressful. Hopefully you will get used to them soon. - Less in-game drawing : You will draw several things, but most of them are only displayed in towns. During the puzzle games, there's nothing you can draw yourself except for your character. If you're a fan of previous games, you'll be disappointed with this.

_childDocuments_.review: You can draw the hero of this tale… and that’s about all there is to say about this. Fun and mildly addicting as that part is, it’s not enough to hide the fact that  lacks the necessary depth expected from a puzzle-platformer. Besides the lack of polish here and there, as well as the unexciting level design, the bland story one has to endure adds to the general feeling of boredom. It’s also sad that aside from the character creation window, painting doesn’t really feel like a big part of the whole experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: It hasn't even been an hour of playtime for me yet as of writing this review, and I already know what I can say about it.So Drawn to Life: Two Realms is the 3rd mainline entry (I guess) in the series released give or take 11 years after Drawn to Life 2. I've been having a big craving for Drawn to Life after this long hiatus and as you could expect, I wanted this game pretty quickly once I heard it hit PC. After playing the game, I quickly realized why the reviews are mixed.The Hub worlds do indeed feel like Drawn to Life and the soundtrack seems to capture a modernization of the vibes of the old soundtracks, but the core levels and gameplay themselves are very barebones and feel very generic compared to what a Drawn to Life game is known for. It almost feels like Battleblock Theater with a different skin, like a spinoff as opposed to a mainline title.I personally don't really consider this a bad thing apart from the fact that Two Realms may have been advertised as a mainline title for the series (I didn't see any advertising for this yet so what do I really know), but at this point we're gonna need a proper Drawn to Life title on Steam. Whether it comes in the form of a proper sequel or a port of this "Drawn to Life Collection" I've been hearing of recently, I care not.TLDR: It's not a bad game, but it also isn't a full-fledged Drawn to Life game.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing through the game, I was disappointed. Basically, there are 2 reasons why I didn't like the game.1) Gameplay is very bland and dry. Every """level""" seems like a mini game level, which is completely boring. The character design is mostly a step backward except for the fact you get full flexibility in color selection.2) Retcons. Rather than to try continue based on the story (where the coma world gets erased), they made so that they're just living off the darkness, which is a pretty lazy excuse to continue the story line.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not the best at explaining things so I'll keep this brief.  This game is a pretty solid puzzle platformer with a few glitches here and there, but it's not a good Drawn to Life.Little references of the previous games, such as certain lietmotifs and the areas based off the villages in DtL2, are nice to see.OST is still a solid piece of work, with a few remixes to some memorable songs.Every human seems to have a Raposa counter part, From memory there's only around 14 things you actually draw, only two of them having any actual plot relevance. nothing that affects gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: Gosh, I was so excited seeing a new Drawn To Life game that I bought it the day it came out, but this is just a let down. It's not like any of the other games in the series, it's more of a mix of Mario Maker with a character you drew.So far in my time playing it there really isn't that much drawing in it, I got to draw my character yeah but that's about it. Everything else I've drawn have been small background details in the world that you hardly ever see or an item that is never seen again any were.The game play is pretty much boiled down to walking to a glowing spot for the next event, characters talk for a bit, and then you do 3 short puzzle platform sections, usually one just to get to the end, one to destroy all toys, and one where you have to place a limited amount of enemies/items to solve the level. And that's it. The puzzle platform sections I wouldn't say are that fun, just kinda eh, but the one where you have to put down items to solve it is the worst since it's just trial and error.The story, at lest so far, is boring. And honestly if you didn't play the other games you would probably be confused on some things I think. Probably not enough for it to matter that much but probably just a bit.Also why do you walk so slow in the over world? Why was that even a thing put in? In the over world there's these fruit you can pick up the speed yourself up to a more normal walking speed for a limited time. But it's just, what's the point of that? It just makes exploring the town unnecessarily tedious.It just makes me sad that this game has changed so much from what the series used to be. I love this series so much, I've played every game up until this point (first and second game on DS, the Wii version and even the Spongebob Edition.) and just to see what it's become, a disjointed collection of short platform puzzles with hardly any drawings that show up in game. In compared to what the other games in this series used to be, an adventure platformer game where you drew your character, weapons, platforms and many other objects that keep appearing though out the game.I don't recommend this game at all. You're much better off playing one of the other games in this series than this one if your able to get a copy of those.
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the first two Drawn To Life games, you'll love this :D But even if you haven't played the originals, if you like puzzle platformers/RPGs with heartwarming stories, this is the game for you. There's also a fun creative element involved in that you get to draw your hero as well as various things like signs, statues, animals etc. which is probably the most fun part of the game. Even if you can't draw, the game gives you lots of fun templates and stickers to make your hero with. The main draw (get it?) for me with this game was the story. The first 2 games had beautiful, heartwarming and sad stories with characters you genuinely got to care about and menacing, cool villains. Two Realms has all of that as well as some beautiful animated cutscene. Honestly, this game is worth it alone just for the story and the characters.There's also beautiful spritework and environments to explore in the overworld, with the visuals of the game being incredibly charming and cutesy :D Honestly though, the actual gameplay missions, which are puzzle/platformer style, get incredibly difficult the further you go into the game, which can become incredibly frustrating. It's no fun to want to see the story unfold but constantly getting stuck on puzzle levels and not being able to progress. The game also has several bugs and glitches- some puzzle levels didn't work at all, leading me to have to glitch my way through.Overall, Drawn To Life: Two Realms is just as good as its predecessors in terms of story, characters, art, and music, but falls a little flat on the gameplay, with frustrating and unintuitive puzzles appearing often. It also has a lot of bugs that need fixing, but overall the game is very good- it just needs some patches and a few bug-fixes for it to be amazing. Additionally, a level skip option for if you get stuck too many times would be helpful :p
_childDocuments_.name: Drawn to Life: Two Realms

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game you will only enjoy if you play the previous two games.- Level design is good, but visually it doesn't match the reason you're playing the level, nor does it feel like playing the levels matter, unlike in the past games. The puzzle platforming got genuinely puzzling. I had a lot of "ah-ha!" moments here for the first time since Portal.- Story is great, but the writing isn't as good as it could or should be, nor does it really pick up until endgame.      - Character development is a complaint I see a lot, and for the third game in the franchise...? The only new characters serve to push the characters we already know and love - that got their development over two games - along through the story. There was no characters to develop here that didn't already get developed to their peak.- Art looks pretty as ever in the overworlds. The stages themselves have clashing art styles with the enemies and literally everything else. The stages don't look as good as they could. - Soundtrack is fantastic as always, but I wouldn't expect any less from good ole Davey.Aldark is a crappy villian, especially in comparison to Wilfre. No bosses at all. Those are very valid complaints. Everything else? I'm sorry, but please reevaluate the situation. Are you sure we even played the same game?I have all these complaints and praises, yet I still gave it a thumbs up. That's because the good side of everything vastly outshines the bad side, even if the bad side is clear. Playing this was an absolute treat. I had a big doofy grin on my face the whole time because, well, Drawn to Life is back. I genuinely enjoyed myself here. Don't let reviews stop you from playing a game if it looked interesting to you before reading anything. Always give a game a fair chance and form your own opinion. But please, if you decide to play this, please play the first two first. Hopefully you'll see what I mean.This game is just misunderstood. It's another solid entry in a series that has a massive cult following. That's more than enough for me. Welcome back, Drawn to Life. Welcome home.

_childDocuments_.review: Just a heads up, if you're expecting this to play like the older games in the series, don't. This takes the approach of a puzzle-platformer with various obstacle challenges rather than an adventure-platformer.How's the gameplay? Well, it's actually pretty decent... for the most part. While about half-way through the game pretty much introduces every gameplay mechanic and enemy, the level design manages to always manages to stay fresh and give you that "Ah-hah!" moment when you finally figure it out. Few levels however feel really janky and were solved by complete accident. The complete lack of boss fights to break up the gameplay routine also hurts, even though the game presents itself as having "boss" encounters.The overworld also feels kind of sterile, for the lack of a better term. When you help NPC's with their optional Imagination Battles, they don't really have extra dialogue, rewards (outside of the star-rating, which is purely aesthetic and nothing else), or even a "Wow, thanks for helping me!" blurb. The same can be said for drawing stuff for the Raposa, it feels like you don't have much impact on the world outside of the story path.For the rest of the presentation, fans of the series should be happy to know that the story does follow up on the original ending from the second game. I haven't really noticed any plot-holes or contradictions, but the general plot is satisfactory, even if there's a little bit too much running around between NPC's to progress the plot. The climax is also a little weak and feels somewhat rushed and sudden. One last note: the music is pretty cool and graphics are nice, colorful and cute. Overall: I can dig it, but after a decade without any new series installments it feels odd to take such a different take in gameplay-styles, and it could be possibly alienating to fans who grew up with the series since they were little kids (like me) and are looking for a nice nostalgia romp. I kind of miss the creative, aesthetic setpieces and various worlds the older titles had also. Some could even find the game boring, frustrating, and confusing if this sort of game isn't their style. Since there's no option for a "Mixed" review, but I had an overall enjoyable time playing, I'll give this the thumbs up if you're either looking for a puzzler to play for the weekend, or are a long-time fan of the series.Hopefully if there's a Drawn to Life 4 (Which I hope does happen), they go back to the adventure-platformer style, but I don't want to see this new style ditched entirely also. I'm sure the two could work together.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game. Drawn to Life is a series very dear to me, and I've been waiting for a new game for over 10 years. Don't get me wrong though. This is nothing compared to DtL2. There are a number of problems in the overworld, imagination battles, and hero creation compared to previous entries in the series. There's no run in the overworld, and it is instead replaced by a bizarre "run fruit" system. Without grabbing every fruit you see, movement in the overworld is a slugfest. Levels, or "Imagination Battles" as they are called, are extremely well-designed, teaching the player how various mechanics and abilities work as you get them--However, you cannot go back to levels you've already completed with new abilities to unlock new paths, like in 2. There are only a handful of preset avatars, and none of them are generic enough to help lay a groundwork for most nonartistic people. There also seems to be no way to purchase more of them. The hero creator also gives you far fewer creative options than 2. You cannot stretch, add, or remove limbs. No Larryboy or General Grievous for you. The writing also seems to suffer a lot. In the beginning, Mari gives you the task of bringing Mike back to the Raposa world in order to prevent... Something. It is presumably something very bad. This is a MAJOR letdown, as previous entries in the series would show you the danger the characters face, and the hero you create is their only hope of salvation. You, the Creator, are the only one who can save Rapoville from its cold, dark fate in 1. You are the only one who can bring color and life back to the world in 2. Somebody needs to get Mike back in 3, I guess.All in all though, I've enjoyed my time with this game so far, and I'm looking forward to what could be around the corner.

name: Grow: Song of the Evertree
detailed_description: ASSETTO CORSA EVO JOIN US ON DISCORD! About the Game Over time, the Worlds of Alaria faded. The Evertree – where many worlds resided on its countless branches – is now nothing more than a sapling, its splendor long erased from memory. No one knows how to make it grow. But you are different. You hear the sun as it sings across the sky. You hear the language of rain against the earth. You are the last of the Everheart Alchemists and it is your ancestral task and privilege to care for the Evertree. Discover a Vibrant Unique World… at Your Own Pace Find unique places, blooming with fantastic fauna and flora as you are encouraged to explore this beautiful world at your own pace. How do you want to spend your time? Exploring caves and solving puzzles, collecting minerals and flowers, fishing or catching bugs … it’s up to you! Grow Your Own Worlds! Learn to craft World Seeds through Alchemy to generate totally new worlds with unique characteristics. Tend those worlds to rejuvenate them and see how they change, and watch as new properties emerge before your very eyes! You can generate unique meadows, deserts, frozen worlds and… oh, well… Alchemy is not an exact science, some seeds may contain unexpected surprises. Meet New People and Create A Community! Get to know interesting and unique characters, listen to their stories, and help them when they need it. You can make them happier by finding a place for them to stay, helping them land their dream job, or gifting them accessories and decorations. Build the Town of Your Dreams Grow offers an impressive catalogue of the cutest buildings and structures to create the town you want. Place them freely and customize them to make sure it feels like home! A Beautiful Soundtrack A Beautiful Soundtrack by games and anime composer, Kevin Penkin. Mystery! Ruins, caves, secret areas… explore and unveil the long-lost knowledge of the Evertree by accessing its very heart.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the style of this game, how you can put down buildings and roadways and see them as you walk around the town. _childDocuments_.review: After almost 14 hours of sheer joy playing this game, I can happily say that there are zero regrets with this purchase. Grow: Song of the Evertree is a charming, low-pressure game that is very easy to escape into and doesn't require a lot of thinking. Life itself has been pretty full on recently and it's wonderful to have something so wonderful to explore and forget about the mundanity of it all for a little while. I love mixing essences to grow different worlds and see what happens - the feeling of actually making a difference to the world is certainly there. If you're a fan of farming/life sim games but haven't yet found the one that scratches all the itches, I recommend giving Grow: Song of the Evertree a chance.

But wasting my time with souls-like and rogue-lite games is defenitely not better from a global perspective. it has no in-game loot and shop mechanics to strip of real world money and is solid in design and concept combined with decent artstyle. so thumbs up. and because of this sweet and sticky fruitbonbon of a game i have to wash my hands before i can continue my rampage in the next stressfull shooter game...

_childDocuments_.review: Grow: Song of The Evertree is unlike other games in the broad genre of wholesome and relaxing titles about farming-adjacent tasks, for better and worse. Though it lacks the social appeal of games like Stardew Valley, it makes up for it by having a strong mechanical core that rewards players for taking the time to dig into it and play around with its base components.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly didn't think I would be this invested in this game.I don't particularly care for farming/repetitive mining game play, but I just wanted something to decompress and ramp down after my work day. The in-game graphics are the exact reason Indie games are so beloved, the goal posts of the game are all tied together so there is no "meaningless" task, and the characters/bestiary are interesting enough to make you want to unlock new characters. Definitely an unexpected, but altogether great buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: So, let me start by saying that I love this game. If you are looking for an action packed, story driven immersive experience then this is not the game for you. However if you enjoy a peaceful atmosphere with beautiful graphics and that somewhat grindy gameplay then check it out. I feel like this game could have some incredible DLC, maybe with upgradable alchemists grotto or useable work station within your house. Definitely worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my all time favorite games. It couldn't get more adorable. The characters are so fun and unique and entertaining, the design/creative aspect of it is so detailed and fulfilling and the story itself is so cute and encouraging. As lame as it may sound, I genuinely felt loved and appreciated through the whole game and it was during a time when I needed to feel that so badly. Lovely graphics, satisfying sound effects, the fact that you can rename people and choose the names of all the worlds you build??? SO COOL!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: You know what? I don't care if the story has a predictable story. I don't care if the outfits are childishly goofy. I don't care if the conversations are shallow, or that the puzzles are simple. I don't care because I didn't play this game for any of that. I just wanted a relaxing game that gives me the satisfaction of cleaning up yuck and restoring wildlife, and that is EXACTLY what I got. The colors are cheerful and the music is GORGEOUS. I don't play this game for a challenge, I play it because it makes me happy. My thanks to the devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: 100% recommend! This game is beautifully designed with a gorgeous world and wonderful music. The game play is pretty fun and the story line is something that will have you wanting to follow along. My mind is usually too busy to keep up with games where you have to follow a bit of a story but so far I'm having a blast. _childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game so much okay. It's so relaxing and cute. Right off the bat when I created my character, the fact that you can be non-binary sold me. I'd buy and rate any game that lets me, a lil enby bean, actually BE non-binary in the game. Representation matters, folx. The exploration is great, i love exploring the new areas and each world and while it can get a little samey at times, there's enough to do where you can avoid the burn out. Had enough of tending to worlds? Build a town! Don't wanna manage a town or tend to your worlds? Explore the mainland! Don't want to do that? Go see the MOST ADORABLE Everkin. There's plenty to keep you occupied all while being so chill and so bright a colourful. The only main downside for me is some of the quests from the villagers. Sometimes (see: most of the time) they want something that is just pure RNG to get. I currently have 4 quests for beards and CAN I FIND A BEARD? No. It's pure luck. Again, it does get a lil grindy, especially if you have a lot of world seeds on the go at once. I can spend 2 solid in-game days tending the seeds and then I get a bit sick of picking weeds and watering things. But I also love seeing my lil seeds expand and grow, and love seeing if I'll get one of those gnome houses which are hands down one of my favourite things in the game. 10/10 would destroy a gnome house again.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: My neighbour actually gifted this game to me since it was on my wishlist and he had a spare key. Mind you, that happened last week. Now I already spend almost 30 hours in the game, finished the story and got 100% of the achievements.Grow: Song of the Evertree is a cute and beautiful game with a VERY satisfying gameplay loop. You can peacefully care for your crafted world, build towns, care for the townspeople, explore, collect stuff. It is very relaxing and still engaging enough that it won't bore you.The graphics look colourful and pretty (the nights in your towns are great), the creature designs are SO cute and yes you can pet them. Cozy soundtrack as well. Performancewise it runs well on my pc, although I experienced some clunky menus from times and got stuck once in a chest and had to restart. Would totally recommend this game if you are willing to relax a bit and mess around in a cozy world.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I personally loved this game, I found it very cute and relaxing. I had a blast taking goofy pictures and building up the towns. the story and characters are simple but fun. There is romance but it is def not something to go into this game for, as it was very minimal. Like others have said the game can be repetitive with the world seed care but i found the variety of seed worlds kept it interesting for me. You take care of your world seeds in the morning (one or two seeds is best so you don't get overwhelmed) and go off to do other things. The game is very pretty and colourful, and the music is lovely. I would recommend this game to people who just want to relax with a pretty game and don't mind if a story and it's characters aren't super deep.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I don't normally review games, but this game was amazing. The story was beautiful, the artwork was even better, the music was calming, and I could get lost in it for hours on end. Somebody recommended this to me because I liked animal crossing, but I don't feel like that is a fair comparison. This game has a few mechanics: growing plants, planting seeds, taking care of "worlds" and then getting essences out of those worlds. Then the other part of the game is tending to a town, unleashing the world from the roots growing around it, and unlocking new towns and getting more townspeople. There are even 5 townspeople you can date, however you can only date 1 of them at a time. This game is a giant mash-up of many game mechanics, and I have never played anything like it before. If you like grinding? They have that aspect. If you like decorating? Boom. Done. If you like getting cute furry friends? Also done. If you like doing quests? They have that. If you like simple puzzles? They also have those. The art is a very necessary side benefit to me, because it is just so beautiful.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Very sweet game. Gets a bit grindy by the end, but all in all, I did like it and I did finish it. I would recommend for a very sweet, cozy game with a nice message. No violence, no stress, super cute animals, nice decorating mechanic, simple and straightforward puzzles. Talking to the villagers was entertaining, and there were some rather funny little easter-egg elements.  The graphics were lovely and the music was very nice. The "romance" element was really not anything to talk about, so don't consider it a major issue. The game could have left it out entirely without much fuss. I probably wouldn't even have missed it: it's that shallow. That said, I  would happily play it again for the first time, if I could. Not sure how much replayabilty  it has, but I was well worth the 121 hours of fun I had with it. I liked it and would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Ugh, okay. This is hard to write. First thing: the rating I give isn't based on whether Grow is a *good* game. It's based on whether I would *recommend* the game. Is the game good? It's passable. A solid 6/10 effort. There are good things about it. But would I recommend you buy it? No. The tl;dr line on this game is that it's disappointing and half-finished, which makes it frustrating to play.First, a good thing and a bad thing: if you're going to buy this game, you MUST understand that "Essences" are used to build "World Seeds", and those worlds, when harvested, will provide *those* types of Essences. The game will give you a few of many types of Essences to start but you will be pressured into using them to build buildings. DO NOT DO THIS. Build ONLY the buildings you MUST to advance the game to the point where you can seed new worlds, then use your rare Essences to build World Seeds for those worlds. Once they're up and running, you'll get a sustainable harvest of Essences from those worlds you can use to build buildings.This is both the most creative and interesting thing about Grow, and super-frustratingly, the thing that the game does the poorest attempt to explain to new players. It's a really nifty idea! But the fact that the game doesn't explain this core mechanic of the game to you well makes the game feel half-finished. If you don't understand this mechanic from the beginning of the game, you can and will "spend your seed corn" and in so doing, wall yourself in and make it very hard for you to procure the Essences you need to build the mid-tier buildings.Other good stuff: the game is very light and sweet, the graphics are cute and engaging, the story is rich and compelling, and the core game-play loop is interesting and varied. And there are occasional puzzles to be solved and those puzzles are interesting. All in all, the core of the game here *is* good, and is fun.But the ancillary stuff that decides whether or not you should buy the game is not here. Key tutorial moments are either handled poorly or not handled at all. There is no in-game help or encyclopedia (the devs are clearly just assuming that someone will write a wiki to document their game). The whys and wherefores needed to find and engage on the core game-play loop are missing. That loop in a fairly short amount of time becomes repetitive (build up one town! okay, build up the next town! okay, build up another! and another!).But the thing that is fatal to this game and what makes me rate it not recommended in the game is that the characters in the game are completely uninteresting and lifeless. Only two are given personalities; the rest are just RNG-derived automatons and not even well-derived automatons. You're just as likely in the early game to get townsfolk demanding to work in end-state buildings that there's no way you can provide. But the charm and life that this sort of game lives or dies on is entirely missing.Overall, it seems likely to me that the devs rushed this into production without completing all the intended features, and may start to build in some of those features (including more characters) as the game makes money. But as of December 2021, I cannot in good conscience recommend this game. It is just too unfinished and haphazard to warrant your full price dollars. If it looks appealing, wait a year and buy it during the 2022 Winter Sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun if you like the type of gameplay of watering and gathering plants, building towns similar to Dark Cloud 2, breaking down items to get materials, (which I do), and a beautiful world.  Singing to the fauna and having a bunch of bubbles burst out to collect is super satisfying.  However, there's some really questionable gameplay design, from minor annoyances to major issues.  It's really annoying when you run up to an object and the marker appears above indicating that you can interact with it, but then you're actually not close enough.  The game is super finicky about where you need to be to interact with said objects.  I spent a few minutes running around a tree, trying to chop it down, and it was very frustrating trying to find the right spot, even though the icon was showing.  This wouldn't be such a negative if it weren't such a major part of the game.  Another instance is when you see glowing objects in the town, but it won't let you interact until you're in the exact right spot.  If you run up to hammer a rock or cut grass, etc, the icon will show above indicating that you can interact when in fact you can't.  You'll need to to move like two steps closer to interact.  There's also no map, so in the introductory area where there's a few quests, you can find hidden locations where you have to come back later when you have the materials to interact, but you have no idea where it is because there's no map.  There's also the minor annoyance of when you are trying to clear areas or build stuff, it costs Myora.  But you have no idea how much you actually have on you when the option to use them pops up, so you'll either have to back out of the dialogue and go into your menus to look, or you will have to just trust that you have enough to do what you want.The writing is also mediocre at best.  I don't expect these types of games to have the best writing, but this one is pretty bad.  It does have its moments, but it's mostly very stale.  Even Harvest Moon has more personality in the writing than this game.  This is unfortunate because when you first load into the game, you have the option to learn about the lore of the world and it's like a middle school child wrote it.I was honestly going to return this game, but it took so long to get through the tutorial and I'm already past the two hour limit for Steam, so I guess I'm going to keep it.  I recommend this for people that just want a game like Harvest Moon or Animal Crossing or want the building aspect from Dark Cloud 2. I'm giving this a NO because I do not enjoy getting lost in games and having to backtrack to areas where there are no maps to at least help guide you.  The above mentioned issues are also incredibly annoying and make the game not as relaxing as it should be, and I'd rather play other games than struggle with chopping trees and getting lost.  I'm really disappointed because I've been looking forward to playing this game since pre-release.  I'm probably going to keep playing since I spent the $20 and give the game another chance, but I'm not expecting it to get better unless the developers decide to patch some of these issues out. I've almost hit 9 hours on this game, completed the first world seed, made a few more world seeds, and started the new district.  The gameplay loop is extremely repetitive to the point where I wondered why I was still even playing, and I'm saying this as a person that was a fully melded crafter/gatherer in FFXIV, enjoyed Harvest Moon: Back to Nature, Friends of Mineral Town, A Wonderful Life, Magical Melody, all the Rune Factories, Stardew Valley, Worlds Apart, Animal Crossing, and the Atelier series since the first Atelier Iris on PS2.  The villagers seem to be randomized and I've already heard the same lines being said by more than one villager, so they don't have distinct personalities or anything.  Only the characters in the main storyline seem to have any type of personality.  The puzzles I've come across are very basic, like hitting blocks with your hammer to move them over glowing sections of the floor.  Decorating the village is fun, but there's such a small limit of what you can place, and it's difficult trying to figure out the limits on some things.  For example, I could only place so many flower/bush items, but when i picked up all my flowers, it still had many counted on my placement and I couldn't tell which items counted as what.  There's no inventory management for what's placed in the village unless you want to manually hunt down each decoration, no glowing indicators on the overhead to show what's placed, and some of the decorations are very tiny.  Decorating the houses is pretty boring.  You decorate the outside and can slap on some new walls or roof colors, things like that.  There aren't any different structures you can modify.  Villagers will sometimes request that their house be spruced up or that they need to update their look, but it's as simple as just putting any random wall on the house or gifting a random item of clothing.  There are no specifications that you must meet, and clothing and housing walls drop like candy when you're gardening, so there's no real gameplay loop for this other than just use whatever random item in your inventory you want and gift it to the villager or modify their house and then you've succeeded.  Speaking of gifting villagers, there isn't really an easy way to find their house unless you click on each house in building mode to see who resides there.  They have their heads as bubbles so you can see who lives where, but many of them look so similar or generic since it seems to be randomly generated that it makes it difficult to remember what head matches what name.  So you're forced to go deep into the menus to figure out who's living where, or you have to run around town and read the placards.I've found a few hidden caves that seemed to have no purpose other than to fish.  Haven't found any temples or anything yet, and I'm not sure I'm going to play any further because this game feels like more mundane work than fun.  This game creates a lot of unnecessary work, so if you're a fan of efficiency, this is not the game for you.  With all that said, I'd rather play My Time at Portia, which I also picked up during the sale and has significantly more personality, better writing, better NPCs, and a better gameplay loop.

_childDocuments_.review: If you do buy wait for a sale.I do like this game but I think it was meant for young children. And I'll explain why: 1. The majority of customization options are terrible and are what an adult would think a 5 year old would like for both characters and buildings.  2. There are several baffling design decisions that I only assume were done because they assumed the target audience wouldn't either understand or forget it after 2 minutes like the taming system.  You can't even access your pet storage properly and you can only place one animal in the areas that can take them.The game feels half complete.  There are masked people who can join you and  want a new style or something and yet you are unable to customize them at all except changing dreamjob/stats.  Also several of the stat/job changing items are bugged or have the wrong labels so you can end up turning a character with 9s in almost every category and maybe 3 wellness  into  a 00007 character just because you wanted to max wellness out and make use of the building boosts that increase production based on wellness.  You can't remove things from villagers once they have something in that slot. So you end up giving a guy one of the 2000 wooden helmet buckets you have gotten you can only ever replace it with another hat.There is a certain cave type that has a floating chest stuck in the air you cannot access and other annoying bugs but sofar nothing gamebreaking although you will have to reload a save if/when you get stuck behind some stalagmites just be careful where you move/jump.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I like the concept and art. I'm not sure this is a game, it seems more like an activity without meaningful choices or challenges. I played for over an hour and I don't think I ever took damage, had to solve a puzzle, or had to make a difficult jump. The levels are very small, so there is not a ton to explore.I hate the constant popups about completing this or that quest which refuse to go away unless you open the quest log, click a box,  watch a bad animation, and receive some doodads. I think having to do those is what pushed me over into uninstalling. I know some good people must have worked hard on this game but it's not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game. I am not usually one for "casual" and/or "wholesome" games, but I was in the mood for something different and this was on special. If you are looking to slaughter zombies/aliens or split some skulls, this is not the game for you. I wouldn't consider it challenging by any gaming measure, but it is fun and entertaining. I enjoy experimenting with what worlds I can create and am often surprised by the variety of the different combinations. The story line is interesting, though a bit predictable. It is fun to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I personally didn't like this game much.After a little it got very repetitive and boring very fast.But, if you like cozy games where you don't need to do much, well you might enjoy this.Basically you create new mini worlds and need to tend to them by eliminating the rot and planting trees and bushes. You can fish and trap bugs while you are at it to satisfy your completionist self - each world will tell you exactly how many things you are missing.Then you have different zones to fill up with buildings and people to go forward with the story, semi-building sim but much easier.There is some fun exploration to find chests and secrets.All in all I can't say it is bad. I just didn't enjoy it and wouldn't recommend it. Other people might find it very relaxing though.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this 24 hour ago and already have 12 hours logged, and honestly, more to come. I CAN'T STOP PLAYING WTF! It's literally a better, fantasy version of Animal Crossing, except you nurture mini worlds before sending them off. This is hans down one of the best games i've played in a hot minute, its such a hidden gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Grow is really two games in one, a world building and tending game and a city management game. I love how the two aspects tie together. The story so far has been excellent, the artwork is beautiful and the game play is good. I lose track of time, which is a good indicator that the game plays well. Again, with 505 Games, I find that the graphics can overheat my poor old system. I have to turn them down a great deal to keep my computer at the safe temperatures, but that's my system's issue, not the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore this game and highly recommend it. BUT. This is very early release and there have been a lot of hiccups with the game. 2 hours of my gameplay was just me, stuck and unable to do anything until the next update came. That said: there is a very active discord group where you can report bugs and the team will do their absolute best to get the game working for you again, and help you recover anything you might have lost. This is definitely a team worth supporting and investing in, but I would suggest that if you are impatient to wait a month or two before you buy the game. If you aren't impatient, get it now, it's lovely.EDIT: we are about a month in and it runs much better, fairly consistently. It is WELL worth the growing pains
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Having cleared the game Yonder on the Switch I was definitely going to check this one out too. While Yonder had more of a wandering with no direction concept, the quests tended to be more vague, tedious, and felt at times pointless. Grow seems to have improved on the good ideas of Yonder, and expanded on them. The game is really beautiful, and relaxing. Exploration is fun because there are actually hidden treasures. It's a town management/explorative/questing game.  There's a lot more direction, and the game feels more complete.Edit after significant gameplay: The unlocking process reminds me of Harvest Moon: Light of Hope. Only much more exploratory. The quests aren't really quests as much as they are suggestions to keep you informed on the tasks you need to complete to progress the storyline; while, the quests from NPC's feel more like errands with repetitive rewards. The being said, I love this game! There is so much to do, the storyline is really intriguing, the puzzles are fun, and the critters are adorable! Aforementioned, when I only had a few hours of gameplay it does feel like a vastly improved Yonder. So if you liked Yonder, you will definitely like this game. Albeit, if you like games like this in general sim/build/farm/relaxing/animal etc. types this is your game :).
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This game has become part of my routine before going to sleep. It's cozy, cute, and a good mix of simple and complex. It has an engaging story that's not too depressing. I especially love playing it on my Steam Deck!I originally bought this game for Switch, which I would not recommend. The game is not optimized for Switch so it runs pretty slow.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Best relaxing game ever played! Perfect balance between a farming, management, RPG and exploring game. I loved the opportunity to design the villages entirely, the customization features, the hidden chests and small dungeons and the worlds creation. It gives you good vibes of creativity and reaches the perfect spot between relaxing and stimulating. It is never boring and the gameplay varies a lot so that you are always busy and engaged.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: The first hour was annoying, the next few hours were rather fun, the next few were a little dull but mildy entertaining, and the rest was very repetitious and tedious.It doesn't get less repetitious and tedious.  It doesn't have several different areas - it has the same one over and over, with slight cosmetic changes - they didn't even give us new cutscenes every time we unlocked a new area, it was the exact same scene played over again.Yonder: Cloud Catcher Chronicles was suitable for children, but kept me (adult) entertained with its very simple, but fun gameplay until I had exhausted every speck of content it had.Grow feels like they made it for eight year-olds, and that is the only age bracket I can understand finding the kind of repetition in this game fun. I kept playing, thinking it was going to get better, there was going to be new content, that something would be different, and I grinded all the way to the end, and have never looked at the game again.  I scroll down my list of titles, and remember the lack of depth, the tedious (VERY TEDIOUS) repetition, and the clunky-ness of the promised but not well delivered ability to grow unique new worlds and arrange towns, and skip over it.It's not one of those hugely expensive games, but I still feel like I wasted my spending money.  If you want to try it, wait until it has a generous sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this game up with little to no clue of what I was getting myself into. I was hooked from the moment I heard the music and saw the opening cinematic. The art style and graphics are gorgeous, it's a living, breathing world that you can nurture at your own pace. Super cute, super chill, and hands down one of the best games of its kind I've ever played. 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: ill preface by saying this game is my current hyperfixation, the world looks beautiful, there is alot of exploration and there is a fair amount of variety in the worlds you can produce. however - i will go on to say that it is rather slow, and gets rather repetitive. Its also really annoying that there isnt a minimap - if you wish to orient yourself and open the main travel map there is always a cut scene with your mount which takes a few seconds but its rather annoying. There is barely any variety with people who can move in, and the friendship quests with some characters are very short. The item limit for towns is too small (not just buildings, especially decorations so its hard to put your own spin on your town. And for me it meant large empty spaces) its worth playing, especially as its free in humble at the moment. But as a sim enjoyer - its not the best ive played.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: The game play is engaging, but it's not very player friendly. No real map other than the stationary map you see when you're on your mount or the little map of each district. The outlying area's are something you just feel your way through.  No map when you discover something and want to relocate it.  Not all of the tasks and management systems are clear and much of it is left for you to figure out how each works.It's a great game but far from perfect. Right now I'm in a cave that you jump over water on to platforms that sink if your timing is just one step off.  Sadly if you get over 1/2 the way through and drown by a misstep you have to start from the very beginning which is very frustrating and not enjoyable. The other puzzles before this one I loved, but this one lack some foresight.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Creating worlds is an attractive prospect but it felt incredibly grindy. There were lots of actions that could affect an area but instead I had to walk to a single plant one at a time.It's.. sort of empty, as there seemed like very little unique feedback to my actions and a somewhat cookie-cutter story. I can overlook that but there was an awful lot of text that felt too childish for me, and constant explaining of things, and very slow minigame mechanics like their version of fishing (It felt a bit like it was just included because 'other games did it!'). It's more childish then I wanted. The 'parent' figures just sorta irritated me as I wanted them to stop talking and it felt like a really loong tutorial. I couldn't feel immersed because they tried humour that I just found irritating, like a character literally saying something "Error 404: Haha fooled you!" How am I meant to feel part of the world with gags like this?I enjoy other games of grinding, and building things in other titles that require some farming but there it feels satisfying, and like I am doing my own thing. Here it feels like "oh no I have to keep going back here?" when only 1.5 hours in, I wanted a bit more adult characters that didn't keep  me throughout the start which goes against the zen gaming goal.Additionally, the pastel colour scheme is nice but over-exposed and honestly hurt my photosensitive eyes a bit, even with gamma down.It's a shame because the creative god-game aspect sounds really cool, but the execution felt like I was playing a slow burning mobile game on a large screen format it wasnt made for that was uncomfortable for my eyes.I only played for 1.5 hours so I could refund, so maybe it's still for you.But it wasn't for me, there's plenty of accessories it looks like and a good portion of dev time on this, but I didn't want to grind for them, ignoring all the babbling dialogue with no voice-overs felt like I was playing an MMO minus any of the good things of an MMO.It felt a bit lacking soul and trying to follow a formula, I'm afraid.

_childDocuments_.review: Settle in, this might be long. (Recommended if you already enjoy the genre and don't mind that it is still rough around the edges). I'd like to start off by saying I really enjoy this genre of game. This title reminds me a lot of a high fantasy version of Animal Crossing but with some better elements in story and game play. No more game breaking bugs so that's excellent! It still feels like an early access title... (I still have high hopes for it!) Graphics - Gorgeous. It's a very pretty game. I don't usually take screenshots in game but I've got a ton from this one. Photo Mode - Easy to access and use, but the programming is weird and if you set everything up before you choose the pose, the zoom gets real funky real fast. A lot going on - It is farming, world-building, rpg, puzzle, and exploration. There is tons going on in this game, easy to get lost but in a good way. I was surprised by the puzzle element of the game, it made it really fun, I did feel they held your hand too much by panning out and showing you where your objectives were (really made it too easy to complete and the panning takes forever and isn't skippable). Town Management - Really neat, but the menus jump around a lot and throw you around the map and randomly zoom in. I think it tries to focus on what is center of your screen instead of where my mouse is pointed. This happens on the world map when you are flying to different areas as well. The top things that irk me: When you build a new world, in certain areas the world tree clips into your world and creates weird walls and issues. The leaves sometimes cover up my world which is just aesthetically annoying. I had the trunk of the tree hiding a bunch of tasks I had to complete because it legit looked like a wall and I didn't realize I could just walk through it. Give the world seeds more space from the trunk. The game is so pretty having clipping issues really wrecks it. A secondary aesthetic thing is if a chest spawns on your world seed, when you open it, it never leaves. It just has the 'withering' animations around it leaving your world with a section that looks gross and diseased and no way to fix it. The 'tutorial' takes forever to complete while not being helpful at all. It teaches you all the basics you probably already know if you've done this type of game before, but the game leaves out literally all the new elements they have added. I've found myself having to learn by trial and error how to do things with the town management, figuring out what the icons mean (since there is no speech but a villager will be walking around with a text bubble with an icon and you just have to figure out what that icon is asking you to do), upgrading buildings, how much of a thing you are allowed to place, and a few other things. The game holds your hand too much on the simple tasks while leaving you hanging on things that you actually need explained to you. I kept thinking it was going to unlock that information later in the game but no. Specifically when you put a villager in their dream job, there is an icon that looks sort of like a business card I guess? Well sometimes villagers just have that above their head, and I'm thinking...okay they are already in their dream job? This means they want their stats upgraded which is done by buying little talismans you can gift to them. A short and simple tool tips tutorial for this might have been useful. Not everything needs to be a long conversation with an npc or a quest. The romance option.... why? I do not feel especially close to either of the characters and the backstory is shallow and told *to* me. I do not feel like I'm a part of it and have no real reason to cultivate those relationships or invest myself in them. I think it actually detracts from the game because it feels very forced and rushed. Also please make some of the scenes skippable. When I get an achievement and claim a reward, it's very long and takes a good twenty to thirty seconds to continue and when you have to do that five times in a row it's annoying. Some of the animations are really cute but also very long and you can't skip them. The first few times I chin scratched a critter was endearing but by the 100th time I'm over it. It takes 9 interactions to claim a critter, 3 per day per animal...you can imagine how eventually even the cutest of animations get stale and there are only 4 total between all the animals... x.x So overall, the game has a lot of potential especially for people who love these types of games. There's a lot of fun new elements going on (though I haven't seen a lot of diversity with the flora and fauna in the game the world seeds are pretty different for the most part). Feels like an early access and needs a lot of polish and cleanup. Hoping to re-review in the future if it ever becomes a complete game.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a Good Game, but only a Good Game.I'd definitely recommend this game due to the fact that the story line is simple and long as ♥♥♥♥ to achieve.You get to create towns, garden, develop minimal relationships with people, and develop relationships between animals and bugs. This game is also great for players who love to explore new areas and also the impatient players to explore new areas lol. There's also a mechanism where you can create new worlds by mixing and match essenses to creating new Worlds.The Withering was such a great antagonist for the game "Harmony vs Discord" which was the cause of the discord between The Children and the Alchemists.Though I feel like there were opportunities where the creators of "Grow: Song of the Evertree" could possibly have improved on. Even though this peaceful game was meant to be peaceful. They could have developed combat into the game, where I have seen a massive amount of potential has been left out, and created certain Hostile Mobs where you attack with the Song and Music whilst also healing yourself with said music. instead of just beating The Withering Gelatinous Blob (filled with bugs) with a hammer with a one time hit. Would've been nice to have seen mini bosses (like a massive gelatinous blob) and actual bosses in the game (like Withering Tentacles). Another opportunities on where the could've improved on, even though this game is targeting the younger audience. I feel as if the puzzles  inside the game to retrieve Fragments of The Song has been too easy to solve, our children in the world are really more knowledgeable than we think they are, and it could've been a bit harder to fit their knowledge expansion. The nature preserve, could've been an area to place said tamed animals (in which i had tamed, but didnt know of the mechanism or controls to place tamed animals) could've been developed further and also the relationships between the pets and animals of The World Seeds could've developed further as well.If I have to give this game a rating from 1 - 100%, I'd give it an 80%, a "B" for effort to where I can see the potential of it could be. _childDocuments_.review: SUMMARY: A mixture of farming/reclamation, townbuilder, explorer, and alchemy, Grow has you splitting your time between growing microbiome "worlds," managing towns, alchemy, trading, and exploring. Gorgeous to look at with great sound, it's one to consider if you like farming/life sims with a dollop of adventure.  It also has an engaging and interesting story.Grow is a game that needs a demo for people to see if they like it.  For me at about 48 minutes I was like "uh-oh" and knew what I'd be playing.Now, as noted it is one of those farming/town/life sims, so the question is "is there a grind?"  I'd say "kind of if you don't find your own groove."  It's a game with a lot of openess, which gives you plenty to do - or a way to turn yourself into a taskmaster.So with the warning "hey, do what you like but don't make it a second job" what's the game got?STORY: Yes, there's not only a story, but a good one.  The last inhabitant of the giant god-made Evertree that used to spawn worlds, you've stayed behind with a sentient book and cauldron with the hope to restore your home.  When your experiments bear (literal, world-making) fruit, you set off to reclaim your home from the mysterious "withering."  It's really a kind of Miyazaki story in theme and appearance.+ The story is great.  If this was a movie, it would be awesome.GROW WORLDS: Literally.  As you reclaim "essences" you can brew them together to grow worlds, which are small microbiomes blossoming from the Evertree.  You end up with lots of essences, meaning you can make some fantastic and disturbing worlds.  Windy deserts, slimy lands bearing rocky outcroppings that have eyes, fairytale worlds, you'll see some amazing things.+ Seeing what the worlds have is fun.- Some stuff gets samey.RESTORE AND CULTIVATE: The worlds you grow need to be restored and culitvated by planting seeds, removing Withering pollution, and so on.  As you restore these worlds you can harvest them and they grow.  You may find caves, devices, puzzles, and so on.  Eventually creatures appear and you can take them as pets or send them to a ranch, and you can hire help.+ Lots of things to do.+ The extra additions like caves, puzzles, merchants, ads more fun especially when you want a bit more than cultivation and cleanup.- You have to cultivate to get resources and extras for your towns, and that lets you unlock more of the game.  You can only streamline so much and times you may need to grind.- Can get repetitious, especially if you're cultivating multiple worlds.  Fully grown worlds feel maybe 25% larger than was needed.TOWNS: As you push back the Withering, you can build downs.  These are where a lot of your money and resources go.  You unlock more buildings over time and can customize them.  Then, you can actually walk in them and even use their services.  Doing the right things helps create "harmony" and further push back the withering.+ Fun to make towns, lots to balance.+ Your actions often unlock other buildings, bonuses, and options.- Controls are simple, but require a little getting used to as nearly ever button on the controller is used.- Sometimes you need specific resources and that can take time to get early on.INHABITANTS: People come to their towns and you can get them houses, assign them to jobs, do random quests for them, and even give them clothes to change their appearance.  Maximizing what they do, who does what, and so on is vital to a happy town.  The townsfolk with the exception of a few "plot specific" characters are randomized down to body language, so you never know who will show up or what they want.  You also want to make them happy to further create "harmony."+ Fun to populate town and figure the right people.+ Random characters and their random requests add fun things to do.+ Play dress-up with your townfolk to find the perfect outfit or make them look like complete goobers.- Character "pool" of personalities seems limited.- It'd be nice to be able to move characters between towns and such.- The ability to customize/revert characters in more detail is lacking.TRADE: Towns provide players to buy things, as do the mysterious "Everkin" who will take unwanted fish, insects, plants, and stones off your hands for "Everkoin" - which lets you buy essences.EXPLORE: The world is enormous, from the Everkin land to the areas you gradually unlock.  Get ready for hidden treasures, caves, puzzles, dungeons, and more.  There's lots of secrets in the world.TASKS: Your sentient book tracks tasks and gives you all sorts of challenges and rewards.  If you love running down quests and maximizing actions to fulfill goals, you'll love it.- Some rewards aren't that interesting or useful.AUDIO AND VISUALS: This is a gorgeous game with great audio.  It also has plenty of settings to make it work right on your machine.So is the game good?  Yes, it's lovely, lots to do, fun, and all the parts synergize.  It feels like a big epic story, zooming between worlds and hidden dungeons, then down to looking to buy someone a hat.  It also is the kind of game you could keep playing to maximize your relationships, building scores, etc.There are some flaws:* As noted, the game can get grindy unless you find a playstyle that suits you.  This is a flaw of the genre, but I think the game could encourage more experimentation.* The random nature of some of the game elements can lead you to miss resources you need for buildings and progress.  Then it's up to brew more worlds OR break down things you may want to hunt for essences.  There's not enough "outs" (for instance, the Everkin should sell 50% or so of all resources at any one time).* The procedural worlds can lead to odd issues like trees so distorted you can't get into position to chop them.* Past a certain point you may have more money and essences than you need.  A real maximizer can quickly get beyond that as a limit.* Some general issues of polish feel like it needed a few more months of testing, such as a janky photo mode.* There's clearly half-finished, not-used, or "leftover" elements of the game.Flaws aside, it's hard to criticize the game as its got a great story, looks great, and has so many fun elements.  It's more a game that "if you think you like it you probably will," which is why I figure a demo would be perfect.Finally, as noted on avoiding grind.  I found the best thing to do is 1) grow a few diverse worlds early, 2) Trade with the everkin for essences, 3) Get towns going to get money, 4) Once you get options, alternate tending, townbuilding, exploring, and just messing around as you see fit.Who's it for, well:* If this sounds like your jam, get it.* If you know people that love farm/build stuff and like the 3D sense of wandering in a world you made, it'd be a probably-won't-miss gift.

_childDocuments_.review: 19.1.2022.As I’m getting older, I’m starting to realize that there simply are some game genres that I simply can’t play. I’m also realizing that for certain game genres I have a real soft spot and those include: platformers, visual novels and farming sims. There’s just something so special about farming sims like Stardew Valley  and My Time at Portia . Well, I got in the mood to play a new farming game but didn’t want to pay too much money and Grow: Song of the Evertree came up so I bought it on a whim. While I definitely don’t think this is a bad game, I can’t say I can really recommend it…The story of Grow: Song of the Evertree is pretty charming in my opinion. You play as the very last alchemist living on the Evertree. The Evertree is basically the source of all life in the world but it’s been taken over by an evil thorny plight. When this came, everyone living on the evertree left except for you. It’s your job to fight the thorns that have grown everywhere on the Evertree and restore your world the way it was. You do this by farming and managing a town. Even though I initially just wanted a game where I would tend a field of crops or a garden, I got a blend of three games that I actually really like. Just like most farming sims, this one has day and night cycles. During the day you can visit certain parts of the Evertree and take care of it. You take care of it by pulling out evil weeds, planting seeds, breaking rocks and singing the Song of the Evertee (which I guess would be fertilizer???). Normally, once farming work is done, you will visit your town where you will use the resources you gathered to rebuild the town. This is where you build houses, put decorations and interact with your residents. After you start building your town a little bit, residents will start showing up and you can make them move to the city by assigning them into a home and finding them a job. The residents won’t do much but they can give you small fetch quests and will help your town thrive.Here’s the problem with this game:  .When I play farming games, I like to feel like I worked hard and achieved something through hard work. I love it when I plant a field of crops, tend to it and then harvest and produce it for a profit. That’s something that Grow: Song of the Evertee never gave me.For example: when you tend to your farming, you already have everything ready. You don’t have to go and buy/collect seeds, you don’t have to upgrade tools and you really don’t have to worry about your stamina either. You just go and do things. It’s the equivalent of “push this button 30 times and you’ll be done”. Yes, sure, you have to switch tools and walk around a bit but it gets old really fast. When you manage your town you just place a building and the next day it will be built. You’ll start with just one district but unlock more as you complete district specific quests. Most quests can be done super easily. You’d think that a quest to build 5 unique buildings can take a while but you can literally finish it in 2 days. Materials aren’t hard to come by and you can easily make more by using your alchemy station. Sometimes you’ll need very specific essences and you won’t have any idea how to get them and you’ll just spend time breaking your stuff with alchemy and end up not getting anything. The residents themselves aren’t more than mere decoration. When they do ask you to fetch them something 8 out of 10 times I already had the item they wanted and I instantly completed the quest. This is also because you have unlimited inventory space which sounds great but then you stop paying attention to what  you are even carrying. See what I mean about feeling lifeless?I almost hate myself for writing this but I simply can’t recommend this game. Even though it technically does everything I wanted from a farming game and more, it does it in a really poor way. During my 10+ hours of playing this I never felt like I accomplished anything through hard work. Instead it just felt like I was going through the motions of pressing the same buttons over and over again as the game “evolved” on it’s own.With that said, I can see why some players would love this type of game and, who knows, you may just be one of those players. Grow: Song of the Evertree simply isn’t for me.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone with autism, this game really, really, REALLY scratches the autism itch. Tending to the worlds is satisfying, with a gameplay loop that rewards you tangibly and visually in multiple ways every time you go back. The static elements of the gameworld are equally satisfying, and while town management can feel a little overwhelming in the lategame, it's still a rewarding experience.Graphically, this game is amazing, and once again touching on the autism, really does a lot with its colour palette to help me relax and just lose myself. Some of the sound design bothers me a little, and my god I can't stand those 'living' worlds with the teeth, but they're small problems that I can't properly place - more personal taste than anything.I'm going to enjoy putting a lot more time into this game. My only wish is that they continue to increase the amount of randomised stuff I can explore.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stunning game that dropped out of nowhere. I'm big on collecting, crafting, building and managing, with tons of hours poured into Stardew Valley, My Time At Portia, Story of Seasons games and this game has just been added to my daily rotation of games I'm currently playing. Amazing soundtrack, amazing signs of growth everywhere you involve yourself in.Towns to be built, seeds to be planted, creatures to be cared for, people to befriend. If you're looking to relax after a long day of dealing with incompetence at work, this game will help cope with mental health. You can listen to your favorite audiobook on the side, wind down, chill and grow with the game.
