_childDocuments_.review: This is the most addicted I've been to a game in a LONG time. I've literally played 10 hours straight since I bought it this afternoon. It is literally everything i have ever wanted in a game. I can't believe I had never heard about it. My Time at Portia was one of my all time favorites, but this game beats it hands down. Such a beautiful and relaxing game. There is SOOO much to do! This game is an absolute STEAL at 20$. Can't recommend enough! GET IT!!

_childDocuments_.review: I had the opportunity to beta-test this, and I'm glad I did.  Even from early beta it was clear that this game had the heart and charm the promotional screenshots and videos promised.  In the same vein as Stardew Valley, My Time at Portia, and other similar semi-casual games, Grow: Song of the Evertree is a story about rebuilding the world from an environmental catastrophe.  Full of cute characters, beautiful vistas and a robust story, this game has the makings of an amazingly addictive experience.The basic gameplay follows the story of the last Tree-tender, an Alchemist who is assisted by a sentient alembic named Coppertop and a sentient book named, well, Book.  To restore life to the world-creating Evertree that is being destroyed by some mysterious blight called the Withering, the three have discovered how to make World Seeds - seeds which, when planted in the boughs of the Evertree, will grow small, encapsulated worlds, which, when tended to properly, can grow into great big worlds complete with their own ecosystem of plants, bugs, fish and creatures, which can then be released to float amongst the stars to repopulate the universe with new habitable worlds.But this is only a portion of the game.  Another large chunk is dedicated to building and customizing your own world, with villages full of buildings to attract population and keep them happy.  Customization here includes not only free-form placement of buildings, but colouring and decorating them and even micromanaging the inhabitants!  Meanwhile, you're also exploring, opening up new areas, cleansing withering, clearing ruins, discovering secrets, taming creatures, farming... the list goes on and on...If there's any complaint to be made about this game, it might be that there's almost TOO much to do.  With a built-in day/night cycle constraining the available time for doing all of these tasks, it's very easy to get involved in one thing, to let another falter.  Fortunately, there's no real penalty for ignoring any aspect of your world(s) for a day or two, so other than pinging the OCD of completionists, this limit only really serves to keep the player moving. There are a number of games out there that have tried to capitalize on the cute factor in world-management games, most do it with built-in mini dating-sims.  Many also penalize you for neglecting to pay attention to your people for a day or two while you maybe focus on building.  This one bypasses the relationship aspect almost completely and focuses instead on balancing work/life instead.  Gender is almost completely ignored (with an option for a third gender for your own character, and little beyond names suggesting gender of any other characters), and while the voice acting is minimal (limited to grunts and "oohs!"), the dialogue is still interesting.  The story is often locked by a complex dialogue tree, but I have yet to find any 'wrong' decisions in this game, certainly nothing that has kept me from learning the entire story.Overall, though the time constraint makes it feel less casual, it truly is a casual gamer's delight, especially for those who like to create and tend worlds.I give this game 5 world seeds out of 5!
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Played for about 6 and a half hours so far. I like the game, but there are quite a few issues I've noticed.The whole tutorial sequence lasts a little too long for what it is, it feels like it should have been shortened significantly. Especially since it's effectively two tutorials back to back about the exact same stuff. The first "tutorial" has your character taking care of their first "world" but it's the size of a regular world, such as the ones you create later down the line, as opposed to a tutorial world. The tasks, if the day timer wasn't frozen, would take about half the in game day potentially longer since you're just learning the game. That said, you also don't get told or shown how each item or tool is useful or what to use them on other than the floating icon above the terrain you're supposed to interact with so it's a long drawn out process of what I think is supposed to be forced "natural" discovery that just feels tedious. Then, once you sleep, you're shoved out the door and told to catch some magic creature called an Everkin. You follow it into a portal and then are slammed with 6 or 7 tasks that are all just telling you how to operate the tools that you were given and made to use for 10~20 minutes, plus a bug net and fishing rod.This whole part could have been reversed or should have been rewritten, even narratively it makes little sense. It'd make much more sense if you had to plant the seed, find out the world is infected by withering even though you just created it and then have the Everkin show up to help and give you your tools and show you how to use them. This would have reduced the tutorial time in half, introduced the Everkin as allies AND shown the player how to utilize their tools properly.The tutorial section also fails at telling you that you can trade items with the Everkin for Evercoins to buy, admittedly, pitiful amounts of essences. If it did tell me somewhere, it wasn't clear.The controls are also clearly designed with a controller in mind. Fishing in particular feels bad with just WASD keys when the fish moves in more than 8 directions, a joystick would be much better for this game. The sensitivity on the camera controls is also terrible by default, but again, would probably be significantly better on a controller. After adjusting the vertical sensitivity to practically nothing the game became a much smoother experience.Inclusivity options exist but don't seem shoved down your throat, so that's pretty nice. You can play as any available body type regardless of chosen gender, there are 3 to choose from Male Female and Believe Non-binary (I'm not personally familiar with the symbol).Hair styles and colors are limited, as are eye colors, "accessory" options such as freckles are extremely limited as well and facial hair only has 4 options, but you can unlock more customization later during the game. Hair and eyes do have this awkward sheen to them almost as if your character has frosting/fondant for hair and literal glass for eyes.The voices are just terrible, it sounds like one person made the voices and then just pitch shifted them poorly.The core gameplay, so far, has been consistent; tend to an island, go to the town and build it up, check anything else you feel you have time for/want to, go to bed, repeat. It's... relaxing. Many may find it extremely tedious, because it is, but that's what some people are looking for. It's calming, relaxing, simple, and could be done with someone's morning coffee.  The puzzles thus-far have been exceptionally simple, push blocks onto the glowing panel, push blocks so you can make a pseudo-bridge. This is either a plus or a minus depending on who you are or who is playing. Good for young children and people bad at puzzles, tedious for everyone else.First and foremost... When you complete an island and have to create a new world seed, or unlock a new town district, Book or Coppertop won't shut up about it. You're constantly reminded at 15 second intervals that there is something you have to do RIGHT NOW! IT'S SO IMPORTANT, IT NEEDS TO BE DONE NOW! This really feels like the devs don't respect the player's attention span, intelligence or time. And is a clear sign that they didn't account for someone to unlock a district at the same time as they unlocked a new world. I was exploring while Book yelled at me to go create her a cheesecake world, after I finally cracked and just went to make the damned world seed and plant it, then Coppertop just starts whining to me about how the new district's airship dock is still broken and we can't have a town without people. Meanwhile I'm trying to tend to my new world that I just created and I have this numpty shouting at me the entire time. Solution to this issue: Just make it a damned objective, don't shove it in the player's face constantly. I get it, you have a story to tell, but you made a semi-open world let the player experience that at their own pace.Edit: Some things in this game break constantly and require a reload or restart of the game to make them work. Disappearing workers preventing you from removing rubble being one of them.Building things too fast or too early will penalize you, kind of. You can't unlock certain blueprints or complete certain rewards until you build/gather x number of buildings/items, but for many of the mini/side quests the buildings/items you have to build/get MUST be new, not one's you've built/gathered before. This becomes an issue when you attempt to unlock a blueprint but you can't because you cannot build enough "new" buildings without unlocking a new district. Deleting an old building and rebuilding it does not count either, so it must be a completely new building.The world feels too big, and too small at the same time. Getting anywhere feels like a chore when you're not using fast travel, there's nothing in the gaps between important areas. Going from district to district or from your home to the Everkin's portal takes forever considering there is literally nothing to do but run there. The character's movement speed is nice though, but it feels like the game was enlarged to accommodate that. It also feels too small in that building space is super limited and the customization options are all kind of crappy and some are poorly rendered.All the "Vaults" are aggravating as hell. Not because they are too hard, but because every "puzzle" amounts to hit a button or drop an object on a plinth and each and every time you have one of those "puzzles" show up you get a 15~60 second unskippable cutscene showing you the object and the plinth it needs to go to or the button and the thing it's going to activate. There is literally no point in these and just extend the time it takes to complete each vault unnecessarily.Book is annoying.It's nice that the world seeds seem to be pseudo-random based on the elements you put into them. This doesn't really add replayability but it makes it so there is more to look at than the same few things over and over again.I liked the fact that Coppertop looks like a tar-slime from Slime Rancher.I like that the villagers have stats in a way almost identical to TinyTower. (same colors and everything, just different names)I would recommend this game to people who enjoy a game that's slow burn and relaxing. But that recommendation comes with the stipulation of don't expect this game to be super polished. It feels like some stuff wasn't really worked on or tested properly. The game works, it's still enjoyable, but some of it feels half-hearted. There are buggy animations and the textures on the characters look terrible. I am happy to see more than two body-types though.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: What an incredibly beautiful game. As beautiful as a Pixar film, and so lovingly designed and programmed. This game is balm for the soul and lets you forget everyday life. The wonderful things the developers are presenting to you here is unbelievable. After the first few minutes of the game, I immediately felt at home in this dreamlike game world and immediately fell in love with my character. I am now looking forward to the many, many tasks that await me. For the current price, the game is really a gift! Really really fantastic
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Really confused by how positive the reviews are on this game. I tried so hard to like this game. Felt myself "forcing" myself to play it thinking "it has to get better, right?" It didn't.I see a lot of reviews calling the game "zen" which I don't understand -- the game is to repetitive and tedious to feel "zen."There are some reviews that called it a "Chore Simulator" -- completely agree. A core component of the game is "cleaning up" worlds where you do really repetitive tasks -- often like 50 at a time -- and you need to switch your tools in between each task. It's a huge pain. Pulling a weed, switching to a seed bag, planting a seed, switching to watering can, holding and watering, then singing to the plant. It would be fine if this only happened occasionally, but you're just constantly doing it. The days feel repetitive and lack purpose and goals.As the other reviews said, the graphics are great. Great scenery and beautiful lighting and colors.The interface could use some work too. There are times when it's not clear what key you need to press. Or you need to press an awkward key like "return" or the up arrow or ESC. Claiming rewards after you completed a goal always annoyed me, because you can't just click "claim" -- the animations appear, and then there's a few second pause, which makes the process of collecting rewards tedious.There's several animations or cutscenes that have elongated animations and pauses -- where you want to just skip through it but can't.On the positive side, the game didn't have many bugs.I appreciate the level of town management -- similar games don't have this level of town management where you need to assign people to homes and jobs. However, it felt a little clunky and unintuitive when you were trying to reassign people from one job to another.Overall, wouldn't recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I had high expectations of this game because the reviews were so good. Different game magazines talked of a "3D Animal Crossing or Stardew Valley". Well, it's not. Yes, the design is very cute and the worlds are beautiful. And in the beginning it's fun to create and decorate the new villages. But it completely lacks the relationships with the villagers that make Animal Crossing and Stardew Valley so great. Most of the people are just people you don't really know and who are just there. There is nothing unique to them, many characters also look very similar like random NPCs and give you quest like "I need a stone, I need a flower, I need an insect" etc. They mostly stay strangers. I also think it lacks a good tutorial, I had to search for help online to figure out some basic things. I was always waiting for an exciting story to begin, but every day was almost the same: Make villagers happy, build new villages, maintain the newly planted worlds. It got very repetitive and boring. If you just want to chill after a long day, maybe this game is for you. It's slow and no rush and there's not really a goal for the day. (Edit: Of maybe you WILL feel rushed because if you need to do something, the kettle will remind you every 30 seconds "You should do XY".)But if you actually want to create "your" city and feel part of a community where you know the name of your neighbour and their story, it's probably not.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Song of the Evertree looks beautiful, the gameplay is beautiful and the story is quite interesting up to a point. I wanted to like this. I liked the previous game Yonder a lot and I love that there are games out there that are about doing quests in beautiful environments and have absolutely zero fighting in the game. In yonder I played countless hours and so did my daughter so I was excited when Grow came out.However after effectively finishing the game I come away rather empty. I am not sure I can point at any one thing that makes that feeling for me. I can point out some things:1. The game is too easy. Yonder was often challenging in the puzzles and things to find for quests. Grow is easy. Apart from right at the start I was never lacking resources for anything, I almost never had to work hard to get enough of something, puzzles were extremely easy both in required skill and in figuring things out. Sometimes I had to look around for a short time to find something but most of the time I just ran right into the things I needed without trying. In yonder I had to work hard to get every district up to the required happiness percentage. In grow....it was usually a matter of a couple of in day games and almost no work.2. Every NPC in the game constantly telling you how amazing you are gets really old really fast.3. The story line was interesting to me at first but then started to feel preachy to me.4. There are never any consequences to doing things "wrong". If you don't take care of a world for a while...that's fine...you can just come back later and continue. If you don't take care of a town for a while the people are just as happy as before. If you don't take care of animals...it's fine. If you don't talk to the people or do their requests...they are fine with that. So there is never a sense of having to balance the different elements of the game.Overall I would say it's an ok game but probably mostly interesting for very young children or if you just enjoy running around doing things in a pretty environment. For anyone looking for even a little bit of challenge I wouldn't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: You know what I need after a stressful day of work? A calm, beautiful adventure, in which I'm able to explore a beautiful world without stress. This is that game.Also, I am a huge fan of Yonder: The Cloud Catcher Chronicles, and have been desperate for a game that engenders the same level of curiosity and wonder as Yonder did. Despite all my efforts, it wasn't until a game from the same studio came along that I finally have something that starts to incite the same feelings.Maybe not a game for everyone, but for me this studio consistently produces games I love.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a bad game. I played about 30 hours before I called it quits. It just has a few key bits I can't get over. On the positive side... it's cute. It has the expected monotony of a relaxploration game. You create world seeds and then look after them worlds until such a time as they're ready to be "released" or you can keep them forever. The exploration part comes in when you rebuild the town and find all the pieces of the Evertree. Building the town is cute - lots of options to decorate all the houses. Now the downside.. it froze quite a few times. But also, and most importantly, some of the NPCs are awful. None of them have any real depth which was fine. I played Yonder and loved it, they didn't have much depth either. The two romance options are awkward, their voice acting consists of awkward sighs combined with repeated gestures and sparkles - I can also live with this. The part that stinks is that some of them are just plain mean for no reason at all... there is no plot or character building to explain their awful personality. Here are some quotes..."Apparently, something has upset Taylor. Bwa ha ha ha! I hope it was something I did. I've done so many things to them""Have you seen Cecil? Have you seen how they dress? How they cut their hair? How they choose to live their life? What a weirdo!""Don't talk to me before I've had my coffee. Or after I've had it preferably."Less awful than those two but still not really fitting the relaxploration genre are.. "Now beat it, kid, ya bother me""You know it's going to be bad when you wake up with a headache""I wonder what I did to make Flavil so mad at me. It must have been terrible, whatever it was!"
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: after trying a refunding so many games the past couple of weeks i was skeptical and even ready to refund before pressing the new game button , but this game is stunning , it's similar to animal crossing but at the same time it has botw elements ? especially that i can hear the same sound effects from botw .i hope i don't get bored as always as i am very enjoying it at the moment , i also hope they keep updating it and add occasional events like animal crossing , that would be very nice .-------------------------------------------------------------PS : also i am not going to complain as i am loving the game but a mini map would be very nice as i get lost all the time because the map is so big for my tiny brain to remember where i am exactly  ..
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: A visually stunning chill exploring and farming game with city upgrading elements? Sign me up!Unfortunately, you soon realize that everything is so very, very basic and repetitive that you do not want to do the tedium of upkeeping your personal tree, day after day after day, cycling through the same 6 tools for what seems like will be an eternity before you unlock the next biome. Even after being bundled, I feel this was a waste of time and money on my part.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: The game is well done. The graphics are good. The sound acting is OK. Stability is there. However, it's just boring.  It's very repetitive.  I mean really repetitive in the sense that you do the exact same things.  Smack a rock, pull a root, chop a tree, water a plant, spin around and do whatever and making your balls fly out.  Oh, and don't forget whacking weeds.  It's not a bad game, but when I had to force myself to play as far as I have and I have no interest in continuing any further. It's just not interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun, relaxing game. I enjoyed exploring and doing The Vaults. Nice character customization (along with villager customization) I also liked the games ending, though I got ridiculed by every tourist in sight. Worth the price with all that the game offers, if I didn't receive this for my birthday woulda bought it myself eventually.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot in good faith give this one a thumbs up. I found myself bored. Unlike other cozy games this one just has a bleh! story. Sure the game is cute, it's got town management, but you have guided 'chores' to do. By the time you finish taking care of the tree world your on, it's evening. And yes, the work on the tree FEELS like chores (take the worst parts of a farming game, without the farming). I just simply grew so bored of the game so quickly.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I could definitely feel Yonder vibes while playing this game.  Similar to Yonder, it feels both wholesome/cutesy and soul-less.  But I can overlook soul-less for a wholesome happy mindless sim management fix.  There was also a touch of Dark Cloud nostalgia with the building placement, decoration, and people assignment features.  Overall: Mechanics seemed to flow into each other seamlessly and create a pleasant, enjoyable experience if you're looking for a happy distraction.  Pros:-Exploration/dopamine spike when you find a secret-KAZUMI!! <3<3 (your flying companion)-Town-building is light and mildly enjoyable, appreciate being able to destroy/move buildings as I get the hang of mechanics and start to customize and try to find the most visually appealing layouts-Variety of town layouts (plains, forest, river, etc)-Variety of building types-Buildings have unique functions and are more than just decoration - i.e. some have shops where you can buy decorations, keys, exploration items, dyes, etc-Tree/world-building was enjoyable to watch seeds blossom into different types of worlds with different types of plants, animals, fish, rocks, and materials; also appreciate that the game rewarded the player for exploration with specific types of seed recipesCons:-Animal care-taking mechanic gets old really fast when you're trying to tame multiple types of animals, I gave up after 3, luckily it didn't matter for main story or other progression-Building decoration mechanic (wallpaper/roof) gets too micro-managey, especially when worked into town customization goals.  I stopped trying and just started picking random colors to meet goals after a while-Quantity of building varieties - you unlock most of the building types early on, so it gets kind of tedious for the last 4 or so maps to keep placing the same buildings over and over to unlock achievements/objectives or place residents in their dream jobs-End game placement of villagers/jobs requires abandoning the "wait to see who comes" or "place one of every building type" model and focusing on raiding temples/bathhouses for job change potions to just make everyone fit a mold-"Romance" was cookie cutter built-in, was not a value-add but... not bad enough to make the game unenjoyable either
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Grow: Song of the Evertree is a beautiful game with a beautiful narrative about how humans effect the world around us and how we can restore it's beauty through kindness. I personally loved every aspect of it. The graphics and the art style were pretty and I loved the Gameplay. I can't wait to see how the game dev's expand upon the story and possible add some more post-game content? - Much love, Bixby
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: The game is rather simple, with no real challenge to it. So if you want to escape to a cute world with lots to do then this game may suit you.I have over 60 hours in this game and at the start was enjoyable, but after about a while I realised there is no real depth to the game and towards the end became repetitive and a bit boring and I only continued to 100% the steam achievements.Most NPCs are generic with no actual relationship building and can be ignored.The town and seed world building becomes repetitive and the once you have completed a town or seed world there is no reason to go back to them.Unless you get the game as part of cheap bundle (I got it as part of a Humble Bundle deal), or it's heavily discounted I'd give it a miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This game is such a great marriage of a few genres, them mostly being Cozy and town building.You can romance select characters, rebuild your town(s) and raise your own little islands to restore your home.There's a lot more involved and this game has so much put into it, it's really amazing. I am very pleased and proud with how far Prideful Sloth has come! I've been following their work for awhile and I can say this game is my absolute favorite.I hope folks can give Grow: SoE a chance; you will NOT be disappointed, this game is literally incredible!
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I have a soft spot for farming/life sims, especially when they take a new spin on the usual format. I found it the day before it launched, bought it on launch day, and have already sunk quite a few hours into it.  Its charming, beautiful, creative, and engaging.  I'm finding it to be one of these games that you love playing so much that you worry about finishing too quickly. I feel that it has pretty good replayability given some of the mechanics I've discovered now, too.  Overall, I love this game and would highly recommend if you love games like Stardew Valley, Harvest Moon, My Time at Portia etc.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I got to the tutorial. First island thing. Immediately bored with far too many monotonous repetitive tasks and very... unrefined controls. Perhaps I'm not giving it a fair shake only playing through the tutorial but if the first 20 minutes were at all representative of what's gonna go on later, not worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: A jumbled and confusing blend of crafting sandbox and life/city management that's been done sooo much better in other titles. It's fun for the first 30 minutes, then it becomes insanely monotonous as you spend the day planting seeds, watering plants and building houses with very insignificant and obscure marks of progression.-SIde remark: As I played, I kept thinking "This gameplay style is nice, but I'd much rather play My Time at Portia or Stardew Valley" as I didn't feel this game respected my time at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I don't seem to be very far in but so far I am having a very good time with this game so I felt obligated to pop a review in to encourage others that enjoy relaxing wholesome games to give it a try and support some smaller devs. The game is relaxing, cute, wholesome, colorful, and though you'll likely do the same tasks multiple times such as fishing, weeding, watering, and expanding your town the freedom allowed in how you go about each day makes the pace relaxed instead of tedious.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: If you like cozy games with town development, exploration, collecting, decorating, adorable creatures, and beautiful scenery, then you should definitely try this game out! To me, this felt like if Breath of the Wild had a sister-game that focused on farming and community development. To be clear, there's no combat. But the exploration, puzzle rooms, music, and little NPC noises all give me those same BOTW vibes. Essentially, you're tasked with bringing the Evertree back to life by creating little mini "worlds" to gather resources from and then you use those to develop your town. As you begin to restore the community, more and more people start coming back and you can give them a home and a place to work. My absolute favorite part is decorating the little communities because in that interface, everything seems so small but as soon as you walk through it as your character, every little detail that you added comes to life and it's just so adorable! If you're a cozy game lover, then I highly recommend giving this game a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: It's quite a relaxing game but once you figure somethings out it becomes a bit boring. The puzzles are good but the requests are very repetitive and they all mostly want the same thing. Building the new worlds is a nice touch and it's interesting to see what they are going to turn out like but each world has 6 new animals to tame and very few places to place them. As a concept it should be good but it somehow lacks depth. Having said that it kept me quiet for 70 hrs
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Reading through the comments, i can see why people say there is a repetitive nature to this game. BUT! That's the appeal to this game. The cozy and atmospheric nature of this game makes those monotonous activities extremely rewarding and pleasant. If you find rinsing and repeating daily tasks bring you peace, then this is the game for you. Not only is there a good story but the world seed creation opens endless possibilities for new biomes. Craft, plant, water, sing, breakdown for essences, rinse and repeat. 10/10 highly recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I found this game at a very difficult time. I was looking for something relaxing and fun that would help me turn my brain off after having to put my kitty to sleep. This game has held my attention for 45 hours and will probably hold it for many more. The different worlds you can create, the beautiful scenery, the cute animals, this game has it all. The main con that I can think of is that the gameplay itself is quite repetitive. I had no issue with this personally, but people who prefer more challenging or exciting gameplay may not enjoy this game for very long.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Love it! Hoping for DLC this was one of my most favorite games I have played in this genre, also it came at the perfect time in my life, to help me relax and heal, and Ienjoyed a lot of it, only thing that could change would be the variety of the dungeon temples, and maybe add some more mechanics and new animations ect. i beat the game, and highly recommend it if you are a fan of games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my favorite games for relaxing or calming down; I neutralize a stressful day with this game! The character is like my kiddo. I want to get her all the fluffy pets and cute bugs, and all the good friends in her village, and decorate her little world.Creating new worlds is a really creative fun way to add to the normal slog that usually happens in farming games (for me). It adds nicely to the anticipation of the game that isn't often a terribly strong point in gathering/farming games. The colors and aesthetic is cozy and vibrant. The character system is fun and adds to the play style nicely.I can save the game at any time. The rewards for achievements and quests are paced nicely.The developers put out updates frequently enough.The story line is just enough to keep me mindful of it and interested (I personally want even more story, but then I'd probably stop the farming/village-building/gathering part of the game if it were too interesting hehe)It's all pretty nicely balanced and easy-going.It's very cozy and comfy.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: *ABANDONED AND BUGGED*A very, very slow paced and quite repetitive farming and city builder. You basically do the same thing over and over, and when you are done, it's rinse and repeat. The world itself is vast and beautiful, but that doesn't help the fact that it's really monotonous.What also doesn't help is the fact that the devs call everyone aside from the MC "they/them", no matter how obvious the gender is. But, that is their decision. Still noteworthy though.Additionally, the game is abandoned, with quite a few game breaking bugs still remaining.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: pretty good game. the main storyline can take you around 10 hours ish to complete, but it serves pretty much as a really long tutorial + introduction to the game.the game really is about expanding your town, exploring the world and collecting all sorts of things.you can really make your own goal whether it is to get a good looking town, a very productive town, a cool outfit, all the fishes or whatever.would recommend especially as its cheap.

_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This game is visually gorgeous with a stunning soundtrack and relaxing, seemingly never ending gameplay. The world is expansive and creative - exploring never gets tiring and the daily tasks don't feel monotonous or empty. Characters and animals are unique and bring a new life to the genre of animal crossing style sandbox games. I highly recommend to anyone who enjoys this type of gameplay!
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Here is my brief review on YouTube: Here are 3 reasons why you’ll want to play and 2 why you might want to pass.#1 PlayLet’s get the obvious out of the way…the graphics. Holy cow are they gorgeous! I am love with this chunky 3D artsyle with a fantasy vibe. It’s a bit like walking into the Shire. Even The Withering, the growth that has taken over the world has an absolutely beautiful glow to it, especially at night. #2 PassYou will have to do a lot of reading…I mean, a lot. They talk and talk and talk….it’s a bit much even for me an I am a fan of reading dialogue and acquiring exposition along the way. And when the game provides you with options to ask questions, when the NPCs answer, they say something which then adds even more options for questioning. #3 PlayThere is plenty to do when growing your world. You most all of the farming sim staples: planting, watering, chopping, mining, and scything. It’s been pretty satisfying. And, in addition, you also get a special skill to help the plants in your world grow even more. I feel so powerful.#4 PassIt might be a bit repetitive (and full disclosure I’ve seen this concern mentioned elsewhere but now I see first hand), particularly as it relates to the quests you have. The quests aren’t complicated as of yet but it it’s basically “hey do this quick task” that takes you literally seconds to do and then they gift you with something random. #5 PlayI hear the main game will take about 5 hours and, with the amount of time it will take to grow worlds and fish and bug hunt and fulfill quests, and all of the other tasks I’ve yet to uncover, I can see this being quite a rewarding adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game 2 days ago and have already sunk 8.5 hours into it. It's a massive game with plenty of content. This game feels like a crossover from zelda, animal crossing, stardew valley and a city builder. I haven't experienced any bugs or issues and I feel like this game is executed really well. It has a cute theme but i feel like it isn't exhausting. I received this game as a gift from my bf <3 but now that I know what it's like I would more than happily purchase for myself.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Grow is a very relaxed and layed back game, in which you take care of newly grown worlds, try to clean them from the "withering", build towns and customise them, complete tasks for villagers, explore to find the so-called song fragments to restore the ever tree.All in all this is a very cute and well made game, i've encountered no glitches or other weirdness, the game saves regularly and lets you load an old save without any issues (this got me out of a situation where i jumped into a hole out of curiosity). The graphics are cute, the music is nice and there is a lot of variety in what you can do. Sure, the gameplay is a bit repetitive because you have to build towns in 7 regions, so some tasks are similar but the exploration is very cool, there are many hidden things to discover and cool regions to climb over.It took me ~20 hours to complete the game. I'm sure you can do it quicker if you want to and rush through it more. And you can also get much more playtime out of of it if you want and take more time creating and taking care of your towns. There are also countless worlds to create and build, so there is a good amount of extra playtime to get out of it :D
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This game is perfect in every aspect. It's a peaceful experience that lets you experiment with crafting world seeds from which various worlds sprout and there's such a large amount of possibilities that I felt compelled to create more and more worlds. I found some truly beautiful ones and also some quirky ones with funny little details. The farming aspect of the game in which you tend to the world seeds is so calming and satisfying as you watch your world grow. And on top of that you can even build towns and see the whole world prosper. My only wish is that the game were even longer so that I could spend eternity in there. You can definitely continue growing your worlds after beating the main story but it would be nice to have more goals after that.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Reminds me very much of Yonder: the Cloud Catcher Chronicles.  I like it so far ... but I enjoy games where you just mindlessly water and plant stuff over and over, lol.  If you dont like that then its not for you.   Update: I never finished the game bc it was too frustrating without very good maps.  A map of each area would have been very helpful.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic little gem of a game and I have very few complaints about it. Let's get into the good.This game is "technically" in the farming sim genre even though you aren't really farming. It's one of the ways the game sets it's self apart.You are the last human willing to bring back the Evertree. Basically this games Yggdrasil. The roots of the Evertree used to create many worlds and creatures. Eventually though humans stopped caring for it, and then came The Withering. These long thorny branches enveloping the world and the tree. Stiffling it's ability to make new worlds and for the ones there are to be cared for.Your character, an Alchemist, is one of the only humans left that hears the Song of the Evertree and desires to help it. This is where the game starts, with your journey of finally helping the tree coming to fruition.Instead of farming you will go to the branches of the Evertree and tend to "worlds". Which are these islands grown from a single seed and a song. You clear them of debre and signs of the The Withering. Planting new plants and trees and bringing life to them with the goal of setting the world free when you are done to become a real world. As you do this you will uncover new elements with which you can make new seeds to make new worlds. These elements are also used for another aspect of the game... city building.As you care for the tree you also destroy The Withering at the base of the tree, opening up new land to slowly bring people back to live around the base of the tree and to care for it. The elements, as well as the in game currency of Myora, are what you use to build new buildings and homes. The more people you have the more Myora you have. The more Myora the more villages you can make.Tending to your worlds is so incredibly relaxing and I adore it, but making the seeds themselves is also fun. You need 50 of any combination of elements (up to 5 different kinds) to make a world seed. Each more unique than the last. Though uh... may I suggest you not make a Squishy, Mushy, Bitter, Spongey world... you won't like it I promise you. I feel for the creators that will inhabit this world when I release it.You also have to get back pieces of The Song to get The Withering off of the roots of the Evertree. Each new area you unlock around the base of the tree will have a new piece of The Song hidden there that you need to find and then do some kind of puzzle segment to get.The story it's self isn't exactly all that original, but it's still very good. The game play loop of making a world, tending it, using resources to get new elements to make new seeds, and in between uncover more of the lower areas and maintain cities... is a REALLY good loop. The game is also incredibly cute and cozy feeling. The Everkin are adorable, but all the animals in this game are so damn cute. Also I can't say enough good things about this games camera mode. This game really sets it's self apart from other farming sims and I love that so much in a genre that can feel very samey at times.There is some bad though....1) It seems as if the game isn't getting updates and there ARE some bugs here and there that I've run into. There's also no way to reload your character to a previous spot if you get stuck on terrain unless you want to lose progress.2) I wish there was a map that wasn't flying into the air with Kazumi3) The management system for the cities could use a bit of tweeking and I REALLY wish I could either kick out some villagers or move them between areas. If this IS a thing I haven't unlocked it yet.4) This game has fantastic music and I'm very disappointed there's not a soundtrack for purchase.5) The animations of gestures and the speaking noise for the villagers isn't all that good. There's also little to no explaination for what the little icons over their heads mean or how to go about helping them. I figured out the badge hovering over there heads means they want to be better at their jobs... but I have yet to find much of anything I can upgrade their levels with.6) The festivals are great, but I really wish that you had more than one day to do them. If I'm doing all I need to do in a day I don't have much time to hunt for the things I need to do for the festival.7) I wish caves were marked on the map after you find them.8) And lastly.... I hate the fishing mini game. It's just not well implemented and it's my only major complaint about the game as someone who loves fishing in these kinds of games. It's fiddly and doesn't make much sense. The game also explains it terribly.Overall though I can't recommend the game enough to people who love the genre but are looking for something new to do in the genre.Works great on Steam Deck

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up, but it's a difficult and complicated game to review (which is why this is version 1.1 of the review !).Overall task: Revitalise a deteriorated and abandoned world using gardening and repopulation to make the place habitable.  You do these two things in tandem, all the while exploring the new land which is revealed.  Eventually (30 hours ?  40 ?) you win.Graphics are good, though it uses a widely-used look that tends to make everyone look like they're made of wood.  The visual style of the game seems designed to appeal to kids.  But there's a lot of grinding,,and there's a need for strategy that takes adult insight.  No kid is going to spend enough time on this to beat it.  (Yes, I know about Roblox and Minecraft.  This game doesn't allow that kind of creativity.)The game has a wide range of activities.  You will gather resources, craft, jump platforms, figure out how to pack buildings in limited spaces, customise buildings and people's outfits, and solve various small puzzles.  None of these things are particularly difficult, and if you 'die' you just lose half a minute's progress.  I'm an avid explorer in computer games but a lot of the optional fun stuff is well-hidden and I was still finding more odd and amusing things after I'd 'won'.You spend a lot of time gardening your new sub-worlds.  Fortunately each ecosystem is different, with different dominant colours, different flora and fauna, and different whacky things to find.  There is inventive humour in the way these worlds can vary and in what you find in them.  It helps relieve the tediuim of taking a new area, clearing the weeds, and cultivating an ecosystem.  To be honest,I think the devs could have cut the work needed per world by 1/5th or 1/3rd, and the game would have been the better for it.The development team have worked to include non-traditional genders and preferences in the game.  Some characters are clearly either male or female, but others are androgenous, or fluid, or non-binary.  You can change your own, and NPC's, hairstyles and clothes during gameplay, and the game has no sex-marking of hairstyles or clothes: it doesn't care whether you mix or match and doesn't use sex-marked language to refer to anyone, at least in the English language.I played the game immediately after release and found no game-stopping bugs.  There were some annoyances which I hope the developers will fix before long, but nothing I couldn't work around.  It was worth the (full) price I paid.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those times where I wish there was a middle "it's just okay" option. The game offers up a lot of potential for creativity and exploration, but it eventually becomes apparent that the game is quite hollow. I was excited at first by the expanse of the game only to realize everything feels same-y and doesn't have as much personality as it appears. Some of the aspects I never ended up really understanding or utilizing much, like the weird village where you can get and spend various in-game currencies, and the townspeople ended up speaking the same five dialogue sentences. This made a lot of the really cool customization options feel kind of pointless.The day-night cycle feels more obnoxious than immersive, though the graphics are absolutely gorgeous! It was also really annoying going into the puzzle caves and waiting five minutes as it slowly panned around the whole thing. It was more frustrating than helpful.It is a fun game in general, but don't go in looking for a deeply engaging and immersive world. That feeling faded fairly quickly for me and eventually became repetitive.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game via humble bundle. Yeah, maybe its okay for many people who like the quiet games, but this is boring. The early game tutorials baby you something rotten, you often get lost doing basic stuff and its repeatitive, but in the worst possible way. Rewards are basically "heres a nice hairstyle" or "here something to put in the enviroment". The bug catching is about the best part of the game as I admit, its the most challenging things per reward while fishing... I think it is tedious at best, its like a more boring version of bug catching wherein the reward is slower. _childDocuments_.review: My main takeaway is: It's kind of like Stardew Valley for children or completely inexperienced gamers. It's a good time sink if you like the genre and need something new, but there  better games than this.The game holds your hand very much and it seems adamant in pushing you in a linear direction despite this being an open-world building/farming sim. When the game wants you to do something, you have to do it to progress in the game. There is a bit of freedom to do whatever you want, but there aren't many different ways to play the game. It's also very linear in that it has a story with a beginning and the end of the game. The story is, uh, a poorly masked statement on climate change lmao.The game is also  repetitive, even if that's part of the grind for a game like this. You unlock a new area, slap down some buildings and decorations, find the vault, move boxes to get the Song Fragment, put the fragment in the tree, unlock a new area, and do this all over again.The game feels a bit unpolished, there are weird bugs littered throughout the game. The biggest one for me was when I created a World that was too close to the trunk of the Evertree, so part of the World clipped into the tree and was obscured. You can walk through the tree wall if that happens though. Even without the bugs the game just feels empty in a lot of aspects.I think the summary is that the game is absolutely playable but "kinda mid", I'm giving it a slight Not Recommended because it feels like I have more bad things to say than good.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a sweet game.  There are components of Yonder that I appreciate making the game very pleasant and consistent throughout.  Objectives are to restore the land via planting world seeds and tending the worlds with a handful of character quests thrown in.  Restoring the land causes people to return and you build the town and businesses for their continued contentment.  The graphics are beautiful and there are lots of activities.  You can't die and it is non-violent.  There are many, many achievements you can chase or just chill and restore the world while achievements dribble in.  The repetition may dissuade some.  I find the predictability beneficial and relaxing in a time where so much of life can be rushed, overly competitive and stressful.  The developers have created characters that are a mix of age and background and gender.  Dialogue is interesting and generally playful.  It is all in text form.   There are a number of guides to help simplify the guessing for "creating world seeds". The puzzles are fairly simple.   I appreciate the time and effort people went to generate these.  The world is very large with lots to explore and occasional treasures to find as well as hints.   Thanks to Prideful Sloth for another lovely game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game.  The art style is great and the experience is well polished.  The story is interesting and town building is great... right up until you hit the very tiny build budgets.  It's like they designed the budgets so that a mobile phone could render the game.  You have 20 decorations in the first district, which can be anything from a tiny shrub to gazebo to a massive tree.  I was really enjoying the game for the first few hours until I decided to make use of all those decoration items I was finding and really put some effort into building a town.  I hit the decoration budget in just a few minutes and it took all the fire out of the game...  why would I got farm up more stuff that I won't even be able to use?  Bleh.  They need to let us build to the limits of our hardware.  We should have no build limits on PC.  I might come back to this game if they change the build limits.  It might be an amazing game with that one simple change.  For now... stay away until they figure out what they want this game to be.  Town building isn't a selling point when you can't build much.EDIT:  If anyone sees this and learns that the limits have been removed or made configurable/moddable, let me know please.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a charming and chill town builder / gardening sim. Graphics look good and really make the world somewhat whimsical and cute without going overboard with it. The game play is really where this game shines though, taking inspiration from games like Harvest Moon, Stardew Valley and Dark Cloud this game focuses on tending to expanding worlds through gardening, fishing, mining and bug catching in order to get the essences necessary to build up your town to the citizens needs. The game as far as I have experienced has no looming deadline for doing this and instead really just lets you do it at your own pace, giving you some freedom to fool around and enjoy the scenery instead of rushing to try and get things done by a set date. The town building is pretty free form with how you can place the buildings and decorations allowing you some decent control over everything, while still trying to appease the citizens that you are trying to keep happy. Unlike a lot of other games like this there is no combat and now way to pass out from exhaustion, letting you have one less thing to worry about while playing. All in all the controls work pretty well, my only complaint would be the jumping which can make platforming awkward, but even that doesn't really sour the experience. The sound design is beautiful and quite relaxing, making it pretty easy to get into a zen mood while completing your tasks. TL;DR: Game good, worth buy.

_childDocuments_.review: Grow: Song of the evertree is a fun adventure game where you can resque and create a whole world without time pressure,this wholesome world-building game puts you in the shoes (or in this case a 'glove') of an Alchemist in the land of Alaria,This world has been hit hard by a dark takeover and as a result the Evertree can no longer provide the world with what it needs to thrive healthily and extensively.Fortunately, you are there to prevent the Evertree from dying completely and better yet, you can repair all the damage,all you will have to do is plant seeds, and sing an ancient song,per seed planted, a region will be covered with green, wild environments and the intention is to do this all over the world.Gameplay: You will have to do all this with the help of a mechanical gauntlet, with this you can find resources and metals that you will need later for items, missions or upgrades,The world is not open but with routes, through these routes are also many hidden locations that take you to even more and also rarer resources, so always watch out.Grow: Song of the evertree also has good support for ultra-wide monitor resolutions, you can see an example of this in this video:

_childDocuments_.review: Grow is a very nice game about rebuilding a broken world.Grow is very relaxing.  There are no time constraints, so you never feel stressed that you have to get something done or you will lose it.  There is a day/night cycle, so you run out of time in an individual day, but there's always tomorrow, and everything will wait until tomorrow.  This perfectly matching what I was looking for at the time.Everything is really cute and funny.  The characters are fun, and I want to hug all the critters I found.  Even the bugs were pretty cute, which is quite the accomplishment.  Some of the worlds you can create are quite odd, but even that is fun to experiment with.  I am not usually someone who spends a long time on aesthetics, but I had fun decorating the houses in town.My one criticism of the game is that the gameplay loop can begin to feel routine.  This is fine if you enjoy it enough, but by the end I was beginning to tire of it.  I think the reason is the atomization.  Each district you make is its own separate town.  I would have liked it more if they were connected in some way.  As it, it feels like you are just making 8 different towns next to eachother.Developing worlds has the same critiqe.  after a little bit, cleaning up each world feels routine.  It's fun to discover how each develops, but I think they need to develop a bit faster as you get deep into the game to avoid them feeling too samey.Overall though, i really enjoyed my time in Grow, and may dip back in as I want.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is enjoyable and adorable, and I find it's great for when I'm feeling stressed or like I just need some wholesome feels for the day.There are definitely bugs (like quests not completing if they come after you've already done what it's asking) and some poor design choices (like not allowing you to transfer townmembers between districts, and there being minimal onboarding/tutorials for some aspects), but it is a relaxing game that I know I'll be sinking more hours into, especially as exam season hits me. The story progress I make warms my heart as I watch my efforts slowly destroy the corruption plaguing the great big tree.My favourite part: all animals are cuddle-able or catch-able and the camera mode also includes many emotes.My least favourite part: it's important to visit your tree seeds early in the day, because if it hits night while you're in the branches you get automatically teleported down to the ground.

_childDocuments_.review: After trying this game from my daughter, I decided to buy it.  I really enjoyed the no killing aspect of the game.  I found the game rather relaxing.  I even bought a controller in anticipation of the reviews I read.    * The graphics are so adorable.  *  Easy to get engrossed in the tasks at hand when cleaning and tending the islands.  *  Great to know you don't loose anything if you drown or fall off the edge.   *  I love the collection aspect of the game.  Too bad they aren't that useful.        Creating new worlds is the best thing to do in the game.  Plant worlds, tend to them, then release them when it's mature.  Rinse and repeat.  The different look of the trees, shrubs, bugs, and animals are nice. It is why I am busy looking for the perfect pets to assign to all the houses in my towns.   I spend so much time using all the imperfect seeds to see just what comes out of it.  That is all I do.  I haven't found much else to do that I enjoy.          Now the not so good things about the game:     *  No mini-map to help me figure out where the heck I am in my town.       *  Being forced to return home, or go to bed.     *  Fishing is too tedious.  I don't like how long it takes to get one fish.          (Catching bugs is so much better,  even though I am deathly afraid of bugs in real life.)    I hate wasting the "active time" looking around the town to find the secret spots and fragment.  I hate neglecting the world seed chores.  After a while I found myself cutting down trees so I could sort of make a path to know which way to go in those islands.  I'm over 50 and really detest having my hands slapped in a game and forced to go to bed.   I just don't understand why game developers have to implement this sort of thing into such games.  I mean I don't eat in this game ...why should I sleep?  Why can't I have a game where I can run amuck collecting everything I can without punishment?  It's the number one reason I stay away from games like Stardew Valley.  I don't like adhering to a clock schedule.  PLEASE take the real life aspect out of my fantasy games!

_childDocuments_.review: (If you got this through Humble Choice/Monthly like me, give it a try! It's worth it!)This game is a mix of cozy farming, exploration and town management.It has a pretty good start where all the mechanics get introduced gradually as your situation improves and feels very nice to play. Then after a while (maybe 10-15 hours depending on how fast you play) it kinda loses steam as the scope of the game keeps increasing but the content that is added is mostly repeats of previous segments.That being said, there are tons of positive things to say about this game, it looks gorgeous, the music is very nice (although gets a bit repetitive), there's some goofy humour and a charming story about respecting nature and taking care of the environment. There's tons of customisation options for your character which you acquire over time and you can swap them at any time which was really fun to me.I had some issues with the game, like clunkiness in the town management part of the game or with the UI, some challenges feeling a bit pointless with lackluster rewards or the overall lack of upgrades for your character (i fully expected to be able to fly as some kind of ultimate reward which would have made the endgame feel a bit less tedious) and very easy puzzles with very long introduction cutscenes that cant be skipped.Overall, I had a great time with this game despite some criticism. It feels very cozy to play and the day/night cycle isnt as stressful as some other farming games. I think this would make an absolutely amazing gift for a nerdy kid. I know that at that age I would have been completely obsessed with this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: It's a beautiful game. I really wanted to love it and dump days into it. I just can't because it's making me sick. Normally I'm not prone to motion sickness. I can play most games to include 60fps and even VR games, but 1 hour in an I had to have a lay down due to motion sickness. I thought surely there's some setting to slow my character down so the tiny lag between command input and character movement won't affect me or to simply slow the running speed down so I can admire the surroundings instead. I dug through settings, tried various methods to reduce control sensitivity, adjust visual detail, everything that was an option I adjusted. No dice.I checked the forums for advice and it's a wide spread issue even among people not normally prone to motion sickness. If you have ever played a video game and felt headaches, nausea, dizziness, sudden sleepiness, or find yourself experiencing these when watching others play certain games, be wary walking in. Give it a try for sure! If you're less than 2 hours in an need a break there isn't a great solution. Consider a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Version: Cute but ultimately forgettablePROS - Procedural world generation has some obvious patterns and limitations, but also a number of delightful surprises - Tons of ways to customize your character's outfit & hair, customizing NPCs outfits and hair, and decorating the exterior of houses and businesses - Positive, sweet main plot and children's storybook-style adventure - Quite a bit of in-world lore and some good tongue-in-cheek jokesCONS - World repetition can get a little old after a time: there are only two basic models of animals with different colors and part swaps, a handful of bug and fish models, etc. - NPC "romance" options seem unfinished, and are therefore completely superfluous; all of the "human" characters look like children or young teens (including the PC) which makes the idea of there even BEING "romance" options all the more off-putting - Town-building dynamic has unnecessary limits on maximum buildings, as the amount of SPACE that's available is and should be the real limiting factor - Actual main story line is very short, just requires repeating the same three general steps 7 times - Lore provided is not explored; hints are given within the Pallas storyline that imply there's more to learn, but nothing ever comes of it - The whimsical children's tale aspect of Book and Coppertop is quickly overshadowed by how incredibly annoying and patronizing they are to the PC - Lengthy, unskippable, repetitive, and often completely unnecessary cut-scenesIn some ways, this game feels like a beta release and not a complete game; I also suspect the initial target audience was for children under 12 but then that side of things was pushed to the side for... some reason. The bones are there for something solid, but it seems as though the developers got bored with creating actual content and threw out a few dozen customization skins, a romance subplot that is so ridiculously out-of-the-blue as to be jarring, and a grindy scheme for acquiring blueprints and the essences needed to build them, and then called it a day. All of the basics are learned within the first few hours of gameplay, so there's nothing challenging in solving any of the puzzles presented later, and aside from some platforming maneuvers which can be frustrating if you're not skilled in such a thing, everything is boringly straight-forward for the final two-thirds of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Introduction:There is frequently a bundle for “Yonder: The Cloud Catcher Chronicles” and “Grow: Song of the Evertree.” I purchased this bundle for Yonder and I considered Grow to be just an additional freebie. Ironically, I launched Grow first and got hooked on it, so I have never even launched Yonder yet.Controls: I play Grow casually, when I feel, as much as I feel. I play it on PC with a controller connected as well as on Steam Deck. This game is not fun to play using keyboard/mouse, in my opinion. The gameplay is significantly smoother, and the mechanics are easier to understand and get used to with the controller/deck.Creating Worlds:The point of the game revolves around regrowing the Evertree. There are these vines that have taken over a significant portion of the land. Your job is to create different world trees, collect essence, and create towns to bring people back to the land. There are 24 different essences to collect and each world you generate can offer different essences. You use essences for certain buildings as well as for creating more worlds – with 6 different “perfect” world seeds you must find the creation code. Spoiler, so skip this part if you don’t wish to see it… an example would be 16 comforting, 12 lush, 11 tranquil, and 11 abundant essences will create one of the six perfect world seeds.Towns:You will have to manage your first town to obtain 100% town satisfaction (make sure there are enough houses, people have jobs that they like, those sharing a home like each other, the buildings and houses are customized with wallpapers and designs, there are decorations around, etc.) Once that is done, you will have to explore the town area to find all the hidden landmarks, journals, chests, caves, fish, bugs, and more. One of the landmarks will introduce you to the puzzles. Once you complete a town, there will be a puzzle you must complete to then be able to start expanding and creating more towns. Each town being completed (check the stone in the center of your town to see your progress) opens this feature up. I have not done every puzzle but so far, they have all been different. One used block as a mechanic where you slide them to open doors. Another used these drone-like creatures you have to avoid as well as portals that allowed you to jump between them and float. Different things to work on:-	Finishing tasks to unlock all the different building blueprints.-	Repair the world to unlock more land, allowing you to create towns, bringing people back the Evertree.-	Finding all 6 of the world tree combinations to create perfect world trees.-	Participate in the “tent” events to earn tokens for different cosmetics and items.-	Perfect different towns to unlock more districts.-	Find all the journals.-	Discover all creatures, fruits, trees, fish, plants, bugs. -	There is more but I can’t remember right now.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game concept. Terrible execution.The basic gameplay is that you grind for content:  travel to pregenerated spots to plant, water, hammer, sickle, etc. different game objects. Working grows the environment (in real time) and gives bonus prizes, which could've been addicting. Once you've finished building a stage, you get more bonuses. This formula would be great if there were content to get, such as diverse worlds/animals instead of re-used ones. The work of farming each stage is excessive compared to the content, even if it were multiplayer. You do less work in Harvest Moon.I should've been done at maybe 10-15 hours, but because the game's RNG prevents you from getting essences you don't already have in abundance, I have been unable after 60 hours to get any Prickly to create a "perfect world" to finish the game.The city-building mode is far less grindy and has better balanced work-for-content. You can build different services and assign workers and level them up, but it doesn't really impact the main game. They just result in more junk in your inventory, none of which can be melted down for Prickly. There are random fetch quests too, resulting in random clothing if that entertains you.The "game" centers on completing the main quest rather than any activity having replay value. So there's nothing you can excel at to do better (or differently) the 3rd or 5th time through. It does run and load very smoothly and has seriously well-designed visuals, but it's like getting a whopper with no meat. You're like...why...is there no burger?

_childDocuments_.review: Waaay better than I expected! It's like an amazing book that you can't put down... I can't stop playing it! This is such a great game!! When I was debating getting this game, it was hard to get a good feel of it from the screenshots and videos. Luckily, it was on sale, so I felt comfortable taking a risk and once I started playing it, I was hooked. The game play is easy to learn and the concept is so relaxing. I don't usually like building towns or villages and decorating them, but the way it is done in Grow makes it fun and not seem tedious or like a chore. The added element of getting to know your villagers likes and dislikes really adds another dimension to it also.As an adventurer at heart, I love that exploration is rewarded! Crafting unique worlds from seeds is such a wonderful idea and tending to the worlds each day is a delight. The game has pleasing sounds and mechanics. The graphics have a cute art style and there are ambient effects that make it feel magical when you play. This game has such a wide variety of things to do and you don't have to worry about what you choose to do during the game-day putting you behind in the overall game. You just pick if you want to tend to your village, world seeds, explore, or decorate and enjoy yourself.It was a nice surprise to find this game had puzzles and other mechanics such as fishing, bug catching, and treasure chests. I have played a lot of games that require you to focus on the time to maximize your day and something I find to be a great quality of life perk is that when you have spent the allotted time tending to your world seed, it will teleport you back to your Alchemist's Grotto and you can continue working in your villages/districts until it gets to be too late and it will teleport you back again so you can hit the hay.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't for everyone, but if you like town-building games, no-stress games about restoring nature, and giving cute, but strangely colored critters belly rubs, this game is for you. It's very cute, and is clearly geared toward young and young-at-heart players. Also players that are sick of dying every ten seconds in online shooter games. Also players that need a break from making someone die every ten seconds in online shooter games. (Why do you have to be so specific? What did Dave ever do to you, huh?) There are some glitches, and it may lock up on you, but if you close the game and go back, as I was relieved to discover, there is an autosave function, so you don't lose very much if that does happen.All in all, I give this game a 7.5/10 based on my experience so far. I do have to say, though, it's a shame so many players drop the game so early. Like 10% as of this writing don't even get to the point of having the Book to keep track of their goals. That's like ten minutes of play. I mean come on, you should be able to tell what kind of game it is from the videos on the store page. If that's not for you, don't buy it. If you do buy it, at least give the thing a chance, people.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming back to my original review some 80+ hours later, I've got some things to say: First up? I still rec this game. It's stunningly beautiful, heartwarming, funny, cute, endearingly random, and made by people who have consumed at least as many substances as I have. HOWEVER. If ever a game needed a mini-map? It's this one. You *will* get lost multiple times on hill and dale -- and deep within caves and dungeon-type areas -- and have no idea how to get where you want to go until you're yanked back to bed and have to start hunting all over again the next day. There is platforming, and it bites. If you hate platforming the way I do? This game has no replayability whatsoever unless you have a friendly person who can take care of the currently-unskippable platforming sequences which advance the plot. I have ragequit multiple times. There are bugs, some game-breaking -- still, the devs are going after those pretty quickly and responsively. The intro/tutorial is both mind-numbingly talky and profoundly lacking in useful information. You *will* be haunting the steam forums and reddit. The game is designed to be all about open-world exploration, discovery, mild city-building, decoration -- things like that. You are not crafting or farming -- get that right out of your head. Unfortunately, as things stand, there are also a few too many hard limits on what you *can* do, like not being able to build up your towns the way you'd like, and not being able to explore much after dark. (Yonder has this game beat to death on this...) Still, even with all that? I'm about to go boot it up and play for another few hours. I'm enjoying myself immensely, and it's a rare game that holds my attention for this long. The fact that it's a game I can share with my even-pickier spouse? A joy beyond all *reason*. Still -- caveats. Original review below: My spouse and I have only played for a few hours, but it's abundantly clear that this is going to be one of our favorite games of all time. Like Yonder before it, it's beautiful, wholesome, funny, cleverly built, and just generally warm. But this is a whole new story with worlds within worlds -- sprawling and vast while still remaining curiously cozy. The lore is deep and focused on environmentalism. You've heard this message before, but not enough of us have heard it well enough -- obviously. Still, instead of preaching, the game gives you the opportunity to fix the problems caused by earlier generations through a farm sim's hard work, alchemy, city planning (!!!),  and a glorious opportunity to wander a truly incredibly rich and detailed world. There's so *much* here to discover for gamers like me, who live for the games which let you take your time and peek around every corner, climb every tree, and peer over every cliff. Every vista is joyously colorful postcard to worlds upon worlds -- a feast for the senses heightened by the score. The screen grabs above do not do this game justice. The video is a *little* better. Listen -- I would've bought this game for 3X the price and thought I was stealing something. If you like games which let you take things at your own pace while also giving you clear, satisfying tasks to perform; if you like games which allow you to wrest order from chaos; if you like games which are made with heart and soul and a desire to bring joy to every player; if you can take a break from killing things for just a *little* while...You have no excuse not to buy this marvel. Bonus: Explicit welcome for non-binary players. The they/thems droppeth like manna from heaven.

_childDocuments_.review: The best way to describe Grow: Song of the Evertree without giving away too much is to call it a rebuilding/ rehabilitation adventure RPG, with a lot of puzzles along the way. The game’s young protagonist is tasked with healing a world corrupted and abandoned by its former inhabitants. Along the way, he/she gets a lot of help. But to get the job done, Grow works the player harder than any other game. And it’s totally worth it. It is a satisfying experience, even though some things could be improved.The first is the in-your-face unskippable tutorial banter early on in the game that stops you in your tracks and breaks the flow. I just started a second run just to make sure, and this still bothered me. There is no reason – and it’s counter-productive - that the game should come to a halt every time these things pop up, leaving the player clicking for air. The UI is intuitive enough to allow doing away with some of the excessive hand-holding.The second issue with this multi-layered game is repetition. There are things that need doing to further the story and they tend to get repetitious. Gamers who play long enough to unfold the early layers of the story will understand the reasoning behind this repetition. But it becomes off-putting after a while. And given the creative license you earn as the story advances, the repetition, which is only a means and not an end, should be addressed, since it also affects some of the game’s numerous puzzles. This is not a game for everyone. There are multiple generations of gamers on the scene today, and not all of them will like this game. Some developers mix and match genres to attract more disparate players. Grow does it too – to a point. But it’s probably a mistake to even try to please all of them. Those who are undecided should consider that this peaceful game is worth playing, albeit with some patience. It is not for gamers who are looking for a confrontational experience. It is an RPG that cares – and dares the player to do the same.
