_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: It's Dark Cloud for people who hated the dungeon bits.  Calm and chill, but with things to do.  Puzzley challenges and exploration.  Also one of the cutest games I've ever played.  Has tools like a farming game, but it's not a farming game at all.  It's much more about the building up of the towns and giving people the things they want in life, while growing your new worlds.  Fantastic but definitely not for the twitch gamers.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: I have a lot of hours in this game, much of them are inactive, but many of them playing.  Rather than going into the mechanics of the game in deail, I'd just like to express something broader, and that is hours not paying off.The game starts off very simple, with basic mechanics that slowly get introduced to you over the course of several hours, including town management aspects of the game.  The payoff of the game is supposed to be exploration and discovery, and while there is a lot of exploration, the discovery portion is underwhelming:The main premise of the game is that you are restoring worlds from a corrupted state back to a prestine state by creating world seeds and planting those seeds upon a tree. In order to restore each world, you have to work, and work you will do.  You will be planting seeds, pulling weeds, pounding rocks and cutting grass.  You have no say in what gets planted where.  You're told where to go, which tool to use.  The only purpose is to waste your time, and the time sink can be intense if you are dealing with multiple worlds.  What is the payoff for this work?  More resources for you to extract.  That's right, there's no satisfaction in exploration because every single world contains the same scenery, save for some will have little caves to go through for you to gather chests.  And you're gathering all of this for resources to build a bunch of districts, the town management aspect.  The town management system involves you placing homes and giving people jobs and trying to align people with their "dream job."  There are some cool interactions with townspeople and it's neat to be able to organize a town and see the residents walking around and doing their jobs.  If this were the thing you spent the most time doing, I'd probably recommend it.  But the town management is hampered down heavily by the amount of micromanagement when your towns get significant size.  You're having to manage what everyone wants in a confusing game of tetris.  In itself this isn't terrible until you realize how much time you're spent managing things as opposed to getting something interesting out of your management.And that's what this game is.  It is a grind that pretends to give you a gigantic payoff, when there is one.  The exploration is meaningless and doesn't have quality of life features.  The time sinks are insane for what littlethere is to get out of them.  The game is one big resource hunt and time management thing with a very shallow town simulation to show for it.  If you're someone who likes the journey, who just likes to grind, this will be a good game.  If you're someone who wants to be rewarded for the grind, definitely pass on this.The whole game is a resource grind, but the grind is only fun if there is a payoff, and there's not a payoff
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This is a cute and fun game with a lot of different things mixed in. There's Animal Crossing chores like weeding and planting seeds but there's also a bit of town management mixed in with learning new building recipes and making your villagers happy. The mix is enjoyable, but it does get repetitive after having to do the same things over and over for each new town and area. Additionally, while this game does say that you can "find love" it's very much not really a thing and you just have a few set characters you can talk to and eventually one falls in love with you and locks you out of the other options so that was definitely a con for me as I would have liked it to have a bit more life and choice to it. Overall though, it was worth it to pick up during a sale. It's a nice way to chill out for a bit.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Way too buggy. Well I had already progressed too far, so it correcting it by putting in the cutscene didn't help me, because I can't finish a quest to progress further in the game now. _childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Agree with a lot of the other negative reviews - this isn't a terrible game (I was willing to finish it) but I hesitate to call it good. Like others, I frequently wondered if it's meant for kids because it's so easy and simplistic. In my opinion, if it was aiming for "relaxing/cozy" it too frequently overshot into "boring". But that's not the only reason I wouldn't recommend this.The core gameplay loop just isn't compelling and many features feel half-baked. Most available activities quickly become repetitive and there isn't sufficient reward for doing most of them; by the mid-game I already had so much money and essence that most of the gameplay had become pointless, and I was sick of going out of my way for a quest or distant gold chest just to be rewarded with some ugly wallpaper or a stupid looking hat. I HATE the fishing system, it feels awful, but thankfully it's not very important. Puzzles range between extremely easy and extremely tedious. As for NPCs, most of them are randomly generated fodder so you can tick off population and job targets to unlock the next area. There are a few characters with unique personalities and interactions, but it's all so short and rushed they still feel pretty lifeless, and the romance system is obviously an afterthought.I did run into several bugs, including the one described in other reviews where trying to accept a certain reward causes the game to lock up, but thankfully that fixed itself after I reloaded the game. The rest were just minor things so in my experience the game was still playable - but I would still recommend looking into other similar games before buying this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This team released another game in 2017, Yonder, which for some reason I've played twice 100% (although multiple years apart) and still somehow enjoyed my collectathon in the second playthrough.Grow: Song of the Evertree came out afterwards, in 2021, and maybe COVID heavily affected the development but this game is a huge step back from Yonder. While Yonder had some quirks, it mostly did feel like a complete game and was decently polished, however Grow is not.There are some fun ideas and concepts but it seems like nothing is actually fleshed out or polished. While I didn't encounter any game-breaking bugs, the game regularly had graphical and audio glitches including the player or insects going through walls, insects usually did not use a crawling animation and just kinda glided along and would run away through walls or objects. Every time you open a chest or something is giving a reward, it spits out the items in a huge burst with way too much physics and causes the rewards to fly through walls or off cliffs. Just a few examples.Yonder was a fun collectathon but Grow was missing a lot of direction in every aspect from story, progression, gameplay, etc. It had a lot of potential but despite a large "Book" (literally a talking book named Book) to track progression, lacked any sort of log or drive to want to collect insects, fish, plants, etc. The rewards from the Book were also typically trivial, outside of Blueprints. The seed islands and reviving the various town areas was a fun idea but quickly got very repetitive with nothing new introduced throughout the progression.Lots of things were just kinda half attempted and inserted into the game that had potential to be cool, like the flying dragon snake things - outside of a random cave I happened to find that had some babies that just flew away, they were pretty much forgotten. Same with the Everkin, where its so easy for players to miss you could go back to their town and trade with them... but again for trivial rewards. But this was also a common theme, where the devs seemingly wanted to encourage exploration without giving any indication of what you're even looking for or might find, but the world was mostly boring, empty, and full of trivial rewards that didn't make it feel worth it. You don't even need to complete the main story to unlock all Steam achievements lol.I got this game on sale but overall I don't really recommend this game unless you really, really want something very chill and very repetitive to play and haven't played Yonder yet, which is a much more enjoyable chill collecthaton game.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

Fencing does not count towards decorations, and can work to better frame the few decorations we are allowed to have.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: In a really stressful time in my life this game is exactly what I need it to be. Everything in this game is built to make you happy and relaxed. I am now addicted to the relaxing vibe of gardening with beautifully composed piano music playing in the background and the town building is a lot of fun. _childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

There were lots of little chests to find, puzzles (nice easy ones thank goodness) and even a little romance, it was so sweet it made my heart melt. Definitely worth the price as I think I will replay it often, so relaxing and lovely a world it is to be in. Well done to everyone at Prideful Sloth! _childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Really pretty world, lovely renders. Plenty of different areas, seemingly infinite combinations of different worlds to create, harvest, and explore. The interiors of most of the buildings are nicely done as well.- Pleasant gameplay for the most part. Cute citizens to interact with and somewhat customize. Cute animals to befriend and adopt, although interaction with them is very limited. Rewarding experience building up your towns and maximizing happiness in each town. - Lots to do, lots to explore. A few different options for fast-travelling. Cons: - Number one complaint is that the 'Everkids' on the worlds you create, are incredibly disruptive and irritating. They're supposed to help you harvest on your created worlds, and they do, sort of. But they also follow you wherever you go, with a constant, loud 'pop' noise and swirly effects, every few steps you take. Worse, they prevent you from harvesting yourself, by 'talking' to you instead of simply letting you select and add resources to your inventory. Super, super annoying. There is no need for them to follow you around, or have a 'talk option' at all. - Some of the caves you need to complete, are crazy stupid hard. The puzzle solving is easy, but the moving and navigating past obstacles is beyond difficult in many of them. Multiple attempts just to move to a different area, only to fail over and over and over again. Not challenging, not fun, just immensely aggravating. They're badly designed to be much too hard for what is supposed to be a relaxing, sweet game. The developers should have paid attention to the cave/dungeon design in 'My Time at Portia'. Tricky, but fairly simple to complete is a far better option for games like this. - Not enough options for customizing your citizens. They all make requests to update their look, which you need to do to keep them happy. There are plenty of clothing and hair and glasses  styles that become available, which is good. Although most of them are more idiotic looking than appealing. But even though you have to update their appearance, you can't simply remove or undo something if you don't like it. Once a citizen is wearing glasses, facial hair, or a hat, they're on for good, All you can do is change the type of glasses, facial hair, or hat. It's a minor annoyance compared to the other big issues, but it is annoying. - Falls don't kill you, no matter how high. Which is nice, and not a problem. If you fall, an umbrella appears in your hand and you gently float to the ground. But it's illogical and really frustrating, that the second you step or fall into deep water, you're instantly dead. If you're protected from one thing, why not the other? Why can't a balloon appear in your hand to pull you back up to the water's surface? If you can run and walk and jump, why can't you swim? Again, bad design and annoying. - You can't customize your character's home at all, yet you can do minor customizations on every other building in the game. Why? It makes zero sense. Overall, the enjoyable aspects of the game are pretty evenly balanced with the frustrating, illogical, badly designed aspects. If it were possible to give a 'thumbs sideways', that's how I would have rated it. This is a new release, so hopefully the developers will pay attention to reviews and feedback, and address these issues in future game updates.

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVE this game.  I just got a PC again and this opened up the magical world of Steam for me.  I've always enjoyed farm/life sim type games like Harvest Moon and Animal Crossing.  After spending hours looking for a game that had an art style I enjoyed and was in the cozy genre, I finally landed on this game.  It has farming mechanics, town building, exploration and fetch tasks, but all with a unique and cute fantasy twist.  Seriously...the creatures are so adorable!The story line, while finite, keeps you sucked in and wanting to learn more.  But not to worry, I would say I probably completed the story line after about 60 hours of gameplay.  I honestly think, and wish, that it had been drug out a bit more.  At the beginning, you focus on your world seeds, but after a few days of that, the quests shift you to more focus on the town and finding the song fragments.  I would have preferred that the game threw in some world seed quests along the way because that becomes more of a "I have extra time in the day" type of task.  I also wish I had held off on completing the story line due to the fact that I hadn't really explored much of the various types of world seeds/biomes the game has to offer.The world seed part of the game has truly had a lot of thought put into it, which is why I wish the quests pushed you to diversify and explore your worlds more.  You can create two world seeds using the same types and amounts of essences and they will look different from each other.  And depending on what type of essences you combine, you will see various qualities from different biomes.  While many would consider this to be more of a "grind" type of task, I don't find myself really getting sick of completing my world seeds.  It's more cathartic and relaxing for me.  So much so, that I have continued playing with the world seeds after completing the story line.  I have a solid 90 hours in this game and I will absolutely come back to play more.I do have a few gripes about this game.  There is no mini map; you are left to try and look closely at the image from your mount in the sky or use build mode to try and figure out what areas you've explored or find things you're trying to return to.  Because there is so much to explore here, it was difficult to figure out where I had been before and where I needed to look around more.  And the other big thing is that some of the achievements are bugged and cannot be completed.  There are 2 achievements in Book that I am unable to officially complete even though I have completed them.  In the world seeds, there are some discoveries that are also bugged.  Specifically, I know that some of the puzzles will not show up as completed when looking at the world progress.  I have also found to possibly have issues with the fruit and insects, but cannot confirm whether that is definitely the case.  I have chopped down every single tree in a world several times or spent days catching insects to try and find the one I am missing, but can't seem to find them.  As a completionist, this is mildly annoying.All in all, I think this is a fantastic game.  Well worth the full price, and most definitely worth a pick up on sale.  I've already purchased their other game, Yonder, and look forward to starting that one soon.

_childDocuments_.review: Wish i could give this a neutral review because its not bad, but not really fun either. Its one of those games that has a very cool idea and some fun, casual gameplay with some mild platforming and puzzle elements, but it lacks in execution.Simply said: it is shallow, simple and bland, many gameplay elements lack depth.Like you can build "worlds" that once there are stationary resource mines that you visit now and then to gain the resources.But resources.. dont do much. You sometimes find materials like wood stoon iron, copper that say they are used for things... but all they do is yield  "elements" that are the actual resources. It is extremely easy to have immense surpluses to the point of making the resources mechanic almost obsolete as soon as you have played 6 hours.You build "towns" that only serve to get unlocks through population and happiness. (the unlocks being next town districts, which act as totally separate towns)  Building a flour mill does nothing except make the miller happy to count towards the happiness. the cafe the same. No one goes there except the barista. The bakery just has the employee and no one ever buys a pie, and the baker doesnt use flower from the mill.All the town expansion does is driving back a dark force called "the withering"This is a nice colorful, casual game that has lots to do but nothing that really matters much. After building a few worlds and expanding the first town, you have enough to never bother with all that and build all the towns. until the end.After 22 hours in i  am kinda bored and just play it off and on to maybe one day see what happens if you end the withering. Its basically like a simple mobile game.If you do get it, get it on a heavy sale. Not worth more than 10 bucks. At a low price it can be a thumbs up if what i described is your thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: Grow is a surprisingly enjoyable game for what it offers.I'm reminded a little of Animal Crossing mixed with the exploration aspects of Zelda. There's small-town building and resident management, but also a large world to explore with various platformer puzzles waiting to be discovered.The alchemy and world seed generation system are interesting in that each "world" you create has elements of randomness, so you're never entirely sure what to expect as each world develops. Some have caves, some have small puzzles, some have unique assets.After 25 hours of gameplay, however, things begin to feel a bit tedious and shallow.After the first few seeded worlds, growing and tending to new ones begins to lose its charm. By that point, I was really just growing them to have something to do beyond town maintenance.The towns are quaint, and I enjoyed developing the first two or three, but beyond that they start to feel shallow and pointless. You stop really caring about making it "your town," and it's really just a waiting game to collect enough residents to fill the meter required to move on to the next area.The residents themselves are basically soulless mannequins. Talking to them is pointless, and none of them feel unique. Even the story-driven characters other than Book and Coppertop are just wildly uninteresting.Asthetically the game is pleasant, but the "cutesy" theme and clothing feel like they cater to a very narrow audience. I felt no inspiration to alter anything about my residents or my own looks. Some of the items are quirky and fun, but everything feels so similar that nothing feels truly special. Even the towns get stale because there's nothing unique about them.In some games, moving to a new area creates a sense of wonder that make you want to stop and drink the new atmosphere in.That is not this game.Once you've seen some of the world, you've pretty much seen all of the world. Once you've seen some of the items, you've seen pretty much all of the items. Same for residents, towns, puzzles, critters, etc.Ultimately, Grow is an enjoyable, relaxing game. The first dozen hours are easy to blow through, but I think what's really lacking here that could have taken it to the next level is more depth and variety. Still, it's worth checking out if the premise sounds appealing to you. I didn't finish disappointed, just a little burnt out from how "samey" everything is.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game because of Yonder (which I played because of Eastshade). Grow is similar to Yonder with mechanics but very different in story--there are quests but also a whole lot of building (towns, new worlds) and thus a lot of farming and maintenance. This type of stuff is new to me but I am able to figure it out as I go along. I am enjoying this game a lot for passing time!
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really sweet, well-paced, creative story/farm sim/world spawner game that I've genuinely enjoyed playing. I just finished up the achievements and all 6 perfect worlds after about 35 hours of gameplay and I have to say that it was definitely time well spent. I'm looking forward to more additions to the game in the future and more from this development team overall. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Grow: Song of the Evertree

_childDocuments_.review: The concept is the only redeemable quality of this game, and it is what got me to buy it. In reality it looks and plays like one of those mobile games you get bombarded with advertisements for.The graphics in game are terrible, and for $40.00 AUD I feel robbed despite getting my money back.Do yourself a favour and get Palworld or ZELDA Breath of the Wild. name: Viewfinder
detailed_description: Challenge perception, redefine reality, and reshape the world around you with an instant camera. Viewfinder is a new single player game offering gamers hours of interesting and fun experiences while uncovering the mysteries left behind. Viewfinder is a mind-bending first person adventure game in which you can bring pictures to life by placing them into the world. Reshape Reality: Beyond photographs, bring paintings, sketches, screenshots and postcards to life while reshaping the world Exploration is learning: You will learn the secrets of the world, the reason why it exists, and the freedom to create. Explore multiple hub worlds that are all cohesive and encompass similar, but complex, differences Experience as much as you want: Viewfinder’s narrative is player driven and will be an approachable experience to someone who just wants to play and solve puzzles, and a rich well thought off world to a player who wants to learn more Find the answer to the impossible, once you step in the world of Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Overall up until the final chapter it was a wonderful game.  However on the last chapter it sort of fell apart, and had to resort to a walk through a number of times.   The last timed mission, even following the walk-through and a finding a short cut, has been impossible to complete after numerous attempts.  Which basically ruined the experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Superliminal, play this. If you like exploring a game's systems to your heart's content, play this game. If you're on the fence but enjoy a rewarding puzzle game experience, play. this. game. It has 40+ achievements and for 75% of them, you're gonna unlock them just by exploring the dynamics of the systems. Yes, the dialogue at the beginning is kind of annoying, but the game knows that as well and makes a point to make it optional after you understand the basic story goals. Also, there's an adorable digital cat. PLAY THE GAME AHHHH-
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very good game with interesting puzzles. If you like Portal, this feels like a very chill, distant relative of those games. The story was nothing mind-blowing but I liked the vibe and how everything resolved. The unique mechanic of using photos to place objects within a 3D space is super cool :)
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: The closest comparison is probably Superliminal.  Clever visual puzzles with a few unique ideas, colorful scenery.  Not too short, not too long.  The story is there to tie the puzzles together, and it at least seemed like it was trying to say something meaningful, even if it may have tripped over its own feet here and there.  In all, worth a playthrough for folks who like chill puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a game with an interesting gameplay idea that is unfortunately not fully utilised.The puzzles are not very challenging and some of the mechanics are very underused and not utilised to their full potential (like the portals or the photocopier). The story is told mainly through voice messages, which I didn't want to listen to all of, but the little I did catch wasn't anything outstanding either.Overall, with a playtime of about 5 hours I can't recommend the game even on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Actually a really great game. Up there with the puzzle greats like Portal and Return of the Obra Dinn. I'll start of with the complaints. The puzzles could be a bit more difficult and the characters are annoying. Now the positives. Pretty nice to look at visuals, and some customization to them as well with the camera filters. The main thing are the puzzles obviously, and they're pretty great. Many very cool mechanics and the game switches to new ones before anything gets stale. The game doesn't overstay its welcome and is fun all the way through.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: A nice experience with good looking and clean graphics, a very chill mood, and an interesting concept. However, for a puzzle game, the riddles are very easy and not challenging at all. On top of that, the game takes only between 2 and 3 hours to complete. For these reasons, I think the asking price is too high for what is offered by the game.It's not really a thumb down, nor a thumb up, but an in-between.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very Q&D review of VIEWFINDER, too early in my experience to accurately do the game justice.But I do wish to reveal that one of my favorite words in the English language is a word that is so rarely used these days that  almost my entire purpose in writing this too simple, too brief review too soon is because I may never have greater justification to us this beloved word.VIEWFINDER (at least so far) is not about painful frustration or mind-melting, ego-crushing obtuseness, as are many puzzle games. It's simply very, very "clever".Thank you until perhaps later (should my mind become too melty to write properly.)
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: For the asking price, you could have a handful of Puzzle games with far more material than 4 hours, or a single puzzle game with far more difficult and satisfying puzzles. Aside from the price issue, the game is good. Short, yet effective. It employs a large number of extremely well-crafted perspective puzzles in which you use your placement and understanding of the mechanics to figure out the solution, but even then it still feels like something is missing. While the puzzles were good, they definitely were not difficult. Personally, I would wait until it was on sale. The story feels rushed and confusing, while having positive reinforcement and a kitty pal to pet and engage with was wonderful, it simply felt like a minor distraction from the main thing. The lack of game play for the asking price. This is more or less a 10-12 dollar game. It's good, but it could have definitely been longer.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: WOW! This is the medium of video games at its most creative. This sort of experience can only happen in this art form. Beautifully crafted, visually amazing, all the different art styles blend to create a world i have never experienced before. The soundtrack cranked just as hard to deliver an ambience i will have added to my personal playlists. Great sound design especially when entering different art styles. All the details around the map had me stopping and admiring for a little too long (the 3D art for the food a major standout). A nice little story added in with some pretty good VO. This game loves you and leaves you a little too quickly... i wanted more. PLAY THIS GAME.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Pity! Just another one of those games with an intruiging concept, but utterly boring execution.I got somewhat excited when I encountered the glitch, as it eluded to a much greater world to be discovered and explored later on in the game, but that was just an empty promise.Also way too overpriced for what it acutally is: A tech-demo with litlle story, less world building and no interesting characters. One audio log is literally someone complaining about having a cookie stolen. You can't emphazise with the characters, as there are none to speak of, neither are stakes present or introduced in a way, you can relate to. The world seems vast and empty, BUT YOU CAN SIT EVERYWHERE and admire the emptiness.But the worst offender for me is the mutilated game mechanic, which did promise endless possibilities but you are restricted to one and only one solution for each and every puzzle, because reasons.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: While the photo mechanic is cool, the game as a whole is painfully easy. Each level lacks any level of complexity and most can be completed with just a cursory glance. A small consolation to anything though is that all of the interactions with Jessie are optional though the telephone booth after the first couple levels. I probably wouldn't have been able to continue if they weren't.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Portal, you'll probably enjoy this. The puzzle design and humor is similar. I appreciate that the game shows you mercy with its final challenges. I played the Portal games when I was new to gaming and never finished them simply because their final boss fights were such a difficulty spike. While Viewfinder does have a difficulty spike in its final sequence, it gives you the option to make it easier for yourself after you've failed a few times. I also appreciate that getting 100% of the achievements is very doable.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: It's an interesting mechanic, a bit like Superluminal, but pushed one step further: you're given a camera that can take pictures, but then you can project those pictures into the world. The effect, when you take a step to the side and what looked like a flat photo resolves into a three-dimensional scene, is very cool.There's a supporting story: that you're in a VR simulation, solving puzzles to... somehow figure out how to solve climate change... or something? It's not clear, and to be honest, I stopped paying attention to the many audio logs lying around, because the people in them just seemed interested in telling each other how smart they are.On top of that, the puzzles start feeling repetitive after a while, and I can't help feeling that they didn't do everything with the game mechanic that they could have. There are a few ancillary mechanics that are tried out briefly, then abandoned, again without exploring them fully. And I'm one of those people who prefer thinky puzzles over twitchy, so the final timed puzzle really rubbed me the wrong way.Final verdict? I didn't think it worked, but if you can pick it up on sale and do your best to ignore the companion cat and the audio logs and just focus on the puzzles? There's a good amount of fun to be had.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Wow just wow. Truly a unique experience and just huge props to the development team for pulling this off. I don't even want to know what kind of coding this required. The visuals are stunning and the art style is pleasurable to the eye. Probably one of the most challenging puzzle games I have played. There are many levels I just sat there and had to think many times over what could I possibly be missing. And there was no better satisfaction after finally putting the pieces together and passing the level. Makes you feel really dumb looking back after you've solve it. The story isn't the most engaging but its cute and wholesome and I believe you aren't really buying puzzle games for the story. Still a good story but just saying it's not anything crazy. Was excited every time I found the cat and got to pet him. I believe this is a must have for all puzzle enthusiasts and it should be appreciated for how truly creative some people are. I had a blast playing this and if they release more levels I will be glad to play more. Might even have to come back and just start from the beginning.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a artsy puzzle game strung along with a narrative. Each of these three components get in the way of each other in Viewfinder. The puzzles are very simple, and two, maybe three are at all challenging.The art is either repetitive, or an easter egg. The narrative is frustrating, with condescending dialogue, and all too easy to have multiple voice lines playing at once.Want to enjoy the puzzles? There's a hamfisted story trying to happen that ends up distracting rather than adding to the puzzles, all while staring at the same beige building material most of the game.Want to enjoy the art? You'll have to go out of your way to be not doing the puzzles, and wait for any story beats to be finished.Want to enjoy the story? Its drip-fed through the levels, making you only slowly get an idea for any of the characters. As soon as you feel like you're getting to know them, perhaps, you're yanked along to the next world!This game has so much that it could offer. The easter eggs of art have some genuinely amazing ideas, and as an experience piece, the photographs could have been phenomenal. The puzzles could have been enjoyable, had the game not try to dress them up with a hamfisted narrative, shallow characters, and saccharine cutesyness. The narrative... well, the less said the better.This is a game of disappointment and lost potential. It isn't offensive, but it is very dissatisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: The writing is infantile, the dialog is tedious, the plot is boring. The single good thing this game has going for it is the (very fun and interesting) main gameplay mechanic - BUT, every level is short and boring, none of the levels offer any challenge, and there isn't much to the game. It's a big let down. The only way I could consider recommending this game is if they dropped any semblance of a story and added like 100 gameplay focused levels in a free update (if they added workshop support somehow, this would be an easy recommend).
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Very boring. The puzzles are simple and repetitive, and you have to solve them on your quest to find a machine which will save the ... zzzz. Sorry, I fell asleep. _childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: As primarily a puzzle game, I think talking about the puzzles first is probably the most important. Overall, they were pretty good! It introduced new concepts with each hub world, and had fun twists on those ideas as those levels progressed.(Un?) Fortunately, none of the puzzles 'felt' particularly difficult. Most of the time, the solution was pretty clear within the first few seconds of arriving in a new level, and when that wasn't the case it was only because you couldn't see around an obstacle.Story was kind of mediocre if only because the topic has been covered ad nauseum; and it didn't really provide anything new to the subject. The cat was cute though.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a puzzle game where you place pictures or paintings in the world around you, which then become interactable and traversable. Later on, you even find a camera with limited film that you can use to take pictures and then place them. The mechanic is extremely cool and actually left me a bit dumbfounded the first few times.I don't think Viewfinder is a bad puzzle game by any means, but I do think it falls victim to it's own mechanic to the point where it almost feels like the game can't ever be anything but simple. The game only has very few mechanics overall, most of them very easy, and with only about 6 hours there also isn't too much of it. There are only two or three levels that stumped me a bit and where you have to think in a slightly different direction, but otherwise the game never steps out of it's comfort zone, which is a bit sad. With a mechanic this impressively cool, I wish there would've been a bit more to it, more ways to interact with the pictures, more layers of puzzling, but most of the puzzles are simple to the point where you could almost rush through the levels if there weren't a few collectibles and bits of audio logs scattered everywhere.Speaking of the narrative, I think Viewfinder is a good example of why a narrative in a puzzle game like this is heavily hit or miss, and more of a miss in this case. The story is easy to follow and not *bad* at it's core, but it also seems a bit shoehorned in. This game did not need a story, but it has it and you will either love or hate that, with no inbetween. The voice acting is serviceable aside from some lines and the soundtrack is chill, so no complaints here. Some commenters have called the game a glorified tech demo, and while I wouldn't quite go that far, I do think it feels like a demo of something that should be bigger, more fleshed out and, above all, more challenging. I do hope another game picks up this mechanic, or something like it, and does a bit more with it. For 6 hours, the game is also a bit expensive. Still, I did really like the puzzle mechanic and it's not a bad puzzler overall, so if you can get Viewfinder for at least 50 % off, I would definitely recommend checking it out, keeping in mind some of the limitations.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Every now and then, an indie game emerges that leaves you speechless. Viewfinder, a puzzle platformer from Sad Owl Studios, is that game for me this summer. This charming game includes puzzles unlike anything I've ever seen before, playing with perspective in extremely baffling and mind-boggling ways, all while remaining simple and incredibly easy to understand. It's a difficult balance to achieve, but now that Viewfinder is available, I can promise you that it mostly works out.The plan is to enter a weird simulation built by a group of geniuses in search of answers and technology that can aid in the salvation of the real world. Granted, the plot isn't really interesting or vital to the Viewfinder experience, and to be honest, it's only servicable. There are audio files, post-it notes, and other environmental aspects, for example, that play back portions of the story and paint a picture of who these "geniuses" were and what transpired to cause them to grow apart. But the plot never gets in the way or makes you stop and think about what's going on. No, you come to Viewfinder for the gameplay experience.Your adventure through the artificial world will be aided by a companion who communicates with you via phone booths. You'll also encounter a cat-shaped AI that will accompany you around the world, and yes, you may pet it. Despite the importance of the subject matter, all three narrative levels, whether from the outside, the inside, or the past, have shockingly little to say. This is a squandered chance that feels fabricated. The creators sought to include pop culture allusions, discuss a contemporary problem, and highlight human connections. In the end, none of this was successful. If the developers had focused on just one area, they could have developed the story far more coherently.The miraculous Polaroid camera, which you'll discover early in the game, is your most significant tool. There are always images, drawings, and even video game graphics concealed among the stages. Most puzzles require you to use the images to solve them. Sometimes, however, they are simply amusing gags that will make you laugh. In one location, for example, you'll discover a picture of Super Mario World that you can explore. Are you often envious when friends send you letters from their trip because you wish you could be there as well? You can just dash into vacation here! There are numerous small gags throughout the game's early stages. Later on, the frequency drops, which is unfortunate because this is when you might have truly let loose artistically and possibly even incorporated mini-games.Viewfinder occasionally intersperses cut-up panels, in front of which you must stand at the correct angle to piece the scene together. Alternatively, you can access the next part by flipping three switches. You'll find a couple levels later in the game where you'll have to sprint through filter portals to remove obstructions and make bridges appear. However, this simply serves to lighten things up because most of the time you'll be clicking images and repositioning them to get to the exit. For the most part, you'll have to flip switches or carry batteries around to duplicate level portals. You do this on the fly with a portable camera and stationary picture stations that provide perspective. In general, Viewfinder increases difficulty by taking things away from you rather than offering new features as the game goes. For example, you can no longer photograph blue structures and objects, drastically limiting your approaches to the goal and frequently resulting in only one answer.Overall you'll be busy for five to six hours if you listen to every audio sample and play every extra task. You'll go through considerably faster if you ignore the talk. The missions are organized into four hub planets that you can visit between levels. They are themed to correspond with the appropriate world builder. In the artist's realm, you'll go through a luxury mansion looking for artist's supplies such as brushes and easels. The gardener's part is all about nature, whereas the engineer's center level is all about machines. The levels are designed differently by each creator, however the hub worlds are just plastered with assets in many areas. The sad part though: you have almost no interaction with any of them. Only collectibles and a few items that are always required to solve a puzzle can be obtained.The game was flawlessly programmed throughout the game. While hardly groundbreaking, the graphics are functional and attractive in many places. Viewfinder is a fantastic indie game, although the plot is a little disjointed. The core puzzle notion is clever and does not tire over the brief gameplay. However, solution approaches are sometimes repeated, which takes some of the joy out of the challenge, and there have been occasional problems that have rendered a puzzle impossible unless I exit and re-enter the level. In the lead-up, the game was frequently compared to Portal, and the gameplay is somewhat similar to Valve's puzzle hit. I personally hope that Viewfinder will follow in the footsteps of Portal and follow up a brief but enjoyable first installment with a truly fantastic sequel that has the potential to alter the field of puzzle games.Gameplay and the delight of discovery clearly take precedence, the first-person puzzle game continues to reinvent itself, astounding with fresh views, concepts, and styles. Although there is a general lack of challenge, completing each puzzle is satisfying because the next puzzle delight with a new concept is already waiting for me around the next corner and sometimes actually flips what I have experienced thus far. In the end, Viewfinder could have done a few things better: a few more stylistic gimmicks, a little more challenge, and a  l̶̶o̶̶t̶  little more depth to the plot. Don't be deceived by the successful but still generic visuals: Viewfinder is a one-of-a-kind gaming experience, and despite its flaws: it was great!

_childDocuments_.review: Poor writing, paper-thin foreshadowing, 5~6hrs gameplay.I was only surprised twice while playing this game, once when I thought the paper-thin foreshadowing was not the most obvious thing in the world (it was, I was just wrong to expect more) & I didn't relies the implications of selfies to the story until the end. . . Which is hilarious because I was still easily able to guess where the ending was heading regardless, predictable.After beating the game you'll be well over 50% in achievements, I suspect an additional +2~4hrs will be required to 100% this game. Luckily I bought this on sale, but at $20, and being very charitable (something which, btw, this gameplay is NOT) you're paying $2.00 or $1.50 per hour of total (re)playability. If you solo the story, without any of the optional challenges, then you'll likely be done well within' 4hrs.The ending was meh, I just felt kind of empty the whole way through. It's hard to content to these characters as written, though it's hard to connect with anything these days. Don't spend double on this $10.00 game, wait until it's on sale with a heavy discount.Very chill experience, interesting mechanics, inspired design, borderline walking simulator: 333/666 final score.To Dev:I just wanted a strong antagonist, but all I got was this sad narrator. Call back the voice actor, have him do additional lines either encouraging or discouraging the player during the very last level in the very final act. Antagonize me, depress me, DO SOMETHING! This character should not disappear during the start of the very last level, just to reappear right at the end (they have a personal stake in how it ends). A solid ending sends the player off with a good experience; you did not send me off with a good experience.I understand that the player will be moving throughout this level very quickly, but having multiple 2~4 word sentences at every other section would really go a long way. That's like 8~16 more words, like really, was it really THAT hard?

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: wait for a sale. I beat this in 3.5 hours and it felt hollow.Look, I get it, we all want a new Portal. I was really impressed by this game's demo when it released for a steam next fest or whatever, so I instantly bought it when it released. However, what I experienced was basically just superliminal with better visuals. To be fair, the core picture/camera mechanic is super cool. There's definitely an adjustment period of discovery where you amaze yourself with all the things you can do. However, each level is so small and self contained that the novelty quickly faded, and it just became a race to the finish. My favorite part of puzzle games is overcoming a particularly tricky challenge, and there just weren't any in this game. Each "world" introduced a new spin on the puzzles, which was useful to introduce some modicum of interest, but each new mechanic was left behind as quickly as it was introduced, leaving each "world" feeling progressively empty. The story is lackluster.Finally, the performance is not great. I have a brand new GPU (GForce 4070) and it was spiking the temperature something fierce. Granted, the visuals are nice, but there's not nearly so much detail that I would expect it to run hotter than God of War.

Soooo neat

_childDocuments_.review: Best puzzle game I've played since Portal. Story can get very vague sometimes unlike most other puzzle games, mainly it's because it's very cryptic or hard to follow, even sometimes out of the way of the player if they're not exploring. But if you're someone who doesn't care about the story at all, then this game is worth every penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say I was amazed by this game. It has a really unique concept where you are able to change the reality by taking photos of things you currently see in  front of you, take sketches, postcards and paintings that are currently in the world and you're able to use them to pass a level. Even though it doesn't last that long, It has very impressive graphics, fun puzzles to solve and it gets you hooked over time. The puzzles in general are not that hard to solve, they just require your imagination, you don't really have to follow the typical ways of solving puzzles; you can always be creative when solving one.  The only thing that really was out of the place is the narrative. I was very confused at the beginning why are there so many random people talking to me and why is this cat creature all over the place, but if you listen to the gramophones that are scattered around the levels, bit by bit you'll understand what is going on.I definitely recommend this game. You won't regret getting it.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: A great, and mostly-original take on the "perspective"-based puzzle genre.Pros:* Keeps the game fresh by using new mechanisms and old, in each successive world.* Chill-out music, except for the last (timed) challenge.* Fun NPC kitty* Each world has its own flavor - art, gamer/engineer, etc.* Optional collectibles are different in each world, which also keeps it fresh.Cons:* Game does a poor job of remembering where you were when you quit. It remembers levels you've solved, just not where you were standing in a hub - which can be confusing.Meh:* The game kinda telegraphed the ending - well, that or I've played too many games. :P* Some puzzles are timed, but for the most part you can entirely mitigate that by being clever.* The final, timed puzzle is... a pain.  Expect to fail it several times before you learn all the tricks to bypass its challenges.TL;DR: If you like puzzles, 8/10; else, skip.

_childDocuments_.review: The spectrum of quality in first-person puzzle games is broad. The universally praised classics like Portal are easy to recommend, but others require a lot more skill and, more importantly, patience. It’s also a huge benefit when they offer some unique design and mechanics that develop with the progression of the game. Few games can meet those standards, let alone surpass them, but Viewfinder is unquestionably one of those few.Abbreviated Review: Viewfinder drops you into its world immediately from the start of the game and doesn’t give you much explanation until you’re already waist-deep in the situation. It is a bit of an interesting reveal, so I won’t spoil it, but I will say that the fantastic world is not your reality. This dream-like world is full of worldly delights like fancy foods, grand views, and a somewhat ridiculous number of comfortable-looking places where you can sit down and chill. I didn’t spend a lot of my time doing that, but it was a nice touch to the overall aesthetic of the game. However, as appealing as it is, this environment is mostly there as a cosmetic backdrop for the actual mechanics of the game.The core mechanic is that you can take a photograph, hold it up in front of your view, and place it – manifesting a new reality in the environment. This is used in numerous ways that expand as you progress through the game. At first, you’ll use it as a basic way to create solid platforms and infrastructure to bridge gaps and get where you need to go. Each level has a teleporter that you must ultimately reach to teleport to the next level and the path is usually the challenge. You’ll initially collect photos that you find in the environment and use them in fairly intentionally designed ways. Additionally, some hand-drawn paintings and sketches similarly present an opportunity for you to dive into these uniquely crafted environments. Ultimately though, you’ll unlock a camera that allows you to snap a photo of any aspect of the environment and use it for a whole new way to solve puzzles.The addition of the camera adds a layer to the experience that makes it feel like you have a lot more control over how puzzles are solved. It’s hard to say if that dynamic nature is truly the case, but when you can take a photo of absolutely anything and recreate it in the environment, it at least seems like that freedom is there. It allows you to duplicate more than just glorified platforms though, you can also make a copy of the goal teleporter itself and potentially give yourself a path straight to the end – and occasionally that’s the intention. This allows for puzzles that seem challenging up front, but once you’ve gotten a good grasp on the mechanics, that challenge is met with a satisfying resolution.Part of the appeal of Viewfinder is that it also has a compelling story woven into the gameplay. The protagonist has an overarching goal and a mysterious third party reminding you of that through voiceover throughout the game, but you discover more within the world. There are recording devices throughout the levels that introduce characters and describe their interactions in this strange environment. Normally, this method of storytelling is easy to forget or ignore entirely, but with a solid performance and a laid-back ambiance, it was much easier to absorb. These recordings along with an odd talking cat that follows you through the levels come together to create a narrative that adds a lot of weight to the evolving landscape and how you interact with it.With the lavish furniture can lounge on, the relaxing views, and the various tools and canvases adorned in artistic endeavors, you can tell a lot about the people that were there before you. As you move into areas that have a more experimental feel to them and start to abandon the warmth of the Mediterranean architecture, it continues expressing the evolving perspective of your predecessors. Each of the five chapters has individual stylings for each to go along with the changes in the design of the puzzles and the ways you solve them with the new tools you’re given.The exploration of the story, environment, and the way the mechanics expand to keep the game so exciting, almost makes the relatively short run time feel even shorter. The five hours I spent in it flew by and, while they were entertaining, I only wanted more. The only aspect that seemed to be missing was more use of painted or drawn images and the unique options they presented. The addition of some of the ‘videogame’ photos was fun, but that too was a bit limited. For as thoroughly enjoyable as Viewfinder is, more of those elements would have only increased the fun. I was also a little thrown off by the collectible items in the game that I didn’t notice until I stumbled onto one halfway through the game. When there were so many random items scattered around, it wasn’t obvious I could pick any of them up. Yet, even with those barely-qualifying complaints, Viewfinder is an easy recommendation even with its somewhat inflated price. If you see it on sale, you officially have no excuse not to pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: A fine little puzzle game. Similar to Superliminal in it's use of perspective, but significantly easier in terms of difficulty. If The Witness is a college course, this is like elementary school.I do wish they had included some more difficult puzzles, or combined some of the mechanics in more interesting ways. I was able to solve basically every puzzle based on my first impression; none of them required much thought. This would be a great game for someone new to puzzle games, but for those with more experience you're likely to be wanting for some more engagement.Good amount of settings and accessibility options. The crosshair options were very welcome, as I'm someone who easily gets motion sick in games without static HUD elements. The game was clearly made with care and passion.That being said, I think 25 dollars is a bit steep full price for a game I was able to get 100% on in less than 4 hours, but game developers are underpaid anyways so that's whatever I guess.I still had a good time with it though, and I do recommend it, even if the price and difficulty make that recommendation less wholehearted. I'll echo what another user said about this feeling like the first half of a great game. It doesn't make that experience any less enjoyable, but it is a little bit disappointing when you realize it's already over.

_childDocuments_.review: Innovative mechanics and a beautiful atmosphere make for a relaxing and rewarding experience. A must play for fans of puzzle games, but I would recommend it to anyone looking for something with a slower pace.You will jump into short puzzle segments from a hub world, using changes in perspective to alter the map in real-time. You manage this by using pictures from your camera, but also paintings, postcards, etc. It's impressive to see the game engine working – pictures can be placed anywhere, altering the map instantly. I never got tired of seeing the environment manipulated in real-time. There are other puzzle mechanics revealed as time goes on, so there is always a sense of progression, and the puzzles stay fresh.The real MVP in terms of mechanics is the rewind feature, without which the game would quickly become tedious and frustrating. Since you can alter the environment however you choose, sometimes you will place a makeshift bridge incorrectly, fall off the map, or destroy a needed item. Fortunately, a quick tap of the rewind button will take you back to exactly where you need to go. It allows for experimentation, making sure you are never “punished” for a mistake – just go back and try again. Combine these gameplay mechanics with a vibrant aesthetic, and music that would fit nicely in a yoga retreat, and you end up with a very comfy game to play. The story, as described by the developer, is almost entirely optional – a wise choice, as those not overly interested might feel bogged down reading notes and listening to voice recordings. For those interested in the narrative, you are searching for a way to save the planet from climate change, entering the world of researchers who were developing a weather altering machine. The story is pretty minimalistic, but gives context to the events regardless; enthusiastic voice acting gives a lot of weight to the scenario.Perhaps my favourite element are the easter eggs – a big thumbs up from me, no matter what the game is. There are hidden collectibles, lots of achievements, and creative distractions that make great use of the game world  - for example, placing a painting and then being able to enter the painting (sometimes to find a hidden collectible). Perhaps my favourite was  It seems clear to me that the developers (as well as the voice actors) had a lot of fun making Viewfinder, and thus makes the game that much more enjoyable to play.My only real complaint with the game comes from the very end.  This by no means ruined the game for me, but it was a little disappointing.I’m glad I stumbled on this one, and I wholeheartedly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really well done. Its central concept--placing pictures to change the world to solve puzzles and open up new avenues of exploration--is one I haven't seen before, and many of the puzzles are quite cleverly executed. The puzzles themselves aren't particularly challenging, but the introduction of new mechanics along with way keeps the gameplay fresh and interesting, and figuring out a particularly unique solution to a puzzle was a really satisfying experience. And unlike other puzzle games like The Witness and Baba Is You, Viewfinder has a complete story and a tangible objective you're working toward beyond the puzzles themselves. That, along with fully developed characters that I felt myself really connecting with by the end, made for a truly immersive experience.My one complaint is that the game isn't particularly long (I finished everything in a bit over 4 hours, aside from the optional collectibles and out of the way achievements), and I would have liked to spend more time with additional puzzles, but the overall experience of the game is one that is going to stick with me for a while, so the pricetag, while a little steep for the amount of gameplay, was totally worth it to me.

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare to find a game with a concept as ambitious and mindbending as the one offered by , especially with how well it proceeds to stick the landing. Set in a lovely soothing environment, the player traverses a few hubs each with a series of puzzles to solve. Travelling with you is the talking cat CAIT, offering words of encouragement as he watches you get to work.In the game's logic, reality can be captured within an image, and released from the player's perspective. The exact rules shift from level to level, each offering its own challenge and limitations keeping the concept fresh throughout the journey.It can't be overstated how polished everything feels, with nothing feeling out of place or being padded. This does mean that the game can be finished rather fast, my personal playthrough lasting just shy of 5 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of great puzzle games start with one core mechanic that they then explore and build around, and Viewfinder is definitely that type of puzzle game. The main gimmick is that you can project images onto the world in front of you, and it's a really neat idea to build a puzzle game around The game is great and definitely worth playing, but it does struggle to challenge you or find ways to build upon its fundamental mechanic. There are 3 major things that they pile on: Timed photographs that give you time to walk in front of a camera, special materials that don't get captured in images and don't get destroyed when projected onto, and a camera that destroys what it captures. These are all cool ideas, but I came out of this game feeling like I was never really challenged and that the puzzles had too much overlap. A good puzzle game will have a progression where levels will ramp up in difficulty, so completing each puzzle prepares you for the challenge of the next one, until you're naturally using all the tools they give you together to solve otherwise complex levels. You just don't get that in this game. At one point they introduce portals, but those only stick around for a few levels and then get forgotten. Same thing happens with the weight scale, which is used in only one level. Neither even shows up in the final level, which is a timed medley of shorter puzzles.I think part of the reason why the lack of challenge doesn't ruin this game is because the game establishes a pretty chill tone from the beginning with an ambient soundtrack. The characters are all cheery and the story has an air of hope and optimism. It gives me the sense that it's trying to be an easier game. The story didn't really do anything for me, and the ending makes zero sense, but I didn't really mind that the story sucked since I thought the levels were fun enough

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. The core puzzle mechanic is amazing. But the game never really explores or grows into it. It just meanders around the same basic ideas. Puzzle solving also lacked creative freedom. The solutions were often far simpler than I expected, and it felt like the real limitation was the dev's creativity, and not my own.What prompted my return was when I encountered a level that relied entirely on misdirection rather than using the core gameplay mechanic to solve the puzzle. After wandering around for 30 min, I finally opened a guide, only to find that the level (as design) softlocks without telling you. Was this just the devs way of forcing me over the 2hr mark?The story, narration, writing are very generic, and I would have preferred the game be entirely in silence. In a first person puzzle game like this the story must align with the puzzle mechanics, like Superliminal or Portal. This plot would be just as at home in an Adventure or FPS game.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool and creative puzzle game. Not too long, not too short contrary to what some people might say. Plenty of interesting ideas in here, increasing in complexity as the game progresses. They really leave no stone unturned. Story revolves around exploring the endeavors of a bunch of scientists who were trying to save the planet from a climate disaster but it's told through short audio logs found throughout the levels, etc. Not very interesting but it serves the purpose of driving the game forward and providing the player with a purpose and a goal. Music is pleasant and the graphics are nice but may cause motion sickness because you're playing around with perspective. Mess around with the FOV, aliasing, and look sensitivity to find the sweet spot.

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a First-Person, Surreal, Puzzle Platfromer made by the Scottish game studio  and published by . The main idea behind Viewfinder's puzzles is the ability to place pictures to bring them to life and I have no idea how it is even possible to code a new, newer before seen idea like that. But aside from a development perspective, the mechanic itself is also brilliant as a puzzle tool. You could watch several playthroughs and almost every time someone would use a different way throughout the process to solution most of the time ending in the same solution which, even though may sound not that impressive, is another achievement this unique mechanic grants this game, though Viewfinder's great level designs also help it achieve this greatly aswell. I even found myself thinking I have cheesed the puzzle somehow while getting to it's ending from time to time. Viewfinder also boosts it's great game and level design by adding new mechanics and obstacles as you progress through the main story and implements them greatly. To expand this implementation, when they add a new mechanic, let's say cutting pictures (Doesn't exist in the game so no spoilers). When they add this mechanic, they first put a really easy room that only requires that you use this new feature once so you can learn how it works and what it does. Then, from there, they start to get both harder and start to also require the use of other features. Now comes my only big" problem with Viewfinder, which could be seen as a positive as well. The game is way too easy and seeing such good and unique mechanics not reaching their full potential is really sad. I think the developers tried to go for the "casual" player base because there was only two or three levels that I could call challenging and I'm someone who rarely plays Puzzle games. It could have been so much fun if they added even only two more level per mechanic, forcing us to use everything to it's maximum potential and stretching the games limits. Though as I said, this could be seen as a good thing as it makes the game way more accessible to people who doesn't like puzzle games that much or just wants to relax while playing. Viewfinder's story is actually good in my opinion. I've mostly seen either people not liking it or just saying it's fine but I think the characters, with the exception of Jessie, are well written for how long they have  a screen time with all having different and sadly shallow characters with aspirations, goals and worldviews. The plot of the game though, is just, there? I guess... Sadly, I don't have anything to say except these as I've said the characters though good are shallow and the events of the game are just there to give a reason for all these puzzles you're doing. Oh, one more thing, I really loved CAIT, by far the best character in the game and I probably wouldn't find it that good without him. Yes, but while it's on a sale. Viewfinder is a cozy and beautiful game with though easy, fun challenges and great puzzle mechanics but it's price is way too high for a maximum eight hour, puzzle game.

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a first person puzzle game, a work of art and pure genius. It is unlike me to reveal my hands so early into my blabbering reviews, but if you’re reading this review, there is a chance you’ve seen the accolades this game has received, as listed on its Steam page. This particular, independently-made lightning in a bottle was captured by  a games studio based out of Scottland, and published by the well-known and profoundly impactful Thunderful Publishing, known chiefly for their SteamWorld universe of games. Viewfinder is even more impressive when you realize that it appears to be the development team’s creative debut.You are an unnamed, mute protagonist, who is part of an effort to rescue the Earth from the death throes of global climate calamity. In this pursuit you have decided to delve deep into a simulated reality created by an illustrious group of artistic and scientific geniuses who tried, all in their own way, to find a solution to the climate change problem by simulating ecosystems and possible solutions in this high efficiency play-space.The experience is divided into 5 hub worlds or chapters, all of which will take you through the work, process and mind of the scientists and artists who made up this tight knit team of eccentrics. The game facilitates its storytelling through Jesse, the woman who monitors your real world vital signs, CAIT, a cat AI once created by the team of now strangely absent tinkers and the various logograms (a neologism for this game’s gramophone-shaped audio logs) which will give you fragmented glimpses into the daily proceedings of the creatives’ lives.Slowly the mystery of what happened to this place and the previous inhabitant’s findings will be revealed to you as you make your way through their puzzles and later the corrupted, discarded recesses of their labor.Viewfinder will have you enthralled with its stunning, often interactive visual design, its unbelievable mechanical brilliance and simplicity, as well as its ability to tell its character’s stories through all of gaming’s modern tricks: audio logs, a guiding voice and environmental storytelling (my personal favorite). Despite you never even catching a glimpse of anyone but the cat-like AI, other than two, highly stylized/blurry portraits of one of the scientists of the team and despite only being privy to fragments of disparate conversations and moments shared among them, at the end of it all, if you have any modicum of empathy, you will leave Viewfinder’s 4-6 hour experience, feeling as if you just spent an evening as a part of a troubled group of old friends.It is thus, perhaps, no wonder that the fragmentary nature of its narrative and world carries over to its main mechanics of reality manipulation through the placement of images, photographs, paintings, drawings, sketches and more. The game takes a paper plane designed to fly no more than a few meters and ingeniously propels it on the world’s strongest ventilator into outer space. I cannot understate how many times Viewfinder made me smile or go “wow!” out loud. You will transgessively slice and dice through the terrain, turning the untouched serenity of Viewfinder’s bizarre island structures into gaudy, unshapely canvases for your mad dash towards the goal of saving the real world… or maybe you’ll stop and smell the flowers on your way, mayhap try out the various camera filters and do your best to find all optional collectibles and lore? Either way, the game will make you think about your approach in the end, as the increasingly melancholic selection of songs from the game’s brilliant soundtrack by Aether, will lull you into the continuously regressive dream you fear waking up from and equally shiver at the thought you need to wade further. These jazzy accouterments are sure to stick with you for a good while after the credits roll and the proverbial curtain falls on your time with Viewfinder.I cannot say anything else, for fear of revealing too much, but I guarantee that if you like puzzle games with open-ended solutions, art and experimentation, you will leave deeply satisfied with Viewfinder, even at full price. It is a short, but intimate and one-of-a-kind experience and deserves all of the praise in this world.

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenally innovative gameplay. The absurd perspective projection mechanic is wild so see in action but instantly intuitive in practice. If you love the puzzle aspect of Portal, play this game! If you love the worldbuilding and characters of Portal, then Viewfinder will likely disappoint on those fronts. I won't go into detail for the purposes of spoilers, but the entire meta-narrative is so divorced from the gameplay that it feels like we are discovering audio tapes left by characters from another, much less interesting game. The most charismatic character in the story is an inanimate roomba. Despite my gripes, I will still emphatically recommend this one as a boldly unique and smartly executed puzzle game, and I would buy a sequel or DLC level pack the day it releases.

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzle concepts were pretty innovative and honestly mind-blowingly cool. I would love to see them explored further, as the game does have this sense - which a lot of modern games evoke - that it must constantly be rushing from one idea to another to constantly please the player. Not a dig on this game in particular, but please, video game people, slow down a bit! We the players (or at least me, I guess I shouldn't speak for anyone else here lol) are happy to slow down and smell the flowers when the flowers smell so freaking cool!All that said, I will say there were a couple things that bothered me. The primary one was the final level was this time attack that was just absurdly short, asking me to solve 9 nontrivial puzzles in 5 minutes - which, as I write it, doesn't sound like a lot, but in-game it was an honest-to-god nightmare. It was just a badly-conceived level in my opinion that honestly really ate at my feeling of reward for completing the game. Granted, my personal opinion is that time trial levels have no place in gaming at all, so I could very well be alone in this, but it was jarring going from so many wonderful puzzle levels into this ridiculous challenge where solutions to each of the 9 puzzles were sometimes hidden in ridiculous places. At the very least, rewinding time probably should have rewound the clock - at least then the player could have some semblance of breathing room.The more minor bother started with a bug where the battery in chapter 4 level 6 stage 3 would not show up in the camera even when rewinding to the start of the level and executing the level properly; that was fixed by restarting the level and executing it properly, so that's just a bug and not relevant to reviewing the game. That said, in my struggle, I consulted the pause-menu hint for this level; since I had a bug, it ended up being useless, but I also found it to be strangely cryptic. The hint I ended up consulting for the final level before finally slogging through it was also cryptic (and frankly confusing and unhelpful), so I wonder about the accessibility and general usefulness of those hints. Perhaps what I would say is, as an autistic person, when struggling through a puzzle, a hint that also presents itself as a puzzle is not helpful in the slightest but in fact is actively harmful to the player.Overall, I'd moderately recommend this game - I would like to see more of these puzzles, and I think the final level is a serious drawback, but there's nothing unforgivable in my qualms, especially when the puzzles themselves are so damn cool.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is alright. A lot of the dialogue is stiff, or just under-performed. The story is kinda generic and could have been presented in a lot of better ways. Jesse gets quite grating after a while as well. The puzzles are pretty good but not that intense. Even the optional levels are kinda easy. A lot of the mechanics don't stick around for very long, and each level is just teaching you a new mechanic.This was made with a lot of love, but for the price point it's not really worth it. buy the game when it's on sale for 5 dollars or so. Defo worth it then. CAIT's VA performed amazingly however. The emotion in his lines is palpable. Very good.

_childDocuments_.review: For the first half of the game, all of the dialog was just characters talking about how cool the technology was and complimenting each other and me for beating the puzzles. For the second half of the game, all of the dialog was just . There was no depth to the characters, beyond a few artificial internal conflicts, despite so much focus being placed on the writing. If you play this game, play with the voice acting volume set to 0 and subtitles off to hide the (in my opinion) poor writing. It doesn't relate to the gameplay. Just be sure to click a telephone if it rings, and then walk away. And don't use any of the gramophones.As for the gameplay, the puzzles were very uninteresting. It's like I was playing tutorial levels for the entire game, just waiting for the real puzzles to arrive. But the real puzzles never came. Only one or two puzzles provided any interesting challenge to me.  If you're looking for a chill game where it's very easy to go through all the puzzles, then this might be for you. But it's not for me.Sorry if this review was too harsh. In my opinion, it's a great premise but with poor execution. I think this puzzle mechanic could have been explored in much more interesting ways, but this game only feels like it touches the surface for me. The only thing I think the game did really well was the graphics and sound design. I also really like the exotic color choices in some of the areas.

_childDocuments_.review: During Steam Next Fest, I fell in love with the Viewfinder demo. Experiencing the tech, the art, and the puzzling potential all felt so fresh and limitless. I knew at that point it would be a Day 1 purchase for me.Booting up the full release gave me that same sense of joy and wonder of playing such a cool and unique experience, that clearly had a lot of passion to function so seamlessly. But after the first hour, a lot of the magic seemed to fade.It became very apparent that there were a lot of good ideas and tech, but not a lot of depth to the puzzles. It simply felt like I was just moving through a walking sim with some neat tricks and gimmicks. I kept waiting for the difficulty ramp up or something that required me to build upon the foundations I learned in previous areas, but it never got there. Outside a few of the optional puzzles in World 4 and and final level, I never really felt like I was playing a puzzle game, but rather the tutorial to one.I was hoping that the saving grace would be a deep connection to the story or an amazing OST, but neither are present in this entry. The story felt fake-deep to me and was told through audio logs forcing you to just wait around at the end of levels or trying to parse out lines overlapping with dialogue from Cait. _childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game with fantastic and fresh puzzle mechanic.  I get portal vibes from playing this game.
