_childDocuments_.review: I came in expecting an abstract puzzle game akin to Antichamber or Manifold Garden (both of which I love). Instead I was truly surprised to stumble upon something entirely unique. I am genuinely unsure if I have played anything quite so genre-breaking as Viewfinder. Puzzles are inherently an expression of logic but Sad Owl Studios has managed to make one in the expression of creativity.I rarely found there to be a "correct" answer in solving these puzzles. In fact, I first wondered if the solution I came up was what I was supposed to do. I've only now realized that it wasn't a question of what I was  to do but something I wanted to do. Whereas puzzles are about establishing boundaries and understanding how to operate within them. Viewfinder instead provides paint & a blank canvas.We're both told to paint a landscape. You choose the ocean & I the mountains. Neither is wrong, none better or worse than the other. Each painting a perfect representation of our individualism.I never imagined a puzzle game in which all of us are presented the same problem resulting in a variety of solutions all of which are "correct." And each particular method, the product of a singular mind, resulting in a finished puzzle? I can think of little as wondrous a sentiment of human creativity than that.There is more for me to play but Viewfinder has caught my attention already.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely wonderful game. I love the aesthetic, the calming music, the cat.The puzzles were simple and did not take much time to solve. The plot is simple but the main point of the game is the puzzles and its unique camera-bring-photos-to-existence and I liked it.The game tries to mix up things by limiting the feature and it sometimes works. But with a creative power/gimmick like this its a challenge to design puzzles around it and I think the devs tried their best.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 game3/10 dialogue10/10 feature to mute just the dialogueI got this game for a "The Witness"-type silent experience, where the only times I would want to hear dialogue would be when there are hidden words of wisdom scattered across the world.Experiencing this game and its special, mind-boggling illusions was much more enjoyable after I muted the audio, which thankfully didn’t affect the gameplay.This is an incredibly relaxing puzzle game with very intuitive gameplay. With it's puzzles never getting complicated enough for me to want to search up the answers.My only gripe with this game is the price. After only 2 hours of play, I was already 80% done. I do feel like that this stems from the lack of difficulty in the puzzles, but as this is suppose to be a very wind down, relaxing experience, I believe that this is forgivable.I am certainly going to come back and finish this game, but a much more fitting base price would be $14.99. The game is simply too short to justify its current price. However, given how revolutionary the concept and execution are, maybe I am being a bit too scrupulous.Either way, get this game. It’s great!

_childDocuments_.review: "Viewfinder" is an exceptional single-player narrative game that seamlessly weaves together top-notch quality in game design, mechanics, and storytelling. From start to finish, the experience is a masterpiece that leaves you utterly captivated.The game's non-Euclidean geometry and puzzles create a truly unique atmosphere, keeping you engaged throughout with its impeccable attention to detail — a testament to the developers' dedication.Upon concluding the final chapter, I found myself sitting in front of my PC, at a loss for words and unsure of what to do next. The impact of the story and the skillful storytelling left me in awe. I remember spending a good five minutes just gazing at Cait in the last hub.What truly shines in "Viewfinder" is its ability to continually expand on its main mechanic, providing players with more than one gimmick to stay intrigued. The constant evolution of the gameplay ensures that there's always something fresh to experience. The puzzles, offering various solutions, are both challenging and enjoyable.Furthermore, "Viewfinder" excels at incorporating great little optional details that enrich the overall experience, making exploration a rewarding delight.In conclusion, "Viewfinder" is an unforgettable journey, offering a masterful blend of innovative mechanics, a gripping narrative, and thought-provoking puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a charming puzzle game reminiscent of Portal, and more especially Superliminal. It throws a number of puzzle mechanics at you over the course of its ~4 hour runtime, with the general theme of perception both affecting and effecting reality. I quite enjoyed Superliminal's perception based puzzles, and there are more like them here if you did as well. Viewfinder does a good job of introducing you to its varied mechanics throughout the game, but will then pull away the training wheels and give you puzzles that require some serious outside-the-box thinking to figure out. The Portal similarities extend to the final level, which requires a synthesis of most of the concepts and will give your brain a serious workout as you attempt to solve it under pressure; I  enjoyed it, even if where the story was going left me sad.Overall I would definitely recommend this game if you enjoy perception-based puzzles. I didn't find the story especially gripping, though it got a bit poignant at the end (poor CAIT!) and the voice acting is certainly quite well-done. It's sufficient to guide you through the levels and keep you going, at least.Edit: oh yeah, and I got to solve a sonic-based puzzle by making a copy of  real, which was pretty cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: You've probably heard about this game. It's probably better if you buy it on sale like I did, but if you really like being made to think in ways you usually don't, it might be worth getting regardless. I beat it in about 4 hours, including the optional levels, but it could take longer depending on how good you are with puzzles. There are some really creative and off-the-wall parts, but that's a given considering how monumentally difficult it must have been to program something as unusual as this. All in all, I give it 8/10. Could have been a bit longer, but each new feature would probably have taken exponentially longer to make, so not too much of a complaint.

_childDocuments_.review: 🟩 Pros:+ The difficulty feels just right, catering to all audiences + The steady pace at which new elements are introduced + How technically impressive it was regarding interactions between photographs and the game world 🟥 Cons:-	The story is somewhat underwhelming, and the narrator is annoying 🏷️ Suggestions:~ A co-op mode would be great In its simplest form, Viewfinder has you taking and placing photos to manipulate the game world. What captured me most wasn’t the easy to understand gameplay loop or brilliant visuals, rather how technically impressive it was. The ability to influence the game world with your photos is amazing, seamlessly integrated, and offers limitless potential for experimentation and problem solving. Without spoiling too much, early on there’s a challenge which sees you traversing through a series of different photographs, each having a distinct art style. From black and white to a 3D rendered world, something akin to an early 90s FPS, all were wildly different and brilliantly presented. This is but one of many segments which had me stop playing so I could take in the world and all its beauty (and creativity)!The story and characters are… Forgettable… To put it nicely. Maybe it's just me, but I was much more interested in the mechanics of the game, and how photographs interacted with the world, rather than the reasoning behind why I was doing what I was. This isn’t so much a negative, more so a thought, as I’m sure many would invest more time into unlocking the secrets of the world.Viewfinder is a unique puzzle game which feels like it came from a longstanding studio with a big budget behind it. Despite the technicalities and interactions within the world, I never faced any issues, be it game breaking bugs or drops in performance. If you’re fond of puzzlers, be sure to check this game (and photograph) out, Nickleback approves!

Obviously not every game need to be 50+ hours, but I still feel this was quite on the short side for the price. I completed the game in 5 hours, and that includes lots of time running around and looking at things. - The puzzles are way too easy. Almost all of the solutions were very obvious. This is a clear contributing factor to the game being very short. If the puzzles had been a bit more complex, they would have been even more fun AND the game would have been longer without adding more puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: They took a very interesting and eye catching mechanic and used it to make a short, overpriced, mediocre game. _childDocuments_.review: Okay, So,  this is one of the games that WILL mess with you and make you feel genuinely amazed at what it can do, and even make u feel disoriented sometimes, at one point in the game it gave me the same weird tingly spacial feeling i felt the first time i ever used a VR, altho not as extreme of course, but still, i thought i won't ever experience that feeling again.I kinda feel a TIIINY bit underwhelmed tho at the PUZZLES side of the game, it felt like there is INSANE potential, especially for the mechanics later on, it felt like a TON more can be done with them but, that never happened. _childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. And of course I will go into deeper detail. And by the time you reach the end of the first level some of the story is revealed or at least its state. by the end the story becomes fully revealed. The ending was kinda heart wrenching for me. Personally i find the money I paid for this game was definitely worth it. I did have to use some help online during some parts because I got stuck in certain levels. But it wasn't the game's fault. I got stuck because i thought inside the box and kept trying to do the same thing. Which made me think about how it brought to my mind how this game somewhat taught me to think about things in a different way. Which definitely wasn't intentional. The core game only took me 4 hours to finish. There are optional levels to do. And I'll probably go ahead and 100% it. this game is a story based game so if that's not for you maybe another game you find will be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible concept, absolutely amazing gameplay! Reminds me of Superliminal and Portal where the very environment bends to your...Jessie "Did you just bend reality!? That's awesome! OH a photocopier!? That's amazing! You're doing incredible solving this puzzle by the way! Are you stuck? Maybe try this!? Maybe you need to do that..?" And here's the problem, I would recommend the game the moment you mute the characters. Thankfully the game does allow that, but why is she here!? Why are these characters constantly adding quips for every single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ puzzle I solve!? "Follow the grey brick road!" Funny right!? REALLY HELPS THE IMMERSION! Who thought that was a good idea!? Who thought that was necessary!? Do I need the equivalent of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LAUGH TRACK for this game!? WHY!? Why isn't the mind melting puzzle breaking concept not enough to stand on its own. It is! Trust me it is. You don't need this, it severely weakens the game. We don't need this verbal enforcement and these god awful quips. It's insulting! The concept alone is incredible, I highly recommend the game for that. But dear god, don't do this, don't include characters that add nothing but quips, backseat gaming, and further enforcement for the puzzle solutions. Ironically half way through the game someone seemed to realize how annoying Jessie is and decided to hide her behind an interactive phone object. That nearly works, except the phone rings. LOUDLY... It rings non stop until you answer or solve the puzzle. Then there's a secondary AI character that's not nearly as annoying, but the problem persists. You killed it, you killed the immersion right there. Portal works, why!? Because Glados isn't backseat gaming, she's an antagonist, the penultimate obstacle to overcome. Why does superliminal work? Because the AI and Dr Glenn Pierce act as further indication for how seemingly trapped you are in the sleep simulation. Jessie isn't needed, the CAIT character isn't really needed. They weaken the game severely. I'm typing this in pure frustration over it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're into puzzle games, this is a must have for your collection. _childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is the perfect example of having a coll mechanic idea and turning it into a game, exploring it's full potential without overstaying it's welcome and building interesting elements around it.You'll explore it's world trough this mechanic, taking pictures to get to the final of the level, simple enough right? and it is, viewfinder always introduces ALL of it's mechanics to the players, allowing them to first learn and them use that knowledge to both solve puzzles the intended way but also their own way and never trying to get the better of the player at any point.With that solid base the game iterate upon it throughout it's five worlds, each reflecting a different style, mechanic and the person who made it. Then add layers of a captivating narrative, some mind bending puzzle solves, gorgeous looking environments and spray some amazing Easter eggs and especial styles and pictures over it and you'll have your game.In the end viewfinder gives the players all the tools needed to have the best of times with it, culminating everything you'll learn into a great ending level and a bittersweet but hopeful ending, and don't forget about the best companion, your feline friend Cait!

_childDocuments_.review: from a puzzle game mechanic, every single puzzle is extremely easy, except for maybe a couple optional puzzles. a lot of the novelty comes from introducing new mechanics rather than designing harder puzzles with the central photo mechanic. even 80% into the game, there are levels that only take 1 braindead photo to solve and are only there to serve the plot i guessspeaking of plot, the story simply sucks. the plot is too obvious and uninteresting. it doesnt help that the story is constantly jutting in with different narrators or the different hub worlds. i think this game actually could have a really cool and interesting atmosphere, but its definitely ruined by the games insistence that you invest in its awful storyline. _childDocuments_.review: This game is $25 for about 5 hours of gameplay, and this is the first time I haven't regretted the purchase. While Viewfinder may be a tech demo, it's a tech demo that wowed me all the way through, relaxed me with its lush environments, and managed to tell a little story with a decent message.I won't talk much about the gameplay of Viewfinder, as figuring out all its little tricks is most of the fun. What I will say is that this is *not* an ultra difficult puzzle game: once you figure out "the trick" then all the puzzles are laughably easy, but it's figuring out the trick that's the fun part.I do feel a little sad, however, at the length. It isn't that they ran out of ideas, it just feels like they ran out of budget to do more. The systems they have hold so much potential for really clever, mind bending puzzles, and some of the optional challenges are actually extremely fun and, well, challenging! They just didn't get to flesh out their concept and it's a crying shame. Just go into it thinking of it as a walking simulator with puzzle elements and adjust your expectations.People often complain about the annoying voice acting and lackluster story and conclusion. While I do agree with them on the annoying characters part, your annoying companion is only in the very first part of the game and she soon gets replaced with someone much more tolerable. And while yes, the ending is a bit of a letdown, without spoiling too much it's about the only way the story could have gone without destroying its own message.All in all, I enjoyed Viewfiner! Would I have liked to get it for half price? Sure. But I waited about a year and it never went on sale beyond 20% off, so if you're on the fence, I would recommend getting it. Also, protip: if the last puzzle is giving you too much trouble there is an option in the menu to turn off the timed aspect to make it easier.

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder caught my eye within five seconds of its reveal trailer, depicting a player who superimposed a 2D photo onto a 3D environment to create new spaces for the user to platform within. This debut title from Sad Owl Studios is one of those rare ‘elevator-pitch’ proposals that would capture the interest of almost any fan of the puzzle genre, or simply novel video games in general. Thankfully, the developers executed this concept with such confidence and creativity that I really hope Viewfinder release is just the start of how this formula is used, as the game offers up some of the most creative and enjoyable puzzles I’ve ever had the pleasure of solving. Let’s get my biggest gripe out of the way first; Viewfinder’s world-building and characters are forgettable at best, and cringe at worst. You play as a nameless entity traversing a series of virtual reality environments with the goal of obtaining information crucial for the survival of humanity. It’s an interesting idea on paper, but there isn’t enough substance behind these narrative-critical moments to draw you into its world. Much of the exposition is delivered via a series of audio logs and documents that are not engaging or memorable to sit through. It’s unfortunate that the biggest marketing this game received was via an early line of dialogue written and delivered by what must be a Marvel Studios employee. Frankly, I don’t blame people for responding negatively as it’s completely out of place with most of the game’s writing, and what’s there isn’t anything to write home about. You don’t gain much by paying attention to Viewfinder’s world, and so you won’t lose much at all if you turned its dialogue off.Viewfinder is split into five hub areas within which you can access a series of increasingly challenging puzzles centered around exploiting its perceptual-based mechanics, with the goal of reaching a teleporter remaining the same on every occasion. The game has a very smart and gradual difficulty curve, where you’ll initially be provided with photos to place, before then being introduced to stationary cameras which require you to create the photos which have to be appropriately placed to move forward. Area 3 is where the game really kicks into gear, equipping you with a camera allowing you to create pictures to place down and manipulate the environment as you see fit. Ultimately, you’re limited not by your creativity with photo shots and placements, but rather by the number of photos you can take per level. This resulted in a series of really interesting scenarios, from creating bridges to duplicating batteries, alongside setting the environment up to be traversed as quickly as possible to overcome the pressure of time. Regardless of how you end up solving the puzzle, the level you’ll leave behind will look incredibly fragmented yet oddly fascinating, where singular screenshots taken and presented to unsuspecting art critics would likely produce some degree of positive response. These mechanics wouldn’t be nearly as impressive if the visual worlds created by your manipulation didn’t look so colourful and detailed, and the relaxing soundtrack to these environments consistently fits the visuals you’ll see perfectly.The levels that really require you to sit back and think are insanely rewarding to figure out, and my mind was frequently blown by just how flexible these puzzle mechanics consistently remained. This is especially evident in the very final challenge which could easily be solved in multiple different yet equally valid ways. It should be noted that some levels are admittedly super short, as their goal is to highlight specific interactions which will become relevant for later puzzles. However, the length of many of these spaces can be extended by searching for hidden photos and easter eggs; these are largely fun because of how different they look compared to the main game’s art style. There are a few 8- and 16-bit inspired photos, a couple of real-life locations, a compelling mini-barcode world where the lines function as trees; each discovery temporarily halted my campaign progression while I fully absorbed every inch of these remarkable locations. This is one of those rare experiences where I’d highly recommend 100% achievement completion to anyone, as there are so many wonderful secrets to uncover that I feel you’d be missing a substantial part of the experience by solely focusing on the main objective. Nevertheless, I don’t think that puzzle game veterans will greatly struggle to complete even the hardest optional content; the difficulty never reached the levels offered by The Witness’ moderately challenging puzzles at any point, but that doesn’t necessarily detract from the experience. Not every puzzle game has to be filled with a series of insanely arduous challenges, especially if they remain this consistently pleasant to solve. Looking back on the original Portal, that game can be beaten in under 2 hours, and no test chamber poses a challenge as great as much of what would be created for Portal 2. In spite of its low difficulty, Portal is still looked back upon as an instant classic due to the creativity of its mechanics. Viewfinder’s photo placement technology is arguably much more flexible than could ever be delivered by two portals; while it does lack a degree of timelessness which Valve’s seminal title will always have, the mechanics in Viewfinder are so excellent that a game even triple the length of this would still not scratch the surface of what it makes possible.I think the biggest sticking point for many people will be Viewfinder’s short length. It took me about 5 hours to complete all the main challenges, then close to an additional 3 to finish the optional levels and clear up every achievement. There also aren’t many reasons to replay the game, unless you wanted to return to previous levels and experiment with various camera filters to create some abstract art pieces. It’s a shame that it’s all over so quickly, as I can’t think of a better example of a game that would insanely benefit from Steam Workshop support. As it stands though, there was not a single moment within these 8 hours that I didn’t absolutely adore. Whether that’s worth £20 or not to you is ultimately down to personal preference, though I personally think the value proposition here is somewhat reasonable if you were already highly keen on playing this title based on the marketing.Viewfinder is one of the most impressive puzzle games I’ve ever played. I’m in awe at how a team could create levels centered around mechanics this flexible yet still present a clear goal to attain for each level. It may not be very long, and I can understand the length will be a dealbreaker to some people at this price point. However, the quality on offer in Viewfinder is so high that it becomes an absolute must-play to all types of puzzle game fans, or enjoyers of unique experiences in general. I really hope Viewfinder receives more content, in particular Steam Workshop support which I can imagine would make it blow up in popularity even more than it already has. I can easily see this making a list of my favourite games of the year, and I cannot wait to see where this highly talented team goes from here. Click  for my review scores!

_childDocuments_.review: Looks really amazing. The story is cool and maybe even a little thought-provoking. Some moments were relly cool and I thought more will come, but it didn't. The primary puzzle mechanic is innovative and just cool. I love taking photos. So, my overall experience was nice. Its just that... the experience is really short. The game is really short, the puzzles never go beyond basic puzzles. The most complex puzzles I had to try one or twice and was done. I guess I was expecting something different. But who would I recommend this to? People who just started gaming often can't navigate in complex 3d environments. People who are more experienced expect something more complex. Something very inbetween. I hope this game finds the right audience.

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a game that you see a cool trailer of and marvel at how such a game is real. And then you play it, and you experience the first level, and you marvel all over again seeing it in action. And then you play it for a few more hours and realize that the initial wow-factor is the highest peak the game ever reaches. The nature of the game's puzzles means that they're usually solved very quickly, and while the eureka moment feels great, it's not a sustainable feeling. We are yet to have a gaming equivalent of the term "Oscar-bait", but when we do, this game will be the definition of it. The story isn't pretentious enough to hold the game back too much, but it is meaningless, and the game would be better if it didn't have any story at all.

_childDocuments_.review: There seems to be some discourse regarding the criticism of poor writing and production decisions being misconstrued as misogyny but we'll put that aside for now.Without reading any articles criticizing the game, or reading any headlines, I chose to play this game with no subtitles, no voice audio, and treat it like a standard indie puzzle game with sick mechanics and a story presented in fragments throughout the playthrough.It was a transformative experience, it gave me a sense of adventure to explore everything, see what I could interact with, see how newly introduced mechanics work and if I could make them work better for the solution, and this approach gave me so much enjoyment. It was a satisfying playthrough, with scattered "Portal" motifs and huge "The Witness" vibes. I wouldn't trade that experience for anything.Then curiosity got the better of me, I wondered, "had I made the right decision to play this way?". So, I attempted to do a second play through,  with voice on and subtitles on. And boy howdy the laminar flow of gameplay I had appreciated and become accustomed to in my first playthrough was obliterated by random interjections by some sort of narrator, poorly written one-liners to serve as exhibition, a talking cat that feels like they put in the game because "hey kids like talking animals, right." I couldn't make it past the first subway ride. The constant interruptions with voice lines just took me out of any immersion I was in and I felt I was being spoon fed exposition and plot and lore, instead of trying to discover it and come to my own conclusions. This is simply a matter of opinion though, my preferences for immersive experience, one that gives players' choices more influence over outcomes, my preferences are ultimately irrelevant to judging the quality of this game for the average player.The gameplay itself is spotless, and it works, and the rules are consistent, and it feels amazing to play.The introduction of mechanics is not spoon-fed to you tutorial style, you have to figure it out on your own.Once each mechanic is learned, they combine the mechanic in an incredibly creative way for the last challenge and it instills a true feeling of accomplishment for having used the tools you obtained along the way to solve your way to the end. And it left me satisfied for having played it.In order to judge this game as a whole experience, we have to talk about the elephant script writer and producer in the room. I just don't think the gameplay and the writing/voicing direction form a cohesive experience, it feels like a high school group term paper where everyone writes about different subjects and instead of editing it to fit together in a logical and cohesive way they just copy/paste everyone's part one after the other. This severe disconnect confused me and not in a good way. It just made me feel like there were two games going on at the same time. I don't know if it is a lack of respect for your audience or an attempt to include all demographics, but having a line like "whoa did you just break time and space?" "Oh look a photo copier" "I guess I don't take fall damage" is condescending and it feels like being talked to like a child.5/5 would still recommend playing it on its gameplay alone, but customize your experience in advance of hitting that start button.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is exactly what you expect from it plus a little more. The puzzles are not that hard so those who are looking for an crindy puzzle game, this is not it. In the contrary this is in its heart a beautiful game. The idea of photos coming back to life, mixed with a meaningful story is all and I mean all that you need from this concept. The story is quite simple and compact but has so much to tell. You need to first of all find the peaces to the story and then connect them. You will be listening to one sad story from the past while a sad story of yours will be building up right under your nose. You will be thinking that the end is sad and it is sad but it will have a happy aspect right when you least expect it. Don't get me wrong there is so much happiness in the game and the mix of all the feelings this game has to offer is something you just have to experience.It is quite pricy to be honest so I would recommend putting it on your wishlist and buying when it's on sale. I almost forgot! The last puzzle was something else and for that alone this game is something every puzzle/story head should play. I won't spoil anything but it is FUN!

_childDocuments_.review: I was really vibing with this game. The puzzle mechanic is cool. The game is extremely chill and forgiving. It has a talking cat that tells you you're smart for solving the puzzles. It's great. Until the end where they put up a countdown timer (that does not play by the rules of the otherwise chill and forgiving rewind accessibility feature) and make you run a puzzle gauntlet. Suddenly, it's not chill and forgiving. Suddenly, the rules are different. I hate games that turn into a different game at the end. "We made a cool game that you've been enjoying for a few hours. We're going to take that away from you!" is a really terrible bait-and-switch.I _despise_ countdown timers. "Hey, we don't think you have enough arbitrary deadlines and meeting and message notifications beeping in your ear constantly in your day-to-day life so we're going to add a super-short deadline and a pounding bass-line to add some stress to your relaxing leisure activity." Seriously: I have two days off a week and you're going to add stress to them? For fun? No, absolutely not. I will not finish this game and I will not recommend it. Maybe I'll check out the end on YouTube. But I'm going to need to find some forgiveness in my heart before I even go that far.It's a bummer. They had a really good thing going. But I guess, in the end, they wanted to make a completely different game. They should've just made that one and saved us all a lot of trouble.

_childDocuments_.review: From a technical standpoint, this is a unique and genius concept. Mechanics are clever and some puzzle solutions are jaw-dropping. Though, it never really felt too difficult except for few puzzles where the "obvious" solution was not so obvious, which may lead the player, especially overthinkers, to frustration. The story was not so great, especially the fact that it ends just as it gets somewhat engaging. A lot of monologues, texts and references therefore feel out of place and end up serving more as an immersion-breaker. The gameplay time itself is rather short and what is there gets a little repetitive throughout. I enjoyed the playthrough, but I think that it is not for everyone. Who expects a great technical demo should not be disappointed. But it is not a full-fledged game.

_childDocuments_.review: My singular and primary critique is probably one a lot of people have mentioned.There is a Character - in the credits she is referred to as "Your best friend".Yeah.She doesn't ruin the game. But she does make it so you have to power through the sections when she talks.The Game is divided into Worlds, each world has a section of levels, and each world tells a particular section of the story.She stops talking right at the beginning of the second world, which is not that far off, as the first world is basically just introductory stuff. _childDocuments_.review: A first-person puzzle game with a conceit that feels truly magical and is pushed to delightfully creative limits.It's relatively easy, at least compared to other games of this type. Indeed, some levels provide no challenge at all and are just there to show off cool stuff. And, yeah, the cool stuff is indeed cool. It works.Where the game falters somewhat is in its storytelling. The basic premise is fine, but the framing and execution not so much. It's arranged a lot like : you're in a simulation, there are tests you have to complete for some contrived reason, and you find various recordings and documents that slowly reveal what this is all about. Unfortunately, the text snippets are not very well written and fail to flesh out the story's characters. Even more unfortunately, poor acting direction (if there even was any) has resulted in somewhat annoying and disjointed over-acting. It seems some reviewers really hate it. I didn't hate it. But I wasn't inspired either. It's OK, I guess, as a way to tie the game together.Another problem is that some of the (many) achievements are buggy. If you do the right thing but not in  the right way, they might not trigger. I had to watch video walkthroughs to get some of them.Also there is a cat and you can pet it!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! is easy to recommend for people who enjoy first-person puzzle games. It's not very long and not very challenging, but it will give you a few hours of joyful brain tickles.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DRVisually stunning puzzle game with interesting mechanics and a few challenging puzzles even if the majority aren't that tough. Quite a short game however so unless you can justify £20 for about 5 hours of game buy on sale. 7.5/10Viewfinder is a recently released puzzle game and one that has very quickly become one of my favourites due to it’s interesting use of perspectives and varied art styles. And that is honestly one of the main draws to the game. It's a visually stunning game which plays with many filters, art styles and perspective shifts in a similar way to games such as Superliminal.For example, you can use one of the games mechanics to walk through a portal to a graphite style filtered version of the world that looks like you've just walked on to the Take On Me music video or place a child's drawing and walk through it to solve the puzzle and continue to the next level. Speaking of mechanics there are a wide variety of them, such as placing and taking photos, the aforementioned portals and even aligning pieces of a photo to make a whole one. Some of these mechanics actually tie in to the games story and they all come together really well in the games finale, as the game tests you on all that you have learnt thus far.The games story probably is the weakest point of the game but is still pretty good. The basic premise is that you are walking through an old research simulation to try and uncover mysteries about the research done within the simulation. You can find various logs and notes within each level that add to this story and really flesh things out but it certainly isn't the main draw of the game. Though I will say the ending definitely got me a little emotional (not that that's very hard)Overall I really enjoyed the game even if I thought some of the levels were a bit easy, especially as you got to the end of a chapter and truly understood the mechanic introduced in that chapter. The game's visual style and requirement of a interesting and often unused set of problem solving skills definitely made the game interesting enough for me to finish.The game is quite short however so if you're someone who feels they need quantity over quality, or just can't justify £20 for a game you can beat in about 5 hours, buy on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: It was alright. Cool mechanics. Nowhere near as brain-bendy as it feels like it should've been though. The mechanics introduced one-by-one throughout do not end up being used together in harder puzzles towards the finish line, it just sorta ends which is a shame.Also, sadly I kind of concur with the reviews suggesting to turn off the dialogue. It just isn't all that interesting and almost takes away from the atmosphere; I do not care for the techno-babble of some scientists, nor a disembodied cat asking my mute character philosophical questions they obviously have no answer to. The game would've felt better if there was merely a hint of some wider story or explanation such as something like The Witness. A lot of puzzle games tend to always be in the shadow of Portal, struggling to replicate its success of having both great puzzles and story/atmosphere, and this game felt like another one of those. Nice first attempt with cool puzzle technology, with what little of a story that there is still seemingly getting in the way.

_childDocuments_.review: I received this game as a gift as I had it wishlisted for quite some time. Viewfinder is like no game I have ever played before. The puzzles are amazing, sometimes difficult and sometimes easy to understand. Using perspective, colors, filters and more to find your way out of a level in the most creative ways. I quite enjoyed them game, even though it made me frustrated here and there. I have to admit that the voice acting of the game is rather poor and that it definitely improved once I fully shut off the sound of the voices. I have to admit that I stopped caring for the story and stopped listening to any of the phone calls or voice notes laying around because it wasn't captivating. Puzzle appeal has been met but I'm not quite sure what the story was even meant to be. There are a ton of reviews and I've read of a few people saying that they don't quite understand the timeline of the story and what it is trying to convey and I'm sadly one of those people.I completed the game in a little over 4 hours with the help of a friend and I definitely recommend checking it out if you enjoy puzzle games and want to experience something new!

_childDocuments_.review: The main puzzle mechanic of Viewfinder is one of the most unique and impressive ones the puzzle genre has seen so far. I would nearly put it up to par with the portals from the Portal series. In the later collection of levels they did something Titanfall 2 also did. They introduce new mechanics practically only for that collection, some exceptions do exist of course.The game may be on the short side for some players with around 4 hours of gameplay. I wish the game would have been a bit longer so that the mechanics could have been explored a bit more.The game is pretty easy arguably too easy, however I think that experiencing the mechanic is reason enough to try the game.I wholeheartedly recommend Viewfinder without a single doubt and hope for additional content.

_childDocuments_.review: Review after 11 hours + full achievement completion.Seeing really is believing with this game. It doesn't quite capture the magic of walking through a portal the first time you play portal, but it comes damn close and it's hard to explain what the experience of taking a picture and then putting it somewhere else in the world is really like. It's an awesome gameplay experience throughout. The atmosphere and level design are awesome and the different camera filters were lots of fun, although they did make me miss my camera even more on the levels i didn't have access to it on.I do wish the game had some sort of challenge mode, i guess that's what the optional challenges are for but even with those it doesn't feel like the game has a lot of content, and the content that is there seems pretty segmented away mechanically. With the exception of the final level there really isn't much that utilizes all of the different mechanics the game has been establishing and it'd be cool to have post-campaign area with extra hard levels utilizing all the mechanics instead of just one or two.I did also experience a few bugs, one of which blocked my progress on an optional level for over an hour because i didn't realize it was a bug until i closed the game and relaunched it after and realized that the idea i had tried earlier in the day actually did work. That was the only major bug i experienced but it made me question the game every level after that i got stuck on, unsure if i was missing something or it was just bugged. That's not a great experience but hopefully most players didn't have that issue.

_childDocuments_.review: The comparisons between this game and Superliminal are inevitable, not only because both puzzle games have unique mechanics that play around with perspective, but also due to the virality of their individual tech demos that ultimately lead to the creation of each game. While Superliminal chooses to focus on the more experiential route towards the end of the game (likely due to the limitations of their own mechanics), Viewfinder manages to present a variety of creative puzzles surrounding their core game-play in a much more cohesive way and deliver a solid narrative around it. The final product is a fun, albeit relatively simple puzzle game that will satisfy puzzle fans.Rating; [8/10]

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there was a mixed review button because by no means is this a completely horrible game. I enjoyed the puzzles and it showed a lot of promise, but the game does fall short of getting an upvote from me. My main issues can be summarized as: I feel like far too much time was spent wasted on a D-tier "for the greater good" story when much more could have been added to the level/art designs. In short, wasted potential. 4/101. The Story/Narration 0.5/10If this game came out before all these strong narrative driven puzzle/adventure games maybe it would have more impact; however, even in a vacuum both the story and narration fall short. I turned off the audio for the voices 5 minutes into the game, and though I kept subtitles on for the rest of the game, I might as well have turned them off too. Not every game needs to have some over-arching moral/ethical dilemma built into it to be good. Shoving climate change down a players throat for no reason other reason than to be a plot point for a plot that doesn't even need to exist is extra and overdone in this case. If you were going to have story, the dialogue on the interpersonal relationships between the "main characters" would have been more than enough, as they were the only interesting part.2. The Puzzles 5/10I enjoyed the puzzles, for the most part. Unfortunately the only challenging puzzles are the optional puzzles, and even then they aren't difficult to solve. I'm fine with a puzzle game having easy puzzles if the gimmicks are cool, which in this game they are. However, when you get the limited amount of puzzles as this game offers while the entire time you get a forced narrative shoved down your throat, it makes those puzzles significantly less enjoyable. I beat the game in less than 4 hours (though the time I am reviewing it I have more because I went afk for food), which I have a hard time justifying the $25 price tag on it.3. Graphics/Art Style 6/10Graphics are pretty good, though one of the first things I noticed when I went to change the FPS settings is that you cannot adjust them (not a major ding imo, but annoying none the less: if you can't change the fps settings don't make it look like you can). I like the art style and as you explore the game, you find that a lot of effort is put into the ones that do not follow the general art style of the game. Therein lies another issue that I have with this game. There are about or less than 10 unique styles that are introduced into the game (apart from changing the color of default textures), and each one has unique sound design when entering them. I would much rather have had those unique styles been part of the puzzles, or showcased more through the game than any of the narration/story.

_childDocuments_.review: The first time I saw the trailer for Viewfinder, I thought it had the potential to be something truly special. Lucky for us, it’s one for the books.The central mechanic for Viewfinder is that you can hold up any picture or photograph to the environment and when you let go, the picture will imprint itself into the environment, even the depth of what was in said picture. This can manifest itself in a myriad of ways and it’s honestly astounding how it works. Giving the player this amount of creativity and non-linear solutions with manipulating the geometry of levels and not breaking the game is worthy of applause in and of itself. Levels are divided up much like test chambers in Portal, speaking of which, I would put Viewfinder’s mechanic in the same class as the Portal Gun, Gravity Gun from Half-Life and the GLUU Gun from Prey. It’s honestly that impressive.The game constantly throws new mechanics and nuances and builds on them in a way that makes this a tight, perfectly paced package. The game does not overstay its welcome at all, and honestly I wouldn’t have minded it being just a touch longer, something I never say about game lengths these days.I don’t really want to go into discrete puzzles or what the game throws at you since I believe it is best to be experienced yourself. That said, I had multiple moments solving a puzzle and saying to myself “That’s f*cking cool.”I personally think Viewfinder is amongst the pantheon of great puzzle games. The only thing that I would say holds it back is its story. It’s coming from a good place and has a good message, I just didn’t find the characters interesting enough or the narrator to be as witty as say a Stanley Parable or Portal 2. But realistically, you’re coming here for the puzzle elements, and Viewfinder is special in that regard. If you in any way have an interest in the genre then Viewfinder is an absolute must-play and my contender for GOTY thus far.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, but pretty short, around 4 hours. Which is weird bc it's not at all a small game. It's almost overflowing with cool mechanics, but where other games would build huge sections around them, Viewfinder very quickly moves on to the next one.One mechanic in particular made it's debut in one level, got expanded on in the next and then finished in the third, never to be seen again. A whole mechanic which one could build an entire game around, introduced and completed in 2-4 minutes.It's an extreme case, but emblematic. I can't help but wish for a version of this game that lingers longer on it's mechanics, creating more complex puzzles with them. Maybe some ppl would have gotten bored by it, but not me. Regardless, I definitely feel like I got my money's worth, and I guess it's not the worst sign if a game leaves you wanting for more.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this review is going to sound a bit negative, so the first thing I want to make clear is that I don’t think Viewfinder is a bad game, I just think its been massively overrated by some of the reviews and awards.While the main gameplay mechanic of using photographs to rewrite parts of the environment is unique, the actual puzzle design is very basic. Most of the solutions are completely obvious, especially for an experienced puzzle gamer like myself.Need to get from platform A to platform B, but they’re separated by a bottomless pit? Take a photo of a wall and use it to create a bridge. Button needs to be powered by 2 batteries but you’ve only got 1? Take a photo of the battery to create a copy. Exit teleporter is upside down on the ceiling? Take a photo, rotate it 180 degrees and place it on the floor.Even though you have the freedom to place photos anywhere, the simplest option is usually correct. And there are a couple of ways that the puzzle design prevents the player from doing anything really creative.Most puzzles give you a limited amount of film, which restricts how many photos you can take (usually 1 to 5 photos per puzzle). Meanwhile, the exit teleporters are usually powered by a switch which is connected by a long wire, and if you break the connection, it won’t work anymore. So you’ll either have to stand in a specific place to ensure that everything you need fits into the photo frame, or place a photo in a specific position to avoid breaking something important.Later puzzles introduce a few new mechanics. Blue coloured objects are fixed in place, and can’t be copied or overwritten by photos. Cameras which operate on a timer allow the player to take a photo of themselves, which can then be used to place yourself past obstacles. And some cameras destroy what you take a photo of, effectively changing the “copy and paste” mechanic to “cut and paste”.But because Viewfinder is really short, none of these mechanics are ever explored fully or combined together in really complex puzzles. It only took me 4 hours to complete the main story, and I’ve just got 3 more optional puzzles to solve. This feels like the first half of a really good game.This is also a rare example of a game that would actually be better without the story. There’s no proper introduction, so I have no idea who the characters are or what they’re actually trying to achieve by solving the puzzles, while the dialogue and voice acting is kind of annoying.

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder feels like a glimpse of the future. Your first hour of play will be marveling at the tech behind it all. You can place environments into the world and see objects get literally sliced away by the new image. Riveting stuff.You then get a bit of story, which is nice enough, before being thrown back into the matrix with environment puzzles. You will be placing batteries on pads, but it never feels like a Portal knock-off, unlike many first person puzzlers of late. In fact, it's hard to slot Viewfinder into the puzzle genre; the levels are rarely hard, and we lose some of the precision of modern day thinking games. Sometimes it's difficult to judge distance needed to place bridging elements into the level. At more than a couple of points, I felt like I was brute forcing some solutions and letting the physics engine pick up the slack.There are however an abundance of mechanics at work that make sure that gameplay never feels stale. A certain mysterious wall type can't be photographed at all, and before too long this camera-shyness spreads to already understood puzzle elements. There are lots of secrets and surprises that kept me entertained and the game knows when to call it a day. I had a good time with it.

_childDocuments_.review: THIS GAME NEEDS A SEQUEL. But not necessarily in a good way.First of all, the core mechanic of placing pictures that you found or took via viewfinder is great. It made for some fairly outside the box solutions and was satisfying to use. I could definitely see it being used for trippy, world within worlds type encounters as well. This is sort of where the good things end.It is hard to not compare this game to the Portal series, solving levels with your reality bending device whilst an AI yaps at you. I think comparing this game to Portal highlights this game's biggest shortcomings: The story and atmosphere. The decision to make this game set in some sort of virtual reality world was odd, although it makes sense to allow the full effect of placing a picture on the world to happen. The in-world motivation to complete the levels made no sense, you interact with terminals to complete sort of "chapters" and are returned to the hub world upon completion. In Portal or Superliminal, similar puzzle games, the reasoning to solve the puzzles was so you could physically move to the next location, to escape or defeat a rather curt robot. This moves us into the greatest sin this game commits, found in the reason the main character is here at all, which is to find some sort of device that exists in this VR world that can ostensibly cure climate change. This is bizarre. This biggest issue with this is that the attitude that all the characters have towards climate change is that it's solution is both unknown, and as the game shows us later on, has no certain solution. This is factually incorrect and a frankly dangerous attitude. We know exactly what causes climate change, and how to stop it. And the answer isn't a giant machine a group of scientists made in the metaverse. Also, many of the mechanics are severely underutilized, with one of the coolest being introduced only in the very last chapter of the game. The is not much combining mechanics for solutions being used either. This makes this game feel like a beta with a bunch of half-baked ideas for levels. TLDR, the plot is weak and frustrating, the motivation is lacking, and the mechanics, while great at their core, are poorly used in many of the levels. Despite all this, if you enjoy games like Portal and Superliminal, I would grab this game on sale. And to the creators, please make a sequel. This has so much potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Reviewing Viewfinder based solely on its innovative technical solutions would result in a flawless score. My jaw hasn't dropped this dramatically during a game since I was a kid.To be honest, though, I'm not thrilled with this title. While the game does invent a number of interesting puzzle techniques, most of the sections feel like mere appetizers because they never attempt to move above a very basic level.The story feels like an additional feature, not something that would give me the drive to progress further. The writing is also passable, filled with soulless characters and an annoying commentator, but the cat at least improves this a little bit.+ A remarkable achievement in terms of game design and programming+ The puzzles are well-made and interesting+ The visuals are absolutely stunning- The story feels like an additional feature and not as the backbone of the game- The price is way too high for the offered playtime- The difficulty in most parts completely stagnatesSimply put, there is no real story in the game. It's there, but it's very evident that it serves no purpose other than a nice extra feature. This is easily verifiable by visiting the game's store page, where not a single sentence is dedicated to explaining the game's plot. I hope you understand that, because of this, I don’t know how much I can reveal about the narrative, even though, as I noted, you can easily enjoy this title by just focusing on the puzzles.The dystopian planet of Viewfinder is characterized by a rapidly shifting climate. As a result of widespread global warming, oxygen is scarce in many areas. Yet, a group of dedicated scientists have created a technology that, if recovered, might drastically improve the future of the human race. The narrative mostly focuses on the past, giving you a glimpse into the group's routine, research, and internal conflicts. Listening to gramophones and reading written logs help reveal more and more about the history of the various structures and worlds as you explore them.You'll also have a helpful feline companion named Cait, who will tell you interesting anecdotes and point you in the right direction. In my opinion, Viewfinder's gameplay mechanic stood on its own without the need for a story, and I suspect that was the case with the developers as well. It adds some flair to the game but raises more questions than it answers. By the end, I had no idea what had happened, and the story as a whole had failed to impress me.Finally, we're getting to the game's meat and potatoes: the puzzle systems. You've probably already had a few "what, how?" moments simply reading through the game's website; trust me, you'll have a dozen more like that while you play the game! The central component is a camera that can capture a moment in time and render it as a photograph; the resulting image is far superior to a "simple 2D one" since it can be positioned in space. But that's not all; Viewfinder never fails to impress me with its technological wizardry, whether it's an interactive rendition of Edvard Munch's "The Scream" or an especially ingenious optical deception. The game heavily rewards those who are interested in exploring the outstanding liminal spaces.In order to advance from one level to the next, you must activate, rotate, or even just find the corresponding portal. The rules will evolve slightly on later levels, but the core concept will remain the same throughout. In particular, the levels that included new types of sounds were fun to play since they demanded creative problem-solving. The problems are initially easy—perhaps a little too easy - but, in the game's second half, Viewfinder truly picks up speed, presenting you with challenges that call for you to change your point of view and, in some cases, launch yourself into the air before plummeting downhill to land on a photograph you have to place in a ‘pro gamer’ way.All of the puzzles make use of this principle in somewhat different ways: as you advance through the stages, the puzzles will become progressively more challenging; nevertheless, a better word might be "denser," as almost all of the puzzles just scratch the surface.While not the fault of the game or its creators, this issue has become somewhat of a norm in the puzzle genre over the past few years, with numerous games featuring impressive yet underutilized gameplay mechanisms. The game's major issue is that the difficulty never rises above a certain point; instead, it consistently introduces new mechanisms every few levels and then stops expanding.The adventure culminates in a time-based puzzle that is a model of what a normal level in the game should have been like: dense, challenging, and offering a variety of unique solutions. My main complaint about Viewfinder is how short the game is; I finished the main and most of the optional levels in a little under five hours, and the game might offer me an additional hour or two if I'm particularly dedicated to unlocking all of the achievements. Seven hours doesn't seem reasonable to me for a price tag like this. - There isn't just a straightforward answer to this subject, despite what many reviews might have you believe.The game's aesthetics are arguably one of its best features. The graphics are stylized with a realistic flavor, and with the addition of flora, the settings come to life; the palettes are rich, and no two images are the same. The developer's insatiable imagination shines through the game's myriad collectibles - which range from posters to portable game systems - and interesting  cartoonish deserts and ancient castles rendered in pixel art. The game's music and sound effects are satisfactory, and the game also features wonderful voiceovers, so there's not much to complain about there. The use of accents by several members of the cast is a nice touch that adds to the overall immersion.My inner child wants to adore Viewfinder, but I simply can't look past its flaws. The game's core mechanism is truly groundbreaking, and it features amazing environments, but it suffers from far too many flaws to be considered a definitive gaming experience. _childDocuments_.review: I was in love with this game after only seeing a brief demo. I found the core gameplay mechanic to be very fresh and novel. Despite some occasional frustration I thoroughly enjoyed it... right up until the last level which has totally ruined my view of the game. This won't apply to everyone, but the best thing about this game to me was that it let you figure out the one of many different solutions to the same puzzle you wanted to use AT YOUR OWN PACE! Then they had to go and stick a timer at the end which saps away any enjoyment and only injects anxiety into what used to be a captivating yet relatively relaxed experience. I'm someone for whom a bad ending will often shatter my view of a piece of media and thanks to a 5 min timer to solve 9 spacial puzzles I'm no longer a fan of this game. I understand restricting the number of photos and even having the player need to feel out the exact boundaries and rules, these elements feel natural. The timer at the very end for the sake of trying to build some suspense and raise the stakes doesn't fit with the theme of this game in my opinion. I might not be so upset if it weren't for the fact that the rewind feature doesn't even turn back the timer. It seems counter-intuitive to the game mechanics and if they amended this but shrank the time allowed I would understand it more as it would then be about finding an effective path through trial and error in the same level attempt instead of having to exit the level and reenter a dozen times to reset the timer and try again. I personally feel that for the style of game they were aiming for, the creators tripped at the finish line with the last level and ruined it. I'm going to keep trying out of stubbornness but I'm no longer enjoying the game and might not bother finishing it if it takes me much longer.

_childDocuments_.review: What if you could take a photograph, place it and then walk into it?It's super impressive to see this brave idea actually working in "Viewfinder"!And the levels are clever, mind-bending even. Sometimes you will have to work with photographs you can find and collect, other times you can take your own ones. But what should you actually photograph? And where exactly do you place it? Is the perspective right? Or do you accidentially remove something relevant? Maybe you need to rotate it - but what will be the effect of gravity, and can you still walk within it? How about placing photographs *inside* of other photographs? It's insane, and insanely fun at that. Additional challenges based on perspective, optical illussions and time itself complement the game well.The seemlessly connected levels are filled with brutal concrete structures, astonishing flora and retro-futuristic tech. Thanks to placable photographs the game is able to explore and combine various environmental art styles in astonishing ways. And the occasional "special" image definitely makes for unexpected and funny situations.Albeit this being a puzzle game, there is a surprisingly deep overarching storyline. It takes inspiration from and comments on challenges of our current time, yet often enough leaves place for interpretation. Levels are filled with paintings and notebooks, audio recordings and sticky notes - this is environmental storytelling at its best.It's rare to see a game that is as creative as "Viewfinder" - I do highly recommend it! I'm sincerely hoping for either DLCs or a successor!

_childDocuments_.review: The game's central mechanic is very clever. Unfortunately, the puzzles are too simple, the story is fairly boring and ham-fisted, and the ever-present AI cat won't shut up already with its patronizing "good job!" whenever I do something clever. It's not like I'm doing some entirely optional clever thing; I'm just solving the puzzle. I like the cat, too. I just wish it would shut up already. Early in the game, there's a brief hint at some potential meta gameplay with error states and glitches, but sadly,  the game never goes there again. Or maybe it does, but I stopped playing in the middle of the timed level, because it felt frustrating to all of a sudden have a timed level, with an entirely manufactured-feeling of urgency, in the middle of what had up until that point felt like a pretty chill experience.Game designers: why add a timed level in at the end of the game? Can you think of no other way to create a sense of urgency? Are you just out of ideas? Was that even the end of the game? I don't know. I may never know, because I'm over it. I didn't bother finishing the timed level, because with the way the story was going, I didn't think the payoff would be worth me redoing the level over and over until I was able to complete it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is actually, sadly, kind of just okay (I too, came from GMTK)This game is quite pretty! You'd be surprised with the shaders that the game displays for you in some parts in the optional pictures. You can literally place what looks like a painting and walk inside it! Or into a pixalated dungeon that truly looks like an older, low-resolution game! It's really cool and just shows how much care when into the presentation of the game.The game is centered around photos you can place in the world, and while this mechanic works well and generally does what you want (despite it being hard to estimate distances), I find that it never reaches that "it's getting real good point".Viewfinder is kind of just confused, you'd imagine the camera, that's advertised in the splash art and in the trailer, would play a pretty central role, but nope! It's not even available in half of the levels, as once you unlock it, it just kinda pops up randomly.Instead, each new hub introduces at least one or two new mechanics that, since they need to be tutorialized, waters down the challenge it might have had, because yes, the game is really, really easy, which you might like! Just a heads up for those that want a headscratcher. One of them only appears in a single level! And it's one of the coolest!! What!!!Most levels only really use 2-3 different mechanics at most as well, meaning most levels stay quite quick and simple.None of the other mechanics are really noteworthy, very standard and uninventive puzzle stuff, all the cool stuff is in the picture placing.I have to say they make inventive use of the picture mechanic, building upon it in interesting ways, though they don't really mix them much.I don't really have much to say other than it works surprisingly well, it really does what you expect it to, even in the weirdest of ways with optional pictures that show cool shader effects. Makes me wish this game was more of a gallery tour, à la Antichamber, than a game with proper mechanics. The potential for this was there but ended up... falling short.I do have to say that the achievements are pretty entertaining, you're encourage to mess around and I love that.Man. I'll be honest they just shouldn't have bothered.You explore this world (that's actually a simulation for an ancient civilization??? Never elaborated upon) in search of a machine that can supposedly change the weather to help stop climate change, because the world turned a bit like Wall-E for some reason (it's even more hilariously apt a comparison after seeing the ending).Thing is, the story is exclusively told through... audio logs. And it's not even anything interesting.First of, the dialog... IS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ AWFUL. Oh my god none of these characters speak like real human beings. It's pretentious, it's trying to be deep by asking fake questions to the viewer, especially your "companion" CAIT that will just say dramatic phrases out of the blue that are incredibly funny by how overly serious it is. Also he just won't shut up, instead thinking it better to comment and praise you on every single thing you do, annoying.Secondly, big case of overacting, especially in the case of Jesse, the girl that follows you at the start of the game. Not only is she written to be as obnoxious as possible, the actress' performance only makes it worse. The other ones also overact, but it's not nearly as noticeable as her, good riddance you don't hear her for most of the game past a certain point.Lastly, none of the characters are really interesting and are quite one note, meaning you'll forget them pretty fast.Everything about it is just, bad. The story premise is kinda dumb but could've worked, but instead we get scenes that are supposed to be dramatic and sorta emotional, but I just wanted the stupid talking cat to shut up already.Also for some reason the game doesn't remove story triggers you've already activated, so they will just always repeat, lovely.It's, a good game, but also kind of, too short. It never finds the ground to soar from, as it seems to not be able to commit to any single thing, making it feel pretty messy despite the actual mechanics being quite refined from how error-prone you would expect them to be.I finished it in around 3 hours, wouldn't feel like playing it again anytime soon, there isn't much that's interesting enough to come back to it.

Most of the early stages, like in Portal, have pre-assigned cameras and camera angles for you to work with, and in the later levels when you *do* have your camera, you're usually so limited by the number of shots per level that, and the important bits are so vital, that you get a pretty good shape of the puzzle pretty quickly. I don't think there was a single time  where I felt like I had "cheated" or broken the devs' intentions, it usually just felt like the devs rewarding curiosity and prodding at their game. The story isn't what you expect, and it ends exactly how I felt it should.

_childDocuments_.review: Good but one huge flaw:This game needs more levels. And I don't mean this in a good way; the game has a lot of great features but the main levels can be too straight-forward and not difficult at all. And puzzle elements seem to be taught but never expanded on.The main levels introduce a good quantity of new puzzle elements, and it keeps a fresh experience. Viewfinder does a great job introducing and teaching new elements to you, nice and easy. But that's it; often, the game didn't go into an advanced degree for these puzzle elements and it sort of just dropped them and carried on to the next one without really challenging me. The main levels were just teaching me new things but never putting my knowledge to the test. The Optional Levels at least filled this role.. But even some Optional Levels were pretty easy and straightforward. There was a lack of Optional Levels for all the puzzle concepts that could have been expanded and challenged on.The Final level was at least able to do this. I really enjoyed this challenge.-For such a well put together puzzle game; it's surprising how little content there is. I only had about 4 hours in this game while going slow and spending time listening to the lore/story and the fun secrets & trinkets.Despite this huge flaw, I still had a great time playing. I recommend this game as long as you are ok with less of a challenge and more of an experience.

_childDocuments_.review: On the surface, Viewfinder is a fun puzzle game with a story about ecological disaster. But it has many hidden layers of meaning.You have the power to change the present state of the world by superimposing old photographs and artwork on reality. This power has limitations, as rewriting history to have two objects instead of one or bringing an imaginary object into reality always alters the surrounding reality, sometimes doing irreparable damage.You are soon granted greater power. You are given a camera, your ability to reshape the present is no longer bound to using existing relics of the past. Now, thanks to your camera, you decide which part of the past is important and deserves to be copied and turn up in convenient places in the present. You then go on a power trip, preserving the past and altering the present as you desire.However, the veil is soon lifted and you are thrown into the real world.You learn that there are some parts of the past and the present that are fixed, intertwined and cannot be remembered and overwritten as you desire. Beyond the malleable phenomena, there are the violet noumena.You learn how your intoxicating experimentations from before were done in a safe environment, and how optimal conditions must be prepared before the present can be altered and rewritten: otherwise, not only the present but also the past is irredeemably damaged and destroyed.The final humbling comes when you happen upon cameras with delay timers, which allow you to take pictures of yourself. You learn then that you are not an entity beyond reality but a part of reality, subject to the same rules and circumstances as everything else.To summarise, this game is secretly a coming of age story.

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a fantastic puzzle game that delivers an engaging experience. Its core concept is brilliant, offering players creative freedom to approach room-solving. The flexibility in solving the puzzles adds a layer of fun without inducing frustration.The game's environment is a standout feature. Every puzzle room feels alive, and are not just boring chambers. What's more, there's a compelling backstory that provides motivation to explore the rooms beyond just solving puzzles. I loved the takeaway from the story with the ending. One of the game's strengths lies in its gradual introduction of new gameplay mechanics. This approach keeps the puzzles fresh, preventing them from becoming repetitive.Props to the devs for including some truly cool elements in certain rooms like However, there are a couple of downsides. The character movements feel slightly stiff, which can affect the overall fluidity of the gameplay. Additionally, some players might find the puzzles a bit too easy. Striking the right balance in puzzle difficulty can be challenging, but except for 2-3 optionnal puzzles, I haven't been stuck on a puzzle for more than 5 minutes (It's still great tho)Lastly, while the game boasts a rich backstory, I found myself not entirely thrilled with the "hub" system and the need to walk to teleporters to access various levels. A more continuous storytelling approach (like portal for exemple), might have been better for the delivery of the story.In summary, Viewfinder is a great puzzle game with a unique concept and story. Although I wished for a more seamless integration of story and gameplay. If you like puzzle games, it's a must play.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a delightful game. I saw a few minutes of someone else playing the game, and the moment I saw the mechanics I knew I had to try it for myself.  *  It's so fun, especially if you like the mixture of photography and puzzles. * The characters are interesting! I loved getting to know the members of the team, not only via recordings, but also how they 'built' and decorated their individual spaces. Aahron and Hiraya's spaces were the most interesting to me - but they all had personality. * When I discovered a couple of the secrets () I literally threw my hands up in the air and hollered. It's so rewarding to find.* The voice acting is great. I truly believed the characters as complete, realised people, especially the scientists. CAIT's voice actor is delightfully warm, which gives the ending a bittersweet feeling.* Speaking of the ending, I was wary of what it would be like - I am used to games like this having underwhelming or disappointing endings. But I liked this one, it was sad but hopeful. It felt like our journey was worth everything we did.    * The friend that communicates with you at the beginning of the game does talk a little bit too much, but I say this lightly because after the game truly gets going she doesn't talk much at all. (in fact I was starting to wish she had more to say on a deeper level - more references to her a person and the relationship between her and the protag. Are they friends or just work partners? How long have they been looking for an answer?)* While the scientists/team is trying to solve a complicated issue, it's pretty clear the core of the game's story is about their interactions and relationships. I do wish their conversations had been more in depth, and that there had been more recordings of them talking to each other as a group)* The time trial at the end does come out of nowhere and suddenly presents new puzzle concepts - concepts I wish we'd seen in other levels. I understand the devs were trying to ratchet up the tension, but some smaller time trials scattered throughout the levels would've prepared the player for it. However, it still wasn't as big of a deal as some other reviews have said. I did enjoy it once I realised what it was expecting of the player.* I do wish the message wasn't directly told to us in the final levels (it's pretty easy to pick up on what the game is saying as it goes along), but I understand sometimes it's safer to just say upfront what the message is(Side note: I saw another review complaining that it only took them 2 hours to complete. If you are REALLY good at puzzles, then don't go into this expecting a really tough puzzler. It's more about the journey and playing around with a cool mechanic. That being said, I feel like I had the "expected" experience - some scenarios I figured out right away and some I was stumped on for a little while. But I never needed the hints, they were all fun to solve on my own, which for me makes a very enjoyable puzzle game.)Solid puzzles, likeable characters, nice background music, pleasant graphics, sweet message of hope in the face of finality at the end. I am interested in anything the developers decide to make in the future.
