_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game cautiously optimistic. I had played the demo and loved the creative game mechanics, but was worried that the game was going to lack decent puzzles and just rely on it's gimmick. I am delighted to say that is not the case. This game is a wonderful, albeit fairly short experience. The graphics are gorgeous, the world is stunningly designed, and very atmospheric. Best of all, the puzzles are very well thought out, some where so creatively put together that I genuinely exclaimed out loud when I realised the solution.Oh, and you can pet the cat.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly innovative core gameplay mechanic that pretty much carries the game. The puzzles are just OK most of the time; they tend to be trivially easy, but the occasional fun challenging level does pop up and the final area in particular is fantastic. The setting was beautiful and relaxing. The plot had very little going on, and the game spent a lot of time repeating a very basic idea that culminated in not much.Easily worth the price for the puzzle concept alone if you like puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: I was excited about this one since I first saw early demos of it two years or so before it was released, and for once the hype didn't leave me disappointed.Viewfinder is a fantastic puzzle game with unique photo physics -- you find or take photos and then project those photos onto the "real" world to cast the 3D world of the photo into reality. There are many different inventive puzzles using this mechanic, from finding objects hidden in the photo's "world", to using blank space in the photos to cut through walls, to climbing or creating bridges by chaining photos together, and more.The atmosphere is also great -- the scenes are very detailed and pretty and they feel very cozy. Without giving too much away, the underlying theme is somber and about climate change and the story is simple but well-told.The game is relatively short, as most puzzle games tend to be; I 100% completed it in under 9 hours without looking up any of the secrets, but the game left an impact and it felt like time well spent.My only complaint is that this concept and this atmosphere would be  in VR and I wish it had VR support, especially since the game effectively takes place in a VR  world in-universe already.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another game that starts out as a series of purely cognitive puzzles, then the designers gave into the apparently irresistible need to put time limits on some of them. And I don't mean you have ten minutes to figure it out. You can take as long to figure it out as you need, but you will then have mere seconds after setting up your solution to reach a goal and make the solution work.Now, this game actually includes an "Accessibility" menu where you can disable on-screen timers. We thought this meant such nonsense as solutions with time-limits could be turned off so people who have challenges with those could still play. Yay!Nope!That's not what it means. In fact, we cannot tell at all what it means. But it clearly does NOT mean you can turn off the time-limits in the puzzles that (long after you have been playing for a while, and therefore thought you knew what kind of game you had bought) suddenly introduce them.This is just wrong. Games shouldn't call for speedy, nimble action after you have been playing them without those skills for several levels/hours. It's a betrayal and feels mean.Not recommended unless you really love parkour games infecting games that aren't parkour games.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: If you like mind-bending puzzle games like Superliminal, you'll love this! Highly recommend!The core mechanic is brilliant and it keeps being expanded in many creative ways.It's very short but almost every puzzle teaches something new or a twist on existing mechanics. A rollercoaster of surprises and wonder!Huge footnote though: Unfortunately just like Superliminal, it's incredibly boring as a puzzle game. The puzzle design is thoroughly lacklustre. Almost all of them are one-off tutorials for a single trick. Each one that follows either doesn't build on top of them or does it in very easy single step puzzles. Rarely is there a mislead or an escalation in the puzzle design. Usually you just need to parse the level, understand the problem and instantly solve it. Or you fool around for a moment and realize you just solved a puzzle. Around 4 puzzles in total were actually well designed and left me thinking for a moment or two.Even the finale, which is kinda great, was just the same but do it faster.There need to be plenty of wrong answers for the right answer to be meaningful! I wish the game took this to heart ...Also do yourself a favor and disable the dialogue and subtitles. The companion monologues and story are not just bad but actively harmful to the sense of wonder and discovery. It never becomes important. I'd even argue the story is stronger if you have to interpret it from just the visuals.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a game along the lines of Portal and The Witness and, in my opinion, as interesting as those two games. What makes the game so strong is that the devs didn't choose to milk out the mechanics until you are sick of it; you are constantly surprised by how it iterates on its main mechanics. The narrative is also compelling and so is its art style. I highly recommend this!

_childDocuments_.review: Well… I genuinely regret wasting my time on this. But we need to start at the… During this review i’ll be doing a lot of comparisons to “Superliminal”, since this game was clearly “inspired” by it. It was also “inspired” by a leaked concept of “F-Stop”, which is my first main grudge - Viewfinder is not a unique game and it lead me to believe, that an entire idea was simply stolen from a multitude of other projects. And it could explain why this game is such a mess. But it is a puzzle game, what can be so wrong with it? Well… Puzzles are the main issue here - they are braindead. Like, there weren’t a single “Aha!” moment through my entire playthrough, and each puzzle may be solved within 5 minutes. And once you compare them to “Superliminal”, it becomes pathetic. See, the core premise here is you taking pictures and being able to place those pictures back into the world. Sounds fun, right? Imagine, that you can make a picture of a wall in a weird angle and place that wall in an absurdly stretched way…Well, keep imagining. It is not “Superliminal”, where perspective matters. Instead, distance - is the only thing that matters. Seriously, no perspective during the shot or its placement, nothing. Nada. Simply step away a bit further and you’ve made a necessary shot. But that makes too much sense, so…Your photo does not only captures what is in front of you. If you photograph a wall, everything behind it is also captured. Like, how dumb this is? And the worst part - there is no consistency. The world isn’t continuous and instead - it is a series of disjointed puzzles. You have a 4 hub worlds, each containing about 5 teleporters to a different set of puzzles. Once you’re done with a set, you simply return to a Hub, walk to the next teleporter, repeat. This might’ve had any sense, if not for the… Yeah… There is a story, unfortunately. The whole world - is a simulation. And you go through it in order to find a technology to save your real world. A technology, that works in an unrealistic simulation, should work and save the real world. A 5 year old written this?But if this game was trying to NOT make any sense, it definitely succeeded. Because you also discover CAIT (an artificial cat, sort of an archival brain of this simulation), which, for some reason, has emotions. And also lies. A computer, that has emotions, that can also lie, that “lives” in an unrealistic simulation, however not being able to interact with his own world. And the worst part about all of it? There is no relief, not conclusion or anything. It isn’t “Superliminal, which felt like a therapy that actually made sense. It genuinely felt like a kid writing his fever dream, and this kid was “special”… And even if this wasn’t enough, you do not actually experience any of the story - all of it is presented in a form of voice memos, scattered through puzzle islands. And “scattered” goes to their context as well. Yeah, i’m loosing sanity by just describing it. So let’s transition to… Credit where it’s due - graphics is very pleasant and nice. It isn’t anything remarkable, but it is good. Most of the assets belong here, and overall it is an eye relief. Also, i liked the artstyle - it is soft, somewhat realistic, with some color painting vibes. It is simply good, unlike… Well, sound should be separated into 2 things: overall sound, music and effects AND voiceover. Sounds are nice, soundtrack is surprisingly decent and I’ve actually bought it to listen. And sound effects, well, they’re there, nothing remarkable. And then you get voiceover… Jesus… There are some actors, who are genuinely trying, and then there is CAIT and your “supervisor” form a real world. Both of them are obnoxious, acting terribly, with a worst sound balancing I’ve experienced in a while. Compare this narration to something like “Superliminal” with an extremely well paced and played acting, or “Portal” with a single GLaDOS doing all the work, and you’ve got yourself a huge disappointment. So… You want to literally waste your evening or a even couple of them? Then it is a perfect “game” for the occasion. And if not - just stay away. There is nothing to discover here, no inspiration, no nothing. It is a student project at best, and it was never supposed to be released. Maybe it is a decent “proof of concept” (i’m being generous here), but it isn’t a finished worthy experience. And if you want something interesting and fun in a puzzle genre - go play Superliminal, both Portal games, whatever game that has puzzles, but not this one. And what rating i would give? 4/10, tops.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a nice little experience. Completed it in a single night (6.3 hours). The story is a little on the lighter side, and the narrator character Jessie is perhaps a bit annoying. Cait is a fuzzy little gem. Here is my main issue: The puzzles, although encouraging creative solutions, don't really feel like they evolved and built up in complexity. And rarely did I find them challenging. The game also has a bit of an issue of introducing new mechanics to keep the game play fresh without exploring them to the fullest.I am recommending this game for the great creativity of the photo mechanic, lovely environments, and the whimsical sense of humor. The developers did a splendid job incorporating the picture/perspective mechanics. Sadly, it's not very long or challenging and I was hoping for more. Great diversion, but did not scratch my puzzle game itch as well as I was hoping.

_childDocuments_.review: Thank you AI for letting me know life is a simulation and now I grow a garden.Viewfinder is probably one of a kind for puzzle genre just like Superliminal, and as a hobbyist photographer, it is mind blowing when you get to use the artistic thought process and get hype when the method clicks to solve part of the puzzle, the coding to make this happen must be fun to create throughout developing process, I can tell devs have a blast to make this, and I enjoy every single moment throughout my gameplay till the end!

_childDocuments_.review: Conceptually, a truly remarkable game. I have been looking for something to scratch the surreal puzzle itch since playing Superliminal, and I thought this might fit the bill.I wish I could say it fully delivers in that regard, but there are a number of things I wish were done differently:- Most of the story is fleshed out via voice recordings and post-it notes. This can be done cleverly, but the post-it notes consist mostly of meaningless science-y jargon. I did not get the same sense of wonder and curiosity about the world that I did with other games that do similar things, like the Outer Wilds.- To compensate for the writing, there are two NPCs that talk at you nearly incessantly. The things they say range from cringey generic tropes (uhhhhhhhhhh did that just happen) to platitudinous redundant statements about the world or little comments on how smart you are. One of these characters is an AI cat you can pet, which is a consolation.  - I would have loved to see the mechanics of the puzzles interact a bit more - it seems the game shows you a new mechanic, then once you fully understand how that works, its on to a new area with a different mechanic. They do converge together near the end, but for a relatively short time.Overall, I would recommend this game if you can pick it up on sale and don't mind a bit of painful exposition (the game does give you the option to turn the dialogue completely off if it bothers you too much) - the concept is really cool and I would love to see a follow-up game that expands on the puzzle elements while trimming some of the awkward story elements.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I'd like to start by saying HOW?? This game has one of the smartest mechanics I've ever seen in an indie game. As a Gameplay Programmer myself, some ideas that's suggested throughout the process of making a game might sound smart, but undoable for most of the time. Sometimes Designers wants something but Programmers says otherwise. In Viewfinder's mechanics, I see myself saying "How would I implement this?"--which I would love to learn because it amazes me to find out about new mechanics and their development processes-- From the look of this game, it seems like Sad Owl Studios doesn't take "undoable" for an answer. After finishing the game in one day, it still blows my mind to think about it because, how and why is this game this bug-free while having these kind of mechanics???? I tested a lot of weird occasions, but no, nothing really bugged it. It was perfectly smooth and still looking good which is annoyingly amazing. But anyways, aside from how good of a game this is as in terms of "Game Development", it's also a pretty good game to experience as a player. I loved how easy it is to grasp the gameplay, I loved the level/game design in each scene and I definitely LOVED the art design for sure. This feels like a really good example to show how each department in an indie game studio works really good as a whole team!   To me it never felt repetitive, with new features coming along the way, it made me even more connected to the game. The only downside was that I couldn't really feel attached to the story that was coming along with me through the journey, I was very intrigued with the gameplay itself, I forgot the story but that might be my fault. Also it ends quick, even though I played it for 8 hours yet it felt quick to me :(. I hope they make new levels at the future but for now, just please experience this game. Especially if you like games like Superliminal and Portal.

_childDocuments_.review: There are moments in videogame history where something is created that changes the industry. For years after that there are hundreds of games and programs that copy, iterate, and push the new concept till something else new comes along to change the industry again. This is one such game. There are a few other projects that implement visual tricks and illusions, (namely Superliminal and Anti-Chamber come to mind). Even so this is a very unique and honestly mind blowing experience that feels like a new level of digital interaction.The player gains access to a magic camera that allows players to take a pic of anything in each level and then place the objects from that photo in 3D space. This singular game element is the main draw for me. There are other puzzle types in the game but honestly most of the time I was just trying to get through the levels without the camera to get back to camera time (and the bonus found photos) cause it's really the best thing by a mile in this game. The ability to rewind and redo any choice is a great tool for fickle puzzlers and curious creatives alike. The game has 5 hub worlds with many puzzles/levels in each, and features some light storytelling in the background. The only negative thing for me personally was that I felt the story, while simple and not in the main spotlight, was still very bleak and tries to tell an environmental warning story but without any solution, call to action (like there is in Terra Nil), or even allowing the player to see work towards a solution in game (Like in The Gunk). I feel the story could have been totally removed or changed and the game would certainly not be worse. I felt it clashed with the whimsical positive magic the game does a great job of creating. I ended up skipping the audio logs in the last act and I think that is a fine way to play the game, but each to their own. Highly recommend ANYONE interested play this, especially art and surrealist fans.Viewfinder will (hopefully) inspire more games to implement this level of technical wizardry and magic. Or better yet, hopefully this studio will create a camera focused sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game. The story (as simple as it was) was a great concept and the game-play is very unique. I loved the partner that travels most of it with you.one critique is with each new mechanic it seemed they would often toss an old one out to rarely be used again if at all. having more intertwining mechanics for the levels would be great.overall a very fun game for any puzzle fan.

_childDocuments_.review: The main mechanic is really cool and the narrative is nice, but I found the game frustrating toward the end when it arbitrarily removes some abilities from you to make the puzzles harder, rather than making the puzzles harder in some other way (like Portal or Talos Principle). The final level is particularly annoying, it introduces a time limit for the first time in an otherwise quite chill game, and the timer ignores your rewind power so you have to restart every time you miss the deadline, and it gives you no indication of how far through the level you are.It's kinda like how Mirror's Edge is really cool until they make it all combat focussed, weird choice for a game to not focus on its strengths at the climax. Honestly I don't know why they did this, the central mechanic of the game is mindblowing and cool and the puzzle design for most of the game is ingenious.I highly recommend playing it because I've never seen these tricks in a game before and for much of the game they're done really well, but maybe not worth finishing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Occasionally a game introduces a concept that makes you go, "Wow! I've never seen anything like that in a game before." Portal managed it, but very few games ever do. Viewfinder does this and it's jaw-dropping how well it is done. Sure, games like The Witness and Superliminal have used persepective-puzzles to good affect, but these are merely a sideshow in Viewfinder. The main conceit is that you can take a photograph - sometimes a painting - and step right into it. It's a simple concept, but a powerful one that opens up endless creative opportunities, which the game exploits to the full. As you progress the game also adds more and more ways of utilising the tools you have so it never gets stale - there are always new ideas appearing.As a pure puzzle game I'd say Viewfinder is perhaps on the easy side compared to it's piers. However, I find what makes a puzzler great is that it allows you to solve the problem in a flexible and innovative ways. Viewfinder gives you this creative freedom; there are often many different approaches you can take. It feels very satisfying to solve the puzzles and this is much more salient to me than having some artificial difficulty imposed. The only time it felt like artificial difficulty was in the very last section with the "timed" puzzles - but thankfully the timer can be turned off in settings,Some people have commented on the length - I found it pretty easy but it still took me 7 hours to complete. I didn't rush, I enjoyed exploring the beautifully rendered vistas and the backstory was kinda interesting (even if Jessie was really annoying). Given it took me only 4 hours to complete Superliminal, that's not too bad. It's also very polished - I didn't experience a single glitch or bug, which (given the experimental nature of the game that allows you to literally destroy and recreate the landscape) is amazing.If you like puzzle games Viewfinder is a must.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful little distraction. Game smacks a lil preachy, or not as thought provoking as it might want to be (nothing big if you're used to it), pretty easy (only needed a hint on one optional puzzle). _childDocuments_.review: Simply fantastic gameplay premise - and this game should be appreciated as a piece of art. However, once the initial novelty of the gorgeous art style/gameplay premise wears off, Viewfinder devolves into a trivially easy puzzle game with a stupid voice in your head which says the most inane and obvious things that will not shut up. Further, this game is not worth the £20 asking price, nor is it worth it for anything less than 50% off. Personally, I think the best way to enjoy this is to buy it, play it, enjoy the phenomenal art style and interesting gameplay loop and then either drop it or refund it if/when you get bored with it.This game is bittersweet, it has so much wasted potential and could have been something so much greater than the glorified tech demo that it currently is.

_childDocuments_.review: A very simple and straightforward puzzle game using pictures to complete puzzles or otherwise mess around with the world. None of the puzzles are particularly difficult but the main fun is just messing around with the photos. The visuals and audio is calming and minimalist but it conveys the overall mood of the game. While there is technically a story with characters, it's mostly in passing and you don't really create a connection with any of them as you only learn about them via optional recordings sprinkled throughout the levels.The game is very short. The story can be completed in about 5 hours, with achievement hunting maybe taking another hour or so, depending on how much you really explore each level when you first visit them. Because of that, I recommend picking up the game when it's on sale.Also, there's a cat.

_childDocuments_.review: This game does things with perspective that I have never seen a game do before. While you can draw comparisons to similar games like Superliminal, which it does seem to be at least partly inspired by, this still feels unique and original in it's own right, and it forces you to think about your environment in ways that I have never done so before. I have seen some say the puzzles are too easy - at the time of writing I am only around halfway through so I can't comment on the whole game yet, but I have already found some more difficult than others so I'm not sure I fully agree. Even if the puzzles are easy, the atmosphere and story of this game, in combination with the novelty of the concept, still make it a must-play game as far as I'm concerned. The comparisons to Portal - which is widely considered to be one of the best puzzle games ever made, and is one of my favourite games of all time - are deserved. This game is excellent. That said, I can also see the price being a bit too high considering what you're getting, so if you're not sure about picking it up just yet I would consider waiting for a sale. If it is on sale though, or if you have enough money to spare, I highly recommend picking it up.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good 3D puzzler for the types who enjoy the Portal series, Antichamber, Manifold Garden, Outer Wilds or maybe the The Talos Principle.The mechanic is interesting and it gets spun in a multiple ways. I kinda just wish the game was a bit longer as I suspect there could have been more and harder levels. I think the mechanic could have allowed for even more.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: ...and that is no exaggeration. Unlike a lot of other puzzle games that have inspirations drawn from Portal, Viewfinder forges it's own identity, and it is one hell of a striking one. There's plenty to adore about Viewfinder, but one big thing for me personally is that it's environments weren't created just for the sake of showing off an artist's skills, they were clearly made with thought in regards to how they interact with the main mechanic of the game with placing photographs into the world (and later on - taking photographs of those environments.)The gameplay feels truly refined and a joy to experience, everything just clicked naturally for me and I was amazed that the experience and puzzles designed still managed to feel fresh the whole way through, there was always something new to be introduced then explored upon through the levels - it never felt stale, and felt brimming with endless potential for new puzzles to the point that I was genuinely sad that the game had ended, and that was after experiencing  I'm especially a fan of how nearly every mechanic felt properly suited for the theme of Photography.If I had to voice one grievance about the game - it was the story, and mostly about Jessie in the first few levels of the game. I did not like the fact a character felt the need to comment on every little action I had been performing when I had just wanted to soak in the world I had been presented with, it felt incredibly infantalising for my first impressions of the game's characters to be very Marvel Movie-tier dialogue (A certain clip with Vinny Vinesauce might come to mind.) but the moment that Jessie had become optional to listen to, I greatly enjoyed everything onward, especially CAIT.And for one final thing about the story - I'm gonna talk some stuff about the ending, All in all however - Viewfinder was an incredible experience, it's rare to see a game carry what I felt was the gameplay essence of Portal and act upon it so wonderfully with a brand new, innovative piece of technology - something arguably more impressive to pull off than Portal's, well, portals. I absolutely recommend giving this game a go if you have the cash to drop on it, it's puzzles are absolutely brilliant and atleast those deserve to be experienced as blind as possible.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: This is a short indie puzzler game that has a fantastic central conceit. In summary, Viewfinder will provide you with an enjoyable, unique experience that you haven't seen in other games. However, it is very short and most people will complete it in 6-8 hours. Therefore, while I disagree with other commentators about it being nothing more than a "glorified tech demo", which is incredibly unfair, the game may not warrant its full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a masterpiece of puzzle and adventure gaming. It is a game that challenges your perception, redefines your reality, and reshapes the world around you with an instant camera. This is a game that lets you manipulate the world around you with photographs and other two-dimensional images. You can place these images in the world to create new geometries and layouts, and use them to solve puzzles and access new areas. You can also interact with the objects inside the images, such as picking up batteries, opening doors, or turning on switches. The game starts with you finding pre-made images that you can use, but later on you get a camera that allows you to take your own pictures and use them in the same way. The game challenges your perception and creativity, as you have to think of different ways to use the images and their properties. For example, you can tilt an image to make a slope, or copy an image to create multiple instances of the same object. The game is visually stunning, and the soundtrack is mesmerizing. The game is a masterpiece of puzzle and adventure gaming.Totally a must-play 9.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

This is one of the premier puzzle games I have ever played, up there with Chants of Senaar and personal favorite The Witness. It has some replay-ability due to the cool Easter eggs throughout the game and how fun it is to do things it feels like you shouldn't. _childDocuments_.review: Once again, another puzzle game with a fascinating and original mechanic cripples itself with a naff story. Viewfinder is frequently surprising and has some pretty decent puzzling, but good lord the story is beyond mediocre. It wouldn't be so bad if it would just shut the hell up for a minute rather than constantly battering you with meaningless audio logs and incessant companions. Apparently, a pleasant English woman talking at you all the time isn't enough, you also need a pleasant Scottish cat to tell you how clever the puzzles are.Even I feel that that was probably too harsh. But to be honest I'm so tired of playing these puzzle games that have such an interesting idea but instead waste time on nothing stories rather than building on the concept with more levels. Viewfinder is only about three hours long if you're experienced with this kind of game, so it doesn't have the room to cram in a saccharine and confusing yarn that could have been pulled from any other middling Portal-like. Just as Superliminal, Turing Test and Light Matter before it, Viewfinder ultimately fails its genius central mechanic.There is plenty to be praised here though, don't get me wrong. The photo placing and manipulation is an idea that is as technically impressive and innovative as the Portals in Portal were back in 2007. The levels are fairly well paced too, but I found the levels I truly enjoyed were the optional puzzles, which were a lot trickier than the main content. Ideally more of these would have been fantastic. Portal can rest on its laurels in terms of optional content because Valve knows they have a willing fanbase who will churn out content an unimaginable rate, but indie puzzle games like Viewfinder don't have the luxury of mod tools, so need to come with more content. As it stands, I can't say that even half of the puzzling potential has been extracted out of Viewfinder's concept.My opening tone is less an indication of anger and more frustration. I'm disappointed that such a great idea feels somewhat squandered, but perhaps I should be analysing what is here rather than what could be. And what is in Viewfinder is largely pretty good. Tune out the story and don't bother with the collectables and you'll find a fun, occasionally challenging puzzler that frustrates as often as it delights.

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to like Viewfinder, but I just can't get past over the game-journalist difficulty. 5/10From a coding perspective, Viewfinder is one of the most brilliant showcases of mechanics in a 3D First Person puzzle game I have ever seen. I was in awe how EVERYTHING behaves naturally and seamlessly. I can't even begin to describe how cool I think that a game like this is even possible in the first place. While Viewfinder is an incredible achievement in programming, it sadly completely fails as a puzzle game, it never explores the mechanics it introduces. It simply skips to the next mechanic before actually doing anything with what you have learned. The entire game feels like a tutorial for game journalists. Even the more advanced puzzles never got me stuck for more than a minute or two. You are also rarely limited in taking photos even though . So most of the time I only used 1 or 2 of the 5 photos that i had access to.Viewfinder reminds me a lot of "Manifold Garden" and "The entropy Centre", where these games have excellent mechanics but never does anything with them. It is pretty to look at, but contains no depth. Which just leaves me so disappointed, because I know you can make an absolutely amazing mind-bending puzzle game with these clever ideas. Even if it was on the easier side, I would've been happy with it. But Viewfinder is so pathetically easy that I never really had to think, the solution was already apparent to me the moment I had explored the level. All in all, I wish these game developers good luck in creating a more engaging experience, because Sad Owl Studios clearly have the technical skills to create something really special. You just need to take more time in designing challenges for the players and you got yourself that masterpiece that will set the standard for all the games that come after it. I still look forward to the next game from this studio just because I know there are some incredibly skilled developers behind this technical marvel of a game. Hopefully, they continue working on Viewfinder and add some hard DLC levels to Viewfinder because I am still down to buy them. Because the concept of the game is just that great.If you came looking for puzzle games, I have some recommendations for you. I would suggest playing "Portal (1 and 2)", "The Talos Principle" or "The Witness" in the 3D First Person puzzle game genre or "Baba is You" from the top-down 2D Puzzle game genre. And for mystery games I recommend "Return of the Obra Dinn" and "Outer Wilds", I really recommend playing these two completely spoiler free, don't even look at the trailers.Edit:As some of the people have pointed out below, Manifold Garden contains additional difficulty when you try solve it without picking up god-cubes. But the game never hints that you can do that, which to me is bad design. When compared to Baba is You's  or The Witness'  it's immediately obvious that you can do some crazy stuff with it. I don't want to have to go through an achievement list or have to look up guides to realise that what i'm looking at is just the surface level and not the entire game.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best puzzle games I've ever played! It is a beautiful, unique, quirky, ingenious puzzle platformer forcing you to explore your own perspective. First 3 worlds feel like tutorials, and even in world 4 and 5 I only got stumped twice, and once was an optional level (the watermelon level, definitely my favourite puzzle in the game. Felt great figuring out that one). It gets pretty condescending having the characters in the game go "Wow you're so smart and cool for solving that puzzle" when it took you like 2 seconds. So buy it if you want to, but don't expect much playtime if you have even a little puzzle game experience. Compared to another perspective trick focused puzzle game i've tried, superliminal, i'd say this one is better in general.Also small nitpick but why on earth would you give a popup for a hint at the very end of the game, in the ending sequence? Not even for a level really, just a complete immersion breaker. All these accessibility options and no option to turn off hint popups?

_childDocuments_.review: Soooo beautiful. Aesthetically and in gameplay. Elegantly scaffolded so that you are always learning and then applying new tricks while also getting you to think creatively. And speaking of creativity... if you got some you will love to do interesting things that may or may not have to with solving the puzzles. And the visual effects are SO cool. The atmosphere is generally great and peaceful though it does pick up with some tension toward the end that my 4 year old started to feel nervous about, but it never got super scary. The narrative, told through audio recordings, writings, and two NPCs who talk to you, was rather nuanced while not having a lot of plot points. I think that's why some people say the story isn't good, but I found it refreshing to take a simple concept and play it out almost like an ARG where there's a lot of materials  that all point back to the same core plot point. I think some people also might not like it depending on their political leanings... My four year old and I just want to play it all again and do more wild things. The ability to visually customize your gameplay (acquired mid-game) also kept things fresh... I never want to see a watermelon again, hahaha. And there were lots of sweet details like collectibles and interact-able things. AND I'm always a fan of rewinding time in games haha.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine this: You spawn into a world and have a look around. There are beautiful things to see, notes to read, recordings to listen to, a kitty to pet, secrets to collect, and of course the puzzle to solve to go to the next level. What do you do first? Specifically, what do you do LAST? Of course you want to do everything before solving the puzzle so you spend time doing them and you're constantly prompted "Are you stuck? Do you need a hint?" like it's trying to force feed the solution to speed you away so the designers could tell their story (which is just a stock standard search for a macguffin to save the world from climate change). As far as I could tell, there's no way to turn off hint prompts.Then you get to the actual puzzle, immediately spot the solution, and do the most obvious thing to solve it. Narrator: "Wow, you sure are clever! Nobody could have ever thought to do that!" Like this game is *very* hand-holdy. Look at this, do this, good girl, next puzzle.I took my time with this game to the point where it was telling me I was taking too long on every puzzle (the last level is actually timed) yet still beat it with most of the achievements in under 12 hours. Probably closer to 8, as I left the game running in the background for a few hours while I ran errands and did other things.The only puzzle I didn't immediately solve using the obvious solution was the one where you had to take a photo of film and a battery in the same shot to duplicate batteries and this is because the film wasn't duplicating. Coming back to this puzzle later it just worked, so the only difficulty spike came in the form of a bug.This game is actually meant for kids.It was neat for what it was I guess. Got to pet a kitty. Might ramp up the difficulty with DLC, level editors, and mods. Also the rewind feature is absolutely just a crutch to cover design flaws. At no point did it add to puzzle mechanics beyond allowing one to scout around to look at things. Maybe have a world where only *some* things are time-reversible?

_childDocuments_.review: It's not only the combination of puzzles and art it is also the mind-blowing tech they have inside the game.This game is otherworldly. The fact that you can take picture of some objects that you can interact with them and then copy and paste ''endlessly'' the same exact picture with the exact same details, it's beyond insane at least after playing lots of game this is something not many have accomplished this tech. Remember you're the one taking the picture you can move 10 centimeters and then retake the picture and the game will replicate this very same thing. I'ts beyond insanity.  I bet there were many ways to pass a level since sometimes you can be creative and do ''things'' game didn't expect you to do.I loved every single Second. Medium? Some puzzles where mostly just tech demo, to show this incredibly world of pictures and copies.But some of them really had me thinking specially 3-4 puzzles.Then End level was amazing!

_childDocuments_.review: rate this game:10/10The first time I noticed this game,I was watching a video from twitter,that video was like showing the basic photo projection concept? The first time I knew the concept of the game,I was like "WTF,that is so freaking incredible" .I played the demo version of this game on steam next game festival,I deeply attracted by the photo projection,and you can even place some post in the game they given.If it is a video game post or screenshot,you place it and you can even play it,although the that are very simple,it still surprised me.Now the game finally released,After I finished the full game,the game is way bigger than I was thinking.The games always teaching you new mechanisms,not just photo projections,the game got a textbook-like in these level  design! to lead you into it,each mechanism came out have a prefect "IPMT" process, IPMT means Intro -> Practice -> Master ->Twist ,which make you fell comfort when you learning or using those technic. _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this. The visuals were very clean, sound design was good and I had no optimisation issues. I really appreciated the design touches in the menu's.I'm not a genius level puzzle solver, but the puzzles did at times almost feel like a walking simulator. It makes up for this by just being really unique with it's mechanics, absolutely adored playing around with the camera and the photos.The "story" wasn't really much, it's more like a background track while you progress. That said, the voice acting was pretty good.If you liked Superliminal, you will most likely enjoy this.Not super long, but it doesn't overstay its welcome. Probably 5 hours (depends on if you just rush through or like to take your time and look at everything), more if you want to get all the achievements. _childDocuments_.review: Sort of yes, sort of no.Pros:Amazing unique puzzle game that takes inspiration from Superliminal and expands upon its core features Introduces new mechanics often enough to keep the game from getting predictable and stale.Cons: 3-5 Hours of game-play... _childDocuments_.review: If I could give a neutral rating I would but alas it failed to meet my expectations. To start off with the positives; it is a rather pretty artistic game with what seems like a good story that does some genuine fun things with the puzzles. I like the art and there is a lot of really fun small parts of the game that are rather enjoyable, such as the more jokey fun pictures that hide stuff or are just for fun.However there is a reason I am giving it a negative review. At it's core it is a puzzle game and the puzzles are usually way too boring and simple. There are some genuinely good ideas for the mechanics around the puzzles but 4/5 times once you figure it out they do a slight variation of that and that's it. There's about 4 or so variations and they don't ever blend together or expand on it too much like you would expect from something like, Portal that uses more simple mechanics to give much deeper and interesting puzzles. There's also unfortunately the playtime which is more subjective for your experience. The game at it's full price is $25 for what most are getting is a 5 hour experience including the small handful of optional puzzles and screwing around. If that matters to you and think you would like a pretty and fun game with relatively simple puzzles then go for it. I'm obviously a minority here and I'm sure others have had a much better time than me.

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder has a charming puzzle mechanic, brilliantly implemented. The puzzles lean towards the easy side, although I had a few nice aha moments. The final level was a really nice test of the skills that the game teaches you throughout. Unfortunately, where the game really falls flat is the story. I simply could not find any part of myself that cared about any of the characters or the world that they inhabited. On the plus side, there's a cute AI cat that you can pet, although sadly I didn't care about anything that he said either. I think I'm getting a little tired of this puzzle game formula where you're listening to audio tapes about the history of a scientist commune and how they fell apart. This has gotta be the fourth game with this same pattern that I've played, and it rarely does anything for me. The Witness was the first one, and the only one that did it well, in my opinion. The last thing I want to mention is the price. Simply put, this game is overpriced. I paid $35 CAD for it, and for the length and what I got out of it, I think a more comfortable price would have been $25 CAD.Check it out if it's on sale, but I wouldn't recommended it at full price.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: I took my time with this one and finished it up in 10.5 hours, I had a pleasant experience with it. It’s a very unique game, with mechanics Ive never seen used elsewhere before. I tried to figure out most of the puzzles on my own and got stuck at a few places, hence the longer playtime. If you ask me, that’s where the fun lies with this one- figuring everything out for yourself without help. Every stage is easily accessible to play through again, so if you have to hunt for trophies, do that afterwards. It’s really so much fun when you’re stuck for a while and the solution clicks into your mind and you complete the puzzle. The visuals are enjoyable too, strong art direction by this team. The narrative is good also, it’s an interesting tale, one that I only understood mostly (because of how it ends). I think I will go back and play this game again in a few months to enjoy it all over again. This is one of the more unique experiences to come out of the indie scene in 2023, I recommend everyone who likes puzzle games (with a narrative attached) should check this one out.

_childDocuments_.review: A fairly good meal of the cerebral variety, so long as you go in with the right expectations.Viewfinder continues the proud tradition of reality-bending first-person puzzlers with its sequence of well-paced puzzles and the interesting story it tells in their midst. The central gimmick comes in fast and early, but the ways in which you use it continue being varied throughout the whole package. The cadence at which these new twists are added ends up in a "just one more level" kind of experience that's hard to put down, and leaves you wishing for more once its over.But therein also lies a common gotcha with this genre: The experience is usually over fairly quickly, and replay value is very light. Viewfinder is no different in this regard, and you need to keep that in mind going in. No puzzle concept gets dragged out beyond one or two iterations, which imposes a hard limit on how long your playthrough can last. So long as you're fine with that limit, though? It's a really good puzzle game.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey look, it's a tree! I've heard about those!Viewfinder is a fun puzzle game similar to Portal and Superliminal, but unlike those OGs it did not live up to its full potential. While Viewfinder is still an engaging, creative game, the core mechanics have the capacity to really open up exploration and secrets that the game just doesn't have.After earning all achievements there are a few interesting areas you can miss, but nothing like the secrets of Superliminal or the back rooms of Portal. Aside from the optional challenge levels, the difficult in this game felt lower as well. Later levels only increase the challenge through artificial difficulty rather than more advanced use of established mechanics, like Portal.There is no reward for beating the game, no developer's commentary which is really missing in a game like this, plus going back through levels for collectibles is annoying when the level select isn't even labeled.But, these complaints are minor. The game itself is brilliant and fun all the way through, with some levels that are open to unique solutions.

_childDocuments_.review: This might be the single most technically impressive game i have ever seen.AnywaysThe story is mediocre and forgettable and the puzzles start out bad and transition into decent towards the end of the game, occasionally sparking some of those aha moments you get when solving good puzzles. The game and it's world look nice but forgettable and the music is there.Yet I still really like this game.There are a number of games based around subverting... physics, a good example being superliminal, but none come even close to the jaw-dropping ridiculousness of this game's picture mechanic and what makes it truly special is that they didn't stop there. New mechanics and features, all unbelievably well-made and seamless get thrown at the player at a breakneck pace and before you even have a chance to relocate your jaw (and the game starts introducing some mechanics made to constrain the player's ability in order to facilitate actual puzzle design), the game is already halfway over.Go play the game, you'll be blown away by what is possible.

_childDocuments_.review: My recommendation for this game is more about how enjoyable the vibes and gameplay are. It's a pretty chill game for the most part--nice and mellow puzzle game. I'd say most of the puzzles are fairly easy to solve (there's a couple I just couldn't figure out which bugged me a bit but I still enjoyed the game). I only really have two big issues with it: 1) Game Length v. Cost: It took me about 6 hrs to complete the game. When I purchased the game it was about 20 USD. I'm not super bothered by the price because the game is BEAUTIFUL and you get this soothingly voiced cat that you can pet on almost every level. But I also probably wouldn't have bought the game if I new the duration/cost relationship.2) Forever Tutorial: The game feels like you're in a part of the game where you're being taught how to play the whole time and never turned loose to solve a bunch of stuff on your own. Every level feels more like a "this is how this mechanic works" and less like "let's see what you've learned" or "here's a challenge that will require you to put everything you know together."Still a great game. I'd love to see more stuff like this.

A slider or even something out of 5 stars would be much preferred.As an Aussie, I will be pointing out this game is (at time or writing) $36.50 Dollarydoos. Which is... Significant, considering how much 'game'you get for it.I would like to point out the game mechanics of what makes this fun and interesting was never brought to question. I quite enjoyed the game mechanics of this puzzling experience, even if on the short side.One annoyance to me was the voice actor and dialoge at the beginning. Was a little harsh and clunky on the ears, but does  improve a little, halfway through and onward. The Second voice Actor though, was enjoyable and fine to listen to throughout.The Story or 'plot'of Viewfinder, however is its biggest weakness. Where I believe a game such as "Sumperliminal" is superier, at least, from my perspective. (yes yes, bad dad joke)To again compare the two games, Superliminal has roughly similar content (maybe smaller, depends how you wish to define it, I do in the sence of what there is to do, how much fun it is, and polish regarding how smoothly everything runs), and a similar level of quality, in general as well.However Superliminal is cheaper & has a workshop. _childDocuments_.review: : Puzzle: ~4 hours to complete.   ~6 hours to 100%.: Easy: Cozy: Heavily Stylized and Stunning: Simple and easy to understand.  SUMMARY: If you want to appreciate this game, look at the creativity of the puzzles, how the components of the previous levels build upon themselves to form something pleasing, and how the game poses questions like "What happens if I sever this wire" or "what happens if I take a picture of myself" and lets you answer those questions yourself.  This game is more a work of art than one of cryptic logic, and I think it understands that, as it starts you in Aahron's hub first to showcase it's beauty and creativity.Don't expect to be wowed by eureka effect moments, as the game is quite easy.  No level took me longer than two minutes and only one optional puzzle stumped me to the point that I had to stop and think.  Don't expect to be moved by the story. It's basic, a little melancholic, and, frankly put, a little melodramatic; but that's not a huge deal because it's quietly living in the background of the game 99% of the time.  I did   All-in-all, when the story is being showcased it has a very "humanity opened Pandora's Box, but we found hope at the bottom" feel to it, which might be someone's jam, but isn't mine.If you're looking for a comfy weekend with a puzzle (which I was at the time), this game is a perfect 7/7. On any other day, I'd still give a 5/7, leaning towards a 4/7, so it gets a thumbs up from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently the top rated review says: "I don't like the phone lady character and I found a good chunk of the puzzles to be frustratingly unintuitive, but I don't think those are things that over shadow the good parts of this game. Got to the cat character and have zero desire to continue.   Also, I wasn't expecting the game to be "levels" that you enter via a hub world.  Based on early cutscenes/moments, they could have made this a tight linear experience with better pacing and less lore filler.   No "hub world/level select" is necessary here.

_childDocuments_.review: A short but sweet puzzle game; the surreal setting works incredibly well and punching holes into reality with photos never gets old. Unfortunately, partially owing to its short length, puzzles never get a chance to be complex - some really interesting mechanics appear only for a few levels to never be seen again. Story is probably best ignored - the underlying message has some merit, but that's the only good thing I can say about it.Regarding a certain timed sequence near the end: while I generally despise timed puzzles, this one is not particularly strict if you utilize the intended shortcuts; it also helps that the time limit is explicitly shown at all times. You probably won't beat it on the first try, but knowing what challenges lie ahead helps you optimize your photo collection. And if you still have an issue with it and would rather keep it chill, timer can be disabled entirely in the accessibility settings.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. The atmosphere, the story telling, the sound design, the little details and funny achievements.. _childDocuments_.review: This game will take your brain and snap it clean in two, and I love it. This feels like a prototype of a Valve game, like something that could have easily been set within the walls of Aperture Science. That said, unlike Portal, the story and atmosphere are not nearly as strong, the game really tries to have a narrative but sadly falls short, The audio logs and narration end up feeling like more of a annoyance than something that adds to the experience, tacked on after the fact to check a box. I'm excited to see more from these devs in the future, I'd be fine if it was this same set of mechanics but in a different setting with new puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: Right off the bat - get this game at a discount. Would recommend, but not at that price.Viewfinder is a unique puzzle game, and a constant rollercoaster of "how was this even programmed"?. If you loved the likes of The Witness and Superliminal, you'll love this too. It's worth playing just for the experience alone, as there's nothing quite like it.The premise is rather simple - you can take any sort of print, be it a photo or a painting, and "paste" its contents into the playable space, overwriting everything that's in front of you. This allows the player to warp the space as needed, and come up with unorthodox solutions and paths, sometimes even completely breaking the levels.  It's easy to pick up and eventually master, and it's clearly been polished to a mirror sheen, as I haven't experienced a single bug or issue surrounding this mechanic.Alas, the puzzle aspect itself is... a bit weak. Aside from about 3 proper head-scratchers (including all of the optional challenges and the very last level), none of the levels took me more than 5 minutes to complete, either because the solution was fairly straightforward and easy to figure out, or because the nature of the player's available tools allowed me to just break/cheese some of the levels. I unironically liked being stuck in puzzles in games like Portal and The Talos Principle, and Viewfinder felt like a breeze in comparison. Perhaps if the puzzles were bigger in scope or more elaborate.The art is pretty, the music suits the game perfectly (if not particularly memorable, but that's ambience for you), and the lore/story are very barebones. As can be seen by my playtime at the time of writing, it's also rather short, clocking in at about 5 hours.It felt more like a tech showcase. One that's definitely worth experiencing, but also one that could be expanded upon with even harder puzzles to realize its full potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Viewfinder

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzle mechanics at the core of Viewfinder are incredible. Unfortunately, upon my completion of the game, I felt like it failed to fully realize the potential of its ideas. There was so much more the game could've done with these exciting and novel mechanics, but in the end it decided to play it relatively safe.The narrative was bland which led to me ignoring it; the setting certainly didn't do the story any favors. On top of that some of the narrators were written unusually and their lines were delivered in a jarring manner, breaking my immersion in the game. The puzzles were always strong, and there were a number of interesting perspective puzzle styles spread throughout the game. But again, it just felt like they were only scratching the surface of what they could do.Overall, I would still recommend Viewfinder due to the strength of its core puzzle mechanics. Hopefully the developers are able to make a sequel that further expands upon its unique ideas.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get this out of the way:  It is worth your money, and most importantly, your time. - The story is one long sigh and eye roll. It attempts to tackle a difficult problem and tries to use big words while coming off as simplistic: it assumes you believe the premise (a rag tag group can solve climate change with a few lines of code), then works hard to prove you're wrong (there are no easy solutions) then defeats itself in the end (...maybe, with this MacGuffin plant!).- The characters are an exercise of "tell, don't show". It is assumed you like the characters, while giving you no reason to like them, save for the cat. Exposition like "this character is very smart and likeable!" is not a compelling reason to think that they are.- The voice of the phone lady will probably sound very annoying to anyone outside of California. The other voices are unremarkable, only the cat sounds good.- Music was very unremarkable.- Sound design was good! Those purple blocks were a highlight in this case.- The visuals are pleasing and relaxing.- The puzzles are very simple, and sometimes you might feel condescended by being told "what a genius you are!" after putting the square block in the square hole. I often postponed the solution just to look around a level and see if there was something to break or a different solution.If you liked games like ,  and , you'll like this, despite what I feel are shortcomings.

_childDocuments_.review: Very smart and unique puzzler. _childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but my initial fears ended up being completely true. It has a very charming aesthetic and a wonderfully unique puzzle mechanic, but unfortunately, it doesn't really make good use of its potential. The whole game is beatable in just a few hours and there's really not a lot of puzzles, especially not at a 25 dollar pricepoint. The puzzles that ARE there are generally very easy, and a solid 4/5 of them are beatable on first pass after just looking around and seeing what tools you have available with no sort of critical thinking required. There were exactly two times I actually felt even a little bit clever about finding the solution, but most of the time felt like I was just sort of walking in a straight line to the end. The story isn't anything interesting either. The "twist" wasn't satisfying or thematically interesting in any way, which assumes I had a reason to be emotionally invested in the first place, which I really didn't. CAIT is a nice companion character, at the very least, but that doesn't salvage the fact that the story surrounding him is a thematic mess and the only moral of the story is that programmers make poor project leads. There's maybe three different ways I could've interpreted what the 'point' was, and none of them were told well. If that was what they were going for, then I guess that's great, because you really nailed writing an unsatisfying nothingburger of a story with no emotional beats whatsoever.All in all this game really just feels like a tech demo for a marvelous concept, put in the hands of people who had no idea how to actually make puzzles with it (or write compelling stories). If this had community levels or something it might salvage my opinion significantly, but as it stands it just feels like a game about a tenth as fun or as interesting as The Talos Principle with one cool gimmick. This is a game I'd feel very comfortable spending five to ten dollars on, because it's going to last you exactly one afternoon and then you'll forget about it forever.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - great game, some wasted potential, but certainly worthwhile and worth its price.Pros:+ Beautiful visuals+ Inspired gameplay mechanics/interactions+ Ethereal background music+ CAIT! You can pet the cat!Cons:- Puzzles are not challenging- A bit pricey for a 3- to 5-hour game- A lot of wasted potential in disposable mechanics- Lacks replayabilityThis is one of the most beautiful games I have experienced, right alongside the likes of Portal 1/2 and Control (despite being in completely different genres and different leagues of difficulty). The visuals was the first thing that caught my eye, and the gameplay mechanics solidified the game's grasp on me. It is achingly beautifully crafted and I can find many scenes or shots that I can make into a wallpaper. The way photos interact with existing environment is mind-blowing the first time you experience it. Some levels are equal parts artwork and mind-f**k. Many levels feel disposable, but there is a respectable level of detail put into them to make the story work. There are also a lot of mini paintings that contain mini games or a sneak-peek into different worlds. I'm sure I missed as many as I found, but they make it worth it to take your time with the levels and not to rush through them in a speedrun.Having read some of the other reviews, I will echo the complaints about the puzzles being too easy and the game being too short (for its price). I didn't find any of the levels challenging - save for one optional level in World 4. Some levels felt repetitive, and the solutions mirror their repetition. Many of the elements of the game are seemingly abandoned as soon as they are introduced (photocopier and visual distortion, to name two), never to be revisited until . Someone called it a tutorial for game journalists, and I find it truthful and reductive. Last but certainly not least, the story is not particularly compelling, and the nicest thing I can say is that it's better than not having any direction or objective at all.Despite all those valid complaints - and the fact that the complaints paragraph is longer than my praises - I don't think they detract at all from how much of a technical and visual marvel this game truly is. I rarely, if at all, write reviews for games, and , ladies and gentlemen, deserve its place in the history of video games for its creativity. The positive aspects way outshines any shortcomings, and I consider the price I pay an investment to help the studio create bigger and better games that hopefully can be as visually striking as this.

_childDocuments_.review: “Viewfinder” is a truly masterpiece and a godsend for all visuals, from the game colors simply impossible to take a look away! It's eye-catching, calming, and magnetic. The color palette truly creates a sense of safety, a dream-like feeling. The spaces (rooms, levels) in this game are gorgeous. It makes being in them more precious and delightful. The plot and passage of levels (for lovers of visuals) can even go to the background, and most of the game time will be spent on the explore such unusual spaces. One can spend several hours viewing every little thing, every plant, and finally be inspire by the views and the overall picture of the level. The game's puzzles are mesmerising in the fact that they constantly need a new attitude, as well as an analysis of the situation and location. Some are fairly simple, while others force to reconsider everything that was before and solve them in a totally new way. Due to the low number of levels, the game does not get annoying, and thanks to the various gameplay mechanics (which are used to pass the puzzles) will not get dull or lose the interest! It's tempting to move forward, go from teleport to teleport, throw a challenge to physics (the game exactly provides this opportunity), crash the levels, fool around and do everything that comes into mind. And the “Viewfinder” will only reward it all! So, don't be afraid to think outside the box, because that's exactly what the game is waiting for ;)From now on, let turn to the plot of this game. The hero is not just sent to the simulation, as it may seem from the very beginning. There is a certain and very important purpose, which changes a bit with the time of staying in the simulation. This goal is unknown to the player from the start, and the friend who accompanies the hero on this journey (outside the simulation) and supports his state of life doesn't quite immediately reveal all cards. The story itself immersion is quite slow, practically unnoticeable.Wandering through the spaces, the protagonist gets to know the life of the creators of the simulation, and namely a group of people of completely different professions and characters, who are united by one goal. Here the player will not be able to see their faces or communicate with them. All the information about the creators is presented through notes, and through recording their voices on a gramophone. It's incredibly interesting to immerse in their stories, to watch them become close, have fun, figure out new things, reach some scientific (and not only) conclusions, but also to notice their slow and unstoppable madness and frustration. Their story is certainly riveting and once again makes an important global issue come to mind. It wouldn't be exciting at all if I continue to deepen into the plot, it's better to experience all these emotions on your own while exploring such an unrivaled game.As well as the protagonist's friend and a group of simulation makers, there's another important character in the game. Truly, how not to mention the charming little companion who will follow the player through the levels - a cat called CAIT. It will not help to solve the puzzles, it will only encourage with a warm speech for their fulfilment. With its low and velvety voice, the cat will gently comment the actions by telling more about the simulation and the people who made it. CAIT will always look at player with a look full of love and kindness, and cheer up the hero with the right, meaningful words. Its voice will haunt throughout the game, and petting this cute cat will become a little ritual (because it purrs very sweetly and loudly)! Finally, I would be pleased to say that this game really has impressed me to the depths of my soul, leaving me with indescribable feelings and bringing a totally unique gaming experience. "Viewfinder" provided me with a lot of joy, an incredible impression, I want to talk about it non-stop! This game really blows the mind, makes all visuals fall in love with it, forces to view the things from different viewpoints, and it's a genuine brilliant among 3D puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: ‘Puzzle game but with a narrative’ is a subgenre that has to deliver said narrative effectively and efficiently to avoid bogging its gameplay down or coming across as pretentious. In Viewfinder’s case, it doesn’t fail in these regards, but it feels like the story was injected for the sake of something to follow along with. Thankfully, the optional nature of Viewfinder’s story doesn’t get in the way of some excellent, brain-racking puzzle-solving that encourages low-risk experimentation.Viewfinder’s main puzzle concepts are twofold: ‘Overlaying’ pictures into the world and playing with perspective. Puzzles are spaced out between sets of levels that introduce these concepts and new spins on them regularly. For example, you’ll find a picture of a walkway that you can overlay into the world to make it usable in crossing a gap, whereas a later level will require you to make copies of a picture to traverse multiple gaps. The game is elegant with introducing a new concept and letting you play around to understand it thanks to the rewind feature, so even if a puzzle is a real stumper, there’s no punishment for experimenting and/or failing.The ‘modular’ format of these mechanics means they can be added or removed to levels, changing the tools at your disposal and what possible solutions there might be. In one instance, you’re taught that overlaying a picture into the world can shear away walls that create new corners to traverse, but shearing electronics or power lines renders them broken. You’re given a camera at one point to take your own pictures, but another level will severely limit how much film you get to play with. I encourage you to watch the trailer for a visual demonstration of some of these mechanics, as it’s hard to explain how delightfully jarring these effects can be by words alone.Save for an instance near the end of the game and occasions where timing is necessary, Viewfinder has a peaceful pace for letting you solve things on your own time and take in the environments. Levels are compact but there are side paths here and there to look for collectibles, optional tasks and explore more of the narrative (despite how swiss-cheesed it is). Viewfinder is backed by a soundtrack that I’d call ‘lo-fi jazz’, sometimes leaning towards one genre or the other depending on the track. Combined with the visuals of a constructed ‘cyber-work space’ with impossible yet pleasing architecture laden with solid, full colors, I was surprised at how relaxed I was during my playtime, even if a puzzle was absolutely trouncing me.Viewfinder’s only real stumbling point is its narrative. Without going into too many spoilers, it’s discovered that these landscapes your player character is placed inside of were created for the sake of a project. Between audio logs, notes and dialogue, it’s apparent that within the project and the people behind it, not all was well and is what leads to the game’s starting point. It’s all fine and good, however there’s so little information shared between such apparent gaps in time that I found it challenging to keep up - Or even really care to. Most of the lore being shared is just internal musings, resulting in disconnects between the story-telling and gameplay that it’s rare for one ever to recognize the other. The game’s overarching theme of trying to find answers when there may not be one is ultimately undercut by its own ending, complete with an illusion of choice that comes across as disingenuous.I finished Viewfinder in about five and a half hours, including going after some optional collectibles/levels. Other than going for one hundred percent completion, trying to solve puzzles differently or going for better times, Viewfinder doesn’t have much by way of replay value, making the $32.50 (CAD) asking price steep. With how levels can be solved in open-ended or unintended ways sometimes, I would’ve liked to see a custom-level tool and sharing system as that’d certainly extend its shelf life. Still, for what’s on offer with this elegant, modular way of presenting puzzles and being a pleasant experience altogether, Viewfinder gets my recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is as if Life is Strange and Superliminal had a child, and that child was raised by the likes of Portal and The Witness (and the games that those two games inspired).  I say that because in this game, you place pictures (like LiS), but the stuff in those pictures becomes reality in a perspective-y way (like Superliminal).  There are other mechanics too, such as this game's version of the ol' box & button mechanic (and others, which I won't mention because it gets spoilery).  The difficulty curve is nice, but it kinda ramps up by Chapter 4 (mid-late game), which is where I'm at now.  Still, there is a (slow — they want you to really think and be creative first and foremost) hint system if you're stuck.Apart from the music (nice, relaxing ambient... kinda like Superliminal), art (dreamy, with lots of places to sit... like LiS), and aforementioned gameplay, one other thing worth mentioning is that the default settings are actually 100% quality for once — I didn't need to tweak a single thing!  And of course most things are fully adjustable if you need them to be.  Finally, most of the achievements are also quality ones, too — they actually reward you for doing little side things instead of your typical "progression" and "secret" achievements.Lastly, the narrative.  Apparently this game takes place in  where , so   Meanwhile,   Also there's a digital cat whom you can pet to your heart's content. All in all, I'd say this game is worth the full price!  I happened to get it on sale, but seeing it as it is, it is a marvel to behold.

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a very cool game that is just plain fun to play!  Armed with only a camera, you are faced with a sequential set of spatial puzzles. You take photos and pick up pictures/documents that can then be used to manipulate the environment.  Need to cross a gap?  No problem! Take a picture of a column, turn it sideways, and use it as a bridge.There is a backstory told through recordings and voice mails. Honestly, I was drawn to the puzzles and the narrative did not add to (or subtract from) my enjoyment of the game. What I loved the most is that, despite many levels with the same goal (activating and using a teleporter to exit), it never got boring or repetitive. The mechanics and landscape change and there are a great many delightful moments along the way. Pick up a postcard or a bar code, apply it to the environment, and step inside to see what you can find. There are collectibles to locate and some funny moments as you earn certain achievements.The 'rewind' feature, which allows you to undo one or more action, is a great tool. It lets you experiment, without penalty, until you find a workable solution to your current situation. The game does a good job of adding new mechanics and helping you build your expertise but the best learning comes from the mistakes you make.  Progress is auto-saved on exit and you can leave or reset a level without losing achievements or collectibles. If you exit a level without finishing it, you'll be returned to the original environment and any modifications you had made in the landscape or pictures you've taken will need to be repeated. Levels are fairly short so this was never a burden.Completionists will appreciate that there are no missable achievements. You can circle back to any completed level, at any time, and perform forgotten tasks or pick up overlooked items. The final chapter has a timed sequence that might sound like a deal-breaker for some gamers. No worries!  The developers provide an accessibility option to turn the timer off without penalty (thank you!).  I take no shame in admitting it took me 28 minutes to finish the final area (instead of maybe 10 that the timer would have allowed).  For me, the victory was in working out the solutions and completing the area.If you enjoy creative problem solving in a very interesting environment, then I highly recommend Viewfinder. For me, my time playing was filled with 'Eureka!' moments when I solved something and big smiles when I encountered the unexpected.

_childDocuments_.review: Viewfinder is a rather difficult game to talk about. If you judge it solely by watching trailers and screenshots, then yes, it seems truly breathtaking. Beautiful. Revolutionary, even. It offers perhaps the most fresh, mind-bending take on puzzle mechanics since the release of Braid in 2008. And, mind you, it works exactly as advertised, no trickery involved. You really do transform levels by superimposing photos, using postcards, pictures on the walls and all sorts of other imagery. Viewfinder sparks almost childlike wonder that is very rarely seen in videogames, and the last puzzle game that managed to do the same for me was Portal.That capacity to dazzle and make the player's jaw drop, to marvel at all the possibilities that the gameplay offers, is a good reason to recommend Viewfinder in and of itself. Sad Owl Studio did a fantastic job at creating an enticing mystery box. It's short, sweet and embodies what all videogames should strive for: raw creativity given form.If, however, you're looking for a good game that will leave a lasting impression, then Viewfinder suddenly becomes somewhat difficult to recommend, and all for very disappointing reasons. You see, it has a truly unique core mechanic, but nothing really to show for it. Viewfinder doesn't evolve, it doesn't challenge the player in the same ways that Portal, or even its many derivatives manage to do. Solving a level rarely feels satisfying: it's more like going through the motions and just repeating the same trick taught by the game at the start of each section.Puzzles are often painfully formulaic and predictable. Sure, the game does introduce new elements fairly regularly, but it never demands player to pay attention, remember previous lessons or look at the problem from a different angle. Which is hilariously ironic for a game that is, supposedly, all about perspective. The only exception to this is the very last puzzle in the whole game, where Viewfinder actually rewards attentive players and allows for clever solutions.Yes, i understand that Sad Owl Studio might have had good reasons for why the game turned out this way. Superimposing photos might be tough to wrap your head around for some people, which is why the devs decided to turn the difficulty down a notch. The problem is, Viewfinder has nothing else to offer. It sincerely tries to tell a compelling story, but falls tragically short and never does anything even remotely interesting with its premise. The game has all the necessary narrative components to truly tug at your heartstrings and make the player question everything they see, and yet... Nothing. Just bland, sometimes too saccharine, sometimes too on the nose messaging.In the end, the only thing Viewfinder really has going for it is a stellar core mechanic that never flourishes to its full potential. It's very easy to praise, but, unfortunately, even easier to forget. Like a curio or a conversation starter in someone's living room. No matter how groundbreaking the game seems in action, it desperately needs more interesting puzzles or a better story to support the beautiful idea underneath. Alas, it has neither. But i hope that Sad Owl Studio's next project will be just as peculiar.
