_childDocuments_.review: The best modern fighting game?Played for nearly 100 hours on PS5 in the first month... came to PC to play more (and with mods and less input lag). Still not tired of it and loving learning more and more. Some of the best 2D-3D graphics you will ever see in an anime fighter. Arcsys absolutely killed it. The animations are extremely smooth, lighting and particle effects are so beautiful, character design is unique and enticing. The cut-scenes when doing supers are outrageous and big, which gives the game even more character. Loading screen is an Eagle soaring to the battlefield, Guilty Gear just  style. From the moment you hop in, you will see how quick you have to think to excel at Guilty Gear -Strive-. They have a burst system to escape from corner pressure and combos, wall-break, and a beautiful EXCELLENT system called Roman Cancels (RCs). There are 4 types of RCs; blue, purple, red, and yellow -- all of which have a specific usage and can slow enemies, guard break enemies, and extend combos. Roman Cancels and wall-breaks is where a lot of the depth comes in and you'll have a lot of fun labbing out combos and finding the optimal way to break walls by canceling moves and extended combos. I've made it to the Celestial floor, which is above floor 10, and let me tell you the matches are very fast paced and entertaining. Even "low-tier" characters have great players up here and if you really love competitive fighting games you'll be right at home. If you're familiar with Guilty Gear, you will know just how awesome the characters are. Returning are a ton of fan favorites like King Ky Kiske, the Super-Speed ninja Chipp, the iron-clad grappling Potemkin, the witch of hard rock, I-No and many more. The new characters are just as unique -- including an undead vampire who has a blood gauge mechanic and a secret service member who fights with a spirit dog by her side. Add in the first DLC character, the defense secretary Gold Lewis Dickinson and you have a really unique cast.There's also a ton of different play styles to chose from here. You got your rushdowns like Chipp and Leo, your grappler in Potemkin, all-arounders like Ky, and big beefy damage dealers like Nago. There's also a good amount of unique characters like I-No and Anji that are hard to classify because of their interesting toolkit. Basically, there's a character for everyone in this game, 15 characters may seem small but there's great variety in that pool and tons of depth with every character. This is pretty self explanatory but ArcSys's netcode is among the best in the industry. Great rollback, even games with 100+ ping can feel alright (assuming they have a  LAN connection). The ranked "floor" system they have makes sure you're against players of the same skill level -- It places you on a floor from 1-10 based on a game with a bot, and you will either go down or up floors based off your matches. There's also parks for more casual games but I highly suggest trying it out rather than fighting such a wide range of skill levels in the parks. It will be hard to learn playing someone from floor 3 then someone from floor 10 all in a 2 match span. So admittedly the game has only been out for a month so metas can still shift, but as far as a first version of a fighting game goes, Guilty Gear -Strive- is pretty close to perfect. There is a couple exceptions to that rule:. To explain how good this character is, you have to understand that Dustloop, the official wiki of Guilty Gear frame data, has Sol listed as having 0 weaknesses. None.- You might think this would be such a big problem that everyone would play Sol and Sol would be winning every competitive tournament. You would be . So far in tournament play, Sol is not the most winning character. In fact, there's a few characters with more tournament wins than Sol so far. Sure, he is the most played character online, but if you really wanted to you could just cancel any match with him (you have to accept to start a match). This really helps exemplify how good the balance is in the base game and how you can outplay a character that is "better than your character".- Anji and Faust need help... Like, a lot of help. Faust players have had a couple deep tournament runs, but with a couple buffs both of them could be a lot more viable. They both have really unique toolkits, so it'd be interesting to see how they'd do with a bit better frame data or damage.  The story continues, just as crazy as the previous games. If you take the time to learn the backstory (the story timeline they provide is GREAT and super detailed), you will learn to love the wackiness of Guilty Gear. From a blind-blonde-dude brought back from the dead that fights with a demon by his side, to the ninja who beat crack addiction with ninjitsu and became president of his own kingdom, this game really will reward you if you learn the lore. This game is excellent. You will find a character you love if you put in the time. If you learn the RC system and how to optimize wall-break, this game will be unlike anything you've ever played. It's both the most accessible Guilty Gear game yet, and a deep game at the top level. Enjoy the rollback netcode. I just wrote a novel about it and most of my reviews are super short. Daisuke puts a lot of love into this game, and it really shows. The community is great and mods are aplenty. Come learn the

_childDocuments_.review: Strive has been out for two years now, and while it has certainly come a long way in that time, it is still somewhat flawed. While the in-game rollback netcode is great, the online lobby system sucks. Much of the flavour & personality of older GG titles is also absent.That being said, the core gameplay is extremely well-thought-out and is what keeps me coming back to Strive. The universal system mechanics are open-ended and fun, while streamlined character kits make it easy to put together a solid gameplan and then refine it with minimal friction. I would consider Strive the best in the genre at making the real "meat" of fighting games accessible to newer players, as well as those who just want to play more and grind less.

_childDocuments_.review: One of, if not THE best anime fighter if you're looking to get into the genre. It has everything, from very simple and fun characters like Giovanna, Sol and Ky to very complex high execution characters like Happy Chaos, Zato-1 and Jack-O, STRIVE has something for everyone. The Roman Cancel system brings player expression to the forefront and the combo system, while still true to the anime fighting game genre basics, is much more streamlined and requires much less memorization.While the online lobby functionality could (and should) be better, you won't find better netcode in any other japanese fighting game on the market. Incredible art direction, amazing soudtrack, fun and expressive gameplay, STRIVE is the generation's best fighting game so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Guilty Gear is a very important series to me and strive has cemented itself as something i will never forget,Seeing friends from all walks of life play and work to better themselves at the game stands as a testament to the success of the games mission. STRIVE is more than a subtitle, but a theme at the core of the game that is reinforced by everything inside it, from the story mode, the music, and even the very useless and cheesy and of match analysis the game does for you. The game invites you through its iconic and diverse characters, stays in your memory from its wide array of fantastic music, and keeps you playing and learning with its simple and satisfying game play, all to reinforce its theme of STRIVE-ing to be better.Strive is not a perfect game by any means, there is plenty to complain about, but at its core lies something to be cherished and remembered, that burning desire to improve that i saw in all of my friends picking up the game, is something that can happen to anyone that picks up the game, and i will never forget the memories I've made, seeing my friends finally kick my ass and being so excited for them despite me losing.Guilty Gear STRIVE is a game anyone can pick up, something that can inspire anyone to improve, pick it up and have some fun with your friends, i promise fighting games aren't so scary.

TL;DR : Game good, lobby trash, please fix and it's the best fighting game experience one can imagine.

_childDocuments_.review: A great fighter for new players but still has a high skill ceiling for advanced players. I am by no means a "pro" at fighting games even though I have played them for a long time, but this Guilty Gear has been the easiest one to get some of my friends into that are worried about getting stomped online. There are few things that help this, the lobby rankings (just use quick match and not the hobbo hotel lobby) actually give people some good match ups and you have to do a tutorial to get placed, which from what I have seen does a good job. The only way you are moving up is by doing better, but you also wont be frustrated because the game essentially has anti-surfing lobbies, so everyone you fight against is around your level too. The other thing that helps this be great for players new to fighters is the Rollback Netcode, no longer do you have to worry about dropped inputs or massive delay, this is hands down the BEST online netcode for a fighting game ever. Visually it's great, Music is great and it's great for new and pro players, if you want a fighting game, buy this for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: A bloody great fighter, a fun as hell metal album and a lengthy anime season all wrapped up in one stupidly pretty package.It's noticeably more grounded than previous games, much less emphasis on long air combos, but it's still unmistakably Guilty Gear. You're still encouraged to play aggressive because that's what rapidly fills up your Tension bar to spend on supers and Roman Cancels, and every character still has their own wildly different brand of utter shenanigans - ONLY May can lock you down with a cacophony of dolphins, ONLY Faust can toss out random crap that confounds both players, ONLY Potemkin can snap your tiny health bar in half with a single command grab.And the sheer amount of effort Strive puts into helping you approach and understand all this is commendable. Your move list has useful text info and video demonstrations of every tool your character's got, and the Mission mode's a rock solid walkthrough that steadily teaches you many genre fundamentals - from how to anti-air, to how to approach a zoner keeping you away, to what do to against a particular opponent's most common attacks.Where it stumbles somewhat is its online performance. Not because of the rollback-based netcode - no, that's doing a great job making matches feel like you're playing offline - but the cube-people lobby system being awfully clumsy and slow to get those matches started. In my experience the "Find Players While Training" button's been much quicker and more reliable.

_childDocuments_.review: Guilty Gear Strive is a good game to get engaged and involved with the genre of fighting games. Compared to previous entries in the franchise, the game has "had the fat trimmed" leading to more simplified basic gameplay, making it more accessible to complete beginners, while the Roman Cancel system allows for very high skill expression for more advanced players to keep the game exciting after hundreds and thousands of hours.If you're interested in becoming part of the FGC, Strive is a great game to learn fighting games. There's plenty of resources to learn and active players. I've personally had some issues with the ranked system because of connection issues and skill gap on floor 10 but the netcode is miles better than most online fighting games,While the generic orchestral score is boring in the story mode, the character themes and the other vocal tracks in the game are amazing, each one providing great insight into what every character's personal struggle or philosophy is. The characters are also crazy and cool and each one is unique while providing vastly different gameplay styles so there's something for everyone, I bet. If you ever get bored, there's plenty of mods available that are easy to install and use, so the game can always be kept fresh and improved.For those looking for a single player experience, I'd look elsewhere. The modes provided are bare-bones and the story mode is effectively just a long movie.

_childDocuments_.review: Ive been a fan of this series since xx and i kinda stopped liking it since xrd. I didnt like the 3d incorporations then, didnt like the roster, didnt like a lot. This game outdoes itself with things I do not enjoy and a small few that I do. I bought this game twice, once to see if it was as bad as I imagined it was going to be while still playing every game in the franchise like a simp and the second to make my friend feel obligated to play and feel the pain that is what GG has become. Now im kinda just playing online to feel like I got my money worth to a degree.1. Visuals: The effects are excessive and I have to look away at the screen sometimes to give my eyes a break. Sometimes watching other people play is clouded with so much ♥♥♥♥ I get lost in unimportant information like the ever bigger combo count or sparks flying over the whole screen. The models arent that great to me, everyone looks odd in one way or another. ky's hands are 1.5 times the size of his head. The screen freezing whenever you get counter hits with giant letters throws me off for sure as well as the constantly changing camera angles. The new dusts capture this very well, took me a few times before i even knew when I could press a button to attack again. These are the same issues as xrd but so much worse to me. It may make me go back to xrd and give it an honest chance at this point.2. gameplay: this game has essentially become street fighter with less technicality and more exaggerated moves. my fingers are like 2x faster than I have to play this game at. I feel so restricted and the characters feel hella gutted. if i do a jab, i can only do a special or forward punch to special (at least for the few chars I played). I keep finding myself just feeling  trapped in my decision making. In XX you could express yourself through when you chose to roman cancel, what kind of gatling combos you did, the movement you chose to do. Now...its kinda all the same, a massive loss of personality to me. The wall splats and wall breaks both being unenjoyable to me but I understand the direction choice. I dont agree with the less hits as a combo choice though, as its just another way to not be able to express yourself. 3. Online. People talk about a good online and I think its good. better than some games i suppose, but man I would much rather play UNIST (which is what i find myself doing). I dont know if maybe its the mechanics of the game, but i get grabbed while my leg is inside their body and other weird stuff to me. The lobby was atrocious and maybe they fixed matching as I couldnt even see people when putting in their exact codes. I couldnt play people I bought the game for to try and find a way to enjoy it so I lost a lot of enthusiasm there as well. 4. What do I like then: well, the roman cancel time stopping is something I do and dont like. I wish there was no time stopping at all, as xrd had projectile issues that made the game feel wonky to fluctuate between speeds all the time. Now its better but I still wish it was removed entirely. The missions are pretty decent for teaching the basics, but if you wanted a game for beginners why not make one than choose something with like 50 missions that require very specific inputs to complete them (Things like the backdash on wakeup is so particular about the timings). This goes to say that the buffering is weird in that there is barely any. Maybe they feel you dont need a buffer when the game is so much slower, but I kinda liked things like jump install. Recommended to Newcomers to the series, it lost its combos for high damage counterhits so its pretty accessible. Just not exactly for me. Fans of the XX series will find it slow and pretty repetitive. This is pretty much the same review that Ive seen getting popular and I agree. To me its a disappointment if this represents where fighting games are going though.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd like to tell you a story. A story that'll show you how it FEELS... to play Guilty Gear StriveBefore I got this game, the first things that drew me towards it where of course, the characters and music. The Guilty Gear franchise is well known for its kick-ass soundtrack and ridiculous, high concept characters, and Strive certainly delivers on those fronts. A 10 foot tall reality warping zombie doctor with a bag over his head, a nonbinary scythe wielding bio-weapon who likes sh*BEEP!*y shark movies, a dead guy voiced by Takehito Koyasu? This game has it all!On top of that, every character has a theme song that plays during battle. They convey the stories and personalities of the fighters through their instrumentation and lyrics, and as such they cover a wide range of styles and emotions. The actual characters do a great job expressing themselves too, with stylish animation and top-notch voice acting in 3 different languages (english, japanese, and korean).Beyond the surface level aesthetics, the gameplay was very interesting to me as well. I had never played a fighting game outside of Smash Bros, and all other franchises seemed far to complicated and intense for me. But Strive features much more streamlined characters and mechanics, which made me want to actually try wrapping my head around them. So I went ahead and entered the mayhem.When I first started playing Strive, the character I chose was Ky Kiske. He's the well-rounded, honest character, with a fireball, dragon punch, all the normal things you'd expect from the archetype. This design and playstyle has lead to the fandom joking about Ky as if he's the boring straightman in a game full of larger-than-life characters, and they're not entirely wrong. Ky dresses quite modestly, and speaks with a calm, forgiving demeanor. As the First King of Illirya, he does his best to maintain appearances, staying polite and offical no matter the situation.When I played as him, I barely understood how the game worked, and repeatedly get my teeth kicked in by even amateur players. Ky has an ability called Dragon Install, a 2nd phase of sorts that can only be activated at low health. It's an incredible burst of power, where Ky's elegant presentation cracks for a moment, and he reveals his absolute destructive power. Of course, that's how *KY* uses Dragon Install in-universe. When *I* use it, it's more like a burglar front flipped through my window, kicked the sh*BEEP!* out of me, and now I'm throwing random crap from my kitchen counter at him while shouting obscenities.I felt powerless, like a cornered animal. I'd throw out attacks at complete random, swinging a sword like a toddler with a cool stick. Dragon Install, instead of being an epic last stand, was more of a temper tantrum to cap off my ass-whooping. I thought to myself, "I can't do this. I don't care about tier lists or fancy combos. I just want my opponent to stay away from me. I wish I could stand back, see where my enemy is coming from, and calmly pick out the right move to counter them."And then I remembered that this game has a zoner.His name is Axl Low. He's a time travelling british guy with two magic extendo sickles and I love him. His attacks shoot out absurdly far, and he's got one for every direction an enemy could approach from. The downside is that his attacks have bad recovery, so you have to pick the right ones for the situation to avoid leaving yourself wide open. It's everything I was wanting.Playing Axl was a far more enjoyable experience than Ky, for many reasons. His playstyle is much more in-line with what I want to do, but his different personality contributes as well. Axl is very causal and laid-back, he doesn't take fights seriously and can't help but goof off during a match. His voice delivery is bubbly and tongue-in-cheek. He's the kind of guy that shouts "Yahoo!" while he throws explosives at you. He even ends his defeat scream with a stupid little "augh" to keep your mood up even when you lose.Forgive my sudden cheesy monologue, but know that that's also right at home in a game like this. With Axl, I feel safe, like I'm finally in control of my fate. I feel like I can handle whatever challenges come my way, if I just stay calm and collected. These feelings help me immerse myself in the gameplay, as well as the story behind it all.In my Ultrakill review, I said that I couldn't handle the story's constant violence and despair, and the world of Guilty Gear is occasionally quite similar. It's a world wracked by an ancient war, and every game seems to introduce a new apocalyptic threat. But the tone of these games and their worlds is completely different. It's because of the characters and how they react to the story's events. They make grandiose anime speeches about the goodness in humanity, they build friendships with people in the same situation as them. They're just trying to carve out a life for themselves, and maybe make the world a better place as they go. Also there's way less blood! That's way more up my ally then "murder robot eats corpses and kills god."All these factors, the music, the characters, the animation, the story, come together to create a world that I can care about and feel hopeful for. This game says that by connecting with each other, by seeing how our "fighting styles" mesh together, we can understand ourselves better, and get each other through anything.That's how it FEELS to play Guilty Gear Strive.

_childDocuments_.review: Most fun I've had learning a new fighting game in a very long time. The game's mechanics are pretty straightforward and quick to learn, but leave plenty of depth to be explored. The Roman Cancel system in this game is nuts. It's actually pretty genius how they've made a game that can please casuals and tryhards alike. All of the characters are completely unique and wild with totally different styles, and most importantly the netcode is GREAT.The game isn't perfect yet, though. There's still people running into bugs with the lobby system, and you are going to become very familiar with the COMMUNICATING WITH SERVER message. It takes literally 60-90 seconds to go from pressing start on the splash screen to actually entering the main menu because apparently the game needs to perform the longest, most over-the-top, 500-step secret handshake known to mankind with the game servers before even letting you into the main menu. It's annoying as hell is what I'm saying. _childDocuments_.review: This was my first traditional-style fighting game after playing smash ultimate, and I have to say that its 10x more fun than games like street fighter. In this game, it rewards you for being aggressive and making the moves and has a couple of really fun mechanics to back that up such as the tension meter. The tension meter builds up as you hit people when you land a hit on a enemy, whether they are blocking or not, this leads to:Red roman cancelling, which is a button you can press to extend your combos or link one of your moves into something else which is really fun in combo trials and learning new routes.Purple roman cancelling, which slows down your enemies during the recovery frames of an attack, so it makes a move that is punishable even more so.They also have defensive uses which you can use as a 'get off me' tool with yellow roman cancelNot only is there this, but players are rewarded for backing their opponent into a corner and hitting them. You can do something called a 'Wall break', this happens when you hit a enemy against a wall multiple times, it can then break the wall and give you a tension meter boost (allowing you to use your roman cancels and super more!) as well as dealing great damage to an enemy and putting you in advantage.This means that the game has a lot more depth to it than other more simple traditional fighting games but also rewards players for interacting with each other a lot more than waiting for your opponent to make a mistake.Not only are the games mechanics really fun and well-tunes but the character art and design is incredible. All of the characters look stunning and so do their moves, making the game really easy on the eyes with especially the stages as well which is really fun.The soundtrack is incredible, the music running throughout the game really creating an epic feel and making you feel pumped up to go in and beat your enemy up with the heavy amount of up-beat rock/heavy metal music that is included in the game.The game also includes something that is quite unique to me in my experience of fighting games. It includes a 'dojo' section. This puts you through mini-levels in which you can complete to learn the different mechanics of the game and the niches of them as well in more advanced versions of the dojo since there are beginner, intermediate and expert levels. This helped me greatly in learning the game, instead of relying on dodgy youtube videos that can sometimes be very confusing. There's also other standard things such as training mode and being able to play against CPU's etc... Oh and online has rollback too! Which makes it a LOT more enjoyable of an experience to play online, feels really nice especially if you're playing against someone in the same country (from my experience). And the game also now has crossplay as well, meaning that PC and Console users can combat against each other, so if your friend is lacking a good PC or a PC at all/ Console then you can still play with each other which is really neat.All in all, I would heavily recommend this game to you if you just wanna pick up a unique fighting game thats really fun, especially with friends close to your skill level. Or, if you want to grind it its also really fun as well being able to climb through the ranking system as well. Its really fun, give it a go I'd say, cause I was at first quite reserved but it was a great decision in the end and I don't regret purchasing at all

_childDocuments_.review: Guilty Gear is of the most unique and versatile fighting games out there, now the biggest  caveat to newcomers it’s its own approachability , GG games were always labelled as “hard games” and it’s true to some extent? Regardless Strive is a reset in the series, it definitely feels like they tuned down the mechanics in favour of approachability, it’s a trade-off that can be controversial for some people but ultimately paid off, especially considering how healthy the player base is right now!One of the biggest changes in this game mechanics are wall breaks, rather than making the opponent getting stuck in the corner, now the corners of a stage can break, kinda similar to tekken, but the biggest difference being, both players land in a neutral position that means the losing opponent can get a second chance to comeback, but at the same the winning side gets the tension meter boost it’s a really well thought balance .The initial character roster it’s really interesting and varied, and I think there’s a character for everyone and most of them are easy to get into, including the newcomers. Even more complex characters like zato were streamlined for better approachability so don’t be afraid and pick any character.My only biggest complaint is how the networking works, not necessarily the netcode because oh my goodness the rollback implementation it’s amazing! But the whole lobby system and how long it takes just to connect the server it’s way too long, hopefully will be addressed in future.Tldr: It’s not your Guilty Gear that you are used to but still Guilty gear, great netcode, play it!!

Strive may have many of the same characters from previous GGs, some decent tunes, the good ol' RC system, and enough modern accommodations to please most, but it simply lacks the speed, the freedom, and the attitude of older titles. Many legacy characters have been pruned and pressed into Strive's mold, with plenty still struggling to retain their identity and some abandoning it entirely. Combine this with the slower restrictive nature and lack of defining moves/tools/mechanics, and it leaves a lot to be desired for older fans and veterans of the series. I cannot change the fact that my friends and I have been enjoying GG for nearly 18 years. This has obviously colored our perception of the game and is primarily the reason why most of us moved on to other fighting games. Objectively speaking, I think Strive is an okay game that tries to play it safe, like most modern fighters, but as a Guilty Gear title, I think it misses the mark.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this game for near 250 hours and comparing it to multiple other fighting games ill leave an honest review. The game mechanics and combos are super unique and very fun to use BUT this game has far, FAR too many defensive options. The newest season 3 update has tried to promote more rush down and less defensive options but in turn has just made the more neutral advantageous characters far better. The reason being, some characters struggle more with neutral than others but can easily be pushed out by a plethora of options. You have Gold RC which can act as two different RC's; one to build tension gauge while also resetting back to neutral and the other to stop an opponents block string, and make the opponent negative. Keep that tension gauge in mind.. Now we have burst. Burst can have the ability to completely stop the opponents confirmed combo OR you can use it to apply a defensive barrier (for the cost of 50% burst gauge) and push an opponent back for a punish or a reset back to neutral. It can also be used offensively to nullify a small portion of someone else burst gauge (so they cant break from your combo) as well as hit confirm/corner carry BUT this move is high risk with little reward in the neutral because you can easily be hit out of it with zoning and good buttons. Then we have invulnerable supers. A character can super to counter a gap or certain types of pressure for a great reward of about 20-30% damage, PLUS the hard knockdown advantage. (Combine this method, Gold RC to give tension gauge, your burst meter, the tension gauge you already had and then you have a large pool of defensive options to reset and reward) Last we have Faultless Defense, a blocking mechanism that will continuously push the opponent back when they hit your guard. Back to characters with great neutral. Their fight for advantage is a lot easier than others so they can use the majority of their tension, burst, and faultless defense simply for push back and reset to neutral. Good neutral buttons combined with zone pressure can easily chip and wear down someones health and mental patience for the fight to get in. To put all of this more simply, the game will constantly give opportunities to reward a "keep away" game play while not rewarding enough for chase down. The highest tier characters are proof of this anyway, look up any tier list. The top 1&2 characters are very zone heavy characters; Happy Chaos and Asuka R. Kreuz. Absolutely love the game mechanics, they are very unique but in the right hands and characters, can be abused rather heavily. I've had loads of fun playing this game so I do think I have my moneys worth as contradicting as that sounds. At the end of the day I want someone to react or fight out of my pressure and not receive a "get out of jail free" card constantly. Combine all of this with option select mechanics similar to DP's and it just feels like a very inconsistent game.

_childDocuments_.review: Now to the review.This game has:Even though its not as complex as it was in the previous Guilty Gear games, it still has a ton of combo routes that allow for player expression and create an interesting learning experience for both new players and veterans of the genre.On top of the standart training and tutorial options the game features a combo tool and a combo library that is made by other players, it is a really good addition to the game that lets you share or learn combos from other players, a great tool for new players to learn the game and for veteran players to help others learn from their experience.Now this one is more of an opinion since art is subjective for everybody. But me and a lot of other people who havent even played GGST agree that the soundtrack in the game is insane. So I still decided to put it as one of the game's strong points.Another point that is mostly subjective, but with the amount of playable characters this game has, and their diversity it is almost guaranteed that any player will be able to find the one that they like. And the story, even though it sometiems lacks in animation quality, and has no real gameplay (its pretty much just cutscenes) is interesting and fun to watch. Although it's best if you've played/watched previous game's storylines.For a new player this may not sound like much, but trust me, you will definitely notice how smooth the game is when playing in online lobbies compared to other fighting games (although many modern ones already use rollback anyway).There still are stronger and weaker characters in GGST but as of writing this review, I beleive that the game is not only much better balanced compared to the release date, but is also heading in the right direction in terms of balance and character changes.Being the main game in the franchise, you can expect guilty gear to get dev support, patches and new content long after release, not to mention the playercount of this game is probably only going to increase with the addition of crossplay (hopefully they will do it right).Now that is about it for the upsides, I may have forgotten any, and your mileage may wary with some of these, not to mention some can change for better or worse in the future.The downsides, or rarther things that I dont like are mostly subjective (duh) but I will list them anyway since it might be something that will turn you off as well.Yes, a lot of people are complaining about it, a lot of veteran players are staying in Xrd or Accent Core because of that, and it IS true. Even the characters that are supposed to have more hp (or rather be more tanky) can ultimately die in 3-4 mixups, and the weaker ones can literally lose 99% of their health in one combo. This makes matches last less and even though I personally am not a fan of that, I came to accept it and the game is still enjoyable for me regardless of this.This is, again, something that I only really dislike because I've played previous GG games and I personally think it was something that was done better in those games. GGST takes a more strict approach to letting players combo neutral moves into one another cS goes into fS and 5p goes into 5k or 6k and some characters have other normals as well but it is still much stricter than before. I definitely prefer how BlazBlue Centralfiction or GG Xrd rev2 did it but with that being said, I still like this game's combo system. I just cant say that it's the best that Arcsys has done.And that's about it for the downsides, or rather things that I personally dislike about GGST.Overall this game is wonderfull, and it doesnt matter if you are a veteran of the genre who played other fighters like TEKKEN or MK and decided to try out GG series, or a new player who is just curious about fighting games and wants to try a new genre, you will have a wonderfull time playing Guilty Gear Strive.

_childDocuments_.review: It hurts me to make this review, but I need to get this off my chest. What happened to guilty gear, this isn't fun anymore. This isn't me whining about "retcons" or there being LGBT characters, I'm fine with that, and there has been gay people (Venom) in GG since Guilty Gear X in 2000. My main problem with Strive, is that it doesn't feel like guilty gear, and feels like a different game. Before i go into detail on the things they did wrong, I'll go over things they did right, and there are quite a lot of those.Things done well1. Animations. Considering this is an ArcSys game, incredible 3D animation is expected, and they delivered again. Every character has incredible animations, and Overdrives look incredible. 2. Character Designs. This is a subjective category, but I think most returning characters have good to incredible design changes. The newcomers don't look out of place at all, and feel like they could be from Xrd.3. Music. I really don't have to explain this.Now on to the things that I have problems with, starting with the small things.1. The UI and overall style of the displays and menus. Guilty gear has always had a heavy metal style for menus and the UI, which makes this new, simple design disappointing. It feels too clean. The health bars are just bare-bones, and no longer have the metal feeling of xrd and plus r. the menus also have the problem of feeling too sleek. there are no chains and steel for the menu like and xrd.2. Online, god the lobby system sucks, just give us a room system like plus r for casual, and a quick-match. the tower hub is tedious. 3. Gameplay. My main problem with Strive. It doesn't feel like guilty gear. rounds end too fast, inputs are simplified, and everyone deals too much damage. this got worse when slayer was added as dlc. Slayer was known as a high damage character in previous games, but strive is a high damage game, so they made him deal even more damage, breaking the game. I would much rather die to multiple long combos than two short ones. at least in previous games, combos were harder. the high damage for every character also ruins balance. the resident grappler, potemkin should not deal less damage with his command grab, his win condition, than one Ky combo. Not to mention the removal of mechanics from Plus R and Xrd. Examples being gutting the gating system of canceling normals into a stronger normal on hit, making burst full-screen so you cant predict them and block, removing full meter gain on gold burst, removing wall combos with wallbreak, removing instant kills, removing burst supers. To top it all off, they removed so many moves from returning characters. and made them easier. Lastly, the new update killed kara cancels for potemkin, gutting his playstyle. It feels like  an off-brand anime fighter based on street fighter with guilty gear characters, not a guilty gear game. Sure they made the game more accessible to casuals, but it dumbed the game down and made it lose its identity. Ironically enough, I was one of those casuals who started with strive, but went back to play the older ones and realized "this is so much more fun, why did they change it?" It sucks that Strive succeeded because it means it's most likely they'll continue with this "accessible" approach and lose more of what made Guilty Gear, Guilty Gear. In summary, buy plus r or Xrd, maybe they'll realize that people liked the old guilty gear as well.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so ridiculous. I'll be ready for a rematch with my opponent, but the game will kick me from our match to announce that my floor has been updated. Not only is it absurd to remove me from the only reason I'm playing this game, but also this achievement is completely irrelevant because literally nobody is playing on those floors. They are removing me from my match, one that I may have wasted a lot of time finding, so that I may know that I can join an empty room.This game doesn't have matchmaking. You need to find your own matches in this idiotic tower system. Most of your time is spent walking around and asking strangers for permission to play with them. If the room you enter had an even amount of players then you're probably SOL because they're all already in matches. You can leave the room and try another one, or you can sit and patiently wait to play the game you paid your hard-earned money for. This game does have one option to find a 'quick match', which is the only real match-making option they offer, but it doesn't work. I had to wait over 30 minutes for a match when I tried to use it. Ugh! Just let me play the game you ******* cowards!Japanese game designers are clearly incompetent. I have become so sick of their games, and I think I'm at the point where I just won't buy them anymore. They are always ruined by painfully obvious problems, ones that can often be fixed very easily, but never will be. They seem to live in their own reality, one where sensibility and convenience are their greatest enemies.I do enjoy the fighting in this game, but that is literally the only good thing I can say about it. Aside from the already mentioned matchmaking problems, I think the graphics are far too flashy which I think makes it really hard to focus on the characters. The characters also look pretty grainy which doesn't seem right. Maybe there's also an issue with the filter that will also never get fixed.I do not recommend this game.

Chipp is faster than ever, though I wasn't as into his kit this time, and I-No doesn't feel quite as nice as in Xrd.  However, the game is beautiful, more visually impressive than ever, and everything is so tight and fluid.  It's poetry in motion.  The greatest fighting game series of all time at its most refined.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan of Guilty Gear for a long time now, and while I'm not an expert at the game I've pretty much played most of them casually, I can say for sure this is the best one for people who are new to fighting games or just new to Guilty Gear in general. The gameplay is not as complicated as in other games, it is much more simplistic which makes it easier for new players to feel like they've done a flashy awesome combo and kicked the opponent's butt and it feels rather satisfying. I've never really considered playing online to improve my skill or ability to win in any fighting game, but there's just something about this game that makes it enjoyable so I find myself playing online more often! The graphics are very pretty. I love the maps and all of the characters along with their music themes (please bring them back to Spotify). It's just a game that is very pleasing to look at!I've also convinced all of my friends to purchase the game so we could all play it together and we're all currently enjoying it! I'm very happy about that as well! If you have friends yourself, convince them to play this fighting game with you! I'm sure you will all have a great time learning and improving be it alongside one another or sharing your experiences and achievements online! _childDocuments_.review: As a beginner in terms of 2D fighters, I found Guilty Gear Strive to be surprisingly accessible and easy to grasp compared to almost every other traditional fighter I've tried in the past. At the same time, it also manages to have deeper mechanics that will take a very long time to master to really separate the veterans from the newbies. Arc System Works' signature art style is the best it's ever been, and has to be one of the most visually stunning games I've seen in a long time. The characters and visual style alone can really suck you into the game to get you to play more, which is not a bad thing in the slightest.If you're new to 2D Fighting games like me, I think Guilty Gear Strive is a great entry point to not only learn the ropes, but have a hell of an experience doing so.

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is solid, and the visuals are gorgeous, but I can't help feeling this is just not enough.  The character roster is incredibly small considering the age of the series, and the fact that this acts as a finale of sorts.  It almost seems as if it were reduced just to sell DLC later on.The story mode is non-interactive, which wouldn't be a problem except for a couple of things.  First, it's incredibly stupid, boring, and unsatisfying.  This is a fighting game series, and over the course of the hours long non-interactive story, there's maybe a total of 60 seconds of actual combat that plays out on screen.  The rest of the story mode is just an anime version of Olympus Has Fallen, but somehow even more lame.Second, the story mode is ugly.  When I went back to playing the game after finishing my viewing, I was surprised at how gorgeous the game was in comparison.  The story is flat, gray, blurry, ugly, and looks like it runs at about 25 fps.Third, and this goes back to my point about the roster, the story mode focuses on only a couple of characters.  There are non-playable characters that feature heavily in the story mode, and a few playable characters that are either not present at all or do absolutely nothing (like sit at a computer the whole time).  It feels so incomplete and non-inclusive of the amazing cast of characters the GG series has amassed over the last twenty years.As a final criticism of the game, you'll find there's almost nothing to do.  Unless you want to do nothing but play online against the same few characters over and over, there is nothing.  Oh, wait... you can't play online because matchmaking is broken.  Also, it takes like 5 minutes to connect to the servers before you even see the main menu.  The arcade mode is very slim, and the game lacks custom dialog between all characters (which was present in previous games).The currency only exists to go "fishing," where you can either unlock songs to listen to (while not playing), art to stare at (while not playing), or clothing for your little 8-bit character.  That is all.  You dress up the 8-bit character so he can go fishing or hang around a lobby.  You fish so you can dress him up.  That's it.Considering previous entries in the series still have visuals that hold up and offer a lot more, I honestly cannot recommend buying this game.  There's almost nothing here.

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay is fun and the population hasn't gone down the road of DNF dual (Discord notification fighter) yet so all in all. Can recommend. The rest of this is just things I wish were better or didn't exist in the game.No single player content outside of the normal stuff (arcade, survival) which is a fighting game tradition at this point.Combo trials are user made which are a mixed bag since you got to shift through “funny” combos and set ups before you actually get to anything decent.Story mode is you watching a cutscene for 4 hours while you pretend to know what's going on.Figure mode. Where you set up little “scenes” of characters doing stupid stuff. Managed to attract the attention of the community for a whole hour before being forgotten about.The user interface is ugly and it's funny to think it could have been worse.Soundtrack is fine but most of the new tracks don't actually fit using them during gameplay. Luckily, they added a bunch of old tracks you can use. What I wish you could do is change the main menu's theme every time you boot up the game. Sounds like I'm attending Blazblue's funeral.Online actually works for the most part. Though, I've had way more laggy matches than I thought I would have. Maybe the people on floor 8 to 10 EU are wifi warriors or the people with Japanese names are actually from Japan. Whatever the case may be. It's a bitter pill knowing that while rollback is 100% better than delay. It can't work miracles.Lobbies are awful. Avatars look like something you get free from logging in daily on a Maple story cash-grab clone.They tried something different with matchmaking and failed. The vast majority of multiplayer matchmaking systems are so bad, it's actually impressive they somehow made one worse.Floors 1 to 11 yet most of them aren't used. You get kicked up or pushed back down floors without even completing the set. Every month people get booted out of floor 11 to floor 10 where floor 11 is where the vastly better players are. Don't think a level 100 player should ever be in the situation of facing a level 5000 player but git gud skill issue I guess. And you get ranked and deranked way too fast.Ranking up means nothing because it's so quick to rank you up. Deranking matters less as you can just choose to play in the higher towers but as previously said it still cuts in to actually playing the game. There is the park where you can just rematch indefinitely. I just hope you can find someone around your skill level and wants to run sets with the character you choose.The last thing I can whine about is character difficulty. Strive was meant to be an easier title in the series. And it is. When compared to the older titles. When you only look at Strive's roster however. The ease of use is crazy to me. You can go from mashing and winning a major. To Zato-1.I guess this is true for all fighting games. But considering strive's core mechanics are simple to understand and easy to execute. The easy characters are made even easier while some characters retain their difficulty and some newcomers are just as hard as well. Ultimately, I guess it's best to have options for people who want a more challenging experience. It just kinda sucks to me that the general consensus to tell new players to “pick the character you want to learn” fails to mention that if you picked a hard character and your opponent didn't. You're gonna get mopped for a hot minute because you picked a character that either has high execution, ever changing game plans or limited in some capacityWhile your opponent can be rocking a character that straight up ignores all that and memes you for a double perfect.Add Dr. Paradigm and Leopaldon to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Game's fun, and has quite a bit of offline content to keep people who don't like pvp satisfied.I found the core gameplay of this game to be a refreshing take on the grounded formula, versus the air focused older guilty gear games. Whether you find that good or bad is completely preference. You are somewhat limited in what each character can do versus the older games, but overall I think I enjoy this game more than the older ones. The two new characters in particular are really fun to play, that being Nagoriyuki and Giovanna. I would definitely say this is most like SFV, so if you are weren't a fan of that game maybe give this one a shot because it feels like a much better version of that game.This would probably be obvious, but the game's look and graphics are amazing and imo, the best the fighting game genre has ever offered when it comes to 3D. I love the animations, character designs, as well as the stages they have in this game. Everything looks awesome.The music in this game is stellar. I rarely bring this up about fighting games, but Daisuke Ishiwatari is a freaking genius. I absolutely love all the character themes and main theme of this game to death. Also, this game has a huge collection of the badass songs from the entire series to choose from and enjoy.Offline has a plethora of missions to help even people who have never even TOUCHED a fighting game the basics of the genre, the mechanics of GG, and even some character matchups. There are over a hundred missions that teach everyone very important skills to succeed in Strive, and I recommend all new players do it. I would argue this tutorial even surpasses the UNICLR one, which used to be the best tutorial imo for new FG players. There's also arcade, 1v1 versus with someone right next to you (and Steam Remote Play works with this too), or you can face off against a CPU (these are pretty staple for all FG).Training mode is what it is, you can adjust position, record what you want the bot to do, etc. There's also a neat little combo recording system where you can record a combo you want to practice and get down, then you can practice it as much as you want with the inputs for the combo on screen for you. The only thing that seems to be questionably missing from training mode is sadly the frame data, which has become a training mode staple in other fighting games such as SFV, so it's a shame it isn't here. Hopefully it comes in a future update.The story mode is more or less a four and half hour long movie, so if you were expecting gameplay don't bother. I found it to be a fitting conclusion to Sol Badguy in my opinion, so I would say it's worth a watch. You can either watch it in one sitting, or let it stop between chapters for you. It also saves in the EXACT spot you want it to so don't worry about picking it up and dropping it later. Also, you should be aware for those seeking collectibles, . I didn't have any qualms with it's presentation (save for the animation and lip syncing) or the fact that you gain nothing from it, but just be aware before starting it what you're getting into.There is also a ton to collect from doing offline activities, including art, music, and some videos from before release (I don't think there are any unlockable player skins to get), which you all obtain from 'fishing' in a gacha system of sorts. Arc Sys does this with every game, and do not worry about needing to spend money or anything like that to get the music you want, but you will need to actively play online or offline modes to earn in-game cash to fish for collectibles. All the music you fish up can be listened to in the gallery, as well as be used as an in-battle soundtrack if you so choose. I quite like this system and I find it rewarding to get all my favorite tracks from the series (if you were concerned with starting with no music, you will start with all main character themes and the main theme of the game to choose from so don't worry).Multiplayer is obviously the meat of the game, and the online connection runs stellar if you can make it past the egregious lobbies. The lobby system is a 2D platformer of sorts where you design an avatar, and use battle stations to que up for battles with people who approach your station. However, as simple as that seems, the connection as of now is quite frankly terrible and you will FREQUENTLY disconnect as well as fail to connect to other players. Also, in general, it's a pointlessly complicated lobby system. It's sad how screwed up these lobbies are, and how excellent the online gameplay experience is. Rollback netcode is implemented beautifully here, even playing a dude from JAPAN (I live on the West coast) I had barely any lag. It really sets a new standard for online in the fighting game genre. Now, you can avoid lobbies (somewhat) altogether by selecting the 'que up for a match while in training mode option' which is definitely a welcome feature here, but it still plops you in a lobby at a station, but at least you can avoid accessing them yourself altogether.Ranked is separated into a 'tower' system consisting of 11 floors. Once you finish the tutorial for the online, you will get plopped onto the floor it thinks you should play on, based on your skill level in a bot match. You can access every tower above you to Tower 10, which you think may sound counter-intuitive, but it locks every tower below yours, so you can't noob stomp lower skill players. As you win, you'll get locked out of higher and higher floors, so eventually the best players will be locked to the top 1-2 floors so noobs don't get wiped out. But, if you so choose, you can challenge the highest floor you can right at the start, so the better players can move up the tower faster if they so choose. Once you beat enough people in the 10th floor, you gain access to the 11th floor and challenge a resident of said floor to gain access. Win 6 times, and you get in. In this mode, you can only rematch up to two times, but if someone ranks down or up mid match, you'll be denied a rematch which can get really frustrating. This system will probably annoy people hoping for a simple ranked experience, but it is what it is.For those seeking a fight against players of all skills, with unlimited rematching, thankfully we have lobbies called 'parks'. There is no skill floor here, no ranking system, and unlimited rematches. This is the classic lobby system from past Arc Sys Works games. You can select a region you want to play in, then you can choose between the 20 or so parks to fight anyone you so please. If you aren't looking for a hardcore experience, obviously I'd recommend this but be aware that there can be some SERIOUS dudes here who could come from the top floor of the tower.For those wanting a more personal experience, there is of course, custom rooms. You can create a lobby with your custom ruleset, and then put it up for people or friends to find it and enter it. Then you can fight whoever you want. It's pretty self-explanatory.Overall though, I would say this is a fun fighting game. There are obviously some hiccups with online functionality, but the content here is well worth full price, and there is more to come in a online combo mode, a figurine mode, and and more customizable features for player rooms. There are also already two DLC characters coming, next month and the month after to look forward to. I would rate this game a 9/10 and say it's worth a buy!

_childDocuments_.review: For those not interested in reading trough 20 paragraphs of text , Ill just come out and say it...this game slaps.Overall its super fun , well made and polished and has some really neat characters BUT...It also has a starting roster of 15 characters (something arc sys has been really pushing it with) and not a whole lot to offer apart from that for the classic AAA game price. MK11 came out with 25 out of the gate and a fully playable story mode and a separate krypt mode, meanwhile the Strive story mode is basically just a very poorly animated anime movie. On the plus side this means the story doesnt force fights as often but on the minus side...well its a movie. If youre the type to skip cutscenes...skip this whole mode and go straight into training or online.  As of time of writing 3 DLC characters are out and playable with 2 more to go (for season pass)Im happy to report all 3 are absolutely a joy to play and this is where I can almost forgive the lack of content.Compared to MK11 yes, there is ♥♥♥♥ all to do outside of playing matches and the roster is almost half the size BUT just about every character is unique and does their own thing.  There is a case of "quality over quantity" to be made here. I guess what Im trying to say is...make your own decision on that. Personally I think there is not enough to offer for the price tag. Im a big fan of fighting games so I know that for my monney there is enough but for everybody else...well , this is not the most generous package in the world.With the latest patch they added player room customization. This is really neat and you can spend a bit of time making sure your room feels unique but even so there is a little bit left to be desired.From a gameplay point of view I actually wont say much. The game is fun , mostly balanced and interesting.With every new game there will be people who say overwhelmingly possitive and overwhelmingly negative things about it.  I personally love how Strive feels and play and my only gripe is the pricing.Loads of playstation exclusive things too. Steam didnt get all the version of the game , we didnt get the soundtrack for buying the game, we didnt get early access when we pre-ordered and most of all we didnt get a special color 12 for all of the characters (including DLC)Things like these do annoy me personally but overall, this is a good game with loads to do an explore.Its got a killer soundtrack, fatastic (tho few) characters , Fluid gameplay and a FANTASTIC netcode.This last bit is huge...the netcode in strive is one of the best on the market and will likely stay the best until Project L finally decides to be a thing...and also stops being called project L...For those few that care about a rating system Id say this game is a solid 8/10Everything present is really well done but there is still a lot missing when compared to some other titles. I fully expect more to be added but ARC SYSTEM WORKS are really testing the waters for how little they can do and still sell the game and all the things that could have been there as DLC anyways.Personally I think we should have the ability to unlock DLC characters with heavy grinding in addition to being able to buy them. I also think characters should be usable in training mode regardless of if they are purchased or not.  Some people will call me an idiot for saying this and say DLC sales would go down a lot but most modern fighting games will set you back a stupid ammount of monney if you buy at release and given the nature of the games at release is the best time to play. Something has to budge because right now only the most hard core fighting game players are willing to spend as much as devs are sking for.Here is to hoping Project L shows the world what a free to play model could do for the FGC....please dont mess it up Riot...

_childDocuments_.review: Guilty Gear had a reputation for being obtuse.Notice the "had". Granted, Strive is still a fighting game, complete with lots of quarter-circle motions, charge moves, and the occasional HCB+F. Thankfully, there's not too many of those, if you don't know what that is.But what it does is move away from is the combomania that defined many earlier games, where a lot of matches banked on your ability to convert a hit into a string of complicated follow-ups and bounces that were your ticket to big damage. If you couldn't have reliable chains, you weren't competitive. And building those combos required labwork and reflexes most players struggled with.Strive turns this on its head by making big damage follow from short combos, power hits, and counters. Timing plays an important part of the tit-for-tat, with well-placed punishes being aptly rewarded. Most characters have been simplified towards their core, avoiding the most complex systems seen in previous games. It feels more satisfying and meaty, and though the cost comes at some of the wilder options of previous games, the options that remain present tend to be more useful than some of the niche mechanics and moves like Faust's tiny little flower. It was an adorable flower, to be sure, but it wasn't exactly something you used out of your well-labbed combo.All of this is pretty inside baseball nonsense typical of fighting games, so the tl;dr is that Guilty Gear is a more decisive fighting game that's simpler to get into. But why get into it, anyway?I don't think it's an exaggeration to say Guilty Gear has some of the best character designs in fighting games, both in terms of visuals and mechanics. And if you've looked at the trailer, you don't need me going on about how good it looks. Or going on about the wonderful collection of buttrock that powers the whole thing. If you haven't, stop this and go do that. The game is just fun and oozes style from every messy pore that it has.All of this makes Guilty Gear one of the best fighting games currently available. The netcode is solid and the fighting is fantastic. What else could one want?Well, single-player content, unfortunately. If you like grinding against a CPU, you'll find things a bit lacking. There's an arcade mode with hints of story, survival, training, and that's about it. There's a story mode that's largely just watching a 3D-animated Guilty Gear TV series, that while entertaining in its ridiculousness... doesn't really interface with the game in any way.And while the netcode in a match is fantastic, the game takes several minutes to. load. up. every. time. There's something weird about how it connects to the server, and also just the fact it demands to do it at the start. You can't even watch the breezy story mode without being lag-blocked at startup. The match-finding system also continues Arc System Works' love of obtuse lobbies, and while it has some strengths--like making it easier to recognize regular foes--it basically makes it just take longer to find a match. While there are ways around it, the game does push you towards it. And sometimes, the game just doesn't want to let you match.Still, those are comparatively modest issues for what's probably the best modern fighting game at the time of this writing. It may not always be the most approachable or the most recognizable, but it's definitely the most rewarding.Experience: played about 60 hours, mainly in online versus, getting up to floor 9 but hovering largely around floor 7-8. Beat the arcade mode but not the hidden boss. Watched most of the way through the story so far. Fished more than anybody should have to fish.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:+++ Rollback netcode+++ Music/Character Themes++ Visuals- Game does not run perfectly with minimum system requirements. Using a i5-4690K 4.0Ghz CPU will still make you drop up to 15 frames in some heavy rollback situations online. (Your cpu needs at least 4 cores/ 8 threads, honestly not a real issue, just do not expect too much when deciding to play on older hardware)-  The Player online lobbies are buggy.Playing does not work when attempting to play with a player from another region (high ping), despite using the right settings.There is a lack of a steam lobby invite function. Instead you are forced to manually copy a code upon creating a lobby. Your friends then need to paste the code into a search bar in the player match search menu.-  The tower lobby and parks also do not allow you to spectate players. A function which would be GREATLY appreciated.- Generally the online lobbies (player lobbies, parks and tower floors) are very laggy and out of sync, which is ironic considering how well the netcode during a match is implemented.You have severe trouble starting a match sometimes, constantly failing to connect. The battlestations are being occupied by players you do not visually see, etc.- Private messaging does not work well, since you need to manually reselect a player, either by walking up to their avatar in the 2d indie-game-styled lobby, or searching for their name in the in the list of players, each time you want to send 1 message.The recipient does not receive any audio cue or pop up. The chat window does not stay open.The messages appear in the same chat window as all the other open messages. The chat history is usually filled with a bunch of automatic responses from players, which are automatically sent each time someone starts a match. "Let's fight", "Thank you very much", etc.There is no way to disable these.- (This would be a positive point if it was implemented properly)There is a system which allows you to add players to a list, and tag/classify them as "friends" or "rivals"When you go into the tower-floor/park selection menu, you will be notified of followed players who are currently in online match mode.You can also see which players follow you back, in another tab of the followed-player menu.Unfortunately this system comes with flaws. Accessing this menu proves to be a hassle. Even though you should be able to open it with just one button just like the news tab and have it open on one side of the screen. Or simply have a shortcut to it.Currently, to get to it one needs to first go to the options and select their own "D-Code" or simply their profile, then press L2 for "useful information", where they can then select "followed played list".It is unnecessarily hidden away.The other lacking feature is that you cannot see which region/server the player you followed is currently playing in, and you cannot select to follow (teleport to) them to the according park/floor via the menu.You have to try each server manually until you can see them in the "followed players"-tab in the floor/park select screen.The last complain is regarding the inability to follow players easily in the case of playing in a park or public lobby. You need to select their D-Code while they are still in the same lobby as you are. You cannot check a players D-Code after they already left, for example, in the match replay menu.The player-profile itself takes way too long to load, up to 4 minutes, which is probably due to some bug.While these are perhaps small flaws, that do no directly affect the gameplay, I still find it insulting that the PC playersbase has not gotten their own beta, or at least an opportunity to voice feedback to ArcSys.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally I was a little worried that Guilty Gear Strive would be a dumbed-down Guilty Gear made super accessible, and was worried about stuff like the wall-mechanics dumbing down the game.  I didn't want this to be the brawl or sf5 of Guilty Gear.It turns out my fears were groundless - nobody needed instant kills, and the wall-break mechanic works for me.  The game looks and plays great - the rollback netcode also works really well and the matches are smooth if you don't play wifi warriors.The game does have problems, but it's entirely possible for them to be fixed or patched-out in the future.  I can live with these, but your mileage may vary:a) Opening the game and navigating the menus / lobbies is suuuuper slow (like on the order of minutes sometimes).  Apparently the game client is making a bunch of synchronous ajax requests to super slow japanese servers.b)  You can't just right click and play someone from your steam friends list, the option is there but it doesn't work.  Oh, and player matches still don't work half the time with some of my friends (we have to go to the park)c)  The lobby system is just super awkwardly designed.  I think it wouldn't be a big deal without the performance issues, but there have definitely been a lot of games with better lobby systems.

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous visuals, awesome soundtrack, fun and fast paced (but not overly hectic) gameplay and the best netcode in a fighting game in a long time (maybe ever). If you have ANY interest in playing fighting games (even if it's just wanting to hit some buttons on a casual level) with/against other people, you just cannot miss this game.The characters are varied and fun, more in depth core mechanics for things like combo extensions make up the complexity of this game, instead of 100+ entries in a movelist for each character.Be aware however: The clear focus of this game is multiplayer. While there is some singleplayer content, such as a servicable Arcade mode, a history of the GG universe, and Mission Trials (which serve as a sort of extended tutorial missions), it is probably not what will keep you in this game in the long run. The story mode is not bad per se, but it is basically 4 hours of cutscenes/movie that will make no sense if you did not follow the Guilty Gear Story up to this point.Another valid point of critique is the loading times and lobby system. While the general "rank" system of tower floors, with a dedicated "heaven" floor for the best players, is very good, the matchmaking in the lobbies is not quite as elegant as it could be. Furthermore, by the time of this review, the time to connect to the servers on initial startup of the game can take quite long.But these are really minor issues, some of which will hopefully be patched out in the future. The only reason they even stand out, is because the rest of the game is so great.The game is super fun (both for people taking it seriously as well as for people that just want to mess around for in a beautiful game for a bit), online is great (Players from Europe can connect to people form the US or even Japan and that stuff just works! It's incredible), soundtrack kicks ***, and as a bonus: It sold really well, so there is a sizable player pool for all skill levels, and you won't have to wait for matchmaking long, no matter your skill rating.

Online modes don't offer a sliver of visual quality the gameplay does, some attack animations are straight up poor (see Ramlethal's super move), and it's easy to break the camera resulting in weird and off-putting angles- Music is good. OST gets a recommendation even though I personally dislike the high number of vocal tracks- Not a lot of single player content. - Online is a joke: the netcode works fine, the online modes feel like a different studio made it, and that studio had no idea what or why they were making. It looks bad, doesn't work, desynchs a lot, and on top of that is designed in a way that encourages rage quitting and matchup avoiding. The floor system is the worst ranked mode I've seen in a fighting game.I'm still looking at updates, and should the system be expanded, possibly along with more varied characters being added, I'll gladly amend the review as there's a lot good in Strive, but it's just not a well thought through game.

_childDocuments_.review: After putting ~50 or so hours into Strive I can conclusively say: It's decent. 6/10. Now let me explain. Strive naturally has the best graphics of the series being the most recent. It also streamlines multiple mechanics of the game for better or for worse (mainly worse.) The music still slaps and the combos are still cool. My issues start with Wallbreaks.In Xrd and all previous installations getting put in the corner was a death sentence like it should be. There was a burst in a few of the games but it wasn't always worth using. If you got put in the corner you were eating damage. . . That makes sense. You made a mistake and got punished for it. However in Strive if you get put into a corner your opponent can just wallbreak you for extra damage AND Positive Bonus (which passively regenerates meter/accelerates meter gain on attacks.) Instead of fixing the "Issue" of corner combos being "annoying" and "unfun" they made the game a snowball fest that depends on who gets the first wallbreak.It's not all doom and gloom. All of the characters are unique and quirky. However unlike previous installments OR BlazBlue: Centralfiction (which I think you should buy over GGST) the characters all fit into distinct categories and play similarly to each other. Not exactly bad but does kinda take away from player expression IMO.And lastly the music. It all slaps. Not a single bad song in the tracklist from what I've heard. The alt skins are good and the modding scene is (While a bit lewd at times) popping and fresh. There's even somebody working on a Goku mod that adds him as a completely new character if I recall correctly.To in two sentences: Beautifully Quirky 2.5D ArcSys Fighter with Archetypes. Easy to master but has issues with snowballing.

_childDocuments_.review: Strive is a very approachable game, though you  to be prepared to lose a lot at the start. This is difficult for a lot of people to accept when learning their first fighting game, but it is a central part of the learning experience. If you go into the tutorial and learn the main mechanics, you should do fine against other new players. Thankfully, Strive has a big population due to crossplay, so it is easy to find people around your level.If you are looking to improve, here are some tips:1. Be willing to change your strategy at the start of each new round. If you keep doing the same thing, you will eventually get punished for it.2. Practice roman cancels. Focus on Red RC to begin with and then look into how other players use the mechanic3. Flawless defense. Negates chip damage and pushes the opponent away at the cost of meter. This helps a lot more than you think it does4. Pick the character you like the most. You do not have to play the best character in the game and the whole cast of Strive is so radically different that anyone is pretty viable.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game to be sure. The combat is fun, characters unique, and music great. But at the end of the day, in it's current state which we can assume to be its first season, the game lacks a significant amount of prior titles freedom, damage on specific combo starters and reversals is ridiculous, and the wall breaks inconsistency prevent it being an easy recommendation for all players. On one hand as a fan of the series in general and its characters, art design, and setting I would love to say buy it with the expectation of it improving in the future. On the other hand however as a fighting game it's definitely got a fair amount of issues and so holding off till future revisions are made would be a good choice for any looking to get into it for the competitive long haul.Overall the game is good and I'll play more in the future definitely, but if you want to hold off and wait for when it gets better in the future then that's perfectly valid. In terms of the networking the rollback implementation is absolutely fantastic and makes even 200 ping matches feel near flawless. The overall lobby experience however is utterly horrific. It goes from being perfectly workable to completely unusable and impossible to match with others. To make matters worse, it's currently impossible to join private lobbies directly through Steam currently.  Very cool Arcsys.Visually the in game graphics are nearly flawless with Arcsys 2.5D artstyle looking drop dead gorgeous. At max settings  1440p at least. I can't speak for lower settings however. However the UI design is... mixed to say the least. Messages like the "GOOD" and "YOU ROCK" look appropriate with the Guilty Gear artistic style with the hard rock edge. Then you have the tepid "Slash!" written in bubble letter that's totally out of place with the painted on look of the games UI. On top of that the Burst, health bar, and Tension bars looking rounded and once again lacking the edge of other UI elements makes them seem out of place. A lot of my gripes can be patched in the future though and hopefully will be. I'll update this review when the inevitable season 2 or rev2 version of the game releases but for now. It's a game that I'm 50/50 on. If I had to choose between this or a populated Rev2 however. I would go for Rev2.

The graphics are great.Yeah, it doesn't play quite like old GG, but it's still entertaining.The game has a few issues though:* outside of battle, anything network related is a mess, you'll often need to restart the game because of network errors, sometimes you can't connect to other players, etc* the game takes like three minutes to reach the main menu if you have networking enabled and apparently a lot of this is due the game making dozens and dozens of separate requests and asking for a bunch of stuff at the start of the game instead of when it's actually needed; if I just want to go into practice mode and lab some stuff, I need to turn off networking* defensive options seem a bit lacking -- GG is famously focused on offense to the point where merely moving forward grants meter, but it seems both too easy to lock an opponent down or to get locked down yourself; also I dunno why they made instant blocking have a 2f window* the floor lobby system is kinda dumb and clunkyUltimately though, I like the game.
