_childDocuments_.review: If you never played a fighting game and are nervous about picking this up. Don't be! Here are some reasons why this should be your first fighting game!There's over 100 tutorial/challenges that cover basic fighting game fundamentals, and guilty gear strive specific mechanics. The game makes sure that they are easy to understand, and has a roadmap of challenges that it teaches you how to complete, gives you the knowledge for, and can get you from absolute beginner to beating your first small town local tournament. There's even in an in game player combo creator where you can create your own or test out other player made combos on specific characters so that you don't need to go out of your way to learn combos for other characters if you don't want to.  At it's core the training arena gives you so many tools to fine tune whatever it is you're trying to improve on no matter the skill level. Online PVP - With rollback netcode as long as you have good internet yourself, matches should feel smooth, and fast paced without the usual stutters all thanks to Rollback Netcode. If you're worried about not finding people or majority of players being too pro then don't worry about it. I assure you this game is still incredibly popular online and has crossplatform. There's also specific lobbies called the "Tower" where it will restrict expert players from joining rooms meant for beginners only giving you room to practice with others.If you're want to get good at a fighting game and willing to put in the time. I highly suggest getting this game and completely the tutorial challenges from noob all the way to expert. That knowledge alone will carry you in most of your games, and once your ready you can start learning combos to min max your punishing game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite fighting game, and the one that got me into fighting games in general. I played a bit of Mortal Kombat and Soul Calibur when I was a kid, but Guilty Gear is what made me learn what plus-on-block and okizeme mean. Every single facet of this game oozes style and the fights are tight and technical. Characters include a black vampire cyborg samurai, the Secretary of Absolute Defense of the United States and his not-an-alien, a crackhead turned ninja turned president of the Eastern Chipp Kingdom (yes, he is the president of a kingdom), and cute pirate girl who yeets dolphins and hits you with a big ♥♥♥♥-off anchor. Among many others, I'd be here all night describing them all. The lore of the game is insane, and while I do think that +R had (a lot) better character interaction with specific lines for certain matchups and so on, Strive is still fine in that regard, I guess, I keep hoping the devs will patch in some matchup lines but everyone always skips the intros anyway so who cares.The actual gameplay kicks ass, it's combo heavy but doesn't overdo it like some other fighters (Skullgirls comes to mind) where you have to reliably pull off 37-hit combos to actually execute your gameplan. Some characters are very combo centric but others have a gameplan that solely consists of "walk up and command grab" with everything else you do basically just being setup for your P-Buster. The online servers are pretty ♥♥♥♥ right now but the devs are reportedly working on making that better. I didn't have a ton of problems when I was playing this game regularly but it was noticeable when you did, you'd drop matches or lag out of the tower and have to rejoin. Playing against your boys on the couch is prime game time, just pick your favorite flavor of busted overpoweredness and pit them against each other.Mostly I love this game for its style, which specifically is just taking something kind of cool so ridiculously over the top that it turns a bit cringe and then wraps all the way back around into being awesome again. Every menu and loading screen have little bits of flavor text that don't mean anything and you see for .8 seconds before the game loads, it's just there for you to ponder over. Every character looks awesome and feels awesome to play. Literally there are no bad characters, you will find mains of everyone on the roster because this game has a fighter for everyone but every fighter has a unique gimmick. The music is insane, some of it I can pass on but several songs I have become so ridiculously obsessed with that they made it into my daily playlist.Buy and play this game if you like fighting games, or if you want to learn to like them. If you're a real old school fighting game veteran and you want something that feels more like that, buy Guilty Gear XX Accent Core +R instead, or one of the older Guilty Gear games if you want, there's been quite a few of them. The franchise is about as old as Street FIghter, and in my opinion it has been heavily slept on by the public at large. It's good, especially so if you enjoy the admittedly cheesy but genuinely cool aesthetic.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit mixed on this entry. Strive is beautiful and plays well, but there are some issues that keep me from enjoying it as much as I'd like. If you're here primarily for Online play (or you play together in-person), and can stomach the lobby system, then Guilty Gear Strive is for you. Otherwise, give it a pass unless AcrSys improves things.Pros:* Fantastic aesthetic* Mechanics and Missions are great for newcomers* Music is good* Solid net codeCons:* Terrible online lobby system* Single Player modes are limited and pretty bad* Classic Guilty Gear music is too quiet* No option to toggle different tracks for randomI love the way this game looks, plays, and sounds. But I also find myself getting bored pretty quickly. If you enjoy playing online, you'll have to suffer through the lobby system with way more waiting between matches than necessary. Once you're in a match, things go pretty smoothly though.If you want a break from online play, then you're stuck with mediocre Single Player options. Endless mode is okay, but it takes too long to get interesting. The real problem is Arcade, which I find painfully easy on the Hard Route. Alternatively, the Extreme route feels like playing against an random number generator deciding whether or not to screw you over. All this is made worse by the dumb route system that encourages you to throw matches to stay on the Extreme Route.But none of this matters, because the real hell is the boss of arcade, whom I've fought a few hundred times without a single match victory. So, at least at my skill level, I can choose between too easy, or insurmountably difficult. And apparently there's an even more difficult version of the same fight after that if you get past it without losing a round. I'm pretty sure that the inevitable heat death of the universe would happen before I could beat Stage 9.If you're someone who does enjoy Single Player, you'll be disappointed by the lack of options and interesting gameplay. There's also no longer unique dialogue between all the match-ups, which makes me sad (at least I don't have to listen to May compare everyone and their grandmother to Johnny). Online could use some matchmaking improvements, but it's otherwise fine, so if that's your focus, you'll be happy.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Game is fun, feels simple, good depth to the mechanics but doesn't feel overwhelming. Its hard not to love the art and characters. Try to have at least one friend who likes to play with you. Memes are quality. Definitely worth your time.Fighting game comparisons:Guilty Gear Strive or GGST is the first GG game I played and before this I have played mainly smash and some tekken 7. This is a very offensive game that focuses on pressuring and putting your opponent in the dirt. There is less neutral than smash ultimate, but still retains really cool neutral tools. I would say that in comparison to tekken you still have the big launchers and nasty combos but there is less reliance on having the oppenent flub into your launcher. Roman cancel allows you to choose and try to approach from interesting angles while rewarding you heavily for choosing offensive options. I personally feel like this stands up as a better fighting game than smash bros. Both are fun but if you have an itch for competition and doing crazy maneuvers that you make up on the fly I would recommend this game highly. Art and Style:This game oozes style and flow. I never played Guilty Gear before this but I already love all the characters. There is the dolphin girl, Doctor Dr., Eddie and his puppet zato, Big Justice, Unga Bunga, Sexy Wolf girl, ♥♥♥♥♥ Sol, the Shoto, Best Girl, Black Samurai, and Sushi Ninja, Oh and they just added Fat 'Merica. The songs are kinda heavy metal mixes which I respect, but if loving a song till you scream it isnt your thing then I guess its ok for you to be wrong. That means its really easy to come into a character and start learning little tricks and techniques that other people come up with. I think the best part is that its clear the developers care about the game and see it from a competetive standpoint by giving suggestions to when a move is useful. _childDocuments_.review: Guilty Gear Strive proves that ArcSys refuses to miss with the GG games. While I don't much care for their other fighting games, Strive has had me hyped since day one of its reveal regardless of some bumps along the road including some delays. While actually getting into a match is beyond frustrating, once you play it, the game becomes super addicting.+Pros:+GOD TIER NETCODE (in matches). Rollback + servers makes this perhaps the best netcode for a fighting game ever, rivaled only by Guilty Gear XX Accent Core +R. Matches run perfectly.+Presentation. The graphics, art and music are completely out of this world as expected of Guilty Gear.+Solid tutorial just like Guilty Gear Xrd+Phenomenal gameplay. Is it XX AC+R? No. Is it Xrd? No. Does it need to be? Absolutely not. Fighting games change, that's perfectly fine so long as the games remain well designed. While this game has some issues design wise, it proves itself that it can stand on its own as another entry in the Guilty Gear series.+If you want to bypass the awful lobbies, you can thankfully enable quick search training mode+They atoned for their sins of making Potemkin mediocre in Xrd.-Cons:-Atrocious lobbiesThe lobbies are barely functional, and at the time of writing private lobbies are impossible to use. As a tournament organizer myself, these lobbies make running tournaments for this game nearly impossible. People can't connect to each other, player lobby search doesn't work as it should, player lobbies can't start any matches even though they are needed for spectating, and without Discord screen share or restreaming it is impossible to stream matches. This is absolutely horrendous performance despite the amazing netcode.-PC port behind on updates. Ugh.-4K doesn't work at the moment, slows the game down-Lacking offline, single player features-Wallbreak is both confusing to actually explain and not rewarding enoughIt's basically either get extra damage, meter and reset neutral, or you get none of that to keep the opponent in the corner (a forced reset). There is literally zero reason to take away the corner after wallbreak when GG is already an aggressive series, that the trapped player should not be given a free pass to escape.-Strive desperately needs frame data built in even though previous GG games aren't frame data heavy

_childDocuments_.review: Light recommend, a bit shallow as far as game modes, streamlined ranked system and single player content in general. But the gameplay is solid and the visuals are gorgeous. If that is worth 60 bucks to you then get it. Really if they just made an addictive ladder system for ranked with seasonal rewards and what not the game would be much improved. As it stands now you just kinda mindlessly play with no real reward or goal in sight other than just for the enjoyment of playing a fighting game. Which is fine to an extent, but it feels hollow given how well past games like Killer Instinct have done their ranked modes.Also, no frame data. Which is a huge negative for those who don't want to have to rely on pulling up some community run information on another screen or alt tabbing back and forth to see it as you play.  Lobbies are also pretty terrible. Really if it wasn't for the netcode and the core gameplay GG would be kind of a mess and all this behind a 60 dollar paywall? Kinda insane in the modern era of F2P multiplayer.

_childDocuments_.review: Guilty gear strive can best be summed up as a high quality extremely confident fighting game. The music, characters, lore, stages and gameplay are all extreme and the developers have so much confidence in its quality that they don't care how extreme or wacky the game is. And they have all the right in the world to be confident.Everything in this game (with 1 major exception which is the online, more on that later) is fantastic. All the characters are really unique and scream for you to want to try them. The game is super welcoming to newcomers, I have tried multiple times to get into fighting games but nothing was as potent as this game. The tutorials are very detailed, easy to go through and fun to replay to see your improvements. Input commands for moves are relatively simple for a lot of the cast and pulling off simple combos can be done by beginners without a lot of research. Even the incredibly long history of 20 years of story telling has been summarized or made very readily available by the devs, on their website they have entire sections dedicated to catching new players up. All of this has made strive an incredibly accessible fighting game and an overall fun and open starting point into the series.The presentation is fantastic. I seriously can not praise this enough. It was enough to make me care about fighting games when I always had extremely bad experiences with those games. Seeing a dolphin girl send a whale after the opponent  or seeing a jojo character use his shadow stand to completely obliterate someone and send them to the shadow realm is absolutely stunning.The music is composed by the director and you can clearly see how that unobstructed vision of his art comes through. A lot of songs have a lot of character and portray the characters they are made for perfectly. The lyrics are also chaotic and weird, especially if you understand English, but in the end it works because once again, the game presents it all with so much confidence that it ends up feeling cool.The characters are equally incredible, a lot of people love talking about the pirate dolphin girl but this game has so many incredible characters. A Brazilian female top class bodyguard that works together with a green wolf spirit, a 3 meter tall mad doctor who went insane and is now trying to make amends for his past misgivings, a black vampire techno samurai, 2 time travelers who have suffered a tremendous amount and went completely different ways character wise. These are just a couple of the growing list of incredibly unique and deep characters with over 20 years of lore history. And they all look, sound and play incredible.Now the gameplay is great, the presentation is fantastic, what else should you know about the game? The online is absolutely terrible. Starting up the game takes minutes even on a pretty good pc. After that you have to wait another couple of minutes just to look for a lobby, after that you get into a lobby with a bunch of people, and then you have to select or wait for an opponent to match with you and pray to god that the game actually works properly, I have gotten stuck trying to fight someone for minutes just for the game to tell me I can't fight that opponent for no reason. If you do get into a match everything works great, the netcode is some of the best I have ever experienced and everything feels incredibly responsive. But actually getting to that point is terrible and its the main reason I stick to casually playing with friends and practicing alone instead of constantly booting up this game and grinding the ranks. Its a big time commitment for something that works as inconsistently as it does.Lastly about the online. Its still a fighting game at the end of the day, no amount of solo practice can help you avoid going online and just getting destroyed by someone that knows more about the game. You will get memed by 1 move, you will get combod from a high percent to death and you will play really long matches of you playing super defensive because you have no idea how to do anything. That at least was the experience for me, but after not giving up I have seen myself improve and slowly beat the things I would get completely destroyed by before. Please be confident that it will get better and don't let this be a game you got super pumped for, just for the first 5 to 10 hours to completely destroy you and make you never want to touch it again.If this game ever improves the out of game connection issues, then this would be a 100 % recommend from me and I will probably edit this review. But for now be warned that this exists and that it is substantial enough to affect a lot of peoples enjoyment.Consider all of this and think to yourself if you are willing to commit 60 - 80 bucks on this title alone. Especially if you are new to fighting games, you might be super scared to get into this like I was. But I promise you this, if you are willing to give Guilty Gear Strive a chance, it will pay you back with a pure kind of fun and level of polish that is so hard to find. It will give you a chance to get into the scary but exciting world of fighting games. And it will give you a game with so much passion and love put into it that you can't help but fall in love with it yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: FIX THE DAMN LOBBIES AND ONLINEEdit: So that was my og review, simply because I had disconnect mid match for the third time in a row. Very frustrating and ever since the crossplay patch at the beginning of March, the game's online experience has become almost unbearable. Minutes upon minutes of struggling to match up with someone, and it teases you by connecting you to someone, almost to immediately break. It doesn't matter what mode you choose, it all ends up the same. Except player match, which is fine, but that means you need to have someone ready to play with you at your convenience, and sometimes, I just want to grind it out quick and easy with others on my floor, but can't. Even since day one, the lobby system was bad but now it's completely broken. The netcode mid match is good, you won't see random teleportation and lag most of the time, but it's actually getting a match started that's terrible. It's a shame because I truly love the game's mechanics, its characters, music, artstyle, and feel. Been playing for almost a full year and was having a blast, but now I honestly don't know if I want to even try logging in if I'm going to spend an hour of disconnects and dropped matches only to get maybe 6 rounds in. There is no worse feeling than getting motivated after a win or loss, only for the game to say "your done for the day." The devs say they were working on it, but still pushed dlc and it's still broken after a month of suffering and the dlc pathc didn't help at all. One more month like this and I'm ready to jump ship, with SF6 on the horizon.Edit 2: The online is still not fixed, but at least the director has made another update, keeping us in the loop. If you can't fix an issue right away, at least keep your community update, which is what's finally happened and I do appreciate that. I'll change the review to recommend when the fix is ready.

_childDocuments_.review: People say GUILTY GEAR -STRIVE- dumbed down fighting games. It's true, executing inputs or combos is a lot easier here (practically effortless). However that's not necessarily a bad thing. It's a great game to introduce people to the genre without the intimidating execution learning curve that you have to get past in other fighting games before starting to feel that you can even control your character properly.For the more experienced, I still believe the game is worth it. If you come from other fighting games, I hope you know your fundamentals and understand the neutral game well because that's all you can count on here as you will feel all the characters are overpowered and have a crazy saucy exaggerated moveset that does tons of damage super fast. However, no one is OP if everyone is OP right? This idea of balancing the cast by making everyone "extra" is really fun and feels dynamic.If you come from older GUILTY GEAR games, just don't see this one as a replacement for Xrd, you can still play Xrd without hating on -STRIVE- and vice versa.Last but not least, thanks ArcSystemWorks for ROLLBACK NETCODEEDIT: Pretty cool also that the game regularly gets balance and QoL patches. My characters get new cool stuff to learn and that's neat.EDIT 2: The "Combo Maker" update is bomb! Every fighting game should have this, it makes learning new characters a lot faster and even more fun than it already was.EDIT 3: Ok now we're getting crossplay, season 2 looks promisingEDIT 4: LOADING TIMES GOT FIXED FINALLY. I don't see how this game can get better now.

_childDocuments_.review: Strive is pretty much anything a fighting game novice could ever want. It has incredibly inviting characters with varied playstyles and personalities to the point where, despite the small roster, it's difficult to choose a main because all of the characters seem too cool. With an extremely catchy yet diverse hard rock soundtrack and a strikingly elegant visual style, the presentation as a whole is superb. The relatively simple gameplay mechanics coupled with the game's visually clear animation allows new players to easily pick it up. That doesn't mean the game doesn't have depth, however; 165 hours in (and a couple more on PS5) and I can safely say that if you like this game from the start it won't wear out its welcome very fast (in fact, I'd be surprised if I don't put in another 100). The only major downside to GGST is that the online lobbies and server connection process can be quite unstable, but this is offset somewhat by the extremely good in-game netcode and ranking system. Basically, if this game looks like fun to you, you are almost certain to enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Story: The story isn't generally what people look for in a fighting game but when it's added (in other games) it's usually not that great. besides some strange stereotypes and questionable dialogue (in older games) i really wouldn't say Guilty Gear's story is bad, it may be hard to follow at times but it's an enjoyable story with actual character development and unique world building.Graphics/Art style: With Strive having a gorgeous 3D anime art style it lends itself toward the category of games "that will never be graphically outdated". I say this because most fighting games have a "semi-realistic" or "photo realistic" design that become outdated in a couple of years and because of Strives chosen art direction it feels like i can always come back to the game and think "this game still looks amazing even in *insert year*". My only gripe is with some of the character designs being either "buff men" or "women with overly *prominent* features". This isn't always the case as with Bridget and Gold Lewis but it's unfortunately a given for most fighting games.Gameplay: Usually with fighting game's, gameplay transfers over from game to game (or IP to IP) and if you're a beginner in the genre it may be hard or complicated to get into but I'd say this is one of the easier fighting games to learn, the basic mechanics are easy to understand and the inputs aren't overly complicated.Music: I sat at my keyboard writing and deleting paragraphs for 30 minutes think of something deep and meaningful to write about but eventually i just came to the conclusion that this game's soundtrack is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. The unique style and meaning of each track makes none of the songs hard to listen to, From "The Town Inside Me" a cutesy pop-rock ensemble about a girl discovering herself to "ARMOR-CLAD OF FAITH" a disgustingly heavy and raw track that catches you off guard with punchy drums and chunky riffs i truly think there a song for everyoneTLDR; Fun fighting game with awesome soundtrack and enjoyable learning curve.

_childDocuments_.review: I got a free movie with my anime tiddy fighting game, huh...In all seriousness this is probably the most satisfying Guilty Gear has felt to me. Hits feel meaty, the movement is easier and more fluid, and the animations and wall breaks look flashy. Could it do with some tweaking? Sure. A few buffs for some characters to open up options would be nice and damage could be ever so slightly lower (though I will say that the reason this game is so satisfying is in part due to the high damage). I'd say for release, this game is pretty solid. It definitely takes some adjusting if you're coming from older Guilty Gear's but overall the changes are nice for newcomers and have definitely encouraged more people to pick up the game, which contrary to what some people believe, is a GOOD THING! (I do agree though that more options is something they should look at.)Weirdly there isn't much to unlock, the ability to get old music is nice but you can't use it outside of fights (no changing menu music etc.) and it seems they gimped character colours in order to sell it off as DLC. In Xrd there was around 10 per character, half of which you had to unlock. They were a satisfying progression based cosmetic that are now relegated to DLC, an expensive one at that. In Strive you only get 6 colours, pre-unlocked for each character and that's it. Don't worry though, you get to fish up hundred's of trash items for your unappealing avatar instead... yay. As much as this bothers me though, it's a minor issue in the grand scheme of things.The biggest issue right now is something you've probably heard talked about to death which is the online lobbies (unwieldy, ugly and lots of connection issues) plus the fact that I can literally go make a sandwich after pressing start to get in to the game as apparently I am trying to communicate with a server on the Moon. Once you're in though, you won't wanna put it down, extremely addicting and an insane netcode meaning I can actually play with my overseas friends with NO LAG! Also the story was fun to watch (especially if you know the lore) and works very well as a movie instead of a more visual novel oriented system. P.S. ArcSys... Don't tease me with saving I-no til last again. I almost had no mains in this game. Jam, Baiken and Dizzy when?

_childDocuments_.review: As with most anime fighters, whether you like Guilty Gear Strive or not is largely going to depend on whether you intend to play online or with offline versus. Offline modes are sparse and all geared towards preparing you for offline/online versus. If you're here to play by yourself, look elsewhere: this game will not give you any bang for your buck whatsoever and you'd be better served by titles such as Mortal Kombat.That said, if you are here for versus play, welcome to fun city my friends.Past guilty gears have been execution heavy, incredibly complicated, and featuring characters with incredibly high skill floors to accompany their high skill caps.Strive goes in the opposite direction:1) Low execution requirements: with few exceptions, if you see an impressive combo done by a pro you will be able to replicate it in your own games.2) Low complexities: Less systems mean better understanding of what systems exist. Better yet, the Roman Cancel system has enough depth to allow you to freestyle in the middle of a fight without hitting training mode. Deep, but not complicated.3) Characters have been simplified: not to a great degree, but enough that their extremely situational (and broken) setups no longer exist and you can focus on the mind games which make fighting games so enjoyable.When we talk execution, what we mean is how difficult is it to  land inputs under pressure. In terms of Guilty Gear, this means being able to land a punish or bread and butter combo in the middle of a round with your life bar in magic pixel territory. Generally speaking, Guilty Gear used to be regarded as a moderately high execution game while Street Fighter games were regarded as lower. I have played Fighting Games all my life and to this day I cannot consistently hit a link combo in Street Fighter 5, let alone Street Fighter 4 even in training mode. Guilty Gear Strive on the other hand? Yeah, I can consistently land everything from the longest optimal punish to the most basic bread and butter and I can even switch routes mid combo like nothing. As far as I can tell, the game has no links and everything is about special cancels and chains. This means, so long as you input the move in a reasonable amount of time during the active frames of your prior move, your move will come out. Contrast this with links where you have to wait for the precise timing in 3 or 4 frames to hit that move.This, more than the netcode, more than the lowered complexity, and more than the more-simplified characters means that I was able to take my online to the highest levels of play in the first month by grinding my way up ranked. I have never pulled that off before: better yet, now that I have achieved that I only feel the drive to just play for the game's sake. The benefit of climbing ranked is you get to fight stronger opponents: matchmaking means you actually have a real fair shot of fighting someone close to your skill level consistently. This is good stuff! Pulling off a punish, making a hard read on your opponent's defense, or pulling off a daring escape under pressure cause endorphin rushes akin to winning a championship: even the tiny things in this game, pulled off well, feel like some legal drug.Prior guilty gears focused on a myriad of systems that most casuals like myself never understood. Teching, the act of recovering quickly and at different angles from a knockdown is downright gone: you either get a hard or soft knockdown depending on the move making for more structured play. Dead Angle Attack is replaced by Yellow Roman Cancel, Hellfire is gone, no instant kill (people likely will miss this), no burst overdrive, no Danger Time, no Blitz Shield, .etcThe list is actually very large: the point is that the skill floor for just playing the game tended to be very high.When people hear the game is simplified, I imagine they're mostly hearing about the stripped down character movesets. For example and in the most extreme case, May is a character with 8 specials and 4 overdrives in Xrd. In Strive, that number has been reduced to 4 specials and 2 overdrives. In a different case, Millia only lost 1 special.  Some characters, termed 'technical' gained expanded toolkits while others had moves merged or discarded for better or worse. At best, this means a lower skill floor, but the argument goes that this also means a lower skill cap. Low skill floors are great: low skill caps not so much. That said, the variety of play I have seen makes me believe this was a step in the right direction. I believe the skill cap is still quite high for this game: just watch different pros play to get an idea of how wildly different play styles can be even with the same character.You've probably already heard, but the netcode is the best yet seen for a japanese fighting game. In my experience, it's the best netcode I've ever seen. Rollback was poorly executed in Street Fighter 5, but this is the real deal here. Playing online doesn't feel like a grind: . Just, stay in your region please. No one likes 200 ms latency even with rollback.Character variety is there: plenty of fighters make their return with improved graphics so all is well there. I'm not of the mind that dlc is a rip off in fighting games: KOF14 has proven, I believe, that you can keep a niche game afloat off of the strength of continued dlc support alone. In Strive, if you like the gameplay then you will be playing regardless of how many characters they give you.I guess the game has a story: unlike BlazBlue (or perhaps like it depending on what you think of that series), this game's story makes zero sense much like Xrd before it. Bullets are the ultimate weapon until they aren't, everyone is a good guy deep down and no one is  evil, and plot holes are a way of life. It's basically a 4 hour anime which doesn't really focus on many of the characters in the initial roster: even the new faces like Giovanna only show up for microseconds and then are never seen again: their presence completely irrelevant to the plot, such that it is.As mentioned, offline modes are all geared into getting you to play online. _childDocuments_.review: First off, my hours logged on this game are misleading as I've played all three PSN betas, early access and time since launch on the PS4 version.Secondly, the most important thing I have to say is this game's fun to play. Fighting games, as much as I love them, have been more work than fun for me lately, but that's on me for wanting to play at a tournament level. Though I'm still try harding, this game has not stopped being fun to play. The tower lobby system for functioning as the game's ranked mode is especially ingenious because it separates players by skill levels so beginners don't get washed every game and high level players get to keep fighting high level players to help them improve further. The amazing rollback netcode they developed for this game really helps to not hinder the fun.Third, obviously, it's visually stunning. The art style and animation really level up every time team red makes a new fighting game. Sound design is just as good, and with the exception of Sol, I even like the voice acting.Story mode's a great TV anime. Even Sol's English voice actor's great in it since he isn't doing his worst growly Christian Bale Batman impression like he does in gameplay.But now that I've addressed the good, let's talk about the bad. I mentioned the game has great rollback netcode, but every time you connect to servers, it takes over two minutes. It's the first thing you have to sit through to access the main menu, and every time you select an online mode to play in. But that's the least of the game's connection issues. The Steam port in particular is especially bad at connecting players with each other. You can pretty much forget about player lobbies atm. Hopefully these things will be fixed soon, but until then, the struggle to play online is still a struggle.From a gameplay standpoint, I miss gatlings. These target combos they still somehow refer to as gatlings only serve to make hit confirming harder, which kinda goes against STRIVE's philosophy of accessability.Also, fishing is basically just free lootboxes. Guilty Gear Xrd had this, too, and the devs' decision to include Anji and I-no in the base roster (despite being planned as DLC characters) after the game was further delayed is a rare example of consumer-friendliness rarely seen in the gaming industry today. Most publishers woulda just made 'em day one DLC, so I wanna give 'em points for that, too.

_childDocuments_.review: Over a year into its life this game still has so many crippling issues that the developers seemingly just don't care about fixing. Updates come and go that make minor changes to one thing or another but never address the things people have been complaining about since release.Half of the terminals for matches in lobbies just don't work, you walk up to them and just get an error message. Probably another half again of the terminals people manage to get onto won't accept opponents, they just give another error message. There's a semi-automated matchmaking system that will place you against people while you practice in training mode so you can sort of circumvent the barely functioning lobbies, but it's unable to handle people who go AFK in the queue or people you've declined matches or rematches with, so if you get matched against someone like that the system will just keep giving you the same exact prompt to play them over and over.The ranked tower constantly interrupts you by limiting you to three matches against someone at a time, presumably to stop people from grinding easy rank off of someone, but doesn't stop you from just getting back on the terminal again against the same person after those three matches for three more. All it accomplishes is forcing you to sit through loading screens. Every few matches it will also stop you completely to inform you you're being moved to another floor so you never get any time to get to known people on any floor, defeating the purpose of a lobby system entirely. The whole system is also set up in such a way as to gradually shift the entire playerbase upwards in level, regardless of whether or not people are really getting better at the game, so eventually everyone will basically just be lumped together in one big pool where the skill disparity is comical. It's already happened for the top half of the playerbase and it's probably only going to be another couple months before it's happened to the bottom half as well.EDIT: They finally added pre-match ping indicators in the second year of the game's lifespan, they take a good 10+ seconds to show up though and are frequently inaccurate, I've had many matches that showed a stable 40-80 ping green connection indicator before the match only to be horrible 8f rollback lagfests. But hey, at least the indicator is there now, useful or not that's a step in the right direction.You'll also sometimes get disconnected mid-round for seemingly no reason, perfectly good matches stop abruptly mid attack with a minute long "please wait" message before you're kicked all the way back to the main menu. Sometimes it doesn't even get as far as letting you start the match and just gives the disconnect message as soon as you approach a terminal.It's really embarrassing that people point to this as the fighting game with the best netcode, if a game in any other genre was released with these kinds of network issues it would be mocked ruthlessly.The game has acquired a reputation for being a good entry point into the fighting game genre but it's vastly overblown, the tutorials are garbage for anything more than learning you can hold back to block and how to extend your combos but the real meat of learning the game is understanding what every character can do and the character-specific tutorials are awful and go no further than "hit the slow move before it finishes" or "jump over the projectile". They added a system for sharing combos with other players to help people learn offense but you can't load those combos into training mode to practice against, you have to manually record yourself doing the combos so if you're struggling to figure out how to deal with something you better hope you're able to do it yourself.It's really a shame because from a strictly gameplay perspective it's an enjoyable game, but when you have to go through such a struggle just to get to the point of actually playing the game and it's fighting against every attempt you make to improve it's hard to feel like it's worth launching at all.SEASON 3 UPDATE: They said in the patch notes that they'd fixed a lot of the issues with the lobbies. They lied, all the old issues are still present but on top of those now when you try to change between rooms you get a network error and get kicked back to the start screen and have to go through all the menus again to get back to the room you were trying to go to.

_childDocuments_.review: This might be everything I dislike in a fighting game in one package. But maybe it's just my age showing.Visuals:Top notch art design with one problem. It's basically screen flashes upon screen flashes. Every attack has extra visual pop. The game hurts my eyes. There is a "bright white" flash between matches which is probably the most offensive decision I've seen in a fighter design. As I have yet to be able to afford a cyber eye upgrade for flare reductions this game has twice triggered headaches after only a short period of time. If you have those yellow goggles / glasses you're not going to 'want' to put them on your going to have to.Music:I dig the new direction the music went with.Game-play:It almost seems like everything has been designed for the spectators. Maybe this is just the way fighting games have gone over the years - but the game feels incredibly cramped. A combination of "poses" / "voice lines" seem spliced into the combat. Level transfer on 'edge' impact may be a good decision to reduce corner cheesing but the animated camera pivots continue to disorient me. Animated 'specials' that pull the camera away. I definitely feel like these characters have gone through a lot of versions and don't have the same consistency. Maybe the complex combo / juggle / burst counter play still exists but it's so hard to see what's going on because everything is like a scene out of a manga. I might grow to like it but my 'out of the box' reaction is that it's a shiny kid's game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first Guilty Gear game I have played seriously and there is a lot to like:Despite *only* having 15 characters on the launch roster this is more than enough as they all feel very distinctive.  Visually the game is absolutely gorgeous and runs very well.  The combat has plenty of depth with various mechanics offering different risk/reward setups.  It can take a while to get used to as it is VERY unforgiving to players spamming attacks as the counters hit very hard and leave you at huge disadvantage.  From what I understand, combo routes have been somewhat nerfed as you cannot chain all attacks in sequence from your lightest to your heaviest - though to me this just means that you have to work for an opening to land a heavy top capatalise off that.  Its still very fast paced for a "footsie" based fighter, however.The ability to sacrifice your meter for the rest of the match in order to access an Instant Kill has been removed in this game.  I think this is somewhat disappointing but can see why this happened what with the shorter rounds and higher damage output overall compared to previous entries.  Perhaps this will be added down the line as a "classic" or "hardcore" mode...A great fighting game, with a fantastic soundtrack and art direction.  The biggest problem is the time it takes to connect initially to the online services - this is still too long in this day and age.  And the online lobbies are quaint to be nice about it and utterly redundant and annoying in reality,  Thankfully they added an option to queue for a match whilst you are in training mode.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fantastic. The presentation is beautiful, the soundtrack is badass (I listen to it on repeat). The gameplay is different from prior Guilty Gear games, but there's a ton of depth in it, especially the revamped RC (roman cancel) system, between the 4 types, there are drift RCs where you can move during the RC in any of the 4 cardinal directions, and fast RCs where you can cancel the RC into a move directly, skipping the burst of it.The netcode is phenomenal, I regularly forget I'm playing online, I even had a game, where I only realized it was 180ms, when I read the ping at the top, I couldn't feel the difference. It's a fixed 1 frame delay, and it's so so good. Rollback is the way.There's also an in-depth mission mode that teaches you everything, even if you're brand new to fighting games, it goes over a ton of fighting game concepts. It even goes into frame advantage, fuzzies, meaties, safe jumps, and matchup tutorials.As someone caught up on the Guilty Gear story (and a fan), this one's story mode is way better than I expected. It's really well written and incredibly entertaining. It's somewhat hard to recommend to a complete novice to the series, but if you watch a lore catchup video like the ones from WoolieVersus or BrendanMushi, I would recommend checking it out.As for the negatives, connecting to the game takes way longer than it should, like 1.5-2 minutes. Lobbies have connectivity issues (which might be better now after the server maintenance that happened at the time of this review. As a recommendation, just queue at a station, DON'T try to chase down people to challenge them, there is too much lag in the lobby, that by the time you challenge someone, they might already be in a match and you can't see that.Finally there are a couple other issues that are in their "known issues" post, like searching for player match lobbies by id doesn't work atm, and trying to view another player's replay redirects you to a completely random replay.I can say though, even with those few glaring issues (which do need to be fixed in a timely manner), the game is just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fun, I don't care, I just want to play it all the time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has the potential to be one of the best ever made but there are some issues that they devs are working on.The action is aggressive and looks great.  This is a game of rushdown.  Defence has to be active and run away is punished by the game.The characters come to life in great detail and animations full of personality.  The backgrounds are also beautiful and detailed but perhaps too eye catching.  They backgrounds are so great that they don't melt into the background.  COUNTER, the game really wants you to confirm counter hits.  It points out each counter hit with a boom, the announcer on a bullhorn shouting "COUNTER" and screen filling billboards.  It's silly and distracting.  I assume that this is a decision to appeal to the esports audiences.The netcode is great the lobbies and servers aren't.  The rollback netcode is the best thing since ggpo.  Smooth and responsive.  With good ISP, and  wired set ups on both sides you can play with anyone in the world.  When you start the game it needs to communicate with it's servers.  This takes 1 to 2 minutes just to start the game even if all you want to do mess around in training mode.  This is of course a great annoyance to everyone.  Another annoyance is the lobbies are still not the best, with matches failing to start, viewing "R-cards" (player profiles) also take one minute each to fetch and trying to find friends a chore.Even with it's flaws this is a 90/100 release.  With fast great looking action and best in class netcode this is a game that all fighting game fans will want to try.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't review games often but I had to put in my 2 cents for GG Strive.  All the hardcore fighting game players already bought this game.   This review is for casual fighting gamers (like me) and new comers to fighting games. -This game is incredibly accessible for the new comer and just out right fun for all skill levels. The balance between simplicity and depth is excellent. So if you did want to grow beyond casual playing, you have plenty of room.  I used to play endless hours of fighting games as a kid.  As I have gotten older I have certainly become a casual.  This game makes me want to start playing for hours and hours again. -The in game tutorials are very good.  The youtube twitch content is also good.  There are so many amazing players you can watch for inspiration. -The netcode is better then anything else I have experienced and I can't say enough good things about it.   The netcode may very well be the best in the industry.  The poor online experience is what has kept me from putting in the hours in previous fighting games i have tried to get into.  I'd just get so frustrated about not being able to pull off combos I know i can do locally.  I just never seemed to get used to the lag.   But with Strive, the online experience is the closest to local I have seen.   -The skill matching system is also good.    You can play better players if you want, but the better players can't go into lower tiers and wreck people like me.   You can let the system match make for you, or you can pick and choose which rooms to join in your tier.  You can also of course create your own room in your tier. -I don't need to sell the art and music, the sample videos and images already have sold many copies of this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I will preface this by saying I've been playing Guilty Gear since it came out on the PS2 some 25 or so years ago.  I've also had many other fighting games under my belt to some degree.If you are reading this review and are 100% new to fighting games, I would NOT recommend this game.  It has a ton of mechanics to it and the tutorial is really hot and cold.  It will tell you how to do things through text then chuck you into a scenario where you need to pass 3 out of 5 attempts and is NOT character specific.  Have a favorite that isn't Sol or Ky and wanna run them through a tutorial?  Yeah nope, for the majority of it, you are stuck learning the basics with those 2 and are kinda left in the wind to problem solve how to do some mechanics with other characters.  The game will even say that some characters can't do a certain mechanic but won't name them specifically, leaving you again in the training mode trying to figure out what in the hell is going on.  I felt the entire experience being stressful, and this is LEARNING the game, not even some expert mode stuff.  That gets crazier later on but anyways.  I'd suggest starting with GranBlue (for simplicity, you can be hardcore or casual in that game and still have fun)  Or BlazeBlue: Central Fiction for being a complicated fighting game with a MUCH better tutorial that IS character specific and really sits you down to discuss things.Now for the people who've been playing this game and are wondering about Strive?  I would recommend it.As for the deluxe version, honestly unless again you play Sol/Ky with the extra fancy colors or whatever, I'd get the base game to see if it flies for you then get the season pass, or heck even wait to see which characters come out of it.The roster is on the weirder side as major staples like Johnny and Venom are noticeably absent.  The new characters introduced (Giovanna and SUPER COOL VAMPIRE MAN) are awesome but don't seem to fill the void of missing out on characters being in the game since 500 years ago.  But that's just me,  I mean even Jam is absent so players like Theresa are sobbing in a corner right now.Gameplay is very smooth and much more refined.  Characters that ARE in the roster either remain unchanged or take notes from Guilty Gear XX(Reload) in how they play.  May is a prime example, in Xrd she felt more like a zoner with her dolphins whereas now she feels back to her rushdown days, getting in your face with her anchor and hitting way more than she probably should.  Millia has done away with her stupid hair projectile mechanic plaguing her in Xrd high level play.  Now she has new moves that compliment her speed and agility with much better mix game.  Other characters like I-No and Zato-1 have more streamlined button inputs making them less painful on a hand if you played using a controller and not a stick.  As for if it benefits them I'm not 100% sure, as I was never great with Zato and only playing I-No to dink around.The new lobby system I have not fully tested out but feels more rigid.  Plus I'm personally not a fan of how they turned the avatar/fishing thing to 2D and very automated.  Most of the stuff you'll be fishing out are just cosmetics for your very pixely avatar where you need to squint to see what the heck it's supposed to be.  There's no figure collecting dioramas like in Xrd so for those who really liked that, I'm sorry for your loss.As for the plot, honestly I never played this game for the story.  Trying to follow it over the years only gave me a migraine.  That being said, they've improved upon the in-game wiki in terms of learning about what happened, when/where and who was involved as well as learning about individual characters and how they're involved.  Even characters who've not seen the light of day (Zappa, Bridget) have their bio up there.My only main complaint is probably how the tutorial is set up and getting into the game itself.  Connecting to the server takes about 5-10min for me and I wish they did a similar system like in DBFZ where you can opt for off-line if you're dinking around in the story or missions.Is it worth the full price?  Honestly, no fighting game is worth the crazy prices, the genre in of itself is a black hole of exploitation.  My only suggestion is if you're hardcore about fighting games, yeah you've already thrown your wallet on the deluxe version, maybe even preordered it and also bought it on PS4.  For others, try another fighting game on sale and wait for this to get more content, as 15 characters with major players missing feels really awkward.

_childDocuments_.review: Aight, let's get into how this thing smells.I'm coming from the perspective of someone new to the Guilty Gear franchise, having played Blazblue and Them's Fightin' Herds as my fighting games of choice before this point. The discourse over Strive being dumbed down and lacking options goes over my head, and considering people have been saying this about basically every fighting game released since 2009 I really am not putting much weight into these statements. If you're looking for a game with plenty of depth and options, this game will satisfy, trust me. Roman Cancels are incredibly flexible, tools in neutral are diverse, and combo options seem to be satisfying.For those on the other end of the spectrum, who have never played fighting games before and are drawn in by the game's industry-leading graphics, fret not. The game's tutorial and challenge modes provide valuable information that will help you get started, and I know many people who are content jamming arcade mode and appreciating all the glowy anime pixels with no intention of ranking or going online. While more advanced players justifiably bemoan the lack of combo training and frame data, Strive has made the fighting game onboarding experience almost as easy as Blazblue's flirting with autocombos and "stylish" mode. That being said, Strive is still a fighting game, and its process of play and growth simply cannot be fully cushioned by nature. You're going to be spamming unsafe moves and get punished over and over again, and you will simply be unable to beat anyone better than you. I can't fault Strive for this simple fact which has towered above the entirety of the FGC for decades now, but it's something for those considering this as an entry point to consider. With that all being said, the netplay has some issues. The much-touted rollback netcode is incredible, and while I feel it's not necessarily better than some other games like TFH or Skullgirls, games feel clean and responsive even over long distances. However, all internet-related things surrounding the actual rounds are so, so bad. Lobbies constantly struggle to get people into games from challenges, and the pace at which one actually connects to servers is glacial on PC. You're going to spend three minutes just on the title screen getting into the game proper, and another three minutes accessing online lobbies. It's simply intolerable, and I hope that ArcSys will continue to fix these frustrating holes in an otherwise great experience.Strive's story mode is also, er, medium. Watching through, the advertised "polished visuals" really kept echoing in my mind as Sol Badguy slowly moonwalks his way through the story. Posing and animation often feels awkward, and can definitely detract from the viewing experience.Regardless of these quibbles, the core of Strive stands as a titanic, generation-defining fighting game title worthy of your time. Its gameplay is solid, its graphics are transcendental, and its attitude and atmosphere are unparalleled.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR:+ Best looking and sounding Guilty Gear to date+ Very welcoming to newcomers- Missing what makes most Arcsys games stand out- No combo mode (to be added later)- Lack of single player contentI want to preface this review by stating this is a great game. Arc System Works are amazing at creating fighting games, and in terms of being the next generation of Guilty Gear, this is near-perfect. I also personally have found it to be worth the price tag, but there are some glaring issues that I feel hold the game back from being worth most peoples' money, at least in its current state.To start with positives, the presentation is absolutely phenomenal. The visuals, the music, the voice acting; these are all amazing and even in sessions when I was playing with the same random person with the same characters (which has happened a few times), I felt like I was playing a fresh match every time. To specifically talk about the music, Daisuke Ishiwatari has really outdone himself, as he seems to do every game, and the vocal talent of Naoki and Aisha shines in every track. Even if you have a few bad matches (or even a streak in my case), it's hard to lose interest when the game encourages you so well.While the mechanics in this game have been simplified over the past entries of Guilty Gear, causing some disappointment in the veteran crowd, this is an excellent starting point for newcomers or even those wanting a more relaxed version of Guilty Gear. Given the large marketing Strive got before launch, I'd assume many people are either coming other fighting games or playing Strive as their first fighting game ever. The mission mode is great in this game; if you are new to Guilty Gear or fighting games in general, this can serve as a good introduction to basics, game specific mechanics, and even some more situational instances.Onto some negatives, the most major is that there is a shocking lack of content in the game, and I don't just mean modes or characters, which is an issue on its own but I hope this can be solved with post-launch content. This one is more targeted towards those who have already played Arcsys games but some newer players might feel disappointed, regardless. Part of what makes Arcsys games great is their focus on character interaction and world. What I mean by this is whenever any character in the roster fights another character, even if they have no interaction in the story, still treat each other as unique when it comes to a win-quote. In Strive, you get a match win-quote (which already appeared at the end of matches in Xrd), a stat summary page, and that's it. Nothing specific to who is fighting who, just the option to rematch or exit the lobby.This point might come off as nitpicky, as it is just a minor part of the game and doesn't affect anything on a major scale, and while I do somewhat agree, was there any reason to remove a notable feature that appears in most Arcsys games? For a less minor change similar to this, just look at arcade. In Xrd, every character had a few cutscenes in their arcade story, as well as an intro and ending movie. In Strive, out of the few arcade runs I've completed so far (as Faust, Potemkin, and Sol), I only experienced two unique cutscenes for each character, and those were only a few lines each, compared to the dozen or so lines per cutscene in Xrd. Let me reiterate that this is something focused at the newer crowd, who might want to start playing Strive by themselves and take a peek into the story and single player content, only to be perhaps disappointed at the lack of presentation in these areas when so much of the game is otherwise oozing presentation in every pixel.(This is to be added in a later date, but until it is, I will keep this section as it is currently relevant.)Another redaction which affects newer and veteran players alike is the removal of Combo Mode. Combo Recipe is likely the successor, which pushes all combo creation and sharing onto the community rather than the developers. While I understand why Strive's mechanics prevent an abundant number of combos from being possible as in Xrd, the outright removal of Combo Mode seems unnecessary, especially since Combo Recipe isn't out yet.To backtrack a bit, the lack of modes is a bit surprising, even for Guilty Gear which never really stood out for single player modes but has always offered it. Aside from arcade, vs, story, training, and tutorial modes, you get survival mode. That's it. No M.O.M. mode, no Combo mode, nothing. Survival could at least do what Accent Core had with the bland but nonetheless more engaging concept of stat boosts, occasional unique items, EX characters, and survival level, rather than the occasional mysterious challenger and win count.I want to finish this review by restating that I do think for many people, this will be worthwhile. Those dedicated to fighting games made up their mind about the game long before the game's release, or are focused on online play and will disregard my points regarding single player. Additionally, I am aware I haven't touched some points such as online, and the reason for each being that many other reviews are summarizing online. For those wanting to get into the story, the Guilty Gear website has a decent summary of events before Xrd, and Arcsys have the stories of both Xrd games uploaded to their YouTube channel. (For those who are up to date on the stories up until Strive, you are in for a treat. The earlier chapters of the story drag on for a bit (but are still enjoyable), but the last chapter alone is such an perfect and heartfelt sendoff that I could not imagine a better conclusion. To quote the ending credits, it's just beautiful.In regards to individual stories, however, there are some problems. Without spoiling anything, anyone curious as to the stories of May, Ramlethal, or Faust will be disappointed, as they do not appear in Story Mode outside of a cameo.)I understand the delays and struggle due to COVID, and I do commend Arc System Works and their team for their dedication and strive (pun intended) to create the next generation of Guilty Gear.  But from my perspective, I wouldn't recommend this game full-price to most people.

_childDocuments_.review: I ended up buying this game for myself and my brother on a whim that tag team might be implemented at a later date and we might have some fun with it.For those of you thinking of buying this game let me explain something to you first. A few of the >>TUTORIAL<< missions require you to react and input controller commands between moves that are measured in frames per second. Some of those moves need to be input within 2 or 3 frames in order for you to 'BEAT' the mission. To put that into perspective and to shed some light on what the developers were thinking when they built this game here it is: An average monitor on an average computer is flashing your eyes with roughly 60 images OR (FRAMES) per second. A single frame is shown to you at a speed of  >>16.67ms<<(that's milliseconds). double that if you are trying to accomplish something in 2 frames. triple it if you want to do the same thing within 3 frames. NOW HERE'S THE POINT ->THE AVERAGE HUMAN BEINGS REACTION TIME IS BETWEEN 150 - 300 MS. You do the math..... There are things that they have designed the game to do that you will never, ever be able to accomplish. Period. During alpha, beta, they had a chance to tweak these things to make it humanly possible. There were some missions that required you to do something within 3 frames. Rather than increase that time to something remotely manageable they instead decreased the frames to 2. Imagine that.... This was there frame of mind and this was what they were thinking about when the crafted a few of the games mechanics ie: instant block and wakeup ect.Will I continue to play the game? I'm a bit of a masochist so ya. Probably will. But you be the judge for yourself if this is worth 80 of your dollars.You've been warned.

_childDocuments_.review: Guilty gear strive is a 10/10 fighting game. Absolutely beautiful graphics and presentation, has an outstanding soundtrack AND all of the old games' soundtracks pre-packaged into the game for FREE. The game mechanically is very newbie friendly, ive gotten several people who would never even TOUCH a fighting game absolutely hooked on this game. Its got a low skill barrier but a really high skill ceiling. The roman cancel mechanics make what is possible basically infinite. If you think you can do it, you probably can.However, this brought a bunch of issues to the forefront as a longtime fighting game player, the game feels very simple. ALOT more simple than the older guilty gears. I dont feel like im using my head and making complex decisions, because most of the time im just pressing buttons and fishing for combo starters. If pressing buttons doesn't work i just rotate between dust/grab/low and i usually end up just mixing the opponent to death without much effort. (Keep in mind im on floor 10, bouncing off of celestial every so often, so im fighting at a level of competence that matters)Alot of characters feel watered down compared to their old counterparts. Sol, the once semi-well rounded character is now a rushdown do-it-all who just mashes slash until he gets a counter hit. May is just dolphin spam with a grab mixup every so often. Ramlethal is just "Push the person to the wall then i win the game". They all have very simplistic goals and dont feel as freeing or complex as they were in Xrd. This leads to alot of repetitive matches, most players blending together in a big mess of characters boiled down to their one main gimmick and then left as that. The online situaion is also pretty terrible. The lobby system is horrible, you get put into a room of only 30 players, even if you use quick start, so instead of fighting against anyone in the world out of a pool of thousands of players, you tend to get matched up with the same 5 or so players over and over again. This adds to the samey-ness of the gameplay and make it feel even more like im just turning my brain off and going numb while pressing buttons.And yet, as bad as that sounds, i still play the hell out of this game and have a blast doing so, because the mechanics of the game are nuanced enough to allow for a level of freedom and experimentation that i have never felt before in a fighting game. _childDocuments_.review: I've been playing fighting games for about 20 years, and Strive might be the only one I play for the rest of my life. Am I bull****ing you? Maybe. Is that bull**** blazing?  I was gifted this game because I didn't have the funds for it at the time, and one of my streaming friends got me a copy on a whim. When my paycheck comes in, I'll buy it for him back as repayment so we can play it together.  Guilty Gear is universally known for its Punch, Kick, Slash and Heavy Slash movements. Usually, they're inputted in a revolver mechanic of PKSH in that order. Sometimes, I like to think that my ex-roommate helped develop this game, because he said "that's a bit extra/too confusing/why can't I just focus on two buttons in a combo." To fighting game fans, you'd probably dunk on him for being a casual. But sometimes? I liked to think he was correct. If you want people to get into a fighting game, make it easy to learn and hard to master. XRD definitely tried to do that with its tutorial, but they one-upped it in this game by knocking in the idea that "repetition is key" and "practice makes perfect."So now, your revolver combos are just Slash and Heavy Slash. If you as a new player want to start a combo, it's just those two buttons. It's a gateway to learning the game without being overloaded tons of info at once. A lot of people (including a certain Steam casual-hater thread) would argue that it makes the game too simple. That's what I thought until I spent 19  hours of this game labbing combos. Hell, I did a deep-dive of characters on stream, and was stuck on what to do with Leo; then, a friend of mine sent me a simple screenshot of their combo recipe--and they barely even touch fighting games--and now I'm hooked on him.Anybody can learn this game, but that doesn't invalidate how technical it is; put time into it, and it'll give you results. Just the same as if you played literally any other game in any other genre.Look, I'm not ashamed in saying that I play this game on a prebuilt gaming laptop with a 1060 in it. The graphics are  It runs at a silky framerate, the atmosphere of each and every stage is beautiful, and the stage transitions were something we didn't deserve, yet got anyway. I haven't had any issues with lag on my machine, aside from the time I did a 3-hour livestream doing a deep dive of the characters, the mechanics, the stages and some of the arcade mode stories. Even then, the lag waxed and waned; I could turn my quality settings down to help ease the issue, and it still retained its shining glory.If you have a potato, it'll be difficult to run it; but not by much. However, if I could give a comparison, if your machine can barely run/can't run Guilty Gear XRD, your chances of running this will be slimmer than that. I knew from the very beginning that when a new Guilty Gear was announced, the music was going to be a banger. I was blown away by "Smell of the Game" to the point where it was my go-to song for everything. Making breakfast, watering my plants, doing both at the same time, hell even doing neither. But when the rest of the soundtrack finally made itself apparent through character trailers, I was sold. "Play the Hero," "Alone Infection," "Armor-Clad Faith," each and every song gave me goosebumps. I will be purchasing the entire soundtrack as soon as possible and make my neighbors feel every vibration through my surround sound speakers because f*** you, it's Guilty Gear time, even if it is 2AM.NOW IT'S TIME!Impressive rollback netcode, but terrible lobby support. That's it. That's the entire online summed up. You don't have to read the rest if you don't want to.I was playing with another friend of mine prior to my stream and we couldn't even set up a private lobby, because when they entered in my specific ID, it would give the lobbies of several other players playing in public lobbies. My lobby never showed up. We circumvented this by making a public lobby, limiting the seats to just two people and letting them rush in as fast as humanly possible. Other than that? We played our hearts out. If we experienced any lag, it lasted for two seconds or less. We played, at most, 10 matches when it was supposed to be 2 or 3. Whoops!I am a huge Ramlethal simp. Ramlethal mains DM me. I just wanna marry you.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who is a fighting game veteran. _childDocuments_.review: is  It got me into fighting games, helped me meet so many wonderful people, and unlocked a competitive spirit in me I didn't know I had. Getting 3rd at a local, place 500th place out of 2000 at Evo, and achieving  a few months ago are the highlights of my gaming career. However, I can no longer recommend  because at time of writing, the game I fell in love no longer exists in any meaningful sense, and it has become apparent that Arc System Works has an adopted a disastrous policy of releasing annual major shakeups to the meta  In August of last year, Arc Sys brought two new system mechanics to the game, and the more notable one, Wild Assault was a toxic snowball enabler upon release. Things improved in a December patch, but adjustments to a Wild Assault subtype rendered it equally noxious, and the flow of the game still revolved too much around obtaining an early advantage in a round. This was finally addressed in early August and aside from a few overtuned recent DLC characters, the game's meta felt healthy for the first time in a year.We were given only three months to enjoy this before Season 4 arrived last Thursday.Season 4 focused on character changes, and a couple of characters had their more obnoxious options tuned down, sometimes inviting an entire rework to accommodate the changes. In many cases, high level techniques have been replaced with more accessible alternatives. From my observations, it seems like Arc Sys' intent is to fill the gap in with new tech but the initial impression many players have is the new options don't have the same juice. One of my two mains, Sol Badguy, has been hit by both of these issues, with all of his approach tools being neutered to the point where he's a different archetype now, a far more polarized and niche character focused on losing neutral but hitting hard when he gets in. Admittedly Sol's damage was toxic when matched with the rest of his kit, but Arc Sys also gutted his pressure with fafnir becoming a new move entirely and bandit bringer being punishable on block now, and the result is a character that is only fun to play when you're doing combos (and his combo structure is entirely different now as well). My other main, Faust, is eating well (literally, thanks to S3) thanks to buffs that entirely outweigh two small nerfs he received , but is entering a meta that renders him competitively unviable. Faust has always lost to many of the top tiers that  has had throughout its life style, and in some cases those top tiers appear to have been gigabuffed, most notably Ramlethal, a character who I am almost convinced is bugged based on the sheer utility of her conversions from any hit and the sheer damage provided by canceling into her super, Calvados. After taking a break from the game after graduating from the aforementioned beginner tournament, I was super excited to return to taking the game seriously over the past two weeks, but now I barely want to boot it up. I sympathize with the pro scene for this game, who don't know whether they'll be playing next year's Arc World Tour finals and Evo tournaments on a stupid patch or one they've barely had time to adjust to. Not to mention the embarrassing lack of key quality of life features, such as a frame data display, three years in and the lack of a true ranked mode. If these issues are addressed I'd be happy to change this review, but for now I can only say 'stay away.'Well, on the bright side, I've been wanting to get more into .

_childDocuments_.review: Truly, this could be the peak of this genre - at least for now. Innovative and refreshing mechanics, well settled and grounded yet fast paced core gameplay - comes with the best netcode I've ever experienced.The visuals are outstanding. It feels and looks like an OVA with the fat load of budget. Soundtrack is simply the best there ever yet. It's just... masterpiece. Almost every character is redesigned for the art direction they are heading (except Potemkin, since you can't make it any better) and the whole cast is fitting so damn good.Classic characters that be a part of the franchise from the start, (such as Sol, Ky, May, Millia, Faust, Axl, Chipp, Zato...) beloved characters from follow-up games (Ramlethal, Leo, I-no..) and brand new characters (Giovanna and Nagoriyuki) are mixed up for a not large, but colorful selection of roster. Definitely feels missing, but I'm pretty sure it'll be filled with more classics on it's life-span (which i hope will be long) - and at the time I write this review; Jack-O returned and they announced Baiken is next.As like the art direction; the gameplay is redesigned as well. Old characters have so different yet memorable movesets - just adjusted for the new pace of the game. At first glimpse it may look like they made game simplier and easier, but I can assure it's not true, even a bit. Roman cancels are now color-coded, and they open a gate with whole load of new oppurtunites. Characters are just feel so good to play with, so I find myself changing between them. It's quite easy to learn a character but really hard to master one.Lobby system might felt bit forced, but it's no means bad. You can customize your 2D avatar and with the last updates, your very own house. Item farming is not hard, but encourages you to play different characters.It has a story mode at launch day. And at this point, GG is just a huge iceberg on lore and waiting for more people to dive in. It's just stunning. And it not feels like "a fighting game story mode" which is filled with pointless 1v1 matches against non-playable or playable characters. It flows like a pure water.Detailed yet not boring tutorial, training and missions mode that makes you better adapt the whole new experience. It even goes for match-ups against every character. It explains a lot of questions you have, it's great to have something like this so you stop googling how to fight against X character over and over again.It's been 6-7 months and it's still alive and kicking on PC. It managed to have a great amount of playerbase to call it a success. Wish there was a crossplay option, though. With each update the game shifts to an even crazier experience with balancing updates that purely focusing on making every character broken - - instead of nerfing all of them down. New characters with distinctive gameplay designs.Unlike most of the other people who hates it's ranked system, I really dig it in. It's encouraging to play with. It's really easy to climb up ranks with consecutive wins and really hard to go bottom with consecutive losses.That said, -STRIVE- has a lot to do to be a one game to rule all. And that should be start at server connection times. Loading times and matchmaking are really fast, that might compensate the initial connection time a bit but it's a huge loss nevertheless. It should not take 5 whole minutes to just boot-up your game. Especially, when it's forced. There is no offline play option at start menu, so whenever you want to play the game, you have to be sure it'll worth your boot-up time. Or just admire you are using the best platform - the glorious PC masterrace and use a custom proxy tools such as Struggle or Totsugeki to shorten it to just a minute.Last but not least, it's highly moddable. You can do whatever you want, if you have enough patience and knowledge. If you don't bother all with these, you can also opt-in for other people's creations with Unverum. There is a dedicated page in gamebanana that you can find countless of mods that alter appearences, movesets, musics, graphics and UI.
