_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has been trying to get into fighting games for a long time, I think Strive really nails it in terms of accessibility while still making every character and every matchup feel unique and complex in their own way. I've tried several fighting games in the past, but everytime I'd go online, I'd feel like I was losing to things I just couldn't adapt to on the fly, and had to either go back to training mode after having already spent tens of hours simply looking for a character to pick up, or straight up google how the character that just beat me worked.Thinking this time would be the same as always (but still having hope due to how the game was marketed as beginner-friendly), I made the mistake of spending my first 50 hours in training mode, trying to learn everything I  I needed to know before ever getting in a real match. Turns out when I jumped into online mode for the first time, I could actually understand what was going on from the get-go, because the tutorials are efficient at teaching you the game mechanics, the characters are not many and are relatively easy to understand (but still very unique, deep and more or less hard to master depending on each case), the animations and the graphic effects do a good job at telling you what's happening on the screen, what hit you, how you should react to certain enemy moves, etc. and last but not least, I don't have to focus half of my brain just on coordinating my fingers in order to  properly. This game's execution/mechanical skill floor is very low for its genre: basic combos are short and not-too-tight but still efficient enough, there are no particularly hard motion inputs, and you get many macros – including one for  Picking a character was far easier than I expected: I just played a few matches with Nagoriyuki because I liked his huge normals, his unique meter and his special-canceling gimmick, but then I realized I was zoning for most of the time, so I switched to Axl  and had a blast with him.If you're picking up this game as a newcomer to the genre, don't worry about not being good enough to go online, because everyone is trash. I know it for a fact because I'm also trash, and yet I can beat other players, but most importantly, I can  even as I get my ass handed to me. Besides, everyone up until floor 6~7 just spams the same approach over and over again, so if you manage to figure out how to get around their favorite gimmick (which shouldn't be too difficult for the reasons listed above), you'll have no problem getting to the point where you have to get good "the hard way" – which is actually not a bad thing, because as I previously said, this is a game that makes losing fun too.As for the things people commonly say to criticize this game: Maybe it's not as deep as the older titles, but it's also far from being shallow, and it's way, way, waaay more accessible than them, so it was a price worth paying IMO. Even for experienced players, more accessibility = more players = larger community and more money for the devs = more attention towards the series. Round length is a matter of preference, although I admit I'd like for them to last longer too; but in exchange, the wall break mechanic isn't too impactful on corner pressure because you'll likely be dead if you get caught in a corner combo after eating one or two mixups. Well yes. The lobby system sucks, the fact that you can't even play more than three matches against the same person sucks, and the time it takes to just go online sucks (the patch made it a bit better but it's still painfully long). But they definitely don't suck enough to make the game not worth playing.Edit: added last paragraph

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:Once I seperated it from expecting more of Xrd, the game started being fun. It's very very different to the other Guilty Gear games, and that's fine. Modding is super cool too, you can make the UI a bit more stylish with it! If you haven't played a Guilty Gear game, but think they look cool, play this. If you're a Guilty Gear veteran, it might off-put you a bit, but underneath it's deeper issues there's an amazing game.Overall the game is fun! I do still have some standalone issues though.Full Complaints here:The presentation is cool, but it's squarely in the territory of going a bit TOO hard on the visuals. Supers take entirely too long for their own good, the growing combo meter is obnoxious, and i've dropped counter combos countless times because of the giant slow down. It's just something I have to get used to because I don't think they'll be changing it, but it's entirely too much. By having everything absurdly over the top, it has the issue of desensitizing you to it, and making everything seem bland.The music is excellent, but we are in 2022, and we still somehow don't have the ability to change stage and music on rematch. No instant-rematch either. Music is great, but listening to the same track for 3 matches in a row is grating. Ideally if the stage/music is set to random, it'd be amazing if it would change per match.Insta-Kill moves are gone, which were a really awesome part of the previous games, but I sorta understand it since you have access to an insta-kill at all times. That being doing any sort of combo.Damage values in this game are a tiny bit absurd, and I really think they need to be toned down. I shouldn't be able to take half of someone's HP with a 4 hit combo. Comebacks aren't impressive in this game, they're common and very likely. It leads a lot of matches to feeling boring because they end from two or so interactions. I might just be scrub-quoting here, but when I feel dissatisfied with winning?? I think something is up.Air-dashes feel awful in this game. There's like, half a second or so of startup when you air-dash, making IADs feel anything but instant. It's probably my second biggest issue with the game.The online experience in this game is actually horrendous, everything that isn't the netplay itself is abysmal. What I mean is, when you're actually playing a match? That feels amazing, the rollback is implemented amazingly and I never think about wifi, internet, or anything like that affecting the match. Everything else however, is terrible, and seriously needs fixing. Even starting up the game still takes at least 2 minutes, which doesn't sound like a lot, but it feels awful for seemingly no reason. If it did this when choosing an online mode, that'd be one thing, but getting into the main menu is horrendous. I've straight up changed my mind about playing for the day multiple times just because of this startup. Yeah, that's probably absurd but it's bad. Outside of that, the lobby system is once again terrible, it seems almost every Arc Systems game arbitrarily has this terrible chibi/pixel lobby system that just makes navigating unfun and tedious. It isn't cute, it isn't funny. Please stop putting in these lobby systems into fighting games, I'm begging you. Just give me a simple list, I don't want to walk around a lobby before a match. It's not just for public stuff, it's the private lobbies too. And then all of these issues make starting a match tedious for no gain. And yet, that's if you can even get INTO a match. Because it seems you have to answer to the game's whims on whether or not you can even play someone. I've seen entire public lobbies softlock before, but luckily it seems that issue is signficantly less common now. At launch it was horrendous. Somehow, these issues seem to extend to private lobbies too, where actually playing a match with a friend is a coin toss on whether or not we actually get to play. With that out of the way...the game itself, when you're actually playing it, is a blast. Despite the gameplay issues I have, the game is really fun to play. I wasn't big on the base roster, I really only enjoyed Zato, once the DLC characters dropped I really started playing properly. The DLC cast is amazing, every single one of them is really fun. I really wish they weren't DLC...hey who knows maybe a majority of my gameplay issues will be fixed in Strive Revelator or whatever. All in all, solid and fun fighting game, just not a particularly good Guilty Gear game. In terms of music and character design though? Really great, I love all of the new designs for the characters, and the full english voice acting. Though I wish the voice acting languages could be toggled per character. Not hearing Baiken in Japanese is kinda...odd. But yeah, if you haven't played a Guilty Gear game, but think they look cool, play this.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a 2D fighting game, from one of the most prestigious fighting franchises out there, and I truly believe that it was built with the intent of removing all of the crappy parts of fighting games that nobody really likes, even if they are used to putting up with them.  Getting stuck in the corner the whole round sucks, now the wall breaks if the enemy goes hard enough and you reset to neutral.  Spending tens of hours in training practicing your BnB combos just to get the damage you earned by opening up the enemy sucks, now combos and routes are streamlined and less demanding but flexible enough to be adapted on-the-fly and still rewarding.  Not realizing you got a counterhit and letting a big combo opportunity pass you by sucks, now there's a time-freeze on counterhit to help you realize what happened and jump on it to get your reward.   The game is more focused and streamlined than past GGs, but this seems to put more emphasis on how you and your enemy interact with each other, rather than testing who has more knowledge or practiced more execution.  And since those interactions are what make a game fun, whether between friends with no clue what their doing or pro players at a national tournament, this game seems like it's trying to make those concepts relevant and easy to understand for players at all levels.  The tech is a bit easier than past games, but primarily to help new players see and understand the actual mechanics behind it, and all other 2d fighters.   As a long-time fan of GG that does not have 20-40 hours available to practice each week, this is my favorite fighter of all time.  And if you've never played a fighter before, i Truly believe that Strive's focus on the core mechanics makes it the best point of entry out there for this genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could put a neutral review for this game, but since I can't, I'm gonna have to give this one a negative.What this game does right, it does incredibly well. You'll have a hard time finding such a good-looking fighting game anywhere else, and the music is among the best you can hear in a genre that's already renowned for having amazing music. The characters all have a unique, over-the-top anime flair to them.My gripes with Guilty Gear -Strive- are all related to the gameplay which, sadly, is a pretty huge deal once you've gotten over how great the game looks and sounds. It took me a while to figure out what I didn't like about this game, but it hit me once I looked at tournament footage and realized I wasn't even finding the game exciting to watch at the highest levels of play: characters in this game are extremely specialized, which makes them most efficient when played like you're following a flowchart.On the surface, having a varied cast of characters that each lend themselves to a really specific playstyle sounds like a great idea. It starts falling apart when you play against ten people that basically play a character the exact same, optimal way, which makes matches repetitive. Some characters become especially matchup-dependent because of this design philosophy. The fact that matches tend to be extremely short, often lasting less than two minutes, is also something that bugged me tremendously after nearly thirty hours of play time.The devs also seem intent on making the player's experience as awful as possible between matches, with the game taking up to two minutes just to load from the start menu (you're not even playing, yet) and forcing you into slow, impractical lobbies full of connection errors.With how popular this game is currently in the fighting game community, I'm fully aware that it's far from objectively bad when it comes to its gameplay. Guilty Gear -Strive- is a gorgeous game and, to be fair, I had fun with it for a dozen hours or two. It simply feels too repetitive and lacking in depth to justify a 80$ price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's Rock. First I wanna say that this is after all my 150+ hours I've spent on the game, even after playing on both PS5 and PC, all the betas, and then on launch. This game literally released on my birthday, you don't know how excited I was for it watching the characters and trailers get released. This game is refined, well made and you can tell that the people who're making it are trying their hardest to create a game in which everybody can participate and enjoy. I respect it. And I respect it so much that though I'm gonna tear into this game, just know that this is coming from a dude who LOVES FIGHTING GAMES, ROCK MUSIC, and overall Guilty Gear.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~REVIEW BEGIN.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~To praise the game, the soundtrack is awesome and so is the graphical fidelity of the game. The UI is fluid, though it doesn't exude that guilty gear awesome metal stuff that it used to. The availability of mods definitely make it a more enjoyable experience. I also have to praise the idea of the Gatling and Roman Cancel changes. For instance; Gatlings were made to be simple, not to dumb it down but to make it easier for newer players and more difficult for older players to learn and reset them both to a state of learning in which it's harder for those who already knew the older games to get an unfair advantage- that's something that as a game dev, you want to avoid. --------------------------------------------------------------------------This game is terrible. Balancing is horrible, movement is sluggish and weird and certain characters have long combo strings to dole out counterhit damage while certain OTHER characters can press a button and do two specials and basically rob you of your health bar. I'm tired of it. By all means this is a scrubquote, from someone who not only played said problem characters, but got the game twice on launch. This is the first fighting game where I can't have fun and I hate it. Thank you.Happy Chaos, though a problem, at least requires a high skill ceiling to pull off his pressure and loops. However, it's still kinda bull how much damage he ♥♥♥♥♥ out. Ramlethal is a problem because she can tap you, corner carry, break wall, then get positive bonus and immediately deal her most damaging links through specials and disjoints with wide ranges. Leo is a character who, though my primary main, definitely has faults as far as making himself PLUS FIVE on his most MINUS MOVE. His runthrough and mixup game is something given to him while other characters have to learn and practice. Sol Badguy, the main character, is a very solid character that once he gets ONE counterhit, it's 70 percent of your health bar. But the PROBLEM CHARACTER, Nagoriyuki, is the worst of them all. Something designed to be a disadvantage turns into more advantages if anything, and creates something that I personally have trouble dealing with; his damage. FULLSCREEN NORMALS. COUNTERHIT THAT LEADS INTO SPECIAL THAT LEADS INTO SPECIAL- And that's not an exaggeration. Nago mains will tell you that they nerfed his one special by making it -3 on block but it DOES NOT MATTER WHEN THE CHARACTER CAN CANCEL SPECIALS INTO OTHER SPECIALS. IT IS UNACCEPTABLE FOR A GROUP OF CHARACTERS TO HAVE BETTER BUTTONS, DAMAGE, MIX, EVERYTHING THAN THE REST OF THE CAST.  INSTEAD OF MAKING 5 CHARACTERS BROKEN, WHY NOT GIVE THEM ALL SOME BROKEN MOVES?MAKE TESTAMENT DISJOINTED AND MORE OF A ZONER!GIVE KY A OVERHEAD!LITERALLY GIVE CHIPP TWO EXTRA POINTS OF HEALTH!There is no reason for people to buy it at full price; as a fighting game fan and furthermore a guilty gear fan, i do understand that a core staple of guilty gear is obnoxiously cool characters giving out ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane moves and tools, but even then this game feels like a pale imitation of the series before-hand. As I mentioned before, the gatlings aren't the problem. But I come from years of time on Rev 2 and XX as a KID, and seeing how much crazy stuff that defied fighting game logic and conventions get stripped from the series is insane. I love kusoge/unbalanced games. They're awesome. Because everything is so random, everybody is unbalanced. Even with the worst character, you can beat the best character w the best player if you play your cards correct. Hell, in PLUS R, the worst character is the BEST CHARACTER. And the 2nd worst, Kliff, is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ COOL and can STILL WHOOP ASS. So why in god's name is it that Anji in Strive gets seven trillion buffs and STILL doesn't budge from being bottom one? Whenever I play Strive, it feels like two games.You're either playing the top five, or you're playing the bottom fifteen. Characters who with tons of skill, can MAAAAYYYYBE catch up and fight against top tiers, but not really all the time against people who picked up the game and thought Nago was cool. This isn't balanced. Not in a fun way of unbalanced either, it's just pitiful and annoying and I hate to see it happen to such a cool series.And to close out, I want to touch on DNF Duel; a game that has some of the problems I listed present. Fullscreen Normals, good ass characters, nice mix. But the difference is that from the betas, all of the characters have access to fullscreens, or frankly broken and stupid stuff. Which sucks to see that there's one game designed for fun, and this game which is designed for...... I don't even know.-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------So, in closing, Strive has balance problems and movement problems, as well as an identity crisis. It's annoyingly everpresent and to see it end up lose the hard rock aesthetic and roots in the UI is really sad to see. But hopefully we see the thought of changing up the meta and characters in a big way, nerfing and buffing, adding new defensive mechanics AS WELL as making the movement something desirable in the LEAST. I don't want my AirDash to have frame data. And I don't want it to be slow. I don't want to have getting in feel like I'm actually not getting in, but rather inching towards a character in a game that's historically about rushdown. If you want people to rush others down, than STOP HAVING CHARACTERS LOCK OTHER CHARACTERS DOWN. If I were to rate this on a scale of 1-10, this would earn a 4 on my list.+Good Graphics+Tight Gameplay+Great Soundtrack+Dope Story/Add on Story-Sluggish and Slow Movement-Simplistic and Closed Character Design that doesn't allow for creativity across the board without the use of Meter-Balance Issues that make most of the cast unviable compared to the rest-Unclear Character Moveset Design(for instance. there's a pattern where if a character have 2 of the same move, one is minus but comes out faster, while the riskier option is plus but is again, longer startup and can be reacted 2. However as of the latest patch, characters like I-No have it so both are minus for no reason.)-A terrible lobby and matchmaking system that works when it wants to-Wallbreak mechanic makes the meta somewhat reliant on it, especially with Positive Bonus which passively refills your meter if you're the one who broke the wall. Characters with excellent corner carry get more and more bonuses off of being good, and then the losers lose harder.-Furthermore, in this game negative penalty should be removed when there's character matchups that require a character to zone and stay far away AS WELL as characters who can LOCK YOU DOWN WITH INTENSE OPPRESSION.4/10- or 4/11 if you wanna really count all of them. It can be much better as a game, and having it be something where I can't learn as I play as well as have fun when i play is a problem.Thank you for reading. If you want to yell at my review i am @nonimegtv on Twitter.

_childDocuments_.review: I had this long review drafted about this game going into depth in various areas, but there's no need. Honestly, it can all be boiled down to: this game is so simple it just isn't fun. Strive is about eliminating features in the franchise. Reducing options. Restricting the player to a set gameplan the devs have in mind. It creeps into every facet of its design philosophy.	The devs themselves have admitted as much. In Patch 1.10 the devs had a tidbit about Sol, and why they nerfed a move: "the high damage and practicality of ->P>Volcanic Viper (HS) in the stage corner was so strong that there was no need to use other combo routes". Whether intentional or not, that is an indirect admittance that their design philosophy has been detrimental in some respects.	Player Expression—the viability of playing a character in unique ways—becomes minimized when the game is simplified. Getting rid of YRC (Roman Cancels with only 25% meter) and gatlings (the staple P->K->S->HS->D combo system) means that in any situation, your followup options are smaller than before. Now you can only ever follow-up P and K with a command normal, a special, super, or crouching dust (typically). Air combat has also been nerfed, which is weird for a Guilty Gear game. From my understanding, they almost got rid of dust as we know it (follow-up aerial combo). 	Even some special moves have arbitrary limitations, like Sol's "Night Raid Vortex" (his uppercut) can't be comboed into from a normal (unlike other specials) because it leads to lengthier combo possibilities that the designers don't want you experimenting with. Sol's "Wild Throw" is now a base 40% damage, instead of leading to bouncing the enemy off the ground and a custom combo. With YRC gone, using specials as movement options has a heftier price and occurs less often, leading to less dynamic fights.	To compensate for shorter combo routes, the developers cranked the damage way the hell up. Walls break and lead back to neutral, with the idea being that we don't want an oki heavy, oppressive corner situation. Ironically this is perhaps the worst the series can be in terms of being in the corner. You easily eat half your health, if not 60 or even 70% when you find yourself in the corner. Off 4 hit combos. Meterless. It can get real bad, and I've seen professional matches end in 7 seconds. 7. This isn't to mention the buff the wall-breaker gets. 	Now, look. It wasn't uncommon or weird for people to begin their mid-screen combos off S anyway. And you could potentially eat half your health in the corner before, and still remain in the corner after the combo ended (so a wall-break is theoretically a better situation). Strive still feels and plays like Guilty Gear, which is a relief to anyone who followed this game's development. At any of the higher levels, you have some mind-games going on and depending on the character, there's a bit more depth than what you see at first glance. 	If this is your first Guilty Gear, it's probably extremely fun. Even if it isn't, there's still the same base experience here. I don't think Strive is, on a fundemental level, a badly designed game in its first incarnation. Which is important, because a game can be bad on launch, but drastically improve 2 years down the line due to how they're frequently updated now. And its important to remember that, because we may see a Strive with more complexity than what we currently have.	This is a review from a fan of the previous entry: Xrd. I think my feelings are best summarized by Snake Eyes (professional SF player) who played a bit of Xrd (for the first time) after trying out Strive. His reaction was something along the lines of: "You can do that in this game? Woah, they let you do that too? Why didn't anyone tell me about this game". Strive is like going from F-Zero GX to Mario Kart. From a Ferrari to a Sedan. You're giving people the same food, only less of it now. Which is typical of modern Arc Sys games. 	I kept telling myself that I should give it more of a shot. There's more depth to it. But everytime I played the game (from the moment it launched) I would stop playing it for 1 or 2 months at a time. I just have to admit to myself what I'm trying not to: I'm just not having that much fun. It can be enjoyable for an hour, but it fails to grip me like previous entries have. What I can do and my routes are reduced, leading to a similar, albeit slower and restrictive experience as compared to what came before it.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I started to play this game, I've heard about the legends of Guilty Gear, and the infinite corner combos that turned you or your opponent into a living ping pong ball. Funny enough, I never even saw much game play of this game until about a week before release, and suffice it to say the visuals of the game were and still are absolutely spectacular.Color me impressed that around 40 hours later, and Guilty Gear Strive is one of the most accessible and frenetic fighting games I have ever played, and probably my favorite fighting game of all time, period. Most of this has to do with the fact that unlike the other Guilty Gear games, this game doesn't rely on infinite combos that juggle you to the next dimension. Now, I know that hard core fans of the series aren't exactly happy about that, but I think it's a change for the better, plus the fact that those combos still do exist, as evident by some of the higher level play that sometimes can have me waiting while I'm sent flying through the air for fifteen seconds, and vice versa to my opponent.Every single character in this game is completely unique, unlike some other fighting games that have different characters, yet almost do the same punch and kicks as other characters. Here, in Guilty Gear Strive, the developers have gone into great lengths to make sure that every character really FEELS like they have weight? What do I mean by this? Heavy characters, such as the absolutely gargantuan Potempkin, actually plays like an absolute unit, giving this awesome sense of going against and playing as a proverbial truck. Every character feels unique like this, such as the absolutely lightning fast Chipp, to my main, Zato-1, which is essentially like playing two different characters at once, which leaves you incredibly satisfied when you manage to start getting good with him.Ultimately, if you have any doubts at all about getting into fighting games, let Guilty Gear Strive be your first foray into such a genre. It's extremely beginner friendly, has a robust mission mode that teaches you basic fighting game mechanics, an excellent ranked system, as well as the best connections I have ever seen when it comes to playing ranked in any type of game. Guilty Gear Strive is, as they say, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Blazing.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best fighting games that released in years with a very refreshing new gameplay and probably the best netcode I have experienced so far in any games.Positives:+ One of the best rollback netcode implementations.+ Super awesome soundtrack.+ Outstanding visuals.+ Tons of mods are made by the community.+ Brings new mechanics like wall break and revamps the game and characters movesets and move properties and their look a lot compared to previous series, so the game feels very fresh and new, even when compared to other 2D fighters,+ Even old characters feel very refreshing and new due to reason stated earlier.+ New awesome character redesigns.+ Good character cast.+ Easy training while you search for a match option, ranked lobbies, then park lobbies for casual play and also private lobbies.+ Story mode is well done with stunning visuals, cool action scenes, nice lore and interesting characters.+ Good tutorial mode and other mechanics and character specific stuff explanation modes.+ You can fish to get items.+ Lobby housing customization will be added soon.+ Has Japanese, English and Korean voiceover, and many other languages for in-game language.Negatives:- A less deep game than previous titles.- Instant Kills are not present in this title.- Some characters might feel a bit too strong while not being hard to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the second fighting game I've invested a lot of time in (The second one being DragonBall FighterZ).Here are some positives:-The visual are great. -The characters are very diverse though there maybe characters that might annoy people.Sound design is great, along with the soundtrack which is a bop.-The combo system is easy to learn and the game does well to teach you how to play the game.-The ranking system is okay (though it's also a double edge sword which I explain in the negatives)*-You can mod it (visually, not much of a positives more of a wanted to point it out)Here are some negatives I have as of making this review:-"Fail to obtain dual station information" is something you see a lot when trying to find a match, it gets very annoying to see every 5 seconds.-Sets are just 3. _childDocuments_.review: I had a lengthy review on this, but I felt it better summed up this way:PROS:- Incredibly beginner friendly. Great entry level game for people new to fighting games, and enough depth for seasoned players to not feel bored with.- Tutorials are incredibly intuitive for new players, and people learning to step up their game.- The absolutely best netcode for a fighting game, ever. Not even debatable. This should be the standard, period. I have played people in Japan and it felt like they were in the same room as me.- Visually stunning. From the character intros, to the movie itself.- One of the best soundtracks I've heard in a fighting game in quite a while. I was apprehensive about it when it was first previewed, but after hearing them in full, I get pretty hyped listening to some of these tracks-- especially Millia's theme.- The Character Select UI is digestable. It's a lot cleaner than previous titles, and I enjoy the minimalist approach.- The almost 5-hour movie that tells the game's story is pretty neat.- The encyclopedia can basically tell you everything you need to know about the Guilty Gear universe. It has a breadth of information dating back to the original Guilty Gear.CONS:- The lobby system, online lobbies, personal lobbies etc. are all incredibly ass. There's no beating around the bush. Hosting tournaments, or even getting a few friends together to play is tedious-- which is sad, given how AMAZING the netcode is. Something as simple as UNICLR's lobby system would have been a godsend for casual play and tournaments alike.- The ranking system is awkward. I had 2 matches and got bumped to the 6th floor, had 5 matches after that, got bumped to the 8th floor, and then 7 more and got bumped to 10th floor, and everyone I've faced is absolutely better than me, I feel. I'm so far 11-3, but feel like I should not be anywhere near the 10th floor at my skill level, yet here I am.- Lack of frame data in training mode. For those who are more experienced or looking to become better, I feel like this should become a standard in fighting games.- 15 Characters to choose from at launch. This may sound nitpicky, but I personally feel in this day and age, the character selection (for an established series) should at minimum be 18 at launch. While I don't play as these characters, Venom, Baiken and Slayer would have been a welcomed addition and given more seasoned players a wider range of character archetypes to choose from.- In-game English character voices on some of the characters (Sol, especially) are so cringe. There are a few shining moments, but overall, I felt like they lacked a lot of personality. I was honestly surprised at how much I just did NOT like it.- Certain features in previous titles are missing. While I'll disagree with some people who say the game is incomplete, I did feel like some of the "fluff" from previous titles like combo makers etc. would have been nice to have for when you don't want to deal with the lobby issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Never tried this series before and from the small amount of time I had before the close of the Steam refund window, I'm pretty disappointed. I had high expectations based on reviews and the relative popularity of this title, but it commits every sin in the book: - An emphasis on perfecting input timing due to extremely tight buffers and less of an emphasis on reading the opponent's intentions (you know, like a competitive game? As opposed to speedrunning a solo game?) - A headache-inducing mix of long and frequent hit-stops in spite of the very tight timing windows (make the game slow or fast, not a confused mish-mash) - Weird and arbitrary rules for each character about which cancels exist/work - Almost every major mechanic seems specifically designed to fix any unforeseen design issues in matchups. There's two separate super meters and Roman Cancels, Psych Bursts, and Faultless Defense are all ways to burn these two meters in ways that arbitrarily interrupt the normal flow of gameplay to "fix" degenerate situations because the authors can't be bothered to prevent such situations. (Or if not that, they're get-out-of-jail-free cards, which are the bane of competitive gaming).It's worth also pointing out that the game is visually not a good fighting game. All of this can be easily watched before you buy, so obviously I was willing to overlook this if the game was good. But it doesn't  that the screen readability of UI elements and characters is bad from a gameplay perspective; and if I may get much more subjective, the animation, rendering, and effects are very misguided. I can say that the environment art is good? But there's gotta be a better way to make the characters pop from the background than making them look like they're in the wrong dimension of the Spider-verse. It's very possible that this game would grow on me if I gave it enough time, but that's an iffy proposition from a fighting game, a genre whose heritage is convincing teenagers to cough up a couple more quarters because the first play was instantly appealing. And sadly, Steam won't give me a refund if I play much longer, so I guess I'll never know.I guess everyone's got their game but I really don't know why anyone would pick this one. If you're reading this because you genuinely can't decide which fighting game to try, start with Capcom (Street Fighter, Marvel Vs. Capcom) or Bandai Namco (Tekken, Soul Caliber).

_childDocuments_.review: In two words, Guilty Gear: Strive can be described as "chaotic fun". Even though I have hardly scratched the surface of what it has to offer, I both love and hate this game. One thing I can say for certain though is that it nearly never ceases to be enjoyable. It is not at all uncommon to find yourself in a situation where the excellent soundtrack blares over the sounds of footsteps and pokes being thrown out, as you and the opponent both search for an in after a reset and it is almost impossible not to acknowledge how well every element of a round comes together so harmoniously. Anyone can find a character to love here too. I struggled to find a main until I tried out Strive's version of Testament, and they are now easily one of my favorite fighting game characters of all time. There is so much *cool ♥♥♥♥* you can make happen with any character with enough practice and skill, and the character cast is highly diverse on top of each and every member's undeniable cool factor. Video games are meant to be fun, and Strive is an excellent reminder of that as it bombards you with bite-sized pieces of concentrated *game* that come together to form an amazingly cohesive whole.

_childDocuments_.review: Strive delivers a thundering success and will be remembered as a revolution in the genre. Plenty has been said about the inarguably beautiful graphics, but it's the accessible game design that really sets this title apart. So many seemingly small decisions coalesce towards this singular goal to great avail. The move list, rather than dizzying players with the usual disembodied display of labyrinthine inputs, details each move and demonstrates their strengths and weaknesses. Counter hits now slow down time, which not only looks cool as ♥♥♥♥, but lets players hit confirm without lightning speed reactions. The training missions, which in other games merely ask you to perform a combo without any context, now teach players an array of broader gameplay concepts using tried and tested terminology from the online community, meaning your in-game study translates well to wider reading. As with any fighting game, Strive has a learning curve, but it couldn't do more to flatten it. The roster diversity contributes massively to that effort. Several characters in the game don't require elaborate combos and advanced mechanics to succeed. Potemkin and Nagoriyuki, for example, play around slow and heavy hits with huge range, rewarding players for patience and space control. Characters like Chipp, meanwhile, demand constant pressure and inventive combo strings to succeed. In the same way calling Overwatch a first-person shooter feels like a disservice to the breadth of gameplay styles available, Strive feels less like a fighter and more like an assembly of playable boss characters from different games. The fact that these characters achieve such distinction from one another whilst largely obeying the same set of universal rules and mechanics is really impressive.Online play is a mixed bag. The rollback netcode is phenomenal; I've played matches between the UK and South America that played like my opponent was on the same arcade cabinet. I will never buy another fighting game that does not have rollback like Strive's. Matchmaking, however, proves more tedious. I actually like the lobby system of finding a cabinet to sit down with another player. It feels like a celebration of arcade culture, and it helps detoxify the faceless, soulless ranked experience of other games by personalising your opponent (yes, they are people). But it needs fundamental improvements. There seems to be a sync issue (avatars are displayed as sat at cabinets when they aren't actually there), and matchmaking feels like a 50/50. In short, getting into a match can grind your Guilty Gears [please clap] but once you're in, it's heaven. Or hell. [Please clap].If you're even remotely interested in the fighting game genre on any level, I recommend you give this a try. It's fun to mash buttons against your boneheaded friends. It's fun to apply yourself against a refined enemy. And most importantly, the journey between those two states of play has never been more streamlined, accommodating, and lively than it is now. Strive's enjoying a roaring success with a lot of new blood, and I trust ArcSys to support this game well into the future. If you've ever thought about fisting someone or getting fisted, now's the time to lube up and jump in.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time Guilty Gear player/ fan, I was initially worried about this game becoming overly simplified and lose its identity.The game is still very much a new spin on Guilty Gear. While the gameplay is different from the past games, it's still enjoyable. Playing it is a blast, especially with distant friends thanks to the rollback netcode. With that said though, the game still feels much slower than it's predecessors, and if you wanted more of that older style, this game is definitely a let down. Some characters are still complex, and the mechanics still lead to interesting senarios, but you'll still feel restricted if you prefer Xrd or XX. Intros and outros are also much more stale in this game, lacking the energy and charisma of Xrd's.If you're a lore fan like me, you'll find that the story is gripping and interesting, and will definitely leave you thinking about about its lore implications.That said, I have two issues with the game, one major and one minor. The major is the lack of singleplayer content. Some people may argue that fighting games are meant to be online multiplayer games, but historically, Arc Sys would always include fun, unique singleplayer content, like the MOM mode of previous entries, to provide entertainment when you don't want to go online or cant. These modes are genuinely fun, and Strives Survival mode just can't make up for the replayabilty and fun you can get from MOM mode. The minor issue I have is that I really miss instant kills. They gave each character a way to demonstrate their personality, and in gameplay, it was a fun thing to do with friends, to see who could land one. It's not game breaking, but hope they make it in someday, because their absence is certainly felt. TLDR, GG Strive is a a different but solid entry to the series, however, it does lack the singleplayer content of past GG games. If you care for that content, I'd say wait for a sale. Otherwise, you're getting a pretty fun fighting game here, and I would recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: The verdict is in; This game smells good.Pros first;-Solid diversity in starting roster, with dev plans to add as many characters from past games as possible.-Fluid gameplay feel; controlling a character feels responsive and intuitive.-Rollback netcode showing off what it can really do; you can have solid matches around the globe if your net is good.-Subjective, but I think the 'Story' mode little mini-anime was entertaining to watch.-The game is approachable, they have taken many strides to present a game that is understandable while trying not to sacrifice depth of skill.-The new Roman Cancel system lets you break the rules in super deep and interesting ways.-While any individual music track is subjective in nature, I've only heard great reviews about the soundtrack as a whole. The music is fantastic and the addition of lyrics was a great choice IMO.-The game is very progressive in it's story/characters, but in a natural way that doesn't force feed *Wokeness* to you. Just characters Striving to be their best selves as the name would suggest.Some Cons do exist though;-Offence is fairly simple to run while defense is very nuanced; While this isn't actually a bad thing for the game necessarily (I find it quite fun), This is one of the larger hurdles for newer players that can cause great frustration despite their attempts to make the game more approachable.-The "Tower" system as the game's premier "Ranked" ladder mode is laughably bad at best. You will find yourself or your opponents being moved floors in the middle of sets constantly. Not only that but being moved happens way too frequently, you can never really sink your teeth into a floor too long without being moved along. Additionally as populations die down a bit as they do, there becomes less people in any individual skill tier/floor in any given region's tower so folks tend to migrate upwards (Sometimes beyond their means, just to get a match). Stick to the parks or battle with your friends :)Don't let anyone try to cry about character balance and scare you off; Anybody talking about nonsense like that wasn't good enough at the game for the balance to matter to them in the first place :)When in doubt, Totsugeki!*Edit notes:-Removed (3) whole bullet points from the Cons section as updates have addressed many issues (yay!)-Added a Con about the Tower "Ranked" (It's bad)-Added (2) Pros, Didn't mention the music my first time reviewing & Daisuke said Trans Rights :)

_childDocuments_.review: This is honestly pretty disappointing as a guilty gear game.Many characters are either missing iconic moves from previous games (millia lost her pin for example, and may retains only her bare minimum moveset), have moves from previous games that seem pointless in this one (leo has his rekka starter but it doesn't rekka into anything), and generally feel like they have far fewer options than previous games. This likely will be fleshed out to some extent in the coming months, with patches and the generally impressive roman cancel system, but overall I do not get the impression that the feeling of endless possibilities of previous guilty gear games will be rediscovered in this one.The game feels really sluggish, owing largely to airdashes having startup and buttons across the board having much more startup than previous games, and often more recovery. The damage is really high in this game, but the combos feel less flexible, crouching punches especially feel the most gimped, most characters really have nothing they can do after landing a crouching jab other than maybe a couple more. Even the big flashy counterhits that the UI emphasizes don't necessarily mean anything, as many of those counterhits either can't be combod off of, or only combo into one more move.I'm not a fan of the soundtrack for this game (vocal tracks don't feel amazing as backing music to a fight), and most of the visual redesigns don't appeal to me at all. The UI is especially bland and minimalistic, which is very odd given how extremely stylized previous titles are, the UI does not look like it was made for a guilty gear game at all.I've played some matches with friends and I've had a good time in them, but honestly I think I can do that in literally any new fighting game, I think the genre is very good at providing a fun casual experience, that's why it was such a mainstay of the arcade era. I don't think this particular game is built to last though in the way that previous games in the Guilty Gear series were. I feel like within a couple months once the honeymoon period dies down, this game will lose its luster because it lacks the mechanics and options to really give people opportunities to dig deep into it.I think for people who have never played a guilty gear game before, or people who never dug too deep in previous ones, this game is probably incredible. If you're someone who loves digging deep into the broad mechanics of previous guilty gears though, I think you'll sadly be really disappointed with this one, and might want to look elsewhere for the experience you're really looking for.

“Guilty Gear -Strive-“ is the latest entry in the Guilty Gear fighting game franchise. Created by Daisuke Ishiwatari and developed by Arc System Works, “Guilty Gear -Strive-“ upholds the series’ reputation for groundbreaking hybrid 2D/3D cell-shaded graphics and intense, rewarding gameplay. There is a fully voiced story mode diving deep into the Guilty Gear universe, new characters joining fan favorites, and robust rollback net code. The cutting-edge 2D/3D hybrid graphics pioneered in the Guilty Gear series have been raised to the next level in “Guilty Gear -Strive-“. The new artistic direction and improve character animations will go beyond anything you’ve seen before in a fighting game!

◆New Revolution in Fighting Games!
Guilty Gear -Strive- brings a number of new and innovative game play mechanics designed to allow players new to the series to quickly learn the fundamentals while maintaining the deep, creative gameplay Guilty Gear is praised for. New additions to the series such as a wall-breaking mechanic will allow for new and exciting approaches to battle.

◆The fate of the universe will be determined…
The story of Guilty Gear, spanning over 20 years, will finally come to a conclusion in “Guilty Gear -Strive-“. The trials and tribulations of the series’ heroes and villains will finally be resolved. Discover the astonishing truth awaiting at the end of all things.

name: Insurmountable
detailed_description: Buzz About the Game ​ Insurmountable is an adventure roguelike with permadeath, in which the player has to overcome huge mountains. Thanks to the procedurally created environment, no two climbs are the same. Make sure that your climber stays alive by always making sure that your vital values don't get into the critical range. This task is made more difficult by a dynamic weather system, day/night changes and a multitude of randomly generated events, where you never know in advance how they will end. Your decisions matter....every single one. Because anyone could be your last. Choose one of three characters with different skills and background stories and start by climbing the first mountain. Search crates, caves and ancient ruins for equipment from past adventurers. You'll need it, because even the first mountain will demand everything from you. But don't worry. As time goes by, you'll become stronger and stronger. Take advantage of a sophisticated skill system to determine which strengths your climber should have. In the course of each of the three mysterious stories, you will meet dangerous animals, overcome deadly abysses, encounter sinister and well-meaning characters, who do not always have to be human. Here, too, each of your decisions decides the following events. Three mountains have to be conquered at the end. One higher and deadlier than the previous one. Divide your forces and your equipment correctly, because you don't have a second attempt and you can forget about learning a route. In Insurmountable you have to cope with unknown dangers, react spontaneously to unpredictable events and realize in the end that, as in life, you can't always know the consequences of your decisions, but you have to cope with them anyway and in the end, it often turns out differently than you thought. Face the challenge of ever new and changing dangers, face snowstorms and the sheer force of nature, always keep your eyes on the summit and overcome the insurmountable. Keyfeatures no two climbs are alike procedurally generated mountains dynamic world with different weather effects hundreds of events with ever-changing outcomes strategic gameplay in path finding, stat and equipment management 3 characters with different abilities

_childDocuments_.review: A solid foundation for a game that feels incomplete.  If this was an early access game I would be excited for the full release, but as is there is just not enough depth.  I was seeing repeated events before my first summit, and rarely saw new ones by the end of my first successful run (attempt 3).  There are hints of a great mystery, but it appears to be all tease and no payoff.  It shows the potential to become a great game if the Dev's keep at it, but maybe give this one another year to fill out.

_childDocuments_.review: Well I don't know even how to start this review. I love videogames since I was a child and I always was a fat boy. When I got 18 years old I tried to lose weight and was looking for any kind of activity that would help me to burn some calories. At the start I began to walk a bit in my neighborhood, but then I found my true love that is hiking and climbing mountains.I did it for 9 years, every single month. Unfortunately last year (2021) I got a really bad injury in my knee (it wasn't an arrow lol) and then suddenly I wasn't able to hike or climb mountains anymore. I got my weight back and now I'm trying to lose it with other activities, but it's really harder than before.For so long I was searching for a game that would join my two passions (games and mountains) a game that could bring me back to those good years again. Last weekend I got this game for free in epic and got really curious to try it. I played it during the whole weekend and then decided to buy it here to support the devs in some way.Thank you to make me feel a bit like before.

_childDocuments_.review: Insurmountable (ISMe) is a turn-based strategy game with a mountaineering theme and rogue-like structure. Players take on the role of an individual stranded on a island. Their goal to scale three successive peaks and uncover the secrets of this mysterious place.Set-up requires choosing which mountain to tackle and preferred difficulty. Opting for one of three routes to take. Followed by determining the class of character to play. Then setting off with naught but their starting attributes, strengths and equipment. While on their trek many dangers will be endured and tough decisions made, while continuously balancing four pools of inner resources. Energy, sanity, temperature and oxygen are all vital in keeping the climber alive and focused. These decline as challenging terrain is traversed, dealing with setbacks and enduring harsh weather. These resources are refilled by resting or using consumables found during encounters. Incidents can occur when in transit causing a multitude of bad effects. Both permanent and temporary.Gameplay takes place on procedurally created environments depicting the mountain being climbed. Several types of terrain and features are modelled on a hex-tiled map to include: rocks, snow, ice, cliffs, fjords and inaccessible paths. Together forming a patchwork of possible routes for the player to take and obstacles to avoid when attempting to reach the summit. Along the way, a number of signposted locations can be visited that provide event encounters. The most important of these are caves, ideal for taking shelter in. Others bestow or deplete resources or equipment. Experience points are awarded on completing encounters. Gaining points allows a skill to be chosen from four, augmenting capabilities for their journey. Passive types are constantly in effect. Actives must be used and then go on cooldown.A day and night cycle complicates matters, bringing with it changes in weather which can reduce visibility and inner resources, complicating the climb even further. To aid them characters can use a small array of equipment. Clothing, picks, torches, provisions and more help keep the climber alive or give them a better chance to succeed. As they near the summit of each mountain, the character must have the inner resources and equipment to overcome the Death Zone. An area of low oxygen and sheer cliff faces below the summit. Getting to the top of the mountain is only half the battle. Players will need the wherewithal to ensure they make it to a sheltered area. Where they can begin to prepare to scale the next mountain.+ 3x mountains of growing length and difficulty to overcome, without dying.+ Choose to play one of 3x characters with different starting abilities and equipment. adventurer, scientist or journalist.+ Procedurally generated mountains with various terrain, day/night and weather cycles.+ Can remove GUI to reveal the amazing scenery.+ A preview feature displays cost in resources to get to a target hex. Useful for pre-planning.+ Tons of strategic dynamics provide a complex challenge: environment, equipment, traits, buffs/debuffs and injuries.- Animations are basic.- Can be a lonely experience. No other characters.- No option to restock between mountains.- No manual saving. No checkpoint reload. Basically ironman mode from start to finish.- High initial difficulty curve. Can be unbalanced to a point.- Inconsequential story revealed in chunks.- Permadeath. Artificially increases difficulty.* Fair number of random events. Many are overly generic in nature. Could do with more event chains.* Rendered terrain: fjords, ice rivers, glaciers, and rocky crags* Dynamic weather system and day/night cycle. Lowers resources and affects visibility and temperature.* Gain XP by completing encounters and levelling-up. Specialise characters through a sophisticated skill system. * Decent setup options: Difficulty (normal, hard and insurmountable); Route; (left, centre and right); Character type - (Climber, adventurer and journalist).* Good flexible camera. Can get stuck depending on zoom and angle.* New difficulties, mountains and climber attributes can be unlocked by reaching mountain peaks.ISMe brings a remarkably distinct concept to the turn-based strategy genre in a very polished format. Every constituent part of its DNA reinforced its subject-matter and theme. Capturing the expectation, trepidation and feel of the experience in a satisfying way. While a medley of related mechanics collectively provided a thought-provoking challenge, with appealing visuals and immersive environments. Making this a contender for anyone's library.There is no combat. That and due to its slow deliberate nature and decision-based exploration, it would appeal to fans who prefer taking their time when strategising. Especially those capable of inhaling its layers of game dynamics and processing them, before making their move. The ability to adapt as situations change would also stand the player in good stead. While some phases of play were almost casual in nature, just like a blizzard ISMe would manage to disrupt the most meticulous of planning, shifting the context of the challenge in an instant.The effect of RNG was limited to the encounters experienced and skills available for selection when levelling up. These could feel unbalanced during a run. Over time accumulating to make for a frustrating experience. At least there were no other major RNG issues. For the most part it really is the character, their abilities and equipment up against the mountain, elements and bad incidents. There was a fair amount of replayability but players would essentially be playing the same game with little change bar what RNG provided. The suggestion of a story never materialised.It very much played like a board-game and what strategy there was worked well but, the action could descend into a lull. It missed having a base camp between mountains to equip anew for the next journey. Equipment that could break during critical incidents. The inclusion of a nefarious entity that would send climbers after the player would have added an extra dimension. Making it more rogue-lite. The imposed Ironman mode and lack of saving, made the game alot less accessible for casual players.ISMe did sometimes feel overly lonely. Perhaps adding characters from a roster to form a team would have added a tactical element that often felt missing. Turning critical incidents into mini-games of their own. Played out on zoomed-in maps. Adding climber related actions affected by ability and RNG with detailed animations that felt missing from the main game. Changing terrain as an effect of weather would have been a great addition.ISMe managed to capture the mountaineering experience in a very satisfying way. For its few flaws it was well worth the time sunk into it. Will suit patient thinkers or fans of the subject matter. I enjoyed it despite a few shortcomings.
_childDocuments_.name: Insurmountable

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game to people who can manage their expectations of roguelites, survival resource management, solitary character experiences, and hiking/climbing, because many negative reviews seem to be from people who don't understand any of these things.So let me explain the core gameplay - Good, bad, indifferent:+Game's look and feel is polished.-The game's sound is limited to serviceable movement & event focused SFX, music, and some ambient environmental sounds. It is consistent with the solitary experience though, and no voices.?If you don't like the relatively slow pace for movement, then walking speed can be sped up somewhat, know that hiking is not supposed to be fast. I personally plan to watch TV shows in the background when I'm less engaged in the movement.?Don't expect a giant variety in events/encounters, though the other two mountains have some new event types, and there definitely are some missions different than "Hike to the summit, then down to a base camp".?Camera movement is intentionally centered around the climber, but there is the ability to press a key ("V" + middle mouse button?) combo to fix the camera location and pan it up higher than usual.+The in game tutorial and help available from pause screen are all intuitive.?Auto pathfinding shows the most direct general path between what ever waypoints you left click. It does NOT optimize for energy consumption, body heat, time elapsed, or least risk. That is your job to determine what you want to focus on in terms of resource costs when you choose movement.+Challenge is by design, though the first mountain was only a light challenge for me given the amount of non-optimal choices I made. So death is normal, but the game provide progression and upgrades between runs using a multi-faceted XP system.+Two additional climber types can be unlocked when going to their areas of the first mountain on the global map and completing their mission by finding them.
_childDocuments_.name: Insurmountable

_childDocuments_.review: In spirit, Insurmountable is a solo board game about the challenges of mountaineering. Not over-complicated, yet thoughtful enough to make one pay attention from start to finish. It appealed to me with soft melancholic visuals and the sheer scale of uniquely picturesque vistas stemming from its hexagonal pocket dimension. I loved how the camera is slightly unwieldy, making the necessity to find good vantage points a mechanic. Or how local nights are so thick that you are physically unable to see without having certain equipment, and it isn't always at hand. This also tightly ties mere visual fleur to the gameplay. I find such technical nuances fascinating and hard to come by.Harvesting a set of compelling mechanics, the game hinges on its raw practical bliss. It provides players with a boost of dopamine on obtaining items, watching the stats grow, and devising perfect routes through treacherous environments to reach the peak, which is usually the main goal. I love routing, and not only in games. It's the pinnacle of miracles like logistics and load distribution. I enjoy planning my grocery runs, so I could kill several birds with one stone, effectively use my strengths and weaknesses, and cut out the redundant parts that waste time. Insurmountable is all of these things gamified. To make it out alive, take your time manually paving the way. Avoid rough terrain while trying to grab as many event tokens as possible on your path since they are the main source of stat boosts, exp, and items. The game will automatically give accurate previews of potential losses and gains for your character.There are 3 of them and each sports a definitive playstyle. Roughly speaking, the Scientist can craft whatever items they want, the Adventurer is pretty good at conquering rough terrain as well as climbing at night, and the Journalist is an experience hog. The latter is pretty OP since levelling happens often, providing highly beneficial perks. They stack up, but it's worth noting that leveling during a mission doesn't transfer to the rest of the game. The abilities are cooldown-based and using them comes at the price of spending time and stats. It's a balancing act, nothing is free. Characters come with separate skill trees, featuring unique active and passive abilities to obtain after getting rewarded for completing missions. Now, they persist, being a part of the game's meta. Progression felt significant initially, but I got all I wanted from it early on, so it stopped being meaningful afterwards. A common problem in this genre.These people's vital signs are yours to look after. This whole affair is about maintaining the status bars: Energy, Oxygen, Temperature, Sanity, Health. Every mechanic in the game serves these Atlantes. Energy gets spent on almost every action, Oxygen depletes at high altitudes, Temperature is self-explanatory, and Sanity loss comes from experiencing near-death situations or the darkness. Because climbing rocks at night is insane, indeed. In the end, all of these meters impact your Health, the only pool that actually matters. If any other bar exhausts completely, you still live, but start getting dangerous random events. They either give you some of your stats back or, if you're unlucky, chip away at your health pool until you die, forcing you to lose a life. Dying takes a while. Sometimes, you clearly see that it's imminent, yet still choose to writhe in agony. I liked that morbid part.But more on death in a minute. There are many ways of mitigating the dangers. Mostly, it comes to your limited inventory capacity and all the management it infers. You aren't allowed to just pack everything with you, having to commit to an inherently flawed plan, relying on the luck of the event tokens. Like a Buridan's ass, I was sitting in the preparation menu for ages, weighing my options. The same decision-making parts of the brain are constantly in use during a mission. Save time and make it to the camp until dusk or take a risky road, which will let you get some items? Concerning the latter, Insurmountable is generously diverse. Tents, consumables, tools, warm clothing - all that good stuff. It isn't an ARPG, you won't see hundreds of items, yet the assortment is impactful. Besides, picking your arsenal is an informed decision. As always, the game gives you enough information about any future endeavor to get things right. Did I get them right? Uh...I died for the first time after not paying attention when I decided to give up and restart quickly after using my skills in the wrong order. It took a life. Then, I managed to lose a few times when doing fourth-tier anomaly missions. I always miscounted these stupid anomalies like I miscount the floors in my building when heavily burdened with meat and vegetables. I give it my all too early, but there's  one extra flight of stairs to endure. In my opinion, anomalies aren't worth it. Having a solid goal of reaching the summit beats shambling between uncertain checkpoints any day of the week. Besides, the anomaly tracker sucks! It's the filter, the disgusting beeps, and how it makes you wrestle with the sticky camera for more than necessary that makes these missions a complete chore. Fed up, I've decided not to bother with Anomaly Hunts anymore, so I could enjoy the rest of the game.And there's much to enjoy, mostly on a mechanical level. By and large, the soundscape is imposing and the atmosphere can be awe-inspiring or oppressive when it needs to be. Insurmountable excels at creating the mood in broad strokes. Simultaneously, it lacks a finer emotional touch the setting is capable of. Yes, being cold fits the theme. To a degree. Does anyone remember Rammstein's Ohne Dich video? This is how you show the mountains! By injecting them with personality. Make your protagonists heroes, make overcoming adversities against all odds feel epic. Oh, how beneficial some drama and character could've been to this game! Instead, it walks a mellow road of blank slates, surrounded by cute barren wasteland. Even the event tokens look lifeless, unnatural, and the dry descriptions within are disconnected from the rest of the ordeal. So is the game's narrative overall.After a while, the only things I cared about when making my choices were punishments and rewards, as shown in the previews on hover. Sure, the stimulus given by getting stuff never failed to incite at least some kind of an emotional reaction in me. I just wish that, outside of dull text boxes, my characters emoted as well. Some exclamations and a few tiny animations like a simple "yay" while raising a fist up in the air after reaching the summit wouldn't stretch the budget too far. Such improvements could go a long way, mending the ludonarrative crevice. I was also upset to find out that, unlike in the trailer, the mountains actually never speak to you. Don't be cowards, give people their talking mountains! Okay, I may be the only one here with that fetish.Even without the mountains kink-shaming me, I ended up beating the game with my last character standing and no revives left. It was a close shave! Thrilling but... what would've happened if I died then? If it meant restarting the game, I'd ragequit since Insurmountable isn't a good roguelite. It's slow, the variety of events isn't great, and having seen one mountain, you've seen them all. The story revolves around time loops, but I don't think I'd want to be caught in this one for longer. However, for the time it took to beat the game, it worked rather well for me. Despite my harsh words, goodness is definitely prevalent. It's a competent little thing. I was allowed to skip everything I hated and, in the end, relished in the mechanically sound, melancholic experience it delivers.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so let's get into this.Overall it's not a bad little game. It's nothing grand but it's nothing terrible either.Honestly playing it the first 10 minutes you're going to be kind of bored. But I found the longer I played it the more invested I became and the more I wanted to dig in and fully climb this mountain.It took me roughly 40 minutes to climb up and then down the mountain completing my first journey or my first level of the game. So if you were curious about whether you'd like it or not you can always play it, complete that first climb and then make you're decision afterwords to keep it or not.I really liked it. It's just a basic survival game. No post-apocalyptic stuff here, no zombies, no monsters,dragons or whatever. It's just the original adventure of climbing up a mountain alone. And it's pretty good. It's survival mechanics are pretty good and it's overal gameplay mechanics are well thought out and work really well to get you into the game.It's graphics are pretty good, it's sound effects are average and it's game length is questionable for 20 dollars but overall I think it's worth it. I'm not going to get a refund. I'm going to keep playing.So if you're into survival games you'll probably like this. Just stick with it though, try to complete that first mountian before you make a decision because it does take a little bit for you to give a damn.But hey if you're still not sure and you want a more in depth look with more in depth information then have a look at the video I posted on my youtube channel (link below). Thanks for reading and I hope I helped some of you out there to spend your money wisely.

_childDocuments_.review: There are two remarkable about this game. One: it has this kind of opinionated, unique design which half its audience will hate, and half will love - and both for the exact same reasons. And two: there's just so, so, SO much wasted potential here, it makes you want to scream. And yes, I'm recommending this game; I beat it on hard difficulty after some 24 hours, and there truly is nothing quite like this. How many games have you played where the only real opponents are attrition and the elements? I mean, I can think of a few, but you know what I mean. Here it's not about your battle strategy, but knowing when to use items, carefully planning your route, taking calculated risks. If that sounds fun it's because it is, but... there's always a but, isn't there.By "hot take" I mean a controversial choice which is nevertheless delivered confidently. Those are some very "take it or leave it" things.The main thing is the camera control. It's very limited, and that's . How do I know? Because there's a skill that gives you a timed ability to zoom out farther than normal; the camera's always centered on your character, by the way. This can be incredibly annoying, in particular when you're climbing down a very steep slope. There's simply no way to position the camera in a way that lets you see how steep a slope is from above. That might sound annoying, and it very much is - but on the other hand it forces you to only plan your routes in very small pieces; also, sometimes you'll find yourself taking a more difficult route simply because you can  the whole thing, rather than trying a flatter, but possibly obstructed path.Next up is the walking animation. You can't skip it. You can make it go faster, but you have to watch every single step you take. Annoying? Yes, sometimes. But at the same time it creates this impeccable, unique atmosphere where travel is not something your character is doing, it's something  are doing; and the entire game is based around this. If you ever went hiking or some other kind of adventuring then you'll be somewhat familiar with what I'm talking about.Finally, there's the hex-based design. It is what it is. It looks a bit crappy perhaps, but it simplifies things a lot, and puts your traversal strategy in focus. If something isn't a hex, it isn't traversable. Also, points of interests are signified by floating coins, which is kind of boring; I'd rather see the stuff myself, but at least this way I'm always 100% sure what I'm going to encounter on a given hex.These "hot takes of design" I wrote about? In the end, I liked them. I liked a lot of things about this game. But there are some things which could've made the game just so much better.First of all, there's the setting and the plot. It's this interesting combination of harsh reality of mountaineering and some sci-fi and "maybe magic, maybe mundane" kind of stuff. It's good. It really is! But it feels like they wrote the plot and then forgot to put it in the game. You get only two sources of exposition: some minor dialogue and event descriptions. They do a good job making you interested in the mysteries, and then just leave you hanging. The ending in particular left me disappointed. Then there are the events. They repeat far, far too often - and usually have the exact same flow. There might be a plot reason for that... but I wish it wasn't so. Especially since the events are quite interesting, decently written and give a lot of colour to the game.Lastly, the terrain. There are three kinds: stone, snow, and ice. Each terrain has three sub-types: normal, hazardous and bothersome. Hazardous has a chance of throwing a dangerous event at you when you cross, and bothersome will slow you down or be more taxing to get through. That's all good, but not only it's a bit boring visually, it's also boring mechanically. You've seen one mountain, you've seen them all. I feel like adding new terrain types with unique effects and events would've made everything so much more fresh.I mostly complained about the game, but I also tried to sneak in the reasons why I think it's actually pretty great. In the end, I was quite happy with my time with Insurmountable - and I was very satisfied with beating it.I suggest playing on hard difficulty from the start - you can't change it mid-game, and I'd say the game would get quite boring on normal, since you're going to have far more resources than you need. The scarcity is what makes hard choices interesting. And no worries, the game's difficulty scales rather well, I'd say. Your characters gets stronger but the conditions get harsher as well.Perhaps the game's price point is a bit high for what it is, but hey, I definitely got my money's worth. If you like slow, meditative yet unforgiving experiences, chances are you'll like this one as much as I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Insurmountable

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from a country where two thirds are covered by high mountains, I was very interested in this game. I didn't play many mountain climbing simulations during the last 40 years, and I never played a good or a somewhat realistic one. This one at least comes close. Simulating the weather, rock, ice, or snow ground, a simple day/night cycle, your body temperature, energy, oxygen level and your sanity you have a straightforward challenge - reach the top and come back alive.The game takes place on a newly discovered island with enormous (+7000 meters) mountains. They look like a hexfield battlemap with different hexfields having different heights. They do not really look like a mountain. They are randomized. I don't really like that, because mountains don't change in reality, only the weather or other climbing conditions change. Select if you want to be an adventurer, scientist or journalist, each one having different perks. Then click on the tile you want to go and watch your character move. Preserve your energy and your food, stay warm, and climb up. You will find animals, caves, plants, natives, other mountaineers (dead or alive), holy shrines and Yeti tracks, and can decide what to do at various points. Help injured animals or eat them, steal ressources from the natives, rest or press on. Sleep in your tent or a cave. Your character levels up and learns new skills during the climb.Is the game realistic? No. You cannot really plan your route before starting. Very careless. You cannot decide what to carry with you, essential things like oxygen tanks are found during your journey. You can climb during the night, although you freeze even faster. You can watch your sourroundings from all angles and zoom out - it is hard to get lost that way. Things I encountered above 7000 meters: a tree, a mountain goat nibbling on some herbs, a holy shrine. Maybe I was already hallucinating?Starve, freeze to death or go crazy in this mounting climbing simulation. A masterpiece? No, but it is the only mountain climbing simulation (more a roguelike adventure than a real simulation) available.
_childDocuments_.name: Insurmountable

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept, Not worth your time. 7 hours to finish it at normal difficulty.Too many things not well implemented. Camera control being the main offender. But the action is super repetitive, the choices you make are always the same and you end up knowing which one to make by heart (like with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sheep).Managing your stats could be more engaging. You quickly find the recipe to make it through the level without too much danger. Level are supposed to be procedural but it always feel like the same mountain. Other games like Steep have done alpine environment much better. the hex system is making the game ugly. the terrain could have been a regular mountain with hex atop of it instead of all those ugly column. There are only 3 types of terrain and the same visual. the floating event coins, could have been replace by scenery, actual animals or people to makes the level feel less empty. 3 characters are not much different in practice, and you are not motivated to try them unless the mission gives extra xp for it. Scanner mechanic is passable, Miss opportunity to have a camera or photo mode with the journalist. Games has a lot of equipment to discover but after 7h I didn't found a lot, and I ended up using the same stuff for every mission anyway. It was on my wish list and I am very disappointed with the final product.
