_childDocuments_.review: Insurmountable is a good foundation for a potentially very chill roguelite. Its slow pacing means it compares more readily to autobattlers like Loop Hero than to action roguelites like RoR or Hades. It's a good time if you fire up a podcast and get climbing.I bought this game after watching a bit of a playthrough on YouTube. I watched it at 2x speed with no problem. The game absolutely should at least have the option to go faster. The current speed options are either "intolerably slow" or "slow."I cleared Normal mode on my first playthrough with very little trouble. I cleared Hard mode on my third try. The game is hard, but very manageable. I disagree with a lot of the other reviews; I think they actually struck quite a good balance between the different resources you need to manage. What I will say is that some skill trees are just blatantly better than others, and that might be part of why some people are having trouble.The main problem is that there is just very little content. It barely qualifies as a roguelite. Each mountain is a set map that never changes - only the event hexes change. You cannot unlock more characters. You cannot unlock more collectibles. The three characters that you can select are all essentially the same with the only variation being the (very minor) starting abilities and equipment. Most of the abilities are purely numerical in nature, and while I don't dislike the resource-management aspect of the game, I wish some of the skill trees had more exciting abilities than 4 different ways to reduce different resource costs. When meditation is one of the most exciting additions to your toolkit, something is wrong.Dying in this game rather severely deflates the tension of the game. The reason is: it's way harder than you think it is to die. Real climbing is risky, and a mistake at any moment can mean death. In this game, you have to make mistakes repeatedly over and over in order to deplete your health. Climbing a vertical face of ice carries no more risk than walking across a flat rock, and furthermore is 100% guaranteed to succeed. You can go to sleep in a tent in the death zone with no oxygen, and just wake up 8 hours later like it's nothing. As a result, danger in Insurmountable doesn't lurk around every corner. Every death is simply the result of 5 or 10 critical interrupt events in a row because a resource ran out. (There is even an ability that ignores critical events. It makes it *completely impossible to die* for the better part of an entire day. ????)If you spend a lot of time on the mountain, you will see a lot of events 3-4 times each. At the time of writing I do still occassionally encounter new events, but the vast majority I have played through over and over. For some of these events, each choice always leads to the same outcome, so once you've seen it before, you know what you can safely pick. Although most events do have random outcomes, they're generally a coinflip between a good and bad outcome. There isn't really much interesting gameplay in terms of risk management. Some events have choices locked behind carrying certain items, but none of them interact with skill trees or character choice (an unbelievable missed opportunity in my opinion).Most of the game is like this. It feels weirdly empty. The "story" is no better: lots of teasing, events that hint at some greater mystery, but no sensible progressive revelations, no answers to even the most minor of questions. Instead of setting up concrete bits of lore that players can piece together, its just a bunch of vague questions thrown out and never answered. It's possible that there are new events that answer this on Insurmountable difficulty - it seemed to me like some events were new on Hard difficulty - but I'm not holding my breath.I unfortunately can't recommend this game. I hope it gets patches or free DLC. The way I see it, basically all the hard work has already been done. It just needs more content.
_childDocuments_.name: Insurmountable

_childDocuments_.review: Played this first day of release as well as one day after update 2.0.Originally, it wasn't engaging enough and after just 2 runs at a mountain, I already started seeing duplicate events. All in all, I didn't like it much, but it was playable.After update 2.0, I played it again. I kind of liked the revision fully embracing the roguelike model as well as the "timeloop" angle. Almost everything was revised, EXCEPT the most important part where you spend most of the time on: the gameplay itself. It's basically the same experience besides some minor revisions which hardly made any difference while you're in the middle of it. Fortunately, I didn't get any duplicate events after two mountain runs now so they improved on that aspect. Still, I was already bored of playing it after just those two runs.There's gotta be some combination of design leveraging the mountain climbing concept that would make this game a lot lot better. I can definitely say though that at least for me, they haven't found it yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Insurmountable

_childDocuments_.review: Played 31 hours. I really want to give this game a positive rating. This game has so much going for it, but I feel like a few minor changes could make this game so much more fun to play.The Good: the game is beautiful. the sights and sounds of being on the mountain are really the best part of the game. It's a fun world to get pulled into. Camera-wise, I know the camera can be a little annoying at times, but I actually felt like that was intentional. The camera will pull in close when you're up against a wall or down at the bottom of a tight valley, and it's hard to tell what the map around you looks like. It's hard to tell where to go. I feel like this just adds to the claustrophobia of putting yourself in a tight, and low place in the topography. In contrast, when you get to the top of a peak, the camera is able to fully extend and you can see everything. It just feels awesome to have such a vantage point.The Bad: the fast-forward option is too slow at times. Given the lack of variety (see the ugly below) even the fastest of options does not feel fast enough at times.The Ugly:First critique goes to the text-based interactions. These are essentially like the text-based "video" games of old with maybe one or two static images to help set the stage. There are tediously few unique options that "randomly" pop up. I put "randomly" in quotations, because there are so few of them, that you easily get the same interaction 5+ times in a single mission if you're attempting to hit as many points of interest as possible. I could easily do away with the images in favor of just adding more interactions (purely text). Seriously, if one person on the dev team sat down for one day and managed to write 3 interactions every hour (24 more interactions) -- that alone would go a long way to making the game feel more "full". That's how few unique interactions there are. I wish that they would have counted up the max number of interactions of a given type that you find on one mission, and written at least 5 times that amount at the very least. No need for images - just the text would be enough to add a lot to the game.Second critique also has to do with the text-based interactions. I don't know how many interactions there are, but I'd venture a guess to say that there are about 50-60. Maybe there's more, but that's about what it feels like. Of those 50-60, I'd say about 20 of them have a variable outcome, and it's just random - there's no point in reading any of the text once you've read it through once because you know that there is one optimal strategy, or it's a 50/50 chance at getting the optimal outcome. I think having more branch points in these text based options could add a lot. I get that branches are expensive in game development, but these would just be text, so dev overhead wouldn't be terrible.Third critique goes to items and inventory. Understand before I say this that items in this game have no 3D representation in the game. They are a single image and a few stat-altering properties. Again, just a little more variety here would be incredible. As is, there's so little variety that I basically stuck with the same loadout the entire game because it just worked. The amount of inventory strategizing that you have to do prior to starting a mission is very minimal. between the lack of variety of items and the lack of inventory space, inventory management feels a little boring to me.**Spoiler Warning Below** Fourth critique goes to the ending. It's about as anti-climactic as you can get. As soon as you finish the final mountain, the game gives you a couple different text-based narrative screens that are different than you’ve had before, and the “twist” is kind of expected, but the payoff is just so underwhelming. After those text cards, the level ends, and that’s it - the credits roll. Maybe they expect me to play through 3 or 4 times before I get the "real ending" but after one playthrough, I'm too bored to go at it again.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has the foundation to actually be really good. Unfortunately at the time of writing this review, it's not there yet and at the current asking price (25 USD), it's not worth it.I have three easy achievements remaining and in the 44 hours I've spent in this game, I've completed a grand total of six playthroughs. The vast majority of the time was spent waiting for walking and climbing animations to finish; the game as a whole really does not respect your time.tl;dr:Full review below, bear in mind that I have only played the "v2" version of the game:Insurmountable is a game where you climb up mountains, represented by hex grids, while managing five resources - health, sanity, body temperature, energy, and oxygen levels. Scattered about each mountain are point of interest nodes where you can gain items, trade for items, restore resource levels, risk resource levels for items, most of which give you experience points to unlock perks that last for that particular mountain. The various POIs are marked with different symbols so you'll know if you're heading towards a shrine, or a trading opportunity, or a cave, as examples.At the end of the mission, you are scored and given experience points across five categories to unlock abilities, new items, and proficiency bonuses that carries over until the end of the playthrough. A complete playthrough of the game takes a minimum of nine climbs, and in between missions you can change your character (when unlocked), your inventory, and proficiency skills. Unfortunately, I find myself taking the same skills every playthrough and the same items every mission because they don't feel properly balanced (pro-tip: bring ).The main plot progress each time you finish a capstone mission, and it feels heavily contrived to fit the game play. . It's not good and the game would honestly be much better without it. The story is also 100% unskippable, even in subsequent playthroughs, so there is an excessive amount of extraneous clicking at the end of and between each mission.The gameplay itself is OK, but needs a lot of quality of life adjustments to actually be good. When you click a tile, you will see the route your character will take to it. You can then click more tiles to add more waypoints. You cannot alter the route at all aside from removing the last or adding a new waypoint. There is no way to clear the entire route, no way to add a waypoint before continuing on the existing route. Given that the basically gameplay loop is routing to POIs while generally heading towards the destination, this could use some improvement.There are two types of missions: one where you ascend to the summit and then descend to a goal tile, and the other where you have to use a sensor to navigate to 3-5 temporal anomaly nodes. The latter is especially unfun; you have to use a sensor to find the vicinity of the node, which doesn't reveal itself on the map until you're about 12 tiles from it. The sensor works by moving the camera around until it pings - the more directly you point the camera at the node, the more vigorously the sensor pings. This leads to some awkward camera angles and it generally feels like I'm fighting the camera, especially when next to cliffs and in valleys. Personally, after the second playthrough, I've actively avoided these missions; they're all optional and not worth the hassle.By the third playthrough, it became obvious that the maps are largely the same and the 'procedurally generated mountains' line is, at best, inaccurate. I've seen about two different start locations per map, one rather centrally located and one left of center. Many POI locations feel the same every playthrough, although the type of POI varies from run to run. Across the 50+ mountains I've done, I expected substantially more variety.Also lacking variety are the events. You will see the same event multiple times across a single playthrough, sometimes even on a single mountain, especially if you go out of the way to hit event POIs. Many of these have one obviously correct option, and the ones that don't are largely avoidable (i.e. "continue my journey" is an option), so there isn't much thought required in terms of risk vs. reward.Which leads me to the final issue I have with the game, which is that it postures as a difficult game, especially with the difficulty modes called "normal", "challenging", and "insurmountable". It's not. Only on my first insurmountable difficulty run did I feel threatened,It's frustrating because underneath all the aforementioned annoyances there's a solid core gameplay loop. I think most people would enjoy doing a couple of mountains or even one complete playthrough. With that in mind, in the current state of the game, wait for a big discount. Hopefully the developers introduce a game mode completely detached from the story, because that would be a game worth climbing for.

_childDocuments_.review: Not enough variation in just about every respect, and the upgrades don't do enough to change the core gameplay. However, what IS here feels extremely polished and is a joy to experience. It feels more like a well-made demo for a larger, more expansive game. Insurmountable is in the board-game style, with your little protagonist trying to reach the top of three mountains, each successively larger and more difficult than the last. The mountains are procedurally generated grids that can form fjords, ice rivers, glaciers, and rocky crags. You have to manage four primary "health" bars (sanity, warmth, energy, and oxygen), with a "true" secondary health bar only depleted during special events or when one of the primary bars is fully depleted. Each of the primary health bars is affected by the environment in different ways, and you try to find single-use items and equipment through the event tiles to keep you healthy. What always happens, however, is that you only really worry about warmth and energy. Warmth is drained at night, during cold weather, sleeping without a tent, and in A LOT of events. Finding the equipment that boosts warmth regen will make the game FAR easier than anything else. Next on the list are the items and abilities that boost energy efficiency. These upgrades aren't mutually exclusive, so you can have a build that has great warmth regen and great energy efficiency. And with every character, that's the only thing I aimed for. Sanity is restored reliably on certain tiles and abilities, and oxygen loss can be mitigated with consumables that aren't terribly hard to find. And that's Insurmountable biggest weakness. It's very easily soved, and the experience isn't different from one run to another. Adding In different environments/themes, like a Volcano level with obsidian glass tiles that would damage health directly, weather patterns that could overheat you, and turn-based pyroclasms that would damaged you if you were on the tiles at the wrong time, would bring fresh variance to the experience. Adding NPCs that you interact with as you're climbing, or an overarching mystery that you solve as you play through successive looks would increase investment and replayability. But as it stands now, I beat the game twice and see no reason to continue

_childDocuments_.review: Well, what to say about Insurmountable? Originally I was hesitant to buy this game because of some negative reviews making it sound dull and repetitive. I waited until it was on sale and bought it for about $7.50. So where does this game stand?This is one of those kind of games that I think will be hit or miss with people depending on their preferred playstyles. Some people are going to absolutely love this game, and some people are probably going to chuck it. Myself, I'm a huge fan of large investment/large payout style games - so, we're talking Farming Simulator 22, American Truck Simulator, and other time-consuming games like that. One of my other favorite genres is the Vampire Survivors/"Bullet Heaven" one, in which each run has a set timer of usually between 20-30 minutes - so, again, something where you have to invest a longer period of time to get the payout.For people like me, who enjoy the long haul approach, I think this game is going to be a huge win. For people who are looking for a quick play, or action-oriented game, I think it will be a miss. That being said, if it wasn't clear from the videos, this is not an action game at all. There is no manual climbing or "action" scenes. You plan your route, trying to be as efficient with your energy, sanity, body temperature and oxygen as possible, and managing multiple-choice "encounters" along the way. It will not be a quick 5-minute climb to the top, so you'll spend a while on each climb.Despite some negative reviews, I thoroughly enjoy this game. I like that the climbs are long and arduous - that's how I imagine mountain climbing IS, after all. It was a very "Oregon Trail 2.0" feel to it - not quite as simple as OT, but it's got that same feel of "I've got to keep soldiering on, managing my resources over the long term to keep myself alive." You may think it's no big deal to invest a ton of energy/oxygen/sanity/body temp to take the short route... until you run into other problems and all of a sudden one of your stats is plummeting, and now you're in a real pickle. You find that it's often much better to take the longer route with smaller climbs to better manage yourself.Along the way, you'll run into all kinds of issues - you'll think you've found a perfect path, only to realize it's a dead end, surrounded by un-climbable paths. You'll encounter problems - avalanches, loose stones, canyons, etc - and have to decide, will I try the quick approach, which is riskier, or the longer approach, which will consume time and the other four stats.. but carries much less risk? You'll encounter item stashes, hermits, bands of people, other climbers, and have either good, negative, or neutral exchanges with them. You'll discover landmarks, which can give you JUST the boost you need to make it the rest of the way. When you have these encounters, you'll be given a multiple-choice response, and depending on how you choose, you'll face the outcome - good or bad.In between runs, you can level up your climbers, pick out new starting inventories (which force you to take just the bare essentials, finding the rest of what you'll need on the actual climbs), and more. Overall, so far I'm having a blast.I haven't yet beat the game, so I'm not 100% certain yet how much replayability there will be... once I beat it, if there is the option to "go back" and do more climbs, that will be great. Or, if there is some kind of generic "climb to the top" mountain you can replay, that will be cool. If once you beat the game you beat it, case closed, then I'm not sure how replayable this game will be. I think I'll come back once I beat it and edit my review - but I felt confident that it should be recommended, because even if there isn't much replayability, the experience alone was well worth the eight bucks I paid. It is a great game for people who really enjoy large-investment playstyles.Is it worth the full $25? That, I don't know. It will be for some folks, and won't be for others. Before you pay full price, ask yourself if you DO enjoy games that don't have a lot of action (besides written, described action), and if you do enjoy games that require a fairly decent amount of time investment. If not, wait for a sale. If you do, I say go for it.But, I feel it does deserve a full "recommend," because this is an extremely visually-appealing, somewhat strategic, fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game per se, but it's . The trailer makes it out to be a strategy puzzler, the shop page claims it's similar to XCOM and also to Ancestors - all three of these claims are BS lies.The trailer promised a challenge, but a played it on hard difficulty and had no real problems reaching the peaks in good health. This game maybe could be challenging, but it isn't and the main reason for it is how the game works:You have to manage the "resources" energy, body temperature, oxygen, and mood and you have to find the safest route to the peak before your supplies run out.So far so good, but you're told exactly what you're gonna lose on your route before you even make the first step and if you don't like that, you just look for another route. That prudent certainty takes out most of the fun the game could've had...Your average run consists of you zooming out and looking for a good route, clicking blindly until the pathfinding finds a route that you like, and watching your character slowly walking over there (you can speed up the walking, but it looks really goofy).Insurmountable disappoints in every way: The trailer promised "1000s of difficult decisions", but neither are there thousands, nor are they difficult. The few "roleplaying" sections here and there appear randomly and are laughably dull and inconsequential. They try to create atmosphere, but in the end all that remains of them is the question "Was that it? What was the point?"And then there's some blatant unrealistic BS. The game tries to be as authentic as possible, but then there's stuff like that climbing gear is not a requirement for scaling a 100-foot wall of ice, but if you use one, it's slightly less tiring. I don't think anyone should climb an icy cliff in the middle of the night during a snow storm 6 km above sea level without a torchlight or climbing gear in RL, but in this game the worst that can happen to you if you do that, is not falling to your death, but just being exhausted...

_childDocuments_.review: On a mysterious island, adventure awaits… You’ll fight against the very forces of nature in your mountaineering journey. If you enjoy an exploration-based game with plenty of interactivity, danger, and an air of mystery, you’ll love Insurmountable by developer/publisher ByteRockers’ Games. I was given the game to review before it released, and I really enjoyed its relaxing, yet adventurous feel. Playing Insurmountable for the first time, I was surprised by the relaxing atmosphere of it. For a game about scaling impossible heights and facing unknown danger, the experience is fairly slow-paced and calming. I played as an adventurer whose goal was to scale a mysterious mountain while keeping myself warm, sane, healthy, and maintaining enough energy and oxygen to make the climb. I did this by managing my scarce resources and exploring the terrain around me to find more resources and tools to aid in my survival. I used items such as tea, canned food, and herbs to keep my stats up during the adventure. The inventory and resource management added another level of interest to the gameplay without being too difficult to manage. I enjoyed the game’s focus on exploration balanced with a need for survival; it made for a slow-paced game that was relaxing, but not boring. Insurmountable was fairly challenging, as well, but not impossibly so. It was just difficult enough for me to feel a sense of satisfaction after finishing each climb. The terrain of the mountainous game world is built in hexagonal sections that you can travel across, which lends a unique board-game-like feel to the game. There are different kinds of tiles- snow, ice, and rock- which can affect aspects of the game such as how much energy it takes to traverse them or the speed at which you travel. Some tiles trigger different types of events when you walk across them, such as encounters with natives, discoveries of ancient shrines, or even dangerous rockslides. Each event is played out in an interactive text-based form. It feels a bit like reading a story- much of the imagery is left up to the player’s imagination, which can be fun, but also may not be appealing to every player. As a player, you can interact with the game in two main ways. One way is the path you travel. You can choose which tiles to cross depending on the danger, energy cost, and events triggered by each type of tile. There are an almost infinite number of ways to reach the top of each mountain. The path you choose may determine how difficult it is to finish the game, or whether you even survive the adventure.The second method of interaction is through the various events you may encounter throughout your journey. Depending on the choices you make in these situations, you may end up with an extra can of food or a broken ankle. These events can mean the difference between reaching the end of the game or dying in the interim. The things I liked the most about Insurmountable were the relaxing pace and storylike elements. It was a nice change of pace from the typical action-heavy games I play, and I enjoyed slowing down for a bit. The story events were also really cool and well-written, and I enjoyed being able to interact with the game in that way. There were a couple things I didn’t like as much about Insurmountable, although they were fairly minor: the player’s perspective and the glitch I encountered. The player’s perspective was a little annoying because of how closely it was anchored to the character- if I climbed down into a ravine, for example, the camera would get stuck very close to my character so I wouldn’t be able to see around the outside of the ravine. This made it a little difficult to choose the best path sometimes, although it didn’t affect my experience too much. One thing that did affect my experience, though, was a glitch that reset my progress. After climbing the first mountain, I took a break before doing the second one; then, after I reopened the game, it reset my progress so I had to complete the first mountain again before I could continue. It didn’t set me back too far, but it was still an inconvenience. However, the same thing happened after I completed the second mountain, so it set me back a lot farther that time. But then, when I played the game a few days later, it didn’t corrupt the save. This means the glitch was possibly fixed. Either way, it was still enjoyable to play because every adventure was unique. Overall, my experience playing Insurmountable was very enjoyable. Every step I took in the game felt like an adventure, in the best way. I’d rate this game 9/10 overall, and I definitely recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: Decent and original game about climbing, but no keybinds for zooming out, and a bad camera. _childDocuments_.review: Overall, this is a pretty solid tactical roguelike experience.In over 5 hours, I've only played normal difficulty, and completed all 3 mountains with two of the classes. I only died once.Considering this is the easiest out of 3 difficulties, I think that's pretty fair. Overall RNG, at least on Normal, seems pretty balanced between "good" and "bad" events happening. The tile-set and graphics look nice.Things that can be improved:There needs to be a clearer representation of the Death Zone, the area where oxygen begins to deplete. Maybe an opaque fog starts to appear as you reach the upper areas, or a opacity colored border marker around the tiles once you reach the zone. Snow and Ice tiles seem too similar and need to have a clearer distinction between them. The UI feels a bit clunky, and while overall it's pretty clean, the information can be presented a bit more clearly. Currently you have to dig around to find specific important stats. _childDocuments_.review: Could've been good, idea is nice, but the execution is lacking.You spend lots of time watching your character move along, with nothing for you to do. You can't even check your inventory while moving. This could've been nice if the game were more interesting to look at, but the terrain makes no effort to smooth out the hex pillars, the sky is a simple static skybox, the props are static, the lighting is uninspired. Overall the audiovisual design is perfunctory and fails to do justice to the majesty of a mountain.The game relies heavily on events, but these are nonsensical in what they present as exclusive choices. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: A unique concept combining role-playing with strategic and tactical decision-making in a rogue-lite package. Although refreshing and engaging, RNG and cookie-cutter events diminish overall experienceEvery once in a while I come across a game that still surprises me, despite thinking I’ve pretty much seen most of the games that the industry has to offer. Insurmountable is one of those games. The game has you play a mountaineer trying to summit various peaks in pursuit of set objectives. Along the way, you encounter randomly-generated events which may help or hinder your ascent -- you may receive useful items, or get injured, or lose time and heat as a result. The game is set in a rogue-lite format, with a single save game and a single attempt to summit all 3 mountains. You may choose one of three different climbers, each with varying starting traits, items, advantages and disadvantages. There are also different difficulty levels. Let’s take a look at the game in detail:+ Insurmountable’s unique concept is a big plus. The challenge of playing a mountaineer is both interesting and compelling+ There are both strategic and tactical choices to be made: Choosing the type of explorer, route, and summit strategy may give the edge you need (or disadvantage you); while climbing decisions, path choices, terrain, weather forecasts and random events are some of the tactical decisions you have to face+ The gaming UI seems to make sense: you have a health bar, but also levels of sanity, oxygen, energy and warmth, some of which can be replenished by items or events. These stats have to be continuously monitored (like in real climbing), as it may mean the difference between life and death+ The audio track complements the game well, is unobtrusive, and adds a layer of immersion to the game+ Once you summit the mountain, you have to make your way back down to base camp. As much as I would prefer the journey to end after reaching the top, this two-way trip is realistic. It also forces you to budget your items for the trip back down (do you have enough oxygen, warmth, etc?)- The game can be frustrating. My biggest grouse is the RNG inherent in the events that you face, and the cookie-cutter format that exists. For e.g. if you ever encounter a cave where you observe a light, always go in and explore -- you will receive some stat increase in addition to being able to rest. Similarly, if there’s a smell, don’t venture any further and just rest. This prefabricated format is kind of lazy and not characteristic of the overall production values in the game- In general, the random nature of the events are the biggest wild card. You may receive outcomes that can be devastating to your climber. While some may consider this to be “realistic”, and yes, random events do occur in life, but the game should more closely mimic the preparedness, supply and replenishment, and detailed planning reflected in actual climbing. For e.g, as you begin the game, you start with some basic supplies, depending on the type of climber you choose. But after you return to base camp, there is no option to re-supply or heal before you’re forced to the next ascent. Seriously? Who climbs 3 mountains in a row without being able to re-supply or heal? - The two camera angles can be limiting as well. Yes, you may be able to see only so far as you’re climbing but what about all the information and intelligence you’re supposed to have on the area, the mountain, etc. (like in real climbing)? Shouldn’t that warrant better top down camera angles? Visibility is everything -- if you can’t pick the best path to the top, be prepared to fail/die - There is no way to replenish energy except by sleeping (for some reason, you don’t need to eat/drink); but if you sleep while in the “death zone”, you’ll almost freeze to death by the time you wake up. There should be a feature that allows you to replenish energy other than sleeping (in “real” life, it’s called eating/drinking)The negatives mentioned here affect the overall balance and replayability of the game (for me, anyway). The format of the events is the same, but the order in which you get them is totally random; you have no opportunity to heal or re-supply (yes, there are no resources at base camp), and the rogue-lite features (only one save game; no incremental or in-progress saving) can be unforgiving and unnecessarily punishing. If there was a way to heal and re-supply in between ascents, Insurmountable would be longer-lived, but as is, I’d likely uninstall it and move on. I understand the need for randomness, but the devs do not reward planning and strategy enough, and some conditions are just outright ridiculous. Insurmountable is a good idea, but still needs to be better balanced and fleshed out before it can be a great game (Insurmountable 2?). In my book, it makes the grade (just barely), as the positives still outweigh the negatives. I would still recommend not paying full price for it though, unless the shortcomings mentioned are addressed.6.0/10.0

_childDocuments_.review: Reading a review is not enough? Want to see some footage? Check the link and watch some game footage for yourself and decide if this game is worth your time:Insurmountable is a rogue like survival game where you climb a mountain and try to survive that awful monster. The Game is using a hex based art style similar to Into the Breach with an advanced Polygon engine, and man does this game look beautiful.This is the third game created by ByteRockers Games who entered the world of Steam  four years ago with VR Frog and Beefense.We need to find the truth by climbing this mountain and probably die.This game is smooth, I need to say this at first before going deeper. The walking animation, the events, the weather and particle effects are wonderful. You start as either adventurer, scientist or a reporter, everyone has a different start perk and equipment. The build up paths and the events are great, the first time that I was curious what will happen after my guy had explosive diarrhea and could just barely get hits pants of to, well take a dump, an explosive spray and prey dump. I had a hard time to manage my characters parameters to stay alive. In this game you have to watch out for your energy, sanity, temperature and later for oxygen. Sanity is a great stat, its more or less a timer to not let you roam and doing every event and becoming to powerful. You also have health, once this drops to zero, you are Dead Meat. Depleting everything else results in an increase of bad events, so you have to watch out, but you are still able to move and try to save you. This brings me to the next point: the animation. It is great, your temperature is low? You will see how your character is freezing and trying to get himself heated up. Low on energy? You see how he is walking in crumpling pain. This tiny things make the game really awesome and its fun to play. Let's talk about the events. Fascinating one, the most event I had been a goat I tried to befriend. It ran away and hurt a bit to be honest. Later the same goat saved me from a jaguar and then later one gave me 500xp by giving me good luck. You heard right, the game has leveling up, and it's the most important thing besides choosing your path. You can nearly level everything. My Reporter was that buffed up, that he would not lose any energy during calm weather and when on the stone path. This is amazing leveling up material, due to this you can customize a lot and play your way. So what's actually bad in this game? Well there is one tiny rant, there could be more events, and it would be great to have an indicator if the event is righteous bad or has a chance of being good.+ a lot of different routes to run and explore+ Great perks and a nice leveling up mechanic+ events are unique and have multiple outcomes+ survival aspect is+ Animations are fun and fun to watch+ 3 different characters to play with- Events are RNG based causing in multiple bad events and death- events placing is not well done, it can either be a lot in one space or nothing for the next 10 minutes.- debuffs at the end of the roads are a too big penaltyInsurmountable offers an addictive game with a unique way to play a survival game. The setting is as amazing as it is deadly, you need to know nearly 300 people died since climbing the Mount Everest has become cool. The game itself feels full of opportunities and looks so nice that I can't stop playing it.So who will enjoy this game? Do you like Hexbased games? Ever wanted to have a strategic survival game? Do you need something new in the survival genre not just building and killing wolves or zombies? Then this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Very unique game about climbing a mountain. You dont have enemies, the nature is your only foe. Managing your resources is important, and visiting as many events as you can to get experience and lvl up is crucial, because of the different skills that you can acquire. I would say that in my first run of the game, i've seen a mayority of the events available, which is not good. There has to be more diversity of events and items. You either stare at an eagle and get some bonuses, an old lady heals you, or you see a dead body and grab stuff (which has happened many times). Spoilers of my run:  The difficulty curve is very steep, you have to plan your path beforehand, see what items you have, which possible items you can collect with the events, and a bit more. _childDocuments_.review: Very solid release with a nice, tight premise and design. You climb mountains by navigating an array of hexagonal tiles that vary in both height and terrain. As you progress towards each mountainous peak, you need to make strategic decisions on what route to take based on your survival statistics (Health, Energy, Sanity, Oxygen and Warmth) and your items. Is it worth spending a quarter of your energy climbing a huge rock face just to see what's in that cave in the distance?There is a wonderful simplicity to Insurmountable. From moment to moment, you are essentially doing the same thing - clicking a hexagon and watching your little anorak avatar trudge further and further up the cliffs and snow, through storms and gales, and hoping you can make it to the top before you collapse through fatigue.This game has excellent presentation. Looking up at the next peak you have to conquer is an experience in itself, filling you with equal parts consternation and determination. The hexagonal design of the tiles you traverse is a constant joy - functional enough to make learning the game mechanics easy enough, but stylised enough to let those same hexagons merge seamlessly with the rest of the mountainside background.The skill and levelling up system has a tangible influence on your future behaviour around the mountain - why do I need these crampons if I'm already a Master Ice Climber? When you level up, you are presented with three choices of abilities to gain. Some are passive, providing a constant effect. Others are active, and require activating in your skill bar at just the right moment to make a seemingly impossible ice shelf become a minor inconvenience.A little gripe with the game currently - there is a stark lack of variety in the random events that occur. As you traverse the landscape, you can step on nodes with certain symbols, like caves or items. I have only played for about 5-6 hours, but already I've encountered about 12-13 wizened old ladies in huts that offer me cups of tea or whatever. There is replayability here in the guise of increased difficulty and different classes of explorer, but the devs need to crank out lot more events to make replaying seriously worth considering.Other than that, Insurmountable is well worth a purchase, and is priced very fairly in my opinion. Hoping that the devs continue to expand on this initial release, as I feel there is a lot of potential for extra content.

_childDocuments_.review: Scale mountains with hextile-based movement whilst managing your sanity, energy, etc meters with items and random hextile-placed events. It's a roguelike, so die on any of the three mountains of your run and that's it. Any game can be summarised as efficiently as you want of course, but what I mean is that  Of course the 'mountaineer roguelike' pitch no doubt inspires thoughts of a 'Strand Game' approach. Direct control, natural looking terrain and all that jazz. When judged on what it actually is, Insurmountable is compelling. Perhaps not lastingly so, but consuming for those first playthroughs nonetheless. It's not immediate Game Over if your energy spirals to nought. Movement and climbing become sluggish and laboured. Pop-ups blare out music that screams crisis whilst intermittently detailing your climber's harrowing descent into vitals failure. Pop-up by pop-up that health meter gets chipped away at and so many temporary reprieves simply mean you're on borrowed time.  Good management and dancing between feeding those meters so you can avoid the dreaded, slow, and panic inducing climb down the death ladder becomes rewarding as a result. Learning all the systems at play is engaging enough. Weather, time of day, altitude, whether you have a tent/cave to sleep in, etc will all affect the meter drain. Events present risk-reward choices, items and good opportunities for meter boosts. Items and skills both present a means to specialise in draining a meter less or boosting them in very logical ways. Some abilities can be activated for a limited time for such boosts, but also perhaps ignoring difficult terrain generating injuries - which affect meters. You get it. Everything comes down to those meters!Those systems are all sufficiently detailed and fun to consider, then.  From what I've played, risk-reward considerations seem to lean massively towards reward in outcome. I learned that it really wasn't ever not worth pursuing a lead on anything. The experience gain alone is worth it. That might well be the difficulty I played on, however. The one - perhaps unavoidable - aspect of these random events is that they're not majorly contextual to the tile you find them. If one thing leads me to describe the game in terms of its systems instead of experience, it's this disconnect between the environment and the mechanics. It's a difficult thing to solve with a small studio and a procedural roguelike. The result is that I know I'm moving between event tiles rather than considering for instance where a cave might be in the landscape.  They remind me an awful lot of playing the Netflix interactive show You vs. Wild with Bear Grylls. Right down to 'should you eat these berries?' At least Insurmountable is kind enough to not yet give me an instant Game Over for being peckish. Spoilers for Bear Grylls' masterpiece there.  Reaching those peaks was so much easier for wanting to prove this rebellious scientist's theory right. It's an ingenious addition. So roguelikes inherently beg to be played repeatedly.  Not currently, no. In fairness to Insurmountable, its concept makes it a difficult bar to surmount. It's hard to compete with the moment-to-moment variation and responsiveness of a typical combat-centric roguelike. Random events and a different environment feel much too much like retreading ground. Presentation is all-around great and the UI is clear and informative. Yes, the very functional hexagonal tiles protruding upwards do look odd, but you get used to it.  A nice touch.

_childDocuments_.review: Great strategic, turn based type game. Has 3 different play "styles" all of which give you different positives and negatives while playing. Mountains do randomly generate but its more of a random rng type generation and less of a physical generation. Learn to use the terrain to your advantage and dont expect to make it to the top every single time without a tiny bit of help from the rng. It can be done but you need to save items you find as long as you can (preferably until the last mountain).I have seen alot of negative reviews about the "immersion" of this game. That depends on which type of immersion is meant. If realism and graphical perfection is the immersion youre looking for and  is a huge deal for you, this may not be the type of game for you. The  terrain is very well done in my opinion, however the actual hexagons that are used for movement are purposefully left that way to give you an easier time seeing the difference between playable tiles and the areas in which arent walkable and are just there for design purposes. I personally had no issue "immersing" myself into the game, however if you are expecting a skyrim type graphical experience you need to watch the videos provided and the images abit more before purchasing. Perma-death is also a feature which i would express to readers before buying. If you die, thats it. No reloading and you must start from the beginning. Be aware of this before buying. I personally find it fun as it makes every decision much more purposeful. Highly recommended for players looking for a challenge and which understand the concept of perma-death and appreciate its relevance in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A creative idea, both thematically and from a gameplay perspective, but a rather lacking execution.Simply listing the, to me, major issues with this game: - The entire challenge of the game lies in the management of your five available resources... but you can completely remove that ressource management with one or two perks each. There's this 'Death Zone', where above a certain height you will start losing oxygen, putting you on a timer. Unless you have a perk that lets you regenerate oxygen whilst on snow (one of the 3 terrain types, and probably the most comon), suddenly it becomes an 'Irrelevance Zone'. Climbing costs you energy? No longer if you combine an item, a perk and a modifier that give you a cumulative -100% energy cost. I'm not certain where the supposed challenge of the game is supposed to come from when you can 'solve' the resource management aspect of the game one third into a run. - Speaking of one third into a run, by the time I was done with the first summit, I had already seen so many repeitions of perks, items and events (not to speak of the same 3 terrain types over and over), that I would dare to claim I've seen most, if not all of the content the game has to offer. Less than 2 hours in. That's not a good benchmark, and is a very bad omen for replayability. - Furthermore, the game feels needlessly slow. You queue a move order... and then you spend 30 seconds fiddling thumbs as your character strolls across the landscape, slowly scaling cliffs and such. There IS a button to speed this up... but only by x2. You could add another x3 to that and it might work out, but as is the game contains way too much waiting. I'm not sure whether this is an oversight or an intent, to encourage the player to enjoy the calm mountainscape... but the latter is kinda not a thing if you ever turn the camera outwards, as the non-playable area is a rather ugly sight of low-polygon mountains. - Semi-related to the last point, next to waiting for my character to execute the movement, what was the 2nd most time-consuming part of the game? Inventory management. But not the interesting kind: See, there's a couple items that give you boni, usually energy cost reductions, for specific terrain types (or conditions). This means, to play optimally, you have to switch out items depending on the terrain you're walking on. So, instead of queueing a long move order and waiting for it to finish, the actual gameplay consists of taking 2 steps, opening the inventory, switching two pieces of gear, closing the inventory, taking 2 steps, opening the inventory, switching two pieces of gear... admittedly, that optimization probably wouldn't be necessary to beat the game on normal difficulty (given the complete non-relevance of resource management)... but this is bad design that will probably hit hard (by becoming mandatory) during higher difficulties. I understand the concept of 'you can only wear one pair of shoes, and have to change what you want to wear!' but it's atrociously implemented from an actual gameplay perspective.Overall, I like the theme and the idea,but the gameplay is dull, the balance seems off, and the content is abyssimally shallow.So, for that pricepoint, I can definitely NOT recomment the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite my overall positive feelings towards this game, I  frankly feel that it should still be in beta/early access at this stage.  The skeleton of a truly unique and fun game is here ... it just needs more meat (i.e. content) and some polish.  For that reason, I can't really recommend buying at full price - AT THIS TIME.  For what it's worth, the dev appears to be committed to content updates and receptive to player feedback, so there's a really solid chance of this game evolving into something worth it's full $20 asking price.As to the game itself, it plays somewhat like a isometric CRPG.. but instead of combat encounters you have several "events" that affect either your four stats or equipment loadout.  The key to doing well is choosing the best path - often tile-by-tile - to get the most out of your four stats.  You'll be juggling your energy, oxygen levels, body temp and sanity.This is not a fast paced game.  If slowly picking (or clicking, rather) your way 2-3 tiles at a time and constantly switching gear to maximize efficiency sounds like a boring slog to you, then you're probably not going to like this game.  If that idea makes your OCD's naughty bits tingle, this is worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: After a grueling series of consecutive summits, low on oxygen and supplies, injured, delirious and disorientated, I summit the last peak, knowing that I won't have the energy or tools needed to make the climb back down to base level. _childDocuments_.review: This game feels like a love letter to old school text adventure games with an updated modern treatment. It feels akin to a few mountaineering board games out there. If you like chill relaxing games, if you like exploration and discovery, love climbing or mountaineering, are capable of suspending your disbelief a little, and know how to remap keybindings, then this game might be for you. If you’re only a modern gamer who expects out of the box perfection and doesn’t like to tinker or doesn’t like game mechanics that go beyond surface levels and maybe aren’t super obvious, maybe go watch someone play it on Twitch or YouTube first. Like many resource management and survival games, there is a little bit of a learning curve. Is it a little rough around the edges? Maybe, but as someone who’s gamed for 30+ years, there’s a certain charm that accompanies games like this that remind me of those quirky games from bygone years. Text adventure and exploration driven gameplay married with survival and resource management, makes for a unique and novel experience that I have yet to see especially for mountaineering.The biggest complaint: The camera was difficult to manage before I remapped the keybindings to better suit my steam deck/gamepad. That was 90% of the wonkiness though. Like any game, once orientated to the controls and gameplay loop, Everything was smooth sailing. Perhaps even on the easy side. However, as I progressed through the game, the difficulty level did improve. Careful planning is needed in order to navigate the terrain and achieve mission goals. I am def fan of these developers: I always check out their Pax East booth each year. They always seem to have some fun concept game going and I remember seeing this one a few years back. For a sale price of $4.99, there’s really not much to complain about. I’m 3 missions in at the time of initial review and will update if anything relevant comes up.

_childDocuments_.review: Runs well on the Steam Deck, however there’s zero gameplay support which the devs on the boards here proudly defend. Their strategy of spamming this on to Epic for free, Prime Gaming freebie, and Fanatical Mystery bundles has really made it have the appearance of a cheap title. It’s not a game I can play a lot of, perhaps a mission a day at best. The camera is janky and sometimes you get stuck right up against the character’s face and you have no option but to somehow pick a random space nearby to move to. There’s a ton of text reading and the text is microscopic for no reason. There’s no option to change it, so they don’t care about glasses wearers, people with poor vision, or as the discussions will show you, Chinese and Japanese players who can’t read it. It’s a very strange accessibility decision. I assume it would be an easy af patch but they have made no indication they care or will fix it. The game is fine but for the length it promises to be events are constantly repeated. Which again, for a story text based game, is a major flaw. There’s one speed up option for the gameplay and it’s woefully slow. Watching our character shuffle along slowly is not content. It’s just artificially bloating the length. It’s a good enough, though there’s plenty better rogues. On Normal you basically have to be a kid to die.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start this review by saying that insurmountable is not a game for everybody. It is very slow in parts and can be very frustrating if you are not good at route finding, therefore, some real world mountaineering experience in route finding is helpful. That being said, it was a fantastic game. As an avid mountain climber, myself, I have to say that insurmountable, for the most part, did a very good job at capturing the essence of mountaineering. While playing this game, it really does feel like it is just you and your wits alone on the slopes of a massive mountain within a majestic mountain range with wind and snow whipping at you at every turn. When I first opened this game, I frankly wasn't sure if I was going to like it. The hexagon shaped tiles at first appear as though they would be distracting and ruin the immersion or the believability of the location that this game is set. However, after spending 9 hours in this game I can positively say that the simplistic art style does not ruin the immersion or the atmosphere. One thing I can say about insurmountable is I wish that the tutorial was a little better than what was in the game. For example, if you want to change the camera angle you have to hold down your mouse wheel and move your mouse, this was not something that was stated anywhere in the game or the controls page in the option menu, I had to figure it out myself. Other than that, the game mechanics are straight forward. I enjoyed the music and the environmental design, and I liked the integration of sanity, body temperature, energy, oxygen, and health and the subtle ways that they all influenced each other. As for the story, it's pretty odd and in parts feels a little slapped together. However, without giving too much away about the story, it does do a very good job at tying together some loose ends that are present at the end of each one of your ascents and descents. Overall, I think I would recommend insurmountable to any of my fellow Mountaineers out there or to people who are looking for a very atmospheric and relaxing mountain experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. Very chill and relaxing.It's alot like a board game with how you move around and you have to manage 5 resources (sanity, oxygen, warmth, time and energy).The normal difficulty is very fair and you can afford to make mistakes, which is cool to see how certain events turn out, because you take more risks.Higher difficulties make the game more like a puzzle where you really have to calculate where and how you move next. And the time resource becomes much more important.There are 3 characters to play with, all at the same time, and they each play very differently. They come with their own skill trees which are very fun and not too complicated. But you can really see the effect right away and this in my opinion is what makes the game more enjoyable overall. Otherwise you would just climb one mountain and you've seen what the game has to over, but now every mountain comes with its own variations and challenges that you can overcome with how you build your climbers and what equipment you bring.Also different events happen that can be more rewarding and also more punishing.The balance of the equipment could've used some tweaking. You can't really take much with you until late in the game. I think maybe if the game overall across the board was a tad more difficult but the equipment costs a tad lower, just so you can bring more with you and feel more like an actual climber.Now you're, for example, bringing a tent, helmet and gloves along, but no boots, no climbing equipment, no rations. Or you take the rations, but gloves.I recommend this game for anyone who loves climbing or loves boardgames.

_childDocuments_.review: It's tolerably good, and I would have recommended it on sale, except... the camera controls.On a lot of maps, it won't be incorrect management of energy/warmth/sanity/oxygen that will kill you - it'll be the wretched camera - disorientating you down the wrong slope of the mountain. At which point you'll have invariably depleted all the items and events needed to survive a backtrack. The new ping direction finder required for some maps .
_childDocuments_.name: Insurmountable

_childDocuments_.review: To be frank, I would prefer to give a "neutral" review to the game, assuming that Steam would support that feature (and what people are crying out for, like for ages now). It is not a bad game, fundamentally gets many things right and most of the problems could be remedied by a major content patch. The reason why I opt for a thumbs down, is simple... this game is on the market for well over one and half years and that "major content patch" didn't arrive. Doubt that it will ever do so.Either way, so this game is like a solo board game about hiking and mountaineering with some mystical / supernatural vibe. There is a story, I would prefer to call it functional, doesn't feel bad, but nothing to write home about. You have to get from A to B (maybe to C and D too) on rugged terrain with some mountaineering mechanics and basically that's it. It's a "peaceful" game in the sense that there is no battle/fight, the variety comes in the form of random events and side missions. Sadly, the pool of the random events feels super limited and (side) missions are simple copycats. Get to a place, then get to another place, rinse and repeat. You can develop your character during a mission, but the skill pool stays the same too (there is an explanation for that in the story, but it still doesn't help to feel the utter grind this game offers). Developing your character(s) out of mission requires you to do the same copycat side missions, which just add to the mind numbing monotony.In story mode the game offers three mountains to scale and a handful of side missions for each mountain. I scaled the first mountain and completed all side missions, then the second. According to the achievement statistics, only one-third of the players successfully scaled the second mountain and the level of player attrition sounds just about right, since that will be the point when I'm going to check out. Especially after seeing that I got offered exactly the same side missions and only encountered a single new random event on the second mountain.It was a fun 4-5 hours with the game and I don't regret purchasing it, but unless mountaineering is your life, I think most of the players will feel what I felt after these hours. A game with tons of potential, abandoned by it's developer.

_childDocuments_.review: offers a lonely climbing adventure, spanning three mountains, shaped into a fun . Tackle the mountains in sequential order as one of three preset climbers and try your best to maintain your vital statistics while also dealing with a slew of random events that help or hinder you along the way. While there's a story, it's pretty much non-existent and feels unimportant.Even with such a daunting name, the game is actually rather  as you start off the run. The game only has Normal difficulty unlocked in the beginning and while it still presents a challenge, it does not feel impossible as there are different ways to manage your resources and statistics, with these methods for you to discover often just off your main path. The game gives you some resources to start as well and those prove critical in tight situations. The game hits difficulty spikes after scaling the first mountain and heading into the subsequent stages. I haven't managed to unlock the other two higher difficulties, but I imagine those are are going to make me pull some hairs out--if only to make a wig and then stick it back on my head to stop myself from shivering.While it is a simple idea of Man vs. Mountain, the statistics that you have to worry about are your  The game does not hesitate to tell you if any of the stats are in critical ranges as you start to have dangerous random events occur. The game is over if your health reaches 0 and so if you can crawl back to the designated safety spot before your health gets there, you will live to tell the tale, or to be able to attempt the next mountain with some battle scars.In addition, as you progress, you will find various ways to gain experience and to level up. Each level up is associated with  of passive or active abilities that will boost your chances of survival.After all, it's a matter of survival, and even planning your feet and a flag atop the highest unconquered peak is not the same as then making it safely home, recounting the adventure with a mug of hot cocoa.The events that you encounter along the way often involve decisions that have  Sometimes you may hit a jackpot and gain a massive boost in the stat that's just about drained, while other times you will end up wasting a lot of time and energy to discover that all was for naught. Even though it's a lonely adventure, you will still find other people and creatures along your way, or maybe all that you find is a frozen corpse and a residual backpack. But your decisions may lead to gathering of resources, spending them, or setting off a chain of events that will affect your game later on.Even though the events are rather interesting and fun, there is a  of these events in general. I think for maintenance of player interest beyond the initial captivation, the game would do well to further flesh out more sets of possible events and outcomes. Furthermore, as the days go by with different weather conditions, it would be great to have more time/temperature/weather dependent events. The store page mentions hundreds of events, but I seem to find myself coming across similar ones rather often in the few times I have tried playing so far. So it could be that I just have not seen most of them.It is easy to expand your camera zoom as far out as possible and only click on the events of interest as you try to climb up. The computer will generate a path for you and you can confirm that selection if you wish. But this often yields in some paths that will waste your precious time and energy, while also taking you across some dangerous random events.  so rushing ahead will often result in regret, if not disaster. Every step is a calculated risk, so planning your paths carefully will likely maximize your chances of survival.You will encounter expendable resources as you move about, but you will also find equipment that will help you in certain situations. Some equipment only help you, while others may have some negative effects. Just as above, pay attention and think your decisions through.Each run will be different as you may choose a different character, the mountains and events will be changed, along with weather patterns in addition to how you decide to move about. All in all, with the difficulty spikes that are built-in along the way, even a run completion in normal difficulty will be a challenge. But I do like the progressive difficulty unlocking to make it easily accessible for you to learn as you play for the first few times. I am still trying to find my footing amid all of the slippery slopes as well as sublime and supernatural events.Nevertheless,  (I would love to see legacy accumulations of previously failed runs in the form of residual equipment and resources become buried to be discoverable later in subsequent runs. Just a part of my own wishlist, of course.) is often an important aspect of why a game is fun also. I would love to see seeded run options or some preset challenges that the player can use to hone skills and to avoid the RNG machine by choice.I recorded myself playing the game for the first time, if you are interested. It was a matter of discovering the game, so be aware that things move along rather slowly.You can play the whole game with a mouse, but you can also use some keyboard shortcuts that you can easily rebind.With the hex-grid modification of the mountains, it is far from realistic, but there's certainly enough of that cold and lonely essence that has been infused into this game by its appearances. It looks pretty cool overall for the type of game and the atmosphere it is trying to present. You can zoom in quite a bit on the climber and the surroundings, so that's cool too.The minimalist music fits the scene and mood, while the sound effects work well also. Nothing too fancy, but it wouldn't surprise me for a climber to only hear his/her own footsteps clinking along the ice while alert and perhaps voices telling him/her to lie down to take a nap or jump off a chasm in an attempt at flight in a delirious state.Potentially playable for anyone who is willing to take on a single-player mental challenge, unless the roguelike nature is just a no-go, which is fine too. I find this game very intrinsically satisfying.The base price of $19.99 US with regional pricing is quite reasonable for this game. It has a lot of replay value.1. More varied/situation-dependent events.2. Fleshed out stories to engage the players.3. Legacy/cumulative caches/deposits from previous runs.4. Preset levels/Seeded runs by player choice.All in all,  is good fun and definitely worth your time and attention. Check it out now or wait until a price that's reasonable for you. Its roguelike nature will deter some players but I think it's quite a reasonable challenge for survival for anyone who is interested.Score: 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: There's not much gameplay to this. It's one of a myriad games where you pick options during a random event, and hope the dice are on your side. _childDocuments_.review: I spent hundreds of hours on other platform so I had to buy it here when it came on a discount! It always brings so much joy and eagerness to play, develop and try out different tactics and ways to play through. Such an uncomplicated but complex game, a true jewel in this hybrid genre. I just adore turn-based games, especially tactical ones so this one is right up my alley! It has decent animations and UI, gorgeous and unique graphics, effective sounds and beautiful music. Game mechanics are very solid and easy to learn, although you need to invest proper time to experience different stuff and learn what skills and boosts are best to use (and when -- so smart planning and understanding how game works is a must). Even then, no game or run is the same since it's procedurally generated (even maps that look familiar are always different in some way), POI are randomized each time as well as map modifiers. You are gonna spend hours and hours being bound behind your monitor and enjoying extraordinarily great Insurmountable. :)P.S. I also LOVED how game was before ver 2.0, followed it since the early alpha builds and it was soooo good. They completely revamped how game evolves, put in the story (writing is excellent) and re-balanced perks, skills and equipment... All in all, it's a must buy (probably one of the top 3 adventures ever made). :)

_childDocuments_.review: I recently purchased Insurmountable, drawn in by its innovative gameplay and the promise of a fresh gaming experience. Insurmountable brings the excitement and danger of mountain climbing to life, with realistic challenges and the need for careful planning and preparation.The game has its ups and downs, just like real-life mountaineering. It quickly teaches you not to be overconfident or reckless; one wrong step can lead to disaster. The mountain's conditions can worsen dramatically without warning, and adequate preparation is essential for survival. Insurmountable captures this aspect of mountaineering somehow.To progress in the game, I recommend taking small, well-planned, and consistent steps. Insurmountable masterfully recreates the perilous nature of real-life mountain climbing, and to my knowledge, no other game has achieved this in such a unique way.If you're looking for a one-of-a-kind gaming experience , Insurmountable is the game for you. It's a testament to the power of innovative game design and a must-try for anyone who appreciates immersive, realistic gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game. It had all the elements I love to make a game I love but a game's rng can only give you the double bird so many times before it's just not fun. Playing as the adventurer was fine. It was challenging but felt very balanced. That's where it stopped. As soon as I started playing with the journalist or scientists the terrain got very rough even when i didn't pick a route with very rough terrain. That's forgivable except the other characters aren't advertised as increased difficulty, just different play styles. The real problem is the events and Item drops. except for the first mountain on adventurer your success is dependent on your consumables. They give you items that are equipment but they're junk. You get 100 points into each stat and the best  and the best oxygen mask I've ever found gives you get this .75 oxygen an hour....you're losing stats on average between 5-7 points an hour and that's the best item they give you??? After almost 20 hours of play I did find a Fire charm which gives you +3 warmth per hours, that was pretty neat.Trait perks are also RNG and are heavily biased for energy reduction which is usually fine if you're getting good items...Events are extremely repetitive and after the 1st mountain on both scientist and journalist just kept giving me the bird. Caves only had biting bears, backpacks you sacrifice sanity to steal only give xp, found crates and shacks and shipping containers are always empty. Meditation events either cost more sanity over time then they rewards or get this...gave +0 sanity...YUP! The event designed to restore sanity started giving me 0 sanity rewards.....Despite all the elements being there to be a great game the rng is so bad that in the end I wasn't having fun. I might try this game again in a year and see if they fix it up. My last playthrough of mountain 3 didn't drop a single oxygen bottle. You have no chance of survival without those on mountain three and only getting .75 oxygen an hour from the 'high quality' mask. Keep the challenge but remember you occasionally have to give the players SOMETHING!

_childDocuments_.review: Only 3 hours of game time so far for me..This game is very easy to understand and navigate. You start out by picking one mountaineer with a different set of skills/abilities. You can only ever have one game save running at a time, meaning you cannot choose one climber - start a game, then later start another game and have two saves at the same time. The game will auto-load/continue from the most recent game you've played. I'm not 100% positive if this changes later? However, be careful if you start a new game randomly, you will overwrite your previous/current game.Each mountain is a continuation of your previous climb with your mountaineer. Meaning, all supplies/health/etc will be carried over. Once/if you die - its over! So be careful about using items too quickly... or not quickly enough. Haha.The game itself has a great understanding of mountaineering referring to "death zone", using crampons/snow boots/etc.. The gameplay is not in real-time. The turn-based style goes well with this new survival game concept.My first run, I didn't make it to the top, as I was making hasty decisions along the way trying to gather how much different things affected different stats. Made the summit, but not the descent.Second run - made it quite easily, then realized quite quickly in the second mountain that everything was carried over. It probably said this in the introduction, though I forgot a lot of what it said. Haha.This is a "wordy" game for the first 15 minutes or so, until you start to memorize the word patterns and no longer need to read all the messages.I definitely enjoyed this game and will be playing it again soon! I really appreciate how this survival game wasn't all about monsters/beasts/scavenging for food/weapons. Great job and I hope to see it grow more! Would really love to see updates for multiple game saves, and also maybe some statistics/leader boards.Thanks for the new survival game!
_childDocuments_.name: Insurmountable

_childDocuments_.review: It's different. A resource management board game about climbing a mountain. Does a good job capturing the atmosphere of a dangerous climb. Not much else. After your first playthrough you've seen everything, and gameplay becomes very repetitive. There's little content, good perk choice can completely destroy the resource management aspect as you go weeks without eating, breathing or sleeping. I clocked my first mountain range at 3.5 hours and don't want to play again. If I had used cheat engine to speed up animations I'd probably be done in 2.Still going to give it a thumbs up for standing out. Give it a try for a chill, short resource management game.
