_childDocuments_.review: This game is addictive and compelling and also frustrating and clunky. But I'm hooked and I have no doubt that future updates will address some of that frustrating clunkiness. They've said on the forum that UI tweaks are high on their list, so I'm looking forward to a smoother experience - especially around delivery routes, which are kind of a mystery at this point.The thing that pushes this game over the edge for me is the relationship system. Everyone has connections, family members, friends, and everything you do affects the way they feel about you. Want to eliminate a rival outfit? Have fun with their families.I think with some extra effort this mechanic could be amazing. I started a game with my outfit just a few blocks away from another outfit and - lo and behold, that outfit was run by my character's father. That just meant we had a good relationship in the game, but I would have liked to explore the possibilities of it more. I'm currently in a game where one of my crew members is related to a few members of an outfit that started snooping around my territory. Once I took them out, his relationship with me became much more conflicted - and I haven't seen any consequences from that, but it opens up interesting narratives. Or, what if you could order a hit on someone, and it's not clear it's from you? What if their relatives were devastated but not blaming you - what might that look like? Or, what if businesses were more dynamic? Ones with more traffic flourish and grow, others can change or evolve, ownership could change, buildings could burn.  Technically feasible? I dunno! But it'd be neat.The procedural map generator is awesome, though not without its quirks. Why does my Chicago have so few bridges, one of which leads to what's effectively an isolated cul-de-sac? Overall, it feels like this is a game from a small team that swung big. Lots of room for growth, and I hope enough people support the game that it has its chance to bloom.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a brilliant immersion into prohibition era gangster economy. It is a deep and rich game with a variety of gameplay options that allow the player to explore how they want to develop their industry and grasp and influence on the city.  It is well-balanced, challenging without being overwhelming - though it may take a few tries to get a good map to start on.  There is a solid in-game tutorial that gets you set up well for your first game and a wealth of guides written by the community to help optimize your experience.  The one downside is that the UIs currently require a lot of clicking which could be tuned a bit more to the things the player does frequently.  For instance, it takes something like 7 clicks just to sell your bootleg wine to a local merchant which is one of the core parts of the gameplay.  The good thing is you can set up trade routes to minimze this but in the early game you end up having a lot of manual clicking until you have the funds to be comfortable automating.  Great effort and responsive devs.  Love this game and what it brings to the genre of economic / city builder style sims!

If you are expecting a shoot-em-up gangster game, this isn't it. This game focuses on production and sale of alcohol during prohibition, and building relationships. Little gets done without knowing the right people, and you can leverage favors you've earned to help you along in the game. As clunky as the graphics can be, I love the style and the vibe. Having to bribe the police,  both large and small scale enemy operations, vehicles that break down, having to pay employees and having a supply of money along with the mission system to unlock more skills and knowledge are all things that I think are big pluses for the game.The devs have mentioned that the game will expand from what is right now primarily just a boot legging campaign and as the game develops I think City of Gangsters will easily become the best modern Prohibition era game out there, would certainly recommend as I would give it 9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely worth a purchase, the overall concept is strong and it's a more relaxed management-style game that rewards forward-planning and careful decision making. Towards the later game it feels very heavily weighted towards the automatic route management system.There are definitely some things that need improvement, and just in case Devs read the reviews I'll post here:- Show the pathing that the character will take before right-clicking. It's not always clear which route the character will take, sometimes it looks like there's a backstreet where there's not.- Have a way to 'remember' things such as who is hireable from where (or better yet, a list you can access of potential hire-ees as long as you've visited a place once)- A clearer vision of what each 'Upgrade' will provide - it's not clear that you might LOSE production in one area by 'upgrading' to another.- A way to cancel 'missions' that you accepted, at a loss of reputation or something.- A way to ensure a specific mission won't come up again (I keep getting asked to drop off 20 of X and 10 of Y, but I don't have and cannot make enough Y).- Add an option for routes to include 'Overall Actions' that would collect any fronts/bottles along the route.- Generally a more intuitive routing system without having to add a bunch of steps on the end and move them up (also number the steps visibly on the map).- A way to completely skip parts of a route depending on conditions.- Make legitimate produce items sellable. Make illegal products purchasable from rivals.- Option/mission to have a delivery company that will deliver from stores for an extra amount (will allow players to choose to focus on management of businesses or self-assigned delivery drivers).- Make dialogue options clearer about what they will do (local groups- If a location will/won't offer to be a front, once you ask remove the dialogue option and instead add a marker.- Make 'drop-off'/'pick-up' actions complete at the end of turns (currently they will arrive at a place with X inventory, but only drop it off at the start of their next turn when they have movement back).- Potential bug: I have bottles appearing in my main/first operation but no drop-offs routed for this place.With a few improvements this could be a super strong replayable game - potentially a good candidate for online multiplayer too.

_childDocuments_.review: It's important you note this is a prohibition-era resource management game at its core; the closest you'll get to the romanticised elements of 20's/30's gangster culture you might associate with Godfather et al, are the extortion of businesses, bribing of law enforcement, and the factional territorialism of various outfits. There are no politics, loansharking, gambling, prostitution, drugs etc, and those I mentioned that do make an appearance are ultimately only there to further your bootlegging operations and logistics in some way or another. So despite at first being excited that this could be the Gangsters: Organised Crime for 2021, I didn't let my disappointment that it didn't turn out so dampen my enjoyment of what is still a great game for what it is. I think it's unfair that people are giving bad reviews because they didn't research the game mechanics well enough and were basing their expectation on the title alone. The devs have been great to respond to honest criticism with patches and I'm positive that the game will continue to be polished into an ever greater state of playability.If you like logistics and micro-management, then you will enjoy it. If you're hoping for a 'gangster simulator', perhaps not.

It's not perfect, but unlike the old days, the developers can actually improve things on the fly which gives me great hope.  It's good right NOW, and I hope it keeps getting better. _childDocuments_.review: *Disclosure: I came upon this game during a semi-regular search for “Has anything like Gangsters: Original Crime come along yet?” But quickly realized through devblogs how this game would be different. I am not going to “not recommend” this game based on what it is not, but I very much will recommend it based on what it is.On two criteria I have decided to recommend this game to others.Firstly on its own merits as a tycoon game. I think that anyone who enjoys this genre of game will have a good time in City of Gangsters.While the criminal organization elements are not as pronounced as in something like Gangsters: Organized crime (the primary source of complaint for many), the theme as implemented provides for an enjoyable roleplay element in a tycoon game that I haven’t enjoyed before in the same way. I am already planning many playthroughs with various gangs themed around their background, what kinds of hoods to employ and how to interact with community, as well as which businesses to pursue.Secondly, I want to recommend this game based on where I see it going. The dev team is engaged and super active, with updates rolling out at a great pace actively resolving issues and adding features as the community discussion is taking place.In their own words they have a long to do list ranging from simple additions to larger mechanic development and along with modding potential I am very much looking forward to it all.

_childDocuments_.review: Great board game but I've got a few recommendations:-Corners that don't have businesses on them or are surrounded on 3-4 sides by your territory should join you either automatically or with a small payment, without a front nearby. Embrace the map painter aspect and allow us to fill in the gaps without paying more for extra fronts, which need around 4-5 businesses under them to turn a profit. I find dead spots of the city with only 1-3 useless businesses in a 3 block radius where the owners don't know anybody except for the people nearby, making it effectively impossible and unprofitable to control them. -Needs a better notification system. I've lost corners before when I didn't see the small red envelope underneath the store icon because it was mostly blocked by another store icon. I've also lost batches of product because I didn't realize I didn't have enough....-Storage space. I've lost quite a few batches of wine because bottle labels take up a huge amount of space, there is barely enough space for two batches worth of production for wine makers. If the ingredients are being used, how do they still take up space? If the product would fit after the ingredients are used the production should go through. How big are the grapes you buy at the supermarket? How large are your bottle labels? I'd rather product instead of ingredients take up larger amounts of space, that way it feels like I'm juggling contraband and not glassware.-Either the map needs to be smaller, you need to be able to take over multiple corners at once, or there needs to be more computers because I'm 150 turns in and only met one other non-hooligan player and they're pretty far away from being an issue. I'm the only one competing for Downtown Chicago and it feels strange. -Learning new skills sometimes costs too much cash or resources, and I have a few missions requesting large amounts of product I need for a skill I already have so I don't plan on finishing them but have no way to cancel them. At least let me collapse the menu. -All businesses should produce something, even if its just extra cash. I find myself hesitant to take control of new buildings until I find one that's likely to produce something, like a fruit store or furniture store. I hate getting a cafe or something similar where my front is useless. Owning the front should open you to new buying/selling opportunities, for ex tobacco shops should let you buy lumber, cafes should let you buy bottles and labels, hardware stores allow you to buy all building materials, fruit stands allow you to buy all fruits and juices etc.-Diversify the computers. If there is a hooligan interested in business they should own a business themselves. Make me compete with them economically too so they don't just feel like pawns to be taken out. Inducting another business into your empire with connections, cash, or intimidation would give it some more depth. -Map maker needs some work. Too many bridges to nowhere, roads that just end, rivers don't connect etc. Get some more of the skyscrapers right too, downtown Chicago had quite a few taller buildings back then.  Adding in some dock yards on all maps would make things interesting, especially if you could use them to store or move product easily. Adding in parks would fit as well. Maybe the map should always be somewhat similar but the businesses get randomized each game?-Seems theres a few achievements not triggering correctly, there are a few in there I should have gottenUpdate: The game was incomplete but they decided to move forward with DLC's. Starting position makes or breaks your game, generated maps are still a mess, and the game is still oddly restrictive, like not letting your main character be a manager.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice Game with a couple of fresh ideas. Pre-Ordered it after already putting quite some hours into the Demo during the demo-week and the full release didn't dissapoint.At the heart its a turn-based management game, revolving around characters. Your own main-character and hired gang-members can be moved around procedually generated cities taking several different actions.Core of the gangs activity is the production and distribution of illegal alcohol, to that end you have to build a network of contacts throughout the city, wich is where one of the really innovative ideas of the game lies. Each NPC character in the game has a network of people he/she knows and through that it is possible to learn about other people on the map and influence them.That one guy doesn't really trust you, so he doesn't let you know if he trades in booze or not? Look through his web of aquaintances, then influence his uncle with whom you already can trade and as soon as the uncle owes you a favor let him put in a good word with his nephew, so that you can trade booze with him too.Fair warnings:- While just bashing in a competitors skull or taking some firepower and go erradicate a rival gang are solutions, combat is turn based and rather simple, the core is, as said a management game, so if you are looking for some action-packed gangster-shooting, this may not be the game for you.- Part of the Challenge in the game is to work with what ressources and customers a generated map gives you where and make the best of it, so if you like total control in how to build a buisness empire you might not really like that aspect, if you like to sometimes work with problematic setups and puzzle out how to make the best of a given situation it can really be part of the fun.The game still has some rough edges, being freshly released, but the developers are really active in the games forum and seem intently listening to feedback from there. The games core is already a solid system and its actually innovative, so I didn't get the feeling of playing just a slightly different version of a game I already knew, like its so often nowadays.

_childDocuments_.review: A very solitaire-boardgame approach to bootlegging with a unique logistic twist. It is a trading and production focused game which means it's a logistic game. The unique thing here is instead of finding somewhere to buy low, then produce something or sell high, the existence of your vendors and customers is in question. The core loop becomes unwrapping the fog of war of the city looking for the new cornerstones of your bootlegging logistic network. These can be new vendors, new customers, or quests or opportunities to learn new skills that let you approach your current logistics from a new angle.Like I mention it feels very boardgame like. I think there's a couple mix ups being thrown around, some from the store page, some from the name, some from coverage or wishful thinking. The social game is very clockwork; it is not grand strategy or Crusader Kings. You turn in favor tokens to generate relationship, or you complete trades etc. There's no complex event systems and the quests recharacterize what someone is to you, but is largely self contained goody rewards.The law breaking you are doing is just bootlegging. There's some brawling and paying off the cops, but it's pretty clockwork again. Less scheming, more combing the city for business opportunity and fighting or paying off other board pieces getting in the way.The UI mostly works but has it's sore spots. It's an info dense game and you will need to ply through several views and reports to make sense of what you can do let alone what you should do.The random map populater seems a bit broke. You can end up in deserts of vendors and customers which can make an early game incredibly frustrating where exploration is so crucial yet expensive. I'm not worried largely because I seem to have a good seed and this is a surmountable problem with player feedback.There's simple route automation almost like Anno 1800. But it's inefficient and unsuited to some of the realities of the games restocking mechanics. You use it eventually because you have to, not because you want to.Overall it's a unique compelling approach to trade and production logistic games. With fixed prices but mysteries about where you can buy or sell things, I am kind of obsessed in a one more turn kind of way. It's almost a logistic puzzler. There's sore spots but I'm taking the sore spots just to get to the unique awesome parts here. I've never played a game where undoing the fog of war is this tense and exciting, let alone because of logistic reasons instead of just being surprised by a tower or Civ goodie hut.

_childDocuments_.review: 13 hours in now, and overall have to say it's a fun game. I will say, for what it features, which is mostly a simulator on transporting booze seems pricey for 30 bucks, or even at 35 bucks if you got the deluxe edition which I did, so do keep that in mind if you're budget strapped, it may be too pricey for what it features. As the others have said it certainly has a more Tycoon feel then I would say Empire of Sin or Omerta: City of Gangsters feel. The whole connection features is a great touch in general too, really makes you feel that it's all about contacts and who you know which is great. However, I will say the Micromanagement is essentially to the absurd, so do keep that in mind too when you play, especially as you expand and get bigger with your territories. There is potential automated deliveries you can set up, but for some reason the action point and movement point are halved when you set that up compared to just running everything manually, which honestly makes no sense to me. I think the Devs said they would look into that, but we'll see. So far I've tried Chicago and Cincinnati and both feel authentic in terms of the period and resources it provided during the time which is another great feature. I do feel they missed out on New York City and Atlantic City (especially those familiar with Boardwalk Empire HBO show back in the day), but I got a feeling if this games sells well, we'll see those as DLC in the future I bet. Combat though is pretty much non-existent so don't go expecting an "xcom" type level experience here, and in fact the dice-roll on combat seems a little weird and hard to understand too, so in my eyes that's probably the greatest negative of the game. Finally, the Music and of course this is more of a personal option here, but figured I would still share it cause, hey, it's my review!, lol... I have to say considering what the game showcases itself to be Tycoon game deep into the simulation aspect and the fact that the graphics are not going be it's strong suit or the reason you would play this game, they really dropped the ball on the music with this. The Music just feels off, and I guess it could feel like 20s music, but honestly it doesn't to me, and it's sounds it's literally just 2 or 3 tracks tops.... Coming also from recently playing Empire of Sin and Omerta: City of Gangsters, I know 20s music can be done really well (probably one of the better praises I can give of those 2 games). So my hope is they also revisit that one day too. Nevertheless, with all these minor complaints and perhaps big one with combat (granted again it's not that type of game) II have, I still have that just another turn feel as I continue to grow my booze empire :). Now does it feel a like a true mob/gangster game? I'm not sure, yea you got the Prohibition in the 20s and you got the Booze as well to sell, plus eventually you set up Speakeasys, but I still don't think it's quite feels like it's truly a gangster game sometimes just more of a booze/transporting simulator with a great connection system, maybe in time the "mafia" aspect can be approved as well. Who knows though, while I am a history buff, maybe it really was like this during the 1920s, heh. So in conclusion, I still recommend it, if you got the cash to splurge, sure get it now but if you don't wait for it on sale for like 15 or 20 bucks. Here's hoping there's a good future in this one :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just plain fun and I recommend it without hesitation. A few people are upset because it doesn't simulate every conceivable aspect of potential criminal enterprises, but no game could. Instead, it does an incredibly deep and detailed job of simulating the creation and operation of an illegal alcohol enterprise during prohibition in America. It's not easy! There's some humor, and a bit of tongue-in-cheek dialogue, but make no mistake. If you're looking for a challenge, one that encourages you to keep track of a spider-web of opportunities while keeping an eye out for the competition (and law enforcement) that's essential for success, then give it a try. _childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot.  It reminds of this game from the 90s called Chaos Overlords where you expand territory in a city and make money through illegal acts in the buildings you control. There is a kind of crafting where you create the booze out of ingredients you have to move around and hide.  There are the cops and the feds hunting for for you.  There is this kind of basic Crusader Kings style relationship system where you have to worm your way into the city and get people to join you in illegal acts.  There is also a team management angle where you control multiple gangsters.  I really recommend you try it.  Sounds like the devs intend to support it and make it even better.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok so I am someone who bought on release played for a bit and kinda felt at the time that it wasn't what I was hoping... (yes like many others hoping it was like Gangsters Organized Crime).  That is the first mistake you can make.  If you go into it hoping it's that game then you will probably give a negative review.  Yes there are SOME minor aspects of that game such as the setting, era.  I didn't hate the game but I wasn't totally feeling it.A few months later I picked it up and gave it a 2nd shot and I figured out what made it MUCH more enjoyable for me and have become pretty addicted to it.  Here's the first rule of City of Gangsters...Learn delivery routes.2nd rule of City of Gangsters...LEARN DELIVERY ROUTES!!!This has made the game much better for me.  The problem I had the first time was I was trying to manage my crew all by myself individually giving them orders and as my crew grew it became more and more stressful because I just felt overwhelmed and always felt like there was too much for me to do and manage.  But this 2nd go I gave the game is way better, once people on your crew are doing automated deliveries you can now have 1 or 2 guys you play around with on your own and things become less stressful.I now have a huge crew doing deliveries and pickups while I have 1 guy exploring the city messing with the other gangster outfits in their territories and 1 other guy who basically stays around my territory doing quests/missions.At it's core this is a micromanagement game, not an action oriented game (there is some minor combat but nothing elaborate).  The game at first can feel a bit overwhelming but if you give yourself some time to understand it, the game becomes really fun and addictive.

_childDocuments_.review: I know some hoped that this would be the spiritual successor to Gangsters: Organized Crime. However, any who saw previews of the game should have known that this was not quite the direction this game was trying to do. This is a business management game with a gangster motif. The business management aspect is pretty well done and it involves supply chains and ensuring your illegal businesses have the right ingredients to continue to turn out goods. This can get tedious but automation is an option for some aspects. It also has a very interesting and decently created relationship mechanic. Business owners will know some people within the city, and with favors, will help you gain favor of others they may know. Without a good relationship of a business owner, they may not sell to you at all, may have a difficulty asking for protection, or even not be able to get it as a front. I think this mechanic is pretty well fleshed out, though improvements can be made.As this is a business management/supply line sim, it is to be expected that the illegal aspects of gangsters will be slim. Though illegal businesses can be had such as speakeasies and gambling, you're not going to find others like loan sharks or prize fights. The vast majority is all about distilleries of various alcohols and beer. I do find it fun and interesting that you must "learn" skills to be able to make bathtub gin or other alcohols before you can begin to distill them.  Combat is also very limited. You have a variety of weapons, some you may need to discover, that you can use to fight other crews. There really isn't any strategy to it unfortunately as it's completely based on luck from a dice roll. Yes, you can have better skilled gangsters that can use weapons better (like brawler), so chances go up, but once you hit attack, it's all a matter of a dice roll. As far as I'm aware, only one gangster per car, so it takes some time and money before you can go and attack with some force. Taking out the boss of a crew will not destroy their crew completely, it will go to another member of that crew. So you must systematically kill everyone to finally end that crew for good.The graphics are pretty decent. There's actually a somewhat alluring aspect that I like about it. It is not trying to be heavily detailed with high graphics like Empire of Sin, but its art style is still very intentional and consistent. I wasn't sure if I was going to like it, but as time went on playing, I began to enjoy it.I haven't played too deep into the game yet, but it definitely has a lot of potential. It will probably never improve its combat system, but that's ok. This wasn't its intention. It would be good if they possibly add more illegal businesses with added resources, and some more quality of life features. I think this game has a bright future and it's absolutely an underdog.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game!plenty of hours worth of making a trading empire and beating other gangs however;Takes patience to really get into, as it's not very intuitive so it's not for everyone.Still plenty of hours before I've explored everything. List of downsides:* progression however isn't very clear, driving around in hopes of finding a resource can be annoying, even more so when it's not easily revealed. * The expansion limit of not being able to make new fronts while expanding is also a mild pain. * sadly lacks other some aspects of being gangster like underground gambling or sexworker industry, weapons industry and so on.* buildings are too random with some doing nothing while others gives insane bonus productions. no market for legal goods or ways to cover illegal once is a bummer too. * combat lacks the depth that the game otherwise maintains.* police is too random and hash, with little to no control. (can't even chose to fight back and make escapes) paying them off has to be done before they move which is another pain.

_childDocuments_.review: So this game takes some getting use to , you have to learn all the mechanics of the different alcohols , how relations works , how to automate deliveries , manage your crews and the other factions , avoid the police etc... There is A LOT of depth to this game and it is pretty rewarding after you understood the Basics of it.Also something that is worth noting , the Combat in this game is ENTIRELY optional , so if you wanna buy this game thinking you will have the same combat system as Omerta - Empire of sin or the original ganster games just don't. This game is about managing on a REALLY LARGE SCALE a booze and racket empire. The Devs are actively working on new contents but for now the main focus of the game is on the management aspect of it , not the combat, so leave the devs a bit of time to work on some new stuff before buying it before you think  you will be able to have an all out war with rival outfits or being able to extort / kidnap / murder you way up ! ( But I hope that we will be able to do it soon ;) ) Of course at the time I'm writing this there's still some bugs here and there but the game itself is pretty well polished and the turn based is pretty enjoyable. I had some reserve at the beginning about it but it gives plenty of time to co-ordinate what you wanna do during your turn and having a big crew with certain skills is important ( not only for combat but for logistic , managing you backroom operations etc... )So if you like gangster theme games and management ones this game is for you ! if you're looking for a combat focus game well wait a bit more for it to get improved !

_childDocuments_.review:
The year is 1920, the start of Prohibition in the USA. With congressional action, a huge segment of the national economy becomes illegal overnight: bars and saloons are ordered to close, distilleries and breweries go quiet, distributors shut down. But a new era is dawning: a gilded age for smugglers, black markets, illegal manufacture, and organized crime.

This is where you come in. You're a new arrival in the city at the dawn of Prohibition, with ambitions of striking it big. Behind many of the city's facades, people are building makeshift distilleries, secret loading docks, nighttime speakeasies. Work your way into this network, and the world will be yours.

But think beyond making a quick buck or two. You gotta be thinking ahead. You gotta be thinking bigger. Much bigger.

name: Wraith: The Oblivion - Afterlife
detailed_description: Welcome to the Afterlife. Play as Ed Miller, a photographer who dies during a mysterious seance and has become a Wraith, a restless undead spirit with unfinished business in the land of the living. Desperate to learn the reason for your death, you’ll use supernatural abilities to explore the Barclay Mansion, the site of your untimely demise and reveal its dark secrets. Eventually, you’ll discover why even the dead are terrified of Barclay Mansion... KEY FEATURES Become a Wraith: Your death is a mystery that you must solve. As a Wraith, you’ll use supernatural abilities to move through walls, track the movement of other spirits, and manipulate objects at a distance to uncover the Barclay Mansion’s terrifying history and the truth of how you met your end. Explore the Barclay Mansion: The Barclay Mansion is an opulent residence filled with Hollywood decadence, occult research, and terrifying monsters. Avoid vengeful spirits while using Relic Items and Wraith abilities to hunt for clues. Beware of Spectres: Hostile Spectres, spirits of wrath and vengeance each with their own background and connection to the bigger mystery, roam the mansion’s halls. With few ways to defend yourself, you must avoid and outwit these lost souls who want nothing more than to send you to Oblivion, the end of all things. Experience the World of Darkness in VR: Wraith: The Oblivion - Afterlife is a first-person VR horror game set in the World of Darkness, the shared universe containing Vampire: The Masquerade, Werewolf: The Apocalypse, and more.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough review for me - I had been looking forward to this game for a very long time and I just found the entire experience to be disappointing. I love VR and horror experiences, but this game is a bore. The gameplay loop is just a series of fetch quests, the mansion is not really scary - more creepy. I couldn't get interested in the story, and navigating the mansion started feeling like a chore. You will run into some boss like figures in the game that you have to stealth past, but really you are just waiting for the dumb AI to walk itself into a corner so you can buy enough time to sneak by. There is not a lot of game skill required. On top of that, the character models and levels are bit - Quest-like. For $30, I would have appreciated some better looking graphics for a PCVR game in 2021.It's not often clear where I am supposed to go next - and while I don't want my hand held for the entire experience, I couldn't stand running around the mansion in circles for a half an hour at a time, trying to find an item. The "indicator" on your hand that leads you to the next objective often lead me into a dead end that had no objective to complete. I made it to the 80% completion mark with about half of the achievements unlocked - and I don't care enough to see the ending. I just don't think this game is worth $30. When I compare that price tag against other top VR games, I believe this game falls short of the mark. If you are really itching for a horror/creepy experience, I would buy this for $10, maybe $15. This game scores a 2/5 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointing, although far from incompetent. Purchased out of desperation for any sort of new mid-budget VR game, Wraith delivered reasonable first impressions. There’s a generous number of locomotion/comfort settings and seeing that a few gameplay elements were lifted from  games gave the impression that Wraith was going to be very contemporary (that is, well-informed on others’ successes). It also runs remarkably well on my increasingly obsolete PC.The unnerving sound design is a commendable source of fear. In tandem with the anxiety from any sort of VR horror, the audio was strong enough to strain my scary-game-comfort-boundaries before the game offered any actual threats. These moments are more akin to  where drinking in the atmosphere without having to brace for impact on scares is an intoxicating sensation. Unfortunately, Wraith’s acclaimed  is routinely interrupted by the startling exposition ghosts. I suppose soft jumpscares might help keep you on your toes, but considering that the story is nothing special, they’re more inconvenient than immersive.Furthermore, nothing breaks the grip of fear like losing several minutes of progress to a climactic scare from janky AI. Monsters may be unbelievably stressful at first, but sparse checkpoints and the creatures’ inorganic movements channel the fight-or-flight fear into fervorous frustration. Sound might be a huge part of Wraith, but it’s hard to know whether thrown bottles had a distracting effect or not. Even if you can stun your pursuers, running isn’t really the protagonist’s forte. At least the game is usually clear about when monsters will appear and lets you tour your soon-to-be escape route before the encounter.As Wraith progresses, the abundance of door/key puzzles and the unremarkable story drains most of the motivation to push past the stress. Most of the later playtime is sadly resigned to painfully slow strolls through the same hallways with occasional moments of being drastically uncomfortable. Wraith is worth it if you're desperately in need of a mid-range VR game, find horror appealing, can tolerate some repetition, and have run out of five-star custom maps in Alyx. Such a low Steam rating isn’t exactly appropriate, although it's certainly easier to criticize here on PC. Its original home on the Quest gave it more appeal. At the very least,  could do with a more appropriate level of sequel-confidence in its titles.

_childDocuments_.review: Bottom Line:  Get this game on sale....NOT WORTH 30.00!  I took my time and did a lot of exploring..thus played for a little over 9 hours.Graphics are not bad; story is average; but game play and controls are bad.  Devs over did it with the stealth required through multiple locations in the game...YOU CANNOT proceed until you have managed to get past the threat (i.e., Spectre, broken woman, etc).  There is no combat and you have to rely on trial and error at the rate of dying at least 6-12 times before you are successful in neutralizing the threat...or should I say before you find a way to get past the threat.  It really is not scary albeit there are some good jump scares...but overall not scary.   Also, this game should have been titled...Wandering Aimlessly in Oblivion.  A lot of walking and not much direction or clues where to go....the task at hand is clearly given in your notes but as far as where you need to go or do, that is a WAG (wild ass guess).  Not a  bad game but not one of the better VR games...I rate it 7/10.  Recommended only if on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I spent over two hours playing this game without much enjoyment, trying to understand why it feels so uninteresting compared to other VR horror games. Despite the evident premium effort and quality put into every aspect, there's a lack of excitement.The game showcases flawless VR mechanics, such as well-designed hands with inverse kinematics (IK) arms, precise finger positions around grabbed objects, and various VR-related options in the settings. However, you may find yourself wanting more to truly enjoy the game, such as the ability to adjust walking speed or disable its somewhat peculiar running behavior. In reality, there's no actual running; the movement is more like baby-crawling for walking, with a brief burst of speed when you push the left stick. While the slow movement might be a deliberate choice for encounters with opponents or stealth mechanics rather than comfort concerns, it often makes the game feel tedious, especially in a desaturated grayish indoor atmosphere.The game makes a notable effort to deliver impressive graphics with consistent lighting and antialiased visuals. The setting features modern, stylish architecture, a refreshing departure from the clichéd choices of many horror games set in old, dusty, or Victorian mansions. The inclusion of quality voiceovers, characters, dialogs, and story is evident. However, despite these efforts, the first two hours of gameplay failed to provide an engaging experience for me.I wouldn't recommend it, especially if you have high expectations considering its price range.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying that I play in VR since 2014 and that I did not get the game for full price (priced 20 at the moment). I will also try to address the "negative" aspects listed in the negative reviews. TLDR at the end.That said, I don't understand the current state of "mixed" reviews. We are full of horrible unimmersive broken VR experiences...yet Wraith is really polished under (almost) all aspects. I tried the game also on Quest 2 / 3 and the PC version is SO much better (I didn't try the upgraded Quest 3 version, not even sure if it's planned). It runs super smooth and it is super sharp in every occasion, even further objects, thanks to its apparently very good temporal antialiasing.Hand animations are top notch and the mansion design is really nice and enjoyable with its different areas and a cool modern looking architecture. Story around it is also pretty cool though not easy to follow (complicated narration). The lore that can optionally be found around the mansion helps with the story.The AI could be a bit weird at times, sure, but really this is not a fighting game and you are not really supposed to run from enemies...every enemy encounter is more like a puzzle, knowing what kind of "behaviour" you have to have in order to "escape" the sequence. At least that is how I consider it and I am having a lot of fun. I am new to VR horror games and this is the right amount of horror for the moment (or "creepiness").Running speed: it's subtle to notice, but the max speed you get only when you are looking in front of you (compared to the analog stick direction). I am pretty sure this is on purpose, because otherwise you could run "sideways" or "backwards" away from an enemy....but no, you have to look forward (where you are going) to be actually fast enough. If you go forward and look sideways, you will be slower. Same for sprinting (which indeed is not very fast, but that's fine).TLDR: cannot really agree with the negative reviews, at least not if you are not extremely picky. Great game for the price, especially if 50% sale. Enjoyable graphics with a slightly cartoonish look (which helps if you are not a horror fan) and super sharp and smooth.
_childDocuments_.name: Wraith: The Oblivion - Afterlife

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant because of the mixed reception, but this game really is the whole package for fellow horror fansThe setting is interesting, the story is fast moving and keeps you engaged and moving throughout the mansion. Both the sound design and voice talent is top notch, the game is dripping with atmosphere and really knows when to pack a punch and when to let you breathe. There are many unique monster encounters, both scripted and unscripted, and i never felt any of them overstayed their welcome.I really couldn't recommend this game enough if you're into VR horror, because lets be honest, it's slim pickings out here when it comes to quality horror experiences.

There is just about enough good stuff here to make up for the bad.

_childDocuments_.review: Played on Valve Index, RTX 3080.In short:Good game, BUT... you need the right approach and either like stealth parts or have the patience for such.Long version:I took an attempt last year and dropped the game after like an hour of being bored. I was awaiting a horror game which will frighten me the whole time. Today I know better and would say after playing Wraith: This is not a "classic" horror game, but a spooky game.I wanted to give it another chance this year and did a bit of reading and people told it is building up slowly, but it can be annoying and frustrating. And they were right. After a bit more than an hour the first stealth section began which got me annoyed so much. After a few deaths I came around it by "cheating" the game and thought that's it now, no more stealth sections... Wrong! There are at least 2-3 more stealth sections coming.I very admired the story, the atmosphere and the whole experience. It was interesting and got me intrigued to find out what happened. But the stealth sections, which I am in general am no fan of and really bad in, were really annoying. Especially at the end I was so frustrated that I nearly rage quit.It is a bit sad as this is a good game, but I feel it has driven quite a few players. I have a lot of people with this game in library on my steam list and none of them has finished this - so I can tell it is not just me. Even if you scroll through the reviews here most negative ones have a playtime of around 1 hour, so I can absolutely see why. The beginning is building up too slow and then it gets hard all the sudden.I wish the devs would have included something to prevent that, may it be different difficulties or a skip option after a few deaths to let all people disregarding of their capabilities see the rest of the game. I know quite a few people who quit after the first stealth section in that game and that is a shame as it is all in all worth playing. After all, apart from my very big "stealth passages" critique, I will give it a thumbs up though as the rest of the game was enjoyable (or rather scary).

_childDocuments_.review: Stealth horror games requiring you to hide until you can get past are nothing new to me. This game though really elevates this mechanic to a frustrating degree. There are no checkpoints or a save anywhere option, only manual save points spaced too far apart, first mistake. The enemies can run very quickly to kill you instantly, your movement is quite slow even when you "sprint", second mistake. Also, third mistake, there's barely any hiding places. Only a few closets that allow you to hide and if you're not near one you can try to maybe duck to block line of sight, because you're certainly not going to be able to run anywhere.After spending a good chunk of time exploring, collecting and even finding necessary story/quest items I was "killed" and was sent back to the last manual save. There were no save points in the area I was in nor did I receive a checkpoint because they don't exist. I won't keep playing a game that doesn't respect my time.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely recommend, but I had a lot of issues with this one..I played about an hour into the game if you'd like to skip through Let's start with the bad stuff..My main issues are that Wraith doesn't support index very well. It doesn't support finger tracking and I had to squeeze the life out of my controllers just to hold basic objects. Wraith also has a sprint on the left joystick, which would be fine, except the index controllers can break from excessive pressing of the left joystick (I actually had to replace my left controller because of this), so I would avoid sprinting when I could.Aside from those issues, I expect this game works great on Vive on Quest controllers, in which case I can highly recommend! Wraith starts out extremely slow, but it does that on purpose to build up tension, slowly hinting at demonic creatures and then you start to see them as you progress, it's truly horrifying and definitely feels like a high quality game (for VR that is).If Wraith worked better with the index controllers, I'd probably push on and play a lot further than I did, but after an hour it was just way too annoying.. but these issues only apply to anyone with a valve index, everyone else should be good.My only legit complaint about the game itself is the lack of checkpoints. You have these save stations, but if you die, you get warped all the way back to that spot. I understand that it being a horror game, losing your progress adds a sense of dread where you don't want to die, right? But it's 2021 guys. If there isn't a checkpoint at the start of a room where I can die, I lose interest, especially if dying means I have to walk another 5 minutes to the same location, only to have the creature spot me and repeat the process.Again, this issue is more of a personal thing, I know some people won't be as bothered with getting sent back to their last save point, but if they added checkpoints or an auto save feature, I think this game would be a must-have for VR horror fans.Despite my review sounding so negative, I still recommend it, and if they can add checkpoints and fix the index controller support, I'll most likely do a full playthrough. Aside from my issues with the game, it's definitely a great VR horror game with good pacing, an interesting plot that slowly builds, and good scares.

_childDocuments_.review: Started off with a good first impression, pretty damn good looking setting and a decent atmosphere but man was my experience so up and down. It's honestly got a few solid spooky sections and the sound design was bloody good but on the other hand it can get really annoying at times with how the AI can act up. Turning around quickly, seemingly at random. Heading straight to where you are and hanging around there so you can't do much of anything for a while. Sometimes not getting distracted by the things you throw.The general gameplay loop of running around and fetching items was fine for a while but when I hit the point where I got to a door and it was somehow magically sealed by 3 items, leaving me to immediately turn back to go on another item hunt, I was quite frustrated.I have very mixed feelings about this game. It does some things well but it gets quite tedious and annoyed me to the point I nearly quit it a few times. That being said, while I feel like the game could have been executed much better, I'm still going to leaving a positive review as I feel like it's still worth playing and it pulled off some good scares, which is what I've been seeking lately. So props to it for that.

_childDocuments_.review: Ngl. Pretty boring.I'll admit though I have been spoiled as I've played some of the best horror games, and some of the best VR games, so it's hard not to compare but there was some unforgivable sins.You're agonisingly slow, the difference between walk and sprint is quite literally a gentle slow stride vs a hurried shuffle. Enemies are vastly superior in speed.Environments are... Okay. Everything is very blocky in style and it's all modern but I can't help but think that the constant use of simple cubed sculptures and simplistic squared off polygonal statues is due to the limitation of a 3D artist rather than a theme? I don't know, it just felt very... Bland.Atmosphere sound-wise was pretty alright, but I never really felt tense.It took far too long to encounter my first spook and it wasn't scary at all, just a dude hanging there talking spooky lines.I think the main reason for things being so slow is to cater to people with motion sickness problems, which I can respect, as they also go as far as providing extensive customisation in the options menu for motion sickness - but if this is the reasoning for making everything so slow it's just crippled the gameplay and flow for something that people get used to after a few hours in VR as it is.Again, I want to remind the reader, I am very spoiled when it comes to horror. You may enjoy this quite a lot, but for anyone who's an absolute horror fanatic like myself I simply can't recommend it beyond sale prices.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty cool and scary, but it is not fun in the slightest. It is a frustrating, unfair slog that does everything it can to make you lose, that's why only about 5% of players have the achievement for reaching the halfway point of the game. It will be very atmospheric and scary until you reach any of the hostile ghosts, at which point it becomes a purely luck based exercise of trying to sneak through an area only for the ghost to "randomly" wander directly to you and kill you instantly, at which point you are sent back to the last save point to do it all again until RNGsus decides to have mercy on you. The ghosts themselves have very spooky designs, but all fear of them will quickly be replaced with rage and frustration. To make matters worse it seems that FTG have seen fit to make the game even harder than it already was either with a post release patch or just for PCVR players as a lot of the bottles that could be grabbed and thrown to distract the ghosts so you could sneak by have since been made non-interactive set dressing, meaning you are completely screwed. Buy Duck Season instead, it's just as scary while also being fun to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually can't remember the last time I have been so bored playing a VR game. I mean bored out of my mind to the point where I just flat out lost interest and quit playing entirely. The dilapidated huge house of a thousand locked doors is not scary in my opinion. Teleportation is extremely wonky, leading you into unintended directions and is insanely slow. This is the sort of teleportation where you hold down a button and stand there watching a marker move along the floor at a snail's pace and then release to teleport. The extremely slow teleportation also makes it incredibly difficult to get away from an enemy's presence. Save checkpoints in this game are also extremely far away. Opening doors with Index controllers is also very awkward and buggy. And it is most often unclear where you need to go or what you need to do next. Gameplay is slowly moving throughout the house taking pictures to trigger past events/memories where you watch characters engage in dialogue, which I found very boring. From watching videos on youtube, this also seems to be a very long game for VR, lasting over 6 hours. There is no way I was going to torture myself for that long. I just found this whole experience to be so dull that I gave up in sheer boredom and moved on to other games.
_childDocuments_.name: Wraith: The Oblivion - Afterlife

_childDocuments_.review: Even though this game has some missteps, I enjoyed it. The exploration is good and intriguing, the story is nice, and the concept of playing as a ghost is good as well. Also the freaky encounters with other ghosts is scary and cool. I think that the "hide and seek" mechanism of the encounters could be done better, it became a bit tedious over time, but yet it was scary and enjoyable.As for the technical aspect, I did not have any issues playing on the Oculus Quest 2, with Air Link, not Virtual Desktop.

name: Observer: System Redux
detailed_description: CHECK OUT SILENT HILL 2! OBSERVER: SYSTEM REDUX - DELUXE EDITION OBSERVER: SYSTEM REDUX - DELUXE EDITION The Deluxe Edition includes: - Observer: System Redux (game) - Original Soundtrack (digital) - immerse yourself in the dark and oppressive atmosphere of the game thanks to the music composed by Arkadiusz Reikowski - The Art of Observer: System Redux (digital) - an official album that will lead you through the dystopian world of year 2084. About the Game WELCOME TO THE FUTURE The year is 2084. The future has turned out much darker than anyone could imagine. First, there was the Nanophage. A digital plague that killed thousands upon thousands of those who chose to augment their minds and bodies. Then came the War, leaving both the West and the East decimated and shattered. With no one left to seize power, corporations took over and forged their own crooked empires. You are a tool of corporate oppression. Feared and despised, you hack into the darkest corners of your suspects’ minds. You creep into their dreams, expose their fears, and extract whatever your investigation may require. You are an Observer. BECOME A NEURAL DETECTIVE You play as Daniel Lazarski, an elite investigator of the future portrayed by late cyberpunk icon Rutger Hauer. As an Observer, you hack into the minds of suspects to extract clues and evidence. Anything they felt, thought, or remembered can and will be used to solve your case. EAT THEIR DREAMS Using a device known as the Dream Eater, hack into the minds of the dead and dying to relive their final moments, to explore their fears and obsessions. Delve into these twisted neural mazes and search for clues that will help you find the elusive killer. But beware: the deeper you go, the greater the risk of losing your own sanity. TAKE IN THE ATMOSPHERE OF 2084 Enter a world ravaged by war and cyber-plague, where life is cheap and hope is scarce. Where most people will do anything to escape their grim existence. Virtual realities, mind-altering drugs, neural implants - pick your poison and drift away into a blissful oblivion. But remember, no matter how deep you go, you can never hide from an Observer. Veteran Observers can dive deeper into this dystopian reality thanks to three brand-new side cases to solve. “Errant Signal”, “Her Fearful Symmetry” and “It Runs in the Family” add another layer of depth to the game’s story while exploring thought-provoking themes of a future that soon might become our present. On top of that, System Redux offers expanded gameplay, which includes new game mechanics, new secrets to find, redesigned stealth, additional neural interrogations, and quality-of-life improvements made with the help of the Observer community. Newcomers get the chance to experience one of the most thrilling cyberpunk stories in all its next-gen glory: boasting 4K resolution, upgraded textures, new animations, models and effects, and transformed with jaw-dropping Ray-Tracing and HDR lighting.

_childDocuments_.review: This is effectively two games. Half the time, it is a deep cyberpunk noir story, where you as a detective use your implants to collect clues and solve a murder inside a small but extremely detailed and complex location. The other half, it is a very bad horror game. When you will stop playing detective and start playing itch.io quality horror is a complete surprise, and sadly the former takes up less and less of the game as the story progresses. I deeply wished I lived in the timeline where the devs picked a lane and stayed in it instead of trying to force a particularly bad version of their usual horror game formula into an otherwise fantastic game concept. The parts that aren't trying to be scary are so great that I'd suggest playing this anyways, but be sure to get it on sale, and expect a lot of your time to be wasted with redundant, poorly stylized and painful-to-look-at imagery that conveys information you already were told through the far better investigative side of the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Observer is a frustrating game.  On the one hand, Observer has some downright incredible writing.  The authorship, art style, vision, and atmosphere are all 10 / 10.  Additionally, the game is absolutely traumatizing, which, if you're here reading this review, is probably what you're looking for.  Observer is that special kind of horror that isn't too directly, viscerally scary, but imparts much more of a slow, cerebral dread.  The game has its gore and it has its jump-scares, but mostly it's just downright  to the point where I was literally dreading my next session, but  to go on to unravel the mystery.  And if you play to the end, this game seriously delivers.  Man, what a finale.  On the other hand, Observer is unfortunately buggy as hell.  And not just getting stuck on corners and weird floating objects.  The game has certain situations that are so severely broken that you can wind up literally stuck in a room with no way out.  More than a few times, I had to google my situation, thinking I was missing some puzzle element, only to learn that no, I needed to re-load the game from my last save and simply avoid this room.  After this happened to me twice, I really thought about ditching the game.  This problem is exacerbated by the fact that a few of the puzzles in Observer are quite frankly very trivial.  When I say "trivial," I don't mean "easy."  I mean, in order to solve certain puzzles, you have to look around the room for one tiny little completely nondescript button in a corner to click.  Often I would simply find myself frantically clicking around wall-spaces, looking for the one dang lever or button that would solve the puzzle.This is too bad, because 1. there are a few really brilliant puzzle moments in the game and 2. Like said, you might be stuck in a stupid bug, and you're never really sure.  What's even more disappointing is that this is the "redux" version of the game.  This was bloober's opportunity to  these bugs and polish up what is otherwise a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ masterpiece of a video game.  Overall, in the end, if you're a science fiction lover, a fan of cyberpunk, or a horror aficionado, you will find these (pretty inexcusable) bugs to be forgivable, if  for the fantastic writing, vision and profound dread that Observer offers.  Had the writing not been so magnificent, I would have never recommended this game.  Also, a lot of people complain about the runtime of this game (for me, about 11 hours).  To me, especially as I get older, this is a LOVELY runtime for a game.  But that's just me.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: Originally,  was released in 2017. The upgraded version is something that came 3 years later. In this review I will be focusing on all aspects of the game. If you are interested in the updates only head over to the paragraph with the appropriate title. The original version I played via  - I also have it here on Steam, however, when completing  I did 2 playthroughs already and I didn't want to do two more again so I decided to just put everything I have to say about the games here.I consider  an interesting game with exciting lore but, first and foremost, this is a walking sim. You play from the first person but you have no weapons at your disposal. And as the development team was  (the folks behind ) expect a couple of jump-scares as well as dreamlike sequences that will test your sensory perception and might disturb you a bit during gameplay.Rutger Hauer, the actor who delighted us in many films, is the main protagonist here. I have fond memories of him as Roy Batty in  or Nick Parker in  or even Harvey Stone as the monster-hunting, cynical detective in . I always appreciate when there is a movie star appearing in a video game. Here he plays a detective who works for the police in Krakow in a dystopian future. While sitting in his car he receives a call from his estranged son which is cut short. He decides to investigate by tracing the signal of the caller.Now, in this future (late 21st century), pretty much everybody is augmented. We know there was a plague called  that killed a lot of people. And Daniel (our hero) is not just any detective but a special one: a so-called observer who's equipped with a special vision capable of scanning his surroundings. He goes to an apartment building where the call originated from only to find a dead body and then a lockdown happens. We are trapped and can only visit the apartments in each floor (the basement is also home to some people) and the courtyard with a tattoo parlor.We cannot - unfortunately - enter every apartment. We will be able to speak with many of the tenants at home, though, as the story unfolds. This means a lot of dialogues with many interesting people. We can pick the order of the sentences we want to say but the outcome won't change as the game is very linear. Things start to get interesting as we enter apartments and scan each room to look for evidence. Our special (augmented) vision either highlights electronic devices or blood (as biological evidence). It's fun looking for clues by scanning everything, opening each drawer, using computers to unlock something or just read e-mails for more information. Now, once a dead body is found we can hack the brains of the individual in question.And this is where our psychedelic experience begins. Such trips are mandatory to progress the story and this is the only part where we can die. It is also required that we pay attention as the hallucinations not only show important information on the deceased person but also on Daniel's past. Lots of material that will all come together by the end. I think this is the most exciting part of the game - something that the  team was always good at and these sections can be familiar to those having already played . With this (and additional investigation due to the side missions) a walkthrough can easily be around 10 hours which is pretty great for a walking sim. Sadly, by the time Redux was released Rutger had already passed away. The game gives us a couple of more quests to do in the apartment building. The one with the dolls is especially great! Another thing they did at  was - as they say - enhancing the graphics. Now, it should be noted that while additional features can now be turned on (ray tracing is one example) the game looks (slightly) different. It's one of those cases where while we can argue as to what is considered next gen or last gen (or even current gen) you just can't avoid the feeling that from an aesthetic point of view this version feels different.I love lighting and in some sections they did a great job (a good example is the small lamp next to a dead body), however, in other sections the lighting differs so much so that it gives an altered vibe to the game. I do not wish to join in on the argument of Original Vs Redux but one thing is for sure: the new edition is slightly longer, it can test your hardware and the game still has a fantastic atmosphere. Perhaps with the new look Observer is a bit closer to Blade Runner and some other works it heavily drew inspiration from. I wish Rutger had been around to see it, too.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly atmospheric dystopian cyberpunk horror mystery 'walking simulator'/adventure game.Unfortunately, i have encountered a progress-halting bug. As the game only has auto-save, i cannot reload an earlier save to try and avoid whatever caused it, as i did for the previous two major bugs i encountered.Also unfortunately, the game has not been supported basically since release. This is essentially an update to the original game (which is no longer listed on Steam). The owners of the original game had to basically petition just to be given a discount on this updated version. Unfortunately, unlike the games made by another famous games publisher who also make buggy games and have a similar unethical practice of selling 'Definitive Editions' as new games, this game has no accessible console commands or mod support, and so i cannot fix my game. It is basically linear, so i won't replay 8 hours just to get back to a spot where i may simply get stuck again. It would be nice if the publisher would either pay the developers to fix the game, or give me a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest. I can't recommend Observer: System Redux. No matter what the devs say I don't think this is the definitive way to play Observer. Starting with the graphics. The game looks better then the last one in some places however In my opinion large chunks of the game look like new stuff jammed into the old. In fact "New stuff jammed into the old" should probably be this games tagline since they do it at every turn. It's weird they'll add little jumpscares and moments that weren't there in the original story that are forced in ways that are unnatural for an example I will list a moment some of you might find to be a spoiler.MAYBE SPOILERIn the Original Observer you find yourself in a basement turning on the power. When you flip the switch the see the shadow of an unseen monster at the end of a hallway, A security door closes and It is implied the monster moves to the door and begins banging on it. In System Redux you see the shadow and then the monster sprints into view in a strange animation that doesn't really look like it was meant for that scene. SPOILER ENDAnd while talking about stuff that does not belong in places Let's talk about the new side missions. These are the only reason I got the game a second time because the devs said they were finishing unreleased side quests that utilised the late Rutger Hauers unused voicelines. >Insert so that was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ lie meme<The voicelines used in these side quests are honestly uncomfortable. A ton of the side quests narrative will be told through the text in the case logs while the main character lets out the odd gasp or "♥♥♥♥" or even in one case a line that just seems completely meant for another scene entirely. It's like when you finish an open world video game and the protagonist just stops talking because there aren't anymore missions for Him to talk in and they become more of a shell of the campaign version of the character just because the only talking they do is the occasional grunt (Looking at you Batman: Arkham Knight)The voicelines just feel weird because the main character is quite chatty in the normal narrative and then He goes dead silent for these new ones only saying "Bingo" when He hits a light switch or Finds a clue. And something that makes these missions feel all the more awkward to play is the fact that they feel 90% finished and are just lacking the polish. Often during the missions I found myself lacking direction so I would end up just stumbling into where they wanted me to go after a good while of wandering. I wanted to like this game. Observer is one of my favorite horror games even with all Its problems and to see It twisted and mashed into something It's not while advertising Itself as a bag of new tricks sucks. Bottom line. If you really want to play Observer and can't get the original then give this game a look but for me as massive fan of the original I can't give this a good review for what is seemingly the same game with new graphics and unfinished extra content.

_childDocuments_.review: Great HD remake of the 2017's observer game.At maximum settings, the image looks really outstanding.The colors and visual effects are really decorative for your monitor and create a beautiful image of a cyberpunk world.No idea what life will be like in 2084, but in 'Observer: System Redux' technology and biology live on an equal level,the futuristic cyberpunk devices and gadgets that you will notice in the game are also very cleverly designed.For example, your main character will have some unique and useful abilities thanks to these ideas.In the game you take on the role of 'Daniel Lazarski', a police detective who uses this cyberpunk tech to hack the brains of others even when they are dead, which has been called an 'Observer'.Observers should try to find out what happened during the last moments of a murder victim by hacking their memory as if you could directly feel, see, hear someone else's perceptions through their senses, ...You will also be able to confirm objects and bio-traces via certain scanners that you also have in you.A good tip is to often rescan the places you have scanned, often you will find a detail that you missed the first time.You will need all of these abilities to further help you resolve the issues in the story.The game also has many hacking jobs to offer, these often require a lot of thinking and there is the option to disable the hacking minigames if you wish.You will also sometimes have to hack keypads, the number code will always be somewhere if you look around carefully, but you can sometimes also decipher all keypad's codes by hacking, sometimes even 1, sometimes none, but it is a great help.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: Let’s get this out of the way: if you’re sensitive to flashing lights in any way, this game will kill you. No joke, it will melt your eyeballs, it will scramble your brain, and you WILL DIE. If you suffer from epilepsy, you’ll be lucky to make it 3 minutes before you start seizing. You’ve been warned.That being said, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with this game. But it’s important to note that this is a walking simulator through and through. The gameplay is mainly just doing chores, with the addition of 1 or 2 tiny stealth sections. The main source entertainment is soaking in the gorgeous graphics and drowning yourself in the lore. For such a short game, Observer packs enough lore to fill a 20-book sci fi series. If you enjoy that kind of thing, then this game is magnificent.As I said, the graphics are just spectacular. I don’t think I’ve ever taken so many in-game Steam screen shots. They don’t mess around: you’ll travel into people’s brains, explore their memories, and it gets visually insane.To sum up: amazing graphics, overwhelming lore, very little gameplay, with a chance of death if you’re light sensitive. I enjoyed it.

_childDocuments_.review: The year is 2084 and Daniel Lazarski is an  -a special investigator working in the police department of the futuristic and dystopic Krakow, right in the beating, biomechanical heart of the Fifth Polish Republic. On a dark, rainy, drenched in green neon light morning, he receives a distress call from his estranged son, Adam. A call that sends Daniel to an apartment building in the slums of the city, in search of Adam and down the rabbit hole: a headless corpse and a suspicious lockdown of the complex later, finds Daniel Lazarski frantically searching for his son while fighting for his sanity and perhaps, his life.     In this cyber/biopunk psychological thriller, humanity has found a way to transcend the physical limitations of the flesh by means of cybernetic augmentation such as mechanical prosthetics and neural implants, among others. Obeying the law of cause and effect, a divine punishement for hubris or, perhaps, simply in a cruel twist of fate, a plague dubbed  afflicts those who have been cybernetically enhanced. The infamous 'AA Glitch' has turned the nanobots responsible for easing the (unholy to some) union of flesh and machine against their hosts, killing thousands upon thousands.  Daniel laments in the prologue -rightfully so.      As if the horror of a digital Black Death wasn't enough, mankind is yet again thrown in a world war conflict, nicknamed the Great Decimation. As West kills the East and vice versa, dead bodies pile up. The losses on either side: astronomical. Winner(s): only one -CHIRON. A megacorporation that seized power as the dust settled upon the ruins and is effectively governing a reforged Poland as the Fifth Polish Republic. In the words of a deeply disheartened detective, it's . The new authoritarian administration implimented a strict societal class system of 3 tiers, where Class A and B are the privileged citizens (as much as privilege goes in a totalitarian regime) and the rest 91.6% of the population is thrown in Class C, the abysmal citizenship status where human rights and freedom are labeled as dangerous, unpatriotic dissident propaganda.     Such an arbitrary goverment needs an equally oppressive unit of enforcement, capable of using advanced (and unethical) methods in order to keep a tight grip on the populace. Enter the Observer: a police detective, primarily tasked with contacting neural interrogations with the usage of the DR-3AT implant, colloquially referred to as the . The procedure involves the Observer peering into the mind of the persons who are being interrogated, with the aim of extracting information from their memories.      As soon as I finished Observer for a second time, I rewatched the original Blade Runner (1982). I was in a hurry to do so, not only to spot the ideas in Ridley Scott's masterpiece that inspired Bloober Team to create the game, but mainly to confirm the impression I was left with, by film and game alike: that of the feverish, maddening visualization of the two dystopian worlds. Both delightfully portraying their noir cyberpunk setting -and also very unsettlingly.     Elements of horror are present, predominantly in the later part of the game. I have read complaints in reviews about the disruptive effect that horror has on the narrative and while I also prefer the 'detective' side of the story over the 'hide and run for your life' one, I disagree with the notion that the shifting of focus to the horror genre in various stages of the game, is inherently a bad thing. Without going into spoiler territory, the aformentioned elements are critical to the story as a whole, especially the biological-horror themed ones and generally the developers did a good job clueing the player in as to why these shifts are happening.     While I haven't played the original Observer, the graphics in this remastered version are amazing. The detail given to the various enviroments that Daniel visits throughout the game is astounding, fleshing out a world of decay. Exploring is highly rewarding since every visual detail, no matter how minute, is memorable. On a sidenote, I played the game with film grain on, but I understand why someone else would be annoyed by it. Personally, I think it added to the atmosphere but you might consider turning it off for a clearer visual experience.     Music and sound design in game are both commendable, pretty much what one would expect from a heavily themed, bleak cyberpunk game. Inspired by similar works in this genre (mainly Blade Runner and Ghost in the Shell [1995] OSTs), the synthesizer-heavy ambient tracks create the ideal atmosphere for the grizzled detective to explore the derelict apartment halls while the choral tracks, albeit few, drive the nail home by creating feelings such as awe and bewilderment, at the right place and time.     My final thoughts on the game are about the Observer's actual job: targeting the poor and desolate third-class (literally) citizens, aiming to weed out potential insurgents. Behind the facade of police officers, the Observers are Chiron's henchmen -whether they like it or not. Dreaded and loathed by the general populace, their semi-prestigious status as law enforcers must mean little to them, especially to those who are conscious of what they actually contribute to society and of the threat, that they are always on the verge of becoming.     Observers are described as "ticking bombs". The constant use of the Dream Eater takes its toll and succumbing to the mental strain from violating minds and meddling with foreign memories is virtually unavoidable, with its outcome being unpredictable: since the mental collapse of an Observer led to a mass shooting incident, carrying firearms is prohibited for the unit of special interrogators. By literally delving into one's mind it can be argued that an Observer is taking an intrusive peek into the abyss of the human psyche and it does come at a cost -the abyss will eventually stare back at the one who observes it.  This is my attempt to entice you into giving this amazing game a try. Cheers!

_childDocuments_.review: This remake of Observer is beautiful and offers detailed visuals and dark atmosphere.I'd call it the unofficial Blade Runner game.Made by Polish developers, Observer is a walking simulator in a cyberpunk setting with horror elements.They actually got the legendary late actor Rutger Hauer to play the protagonist! Absolute mad lads!Hacking people's minds and having a psychedelic trip is the selling point of the game.The techno weirdness is cool. The horror made you confuse reality from dreams. Flaws:The game touches some philosophical topics but the devs did not invest into fleshing them out.On that topic, you talk to most people only through closed doors and animations are minimal.Beside the janitor Janus, you won't see anyone actually move, they are mostly expertly covered by scripted scenes but sooner or later you start to notice.This was supposed to be a REMAKE/REMASTER, can't believe they haven't fixed the bugs!The game soft-locked me multiple times in my single playthrough:1) A cable that you have to drag dropped beneath a grate and was completely unreachable/unclickable. Reloading did not help, had to load an older save before the cable cord was dropped. Progress lost.2) On two different occasions was stuck in a locked room. Looked up video and there was no issue there. Simply reloading helped in the 1st case, in the 2nd had to load older save but luckily not much progress was lost.Lack of manual save could have saved so much trouble, wtf devs!?Also some achievements and collectibles are locked if you progress too far. Only way to get is start over, ew.Overall a unique experience.Lose your humanity and get lost in a maze of cables and screens.
