_childDocuments_.review: I do hope Steam has a neutral button or something.I really want to love this game, and I do love its world building, its lore, and of course, Rutger Hauer's performance as Detective Lazarski. The first few hours into the game were quite good and immersive, but the gameplay soon became dreadful and boring, plus the bugs that deeply affected the experience. Still, I do think it will be okay for players who love this genre and have more patience than I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure if I can find the words to describe how amazing and incredible this game is.Apart from being technically incredible and flawless, from an artistic point this game is kind of a masterpiece of the Cyberpunk Genre. ALL the art design is absolutely incredible and unique.It's tackling deep, complex and serious issues, in a fully adult tone.So you're investigating a series of murders in an apartment building, looking for clues and most of all you'll be linking to the victims brain chips, in a sort of VR experience of the victims' persona, memories, traumas and most of all their last moments before getting killed.But what spices things up is that your own traumas might sift in those VR memories, but maybe also in the real world...Anyway I have now immense admiration for Bloober Team because this game clearly comes from the guts and minds of those developers. It's in my opinion just as major as the Deus Ex games.And I really really hope that one day Bloober could come back to the world of Observer and make an even more ambitious game. Because with their talent and the amazingly credible world they've created here, if they could make an immersive sim game I would just throw my money at the screen !

_childDocuments_.review: A strong game with remnants of SOMA, Control, I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream, and elements of trans-humanism akin to Nier Automata. My only issue with the game is that there is no option to run it with separate GPU other than integrated, so if you're running it on a laptop with dual GPU (Integrated HP and a Nvidia), it'll always default to integrated even if you set Nvidia control panel to always run with it. Story and lore wise, it's a satisfying game, and a relatively short play-through. I did all side quests and beat it in 9.2 hours. Overall a great game, and I would definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoyed games like SOMA.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing as the original one. I like the visual improvement and all. Also the game looks good with or without Ray Tracing. _childDocuments_.review: So, 3 years after the original game's release we got its remaster for the new console generation with improved graphics, new features and some new content. Nobody asked for that, but still many awaited it. And because the original was deleted from Steam, so you can buy System Redux version only, this review will be divided into 2 parts: in the first one I will speak about the game itself, and in the second one particularly about the changes brought with System Redux. >observer_ is one of the few games that after all that time kept true to the original pure cyberpunk: high-tech, low-life, dystopia, eternal neon night, and lots of trans-humanism philosophy. And I don't say that it's the only true cyberpunk, it's just very unusual to see such a piece nowadays. But what exactly creates its "pristine" nature? Well, a lot!First of all, the design and atmosphere. All these retro 80s PCs in futuristic dystopia coexisting with the various advanced technologies of the future, constant neon rainy night, low life rundown districts with corporations' skyscrapers looming over them. Soundtrack, which was seemingly composed by taking the best from both Blade Runner and Ghost In The Shell. And the voice over with the main hero voiced by legendary Rutger Hauer. All this blends in together creating just the new iteration of classical cyberpunk straight from the 80s. And though it's not all that perfect, graphics are weird in some places, there is not that many tracks, and in some places, actors could play better, but, overall, you don’t really notice it, when you dive into the game. Now, what about the plot? Well, all of the above is genuinely the same for it too. Though I cannot really call this story a truest masterpiece, because some twists are kinda predictable, it still very outstanding in comparison to the simple narrative most of the modern games tend to have today. It has a decent number of good twists, several layers, raises a lot of complicated questions, and really makes you to think all of this over. But as for the gameplay, well… it's not that great in terms of it. I mean, you don't expect some large action and deep mechanics from a philosophical cyberpunk game, but even the existing mechanics could be improved for better. Like diving into the people's minds, which is one of the features of the game, could be implemented as non-linear sections, where you would actually travel through person's memories trying to find the exact clue you need. Or we could actually interact with some objects and not just pick, rotate and scan them. However, despite of the lost potential is the gameplay bad? Well, not really, it's not something great but it's also not irritating. It's something like a usual walking simulator where you just witness the unraveling protagonist's story, but with a few choices and additional options.And, last but not least, the horror aspect of the game. I'm actually not a big fan of this genre, but I know that many are, and if you are on to some unusual horror, well, I'm afraid you will be disappointed. Though the game is far from peaceful and vivid, it's not really that scary: there are some tense moments along the way with a bunch of "screamers" (sudden change of scene or actions, which make you jump but not scare), but that's not enough for a full-fledged horror. The game is just creepy at some moments, and more about the dark atmosphere, rather than a horror and terror. So, all in all, Observer is a great game, which through all those years brings back good old pure 80s cyberpunk. If you are a fan of classical artworks of this genre like Blade Runner or Neuromancer, you will definitely like it. However, if you are looking for something gameplay-diverse piece or true horror experience, I would recommend checking something else.And now about the "definitive" edition of the game. Well, the most obvious change is improved graphics and in terms of that the game looks great. New textures and lighting definitely look better and more realistic than in the old game, however, they alter the visual style of the original game a bit, which is not that good, and I personally prefer the previous gamma. The second addition of the remaster is 3 new side-quests, which were one of the main reasons to buy and play the remaster for many players. And I was curious about them too, because, as you may now, Rutger Hauer passed away in 2019, long before the remaster release, and I was wondering how they will perform the voice over. Will they hire someone with a similar voice and then post-process the records to resemble Rutger Hauer? Or will they take the already recorded lines and chop and merge them into new sentences? Or will they simply use unused voice lines for cut quests and build new ones around them? And, well, they did neither of these! For the whole game the character comments on one or another thing but in those 3 he just goes silent, with only few simple phrases spoken, which are copied from other parts of the game. As for quests themselves, well, they are not really outstanding and needed: cut them out and nothing will really change. One is fine but too short and obvious, another one is simply unfinished, and the last one, though being interested is totally ruined by complete silence from the character. Ok, remaster didn’t bring that many good changes, but who cares, it gives, not takes, right? Well, I would be glad if this was true. The remaster has a ton of bugs, some of which weren't fixed even after half a year since the release. Light can glitch, quests can soft-lock, collectables can vanish and, in some cases, you might even break the main story line and have to restart. I understand, that making a good remaster takes a lot, but in half a year they could definitely fix all this up, considering that the original was nearly flawless in terms of bugs! The only really good set of changes here is trackable collectables, which also transfer between saves, and manual load of crucial checkpoints. Though, still they are not perfect: collectable cards are always randomized, you can't instantly tell which one you missed; instead of just manual load they would better just make a chapter selection menu or simple manual saves. So, all in all, do I recommend the game? Yes. Do I recommend the remaster? Not, really. Though, as I already said, you don't really have a choice, because original was deleted from Steam (which is also a bad move, I think situation with Warcraft 3 Reforged showed why). But anyway, if you didn't play the original and look for some classic cyberpunk – buy it without hesitation and godspeed with not encountering any critical bugs. If you played the original and hesitating about buying a remaster I would recommend not to, unless you really-really need new graphics and quests (but at least wait until the major bugs are fixed, if they ever gonna be fixed, of course). Instead, I would rather encourage you to replay the original one more time and maybe get all the achievements there if you haven't already. The game itself deserves a second replay, because, already knowing the plot, you really start to rethink and analyze all those tiny bits of information, which you skipped during the first playthrough.  P.S. According to many reviews the remaster is at full price even for the owners of the original, which is really weird and definitely not worth it. So, if you already have the original and there is no at least 50% off the remaster, it's another good reason not to touch it.

_childDocuments_.review: Observer puts you in the place of a police investigator in a not-so-distant future where the poor are put into decrepit housing districts and often seclude themselves in Virtual Reality as a means of escape from their bleak existence. Your primary gameplay is investigating and solving various crimes, there is no shooting or fast placed action gameplay here. Observer is a deliberate, slow-paced detective story with a Cyberpunk bend to branch the narrative into something unique. I don't find myself often playing games with minimal "gameplay" however Observer, with it's unique environment, unique characters and fantastic storytelling was compelling enough to have me hooked until I finished the game. You feel compelled to solve every mystery you come across. With the System Redux version you get three additional cases to solve, adding some very enjoyable content on top of the original game which was already quite enjoyable by itself. New cases, new neural interrogations and some new secrets justify the new release IMO, other reviewers often fail to mention the new content added and only seem to highlight bugs.If I had to give negatives to the game it would be that some of the "horror" aspects, mostly in the dream sequences could be a little stereotypical and played out. I'm happy to say the game is more creepy atmosphere than jumpscare central however I felt like when there WERE jumpscares or the screen "shook" around uncontrollably it did not add to the experience but detracted from it. Observer is a master of a horrific environment and thankfully the experience is  that. The game has bugs, some will crash your game and some will halt progress however the save system is generous and you can usually rollback 0-10 minutes of progress and continue going. During my playthrough I had no gamebreaking bugs just a few crashes that took minimal time to recoup my progress. At the end of the day I would absolutely recommend this title to anyone interested in a Cyberpunk detective-style game, it's a wonderful final performance from Rutger Hauer that I believe only serves to add to his legacy.

The other half is a really bad horror walking simulator, that just drags on and on. _childDocuments_.review: Surely it is a (very) good game but this Redux doesn't add a lot. It looks a little better. But I don't have a RTX gpu, so I can't take advantage of RTX here. It adds three new "quests". But that's it.One thing is actually worse: the performance. I mean most of the time it's fine, usually like 90fps on highest settings. But especially in one of the new quests I had really low framerate, it was barely playable. Also on some other points the framerate drops.If you haven't played the original, sure go for the Redux. If you have, there is not a lot of new stuff here. I got this game for 5 bucks because I pre-ordered it while owning the original and I guess that is fair.

_childDocuments_.review: Someone told me this game was the underrated indie cyberpunk game of the year that got sidelined by, you guessed it, Cyberpunk 2077.So I got into it, expecting a philosophical game about a cyberpunk dystopia, similar to Blade Runner. Instead I got a psychological thriller that takes place in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ neighborhood of the future.Instead of a fun cyberpunk experience, this game gave me a headache, motion sickness, epilepsy, fear of the future, fear of tech, fear of cyberwerewolves and probably a reason to have nightmares today, all while staying true to the roots of the cyberpunk genre. In case you haven't noticed, yes, I'm talking about the good parts.The art direction in this game is incredible and more creative than I could ever expect. It's definitely the best I've ever seen in a horror game, and might be one of the best in general.You can experience the story of an Observer who winds up in a ghetto apartment complex where every single room is either filled with a different kind of psycho and try to solve a case of an inhumane serial killer. It's the slowest game I have ever played, yet the lack of distinctive chapters, parts, objectives or any loading screens made it hard to quit the game at any point. Without realizing it, I spent 5 hours in the game in one sitting. Which is good, but then again, it also did give me a serious headache. Which brings us to the last point, that is something about this game that truly did not appeal to me. While being the most creative dream sequences you can ever experience (they even include puzzles of different kinds when you least expect it) the excruciating nature, the sheer length, and the overall psychodelic effect of them makes it hard to get through on all points. I even thought of quitting the game entirely at 3 different points of those sequences. Considering I spent 5 hours of my night on this game while simultaneously thinking of ragequitting on several occasions, it feels like that's an amazing contrast. Thankfully the building was filled with different type of mysteries that made me want to stay and explore them further until I got to the bottom of some stuff. Seriously, side quests were the saver of this game for me. Bottom line: I know they provide lots of context for the story but I wish there was an option to shorten the Observing sequences that didn't include the puzzles or the dialogues. Other than that, it's an amazing game. Give it a try if you like cyberpunk dystopias and horror-mystery games. It's not everyday you see a game that's ballsy enough to explore all the horrors a cyber future can hold in small-scale environment.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: I should not be recommending this game, but its just too good not to – HOWEVER:You're going to be walking around in the same 3-story building for 5-8 hours, and you're going to be backtracking for most of that time. Additionally, the developers either decided against or don't have the experience to create a natural flow to the challenges you face, most of the time. This often puts you in a situation where you can put all the puzzle pieces together and know where to place them – but now have to spend time searching for those pieces. Which, when frequent, quickly becomes aggravating.Adding in plenty of cheap jumpscares, then it's suddenly becoming increasingly difficult to recommend Observer to most people.However, everything else is of a high caliber: Especially the writing. Everything from minor dialogue to the overarching plot is fantastic.The aesthetics work wonders – and there’s clearly been a lot of care and work put into creating a unique environment in an otherwise oversaturated market. There never was a voice I thought sounded “off” or had a heavy accent that made me think they were of some nationality: All characters felt genuine and authentic – and that’s something most triple A titles fail to do.EDIT: Steam' recorded hours doens't reflect my actual time playing the game
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: As a lover of the original version of the game (and of Cyberpunk in general) I am glad to say that this truly is the definitive version of the game. The extra game-play does flesh it out a bit more, and the general visual upgrades/tweaks really brings the original vision of this dark future to life. One point to remember, you may depending on our actions receive objectives from cases that you will not have access to for completion until later in the game. It's not broken, you just haven't reached that part yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: This game should have been free or discounted permanently for all owners of the original Observer. I am leaving this review to raise awareness about Bloober Team's greedy and anti-consumer practices. "A tool of corporate oppression." Yeah, they really meant that.I gave the original Observer a 4/10 and could not recommend it in my review as I felt that it was just not scary or interesting, especially when compared with Layers of Fear (that was not interesting either; just a jumpscare fest), or better yet, measured up to SOMA, from which Observer draws a surprising amount of inspiration. Observer lacked depth and felt very shallow/superficial, in my opinion. I nevertheless enjoyed the cyberpunk setting and found Janus, Rudy, and the protagonist to be likeable characters. I was still interested in checking out Observer: System Redux, but owing to the greedy business practices of Bloober Team, I really don’t feel like supporting this studio anymore. In fact, this has dissuaded me from buying The Medium.Essentially, Observer: System Redux is like an AAA game that, instead of having a free High Resolution DLC and a few DLCs, gets released again as a standalone experience for the price of a brand-new game with near-complete disregard for its loyal fanbase. Even AAA studios would not resort to such egregious practices. Besides, this ain't no Skyrim.Admittedly, there was a short time window during which a discount for owners of the original game prevailed. I did benefit from that discount, but I realize that I am in the minority. Most people were not even aware of said time window and discount. At the very least, the discount should’ve prevailed indefinitely for all owners of the original Observer. A timed discount reflects poorly on the studio and is quite frankly a laughable excuse from a loyalty standpoint. This ultimately proves to be disrespectful to the community. If anything (and in all fairness), Observer: System Redux should have been released for free for anyone who owns the original game.As an indie studio, they need to harness all the goodwill they possibly can, so it's even more surprising they're resorting to bureaucratic, anti-consumer tactics to operate. The studio is working on a solution, apparently.But, this is not unreasonable in the slightest. Take CD PROJEKT RED. They’re working on a next-gen version of The Witcher 3 with all DLC content that will be released for free for all owners of the game across all platforms. Think CD PROJEKT RED is too big for a fair comparison? Fine, they got their hands full with the Cyberpunk 2077 situation right now anyway. But still... They give it to the people for free.Take SUPERHOT Team then. They gave out SUPERHOT: MIND CONTROL DELETE for free for all owners of SUPERHOT across all platforms. This is a very small studio and their new game was in development for at least three years. But still... They give it to the people for free.There are countless other gaming studios that are leading by example and doing what’s right for the people and the community by creating value that will ensure goodwill. These studios value and respect their fans and loyal supporters. They did not forget where they came from. Why? Because charging full price for the same game, albeit with "new" content is not right. Because a timed discount for owners that went largely unnoticed is unfair to those who did not know about it.Give it to the people for free. Or, at the very least, make the discount applicable for all owners of the original game.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels a little odd that Observer has already received the "redux" treatment since it just release abit more than 3 years ago but I was a fan of the original and was eager to see what changes/upgrades would be made. This is more a review of the entire game vs just of this new fancy new version if i'm honest, I do appreciate the changes in System Redux but I truly feel this didn't need to be a whole paid separate steam title and should've been just a patch/DLC for the existing game. The visual upgrades are hit and miss, while I was glad to see Ray Tracing added since I recently scored a 3080 but honestly only really noticed the graphics overhaul in certain aspects/sections of the game and I expected much more. It's great to see a little more content added to the game but it's nothing crazy, still pretty rad. The redesigned segments seemed to workout and the game's pacing and stealthy areas more fluid so I see the improvements but they arn't worth 33.99 CAD in my opinion, kinda steep. So the "redux" I give just an okay could be better score but the game itself if you havn't played it yet is in my opinion is Bloober Team's best so far and I really hope The Medium turns out great but we shall see. Just the fact that they got Rutger Hauer as the main character in Observer is so amazing RIP you legend. Really enjoy the overall setting and atmosphere to this game it's really unsettling if you get disturbed easily I'd stay away from this one. Interesting story/narrative and subject matter nothing we havn't seen in science fiction many times before but it's intriguing to me personally. Def want to crank up the headphones on this one lots of tension and hair raising sounds and music. Gameplay wise it's not great but atleast we get some puzzles and detective tools much more than many other games in this genre. Had a bug in one section which I think is one of the new ones in the System Redux that tank'd the fps completely but restarting the game seem to fix it thankfully. Some frame pacing issues and other graphical problems that seem to plague all of Bloober Teams releases, hate to see it. Was expecting more polish from a "redux" didn't fix some of the bugs with the original game seems like this is kinda them milking it for some cash. But overall it's a immersive game and I feel the devs are certainly capable of giving us a real horror masterpiece they just havnt gotten there yet but are improving with each title.  So if you like Blade Runner or anything dark sci fi/horror I highly recommend this game. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you are up for a dystopian cyberpunk adventure delving deep into the darkest corners of human psyche, Observer: System Redux is here to fulfill your dreams. Perfected with unbelievably artistic visuals and creative environmental details, this game will offer you an experience like no other. The characters’ life stories are engrossing, some of them containing extremely dark and disgusting topics that could as well be reality in the near future.The gameplay is nice enough to keep you invested, varying from inspecting the gorgeous game world by using Daniel’s special abilities to interrogating tenants, finding collectibles and hacking into people’s minds. There are some stealth sections here and there involving a creepy enemy, but they’re no nightmare fuel. Still, I would say Observer: System Redux is the scariest Bloober Team title so far - the way it creates a constant sense of uneasiness is truly worth mentioning. The clunky controls irked me to some extent, because the protagonist’s slow reactions sometimes resulted in frustrating deaths, but they didn’t hurt the overall experience.In a nutshell, Observer: System Redux is a great and entertaining horror game with some minor flaws in it. It’s that type of game where you must stop and marvel at the genius execution of the cyberpunk-themed work of art. _childDocuments_.review: Observer Systemn Redux (2020) is a refurbished version of Observer (2017) both developed by a polish development company named Bloober . This walking horror simulator is based during a cyberpunk era, 2084, when a deadly disease known as ‘Nanophage’ has already become rampant in the past and manifested itself among the slum C district of Krakow Poland. Due to a nuclear holocaust from both east and west, a mega corporation known as Chiron was able to usurp control by segregating the nation from the rest of the world (the great wall) and forming the 5th Polish Republic, further divided into three classes. A-district upper class, B-District working class and C District – slums.To help maintain order, a police unit working for the Krakow Police Department (KPD) known as ‘Observers’ were established. These officers through the use of devices on their arms called ‘Dream Eaters’ are able to connect themselves to other people’s brain implants and with their permission witness the events preceding a crime. Observers also have the ability to switch to augmented vision allowing cloud base scans of either electronic equipment or biological matter.Due to the unsettling nature of the work when an observer taps into the conscious mind of an individual, they often also tap into the subconscious memories of that person too, presenting a confusing cesspool of frantic thoughts, fears and recollections. This can be disorientating and dangerous for the sanity of the observer and is often controlled by a supplied drug from Chiron known as ‘Synchrozine’ which of course is to synch the observer back to reality.Nanophage is a digital disease which transmits the ‘AA Glitch’ into nanobots causing their coding to go off by at least 1 percent causing them to reject biological tissue. As puncture wounds appear and internal organs start to degrade, the disease turns biological, causing flu like symptoms where the disease becomes again highly contagious in both fomite and airborne transmissions. In order to prevent outbreaks of this dreadful disease, tenement buildings were constructed in the C district. These buildings internally scan their tenants for any anomalies and if one is detected they can go into full lock down preventing movement within building and electronic signals from getting out since the ‘Nanophage ‘is digitally transferable too. The KPD and ‘The Cleaners’ responsible for investigation and clean-up will become automatically notified when a building goes into lockdown.You take control of an Observer Daniel Lazarski (Rutger Hauer-Blade Runner) who has received an incoming distress call from his estranged son Adam. When Daniel traces the call, he is lead to a C district building and happens to witness a crime scene of a beheaded corpse where his son was calling from. Not being able to establish identification of the headless corpse we continue to follow the blood trail of a serial killer known as ‘The Splicer’ who is terminating all colleagues working along with Adam on a secret experiment which Chiron was not aware of at the time and immediately fired Adam and confiscated all his research when they were. What our son was involved in, where our son actually is and why is the Splicer now targeting us is what pushes a player forward looking for answers. The original (2017) version had a hopeless save system which infuriated players trying to unlock all achievements and collecting all easter eggs particularly the nanophage cards since missing one often meant restarting the game completely from beginning. Likewise, the voxel runner achievement and the no death achievement equally vexed many players. While the (2020) version has a much-improved save system with chapter select options amazingly it doesn’t do any better sparing players from the tedious frustration of the glitching card mechanics. I had several card glitched out of existence with no possibility of future attainment wherever I loaded in chapter recall (Pieta card an example), forcing yet again a complete walkthrough by me through the entire game. This I would have thought to have been solved by Bloober by now. While the no death achievement is much easier this time, the voxel runner achievement is still as infuriating and completely unreasonable to players like me, who may not be as quick in being responsive. Life is short as it is, who has time spending hours on these fruitless frivolities? Other than enhanced visuals and sound effects, the 2020 version has 3 additional stories containing what happened at the exact moment the building went into lock down. These follow Stanley Tkacyzk tenant from 208 and the tragic toll of what the lockdown did on a hypochondriac. The sad conclusion of tenant from 207 an architect passionate about the buildings internal network and the bloody conclusion of tenant in 108 who went against protocol and turned on a sexbot proven to be faulty. All 3 stories reveal that the nemesis revealed at the end of the game, may more than likely had a hand in their deaths too, revealing how narcissist and blood thirsty this villain may be. Don’t be fooled by the Stockholm Syndrome question at the end of the game.The expert story telling is where the game really shines for me and there are still many possible fan theories and questions begging for follow-up. I’ll list a few of my own. Big Spoilers Below…In final, there was many adult thought-provoking concepts to this game, that in truth with human advancements the way it is, we may be on the threshold of finding out soon for ourselves anyway. Looking down the double barrel of quantum computers and artificial intelligence we may be forced to surmise these ethical issues more sooner than later.Sample Below...If you enjoyed reading this review feel free to subscribe to my curator page. Thanks...

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've ever played. I have a background in Cyber Security and Ethical Hacking so the subject matter is right up my alley. I have never, EVER seen a team create such a vivid and realistic dystopian future as Bloober Team has with this game. _childDocuments_.review: It hasn’t been that long since I’ve decided to play Observer (or as it was stylized >observer_) and I wasn’t considering revisiting the game that soon. It was undoubtedly the best game from Bloober Team, despite still feeling like a visually cool project made by a team of visual designers with little knowledge on how to make games fun to play. And it still was way too copy/paste with its influences, but at least it had a lot of interesting takes on familiar ideas. But, System Redux promised new and improved gameplay apart from updated visuals with ray tracing, so I decided to give it a check.And my general feelings on the game remain unchanged. It’s good at the start, when it explores the dark dystopian cyberpunk world, ugly and paranoid, where people have no privacy or escape apart from drugs. The new edition adds several new side cases which explore this in new ways. Though, to be fair, only one of those feels like a fun case while the other two are either poor in gameplay or half-baked in their themes. And the updated visuals improve the way the game looks and feels as well, with the ray tracing, predictably, making some scenes looks absolutely fantastically.But the old problems remain unchanged. Few sections seem to have been somewhat tweaked, but I didn’t feel that the change was actually meaningful. Some of the old bugs are still present and the new sections have their own. The visuals can still be too much and nauseating, and sound design still full of jumpscare approach, which often feels at odds with the rest of the game. Some sections remain poorly explained. And the main story is as poor by the end as it used to be, deflating the really interesting side-stories that the game provides up until then.It’s a game that could be fun to check out, and this version is undoubtedly the superior one to do so. But it’s still not something I would outright recommend playing.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the first few hours of this game.  It puts its best foot forward with beautiful, detailed visuals, a cool (and VERY grim) cyberpunk world, and an intriguing detective story.  But the more time I spent with it the more its many irritating qualities started to show through and dominate the experience:- The investigative gameplay soon reveals itself to be little more than pixel hunting with a muddy filter on the screen.  There are a few puzzles but the most challenging ones are challenging for the wrong reasons, usually that it's not clear what you're trying to accomplish or what parts of the environment are interactive.- The "mindhack" sequences, which comprise close to half the game, seem cool at first until you realize they're mostly just overlong linear sequences full of freaky imagery with a jump scare thrown in every 30 seconds.  The game has a very small number of audio and visual tricks that it throws at you over and over again until they induce boredom more than terror.  The only real gameplay in these sequences are a handful of awful stealth/maze sequences.- Objects have a physics-based interactivity, which is cool until you realize this means you're spending a lot of time click-dragging on basic doors and drawers and cabinets, most of which contain nothing interesting.  This feature also seemed a little janky, sometimes puzzle-related objects wouldn't move as expected.- The story is just OK.  It's fine.  I found the conclusion satisfying enough, but the pacing isn't great.  A lot of time is spent on elements that feel inconsequential by the end, and it would have been nice to see a little more of the larger world that is implied.

_childDocuments_.review: Anyone that has been into gaming for the past few years clearly knows Observer. As a fantastic dystopian thrilling adventure, the game left us all impressed by its story and aesthetics. There was however, a lot which was left behind, and in that regard Observer: System Redux fulfills every aspect, including in the technical department.But let’s not get ourselves in the optimization just yet, because first I want to assure everyone that no story-related detail was altered or manipulated. System Redux remasters what was already present. This is obviously good, as the story itself was already top-tier, revealing a world where augmented electronics embed in the human body created an easier but also tougher verdict for citizens.  We play as Dan Lazarski, an observer, part of a police task force with an amazing ability: The permit to hack and invade suspects' minds, and relive their memories. The year is 2084, but it seems no one has ever left the 80’s, instead, they improved it, delivering a retro-futuristic cyberpunk reality where technology fuses with the human body.For detective Lazarski this was a typical day until a phone call changed things, turning it into a personal quest, across digital demons, psychological choices and flesh that still bleeds as it always did despite the metal in it. One of the aspects which I really like is how the whole game is set in a building compartment. One would think such design would limit players, or even create barriers for the plot, but no.The narrative and placement of events are just good, almost like a fantastic movie you can’t stop going through it, until you decipher all the events. Each room, each tenant and each side-quest delivers more information about a world you can’t stop diving with full curiosity. if by some strange and bizarre reason the story doesn’t convince you, maybe the visuals will.This time, visuals and optimization have to be described almost at the same time. It’s no doubt Observer: System Redux ets itself for the future, aiming at next gen GPU’s but also, keeping it cool for what should now be standard hardware. Some options that were previously only tweaked through the .ini files can now be chosen directly in the game’s menu.Chromatic Aberration, Field of View, Ultra-widescreen and increased Frame Rate are just some of the options that were adjusted to fit the new demands. It’s now much easier to enjoy the game if you’re having a low tier card, or even medium. In my case, with a RX 580, and by disabling special effects, chromatic aberration, and adjusting shadows, I can almost keep stable 60fps with everything else on Ultra. Visually the game definitely delivers an improvement, but maintains the same structure you came to know very well from the original. Character models are solid, and the same can be said about effects, lights and scenery. With no impact on the gameplay, and absolutely no compromises when it comes to visual quality, Observer: System Redux is definitely a welcoming remaster. If you never had the chance to play it, now it’s impossible not to.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm conflicted on this one. The visual and production design on this is fantastic. The way this world was built, the layers, the textures, etc. Visually, this has a lot going for it, especially as a Cyberpunk game. Yet I guess when I read what this game was, I expected more of the investigation part, but quickly, this game doesn't make me feel like I'm investigating at all (at first it seems to, but then quickly that idea fades), so much as just following a very linear story with no real meaningful choices. The games that made me feel like I was investigating a scene: Arkham Knight, The Sinking City, and to a lesser degree, the braindance sequences of Cyberpunk 2077. In these games, the investigative parts felt meaningful, like you were uncovering a deeper mystery that would lead you somewhere. I would have liked if with Observer, we started off at the hotel, gathering some clues, maybe look up a few connections on our pda or vid thingy in our car, and let that guide us to other locations. With that aside, Observer feels like an updated adventure game with minimal puzzles along the lines of the Telltale Games with more atmosphere and horror, and it has some big story strokes that are cool. The lack of any real investigation and very constricted to this one very limited location really hamper this (this hotel), albeit with more parts of the hotel opening up as you go and do things, many of these areas still have a sameness to them. Also, the mechanism for interacting with objects, where you have to hold the mouse to say open a door, that's cumbersome. Accessing your little PDA or whatever you call it, was also a bit cumbersome.  The time commitment is low, though, so it isn't like I'm wasting so much time playing this only to be dissatisfied, but even then, it starts to wear by the end because of too much that feels the same. I really loved the idea of jacking into people's minds to uncover the story, maybe root around and find clues, but these sequences quickly feel repetitive. You are mostly just going straight or wandering a space that repeats until you go the right way or whatever, and when it does stop you, then you are pixel hunting for the right interactive spot. That is a very old adventure game flaw. That was great about the Deponia games, you could click a key and all interactive spots are highlighted. I shouldn't have to find interactive spots in an adventure game, anymore. Yet you have Rutger Hauer voicing the main character. The atmosphere and graphics are definitely top notch. It gets very tense in parts. So I guess it is a mild recommendation, if you are enjoying the story and the setting and the horror aspects. I probably won't ever play this again, though.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games I'd wish a "maybe" option for Steam Reviews was a thing.Graphically this game is fantastic, the environment design is just beautiful and the concept of the game is super interesting. However the SFX and music do sometimes stumble, often times it was the SFX that really pulled me out of the immersion in this game. Especially when the SFX goes "boo jumpscare" and you have to look around as to what actually happened. Other times you're stuck in a room somewhere not knowing what do to and there's these few noises keeping on playing being a lot more annyoing than scary. Other than that often times the ambiance music stays the same for much too long.The gameplay is simple but at times unintuitive. This game suffers under "I clicked everything already I don't know what to do" only to find out you have to interact with objects from a certain angle for it to work. There's been many times where I looked up walkthroughs only to find that the thing I was missing was an object I already inspected but the "click me" icon just hasn't shown up because I wasn't standing in the right angle. Often times, especially in the dream eater sequences this can become quite the problem, as these sequences are already very surreal so not knowing what the heck to do happens more than I'm happy with. Bug-wise I've gotten stuck in the geometry multiple times, one of the bots in game gut stuck between a door-frame keeping me from pursueing one of the side quests and finishing that quest.Other than that though the detective gameplay is fine, nothing special. You're not made to make your own deductions, everything is done for you so that's that. But that is only a minor gripe with it. The story starts off semi-interesting and becomes extremely interesting fast. The dialogues are really well-written and are almost always making me feel uncomfortable in the best possible way and the voice actors chosen for the entire cast were chosen well, too.I do recommend this game, as I personally really enjoyed it, but I'll add a slight maybe because I also know lots of people who really wouldn't enjoy this game for the reasons mentioned.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first time playing Observer. I have never played the non-enhanced version. My views and opinions are solely based on the current generational standards with regards to graphics, sound, and design. You play as Daniel Lazarski(voiced and acted by Rutger Hauer), a detective working for the Krakow Police Department. The story consists of going to an apartment complex, firstly to investigate after being called by your son Adam of what seemed to be a dangerous situation. Arriving at the location, you realize quickly that your son's call is a just small fraction of the secrets that lay behind apartment walls. Everyone has a story in Observer; some tragic, some freeing, and some disturbing. As the player, it is your choice to investigate the tenement building and learn more about the individual residents and the problems or experiences they may be facing. The gameplay loop is simple; investigate points of interest using both electromagnetic and biological scanners to gain evidence and learn more about the situation you are facing with. As you discover more clues, the individual stories open up and show more of their inner workings.I have always been a fan of the neo-noir aesthetic. It is clear Observer draws heavy influence from the movie Blade Runner as well as themes and tone from Philip K. ♥♥♥♥'s . From your first moments with the game, you can feel the oppressive environment pressed upon you as the player character. Before you even step foot into the game, a part of you knows what kind of delivery this game is shooting for. With that said, aesthetically, I believe Observer succeeds in making you feel immersed in it's dark and sick world.Looking through the lens of the our world currently, it can be easy to assume some of the actions and thoughts the characters in Observer have are sick, selfish, and twisted. In actuality, Observer presents itself in a way that actively encourages you to think as if you were living within the set time period of Krakow in 2084; a city with rampant drug use, mega-corporations controlling large faculties of human life, and augmentations that are interwoven in everyday living. All of this coupled, driven even further with heavy themes such over-indulgence in sex, extreme violence, and moral grey areas such as human trafficking.The story of Observer is good and most of it, in my opinion, is carried by it's phenomenal world building and emphasis on the quality of interaction over quantity. Most of the stories, both the main and side cases, will have you venture through the different facets of life within Krakow. Earnestly, both types of cases are fully-fledged out and whether you choose to progress the main or side cases, you will be satisfied on either end. I personally found the side cases to be more interesting because they were a bit more dense in their storytelling. The side cases tended to investigate the sicker, more outgoing ideas that one tends to expect from a world like this. Without giving too much away, I found the story in an overarching sense to be suitable and a clear step up from Bloober Team's previous works.The  in this game are beautiful, plain and simple. I don't mean beautiful in just the technical sense, but in creating something special within in genre with it's world building. Don't get me wrong, this is not an ugly game. It's just as much a technical beauty as much as it is an artistic one. There were moments within this game that I felt were completely jaw-dropping in terms of it's use of colors, lighting, and art direction. The crackles and sparks of loose wiring, grime and dirt festering between the wooden cracks, and use of blending both the human and technological. Bloober Team, in my opinion, have doubled down on their strengths from Layers of Fear. They have the ability to create amazing visual images to look at, and they used them fully to flesh out the world of Observer.  design is also incredible, many of the sounds you can tell were made in-house and it shows. Visual glitches, sound-screeching, technological hiccups and distortion all play a role in making you feel like you stepped into a environment that you know is unsafe, but is oh so sickly sweet in making you want to see more. I do feel however it should be noted that the mixing could have been better fine tuned, something that Layers of Fear also seemed to struggle with. I do not mind loud jump cuts, but sometimes I felt that certain sound effects would just completely overpower others when walking through the tenement buildings. The  is where I found my only issues with the game. Before I go deeper, the story is not bad; that needs to be clear. I was completely satisfied with how it started, continued, and ended. When I say issues, I usually mean with delivery. It should be noted that all of my issues come from  the main story case. The side stories in my opinion, were actually perfect. Not, "Wow these are neat and interesting!" but actually perfect. The side cases explored a theme, person, or event, had a good character or idea behind it and gave you usually a thought-provoking choice at the end. Sweet, simple, and really helped push forward that the world Daniel Lazarski is in, is a real twisted and sick one. The only issue I have with Observer, is it's overuse of jump-cutting and the induced visual hallucinations. Don't get me wrong, I loved observing into someone's neural network and the constant jump-cuts and glitches made me actually feel like I was relieving the memories of those I had chosen. It just becomes mentally taxing after 30 minutes of constantly switching scenery and soundstage. It reached the point where every lapse of sound was an easy tell that I could expect a loud "jump-scary" type noise to break the silence shortly after. I wish sometimes Observer would just let the story tell itself. To me, the highlights of the game are walking around the dilapidated apartment and letting the world grab you and tell a story. Seeing those needles and pills on the ground, hearing people yelling behind their doors, and investigating those distant sounds that seem jarring; that's the strength of Observer. When hacking into the brain of someone, everything kind of loses its sense of mystery and wonder if I'm constantly jumping between worlds or environments every second. Again, visually it's beautiful, but it ends up showing too much without having much substance.Performance wise, this game runs mostly flawlessly. My specifications are as followed:CPU: i7-6700k @ 4GHzGPU: GTX 1070 RAM: 16GB 3000MHz DDR4The only time I had performance issues is when transitioning from the main compartment to the basement and vice verse. The game would literally tank in FPS(~sub 10) and would more often than not freeze(0-1fps) for about a second or two and then fix itself. This would always happen at the bottom of the staircase connecting to the basement.All in all, Observer is a really good game. I'd recommend this game to anyone who loves a neo-noir aesthetic with some truly phenomenal visual design and strong story-telling. Some of the themes can be heavy, and a lot of sick imagery is found, and that makes it all the more tantalizing. I can only see Bloober Team going up from here. This is Bloober Team's magnum opus. It is a clear standout in all their games. If I were to give one recommendation, it's to let the world breathe and the story will tell itself. The jump-cutting and silence shattering spooks feel like remnants of Layers of Fear's horror design. I am aware, this may just be the Bloober Team "aesthetic" and could be what they are going for. It is their game after all, not mine. To me, the scariest parts were when I chose to investigate that creepy sound, or that odd compartment; not when I forced to sit through it. Thanks to everyone who made this wonderful game at Bloober Team!

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who is always looking for quality detective games (see my hours for LA Noire) - I somehow never came across this game. I've been browsing detective games since 2011 to scratch that itch, and not once did I come across this gem of a game.As soon as I saw the trailer, I purchased it, and even though I'm just an hour in, I feel like my purchase is justified.If you like horror-esque games (not straight up horror; more like Alan Wake II), love the cyberpunk aesthetic, and love detective games... then this is the game for you!**UPDATE**After finishing, I can say this game is definitely worth a playthrough. I don't mind that it's mostly a walking simulator with a few puzzles thrown in, as the story and protagonist are enough to keep you hooked.The world is vibrant, alive, and feels real. The characters have depth and history.There are two downsides for me. First, is that this game falls into the lazy trope of "hide from monsters" like Amnesia or Outlast. It's an identical mechanic that the game doesn't need to make you feel in danger. Without divulging spoilers, there's enough tension that something MIGHT happen that it's not necessary for something TO happen. If that makes sense.Second, the mouse controls are incredibly frustrating. Doors open slowly and all mechanics that require the use of the mouse require me to move my mouse like 50 times. Sometimes I'm approaching a door, I click and drag my mouse and nothing happens, and I have to do it multiple times. It's frustrating and immersion breaking at times.If you had told me that Fictional Games had created a version of Amnesia that was cyberpunk and dystopian, and then presented me with this game, I would have wholeheartedly believed you without a second thought.This game is definitely worth a playthrough if you don't mind the hiding-from-monsters thing. For me, it feels cheap and really takes me out of the game. In this instance, it damaged my perception of the game but it was enjoyable nonetheless.I'd give this game a solid 7/10 because of that.

_childDocuments_.review: I was curious about Observer System Redux for two reasons - its strong score on Opencritic (80/100) as well as the hubbub that Bloober was developing the next Silent Hill (this was when it was just a rumor).  I didn't know much about the game going in, so I was surprised to find that this is basically a walking simulator - a genre which I don't have issues with since I've enjoyed Gone Home, What Remains of Edith Finch, Firewatch, The Stanley Parable, The Beginner's Guide, etc. But...honestly this game is very underwhelming, aside from its at times flashy graphics (more on that later). For one, the story and more importantly the dialogue is a mess - badly written and incoherent. Communicating with the only notable human, Janus, was a real chore with dragged-out lines that unnecessarily hang on every word. Worse, the performances were super flat - Rutger Hauer's final starring role here didn't do him much justice as his delivery was super flat and uninteresting. Basically, in the end I just didn't care about anything or anyone at all, nor are the myriad of "cases" all that interesting to explore. Most are red herrings, like the doll room for example. Worst are the parts when you "jack" into the victims - they become headache-inducing trips with way too much flashing lights and very little in terms of interactivity. For example, I got stuck because I had no idea I could turn those knobs on the radios - I was wandering around aimlessly for ages, unsure of what to do. It's exactly these empty rooms and corridors with ONE specific thing you must interact with that really shows the game's flaws, especially when it gives you no clue what it is that you are supposed to interact with. Then there are those insta-death sneaking sections that are utterly lacking in suspense, and only serve to annoy you. Once I even somehow got stuck in a loop that I had to hard quit out of - not sure what bug that was, but it was super frustrating as I didn't know the game was basically freezing. Even the graphics, at first seemingly flashy, ends up being less impressive as you go on - humans are really not well-modeled or animated, for example. All the hallways and sewers and glitching graphics just got super old once you see it umpteenth times, and admittedly I really had to force myself to finish the game as I basically stopped playing twice. And the ending's two endings...disappointing as neither has any impact at all, emotionally or intellectually. Overall I give this a 4/10 - not sure how it got 80/100 on Opencritic as this game left me quite underwhelmed.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I would like to point out that the game is magnificent in terms of visual style. However, it cannot show this magnificence in terms of gameplay everywhere. I saw that there were small bugs here and there. To give an example of one of these. There is a place where we need to update the computer version, right next to the tattoo parlor. When you enter there, after a certain period of time, the janitor outside gets stuck listening to music and it becomes impossible to get out. There are only a few bugs like this in the system redux version. But automatic registration generally solves the problem. It's not often that you get stuck. The game does not offer much to the player in terms of gameplay, but overall the gameplay is enjoyable so much so that I did not enter the game expecting much anyway. The graphics look very nice for its time and in the new version. I have always loved the Cyberpunk theme. It makes me feel tension in places, so much so that I actually had goosebumps in some places. The game gives the feeling that someone is secretly spying on you very well in the lockdown center. The last thing I can criticize about the game is this. The parts that connect to people's brains are too long.  They are unnecessarily long. After a while, it really strains your eyes and gives you a headache. Even though I don't have any illnesses, the lighting effects in this game are incredibly challenging. Overall I liked the game. I hope we see the second game soon. In these times when the gaming market offers the same garbage a billion times, every player will want to see such rare works.

_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: I really love the scenario, the art design, the sound design, the graphics and obviously Rutger Hauer's performance. However, the gameplay is a different story: While I had some fun exploring the building and its secrets, I quickly got annoyed by the many dialogues at the doors and the reading of so many emails etc. Still, if these were all my gripes I would have stuck with it. However, the mind-exploring sequences were just plain horrible - both horribly boring and horribly annoying. I really did not enjoy running through moving and changing corridors till you figure out some arbitrary sequence to proceed or solving abstract and tedious trial-and-error puzzles. Also, I did not like that forced "lynchian" design - I get it, you're supposed to be in someone's mind, but it did not work for me. Also, the sneaking was just a pain...Too bad, I would have really liked to see the entire story and listen more to Rutger Hauer's voice, but after 3 hrs it just felt like I was forcing myself to continue and hence wasting time.

_childDocuments_.review: Observer offers more of an experiential journey than a traditional game, making it a must-try for those immersed in the Cyberpunk genre. Unlike Cyberpunk 2077 or System Shock, this is a detective thriller with a touch of horror, emphasizing storytelling over a shoot-'em-up style.The game is notably surreal, immersing players in a heavily story-driven narrative. While most puzzles aren't overly complicated, attentiveness is key to navigating through the experience.However, it's important to note that the game does have its challenges. The game mechanics are somewhat dated, and the dreaming scenes can be intentionally disorienting, adding an extra layer of complexity. The absence of a map can contribute to a sense of getting lost.Despite these drawbacks, Observer becomes a worthwhile investment for those able to look past these aspects and appreciate the unique experience it offers.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: one, single word.M A S T E R P I E C E.Cyberpunk 2077 can't even come close to what this game has done in terms of cyberpunk theme.i made probably over hundred screenshots. it's that good and beautiful, even that i played it without ray-tracing (i have 1080 Ti). Very good optimization (there is rarely any areas where you will encounter FPS drops).If you love cyberpunk stuff, this game is the best game there is! A must play!
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: Observer is a psychological Cyberpunk game with a bit of horror. You play as an Observer which corresponds to an officer that can deepdive into the memories of victims and criminals to find clues to what happened. In the game one investigates events in an apartment complex that is under lockdown and asks many different people to find clues etc. You have different dialogue options and dependent of what you choose you get other informations or reactions. The voice actors did an excellent job of bringing the characters to life. There are some little stealth sections that are short but can be a bit annoying because it disturbs the pacing a little imo. Especially at the end it feels like a bit dragged out, like they wanted to show what they can do effect and artistically. But the story and secrets you can discover in the game are amazing, It took me a while at the start to get really into it, but after a while i got really hooked to figure out what happend. Graphically and in terms of art style, the game looks great. It seems like they were heavily influenced by the Bladerunner movies. Its more gritty and dark in terms of the atmosphere and world. If you want to dive into a more sinister cyberpunk world with a lot of secrets and lore to discover, you should definitely give this game a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: This was a really interesting experience and I really liked it. I think they nailed the cyberpunk horror and detective themes very well. The atmosphere is especially amazing. It's really immersive. The main story and the side stories are interesting as well. The main gameplay loop is investigating what happens on the main story and the side stories by going door to door, interacting with the tenants and searching the apartment the game takes in with occasional puzzles.At some parts, I was a bit lost but it did not take away my enjoyment from the game. I'd recommend the game if you like cyberpunk settings and/or detective games.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: Bloober Team did a great job at creating an incredibly detailed cyberpunk world. The futuristic dark setting and Rutger Hauer's stunning performance really increase the level of immersion, but the horror moments kinda ruin everything. There are too many wanna-be surrealistic parts that are just repetitive and annoying (lights flickering and constantly teleporting) and when they are not you know it's gonna be another  boring section. After playing most of Bloober games I think this is one of their biggest weakness. I couldn't find it scary and it's sad to see they still rely on stupid jumpscares (pigeons, right...). At the end I think I played it more like a walking sim in a detective drama rather than an horror game, but it was still a good experience, 'cause the writing is great and the old and new optional cases are really interesting to solve. That said, I am still disappointed about the story endings and the useless cliffhanger. Why can't writers write a self-contained story nowadays? I would have preferred a great ending rather than a hint to Observer 2.Anyway if you already played the original Observer I would only suggest getting the Redux version with a 80% discount. The graphic improvement is cool and the game looks good with or without RTX, but that's about it. The additional new cases are kinda short and end up using the same reskinned location. If you never played Observer I would still recommend the game cause it's a great cyberpunk experience and the story is good.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! You investigate a slum tenement building in the year 2084, full of crumbling cyber-infrastructure and strange characters who exist on the margins of society. Everything is "enhanced" with tech to the point of disorientation, and as a police "Observer" you have the ability to hack into peoples' minds, which results in surreal, nightmarish excursions deep into the psyche and subconscious. As you go door-to-door, exploring each floor of the building, solving puzzles and chasing mysteries, the game is like a sci-fi version of "Silent Hill" in many ways (minus the combat). The tech-nightmare world is also the best argument against transhumanism that I've ever seen.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: Visually looks great , the idea behind the story is an interesting concept ( no spoilers ) although it can get a little disjointed when you are playing multiple investigations at once . To be honest it is a game that will probably be overlooked by many people as it’s not resident evil or silent hill , and that would be a shame , as it deserves to be played . It’s not too long and does make you want to see it through to the end .
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: Was looking for a good horror game, and purchased it when it was on sale. First of all  but a walking simulator with an interesting story. And that's the great part. The story is solid and has great turns and twists. The dialog is well written and the characters are mostly great. However game-play wise, the game falls a bit flat for me. There a several mechanics introduced, however they aren't implemented a lot.  The last part of the game is great, but it is over so quickly, leaving me personally unfulfilled craving more. And that is this game in a nutshell, very good but ultimately leaving you wanting more, which is usually a good thing, but not really in this case. There is a lot of good stuff here, but aside from the story, it doesn't find its potential. I think I would have enjoyed it a lot more if I knew what I was getting into, the tags personally for me set my expectations to a completely different place. This is a great walking simulator with a horror elements and a solid story that ultimately unfortunately leaves you feeling unfulfilled and wanting more. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Rutger Hauer's voice acting here sounded different from his voice in Blade Runner surely due to his age at the time of this game's development. But with the added deepness coming from age, his voice sounded like poetry here during his dialogues. Now if you'll excuse me, I need to watch the famous Blade Runner tears in the rain scene (there is an easter egg secret of that in this game!) and listen to that legendary "rain monologue".

_childDocuments_.review: I wish Steam's recommendations for games were set on a scale. Observer: System Redux started off strong. It's a slow going Dark Cyberpunk Sleuth set in a single apartment complex. Fell off hard a little bit over half way through. It definitely overstayed it's welcome. I'd recommend it for people who are die-hard Cyberpunk fans. There is no combat, you essentially go room to room interrogating residence and stumbling upon crime scenes all while trying to find your son. Switching between electromagnetic and organic visions to scan evidence. Jacking into the minds of the deceased as an Observer is cool though. Without getting into any details, the game is super grim. It is a very pretty game but heavily overwhelming with visuals. NOW, here is the main reason I can not recommend. I encountered 3 bugs during my play-through, actually 4. The big one that hasn't even been fixed yet literally would not let me proceed. I got the "bright white screen" bug on a computer screen that you need to use to proceed, not allowing me to see anything or interact with the in-game computer screen. Loaded my last save and fixed the bug. Interacted with the in-game computer screen again and my mouse disappeared and I couldn't even use my keyboard to navigate the in-game computer screen. I had to plug in a controller to proceed. If you don't have a controller and encounter this bug, good luck. Restarting the game and reloading checkpoints multiple times didn't even fix my mouse disappearing and keyboard not working. If the future is anything like what this game portrays, I want no part of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, where to start? Unfortunately what many call Bloober Team’s best isn’t very good. A decent opening and the gameplay loop of checking in on tenants works as a good hook. Though the plot moved at a slow pace from me taking my time with the side stuff, the first half felt much more engaging than the latter. The side content here is the highlight, with some stronger (but still derivative) ideas than the main story being allowed to come and go like short stories that don’t waste your time. Once you reach a point of no return however, you’re basically following a straight line through an exhaustingly long haunted house where the game continues to try and one up itself with the dream eater sequences.The first of these sequences I saw made a good first impression with an environment made from what looks like broad paint strokes, a blunt but expressive way of contrasting this fractured childish mind from the reality you lose touch with. The following dream sequences really begin to drag with unintuitive puzzles, obnoxious and downright silly scares. Did I mention this game is too long? I would probably at least like this game if it was two hours shorter. Narratively it’s a series of vignettes that play out back to back until the main story takes the wheel and railroads you. Unfortunately the structure that makes the side content stand out completely kneecaps the core narrative because there’s essentially no narrative clarity until the last act and then it rushes to resolve the personal stakes at the last minute. It doesn’t help that everything going on art direction wise feels like a ripoff of something else.Truly some baby’s first cyberpunk kind of stuff going on here. Some shallow anti-corporate stuff, generic police state (1984 copy on a shelf made me gag), sexbot ethics, transhumanism, mishandled mental illness narratives, a collage of familiar ideas given no room to be fleshed out. If Bloober Team deals in haunted house attractions, this is a limited event on their lot where they swap the old paintings for holograms and coat their skeleton props in chrome paint. It doesn’t help that they can’t tell when the screaming and showers of fake blood get old.I feel bad. I liked this enough in the early hours but then the game went and spoiled all the good will it built at the end. The game brings out some pity in me, mostly thanks to Rutger Hauer’s presence. Hauer obviously thrives more as a screen actor than a voice actor, but in spite of some weird deliveries the frail ache of his voice carries a kindness in it that you hate to see punished. It’s a shame really, the man deserved better than this.Rest in Peace, Mr, Hauer.

_childDocuments_.review: The beginning was very hopeful for me but it went downhill real fast.My biggest annoyance with it was how on the nose it's been throughout it all. You can't get any more of a cliché cyberpunk sob story than this. "Big corpo bad, transhumanism risky, life bad, job bad, government bad, drugs bad, war bad, maybe robot human?" The game literally begins with you finding a 1984 book ffs, and there are "big corpo is problem not solution" graffiti all over the place. Not to mention all the Bible references with the names and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ apple.Also forget about scary, it wasn't even creepy in the slightest despite all of its extremely obnoxious efforts with its sudden loud noises, screen shakes and visual distortions. The dream sequences were also a letdown. They always went on for far too long and were just... stupid. There's no other way to put it. They had some classic Bloober 'baby runs into wall' tier unintentionally funny moments in them. I'm not even sure if the last half was even playtested. I was begging the game to let me finish them so that I could continue exploring the apartment complex.And on the technical side, the game is littered with stutters and micro freezes despite being the 'System Redux' version. The stutters were kinda manageable after turning on vsync and locking framerate but the freezes kept on happening.Just talking to the tenants of the apartment complex, exploring rooms and solving small mysteries was the best part of the whole game, but they last unbelievably too short. You only talk to each tenant once and there were only like 4 side quests from them. There were a couple scenes with good writing and cool visual moments, but it's not worth this slog.

It's regrettable, because I like the game, I enjoy the aesthetic and the vibes as well as how good it looks.  But holy hell, does it have problems.  From certain abilities simply not functioning for no reason at key points to doors refusing to open NO MATTER WHAT, this game is broken.  It's so sad.  But it's true.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the 10 hours I spent wandering the corridors of this game. However, under the tattoo parlor the keypad didn't appear, a bug that I got around through a reload, after spending way too much time trying to figure out the issue. Then later, in the doll room, the game froze completely when exiting the computer. Reloads didn't help. A shame as it was good while it lasted. _childDocuments_.review: What an amazing journey!Observer has definitely left it's mark on my memory as one of the best games I have ever played.The atmosphere and environment sucks you right into a dystopian cyberpunk world, where you are faced with intriguing and often horrifying encounters and choices to make. It would seem Sherlock Holmes was having an affair with Cyberpunk and Observer is that bastard child that flourished in life, becoming a hidden gem among the masses.I can easily rate this game as a 10 and would definitely recommend this!

_childDocuments_.review: + Immersive setting+ Visually beautiful+ Dystopian Furutre Detective on a personal case has so much potential+ The building block does build a pretty good atmosphere+ a few side stories have enticing ideas- Chase/dream sequences that have you running/evading in corridors get old  fast and drag on too long- Environmental design/Symbolism in those segments is either very heavy handed or makes barely sense in the context- Main story is overall a letdown in regards to the character's motives and the 'ideological/moral' choice the player has to make- Dozens of dev portraits as collectibles just break the immersion- Anachronistic minigames and hardware make little sense in a world where VR, mind hacking/uploading and similar concepts exist- So many jump scares that are more annoying than frightening/atmospheric- References just for references' sake may take you out of the experience- The voice acting may be an hommage, but more often than not it really misses the markAll in all it's not a terrible game, but the premise could have turned into soo much more. I guess that's on par with other bloober team releases.

_childDocuments_.review: A splendid graphic update of Observer. The story remains the same, with the addition of a few side quests, but the introduction of ray tracing and improved models and textures makes the experience even more immersive, claustrophobic and visionary. If you have not yet had the opportunity to experience its excellent story, dive in without hesitation. Not suitable in any case for those who can't stand walking simulators, because, with the exception of some short stealth sections, the title fits perfectly into that category.

_childDocuments_.review: While this game is good just like the original release; I find it highly disrespectful from the developers not to give the people who bought the original game already a discount on this enhanced version of their game to show their gratitude to the people who supported them in the past.Having to buy this game for nearly 30 Euro'es all over again for the simple fact of getting a few more side missions and ray tracing is a bit of an over kill.So if you've played the game before and simply want to experience the new puzzles, hold until there is a sale.Trust me, you'll thank me later.Most of these new puzzles are so insanely hard that you will be standing looking for the answer and giving up an hour later anyways.SADLY.6.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest. This game is good. The psychological horror is on point. However, there was content in this game that I, myself, couldn't handle and found myself very depressed after playing. There is a lot of content about drug use, sex trafficking, pedophilia, rape and sexual violence while investigating the potential of a serial killer in the apartment complex your character is in. This is only within the first 3 hours of this game. Most of the time I can handle content like this. I recently played The Medium, and the psychological horror within that game was beautifully written, leaving me wanting more of it.Take this as a fair warning. This game is much darker than what the previews show. If you're into that kind of stuff, then you'll enjoy this game. I was blindsided and couldn't handle it. I had only wished someone wrote this review before I considered playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: You know those crash montages of spooooky, gory imagery in early 2000s horror films that were supposed to show you how crazy some serial killer was? What if you had a movie that was 9.5 hours long and was ONLY that and your VCR was on the fritz so you had to hold down the "play" button to keep the movie going.  That's Observer.
