_childDocuments_.review: Observer is a psycho crime cyberpunk experience blowing your mind.Difficulty ★★☆☆☆☆☆☆☆☆ (only few parts in which you can actually die)This game does take you on an awesome trip. I am not a cyberpunk style fan, but the crime topic and how the devs worked them out made me play the game. And I was well entertained. Though I do love the first part of the game more (more crime investigation themed) the latter part changes more into a narrative mind twisting plot.This game urgently cries out to go VR. The whole experience would be even more immerse. And most game mechanics and elements are already fitting perfectly for VR. Should be not too hard to implement. So if they bring out the VR version one day, I am up for another ride ;)And, I absolutely loved the voice actor of Daniel. He was doing a fabulous job. Totally fitting in to the observer role.

_childDocuments_.review: I can see why this game would be appealing to some, and it's almost something I'd look forward to playing. Unfortunately, this game is extremely limited in ways that its fascinating story and creative aesthetic can't make up for. The more you play, the more "on rails" it feels. There are very few actual game "play" (or choice) moments to look forward to outside of picking up some meaningless clues and mini-games here and there. It tries too hard to be deeply unsettling in a variety of ways, mostly missing the mark outside of the over-used glitchy, flashy, disorientating effect that they heavily rely on through-out. You will find yourself squinting, grimmacing, and wanting to look away as the migraine-inducing storm of shapes, sounds, and lights overwhelm your senses. I don't know if the game ever opens up enough to be worth it for me, but the experience isn't good enough to waste any more of my time trying to find out. It seems to have a pretty good rating, so I guess people like it... if you're like them, I guess you'll like it too, but if you're like me and want a less constrained, investigative  game with lots of options and actual puzzles, without being brought to the brink of a grand mal seizure, you should pass on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Observer is a game I wanted to enjoy, but did not actually get to play. While the game may look decent and has solid atmosphere out of the gate, I cannot recommend this game based off of my experience purely off the fact that there are bugs that should not be present in a remaster that was released 4 years ago. While you may not encounter these bugs and may have more patience than I do, the two bugs I encountered were enough for me to pursue a refund.The game was running fine for almost two hours until I became permanently stuck on the stairs going from the ground floor to the first floor which lead to me having to reload to my last save. Immediately after I ran into an even bigger bug that effectively killed my playthrough.A game breaking bug in which neither vision modes or the action wheel was brought up 4 years ago is still present: I attempted the solution using a Hex editor plugin in Notepad++ as outlined in the PC gaming wiki for this issue but unfortunately this did not resolve the bug. Sure I could just boot up an old save file, but the problem here is this is a 4 year old game breaking bug.

_childDocuments_.review: It's really a shame that this game has some fatal shortcomings because it often oozes the perfect dark cyberpunk atmosphere, plus has incredible voice-over work from the late Rutger Hauer.Where to begin with my beef with Observer: System Redux. For starters, this game runs like crap on my machine, which is more than capable of handling RTX.. Random stutters, fps drops are frequent and just plain infuriating. There have been times when I've walked down a random hallway with not much going on visually and my fps will tank by 50%, even with frame-caps and raytracing turned off. Really a shame because this game has some absolutely gorgeous graphics and art direction..Onto the story and voice acting. Again, Rutger Hauer is phenomenal as the playable character/detective, but every other character ( there aren't many NPCs in this game ) have laughably bad voice over performances that really spoil the cyber-horror atmosphere and make it so much less scary.I would say that Bloober Team had a really good game hidden somewhere beneath the jank that is Observer: System Redux, but this is already a revision of a version from 4 years ago. Maybe they'll get their act together for The Medium: RTX System Redux? Or Silent Hill?
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: Some great setpieces and a decent mystery, but lacking in gameplay. Rutger Hauer is phenomenal and really carries the game. BIG annoyance: finding the thing you need to interact with in a room. The interact icon is very small and only appears when you're basically looking right at it which leads to near point-and-click levels of trying to interact with everything in a room. Can be very frustrating and ruins the pace/flow of what are pretty great setpieces.Story has some really big highlights in the side stories and the main plot BUT has some awkward hamfistedness and silliness tucked in there. I don't know if this game/story needed a werewolf but I can't lie and say it wasn't entertaining at least

_childDocuments_.review: This is a no for me. The horror/dream sequences others have mentioned in reviews make up a significant portion of Observer’s runtime, but are only loosely related to the cases and story, and are arbitrary, haphazard mazes or puzzles. They can be difficult to solve, which on its own is fine, but the soundtracks for those sections are grating - glitch sounds, a baby crying, a very short looping music track - all of which become annoying when heard over and over. The game looks great, the detective sequences are fine, but neither makes up for the frustrations. I also found the performance to be lousy on steam deck, even at mid to low settings and frame rate capped at 30fps, performance was erratic.

_childDocuments_.review: Observer: System Redux First Impression Review - 1.5 hours Sure.. no problem I will just go to the F*cking Eye store.. speak to the eye salesmen and buy a new pair of eyes.This game starts off very promising, Detective Observer Lazarski, you go to check in on your son after he calls you out of the blue. The suspense is there, very compelling stuff so far, graphics look awesome... then... you step out of your car heading towards the C block rentals and holy Sh*t, everything is flashing and going nuts, huge neon signs and lights blinking a million times a minute...Get inside and it's just as bad... your two Detective visions are hard to use as well, dark and you can't see what your doing half the time.. once again, very f*cking hard on the eyes...So ok, i am pushing through so far, can't get worst right?... well, I finally find Amir, a man dieing from a mortal wound and you need to jack into his mind and see his memories...Well, just shoot me in the go*da*m face with a point blank Shotgun round.. just when camera shake and flashing lights couldn't get more crazy the whole f*cking scene takes a kanip sh*t.. I turn my computer off, like hard turnoff mid game because I became dizzy and eyes were very sore...Wow... just blows my mind, what were they thinking.Otherwise interesting ideaUPDATE I reduced the brightness significantly and it has helped a bit, still the screen shake and flashing lights are nuts, review still stands but reduce brightness to help with the neon lights

_childDocuments_.review: I played the original Observer when I was deep in alcohol abuse. The game was a huge part of my life during that time, even though I'm not proud of that time at all. The alcohol helped me get through the scares, but it also had my head all scrambled up about what was going on by the end of the game. (ironic, considering the whole story of the game is about your mind being f'd.) I've come out of my alcohol abuse and have had Redux in my library for some time, but I didn't have the guts to get into the scares without my drunkeness to lean on. This week, I decided to test out Remote Play on my phone and I used Redux for this. I suddenly found myself engaged in the story again, wanting to explore the building that I felt like I knew so well and before I realised it, I was hooked again. I just finished the game while writing this. It feels like achievement in itself to be able to get through this with a sober mind. I've always called Observer my favourite game and that has not changed. If anything, I love it even more now that I understand the story better. All of this being said, I gotta be honest and say that I was a little disappointed with the new interrogation sequences.  Although,  Lastly, I continue to reserve a special place in my heart for this game. It's my all times favourite game. The imagery in this game continues to leave me breathless and the stories of the characters takes me on a rollercoaster of emotions that I don't want to leave.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best Cyberpunk horror game you can get. And maybe even the best psychological horror game you can get. It's one of the best I've ever played. Never was a psycho trip as intense as in this game. If you are a horror fan or a Cyberpunk fan, you definitely should give Observer a shot. It's more an experience rather than a game. An amazing experience with an intriguing story that is told through fascinating visuals and shock moments. Not to forget the great job that was done by the famous actor Rutger Hauer with his atmospheric and fitting voice for Daniel Lazarski.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute experience. Observer refines the cyberpunk genre down to its very most dystopian, with a small-scale yet harrowing story and incredibly grungy visuals. As both a huge cyberpunk fan and someone who is usually unfazed by horror, Observer managed to legitimately awe and unsettle me through about half of its roughly 7 hour run-time. Don't go into Observer expecting "just another" experience of any kind. It's an absolute trip, with a truly unsettling world, premise, and story, beautiful but headache-inducing visuals, dream sequences that you will dread entering, and come out of questioning reality. By the end of Observer, I had no idea what the ♥♥♥♥ was going on. And that makes it great.
_childDocuments_.name: Observer: System Redux

_childDocuments_.review: I never get tired of the title sequence, the digital memories are mind blowing, I just love the creativity and the way they went about it, digital glitches of the mind. The dreams are super immersive and so physically emotional to me. So good. Loved actually being my own investigator and having a little clipboard/inventory system to kinda guide me through what I should do next or consider. Loved the organic and electronic scanner ideas! So futuristic. Really thoroughly enjoyed this game. Was such an adventure at least for me! 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Before anyone buys this, this is not a typical game and more like an interactive walking sim. There is no open world here or a combat system. You play a detective from the near future and you are responsible for accessing the minds of the dead using a device called a dream eater. Despite its simple gameplay, this is an immersive experience and I recommend it to anybody who wants to try something a little different. The graphics are amazing, voice acting is awesome. Rutger Hauer's (Rest his soul) performance is superb here. However, as a game, there are flaws with it and it feels overall empty and boring.Its freaky at times, its scary. You will jump out of your seat. The horror elements here really do click. It's flaws are mainly the fact that it's fairly short. Not much complexity overall as a game. The story starts off right but ends up being very dull and lack luster. Not gonna spoil the ending, but you are given choices which ultimately don't really matter. The graphics and design are beautiful, but you are stuck in a depressing ass apartment building through the whole game. After a few hours of play, everything feels the same, nothing fundamentally changes, and the game starts to feel like its dragging. Some of the environments change, but that comes towards the very end and doesn't last very long.The dream eater sequences, when you jump into the minds of the dead, are pretty cool. BUT, you only get to do that maybe 4 or 5 times in the whole game, that's it. The rest is walking around, buzzing apartment doors to talk to tenants, eventually finding a crime scene or clue that moves you to an already designated area that you are guided to.Not much replay value here, once the game is finished there is no reason to come back again. This recommends a rx590, played on a rx580 on medium 1080p, no drops. Also played on a 5700xt 1440p max, no frame drops. The only couple of drops happened when walking into another new area for a brief moment and some texture pop ins but that's the Unreal Engine for you lol. 60% - C

_childDocuments_.review: It was pretty nice to get the upgrade just for owning the old one, and while they're not the only developer to do this, it's always nice when it happens. As for the contents of the upgrade, the visual redesign looks great. I really didn't have an issue with how the original version looked or anything but the System Redux just has a much more imagined cyberpunk look to it. The three new side cases are also good. Maybe it's just that I had played through the previous cases twice already but they were just genuinely interesting and unique. Well two of the were. I thought that conclusion of "Errant Signal" was completely lacklustre which was in stark contrast to the new cases in particular, but even to some, if not all of the original ones. Maybe I did something wrong and got the bad ending to it, but from my 5 minute google search I couldn't find anything. The last thing I want to mention was the "Redesigned Stealth". I didn't notice anything new or different about it, but then again, they are by far the weakest sections of the game so I was just trying to get past them as quick as possible to get to the actually interesting parts again. Really enjoyable atmospheric, cyberpunk horror game. Probably wouldn't recommend at full price, but would consider at a 25% discount and definitely buy at anything 30% or higher.Also, whoever's idea it was to add "new secrets to find" ♥♥♥♥ you. You know the "secrets" I'm referring to. Here is an hour long guide to find all of collectables, some of which can only be found at specific points in the game and completely break up the pacing and suspense of it.

With so much love and care for the genre aswell as talented writers and actors like Rutger Hauer, RIP. Totally worth playing. Great trippy visuals and a really interesting story and world. _childDocuments_.review: Just to be clear, the game is more of a walking simulator with a linear narrative. That's OK, but definitely wasn't the more detective/investigation oriented gameplay that I was expecting to see. Not to give too much away, but much of the game is centered around dreamlike sequences that seem to bend reality. It's really cool at first, but it tends to get drawn out way too long, and the constant distortion of the screen and sound ended up making feel like I was on a bad acid trip.Graphically, the game is a really beautiful and dark vision of the future. I had only minor issues with objects in the distance popping into view suddenly as I approached. Overall, loved the look and acting of the game, but it just wasn't enough to overcome the uneven pacing and issues with the "dreams." I would not recommend to anyone other than fans of the cyberpunk genre...but, I did see enough potential in the game that I'd probably try out another Bloober product.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a crime. No seriously, making a game like this should be illegal. The devs had EVERYTHING to make this into an amazing game: a famous actor, an amazing setting, a great graphics engine, a murder mystery which SHOULD come all together into a marvellous sci-fi crime solving story. That's also what it starts out as -  you enter an apartment and quickly are set to tracking clues.But ... then it all starts falling apart. Here's a list:- the game is extremely short and is mostly limited to an apartment building- the apartment building is a MAZE and horrendous to navigate through- you don't REALLY hunt for clues - you can scan stuff but you only need to scan the right item for the game to tell you what to do next. - mind hacking = walking for 20 minutes through memories which is as tedious as it sounds- the devs decided adding tedious "puzzles" to an already tedious mind hack would be a good idea- have fun going from hotel room to hotel room- there's all kinds of small technical issues such as rebound keys not working properly- loads of disability settings but no way to reduce the seizure inducing flashing & flickering?- the story is nowhere near as interesting as you might expectThis whole game feels to me like an art project that was forced to be a game. THIS is a not a murder mystery game. It's a walking simulator in one of the worst most tedious settings possible with an occasional interaction. It also doesn't help that Rutger Hauer sounds extremely tired. He's a legend but near the end of his life he clearly lacked the energy for a project like this.It's such a damn shame but despite the game looking brilliant from the screenshots, it's all looks and no depth.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a point in the game that bricks the gameplay. until that's resolved, I don't recommend this. There is no alternative solution. I've tried variations of the 'method' and still get locked in a portion with no response from the one clickable. Discussion solutions have no assistance, just linkouts to personal guides.Update: the issue, without breaking spoilers, is using the clickable in a way that was not really indicated. You're led to interact with previous versions one way, but keep in mind what the clickable is. When I realized that, I moved on through the game pretty fast.In the fast pace of life these last 3 years, hearing that Mr Hauer passed on like so many other great actors was a shock. This is a fantastic narrative to follow through. The visual aspects and story-driven puzzles are perfect for the theme. The outcome is, as they describe, dystopian. In that, you don't so much win, as move on, and it's up to you whether it's for better or worse. To be honest, I think a major positive of the game is that it's not tailored 'American' Being in another part of the future world, where the language is different, and even cultural expectations are foreign, really expands perspective. We're so trapped in our own narrow view of things, on so many aspects, being drawn away from our norms both showed me not only how different it was, but how we're all still the same at the core.

_childDocuments_.review: After a full playthrough experiencing all of the content and careful deliberation I would say that I do not recommend this game under the vast majority of circumstances.Pros:Main story is somewhat decent when it stays on track.Side stories are unique and interestingGame has a good visual flair to it and the new graphics in Redux are fantastic.Good setting and great overall tone being attempted.The ending is great.Cons:There is effectively no gameplay. The gameplay is walking around, listening to things and clicking on buttons. There are a few moments where you have to hide from an enemy but the AI is so rudimentary it could exist on the SNES.The story meanders a lot and has no real cohesion until it wraps up close to the end in a giant dialogue dump.Some of the side stories end in cliff hangers or have no true conclusion. For me, two of them failed to be removed from my quest log when they were completed.The game could not keep me immersed as the developers put pictures of themselves all over the place as collectibles. And I mean ALL OVER THE PLACE, there are over 60 of them in a game that lasts seven hours. Many times I would be finding myself immersed in a section of the story or an environment only to be snapped out of it when a picture of a smiling Polish person shows up. Additionally, some of the content thrown into the environment are so absurd that it ruins the tone they're trying to set - references to Big Black ♥♥♥♥ and literal Drilldos (dildos attached to a drill) thrown into rooms.Voice acting is rudimentary at best. I understand Rutger Hauer is world renowned and has sadly passed, but his dialogue is off-tone and stunted for most of the game. He doesn't sound like he really cares and his delivery is really flat even in highly emotional moments. I started playing this game because Rutger Hauer is in it and I was incredibly disappointed in the vocal direction they gave him.The puzzles introduced in the new side stories are horrible, mostly consisting of finding the right item in an extremely vast space that you need to left click on in order to hear the next info dump.Corners were cut in a lot of regards and it shows. Very few characters are modeled and animated, you generally find no NPCs whatsoever for the whole game and people who speak to you do so from behind a .png in the wall or over the radio. Multiple times you can tell they avoided lip syncing by distorting or hiding the face. To add to this, almost all of the environments are attached at the hip. When you're told you need to go to another building that building is very conveniently attached to the apartments you're already exploring. I imagine this was done so they didn't have to make a city block or back alley you have to walk through.The game was not scary and relies on loud noises and popscares to startle you, some of the sidequests that began to get interesting and horrific came to a conclusion right before they got good.Lastly, this game did not run particularly well on my computer. I have a Ryzen 3700x and an Nvidia 2070 Super with 32gb of RAM, my drivers are up-to-date. I played this game at 1440p maxed out and it failed to exceed 80-90 FPS at its height and dipped as low as 50 in some areas. This didn't change much with RTX on or off, and I barely noticed a difference in visual fidelity with RTX on.So yeah, I wouldn't recommend it. Unfortunately. It looks good, but it just isn't. I doubt I will be playing any Bloober Team games in the future as they appear to have promising trailers and premises as well as high visual fidelity, then fail to deliver once you've delved into it.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: It's a very pretty, ambitious and well-put together game that simply wasn't to my taste.While the game is extremely pretty (even if everything is disgusting/ugly/dirty) and there is a really strong sense of art direction that is to be commended, I mostly found this game an exercise in frustration. Perhaps the biggest problem the game has is that it is distressingly common for prompts to continue gameplay to be hard to spot: a small white reticle that may only appear on an already viewed object AFTER an arbitrary point is reached, easily missed on another sweep or due to frequent (deliberate) glitches in the players POV/position.  It doesn't help that the game also wants you to frequently be switching between vision modes (and doesn't tell you that you have night vision until 80% of the way through the game, unless I missed it earlier?) that can turn a lot of the high fidelity graphics into a murky red or green fog that also makes it harder to spot prompts.Rutger Hauer (RIP) as the titular Observer, Lazarski, doesn't phone it in, but nor does he give a particularly fired up/notable performance.  Voice acting wise, he sounds old and tired which works in character, but it means he lacks a certain urgency or emotional investment in a lot of what he says or how he reacts to events.   The climax of the game really falls flat because of this, and in an odd way it is mirrored by how the character moves in game as well: at best you can move at a brisk walking pace and usually you're just kind of meandering your way about, which makes some of the larger levels a bit of a chore to navigate: an incredibly brief section of the game where suddenly somebody you are controlling can run just makes the slow pace stand out more.  It is presumably deliberate, to allow you to really drink in the atmosphere or to build tension, but for me it just kind of got frustrating.The game doesn't really explain much about the setting, which to be fair some players may find laudable/preferable to exposition dumps.  You're just kind of dumped into the world, never really get more than brief glimpses of the wider society and even less of the history of how it came to be.  The game is NOT uplifting, seemingly deliberately so based on a note from the developers at the end of the game, and that in turn added to my frustration as the "best" ending of the game is a real downer and kind of miserable.  With a bunch of collectables thrown in for no real reason, a ton of interactivity in the environment that doesn't really seem to serve any purpose beyond the interaction itself, this very much feels like it probably should be or wanted to be a VR game but just wasn't.  It's very much a style over substance game, and the plot is kind of ridiculous, but there was still a lot of enjoyable moments in the game, mostly around Lazarski investigating cases unrelated to the main one.  There was a ton of potential in this game, I personally don't think it was realised but that just may be my own personal taste, I'm sure there is plenty here that others might enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game but unfortunately I didn't. A cyber punk detective story, a murder mystery, Rutger Hauer...the description checked all the boxes for me. Imagine a horror movie with loud noises and jump scares but instead of delivering them in small doses to scare you the game throws them at you every 10 seconds. At one point I had to turn of the sound because I just couldn't stand it anymore. Instead of being scary it became a nuisance very quickly. I mean I give the developers credit for trying something new but they really overdid it with those constant glitching effects and screechy noises.The story didn't exactly knock my socks off either.  Yes, it's bleak and dark and the ending in and of itself is terrifying but 'Soma' did it all before and with a much much better approach to the topic. Overall, Observer isn't a bad game but it isn't a good one either. If you're looking for a game with an existential horror theme, play Soma.

_childDocuments_.review: There are many things right with this game, and many things wrong. This is, on the whole, a mid-quality horror, where some aspects have been treated well, and some have been disregarded entirely. A great game, as any other piece of art, is shaped by a narrative (or a ludonarrative) and the general experience; in this case, a lot of attention was paid to minor details, such as furnishings of the forlorn slum where the action takes place, several characters and the dreams that you get to explore. Some of these are actually very impressive and convey a feeling of abandonment, deprivation, misery and the textbook definition of dangers that come with human modification and eugenics. The horror here is just the sense of desperation that feels somewhat synthetic (like the human augments in game) given the excessive effort at shaping a totally messed-up building. That said, everything on the meta-level is very raw. Gameplay fails to adequately address the investigative part and doesn't treat your special super-detective abilities in any meaningful way, so if you are looking for an investigative game that's not going to feel satisfactory. The game never focuses on any larger problems, it's just a statement that "this version of the future is a total mess". That alone doesn't impact the player significantly: no story lines or problems are researched in-depth, you are basically given a sampler dish with a ton of themes that don't really go beyond skin-deep. The story itself just happens in the last hour or so of the game, rest of the time you are just slowly creeping behind the dangerous entity that hardly ever interacts with you, ever on its heels but never even touching it before the key storypoint is triggered. It feels somewhat superfluous.On the whole, it's just too many things mixed in a single bowl with not enough attention given to shaping an actual game. Which is a shame, because many bits and pieces are crafted masterfully.

The last act was a drag and really exposed the game's core problem as a walking simulator through doors and corridors. Its only saving grace is that at least it wasn't pointlessly long and ended just as I got bored with it.2/5

_childDocuments_.review: A crappier SOMA. There is a really good premise here; I LOVE the idea of being a detective who hardwires into victims and explore their mind either as they are awake or as they are dying. That sounds fantastic.Unfortunately the way it's implemented is just not scary or immersive. You are essentially thrown into an on-the-rails modern abstract art gallery full of parlor tricks, and you are to derive meaning from things happening and figure out yourself what to make of what you see. Did you ever see The Cell? It's like that, but nearly zero disturbing elements and mostly just going down a linear path from A to B. Look at the trailer; there is a moment wherein a bunch of children with monitor-heads turn toward you. Does that scare you? OK, then buy the game. If it doesn't, then I would say pass-- at least if you are eyeing this game for horror. At no point was I ever scared, except for the WAY TOO MANY jump scares accompanied with ear-destroying mechanical stingers, they really just cheapened the experience.Also what cheapens the experience is the half-assed models and assets. You interrogate people's apartments and see nothing but their eye(?) in the monitor on a loop... for some reason. There is one part of the game that would've been very powerful but is very much hamstrung by the fact you are talking to yet another monitor with a looped asset on it. There is no practical reason for that to be a thing in any world; why would you ever want to see a video of an eye in a peephole? It'd have been much better if they literally just had today's peephole experience; you just see a shadow block out the other side of the door. Another thing that bothered me is just how bluntly this was inspired by Blade Runner down to the Vangelis-rip-off-music and the obvious choice of Rutger Hauer, who-- as much as I love the guy-- was very much phoning in his voicework. Compare this to his work done in the Alien Audiobook and he just sounds like he doesn't care.tl;dr digital glitchy effects are not scary, and the story would've worked better had it done it in a more straightforward way and not just have nonstop abstracted environments.

_childDocuments_.review: The game basically consists of 2 parts.1 being great 2 making me puke. + A overall lack of polish, weird game design1: Interesting and atmospheric exploration of the complex in which you spend most of the game in, including cool side quests with decent enough puzzles/choices/scary sections. 2: Boring and overstimulating dream sequences, which are a very big part of the overcomplicated but simple and dumb main story. The game lacks any exciting gameplay, the few "enemy" encounters are rare, bad and meaningless.

_childDocuments_.review: BLUF: Observer is not a game despite the fact it  tries to pass as one. It should not cost money but, rather, should be something you're paid to experience.Walking simulators (Firewatch, Vanishing of Ethan Carter) are games, but Observer is not even a walking simulator, it's a post-realism art piece which, unfortunately, lacks vision, coherence and respect for the   unwilling and unwitting participant.The cyberpunk aesthectics are promised but not really deliviered. Observer is as much cyberpunk as Outlast is. It's claustrophobic and has a slightly retro look. The presence of "vision modes" (which helpfully show everything, making the detective work moot) and a mention of "nanophage" (which is a bad thing, but nothing is clear beyond that) and "class a/b/c citizens" does not make a game cyberpunk. Neither does hiding every character behind a door and only representing them by a voice. Observer looks and sounds quite nice. though, as long as you are outside the brain scan sequences...... Which are downright nauseating in every way and sense. Firstly, they have no mercy for epilepsy, as the amount of flashing lights, jump scares and instant location switches is way too high. Secondly (and that is where the lack of respect for the test subject comes in) they are needlessly long and carry a significant risk of blunt metaphor trauma, by hammering the same ideas about the character you're scanning again and again and then again some. And then they continue for some more, oozing some more metaphors for your viewing pleasure,The product could absolutely use some actual world building, involved gameplay and serious restraint in the unfettered surrealistic self-expression of its makers.Don't buy at full price and save your sanity by also not buying at a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok so you sit down at your PC after a long day, and crack open Steam to find a game to play. Why are you doing such a thing? You want to have fun of course! That is exactly why you should avoid this game like the plague.I love adventure games, I love mystery games, I love dialogue heavy games. They are MY types of games. So this game SHOULD be right up my alley. But it really isn't. It's a 'slog' game that you only persevere with because you're semi-interested in the story and want to know how it concludes. There's no objective markers and progress is most often a guessing game, but my god don't get me started on the 'dream eater' sequences. They go on for far too long, they don't make any sense and they're just a mess of flashing lights and random noise. I persevered through the first one, but with the second one I ended up in an office filled with random shadow glitches and no path to move forwards. I gave up here and I won't be playing the game again.Pros: Great graphics. Ray tracing is decentThe voice acting is fantasticThe story is intriguing and I really want to know more.Cons: There is no fun to be had with this game. It's a depressing slog and you'll be over the moon when it comes to an end, only so you don't have to play it any more.No help when it comes to objectives at all. I searched room 108 for what seemed like years but I never found what I was supposedly looking for.The 'dream eater' sequences are far too long and soul-destroyingly boring.The cyber punk aesthetic is wildly inconsistent. At times the environments look great, but then most of the time the environments are covered with matrix-like glitches and it just looks a bit rubbish.Conclusion: If you like punishing yourself and forcing yourself to play to the end of a game despite it being as fun as trapping your gooseberries in your zip, then this game is for you. If you play games to actually have fun however, then please save your money and stay away from this monstrosity.

_childDocuments_.review: I have this image of the Bloober team, they have interesting ideas for games, but they miss the mark in execution. I think this best sums up Observer. It is an interesting concept that starts well, but as the game goes on, its flaws become apparent. The narrative has the legs to keep you interested till the end, but it is the gameplay and the unnecessary padding that make it less interesting, it might even discourage some players from completing the game altogether.Visuals & PerformanceThe game has personality. The art style and the visuals, especially with Ray Tracing enabled, really bring the game's world to life. The setting feels lived in and accurately conveys the class divide. On top of that, the performance is good too. The game runs well even on a mid-range PC, probably because it is a slightly older game. However, there is one glaring issue, the traversal stutter. Every time you go to a different location in the game, a stutter occurs, which can be annoying. 7/10Narrative & GameplayThe game's story is basically a murder mystery. You play a detective trying to find who is committing them, while also looking for his estranged son. As I mentioned, the narrative has meat on its bones, as the twist is really good, or could've been if the gameplay sections leading up to it didn't make me hate it. Not to mention the unnecessary gameplay sections that force stealth, and annoying sound effects, that were clearly put there to scare you, instead, they make your ears bleed. If they had just nerfed these sections or cut them all together, Observer could've been a very good game. Other than that, it is a fairly simple game where you gather clues. 5/10To sum it up, Observer: System Redux could've been a good game. It hooks at the start but loses you as the story progresses. Final score - 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game thinking it's some cyberpunk noir detective story.It was, however... I started to realize it's also a horror game and not the usual type. This psychotic roller coaster is something really beautiful but also horrifying. The thought of a cyberpunk dystopia always scared me a bit with it's implants and trans-humanistic ideologies. This game takes the concepts and throws them at you in the most brutal and scary way possible. Someone really put deep thoughts into this and yes I have encountered a few glitches but overall the beauty and interactivity of this game puts many other titles to shame.It's been a fantastic ride but I'm sure as hell not coming back, one playthrough is enough, at least for this year. P.S. Would not recommend to people with mental health issues, especially psychotic or schizophrenic disorders.

Everyone interested in Sci-Fi must play this. Just by atmosphere and world building alone, The Observer: SE is one of the best things ever made. Just narratively it's a bit like Swiss cheese.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully crafted game that is cinematic enough to play with non-gamers. I played this with my wife and we thoroughly enjoyed the experience together. This game definitely is a labor of love and is a must for anyone who enjoys adult-oriented narratives with psychological horror themes. It can take a little while to get used to the style but it pays off quickly.* Masterfully crafted visuals/ animations (can be extremely trippy!)* Engaging narrative that is executed professionally* Scary without relying on jumpscares (but there are some jumpscares...)* Satisfying puzzles* Beautiful soundtrack*- Adult themes may be too disturbing for some... (18+ for sure)*- Jumpscares definitely will get you (may be a bit much for some)*- Optional missions (you can finish the game without completing all)*- Graphics are beautiful (but require trial and error to run smoothly)*- Game mechanics take time to get used to (don't forget your pills!)- Audio can get overwhelmingly loud if you play at higher volumes (studio monitors + sub used in my playthrough)If you are looking for an experience that is scary but also very thought through, and you can handle mature themes, I highly recommend Observer!(Major Soma vibes....)

_childDocuments_.review: Observer translates, through its fascinating lore and disturbing intrigues, as a masterpiece of writing, voice acting and storytelling through leveldesign. Everything has a purpose, the attention to detail is striking, and the gameplay remains very accessible. The whole plot happening in a single complex building (and in people's mind !) with so much background is a brilliant idea, making the exploration surprisingly thrilling and entertaining despite the apparent lack of life. The visuals and rendering of the redux version is enjoyable too.My only complains about the game are the annoying doors physics which is both slow and useless (a simple tap on a key to open anything would have sufficed).And the fact you can't save manually. The checkpoint system is terrible imo.Finally, thanks to R. Hauer for delivering an amazing performance in this game. RIP, you worked well.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't like it. I wouldn't recommend it.The gameplay is split into two larger parts:1) Pixelhunting as a detective (puzzles are NOT always displayed in Forensics and Bio view) in a confusing map2) Dream sequences from the Russian hell. Interrogations where you learn absolutely nothing new or understand what's going on. (Except for one, to be fair.)The dream sequences in particular are a pure nightmare. Not in the scary sense, just annoying to play. There is constant screaming, something explodes or makes some other kind of noise. Hearing the same caughing sound of a kid in a 2 second loop is really annoying. I always turn the volume down a bit during these sequences because otherwise I get a hearing loss. Visually, it's the ultimate cluster♥♥♥♥. People who have epilepsy die when they're in the same room as me. Nothing about it is scary. It's just loud and incredibly tiring. I wasn't scarend ones in the game (especially because there is nearly no fail state). Even Bioshock was way more scary. I don't want to spoil anything, so I can't really say how mind-bogglingly stupid the solutions to some of the puzzles are, but yeah. I'd have to stick my head in the microwave for 3 minutes to figure some of them out. I really never felt this clever NOT finding a solution instantly.After completing the game I realize that I couln't go back to the side objectives in the last few hours. _childDocuments_.review: In the neon-lit dystopia of our future, you don the digital mantle of an FBI agent with a twist: you’re not just an investigator; you’re an observer. Armed with cutting-edge technology, you can jack into people’s minds, reliving their memories, and piecing together the fractured puzzle of a city plagued by mysterious deaths.The stakes are high. Your son is missing, and the trail of bodies leads to a shadowy conspiracy. As you delve deeper, the line between reality and illusion blurs. The game’s cyberpunk setting sets the stage, but it’s the mind-bending experiences that steal the show.Imagine diving headfirst into someone’s consciousness—a kaleidoscope of fractured memories, distorted realities, and hidden secrets. Each neural connection reveals a new layer of intrigue. Was it the rogue AI? The underground syndicate? Or perhaps something more sinister?The beauty lies in the unexpected. This isn’t your run-of-the-mill detective story. It’s a psychedelic rollercoaster where you ride the synapses of the damned. The visuals pulse, warp, and glitch as you unravel the truth. You’ll question your sanity, your purpose, and the very fabric of existence.And then there’s the emotional weight—the gnawing ache of a missing child. Every revelation inches you closer to answers, but also deeper into the abyss. The game doesn’t hold your hand; it drags you into the abyss and dares you to emerge unscathed.So, fellow observer, buckle up. The rabbit hole awaits. The killer’s identity, your son’s fate—they’re encoded in the synaptic sparks. The TRIPPY EXPERIENCES you’ll encounter? They’re the heart of this cyberpunk odyssey.Verdict: If you crave a narrative that defies conventions, if you yearn for a game that leaves you questioning reality, dive into this digital maelstrom. Just remember: when you jack into someone’s brain, you’re not just solving a case—you’re rewriting your own destiny.Enjoy the ride, agent. The mind is the ultimate battleground.

_childDocuments_.review: I really loved this game, I played the first version of this, then someone let me know there was a Redux, and WOW.It was hard to understand what to do at points, I will say that.I think this has to be one of the best quality Cyberpunk-ish games so far, in my opinion.I'd really look forward to any more games of this genre by Bloober Team!Amazing work.Gameplay: 6/10Visuals: 9/10Optimization: 10/10 (Ran super well, even on highest settings without DLSS!)Story: 5/10, 8/10 towards the end, the beginning was quite hard to understand what was happening.Sound Design: 6/10 Ambience felt really good, helped me get quite immersed.Controls: 7/10, Very quick to grasp, the way the game just locks your view in some cutscenes was a little jarring though, and when the game gave back the controls to me, it would sometimes rotate in weird ways which made me quite dizzy sometimes, and crouch felt a little slow to toggle.VFX/Post processing: 8/10, I loved the look of the glowing displays a lot (advertisements, signs etc), they quite well delivered that they were hologram based! The camera shaking was VERY jarring though, I personally think the camera could have used less positional shake, and more rotational, as the positional shake really made the motion blur go haywire, and I would miss some things because of it.Overall: 7/10.Definitely will be replaying this a few times.TLDR; Good game, a few small details I didn't like, recommended though.

_childDocuments_.review: I have an obsession with dystopia, particularly of the cybernetic kind. My relationship with sci-fi goes all the way back to early childhood and much of this game resonates with some of the early flagship novels in the grenre.There's just  about the atmosphere of Observer that I find potently spine-tingling. The level design is simple, but elegant in its display of coiled cables and flickering monitors. Just the sight of such a complex infrastructure of tangled wires causes me the slightest bit of distress at the implications of a world in which these sorts of things are standard.The sound, to me, is an electronic masterpiece. The music is just heavy and disjointed enough to make you uneasy, yet simultaneously curious about the environment in which you tread. Acting was overall in the margins of... well, just acceptable. You can tell that Rutger Hauer really tried to give the performance his best despite his old age at the time. He will be missed.It's possible the number of voice actors were limited, because I swear I could hear the same actor pitch-shifting for different characters, which aided in the game's surrealist atmosphere but could get a little too on-the-nose to be believed.Yes, I thought this game was unsettling, but not for its obvious jump-scares, that despite being telegraphed still gave me a fright every damn time. All of the elements that turn what seems to be an ordinary apartment complex into a digital nightmare was what made my stomach tense up. I do love dreamlike, surreal sequences in a variety of artistic media (again, sans the jump-scares), so maybe this aspect already appealed to someone like me. I just appreciated its tone.With all that said, though... the game could be longer. I'd pay extra for more content, no problem, with a preference toward elaborating on the ambiguous ending I got.The story is a bit on-the-rails, but that's kind of what's expected from Bloober. I don't mind it all that much, since I love the atmosphere enough, but once I realized I had wandered into a point-of-no-return, I was disappointed that I couldn't catch up on my side-quests. I didn't realize the story was ending so quickly. I have no issues replaying the game, but some warning would have been appreciated.Hide-and-seek sequences are a little played out(last) and I can do without them at this point in the horror genre. However, this game sort of predates the mundanity of the Chase Sequence, so I forgive it for this. Because games like Alien: Isolation had done it so well, not many have been able to live up to that level of lurking horror for some time now. To my knowledge, anyway.I never had a chance to finish the story when the original version of Observer released, but I'm glad I saw it through to the end in System Redux. I'll be ruminating on its effect on me for some time. I only beg Bloober to make a sequel or some DLC to satisfy my dark cyberpunk itch some more.

name: Yakuza 6: The Song of Life
detailed_description: In Yakuza 6, Kazuma Kiryu will find out exactly how much people are willing to sacrifice for family - be those ties through blood or bond - when he investigates a series of shadowy events that involve the ones he holds closest to his heart. Fresh out of a three-year prison sentence, an older and weathered Kiryu comes to find out that his surrogate daughter, Haruka, has gone missing from the orphanage he looks after. The trail leads him to his old stomping grounds in Kamurocho, where he discovers that she has been struck by a car and now lies in a coma. To make matters worse, Kiryu learns that Haruka now has a son that he must look after. With baby in hand, Kiryu journeys to the seaside town of Onomichi, Hiroshima to unravel the truth about Haruka, her son, and a sinister secret that the Hiroshima yakuza are harboring. From the unparalleled realism of the new setting of Onomichi, a beautiful, sleepy port town in Hiroshima Prefecture, to the latest evolution of Kamurocho, the biggest red-light district in Tokyo, Yakuza 6 is the ultimate iteration the game's blend of gritty crime story, hyper-explosive combat, and all the vices and distractions those locales have to offer. Enter the “Dragon Engine” - Explore the world of Yakuza like never before. Yakuza 6 is the first current-gen Yakuza title that was developed from the ground up for the current-gen hardware, introducing the seedy Japanese underworld with detailed visuals, lifelike animations, a new physics engine, interactive storefronts, seamless transitions and more. Explore Kamurocho Reborn and the Scenic Views of Onomichi - The hypnotic lights, opportunistic inhabitants, and hedonistic distractions of Kamurocho look better than ever. Revamped minigames like karaoke, batting cages, darts, hostesses, and the SEGA arcade have been streamlined for maximum pleasure, and new additions like the RIZAP Gym, Cat Café, and Clan Creator are the purrfect distractions after a long night of bashing heads! But it’s also time to get away from the hustle and bustle of city life to play tourist in beautiful Onomichi. This tranquil coastal community is home to plenty of local activities like bar mingling, spearfishing (think action-packed rail shooter … with fish), and more! Let the Bodies Hit the Floor - Yakuza 6 Kiryu is a 100% certified badass, so that means he’s a battle-hardened veteran when it comes to the art of street fighting. Although he utilizes one fighting style this time around, you best believe Kiryu hits like a truck. Devastating combos and bone-breaking Heat Actions make a return, but now the Dragon of Dojima can fill up a meter to engage Extreme Heat Mode. When activated, Kiryu glows blue and unleashes heavy-damage combos with his fists or any “tool” that’s close at hand. Fully Voiced Japanese Audio - For the first time in series history, every line and piece of dialogue is fully voiced in Japanese. Let the dramatic story and absurd humor of the series unfold like an interactive foreign film experience.

short_description: Step into Japan's criminal underworld in this explosive action brawler starring legendary yakuza, Kazuma Kiryu, who is hellbent on unraveling the truth around his daughter's tragic accident.

_childDocuments_.review: Damn, where to begin?7 games, 930 hours and about a year later here I am at the end of the saga of the Dragon of Dojima. What a journey it has been. Has it been all sunshine and rainbows? Heck no, there were times I cried like a baby, there were times I laughed till it hurt, I still hate fishing with every fibre of my being, and I never ended up learning Mahjong. Still I am so very glad I got here. I will be going through my general opinion on the game. I am by no means a critic and this is purely from a standpoint of someone who loves the story of Kiryu. I will hold it in relevance to all 6 games that comes chronologically before this. (I know Kiwami 2 came after this). I am not going to do a proper Pro and Cons list. I will just list the things of interest that I found:-•	Dragon Engine visually – Kamurocho and Onomichi comes alive with this new engine. Crowds are heavy and always bump into you and I love it. Walking down Tenkaichi Street is nothing new but this time it feels special, the sounds are deafening, the light from signs practically fight with each other to grab your attention. Its amazing. •	Dragon Engine in action – Here is where it all falls apart. Combat looks flashy as hell but lacks impact. Each hit feels like grazing the enemies. The physics are all over the place. A single hit can mess up all of your combos and effects. God forbid if it’s a heavy attack, you will be flopping about like a dead fish. The ragdoll is crazy. Kiryu also feels like he is floating all over the place, there is no weight to his movement in combat. It’s clear they didn’t get the chance to test out the engine before this game like they did with Kenzan for 3 and Ishin for the 0 engines. •	Fully Voiced – For the first time in the series, each and every spoken line is fully voiced. This adds a whole new layer of intimacy to the game and adds a bit more life to the world.•	Kiryu is Kiryu – The Dragon of Dojima has not lost his claws. He proves once again why he is a living legend, the way he does best, beating the ever-living daylights out of everyone. This time, he takes no ♥♥♥♥ from anyone, and I love it so very much. •	Green Exp – The green xp will be the bane of your existence. •	A LOT of cut content – I mean a LOT LOT. If you are like me and have come through 0, Kiwami, Kiwami 2, 3, 4 and 5, you will notice it in an instant. Here are some of them – o	No weapons – You can no longer carry weapons on you. All you can use are the ones you find during fights. Lame.o	No Armour Sets – Gone are the old armour sets which gave you any set bonuses, heck there are barely any accessory item with significant boosts, its all just stat boosts. Also you get 2 Accessory slots, that’s it. o	No Masters – Maybe a good thing, maybe not. You choose.o	Blocked Map areas – The entirety of Park Boulevard (The street in front of Kamurocho Hills) and the Champion District are blocked off. Dude why? It’s the last time I get to walk about as Kiryu, let me have the whole map. I would have loved to just sit down and have a drink one last time at Earth Angel. The okama has been there since 0.o	No gambling – With Park Boulevard blocked off Ryugajou is off limits. So no gambling.o	No Purgatory – I has vanished. I am not kidding; it has just straight up vanished. In fact, neither Purgatory or The Florist is ever even mentioned once. So, you guessed it, no Coliseum either. o	No Locker Keys – You no longer get to pick up the billion keys you used to before. So, there are no cheat items either.•	Messed up map – The map is all over the place. The streets are not where they used to be, buildings have also moved all over the place. I know that doesn’t sound like much but I practically had Kamurocho memorised like the back of my hand and now it’s all different so it feels weird.•	Reduced Substories – You get a grand total of 51 substories which is tiny compared to older games. •	Drinks – Vending machine drinks are quite useful in a pinch early on. Problem is, you buy one and you can't store it, you carry it on your hand, and you have to drink it as you buy it. No keeping it for when you need it. Kiwami 2 fixed that but come on, story wise it was 4 games ago. •	A billion pockets – You no longer have to worry about inventory management on what to bring with you to battles, every kind of item is available for you to use. They are all there, only you get a certain amount of each kind. •	Restricted Moveset – Heat Actions, which are the staple of the series are very limited than what Kiryu had access to in older games. Also, most of your Heat actions wont work unless you invoke Extreme Heat which is stupid. That means you will have to repeat the same 4 or 5 heat actions unless you activate Extreme Heat. •	Amon – Gone are the days when you had to complete all substories to get to fight Amon. That was the testament to your dedication to the game. Now you can fight Amon only after finishing 2 specific substories. Yes, just 2. You can just ignore all others. Now, Story wise I will not spoil anything. Its touching, not the best, 0 has that spot, but its not that bad. It follows the Yakuza tradition of taking a word and hammering it in your skull over and over. 0 had ‘Empty Lot’, 4 had ‘Rubber bullets’, 5 had ‘Dreams’ and this game has ‘Secret’.There are a lot of important recurring characters missing. If this is supposed to be Kiryu’s swan song, I would have loved to see some of the characters that we have spent so much time with. No Komaki, no Florist, No Tojo allies, no Kazuki, no Kamiyama, no Minamida to name a few. Sure, don’t give them full-fledged mechanics, but let me have a substory with each of them, to say goodbye to the allies and bonds we formed over 10 years of Kiryu’s life. But hey, we do get our blazer wearing kicky boi, Akiyama so that’s a blessing.However, that one this I will say is that WHERE IS MAJIMA?We went from Majima Everywhere to Majima Nowhere. Till 3 he was such and important character, a flip side to Kiryu’s coin but it’s a shame that from 4 he starts to appear less and less. Here he is there for 2 minutes during the Prologue and 2 minutes in the Epilogue. That is. THAT’S IT? I figured after 0 they would have realised just how popular he is but no. So if you expected the Dragon of Dojima and the Mad Dog of Shimano, two legends that you have been playing as and following since they were 20, to fight side by side one last time, sucks to be you.  All in all, it’s a decent game, nothing ground breaking nor something to hate. It’s the end of a saga of a beloved character and I am happy we get to see it through. I would give this game a generous 8/10, but that may be tinted by my love for Kiryu and the whole series. Play the game, laugh, feel excited, angry and then cry. Let the credits roll. Then load up Premium Adventure. Walk around Kamurocho in that grey suit one last time. See the city you have walked through for countless hours before this, fought in, fought for, bled for, played though and lived though, one last time though Kiryu’s eyes. Once you are satisfied, head to Karaokekan, choose TONIGHT, sing it, see the pictures of a young Kiryu and Nishiki and let it take you back to the memories of Yakuza 0, back in 1988, where this journey began. So long Dragon, thank you for everything!

_childDocuments_.review: This. Is. The. End.6 mainline titles, 3 spin offs, 9 games in total and more than a decade of hard work and dedication has finally come to an end for The Dragon of Dojima's final chapter. This game has blown me away into an emotional wreck. The journey I've been through, the friends I've met along the way (part of the Yakuza community and in-game), the time and energy put into experiencing Kiryu's journey was all worth it, every second of it. From a young, Yakuza climbing the ranks in hoping to succeed in the Yakuza world to becoming a loving father figure who's down to die for his family. The Yakuza franchise is by far the best franchise of ALL time due to the sheer amount of emotion and wild rides it takes you on. Everything about Yakuza 6 was INCREDIBLE, there wasn't a single flaw for me. I loved it from the beginning to the very end.This is Kiryu's final chapter, cherish it like nothing before.

_childDocuments_.review: the game can made a man laugh as loud as a man doesand cry as hard as a man does.Edit: It has been around 22+ hours so i think it is safe to say that i can give my complete opinion. Do note that this is my personal opinion.PROS:The first impression i get is that how the graphic aspect of the game is so beautiful, the "new" dragon engine really brings Kiryu and the life around him to life. I can't help myself having one of my hand standby on the F12 button to capture all the amazing scenes as much as i can. The environtment is nice, i love how beautiful both the modern Kamurocho and the laid back seaside Onomichi is. They really done a great job on giving them appeal. My favorite are the Kamuro Theater and Little AsiaNext one is how the story is really touching.  I really like this approach like how they touches more on Kiryu's human side in 3. Or to be exact they call back that side in Yakuza 6. And with the Dragon Engine graphic helping the storytelling even more touching with the details on Kiryu's eyes in the cutscenes. I can feel his emotion (thus my first review). Aside from that they also manage to balance between the drama, action, and comedy part of the story. Making it really engaging.Gameplay wise i love it. Fighting is trickier in here but also still fun (im around 200-ish stats and the random battles are still quite tricky at times), the ragdoll is hillarious, Eventhough the heat-mode isn't as over the top as previous title, the battle are still a fun to do. Also the best part is how we can smoothly get into building now, and even bring the fight into the innocent stores, then we cant use the store and get "kicked out". Maybe many didnt like this, but its hilarious to me every time.Minigame wise it never a letdown for Yakuza series honestly. there's Dart (my favorite), Baseball (it become my favorite too), the arcade games, karaoke, cabaret dating, SPEAR FISHING (dont miss it), and a "dad hanging out with dads" simulation. Even clan creator which i didnt really like in Kiwami 2, i like it here (although aside from the gameplay, theres another reason) I didnt need to say many thing here i guess other than, its Yakuza. Substories, i love the substories (or stories) that ties into Clan creator and baseball team. The clan creator maybe im just too biased because they include NJPW's top wrestler to participate in the story and we can fight them  (both in Clan Creator and after fist-to-fist). But the baseball one, i have the urge to help the team build their roster and made them the "champion" (though i havent progress enough at this point because i need wait to return to Kamurocho to finish some of the fetching member quest then come back to day time Onomichi). I feel the baseball team story and minigame really adds a lot narrative wise and gameplay wise.CONS:alright, first thing first is i understand that they have limited time and resource to develop this game, but i think it can be better.First up is the map, i dissapointed that this is probably the least of Kamurocho we possibly have. The underground portion of it are completely ommited (aside for one tunnel for plot wise). Champion District and West Park area (Kamurocho Hills?) are also blocked completely (but at least they have a reason for this). For the lack of overground area (similar to 4) i didnt really mind because they compensate by letting us explore the buildings inside and i dont really like 4's overground anyways. I mostly dissapointed with the ommision of the underground area because i felt it become a very missed opportunity to bring more life into Yakuza 6's kamurocho.Next one is the substory. Although i still enjoy it, it still kinda dissapointing that we have less, and it also not a lot is a hilarious diversion from Yakzua 6's story. Also how we cant move from Kamurocho to Onomichi freely. Later in Kiwami 2 they fix this by allowing us to switch city by taxi before premium adventure. Though this is a minor issue, still kinda infuriating that i must made the story move on before i can bring Saigo his Tonkotsu Bento lol. Another slightly infuriating thing is that how Onomichi has not much thing to do especially at night. (Yes its more like myself nitpicking for the cons part lol)Overall, i love the game. _childDocuments_.review: Overall: 8/10Story:Yakuza 6: The Song of Life delivers one of the series' most personal and intimate stories, standing out as a refreshing shift in tone and scope. The smaller, tighter narrative feels especially well-paced, particularly coming right off Y5’s sprawling, often bloated storyline. Here, there’s little to no filler, and the story unfolds with a clear focus that avoids the labyrinthine web of twists that defined the PS3-era games. The twists that DO appear felt impactful and well-executed, providing intrigue without feeling overwhelming.I thought that the central mystery of Onomichi and its “secret” was a very cool plot element without feeling unrealistically spectacular. As someone who loves history and alternative history, I found this plotline deeply engaging. Initially, I thought the Hirose Family would be knockoffs of Y3’s Ryudo Family, but they quickly proved to be their own unique group. The game invests time in showing, not telling, why you should care about them. Their individuality, chemistry, and balance of humorous and heroic moments make them some of the most captivating new characters in recent entries.However, while it was nice to see fresh, memorable faces, I felt that Y6 fell short as "the end of Kiryu's saga" when it came to the series' staple characters. Additionally, the finale itself, while thematically appropriate, lacked the spectacular, cathartic energy typical of Yakuza climaxes. Finally, the ending left me unsatisfied. Gameplay:Y6 marks a major turning point for the series as the first game built on the Dragon Engine, and it shows in both its strengths and weaknesses. One of the best features is the ragdoll physics, which i prefer over YK2's, as they feel far more weighty and grounded here. Every punch, throw, and collision has a visceral sense of impact that adds to the immersion, though the game is not without its flaws.Unfortunately, the combat variety takes a hit. While I may be in the minority that actually enjoys Kiryu's early Dragon Engine combat (despite them nerfing Tiger Drop), Y6 does severely lack the plethora of Heat Actions you'd expect by this point in the series. While the Heat Actions that are present are undeniably cool, they are pretty much the same as in YK2 and the Extreme Heat Actions feel pretty unrewarding, leaving the gameplay feeling somewhat repetitive. This is also the debut of Extreme Heat Mode, which should have been a game-changer; However, it also feels much weaker and less satisfying than in YK2. The combat often feels designed around Extreme Heat, but its underwhelming implementation leaves much to be desired. Additionally, the bounce-back mechanic when attacking a blocking enemy is just as irritating as it was in YK2.On a more positive note, the Dragon Engine introduces several quality-of-life improvements. Random encounter enemies are now marked on the minimap, making it far easier to avoid unwanted fights. When you do engage in these battles, the transitions are seamless and natural, eliminating the jarring load screen/setup of previous entries. Y6 also introduces the hunger system previously seen in YK2.My favorite gameplay highlight of Y6 is certainly its fully voice-acted substories, which is a first and only for the series. This elevates the storytelling and makes every side quest more engaging to experience. It’s a shame, though, that the game lacks some of the best minigames from the series. The absence of staples like gambling, fishing, bowling, and others is a glaring omission that detracts from the overall experience.World:Y6 does an excellent job of breathing new life into its world, delivering a mix of nostalgia, innovation, and detailed immersion. While it’s a bit disappointing to lose access to certain parts of the map that we’ve explored in previous games, I personally feel like Kamurocho makes up for it with its vibrancy and attention to detail. The sheer number of enterable locations brings a living vibe to the city that surpasses even YK2. There’s just something special about returning to familiar locations with updated graphics. After playing through Yakuza 3, 4, and 5, stepping back into Kamurocho feels like visiting an old hometown, but it's now shining brighter and more alive than ever. The visual fidelity in Y6 is very fun to explore, as every neon-lit street corner and gritty alleyway feel more immersive than before.Onomichi, while not my favorite city in the series, deserves recognition for the variety and character it adds to the game and to the Yakuza universe as a whole. Its charm lies in its slower, more intimate atmosphere, providing a contrast to Kamurocho's urban chaos. It might not top my personal list of favorite cities, but I can’t deny how much it enriches the game’s universe and narrative.One of the most significant innovations in Y6’s world design is the seamless transitions between interiors and exteriors. For the first time in the series (and chronologically, the first since YK2), moving in and out of buildings happens without loading screens. This feature not only enhances immersion but also makes exploration smoother, more engaging and more natural.Visuals:Despite Y6's status as the engine's debut, the game delivers visuals that are nothing short of stunning. From the vibrant streets of Kamurocho to the serene beauty of Onomichi, every environment is brought to life with incredible detail. The lighting, reflections, and environmental textures all work together to create a level of immersion that's breathtaking, making it feel like you’re truly walking through these beautiful cities.One of Yakuza's long-standing strengths is its masterfully crafted cutscenes, and Y6 proudly upholds this tradition. The cinematic sequences are impeccably directed, with a level of polish and attention to detail that rivals films. The character models are rendered with extraordinary care, capturing subtle facial expressions and emotions that elevate the storytelling to another level. Music/Sound Design:The OST is an absolutely underrated gem in the series, delivering a perfect blend of emotional depth and high-energy tracks. The music elevates every moment and perfectly captures the game's themes of family, sacrifice, and resilience. The sound design is immaculate too, with ambient city noises and impactful fight effects immersing you in Kamurocho and Onomichi like never before. "Destiny" is one of my favorite songs in the whole series, and for me, the OST is probably one of the best in the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: I've finally finished the Kiryu Saga, including Like a Dragon, and I can safely say that Yakuza 6 is a fitting end to the beloved Dragon of Dojima. Yakuza 6 is way more self contained than the previous entries and features two playable cities, Kamurocho and Onomichi, both which are beautifully recreated in the first ever rendition of Dragon Engine. The game feels modern both in terms of the setting and gameplay as it now has autosave, smoother animations and photorealistic graphics while the combat has been simplified, which could be a con for people who were used to Yakuza 0/Kiwami/5's combat system. The story itself is straightforward, without the unnecessary twists and turns that we've experienced from Yakuza 3-5 and the new characters are quite likeable. Yakuza 6 also brings new mini-games to the series along with interesting sub-stories that'll make you go "WTF?!?".Overall I enjoyed my time with it and I can't wait for Judgment on Steam, SEGA PLS.

_childDocuments_.review: So my time with Yakuza finally ends.  After 8 games on PC, I’m caught up and ready for wherever the series will take the player in the future.  While Judgement and now Lost Judgement is hopefully coming to PC, for the moment I’ve arrived at the temporary end of the journey. And Yakuza 6 ends what I consider the main arc of the franchise, ending the games that star Kiryu Kazuma in one final epic tale, at least that was the hope. Yakuza 6 is probably not what fans expected, and unfortunately may not be what fans want, but many issues with Yakuza 6 come from this potentially being the final time players take on the role of Kiryu Kazuma in the franchise. With Yakuza 0 releasing the year before Yakuza 6, players now had taken on the role of Kiryu in six previous titles, each time Kiryu finds a new way to get involved with major conflicts that trouble the Tojo clan.  Yet in Yakuza 6, while the Tojo is important to the story, pretty much everything the series has built up about the Tojo Clan, and the Omi Alliance is wiped away or ignored. Instead, Yakuza 6 revolves around a new group, the Yomei Alliance, and while this new organization does have an interesting and unique story, it struggles when compared to a group that players have been associated with for so many games. It also doesn’t help that the first half of Yakuza 6 focuses quite a bit on a new baby in Kiryu’s life.  A baby who appears to be born to a certain character and in a very un-Yakuza-like fashion is proven correct, rather than being a mysterious plot point. Much of Yakuza shoots straight. X person appears to be married to Y person, that can’t be… except it is and it’s just treated as fact.  The baby is found with Z.  And sure enough, Z’s the mother. It’s a shame because the Yakuza series has found ways to tell and experience complex stories that surprise players, but Yakuza 6 seems happy just to tell a straightforward story, and it loses something important for the series. That’s not to say there are no big reveals or bombastic moments.  Once the game gets going, the final third of the story is one giant roller coaster, but the problem is that the first two-thirds are dry mostly because Yakuza 6 has to establish new characters, relationships, locations, and storylines which feel all unnecessary considering the wealth of history this series can draw from.About half of Yakuza 6 occurs in a town called Onomichi, located in Hiroshima, and while Kiryu returns to Kamurocho often, it’s not the Kamurocho that fans remember.  Part of the reason is the upgrade to the new Dragon Engine, but the other more important side is that the Tojo Clan and friends Kiryu has made over the six games are suddenly absent. Daigo Dojima and Majima Goro are fan favorites and neither character gets more than a couple of minutes of screen time.  Worse, there are side characters from previous games that get more development such as Yuya, the host of Stardust.  But even those characters only appear for a couple of minutes apiece.  The lack of core characters that have been series staples is noticeable, but it also contributes to the fact that Yakuza 6 spends so long introducing its new setting because that’s where the story will take place. This is only made worse by the fact that Yakuza 7, also known as Yakuza Like a Dragon has a more appropriate story for Yakuza 6, and includes those characters that fans want to see even though that game has a brand new protagonist.  Yakuza 7’s story is the story that should be in Yakuza 6 and where Yakuza 6 attempts to branch out, Yakuza 6 fails because it also attempts to give a final game to Kiryu, but even in this, it feels like it’s all stuff we’ve seen before. Without spoilers, I can’t say too much, but the ending of Yakuza 6 upset me mostly because it was predictable, and something I had already seen twice in this series. With that said, Yakuza 6 still has a typical Yakuza story, which contains all the same elements, and while it focuses on a new group, the Yomei Alliance, Yakuza 6 still keeps fans interested. The story for Yakuza 6 is well told and works perfectly well, involving many groups.  The problem is it never really feels like Kiryu’s story.  Where Kiryu has a tie to the Tojo which explains his participation, it almost feels like Kiryu forces his way into the major conflict here and should have been rejected, even with his history from the previous games.  At the same time, Yakuza 6 is a major accomplishment for the gameplay.  While Yakuza 0 and Kiwami were previously on the Dragon Engine, Yakuza 6 was on a vastly improved Dragon Engine and is unbelievably smooth.  There are no loading times or broken-up scenes when it can be avoided.  Walking into most buildings is a single continuous shot as is battle. and the battle system feels far more fluid than ever. There’s a huge technical step up for Yakuza 6, and it’s a noticeable one, though there are limitations, most noticeably, some sections of Kamurocho is “locked off” and players are unable to venture into the Champion District or the north end of Kamurocho, which is a strange limitation since it’s just a single block along the top of the map, that is blocked off for no reason. Yakuza 6’s battle system feels excellent as well.  This is familiar territory for fans of the series, though the battles will feel slower at first. By the end of the game, the Yakuza 6 battle system feels excellent, though the combat in Yakuza 6 is frightfully easy, playing on hard I only had to continue a couple of times in the entire game, and abusing health restorative medicines would remove even that difficulty.  But after the previous games, much of Yakuza 6’s systems are what people will expect.  Sidestories are back to distract and entertain the player like always, though similar to the writing many of them feel like they’re lacking the level of depth as the previous games.  However to even find many of them will take a decent amount of time, and some of them are linked to side activities. Where Yakuza 2 was stuffed with side activities, and Yakuza 5 had so many they were forced into the story, Yakuza 6 seems to take the right approach of having so many activities players might miss, but not required.  I missed one of the large activities of building a baseball team until after finishing the game, and once I found it, I enjoyed it immensely.  Clan Creator, which is also playable in Yakuza Kiwami 2, was introduced in Yakuza 6, and it’s also another side activity that will require hours of work but is an enjoyable form of a real-time strategy game.   There is also a drinking discussion mini-game, a workout simulator, and even a strange online chatting mini-game where Kiryu ends up typing “BOOOOOOBS” and I still can’t believe that isn’t fan-fiction. But ultimately Yakuza 6 gameplay is the culmination of a decade of games at that point.  Yakuza 6 is what players have come to expect from Yakuza’s style, large worlds, tons of different stories, and variety where players can stumble on something new.   From the gameplay perspective Yakuza 6 succeeds. But that expectation is a double-edged sword because Yakuza 6 fails to deliver what is important to fans, a satisfying ending for Kiryu’s arc, and what’s particularly strange is that it’s clear RGG made the game to give Kiryu a send-off but then didn’t make an attempt to make that sendoff particularly poignant or tie in with the series as a whole. What a shame and missed opportunity in Yakuza 6, yet I still enjoyed my time with it.  I’ve thought a lot about my score and for Yakuza 6, I’m going to give it an arbitrary 7/10.  Yakuza 6 probably deserves an 8, it’s a solid game, and if you’ve enjoyed this series there’s no reason to stop at the previous game, but Yakuza 6, fails to give fans what they deserve and it fumbles what should be either closure or a continuation of the Kiryu Saga.
