_childDocuments_.review: I'll review the story for this game. The gameplay itself is fine. All the Yakuza games are good. I can't not recommend this to a fan of the series. Combat is neutered, but it flows well. There's less minigames, but the ones that are back have gotten an overhaul and are more fun than they were before. Instead, let's talk about the story.Without giving anything away: it's a mess, plain and simple. But it didn't  to be a mess. There's some things this story does right. Let's rewind back to 2005: Yakuza is released. The story is very personal. The Yakuza/real world politics take a backseat to the relationship between Kiryu, Nishiki, and the other cast members. The stakes Kiryu has to face are personal, they involve people he consider his own family and even the woman he loves. Things are constantly moving, it's never stuck in one spot with a bunch of executives and Yakuza big shots dumping exposition on you for what feels like an eternity. This approach continued for Y2.Then Y3 happened. And that's when the plots started getting  political. The CIA, the military-industrial complex, the cops, politicians...all of it is based on real-world events happening in Japan at the time, which is kinda cool, but that doesn't make for the most exciting story, and unless you're actually Japanese, it's not going to do anything for you. Kiryu had the orphanage and all its drama, so they  tried to add personal stakes, but starting here, said stakes really took a backseat to the overarching political drama involving the criminal underworld. Yakuza started out feeling like they meant for it to have mainstream worldwide appeal, but I guess when it didn't, they went all-in on the Japanese aspect of it. This continued into Y4 and Y5, the latter of which had so little in the way of anything for the player to actually give a ♥♥♥♥ about that your eyes will glaze over while playing. It still had very likable characters, like Saejima and especially Akiyama, but the things they do in the story don't actually involve them on a personal level, and there's not much character development for them.But then, Y0 was released. Sega's last-ditch effort to appeal to the American market. A fresh start for our characters, an appealing setting, a new (amazing) localization, and dialing things back to Y1's storytelling. And wow, it paid off. There are so many fans that consider it the best story in the entire series, that they were invested in what was going on, and while Kiryu's half still had a fair bit of politics in it, they didn't overstay their welcome, and his relationship with Nishiki and Kuze were enough to pull it through. And Majima's half was just fantastic, there was romance, real character development, loss, redemption, tragedy, a true hero's journey. THIS is the stuff Western fans want in their stories, and what was missing from the games for so long: So now we arrive at Y6. The writers at Sega have seemingly learned their lesson, and are going to add some real emotion and interpersonal drama between the cast this time. The Yakuza are no longer the subject of the story, it is simply the context. Except, not really. It takes one step forward, and two steps back. They learned the wrong lessons from Y0's success. They tried to do what Y1 and Y0 did and have a new plot, new setting, a new cast, and few returning characters. Ok, well, here's the problem there: this is Kiryu's swan song. This was consistently marketed as the big finale, the culmination of a journey Kiryu's had for 10 years. He's had an (adopted) daughter, he's raised a bunch of kids in an orphanage, he's singlehandedly taken down several organizations and saved not only the Tojo Clan but Japan itself multiple times. He has met and become close friends with a lot of people in that time.So he gets closure with all those people, right? I mean, this is Kiryu's final game. You want it to tie up all loose ends and see all your favorite characters back for one last showdown, the most fan-satisfying conclusion possible, right? Well, forget it. All those characters you like? Majima, Saejima, Daigo, the kids, even freaking Haruka? They're not present for 90% of the plot. Some have no interaction with Kiryu at all, and the ones that do were never  close to Kiryu. You get Akiyama and Date. That's it. And Akiyama feels like an afterthought, he never feels like he needs to be there. Even series mainstays don't show up at all. Where's the Florist? Where's Komaki? Where's Hana?Instead, you have new characters, the Hirose family and a woman in Hiroshima. I like them well enough, especially Beat Takeshi's character. They're certainly more likable and deep than a lot of other Yakuza characters over the years. But they're the kind of characters they should've been saving for a spinoff or a prequel or Y7 or  other than Kiryu's big finale. There's a new villain who's fantastic and could've easily been the main conflict and the final boss, but he gets shafted halfway through for a villain who doesn't parallel anything about Kiryu's character at all.But I'd be fine with that. I'd be fine with the new characters and making it mostly about Kiryu himself, if it wasn't  It really, really tries to humanize Kiryu and make the conflicts in the story more relatable. He suddenly realizes he's a grandfather, has to take care of a baby, and his daughter is missing. That's a great setup for a Yakuza story. It had a lot of mystery and intrigue into what was going on. There were new twists at every turn, and questions kept getting answered with more questions. I was confident that the game would answer all of them by the end, but boy was I wrong. By the last third, the story gets so convoluted, so confusing, so political, that I just stopped caring. It keeps throwing new, exciting setpieces at you, but they're fleeting.Hitchcock once described so many films as being just "photographs of people talking" with very little cinematic camera work. For a game that prides itself on being like a Japanese crime movie, there's very little cinema going on here. Scenes just go on and on and on with static camera angles of characters dumping so much exposition on you, I mean good god. It got to the point where I was speedreading and skipping through the dialogue not even bothering for the voice acting to catch up. Another thing is that it feels like 20 pages of the script got cut out. I won't spoil one of the game's biggest twists, but a major character is ruined in a way that absolutely should not have gotten past an editor, with their actions never being explained nor justified despite so many characters bringing them up, and it made me want to pull my hair out. They added romance as an element, except the romance here was just creepy and awkward.All that makes me want to call this the worst story in the franchise, but I can't, next to Y4 and Y5, because there are moments where I actually found myself invested. I cared about a lot of these new characters, and I cared about Kiryu, enough that by the end, I got choked up, purely because they injected real, relatable emotion into it and had that emotion explode on-screen. When the cinematics are good in this game, they're  good. And if none of the other characters were treated well, Kiryu totally was. His ending was fitting for him.Basically, Y6's story left me conflicted on whether to feel satisfied or not at its conclusion. It's inconsistent, and convoluted, and yet it has more personal stakes and emotional storytelling than anything in Y3-Y5. It feels like it deserved a lot better than what we got. This, plus the lack of returning cast members, can probably be attributed to Sega's budget being blown on the Dragon Engine, which while technically impressive was not worth sacrificing the game's story (nor its gameplay for that matter, which I can't go into much here due to character limits).

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this for the most part, but I think that mostly has to do with the narrative, characters, the fidelity of the Dragon Engine and just the simple fact that it's another Yakuza game on PC.However, In terms of gameplay I had some frustrations. The dragon engine's combat has received quite a lot of criticism from the Yakuza community, and I don't want to repeat all of that, but the short story is that there is much less variety than in previous games, as well as the physics not always working properly. I don't exactly know how to explain, and I am sorry for these vague generalities, but...the combat just seems so awkward at times. Like attacks sometimes don't connect, you grab an enemy and start swinging it, but for some reason Kyriu will drop him, etc.What really angered me, were some of the moments where the game wouldn't register my inputs. This was especially infuriating during the final boss (no spoilers) where he grabs you and you have to mash A to get out of that grab. For some reason the game wouldn't register my inputs during the grab and I ended up having to watch helplessly, as the Dragon of Dojima got slowly beaten to death. So I had to make sure to avoid that attack at all costs, otherwise, it was basically a one-shot game over screen. Did anyone else have the same problem? Do let me know pleaseOther than that, I really enjoyed the story and the substories as well, but the side activities were a mixed bag. The dragon engine looks great, Kamurocho is BEAUTIFUL, especially at night, and this game does not have the same weird green filter, that Kiwami 2 has. What I commend SEGA for, is having dropped the price of the game to 20 EUR, I think that was a very consumer friendly move from their part.Overall I do recommend this game, but mostly just for you to experience the final chapter of the Dragon of Dojima. Man what a great feeling that now all of the Kyriu-saga games are on Steam. Now, SEGA...

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 6 marks the end of Kiryu’s journey as the protagonist of the series. This is the finale of nearly 30 years of game events, Kiryu’s sendoff party, as well as the first steps of the new Dragon Engine. Although there are definitely some missteps in this elaborate dance, the underlying song that guides the game is very bittersweet yet enthralling. This entry’s story is centered around the aftermath of Haruka’s actions at the end of Yakuza 5 and the appearance of a mysterious baby. Yakuza 6 is a much more personal story revolving around Kiryu and the ones he loves. It’s up to him to solve the mystery, traveling to Onomichi, Hiroshima to track down the baby’s family and getting caught up in Tojo Clan drama all over again in the process. The baby’s origin is inexorably linked to multiple crime syndicates; dredging for the truth further fans the flames of war between them. Overall, I liked the story, but felt that the truth bomb of the baby’s origin and some other plot points were confusing or weird. The new characters as a whole were pretty good although some could have been fleshed out a bit more aside from being “stone-cold boss” or “suddenly the smart one.” The pacing was okay overall, moving at a fairly consistent rate so you don’t get bogged down too often while playing. The only real exception is the late-game exposition dumps to fill in the gaps the mystery left behind. As the subtitle implies, the game’s main themes are of:  With this in mind, a baby is the perfect symbol. Kiryu makes sacrifices to ensure the baby is safe and can grow up normally, his struggles are what make the story really engaging. I do think that the story is good but not as good as the previous games. Yakuza 6 makes various tweaks to the formula but not all are for the better. One of the biggest changes is how combat plays out. Kiryu has some new moves but has also been stripped of some. He can now parry attacks, then do a counter Heat action. However, he lacks Heat actions against grounded enemies, a series staple. Other Heat moves were also removed and input windows are a bit finicky. Similarly, new move Revelations and any trainers (such as the beloved Komaki) are notably absent. Nonetheless, Extreme Heat mode, a temporary powered-up state, gives access to some exclusive Heat moves if you have them unlocked. EH mode also has new QTE attacks if you hit an enemy enough, dealing good damage but reducing the gauge significantly.  The XP system has been completely redone. There are now 5 different types of experience, each corresponding to a color. You now have more freedom in choosing upgrades (including baseline stats) but need the associated amount of each type of XP to purchase it. However, XP distribution is very uneven. The first 3 types are overly abundant, whereas the last 2 require quite a bit of intentional grinding to get. This got annoying in the late game where upgrade costs skyrocketed.  Actual combat was surprisingly consistent due to the enemy AI being pretty competent. They dodge and block frequently which prevents you from spamming attacks brainlessly. Their ability to swarm and overwhelm you is also dangerous as you can get stunlocked fairly easily. The average enemy count is also higher overall, basic street fights usually having 5 or so enemies at once even in early game. Story encounters can also have at least 10 or so in a given encounter room. Nonetheless, having basic enemies consistently stop your combos with blocking and having to face multiple at once definitely gets annoying. However, since enemies have only one health bar, encounters can also be ended quickly. This is especially so if you max out attack and stack attack-boosting equipment.    In terms of other gameplay elements, I felt the game was a bit lacking. Portable weapons and crafting are gone. Gear has been nerfed a bit; you only get two slots instead of three, but can stack armor-type gear. Some minigames were removed, reportedly due to engine problems (e.g. bowling). Likewise, some staples, such as the coliseum and western gambling, are absent for some reason. There are fewer substories (sidequests) overall but most were good. The RTS-lite Clan Creator, baseball sim, bar chats and other new minigames were okay but don't fill the hole enough.I finished the story around 27-ish hours, including grinding and most substories, so the game is a bit short. Granted, going for 100% will likely take significantly longer. Overall, you’ll definitely get the Yakuza experience, but Six fails to live up to the rather high standards Zero sets.    One thing the Dragon Engine does fantastically is the visuals. The overall quality is superb and truly feels like a step-up like for the series in almost all areas, especially Zero which came out before this one. Kamurocho and Onomichi look breathtaking in the pre-rendered scenes as well as when walking about. Pre-rendered faces are absolutely insane in terms of detail; it is really close to photo-realism at times, and the facial animations are great. In-engine cutscenes are a bit iffy, however. Mouth movement/ lip sync can be laughably bad and having characters with almost perfectly still faces and default breathing animations talk to each other is disappointing. Overall animations and VFX were really good though.  The series retains its strong sound design here as well. The voice acting is superb for the main characters and really helped sell them. There is also considerably more voice acting available, which is a big step for the series and made the world feel more alive. Child VA in some substories was a bit dodgy, as they sounded older than the models looked. Overall SFX were great - combat felt weighty and cities felt alive. The music was also very strong with a pretty nice selection of genres and instruments. Boss themes definitely stood out, giving each encounter some great depth. I had some weirdness with the Discord overlay and launching initially, but no other issues afterwards. The game also features a nice variety of graphical options to tweak things to your liking. I averaged 60 FPS or above consistently.  Despite hearing that 6 was the worst in the series, I was surprised at how good it actually was. All the hallmarks of a Yakuza game are present: gritty crime-drama story, wacky and light-hearted substories, and fun overall gameplay. However, the overall package lacked impact due to the aforementioned issues; writing issues, removed content, and altered combat were my biggest gripes. Nonetheless, the overall game was a fun ride. While not the ideal conclusion to the Kiryu saga, it was gratifying to see him off from the series and get closure on his story.

Kiryu has to atone yet anew for his sins, washing himself clean for a different future however we all know how that always ended up like. Many of the major characters are showcased through a strenuous stage some even unable to do anything meaningful but let time pass. Visually it's pure enjoyment to see Kamurocho again in Dragon Engine, the details are staggering with few words being able to describe it both in Kamurocho's glamour and Onomichi's nature & ocean. It takes a while to get everything started in Yakuza 6 amidst very uncertain tragedies that seem to not stop, after you learn enough and begin another arc of being a lone wolf as usual you'll see the akin Yakuza 3 setup where you one way or another are being introduced to a far away independent family. It's do or die.The sound design feels a ton more personal indicating the weight of any decision being made or unmade, can't go back to past to undo nothing. OST as always top notch completely fitting the atmosphere & mood at all times. Combat is extremely fluid even though it doesn't involve 4 stances like in the first two installments the new heat mechanic can make you an unstoppable fury, containing intense, diverse & flat out fatal volleys. Clan Creator is also making its debut with absolutely over the top hilarious but believable characters and their sincere & savage battles, advancing past adversities and realizing the true meaning of each one's path. Nothing more to be said and done, incredibly long adventure of everyone to conclude a worthwhile exit.- visuals & artwork- characters & story- OST & ambience design- voice acting quality- hostess dialogue massive improvement- unsynced minigames

_childDocuments_.review: In Yakuza 6: The Song of Life we once again take on the role of the protagonist Kiryu Kazuma, who has spent the past three years in prison. He voluntarily took this upon himself so that his foster daughter Haruka could live a peaceful life. His ties to the yakuza in particular did not make this easy. So a break was bitterly necessary. Actually, after the three years, everything should finally be fine, but as fate would have it, it is not quite so easy to escape the clutches of the underworld.One look at the protagonist's face reveals that this game is all about aging. If Kazuma still looked blood-young and swashbuckling in the 80s of Yakuza 0, deep wrinkles have now formed around his eyes, which look tired and have seen a lot in the meantime. After all, Yakuza 0 and Yakuza 6 are about three decades apart in the game.After the events of Yakuza 5, Kazuma has spent three years in prison, but he learns just how quickly the world can move on when he is released: his foster daughter Haruka has since become a pop idol as well as a mother, and has a son named Haruto. Hard for Kazuma to imagine, since the last time they met she still seemed like a child herself.However, the reunion celebration with the offspring comes to nothing, because Haruka was hit by an unknown person. The hit-and-run driver, the mother in a coma, and the father of the bundle of joy have also disappeared. Kazuma doesn't believe it was an accident, and a thrilling detective story unfolds in search of the lost father and the background of the suspected attack. Did someone want to take revenge on Kazuma from his criminal past?You don't only get experience after fights, pretty much every action, such as eating, throws off the coveted points. A hunger indicator provides additional motivation to settle down in the lovingly designed food temples of Japan (just like Yakuza Kiwami 2). You get bonuses on regeneration or experience points when you fill your stomach. If you want to do without, however, you won't have to endure an annoying hunger warning message, so you won't be forced to spend money on treats. Other sources of experience points are side quests, mini-games and progressing through the main story. On top of that, there are plenty of challenges that land in your points account in the form of a reward when you reach certain milestones. These range from conventional, passively achievable goals like "run a certain distance" to "hit ten home runs".Gameplay and side activities in Yakuza 6 are unsurprisingly similar to the predecessors. In comparatively small, but extremely detailed and convincingly designed areas you'll fight with brawling drunkards or gang members, meet attractive hostesses, sing karaoke, gamble in arcades or devote yourself to games like mahjong. You'll also now manage an amateur baseball team and build your own street gang in a sort of real-time tactics mode. The former, unsurprisingly, is primarily of interest to those who are familiar with the sport. Only when it's your turn do you have anything to do in this mini-game, the rest of the innings run automatically and are presented in simple cartoon graphics. The Clan mini-game, on the other hand, is more crowd-pleasing; you recruit new "heroes" by defeating crooks lurking around the game world, who join you from then on. From the bird's eye view, you'll send your men towards the enemies, accessing different fighter classes. You can give special orders to the heroes, the cannon fodder acts fully automatically and attacks what is near it. You can still meet hostesses and get closer to them in conversations. This time, you choose from conversation cards at the bottom of the screen and build up combos that increase your partner's affection bar. In Arcades you'll once again play classics like Outrun, in the gym you'll shape your body and for the cat cafe you'll search for escaped house pets.Another standout feature of the series is the fantastic character models, which actually look like people and not like computer-generated ideal figures - Kiryu is an exception, he looks too young for his age and his features bear witness to the aging design template. The movement animations during running and fighting are great, but during conversations the facial features seem stiff, and the camera angles during dialogues could be more exciting in view of the sprawling conversations. Those who are used to western RPGs might be surprised at how little influence the player has on the course of the story; there are no alternative endings. However, since Kiryu is an established character with a fixed nature (and Yakuza is also not a pure role-playing game), the linearity of the narrative is quite logical.Yakuza 6: The Song of Life is a solid title that scores especially in terms of storytelling. The staging of the different locations also comes across very attractively, as does the great degree of variety, especially when it comes to the numerous activities in the cities. But at the same time, the game also weakens in aspects that could have easily been avoided. Almost every quest ends in a mass brawl, emotionless facial expressions make for yawning emptiness and the combat system turns out great at best while it definitely could've been exceptional. Yakuza 6: The Song of Life is well worth a look and can provide many entertaining hours, but likewise you can't experience an absolute stroke of genius here, the mafia life is too monotonous for that.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 6 is the final chapter in the story of Kazuma Kiryu. After the events of the previous game, Kiryu is searching for Haruka, who has disappeared, and eventually finds himself involved in another complex war between the Tojo Clan, Yomei Alliance, Saio Triads and the Jingweon Mafia, which takes place across Kamurocho and the small town of Onomichi.This game has a smaller scale than the previous two games, which featured multiple playable characters and several locations. Kiryu is the only playable character, but I liked being able to focus entirely on him for one final time, and this also helps to improve the pacing of the story.Endings can be hard to write. I’ve watched many TV shows and film franchises that failed to give its characters a satisfying finish. But the conclusion of this storyline is very well written, and gives the Dragon of Dojima the epic finale that he deserves. Many characters from the series’ past make an appearance, in addition to some interesting new characters, there are lots of twists and turns, and many exciting cinematic cutscenes. Each game’s combat has a slightly different feel, here the physics felt a little weird to begin with, probably a result of moving to a new engine, but after getting used to it, and learning how to make best use of heat finishers and extreme heat mode, Kiryu feels like an unstoppable badass.There are other improvements which make this feel like a more modern game. Graphics are much improved, and the environment looks especially great in first person mode. Every line of dialogue is fully voiced throughout the main quest and all sub stories. And you can save anywhere instead of just at phone booths.There are of course lots of wacky sub stories to play though. One minute you’re fighting ghosts in a haunted cemetery, and the next you’re feeding cats to gain their friendship in order to recruit them for the owner of a cat cafe.As usual there are lots of minigames to play, including Sega arcades, baseball, karaoke and mahjong. Bowling used to be my favourite minigame, unfortunately the bowling alley has closed and a gym has opened in its place (where you can do a few minigames like weight lifting to gain XP), but fortunately the controls for darts are much improved, especially using mouse for precision aim. There’s also a lengthy storyline where Kiryu has to build a clan to fight against a rival in a kind of basic RTS minigame.Its taken me 37 hours to finish the main story and around half of the sub stories. I haven’t noticed any bugs, crashes or framerate problems. The controls work great on gamepad apart from my one minor complaint where the default movement speed is walking, and you have to hold a button to run. It would feel more comfortable if it was the other way around.Yakuza 6 is a great game, which shouldn’t be a surprise because all of the Yakuza games are great. But as always, my recommendation is to play these games in order, starting from Yakuza 0, to get the most enjoyment out of the story.

_childDocuments_.review: After 7 games, and a combined 172 hours of my life, I've finished Kiryu's journey. Yakuza 6 manages to close off the series on a very strong note, and although the story is quite short (my 2nd shortest after 3), it is still a great finish to my favorite video game series of all time. A lot of people are ranking the series in their reviews, but I can't actually give my overall ranking because it's way too hard. So I'll give my ranking for each category as I review them.Firstly, the story. In my opinion the story is the strongest part of this game, very solid all the way through with plot twists that you won't expect but also don't qualify as actual asspulls. The plot of this game is quite ambitious, involving 3 main organizations, but the story does a fantastic job at balancing them. My main complaint with the story is how certain characters were thrown to the side for the entire story. Main characters built up throughout the whole series, yet they're given a lame excuse to not be present. I wish that they had a bit of closure at the end, but it is what it is. My ranking for the story is 0>6>3>K2>4>K1>5.Now, the combat. As you may know this is the first game in the series using the Dragon Engine. And to be completely honest, not a big fan of the combat in this game. The "Dragon" engine doesn't have you fight with the "Dragon" style, getting blocked by enemies in this game is more painful than in 3, and ragdoll physics aren't so fun either (I think they're better here than in K2 however). Heat actions suffered the most, with so many iconic and reliable moves simply gone. Literally the most basic heat action, "hit the enemy lying on the ground", isn't there. I got pretty tired of spamming the weapon slam and 2 person combo as well. It gets bearable with  some grind, but I will forever mourn the older combat. My combat ranking is 0>1>5>4>6>K2>3.So, onto the main villain of the story. I think when ranking the series, the villains category is by far the closest one for me at least. 6's villain is pretty strong, although not the strongest physically, he still does his job well. Built up decently over the latter half of the game, and the story does a great job at making you genuinely hate this guy. Compared to the previous games, you'll probably get the most satisfaction pummeling this guy's face into the ground. My villain's ranking is 3>2>1>0>6>4>5. About the final fight, it's a bit unconventional compared to the rest of the series. But the challenge is good and as I said before, the satisfaction is definitely immense. The boss fights in this game are pretty good, but I just wish that there were more QTEs (especially finishing off a fight). Most of them are also just "avoid taking damage" ones, so I wish there was more payoff in landing them. Obviously I can't be bothered to remember the boss fights from every single game, so I'll just rank the final boss fights (atmosphere, OST, challenge) as 5>0>1>6>3>2>4.I'll make this last section quick, it's just the side content and exploration. There's notably less content in this game compared the previous games, which is a disappointment but not a deal breaker. There's only places to explore, and to be honest Onomichi is one of the weakest towns/cities in the series. Kinda makes sense since it's a kind of "out there" place, but still a shame how much it pales in comparison to the other iconic spots in the franchise.Well that's it. I can say farewell to the beat em up Yakuza games, and move onto a new protagonist as well. If you told me at the start of this year I would have finished even just 0, let alone the entire Kiryu saga, I would've laughed. If you stuck around this far into the series, then I promise that you will not be disappointed by this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 6: The Song of Life is neck and neck with Yakuza 0 as a narrative, and it is a worthy ending to Kazuma Kiryu's story. The game's most gaping weakness is its combat, and even that remains satisfying. Physics and movement ends up feeling a little heavy for its own good, as opposed to the buttery smooth combat at the best parts of Yakuza 5. Yakuza Kiwami 2 repairs some of these issues, but the Dragon Engine lacks some of the arcadey charm of the other Yakuza titles. Even so, going into Extreme Heat mode and laying waste to hordes of enemies remains extremely satisfying, fret not. Besides these issues, it learns a lot from Y5 and satisfies in the most important of narrative.The disjointed nature of Y4 and Y5's plots became more difficult to follow, and to an extent less compelling. The singular focus on Kiryu for the final title works wonders, and it is easily one of the most compelling stories Yakuza has to offer. Characters are given so much more time to grow and react to events that Y4 and Y5 couldn't do with its multiple character narrative. The dynamics present put Y3 to shame, Rikiya can be compared to Yuta or Nagumo, but both of these characters are far superior in being both believable and unique, while also having fantastic interactions outside of their dynamic with Kiryu. The theme of Y3 is family, but the theme of Y6 expands upon this in every sense of the word. Literal family in the sense of fatherhood for Kiryu and Haruto's father, and familial bonds within the Hirose family, and far more to expand upon here. The ending speech by Kiryu puts into crystal clear view, all the themes and ideas present in Y6, leading to arguably the best and most compelling ending of any Yakuza game. Kiryu's final adventure is a rousing success and a worthy ending to the story of the Dragon of Dojima.

_childDocuments_.review: Is what I would describe Yakuza 6 as. I ought to say "Jankier" and add "Slightly Hollow" but that would make the header title slightly too long. Yet those terms would also describe the game quite well. This came from having played Yakuza Kiwami 2 first as my first Dragon Engine game, which I will elaborate in a bit further below.Yakuza 6 is a , the 7th and last entry of the Kiryu saga in a long established game franchise. It is also the first game to use the new graphics engine dubbed "Dragon Engine" developed in house by RGG studio for the game. You play as Kazuma Kiryu as he tries to find out the truth regarding his adoptive daughter Haruka being involved in an accident which left her comatose, while looking after a baby that is seemingly hers at the same time.To put it in a way that won't spoil things for readers more than they already have been via the store page and/or other reviews, Yakuza 6's story ranks itself pretty high among all the Yakuza games I have played so far, on the basis of emotional impact. The story itself has quite a few instances of bait-n-switches, as well as some very subtle foreshadows which turns into shocking plot twists. As always, the plot is linear and as such you don't decide how the narrative ends. Even so, the linearity does NOT detract any complexity to the plot at all. In fact, there have been times when I've felt that the plot was getting too convoluted. But past that, when the emotional bit comes, it does so very hard. I did not cry playing the game, but I will be lying if I said I didn't feel very emotional and sad because of things that played out on screen.Overall, after considering what others have said about the story, I can say that the writing has its ups and downs and not always consistent, but nothing like sky high to an out the window trip then back again. But the execution? Voice acting, the facial expressions, the general delivery of the scene is as superb as always. Maybe even more so because the Dragon Engine brings out more of everyone!Yakuza 6 is the first game that uses the Dragon Engine, and it leaves a pretty strong impression on first look. Kamurocho and Onomichi comes to life in an ever so vibrant manner that makes Yakuza 0 and Kiwami looks almost dull (though to be fair, Kiwami does kinda have that depressive tone especially at night time). Everything looks more detailed and photorealistic, enhanced by improved lighting effects and shadows.This comes at a somewhat relatively steep cost of extra computing power required to run the game at 1080p 60fps on HIGH settings, and it has some kinks regarding anti-aliasing. But these are nitpicks that doesn't majorly detracts from the experience, if at all. As for the GAMEPLAY, Yakuza 6 continues the well-established hand and leg throwing gameplay tradition of the previous games. In 6, Kiryu uses his legendary and iconic Dragon of Dojima style to thrashes his opponents in myriads of ways. And owing to the Dragon Engine, it looks so  and . The sounds and visuals accentuates this such that it feels very satisfying to pull off certain maneuvers, though I will say that I have some mixed opinions about it considering the other games I have played. Outside of fighting, Yakuza 6 has a pretty good variety of side quests and minigames that can occupy quite a decent chunk of your time, though I say this as if it is a plus, but that it is in true Yakuza fashion. Not having enough of it, never mind not having it, would be doing the name of Yakuza a disservice. Some of these minigames include hunting fishes with megafauna boss battles, baseball manager 2016, hostess club talks and dates and being a simp for racy ladies (real model actors) in an online chatroom. Overall, it leaves for an experience that doesn't feel hollow at all, though it pales relative to its probably magnum opus predecessor, Yakuza 0.Yakuza 6, being the first Dragon Engine game, has a few differences vs Kiwami 2 that I noted, many of it negative:1. Kiryu's heat meter is inferior in 6. The straight bars in Kiwami 2 is a better and clearer representation of his heat gauge than 6's heat orbs2. Kiryu's has substantially LESS combat tricks in 6 vs Kiwami 2. There is no counter throw (vs one learned from Kawauchi in Kiwami 2) and there is no 4 direction counter heat move, just to name 2. There are others that I haven't mentioned yet.3. There is NO carrying weapons on yourself in 6. You can use the environment with the pots and signboards or enemy's weaponry, but there is no procuring weapon for yourself to carry. Gears are also LESS fleshed out, with only 2 slots and there being no set bonuses for wearing matching gears.4. Opponents bodies despawns near-instantaneously after battle, often in front of you. Whether or not this is a con and detracts from the experience is up to you.5. Kiryu can enter Extreme Heat Mode without requiring an entirely full heat gauge. This is the one aspect of 6's gameplay that I liked over Kiwami 2.6. Menu items in restaurants are not marked for having been consumed already, unlike Kiwami 2. This means you have to revisit the awards section frequently to make sure you get every single item on a menu list. This is a bother for me personally.Overall, Yakuza 6 is a very great game. I personally loved that EVERY single dialogue interaction in the game is VOICED with NO dialogue boxes, meaning I can just kick back and just enjoy the conversation that follows. Though this was clearly an experiment that was potentially resource consuming and divisive so I can see why they went back to old ways in Kiwami 2 and 7.  The game has its janks here and there and sometimes, it leaves quite a bit to be desired. But it is definitely NOT a game where you feel that you don't want to see it to the end. It is highly compelling, and very much worth its price tag. If you can get it on sale, even better. But please......if you haven't already noticed the number 6 in the title, please DO NOT PLAY THIS AS YOUR FIRST YAKUZA GAME!. Do so with Yakuza 0, and go on with Kiwami 1, 2, etc...8/10[EDIT CHANGELOG]30 - 01 - 22: Proofread and grammar fixes, added a word

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 6: The Song of Life is the final installment in Kiryu's saga. That makes it an ideal point for my current Yakuzathon to come to an end. Newly out of prison, legendary yakuza Kiryu Kazuma returns to Okinawa and his orphanage only to find out that his ward Haruka has gone missing while he was away. Haruka resurfaces in a Tokyo hospital, lying in a coma after an apparent car accident. What's more she now has a baby that needs a carer. Kiryu yet again takes on the role of guardian and sets out to investigate Haruka's accident. Meanwhile, another mob war is brewing in Kamurocho and Kiryu's presence can only complicate matters further.The main plot of the game is unusually decent. That's not to say there are no flaws, or decisions that feel forced for drama. In fact, there are several. Kiryu willingly going to jail to wash away his yakuza shame sets many of the events that follow in motion, ie Haruka's disappearance. But that choice is invalidated when Kiryu immediately gets involved in another mob war as soon as he is out. Haruka having a child via some one-night stand is totally out of character. Haruka, the responsible. Haruka, the level-headed. Haruka, the stupid teen that doesn't know condoms are a thing. The game also delivers a few strong gut punches, only to walk back on them in the finale. Despite all that though, the main plot manages to remain engaging throughout, it introduces some great new characters and keeps you guessing. For a Yakuza game, that's quite a rarity.The game was created using a whole new engine, the same that later on would be used for Kiwami 2. This is clearly evident, the game feels a lot more modern than previous entries. There are many seamless interior areas, combat happens in place and in fact enemies are visible on the map. This finally addresses a classic Yakuza annoyance, the ridiculous amount of random encounters. There are though several teething problems too. For starters, some locations in Kamurocho are missing. Apparently the devs couldn't recreate them in time. Combat is another example. Yes, old annoyances like excessive blocks or grabs have again been soothed. But combat doesn't really feel bombastic or over the top enough. Kiryu is nowhere near what he was before. His attacks feel less impactful, more sluggish. Maybe some will accept the trade-off, but for me it was a bit disappointing.Content wise the game is generally more sparse than previous entries. Fewer mini-games, fewer substories, less everything. Kamurocho in particular feels pretty barren. On the other hand, what content is there is great. There wasn't a single mini-game I didn't have some fun with. Furthermore, the new area the game introduces, Onomichi, is one of the best areas in the Yakuza series. It is a small port town, near a hill with beautiful shrines. The landscape has lots of elevation shifts and a very unique layout. Its small size works in its favour by making it feel more packed, despite the relatively small number of substories available. All in all, it appears the devs opted for quality instead of quantity here and it shows. Yes, I would have liked it if there was some more content, especially after Yakuza 5 spoiled me so much, but it is what it is.In conclusion, despite a number of shortcomings, I found this to be a worthwhile experience. Yes, there are better Yakuza games than this one, as usual I will recommend starting with Yakuza 0. Whatever the case, this game offers a decent plot, a beautifully rendered world, some great new characters and of course the conclusion to Kiryu's story. All that is enough to make for an acceptable package. I recommend trying it out. For fans in particular, it's unquestionably a must.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 6 introduces the new dragon engine to the series that was used to make Kiwami 2, so people playing the games in order will be familiar with the combat, physics, and upgrade system already.This game marks an important part of the series as it wraps up Kiryu's story, and the stakes are higher than ever this time. I found myself enjoying the story this time around, minus one short but awful segment where you have to calm down a crying baby.This game's most biggest flaw might be in the combat, which I feel lacks variety. After being spoiled by 4 and 5's multiple characters, or 0 and Kiwami's styles, it feels like Kiryu is missing something while he's fighting. On top of that, he staggers when he attacks an enemy that's blocking. Extreme heat mode spices it up a little, and is a more logical version of his Dragon Spirit from 5. Rather than invulnerability, Kiryu will take damage, but he will not die while in Extreme Heat mode, and rather than a new, but limited moveset, he can power up his combo finishers as well as access a couple new heat moves. There are a lot of substories in this one, but a lot of them are behind long grinds. Like maxing affection with every hostess in Kamurocho, or being friends with every guy at the bar in Hiroshima, or completing a boring baseball simulator. The good news though is you don't need to do EVERY substory to unlock the secret boss fight in this game. Plus aside from the grindy ones I mentioned, many of the sub stories are as entertaining as you'd come to expect from the series.It's a solid entry to the series, and a great way to send off the beat em up style they had going for so long before trying out the turn based RPG style in Yakuza: Like a Dragon.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fitting and conclusive end to Kiryu's saga that started all the way back in 0. For a basic overview, while combat feels a bit simple compared to previous games, it still feels very fluid and fun, especially when using Extreme Heat Mode. Graphically, the game looks great, with the Dragon Engine providing a major upgrade compared to previous games' visuals, especially with character models and cutscenes. Side-content such as substories and minigames are also here in abundance, with the expected Yakuza series charm and light-heartedness fans have come to love, though toned down some likely due to adapting to the Dragon Engine and fully-voiced dialogue.Story-wise though, the game's plot provides a good amount of fresh air compared to Yakuza 5's very overwhelming story, but still ends up feeling a bit lacking compared to other games regarding certain characters, yet is still fairly solid. Emotionally and thematically, however, is where 6 truly shines, with some of the most emotionally-engaging stakes of all the games, and an ending that made myself cry multiple times, something I can't say a lot about other games I've played, including any other Yakuza games so far. Overall, while being a bit rough around the edges, Yakuza 6 is still a phenomenal game and one of my favorites in the franchise, with a conclusive thematic end to the Dragon of Dojima we've known for seemingly so long.

_childDocuments_.review: This finale to the "Kiryu saga" is particularly strange to me, because there is less of the bad things that were starting to get tiring in 4, let alone 5, but a lacking substance all around. In better words, maybe a bit too focused.Much of the lessons learnt over the years are pretty noticeable, as not only the pacing is actually even and allows a healthy balance, a significant amount of the narrative is clear enough and avoids much of the good ol' asspulling people would expect. Hell some of it's best scenes are to me highlights of the franchise as a whole, with the music, acting and combat all falling nicely into place to form skull-cracking fun.It is however tad dissapointing as a conclusion tale to an extent, even if I personally was engaged the entire time. Even if you like the story as a whole, I promise without spoiling you will think it could have been better.The renown Takeshi Kitano in particular delivers a surprisingly great performance in a character that fits him like a glove. The ending might be lukewarm but overall I personally believe they did an okay job, despite under using other allies of the franchise. That and the "secret" is absurdly idiotic.One aspect of the game that received significant injury was sidecontent. Kamurocho has most of the known minigames but a lack of some smaller interactables (like skill machines) and particularly some entire areas are sorely missed, and Hiroshima is particularly barren of stuff to do at first. Some new side activities crop up but I don't think Troublr or Clan Maker have much variety or enjoyment to go for them that isn't XP or money.At least the port is pretty much alright with no denuvo or technical issues in my run on hard, so in general all I'm saying is if you just want to get this over with, pick it up on a discount.If you already know what to expect here, after such a long haul, maybe the focused and condensed experience will be what you prefer.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this game is a great return to being Kiryu focused as well as paying off a lot of his story that has come before. I was sad some core characters of the series didn't really have much of a place in the story of this game but all the new additions are more than welcome. Moving on, Yakuza 6 is a huge step up when it comes to graphics from Yakuza 5, thanks to the new dragon engine and not being bound by the PS3's hardware. The way the open world flows and is presented is also vastly improved and is that much more immersive. The combat is the only real negative I have when it comes to the changes. It isn't bad by any means but some fights just feel awkward with how some Extreme Heat mode interactions work and how the enemy AI acts sometimes.The only other negative I have with this game is the lack of some very important music that is left out of the western versions. Luckily there is a very easy to install  that remedies this and restores Tatsuro Yamashita's work that is pretty key in driving some emotional scenes home.If you are a fan of the series this game is a no brainer pick up, especially at $20. If you are new to the series I would recommend going through the earlier games first to get better context of Kiryu's journey since this game is pretty much all about that.

_childDocuments_.review: After all these years I can finally say that I’ve played through all of Kiryu’s story with the exception of Kenzan and Isshin at least. Maybe you can throw in Dead Souls too, if they come to PC-Steam I’ll definitely buy and play them. So, what do I have to say about Yakuza 6…not much…actually…I honestly found the story in 6 to be kind of meh. I’m not going to go over the story in detail, but I’ll give you a brief summary, at least to the best of my ability. I’ll do it in bullet-points, just easier for me. 1- Kiryu was in prison for some years for the events of Yakuza 5, he gets out and Haruka is missing.2- Goes to Kamurocho to find Akiyama to find Haruka.3- Haruka in big accident.Haruka has child.4- Kiryu goes to find who hurt Haruka.5- Goes to Hiroshima because Haruka was hiding there.That’s about as much as I’ll say on the story, don’t want to spoil it for people. So due to Haruka Kiryu once again goes down a rabbit hole in order to find out who hurt Haruka and who the child’s father is. The thing is that the story is really just kind of meh, I’m not very expressive when it comes to my opinion and I do recommend the story if you are a fan of the Yakuza series. But keep in mind I’ve played all other main-line Yakuza games up to this point and there are much better stories from previous games. I think this story is better than 3 and 5’s but nowhere near as good as 4 and all the above ones (0, Kiwami & Kiwami 2). I think the main issue is the whole baby thing because Kiryu ends up carrying it around for a big chunk of the game and its really just kind of there. Big conflict? Oh, can you look after the baby while I smash these punks faces in. Really bizarre to be honest. Anyway, the story is just kind of meh to me, I’m sick of talking about it anymore.Gameplay is what you’d expect, it’s no Zero but still pretty good. World looks really nice graphically. Keep in mind this game came out after Zero and the two Kiwami’s so it should look really good.Substories are good. Made me laugh whenever Kiryu went into the sewer because he would just yeet the hatch when in previous games we were told that only Saejima could lift them due to being too heavy but in 6 Kiryu just lifts it like it’s nothing. When coming out of the sewer with one arm as well. Makes me laugh. Actually…this game has a lot of weird moments in the story, like the same thug getting beaten down and then acting like that never happened. Yakuza thugs using RPGs in the story? Using the baby like a rugby ball. An old man with honestly no power being an assassin that could potentially kill like 100 armed men with guns with just one gun. There are other stupid moments which made me laugh but these ones came to mind while writing this. I guess Kiryu did fight two Tigers in Kiwami 2, so I guess it’s fine. The whole game was about family and blood bonds and some instants within the story were pretty good but overall it was just fine. As a conclusion to Kiryu’s story though he kind of just fades away quietly which made me kind of laugh. I won’t spoil the ending but it’s not great.Overall this game is average for a Yakuza game. A solid 6/10If you want to know my Yakuza ranking out of curiosity or just so you can tell me I’m wrong in the comments. Here you go.1) Yakuza 02) Yakuza Kiwami 23) Yakuza Kiwami4) Yakuza 45) Yakuza 66) Yakuza 37) Yakuza 5

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, I LOVE the yakuza series. However, 6 was just lacking in many areas. The new dragon engine does give it better visuals, and gameplay (more to the fact that you actually run from the random encounters now.) And going into buildings is seamless. However that's where our good time ends and the problems begin. If you've play the other games, even the PS2 ones, then you're familiar with the combat. They've changed it in this game. It feels slower, Kiryu feels weaker in both attack and defense, heat mode is a little different, instead of a bar you get heat orbs, which can activate the new extreme heat mode if you have a certain number filled. Extreme heat mode is technically beast mode from 0 and kiwami, but you can attack at a constant rate while in extreme heat mode. there are no carry weapons, just the ones you find on the street. Armors are practically non existant. I found maybe four armor types through my playthrough. And they didn't do much in defense. There are many more bosses and mini bosses, which is a good thing, adds challenge. And the story is probably one of the best in the series. I will not spoil anything storywise for those who have not played it yet. But I can absolutely tell you that it's missing one end game bonus that the rest of the games have. There is no premium adventure mode. So buckle down and 100% the game on your first playthrough, or do it in new game+ mode. There are few mini games. Most notably is the arcade version of puyo puyo and virtua fighter 5 final showdown being playable. Karaoke has also changed up a little too, but it still feels the same as past games. The cabaret club is back and it's still fun to play, and there's a new mini game where you can work out with Rizap. However that game was tedious and kind of boring. The reward wasn't all that worth it either. And one new mini game where you do "live chat" with adult web cam models on a japanese website. Other than that, there's not much to do on your downtime. Money is also incredibally hard to come by in this game, since there is no Coliseum or much of a way to get pawnable items. You have to grind for money in random encounters, but they rarely drop yen unless you upgrade a certain ability. That's about it for the game.

_childDocuments_.review: + Great improved graphics+ Great overall story, probably second best next to Y0+ Well written substories with many throwbacks to previous games+ Cool and fun new minigames: Clan Creator, Spearfishing, Baseball manager- Many old areas in Kamurocho are inaccessible- No coliseum- Less than half the content of Y5- Dragon engine physics is rough- No equippable weapons- Limited heat move options+/- Ending works, but boy could it have been betterI have mixed feelings about this one. Don't get me wrong, as a standalone game, Y6 is great. But as the final episode of Kiryu's story, I must say I was expecting a lot more in terms of content, a better game engine, and a better ending for Kiryu. I tried taking my time with this game, but I was shocked to have completed all but one of the substories just halfway through the game. Coming from Y5, this felt like a huge disappointment. It would've also been nice to explore Kamurocho Hills after so many games talking about it, but you couldn't even get anywhere near, since many areas of the city are blocked off. What a wasted opportunity.And since this is the first entry to introduce the Dragon engine, it felt really rough. Enemies spinning around into space, Kiryu getting kicked all over the place, enemies knocking you back when they block... For most of the game, I had to run around picking up bicycles, because they were by far the best "weapons" to use against crowds. Otherwise, they'd just mob and knock you down repeatedlyBoss fights also kinda felt cheap in the sense that in order to beat them effectively, you kinda have to use cheap tactics. You couldn't even land proper combos even while attacking bosses from behind, since they'd just randomly turn around and hit you. Instead, you had to rely on a few hits at a time. Dash punching would be the bread and butter, since speed is everything here. PS: secret sub-story boss is quite a nightmare in this one.But overall, this is still a must play for any fan of the Yakuza series. Onomichi is a really nice and quaint town, and the dragon engine makes everything look great. And after 6 games of watching Kiryu and his friends suffer, it's only apt to stick with him and suffer for the last time in his final chapter.

_childDocuments_.review: After the massive , which was ,  switches things up: We’re back to one playable protagonist and only two locations to visit but also made the move to the new Dragon Engine in return. Additionally and most importantly,  is about the end of Kiryu’s journey – but with all these changes, can it really succeed as a finale to six mainline games?The most visible change and thus the first thing I want to talk about is the new engine. Now that it has also been powering more recent  games as well (), it’s use in  has often been regarded as a “beta test” by fans – and there’s some truth to that, unfortunately. There’s some good to it, without doubt: cutscenes look fantastic for the most part and entering shops, restaurants and more without loading screens makes for a more immersive experience.On the other hand, besides the obviously higher hardware demands, it also introduces some graphical and physics related issues. For one, the anti-aliasing in this game is really bad. Unless you’re playing on extremely high resolution to begin with, you’ll notice a  of shimmering which can be downright distracting. And then there’s physics, often glitching out in fights with bodies flying around or weapons breaking for no reasons. Lastly, defeated enemies now despawn immediately after a fight ends – turning a battlefield back into an empty alleyway in seconds. With the added immersion of the reduced loading screens, this one’s a real bummer.Speaking of alleyways, the two explorable locations – Kamurocho and Onimichi – do look great, really showing off the technology shift to a new generation. Problem is, they’re both limited to some degree. Good ol’ Kamurocho got a lot of closed off locations, meaning you’ll only be exploring a smaller part of the map than you might be used to. And Onimichi, while boosting a reasonable size, only features a really small amount of interactable buildings (shops, restaurants, etc.) – leaving most of the map to the cruel fate of being nothing but background decorations.Anyway, as for what you – or Kiryu, to be more precise – can actually do in these locations, you’ll get the usual mix: Story missions, side missions, mini games (the karaoke minigame does not feature bake mitai – a criminal omission) and of course a lot of fights. A new addition is the so-called “Troublr” app, which basically marks quick fight missions on your map if you pass by them – nothing major but makes for more lively cities.The big minigame questline this time around circles around the “Clan Creator”. Kiryu is basically acting as a commander of sorts, telling clan members where and how to strike instead of just ending fights himself. While that for itself seems a little out of character, my main complaint about the minigame itself is how much of a non-challenge it turned out to be. Even without farming missions to level up my clan, I easily beat the questline without even getting close to a defeat. I’m all for minigames not being too punishing - but just spamming troops without any need to strategize is not really the goal of a strategy minigame, no?As for fighting, we got a new RPG-style upgrade system that also allows for stat improvements (attack, defense, etc.). Reward points are now awarded in five different categories (strength, technique, etc.) and upgrades require certain points of each category. I like the upgrade system (allows you to get to max combo speed in mere hours!) in general, however, I felt like point distribution was a bit uneven. I quickly reached max points in three categories thanks to a lot fights but as those don’t reward technique points for example, I was still locked out from a lot of upgrades which required points from all five categories. I played a lot of Darts to get those missing technique points – but it feels weird to farm for one point category specifically while the others are basically rewarded at every corner.The fights themselves got a lot of “oomph” to it, thanks to the new engine. Some cuts have been made here as well though: we still only got one fighting style for Kiryu but  also cut the feature to carry/equip weapons – meaning you can only use weapons if you pick them up from the ground during a fight. Also, as soon as you got access to a few moves, many fights in  become significantly easier to beat. Running around and continuously dropkicking enemy groups for example quickly served as an easy way for me to decimate enemy troops, on normal difficulty.As for the actual story (& ending),  might not deliver what one might expect for a finale of this size (remember, six games leading up to this one!). It works with an almost completely new cast, meaning many familiar faces that franchise veterans expect to show up won’t – or at least not to the degree you might expect. This does make this game more approachable for newcomers, there’s even a flashback in the beginning of the game explaining who some characters are. But personally, I’d have preferred this to be more of a best-of finale, featuring characters from all over the franchise. There  reappearances happening, during substories as well, but the game feels less like a big finale and more like just another new chapter in the life of Kiryu quite often.Even more personally speaking, I was actually quite disappointed by what I got as a final chapter in terms of story. There’s significantly less Kiryu – Haruka moments than I hoped to see after all their history. The orphanage is brushed aside expect for a few instances. And lastly, some story moments (especially during the last few chapters) made me legitimately want to hit my head on my desk due to the amount of unnecessary stupidity going on – and of course, guns still remain one of the worst plot devices in this franchise. As you probably already know from the other Steam reviews though, this is not the popular opinion – so the chances are high you might enjoy it more than I do.Those were quite a lot of negative points, you might say at this point, so why did you still give  a thumbs-up? And to be honest, I thought about changing that quite often as well. But if I look back at my time with the game, besides all these criticisms (of which I could probably find even more with a bigger character limit), I still enjoyed walking the streets of Kamurocho with Kiryu one last time. I love that I can now drag enemies into a convenience store and throw them in the microwave, only to be told by the manager to leave afterwards. I love that Kiryu’s story did receive an ending instead of going on forever. And most of all, I don’t regret playing through the entire franchise just to reach this point.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 6 is a superb game and a great final chapter for the story of Kazuma Kiryu. It's hands down one of the best games I played in recent years. The story is intriguing, emotional and entertaining from start to finish. The characters are really well written and likeable  - the new ones as well as the recurring characters. Also the game has some of the most despicable villains of the series. In terms of game, Yakuza 6 was also really good. The combat feels more smooth than in previous installments. The number of side activities and substories is lower than in older games, but in turn all the substories are voiced. And unlike in the older gmaes, I enjoyed almost all side activities (baseball wasn't really my cup of tea). The graphics look really gorgeous, Kamurocho never looked more impressive. Same goes for the face of the characters, which are extremly detailed. The soundtrack is really on point and adds a lot to the atmosphere of the game.  To sum it up: Yakua 6 is an excellent game, which I highly recommend to any fan of the franchise or anyone who like action games. In my opinion, Yakuza 6 is a high point of the series. I'd even say it's the best game in the franchsie alongside to Yakuza 0.

_childDocuments_.review: Warning: There may be some spoilers!In all honesty the Yakuza series so far has been a hit for me, although I started with Yakuza: Like a Dragon the story of this game can really make you feel emotions. This game really does not wait until the end for sad stuff as they show it right off the bat, making you really feel sympathy at the very beginning of the game which in turn makes you intrigued in the story only wanting you to continue furthermore. Overall this game has a very interesting story with major plot that enchants the person playing this game.If I had to put this in words I'd have to say this game is very emotional and is putting you through a roller coaster of all the emotions. Throughout the story you can find the game makes you go "Oh this is so sad" to "what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on" in the span of 5 seconds, and it doesn't hesitate to throw you for a loop either. All the characters in this game (including the new ones) are all extremely well designed all with meaning to the plot. I must say one of the new characters you get introduced to really made me laugh, he was really well detailed and threw everyone for a loop as the story progressed but he was really my favourite character besides the main character. Yakuza is a very story-rich series, with many plot twists and plenty of cutscenes to keep you going into this story, many substories to laugh over and give you comedic relief. This game especially REALLY gives you that comedic relief in the substories as it points towards the main story a bit while also involving the background of places you're in, really enhancing the story-line completely. I am now a complete Yakuza fan because of these reasons.I experienced this game with a friend of mine and they enjoyed the story very much, as well as I. I recommend you play this game if you are interested in the Yakuza series or have been for a long time :)

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 6: The Song of Life was ostensibly the last game in Kiryu's saga when it released, and while that may not quite have panned out, it's still a strong send-off for the Dragon of Dojima. In contrast to Yakuza 4 and 5 with their multiple protagonists, Yakuza 6 is very much Kiryu's own story, with the stakes largely being much more personal and the game explicitly being about the nature of families. Putting that aside, this was also the first game in the series to use the Dragon Engine, which upped the graphical detail and made entering and exiting buildings seamless. This game also had fully voiced dialogue for not only all main story cutscenes but also for all substories. This particular changes slows the pace down, however, possibly too slow. On the other hand, the new town of Onomichi is a delight with its coastal charm, verticality, and introduction of some very fun new minigames.Ultimately, Kiryu's story goes out on a high note, even if not quite the series' highest.
_childDocuments_.name: Yakuza 6: The Song of Life

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 6: The Song of Life is the 6th mainline title of the Yakuza/Like a Dragon series and is a bearer of many firsts. For starters, it's the first game that carried its byline from the Japanese title to the English one (4 was Successor to the Legend, 5 was Fulfiller of Dreams, and 0 was Place of Oath). It's also the first one to feature the Dragon Engine, which will become noticeable in a while. To start it off, the story is by no means bad. This was meant to be the last game where Kiryu will be playable so they took extra care to ensure he goes out with a bang (and no, I'm not talking about the Millenium tower). What many people find problematic about this title is the gameplay. Sure the Dragon Engine definitely looks way better than the engine previous Yakuza titles had, but the combat just doesn't add up to expectations. If you played Kiwami 2 before this then don't expect anything like it as K2 improved the combat a lot. Yakuza 5 and 0 showed us just how good the combat can get and they give us a complete downgrade in this regard. Sure one may argue that it's because Kiryu is getting old, but that doesn't mean you have to take away the fun in playing as him. It felt like almost all of the resources they had for this game went to making it look good and they kinda forgot everything else that also needed work. This game has the lowest substory count of all Yakuza/Like a Dragon/Judgment games and only the Tiger Drop remains of all the Komaki techniques (Komaki himself doesn't even appear). The plot twist in this game is definitely better than rubber bullets, but it does disappoint. The final villain also disappoints as he isn't exactly as great of an antithesis to Kiryu than say, Mine or Ryuji. But taking those away, this is otherwise a solid RGG studios game. As I've said before, graphics are amazing and still hold up despite being originally released in 2016. The minigames are a hit or miss depending on how much you love micro management. Despite the low substory count, all of them are completely voiced, which is pretty cool if you ask me. The soundtrack is divine in both Karaoke and battle themes (Hands and Destiny da GOAT). And the characters are all great really. You'll find yourself attached to one villain after fighting him 3 times, sympathetic even. At one point you'll notice some sort of a role reversal between the two, but I'm gonna stop right there. TLDR, Yakuza 6 isn't a great game. It's a decentish game at best. But if you're a diehard RGG fan who already played through The Remastered Collection, then why stop now? After this title you'll find no major flaws in any of the future games you'll be playing, which I assume will be LaD and the Judgment games. (P.S. I highly recommend using the Japanese Music Restoration Patch as the scenes just hit harder with it)

_childDocuments_.review: Ah. Another controversial game in the series, Yakuza 6.But unfortunately, this is my favorite games in the franchise, along with 0. Let me tell you why.- The punching thing is not refined as Kiwami 2 but I think that's the charm of this game and kinda "make sense" when you considered he's 48 here and 38 in Kiwami 2 so he doesn't have that kind of vigor anymore.- Some said the story caused Haruka's character regression. I somehow disagree. Remember, she doesn't have a proper education until Yakuza 3 when she's 10 and by 15 she left the school to pursue an idol career and by 16 she's the target from SNS. I mean if you want to call her character regress then it's probably her decision in the ending of 5, not 6.- I do agree that things happened after that with a certain character feels rushed and too convenient.- The scheme they plotted, whatever fractions are, makes sense. With how messy things happened in 5, I think it's not too over-the-top for what happened in 6.However there are parts that I disliked and I think they did a great job fixing these in Kiwami 2.- Extreme heat mode feels fun in early games but feels to repetitive and inconsistent. You mashed the button, hoping that button will pop up to trigger the QA, but it's not always there. They fixed this in 2 and tbh that's big QOL improvement.- Charging atk is much better in K2 as you're not standing still to do so. In 6, you probably have to do that against guarding foes.- Overall, I think they did nearly everything better in K2 in terms of fighting. Probably except "Feel the Heat!". I think that's way more dumb than 6.Overall for this game? I think it's absolutely bargain if you can get it around less than $10.- The graphic ages so damn well. I plugged my laptop with a larger screen in living room, lay down on sofa and played. My family thought this is a CG movie. - You might not like the fighting mechanic but sometimes the ragdoll can pull a few laughs.- The story is somehow borderline make senses and nonsense but I think it's a decent story, much improved from what they did in 5 or even 4.- No green tint filter like K2.

_childDocuments_.review: While I do recommend this game, I must clarify that I'm only recommending it for the story. I completed only one substory and, while the outcome was cute, it just wasn't fun to do, so I made the ultimate decision to skip the rest and I have no regrets. I also didn't play any of the mini games because they just didn't interest me, so my ~20 hours on record is just the main story. And I'd like to further clarify, that I usually  complete all of the substories and play all of the mini games in this series, but for Yakuza 6 it all just felt like it was lacking...something.Pros:+Gripping plot+Great graphics+Interesting cast of charactersCons:-Combat felt weak-Almost nothing to do in Onomichi-Felt pressured to do substories, mini games, etc.-Some of the cutscenes were painstakingly long for no good reason-Well-loved characters not included or added briefly for fan service*To elaborate on "the combat felt weak", it just felt lifeless compared to the combat in other Yakuza games. I even had max stats and was barely shaving off enemy health, unless I was in heat mode. And instead of getting in quality fights, it was just wave after wave of 20+ enemies, which was more annoying than any of the boss fights after.Everything else aside, this game had me on an emotional roller coaster and I'm so relieved it's over. I know that Yakuza games aren't "butterflies and rainbows", but the addition of a baby was just so stressful to me.  As a mom of a child that's not much older than Haruto, there were some moments and dialog that just hurt my heart. I'd go from happy/sad/stressed/angry in such a short span of time, it was like the story was pulling me left and right. And while most of the characters had good intentions, some of them were just acting out of stupidity or selfishness, which was very frustrating at times.However, my biggest beef with this game is If you MUST play this game, I'd say the story is totally worth it, but you might be disappointed with everything else. To anyone that's on the fence, maybe you're better off watching it on youtube.

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy end for Kazuma Kiryu, Dragon of Dojima, 4th Chairman of the Tojo Clan, Judgment Kazzy, Kiryu-chan and Suzuki-san.Experience breathtaking visuals and beautifully re-created scenery for that itch of virtual tourism while getting lost in the plethora of mini games such as Mahjong, Virtua Fighter 5: Final Showdown, Puyo-Puyo, managing your own baseball team, going deep-sea fishing or playing tower defense.Embrace the Way of the Grandfather as you take care of Haruto and find out who his father is while meeting familiar faces along the way and tying up those loose strings of the past, become a loveable mascot of a quaint little seafaring town called Onomichi (Which is a real place btw, Yakuza's first real location) and teach baddies some manners with your fist.10 out of 10, would wear charming Hasaku face, a cute fish pouch, cool boots, vital for any fisherman and a bold and trendy Ono shirt again.For 20€ seriously a steal, just buy it already!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving this a positive review because I had fun, and it's still a Yakuza game at the end of the day, but god was this game disappointing. It's obviously still worth playing if you've played the previous games, but it's definitely one of the weakest entries in the series. Combat feels unsatisfying in the new Dragon Engine, though they improved it a lot when making Kiwami 2. There's way less heat actions available and extreme heat mode feels incredibly braindead to use. The story was also not as exciting as 4 or 5, though there's still just as many plot holes (which you should be used to by now). The quality of life improvements are pretty good though.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing through Yakuza 6 I'm still stuck on the decision on whether I like this game or not. I find my self flip flopping so hard on my choice that it is actively giving me whiplash. The game is Reuse Ga Gotoku at its absolute worst most of the time, but it starts to gain it's own identity later on. The new side content added is not compelling whatsoever, but a Yakuza game not focused on side content may have been what the series needed after having 3 of its most grind intensive games released back to back. The game is gorgeous and seamless but at the cost of a lower amount of development time, which results in some of the jankiest and slowest brawler combat seen in this series. I feel for every amount of good in this game, there is just 2 times more off putting things. Never bad things mind you, but I just don't see how they went backwards in so many departments. I will say this though, I loved the story, It got about 20 hours out of me and satisfyingly concluded the main arc. Now I know that the ending is rendered moot now (ffs Kiryu is on the cover of 2 new games now its not hard to spoil it), but the entire game itself was a necessary ending to Uncle Kaz's story. Reiterating on the strongest parts of his character, re-contextualizing the original Yakuza story for a new generation, and taking the time to attempt plot points and character arcs that were blundered or never expanded on past the surface level. I will admit though, the first half of the game has a frustrating plot, but it all connects nicely and I found myself emotionally attatched to everything new by the end of the game.While Yakuza 6 may not be the best video game out there (and at the time of writing this DEFINITELY my least favourite RGG mainline game), it still has an endearing plot that needs to be experienced at least once. Whether it is a good game or just a fluke is something for a replay in the future to decide.
