_childDocuments_.review: After finishing Yakuza 0 way back in late May, here I am at the conclusion of the Kiryu saga. My 0 review popped off, and that convinced me to give reviews of the series as a whole after beating them.  As such, I hope this will be short and sweet just like that one was, and convey my feelings as well as that one did.Yakuza 6 is notable for having a title associated with it: The Song of Life, and honestly, I think that's very fitting in a lot of ways. It's the final hurrah for series mainstay Kazuma Kiryu as a main protagonist, and it both feels like a fitting end, and not so. There are some parts very reminiscent of earlier games. The foundation for Haruka's leave is shaky at best, if you liked Haruka as a character in the previous entry, you might not be so happy with how they took the direction for her in this one. While the foundation isn't so great, the way they go about executing things despite that fact, was still very well done, and I can't fault them in that regards. Kiryu has less patience dealing with things at this old age, and it's kind of refreshing to just see him punch first and ask questions later for the most part. Him being an actual father to a literal baby is also not a bad fit, unsurprisingly.  Since Kiryu has once again spent a decent amount of time in jail yet again, Kamurocho has underwent a facelift evident by the Dragon Engine's ground up rendition of this classic city. Things aren't where they used to be, and the Champion District and the top portion of the map is blocked off for construction. It feels familiar, yet also not at the same time, which leads into the small, and very traditional second space of Onomichi. It feels very much in line with where I'd envision Kiryu in his late 40s would retire to if he could ever get rid of his yakuza shackles. There's a variety of new characters introduced in this section, and they are a good fit, very much so for the last title featuring the main character of series old. While the new stuff is all well and done, there's odd places where the callbacks, especially considering the relations Kiryu has with some of them, is either absent or almost non-existent. Majima fans must be seething to see so little of him in 5, and now in 6 as well. We do get the returning favourite, Akiyama once again, but it's weird to not see Majima helping Kiryu out in his final outing, considering their relationship. Saigo and Sodachi make returns as side quests to beat them up, and even Yuya makes a return, though many others don't even pop up at all, or are briefly mentioned.The combat feels very much like Kiwami 2's combat, since this one came first, it doesn't have quite as much in the way of contextual Heat moves outside of Extreme Heat mode, and you'll be popping that off to get much mileage out of going ham on enemies, with Extreme Heat acting as a beefed up Beast mode being able to auto pick up weapons, throwing motorcycles and other large objects, and dealing more damage overall. There's an odd lack of storeable weapons as well, though it's compensated somewhat by most weapons actually doing decent damage for once, at the cost of very low durability. Substories are all voiced, which feels great for people that find it boring to sit through texts during these segments, and it's very nice to see it, though the substories aren't quite as numerous because of this. There are some cool and even heartwarming ones in this area, and you don't need to do all of them to fight Amon this time. Not too bad for the final entry as Kiryu as the populace's problem solver.There's a complaint that a lot of minigames are absent, either due to the Dragon Engine's limitations or lack of time, but those are usually people who don't do the Completion List anyways, and who really laments the fact that there aren't godlike AI going against you in pool? It's really only the novelty of those things missing. Though in that defense as well, it's nigh impossible to actually 100% the Completion List if you're doing it because of the accursed Puyo Puyo requirement. If they ever bring Judgment to PC, pray it is the remastered version without the Puyo Puyo curse. Otherwise, the achievement cleanup here is probably the easiest to do in all the series, and would most certainly the hardest if you actually needed to do the Completion List. Kiryu Clan is an enjoyable romp where instead of playing defense in Kiwami 2, you're doing offense, and as an off hand note, the DLC is literally pay to win, and there are free codes you can use to make things easier too, so don't feel like you need to get the DLC unless you really want to steamroll this aspect of the game.The story may be shaky at its core, and the final villains are just more of the same smarmy evil forms that lack any real character or motivation outside of power grabbing (conversely for once, the side villains are actually interesting this time around), but the story is still very solid and it both feels like they did the end justice, and didn't. It still succeeds more than it doesn't, and it's been a damn fine journey going along with Kiryu. So long, Dragon of Dojima, until we meet again. And I think it'll be very soon.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all - I dislike ending which Nagoshi served us, long time fans. I never liked it to the point, when I've played this game back in the day after PS4 premiere, I had depression afterwards and I had to have a long break from videogames in general. This time, while replaying it on PC I was somewhat prepared...but still, this title makes me deeply emotional.To the core and mechanics. Game is made on Dragon Engine (first one which uses it) so it looks noticeably better than previous entries in the series chronologically. Gameplay is common to the series as well, pure fun beat'em up while usign different kind of objects and people (yes, people). Player have a time to explore sidequests and time to go deeper into the main story and mostly it's up to us to choose what we want to do at the time. It is good old Yakuza with very good substories (I strongly recommend fishing related story and minigame) and minigames. The latter ones are significantly reduced due to the lenght of the game overall. This is one of the shortest entries in the series - there is no need for long and convoluted plots as main focus was to end the story of Kiryu and Haruka.If you've played previous games in the series, you don't need my review to decide if you should play it or not -  But be warned: have some tissues nearby while playing. PC port looks amazing and performs well, so I can recommend it. Ultrawide resolutions works well (except for cutscenes, where we have black bars). There is autosave and save on the fly option. If you want to play this game straight after Kiwami remakes - DO NOT. Play them in order, Yakuza 6 picks up straight after what happens in Yakuza 5. You will learn more about characters and get attached to them before reaching conclusion.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 6: The Song of Life is the final chapter in the saga of Kazuma Kiryu, the legendary Dragon of Dojima. It is a fantastic ending to his story, with emotional moments, thrilling twists and satisfying closure. The game also boasts great graphics thanks to the new Dragon Engine, which makes the world of Kamurocho  immersive and realistic than ever.However, the game is not without its flaws. The combat system, while decent, feels downgraded from previous entries, with fewer moves, styles and heat actions. The game also lacks many fan-favorite characters, such as Majima, Daigo and Saejima, who barely appear until one scene at the end. This is especially disappointing considering that this was supposed to be the last entry in Kiryu’s story, and it would have been nice to see more interactions and closure with them.Another issue is Haruka’s characterization, which seems inconsistent and out of character at times. She acts recklessly and selfishly, putting both Kiryu and Haruto in danger. She also does not call Kiryu her father in what she believes to be his last moments, which feels odd and disrespectful. The game also removes half of Kamurocho, which makes the city feel smaller and less diverse. The game also changes the heat aura colors and gameplay flow, which may annoy some fans of the series.The game also suffers from poor optimization, with long loading times, frame drops and glitches. Some of the new characters are also disappointing, such as Yuta, who is bland and annoying, or Someya, who is underdeveloped and wasted. The game also has some questionable plot points and decisions that may leave some players unsatisfied or confused.Despite these flaws, Yakuza 6: The Song of Life is still a good game that deserves to be played by fans of the series. It has a lot of heart and charm, with memorable scenes, characters and minigames. It also has a great soundtrack and voice acting that enhance the experience. It is a worthy farewell to Kiryu, who has been one of the most iconic and beloved protagonists in gaming history.As a joke, I would say that Akiyama should have been everyone in this game. He is one of the best characters in the series, with his charisma, humor and skills. He barely appears in Yakuza 6 and is completely absent in Yakuza 7. I hope that his lack of appearances could be a sign for him to be in Like a Dragon 8 or his own game. He deserves more spotlight and recognition.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna start with this. I was expecting to just glide through this game, and learn what I need to learn for LAD. I seemed to be liking the games less and less as I plowed through the series. Kiwami 2 was a great sightseeing tour and introduced Daigo and had the spectacular antagonist (Ryuji), but the overarching story felt like it went nowhere and forced a relationship between Kiryu and Sayaka outta nowhere. Then Yakuza 3, which I did enjoy, but I just hopped from story beat to story beat, didn't really feel like a Yakuza game. Then 4 and 5 were just a mess, I can respect the games, but I just did not enjoy my time with them as much as I did previous entries. And this entire time, LAD was tempting me. I love turn based combat/the whole JRPG setup, and the supposed twist into the more humorous side of the series looked like it was right up my alley. I could have easily dropped 5 and skipped 6, but I dug my heels, and powered through 5 and 6. And boy oh BOY do I not regret doing that.Yakuza 6 is absolutely fantastic, I can barely think of any flaws in this game. The new Hiroshima map is unlike anything we've seen, the calming Japanese rural suburb was just a treat on the eyes and looked stunning in the Dragon Engine. The characters, story, twists, and reveals are  some of the best in the series. I found myself falling in love with every main, side, and reoccurring character. And the big twists in the second half of the game literally had my jaw on the floor. This is introducing some MGS LaLiLuLeLo type ♥♥♥♥ and I LOVE IT! Its full of confusion, tension, laughter, tears, it sends you on a roller-coaster! Music is phenomenal, gameplay is great (but still not better than 0/K1), and that ending is one of the few endings to make me shed a tear.I beg you, ANY of you, who are planning to get into the series through LAD to please reconsider. Please, play the Kiryu saga all the way through. Just do it for this absolutely spectacular ending, and heartfelt sendoff for one of the most beloved and revered characters of all of gaming.

_childDocuments_.review: Since the release of Yakuza 0 for PC in 2018, I´ve played every Yakuza released on PC, I´ve even completed Kiwami & Kiwami 2 twice, because Sega thought it is a great Business decision to not release any PC-Ports for 2 years. Yakuza 6 carries the weight of having 6 predecessors and as the final game of a Saga, which lasted for more then a decade, it needs to conclude all of its Stories. This is not an easy task and despite that this is the best Game out of the franchise. And those are my reasons, why I think this is the best Yakuza-Game:The Game Engine used in Yakuza Kiwami 2, 6, 7, Jugdment and also Lost Judgment is just top notch. We have great looking Graphics, uncapped fps, decent lighting and one of the best face capturing technology in the industry. Thanks to that,  this game looks new, even 5 years after release, you can´t say the same about Kiwami 1, which release in the same year.With the Dragon Engine the fighting feels smooth and responsive as ever. Animations are smother, Kiryu looks finally like a human being when walking and running around and the ragdoll physics are just hilarious. Actually they show of Kiryus strength perfectly how he can launching a goon halfway across Kamurocho.Also in contrast to Yakuza 7, this game has a proper fighting system not that JRPG nonsense we got in Y7. Finally with Yakuza 6, all Substories are voiced. This makes the game feel more high-quality and actually more like a AAA-Game. This was something that always bothered me in the older Yakuza-Games. It can get tiresome really quick if you try to do all of the Substories to unlock and fight Amon.Some of you may think of this as a bad thing but with Y6 the series got finally back to its roots. We got the mess of Yakuza 4,5, when they tried to include more characters then just Kiryu. Yakuza 0 was great, but this is Majima we are talking about as a playable character, that´s whole diffrent Story. Kiryu was one of the last cool character left from the last decade. I´d call Kiryu oldschool. Chracters designed for todays games need to be shiny, bright likable for everyone and in need for friendship-power. I prefer characters like Kiryu: badass, One Man Army, respectful and someone you would respect. Some Examples: Kratos, Joel (TLOU), Sebastian (The Evil Within), Niko Bellic, Max Payne, Geralt (The Witcher). Unfortunately characters like those are dying out and except of Kratos, it is very unlikely that one of them will ever return.Those were the most outstanding points, there are some more like the well-written Story, the great Minigames (Speerfishing, Baseball), the atmosphere, especially Onomichi just looks beatiful, all Story Cutscenes are voiced and (ingame-)rendered (wasn´t the case in the older titles) and the Substories itself are really well written and interesting. _childDocuments_.review: Kiryu's final outing lives up to the saga.I felt that Yakuza 4 and 5 were weaker entries; the unfocused story and the sprawl of the content meant the games collected no momentum. The games would pivot to another side story, none of which were meaty enough to carry the player forward. Meanwhile, 1, 2 and 3 were simply older games, difficult to hold up to the standards of today. Yakuza 6 delivers on the focused, nuanced writing that made Yakuza 0 so special. You can tell this was made after 0 and Kiwami 1; the character work is really the focus and it pays off big time, both for the good and bad characters. It may not be as epic as 0, but the writing really stands true to the series, delivers the final beats you want from these characters, and does so with thematic gravitas. Hell, it even has some great acting, including a fantastic performance from Beat Takeshi. When Kiryu finally gets to the big bads in this game, I was whooping and hollering, and the emotional payoffs hit as hard as they deserve to in a series this long.Meanwhile, the combat got a boost. The Dragon Engine combat is just fun to mess around with, it's very silly as everyone ragdolls around and the hitboxes/locking animations are a little generous, but it still feels suitably punchy. I liked the heat mechanics here, there's a good level of management and reward. This game doesn't feel that great at 30 fps though, it's a bit mushy and unresponsive compared to the rest of the series. You get back most of that proper brawler arcade Yakuza feel if you can push it to 60 fps. For that reason alone, I really only recommend playing Yakuza 6 on PC or on Xbox Series consoles. Once you get that smooth feedback and snappy input, it's pretty solid and enjoyable to play. I found parts of 3-5's combat irritating and incomprehensible, but I didn't have any frustrations here.On PC performance. The Steam Deck is currently marked as Unsupported but I did not see any issues in my brief (1-2 hours) playtime. The Deck can't do a full 60 fps when I tried it, but it can manage a 40 fps lock on low, and dropping the resolution can help with battery life. As far as a big screen experience is concerned, the game is extremely GPU heavy. On an RTX 3060ti I got a solid 1620p (75% res scale for 4K) at 60fps on High, and I thought it looked great on a 10 foot projector screen. I hope the dev team considers adding some upscaling tech (DLSS, FSR, XESS) to the Dragon Engine eventually. This engine has always had issues with aliasing and it's on full display here. Oh well.Of course, as with the best of Yakuza, we also get the side stories and mini games that make the series so great. They all deliver here and I didn't find any of it too annoying like pool in Yakuza 5. And thankfully none of it is shoved in your face - there's a few side story cutscenes that trigger and take up a bit of time through a rushed playthrough, but I found it all pretty great and the game does not waste your time. Many side stories deliver a few laughs and quick combat experiences in just 15 minutes or less.All in all, I'd rank this game as the second best Kiryu game after Yakuza 0. Everything's just done right. Well done.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a classic Yakuza game and I think it's one of the better ones.Yakuza 1 & 2 Kiwami were good games but also disappointing after Yakuza 0. There was a lot there left from relatively simple original games, and the story and especially sidestories were not nearly as great as Yakuza 1. Yakuza 6 was made after Yakuza 0 and it shows, the quality of the storytelling is similar, and this is probably the main draw of Yakuza series. I would recommend skipping Yakuza 1 & 2 Kiwami and going straight to 6 after Yakuza 0. Or maybe you can just play Yakuza Like a Dragon which is a soft reboot and also turn-based RPG instead of beatemup. Also, the games are independent enough so you can play 6 straight away. There's a lengthy introduction that explains everything and the game doesn't have a lot of stuff you have to know to play it.Enough comparisons, let's talk about the game itself. It's a beatemup with character progression and a lot of mini-games and a story that switches between pathos and absurdism. It's great. As I've said, the story is the main attraction of the game, and it's highly recommended to play the sidestories you find. I don't think the hero Kyriu works well here as a protagonist, he always felt like a blank to me, which was appropriate in the early games where he was reactive force of justice. Still it has a great cast of characters, some of them are internationally recognizable actors which can surprise you.In some of the previous games I eventually got bored with the combat, and this is partly why I appreciate turn-based gameplay of Yakuza Like a Dragon. Here I set the difficulty to Hard and this might be one of the reasons I've enjoyed the combat more. It's not hard anyway, you can still obliterate a crowd of enemies with a single swing of a bicycle, and it doesn't matter how hard a boss strikes when you have hundreds of healing items available at any time. But on harder difficulty, I felt the need to be aware of what happens around me, reposition to not get stun-locked, and look for items on the ground I could use against tough foes. I still wouldn't play this game if not for the great story, but unlike Kiwami games I didn't wish for combat to disappear.It's the first game with an updated engine, and it looks good, especially in well-directed mocapped cutscenes. It's a little rough around the ages though, and there are performance issues and not as many options as you'd like. On normal graphical settings, the game tries to lower render resolution - and I needed that on my Steam deck - but usually, games that do that have some sort of temporal reconstruction processing, and here it's just SMAA. One small irritating detail is that the game is fully voiced which sounds good, but it's not like Mass Effect game where they've added camera work and animations: this means that several hours of the game is spent looking at the completely static scene where characters stand still and open their mouths to say stuff. It looks bad compared to proper cutscenes where characters are animated, and it's not as convenient as the usual JRPG text prompts. Plus it probably required a lot of work, and some of the lines sound like a first take. Later games went back to just having proper cutscenes and text for less important conversations.Anyway, if you know what a Yakuza game is then this is a good one, right there near Yakuza 0. If you don't know it's a decent place to start if Yakuza 0 graphics look outdated to you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute mess. I used to think it was the worst game in the main series, but I've since reviewed a lot of my criticisms of this game after both Gaiden and Infinite Wealth came out and produced two absolute trash games in a series that I used to think always produced great games, if flawed at times.Gameplay is the easiest thing to talk about when it comes to 6, because it's just complete rubbish. It's the first game on the dragon engine (By FAR the worst thing to happen to the series gameplay-wise), and where 3 had a sort of experimental game (Kenzan) beforehand to ease the transition and fix any major flaws with the gameplay, 6 IS the experimental game and the combat is just atrocious. Kiryu's moveset feels incredibly unfocused and sloppy, it's a huge step down from 0/Kiwami 1 - which themselves were a noticeable step down from 5. You'd be hard-pressed to find someone willing to defend 6's combat, as the only thing it provides is some mild entertainment in the first few hours at the new physics the dragon engine has, but the novelty for said physics quickly wears off and often ruins the tone of any serious encounter in the game when you practically have a seizure on the floor every time you get knocked down.The writing is the most frustrating part about this game. For every good thing the game has going for it, it has something equally bad alongside it, which prevents it from feeling like a satisfying story while also saving it from feeling like complete trash like Gaiden or Infinite Wealth; some examples:>The Hirose boys and the people of Onomichi are great, but 90% of the characters involved in the larger conspiracy are some of the blandest and most unremarkable the series had ever seen up to that point.>The game carries on directly from the ending of Yakuza 5, yet it feels utterly disconnected from 5 to the point of absurdity. Once the story gets going after the first chapter or so, virtually nothing about 5 and the events in that game are even hinted towards.>Kiryu's interactions with Haruto are great, but Haruto himself and everything to do with Haruka's story in this game absolutely should never have happened, and it's no wonder this game is the reason why so many people came to despise Haruka as a character. >Kiryu himself is pretty good in this game, but you can tell the writers were struggling to go back to writing a story with one protagonist after the last 3 main games had 4, 5 and then 2 protagonists; the pacing is pretty poor.>The ending is by far the best thing about 6, being probably the best moment in the series. But it's been continually ruined as RGG keep walking back on it over and over again as they just can't let Kiryu go and a lot of people got filtered by it. I know you can't really blame 6 for what 7, Gaiden and Infinite Wealth would later do, but it does end up souring what was the perfect sendoff for Kiryu.Overall, despite the complaints I'd still say it's a 6/10, and it is worth playing. It isn't a bad game by any means, but it does pale in comparison to most other games in the series in terms of writing but especially in terms of gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Yakuza 6 is a wonderful game to play as the dragon engine makes its debut in this title. The combat is crazy fun and a spectacular change from the more clunky PS3 remasters that I played through before this. The rag doll and psychics in the fights are really fun, with each boss fight feeling just as fun as the last. I honestly only had one boss fight in the entire game that frustrated me a little bit, so I'd say that's a positive improvement from the last 3 titles I played. However while this game was fun to play through, it felt incredibly short due to the previous two games having very long stories, because of the inclusion of multiple playable characters. Even playing a bunch of the mini games and doing a few sub stories here and there didn't really draw out a huge playtime of mine. The story for this game is the most confusing one yet, nothing made sense and all of the traditional twists and hyper connected story elements weren't really here for this game. This is definitely one of the weaker plots in my opinion however, don't let that ruin your experience as this game. While I didn't necessarily enjoy this games plot it's still a great game that you should play if you are a fan of the series and are playing chronologically. I'd even say you can play this game without playing the previous 5 titles as the main menu features a "Memories" section that will give you the rough plots of the previous 5 games, (But I still recommend you play the others in the series.)
_childDocuments_.name: Yakuza 6: The Song of Life

_childDocuments_.review:
In Yakuza 6, Kazuma Kiryu will find out exactly how much people are willing to sacrifice for family -- be those ties through blood or bond -- when he investigates a series of shadowy events that involve the ones he holds closest to his heart. Fresh out of a three-year prison sentence, an older and weathered Kiryu comes to find out that his surrogate daughter, Haruka, has gone missing from the orphanage he looks after. The trail leads him to his old stomping grounds in Kamurocho, where he discovers that she has been struck by a car and now lies in a coma. To make matters worse, Kiryu learns that Haruka now has a son that he must look after. With baby in hand, Kiryu journeys to the seaside town of Onomichi, Hiroshima to unravel the truth about Haruka, her son, and a sinister secret that the Hiroshima yakuza are harbouring. 

From the unparalleled realism of the new setting of Onomichi, a beautiful, sleepy port town in Hiroshima Prefecture, to the latest evolution of Kamurocho, the biggest red-light district in Tokyo, Yakuza 6 is the ultimate iteration the game's blend of gritty crime story, hyper-explosive combat, and all the vices and distractions those locales have to offer.

name: Arcade Paradise
detailed_description: WISHLIST MEOW! 😻 BUY ARCADE PARADISE VR NOW! About the Game Welcome to Arcade Paradise, the 90’s-fuelled retro arcade adventure. Rather than washing rags for a living, you decide to turn the family laundromat into the ultimate arcade. Play, profit, and purchase new arcade machines, with over 35 to choose from, to build your very own Arcade Paradise! Take the laundromat business made up of dull chores from washing clothes to throwing out the trash, and turn it into a booming arcade with the coolest games in town raking in all the money! Over 35 arcade games, each fully realized with its own gameplay, stories, missions, and high scores to set! Inspired by 3 decades of gaming, from early vector games right up to the 32-bit era. Insert a second coin and play against a friend in a number of co-operative & competitive arcade games with up to 4 players locally. Prove yourself across each game, set your high scores, make your favourite arcade game more popular and upload to the online leaderboards. From the individual games to choosing what song to put on the jukebox inspired by some of the great records of the early 90s, the soundtrack captures the heart of a bygone era. Hello 90’s. If you could smell this game, it would smell like memories. Everything from the look and feel of the arcades, to using the latest PC connected to the mind-blowing dial-up connection, all have been recreated with pure love. Doug Cockle (famous for his voice acting in Victor Vran and The Witcher series) plays the role of Ashley’s berating father. Being too busy in the Riviera to see King Wash for himself, you will receive many phone calls from Gerald sharing his wise words of advice and constant reminders to fix the toilet.

short_description: Manage profits, pick up gum, do the laundry and get coin to unlock arcade units and flip the family laundromat business to become an Arcade Paradise!

_childDocuments_.review: While I do recommend this game, there's some things to keep in mind.This is NOT a business management game.This game is a collection of minigames.You do not have any costs to manage or decisions to make. The only impact the business parts have is how quickly you unlock new games to play, and in what order. It is impossible to fail, you will eventually succeed and unlock every game even if you do not do everything "optimally."This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but if you go into it expecting one thing and getting another you might be disappointed.Now, as a collection of minigames, it's pretty cool. The environment of the laundry/arcade is really good, and every game has a series of goals for you to accomplish. (and their profitability goes up when you do) The story is pretty minimal but does add some extra intrigue and kept me motivated to keep progressing. The games themselves are mostly decent, although there are a few stinkers.Overall, I still recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like i have to rate this negative just because of the DLC.  I bought this game with the understanding that the developers were going to continue adding cabinets.  Did not realize they were going to be paid DLC.  Smoke Em 3D & Penguin Push are in the original title screens and art.  Asking users to purchase mini-games that were assumed to be included is a bait and switch.  Do not support this game.Kung Fury has been available elsewhere for years.  At this point they are asking users to purchase a storefront.  For the content, and depth of these mini-games, they should have been included in the original purchase price.
