_childDocuments_.review: As a person with ADHD and depression its often hard for me to stick to games for long term goals. I love playing strategy and simulation games, but after a week of obsessive play usually I have an episode and get overwhelmed. I start to feel the weight of keeping up long term goals, of maximizing my time and making sure I check every box, and eventually lose interest or have a sea of "new game" files (Stardew and Rimworld, I'm looking at you). This game is the perfect mix of business simulator and mini game hub. Everything is gamified - I feel good about picking up gum or unclogging a toilet. The long term goals feel like a surprise bonus to a genuinely fun arcade simulator. Each day is segmented into manageable goals, making it easy to jump back in after not playing. Despite this I don't feel any pressure to necessarily complete the daily goals - if I don't enjoy the game it asks me to play, I can spend time doing something else. I never feel guilty for not completely any laundry in a day, instead of other games where I feel a looming sense of dread for needing to complete all the unique daily tasks that stack up over time that add complication to the game. There are gentle reminders to help you keep organized on the business side, but it's not the end of the world if you leave the toilet clogged for an hour while you try to beat your high score on Zombat. There's a trickle of a story that comes through voicemails and chat messages with your family and friends that is engaging and keeps me wanting more. But at the end of the day, this is a killer arcade simulator where you will never be bored with the large variety of takes on classic games that add a twist to improve the basics. This game is nostalgia packed with game references and the aesthetic is unbeatable. Honestly going to be one of my favorite time killers from now on.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Early impressions are AMAZING. Finally an arcade simulator that I can both run the business AND play the games.It follows a lot of other "simulator" games that end up half baked, but instead... this ones full baked to perfection. -Original Arcade games (Clearly inspired by classics, but all have their own twists)-Best graphics out of all of the "simulator" genre-The style is nailed to PERFECTION from the mini-games, the arcade games, to the UI. This has Identity which so many games lack today.-Playing the arcade games themselves are not only fun on their own, but they improve your business by completing challenges making it beneficial to play!10/10! Best arcade game on the market. Already worth my 20 bucks and I'm not even 2 hours in.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Friday afternoon, 1994. Finished mowing the lawn as fast as I could, grabbed my allowance from my dad, and I was out the door, on my bike, headed to the bowling alley arcade. I scraped and rubbed that ten dollar bill, praying to the change machine to accept my meager offering. Once, twice, three times, an eternity, and finally, ka-ching, as quarters rained down into the coffer. It was on. Street Fighter, Smash TV, Super Off Road, NBA Jam, Turtles in Time, Killer Instinct, Space Harrier, After Burner, I poured my allowance into those machines in an ecstasy of colorful lights and explosions.This sim captures that essence perfectly. The arcade games are mostly all clones of the classics, but with enough uniqueness to make them feel like a new experience. The goals and daily tasks keep me coming back to beat my high scores. It's all painstakingly recreated, like a love letter to a bygone era, Arcade Paradise is a warm nostalgia trip, like being wrapped in a blanket that smells like cigarettes, fry grease, and spilled Coca Cola.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: You never get a second chance to make a first impression. So the devs took a very risky gamble here!We all come to this game for the 'arcade' aspect. But there is very little of that early on, as they front-loaded it (pun intended) with all the most boring tasks in life: i.e. Picking-up garbage, unclogging toilets, and doing laundry. More precisely: Other people's laundry! And loads of it, over and over again!!As such, the first few hours are mostly just a real grind. And sadly many players will lose patience and abandon this game well before getting to the good stuff!HOW-EV-ER, for those not afraid to get their hands dirty and put the effort, the rewards seem immense!Once you start expanding and buying new arcade cabinets (and even better: playing them!) you finally begin to see the light at the end of the...tumbler!As the somber days of the tedious laundry routine give way to the bright neon lights of the Arcade, you discover the many games you are slowly-but-surely adding, each playable and having their own objectives, upgrades, and achievements. There are even real-life leaderboards for each one of them, accessible from the main game menu (a.k.a. the unrealistic cell phone for this era)!Getting multiple games in one, while being able to manage your expansion and enjoying your success, suddenly becomes all the more enjoyable especially when you remember where you started!I am still not decided if the early grind was all that necessary. And I am sure there are ways to make this phase a bit more entertaining. But if you approach it with the mindset that this is as much of a 'sim' game than it is a 'tycoon / management' one, and understand that the whole point behind it is exactly to have you move AWAY from the boring laundry life and not to trap you in it, then your perseverance will eventually be rewarded with a wonderful trip down memory lane, when everything was only neon lights, hairspray, ...and arcade high scores!!
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute blast. Hours of fun and nostalgia to be had. The story is surprisingly impactful, and I found myself growing really attached to the characters; despite never actually seeing them. When it was over, all I wanted was more. If you're reading this trying to figure out whether or not to pick this game up, here's a few tips. 1. Your first upgrades should be the radio ad and the book that slows down time. These will make a huge difference on your daily income and give you more leeway with some of the peskier daily challenges. 2. Make sure to use the konami code(Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A, Start) on the title screen, so that the washing machines will turn gold and you will get an S rank no matter how long you take.3. In the beginning chores and laundry are your primary source of income, but you can buy the book to reduce the frequency of chores and just ignore the laundry once you start to really get the arcade going. 4. Completing the set of goals for each machine will make a huge difference in how much they pull in; between 2-4 times as much in my experience. 5. When you get to the point that you are having to empty the hoppers multiple times per day, the assistant manager is another really nice quality of life upgrade. 6. Don't bother with the book that makes machines more reliable until later in the game when you will sometimes have 3 machines break down every hour. I think that covers just about everything. Enjoy your stay at Arcade Paradise.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing for four hours and am really trying to find the fun but it's just not there for me. It has a lot of STYLE, but I cannot find the fun, if I'm honest. At least in the first four hours. Some have said "it gets better later", but I shouldn't have to play for 8 hours to get there.This is not really like Gas Station Simulator where you have different inventories to manage and a variety of tasks to accomplish. You just do laundry and wait for laundry. Sometimes you pick up trash or unplug a toilet. But mostly you just load and unload laundry.It's supposed to be about doing laundry to make money, but also playing around in your arcade "on the side", but there are some problematic conflicts with that, which I'll describe below.--You get money for completing loads of laundry, but you get "graded" for how fast you deliver the laundry to the table after the dryer timer hits zero. If you take your time unloading the laundry after the dryer hits zero, you make less and less money very quickly, so you need to unload the laundry fast. That being the case, it discourages you from playing the arcade games because you'll either have to constantly quit in the middle of your game to unload the laundry fast enough or constantly get a bad grade / less money. So rather than using the arcade games to "pass the time", you instead end up standing around the laundry room waiting for loads of laundry to finish.--Whenever a washer finishes, dryer finishes, new basket arrives, new chat message is received, toilet plugs, etc, the game shows an animation of you checking your watch, which has a notification on it to let you know what is happening. If you are playing an arcade game, this animation of your arm coming up to check your watch repeatedly plays as different things are happening, but the animation of your arm covers the screen, blocking the view of the game you're playing. And it's not just your arm. Various UI messages can cover the screen while you play, blocking your view of the game you're playing. It's like someone repeatedly covering your eyes while you're trying to play. It's basically griefing. This discourages you from playing the arcade games during business hours. So rather than using the arcade games to "pass the time", you instead end up standing around the laundry room waiting for loads of laundry to finish.--Really the only time it's worth playing the arcade games is at night after the business closes when you won't get penalized for it and the constant notifications won't grief you while you try to play. But... unfortunately the game kinda ruins that for you, too.--Staying after close is the best time to play the arcade cabinets, because you won't get penalized on your income for "taking too long" to respond to laundry and there won't be any watch-checking griefing while you play. But you're told that if you stay too long after hours, you'll pass out, which is a DIFFERENT kind of penalty, so here too it discourages you from playing the arcade cabinets. (The game does not tell you when passing out will happen, so it's either a surprise or you  have to take it up the ass once to find out.) It sounds like what you should do is go home to sleep as soon as you can rather than hanging around too long and risking this penalty that could happen at literally at any moment (you don't know). So even during the time when you can finally play the arcades without nags and penalties, you still can't really, because you are under time pressure to hurry up and leave.--Remember above when I said you get penalized for taking too long to unload the dryer when it's done? Well your business closes at 11pm, but customers will sometimes come in and give you laundry really close to closing time, so there is absolutely no way the laundry is going to make it through washer and dryer by closing time. The game is unclear on what happens when there is still laundry in the building when the business closes. It tells you that no more profit is generated after closing, but you can still complete the load and are shown a message that you received money. So did you receive the money or not???  Also, if a customer comes in very late in this way, and the laundry can't be completed by close, and you don't want to pass out, so you just leave and come back the next day, you will still get penalized for "taking too long" with the laundry, even though by the "rules" of this game, you were not supposed to hang around too long to finish, and it's not clear you would get money for it anyway, if you consider the previous point.--But suppose you do decide you are going to stay late and push your luck to make sure that laundry gets all the way done on the day it arrived. Well, at 2am the game for some reason locks you out of all your controls. You can't interact with washers, dryers, the safe in your office, or anything. I don't know why it does this, since it already threatens you with passing out if you stay too long, but it does this for some reason. So even if you want to try and finish the laundry, it might simply not let you. And then it will tell you the next day that you did a bad job.--There are actually two different currencies in the game. One is dollars, which you earn by doing work in the laundromat or cleaning out the coin hoppers on the arcade machines. The other is pounds, which you earn by completing random "objectives", usually pertaining to getting achievements or certain scores in a random arcade game. Some of the upgrades can only be bought with pounds. While I appreciate this in theory, by giving players more reason to engage with the different games, if you're not a player who is really interested in cheevie hunting or don't like all of the games, it feels annoying to have to play games you don't want to in order to get certain upgrades or rely on the RNG to give you a task in a game you actually like.--Some of the gripes above can be eliminated / relieved by sorta "cheat" upgrades you can buy later, but they are locked behind pounds (see previous point) and it takes a long time to get them. Some of them don't feel like "upgrades" so much as fixes for things that felt like bugs.There is a lot of charm going on here in terms of just loving the vibe of old arcades. That's what brought me here in the first place. And I like the idea of playing around in my own arcade at my leisure, but the game never really gives me the freedom and peace to do that at my leisure. I also like the idea of running a business to help support the arcade, but the "running the business" aspects of the game just are not very interesting. You don't really get to make any kind of decisions. You just grind loads of laundry for money. There are "upgrades" to buy, like room expansions and new arcade cabinets, but it's all pretty much on a track. There is no real "management" to it at all. It's just grind and unlock.[UPDATE: Some other reviewers / commenters have argued that the problem is "I'm playing it wrong". They are saying I'm supposed to ignore the laundry and just play games all day. If that's the case, I don't think the game makes this clear. I'm a person who tries to do a good job, so my instinct is to try and do well at "both of my businesses", i.e. run a good laundromat AND a good arcade. But people are telling me I'm *supposed* to *neglect* the laundromat.  I don't feel like the game's instructions or feedback point me in that direction, and even if it did, that just doesn't feel good to me? Anyway.]Ultimately this game feels like it has two components, both of which I would enjoy in theory, but both of them just kinda trip over each other and get in each other's way.The fault may be entirely with me. Maybe I'm just unable to find the rhythm this solomon's child of a game is marching to. But... it's been four hours and I just can't find it.It looks like the game is finding its people, though, and I wish the developers well. Just wasn't working for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: I recall reading a bunch of negative reviews on this game and going in very hesitant because of it. I've binged this game for the last couple of days so here's my thoughts.Overall a pretty fun and kind of addicting game. If you're like me and enjoy trying to optimize your management/sim games, this can keep you hooked for a while. Each in-game day you're very limited on time so, to optimize, you have to do all of your tasks very quickly and efficiently. Pros:- Can get addicting after you get going- Some of the arcade games are quite a bit of fun- Good feeling of expanding your business and accomplishing a bunch of goals- In-game dailies and machine-specific goals are enough to keep you super busy for quite a while- The feeling of your business growingCons:- I've had a number of goal-tracking bugs where I do the goal but it won't register it as done so some of them have to go uncompleted. It can be kind of frustrating but it's not the end of the world.- Some of the arcade games are super boring, but you can get plenty of goals for them. Making me play a boring game for 10 minutes as a daily can be....not fun. I think "play game for X time" dailies are kind of silly, but they at least have an easy work around of just walking away for a while.- Early game isn't super engaging imo.- Some of the trash is really hard to pick up. Like it doesn't matter where you look or how close you are to it, sometimes it just won't let you pick it up.To conclude, I wouldn't pay $20 for this game, but I am very picky about spending money on games. I'd pay probably $10-$12 for it, so maybe catch it on sale. Try to find the good in it because there genuinely is a lot of good in the game. It just has some obstacles you need to overcome.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointingly shallow - there is no management aspects beyond where you place your machines, and all of the chores quickly become tedious. The games are decent enough, but the obnoxious nickle and dime tactics of the dlc means the game is over double the price if you want the full content - because at the end of the day, the arcade games are the only fun parts of Arcade Paradise. Even then, they're *just* arcade games, and are hardly capable of being entertaining for more than half an hour each.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: The LaundCade Simulator has ArrivedAs soon as I was crawling around on a Laundrette floor searching for chewing gum and plastic bottles I knew this game had me by the Sean Kerlys’. Arcade Paradise follows the story of a son who is given the opportunity to make something of himself by his dad by taking over the family laundrette business.Every day you will drag your arse into the laundrette on the bus and then the day job will begin. You’ll be presented with the benign tasks of running a laundrette such as unblocking the toilet, emptying the cash hoppers, taking the rubbish out and filling the safe with last night's takings. Once you’re done with that you’ll have to get as many washes on the go as you can and then be ready to pop those washes in the dryer as soon as the wash cycle ends. Once dried you’ll need to get those clothes back into the collection area for your customers to collect. Spinning all these plates will ensure that your laundrette business keeps the money rolling in.On the face of it, this daily grind sounds monotonous and boring and yes it would definitely become very monotonous and boring if it wasn’t for the fact that every task is gamified in some way. Pulling chewing gum from surfaces is a game of golf game-style timing in order to get maximum pulling power and purchase when trying to collect these little sticky rewards from the premises. Picking up rubbish from various parts of the laundrette fills your rubbish sack as you add more to it and then when it’s full it’s time to see if you can hit the bull's eye of the dumpster outside the shop with your bag of litter. The speed in which you wash, dry and return the dirty clothes to your customers is rated in order that they can give you more cash for a better level of service, unlocking the safe also requires you to do 3 left and right combinations to crack the code each time you fill up with the day's takings and the grimmest of all the jobs, unblocking the toilet, is all about finding the sweet spot on your analogue stick and pressing the trigger to defeat that blockage.Then comes the main event, the arcade machines!Out the back of your laundrette is a stock room that has seen better days but it does contain 3 arcade cabinets for your customers to play that can generate cash for the business. You can also play these games yourself! Here comes the thing that hooked me most about this game. There is a constant battle between trying to run your laundrette and earn cash for new machines and also to play the games in your stock room to enable you to complete tasks that are baked into the game. Can I just say one thing, these games that exist in the arcade room are bloody marvellous! All of the games are made with love and care and obvious nods to the classics. It’s a miracle of gaming that these games exist within an already intriguing and amazing video game. There are actually 35 games in the game plus the overall game, take that in for one moment…At the moment my favourite one to play is Wood Gal's Adventure which is massively addicted and normally sees me miss the drying cycle timer in order to play just one more go on Wood Gal!In order to build up your arcade and make it a success, you will need to think about the placement of your existing machines and also which machines to buy next with your hard-earned cash. Placement is a consideration as placing a popular game next to an underearner may increase its potential for earnings. Once you have enough cash in the bank you can then hop onto your old school PC to order a new machine and have the anticipation of waiting until the following day to take receipt of it into your LaundCade.When I think about my experience with Arcade Paradise it’s the little things that make it a classic. The PDA that you use to track goals and make adjustments to how your shop runs, your Casio watch that reminds you of key events such as wash reminders and hammering home the need to unblock the toilet, the perfection in the setting and how it portrays that time in the 80s and 90s when arcade machines lived in laundrettes and taxi rank, the game of Llama on your PDA and of course the arcade cabinets in the game being just perfect!When I originally saw this game I knew I was going to love it. Playing the game has proven to me that not only does this game tug at my nostalgia and my dream to run my own Arcade, but it also delivers more than that and that’s the genius of the devs right there. The words above only scratch the surface of what awaits you in this video game and I don’t want to take away the wonder of playing the game by giving away anything more as you deserve to experience this labour of love for yourselves. This game is a pure joy to play, so just go buy it.See The Full Review Here: P.S - Devs if you are reading, please put a Ker Ching till noise into the game when you place money in the safe*Full disclosure, this game contains a tune from the Senior Reviewer Britt’s band Recluse and in no way does that sway our judgement of the game. Plus the tune is an absolute stone wall classic, so go and get the soundtrack when that’s released! Right, I’m off to sniff some washing detergent while playing Knuckles & Knees with may last remaining 20p!
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: I was really hoping for more out of this game. I wanted to have something with lots of customization options, but this game is mostly just a grind that has very limited options for what you can do with your arcade. You don't really get to choose the layout of the arcade, and all you can really do is change where the machines go and even that does not really make it feel like your arcade.The loop of cleaning clothing is not that fun and the games don't really have that much replay value. The upgrades do not seem to add to much to the game, all they really do is make a mundane task faster, but that does not mean that you still don't have to do it.This game had some hope at one point, but really just seemed to fall flat, at least for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Easy recommend, 17 hours for me to beat the main storyline.The overarching game is where you manage a laundromat as a front to build an underground arcade in the back, slowly pushing the arcade to the forefront.  I won't go into plot details, but I will be SPOILING the complete list of playable games and their real world allegories since I've had so many friends ask.Yes, every arcade game in this game is wholly playable.  I will be listing all playable machines that I've unlocked (there's still some locked spots, probably DLC) in alphabetical order, their real world equivalent, and any following notes.  Then listing DLC cabs.You good?Alright, the list...Air Hockey - Air HockeyAttack Vector - Battlezone (top-down)Barkanoid - Arkanoid (but the paddle's a dog...very clever)Blobs from Space - Space InvadersBlockchain - Drop7Bomb Dudes - Bomber ManBugai - Bust-a-Move (aka: Puzzle Bobble)Championship Darts - Darts (301 rules, mechanics similar to the Shenmue minigame)Communists From Mars - Missile CommandCyber Dance - Dance Dance RevolutionFruit Crush - Puyo PuyoGraffiti Ballz - Merge BallsGravichase - Super HexagonHustler - Pool (pocket billiards for specifics)Jukebox - (Plays Music)Knuckles & Knees - Final FightLine Terror - Qix (aka "Bad Area")Meteor Madness - Asteroids (but with turrets that shoot back and gems to collect)Racer Chaser - Pac-Man (but with GTA inspired graphics)Shuttlecocks - PongSlime Pipes - Pipe Dream (pipe mania)Space Race Simulator - Outrun (but looks like F-Zero)Stack Overflow - Original? (it's a sorting game that's mechanically Lucas' Tower, but you sort by color instead of by size)Strike Gold - Mr. DrillerTable Football - FooseballThump-A-Gopher - Whack-a-MoleToad & Turtle - FroggerUFO Assault - Blitz (C64 game, those systems were popular in Europe)Video Air Hockey - Air Hockey (similar to Laser Hockey from WiiPlay)Vostok 2093 - Galaga (but with a splash of U.N. Squadron through upgrades, different weapons, etc)Woodgal Jr - TimbermanWoodgal's Adventure - Candy Crush (with RPG mechanics.  One of the longest games AND a starting cab.)Woodguy Golf - Mario GolfWoodguy Jr. - Timberman (the only clone-cabinent in the base game)Zombat 2 - Total Carnage (and the sequel to the Zombat minigame from The Hungry Horde - same company)-=DLC=-Cyber Dance: Euro Mix - DDR again (but with eurobeat - a clone cab)Empathy - N/A (ASCII graphics and designed like ShockerKung Fury - One Finger Death PunchPenguin Push - Mario Bros (1983)R.O.G.E.R. - Chase (top gun inspiration, you have to run away from an ever growing number of missiles for set time limits.  Reminded me first of Hungry Hungry Felhounds)Smoke 'Em - Shooting Gallery (light-gun target shooting in style of Namco and Taito games from the early 90s)Summer Of Sports - World Class Track MeetVoxtok Inc. Pinball - Pinball (Original machine - 70s design - appears to be an "Electrifying" machine, mechanically you alternate left/right to walk)And following the game's credits message, this review/recommend/compendium is in loving memory of my Aunt, who first introduced me to video games, arcades, and bought me my first system - a PS1 (and thanks to my mom for giving me a used Win98 office PC when they upgraded to Win2000 - while "Gaming" is my passion, I still prefer PC to Consoles for their modularity.)
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Do NOT buy this if you just want to play retro arcade games. Many of them are broken, and most are inferior novelties based on the classic, but they're not executed well enough to stand on their own.The real fun of Arcade Paradise lies in the business management aspects of the title, and the story of running an arcade against the will of your father. You'll want to finish it to finally prove him wrong. It's also weirdly satisfying to do laundry and pick gum off the seats.6.5/10 - definitely worth your time but not for the reasons you'd expect
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Microtransactions for each new individual cabinet? No thanks. I loved the game on release and recommended it to friends, but this is not a model I can support.  There were cabinets in the trailer and in the main menu screen that are not available in the game, and there was clearly intended room for aditional cabinets. This just makes it look like the developers intentionally cut content to sell it as individual microtransactions later.Edit: Due to the developer response I would like to clarify that only new cabinets released after the main game are microtransactions. The base game is still amazing, it is only the microtransaction model that I have an issue with, as I generally dislike microtransactions in single player games. A model I would have supported for this game would be a larger DLC that adds 5+ arcade cabinets, a new expansion to the building and some other minor content, like new upgrades and mail/messenger conversations priced at 10€/10$ instead of selling individual cabinets or bundles. Starting up Arcade Paradise to play one individual new cabinet just feels like buying a port/remake of an old arcade game and going through hoops to play it, especially after you've completed everything else in the game. Arcade Paradise as a whole is an entire vibe, going from a person with a dream picking up socks and pulling bubble gum and dealing with an overbearing father to the owner of an arcade empire set in the beautiful carefree atmosphere of the early 90s. Playing arcade cabinets is just a minor part of that, so only adding individual arcade cabinets does not add more Arcade Paradise for me.I do love the base game and I do hope I get enticed back in the future and end up recommending the game again, but selling individual cabinets is not it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve always had a bit of a fascination for arcades. It might be due to the fact that there aren’t many in my city, as they were slowly closing down when I was still a child, but the fact remains that I’ve always loved going to them and playing whatever games they had. Air hockey remains, to this day, my favorite. Recently, I’ve been craving going to an arcade again, but it’s tough to find the company to do so, especially nowadays. Imagine, then, my surprise, when I decided to look up online arcade experiences and found this game. It seemed to tick all my boxes, so I got it. 25 hours later, I have to say… I’m not at all disappointed. Quite the opposite, even. Let me explain why.—---------Arcade Paradise has 19 year old Ashley - that’s you! - running a long-forgotten family business: a laundromat called King Wash. On her first day on the job, though, she finds some arcade cabinets in the back, and after running the numbers, decides that it’s a good idea to turn the laundromat into an arcade. However, her father strongly disagrees, and she disagrees with his disagreement, as any sane person would (I mean, a laundromat over an arcade? seriously my guy????). So what’s the solution? To start a hidden arcade in the back of the laundromat! And so begins our journey to set up the best arcade ever.The first thing I want to mention here is that this game is about a 90s arcade, and it SHOWS.  From neon lights in multiple colors to black floors covered in colorful shapes and forms, complete with a jukebox full of early 90s tunes and even an internet dial-up tone, the developers took great care to make it feel like a trip down the memory lane. I wasn’t alive for half of the 90s and too young to do anything on the other half and even I was enamored by everything they managed to do here. And that’s not to mention the main attraction of the game: the arcade cabinets themselves.  You may recognize, for example, an Arcade Paradise version of Pac-man, air hockey and even dance dance revolution! I’ll stop here because I don’t want to spoil them, since buying and testing the cabinets yourself is potentially the most fun part of the game, but still, take my word for it when I say that they’re mostly pretty good. Quite a few of the cabinets also allow for multiplayer and online leaderboards, if you’re one to chase high scores (which I understand is the reason lots of people played arcade cabinets in their lives - or at least that’s the case for the people I know anyway).At this point you may be asking yourself: “is that it?”- or maybe you’re not asking yourself anything and just finding me crazy for assuming. But humor me and pretend you asked the question. The answer is no, that is not it. See, as I mentioned, you build the arcade from the ground up. All you have when you start is around 3 cabinets and a stinky laundromat. So how do you grow and get more cabinets? By doing the management bit of the game, earning money and buying more cabinets and expansions for your building!In Arcade Paradise, your arcade cabinets are the star of the show. That means they are your main method of making money, as people have to pay to use the cabinets. Aside from buying them and expanding your space in order to buy even more of them, you can also level your cabinets up, per say.  You can directly influence the popularity by playing the cabinets, but there are also other ways to do so.  If you place a less popular cabinet next to one of your better performing ones, the less popular one also receives a boost. You can also individually change prices and difficulty settings for each cabinet, and the game will automatically calculate the hourly profit from each combination. This is what you will spend the most of your time in the game doing: playing arcades and optimizing their profits. Well, that and… chores.Yep, the game has chores. Remember the laundromat side of the business? In the early game, it will serve as a really good source of income for your commercial adventure. However, the process for earning money this way is very boring. I know some people were into it, but it actually felt like a chore to me. You basically pick up clothes, put them in a washing machine (by holding E for a second or two), then wait a few hours, take the clothes out by holding E again, put them in a drying machine (holding E…), then wait a few hours, then get them out using the same process, and then you’re done. However, some of the chores in the game have a letter grading for how well you did the task, and this is unfortunately no different. So basically, if you want rank S (and the decent cash boost from it),  Still, the process doesn’t seem too bad, right? Well… keep in mind you usually have 3-5 sets of clothes going at any given time, and some with different timings.Thankfully, this specific chore can be ignored: if you don’t like it, my recommendation is to just stop doing the laundromat activities when your arcade cabinets start generating enough income to get you by. The other chores, however, can’t be ignored. You need to clean the place, unclog toilets, squash bugs from cabinets… all with their own accompanying minigames.  These missions can encompass all arcade cabinets, and like the goals, vary from easy to hard. The daily quests give very little of said currency, though, which makes it hard to save up for the more expensive upgrades. Extra tunes for the jukebox also cost upgrade currency, which breaks my heart, as I haven’t been able to buy any due to saving up for upgrades.In terms of issues,  The whack-a-mole cabinet, for example, didn’t actually spawn any moles when I first got it, which made for a very awkward 30 seconds (60 when you consider I tried it again). A few of the cabinets, like this one, ended up glitching upon their first few uses, but these glitches were all fixed by restarting the game. Some trash is also hard to pick up. But really, these are minor grievances that are a worthy trade-off for the awesome experience that is this game. I just wish the beginning wasn’t as boring with having to manage the laundromat, but oh well. There are people who are into that, I’m just not one of them. Still a great game though!
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game to build an arcade and enjoy playing the games in it.  Instead, I am addicted to running an efficient laundromat by doing laundry and picking up trash.  What the heck?  Recommended, but leave the gum alone, that's my job!EDIT:  So I have bought both DLC, all the arcade games added to the main game, and everything is working okay.  When I bought the first DLC, I had room in the arcade and added all of them.  With the second DLC, I just bought it before this review edit, and read in the discussion that players were encountering a bug that stopped them from continuining the game because they bought the DLC but had no room to add the games.  I don't have room for the new games, but I got a message in-game saying I didn't have room and needed to expand the floor space of my arcade to add the new games.  So I assume the bug is fixed.  Still, stay away from the gum, that's my job!
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: This game is actual amazing and very addictive.I absolutely love the different Arcades, yet i still miss a variant of Tetris.This game is not about realism, if you expect a serious Arcade Management Game, this is not the game for you.You CAN manage your Arcade, that's not the problem, but you don't have any "Problems". You don't have to pay workers (you can hire one as an "Update" but that's it). You don't have to pay for power or other expenses - quite the opposite, you get Money for EVERYTHING, even taking out the trash. You play your Arcade Games, empty the Hoppers once or twice per day and make a lot of money. That's basically it. You can optimize your machines for maximum profit.I think the important part of this game is it's message about abusive Control-Freak Parents. The type of Parents who like to ruin any of your dreams if you don't do as they want. No matter how good you are in the thing you love, they have to ruin it. So, i would call this game more like a storybased game instead of a Simulation.I really love this game. Well made Arcadegames which runs smooth and have sharp controls and a nice story to progress in.You may ask now, why i don't recommend it, if i love it so much?Because the most crucial thing is missing. If you finished your game and want to start over - well, YOU CAN'T.Because there is NO FRIGGIN NEW GAME BUTTON after you started a game. No profiles, no saveslots, so you could save your game in a current state and load it, whenever you want to experience that state again. Yeah, there is an emergency solution, you can turn off cloudsaves and then delete your savefile, blablabla. NO. Saving is a feature we know since the friggin nineties. So this developer can't add it in 2023?! That is very sad.SERIOUSLY DEVS. FIX IT.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Got this in a Humble Monthly. The amount of content you get for the price they're asking for the base game is criminal. It's like a Warioware game with how many different mini-games you can play. They sell new machines as DLC but those are optional and only if you've overplayed all the base games or you're a completionist like me. Not sure if I'll 100% this, but there's definitely content there for those looking.EDIT: My ONLY gripe is how slow or tedious completing the "To Dos" are to get the pound sterling required for upgrades. I have $20k+ sitting in the vault but I need to do 6+ days of To Dos for 400 pound sterling for a car? Why no conversion mechanic? I can see it being a mechanic to lengthen the hours of gameplay but it can be frustrating especially as some To Dos are significantly harder than others.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: I thought it was a great game for a week of playing, I've wanted to come back and play through it again for fun, but its impossible to just start a new game, a simple feature that I guess I've taken for granted until I couldn't do it anymore.It's a fun game, would like to see some more work go into it instead of just more DLC, like updates to polish it up and at least add the new game option.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: While I would love to recommend this game, with its current options I'm unable to play for more than a single day without feeling incredibly motion-sick. I love the premise and believe I would enjoy the game, but with a maximum FOV of just 60 and a slew of faked nostalgic screen effects, this is one that I'm currently unable to play to its full potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: I'm bummed out on this one, I should LOVE this game, but I don't.  The laundry gameplay loop is what kills this game for me, and unfortunately the arcade aesthetic doesn't save it.  You don't really have time to enjoy yourself and play the arcade games due to losing your cash and time to laundry. Wait 3 mins to wash - transfer - wait 3 mins to dry - place on counter. If you're a few seconds too late on doing your laundry duties then you earn barely anything.  I get it though, main premise of the game is you're taking over a laundromat, I expected to do some laundry...just didn't expect it to be worse than doing it IRL.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: A smidgen of today's technology overlapping a heavy dose of 1980 arcades. Performing daily tasks and managing a family business will provide access to variety of custom arcade cabinets. Each cabinet is a unique mini-game poised to capitalize on the look and feel of the 80's.There's an initial quirky feel to the game-play. The odd feeling fades to appreciating when the creativity of the developer shines through. The variety of machine designs and shared mini-games are truly fun to experience. In fact, they divert attention away from the business. The same business that provides income and enables the purchase of more arcades. Hopefully the growing collection arcades can provide a lucrative coin-drop to offset the laundry's losses.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked how this started. You get a job in your dad's laundromat and at the beginning you're mostly doing laundry, collecting coins out of the change machine, cleaning gum and trash - normal laundromat stuff. Once you get your arcade machines and start working towards an arcade, you're still expected to do the day-in, day-out laundromat stuff. Eventually you can unlock an assistant manager who handles some of the boring stuff, but at that point you realize that the gameplay loop is kind of built around this mundane stuff, and the actual fun challenges that are provided by the arcade machines are constantly interrupted by things like, "WASHER NEEDS FILLED", "YOU LEFT CLOTHES IN THE WASHER". I don't know about you, but I don't really like it when the game I'm playing puts up big red warnings that I'm not doing enough of the boring tasks. At a certain point the laundromat should become a non-issue, but instead it permeates and ruins any fun Arcade Paradise might build towards. You're constantly (and I mean constantly) interrupted from doing anything enjoyable by the game's systems getting upset that clothes have been in the dryer too long. Neat concept, holds up for about 4 hours. If the boring stuff sounds fun to you, get it. It just gets too repetitive to be fun to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Here's my top 5 problems with this game, if any are dealbreakers just pass.No sense of humour, aside from a very stylish and MTV-esque opening cinematic the game is incredibly dull and dry with any plot or dialog delivered via the games one voice actor monologuing at you over voicemail or pre-scripted text messaging.The game looks like it takes place in an old payday 2 map, with no particularly fun or interesting interactive items aside from actually playing the arcade games BUTThe game doesn't let you really sink in and invest time on the arcade games as you're constantly having to quit them to do chores/will literally pass out after a certain amount of time.You're never given enough data or freedom of customization to really enjoy this as a business management game, but as an immersive sim it gets incredibly tedious.The U.I and controls for things like the computer and PDA are totally messed up. It's possible to not see options for things you can buy (arcade games, upgrades) because you actually can't scroll the in-game computer windows properly. Also, the time-wasting flappy birds ripoff on the PDA still keeps time paused so it fails as a time-waster.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a emotional treat for me and a personal trip back to a better time.  Most of the games are clever re-works of arcade classics and the rest of the sim keeps you on your toes for a long time (be patient with the tasks, it's not forever.)  Just finished the game and I just want more!  My love to the developers!  You really made something special.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Though a few aspects of the game differ from reality, the game is not far from the reality of working in an arcade.I have nearly twenty years experience in the electro-mechanical industry and I would trade it all in just to go back to the days when I managed a number of micro-arcades (ones in hotels, cinemas, but never had one in a laundromat). Most of my day was spent maintaining the machines (yes, a ton of playing games) and ensuring the place is clean. This game is a great reminder of what once was a thriving industry that somehow clings on from becoming a thing of the past. If I could change one thing in the game, it would be the naming of the "hoppers" because they're supposed to be called cash boxes, hoppers dispense tokens (or coins in gambling machines).If in the extremely rare chance one of the developers sees this review, I would like to offer my experienced consultation if there ever be a sequel to this perfect game.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: For a game called "Arcade Paradise", I'm having to do an awful lot of laundry.  I guess it's ok for a startup business simulator, but I got tired of the grind pretty fast.  The mini-games are boring and easy.  Playing the arcade games is fun, but takes away from your Making money time.  I can't even imagine how long it would take to get to be an actual paradise... too long for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: This game kept feeeeeeling like it would be fun once you get the next upgrade, the next upgrade, the next whatever. I ended up just doing a ton of laundry because it feels like an item that SHOULD be checked off a list. I get that you don’t *have* to do it at all. But why can you not hire an employee to take care of it? Not even about the money making aspect, it just doesn’t make sense that you become crazy profitable with one business and just let the other one rot. Also, ♥♥♥♥ the dart game.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: This game is brilliant. But it has so... many... bugs... I guess it is understandable since there are so many things to do in this game, but it is still takes you out of it whenever it comes up, and it comes up a lot. Sometimes garbage or gum cannot be targeted due to object overlap. Many of the game specific objectives are busted and cannot be completed. Some of the games have bugs while playing, like bomb guys where you can get stuck behind the bomb in a dead end or space racer where, even while skidding, you cannot make many of the turns. And the bounce prediction algorithm is off by quite a bit so the pool balls won't bounce where it tells you they will and the same for Bugai. I even had $300k at the end game when you have to spend $150k, but it wouldn't let me make the purchase till my investment came in. I get that it was a story beat, but they easily could have made it cost $50k more than you had no matter what and the investment gives you exactly the right amount.I so want to 100% this game, but it is impossible in its current state. Regardless, it is a ton of fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Arcade Paradise just wasn't for me. The game play loop was tedious and boring, I spent more time worrying about laundry than actually having fun. The arcade side I was hoping for some customisation options for your arcade, but there where none apart from buy, place and play the machines.Maybe it was just me but I didn't have fun so I refunded.Good luck to the devs with the game though.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: A nice experience ruined by bad design choices and bugs. The path to victory is to play arcade machines and try to complete all the challenges for each machine. Complete a few arcades and you won't have to worry about the money. The issue is that challenges go from easy to impossible and broken. Some challenges reset when you quit the game, others are so ridiculous that nobody can ever reach them. Grind is also a common theme that almost borders on insanity in some machines. When you have this in the first hours of the game, there’s no desire to continue playing or even finishing it. I hope there’s a big patch coming that will fix some issues, because it would be a shame to let this die.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance, Arcade Paradise seems like another entry into the veritable mountain of Sim-Jank titles we've come to expect from Steam's liberal view of curation. And to be sure, there will be some of that, especially when you get your first glance at what appears to be the usual collection of prefabbed assets (it's on Unity, and you can definitely tell). But if you give the game a chance, and put up with a few dozen loads of laundry for a bit, you'll find there's a bit more under the hood than expected in terms of gameplay, narrative, and the satisfaction of growing your business from a crappy laundromat to a nostalgic Arcade refuge.In the beginning of the game, you start off working in a dilapidated laundromat which happens to have a handful of arcade games in the backroom, a room that frankly looks like no customer should assume they're allowed back there. During this time your primary focus is on maintaining the laundry business, putting in loads, switching them (why aren't customers doing this themselves? What the hell is that token machine for, then?) picking up trash (they're animals), unsticking gum. and unblocking the toilet. The immediate thing you'll notice in all of this is that everything is treated like a minigame. Laundry tests your speed in completing it, gum challenges you to pull strong enough in quick succession, and the toilet has you looking for the 'sweet spot' for the most 'damaging' plunges. None of it is particularly compelling on its own but that small bit of presentation goes a long way in keeping you here longer than expected.Of course, your primary motivation is to make enough money to buy more machines and ultimately manifest your dreams of a personal arcade into reality. This creates an interesting 'work-life balance' because the primary way to make your arcade machines profitable is to play them often, and complete the goals therein. This increases their traffic and allows you to set the price and difficulty higher, owing to their popularity. But you only have so much time between loads of laundry, which will be your primary source of income for the early goings of the game. For some players, the laundry is viewed as a chore. And I'm conflicted on how to feel about that. Because I agree - laundry gets annoying, and just interrupts you from what you'd rather be doing. But at the same time, it is a  That's the point. You'd rather be playing arcade games, and you can only do so between laundry tasks, and as annoying as that can be, it adds another layer of...thrill, perhaps? It adds some thrill to the arcade gaming experience, where the otherwise simplistic games take on new urgency when you've only got maybe 2 minutes to do whatever it is you need to do with them. And ultimately you dream of the day when you don't have to do laundry at all, a primary motivator for success. In this way, the game works as intended, even if that means grumbling to yourself whenever your wristwatch (don't get me started on that damn watch) beeps WASH at you while you're trying to get those last few money stacks in Racer Chaser.The arcade games themselves are a mixed bag. They seem to span an era of roughly between 1972 and 1998 (the game itself is set in 1993, so that knockoff Dance Dance Revolution should really be blowing people's minds). Some of them are okayish, others kinda boring, and a choice few are genuinely addicting. Many of them are recognizable as being based on something more famous. Shuttlecocks is just Pong, with no real variation from the classic formula. Communists From Mars is a pretty close approximation to Missile Command. Line Terror is a somehow more annoying version of Qix (we have history). Other games are recognizable in their inspiration but with a new twist. For instance, Racer Chaser's gameplay is overwhelmingly based on Pac-Man but is thematically also inspired by Grand Theft Auto. It adds the new element that once you're caught by a cop car, you jump out of your vehicle and make a run for it to another vehicle to continue the game. Another example would be Meteor Madness, quite clearly based on Asteroids but with the added element of tasking you to grapple crystals blown out from the rocks and bring them to the delivery point. There's a pretty wide variety of games just in the base game alone, and I won't speak to the quality of the DLC games as I only purchased one, the pinball machine (Which is...fine).Somewhat surprisingly, the game has a narrative woven into all of this, surrounding your disapproving, business-tycoon father's reluctant decision to let you run his old laundromat, and your collaboration with your sister working at City Hall to help you transform the place into a thriving arcade without the old man's knowledge. The story beats are a bit predictable but I appreciate that some effort was put into it, as it's not really what you expect out of a game like this. The only voice acting you'll hear is from your crankshaft of a father, and the actor is putting on this very comical hoity-toity voice ("Hello Ashley...this is your father." Very organic). Proving your dad wrong might not motivate most players to move forward as much as the simple promise of buying a new cabinet but it does give some sort of context to the whole thing, even if the game tremendously glosses over the actual logistical challenges to owning an arcade (there is literally no overhead. That's very convenient!)Overall, this is a game I picked up on sale for $7 in the hopes of distracting me for a little bit from existing in America, in October of 2024. What I figured I'd get bored with in two or three days turned into something that I honestly couldn't put down, with the allure of the delivery truck recklessly dropping a new game at my doorstep always keeping me playing for just one more business day. I don't think it's a game for everybody, and I think it's something that might appeal to a more 'oddball' demographic, or at the very least, nostalgia seekers. But for a game that greatly exceeded my admittedly modest expectations, I am more than happy to award it the prestigious Blue Thumbs Up of Quality.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: I was part of the previous closed beta, and oh god I *loved* it. There have been a few arcade management sims in the past, but all of them seemed to have different failings that prevented them from reaching true greatness. Not this one! It seems like Arcade Paradise absolutely nails the atmosphere, the style, and the management sim sections without being dull or unpleasantly repetitive. What truly sets it apart from all the others is that this time, the arcades you buy and fine-tune for customers... they're playable! Fully playable minigames that ape popular titles of the past and the modern era too.I've "only" put around 8-9 hours into the game so far but gorram I love it and I can't wait to sink even more! Fabulous music, gorgeous visuals, playable engaging arcade games, and absolutely rock solid top-notch performance (something of a true rarity in the usual "sim" genre, where performance routinely falls by the wayside)~edit~Updated review, now 40hrs into it :) Such a fantastic game, thoroughly engrossing with gorgeous visuals and a surprisingly emotive story too. I truly hope Nosebleed Interactive continue to support the game with post-launch content \o/~edit~Voted in the "Sit Back and Relax" category, such a blast of a game deserves it!
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: I was gifted this after having it on my wish list. Took a couple weeks to get around to playing it but i really enjoy it! I used to work nights at a laundromat with a pinball table and a couple claw machines and used to have dreams of opening my own, but with an emphasis on arcade cabinets. This game is as close as i ever got to realizing that dream lol.As a 80's and 90's kid it feels like a personal love letter to my generation as well, so it's just a perfect match for me personally. I'm hoping the VR version due out soon, will also make it's way to PC! I said the moment i saw this game "That's perfect for VR!!!" The only thing that is missing to take this game to the next level (pun intended) would be a way to mod real arcade games i grew up with, into the game. Maybe in the future? Who knows. But right now i'm enjoying my self a lot! Definitely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: To those of a certain age and temperament – which, if you’re reading this review, I sense will be most of you – the glory days of the 90’s video game arcade are something that you probably recall with a wistful smile. The cacophony of lights and sounds that assaulted the sense as you entered its murky depths, the thrill of achieving a new high score or besting your friends… And that worrying sensation of not knowing exactly why your feet were sticking to the carpet with each step. It was the best of times, and chances are your older and aching body wants to recapture those moments. And so enters Arcade Paradise almost on cue, perhaps on a skateboard and wearing pants that are far too big, with the promise that it can deliver this and more… But it’s going to make you work for it, first.  You see, a bustling metropolis of video game nirvana is nothing but a dream in your mind’s eye when the story of Arcade Paradise begins. Instead, you’re down on your luck, forced by your father into the glitz and glamour that is the wonderful world of… Laundromat management. Yes, the first tasks that you face, and the ones that you’ll have to complete a not inconsiderable amount of times, are as follows; Get clothes. Put them in the washer. Take them out. Put them in the dryer. Take them out. From there you simply rinse and repeat, and I mean that in the very literal sense of the words.  Now, I can see the confused frown forming on your face already. Yet in all honesty and sincerity there’s a strange sense of calming therapy and routine to be taken in keeping things running over, which even extends to picking up the trash and slowly peeling gum off the seats. It’s all presented in a video game style as well – you’re graded on how fast your laundry loads are, the speediest of the cleaners earning the fabled S rank, earning a round of applause and suitably 90’s victory music to boot. Heck, the simple act of unblocking a toilet in presented with the pomp bravado as if it was an epic boss battle, health bar and all.  It’s charming and engaging, and that’s before we even get to the arcade cabinets that are tucked away in the back of the store. As you’d expect, these are the real money makers of your enterprise – as punters roll in and spend their hard earned quarters, that combines with your heard-earned laundry takings, and slowly but surely the world opens up to you. You can purchase more cabinets, instantly providing you with better cash flow. This can be then spent to bust down the walls of your humble little abode, opening up the space and in turn letting you fill the walls with more of a weird and wonderful selection of games. In all honestly it’s a fairly bare-bones management game, even taking into account the advanced tricks, like putting less popular games next to the popular ones to boost their takings. After all, the gameplay loop essentially boils down to slowly but surely waiting for your earnings to tick up towards the next big investment. But you know what? That’s ok. Because you’ve got a few things dotted around you to help pass the time…Yes, the big selling point of Arcade Paradise is the fact you can actually play the games you buy, and there’s a mad selection of over 35 titles for you to sink your teeth into. Many are essentially riffs and copies of classic titles, I’ll concede; ‘Racer Chaser’ is Pac-Man with a GTA skin, ‘Cyber Dance’ is Dance Dance Revolution in miniature form, and ‘Shuttlecocks’ is quite literally pong in everything but name. But there’s some original and clever stuff in here, too – my personal favourite is ‘Blockchain’, a weird number based puzzler that sees you playing a hacker. This is both infinitely more addictive than that premise might sound, and comes with such a compulsive background tune I’m dancing away in my chair even thinking about it. Opinions may vary as to the best games on offer, and you’ll certainly come across some stinkers you’ll play once and never touch again. Yet it still creates a situation where every new cabinet that explodes into your cabinet in a glorious fanfare creates a situation where it’s not only a pleasing boost to your profits, but also carries the excitement of seeing what its gameplay has in store. Each title also has goals, varying from the simple to the complex. Beating these not only gives you a slight fuzzy sense of pride, but boosts the revenue that game will earn. There’s also your daily to-do list, which tasks you with completing separate objectives that go towards funding personal upgrades. Some are basic, such as sneakers that allow running around your arcade like a child on the best sugar rush of their life. Yet others have dramatic effects that really can make things much easier; perhaps the best is the car, which in real terms simply provides more time per day, but also comes with the buzz that you're allowing your character to escape the drudgery of the early morning bus commute. Bundle this all together and for a good while this is brilliant stuff. Yet - oddly enough - the greater your success, the more the charm seems to wane. Remember the Laundromat? It might seem like a blessing your arcade rapidly begins to eclipse it, but it reality in removes the interesting plate-spinning mechanics of the early stages, where keeping your washing going was as important as investing time in your cabinets. The game’s unique nature slowly fades away into what is, essentially, a selection of mini-games… And it’s only so long you can play the same basic shooter or racer before the novelty really start to wear thin.There’s also a problem with Arcade Paradise's progression and objective systems, specifically the goals and to-do list mentioned above. Let’s start with the former – some goals on the games just have off-the-wall or absurd requirements, requiring massive inputs of time and effort (Or, in some of the worst cases, pure blind luck) in order to achieve them. Many of them are tied to the games which simply don’t enough substance to warrant such an investment, and as such both the game and the challenge it presents begin to grate very quickly.  The to-do list is even worse, and that’s primarily due to the fact you get a max of three tasks to do a day. No more, no less, and often they can be whittled out in a matter of minutes. This wouldn’t be too bad, but the upgrades you get from completing these tasks almost become critical in the end-game if you want to maintain both your pace and your sanity. It leads to the odd situation where you’re best off completing the easiest tasks, and then immediately heading for the door and starting the day anew to get a new set. I’ll be honest and say it’s good the story ends when it does, because trying to navigate such issues really wears away the charm the rest of the game has in spades. Still, in many ways I’m being overly critical. Even if I have no real intention to return to Arcade Paradise any time soon, I still found myself compelled and entertained by it for over 20 hours – a healthy playtime considering the asking price. I also can't deny it perfectly captures the spirit of those 90’s arcades we all spent our childhoods in, and it’s clear that was the game’s main goal from the outset. It’s a tiny bit of a shame that some odd design choices drag the experience down, then, but if you’re looking for a good time with a burst of 90’s nostalgia to boot you won’t go far wrong with this. Just… try not to get stuck to the virtual carpet, yeah?

_childDocuments_.review: In the beginning, I was getting a bit frustrated between running the laundromat and playing the games - but after I started getting daily tasks, I started believing that game is tuned that way on purpose. You are never being TOLD to neglect the laundromat, and the arcade is basically generating money on its own... however - neglecting the laundromat and actually playing arcade games instead will bring far bigger gains, AND the upgrades (once you get to them) and nearly ALL tuned towards getting you more gaming time.Now, with that realization, I absolutely love how the game, intentionally or not, showcases the philosophy of mindless employee drone and its grind vs. entrepreneurship, and the fact that you have to sacrifice illusion of stability and security in order to get big gains.These philosophies aside, its a really cool game. Nearly everything you do is a small minigame, like collecting and throwing the trash. Absolutely amazing is the fact that all arcade games I tried - are actually FUN AND PLAYABLE. They aren't just a gimmick that you'll play for five minutes and go "he he fun retro game gg", but I legit spent solid 70-80% of my time playing most of the ones I own.It is not much of a management game, so don't get confused there. It really just moves you from grinding repetitive tasks, towards playing retro-feeling games all day long and earning cash on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this game for the first few hours will seem like quite a chore as you will be managing a laundromat. The laundromat stuff is pretty easy, but also very tedious. For the first few hours it will be a pretty rough grind of loading machines and setting out the dry clothes for customers to earn profits to build up what you really came for which is the arcade. The arcade starts out small, and before too long it overtakes the game and starts to become the main source of daily profit for the business. At this point you can pretty much ignore the laundry machines and just focus on the arcade. There is still some daily tasks to keep in mind, such as cleaning up trash, occasionally fixing broken arcade machines, doing optional tasks for special currency, and more. That stuff though is pretty easy to knock out. Once you get to the point of not needing to focus on the laundromat, you can do your daily cleanup tasks which you can knock out quickly and then just focus on playing games in the arcade for the rest of the day! And there are some great titles here and there ranging from a multitude of genres. Not everything is going to win you over course, but its worth trying everything out at least once. And playing games also to meet certain tasks will reward the machines with a popularity bonus that  can increase money earned per hour to help maximize your daily profits. There's also some minimal micromanaging for the cabinets such as where you place them in the arcade, like having an unpopular machine next to a popular machine will give a boost to the less popular ones, and also setting the difficulty and price per play for customers for a variety of different hourly profit possibilities. And you'll want to look into the optional micromanaging to get things going as there are over 30 different cabinets to buy, as well as business expansions, and more. Luckily this part is not as tedious as the previous laundromat stuff was in the beginning. The game has an nice aesthetic to it matching a cool retro 90s vibe. The music is also great! I'm not really familiar with the artists they picked for the game, but they nailed a lot of sounds that feel straight out of that era. The variety of arcade cabinets and other games is also amazing, with lots of them being nods to classic arcade games. Like I said before not all will win you over, but some definitely will. I found myself playing several of them for quite a bit literally running through the entire in game day on several occasions on quite a few titles. What's better is that this game works wonderfully on the steam deck which is where I played most of it. Definitely check this one out if you are a fan of retro arcade games or want a simple but fun business management game with a nice twist.
_childDocuments_.name: Arcade Paradise

_childDocuments_.review: Arcade Paradise does many things, but all of them follow the principle "do one thing and do it well". Picking up laundry, putting it into a washing machine, getting it out, putting it into a drier, picking up trash, cleaning a toilet - everything in this game has a haptic feel to it, a nice animation and super clean, nicely done UI elements.The basic game loop is doing the laundry for customers, collecting money and upgrading your shop. While waiting for the machines to finish you can collect trash, or go into the back room to play some arcade games. All the games are custom programmed, all with their own unique UIs, and they are extremely simple. All games I played so far only need the WASD keys and space key. They are of the caliber of Pac-Man and Match-3.Everything in this game is easy to control, you are never confused about what to do next and you can choose to grow your two businesses as fast as possible or procrastinate. There is even a minigame in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pause menu. A nice touch is also that most of the arcade games have an online leaderboard. And each game has "goals" (in-universe achievements) that boost the respective machine's popularity / income generation.Arcade Paradise is repetitive - that's kind of the whole point. If you enjoy glorified, gamified simple-minded tasks and enjoy some grind to unlock more minigames - give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: There's something bizzare about this game.  In the UK, I  never felt there was this arcade build-up the way there seemed to be in the US - the arcades went into gambling parlours and you snuck in as a kid, feeling somewhat guilty.  They weren't in "laundromats" (I never even knew you could have places where you rented a washing machine by the hour).And yet... this game feels nostalgic, because it hits the time period so well.  The games are there (Though I played them on home computer knock-off versions), the sounds are there, the look is there... it just feels so right, and nostalgic for something I never had.I assume that this means that for someone who did have this experience, this will be a real kick in the nostalgia nuts :D  Well, enjoy.There are some bugs, and it's a bit slow and janky, but... it feels really, really good so who cares?

_childDocuments_.review: I don't get why people complain about this game. It caters a bit to the simulator types that tier up for their rewards. The games in the game are not something you get often and they are quality meta games. GTAxPACman, TetrisXMeanBeanMachineXSudoku, i mean it isn't a breakthrough per se, but these are mobile equivalent that people sit through ads for.  I was VERY happy to see the attention to detail in some of these games even though they aren't perfect. Overall, the textures, the sounds, the music; they all vibe with the generation that grew up on arcades (especially the few that experiences arcades in the laundromats!) I grew up in Detroit and when I was forced to go to the laundry with my mom, I made sure she handed me some quarters for Pac-man and Centipede.The only gripe I have is that there are some bugs like I couldn't go through doors.You can go on the computer and time freezes, but the time for laundry doesn't freeze (kind of a hack to cheat for more money)and of course the other games come as dlc. I want to get the dlc for the other games, because they are really good. But because they are games within a game, it eats my system up and the price isn't worth the extra games. If they only made them a little better...HOWEVER, as a resource management/simulator with games in the game, it is well worth playing. I spent a lot of time playing solitaire but I gotta say the soundtrack bumps! With very similar rips to artists like Deftones, Nine Inch Nails, Rage against the Machine, Beastie Boys, Kylie Minogue, Queens of the Stone Age, et al. Good stuff!I have found some bugs that also detract from the value, but they are not gamebreaking. Usually regarding goals or not being able to interact with trash/gum easily. I also hate that the wristwatch reminder (or any reminder for that matter) comes up and distracts you from trying to make a high score, specifically for the email punks.The best game is the pool/foozball/puzzle bobble clone, but i spent the most time on the woodgal jr game for that high score. The only thing stopping me is the performance lag that hiccups my system sometimes but that could very well be a me thing.The DDR clone game could also use some tweaking especially since it is often out  of sync. It's not challenging at all and quite boring despite it replicating the game quite well. I still highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot to say here. Clearly the developers put a significant amount of energy and thought into the creation of this game. It combines the mundane sim genre, a good sense of humor and a love for the arcades of the 1990's into a hearty stew. If you are approaching 40 or have a fondness for the days the game references you will suck this down like a chili dog. Clean and operate a dump of a laundromat for your absentee rod of father and sneakily create an arcade in the back.  The overall game (operating and creating the arcade) does have a story, and I think, a rather satisfying one, with a couple of surprisingly poignant twists.The games within the game:Look here's the thing - many of us who went to arcades (especially if you weren't loaded with cash) ended up playing whatever we could afford. This means that I remember a lot of arcade games being hard, unplayable, not great, just blah. Over the years, prior to founding GameGerry(tm), I was known to say "All Games Are Bad." I still stand by this sentiment - because they still are usually a waste of time, kind of half-baked and particularly from the 1990's a product of rabid consumerism (like He-Man action figures - these lil $$%%$$ will eat it up).  BUT Arcade Paradise captures this so perfectly - the games are not all good.  There will be ones that you enjoy and ones you detest. If they were all bangers, it wouldn't feel right.  Some get better as you play them and learn to deal with their quirks, others you will love immediately, and some you will just play once. I don't know how they did it, frankly. It captures that feeling of the real life arcade so perfectly, I cannot even really put it into words.Would I truly recommend this game to anyone? YES. But - you have to be ready for a slow burn. Some of these first games are stinkers, some take time to get into. The tasks to earn money are a grind at first, it pays off though. You will find a few of the games you like and make big bucks managing the arcade with your Palm Pilot.  If you are like me, and enjoy mundane sims, but are put off by the hyper-realistic/humorless nature of some of them, this will be right up your alley. If you are looking for a fully fledged arcade from the jump, look elsewhere.Last thing - considering the amount of effort and craft expended on this game, the music, the art, everything here - I am hoping that at some point this game gets some kind of accolades from video game media. It is truly a touching love letter to the 1990s when, even though we had to live in a consumerist hell, purchasing unlicensed David Letterman POGs and throwing our money away on 3DO games, we managed to thrive.

_childDocuments_.review: Arcade Paradise, while not a perfect game, is still entertaining and worth plying in my opinion, I am Arcader from long ago and I find this holds up to that.Essentially,as many others who have played this game before me have cited, you start out more or less a flunky for your father who owns a laundromat, where you wash, dry, clothes, pick up trash and other odd jobs to make the green and progress through the game.  The main goal that I have found is you have an Arcade in the back room in which your character seems the money made from the Arcade to be much better in the long run than laundromat and therein is the goal.  Through completing the menial tasks and completing game goals (like playing the actual games in the Arcade) you get money in various ways to either improve your laundromat/Arcade, self, and whatnot.  At times I have notices some pain with the clothes either from my own ineptitude or the actually engine the game uses, controls are fairly direct but can be buggy at times, picking up trash most notably, you sometimes cannot pick up certain trash due to is proximity to a video game in the Arcade (as an example).All in all as I said, this game is still being developed so it is only get better I am certain, but as it stands, its playable, its fun, so what are you waiting for Arcaders, build you biz in the Arcade industry ;) - Cheers - Darkendone - {LDH}
