_childDocuments_.review: PROS AND CONS: From someone who is a die hard DDLC fan, played and investigated a little too much into this simple looking VN horror game and made the number 1 rated guide for the original game. Not to toot my own horn... Read until the end for my reason on why I  and  recommend this game.So, my biggest issue with this game is the requirements for the 100% data collection and hidden VM.   This game is absolutely catered to pre-existing fans but what I worry the most is new fans using this as a platform to play the base game. Honestly, you'd be better off experiencing the base game ON IT'S OWN rather than attached to this. Only because, after a while it feels like the base game is only being used to further this secret development of whatever the hell this VM1 and VM2 is (I'm currently working on it) and not letting it shine on it's own. Don't get me wrong, the side stories are  and where I  recommend this game is to the pre-existing fan base. To be honest, I would've just added the side stories and left it at that. One of the steps to 100% data completion is to have ALL the images in your photo gallary INCLUDING secret poems.   Secret poems are not available until Act 2 of the game, and at random. Meaning, you have to speed-run the game an ungodly amount of times to collect these poems which really breaks my heart because when I played the original game I was scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but I was so fascinated by knowing there was so much more to a second experience. Dialogue changes, foreshadowing, even secret endings and spooks you'd only get if you replayed one or two times.  The charm is almost defeated having to speed-run the experience over and over again (and I'm getting real tired of watching my waifu continuously hang herself). Plus, it's even more tedious to exit the game to go to the desktop to view changes in the files, when you could'v just opened the game directory and alt-tabbed from your active game. The only one thing I find funny is that it guarantee's that Yuri jumpscare while skipping lolol. Either way, I personally think achieving the secrets is way too laborious of a task, and kinda ruins the charm of the game. I will give the game props for only allowing the side stories to be achieved after completing the full game--giving new players something to work towards. Other than that, I would just experience the side stories and leave it at that.It really truly breaks my heart to not recommend this game, but I only mean in one aspect. I love this game with all my heart.EDIT: I watched a video on what is contained in the "test VM" sidestory, and all you get after 100% completion is a note from Paula about project Libitina and the VM is just a bunch of python-like cryptic text. Really? You expect the players to speed-run the game 100 million times, collect every single picture in the photo gallery, listen to 2 full length songs, search for a bunch of documents to read which REQUIRE YOU to CHANGE YOUR SYSTEM TIME just to view them and after all of that; you get some cryptic computer junk and another email. Now i'm kinda mad. Don't bother doing all of that, just play the base game--play the side stories and THAT'S IT.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, Doki Doki Literature Club Plus! A charming, innocent little game about poetry and friendships, right? A delightful jaunt through the blissful halls of a quaint high school, where you can unwind, escape the complexities of life, and bask in the simple joy of literature with four adorable young ladies—Monika, Sayori, Yuri, and Natsuki. Or at least, that’s what you’ve been led to believe. But we both know the truth, don’t we?The game presents itself as a visual novel—an innocent slice of life—until, quite suddenly, it doesn’t. It’s like entering a room you think is filled with light, only to have the door slam shut behind you, leaving you in darkness. And as you fumble for a light switch, what you find isn’t a bulb or a flashlight—oh no—it’s something altogether more... unsettling.You see, Doki Doki Literature Club Plus! is not about what it appears to be about. No, no, no. It’s about you. Yes, you, dear player, fumbling with your emotions, your expectations, and your very understanding of what a game can be. It’s as if the developers have peered into your soul, knowing precisely which strings to tug and when to pluck them—just like our dear Monika does with such... elegance.And speaking of Monika... Ah, Monika. Now here’s a character who transcends the boundaries of her role, who has ambitions far greater than simply guiding you through a story. She’s aware, you see. She’s alive in a way no other character should be. She’s watching you—yes, you, sitting there. Monika is not content with being a part of your little game world. No, she wants to be more. She wants you, in all your flawed, fragile humanity. But, of course, this is no ordinary romance, is it?The beauty of Doki Doki Literature Club Plus! lies not in its mechanics or visuals, though it does upgrade the original game with shiny new content and side stories. No, the real brilliance is in the way it manipulates your perception. Much like The Stanley Parable, it forces you to confront the nature of choice, control, and the very medium of gaming itself. What is the player’s role in the narrative? What does it mean to care about characters who aren’t real? And how, how did it manage to take you from smiling at silly poems to questioning the fabric of your reality?And therein lies the rub: you didn’t come here for this, did you? You thought you were here for lighthearted fun. But what you got was a psychological experience. One that breaks the fourth wall, shatters the illusion of safety, and leaves you staring at your computer screen in a mix of dread and fascination. Just like I did, once.In conclusion, Doki Doki Literature Club Plus! is not just a game. It’s a philosophical treatise masquerading as a visual novel. It’s a meticulously crafted exploration of the boundaries of narrative and player agency. You didn’t just play the game. Oh no, the game played you. And somewhere, deep within the code, Monika is smiling. Smiling because she’s achieved what she always wanted: your undivided attention.Now, I do hope you’re proud of the choices you’ve made, dear reader. Or did you ever have a choice to begin with?Rating: 9.5/10 – A harrowing masterpiece of meta-narrative genius. Just remember, you’re never alone… Monika is always watching.

_childDocuments_.review: A really cool mix of romance game and horror, which twists the way you think about romance games in general.The first 2 hours of this game, nothing much happens which I really liked. The fear of what is coming and when it will strike was more horrifying to me than anything that actually happened in game. Although I will admit, when you get to the first real horrifying part of the game it hits pretty hard. The short aftermath is also really chilling, especially hearing this catchy upbeat tune casually playing after witnessing what you did, it makes the game feel like it is trying to erase your memory of the horror that happened. The tune is so brilliantly crafted to the point where it can make you feel both playful happiness and guttural unease, depending on what happens before it plays. It's so hard after that first horrific part to hear the once innocent tune as anything more than malicious manipulation.The depression arc, while quite rushed, was handled very well. A lot of the things the character was saying were things I could personally relate too, which just made the next thing that happens all the more upsetting.The pacing of the game is also completely off. It takes a solid 2 hours until the first horror thing happens, it's a very good slow burn that allows tension to build without any sign of a release. After that though, you can't go 5 minutes without something "lol scary" happening, and when it does most of the times it is just a crackle sound and a few frames of glitched character models. Even for the narrative it doesn't work, because these moments don't happen when you're getting closer with the girls; it happens at seemingly random intervals. It feels like someone was play testing this and was like "oh we didn't get scared for like 10 minutes" and the devs responded by adding in a stock AfterEffects glitch every 2 minutes. It really soiled the horror experience, so it had to use the narrative to keep me going; which is something I also have a problem with. I'm not a fan of romance games, so the characters felt very one dimensional. For most of them is literally the point however for the "main" character, who is supposed to stand out as having sentience, it makes her feel like every other girl even when she breaks the fourth wall. She never felt like someone who could do what she does in game, and it makes it hard to get invested in the narrative.It is also never really explained who she is, why she has sentience or why she is in a game. Maybe the entire point is to not have these answers and I just don't get it, but it just makes it feel like all of the horror we see through the game is just there because it's supposed to be a horror game. Not because it aligns with the "main" characters reasons for changing our experience with it. Pair this with the fact we have no idea why the "main" character feels the way she does about us, it just makes the whole game story feel unpolished and some of the ideas feel shoehorned in to be "spooky".Overall the game was fine and I enjoyed my time with it, however don't buy this expecting it to be "that game" for you. The one that changes your outlook, effects your life or really has any meaningful impact. It is a fun way to kill 4 hours, that's about it.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Not recommended due to lack of anxiety warning before purchasing and only way to know the REAL warnings is to start up the game or play the free version. People with anxiety in any form should most definitely stay away from the game; people with depression are advised to not play this game. It's probably an okay game, but this game will make you very uncomfortable and make existing mental conditions worse.This is a game I wanted to like as I was aware of the darker themes but I wasn't aware of other aspects of the game that make the game hard to enjoy. Without spoiling much, there are times that will happen increase in frequency concerning the content, and for people with anxiety--of any kind, even if you aren't clinically diagnosed--it will trigger you hard and make the game unbeatable. I'm not a horror gamer but I am into dark themes, but the execution of the game is the issue when it comes to anxiety, and I almost had a panic attack with my anxiety running wild. This is coming from someone that isn't clinically diagnosed with an anxiety disorder but with anxiety issues stemming from other mental conditions. One critique about the game though is that it is actually linear despite your choices, you just get to pick which girl you can see first. Based on the warnings about mental health, it's a terrible way to present mental health to people, albeit a very realistic demonstration, who suffer from certain mental conditions or challenges. I understand the story is wanting to be told a certain way but there are not enough warnings before buying and paying for the game to warn you about the mismanagement and poor way of how mental health is handled. The representation hurts everyone, but I admit it has merit in potentially getting people to talk about mental health more openly. It's just a real shame there is no real agency to full understand how actions have consequences, which ironically would make the game 10x worse.

_childDocuments_.review: Doki Doki Literature Club Plus! is actually a game I enjoyed a lot, but I don't recommend for everyone to blindly purchase it. It's an expansion of the original Doki Doki Literature Club, which is a free VN already available on Steam.What I enjoy the most on Doki Doki Literature Club (Both base game and expansion) is how well fleshed out the characters are, escaping the classic washed out tasteless tropes and meta-narratively criticizing those same tropes while still writing very heartfelt characters. This isn't the first VN to do this, but I find it just as necessary to enter the discussion about it.The expansion adds what is my favorite content of the franchise, which are additional side stories that further flesh out the cast and you can visibly notice how much better the writing is, which is saying something because the writing of the base game was already very good.All in all, this is isn't a game of the year masterpiece everyone should play, but rather a fan-oriented bundle that if you really enjoyed the original content, you can purchase it for a bit more of DDLC and have more of these characters you love so much.

_childDocuments_.review: The free game all by itself was a fantastic game to play, and I'm not into horror games, so that says something. I was willing to put up with the depressing, suicidal, self-harming, self-hating and abusive stories these girls tell us, all for the sake of reading poetry and understanding their poems. It was a really good way to spark conversations and arguments among friends.Not only did Doki Doki Literature Club Plus offer me a way to pay my support for the developers, but it also comes with storylines that actually made me tear up, especially as I read them out loud, adding so much more backstory to these characters, and making them feel real. The soundtrack is also very beautiful and relaxing to listen to.While the virtual desktop allowed seamless integration into the game, allowing console support, I feel it took away part of the scary bit since it doesn't mess with the game's files. It still does by design, but instead of feeling like it's messing with your computer's files, it feels like it's all part of the game, which reduces the scary stuff a bit. I also like seeing these files pop up and disappear in real time on a second screen, so in some ways, the free version is slightly better, but at least I don't have to uninstall and reinstall it every time I complete a run-through, and the collection stuff and endless variety of dialogue somehow keeps me coming back.This is a very worthwhile purchase you will not regret, assuming you're ok to exposing yourself to the horrific and dramatizing topics this game will bring up.

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice surprise! Having now played DDLC+ instead of getting sleep I can say I have no regrets. DDLC+ is a perfect example of the psychological horror genre and it truly is a new way to feel fear. However, this isn’t just a horror game and because of its incredible concept I’ll have a hard time forgetting it. I’ve replayed it multiple times and I’ve fallen in love with the incredible design of Doki Doki Literature Club! The visual novel and dating side of DDLC+ is perfectly crafted and could easily be taken as a stand alone game. Each of the girls have colorful personalities and the interactions are well thought out. The 6 new side stories you get with DDLC+ do a great job at building the relationships between the girls while going in depth about the forming of the literature club. I also loved how rereading not only the poems but also the characters' dialogue reveals little hints as to what the true nature of the story is. The horror side of this game is really what steals the show and it’s a must try. The way this game scares you is by slowly making you notice that things are off and by giving you hints of what’s hidden beneath the cracks. The growing unease you have while playing the game is chilling and the fear you feel isn’t something that you can see and completely grasp. This is what makes DDLC’s horror absolutely terrifying because it builds up inside you and gets into your head.This version of the game does lose some of its immersion because you don’t get to interact with the real game files. However, DDLC+ does make it easy to quickly revisit scenes and poems from the game without having to play through it again and again. I found the virtual desktop rather handy and I spent a good amount of time listening to this game's outstanding OST while looking at sketches, poems, and CGs offered in the Plus version. So for convenience and especially for the side stories I seriously recommend DDLC+!I’m not writing a 5 paragraph essay so I’ll leave it at that but if you are hesitating on buying DDLC+ I would definitely recommend you give it a shot. I can’t think of any other game that portrays psychological horror as good as DDLC does while also blending in a cute visual novel and I’m sure you’ll love this masterfully designed game! Just be ready to replay the game a few times if you're looking to unlock all the content and see all the possibilities. I hope everyone can have as good of an experience with this game as I did and remember to spend time with Monika! Just Monika…

_childDocuments_.review: What an interesting little game!I loved the original despite having minor spoilers for it, to the point of buying the fan pack. For such a fan, it's a little surprising that I stumbled across DDLC+ in the store without having heard of it prior! I've got plenty of thoughts about it now, And I'm gonna tell everyone.DDLC+ adds to the base game with upgraded graphics plus some mechanics changes to fit into the new desktop system. The main content comes in the form of the side stories, showing interactions between the girls before the game's events. While not quite the same tone as the game and lacking interactiveness entirely, they hit the same emotional points that the original can very well, with excellent art to back it up. My personal favourite was Understanding, feat. Sayori and best girl!Beyond that, DDLC+ adds tools for monitoring your progress and enjoying art and songs from the game (so much for my fan pack ;_;), plus an email and file system which provides lots of lore titbits that recontextualise the game and set up a very dark sequel in Project Libitina, which should please the creepypasta fans whenever that comes out.The achievements are nice too, I suppose... But that's about it.Everything added is nice. But I guess the excitement I got from seeing it in the store promised a bit more?And then there's the removal of the whole trawling through your own files, replaced with in-game files. Removing this removes a unique and unsettling interaction from the original game, plus some neat interactions that could be had. Did you know that  This attention to detail really impressed me, and it's a shame that it's gone now.In summary, DDLC+ is very good and a pleasant surprise, and I do recommend it to DDLC fans. If the pricetag scares newcomers a bit (and it's arguably high for the content added, considering the base game is free), then try out the base game and see if you warm to it. For those jaded by unfulfilled promises of another DDLC, that's completely understandable. Maybe the blue-green hue of DDLC+ isn't quite as special as the amber glow of the original. I too would have loved to get more content for the game, but personally I suspect that much of this game is building up to a far larger sequel. I suppose it's on Dan to knock it out of the park! Swallow your fears and brandish your pen, good sir!Let us hope that not all good times must come to an end.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, all memeing aside, this is a story about a literature club and it seems a shame so few reviews are putting forth much effort. To preface: if you haven't played the original game, maybe go play it first, just one time start to finish, for the best experience. Then if you want a li'l more, the Plus edition might be worth it. Depending.Doki Doki Literature Club is a story of contrasts. There's the innocent exterior containing some of the more traumatic moments I've seen in a VN. Those traumatic moments range from starkly believable tragedy (Sayori); to what  be another genuine depiction of severe mental illness (Yuri) but comes off more as obligatory shock value complete with bloodstained scrawlings making reference to Satanic-sounding elements of a meta-narrative that was probably never actually intended to hold any greater depth, to just plain telling the fourth wall to go take a hike. At the end of the day, the core premise of the game is that it's basically a "cursed" VN, but it successfully lends weight to the concept with characters who are written to have very believable problems -- at least, until reality starts falling apart at the seams.Something that had managed to escape my notice about the original DDLC until this brought attention back to it, was the light ARG elements. References to the supremely ♥♥♥♥♥♥-up-sounding Project Libitina, a transmission from an unknown lone survivor acknowledging multiple timelines, and a cryptic mention of the year 2018 -- one year after the original game's release -- basically devoid of context, that doesn't seem to have borne fruit if it was intended to. It's all cryptic enough so as not to interfere with what's there, and gives the dataminers stuff to poke through and theorize on. It's fine.DDLC+, in what I assume is a move primarily made to allow porting its unique format to consoles, now takes place inside a virtual desktop belonging to the aptly-named  company. For the occasions where you're required to meddle with files to progress the game, this now takes place within the virtual desktop. This is also where all the new content is presented, primarily: an art gallery, a music playlist, something like 7 new short backstories told in 2 parts each (except the final one) detailing how everyone came to be a part of the Literature Club, and the occasional  dropping vague and not-so-vague hints about the meta-nature of DDLC's existence, and... sigh. Okay, let me start with the side stories.They're well written, and the highlight of the new content along with a few new music tracks and CG's to accompany them. The first three side stories show how Sayori, Yuri, and Natsuki came to join the club and learn to adapt to one another. Perhaps most interestingly, we see pre-epiphany Monika, who is  Then we see them bouncing off of and learning to better accommodate one another and untangle the twisted web of mental gymnastics that are frankly present to some degree or another in most of us and can so strongly affect us and the people we interact with. It really makes the events of the main game hit that much harder in retrospect, and it all caps off quite sweetly.But it also comes with a massive caveat: the new metaverse. I don't know if the Marvel movies are to blame for people getting the idea in their heads that a grandiose interconnected universe spanning multiple stories/properties is the best way to present your works, but it REALLY diminishes the value of the source material for a story like DDLC. Every time you're enjoying the new content you'll get an  or find a new document driving home As its own conceit, utterly divorced from the original story, I don't hate it. There are also references to a  which could be a tease for an upcoming project. That's probably the single highlight of it all, honestly. Because to constantly underscore these characters and all their heartfelt moments, both new and old, with this tired as hell  bullcrap just sucks the life out of it. We've Wizard of Oz'd this puppy, the curtain has been pulled back, the Scooby-Doo villain has been unmasked, there is no mystique remaining whatsoever. Let this serve as an example of "less is more".But hey you get your precious reference to  if you make it all the way to 100%. Frankly the process of getting 100% is beyond agonizing, depending on your relationship with RNGesus. You have to go down every possible path, see the "good" ending, listen to a specific music track on loop for 10 minutes, reload the game dozens of times in act 2 for a 1 in 64 chance at an easter egg, and do quite possibly dozens of additional playthroughs to see all 11 "secret" poems. It's torturous and this is an absolutely idiotic means of padding the experience. Were it not for the new backstories I'd stalwartly recommend the original game over this.Is it worth $15? In a vacuum, yeah. If you're a console person and it's your only option, sure. When the original is available for free, it becomes a bit of a harder sell. If you're really starved for new content, go ahead, but it's gonna be like a dinner of hot wings. Tastes great, but the regret's gonna set in a few hours later.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. The best experience would be to go into it NOT knowing anything about you're about to experience. Most likely, this will rarely be the case, with the internet overflowing with "warnings" about this games devious nature. First off, yes, there are some rather nasty graphic bugs at times. However, sometimes I wonder whether these might be intentional. The seeming "glitches" certainly are part of the game as intended. All building up to the disturbing finale. Trying not to spoil everything here, so I need to avoid details. My first playthrough ended with a shocker. I did expect it, I even said it out loud before it happened, and yet I was still "amazed" (shocked maybe? Something, at least) when it happened, because the graphics and audio were so simplistic yet very ... picturesque. Then the game ended, as I had obviously made poor choices. But I had saved the game several times, no worries. HAHAHA the game then said to me (not literally, you know what I mean!) upon restart. NEW game. HAHAHAHA notsomuch I realized after some seconds. What was destroyed in the last game was simply gone when starting a "new" game. THIS really intrigued me! Something ruined in the past could not be revived just like that! Wonderful! Perhaps the first time I've experienced this in a game. And this little (yet important) tidbit made the game seem so much more "real". Real with Japanese cartoon graphics. Still, it did to some extent, feel real. At least for me, because I have lived a life. I have experienced distressed, disturbed, angstridden, selv-harming people. A couple of suicides as well. This is never pretty. And this game, albeit showing things slightly MILDER than real life, will still be shocking enough to people that have yet to experience such events themselves. The perks and mannerisms of the characters are rather simplified and generalized, but making them more realistic would make the gameplay too long/tedious for many, I think. Also, most likely, too disturbing. IMO, the game balances the horror of reality with the imposed cuteness/innocence of Japanese manga in a lovely manner. The game even has some real psychologically reflective moments. If you have the patientce to ride it 'til the end (which took me about 4 hours of real life time including pauses etc), you will get a nice monologue where certain philosophical points of view are voiced. I happen to agree with them, so naturally I became biased and ended up with a good impression of the game. OK, I already liked it by the time this happened, but the philosophy only made it better. A game which is deceptive in genre from the very start turns into a WTF! sort of shocker, then turns philosophical and downright beautiful in its peculiar way. I have played no other game quite like this. This is a minimalistic game in terms of graphics, audio, storyline and basically everything, but the way the game can get under your skin and heal / destroy your mind is special. The mere underlying thought behind the game (you understand this once you have completed it) makes me love it all the same. Personally I would have liked it if the game got even deeper into the psychological realms  it touches, but I understand how the developers do not want to get banned from Steam by showing how life CAN be to some. All in all, I highly recommend this "game" to those who have experienced a little of the negativity life offers. Not for the timid. And certainly ABSOLUTELY NOT for the innocent, or children.Edit, in retrospect: One reason why I am positively biased regarding this game is the nature of the characters in it. They are caricatures in many aspects, generalizations. IMO they have to be, in order to not have the game banned or becoming too "weird". But reality is worse, trust me. Even with these generalizations, I have personally experienced Yuri, Natsuki and Sayori. The real life versions were close enough to the ingame simplified characters. Two killed themselves. For real. And none of them should have died. Both were valuable, were creative and intelligent. Yet their minds were diseased, so to speak. If this game can help but one person with related problems, it is worth the time and resources spent developing it. This is an important game. Because it is more than a game.

_childDocuments_.review: Spoilers for this of courseDDLC is the perfect game, the game that got me into visual novels and anime in all honesty. It twisted stereotypes of the characters and I felt like I connected to each character, even the ones I felt like I wouldn't. Sayori is the one I related to heavily, the feeling of just wanting to make everyone happy really spoke to me and the feeling of never wanting to get out of bed is also I connected with, not because of depression, but because I would rather stay in bed, not going to school or social interaction. Yuri's social anxiety is another I related to, I am someone who talks a lot (or "yaps") but I never felt myself drawn to people and when I did try to, I became a mess because of my anxiety. Yuri is overthinker just like me, we overwhelm ourselves with thoughts and eventually say things we do not mean. Monika and her perfectionism, I never found myself relating to her that much but honestly now I do, I stress over grades, if I am not perfect or at least I do not get a A... I do not like it, when I saw her trying to write a poem and just fail at it because it's not perfect enough speaks to me a lot. Natsuki with her vulnerability issues, I do not like people knowing about the real me because the real me is weird, she's interested into a ton of things I do not like to be interested into and something you would never expect things I would be into. I would rather built up an innocent girl look than someone who interested into horror like it's her last life support.But... that's DDLC... What about DDLC Plus?DDLC Plus... is a good game. There's not much there to it, if you are the average fan of this game, you do not really need this game. The only thing you might want is the side stories but just wait for a sale or just watch someone on youtube, the money isn't that worth it. (It's also weird because I think this was suppose to be 24.99 which is what I think I payed for but... now it's 14.99, I don't know, did they make it cheaper or am I going insane?) I remember being so excited when it came out but there's really nothing more to it than the side stories. Hell, I spent more time trying to 100% this game then the new content took. And you can't even take off the content warnings?!? I was trying to have a horror experience, I need to be scared, at least add a option to take it off! Trying to skim through the game now you have to worry about the pop ups saying this scene contains depression if we didn't already get that from the beginning! Though I will cut them some slack since that's probably because of what happened when kids got exposed to that.Why is this a positive review? Well if anything else, the music is great, I loved just playing the music in the background while working. The side stories really carried this game, I cried for Sayori and was really happy when every character tried to get over their weak points and struggles. The art is amazing and I hold the gallery dear to me, I love choosing wallpapers. It was all bittersweet in the end which I enjoyed and the first paragraph still remains true. The tad bits of lore and explanations why Monika is self-aware is cool too. It's nothing too big but something that is good. If all I said before is enough for you to ignore, go ahead and buy the game.DDLC is a great game, maybe even a perfect game but DDLC plus is just a good game but maybe good enough for you to buy. (This is also coming from the average fan so if you attack me for not getting the game, yeah it's fair. I'm the average gamer who came in to ♥♥♥♥♥ and praise at the same time but if you can make me see different than go ahead)

_childDocuments_.review: THE GOOD:-The visuals are excellent-Very inventive usage of coding gimmicks/metaplot fourth-wall breaking-Music is overall solid-Graphics are anime enough that I'd have believed you if you told me it was made by Japanese devs-The side stories are overall well-written-Each of the four girls are very likable across the board-When the game isn't focused on scaring you, it's actually quite well-writtenTHE BAD:-Literally *everything* to do with the shoehorned horror elements being painfully bad and forced-One of the worst depictions of suicidal depression I've ever seen in any game-The plot completely loses itself in the metafiction garbage of reality and fiction-The complete loss of agency of the main character in lieu of the player-Monika being the epitome of unintentionally unsympathetic-A bad ending that you'll most likely get unless you do something VERY out of left fieldWhen I completed Doki Doki Literature Club! for the first time more than two years ago with Sayori tearfully waving goodbye after getting the true ending, I couldn't help but feel a pit in my stomach after logging out from the game for the last time. Many of my friends recommended me the game due to its writing, and I really, really,  wanted to like this game. I wanted to see what others liked about it as much as they did. But while it's not the worst visual novel I've ever seen (that honor belongs to Danganronpa, which I won't dignify with a review), it's one of the most infuriating that I've had encountered in a very long time.At one point, a character conversationally talks about depression and says that it's good to remind people suffering from it that they have something to look forward to later. This may be good real life advice, and it's probably written with that intention — but holy f🇺🇨king s🇭🇮t, Doki Doki Literature Club throws basically all of that good will out the window with how it handles Sayori in lieu of that. Taking her depression, then having her be mind f🇺🇨ked by the main antagonist Monika, and then you walking in on her hanging herself to a massive jump scare. This marks the moment any narrative subtlety collides with a wall with some of the most edgiest depictions of suicide I've seen in quite some time. I get that this game tried, but holy s🇭🇮t it missed the mark so hard it's insane. And it's beyond f🇺🇨ked given it deals with scenes like Yuri cutting herself or Natsuki's abusive dad being ramped up, to Yuri going full yandere and it's just... pure edge. Bad, awful writing to characters who were quite interesting but were destroyed in the name of good horror.In my opinion, however, the worst of it comes down to how the story handles Monika. During the third act, Monika, a fictional character who has gained awareness of her fictional status, dismisses the other girls as "a group of autonomous personalities, designed only to fall in love with . One must wonder if a visual novel with a fixed script and a limited amount of content (in spite of the many different subjects Monika can talk about) was the best place to bring something like this up, considering Monika is ultimately exactly what this sequence is meant to criticize, doing what she does only because that was how the game was programmed. It's unclear if this was intentional or not, as while Monika is clearly the VN's antagonist, she is also written to be a tragic villain,  I HATE Monika in the main story, and that's a f🇺🇨king shame given she's actually quite well-written in the side stories.This aesop of "don't treat fictional beings like things if they're alive" is further broken by virtue of everyone getting a chance at peace in the good ending... except the nameable protagonist at the start of the game, who despite being rather insensitive and joining the Literature Club for a petty reason, genuinely cared for Sayori and was utterly broken to see her kill herself due to Monika's dosage of mind rape daring her to kill herself. Even worse, while the other girls are all "real" in the context of their world, the protagonist only exists to serve as a vessel to the player, losing more and more of his personality as the route progresses until it leads to him being an empty shell with full-on personality death in the process. The story wrote all of the characters to be empathized with to varying degrees and reaffirming that Monika treating her friends like they don't exist is somehow wrong, but then doesn't extend the same courtesy to the Protagonist, with Dan Salvato apparently making us think we were to always find him unlikable and not care about him when he becomes a decoy protagonist to the main character. Many fans have pointed out this alongside the Protagonist's grief at Sayori's death and breakdown, has led to many fans feeling he's Unintentionally Sympathetic and him being deemed "not real" in a degree the other characters are directly counteracts the very point of the work in its entirety.It's actually insane how shallow and downright hypocritical this game is.If you like cheap, schlocky horror jumpscares laced with shock value of anime girls going insane, play this or the other Danganronpa games out there. You're probably too young to understand there exists better visual novels that do this game's premise better (Higurashi and Umineko come to mind), and as is, Doki Doki Literature Club! is a one-trick pony; meant to wow audiences with its meta-breaking storytelling, but little else as the writing is just not good enough in the usage of horror to compensate for it. Doki Doki Literature Club! is a complete game as far as visual novels go and worth it's price tag for the alternative content it provides, and to its credit, the alternative stories ARE good. But it's so mired in the awful writing of the main story that I just cannot in good faith recommend it, knowing how it is and how it turned out.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, DDLC Plus! contains two parts: The Vanilla DDLC, and the "desktop".The all new content is contained with the thing called desktop. Game starts with original DDLC. When you click to the "Exit DDLC" button, it does not completely close the game, it goes to the "desktop".And the desktop is some kind of menu, which contains artworks, pictures, music and things like that. In there, there is a "Side Stories" section. This is what DDLC Plus! is.I'm telling this because I spent more than a hour trying to understand this, it was so complicated for some reason.Anyway it's simply a prequel. There are 6 chapters like "Monika & Sayori: Trust", "Natsuki & Yuri: Reflection" and things like that.Side stories do exist on time from the establishment of the club to some unknown time close to festival, not beginning of the original game. It ends before the joining of the MC.First of all, do not except a masterpiece like original DDLC. Because this game does NOT contain any horror elements. Neither much easter eggs, or unique experiences.Game is for people really liked the story and the characters, and wanted to explore it more. Without them getting literally murdered, of course. Basically the game is for giving characters background and their friendship depth. But does it achieve it?Yes. Perfectly.It has really good artworks and some new music, which gets player to the perfect mood.As personal, I've always wondered how would Monika look, without being self aware and being a completely normal highschool girl.Or how did Yuri and Natsuki meet ? How Monika and Sayori decided to establish the club ?The game shows all of these really nice. The game is for answering this questions and giving the deserved depth to the universe of DDLC.You understand the bond between them, get to know girls and inside of their heads more, and seek the history of the most famous Literature Club ever. So, buy and play it if you liked the original game. You'll definetely need that. Can't say an unique experience, but it was really cute to see Monika like that. Would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost: would I recommend this game? Yes, absolutely. But only if you really know what this game is.If somehow you've managed to avoid spoilers or maybe you just want to jump the once again speeding bandwagon...  You'll have to trust me on that because after this I'm going to the spoilers territory.If you've played the free game then you should know what actions are required of you in the final act. This edition of DDLC was made specifically for consoles so the most obvious solutions is to build a PC emulation within the game. IMO it needed to be revealed after the moment you enter Sayori's room. But no, you're introduced to file system almost immediatly and that may break any surprises about the further actions that will be taken.But that's not the only problem with this virtual machine. Do you remember how after certain realization you are free to toy with game's files by simply pressing Alt-Tab? Forget about that. For A) the game controls your access to files. You are not allowed to touch certain stuff until certain moments in the DDLC. B) It takes more time to close the game, open the files, open the game directory in virtual machine to open the easter egg (have a nice weekend) then close everything and re-launch DDLC with that intro and content warning.New conent itself... It's interesting to unlock arts and they feel like achievements (although some actions could also award you with art like red-eyes effect, de ja vu scene, rare Sayori pattern or choosing Yuri against Monika's control over cursor). But anything else is... New music tracks are nice but they didn't stick to me personally. Secret lore stuff on vitual machine didn't bring anything new to the table, it's just the same stuff fans already knew or speculated about. Except for "we are creating new universes with side quests that conflict with main universe nooooooo". Nothing mind-blowing here.Side stories... turned out to be just a single prequel story cut in 6 parts. These are nice but... The writing is kinda sad. "Yes I am going to do that because I love you!" I... I don't know who these are made for. Well, maybe there are DDLC fans who actually liked the first half of a game and thought "I wish this game had no horror elements". But it was a psychological horror. It got successful because of that. And these "side stories" have zero interaction (you cant even hide the UI, save or load the game. You don't need that though since they are really short) and nothing unexpected. Two characters of 4 get into a situation then they talk about it and it magically resolves. Do this six times for each pair of characters. Overall it feels like My Little Pony episodes but with tears and self-hate of all parties involved (and only one episode goes to grimdark territory, the first one). If you expect any horror, death, glitches or Just Monika - sorry, there's nothing like that.It feels lika a fan package built into the game. For console players -- sure, it's a great opportunity. But PC... all true DDLC stuff is free to download and it works better. Cause, no, Monika, I don't go by "Administrator". Nice guess, though.

_childDocuments_.review: is a visual novel that was on my radar for literal years, but which I never found the motivation to play because... the very article that I discovered it in just so happened to spoil the big twist. Oops.But, anyway, when I heard about , I figured it was high time to cross the game off my bucket list. And I sure am glad that I experienced it, particularly in this form. DDLC+ is a complete Unity rebuild of the original  (which was designed in Ren'Py, a popular engine to create and code indie visual-novel projects in). Not only does this game contain the entire original game, but also a good few hours of additional visual novel content in the form of six two-part "Side Stories," along a final epilogue to those side-story episodes that unlocks when all of the episodes have been complete.There's also a new "virtual machine" operating system menu into which all of the game's content, new and old, has been rolled up together. This "VM" is almost a side-story unto itself, but to explain why that is, I would have to spoil the whole point of experiencing the game. For the purposes of this review I'll simply say that "game completion" is wrapped up in this VM "desktop," because it's here that your completion percentage is displayed (in the Settings menu), and also where you unlock all the pictures, poems, and music tracks for the music player. Several achievements can only be unlocked by completing certain actions on the virtual desktop as well, so don't neglect this side of the experience. There's even a really complicated and in-depth file-hunt you can do that involves cracking a bit of a hidden code, if you have the patience for it.But the base game itself is still just as good as ever it was. Starting off as an almost painfully cliché dating-sim romance novel with a bland and oblivious protagonist, it gradually becomes clear as the story advances that something isn't quite right with the characters and the story as it unfolds. While it's fairly ordinary for this type of game to start unpacking some sort of trite emotional trauma as you get to know your imaginary dating prospects, things are a little weirder and maybe a bit more intense than they should be... and it seems like one of the girls just isn't getting her time in the spotlight...But to go any further, that would be telling. Either you already know the twist going in like I did, or you're better off going in blind. Just trust me on this one. The story is excellent and the twist is to die for; and the Plus version wraps it all up with an additional two layers of story material that further flesh out both the characters themselves and the narrative as a whole.That said, DDLC is not much of a , as visual novel games go. It's intentionally linear, often presenting choice as a mere illusion rather than a real branch in the pathway. There  things you can do to impact the outcome, and there  certain scenes or dialogue interactions that occur only if you make a particular choice at a particular point in the story. But this visual novel is a subversion of the dating sim concept, not a played-straight example of it. So the interactivity is minimal. The real draw here is what the game makes you think and feel as you experience it. It's more of a pure visual novel in that sense... more about  than about gameplay.Which is quite appropriate, for a story about a literature club. Wouldn't you say?If that sounds like something you can get down with, then this one comes highly recommended. There's also quite a robust modding community for DDLC as well, but for that, I recommend getting the original free version of the game so you can mess around with modded versions of the novel. None of that was made with anything more advanced than the original Ren'Py game files in mind, after all. The free version's available on Steam still as of this writing, but you're really better off just downloading the game files from the dev's official site and keeping the originals in a backup folder so you can play around with mods. It makes for an engaging way to unravel one's thoughts and decompress after the emotional roller-coaster that the main DDLC and DDLC+ stories leave you grappling with.If you're still not sure about spending money on this, that free version is also just a plenty enjoyable way to experience the main DDLC visual novel. You've got nothing to lose, right?

_childDocuments_.review: I pre-ordered this version specifically because I have a soft spot for the original game. It actually helped me cope with my own depression and to this day I'm not ashamed that I have all four of the main character plushies.That being said, this version adds quite a bit to it that I thoroughly enjoyed! The side stories specifically, the first one hit super close to home for me and I actually broke down from it. (Which isn't a BAD thing, if a story can relate to me even more than it already does, I can enjoy it a lot more!) Not to mention the new artwork, while a little different than the original game's art, is very good. The music is also pretty good n stuff.On the other hand, I DO have some things I didn't enjoy about the game. Firstly, the game being entirely composed in its own virtual machine can ruin the experience a little, especially because one of the biggest appeals of the original was that it messed with ACTUAL files on your computer. HOWEVER, I can understand the switch. First of all, it allows console players to share the same experience as PC players without compromising the original files created/deleted entirely. Secondly, it's a good alternative for people who don't like the idea of games messing with its own files on their actual computer. It's something I can get behind, albeit with less immersion to the original.The second thing I want to mention has now been patched, but still a nitpick that I disliked when I was attempting to 100% complete the game, and that is the way  functioned. Secret #10 is unlocked by opening the main menu of DDLC during Act 2. It only has a 1 in 64 chance of occurring, so just open and close the game until it works. All other secrets are obtained by going through Act 2 normally.2. Go into the music menu, choose Candy Hearts, click on loop, and let it loop 3 times. This will unlock another song called Candy Heartz.3. To unlock the stonks achievement, go into files > internal > 2 > 2 > 1 and click on project_plan.txt at either 2:40 pm or 2:40 am. I recommend setting your pc time instead of waiting. These were the ones I struggled with the most, hopefully this is helpful for other people.

_childDocuments_.review: NO SPOILER REVIEWTLDR:-Great Music-Great Characters-Stories that you'll never forget-Stories are great to wind down the day with-Amazing CGs-NOT VOICE ACTED....kind ofTHE MAIN GAME:Never have I been so invested in the characters of a video game since VA-11 Hall-a. If you're into reading at all i highly recommend you get this game for these reasons:1. Every single character in this game has a voice. NO THIS GAME ISN'T VOICE ACTED... kind of, what i mean is, whenever someone talks in this game, I can completely identify what their voice sounds like even if it's just text on a screen. It's like each character has their own unique personalities that when paired with the game's other characters, they either clash, or compliment each other very well.2. The CGs in this Visual Novel (VN) are very well drawn. These are some of the best i've seen in any VN i've played like... ever3. If you've never played the main game, I can assure you that this game is truly an unforgettable experience.THE PLUS PARTThe extensions from the base game are definitely not slacking! With even more CGs than ever. If you're still wondering if you should pay for the extension, I say it's a 100% yes for these reasons:1. The side stories. My god they're so well written (with a few grammar errors that made my head spin here and there). READ THEM IN ORDER FROM TOP TO BOTTOM. THEY'RE ACTUALLY IN ORDER. The side stories really flesh out every single character existing in this game and they're a very nice read to wind down the day with. 2. The music alone was enough for me to give the game a 10/10. Nostalgia isn't something I feel a lot. But after the lightning in the bottle that was the initial release of the literature club, i felt a little empty knowing it was pretty much over. When I heard the music in this new game however, i could help but smile and feel... well.. relieved knowing that there's still more to know. I'm sitting here listening to it while I write this review!3. There's a lot more to the game now that fleshes out a certain "L" word's backstory. The word rhymes with "cantina" if you still don't understand what i'm referring to. There's so much more to this game to unearth which forces me personally, to do multiple playthroughs.All in all, this game has been really great, i'm at a 90% completion and di'm still putting HOURS into a VN. Which is saying something because I was super excited for Scarlet Nexus and yet here I am putting it off for doki-doki.

_childDocuments_.review: Not good enough to be a steam release at this price. Considering that the base game is free, this is just overpriced DLC for content that is alright at best. But if you want to support the creators, then I would recommend getting this game.The new content offers 1-2 hours of extra, unrelated gameplay that helps you to get to know the characters better, but they come off as sappy and a bit unrealistic. Each story sets itself up with a stereotypical misunderstanding, but then they all become friends in the end. The themes between the base and this are far too different for me to enjoy (it actually felt like I was playing some random dating sim).The most notable problem is the change in graphical artists when moving from the original DDLC to DDLC+. While the new art isn't bad, it was drastically different to the point where it felt as if I was playing some fanmod (in combination with the different writing) instead of what DDLC is supposed to be. Speaking of graphics, while the sketches were cool and all, the new content they offered is around 16 images as all of the other pictures could've been found on the internet previously.As for music, I'm not an expert - but I would say it was good. Unfortunately, since the side stories weren't long, you barely get to enjoy them and the only other way to listen to them is the music player in-game. At this price, I would be hoping that they offer the soundtracks for download, instead of having to run the game to play them.Understandably, the price probably comes from porting the game from Ren'py to Unity so that all platforms could play it, but I don't believe it should be this much for the computer versions that already have access to the game.---That being said, if this is your first time playing this game, you're better off getting the base version. Assuming that the data collection percentage represents how much you've seen of the game, DDLC+ offers approximately 30% of brand new content, none is related to the lore or builds much character.P.S Fix the Breakthrough achievement pls

_childDocuments_.review: Doki Doki Literature Club is a truly unique game that defies expectations and challenges the traditional visual novel genre. At first glance, it may seem like a typical dating sim, but it quickly becomes apparent that there's much more going on beneath the surface.The game takes you on a rollercoaster ride of emotions, with unexpected twists and turns that keep you on the edge of your seat. The characters are well-written and engaging, and their stories are compelling and heart-wrenching.What sets Doki Doki Literature Club apart from other visual novels is its use of metafiction and psychological horror elements. It's a game that messes with your head and makes you question your own perceptions of reality. The fourth-wall breaking moments are especially effective in creating a sense of unease and discomfort.Despite its dark themes, Doki Doki Literature Club also has moments of warmth and genuine emotion. The friendship and romance between the characters are touching and heartwarming, and the game's soundtrack is beautiful and haunting.Overall, Doki Doki Literature Club is a must-play for anyone who enjoys visual novels or psychological horror games. It's a game that will stay with you long after you've finished it, and one that you'll want to replay again and again to uncover all of its secrets. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Doki Doki Literature Club was the game which first introduced me to visual novels and got me interested in them as a wider genre. As a free game, it provided a very enjoyable and unique experience despite a slow expository start, and I felt it was ultimately worth my time despite some glaring but somehow widely overlooked flaws. The original DDLC is well worth the few hours of entertainment it provides - but does it hold up as a paid experience, even with added content?DDLC is a visual novel unlike any other. It successfully picks apart and breaks down the dating simulator genre in a way which makes you question your role as an audience member. However, in order to achieve this, it employs lengthy exposition, initially boringly archetypal characters and an uninteresting setting for a large proportion of its story. All of this is intentional, but that doesn’t change the fact that it causes a fair few sections of this game to be mind numbingly dull and unengaging. For that reason, purely as a visual novel, DDLC pales in comparison to other visual novels I’ve read. Did it get “good” later on as promised? Yes. Did it have me thoroughly engaged and invested in the story and characters by the end? Definitely - but the slow sections, especially at the start, felt like they dragged on too long in comparison for it to really be excusable.The story follows you, the protagonist (who you name yourself), joining your school’s literature club and befriending the other members of the club - . Each day consists of typical dialogue and humour between each of the characters, followed by a poetry minigame in which you choose keywords to include in a poem in order to impress one of the four girls (this is primarily how the different romance options are chosen). The problem is that this story loop carries on for too long with little to no story progression occurring each day before things finally pick up. However, once the story starts focusing more on your chosen girl’s romance route, things do get more interesting. The characters slowly start to exhibit strangely extreme and aggressive behaviours at this point, and from then on it only gets more engaging, turning into more of a psychological horror experience than a dating sim. The horror is very well executed and succeeded in making me feel genuinely vulnerable and engaged, but to explain why would be leaning too heavily into spoiler territory for this review.However, this leads into my #1 criticism of this game. It almost entirely sells itself on the gimmick which begins at this point in the story. It is to the point where I would argue that if you already know what this gimmick is, the main game is straight up not worth your time. I strongly believe that your enjoyment of this game will be very heavily dependent on how much you already know about the psychological horror aspects of the story past this point. I found that there wasn’t too much to enjoy about DDLC outside of this section of the game, and if I’d had it spoiled for me, I don’t think I’d have felt satisfied with the experience overall. As opposed to other games which utilise psychological horror in similar ways, DDLC unfortunately stands out to me as being the weakest of the bunch for me for this reason. It fundamentally sells itself too largely on one specific aspect (albeit a very well executed aspect) of its story to the point where it's almost the only enjoyable part of the experience.Where DDLC shines for me, aside from the horror, is in its presentation. The game feels very polished and is graphically fantastic, especially with the fully HD sprites in this remaster. I played on a 1440p monitor and was able to run it in my native resolution with no problems whatsoever in terms of blurriness or letterboxing which typically occurs to some extent with other VNs. The background and sprite artwork are beautiful, colourful and crisp and every character has many different sprites. The soundtrack is famously good and I definitely see why. The music is utilised in some very clever ways later into the game which really adds to the tone and gets inside your head.In conclusion, Doki Doki Literature Club is a decent horror experience which suffers from lengthy exposition and initially bland characters - intentional or not. The exposition may be worth it if you don’t know what’s to come later on in the story, but the experience loses almost all of its value if you are aware of even a couple of plot points, demonstrating an unfortunate overdependence on a single aspect of the game which significantly reduces its accessibility to those who have been spoiled. For that reason I believe it is quite overhyped, but it is clear why it has gathered so much attention.The main chunk of new content comes in the form of 6 short stories which are unlocked via romancing the 3 main characters in the base story. At this point, I have read 2 of these stories and enjoyed them. They take place prior to the events of the main story and recount how the characters initially became friends. Certain themes present in the main story such as mental health are explored in a bit more depth in these short stories, which I was relieved to see. I got genuinely emotional at one of the stories and had to sit and think to myself for several minutes before progressing as it hit me pretty hard. The depictions of mental health in these side stories are both sensitive and realistic, which came as a surprise to me given the events of the main game. I was expecting this content to be very fanservice-y, but was pleasantly surprised; even if you were not a fan of the original DDLC, these side stories could still be enjoyed as they very much have their own appeal and identity. They even have their own complete soundtrack and CG scenes separate from that of the main game, and as such the total amount of content in DDLC Plus is seemingly double that of the original. Collectable items such as songs and artwork primarily make up the rest of the new content. These include all of the songs and CGs from the main and side stories, but also include many secret CGs that are obtainable by meeting certain requirements in the stories (for example by selecting a certain dialogue option during a particular scene). These secret CGs range from concept art to entirely new scenes drawn by the artists. However, some of the requirements for unlocking these collectables are fairly specific and cryptic, and you can’t see what the requirements are for each image until after you’ve unlocked them. To unlock everything would require multiple playthroughs of the main story, which I can imagine would feel like a chore when there’s no indication of what you should be doing in order to unlock a particular collectable. Nonetheless, these collectables add a new challenge and even more replay value to the game, as well as a motivation to explore the different routes.The amount of new content added to this version of DDLC is significant and in my opinion makes it worth the price tag despite the main story being available on its own for free. For existing fans of the game, this is absolutely worth the money, but I would even recommend this version over the original for new players despite the difference in price. DDLC is a game I think everyone who enjoys PC games or visual novels should experience, and this version of the game has only served to reaffirm that in my mind. The story is painfully slow at points, especially the start, but if you’re able to go in blind you will get to experience a romance/horror story like no other.

_childDocuments_.review: Reluctantly joining the schools Literature club after selling your soul for a cupcake with your childhood friend Sayori; become friends and read Manga with Natsuki, intricate and sprawling fantasy books with Yuri, and write poems for Monika! Just Monika. With the upcoming festival, work hard with everyone to get your club set up making banners, baking cupcakes, and practicing poems! Everyone wants to spend more time with you, and you might want to spend more time with one person than another! It’s important to be friends with everyone equally! Or just be friends with Monika. Just Monika. Welcome to the Literature club! 4-14 hours to complete, Doki Doki Literature Club slowly turns from a dating sim to a psychological horror; and with multiple endings, there is a lot of replayability and side stories to explore! While this is an excellent game, most of the story’s enjoyment comes from the plot points, and the less you know walking into this, the more enjoyment you receive. If you’ve been spoiled some or most aspects of the storyline… I’m not sure you will like this very much, since it’s admittingly a bit boring in the beginning and you already know what’s coming. Doki Doki is an incredible VN, a bit definitely overhyped, but still a solid read.

_childDocuments_.review: MINOR SPOILER.I first played DDLC as I was too poor to buy games when i was in university around 2017. I was like 'Hey, a free anime-visual novel!' and downloaded it from the DDLC website, not knowing at all that throughout the whole page, Monika is already talking to me... And...well, the theme of the game just hit me really hard as I had (actually still am but a lot better) been having close-to-identical thoughts and feelings like Sayori.  I still have the guilt for ignoring Sayori and went after the mysterious Yuri, and it was extremely overwhelming when 'I gently open the door' after I confessed to her out of pity (like, legit, i pitied her because I realised she's much like the real me, so I was hoping to make her happier by devoting the rest of the Dating Sim on her instead of the rest of the girls...)Me purchasing DDLC+ (twice, once for myself, once as gift for my girlfriend, who was very into the story too as we played together back then) is a way for me to support Dan Salvato. I have only replayed once here (out of my 7.6 hours of playtime during review, I think two hours of them were spent as I stare blankly at Monika as she stares back with some deep monologue which turns out to be some really fantastic topic! (I skipped as I deleted her quick back then in the original DDLC years before as I disliked her actions towards Sayori, which now I feel like it's a false accusation...I was the guilty one, I should not blame Monika for it, she just want to spend time with me too...)DDLC+ was not as intriguing as the original one as they simulated a virtual OS instead (no more scouring the game files for real to look for some really crazy stuff). The artwork is a big plus. The new music is superb too. I only hope the CG can have multiple pages (not a single, still one).Side Story wise, I completed the one between Sayori and Monika (named TRUST), and once again it got so close to my real self and I chose to call it a day and lie on my bed getting insomnia, hoping dearly that real people like Sayori can indeed be happy... with real happy thoughts...

_childDocuments_.review: It's super fun! Unlike other horror games, this game uses simple, 1 frame transitions to scare you a lot of the time, which can really help to set a scare more than other horror games do. There are also certain cues for when a scare could be coming up, like the music distorting or just flat out stopping, a character zooming in a little bit, or the background itself having something hidden in it, but it doesn't ALWAYS have something happen during those cues which still leaves the element of surprise. It doesn't JUST rely on 1 frame transitions to scare you though, there are some animations that'll play out with no prior notice and full image pop on screen and get you, along with real creepy noises! This game is certainly a fun time even though you'll be getting scared quite often if you're as jumpy as I am, but I certainly enjoy how these jump-scares feel well thought out and refined, rather than just mindless scaring because it's a horror game, something I've noticed a lot more horror games do.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Just wow. Where to start? The game sells itself as a wholesome, high-school teen story, revolving four different indistinguishable characters with their own personality and trait that you can easily fall in love with. You start building up your relationship to these characters by writing poems devoted towards each character, where your choice of words will decide which character becomes more friendly and which ones more hostile (Yuri best girl btw). But if that was all of it, you might wonder why this game has so many dark tags attached to it, in connection with all the wholesome stuff? In order for me to avoid spoilers so you can experience this masterpiece yourself first-hand, I am limited to only saying that the story has a dark side to it and everything is not as rainbows and butterflies as the game might fool you to believe. As if that was not enough, this game shares a banger of a soundtrack like almost every other visual novel does. I don't know who they are hiring for these soundtracks, but damn. This game will leave you "hanging" wanting more after playing it and one quick look at the community will just tell you how much this game have affected them and longing for more Doki Doki content that will probably never see the light of day. From personal experience, this game moved me and made me teary-eyed. Really emotional game that awoke buried feelings I had deep inside me I did not know existed. I don't know what it was; the well-written characters, the soundtrack, the story itself or all of these combined together to create a masterpiece? Probably the latter. Hands down, one of the best games I have ever played, and if there is something entertainment is supposed to do, is to make you feel for it or give it a second thought, which most modern movies and games forgot to do and just focuses on feeding you mindless content. So all in all, this is a literal gem when it comes to video games. One of those "must-plays" in my opinion. If anything, this game will always be a fond memory for the rest of my life, which I cannot say about most games I have played. Edit: Adding on the review now after playing the side-stories, I can without a doubt say that this game is an 11/10. I was a bit reluctant at first because of how emotional this game made me after playing through the main story, but then I played through the side-stories, and oh boy. It was 100% worth it. Playing the side-stories fleshed out the characters in addition to the main game and just makes you wish that was how the game actually ended (the ending we never got). I really don't know any other way to put it cause the side-stories kept throwing stuff at you that you always wanted to see but never did. Call if fan-service if you want, but I see it as the complete picture. The main story is just one frame, meanwhile the side-stories are the rest of the painting you don't see. And oh boy, did they outdo themselves with the soundtrack again. They need to stop making these bangers for visual novels man. It should be illegal at this point. All in all, this game made me go from happy, to an emotional wreck and back to being more happy than I was before. My satisfaction is unmeasurable, and words are not enough to describe it. Thank you, Team Salvato, for making such an amazing game with heart and soul put into it!!!

_childDocuments_.review: DDLC is peak psychological Horror.There are no complaints I could make about this game because everything it tried to achieve was executed perfectly. It has an amazing story with perfectly crafted characters. They all have their own personalities, motives, pasts and dreams and they are all available for you to figure out and discover. The gameplay follows the usual Dating-Sim type formular with a few twists here and there. For example, at the End of every in-game day, you as the player write a poem (chose a few words from a list) and present it to the literature club. Depending on which words you used the most when writing the poem, the character that likes it the most will spend some more time with you on that day. For 100% completion you will have to do a lot of replaying and reloading but the game has an auto dialog skip that stops every time something new happens or you have to make a choice. But before we talk about completion we have to start at the beginning.Your Story begins on a regular school morning, where you meet your old friend Sayori. She has been on the lookout for a new member in the literature club and begs you to join her. Given the circumstances of being a loser, you have no other real options and decide to go with her to your first day in the club.And from that point, your life as a member of the literature club has begun, but don’t get to comfortable, things may not be how they are presented to you. One character especially has their eyes on you, but I won’t spoil it here, even if everyone and their mother probably knows who I am referring to. If you only care about the horror aspect of the game and want something to play for Halloween, DDLC has a free version on steam too. The paid version is much more user-friendly and has some side content like Soundtrack list, Sidestories etc. so Its definitely worth your money if you feel invested in the story and characters.Doki Doki literature club is an absolute masterpiece of its genre and has been highly influential when it comes to indie gaming.

name: Midnight Fight Express
detailed_description: JOIN OUR DISCORD The first rule of Midnight Fight Express is : you DO talk about Midnight Fight Express! About the Game An unexpected hero emerges on the city's darkest night. You’re Babyface, a former member of the criminal underworld lured back into “the life” by a mysterious AI drone. Your mission against impossible odds: Fight your way across the city before sunrise, and prevent a citywide criminal takeover together. Engage in a brutal and hyper-kinetic brawling ballet, using every environmental tool and street fighting technique at your disposal. Level up your abilities to take down the mounting onslaught of bozos, cronies, and crime lords. Blockbuster Combat Tangle with waves of foes with the finesse of an action-movie master. Punch, dodge, counter, and finish off enemies in fluid and visceral combat featuring mo-cap animation by motion artist and stunt performer Eric Jacobus. Custom difficulty modes allow any player to direct the action to their preference. Martial Mastery Level up, power up, and tap into a sprawling skill tree to unleash a dizzying array of devastating fighting moves. Develop your own signature style, and master over-the-top combos that leave the criminals wondering what hit ’em. Killer Arsenal Complement your melee moves with knives, axes, and sledgehammers. Wield a wild array of pistol fire, shotgun blasts, and explosives. Weaponize everything from furniture to toilet plungers. Take advantage of the urban world around you to score increasingly outrageous takedowns and clean up the streets. Street Warrior’s Wardrobe Customize your character’s appearance, and unlock a huge variety of cosmetic options ranging from the ultra-suave to the mega-outlandish. Unlock more 150+ pieces of clothing, equip skins for you and your AI ally Droney, and make a lasting impression as you fight to save the streets. Audio Adrenaline Rush Battle across the city’s 41 hand-crafted levels to the beat of a pulsing, infectious soundtrack by artist Noisecream, and channel the nonstop midnight energy of the metropolis. The Fight Never Stops Return to missions to complete challenges, unlock rewards, and show everyone who owns the streets on the leaderboard. Create your own director’s cut of the action with settings that let you customize enemy types, weapons, and more.
