_childDocuments_.review: It's a very decent little zelda clone. It gets the style down, combat is pretty similar and it uses a few similar items (bow, bombs, boomerang, etc) It's kind of charming but never quite reaches the level its going for. It's not bad by any stretch, but it could do better in a lot of areas. There's a relatively large inventory but you don't really need most of it, The combat potions are useful but the normal difficulty is such you can ignore them and not think about it. Honestly once you upgrade the spear you can mostly ignore the sword and the bow is never really needed except for puzzles (which makes you wonder why you even need to upgrade its damage) The deflect spell was kind of novel but it doesn't see a ton of use unless you just want to spam it since it hits in all directions unlike the sword. The sword even gets an upgrade to charge up but it's so slow and can be interupted it's simply not worth it. The ancient spells are sort of interesting but all basically do the same thing, as a kind of screen clear but again you don't really need it given nothing is that hard. The warp charm was neat but comes so late and has so little use it seems like it was added as an afterthought. And then rock salt candles, ether bombs, and seekers are just there. They all have some use but they mostly just sit in your inventory. I did like rock salt candles as an idea, frankly I think they would've been better to save as a late game item because they're ridiculous and strong (and you can murder just about every boss with them) Boss fights are largely uninteresting, they have some mechanics but honestly I just threw rock salt candles at everything until it died. Admittedly, being able to heal at any point is part of what makes the difficulty so low as it's not hard to keep stocked on breads and fruits. Money is initially hard to come by but it's not too hard to keep scavenging, really you can probably sell most of the alchemy ingredients since by and large you don't need most of what you can make. But once you can access the tournament in Oakhaven Port you don't need to worry about money, ever, because for 20 currency you can repeat any level for tons of items and money. Honestly probably should've been a one and done deal. The world and dungeon design is okay, it's a big sprawling world with lots to explore and it's not hard to miss some of the side quests and things (I'll admit I missed the lightning spell for quite a while simply because I never bothered to interact with the fountain that starts the quest, not that I think I would've used it much except for the sidequest to upgrade it) It can be a little tedious to get around sometimes, there's a bit of backtracking and just 'okay, where do I go'. You get general directions but there's times later on when you have most of the world open when it's just a bit of slog with how far you have to travel and find the one particular thing you're looking for. It does the typical zelda/metroidvania thing where some things are gated behind getting the right kind of gear, but Ocean's Heart doesn't utilitze it much, I was particularly disappointed with how few places the Flail and the Warp Charm actually open up, they're mostly used in the dungeons you find them in and the final one, there's some very isolated instances out in the world to use them but that's it. The bow and strength charm early on gate a few things but that's about it. I get the sense this was more of a 'well zelda did it' and checked the box rather than really thinking of how to integrate some of these items and gating things with them. Dungeon design is fairly short and has some okay puzzles, find keys, hit switches, open locks and find treasure, that sort of thing. I would have liked a dungeon map feature but then few of them are really so long you really need it. The story is, unfortunately, the weakest part of the game. It isn't bad, Tilia is an okay protagonist, but it's all very simple. She wants to go find her friend and Dad, so she sets out with sword in hand. She uncovers a bad guy and despite being introduced fairly early on, Blackbeard remains just a cardboard cut out villain. Not that I was expecting some huge twist or amazing depth, but everything is presented very plainly and matter of factly. The ocean king/sea goddess lore is okay but again, it's all just very straight faced and there's not much depth or surprise. Honestly the whole sword subplot could've been dropped without much issue other than 'zelda had a magic sword'. There's a kind of interesting evil presence in the world called 'the abyss' but the game never really does much of anything with it except it's where monsters come from and it's used in a sidequest or two. Again, none of this is bad. It functions well for what it's going for. But its all pretty basic and tropey, a very 'knight rescues princess from dragon' set up and pay off kind of story. I will say the humor doesn't land very well. It tries to be kind of genre savvy but it's not that good at it (Tilia's basic response to most quests and plot updates is 'well time to go beat up pirates/monsters') There's puns but.. they're puns. The best thing I can say about the humor is it -tries-, the writers definitely attempted to be funny. Before wrapping up I want to give a special mention to a sidequest later in the game that is just beyond obnoxious. Without warning, you're taken to a new area with no ability to return to the rest of the game and the bulk of your items are robbed from you and you'll spend the next about 30-40 minutes scouring this small island going back and forth retrieving your equipment (which some of it you can miss, particularly the boomerang) and it's just... so so annoying. It doesn't really add much to the story, it does eventually give you one of the best weapons in the game but I -hated- being stranded and losing all my items just, out of nowhere and being locked out of the rest of the game until I finished it. That said, I'd rank it like a 3-3.5 out of 5. It's definitely not a 'must buy' experience, but if you're looking for a 2-D zelda-like, it's okay for the price range and you can burn a chunk of time on it. If it's on sale absolutely grab it, it's well made but doesn't live up to the potential it has and misses the mark meeting what it was paying homage to.

_childDocuments_.review: Great great game, one of the best Zelda 3 like I've played in recent years!Protagonist character is a girl who decides to go after her father and friend who have been gonne for a month following a pirate's attack on their tiny remote village.Lots of things reminds of Zelda: A Link to the Past, closer than other Zelda-likes might... the pixel graphics, some of the lore, some of the scenario.There are some things that I'll warn people about because some people might not like it, but it wasn't a huge problem for me. First of all, this game isn't exactly hard. It's easier than most Zelda games, particularly if you are a completionist like myself. Put simply, if you go after all sidequests and explore every nook and crany, by the end of the game you'll go through final bosses just by repeatedly slashing them... you have so much HP and your weapons are so powerful that nothing really poses a huge threat.Which is fine for me... it's one of the reasons why I didn't get to finish a bunch of Zelda-likes and Zelda titles myself, so this is great. I kinda hate getting stuck either because of too hard to beat bosses, or too difficult to figure out puzzles, so no complaints here.The game has a curse mechanism to make it harder for those looking for a challenge, but I'm not sure how much of a challenge it becomes as I didn't test it much.The other thing is that if you have no memory like myself, prepare to get lost a whole ton. :PAt least for me, this game could've used a more detailed map, a more comprehensive fast travel system, or some way to tag and mark points that you know you have to visit further along because the first time you went there you were missing some item or something to open the way.So really, even though I took 24hrs to finish it, if you just rush through without trying to get everything in the game, you'd probably take half the time... but I'd still recommend it nonetheless because it's just a fun adventure.It has a sorta dry sense of humour that I kinda like, and the variety of story, lore, weapons, puzzles and whatnot are satisfying.While I don't think it's perfect or that most people will like as I did, I personally think it's worth giving a try!It's really a game to play with gamepad, but I'm stuck with keyboard only, and even that didn't subtract from my enjoyment, so there you go. :DKudos to the apparently amazingly small team that created the game! Impressive stuff!

_childDocuments_.review: The controls are very obviously not optimised for game pad. You walk over edges, the menu works terribly, the hints reference the keyboard only. Pause isn't pause, it's "open the last menu".But even with the keyboard, falling down - or actively jumping because the action key does that if you are not exactly facing a person to talk to - is really annoying. Edges are hard to judge - at least falling down isn't a instant death.Manual saving is alright, but what happens at death? "Save and continue"? Why care about health items if I don't go back to my last save? Why have manual saves if I go back to a far away checkpoint anyway? This breaks the whole combat part into just tanking damage and running through. Enemies respawn anyway and healing is useless except for some boss fights that take more then a few hits. Basically, dying after a room transition is more efficient then stocking health items. Items/Progress are also persistent if you die, so health in this game has no purpose whatsoever.Moving boxes has fake difficulty by allowing you to move only in specific directions (and not moving back). Pressure plates also seem to only activate if you move in the right direction. The temples are fun if they contain some puzzles and rooms to unlock, but most of them are really short.The story is fine - in fact the beginning is really good with some neat details. It keeps you moving through the world. There are a lot of (more or less obvious) secrets strewn through the world, which makes exploring fun and engaging. Fast travel is also an option so you never need to walk that long.The writing tries to keep it light and doesn't get to serious but it's neither surprising nor terribly funny or interesting. From a world building standpoint, we get some bits of history, people produce different foods, towns have markets - it's believable enough. It's a pity you can't interact with some of the statues/monuments you come across. While it explains that our protagonist has had some sword training in the past (good detail!) and everybody knows the "voluntary navy", we seem to be the only one in the world from that group.From controls to combat, the core elements of this game are flawed. Exploration saves it to be mildly compelling. You are not missing much.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr The gameplay is good and so is the art, but it's too cynical. To me, that ruined the game. There is so much that goes right in this game. It probably deserves at least a recommendation for its fun gameplay and very solid construction and design, not to mention the unique and well thought-out art style-- but it has a soul-destroyingly cynical spirit that had me dreading playing it.First: gameplay-wise this is one of the most complete Zelda adventures that doesn't also have Nintendo's name on it. It's that good! The sense of exploration, powering up, the size and depth of the world itself, and the number of secrets in it are all excellent, and handled masterfully. Especially considering that this was made by one man. Heck it even makes backtracking sweet due to the amount of unique and needed consumables you tend to find. I had lots of fun with most of the enemies and bosses I've seen so far. Truly hats off to Max for that, he really knocked the gameplay out of the park. The art style is also fantastic, this is what drew me to the game at first. Max has a good understanding of subtlety, which I think is needed in good pixel art, and though it isn't quite perfect, it's better than most (even the vast majority) of games of this type. I appreciate that the biomes are all different, but also similar- it seems more realistic, which can be good or bad depending on your preference. There are also biomes in this game that are, as I said, subtle, and not like any I'd seen in a game before- think of the difference when walking between a coniferous forest and a marshland, in real life- there wouldn't be a huge difference, but yet everything would have changed. Max does this well.So what's not to like? For me, I play a grand adventure narrative in order to feel, like, hope and wonder. People have commented that the story is sparse, but I wouldn't mind that if its treatment of everything the protagonist is doing wasn't so cynical. The constant refrain is Tilia (the protagonist) saying something like, "Oh, forgotten temple, vital to the history of your people, yeah, yeah, uh huh, when do I get to blow stuff up and then you pay me?"That's the game's orientation towards itself. It's a weird contradiction, because Max has obviously put thought into the world he has created. As I said before, a pretty impressive amount- only to have it ignored, downplayed, or mocked by Tilia, the main character. Like it's all some idiot joke. I get that he isn't writing Dostoevsky. But I also don't think a quest should be meaningless. And here, it's presented as exactly that. So then why am I playing?In Zelda, the game this is based off of, the protagonist Link is an unlikely hero, often barely capable of getting out of bed on time, and yet he's called on to complete a grand quest, a task seemingly too great for him. Through his trials he becomes stronger, meets friends, helps people who he cares about, and purges the world of evil. Tilia? Tilia's cooool (Picture her wearing sunglasses and doing finger guns for just a moment). And what is she doing? She's aimlessly wandering in search of her father. Would he probably be found if she wasn't doing this? I don't know, it kinda seems so. Is she challenged, does she grow? Cool guys don't grow. Nothing is difficult for her, and she lets you know that. Then why, Tilia, am I accompanying you? Please do it yourself. Why do I care if the main character doesn't? Again, I applaud Max for his game design and the great art direction, and not only that but pulling this entire massive project off by himself. But... man. It's like three steps from alcoholism.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey, do you remember Minish Cap? One of the best, if not the best handheld Zelda game? Wanna play a game that looks like it belongs on the GBA? Then Ocean's Heart is the game for you!Now I have only spent a short amount of time with the game but it doesn't take long to understand and figure out what type of game this is. Ocean's Heart wears its Zelda inspiration/influence proudly, from the way the game plays, to the roll when you press the 'Interaction' button (A on the Xbox controller), to even the art for the main character. However do not go into this game expecting it to match Zelda in quality. That's not an insult to the game or to the developer, Max Mraz, that's a testament to how impressive the Zelda series is. I'll stop talk about Zelda now and focus on Ocean's Heart.You play as Tilia, a young Navy volunteer who must track down her father after he disappeared at sea. The game has an okay challenge to it from what I have seen, again it pulls from the SNES/GBA style of games so it pulls their difficulty as well. The game does have an open feel to it but I wouldn't call it open world. I hate to sound like a broken record but if you have ever played these types of games on the GBA, you pretty much know what to expect. Perhaps I'm jumping too far ahead with making this review. If that's true, I will edit this review. If you are like me, seeing this art style should feel you with determinat-err-nostalgia.  Everything about the game looks and feels inspired by the Zelda series. Depending on your opinion of the series will also depend on how you like this game. I have said it again and again through this review, in fact I think I have talked more about the retro/GBA feel than the game itself. It's still a Pro for me. So some of the control decisions are odd. LB opens the menu, right RB scrolls the menu to the right but LB closes the menu. Why doesn't Start open the menu? So this is a big big Con for me. In an attempt to be as GBA as possible, the game uses a font similar to that era. However, on my monitor it makes the font, idk, like bleed? It's a strain on the eyes to look at it. I am unsure if you can change the resolution, because when I played this on my laptop, I didn't have that issue. So this is a weird Con. I see a lot of reviews either taking off points or down right not recommending the game because of this. So I wanted to address it. Yes, there is no Auto-Save. The game uses an old-style Go-Through-Menu-Click-Save to save. If you aren't use to it and have become accustomed to auto-saving, this can be frustrating. The game does remind you to save at least once and since I'm old, I save almost every time I'm in the menu or before I quit. So while not a Con for me, I did want to make people away.I have also read that their are bugs present. I haven't played long enough to encounter any so I'm not sure. However the game is being worked on, I think, so hopefully they can patch out any issues. If you are looking to scratch that Retro/GBA itch, you could do far worst. Ultimately, maybe get this one on sale like I did? Although $14.99 isn't a bad price.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a really solid game for me.  It definitely feels like a Legend of Zelda style game but it does need some fine tuning to make it even better.  Even so it was very fun to play and I enjoyed the story line and art style.  Some things need a little extra attention but they're minor details that didn't affect how I played the game.  Some things I would have liked to see were:-An autosave feature: I constantly forget to save even though it told me to and I actually ended up losing a lot of progress at one time due to the game freezing (though I still went back and continued!)-The magic items should probably drain less mana than they do, but I didn't use them much.-Minor corrections in the dialog, not many though.-Ability to adjust the sensitivity of controllers: I used an XBOX 360 controller and noticed that the sticks were way to sensitive for me to use the menus or walk straight, but I was able to re-map them to the D-pad and it worked a lot betterStill, I loved playing this game and I would recommend it to other fellow Zelda-style lovers out there.

_childDocuments_.review: At 2 hours of playing I thought: "It's alright. It'll get better. It's not that bad."At 4 hours of playing I tried to refund it. No success (obviously). 2D Witcher with no navigation whatsoever and wonky controls. You click the wrong button, you die. The developer thought that allowing the player jumping in the water and die a few times in a row is fun. Doesn't look like that to me. Just erase this oppostunity & it will get better already. The game gives you a mission. You have to go back and forth through the map again, and again, and again. Talk. Go. Do. Go back. Talk again. Go again. Kill a monster. Go back. The games doesn't count the mission complete even when you did everything the game asked of you. There is either no monster you can kill or there is a monster, but you have to do what you just did but a second (and maybe a third) time. I had to spent at least 30 minutes on youtube to undestand where I need to go (people were just as confused as I was). Some roads are closed, so you have go back and forth again. All of that through the monsters that respawn again and again, but don't give you any resources. This rock is too heavy for you to move and open a new road. This rock can be moved, but not this one (that looks exactlly the same). This brick can be blown up, but since the controls are wierd, I wasted all the boms & I can't buy or create more because there are either no resources (some kind of uncknown flowers) or there are no bombs on the market. This way I have to probably restart the game & run trhough the entire map again, and again, and again, until I'm out of my mind and have a very real headache. No proper saving system, so I can't start from a point I would like to. It's either a new game or you suffer with what you currently have."Go to east." First of all, where?! Second of all, the road is closed! Now you tell me I have to go back and find another path??? Where there is no path?? No marks on the map, no functional map of the world. Barely any travel points (only 3 for me right now when there should be at least 6). I thought this is gonna be Stardew Valley. Boy, I was wrong. At least Stardew Valley is clear about where you need to go, who lives where, what can you get where, etc. I bought Ocean's Heart on sale & I regret it so much. I would refund this if I could. I would not recommend it at all. Considering everything, I'm not invested in the story at all.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very solidly okay and generally pleasant.  The graphics are cute, the puzzles are generally interesting, etc.  Gameplay-wise, it's a mediocre throw-back to GBA-era 2D Zelda games.  Story and dialogue is a bit heavy on tongue-in-cheek jokes about game tropes but generally leans on the amusing side of that line.The most frustrating things, personally, were the heavy knockback when hitting certain enemies (we're talking launched at least 3-4 blocks back), the wonky hitboxes (some are too small, some are too big), and enemy placement when entering rooms/enemy behavior in general (on multiple occasions I took 3-9 hearts of damage entering a room because I was immediately barraged by enemies, and enemies tend to be very quick to punish you if you don't learn their attack patterns).If you don't like 2D top-down dungeon crawlers (i.e. 2D Zelda-esque games), this probably isn't a game you'll enjoy.  If you do, you should probably wait for a sale (or a price drop to less than $10).  I'm expecting to get about 10 hours of mild fun out of it, so weigh the price accordingly.

It's not quite as irreverent as Link's Awakening, but it has a similar charming silliness to the characters and storytelling that implores us to not take things too seriously. And if you like 90's-era Zelda-style overhead gameplay, and you're not terribly bothered by games with occasional frustrating periods, then you might enjoy treating yourself to Ocean's Heart.

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up playing Zelda games on the Game Boy Color and Advanced and bought Ocean's Heart hoping for a similar experience. I was not disappointed! The Bad:It's not quite as good as the old Zelda games in my opinion. Gameplaywise this is because most of the dungeons aren't nearly as big. The controls also feel less polished with the character falling into water or pits far more often then in the Zelda games. I also feel like a lot of the spells and late game items were underwhelming. _childDocuments_.review: Worth a look! The presentation is really nice — the pixel art is terrific, and it goes a long way having something nice to look at all the time. I appreciate that the story is fairly straightforward (meta-overload that was Blossom Tales this is not, and that's refreshing). But there are certainly nods to video game history peppered throughout, and the writing is generally pretty amusing. (Nitpick: the writing is very comma-laden — throw in a few other forms of punctuation to punch it up a notch!)The sense of exploration is probably this game's other great asset. After a brief intro, it sorta just sets you loose and you can really go off in whatever direction you please. There's still plenty of gates to prevent you from going certain places all at once, but you can certainly wander into brutal monster territory as soon as you please, which I think is really true to classic Zelda form. There's also a handy sidequest tracking system: just enough to be helpful, but we're not talking Cyberpunk levels of disorganization here. That's a good thing.I do wish the game's control feel and enemy AI were a bit more polished. No denying there's some nice animations at work, but it seems all too common for enemies to follow a simple movement pattern with a basic attack. You can lure them to get stuck on corners sometimes, and it's just a matter of patience. The key really is not to get hit, since the enemy attacks can be harsh. The sword attack also could feel better. Stand in front of a group of bushes and you'll see what I mean: you can only effectively hit a single one at a time, directly in front of you, even if it seems like your blade is making a wide slash. It could just use a little bit of polish to feel more fluid. (Oh, and button mapping aside, having roll and inspect on the same button is irritating. Too many times have I wanted to read a sign and rolled away from it instead.)I'm not very far in, so these are just impressions. But there's definitely enough going on here to keep me interested - and I'm actually glad I'm not looking at a 50 hour, dragged-out, milked-to-death thing. It's fresh, it's concise, the scale feels just right, and you're helping out a solo developer who clearly poured a lot of heart into this. Is it perfect? No. Do I want to see more from this guy? Hell yes.

You can find the original one below.Ocean's Heart is basically a GameBoy TLoZ clone based on an engine (called Solarus) that was specifically made for these kind of clones. The graphics are great, the music is alright (but sometimes a bit annoying tbh) and the world is pretty neat. Actually it is pretty beautiful and feels very much alive. I think you could compare OH more to Minish Cap or Phantom Hourglass, because the whole world is a group of islands within a big ocean, you will see water very, very often, so I hope you like the colour of blue.The gane is far beyond being perfect. name: Orwell's Animal Farm
detailed_description: “ All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others. ” In Orwell's Animal Farm, the animals have fought off their exploitative human masters. Now they're in charge. In this text-based choice-driven narrative game you can assign their tasks, manage their resources, choose their laws, and direct their propaganda. Determine which of the animals will make sacrifices and which will be 'more equal than others.' George Orwell's 1945 novella was a scathing critique of totalitarianism in the early days of the Soviet Union. Since then, it has spoken to people of many ideologies in countries around the world. It offers a powerful awareness of how power can be abused – and of how generation after generation seeks a more just and equal society, where the many do not suffer at the hands of the few. Orwell's Animal Farm brings the familiar characters and situations to the medium of a game, and to the context of 2020. Depending on how you play, you may encounter situations very close to those in the book, or others influenced by events Orwell never lived to see. Play it to explore a classic tale from inside. Play it to try your hand at running the farm – or because you dream of spreading Animalism across the world. Play it because you've always wanted to oversee a construction project by a herd of cows. Play it because Boxer deserved better.

_childDocuments_.review: "Four legs good. Two legs bad."Boy if that sort of division doesn't sum up the current time.This was required reading when I was in school and I'm starting to see why, however I wonder if the game truly captures why the book is so important.This is a sort-of visual novel with both more choices and fewer choices than I expected, although that's a contradiction.  In the destiny of the farm, I did feel like I had a decent amount of choices, but only in the vein of the original story.  If you're expecting a variety of outcomes, then perhaps this isn't the game for you, as we get 8 finishes, and I just completed one, a very very bleak one.Bleak is how I could describe both the original novella and the game.  The spirit of weariness is there, but some of the moments in the book that strike most powerfully are glossed over in the game as simple dialogue boxes.  The death of beloved characters lasts a handful of seconds, has no artwork or animation to accompany it, and triggers a loud "thumping" sound effect and a game "achievement" (if that's the right word) to pop up.  I thought that took a lot of the bite out of those moments.Napoleon didn't seem as sinister as he has in the book or the various adaptations on screen and television, not sure why.  He's more intelligent than the drunken slob portrayed by Sir Patrick Stewart in the television adaptation and yet not as eloquent as I remember him from the novella.  This Napoleon would be right at home in the modern-day US Senate screaming about going to war with countries over oil and trade.  This is no Joseph Stalin.That being said, the game is very pleasant, if somewhat limited.  It would be nice to have some audio options to help make the narration a bit easier to hear.  it would have also been nice to have a bit more voice acting in the game as it's essentially an all text game.  I do wonder how much the choices truly change the narrative, and at times I felt like I was on-rails to a certain extent, but I guess that's to be expected.Overall, I thought the spirit of the book was still captured, though I'd like to see some fixes and changes so that this feels more like a game and less like a visual novel.People in 2021 should still pick up this game, though, as it's very important to learn the story.  But Boxer deserved better than a dialogue box. 7/10Pros: Very relevant message, captures the basics of the book in an engaging manner, does manage to hook you into wanting to unlock all endings and destinies for the animals.  The game still bears all the weariness and darkness of the book with a few small grisly details glossed over, but the basics are all there.  For an adaptation from a novella, surprisingly complex.Cons: Events felt on-rails at times, lack of game options such as audio levels (unless I'm just dumb and I couldn't figure out where they were), and a lack of animation or variety of visuals, overall making this game seem more akin to the Oregon Trail than a game made in 2020.

_childDocuments_.review: Although it’s been several years since I last read  in an English class, I still vividly remember the strong feelings its bleak ending line evoked for me. This may seem a strange reason to choose a game, but I was curious to see how the developers would adapt, expand upon, and possibly diverge from the source material.  is described on its Steam store page as a text-based choose-your-own-adventure game, and I would say that description is fairly accurate. Although more complex in its gameplay than a visual novel, it’s still prone to the same limitations of that genre, and despite having multiple endings, in none of them do the developers stray as far from the book’s original ending as I would have liked.As one might expect from the title of the game, the game universe is built around the political allegorical novella  by George Orwell. Certain portions of the text heavily reflect actual content from the novel. However, with eight possible endings, the story is not merely a retelling of the book’s plot in game form, and it is possible for characters to have different outcomes in the game than their fates in the book. Unfortunately, it  is clear from the achievement name for reaching every ending that all of the endings stick with the source material’s bleak tone, which I feel was a missed opportunity to more critically explore and evaluate the political systems under scrutiny in the novella.There’s no tutorial or guidance on how to play, but I feel I was able to mostly suss it out through experimentation. Gameplay takes place in four locations: farm overview, barn meetings, battlefield, and inside the farmhouse. When on the farm overview, the cursor is a magnifying lens that pops up actions on any available character. Different actions will increase or decrease an individual animal’s health, the amount of food in storage, the level of Animalism, and/or the farm’s population. The color green is used for increasing effects and good health, while the color red is used for decreasing effects and poor health.Despite being somewhat intuitive, I wish that the specifics were more clear-cut sometimes. For example, the number of actions that can be taken each turn is not consistent, and it would be nice to know how many actions I’m able to take before I start making decisions. Also, what does the Animalism level really mean? Does it simply mean the animals have a better attitude even when the situation sucks? Or does it also affect outcomes in other ways? Without a more clear way to track progress, after enough years have passed sometimes gameplay can start to drag a little because the same text starts to repeat as the seasons change. One playthrough to the longer endings takes about 2 hours, spanning over 7 in-game years.The art style is hand-drawn like classic English children’s storybook illustrations, but there’s not much in the way of motion animation due to the game being text-based and similar to visual novels in presentation. The soundtrack is orchestral, musically pleasing to the ear, and possesses enough variety in theme to not get repetitive. The only voice acting is the narration done by the storyteller; all character dialogue is text-based. There are also animal sound effects when a particular animal’s action is selected, and stamp sound effects when a stamp is made in the handbook. All of these simple effects combine into a charming whole that contributes to the story being told.There are five possible achievements, ranging from very simple to complete (e.g. it’s unlikely you’ll fail to click on the handbook at least once during a playthrough) to ones that will require multiple playthroughs to complete (e.g., collecting every stamp in the handbook and seeing every ending). You’re able to see your progress towards some of these achievements in the handbook (e.g., stamps earned previous playthroughs have a watermark version of the stamp) or in the stats screen at the end. I’m still working on some of the more complex achievements at the time of this review.I frequently encounter a bug when trying to launch the game where it says there is a missing executable. When I encounter this bug, the only solution has been to verify the integrity of the game’s files AND restart the computer. However, since this error doesn’t occur during gameplay I don’t find it a detriment to the overall experience.Priced $9.99 at the time of review,  is an outstanding interactive exploration and tribute to the classic book, and I would highly recommend it to any Orwell superfan or student seeking to spice up their English class experience. For those who don’t fall into those two categories though, the game is probably better purchased at a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: dystopian and satirist literary work undoubtedly influenced, and still influences, a lot of other creative people, who are inspired by his themes, and use them for their own work. However, having a full videogame adaptation of his work is something else, and now we finally got it with , which adapts the original allegorical novella. This text-based game tries to capture and expand the book’s themes and experience a bit by adding several story choices. There is not much more to this game, as you could say it is similar to a visual novel. Is it a good addition, though? Well, let us dive into the review to find it out!It all starts in one of the many farms in England, which is poorly and irresponsibly run by an alcoholic farmer, . Most of the animals got fed up with him and started to think about overthrowing their master. They finally do it one day, under the leadership of two sly pigs,  and , with whom they successfully drive  out off the farm. That is only the beginning, as now more important task awaits them. They have to run the farm on their own, and their success relies on your decisions.However, the game strictly follows the book’s plot only in the introduction part. After that, it is up to you, which direction will farm and its animals take. Your journey will eventually end in one of the eight endings, which quite suit the book’s theme. It is not that hard to reach one of those, as one playthrough takes around an hour or two, depending on how fast you read. Yet, with so many endings, it feels like this game has an identity issue, as it tries to both faithfully re-tell the book’s plot as well as forcing you into choosing from story-changing choices. Unfortunately, the game fails in both of those parts.The problem is that the way it tells the original story is very simplified after the introduction, and most of the added scenes with choices replace some parts completely. So, while you will reach throughout the years the main events of the story, you will spend most of the time deciding about which activities should animals on the farm do. And that would be a great addition if it did not overshadow the main plot, which is the main issue here. It is just way too repetitive and uninteresting this way, so I just skipped through it in the next playthroughs.For example, as in the book, animals discussed in the barn, whether they should build a windmill or not, and after that event, you return to the farm’s overview and return to the chore of choosing from monotonous tasks. And they represent all of the farm’s activities, like food harvesting or battles. They are totally random in every playthrough, and I have to say their arbitrary appearing ruined at least one of my six playthroughs. How? The game wanted me to choose between birds’ spying and singing three times in one year. Both waste your food supplies, and even though I ploughed the field in the previous year, I only got an option to harvest it for food once! That lead to marvellous starvation. Well, at least  was happy with himself…That leads us to another problem, on which developers are apparently working now, which is that the game’s mechanics are not properly explained. While I know how much food I have left, I am not that sure about other aspects. Like, does Animalism influences overall morale, working effectivity, or battles? It is also unclear whether there is a set number of animals or not, as I lost two sheeps during a battle, yet I could still use them. My playthroughs were also a bit buggy, as a goat  died during the battle, and reappeared afterwards even though she was marked as deceased one. Things like this just add to the overall confusion on how the game actually works.What  excels in are its audiovisuals. The colourful, hand-drawn art style is beautiful to look at, and it fits the game’s premise a lot. Animals are also portrayed very well with specific traits, and their facial expressions change a lot too. Including more animations for animals would not hurt, but the lack of them does not ruin my experience.While there are not many sounds, the game still shines with its soundtrack, which is varied enough and at certain parts, it manages to deliver those nationalistic tones you would expect to hear in your tiny, animal kingdom. Definitely a great choice! It is a bit of shame that animals are not voice acted, as the only voice you will hear is the narrator’s one. He is doing a fine job, though.To be honest, even if it was not for annoying bugs and repetitiveness, I would still bee bored with , as the plot is not that engaging as in the book due to all the unnecessary distraction by various choices. I also do not recommend playing this game if you did not read the book because the experience is barebone. I have no doubts that the developers are fans of  work, but this does not work for me. It is a shame, and I am honestly a bit disappointed, as I was looking forward to this title.
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: Got a copy from Nerial to review this - thanks! Orwell's Animal Farm is, at first, a very straightforward adaptation of the literary classic. But as the game goes on, through a series of Reigns-like we decide the outcome in certain situations. This means that the narrative can branch off, but that's where the game disappointed me the most: I wanted to reach certain scenarios or endings that I knew were possible (the game itself tells you what happens in each of the 7 endings), only to find out that the story kept railroading me towards a certain point. I only managed to get 3 endings having played it more than a few times, and they were all pretty similar. I wish they had taken some more liberties in this regard; nevertheless I commend it for being unapollogetically political, even knowing how gamers are about these things. I should also point out that the graphics are charming, the OST is great, and the narration is hypnotic. Overall, it is worth playing and experiencing, especially if you've read the novella (I encourage you to do it before playing, it's not long). It just needed some more ambition behind it, because as it is it's fine but there's not much more to it once you've played through it a couple times (which takes about 2 hours).
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: I do not typically review a game with only 12 minutes playtime. But, I made an exception here due to the gameplay. The concept is built around a beautiful book. Animal Farm the book is a classic much loved, as it should be. But, the execution ends up being nothing more than a click click visual novel. That may be what a few people are looking for. But, my imagination had taken the word 'choice' and ran with it, so I had expected a text-based choice game. Instead, it is more like the little anime novels where you read and click to advance, with an occasional choice of which animal will respond to the previous script with a neigh or something. That's fine if that's what you are looking for, but if you expect meaningful choices, then you are probably looking for something along the lines of say , which was a text-based choice game which I loved. But, I don't see this as something that even kids would enjoy, as it is currently executed. That is just my opinion. But, for the positive. The soundtrack is good. I kept the game for the soundtrack. It is a nice change-up in sounds to add to my gaming playlist on my phone and pc. The tunes are somewhat classical, and remind me a bit of Tchaikovsky's Peter and the Wolf, or other classical pieces. No hate intended. If this is what you are looking for, by all means buy it. But, just so you know what the gameplay style is... here's my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting text style choose your own adventure game based on George Orwell's short novel, Animal Farm. Here you delve into the world of farm animals where they have fended off the humans that have shackled them and are now managing the area. With the wide range of animals from rats, horse and dogs etc, things can get political within the game depending on how it is played and how the animals are governed. There are many paths to lead because of the choose your own adventure way of playing. Whether it be focusing on administering the farm or spreading the ways of the animal. Gameplay is pretty fun, especially when you get invested the the story and direction that which is chosen. There are also some puzzle and point and click elements within the game as well where going through certain spots or certain characters are required for that scene. There is a good amount of replayability to the game because of the various endings that can be seen. Visuals are also quite appealing too with the hand drawn art style of the of the animal characters as well as the background environment. Overall, is a neat text based game with an interesting story that absorbs you into the world. I haven't heard of the author nor the novella before but do feel like checking it out as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: I finished reading For Whom The Bell Tolls because it was mentioned in Cyberpunk 2077. Likewise, I wanted to read Animal Farm because it has a reference in a pretty little game called Inspector Waffles. Before visiting the local bookstore, I browsed Steam and found this game with the  same title. I know video games are not the best way to read a book, but it was so delightful playing Ken Follett's The Pillars of the Earth, also Bobok the game (by Fyodor Dostoevsky), I decided to give this game a go.I expected an original read with some graphics, however, this game is kind of an easy farm sim, where players get to choose which animal to do what, build up the stocks, react to emergencies, etc. The story is related to the book, there are multiple endings depending on which options the player chose.I do not blame devs for not being "true" to the author, nothing wrong with being creative. I am glad to read the rules made by the pigs are the same in the book, what I do not like is that the player is given too many opportunities to choose, not to mention I have a year almost identical to the previous year. I wanted to see how those rules are altered, however in my run I only see 2 out of 7.This game has satisfying graphics, clear lines, and good music. It does not meet my expectation as a shortcut to the original book, but it would be unfair to give a negative review just because of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.”― George Orwell, Animal FarmI remember when I was younger we had to choose a book to read and write about. I chose Orwell's Animal Farm, because I was a teenager and liked animals. Oh boy, is the book and this game based on that book, more than just about animals. This game is a visual novel type of game where there are lines from the book and it follows the story of the book somewhat. There are choices you get to do and multiple different endings you can achieve, though none of the endings are particularly happy or good, nor did they have too much variety in them. The art is beautiful, the narrator's voice acting is great and it fits the somber mood of the game. I can somewhat recommend this game, it was short and fun, but I do really recommend reading the original book. It's short and not too long, just like the game, but you might get more insight on the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: This game explains nothing about its gameplay (after multiple playthroughs I'm still unsure of what the Animalism stat does) and appears to be a buggy mess of RNG. Dead animals can still comment on events occurring (Napoleon and Boxer appear to be the biggest culprits) or show up at the gravesite despite being dead (such as the Cabal of Pigs ending where Snowball and Napoleon have died, but Napoleon is at the grave). You can run into problems where you have plenty of supplies and want to repair the buildings but you can't until the option presents itself, or similarly where you had the opportunity to harvest with multiple animals to fill the supplies to their maximum but suddenly only one animal can be chosen and you have far less than usual. Sometimes it skips letting you plant for next year which makes supplies much worse and no longer lets you plant on subsequent years, even if you have the supplies to do so.Some events, like Snowball being chased off by Napoleon's dogs that he's raised and trained (as per the book) seem to be tied to the dogs giving puppies that Napoleon takes away for that purpose, but the event still occurs even if the puppy event never triggers. Instead, to avoid Napoleon driving Snowball off the dogs must be removed from Animal Farm (either from fighting humans or choosing for them to leave if supplies are low in the winter), which keeps both leaders on the farm even if you got the puppy event.Boxer is a fragile china doll who drops dead pretty fast or sold off for slaughter (as per the book) if you use him for work (other than ploughing the fields or harvesting under good circumstances). Story-wise it doesn't really add anything to Orwell's story. Other than four game over endings, the four successful endings just checks to see which leader is alive: Snowball, Napoleon, both, or neither. Both/Neither has all the pigs die and the birds talk about how Animalism is past even if the farm is successful, while Snowball/Napoleon solo endings have the same event per the book (inviting and dining with farmers), but with a slightly different motive for Snowball.It's not a terrible game, but I was kind of expecting more.
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: A good game to play after reading the book. It would be nice to see further novels adapted in this way. 1984 would make an amazing choice based game.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically a visual novel, not really what I would call a game in the classic sense. However, given the brilliance of the material it is based on, I cannot justify a bad review. Be aware of what to expect though, this won't become a game you're likely to play/replay very often. But it's a great way to introduce the novel to kids, and a joy to see for every true fan of the book. If you approach this game with any high expectations in terms of gameplay, you'll be bitterly disappointed though. Make sure this is what you want before purchasing.
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: in 1945 George Orwell released an allegorical novella called Animal Farm, it is often hailed as one of the greatest books of all time.Written during a time of war, and Stalinism, its basic premise is one of a critique of the rise of Communism. Pretty light stuff for a video game don't you think?Well, some 75 years later a game has been developed whereby you can take the decisions, make the important choices and basically be part of the revolution.The game itself is not really a "game" in the classic sense, it is more of a visual novel but with defined journeys and outcomes that you decide.You are in charge of Manor Farm, and you have a group of various animals, you chose who is listened to, who is ignored, who works what job on the farm and so on, every choice matters. The main purpose is to last 7 years, of course the wrong choices will end up with everything going wrong. Everything is about balance. Keeping everyone happy or at least content.With the game being released now, I suspect that the game makers think they are pointing out a certain set of issues that exist in 2020, but perhaps inadvertently they are actually exposing what is to come. Either way this is not a kid's game, and I think it would be hard for anyone who has not read the book to take much out of this game.The GoodThe game is very well drawn. And you will replay the game to see the different outcomes.The BadFar too often you will find yourself not really paying attention and instead just clicking through actions to see the different outcomes. So good and bad in that respect.There isn't really that much to do, you are just making the odd choice and seeing what happens.OverallThis is a tough one to judge. I understand what the game makers wanted to achieve, and in many ways, they have achieved what they set out to do, the problem is that in many ways it is all a bit dull. The lack of actual game play is a problem here. This is basically a "Choose Your Own Adventure" book, but stripped down to the absolute minimum to fit into a game. I actually think this would work better as a proper book.I Score the game 4/10By Jon Donnis

_childDocuments_.review: I think the gameplay is too one-directional and repetitive, and the dialogue is too shallow, and incohesive to be a game with 8 different endings. I played though it twice and I'm already very tired. Things don't change that much with what you choose and I'm tired of the game pausing the gameplay for the animals to talk about the windmill, or the rats, or the rules, all in the same fashion, over again. too slow. The game is more survival than narrative (if you are buying the game thinking it will be a visual novel with options you are mistaken and should reconsider buying the game).The survival part is not well explained either. My farm keeps dying of depopulation but there is no meter that tells me the amount of animals I have. Animals seem to die at random, and they don't tell you. The horse keeps dying on me even if I use him sparingly. There are a handfull of fighting options, but it is not very clear to me they change anything.As I said, the narrative tramples on the gameplay. And, In the end I didn't feel I was living the "comunist revolution leads to tyranny" thing of the book, only something like "surviving against nature is hard".Also, and maybe more important than anything else... They didn't had a sung version of "Beasts of England"! To sum up, this is an average management game with the thematic of the book, butnarrative and gameplay are not well consolidated together.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun and faithful interpretation of the book Animal farm, and I enjoyed it wholeheartedly. However, it's not without its bugs. _childDocuments_.review: Visually it is fantastic. Progression is slow and also although it's a bit shortened, just about the whole book is crammed into the game so it's technically a visual novel where you pretty much only read and don't actually play a game.Refunded and giving a low score because my expectations for this "game" weren't met. Highly recommended for children (even if they don't know English, the visuals and sounds are awesome enough to keep them entertained) and for people who haven't read the book. _childDocuments_.review: I am incredibly disappointed by this 'game'.Calling it a game is an insult to actual games. _childDocuments_.review: Fun little game for while but it seems that whatever you do the fate of the farm and the animals is doomed to an extent. I don't know that this necessarily reflects Orwell's meaning but it makes for depressing gameplay, particularly because it's not clear who you are playing as/for: Am I just trying to make the farm survive? Am I trying to liberate the animals? Am I trying to keep the pigs in charge? It just makes your decisions feel meaningless and makes for boring gameplay. I've played other "based-on-book" games and games where you can't really change the outcome which have nevertheless been much more entertaining than this one sadly. I was also surprised at how much disk space it occupies.I stopped when I noticed Snowball had decided to come back to life to speak at the funeral for one of the sheep.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting way to interact with Orwell's Animal Farm, allowing for the "what ifs" that would challenge the events in the story.Have you read the book? If not, it is not a big deal, just take to heart that this in an allegorical game world of political and social critiques from the time. So while you do impact the narrative and manage Animal Farm, the real takeaway is self reflection rather than the ending. The way it is set up, I doubt it would be much fun as just "a game."I had not read or watched Animal Farm since I was a child and still remember thinking about if only Snowball had prospered. Through this game, I sort of got my answer. For better or worse.

One I could open up on the spot and play for 15 minutes, get back to it later in order to eventually get the full extent of what the creators intended.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautifully made, family friendly game which brings Orwell's increasingly relevant masterpiece to new audiences. It is rare to find games that provoke thought and action. If you like games that make you think, have enjoyed the simple but compelling mechanics of REIGNS (developed by the same team), the social satire and moral choices of the multiple award winning PAPERS, PLEASE and have made tough decisions in Osmotic's excellent ORWELL series of games etc., then this is the game for you. It could also serve as a really great learning tool and an interactive "bed time story" to enjoy with kids during lock down. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: Really unique game that just sucked me right in,  The whole dynamic of it just kept me beyond captivated. You just become so invested in everything that's going on seeing your choices come to life. A fascinating theme with super fun gameplay matching a beautiful game. I couldn't stop until I played it through, and made me already plan how I am going to re-play it before I even finished. Should I choose what's good for the farm? Or the animals? Or actually for Animalism as a whole? What does good even mean here? _childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: A faithful and timely adaptation.I first encountered Animal Farm many years ago at school. It was the annual school play and I ended up playing a bull that got ripped to shreds by dogs for breaking the rules. I was too young to really grasp the real world commentary but now, many (I’m not saying how many) years later, it all makes a lot more sense....So, the game - it is, on the face of it, a very simple point and click, PYOA. There is a basic introduction to the mechanics and then off you go. Much of what entails is discovery, you find your feet and pick up on the dynamics and the implications of your decisions. It’s the up to you to chart a course to the end. It’s a balancing act - managing the demands of supply, personality and power. Your morality will be tested. Being acutely aware of the original narrative, I could see the path ahead of me and what would be the likely outcomes - I was essentially living the story. But that is to do the game a disservice, there is more to it than that. The game forces you to think. And not just about the mechanics and the quest to the end, but also about just how frightening the relevance of the game is to the world we live in today. How we can be manipulated by words, how we can become monsters and enforcers for those who tell us what we want to hear, not what we need to know. I played the game with an impending sense of dread - uncomfortable but necessary.Kudos to the game designers, a brave and relevant project to tackle. Playing games are an integral part of how we learn. Play this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: I have always heard good things concerning the original novel, but I never read it. One night while stoned and curious  I ended up giving this a chance and I was truly satisfied. After playing it once, I ended up reading the original story and it gave me greater appreciation for both game and the writing. I think walking into this game with an unbiased perspective made it incredibly interesting and honestly this would be great for students in middle school/high school. Animal Farm's themes are incredibly thought provoking and abstract and with the interesting writing this makes for a worthwhile experience and investment. I never make reviews on steam, but I think it's important games like these receive deserved praise for their excellence in putting an interesting spin on great story. I hope more valuable writing can be turned into games like this in the future, I think this is a great way to expose people to literature.  Also, I would definitely recommend playing this with someone. I did and it made the experience very fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Orwell's Animal Farm

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty faithful to the novella without railroading the player. It seems to be designed in such a way that making the obvious choices will tend to result in the same outcome as the novella. Perhaps that's as it should be, if Orwell's message is to be preserved. Still, it is possible to make different choices and steer Animal Farm, and its inhabitants, toward a different fate.This isn't a VN to play through just once, though it's not bad for that (especially if you're unfamiliar with the original work). It's rather short; I think my first playthrough was about three hours. But it encourages you to play it again and see how things might happen differently. So if you're looking for a "one and done" experience, this may not be the game for you, but if you're at all willing to replay and experiment, I think you should give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Orwell's Animal Farm is a game developed by Nerial and published by The Dairymen and is based on George Orwell's book of the same nameAs an avid fan of George Orwell's works such as 1984 and Animal Farm, I was slightly excited to see Animal Farm be turned into a game, but at the same time, I was quite concerned and questioned myself, "can Animal Farm  be turned into a game in the first place?" and although Nerial, the same people behind the Reigns series, tried their hardest, they slip and fall big time and that's a damn shameThis is not going to be a game for everyone, and you can clearly see that with the amount of reviews this game currently has, sitting at a measly 40 reviews and, not going to lie, although I'm a somewhat fan of visual novels, I was not a big fan of this oneThe game offers some nice graphics and aesthetic, although some ugly glitches here and there, such as text automatically jumping to the next set of text without me clicking on the text box or the narrator's voice continuing to talk even though I skipped it (because I was incredibly bored), it is pleasant all the same. However, I cannot understand why there are black borders on the sides for certain parts of the game, but then in others it isn't, it is incredibly annoying and does not fit any aesthetic purposes whatsoeverThe sound mixing in this game is also awful, with music either being too loud or too low and the narrator's voice being too damn low - what on Earth happened? However, to give credit where credit is due, the narrator's voice (from what little I could hear) is good and gives some emotion to the otherwise bleak scenes (not in terms of setting but in terms of what the game actually offers)Also, this game's repetition is horrendous, although they took Orwell's Animal Farm and made some alternate endings, the same amount of text and voice bits that constantly repeat over and over again which is incredibly annoyingThe gameplay... isn't really gameplay to be honest, it's just you clicking a bunch of times and seeing the outcomes of said decision - that's it... if this were just a straight up visual novel, I would have turned a blind eye, but then again...It seems like Nerial did not know what they wanted out of this, did they want to make a visual novel or a different take on Animal Farm, but then again, can you actually adapt Animal Farm into a game in the first place? Especially when it has such complex characters and settings and deals with incredibly heavy topics, especially when it dabbles in politicsOrwell's Animal Farm overall, is a massive disappointment and that's a damn shame, however, for the little it offers, it is an okay game to play, and it does get incredibly boring if being played for a long time, but is an okay-ish to meh casual visual-novel game and to play in short burstsIf you're expecting a different take on Animal Farm, or even a sort of political sim (which would have been incredibly interesting if done well and especially in the setting of Animal Farm), then this isn't sadly it...

detailed_description: The DioField Chronicle DEMO Presenting a free demo of 'The DioField Chronicle', that allows you to carry over your progress to the full game. In this demo you can play from the game's opening through to the end of chapter 1. *This demo consists of a section taken from the full game. *It is possible to carry over save data from the demo to the full game *It is possible to carry over game progress and character levels to the full game. *Content may vary from the full game. The DioField Chronicle Digital Deluxe Edition ■The DioField Chronicle Digital Deluxe Edition contains: ・Main game ・Weapon: Knight's Spear (*1) ・Accessory: Mystical Ring (*1) ・The DioField Chronicle Original Soundtrack (*2) ・The DioField Chronicle Digital Artbook (*2) *1: These items can be obtained in the second half of the game, but they can be received during Chapter 1 Episode 2. *2:These are identical to the 'The DioField Chronicle Original Soundtrack' and 'The DioField Chronicle Digital Artbook' sold separately. Please be careful about making duplicate purchases. About the Game The era of myths gives way to an era of great turmoil… The world of men is mired by an age of war which rages for year on end. A band of elite mercenaries calling themselves Blue Fox arise amidst the flames and the chaos, their fates and valiant deeds to be sung of in ages yet to come. But when all is said and done, will the name 'Blue Fox' come to signify hope or darkest tragedy? Featuring a unique and beautiful world that blends fantasy, medieval and modern-day influences, and a deep yet innovative real-time battle system. ■Deep, strategic, real-time tactical battles The battles in this game are defined by real-time assessment of battlefield conditions and issuing decisive orders that take advantage of your troops strengths and weaknesses to gain advantage over your foe. Make clever use of a variety of skills, classes and equipment to complete your mission. ■Realistic 'diorama' style battle scenes Richly detailed depictions of the environments of the island of DioField combined with unique 'diorama' style visuals as you command your forces like a general.

_childDocuments_.review: The actual gameplay loop of Diofield is pretty grim - it promises a unique take on the tactics game but what you actually get is pause-based combat akin to Baldur's Gate, with less complexity and less difficulty.    This is not a new and fresh take, it's been around for decades in the CRPG world and it was done better at the very first jump. On top of this the controls are mapped weird, you are constantly popped in and out of pause when you don't want to be (there is not a generic spacebar to pause function, possibly the easiest thing to implement to make the game feel less slippery) and units will occasionally pick up the wrong orders or get mass ordered in a way that redirects them from their intended targets.  It's friendlier to controllers than keyboards.There's been a lot of improvements in pause-based real-time combat over the years and this implementation has all of the weaknesses of the format and virtually none of the strengths or lessons learned (and in cases like Larian's Divinity, a lot of the lessons learned have been to pivot back to turn-based and streamline that combat instead).  The game fights this management by limiting the player to four units, which virtually turns off the strategy element and is still somewhat difficult to keep tabs on.   All the tactical elements that are implemented are broken by the floatiness and lack of precision - for example, backstabbing is critically important but enemy facing is determined by a vague circle with an arrow, making you long for an actual tactical grid, and whatever circle-based system the game uses for indicating vision isn't particularly accurate.  Frequent time limits prompt you to rush through most stages thoughtlessly and the mana system allows you to easily burn skills at short cooldowns, with the only measurement being how many enemies you think will magically spawn in after you finish your current batch.  On hard mode, you can perfectly clear each mission in the first five hours without the user having to strategize anything. Several of the usual Squeenix JRPG port issues apply - no widescreen support, fairly barebones customization and poor interaction with Windows in general.  It at least runs with no visible framerate drops on high settings.This game evokes Final Fantasy Tactics fairly hard in map design, art, story and its fairly exaggerated claim to the tactical strategy genre.  But so far it has none of the depth of strategy or story that really pushed those games to the top of the list.  It's not bad, it's just extremely lazily executed and a huge disappointment to its predecessors.  I might finish - there's some good design here that's decently thoughtless fun and could pay off as things get more complicated - but it currently feels like about ten bucks worth of game in a sixty dollar package.

_childDocuments_.review: I can barely recommend DioField Chronicles. The bones are in place for a great experience, but each of its systems are frustratingly missing the meat needed to flesh out the whole. I played DioField Chronicle on Hard with no additional grinding outside of the main story and all side missionsOn paper the combat for DioField sounds great. It wants to be a real-time counterpart to Fire Emblem. Unfortunately due to how the game is balanced the need for strategy is unnecessary. The core of the combat is similar to MMO dungeon gameplay. Round up a pack of mobs with your tank and AOE the trash to oblivion. Beefier enemies and bosses may have additional health breakpoints which mechanically means that you will have to use a single heavy hitting skill for each breakpoint until they finally fall over for good. The game's hub is reminiscent to newer Fire Emblem titles and older Bioware titles. Unfortunately DioField fails to really flesh out the out of combat experience. You can use your various currencies to purchase new equipment and research upgrades for your skills, weapons, and summons. Upgrading your skills and summons is straightforward enough. Give money for more power or utility. Unfortunately the weapon system is a mess. Each weapon archetype has a single best in slot option which normally wouldn't be a problem except that weapons determine what skills you can use in combat. Since you can see which skills those weapons use as soon as you get access to research there is no build diversity. You will be funneled to those default best in slot skills for those best in slot weapons. with a little more effort to flesh out the system it could have been a great way for players to express themselves in the combat portion of the game. Each of the characters you recruit over the course of the game's story have minimal interactions with a couple of dedicated side missions for each. These side missions do little to explore each member of the Blue Foxes. Nothing more than a line or two of dialogue to try to make you care for your comrades. Which also resembles how the story of the game is handled. The story of DioField Chronicles explores the career of the Blue Foxes mercenary group. Told in a documentary style the actual story, like the rest of the game is woefully lacking. Major events that take place on the island of DioField are just skipped over, dismissed with a line of dialogue. They try to build up various antagonists but they are typically introduced and then killed in the next mission or two. It reminds me a lot of early Marvel movies without having the payoff that the following Avengers film would give. I want to love the game. I like it, all the pieces are there for something great. But it really just needed more time in the oven to iron out all of the disjointed systems, and expand upon the great story and characters that are just out of arms reach.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. The demo made me fall in love with it and I bought it on preorder.I was really looking forward to this, but it failed oh so badly.They failed so badly on so many things and managed to make the wrong decision about literally everything in this game.The combat is cool, it's what made me like the game in the demo. While the controls are a bit clunky you can wrap your head around it quickly.Problem is the rest of the game as a whole.Plot: it exists. It's presented to you in some form of "documentary-like" narration and some quick cinematics between the characters that don't last more than 30 seconds and it's mostly briefing for missions. The important stuff happens in the narrated part. And I mean REALLY important events are just dismissed as "this happened and was resolved this way", and proceeds to introduce you to a sudden new event you never heard of before, like a point where suddenly in the same narrated cinematic you apparently repel an attack and then "yeah btw in the South there were this people, now they are angry because this other stuff happened". It detaches the player from the story, makes all missions feels like just a chore to proceed to the next messy development in the narrated parts.Gameplay: Combat is good, told you as much already. The rest is bad. Skills are bound to weapons and that makes the party feel really stale because who you pick makes really little difference as long as they can equip that weapon. Also you can upgrade skills spending points but sometimes are forced to just not be able to run that skill if you want to bring a stronger weapon as there is no way for a character to learn that skill "forever". You must equip the weaker weapon to the supporting character but that locks you out of trying fun combinations or even just use the switch mechanic in-game.Also upgrading characters costs A LOT so good luck trying to switch a character out of your main party.The game is REALLY easy. I'm playing on hard mode and decided to just not use some skills to make life harder but still midway through the game only one character so far died on me and that's because I shot an explosive keg by mistake.With characters having really low screen time to not only develop but even just SHOW their personalities, you end up not caring about them and the war they are fighting at all, and all the missions (which, btw, have LOTS of repeated enemies) just end up being a long checklist to complete to proceed from chapter to chapter.All in all I had high expectation for this game and now I'm just sad I didn't ask for a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think anyone in Square Enix will bother reading this but I pray to god they do.Let me start off by saying that it was a distinct displeasure to sink 13 hours of my life into this absolute embarrassment of a game. As a diehard fan of Square Enix games who played every FF game ever released I really tried to like this game, I really did. But a 20-hour long title with pretty but repetitive music and nonexistent plot/gameplay variation does not deserve an AAA price. I don't know what exactly went on that led to the publishing of this game--either this was an experimental Fire Emblem Three House-esque copycat (you really can tell the similarities if you've been attentive to FETH plot. Empire vs Kingdom vs Alliance and a mercenary company in between) that they wanted to profit off when they shouldn't have, or they decided to milk some more cash by making low-budget, high-priced games. Honestly I'm more convinced it's the latter in this case after seeing a similar situation in Valkyrie Elysium--another 20-hour long game with pretty music, nonexistent plot, and braindead combat.These game companies should learn the hard way that they can't just blatantly scalp players with impunity. We--I-- don't mind paying lots of money for a game, but I want my money to get something with more flesh on it.

_childDocuments_.review: What could have been a fantastic comeback of the Tactical RPG genre ended up being one of the worst games released in the past years.The list of things this game does wrong is too long so I will just mention a few and I won't dig too deep into the whys.- The story is bad, really bad, a lot of things feel disconnected and some other just happen because they wanted to fill up content.- The characters are also bad, specially the main ones, which makes it worse. With the only interesting character being removed from the game halfway through. The game doesn't even care to dig too deep into anyone's story save for the two main characters.- The gameplay is boring. The developers made a pretty good job building the combat framework, but then the level designers decided to make each and every mission the same, you just need to kill X amount of enemies, also at some point they stopped bothering and it starts always being three waves of them.- Characters outside of the party earn no experience, so trying out different party compositions has its limits. To make it worse they decided to permanently remove character from your roster at specific points in the story, so if they were part of your main party, tough luck.- The main character is the only one with the most OP class in the game, so if you don't like him and want it out of your party, you are shooting yourself in the foot.- The second most OP class is the ranger with guns/crossbows. They are so OP they make each and every enemy a joke.- The game on normal difficulty is a joke. Missions that offer bonus rewards for being cleared under 6 minutes can be completed in less than 1 minutes most of the time, the longest they take is 2 minutes. By the time I noticed it was not going to get any harder I was too deep into it and changing difficulties is not an option once you started your playthrough.- New Game Plus is there because it was free to add to the game. They should have removed the "plus" part from it because it adds absolutely nothing. To make it worse they don't even make it harder, so you have your level 40+ characters one-tapping level 3 enemies.- The story doesn't properly end, so if you want to know what happens at the end, bad luck, come again some other day to see if they released a DLC with it or some sequel.TL;DR: Don't buy it, even if it was free, you'd have more fun replaying Disgaea 1 or Final Fantasy Tactics for the 263547th time than this malformed child Square Enix put out.
