name: Reverie Knights Tactics
detailed_description: Reverie Knights Tactics is a turn-based tactical RPG with strategic battles in isometric grids where every decision you make can alter the story and the way you configure the characters. Lead your party of heroes, each one with distinct, special abilities and skills, allowing you to use multiple battle strategies to defeat your enemies. Craft new items and accessories from the treasures you collect and use them to further customize your characters and gain a tactical advantage! Discover the Tormenta RPG setting Delve into a unique fantasy world featuring deep map and scenario exploration in an epic adventure, stylized as a visual novel and set in the Tormenta RPG setting, drawing inspiration from more than 20 years’ worth of tabletop RPGs, comic books, novels and audiobooks. Embark on an expedition to find Lennórien, the long-lost elven city, to save your loved ones, while fighting the goblin menace that spreads terror across the continent! Key Features: Beautiful Hand Drawn Art: Meticulous multilayer artwork from pencil sketch to full detail color. Decision-driven Storyline: Make several decisions through your quests, affecting the story and other characters` reactions. Character Customization: Customize character`s performance attributes, skills, and accessories for heightened abilities! Item Crafting: Collect powerful items as you explore the world and discover combinations to create new items. Exploration: Travel your way through an expansive map, unlocking secret quests, solving puzzles, and exploring scenarios and evil dungeons! Up to Four Hero Characters: Control 4 different heroes, each one with distinct, special abilities and skills, allowing multiple battle strategies. Battle Phases: React to your opponent's strategy and come up with the perfect tactic every turn, challenging you to think ahead. Interactive Battle Scenarios: Manipulate parts of the battle environments, and use scenario effects to your advantage! Multiple Battle Grids: Each battle contains a different isometric grid, making every battle an unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really excited for this game. Looks like Fell Seal Arbiter. But the game immediately in the first few hours left a bad taste in my mouth. The progression in the game is based on attrition. So you can't just heal your characters. This will immediately result in you possibly becoming permanently stuck in the game, which is a horrible design. Then the maps have extra goals on them that give you points to progress your characters. Achieving these goals requires being risky, which makes the game harder, or you progress slower. I have already seen the developers in the discussion forums suggesting that if things don't work out just reset the level. Which seems to me that they just have one design on how users complete the levels and it's up to you figure it out (no thanks).Then to top it all off, the game puts a band-aid on this "one way to play the game" by adding a story mode, for those that just want an easy difficulty. This just reeks of bad design. I wanted a balanced campaign, a normal mode, similar to other grid-based tactics games. Leave this attrition crap in a hard mode, and stop pushing people away who want some flexibility in their gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Reverie Knights Tactics is a turn-based and story-rich strategy game with RPG elements. Goblins conquered your lands. Now it's your turn to conquer it. That's about it in very short. I don't think the story is very good nor original so I'll keep it at that. It's pretty generic but not that bad either.The good thing is, that you have several decisions to make. In conversations, you can decide what to answer (there 2 or more options available most of the time). Sometimes there are 'important' decisions to make (Whenever a blue-red yin yang symbol is lightning up). These will change how the story goes. There are two different possibilities: Chaos and Order. Are turn-based. They are also divided into preparation- and battle-phase. The preparation phase allows you to move your units on the battlefield however you like.Most of the time, you will start your turn but if enemies ambush you, they will start and the preparation phase will be skipped.All units of a team will act in one turn, after that, the other team can act. Every character has 2 APs per turn. Aside from that, they have HP, Mana, and Focus. They are pretty self-explanatory. You have several different attacks per character. You can also do team attacks if both of your units are nearby an enemy. For every move, you build up Focus. For a certain amount of it, you can do a special attack. Overall, there are plenty of attacks and possibilities to make it as tactical as you wish. The position is another important thing in RKT. After your turn, you need to decide in which direction the character looks. Based on that, enemies could attack you from behind and you get more damage, etc. The same goes for enemies. Your characters get EXP after every battle and thus level up after a certain amount. For every level, you can choose one of two new abilities and they get 1 point which you can then use to level up their fitness, defense, or strength. You can also use equipment that will strengthen your attributes in return.Aside from that, you have items to use within and outside of battles.That's about it. It's pretty basic, with no skill tree and nothing else involved. Different tents are in your camp. For example, in one tent is a cook, which will cook different items for materials you have. It works like crafting in other games. In another one, you can buy "foliants" which is basically equipment. There's more to come during your journey and you can bond with other units in your team.   Reverie Knights Tactics is a fun turn-based strategy game. When it comes to the story and RPG part of it, it just scratches on the surface of what other story-rich games or RPGs have in store but the tactical part in the TB battles makes up for it. There's nothing really bad about the game and the art style and the cutscenes are gorgeous. Some fun mechanics like bonding with mates, deciding what to say in conversations, or team-attacks in battles spices things up a lot. If you lookout for a new turn-based strategy game, I definitely recommend taking a look at RKT. The price is a bit high and I would suggest waiting for a sale.  If you lookout for a story-rich RPG and aren't much into TBS, I wouldn't really recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm all for a good, addictive isometic turn based strategy RPG.  Though, with this one I'm very much on the fence.  It looks like it's setup for some nice things, but once you get into it, you notice it needs some improvements right away.  Graphically it reminds me of Fell Seal, but looks better.  You can customize characters by unlock skills as you level up and then you can choose which skills to equip (up to three).  There's also a 'choices matter' system which supposedly affects dialog and more (who will join you?).  Obviously, I can't validate that right now.What I don't like:No way to undo your moveNo way to undo your attribute allocation (on level up) - once you accidentally pick a stat, you're done, that's itNo 32:9 supportMinimal voice - doesn't quite get to FEH levels.  And, to be perfectly honest, the "NO" sound effect is annoyingCharacter art is Ok-ish, if not a little too comic geared towards the younger folkBalance - the game is certainly not balanced - be prepared to bring lots of items and spam themNo map rotation - just like Fell Seal (all TBSRPG's should have map rotation)Character personalities are really weird.  (female knight is basically dumb (which is jarring), but hey, why not keep to the brawny knight tropes)What I like:Music isn't badGraphics in maps are pretty goodDecent enough strategy - there are combos and environmental hazardsI'll be honest, I played the prologue and didn't really get into it.  I figured the full release would be better, but I guess not. I'm not sure if 1C was riding Fell Seal, but Reverie definitely needed some more time to cook.  It really needs balancing and then QOL fixes.   Can't really recommend this right now.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what the other reviewers are whining about, this game is not difficult at all. In fact, compared to other tactical games such as Advance Wars, Fire Emblem and Final Fantasy Tactics, this game is very simple while offering a decent challenge. There are no time limits, no permadeaths, no min-maxing, no "statistics", just an overall pleasant and stress-free ride. If you're someone used to tactical RPGs you'll likely breeze through the game even on hard. For those not used to the genre, the developers added a new difficulty level in response to player criticism, so the game can be even easier for those who prefer it.Sadly, the game does lack many quality of life options, some of which have already been mentioned in other reviews. The worst thing for me was the lack of information, there are many interactions between skills and enemies and obstacles that are not immediately clear until you try them out, and since there is no undo option you might have to restart a whole fight, which can get old quickly. Also there's barely any room for customization, the stat distribution is as simplistic as possible (basically put all your points into increasing damage) and there's little skill variation, some of the starter skills can be useful from start to finish for lack of something better. The plot is decent enough, but instead of a complete story the game presents more of a "chapter", and the ending leaves a lot of room for a sequel that may never come. For these reasons I wouldn't recommend this game at full price.All in all, a tremendous effort by a small indie studio with lots of room for improvement, but that in no way deserves such harsh reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: Just nothing about this game makes me want to play it.  I love SRPGs any can usually overlook things like bad story or difficulty spikes if something else keeps me engaged but there's nothing "good" about the game.  It's not all bad, it's just a mix of "average" and "bad".  Strategy is supposed to be about the choices you make but this game ruins that.  Some enemies have an alert range and will become aware of you only if you enter their range.  That's fine but even if you walk through it, you will alert them and you don't get to pick the path you take.  So if an enemy's alert range is 3 tiles north of you and you want to end up 3 tiles north, one tile east (a tile that isn't in the alert range), your character will walk 3 tiles north, alert the enemy, then one tile east.  If you were able to move 1 tile east then 3 tiles north you wouldn't alert the enemy and you'd end up in the same spot but the game won't let you.  It picks which direction you'll walk first to get to your end tile which is such a bad choice when even crossing certain tiles matter.When you level up you pick a point in either defense, finesse, or might.  The game says some skills use finesse for damage and some skills use might for damage but it doesn't say which skills use which so I'm being forced to make level up decisions for my character with no clear explanation on the impact.  Since you can't respec skill points you can end up wasting them.With such a limited character roster, the fights all feel the same.  There seem to be about 10 or so normal maps and then a difficult encounter (so far).  The normal fights are just throw away fights.  Each fight has bonus objectives that seem to be based around wasting time.  Like "destroy 3 objects", "push an enemy into an object".  It doesn't make the fights any easier/harder, it just makes them longer as you have to sometimes ditch the most effective strategy in order to waste time setting up hitting enemies into a tree.The boss battles seem to be difficulty spikes.  It's not that they're too hard, it's that the game doesn't really force you to consider any kind of tactics normally so you tend to go back and forth between brain-dead kill all you see to then entering a boss battle and not having experience using your characters, their skills (and load outs), and the terrain effectively.I almost hate to bring up the story because I tend to not care so much about SRPGs for their story, but it's been pretty forgettable.  I usually find there are 3 reasons to have dialog, to develop the plot, to develop a character, to entertain the viewer.  This game was just looking to fill space, most of what's said in game could be removed and no one would know the difference. I won't say the game is horrible or unplayable, I simply don't recommend it.  There are much better SRPGs worth the time.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a fan of Fell Seal, having done multiple playthroughs, so I was quite excited when I saw this game come out.  After a few hours playing, I found this game to be a bit of a let-down.  The characters are rather one-dimensional, and having status (health/mana) progress maintained between battles means that you need to do regular replays of maps to avoid getting into an downward spiral for managing items if the battle didn't go well.  The resource management aspect of the game is a cause of frustration for myself.  Removing this would allow for smoother gameplay, and permit more involved battle variety.  I really had high hopes for the game, but based on my initial experience, this will sit on the shelf for me, unless this is changed in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Reverie Knights Tactics is a new tactical role playing game which was developed by 40 Giants Entertainment. You are Aurora, a young cleric of Tanna-Toh, who is on an expedition to the city of Lennorian to find her father. He was sent there to gather Elven knowledge but is stuck in the middle of a war between the Elves and Goblins. He has been missing for quite some time and there has been no contact with his group since they left. Through this coming of age journey, you meet 3 other companions who help you on your adventure. The game features interesting battles and a story that is affected by the choices that you make.During conversations with your party, you can gain a shift to either Chaos or Order by your dialogue selections that will impact both your skills as well as the events of the story. After each conversation, you click on the next battle node on the map. Once the battle is over, you have another conversation and continue to the next battle. Every so often there are nodes that are puzzle areas such as picking a lock or solving a pattern that rewards you with items. In between fights you can go back to the town hub to craft different items or have more conversations with characters. The conversations are told in static images with text and very little voice acting with the occasional cinematic at key points of the game.The battles themselves are a standard affair. Your characters have 2 action points to spend each turn that can be used to move, use an ability or item, and defend. Characters can move a certain amount of squares to position themselves within range of enemies and can perform backstabs if they are behind them. Different abilities can push and pull enemies into or onto hazards for an additional strategic layer. If more than one member of your party is surrounding an enemy, you can perform a team attack. These are more powerful versions of their basic attacks. Battles also have additional bonus objectives such as collecting all treasures, pushing enemies into hazards, and performing team attacks against an enemy. These bonus objectives provide you with additional experience and currency to buy tomes.Upgrading your characters comes by leveling them up. Each character can reach a max of level 12. As you gain levels you get a stat point that you can allocate to one of three stats. These stats increase passive gains as well as increase damage of abilities linked to those stats. Each of the four party members fill specific roles such as a tank, healer, support, and DPS. It’s fairly obvious which stats you should fill on each character and while it seems like you can have different builds, the character abilities really push for one specific stat per character. Besides skill points, every few levels you gain additional abilities that seem to be influenced by your team’s morale shift towards Chaos or Order. However, by the end of the game, I seemed to be getting skill selections from both sides of the spectrum. I’m not sure if it is a bug or that your balance just influences the power of these specific abilities. You can also equip tomes to your characters that provide bonuses to your stats as well as immunity to certain ailments. These are purchased with currency gained at the end of each battle or sometimes by finding them in a locked chest or story event.One major difference with Reverie from most TRPGs is that you are not allowed to go back and replay battles that you have completed. There are no opportunities to grind for experience or items. You have to make the most of the time you are given in each battle and collect as much as you can as you move through the world. These limitations can make using healing items more risky because you can find yourself in a tight spot as you aren’t fully healed in between battles. The only way to heal outside of items is to level up or by using healing abilities in battle. If your characters die they are resurrected with a single HP, but you can use items before the next battle to heal everyone to full. If you do happen to find the battles a bit too challenging, there is also a story mode which should make things very easy for you to complete the game and see the full narrative experience.The graphics in battle are very well done and they are nicely animated. You can also speed up the battles if you feel they go a bit too slow, which admittedly I did. The environments at town hubs are interact-able which is an interesting addition. For instance, you can pick mushrooms and herbs from the map and they become usable items. This was much like a Scholastic Hidden Image picture from my childhood. Outside of battle, everything is just a little too static. You can move your view in hubs and also click on characters to talk, but there is a just a lack of energy and life to these moments.Overall, the game took me about 12 hours to complete. I finished all bonus objectives for each battle except the final two. I had already obtained the max level for my characters and bought the best tomes, so there was little incentive. While there are interesting concepts such as puzzles and dialogue choices, this game might be a bit simplistic for veterans. Players looking for a game such as Final Fantasy Tactics or Fire Emblem might find Reverie Knights Tactics lacking. If you want a story that is focused and you aren’t seeking a ton of customization options this might scratch that itch!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall Reverie Knights is a fun, short game with flaws.The good:Combat is well done and enjoyable.Soundtrack is lovely.Art is beautiful.The characters are distinct and their personalities pop.The order/chaos system of decisions is neat. It's not as fully developed as Dragon Age for example but for how short the game is it's a cool feature.The bad:The game is really, really short. I beat it in 12 hours on normal difficulty.The game tries to get you to utilize the terrain in combat without providing much reward for doing so. The damage/effects they cause are often minimal.The story line is one dimensional. Goblins bad. It doesn't bother me but it also adds very little.The meh:No real stat customization for the characters.The crystals in combat are fairly useless unless you're playing on hard difficulty where they might make more of a difference.The difficulty between Normal and Hard mode is insane. Normal is very easy while Hard is VERY hard.Overall:It's a fine game. It's nothing amazing but it's definitely worth playing if you love tactics RPGs and get it on sale. Keep in mind it's VERY short with no replay-ability but it is worth playing in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: ok, first up don't look at that hour count. There was a discrepancy from Steam Deck and the PC (I played it all on Steam Deck) and it cut the hour count to match the PC. I finished the game around 7-8 hours. Reverie Knights Tactics is a strategy RPG from 40 Giants Entertainment, from what I can tell this is their first outing. This game is fairly short by srpg standards, but I actually think that helps them in this case. But I’ll get to that.Technically, it runs perfectly fine. No problems whatsoever. I ran the game completely on steam deck and no issues, except for Steam Deck not accurately showing my hours played. I don’t know what that crap is, but it’s annoying. Otherwise, this game isn’t super demanding and it shows in the technical performance.The visuals are a highlight of the game I think, the colors are incredibly vibrant, the backdrop cities or forests are gorgeous. The characters are definitely not my favorite style, but they’re still well done. The animations are a little unique and different, some of them are really cool and others are kind of awkward, but overall I thought the visuals were outstanding.Story wise, it was interesting. Basic idea is that you are from a magic academy that both studies magic and works to keep people safe from the dangerous side of that magic. Your father took a team and went on an expedition and hasn’t come back so you are taking a team to try and save them. Along the way you learn of a deeper issue and a more sinister plot. The story doesn’t pull punches, and has some darker moments. But partly because of the visuals it never felt that dark or serious, even though the plot points kind of were. Gameplay is, as per the usual, the focus of this srpg. Ok, so this game is broken into two parts. Camp, and battle. Camp is where you talk to your companions, and craft bombs, potions, or other items. This part was rough to me. The writing is mediocre at best, and the crafting is serviceable but not exciting. I do appreciate that they tried to build something to do outside of the battles, but there is basically no building the characters, so this camp stuff did nothing for me. Speaking of building your characters, essentially the way this works is every level your characters get one point to put in to either physical attack, magic efficiency, or defense, and every so often you get a new special move. But you can only equip 3 moves, so most of what you learn is left on the cutting floor and the points put into the 3 stats if you will, feels pretty pointless. You can buy or find equipment of which each character can equip 3, but again, outside of the late game ones I found that grant immunity to certain status’ they really didn’t do much. Ok, battles themselves were pretty fun. You have your standard strategy rpg fair, moving on a tile based level, utilizing attacks, buffs, debuffs, and such. You can use team attacks if you have more than one character next to an enemy, if you have 3 or more, this is very useful. But it uses up actions from everyone, so it’s not always the best move. Reverie uses obstacles in each level that can cause damage or just give items. Using these to your advantage is always smart as they can do damage, cause status effects, or even outright destroy whoever gets pushed into them. Using moves to push or pull enemies is vital to using these strategies, and are usually important for challenges that each level has. Those challenges are in every level, typically 2-3 challenges per level, and tend to be things like pushing enemies into traps or defeating enemies with team attacks, etc. at first I was obsessing over these, and there is an achievement for doing so, but eventually it got too frustrating so I just did what I could without sacrificing too much. Completing these challenges gives you extra experience and currency that you use to buy that equipment I talked about earlier. They’re fine, but it gets old pretty quick.So here’s the thing, I enjoyed the combat, but it got stale. I really wish there were more characters, or classes or something you could try to build. A few more enemy types would have been nice as well. All that said, in total, and I did every battle just not every challenge, and I beat the game in about 10 hours. So right when I was lamenting the enemy types, it pretty much finished. I still think other characters or classes would have been beneficial, but that might have been too much for the small team. Reading earlier reviews it seems that the characters didn’t heal in between battles, but that seems to have been updated because that wasn’t an issue for me. It was a nice, punchy experience that didn’t hang around too long. As so many srpg games are super long, this was kind of refreshing and unique. I really love the depth of those longer games, but this was a cool experience.The king and short of it is this, it’s a fun game and worth the experience if you can get it on sale. I think the $20 asking price is a bit too much for me personally, but I got it on summer sale for a few bucks and it was definitely worth that. It wasn’t too difficult, so not bad if you are just starting out on strategy rpgs, plus it has an easy mode. It’s a nice, punchy strategy rpg experience, thats well worth a romp at a discounted price.That’s it for me, let me know what you thought in comments below!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving this one a thumbs up, because there's nothing negative about it, but it's very bland compared to many other tactics offerings. The story is straightforward and not very long (10hrs), with only a small handful of optional quests (3?) and some dialog choices. The max level is 12. There isn't tons of monster variety or skill options and it starts to feel repetitive, but ends before it gets too bad.Overall, a simple turn based strategy game that feels like a part 1 in something that could be two or three times longer. I'd recommend Fell Seal: Arbiters Mark, Fae Tactics, or any of the Disgaea games much moreso.

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics are beautiful.  I have seen one or two glitches (animations facing the wrong way based on the attack), but no significant bugs.  I like the ease of controlling everything, it is very intuitive.  On Normal mode, it is challenging.  You likely will die and repeat battles often, but nothing that can't be beaten eventually.  Haven't finished it yet, but close to the end.  It is definitely good for a few days of play.  Not sure how re-playable it is, especially since there are four static characters.  You can't swap out team members.  And realistically, you'll explore every nook and cranny for resources.  You can usually gather up everything by leaving one enemy alive then loot everything before you kill them.  You definitely never feel all-powerful, but you don't feel helpless either.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid little mid tier SRPG, its takes roughly 10 hours to see the ending.It is a game not without it flaws but I feel the current version is fun shorter experience in the genre.We take on the role of a team of 4 battle goblinoid creatures for the elven homeland the story is quite simple but passable and some of the characters interactions are fun.The battle system is a quite standard for the genre, using an "I go You Go" formula and a 2 point AP system (Action points) to manage you actions which allows for some flexibility in team coordination as you can jump around the team you don't have to completely use one characters action points before moving on to another.I played through the game on normal mode which from my reading is a updated mode that causes you team to heal between battles which wasnt in place when the game was released meaning that some people got softlocked due to running out of healing - this is still in the harder difficulties but hey that a challenge you would expect from  a higher difficulty.Overall its nothing flamboyant with a unique art style and simple story and battle system that doesnt out stay its welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the better SRPGs I've played in a hot minute. Everything, from the graphics, to the music, to the story, to the level design and core gameplay - is all outstanding. It's very obvious how much effort and care was put into EVERYTHING in this game. I've played many soulless, uninspired SRPGs, and this is not one of them!I particularly appreciated how the game varies things up a bit with puzzle segments and point-and-click segments. Those were pretty fun, and I could see them making the game more accessible for SRPG newcomers. My only problem? It's too short; I finished the entire normal mode with all optional objectives in under 10 hours. Still, I'd much rather play a game which is short and excellent, rather than one which is long and just "ok." There's also a hard mode which I'll have to get around to completing eventually, so this adds to the game's replay value.By the time I finished, I was very satisfied, but I also felt like this was just the beginning of something greater. The entire game only features 4 characters, and while they're all decently developed (both in terms of story and gameplay), I would've liked to see more options. The entire game takes place on a single island, and although it's a great journey, it feels like it's merely the beginning of a wider narrative. Given all this, I'd love to see a Reverie Knights Tactics 2. I'd love a sequel with more characters, more battles, more story, and more of everything which made the first one so good. Open the floodgates and give us more!!!It's possible the game had some bugs and issues when it first came out (hence the mixed ratings), but all the actual issues I saw people mention in other reviews have all been fixed. The game's now basically bugless, and free of pesky loading screens, which is an utter rarity as far as Unity-made Indie games go. RKT essentially feels like a AAA effort. It's that good.

name: Kapital: Sparks of Revolution
detailed_description: NEW GRAND STRATEGY - WISHLIST NOW About the Game Kapital: Sparks of Revolution is a sandbox city-builder focused on crisis management. It is a game about crisis and permanent conflict in human society. You will run out of vital resources in times you need them the most. People will protest and riot despite your best efforts to help them. Not everyone will survive. There is no way to avoid the crisis, you have to live through it. You’ll have to run a city with limited resources. To balance between people's needs and city development. To deal with angry crowds on the streets. You are the one to shape the future of your people. Just remember - you can't make everyone happy. The population of your city consists of 3 classes: nobles, bourgeois and workers. Each class has a unique role in the city economy. Nobles serve as officials and policemen, bourgeois pay taxes while workers provide the labor force. Their vision of the future is very different and they are ready to fight for it. Running the city is not an easy task. Your resources are limited while people’s demands are high. You have to decide who will get food and shelter first. Be prepared to face new threats on a regular basis. Epidemics, accidents, sabotages, hostage situations - the city will fall apart unless you make a difference. People whose needs go unsatisfied will hold a grudge against your rule. Some of them will become dissidents and radicals. They will form secret societies to overthrow you. Protests on the streets will turn into massacres and riots. You have to make a tough choice of which class to support and which to suppress. You will research new technologies and adopt new laws to improve the lives of your citizens. You will fight crime, tackle corruption and maintain order on the streets. As a ruler of the city, you have the ultimate power to shape the future of your society. The question is how far will you go to reach that goal?

_childDocuments_.review: To me its too less.The game has one major problem besides the lacking content: Its a lesser version of Anno 1800 or Frostpunk.Both games go more complex and provide more depth and replayability. Frostpunk has the same balancing act of your actions, the resources you have and what people want until they get mad at you.Anno 1800 has the similar orientation of harvesting resources and balancing population classes.Both games are far better, far more expansive and have far more content.Which gets me to the nail in the coffin:It only has one map.I was kind of accepting that it is a limited, kind of  "poor mans Frostpunk", if you so want. And i was also accepting the somewhat cheesy story,  with  people who would just not talk the way they do here.But the game is so limited in its options. The "Sandbox" Mode offers you the same map from the campaign, with 3 options to define how your start is.Beyond that, nothing.The campaign is just a glorified tutorial, with a cheesy story on top, having you play the same map as Sandbox Mode. For the price asked, there are far better games with far more stuff to see and do.The mechanics also arent unique enough to warrant playing it for longer than an hour or two.Its prime selling point is social conflicts between societal classes.Yet the "Tropico" Games somehow managed to do that far better with far more complexity.Here it simply is poor versus rich, workers versus entrepreneurs, bourgeoisie versus proletarians.Tropico has like 10 different classes with their own buildings, policies, effects and mechanics, that you have to balance out.Anno 1800 at least has you balancing the amount of workers, making clear that you only need a few rich people but many making them rich.Kapital:Sparks of Revolution catches the visualization of it, but not the experience.The visual style is lovely though. You can really see the people sleeping around a campfire if they have no housing, walk around and stand in line for food, noticing their social affiliation by observing their clothing.I also like the trains a lot. Too sad they dont play a major role in terms of gameplay (aka you building the tracks, the station etc).You can just do some flat upgrades (Number tweaking and Stats raising).It might sound harsh, because overall the game is kinda there. It has its mechanics of building, of resource management, of organizing space, of dealing with demands and so on.Yet its kind of too less and personally i am currently not seeing it being overly special doing something no other game is doing far better.Societal dynamics, people and their "class" affiliations, ressource demands and satisfaction isnt all too new.And i kind of think that for a game making this its most crucial focus point, the societal mechanics are more flat than i expected.I will keep an eye on it, as i rarely skip a strategy and management game, especially one that generally has the quality.Kapital is not a bad game per se and its polished, but mechanically and content-wise its not where i it should be.Maybe later, with some heavy work.Its one of those games that should have better been released into Early Access, because it feels like it is an Early Version.

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially quite enthusiastic about this game. It looks beautiful, runs well (even on Mac OS) and if you actually read the dialog you can tell there is a great sense of humor behind it ("The whole town was completely destroyed.. quick, we must repair the palace!"). I really wanted to like this game for the art-style alone.Unfortunately there are too many things that in my opinion are not quite ready for primetime. Here are some: The game is a constant struggle of getting the resources you need and keeping the people happy. Both the way and speed at which you gain resources and the degree to which your actions influence the mood of your people can feel very arbitrary and sometimes out of your hands completely. Not managing your initial set of resources correctly seems to ruin the rest of the playthrough, but you only really notice this later in the game resulting in a lot of time wasted. A lot of the actions in this game revolve around waiting for timers to elapse. You queue the building or demolishing of some buildings and then you wait for all the queued timers to run down. You sign a new law (like a tech tree), you wait for the timer to elapse until you can progress with the game. You run out of wood, you fast forward and wait for your factory to produce more wood. This might get better in a later stage of the game but after a little while all this downtime gets very tedious and - unfortunately - boring.One of the strengths of the game is the great sense of humor that can be found between the lines of the dialog that the recurring characters throw at you. Unfortunately, every time you start a new game you are interrupted by the same lines of dialog - which you can skip - but the interruptions are so frequent and abrupt that they become really bothersome and pull you out of any sense of immersion you might have. It feels like playing the tutorial over and over. I know this won't be relevant for everyone but this game is not really playable on Ultrawide monitors. UI Elements scale in a weird way at wide resolutions; they end up being too large and partially overflowing which results in important buttons being inaccessible. Additional resolutions were limited a to a selection of quite low resolution 4:3 options for some reason. On a 16:9 monitor you probably wont have any issues with this but a way of adjusting hud size would still be a great thing.The options are also quite limited, with no way of changing keyboard bindings (not that there are so many, the game seems to have no keyboard shortcuts for anything other than pausing the game with space) or even adjusting resolution once a game is started. I really like the idea and concept and I love the art style, I hope the developers still see this as a work in progress and maybe with some much needed adjustments and additions this could still end up as a fantastic title. In my opinion this game is a great example of a game that would have benefited a lot from an Early Access phase with lots of community feedback. I hope at some point in the future I can come back to this game and get the experience I was hoping for but unfortunately - as a full release - this game feels unfinished and unpolished and in it's current state is not something I'm willing to pay the price for and I can't in good conscience recommend it to most people.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played a great many newer city builder sims that look to the past, including the excellent Anno 1800 and Surviving Mars, I have to say that while I initially found Kapital: SoR a bit lacking, I ended up spending 18 hours of challenge and several chuckles at its poignant humour. It feels more like a challenging tabletop with a very competent narrator, which will keep you going for 3-4 campaigns that will take you to fully explore, which translates to 20 hours of fun for a genre devotee.A raw, not without its problems, but honest indie city builder that offers the special atmosphere of the crisis and political ferment of the early 20th century.Read more at: ragequit.gr

_childDocuments_.review: (applies to game v1.0.3, May2022)I don't usually post reviews, but will make an exception in that case.On the graphics:- not 3D but well drawn by a professional artistOn the game engine:- almost complete- lack of information (I have no idea why people are starving when there is bread everywhere and restaurants are half empty, no idea why people are falling sick when there are pharmacies everywhere)- crematorium seems to not be working (need to cremate nobles and workers separately, the number of bodies is not the same as the main interface)- two random events that require clicking (hostage and loyalty rebalance) which is not a lot- this game likes clicking around (you have 500k gold and 5k wood, you need to click to repair the train for 300 gold and 100 wood)On game balance:- three thumbs down- immigrants keep arriving, whatever you do- I finished the game with 600k gold, people were dying of starvation and illness everywhere although I had empty pharmacies and restaurants, all my stocks were full of goods- all buildings do the same thing (sawmill III is exactly sawmill II with 'efficiency +10', I have no idea what that means), in Frostpunk which inspired this game the next building is twice as efficient- everything gets built almost instantly, research takes a very long time, since all versions of a building do the same thing research barely matters- if I wanted to balance this game, I would build a strategy tree (game state at time t+1 = game state at time t + some chosen action among 100) and see how many branches are viableOn the subject matter:- I like the history of political economy, if you are a hardcore commie wanting to make things right or a malicious business tycoon who bought the game to let the population die for a laugh, this is a huge disappointment- I was expecting standard elements of political economy: bartering, debt, interest rate, minting, goldsmith letters of credit, etc...- I was expecting left wings elements of political economy: you start with small workshops, but soon you have to replace them with factories or die, the workers who had a workshop (capital) and pride in their production are replaced with capitalistic factories, thus creating Marxist angst- I would have hoped for new left wing political economy: shared school between rich and poor, inequalities giving rise to unrest, the old school debate about whether merchants are useful to society as a class of citizen (also marketers today) (also bankers today or Jewish money lenders before), people leaving the countryside for the city because of poverty- I would have hoped for a bit of left wing turned right wing: Marx recognizing the usefulness of capital accumulation, Mao saying getting rich is glorious, and all that goes with accepting free markets while recognizing their limitations (with a keynesian dessert)- I got: poor and rich are in separate houses and separate food halls- this game would really require the attention of a very talented economist (with lots of knowledge of history and no political slant), Frostpunk gave me chills with every house built near a fire and every child that got sick, in this game I never close a workshop in exchange for a factory sending a guy I know to wage slavery, I never send a tycoon to the (American) gulag despite his loyalty to please the populace who want collectivisation, this is just click click build two different houses for rich and poorAll in all, my current rating is 'still an Early access game' (and priced approximately there)

_childDocuments_.review: If you are expecting an economic class struggle simulation, this game is not for you. There is a lot that Kapital: Sparks of Revolution has going for it. The art style is by far the best thing about the game. I also genuinely enjoyed planning the layout of my newly rebuilt city.While the city building aspect is a lot of fun, it loses its novelty after the first few hours. It took me about four hours to figure out how to play the game, and, once mastered, the challenge went away and tedium set in. I really wanted to experience the class struggle of the working man, but there is very little to impact the relations of each class aside from mandating extra work hours or running PR campaigns. If the proletariat do rise up, the penalty is a quick burning of your palace, which can be repaired with resources amassed in about sixty seconds of game play time.My biggest problem with the game is that it is nether challenging or rewarding. I'm not incentivized to keep my citizens happy nor is there harsh punishment for their revolution. In summary, the game is a very simple city builder that remains surface level. It's fun to play, but not worth $25 in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: This is still an early release even though technically it is past the 1.0 release version.  That means there are still a few bugs that need to be worked out, although from my experience there tend to be ways to work around the bugs and still mostly enjoy the full experience of the game.For the money I paid for this game, it seems to be worth the money overall and is a pretty good time for me where I started playing this game and literally lost track of the time.  This is a classic city builder game....not the best on the market but it is better than some.  I know that this is subjective to many, so I will go onto the good, the bad, and the ugly about this game.What I am mostly impressed with this game is the overall theme of trying to build up a balanced city where you provide basic services of food, entertainment, and housing for your citizens.  The game is themed to be late 19th Century or early 20th Century (roughly about the time of World War One) and depicts the social unrest.  Housing is pretty abstract as it isn't really homes for individuals and their families but rather simply dormitories....although from a gameplay perspective this is actually a good thing so you aren't really micromanaging that aspect of your citizen's lives and I understand why the developer went for that level of abstraction.I really like the attention to detail that has gone into the lives of the ordinary citizens where they are happy, sad, suicidal, disease ridden, and angry.  When the citizens get very angry they even start to form protest groups and start riots including potentially sacking the mayor's palace with molitov cocktails.  You can attempt to control those riots with police...and the police don't always win either.  I am still not really sure about the game mechanic of the secret service where you can kidnap or execute random citizens in a vibe similar to Tropico.  Still, this aspect of the lives of the citizens is one area where this game really shines and is done very well.  Citizens are both men and women, although on a practical level there is no difference between the sexes in this game and that is mostly flavoring.I especially love the homeless camps that surround your city when citizens have yet to find a home for whatever reason there is a housing shortage.  It is a nice touch and helps to remind you to get them into proper housing eventually.I am also impressed with the depth that the developer has put into the various mechanics of this game as you progress through the various elements and the "tech tree" after a fashion.  There are multiple game options where you can influence the city and so many other buildings that I have yet to build all of them.  Drilling down into each broad category of buildings and game play has you exploring various menus and control panels that also expand as you progress through the game and have more and more options available to you as a player.  I think this is also a good feature overall.The bad aspects is mainly micromanagement.  There are several aspects of the game that seem to be mostly grind and delving into dealing with repetitive tasks and constantly checking to see if you need to perform that series of tasks again.  I wish there was some way to automate that aspect of this game where I'm constantly checking for these routine maintenance tasks.  I want to concentrate on building new things, not really reworking a factory with fresh tooling or worrying about starting and stopping the train service.Related to this is upgrading buildings.  As you progress with research and the tech tree, upgraded versions of existing buildings can show up as an option.  These upgrades also chew up resources in the game (that part is good IMHO) but they also occupy a regular building slot in the building queue.  At least I don't need to tear down the old building and replace it with a new upgraded version of that building, but it can be tedious when you are at the late game of this game.Map size is also very small.  While there appears to be a RNG (random number generator) that sets up the land where you can build, it is all mostly the same map with just a random assortment of lakes.  And I find toward the mid to late game that I am having to be very conscious about where I place new buildings or even what buildings I construct.  This seems to be an artificial restriction though where the map feels like it should go on forever but in reality the land upon which you can build is very limited.  I would personally prefer a much larger canvas upon which to build a  part so I can even just build everything that is included in the game.  As it stands right now, the endgame is really when you run out of plots of land to build the city.The game play is also at the moment very linear in terms of progression.  I prefer to have multiple paths to have a game which plays differently each time.  Instead, it seems like there is definitely a min-max set of scripted tasks you must perform in a clear sequence and only minor variations are possible.  There are three possible outcomes for end game content but even that seems to be mostly irrelevant to actual gameplay as it is all mostly the same thing just with a different "boss" in charge.The ugly really is the bugs.  Some of these should have been fixed before release as it is an advertised task that even has a steam achievement related to it.  Or a real show stopper where the building queue for new buildings is simply not working.As I alluded earlier, the "secret service" or "special agents" of your internal security bureau is a really odd and disturbing aspect of this game.  There is a common prison where you put ordinary criminals and a whole aspect of a police officers and even the idea that various parts of your government can be so corrupt that you can eventually lose control of your government from graft and bribes.  Then there is this whole extra group of people that act similar to the Stassi, Gestapo, or KGB who can randomly raid the homes of citizens and put them into a special holding cell in the basement of that secret service headquarters where various kind of torture is happening to those citizens.  Fortunately this is abstracted away so it doesn't go into details although your imagination can run wild.  Just be aware this is a game option...although fortunately you aren't forced to use this gameplay mechanic if you choose not to use it.  You can unleash your inner Hitler/Stalin and inflict cruelty upon the citizens of your city as you are building it.  I really don't think this is necessarily a good gameplay mechanic at all and perhaps is a bit too much realism?  I'm really surprised this isn't more controversial.On the whole this is a good game.  It reflects that turn of the century (from 19th to 20th Century) era with some good vibes that I really like and the campaign mode really gets into the spirit of that time period.  It is a mixed set of gameplay that plays out very well and is quite engrossing.  I admire the hard work that the developer has put into this game.  It shows that it is a labor of love for the developer.

_childDocuments_.review: In its current state, there is little to do but wait for new buildings to appear. Mechanisms that unlock social unrest seem to be placeholders at best, the problem is that there is little to do in the game. Even the basic ability to build an aesthetic city which is important to many who like city building games is at best lacking. There is no variety for buildings every building looks exactly the same and does same thing. There is no statistics to support player agency, migration cannot be stopped or managed effectively, resulting in boring grindy gameplay that has no meaning other than to wait for the next unlock. It has potential for growth but for now, as the developer has not replied to any feedback or suggestions and has not announced any plans I have little hope to see it improve. This should be an early access title rather than a full game.

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions, because this game needs more reviews: So far, this is absolutely great. Games like Anno were, to me, always lacking in the narrative department and Kapital: Sparks of Revolution fixes that without relying too much on dialogue boxes. Games like Frostpunk have already proven how city-building sims can result in fascinating stories about struggling societies that emerge through gameplay in a natural way.The stakes are definitely high (I ran into my first financial crisis after just one hour, because I didn't see my train was broken, and from there my people spiralled into a full food, health and depression crisis). The class struggle is also palpable right from the beginning, albeit with a somewhat hyperbolized tonality and black-and-white caricature logic. It fits the game though - because of course noble and bourgeois people would rather freeze to death outside than sleep one night in a dingy working-class shack.You can definitely tell that this game focuses very much on this class aspect. For example, there is no regard to infrastructure or logisitcs in a way that certain buildings have to be arranged in a certain proximity to each other. As long as there is a connecting road, you can place the alehouse for the workers' district a mile away. However, the game seems to know where else it needs to put in effort and that results in a focused experience that is still just very refined in the ways that matter most for what it wants to convey.
_childDocuments_.name: Kapital: Sparks of Revolution

_childDocuments_.review: What's weird is that the trailer makes the game look like some sort of city building strategy game that involves politics and intrigue; but the game I ended up playing was a generic farmville clicker game with stupid spoiled rich kids complaining while I did all the work. This is what happens when indie devs pretend their dookie don't stink and try to pass off a mobile game as a PC game, you get sub par generic drek like this. This is not the game that is promised by the store page. The game limits you with arbitrary numbers of structures in order to outright force you into not having enough resources, all the while screaming at you that you can't protect everybody even though the game is the one forcing them to not have enough resources. You have to research the concept of warehouses, and like any other terrible farmville game your people automatically burn/throw away any resources they can't immediatly put in the warehouses. So yeah it's easy to say "You will never have enough! YOU SUCK AT GAMES LOLOLOL" if the game outright forces you to waste excess resources and refuses to make it easy to store more. You are a mayor after some sort of disaster that paradoxically left just a ruined train station, palace, and a bunch of ruined buildings. Your workers do everything ONE BUILDING AT A TIME like in a mobile game, you can only have so many of certain buildings like a mobile game, you can only have X of this item and X of that item like a mobile game, etc. Basically they designed a really trashy mobile game and then in a last ditch effort to make sales wrote a "story" where a bunch of idiots argue infront of you, and then lied to people calling it a simulation game. I could only play this for an hour on my stream before I had to return it for being so criminally bait and switched. If you were expecting a city builder game, this is not a city builder; this is a mobile game where you spreadsheet numbers and build the perfect farmville.Edit: I was responded to by the mobile game company that made this game, who wrote a canned response ignoring all of the issues with the game; instead it's somehow not my fault. As a generic farm building game, Kapital is as deep as a puddle and I ran into every mechanic/system in the first couple of minutes. I don't know why they are lying to people saying this is a strategy game, or why they are pretending there is more to the game than I played. Thankfully Kapital is a failed game from a failed mobile game company and we don't have to worry about these losers sticking around.

_childDocuments_.review: Keeping everyone happy isn't an option in this game! In this society simulation, peasants carry the burden of protection, agriculture, and public services. Borgovasie controls the flow of money, business, trades, means of transportation, law enforcement, and the stock market. Nobility stands above all, demonstrating total monopoly over education, healthcare, and governing. The hand-picked policies and the ratio of powerhouses' influence dictates the outcome. What could be next? That's up to the player. A socialist utopia run by the peasants, a real estate powered by the bourgeoisie, or a totalitarian regime in the claws of nobility. Nothing is simple, and there's always a punch in the gut. Flue, pox, famine, fire, waves of migrants, public demands, civil unrest, crimes, insurgency, and external enemies tighten their hands around the neck, adding to the pressure of building a stable and prosperous society. Even neighbors may ask for favors. Infrastructure, utilities, security, and healthcare, all need extensive attention. You are building a community with every bit of your resources. There will be compromises, failures, and people may die. You should make sacrifices. If you are ready for a new governance challenge, this game is for you!

_childDocuments_.review: Challenging management sim with some significant balance considerations.  This game isn't for filthy casuals, this game is for those who want to be put to the test.  In fact, the devs even changed the names on the difficulty levels from Easy, Normal, Hard to Normal, Hard, Very Hard because people were complaining.  That doesn't mean the game isn't good, just that you have to have some skill at these types of games to make it work. I guarantee you will NOT succeed in your first game.  This is in part due to learning the mechanics, and in part due to a problematic campaign that doesn't give you all the clues you need to make your city survive.  While the campaign guides you through some basics, if you ONLY do what the campaign says, you will not succeed.  When it says to build one Sawmill for instance, you will eventually need two.  Things like that have confused folks and they've left poor reviews but it becomes pretty obvious during your first playthrough what is necessary.  I've played mostly on the middle (now Hard) level and found it pretty easy to get significantly far into the game without much issue.That said, others have compared this to Frost Punk. The choices you make cannot make everyone happy.  The game can get pretty dark in that sense.  You will be making everyone struggle - some more than others.  Like Frost Punk, you often feel like you are on the verge of collapse at all times.  You're constantly bringing your town back from the brink of chaos as you adjust what is working and what isn't and who to work where.  Fun game that takes some serious strategy gamer chops to play! Recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the concept but the game is a little flawed. I could still enjoy it though. To survive the start you need to focus on wood, food and alcohol while making sure you get enough income from alcohol and shops. Each in-game day you get more residents who also need food and housing. But there is a migration building to limit the number of new residents which can be enabled by enacting the corresponding law. You will need this building mid game to limit the incoming residents.The main problem: the idea is that you need to balance the needs of the three classes: nobles, bourgeois and workers. And you should not be able to satisfy all needs. This should create conflict. But in the game it is only really related to money. If you have money you can manage the needs more or less. But without money the production buildings stop working and everyone will starve once food is low.Smaller problems: infographics. There is no overview of daily spendings/production.
_childDocuments_.name: Kapital: Sparks of Revolution

_childDocuments_.review: This has been on my wishlist since it came across my radar. It reminds of the game Frostpunk, but in Kapital you have greater number of resources you have balance than in Frostpunk. I have not played much of it, I love the game. Coming from Frostpunk, a rebellion does not equal game over, you can survive a rebellion, if the palace/city hall survives. But keeping in mind the message than opens with the game, rebellion is inevitable one of the three classes is going to be unhappy and will rebel. Which I think is the beauty of the game, it both conveys it central point in its story's flavor text and in the gameplay. Many games have a hard time dealing with this. I can even say it does this a bit better than Frostpunk, I play a lot of endless mode but at certain point the eternal winter apocalypse isn't scary at all, it like dealing with a seasonal hurricane. But Kapital you constantly judging the needs of people and the city simultaneously and you don't have infinite resources, something will have to be undercut. Any real problems is more of me still learning the game: I do constantly find myself out of money or the negative but that might be because I'm still learning balance of the game's economy. I will say this game has a similarity with Frostpunk, you need try and fail, then try and fail again to succeed. As this game reminds me much of learning how to play Frostpunk, but I will say Kapital it was easier to early decision making; whereas in Frostpunk it you unintentionally collect all the wood, then be unable to build the wood production buildings. In Kapital, I generally got all my major buildings down before my problems really started (i.e. a flu hit the city before I had the ability to research medicine to cure it).I have high praise of Kapital, I don't have much bad say to about it. I'm surprised at the time of writing it has mixed reviews on steam. My problems are based on I'm still learning the game, and the game has a specific point that devs ingeniously tied the game's central point into the story and gameplay, your decisions have consequences in very organic way, you have pick the needs of one class over another or sacrifice the needs of your people to improve the city. The people or city reactly very organically: uncutted classes get unhappy and will eventually boil over; neglect of the city will leave you economically or generally inable to address certain crises (ex. having a epidemic disease breakout with no way to research a cure because you don't have the building that allows you to research a cure.) If there is anything I would add is maybe for the devs to add a map maker/editor because the criticism I've seen is there is only one map.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game conceptually, but as others have said, it's just not particularly fun. The bickering of your advisors and the dialogue in general are brilliant, but the game itself is just... messy. It's a neverending stream of your resources being stolen, trains and production facilities breaking down, and people rioting and burning down the houses of other classes. And the worse off things are, the more often these things happen. No more grain shipments due to a story event that got sprung on you and  which requires two in game days to complete? Have fun not producing anything because all of your workers have decided to leave their jobs and firebomb the nobles, bourgeois, or your palace instead!If these events were scattered out more to give the player a breather, they'd probably be fine. But when the game becomes one disaster after another, they stop feeling like a challenge to overcome and just a permanent nuisance. You know how in games like SimCity, if you horribly mismanage your city, it becomes a disaster of constant traffic jams, fires spreading, etc? Well, that's this entire game. There's nothing you can do to fix your city or to avoid these disasters. You spend the entire game slapping bandaids onto problems while new ones spring up faster than you can deal with them, and all the while you're constantly stuck waiting on mobile game-esque timers to get resources, with every other disaster interrupting or outright halting said timers, which renders you unable to deal with those disasters and future ones. It's just a mess.I *want* to like this game. I really do. I think it's conceptually pretty cool - building a city back from ruins while managing delicate class relations and progressing through a linear sort of story. I restarted the game three times trying to finally get a run where I didn't just descend into complete chaos immediately. Last night I got so tired of it I figured I was done with it. This morning, I opened it up again, and it took me an hour to consider uninstalling it again. Again, I *want* to like this game. Maybe I'll try playing it on easy just to see the story through.As is, I can't really recommend this game to anyone unless it's discounted by 80% or more and you're willing to take a gamble on a unique, but extremely frustrating game.My best to the devs, and I sincerely hope their next game performs better.

_childDocuments_.review: Usually don't leave a review, but I wanted to combat the other negative views. Is it the best city builder out there? No. Is it a fun and unique one? Yes. The art style alone makes me say keep an eye out for a sale. The campaign is at least interesting and provides an exaggerated view of class antagonisms that existed and still do. Just don't go in thinking you are getting a tutorial. The sandbox is also great fun once you know what your doing and able to make large sprawling towns. That being said its not perfect, I would like more map variety and the ability to better control just how much migration I get. The UI could use some work too, I did not realize the train was broken my first time and my city starved cause I repaired it too late. As it stands I would say wait for a sale or a few updates the devs seem keen to take feedback and improve so hopefully the game would be worth the $25 price in a few updates time.

name: Neptunia Virtual Stars
detailed_description: Story Enter Virtualand - a digital world that exists alongside the networks of various dimensions. Within Virtualand lies the planet Emote - a planet faced with extinction due to the maleficent group of Content destroyers known as Antis. In an act of desperation, the Digital Goddess of the planet Emote, Faira, sends a distress signal to other dimensions in hopes to find a savior of this planet. And the saviors that were reached? The rising Vtuber stars, Me and You, members of MEWTRAL, as well as the Goddesses of Gamindustri: Neptune, Noire, Blanc, and Vert! Can MEWTRAL and the Goddesses band together and save the planet Emote from complete destruction? Key Features Switch Up & Keep Movin' – Seamlessly switch perspectives between the four Goddesses & playable VTubers in fast-paced hack 'n' slash battles. Rock enemies with lightning-fast combos and glide across the map to dodge incoming attacks. Feel the BeatTik Rhythm – Keep tempo in the BeatTik rhythm game! Accessorize your favorite characters and have them groove to your favorite Neptunia Virtual Stars tracks. Record your BeatTik performance, then use the video on the Video Battler section to unlock unique items, songs, and even more dance moves! Take your EMOtions to Overdrive – The Emotional Overdrive special attack can bring the Goddesses and Vtubers to a harmonious victory. Fill up the Emote Gauge to activate your Emotional Overdrive and watch the Vtubers come to life. You may even find yourself receiving extra loot for your stunning performance! Rescue a Vtuber, Save the Planet – Find and save the Vtubers scattered throughout Virtualand! Do you find yourself falling flat in battle? With the Guest Connect System, Vtubers can support you with their special powers to topple any enemy!

_childDocuments_.review: Important disclaimer:There are two main reasons I dislike this game,  check the second point if you have the time.I don't believe is strange to think that the target audience of this game are Neptunia fans, people that know the characters, franchise and enjoy them.Virtual Stars will offer nothing of this to them.The game main focus are Vtubers, Neptunia characters are treated as guests that, yeah, they take part in the main story and interact with the rest of the cast, but are just placeholders with few lines and basically one recurring gag for each of them (seriously, Neptune's character is more than just "I'm the protagonist" during ~6-8h of story).If you came here wanting to enjoy a story about the goddesses go search for a different spin-off, the developers want you to like the Vtubers, play with and focus on the Vtubers.This game has one clear mindset. , but that doesn't mean that it will be as rewarding as playing as the Vtubers. The game mechanics can be summarized as another musou Neptunia spin-off.When playing as the Vtubers you will control the one you have selected while the AI moves the other member of the pair same style as 4GO. Vtubers play a H&S style, usually with one of them focusing on meele and the other in ranged. You have two types of basic attacks, a special version of them, 3 skills and both jumping and dodge. Leveling, HP and MP are the standard, honorable mention MP always on autoregen and the ability to regenerate life in any moment without using items.The CPUs are nothing like that. They play some kind of on-rails shooters where if you are close enough you have lock-on feature (that barely works). Unlike their Vtuber counterpart, there's only one CPU active on time, the AI won't follow you with them and they only have one attack (that can be triggered with 3 buttons because all of them were used with the Vtubers) and 3 skills.Each CPU fills, basically, the role of one of the attack-types the Vtubers have, Neptune being the fast light attack, Noire a slower more powerful version, Blanc the slow (with charge option) but high damage and the biggest loser of the 4, Vert, who has some kind of (in theory) status effect attack but in reality is slow, weak and has the shortest range.Outside of that, instead of the dodge ability, the CPUs get some kind of fast movement through the map, which is way worse than how it looks at first glance. The duration is predetermined but there's no visual indicator, you need to learn by yourself when it stops. When it ends, the CPU makes a slow, vulnerable somersault that can make you lose life against a lot of enemies (they always have a bigger range of attack than you).Talking about life, the goddesses have their own life system, which is based on hearts (starting with 5 and a max of 30). Each attack deals between 1 and 3 of those points as damage, so it feels like a simplified version of the classic HP bar that the Vtubers have.Lastly (despite the in-game story saying you can't) there's a special move where they transform and you button mash your way during 15-30 seconds to deal with all the enemies in the arena. This makes a game where you can be 10 levels below the enemies and still kill bosses without losing more than 1 or 2 points of life even easier.If there's something that I find hard to understand, is how the game designers decided that the UI and interactions withing the game were a good idea.If we divide the screen in a 3x3 grid we find, at any moment, that 1/9 is dedicated to the map, 1/9 to the meter of the special move, and 1/9 to HP/MP/etc. The enemies have a meter with the percentage of the life lost in a dialogue box similar to P5 in addition to their health bar, another bar with level and name, and another marker in the center of their body with the TKMK (basically a meter for stagger).During the fight, drops, leveling, etc will appear in a box that takes another 1/9 of your screen even if you just dropped an item, in addition, a real vtuber (not one of the playable characters) will appear in a screen taking another 1/9 just to say one ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ line and stay there while making a sign, dissappear or be replaced by another Vtuber doing the exact same ♥♥♥♥ (my record is chaining 6 of them), this means that your screen is almost filled with trash information in an environment full of enemies in 360º (enemies that are, in a lot of cases, small or can teleport so I have ended shooting just looking at the minimap, it was more effective than moving the camera which most of it is rendered useless anyway thanks to all the props). On top of this, comments will appear through all the screen, useless text that gives you nothing but is there taking space.In top of this, we have the hit count meter and the extra elements from boss battles, with the boss health, the finisher meter, song information, THE LYRICS THROUGH ALL THE SCREEN, etc making following what's happening on the screen a nightmare.Some examples:You can turn off the comments and the lyrics, but the game doesn't explain it, you need to dig it yourself.Sidequests are another heavy deal for me. There are two types of sidequest, the basic ones get autoacepted and autoturned once you complete them. How do I complete them? Good question my fellow reader, because I don't have a clue. This sidequests have an obtuse description like "I want to see Neptune shine like never before", "Blanc makes my heart race" or "I want to see Vert having fun", like WTF? So your real option (like almost anything on this game) is to just mindlessly go forward annihilating everything until something pops up (not like you need it).The second type are the ones provided by Vtubers. Despite this ones being straightforward (go to X map in Y floor, kill Z thing and get the drop) you need to watch an unskippable video of the Vtuber doing its thing to asks for the quest and deal with a second annoying unskippable video if you turn it in (also, for some reason, they don't last long before dissapearing). But don't worry, those rewards are not needed.Like the initial title said, this game feels like a big glorified commercial.Every loading screen features a Vtuber introducing itself and asking you to suscribe to their channel, while in the game, those said Vtubers will appear in TVs all over the levels.The loading screen shows a badge "bonus for watching the full video", reality is that there's no such bonus and you'll end up mashing the skip button.There's also a button to look directly at this TVs, which is a nice touch, except because a lot of them are near chests and floor changes, so when you try to interact and get the loot, you end up, instead watching the monitor.So, if you buy this, I hope you are ready to watch a lot of selfpromotion instead of spending your time playing a game.And I will stop here because I've hit the max-word count twice.If you have any doubt feel free to ask.

_childDocuments_.review: Worse than Super Neptunia!Do you like Neptunia games because...They're cute...They're funny... and because they're video games about video games, where the main characters are video game consoles in the form of anime girls...and they have some light fan service here and there...Well prepare to be disappointed on every front.While the graphics are better in this one, the girls aren't as cute. If you don't believe me, just compare the images in the store page for this one and rebirth 1. I'm sure most will agree.Next, the jokes! They're rather dry, some are decent but I never let out more than a ha ha. This has been a problem since Super Neptunia. The spring ran dry, it seems.It's not about video games! This time around it's about vtubers. Like I care, if  I want to watch youtube videos, I'll go to youtube. Nep games should always be about games, even Super Neptunia was about games, at least.Lastly, as far as I have played I have not seen an ounce of what one might call "fan service" in this game.Pretty much everything the Nep fans love about these games has been viciously ripped apart or just plain removed.Verdict! If you're a Nep fan, I'm sorry to say but it looks like the series is just about dead. I can hear the funeral music now and I weep for it...Oh well, it was good while it lasted!Update!So I forgot to mention the poor performance in this game. No matter if I run it at 1080p at 30 fps or 4k 60, it lags and stutters and my pc is at or above the recommended specs.Also when I try to record a beattik (A game mode where characters dance while you press buttons kind of like DDR) the game crashes, every time I turn on record Beattik.Last Update!Finally beat the game and I have to say that this is quite the slap in the face from Idea Factory  and Compile heart.They say in the game how it's important to listen to the people in order to make beloved content and then near the end of the game, one of the characters talks about how they think it's sick how some developers of content "pander" to certain groups ( referring to the people who enjoy a little fan service. By the way this game has none ) and how they're scum for it..It's all very hypocritical since this series has had that sort of thing in it for the longest time and to call other devs scum because they want to make the fans happy. That's messed up!Fans tend to expect certain things from a series. After you make one game, you set a sort of blue print for what people will expect from future titles in the series.If they didn't want to make the game this way, they should have just made a new IP and let this one die with dignity.Originally I was gonna say, if you wanna buy this game then buy it on a steep  discount ( 10 dollars, maybe ) but now, seeing how Idea Factory and Compile Heart have made it very clear that they hate the people who built them up ( the fans ), I can't recommend this game in good conscience.I'm very insulted!
