_childDocuments_.review: was very excited for the game's full release and bought it immediately on day one. after an hour of playthrough, up from the beginning, everything was gimmick-y, and combat was underwhelming. better to do a jump attack to a 3hit combo than doing the charge attack or finishing with strong attack. first boss fight was bugged. it got me cornered then just stopped dead in its tracks and didn't do anything and had a staring contest with me. didn't move till i moved. hammer boss was also boring with the repeating pattern of attacks. i guess i'd recommend this to casual fans of metroidvania, but for the hardcores, replay Hollow Knight instead.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: short game, expect crashes, very linear, no replayability, Enemies felt easy and some can be skip entirely, few steam achievements is either glitched or currently unavailable. I truly want to love this game and I see it has great potential, from the gameplay, the art style, and music, but I cannot recommend it, for now.I want to first express that do not let the hours I put in this game fool you, I was away on several occasions, other then that, the game is at least 4-6hours long, give or take if you backtrack.Speaking of backtrack, the game is very linear in comparison to other metroidvanias. In most games, you may have to obtain an ability later down the road and revisit old stages to obtain newer stuff, but this game doesn't give too many reasons to do so. Yes there is a few here and there, but most maps can be clear in one swoop, giving almost no reason to go back.The game felt a bit easy and gives no reason for replayability. A lot of the enemies AI just felt very similar from one to the next, to which in some cases,  they can either be cheesed off or skip entirely, especially after you get double jump.This is one of my biggest grips because there's more then a few stages where fighting enemies is kinda meaningless.If I may suggest, I feel part of this could be fix by having enemies drop items needed to buff Europa at the workshop, and/or change/add more difficult AI.The game had crashed on me on several occasions, but I don't think it's that big of an ordeal, especially since the first version is going to be buggy, and the crashes I had was after I died.Lastly a few steam achievements seems unavailable, or may be possibly glitched.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best Metroidvanias I've ever played, after Ender Lilies.It does have a rough start. But once you unlock some stuff and start understanding the design language of the game it becomes a lot more fun.By the end I loved it.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just okay, and that's about it. It doesn't quite hit the mark of being good or great; it's not some hidden gem waiting to be discovered. It's simply okay.If I had to sum it up, I'd say it's 'vision without purpose.' Visually, it's nice to look at, and there are game mechanics that could be satisfying if they were given more depth beyond the basic 'this thing helps you get there.'As I'm playing, I can't help but ask myself, 'Why?' Why do I need the green armor? Sure, it lets me navigate poison areas, but those are so few and far between that it makes me wonder why they bothered including them or the armor in the first place.Why have I been collecting coins since minute one? Because they're used for health and armor upgrades? Well, those upgrades require more than just coins, and by the time you actually have everything you need, you'll have amassed ten times the amount of coins the game ever demands.And why did I just defeat a tomato-throwing minotaur? Because it's a mini-boss? Okay, but what does a tomato-throwing minotaur have to do with this setting or story? Why are there so many mini-bosses for seemingly no reason? You can't tell which battles will progress the story and which can just be avoided entirely. It's filler, plain and simple.It feels like the developers had a story they wanted to tell, but because it couldn't just take place in a single room, they created gameplay that's inconsequential, and merely a means to move you from one plot point to the next. The artwork is nice, but the areas and backgrounds lack cohesion; there's no sense of connection in terms of layout or purpose.Even the combat isn't unique or engaging enough to keep you hooked. Eventually, you'll find yourself just running past most enemies unless they're blocking your path.This game commits one of the biggest sins for a new Metroidvania. It's only towards the end of the game that you actually feel any sense of progression, and even then, it's not all that different from how your character starts the game.  Despite this game being okay, I don't recommend it simply because there's better metroidvanias to spend your money on.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game as part of Humble's Metrodvania bundle, but its been a game that I've had on my wish list for some time.  I'm a fan of the metrodvania genre, and have played most of the major hits in the genre over the years.  Unlike some folks, I'm mostly a fan of the "vania" part of metroidvania having bounced off pretty hard off Metroid in my early years of video gaming.  I can safely say that the first Metroidvanias that really captured me were both Symphony of the Night as well as the GBA games Circle of the Moon and the like.All that background just to say why I really wanted to play 9 years of Shadow.  Just a look on the store page shows you beautiful background and pixel art that evokes the type of gaming I used to thoroughly enjoy in my misbegotten youth.  Then I got the actual game and started playing it.  The best thing I have to say is that, its mostly a competent MetrodVania.  The combat is quite tight, the various unlocks you get isn't bad, there's a mini map and the boss fights are also quite servicable.  As I said, competent.  The highlight is that the art is very good, and the animations that pop up once in a while are all quite well done.However, if I have to balance the bad with the competent, the bad mostly wins out.  The first of which is that there's only one weapon with not much modification to it.  There's probably nothing wrong with that, as some of the more memorable Metrodvanias over the year also had that (Ori and Guacamelee to name a few), but there's also no real modifications to the weapon.  You can't make it longer, and whatever power you add to it is barely noticable.  Then there's the lack of fast travel.  If you found out you missed a section on the map, you're gonna be slow traveling to that location.  Sure, you can skip fights, but you're still going over a lot of ground for probably the last upgrade shard or something.Then the upgrades themselves.  They're extremely unnoticeable except for maybe the health upgrades.  Each time I upgraded my Halberd, I couldn't really tell that I was doing more damage.  I'm sure it was, but given that the normal enemies were no challenge with no upgrades and the bosses were damage sponges, i'm not sure doing 10% more damage made any difference in the game.Then that the entirety of the game's challenge comes from the bosses.  There's no challenge from your normal traversal of the castle, and the only challenges comes during the boss fights.  There's also a huge unevenness of how difficult the bosses are.  Some bosses are ludicriously easy, and others require you to die and restart multiple times to even get a sense of their patterns.  There's nothing wrong with this, per se, but when you hit 5 bosses within 10 minutes (and its not an Arena), it does get tiring.There's also changing how you play the game in the last 5% differently from how you've played it the previous 95%, but given that its mostly just 2 bosses you fight, you get the hang of it after a while.All this to say that this is one of those games where a thumbs up/thumbs down isn't good.  I need a thumb sideways to represent this game, but given that it doesn't exist, I'll have to say, only pick it up on a really good sale.

_childDocuments_.review: A competent if fairly unsurprising metroidvania with some novel mechanics. A solid 7 - held back by two cardinal sins of the genre: (1) a final boss which is 4 phases long and (2) unskippable dialogue scenes before bosses. So if you're fighting a boss multiple times you gotta mash through the (short) dialogue beforehand. On the positive side, I love the art, there's an interesting story in here even if it  is a little obtuse at times, and while the lack of enemy variety lets it down each biome does feel pretty distinct and each armour set has fun specific abilities.

_childDocuments_.review: What could have been a good game is instead ruined by one horrendous design flaw. Your health in this game is tied to you ability to move throughout the map. Run out of the first bar of your health but still survive? You're stuck in the map and will have to restart the portion that you juat played from the last time that you saved ALL OVER AGAIN. It's especially bad when you defeat a boss (which does not authosave) and then are forced to restart the whole boss anyway because you can't move due to the health you lost during the battle. Huge disappointment. The game also crashed way too frequently.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:-later bosses have questionable design choises/are borderline unfair and frustrating-game strips you of a core mechanic at the 90-95% mark and does not give it back-the general theme around colour is kinda underdevelloped in game.-buy on sale if you want to play itIts a fine metroidvania, with some unfortunate design choises. I would like to give this game a neutural recommendation, but steam only gives me good or bad as an option. Its not a bad game but also not an very good one. Its just there I guess. I really enjoyed the game untill all bosses started being really annoying for no reason at all. My main gripe is that some of these later game bosses should not have a collision hitbox. That becomes a real problem when you can not predict where the boss is showing up again and you have to flip a coin and hope he does not spawn right into your face. Also some bosses are airborn an require you to jump up in order to reach them, but most of the time when you get hit in the process, by lightly touching them. Next up, all bosses have this thing where they get faster and attack faster, the more damage you deal to them. This does not allow you to get out of danger or even react at all to some attacks. Also really anoying is the fact, that the game strips you of an core mechanic and never gives it back to you. The replacement is mostly worse and throws the gameplayloop, you learned and used for 90% of the game under the bus. This is just a personal thing, but I wish they did more with the general colour theme of the game. Its a thing until the tutorial ends, one more time at the end of the game.I guess go for it when its on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I am saying negative because I would not recommend it to a seasoned metroidvania player. This is a solid metroidvania with all of the pains a classic comes with. I dislike the the combined mana and health\shield bar. It takes too long to recharge in the second half of the game too. The Boss battles are mid, I had one memorable battle, the rest were simple to do. The story wasn't that engaging to me. The introduced a lot of characters that were somewhat colorful but it didn't really expand the world. The design is pretty, but that's about it. There isn't a diverse set of enemies. _childDocuments_.review: 🎀The initial healing system is very frustrating. When Europa's health runs out at the beginning of the game, there aren’t many ways to recover it directly during combat. Europa starts with a health bar that can only be regenerated by collecting health orbs scattered throughout the game world or dropped by defeated enemies. This makes the early moments of the game challenging, as you can’t yet rely on the rhythm-based healing system that gets unlocked later on.The Music Box healing system becomes available later in the game and introduces the healing mechanic through music, but I haven’t been able to reach this stage yet, having died several times in the first level. Additionally, the checkpoints are too far apart, forcing me to retrace my steps instead of teleporting, as you can in other metroidvania games. Moreover, you have to re-explore the entire map after dying because the game reloads the previous savegame. The art style is beautiful, but the scaling of the initial difficulty has really worn me out, I don’t have the patience to keep repeating the same level due to a new healing mechanic that can’t be used right away.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: It was fun. Art style and music were fantastic. The story is fairly basic, but still sweet. Bosses took 2-3 tries for me to beat in the latter half of the game. 100%ed it on the first go without a guide.I'm not a huge Metroidvania person, so if you like super intense Hollow-Knight level experiences, this might not be enough, but for someone like me who just wants a casual MV experience, this should do you nicely.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: As soon as you get in a fight, you realize that there was the weirdest mechanic design you might ever witness in a game with combat. Your dodge/dash is only backward. I am legit confused by this decision, why? It's counter-initiative (unless this is literally your first game ever), it makes the game unnecessarily hard as you end up dodging into the enemy rather than away, and it limits your combat, as the only effective way I can think of to use it (and probably what the devs had in mind), is to literally stand still and as soon as the enemy hits you dodge back! Why do that to your game? Your combat is already limited dodging and fighting wise.What a game mechanic flaw! I kid you not, I am moving my L3 the opposite way and dodging to make it better, and faster, not to mention you can't dodge to traverse faster! I am baffled that someone would intentionally implement something like this! It really does hugely negatively impact your game.So I went to the left side of the map, and I think I am soft-locked, that or there is a mechanic the game didn't bother telling me about, either way, it's not worth my time.

_childDocuments_.review: Just some odd choices here that so far make the game not that enjoyable. Combat feels pretty stiff and most enemies have weak animations so far. The main character is animated fantastically tho. piano save spots kinda annoying having to restart all progress (collectible items and all). Just makes for boring unneeded backtracking.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: The art & music are great, but the game's design has a lot of issues. Upgrading your health bar doesn't actually give you more health because so many sources of damage in the game will empty a full health bar regardless (like spikes & bosses). For bosses this is particularly bad, as it means you have to almost completely avoid damage against the hardest enemies. Technically there's a way to heal, but it's a bar that pops up for less than a second. By the time you see that it's there it's gone, which means you need to react to it before it even appears. When I'm playing and get a game over, my most common response is "There was absolutely nothing I could've done about that", which isn't a problem I often have in other games. Its common when developing a game to feel like it's easier than it is because you're creating the hazards and timings. You know exactly what to do when & how. This is part of why it's important to have new people who haven't been working on it playtest a game before release.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a lot of fun up until the last boss and the boss for the last mission. I grew up in the 90s, had an NES, i know all about hard games like Ninja Gaiden, Contra, etc. I also love souls likes with Nioh being my favorite. This last boss battle was just poorly designed. You have your health bar, and during the game you can recharge it, well that ability gets taken away, it sucks but i can deal with it. Got to the last boss, defeated his first form without getting hit after numerous tries, i got gud. Then the battle changes, the boss quickly turns into a shmup level, you have no idea what's going on, no pattern, and just die because everything hits you. I whaled on him with full health for a solid minute or so and gave up.*Edit. Originally gave this a thumbs down, changing it to thumbs up. Just finished the game by upgrading the last armor set. I was able to beat the boss much more easily, and on the first try, while only using 2 vitality points. You have to upgrade everything to beat this. Overall the game has excellent music and art. Feels like one of those budget games you get when your parents couldn't afford Castlevania and got you this instead and it ended up being awesome. It was fun. Wish there was more than one weapon. And the last boss was poorly designed.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Recommendish,It's an average metroidvania with good art but an obstructive story.The game map has a nice layout, the game flows around to various small zones in sequence and there is almost zero need to backtrack, and if you do it's usually with a traversal ability to speed up the return trip.The moment to moment gameplay is fine. Your primary attacks are melee, ranged attacks cost you HP that you recover by standing still or hitting/killing things in melee. There are a number of traversal modes you unlock that the game uses as keys and backtracking.Enemy difficulty is uneven in some parts.Flying, zero warm up, 360 degree shooting bugs are some BS.A couple of later bosses like to spam slow homing projectiles that overlap with other attacks, but as a melee character you don't have much to do while forced to evade fire.A story is present in the game, it's not terribly exciting and that's fine. The issue is that it gets in the way of the game part of the game. There is a fairly long series of text boxes in the games intro but nothing of importance was conveyed that wasn't in the animated opening before the title screen.Also, every time you use an elevator you have to tap through a number of text boxes to continue playing. Even when the protagonist runs out of dialogue, you get a single ... text box you must tap through.Each boss usually has some pre and post fight dialogue as well, which can't be skipped and must be tapped through.The game has a small indie difficulty problem, where the final boss is a much larger roadblock than everything before it. So the climax of the game is some sort of weird denial play instead of having a satisfying conclusion.I did get stuck after you are meant to use the yellow generators to activate the lift, since it wasn't obvious that the generators controlled lifts. The red generator before it was meant to be a tutorial, but it's tutorial popup was very vague about what it did.There are a number of bugs in the game, nothing major I encountered though.The horned gods lasers damage you during their prefire animationSometimes enemies elemental auras would not display upon reentering the room.The game will 100% crash if you attempt to continue after a death.It also crashed after the credits finished, but I guess the game was done anyway. Hope there wasn't anything after that!Very nice pixel art though.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Good metroidvania, good mechanics and controls feel very good. The world looks nice and vibrant, the characters are fun and cute. I will complain now but I do think people should play this game. That being said I am getting a bit annoyed at the game. The game strips you of your normal healing/ammo regen systems to give you a slow, very slow, health/ammo regen at the end of the game. It makes using ranged attacks very inefficient and make the final boss (what I believe to be the final boss?) or any bosses you encounter near the end of the game very challenging. _childDocuments_.review: Saw some weird negative reviews, so wanted to balance that out with a positive take, because I think the game deserves it. This is a really really cool game, and I think it's a bit misunderstood.This game is NOT inspired by Dark Souls, and is NOT Hollow Knight. If that's what you want in every Metroidvania you play, that's ok, but this game might not be for you.This game IS a love letter to GBA Metroidvanias. Have you always wanted more high quality GBA-style Metroidvanias? Did you ever wonder what Castlevania would be like if it was made in the style of a Metroid game?? Then this game is absolutely for you.Pixel art and animation are first-rate, and the story and world building really come together in the later half of the game. Controls are very fluid, and you'll be constantly getting new tools to switch up traversal. 9YIS does take a more modern approach to level design, in that it's made to be easy to progress linearly(similar to Metroid Dread), but the game certainly doesn't railroad you onto that path. Combat is relatively simple, but has some depth for you to explore(like the Castlevania classic of canceling a jump attack into a ground attack for a double hit, and a fun crouch-cancel infinite attack loop). Enemies in the world aren't hugely varied, but the bosses are all unique and fun, though not particularly difficult. I can't speak to earlier versions of the game, but currently the "Health As Ammo" system is well tuned, and isn't punishing as long as you take a few minutes to actually learn the system.Music is a key theme of the game, and the soundtrack is really incredible. For any music nerds out there, the soundtrack is primarily Jazz inspired, but the whole game is tuned to 432 Hz. As far as I'm aware, this is relatively novel in the video game world, and adds a relaxing, dreamy quality to every song. You also meet various musician characters throughout the game, and they each have a musical theme that highlights the instrument they play, which is a cool touch.The game took me 7.5 hours to beat 100%. Some reviews were saying this is too short, but that's a pretty expected length for this style of Metroidvania(each GBA Metroid game takes about 8 hours to 100% as well). It's a well paced game that doesn't outstay its welcome. As far as value goes, I think the game is accurately priced at $20. If you get this game on sale, it's a steal.All told, if you're a fan of Metroid games, or GBA Metroidvanias in general, I can't recommend this game enough! If you're more interested in the visual or musical aspects of the game, I'd also give it a strong recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, I get it. Games for many are hard to drop a bunch of money on for some players out there if you don't get a lot of hours out of it. It's a valid criteria, but I always have to point out that quality of those hours are important. We've seen games that have stretched out their content so far that the slightest of pressure will cause it to snap. Well, 9 Years of Shadow is the opposite of that, and quite frankly, was fantastic for the time that I've played so far.Obviously, you're probably here for the visuals and presentation, which are absolutely gorgeous. The game shows a variety of environmental designs along with fun characters that let's you appreciate the small details on each of them, without getting lost in the big picture of functional gameplay. I love the weaving of elements into each character and how you can tell who they are just by looking at them. In addition, the game emphasizes key moments well with beautifully constructed screens: like those that you get when getting a new armor. The music may be a slight step down compared to the overall visuals, but that's like saying the great fries are a step down from the big juicy burger next to it: it does more to complement the visuals more then anything.The gameplay is up my alley to: a focus on basic positioning and simple attack/defense strategies in metroidvanias. The element system does enough to change encounter, and the movement options that are introduced (especially the water siren form) really feel fantastic and just wants to make you move around. There's ok enemy variety but great boss encounters, and the game hits the level of pushing you into situations that will get you tense, but not to the point of frustration. Exploration is easy yet can get you confused at times, but you'll want to keep exploring this world as much as possible. Look, the biggest knock against this game right now is the length based on other reviews, but the impression it leaves from a gameplay perspective does a lot to justify it's cost. If that's important to you, then keep an eye out for it in the future at least, but for others, this is a great example of a polished indie game that you'll be thinking for days to come, and just want to see what the world has to unveil next.

_childDocuments_.review: This game looks beautiful, but is unplayable with a keyboard, although I have happily played dozens of other metroidvanias with a keyboard. As some examples of the lack of effort put into keyboard support:--There seems to be no user interface to indicate what key to press for various purposes. For example, when I first started the game, I had to guess that the movement on the opening menu used WASD and that spacebar was the confirm key.--The arrow keys are not used for movement or menu navigation, which is awkward and counterintuitive.--In the options menu to rebind keys, many critical controls are hidden, so that the user can neither see what key is used for them nor change that key directly. If the user changes a visible key to match one of the hidden ones, the hidden one seemingly becomes unusable, short of resetting all key bindings and starting over.--I stood in front of a treasure chest (for which the game indicated that I should press an up arrow) and pressed every key on my keyboard and mouse, but was unable to open the chest or trigger any dialogue. I had the same issue at what was probably a save point, though it was hard to tell, since I couldn't guess the hidden key to activate it.

_childDocuments_.review: Written after 100% Completion* (one achievement is bugged out currently and thus 1 achievement is missing.)TL;DRA good solid, Simple Metroidvania. Wonderful art, good music, decent difficulty. Worth a play, if a bit short for my taste. Why no more Transformation sequences like the Opening? It's good, more please.The greatest complaint I can give is that I want more. More forms, more armors, more depth to combat, more levels to complete, more things to collect. But, what is there is good, if simple.Combat is simple, but solid for the most part. While there were many times during the game that I wanted some more variety, what is there is made for purpose and function. You have a basic quick combo, and a heavy attack that can be used in a finisher for a bit of extra damage. That's about it. Aerial combos aren't a thing, which I think is the first obvious miss. Second is the lack of any combo but light-combo-> heavy finisher.The healing and recovery for most of the game is fairly forgiving, while slow you have infinite healing. Since the game doesn't have checkpoints, it's easy to see why.With the armor, I wish there was more interaction with them. Many regions lock you into a specific set, which makes traversal and security nicer, but I think it limits the ability for each to feel unique. All uniqueness for each is limited to traversal, and there could easily be more. One could be defensive, another offensive, another have DoT effects, etc. Art wise I like it, it's a kind of modern throwback style, reminescent of the 70s and 80s era of anime. A good comparison would be Space Battleship Yamato for a good original/modern comparison, though this has much more style and for good reason. The music was always good, tending around a kind of lo-fi style through most of it, though no singular track stands out to me. Few do in any game though.I feel the story is a bit weak, or perhaps not as explained as I think it should've been. Many bosses feel kind of shoehorned in, no real explanation given as to who or why they are there. The musicians are a bit scattershot, making them seem a bit out of place. That's not to say it isn't effective though and the reveal for the final transformation did get to me a bit, but it otherwise feels disconnected.Still, any grips I have are small and wishes for a possible expansion. I still give this game a thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: A decent Metroidvania with a great visual look and a superb soundtrack. There aren't any surprises with this one, it has the standard upgrades and backtracking you would expect, the difference is that the presentation is spot on. Lots of games in this genre just can't stand out in a sea of copycats, and though I wouldn't describe this one as exceptional, it does everything right and doesn't overstay its welcome. Overall, not many complaints, just don't go in expecting a masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: This is the type of game i would like to love but it's so hard. I don't know if it's just me but some of the battles feel completely RNG and i can notice it, i can see what a different number does to the gameplay of a battle. I also suspect there is some kind of difficulty auto balancer because, sometimes, the life of the bosses feel smaller after a certain amount of player deaths. Also, most of the cutscenes and dialogs before a fight are unskippable, making the gameplay more tedious. Of course, this is me, i might not be a good player at this type of games, but still...The art is amazing and the soundtrack is pretty good for this aesthetic, SOME upgrades the player has do seem to be coppied from other games but at least they try to integrate them in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: The best way I can summarize  is as a largely competent, gorgeous metroidvania that ever-so-slightly overstays its welcome even with me 100%ing the game in 9.5 hours. I do recommend it but with a massive pile of salt, so hopefully the devs will address some of the issues I had with it because while it's good, it could be even better.The main reason I say this is because everything feels like it takes longer than it should - combat, exploration, area transitions, cutscenes - and not enough is done to diversify or expedite any of it before the tedium sets in. The final armor upgrade, , is also one of the most baffling design choices I've ever seen in a metroidvania, but I'll get into that later.When it comes to combat you have a light and a heavy melee attack with a four hit combo (3 light + 1 heavy) which you can use to slowly refill your light bar (i.e. mana), plus a light element projectile attack from your bear companion that uses a part of your light bar with a (mostly) accurate lock-on system. Later on, your projectile is replaced by a charged screen-wide explosion that deals heavy damage to all enemies (17+ damage compared to 2-8 damage from melee attacks).Throughout the game you collect various elemental armor sets - thunder, water, fire, and earth - that outline your character in the armor's respective color and give you different movement abilities that are fun and satisfying to use. This outline also applies to certain enemies, who take double damage if you match colors when attacking with melee along with purple enemies that can only be damaged by light. Thankfully non-purple enemies still take regular damage if your color doesn't match instead of half, which is definitely a plus.While you can upgrade each of the different armor sets once, the upgrade adds an additional one (yes, one) damage to your attacks, meaning enemies that would normally take two hits to kill... still take two hits to kill. You don't get a defense boost for upgrading your armor either, which seems odd, so the only way to increase your survivability is by collecting Red and Blue Note relics which can be traded to an NPC along with the in-game currency to boost your vitality and light bar respectively.By the end of the game I had the max of four vitality and a light bar that went 2/3rds of the way across the screen (it isn't quantified in game).Now for the main issue I had with the combat: your light bar also acts as a shield, meaning that if you get hit too many times you can no longer fire light projectiles and are vulnerable to vitality damage. You can recover your light bar via a quicktime event as soon as it's depleted, but if you fail you have to hug your bear companion to slowly refill your light bar (which is kinda cute, not gonna lie). However, if you are hit at any point during this animation you lose not only one point of vitality, but the light bar is also reset to zero.This wouldn't be such a big deal if it weren't for the fact that most bosses  you to break dark crystals using said projectile before you can damage them with your melee attack. And if you use the last of your light bar to make them vulnerable  fail the quicktime event, you're better off not attacking to replenish your light bar, making fights take longer than they should. Oh, there's also contact damage in this game so if you're trying to recover your light bar and an enemy lands on top of you, you'll potentially take multiple hits or die despite there being a few seconds of invulnerability after taking damage. (Seriously, unless it makes sense for the enemy to deal contact damage, why do enemies deal contact damage?)Compounding this is that some bosses have an unskippable intro cutscene that plays every time you enter the boss room, which is further padded by the game taking you to a "Game Over" menu before you can load your save instead of placing you outside the boss room or loading your last save automatically. Finally (for comabt at least) is the final armor upgrade in the game, which actually makes you  by replacing your quicktime event and hug mechanic with an incredibly slow regen that stops whenever you take damage. As a plot device I get it, but for a supposed end-game upgrade it made the final few fights a lot harder arbitrarily. I feel like if they had let you keep the quicktime event or even doubled the melee regen it would have worked better, but as it is it's an awful design choice.When it comes to the exploration there are 10 areas including the final area, each with a distinct look and armor-related traversal mechanics to set them apart from one another. Again, the visuals and overall presentation are fantastic and the music did a good job at setting the tone for each area. However, most of the exploration in this game is done on foot with the exception of a main elevator that takes you to the center of the few main areas and smaller elevators between the few side areas. There is no fast travel mechanic that lets you warp between save points and, while rare, there are a few passages that are one way only, so if you aren't paying attention then it's more backtracking for you!The smaller elevators are also used to play a cutscene (the same one every time) with some plot exposition overlaid on top, though eventually all that appears is a "..." that you have to manually skip before the cutscene ends and the next area loads.There are also no map icons to indicate where missed collectibles are and no hint system to point you in the right direction, so for the last hour of my playtime I had to manually go back through each area with a map I printed out to nab the ones I missed. Considering even  had map icons, I'm amazed at how many modern metroidvanias don't.Lastly, even though effort was put into making each area unique, this effort was not put into the bestiary, with the same handful of enemies being pallet-swapped between 9 of the 10 areas with little to no change to their attacks.But despite how harsh all of the above is, I did overall enjoy my time with .You can tell the developers put a lot of heart and effort into the game and with a few more QoL fixes it could be one of the better metroidvanias out there.It seems like the devs are still putting out patches so if it looks interesting grab it while it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: It's a little on the short side but I think that works for it, especially given the lack of a proper fast travel system. The upgrades/map parts aren't too difficult to find which absolutely helps you out in the long run. The story and characters are charming, the visuals are stunning and the music is fantastic. It's got a nice balance of difficulty, minus the somewhat small spike with the final boss - which I feel was down to the lack of a checkpoint if nothing else.Overall, I loved this game. Sure I have my gripes with it, but it was very enjoyable throughout.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Couldn't stomach finishing this, its a fine game but its not what I look for in metroidvanias. Its your run-of-the-mill castlevania clone with an uninteresting progression system, the combat is barebone and movement options are pretty non-existent. Nothing felt like a challenge, you're just going through the motion without much hassle, especially going through the zones by platforming or with the different "door-unlocking" powers. It actually felt that it wouldn't let me miss a jump or punish me at all for not platforming well. You're just kinda flowing through everything, which can be good for some but it was so boring to me that I personally can't abide by it. I'll give it that it as great flair and the music is nice, but the whole "theme" of music doesn't really matter or makes sense. No enemy or boss cares about the music part, theres no music mechanic that really tie all of it together. You just simply pick up musical notes (upgrade material) and meet musicians for whatever reason (I'm sure it might pan out to matter in the end, but throughout most of the game, it doesn't), also the save station is a piano I guess. I did really like the "big" bosses however, some great set pieces and exotic gameplay made them memorable and fun to figure out, but again without much difficulty. It all boiled down to that for me; the mechanics were solid enough that it could have been made harder without frustrating the player, I could even see the platforming puzzles being revisited to add challenge without breaking the flow. I would have really recommended this game by putting aside my opinion on the difficulty if the world and gameplay was at least interesting. Right now it just feels like a disconnected pile of metroidvanias' tropes and I couldn't care about it at all.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: I play a *lot* of Metroidvanias, and I really enjoyed this one.  It's a fun and well executed mostly-melee Metroidvania - the controls and combat most closely reminded me of Order of Ecclesia.    Pros:   - Gorgeous pixel artwork and great animations. The game is appropriately bright and colorful  - The soundtrack is great  - Controls are responsive and combat feels good  - The elemental armor system is interesting and leads to some creative movement options in some areas  - The story is nothing mind-blowing, but it is interesting enough and all of the dialogue is well written. Europa's elevator monologues fondly reminded me of Metroid FusionCons:  - Some technical issues at launch time.  Certain achievements do not work.  Also there is a memory leak that can lead to crashing, mostly during loading screens but occasionally at other times.  This will hopefully be fixed in the first patch.  Other Thoughts:  - Length: It took me ~9 hours for my first clear.  Perfectly acceptable for a Metroidvania IMHO - this is longer than my first playthrough of Metroid Dread took.   - Difficulty: With the exception of a few late game bosses, this game is on the easier side for a Metroidvania.  The way light recovery works means you can brute force many encounters without really learning the fights.  I wouldn't mind if they added a hard mode at some point down the line.   - Linearity: On the linear side.  Major areas have to be tackled in the intended order.  Areas interconnect and backtracking is allowed, but backtracking is rarely required unless you miss an item.  All told: very enjoyable and I'd definitely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could sing this game's praises higher than I'm about to. As one of my most anticipated games of the year, I'm already coming into this with bias, but even I can't deny that this game could've used a bit more internal testing before launch. When it runs, it plays really well. It has some of the best pixel art I've ever seen accompanied by an amazing soundtrack. It's aesthetically one of my favorite games of all time. And on top of that it has some awesome movement in thanks to the collection of armors you gain throughout a playthrough. But sadly, I experienced more glitches, lag spikes, visual bugs, and crashes than any other game in recent memory. Even after a patch to improve stability and the memory leak, the game is still prone to fall apart the longer you play, whether that be boss attacks not appearing right(or at all), or the game crashing at the next load screen. I still heavily enjoyed my time with it, but I think waiting a few months for more patches is a good idea. Hopefully a year from now I'll be able to recommend it without a "but" in my sentence.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: A very competently made metoridvania. Graphics and music are nice, I like the element-switching mechanic, and the smooth transitioning between transformations is greatly appreciated. Enjoyed my time with it, and will likely play it again sometime in the future.The game is a good size and length, though it is a bit linear (especially the "portrait" sections) and maybe a little bit too easy overall. That said, the difficulty spike on the final boss is ludicrous.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Despite what some other reviews are saying, I would wager this game easily weighs in at about 10-12 hours. I'm not exactly a speed runner but I'm not exactly a slow gamer either.Pros:Beautiful visuals, artwork, animations and colors.Unique and iconic levels Snappy, reactive game play which coordinates well with its platforming and puzzlesMultitude of different bosses littered throughout the game which all give a unique experience.Fun and diverse cast of NPC characters which provide a sense of joy when helping them.Curious exploration by the player is almost always rewarded.Offers some challenges, however is neither boringly easy or hellishly difficult.The story is told clearly with a clear and realistic motive by the main character (Europa).Cons:No Autosave featureFast travel option does exist but its not great.Save spots can sometimes be far apart which can be frustrating.Does not really have an RPG element to it which, to me, does not offer much incentive to replay the game.Contact damage from enemies and bosses can sometimes be confusing.Almost no post-game content or higher challenges.In conclusion if you're a fan of Metroidvanias and you're looking for something to sink your teeth into this would be a great addition to your library. I do not regret buying it for the experience as it was a fun and colorful game that kept me occupied.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: This game is neat. The energy mechanic gets some getting used to but it adds a sort of tension that I haven't really seen in a game before. It forces you to identify moments of rest and really pay attention to boss patterns. I think the abilities you get a pretty uninteresting but well designed around. The story is fine. It gets the job done and has some unique things going for it. I would recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to like about this game; I love the music, visuals, and the interesting set of mechanics that generally mesh well. I felt engaged during my whole play through. On the other hand, it heavily borrows from three key Metroidvanias without much self-contained cohesion. Inspirational titles I can most directly pinpoint are Metroid Fusion and Castlevania: Portrait of Ruin. There are definitely nods to other titles as well, but you can see a lot of aspects from these two in particular. The way elements are fused together isn't bad, but other than the Portrait of Ruin styled painting sections (these seem to exist for no reason but to copy; however, they do not overstay their welcome and are decently done), the mechanics/gimmicks are often worse than those in the predecessors in some way. A good example of this is the elevator scene, which is a cool and uncanny recreation of how it's done in Fusion, but there are many of these in the this game, and they kind of overstay their welcome during elevator transitions until they are replaced entirely with, "...". It's almost like the game listened to the player and the inner monologues stopped, but then why make the text appear at all at that point? While on the topic of Fusion, why bother calling the areas "sectors" if the areas already have their own names? It's not a space station and traversal isn't entirely linear either. The game's story is blatantly Castlevania like, but with a narrative and setting switch-up that is pretty solid if you want a similar vibe and don't think too hard about it. Otherwise, you start to see how elements just don't really add up to a very cohesive universe (. Some enemies and bosses are also practically Castlevania re-skins, with occasional cool reworks, but mostly the same stuff.Game mechanics/upgrades are a welcome mix from the three games I highlighted, and they actually feel quite responsive in combat (albeit sometimes actions feel like they don't trigger in some tight spots). Probably the silliest quality of life inclusion is the extensive reach of the snake upgrade when exiting and entering holes in the wall, because in some tight corners you might find yourself accidentally going back and forth into and out of these passages for no reason. A worse issue is the fact that with the exception of two major bosses (, the sort of Hollow Knight like healing mechanic can take away from the tension of fights, since you virtually have infinite health if you can manage your magic. The chance to regain partial health can be annoying since it's easy to forget it is happening. Then you just try to hold to regain before realizing you didn't regain any magic back and immediately die. The caveat there is that . I wasn't a fan of how the boss fights compensate for difficulty with healing mechanics, but it does balance out in my opinion.Progression feels Fusion like, because it is semi-linear and "boss rush" styled in pacing. Some complained the game is too short and has a lot of boring backtracking, but having played many Metroidvanias, I completely disagree to both of these complaints. There is almost no backtracking, and if you do all the optional bosses, there's quite a bit of solid content. The boss progression can sometimes feel purposely out of order, but it's also important to keep in mind that they probably thought about nerfing some mini-bosses to account for the fact that save stations aren't usually immediately close by to them. This probably could have been reworked a little more. Side content is worth your time, since the core game ends up being pretty concise. Although quests are repetitive in nature, it boils down to more unique fights using the game's combat system. Probably worth working towards the last optional upgrade in the game too if you want some piece of mind in the final fight.One major complaint I have is that skipping cut scenes already seen could be a little quicker, as the current option still takes a bit of time to get working, and cut scenes repeat themselves every time. As other players mentioned, there are a considerable number of possible glitches. Mine weren't quite as severe, as I mainly noticed that the camera glitched upon loading one of my save files. The skewed camera made it virtually unplayable, but this was quickly resolved by leaving and rentering my save file.All in all, if you are looking for a vibey game with some recognizable metroidvania nostalgia and new twists on them, this is pretty solid. Story is hit and miss, but emotional at times too. Probably won't play again, but I am glad I did!
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some extremely difficult bosses. We are talking multi phase, enormous health and bullet hell. It is strictly for those who like old school bosses like in Megaman games, but there is also a unique health/mana system that adds extra difficulty. Health and mana are practically the same, so when you shoot magic you are doing self damage and getting hit by bosses leads to ammo loss. Recovering health/mana requires you to hold down a button for a couple of seconds while not moving. This is risky to do during boss battles and it can be frustrating to get hit while trying to recover. Fighting against regular enemies is pointless because you can shoot them all from a safe distance and then recover your mana without limit.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: The games art, boss design, music, characters and (to some degree) story are straight up fire.But the metroidvania aspects are far too linear. And the backtracking - really needed to be more generous with the fast travel system.If you miss an item in a corner of the map, you could be in for a trek. I was missing two notes at the end and getting back to them was painful. While we're on the subject, the map is okay for navigation during the base game. But it becomes pretty useless when trying to find anything you may have missed - I was scanning it for ages trying to find where the remaining notes were and had to cross check with other online maps.Having said that, can't stress how cool some of these bosses are - the dialogue is super clean as well with a very likeable (and dope looking) main protagonist.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: PLAYED ON STEAM DECK and it worked FLAWLESSLY!9 Years of Shadow is a rare case of simple action for maximum execution. The game is not brilliant or varied in combat, for instance, but it's incredibly engaging once you understand the system behind it. Took me some time to understand the relation between the blue bar and the health, but once I got it, that was a game changer to me and I started to appreciate the elegant design behind many of the decisions in this game.The best part is clearly the platforming and I will not tell you why. It manages to keep it fresh during the whole game. Right in the moment you're getting bored of your current traversal moveset you get a new one opening possibilities you weren't expecting.The weakests points to me were the absence of teleports or quick travel and the save system, which we can only define as "very classic". I had to repeat a couple of sections because I died in the most inconvenient moment... but you get soon into the mindset of "i just did something important so I need to find a save room ASAP" which, by the way, are frequent enough.In conclusion: if you love Metroidvanias and you miss a more classic approach to the genre with beautiful visuals and great platforming sections, YES, this is your game.RECOMMENDED.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely gorgeous game with a great soundtrack. Map design is fairly linear for a Metroidvania and combat doesn't evolve as much as I would like as the game progresses making it feel a little repetitive near the end but I still had a solid time exploring this and taking in the beautiful pixel art. Had some technical issues and crashes while I was playing but a recent patch seems to have been resolved those issues since finishing it. Solid game that I think is definitely worth playing for the aesthetics alone.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Despite billing itself as a Metroidvania, 9 Years of Shadows is in reality a rather perfunctory and linear puzzle platformer with basically no backtracking or worthwhile exploration to speak of (and what backtracking there is often hampered by locking you into certain areas of the map until specific bosses are beaten - NOT good design there). Most of the gameplay is underwhelming, with regular mobs being little to no real threat - making boss battles horrid difficulty spikes in comparison, made worse both by the way how health recovery works in the game and the absurd amount of health most of them have. The game has a currency system, but it's basically moot - you'll end up with far more coins than what you need to max out Europa's upgrades, so why has this not been leveraged as a means to purchase consumables for boss fights is quite puzzling. The elemental armor gimmick, while in theory offering interesting design space, is not utilized very well - it's pretty much solely offensive, with no defensive counterplay, there are very few places where you have to actively switch between armors to solve obstacles, and boss fights basically don't use it at all, quite a few outright locking you into using one specific suit. This makes the  fight that actually does something with it (Maelzael) stand out even more, as a testament of what could have been.As much as I want to like the game, the stellar art and music direction can't compensate for its' at best half-baked gameplay. And so I just can't recommend it in good conscience.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Metroivanias and Platformers are not my favorite game genres, however I loved this game, it is a great introduction to the genre as is easy to play and is not that hard on most parts (though I really suffer with a couple of bosses).I have played some like Hollow Knight and Blasphemous in the past, but I never completed any, but now I have a pending list of metroidvania games to play!
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: I play a lot of metroidvanias, so I feel like I have at least some kind of grasp on what a good one is. And unfortunately, the beautiful art style, graphics, and music aren't going to save this.  The SOTN influences are present and welcomed, but it's the divergence from it that hurts the game.Like, your magic bar is also a shield for your health, and in a boss fight were you HAVE to have that magic bar present means you will get a boss in a weakened state that needs that magic and you and the boss are just awkwardly staring at each other while you try to generate your magic back, only to miss your opportunity to damage the boss this cycle and have to go through another just for another attempt.  And this feels really bad.  On top of this, there are many bosses where the run back from the nearest save point is absolutely brutal.  I mean, some are near by, but so many times you're going to have to fight your way back for another attempt.  And tack that onto the fact you can not skip dialog just adds to the frustration ever attempt.Enemy variety is the game is terrible.  There are only a handful and they get recycled the entire game.  In fact, in the bestiary, there are different enemies that visually look the exact same, palette and element border and all.  You will see all the enemy types pretty early one and never experience anything new outside of bosses.  On top of that, there's no levels or experience in the game, no gear, or items.  And enemies rarely drop any currency, so there's hardly a reason to fight anything and just try to get around them as some enemies can be very tanky even with the appropriate element.The elevator transitions are aggravating as well.  You get stuck in every transition if you don't mash through the dialog.  And the lack of warp points or SOTN equivalent of library cards makes traversing a legitimate pain.  On top of this, there are room transitions where you will not be able to avoid damage without knowing ahead of time what's in it.  And while speaking about moving around, down right and down left prioritize walking instead of ducking, so you'll take otherwise avoidable damage from not pushing  PRECISELY down.::Minor spoilers::Towards the end of the game you get a final set of armor that actually makes you weaker instead of stronger as it takes away your ability to heal back your magic bar.  It auto-gens, but it's very slow and and you have no control.  It's objectively worse than just being able to heal it on your own.  And in a metroidvania, making your character weaker feels awful.The final form of the boss is an absolute ♥♥♥♥ and it's so unfair to do all it's previous forms with full health only to get absolutely blasted by things you can not avoid only to have to start over from form 1 all over again.  And if you lose ANY health before the final form, you might as well just die on purpose and start over.::End spoilers::Ultimately, it's a pretty package but takes too many missteps on what makes this genre good.  I came away from the game frustrated and wishing it was something else.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could recommend this game. But I can't. 9 Years of Shadows is a pretty game with gorgeous art, responsive controls, ever-expanding mobility mechanics, and not much else going for it.Outside the visuals, the first thing you notice is the story, because 9 Years of Shadows wants you to. There's quite a bit of dialogue throughout the game, some of which in flashbacks and cutscenes, including at the very start, and not a bit of it is skippable. The story is up for personal opinion, I was interested at first, but the increasing number of faces that were not interesting pulled me out of it. I stopped caring about the story very early on, so every unskippable dialogue box just became another forced stop in the gameplay. Some people may find a cute doll that only says a single word that other characters can understand full sentences from acceptable. I do not. These unskippable cutscenes even happen every time you get into an elevator, the main character will have some inner thoughts about what's recently happened or what she's generally feeling while waiting to reach the destination. Later in the game elevators appear frequently and you'll eventually run out of inner thoughts, SO SHE THINKS NOTHING! You're still forced to sit through the elevator scene while she thinks "..."! And the game has the gall to say "hold start to skip" but all that does is press A for you at every earliest frame possible: it's still unskippable.The gameplay shines in some areas, but not in others. You begin with a light attack that can be chained three times and a heavy attack. Doing a heavy attack after any number of lights turns it into a combo ender for a little extra damage. Sadly, combat hardly evolves beyond this. You gain additional armors over time, which change the way your lights and heavys swing, and allow you to hit elemental weaknesses... when you're actually allowed to. You'd think being able to hit elemental weakness would be important, but it's not. Each unlocked armor grants you the ability to traverse a type of area, Water for wet, Earth for poison, and Fire for hot, and this is FORCED! Whenever you enter these types of areas, if you have the necessary armor, you're automatically swapped into it. And in these areas you'll see plenty of enemies with different elemental weaknesses than what you're being forced to use. And bosses don't have elemental weakness, so the only real use of it is when you're traveling between biomes, because every single enemy respawns when you leave a room, so be ready to fight things over and over again.What's actually more important are the different swings in the different armors, and exploration. The different armors do attack fairly differently, I found myself using mostly Water for the thrust attacks because it let me fight at a longer range, or Earth when I wanted to use the heavy attack to hit airborne enemies without jumping. Your starting Light armor very quickly becomes worthless, except for those times where hitting with Light is required to open a door. Each armor (except Light until the very end) does eventually gain it's own exploration tool, and it's fun to speed around with them, especially when they can easily blend together which happens a number of times. This is the one instance where the forced armor switching makes sense and works, I just wish it was handled better.9 Years of Shadows' other form of combat is also it's biggest mistake: Shooting. Which honestly ties into my biggest issue with the game: The Light Bar! I HATED everything, every single mechanic tied to the Light Bar. The Light Bar is the standout feature of the game, it essentially acts as your shield. The monsters in the tower hurt like hell, at the start you can only survive a single hit; taking two hits equals death. If you have any amount of Light Bar left, it will take the damage instead. Shooting ALSO drains some of your Light Bar, meaning you're spending your own safety net to attack. While most monsters have an elemental weakness that can optionally be exploited, some monsters are weak to Light Shots and IMMUNE to everything else! Shooting them is required and shot-required entities can appear in boss fights too. It's very easy to find yourself in a situation where you have shot-only entities coming at you, but you're low on Light Bar so shooting them means leaving yourself vulnerable to taking actual damage. The Light Bar can be regenerated in a number of ways, including a nearly unreactable timing window when it hits empty, but health can only be restored at a save point. At the end of the game you get a new Light Armor with a "regenerating Light Bar" but this actually makes you weaker, the regeneration is slow and enemies still hit hard, so it actually becomes EASIER TO DIE at the end of the game! The Light Bar was a mistake, through and through.Shooting also just has its own problems. The Light Shots come out of a teddy bear hovering around you and aiming is controlled with the right analog stick. The bear will always aim in the last direction you held on the right stick, regardless of how long ago that was; the left stick is ignored entirely. This easily leads to wasted shots, but when you try to aim your shots you'll discover lock-ons. When you hold the right stick towards an enemy, the game with lock onto it to ensure your shot doesn't miss. Makes sense in theory, but very early on the game throws a large knight monster with a massive sword and shield. The sword and shield have their own elemental weaknesses, and hitting either with that weakness is the only way to damage the knight. The first one you fight has Light Shot-weakness on his sword, which he holds behind him. The trick is to shoot his feet, this seems to register hitting his sword, but trying to aim at his feet results in the lock-on, forcing you to shoot the shield instead, which does nothing. You have walk into the corner, hope you can position the bear without triggering the lock-on, and shoot his feet without touching the right stick again. It's bad, it should've just copied Super Metroid's shooting controls.Enemy variety is okay. Most of the bosses are pretty cool and interesting to fight and there's a good number of them; this is where the real fun is. But tower monsters are mostly jokes to slow you down and hinder movement until you defeat them. A lot of enemies are placed in spots in rooms where you can't just jump over them, you'll take contact damage if you try, but with the limited variety you'll quickly see all the fodder the game has to offer. With no experience to be gained and currency dropped like candy, there's really no reason to keep defeating these enemies blocking your path, yet you have to just to advance forward. By the end of the game I had over 1000 currency: there is nothing in the game that costs 1000, or even half that!The lack of mob monster variety and the unskippable cutscenes in elevators bring another thing to note: just how big this tower is! Most elevators in the tower only go to specific points, but there is one elevator at the center that does serve as a "fast travel" of sorts. But it's clearly not intended to be used as a fast travel mechanism, so to get anywhere you'll be walking and fighting a lot! I don't think the amount of walking you'd have to do to get from one corner of the map to the other is really that different from other Metroidvanias, but with the mob enemy combat that gets old fast it noticiable how long it actually takes. When you get the final Light Armor upgrade you'll gain a small constant AOE damage around you to kill weak enemies on contact, but this really only works on those with Light Shot weakness or those in the starting area, it doesn't make any of the other enemies any less annoying.9 Years of Shadows had promise, it looks great and plays great, and it knows how a Metroidvania should be, but where it tried to innovate and stand out became its undoing. I do not recommend this to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I gave this game a recommended rating, more detail is necessary. Overall score 6/109 Years of Shadows is a fine game, but it's just that. It doesn't do anything to particularly break the mold or revolutionize the genre but that's ok. The Armor System is actually really neat and fun (although I wish there was more variety between the different armors) and the music and artstyle is amazing, as well as the boss designs (visually) but that's about where the good things end.On the negative side, as a metroidvania, backtracking is one of the biggest aspects of any game in this genre and to be honest, this game suffers from both underwhelming movement options to an infuriating lack of fast travel options. Getting around is not enjoyable, it's a slog and with enemies respawning every time you leave and re enter EVERY room it can just be downright annoying. Additionally, this game has no quick save or even true "continue" options; when you die, you can either reload the last save or just exit out of the game. Normally this isn't too bad, but since there is no auto continue or quick save. If you die to a boss with a long intro speech, you have to sit through it every single time you die. Did you run into a boss room after unlocking most of the map or secret rooms since your last save? Better hope you don't die because if you do, you have to go back into all of those secret rooms and unlock all of the map again. Just make it so that dying to a boss doesn't add to the tedium and I can just challenge it again instantly. I actually really enjoyed the boss fights and learning their patterns, but having to basically replay up to 20 minutes of game time because I wasn't able to recharge my shield and died to a rogue projectile is frustrating.That leads me to another negative: the health system. Basically, you have a resource bar that is both your shield and your projectile attack (at least until the last 30 minutes of the game). If your shield runs out from taking hits, you can recharge it by holding a button or hitting a mini quicktime event, the problem is for the quick time event, its always random and trying to charge is incredibly slow. Some boss patterns make it almost impossible to find a window in which to charge your shield which will lead to A LOT of annoying deaths which compounded with the saving and backtracking only make the game become tedious.At the end of the day, did I enjoy the game? Yeah it was ok, a solid 6/10. Would I replay it, given the chance? No, I don't even want to fish for all of the achievements because there isn't enough good to make it worthwhile compared to other metroidvanias but still a fun 12 hour sink for fans of this specific genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I normally don't review games until I finish them, and I'm not quite done 9 Years of Shadow.  I feel like I need to get some of my feelings out, though, before I forget all of my thoughts.To start with, this game is very pretty.  It has fantastic pixel art and pretty good animations.  That's really the only thing I would say was actively good here, though.First, it's a metroidvania that features very little exploration.  It's mostly linear with a few spots you can backtrack after getting new upgrades.  The upgrades come fast and heavy, but they aren't very satisfying; it's basically go to a new area, go around a section that you can't pass, get an upgrade, circle back.  One upgrade every few minutes, but none of them feel good or give a sense of discovery.Then, the combat.  It's fine, I guess; it sucks you can only dash backwards, but otherwise it's just very basic.  The problem here is some really weird decisions, though; your shield is also your magic, but you have to use magic in a lot of places.  You can't regenerate the shield manually unless it's completely empty.  You have armor that makes your attacks hit same-colored enemies better (which is weird anyway), but you're frequently forced to use non-optimal colored armor because of the environment.  Many attacks just strip your whole shield no matter how much you upgrade it.  The bosses all have extremely simple patterns and are only difficult because they hit hard.  It all just smacks of being different for the sake of being different; none of the elements come together in a satisfying way.Add this to the fact that the story is fine at best, the characters all have only a couple looping lines, and you hit for piddly damage even after your upgrades, and it all just comes to a game that is honestly very frustrating to play.Edit: Having now finished the game, I'm honestly even more frustrated.  The very last upgrade you get actually makes a lot of things about this game better, but you only have it for maybe half an hour.

_childDocuments_.review: Terrible game design. There are some interesting ideas but badly executed. The worst part is the way life works. So many times you spend all your shield trying to hit the enemy only for it to hit you back and take away one of your lifes. There are two ways to heal. One is a quick time event that occurs right when your shield drops to 0. And another by holding a button while you have no life. This second option can be hard during boss battles where you get hit while trying to heal and have to start over again.The worst part of this, is that both ways to heal are taking away before the final boss, so you have to deal with a subpar way to heal on a very tedious fight.  Honestly I gave up at this point. I was a KS Backer and while the game showed promised, it doesn't deliver. A extremely linear game, almost impossible to lose a collectible, no retracing sections of the map once you get an upgrade. And no way to track which items you have collected on the map or put your own.This game showed promise but didn't deliver it.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, that animated cutscene sure looked good, huh? Wish the rest of the game was at the same level of quality. Character and boss designs are good, but level designs, and combat mechanics are lacking. The rooms don't feel like the inside of a castle, they feel like a bunch of game mechanics where everything is just there for "gameplay" - which in this case, is a bunch of crappy platforming. Its not even challenging platforming, its more like just a change in movement animation where you swim or float through a room instead of jumping. The combat is the biggest weakness here. Setting aside the button-mash combat against brain-dead enemies that don't even chase you down when you're low on health, the health system undermines any chance of failure. You've got pips of health which are protected by a shield you can recharge at any time. That alone would be okay, since you have to pick your times to charge, but then they give you an item that does a quick recharge if you complete a QTE at the moment your shield is empty. From that point on, boss battles started ending on the first try simply because I couldn't die. Even playing more recklessly didn't matter much as long as I got the shield charge. And after blasting through a dozen bosses that all died in the first attempt I quickly started losing enthusiasm. The combat doesn't have any depth with combos or puzzles that might keep you engaged, its just a mash-fest. And with a mechanic that almost guarantees infinite health, there's not much else here besides seeing the design of the next boss.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid Metroidvania that leans more heavily on the Metroid than the 'vania.It's refreshing to see more indie games drawing inspiration from classic Metroid when so many lean towards Castlevania and Dark Souls influences these days. Right off the bat, it's very apparent that 9 Years of Shadows is calling back to Metroid Fusion, and its open-but-guided zone progression reminded me a lot of Metroid Dread.The combat is probably the strongest part of this game, feeling fast-paced, snappy, and satisfying. It manages to wring a surprising amount of depth out of the basic 2D formula by adding in a heavy attack that can be chained in as a combo ender and a charge move that can be powered up while you dodge enemies. It's the defensive mechanics that make 9YoS *really* interesting, though. You start out with just two pips of health (which can be increased later, but only up to a maximum of four) with no way to recover them outside of hitting a save room. Fortunately your health pips are protected by a generous shield bar that can be recharged very easily through normal gameplay. The fun part is that in order to use your ranged attack (which is often required to make bosses vulnerable), you need to expend some of your shield bar for each shot. When your shield bar depletes fully, you can partially replenish it by either stopping to go through a short animation that leaves you vulnerable, or hitting a skill check that recovers a smaller chunk instantly.Needless to say, this makes for fairly relaxed moment-to-moment gameplay offset by far more intense risk/reward boss fights. I had an absolute blast with this combat system, and it stood out as a genuinely fresh take on a genre that often retreads the same ground.The boss battles also stand out as worthy of praise. Mostly they're quite simple - only a handful have more than a couple of attack patterns to worry about - but they do a great job of throwing such a broad variety of bosses at you that it more than makes up for it. Combined with the novel combat system, I felt like I was running into fresh new challenges every few minutes.The exploration side of the game is solid enough, but fairly basic. While you're rewarded for hunting down secrets, it's far from mandatory. You get a good set of movement abilities over the course of the game that blend a decent amount of Metroidvania staples with some fresh and original ideas. None of them particularly blew my mind, and a couple felt a little clunky and flow-breaking to use, but for the most part they do their job well.The only real gripe I had was the final stretch of the game. It feels like you run out of new content to see (besides bosses) after you get all your upgrades, which I want to say happens close to the 60% mark. From that point on you're just interacting with variations of the same enemies and puzzle elements you've seen before, which started to drag a little in the last couple of hours. The final boss, too, feels a little weird and out of sync with the rest of the game. 9YoS is fairly forgiving compared to a lot of modern Metroidvanias, but the final boss is a massive difficulty spike compared to the rest of the game, occasionally in unfun ways with attacks that are unavoidable if you happen to be in the wrong part of the screen when they wind up. Your regular healing mechanics are also taken away for narrative reasons and replaced with a slowly regenerating shield bar that I think is supposed to feel more powerful, but ends up being far weaker and less interesting than the active recovery mechanics you've had for the rest of the game. This left me with a weird taste in the end, with the final boss, while being a good challenge, feeling a little sloppy and jarring.All in all, though, this is a fun, snappy, fairly short Metroidvania that does enough to feel fresh and unique while still playing into lots of familiar ideas. The movement feels great, the combat feels great, the art is great, and the pacing is pretty solid most of the way through. Definitely worth a playthrough for fans of the genre who're looking for a slightly different flavour of action platforming.

_childDocuments_.review: A great Metroiodvania, and a bit of a hidden gem. Good story, controls are tight, and the combat is satisfying. The protagonist, Europa, is a well trained, highly skilled warrior who moves with grace and swings her halberd with finesse, and this is extremely well communicated to the player. The overall "feel" of the game is excellent!Difficulty is moderate. The bosses are not too punishing. It may takes a few tries, but you learn their attack and movement patterns and your victories will feel earned. The game does a good job teaching you how to use your abilities, and if you're mindful of what the games gives you, no fight will seem unreasonable.  This game has a system where health and mana are shared, and it's the most controversial topic I see in other reviews. Taking hits and using ranged attacks will deplete it, and successful melee strikes will slowly fill it, and you can regenerate most of it once depleted by holding RT for a few seconds. It took me a bit of time to warm up to it, but quickly found that it provides a good balance - ranged attacks are unlimited, but the more you use them, the more vulnerable you are. It encourages using a mix of melee and ranged, and allows you to "heal up" anytime when in between fights. Later, you can unlock a Gears of War style "quick reload" which allows for very aggressive play style when mastered.Is it a good system? For this game, I think so. Could it use improvement? Probably. Could the devs have used a more traditional health mechanic? Yes. But it's refreshing to see ideas like this, and it fits this game well.And of course it has to be said - the sprites, artwork, and music are amazing! It'll hold up forever.
