_childDocuments_.review: With a plethora of Metroidvanias in the market, why would anyone want to play 9 Years of Shadows? Well, this one has aspects that help set itself apart from the crowd. First, instead of a typical health bar, you have a shield gauge (called the light bar) that can either be recharged once depleted via a QTE or by hugging your teddy bear companion (it makes more sense once you play). You also replenish your light bar by damaging enemies.This might sound like it makes you invincible, however, enemies hit hard. Even walking into some enemies is enough to completely drain your light bar. So this helps balance things out. Additionally, unlike in games where you have a separate gauge for magic, your light bar is also tied to your magic, so any abilities that use it will drain it.Another unique addition is the pseudo-Mega Man armor aspect. You have four (technically five) suits of armor that each apply to a certain element and are needed to get through certain obstacles areas. You can switch between them on the fly, so it's not like Castlevania where you need to equip a certain soul to use its ability. Certain enemies are also weak to a particular element, though a lot of times, it's the same enemy but reskinned to be weak to a different element. There's no other gear besides the armor sets and halberd, so if you want to create your own kind of build, this game will not provide that for you.The combat is pretty simple. You have a basic attack that you can create a 3-hit combo with and a single strong attack. That's about as deep as it goes apart from shooting light magic. This is a bit unfortunate, as there are no RPG elements like in an Igavania, so you can't do anything more than this and you're most likely going to be dealing between 2 to 9 damage to everything.The one saving grace for all this is that the game is not long. My clear time was about 9 hours (of shadows), though that was mainly due to looking for the last few items, which is another thing to discuss. Unlike the Metroid games, Igavania games, and the Metroidvania games that I've played, there is little backtracking involved in this game. At most, you go back some rooms to access a point you couldn't before, but it's still in the same area. This is great for making progress, however, it's a nightmare for collecting all the items.The main problem with getting items is that you're likely exploring each area that you visit, so you're filling up your map as you traverse. Once you're in the final endgame, though, it's really hard to figure out what four rooms you missed. Even when I looked up a map online, it was extremely difficult to find those rooms. And the last item I needed was in an early-game room that I had already visited but couldn't get to because I needed the fourth armor skill. This is something that none of the other items did, so this one being set up the way it was is outrageous.Moving on to the plot and characters, the story is simple. It doesn't do anything extraordinary, but it's not bad. Europa is a decent character, and her idle artwork in the elevator reminds me of Samus Aran (which is AWESOME in my book), but unfortunately, none of the other characters are really much interesting apart from maybe Apino (the teddy bear spirit that I mentioned earlier). They're just there, and even Draythus (Europa's rival) is uninteresting. The opening cutscene made it seem like there was something profound, and while information is given, the execution fell flat for me.There are a few main gripes that I do have with the game, mainly due to backtracking for the items. First, while hearing Europa's internal monologues in the elevators are nice, once you run through them all, you only have the "..." speech which you have to advance or skip before she can exit. This is very tedious when you're backtracking like I was, and I'd much rather have an automatic loading screen than have to manually advance this "loading screen." Also, there's a weird bug where several bosses I defeated came back, so they caught me off-guard, and I had to beat them just so I could continue searching. My last one is that there is no marker indicating that there's an item in a room that has not been acquired. This would help cut down searching tremendously. Metroid gave a good template to help remind you that there's an item in a room you've visited. This game needed that.All in all, I enjoyed this game despite my criticisms. Had I played this last November this would most likely have qualified as my game of the year. If you enjoy Metroidvanias, this is one I recommend. And even if you're skeptical about this one being different from all the others, it's truly a unique entry.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely gorgeous Metroidvania with a nice, heartfelt story to tell.It initially felt a bit on the easy side with its regenerating shield/light system (which I was *FINE* with, to be clear), but then the difficulty was ramped up considerably. Some bosses felt like I was playing a bullet-heck game, and... there's a reason I avoid those. I'm no good at them. Still, with some perseverance I managed to make it through even the optional bosses, but to be honest the final boss was too much for me, so I cheated. Maybe I'll have the skill to defeat that boss one day, or maybe the days when my brain and body could do something like that are firmly behind me. Regardless...The art is top notch, and I'm pretty sure I'm seeing some magical girl, Gatchaman and Super Sentai inspiration in places for the armors and transformations. Possibly some Kamen Rider as well. The music is also great, and I really adored that the game's save rooms had Europa playing a little tune on a piano to save.That said, the criticisms come here:- The accessibility menu is pretty barren and really could have used some options to make the game easier.- The map's color-coded sectors don't always work, and would have benefited greatly from either an automatic or player-controlled marker system. Super Metroid marked items on the map in 1994, after all.- There's a potential soft-lock in the Portrait of Demise area, as well as some other game state issues not being saved, and the Horned God boss unexpectedly respawned when I revisited his room later.So not a flawless game, but still one I warmly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: This game is wonderful. The art style is lovely, the mechanics are creative, the Metroidvania influence is clear, the gameplay is fun and (at times) challenging, and the music is good. The storytelling is... okay. It's not bad necessarily but it's definitely the weakest peace of an otherwise stellar game. One of the best features of a Metroidvania is, in my opinion, that every death feels deserved. I never die and go "OMG that was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!" -- every time I die I know exactly what I did wrong and what I can do better the next. Not all of the bosses are difficult, but the ones that are are very fun and good fights. The exploration is satisfying. The way you progress through the zones is satisfying. I've played a lot of mediocre-to-bad Metroidvanias, and this is absolutely not one of them. It deserves a place in your library if you like this style of game at all.

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely Dark Souls + SoTN.  I do like the game, and the direction it took. the art and music are great. I bought it on sale and mainly play on steam deck, so its worth checking out.  But beware, the difficulty is brutal.  I'm more of an exploration fan over pinpoint control attack mechanics or brutal bosses one shotting you kind of games. Not going to lie- I ended up hacking the game with cheat engine because i get annoyed when i die to dumb things like hitbox detection or very subtle lag I just wanted to unlock new areas.   The game feels good platforming, but the combat has a tiny bit of lag/animation at times which can kill you.  Maybe its that I am just old now.  I'm over 40 and ive lost my gaming reflexes.  This game reminds me of Ninja Gaiden difficulty on the NES.But I like playing these kinds of games to feel more powerful as I go exploring and unlocking new areas,  I don't seem to feel more powerful as i progress, i like to plow through old areas to explore, and getting gibbed for half my health and thrown in water while things are shooting at me from 2 directions then die kind of kills it for me.  Yeah "Git Gud" i know ...  its like the game just needs a little more tweaking to be a 10/10. Maybe patch in an easy mode for casual people, who are the ones likely to give games like this a try and grew up playing Metroidvanias.

_childDocuments_.review: It's very much Metroid Fusion, in so many ways, and it's absolutely phenomenal for it. The story is incredibly cute and sweet, being very much about redemption and recovering from trauma, and the combination of your health and mana bars, meaning that your spells bring you closer to death but that you can always heal with a well timed auto reload or by hugging your teddy bear ghost results in some very interesting and rewarding combat. _childDocuments_.review: The game railroads you into exactly one path at all times. Backtracking is often impossible, and the only time it is necessary is when passing through in order to reach a new area you unlocked. Metroidvanias are greatest when you need an upgrade to reach an area, multiple upgrades do the work of reaching it. Maybe there's two paths to the new area, using two different powers. Or maybe it's locked behind difficulty which is lifted when gaining a new powerup. None of that is here, because this is not a metroidvania.The movement is snappy and works well with stretches of tension without checkpoints. However, huge majority of the fights can be basically skipped by standing outside the range of the enemies and shooting your infinite bullets into them. There are few enemies which are immune to bullets, thank god, and are the only source of meaningful combat outside of bosses.But the bosses? All bosses are huge difficulty spikes due to overworld lacking any meaningful combat challenge, they are still easy, don't get me wrong. You have basically infinite health as you can hold m2 between enemy attacks to recharge your health bar.The game especially becomes a slog at the end. Only 9% of players have unlocked all powers, which happens at about halfway-point of the journey. It's clear why the game lost everyone: All your powers are used in the same way they were used when they were introduced. Even when used together, you are doing nothing new with the mechanics. The game never starts throwing out more complex uses of the powers or requiring better timing, platforming, combat or puzzle solving.The plot is... Fine? The characters aren't uninteresting but never elevate above their archetypes. None of the attempted plot "twists" change the perspective of the story. So the entire storyline is more flavor text than anything else.This game's world makes no sense. I can understand a cowboy character with a real world revolver if we assume that bullets can be as avoided easily as in gameplay. But you can find a musician with electric pianos. So this world has handguns and electricity, yet we walk around with a halberd. It's not even enchanted, just a normal piece of metal. Where are the helicopters to take down this ancient evil? Did nobody just come up with the idea of using electricity for anything else than an EDM kit?Pixel art is made of abstraction. Due to the limitations in pallet size and smallest possible detail, you cannot represent anything perfectly. For example, the main character lacks eyes and mouth in the overworld sprite, leaving nothing but mess of pixels for the mind to fill in....So why does the game flip between detailed comic style for character portrait and these abstract pixel art style in-game? Why use pixel art in the overworld if each pixel must represent a detailed face or garment? This isn't a big issue on it's own, because the pixel art is mostly incredible, however:The game likes to rotate pixelated objects so that they leave the grid. I understand that they want to have smooth rotation animation for some attacks, but doing that the easy way by ignoring the pixel-bound aesthetic of the game ruins the entire appeal of pixel art. Go for hand-drawn aesthetic if you want to do that: The artist(s) of this game clearly know how to draw anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: A by-the-numbers metroidvania that looks absolutely gorgeous and features an interesting health system that does work though takes time to get to grips with. I had a great time with 9 years of Shadows; largely carried by the visuals with the rest being plenty good enough but not much beyond that. The other standout IMO was the number and variety of bosses; they try a bunch of stuff some of which works and some doesn't; but they are always interesting and good fun.

I don't want this to end ...I miss the Teddy-Hugs already ... even though, I was this Monster-Killer Machine Assassin Rogue in the end ... Such a beautyful piece of art .... I will see, how often I am going to replay this ... I cannot not replay this!...Edit:I come bac from time to time to beat the endboss.It is incredible, how the game taught me, to do it every single time.It is like a sport now.A warm-up.A friendly play-fight wth an old friend.And I still cry everytime at least once or twice, while the ending is scrolling ...I sing to the end-song. It is great to warm-up my singing voice for any particular day.To tickle my inner emotions and wake me up.(I just did ... and sth happened.My character was auto-dodging while I was hitting the attack-button. But at random ... still ... I went on ... it was so weird ... I had to learn the boss new in a way ... while my character was RANDOMLY auto-dodging ...and still, somehow, with the last sliver of my life ... I made it through the boss-fight ... it felt like the game was giving me AGAIN a new taks to deal with ... ...and I was able to overcome it ... Immediatly.I dunno. WHat. Is. Going. On.With this game ...even after all ths, it keeps giving me riddles and tasks to solve ...(maybe I have to check my controller ... dunno).)Gr8 game. AWESOME experience!And the music. The music keeps giving as well.( I still listen to the Portrait of Hope Soundtrack practically everyday. :3)Thank you so much, for being there.For creating this.

_childDocuments_.review: This is soo good. I know Plano de Juego since 2 years ago, I can't believe this game is finally in my hands. The art and the music is very unique, and you can tell the references to other videogames such as Castlevania, Hollow Knight, Zelda, Metroid, etc. I've only played for 3 hours so far, but it got my heart since the first second. It does has some bugs (i.e. sometimes the coins go below the floor and become unpickable) but they don't affect the overall experience. I LOVE IT!! Makes me want to continue my video game project from a year ago.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this. The character design and color thing is a cool idea. But then they really don't do anything with the color. You see it all for 98% of the game. I forgot about it for a moment until it happened.Some of the bosses are just annoying with attacks that really don't let you attack.Speaking of bosses. I've had FOUR incidences where the bosses are just randomly back. There's the same exact conversation before the fight as the first time you fight. 3 times was the gun dude and 1 time was the necromancer or whatever he was. It's a pain in the ass when I just want to pass through the area.Then there's the end game. You lose your ability to self heal and in it's place is a constant heal. That's great for exploring and can sorta let you keep boss fights going longer. But it takes getting used to. I do dislike the time it takes to actually start the self heal. Ultimately though, losing the active heal isn't too terrible since any bosses you run into at that point will just smack you enough to get rid of what you healed anyway.I'm still going to beat it since I just have two bosses left in the game including the big bad end game boss. But it's just disappointing.I finished it and 100%ed it. The story is cute. A lil predictable after the half point but good.I know people complain about the final boss. But after upgrading the final armor, it took maybe five more tries. It was kind of annoying. But it wasn't THAT bad.It still didn't feel near as good as I'd hoped.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good, it's an indie Metroidvania.  The health system is a bit weird but you get used to it.  You start with only 2 health, and mostly rely on a shield.  The caveat is that shield refills as you hit and kill enemies.  In addition when your shield is fully depleted you can charge it to about 90% in a few secs.  This can be done in battle but requires timing.  The level design and music are good quality.  The only thing I didn't like was that the dash is backwards like some vampire style games.  A directional dash would have been more fluid.  There are a few particular enemies where this gets annoying and ends up making you get hit when you meant to dash away.Overall worth playing and supporting.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: "5 hours of competence" was used in a review article and I think that is apt. The game looks beautiful, but it's nothing more than "well executed" in all areas and doesn't excel anywhere. I didn't even end up beating it because it just got boring after a while and it's never fun when a game like this slowly becomes a chore.Saying that; I would give this something in the range of 5-6/10 and would only recommend it on a steep sale.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, the art direction is amazing and it plays very tightly, which made it very enjoyable to complete. Its not trying to reinvent the Metroidvania genre, it does have some original ideas but it still flows similarly to an old Metroid game, which isnt a bad thing in this case.Difficulty-wise, I found the game to be on the easier side, with some tough fights (and some kind of BS fights lets be honest). Its not easy in a way that is negative, its more like it was easy or casual enough to go through the game in a good amount of time without burning out. I personally liked the life bar system, while it was frustrating at time, it also allowed you to look for openings and safe spots to recover either to deal bursts of damage or to not lose vitality.The story is coooooonvoooluuuuted. I had some thoughts at the start and midway but by the end some things are revealed while a looooot but I mean A LOT of basic plot points are never explained or fully addressed.The OST is amazing, its jazzy at times, atmospheric at others; but always very fitting.The quest system is alright, if you explore things fully, you'll naturally get the quests and clear them.Definitely would recommend to play this if you're looking for a more casual Metroidvania experience that is not going to try and suck 20-30 hours out of you.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: I know only a little about metroidvanias, yet I have thoroughly enjoyed this. After playing for a while, it exceeded all my expectations. The controls are fun and easy to use. I love how quickly you unlock new abilities and powers, some of which open new gameplay forms (I worship the Mermaid form). The art is the best part; it's all so unique and detailed, it feels so unique compared with other pixel games, and the  VFX brings everything to life. The music is so good, and every sound fits perfectly. I would say not to expect perfection, but this game is far from a "broken mess," probably, patches will improve whatever early issues, so don't worry. This is your game if you want to have fun and enjoy an exciting but not annoying story.For the price, it's worth it. So many games are released every year, yet, this one feels different; you can tell how much love and dedication the devs put into this game, and after seeing how kind they have been to their community, I'm more than glad to support such a fantastic team with a delightful game.And if you are unsure if you should buy this game, as a tiny ghostly bear called Apino once said, just "Twizzi." And I felt that in my heart.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: The game started out just fine.I did run into an early bug where my gamepad would not let me proceed with some conversations.  I had to use my left mouse button to do it.  Which is weird because the button that connects to is not the button you use to progress with all other conversations.The first portrait boss though illustrates the biggest problem with the game, there is not progression difficulty scaling.  That boss is harder than the last boss by a huge margin.  The bosses before it were really easy, but it was immensely annoying to have that large of a jump in difficulty and then it go back down to easy for the next few bosses.Another example is a late game boss where it is a ninja.  The whole fight is to hit the one that is completely different looking from the clones it summons.  You never take damage if you hit the right one.  There are normal enemies that are harder than this boss.In the end, I just decided not to finish the game after a crash on the last boss, who was not hard.  It was the last frustration and since there was no reason to try again, I just watched the ending on youtube.  It has a random plot point that just feels creepy to no end.  I mean professing your love for a teddybear is just not right.So, I would not recommend this game to anyone.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent first entry by a Mexican developer. (viva mexico ;])However, I have criticisms and one of them being random crashing. Beat it but sadly the game "froze" during the end credits which also mysteriously did not reveal themselves. What saves this game from these game breaking crashes is the art direction and soundtrack.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: The one positive point i give to the game and the only reason I bought this game is the amazing art style. The pixel art is great, the characters look great and the music is nice and chill. HOWEVER!, this game feels like a really long DEMO. Enemies are brain dead and serve no other purpose that to block your path. The story is very much rushed and the pacing is all over the place. Characters barely have anything to say and the bosses have no rime or reason to be in the story. The armors and color matching enemies seem like a nice game mechanic but they only difference is how fast you can kill an enemy. whats more the armor abilities are bare bone and very niche to use (except the Poseidon armor that has a fun movement option)  The game play is mediocre at best, bosses are just boring to fight since you can infinitely heal if you are fast enough EXCEPT for the last boss where the mechanics you have relied for the whole game is taken away from you. At the end you get the "best" armor that in reality is the worst of them all. Your healing is automatic and all other armors become obsolete because of the damage calculation and invulnerability mechanics. The game also has lot of annoying bugs that soft lock you when you get items or get to a room with an enemy you cant hurt so you have to die and good luck if you haven't saved in the last 30 mins.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: This game has wonderful art and music. The gameplay is good enough, though I was expecting some larger differences in the combat between the different armours. It would have been nice to have indicators on the map that show collectibles that you've already collected so that you don't have to scour the entire castle for notes blindly after the fact. I had 3 crashes throughout my playtime which isn't egregious, but for the best experience I might recommend waiting for a stability patch. All in all, I had a great time playing this game and if you like metroidvanias I can only recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable SotN clone. Spikes in difficulty when facing a boss but most of the game is easy mode. Some of the mechanics are cool but not well implemented and fully thought out. Controls are pretty tight and game-play is enjoyable. Would benefit greatly from some more/better fast travel points. Will say this: The music is absolutely fantastic and the graphics/aesthetic is great. The world the developers created is very interesting as well. Overall very enjoyable and rating it an 8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: So like.... I'm torn. I picked this up after backing this studio's new game to see what their first game was like, and it definitely feels like a first game. Let's start out this way - I would recommend this game. It's a fun game, the music is really good, the art style is cool, the character portraits look good, the combat is overall fun, the different armor is neat, the traversal is enjoyable, and some of the bosses are a blast. If you like Metroidvanias, you'll like this! ...IFIf you can deal with the whole 'first game' aspect. Bosses are fun... except some have awkwardly long runs back if you die, and unskippable too-long intros.Bosses are fun... except when you just have back luck and they chain strings of their most annoying attacks, and it stops being about fighting the boss and just repeating the same jumping pattern until they calm down. The music is really good... and you'll hear the same tracks a LOT. Traversal is enjoyable... but there's not really a good fast travel system, so the game feels padded out by the traversal. The different armor is neat... but ultimately kinda same-y. Each one gives you a different traversal skill, but doesn't really change combat in anyway other than matching colors up with enemies. By the end, I was honestly kinda hitting a wall. Instead of scouring the map for the last couple items I missed, I just went to the end boss and banged my head against some of the things I mentioned before (Thankfully that one has a short run time) But lemme be clear - there's AWESOME stuff in this game too. Some of the boss fights are absolutely fantastic, and the controls are tight enough to make you feel like a lot of close wins are super earned. I really liked the overall look and sound and feel of this game, it just got a little long in the tooth trying to cram in a bunch of extra boss fights without making the core of a Metroidvania--going back and forth across the same map--more engaging. Still pick it up if you love Metroidvanis though!
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful Pixel Art, smooth gameplay strange and unique characters and well realised lore, Fantastic OST  and just an over all well realised Metroidvania with some smart map design that lets the player know where to go for the main story while offering plenty of chances to go off on your own to find secrets.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: This is not an easy recommend.If you aren't prepared for ten minute boss fights that demand your focus with little room for error every time you walk into a boss room, you are going to have a bad time.The bosses and even regular enemies feel like they have just a bit too much health. Every fight feels like it goes on for two or three minutes longer than it realistically should. The final boss especially has such a punishing array of awkward attacks in a four phase fight that takes literally seven or eight minutes of straight combat that leaves very little room for error. If that doesn't sound like your kind of game, don't even bother.If it does, the game is pretty, the music slaps, and the harder, more interesting fights might give you a sense of satisfaction if you manage to persevere.Even then, temper your expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best metroidvania i played in 2023 so far. I love the Art direction, the Spritework is gorgeos and the writing as wall as the music. When it comes to the difficulty i would say the game is definitly easy for veterans of metroidvanias but i had a couple of bossfights that i had a few deaths on. There were a lot of Boss fights for a game of this scope which i appreciated a lot. But outside the big progression encounters a lot of the minibosses were definitly too easy. Exploration feels limited but never empty. At the end i had a maxed out character without trouble finding the little secrets. I ran into a couple of bugs. Most notably one where i could not move my character after a dialoge trigger and had to replay from my last save. But other than a few minor hicups i really enjoyed my time with 9 Years of Shadow a lot. In the End i would for sure recommend this game to any fan of metroidvanias.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a completionist like I am, stay far away from this game. The game keeps freezing up during the cutscene after the final boss. and tbh, within the genre, there's a ton of other games that are way more deserving of your time. _childDocuments_.review: Pretty decent.  Has a great original art and music style.  There's a kind of color theme that is not super important but it's stylish.  The HP/MP mechanic is unique, your HP and MP share a "light" bar.  When it gets to zero you can hit a QTE to heal about 66%, or if you have the time you can break away and smooch your Estus teddybear for a 75% heal.  If you get hit while your light bar is at 0 you lose an HP, and you only have a few of them.  It's original but it makes the game pretty easy overall.Worth a play if you play every single Metroidvania but want a little fresh flavor.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: This is a Metroidvania.  It ticks off all the boxes for what a Metroidvania should do.  It's not particularly challenging, and it's fairly linear and fast-paced (I 100%d the game in about eight hours).  If I had had higher expectations, or it had tried to stretch out its gimmick longer, I'd probably have been disappointed.  As it was, it was a good popcorn game -- buy on sale, play through once and enjoy its lush visuals and sympathetic characters, move on.  It's a very soft recommend -- if you're not already a fan of the genre, start with one of the genre standouts like Sundered or Hollow Knight -- but it's pleasant enough.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this was definitely one of the (if not the) best experience I had in a Metroidvania for a long time.Outstanding graphics, amazing OST and a good character development, so please... Just play it when you have the $, it's worth it if you like Metroidvanias and mandatory if you like Greek Mythology.Final Score: 9 crystals and one teddy bear. 10/10!
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: I originally was going to give this a thumbs up.  Then I froze on the last boss, got angry, and submitted the review w/ a thumbs down.  Now that I've finished the game and cooled down, I've decided I shouldn't give the final judgment based on crashes.  It's fair if others do, I obviously understand.  But the game is over for me now, so I'm trying to look at it as a whole experience.But man...the crashes during screen transitions and when I froze on the last boss was EXTREMELY frustrating.  Game has been out for a month and crashes are still a thing and now freezing mid-boss fight???  PLEASE FIX THE CRASHES.Anyway, I'll still do a pros a cons.Pros- Great music.- Amazing visuals, both in terms of the pixel art quality and general aesthetic.- I dig the story and the main character Europa.  It's a fairly touching story.- Interesting combat in concept.  The combat mechanic of ammo=health is neat.  I don't dislike it in concept.  I do think it needs some tweaks (see below).  Melee'ing and shooting any direction simultaneously makes some encounters more fun.  Swapping between "forms" can be fun and intense at times too.  Kinda tedious in other encounters.- Some cool upgrades.  And the final form is a neat idea to change up the gameplay.  Although I know some ppl feel it's a big nerf.- Some bosses have some real neat mechanics.Cons- Ammo=health needs to be tweaked.  It totally gimps you in some boss fights.  You can only reload (read: heal) while standing still on the ground or by having a randomly placed insta-reload gauge on your reload timing meter (if that makes sense...Gears of War I'm told is similar).  But some boss fights force you to NOT be on the ground.  So one slip and you are unable to heal and just take damage.  Let us do the charge heal in our various non-land forms and don't make the reload meter randomly placed.- No directional dash, just a backdash.  This is a preference thing, but...I REALLY don't like it.- No shortcuts (no REAL shortcuts) or meaningful fast travel means traveling or backtracking can become tedious.- No camera control (i.e. look down) can lead to some spike damage from falling you cannot see.- Questionable hurt/hitboxes at times or on some bosses.- Crashes.  I crashed maybe 10% of the time during screen transitions (entering new areas or dying).  I know for sure I have crashed more than 5 times and my save file is 5.5 hrs, so that's about once per hour from the save file.  I have probably crashed closer to 10 or more times, which still fits the 1 crash per hour rate.  I think my freeze on the final boss was due to a screen transition between his phases/death.- No autosaves.  I get it, most MV's don't have autosaves because of "difficulty".  But when a game crashes, it's necessary.  Especially when it crashes after a boss fight and welp, time to fight that boss again!Neutral- Overall map, MV elements, and enemy design is meh.  Nothing great.  But not bad.  Anyway, I recommend this game if you don't crash.  The combat is interesting, though has some things I really dislike.  The story and overall experience is good for a shortish game.  My save file is 5.5 hrs, but my play time is double that, probably from all the crashing and having to re-do sections (and just dying to bosses lol).

_childDocuments_.review: It’s already been said, but to sum it up: boss fight difficulty spikes are frustrating, exploration isn’t rewarding, upgrades are underwhelming, ranged attack aiming is bad (maybe just on the steamdeck?), and the elevator transitions will have you mashing the A button. The game is beautiful to look at but that wasn’t enough to keep me playing. I might come back to this one.

A lot of effort has been made on the design. I really like the theme.Combat so far is OK.  I only did one boss fight and it was ... weird ... but I've managed.I recommend this one more for the ambiance than the gameplay.  That's a first I believe.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of metroidvania games, especially ones with a female protagonist, and I would say that 9 Years of Shadows is a pretty fun addition to the genre that had the potential to be a lot more. The combat in the game is quite fluid and the art is gorgeous. The concept of the switching elemental armours, each with their own special movement mechanic, is quite well done and satisfying to navigate around the map in.  There is also a very interesting story line with the MC voicing her inner thoughts during elevator transitions. All in all the design and mechanics of the game are very solid and the controls are nice.The problems that I have with the game are in it's rather short play time and overall difficulty. This game is very easy. The enemy variety is lacking with very simple attacks that are easy to dodge or avoid. Even the bosses are straightforward with only a couple of them giving any noteworthy challenge that only lasted until you figure out all of their attack patterns. There isn't any fast travel except for an elevator in the middle of the map so back-tracking is kind of tedious; though there is also a distinct lack of motivation to do much back-tracking, which is a core staple of metroidvania games, anyway since there are only a few collectable power-ups, most of which you don't have to go far to get. Some people have complained about the health system but it's honestly not bad. You have a shield and a couple points of health. The shield energy is also what you use to shoot with so part of the game-play is managing it but it's not hard to do. Getting hit depletes it very quickly but you can recharge it most of the way by pushing the right trigger for a second or so. Honestly this is easy to do and only the most difficult boss fights prevent you from doing this easily when needed. The shield will also completely negate any attack even if there's only a sliver of it left. This contributes to the ease of the game since I felt there was little risk of dying unless I screwed up mid fight.I would rate this game as a solid 7/10 Metroidvania. It has everything in place to be a 9-10/10 game but unfortunately it isn't there.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: In general, a good, enjoyable game, a little bit short tho. I enjoyed the music, the art and the story. The gameplay is fun when you have all the upgrades, but before that the game goes a little bit slow.Charming characters, but I feel like they could have said more or in particular cases appear more.It has some achievements that are bugged, I fought every boss in the game but still have some achievements not unlocked, same with the achievement related to unlock every ability.saying all of the above, I find this a great game, also considering this is the first game developed by halberd studios. I was waiting for this game since it was announced by Champ, the owner of the YouTube channel "Plano de Juego", and I, who has some hype, think the game's worth it. If you come without expectations, you'll find an entertaining game and a good story.101% completed in 10 hours ( I'm a slow player)P.S. I almost never used the back dash
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like 9 Years, I really do, unfortunately there are a couple of glaring and minor issues that I'm hoping will get addressed in later patches.First, the minor annoyance. The level design is, in a word, "fine". Nothing memorable, nothing to get you excited and nothing that really sets on area of castle apart from the others except for maybe "this area has plants" or "this area is partially submerged". It serves it's purpose, but relative to the games in the genre, the levels feel uninspired and bland, fairly rudimentary even.Now the two biggest issues I've had with the game are the number of unity crashes and the cheap deaths. The unity crashes seem to come at weird times, but usually when loading in from a save, or respawniing. It's not a constant barrage, but enough to get irritating.The second are the cheap deaths. The game isn't really difficult per se, there are some nice boss fights to be had, but nothing that ever made me feel like I was being pushed too hard. The issue was I was more often dying because of some wonky hit-box detection, or a mechanic that wasn't tuned quite right. Using the Portrait of Hope boss as an example, dying because you were apparently clipped by one of the mid-round bullets when you were a good three or four pixels away felt bad. Also, getting clipped by the phase 3 mechanic, utterly depleting your meter and having almost no breathing room to recharge it if you happened to miss the timer because you were busy avoiding getting hit again also felt bad.There's a good foundation here, and I like the take on the elemental mechanic al a Deedlit, I just hope some future patches can address some of the crashing issues and tightening some of the nuts and bolts could probably turn this into a really great metroidvania. As it stands right now, it's hard to enthusiastically recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Do not buy this, if you want a Metroidvania that's tough and/or long, it isn't. (Approx 6 Hours)It has a very Linear approach, and most stuff to progress is very gimmicky, it's still fun to see the flow between the Forms in the later Part of the Game, Bosses have relativly easy to learn patterns, maybe one or two moves that take you more by surprise than others.I wouldn't say that there is much wrong with the Game (read some People had crashing Issues, but only had a Single one myself), for the most Part everything is solid enough, it's just the Question on how deeply you're in the Metroidvania Rabbithole, and if you are a Beginner or a Veteran, and actually want Veteran Difficulty, if so just avoid this one.So what most People would put into negative with the Game apart from Crashes, is exactly what a newer Player to the Genre actually might enjoy:Enemies don't have great Variety - so Movesets are well known earlyish onProgression is more or less Linear - easy enough to find your Way around, not to much has to be rememberedNo alternate Weapons - So there is not much you can alter in terms of combat Style, so by the end you're used to the pattern.Story is pretty generic, but that's rarely a strongpoint for the Genre anyways.Graphics are great, sound does it's  Job.Only thing I myself would mark red:Dialoge/Cutscenes can't be skipped after having seen them.Elevator Animation still shows even with no more Monologue available.So again if you are a Veteran and want some Hollow Knight level of Gameplay, this might not be for you.If you are more of a Casual or Genre-Starter, or you just wanna have something you can play with your Kid, you  will most likely have Fun with the Game.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: The game is half-made and you can see that from the first minutes of game-play. Overall is just disappointing and not fun at all. Structurally there are so many bugs and resource consumption even after all the updates that were supposed to fix it.There is a lacking of enemies, they just recolor the same over and over using different elements. This is one of the most lazy ways to try to add variety. The gameplay is boring since you will find one or maybe two enemies per room, even the larger ones.; They drop coins that later in the game you will find that you cannot do much with it.Its sad to see a new Developer publishing a half-baked product and just taking the money, they announced a new game that they are working on and i wonder if that will be equally as bad as this one.Please read all bad reviews before purchasing this one, steam just hided all problems and complains.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately despite a number of cool features like the armour changing and a few fun mechanics, I have dropped this game. This game doesn't respect your time and is so convoluted by poor checkpoints and massively long unskippable cutscenes for boss introductions that completely punish you for failing a dodgy Gears of War active reload system for your health.I wouldn't recommend this game as the metroidvania scene is full of other, more competently made examples that do not have the same short-comings of this entry.
_childDocuments_.name: 9 Years of Shadows

_childDocuments_.review: Been a little hesitance about a new metroidvania but this game is like a really an evenly Castlevania and Metroid game. It has a Metroid atmosphere but with controls like Aria of Sorrow or Order of Ecclesia. Although its short, I think the game stands out with other of the genre. Definitely will keep playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Smaller metroidvania game (~5-6hrs) which had me enticed from the beginning. Has a risk reward combat system that did originally put me off, but came to love in the end. Art style and music are damn astounding. _childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Nailed it with the graphics. The game is vibrant, well animated, and extremely polished.-The soundtrack is also excellent.-Several bosses reward paying attention to game mechanics, as just beating your head against them won't end well.-The plot is interesting and the protagonist is likeable enough.Cons:-No fast travel. The closest thing you'll get is an elevator that runs thru the central area.-Linear gameplay, as you venture into new areas many of the collectibles are found behind very obvious and breakable walls. The maps you unlock for each region even highlight rooms you missed. Backtracking to explore previously unreachable areas is something severely lacking in this game. You'll clear out an area and won't have much reason to return later.-Bullet hell towards the endgame. Several lategame bosses will eschew telegraphed attacks in favor of PROJECTILES EVERYWHERE HAVE FUN.-No replay value. This game would benefit greatly from a randomizer mode or an alternate character run.Despite the flaws I did enjoy this game. It's no Hollow Knight or Ori and the Blind Forest, but those games raised the bar way too high. I wouldn't pay full price for 9 Years of Shadows but definitely scoop it up from a sale/bundle.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel very disappointed about this game. It is SO BEAUTIFUL DANGIT, but there are so many flaws along the way that it just becomes a dry, boring play. Positives:Probably the single most gorgeous metroidvania I've ever seen. EVERYTHING is beautiful and incredibly well crafted as far as the graphics go. The various suits of armor are flashy and cool-looking, and add a nice elemental twist to the combat.The animations of the character and the enemies are all beautifully done. The bosses are absolutely beautiful, especially the main bosses of each area - they are imposing, gorgeously designed, and quite intimidating in a number of cases. Negatives:The combat is severely lacking. Everything feels too fast - you can attack, attack, and attack, but you really don't deal much damage. Most of the enemies are fairly spongy, and there's simply not enough reward for fighting or attacking them. You get currency that you can use on a handful of upgrades, and the upgrades simply don't do enough to be meaningful. The damage boost you get from them is dismal to say the least, and the gameplay makes these upgrades entirely optional to obtain. There is a secret final upgrade, but it is likewise entirely missable. By the time you can get it, you simply don't have much use for it. On the note of the combat, changing between suits of armor bears the promise of entertaining new animations for attacks, but these are tainted by the fact that nothing else changes about them. They all attack at roughly the same speed, and there is no damage boost for using one or another unless you are fighting an enemy weak to your element. This makes using a "favorite armor" practically worthless, as none are really better than the other, combat-wise. Additionally, in a game where beauty is clearly of the greatest emphasis, I found the solid elemental color outline of the character and enemies to be downright distracting and bland. There are so many ways to make that look more attractive and interesting while still getting the point across about what element is being used. It feels like the developer took a significant shortcut there, and it simply wasn't merited in my own perspective. The story has the potential to be intriguing, but it simply is not the majority of the time. The main character is pretty bland, her dialogue doesn't feel particularly meaningful, NPC interaction doesn't feel like it furthers the story that much, sidequests are frankly pretty boring, and there is a massive amount of REALLY interesting lore that is just not catalogued or explained in a satisfactory way. There's a lot going on in the game that would benefit from additional explanation of some kind, even if only in the form of "scans" like those of Metroid Prime.The level maps are not particularly interesting in design. Tons of platforms with little variation. Platforming challenges are somewhat limited and require a minimal amount of effort to complete. The bosses, despite their incredible design, are frequently too easy to defeat. That's not to say that there is NO challenge - I died at least once to several of them, especially to the minibosses. But their patterns are too easy to figure out, and bear little challenge after doing so. The main character's backdash ability is all but useless. Where most games with a dash/dodge mechanic add invincibility frames to ensure you can dodge anything with the right timing and skill, this game does not. You are vulnerable throughout the entirety of the backdash, and it doesn't move you that far back to begin with, making dodging with it painfully unpleasant. This game has so much promise. I love the general premise, and I think that there is an incredible amount of growth that could happen here. As it is, I cannot recommend the game in its current state. It simply does not meet many of the criteria for a quality metroidvania.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought this game was great up until I got to about 90% of progress. As much as I wanted to leave a positive review to balance out the negative ones on here, I simply cannot. While the graphics/animations are beautiful and many bosses very creative and fun (Mask of Hecaté and the chess boss especially), the main problems that the other reviews mention are present - the lack of fast travel (which results in repeated and therefore boring traversal of the world) and the sudden change in mechanics by the 90% progress mark. The game becomes simply unplayable, because whenever the player gets hit by virtually anything, it is necessary to stop and wait for good 10ish seconds before the Light bar starts filling up again. This makes the game incredibly unfun, plus unncessarily difficult.I really enjoyed the game for the most part and I can see that a lot of care was put in it. But it is very frustrating for me to simply have to uninstall the game before finishing because of the aforementioned issues - has anyone beta tested the last section?Once a patch comes out, I will be happy to finish the game and change the review to positive. Up until then, I recommend you only purchase this game as long as you are happy with dropping it right before the end of the story (or grinding it until you beat the impossible mechanics).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is honestly pretty good, which you can't really tell by the first couple bosses (and reviews).  It takes a while for the fluidity of the level design to pick up, but once it does it starts to make the game feel like less of a chore when you're backtracking and more like something that was meant to be in the core gameplay.With that said, I hate some of the mechanics and while I haven't finished the game yet, I hope that if there aren't any difficulties unlocked upon completion that there are mods that bar off the use of the quick-time event that gets all of your "ammo" back.  The reason I say "ammo" is because this mechanic can be greatly abused against bosses to store hp and makes what are pretty well designed boss fights into a mashfest until you have a sliver of your temporary health (ammo) gone.  As long as you aren't losing permanent health, there isn't really much risk.Otherwise, the powerups are well designed, while I'm not a story person with games, the character dialogue isn't just total nonsense and I appreciate that other characters are in the tower that add to the world building such as the painters.  This game really showcases what a competent developer can do when taking the right concepts from the right games, and I encourage anyone wondering if they should give this game a chance to give it a shot.  The art, soundtrack, and long-term combat are really made with a labor of love for the genre and overall this game is a success for its time.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is a mixed bag, so I supposed I will break it down.Story:There isn't much, but in short. Europa enters into a tower or something, and encounters a bear. Who is tied to the events on what is happening. For the longest while, there isn't anything going on until near the end. Sure, there are dialogues and whatnot, but nothing really links together until a proper story forms near the end.Mechanics:Europa can use five forms. The fifth is obtained near the end of the game, and replaces her first. Anyway, this game works with elemental affinity. However, there are quite a bit of times when you cannot match the correct one, due to the environment. Aside from this, there are also a variety of skills obtained. And music notes is collected to upgrade your light bar and health.Dungeons:These were actually well made, given how the platforms links together well. It is a smooth experience on this end.Boss Battles:This is where we get into the main issue with the game. Starting off, collecting the forms. The boss battles are time gated. This means, you have to survive until your opportunity arrives to break their shield with light to be able to damage them. Some of these ones are so long, that it is just annoying. On top of this, some attacks are impossible or near impossible to avoid. And if you do not have any light, well. On top of taking damage, you can miss opportunities to break their shield and have to sit through a long stall session.This shifts around 60% into the game, where it takes on a more traditional form of combat which is nice. Though, once again suffers major issues with the last battle. With it being four phases, a lot of things on screen, and sometimes you are just unable to avoid attacks. You are not healed between phases, and the last phase was just poorly designed. With everything just being thrown on screen.To this note, it does appear every time you die and continue, the fight gets easier. And on that note, why wasn't the game balanced better?Damage/Defense:Damage is essentially fixed, no crit or anything. This plays into elemental affinity which is kinda worthless, especially near the end. And you can increase this by upgrading your forms. Defense also doesn't matter, as there isn't a defense property. Just a light bar that takes hits, and each enemy will knock away a set amount before getting to your life.Before you could have used a feature to instantly get back your light bar to a certain extent, with each one giving less. As well as you had a manual charge to recover a lot. Near the end of the game, this was replaced with a vastly inferior one. You get a slow auto regen for the light bar, which can make battles a lot more frustrating. Once again going into how the game isn't balanced well.Music:It was good, could be better.Art:The art in the game is amazing, and they do well to show this throughout the game.Overall:I can recommend it, but know the issues you are gonna encounter going in. If the game was better balanced, it would have been much better. Needless to say, it was generally good. And I did enjoy the characters, and the story once it got started.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is good. Controls are tight, exploration is satisfying and rewarding, the bosses are interesting, and the depth of the gameplay really opens up as you complete your arsenal, as is proper for any Metroidvania. Generally speaking I'd rate it an eight or a nine out of ten, a deeply satisfying experience, but I'm missing a boss from my beastiary and that's the only thing keeping me from 100% the game, so that's kind of driving down my enthusiasm for the game at the moment. Don't let that deter you from playing - I encountered no real bugs or glitches while otherwise playing through, and I will be revisiting this game one day.EDIT: Less than an hour I may update this review to be uniformly more positive because, apparently, the boss respawned and I just had to kill it again. This was not intended, but I'm just happy to say this game is done and dusted. Satisfying narrative, satisfying exploration, gorgeous art and music - I look forward to this team's next game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tragically underrated game, a victim of its own innovations. A metroidvania with a heavy emphasis on its unique gameplay mechanics.  Exploration is intentionally streamlined, each zone is explorable and full of secrets, but once cleared is never returned to (unless you missed something). Hidden walls show up on the minimap, making them easier to catch the first time around and reducing backtracking. The areas feel like "levels," and are very well-designed, but basically disconnected from each other in practice. For some, this is a negative, but for me, it makes the game much more relaxing to play so I can focus on what is NOT streamlined -  The mechanics! This game has an incredible set of unique gameplay mechanics to juggle, and understanding them is CRITICAL! There is an elemental system, using the right element at the right time grants bonus damage. Your health is extremely limited, but you have a permanent mana shield. Spending mana unleashes a powerful projectile, but also flirts with death if you don't use it wisely. When your mana is depleted, there are a variety of ways to get it back, making you essentially invincible if you juggle them properly. All of this put together means that once you really understand the combat system, you'll be waltzing through enemies (and even bosses) that previously 3-hit combo'd you to death like they are nothing, and it feels GREAT after struggling to find the balance of offense and defense. Think of the combat as a puzzle - if you brute force it, then it's hard; if you use the right tools at the right time, it becomes easy.  To top it off, the art and music are superb. The music invokes Michiru Yamane's gothic jazz vibes, and the art - well just look at the screenshots. The story and writing are not incredible, but not offensive either. The world and characters are believably held up by what is there, and the game doesn't attempt to waste your time with anything more than that.Gamefeel is good, controls are responsive, plenty of boss and enemy variety, healthy pacing of combat to traversal puzzles. Long enough to be worth the price, short enough to not overstay its welcome or feel padded.tl;dr: Excellent game that has a clear goal of being a streamlined, gameplay-focused metroidvania, absolutely crushes that goal, and then brings in gorgeous art and music to make it even better.

_childDocuments_.review:
For 9 long years, the world has been submerged in the deepest of shadows, robbing every object and living creature of their color. Once a thriving civilization, the people have forgotten the warmth of the sun, the joy of laughter and the promise of a prosperous future.

Many brave souls have tried to venture inside the corrupting depths of Talos Castle, a long-abandoned orphanage from which the curse stemmed, but with each futile attempt, resignation became the daily fare for the people, all hope lost. Except for one person.

Armed with little other than her halberd and sheer nerve, Europa's daunting quest is clear: enter the castle, find the source of darkness, and return color to the lands before it is too lat

name: Broken Roads
detailed_description: Born of a love for traditional computer role-playing from franchises such as Pillars of Eternity, Disco Elysium, Fallout, Wasteland, Tyranny, Pathfinder, and Baldur's Gate, Broken Roads provides a rich, engaging narrative in which players make their way across a desolated future Australia. Blending together traditional and all-new role-playing elements on top of a classless system offering nearly unlimited character development options, Broken Roads presents players with an original morality system: the Moral Compass. This novel design sees dialogue options and questing decisions influence, and be influenced by, a character's philosophical leaning. Immerse yourself in a game world set in post-apocalyptic Western Australia filled with intricate lore, deep history, and compelling characters. As you embark on your epic journey, complex storylines, branching quests, and memorable encounters await. Uncover hidden secrets, unravel political intrigues, and confront moral dilemmas that challenge your assumptions about right and wrong. Every decision you make shapes the rich narrative, leading to multiple outcomes and ensuring a truly personalized gameplay experience. From the grand overarching plot to the smallest details, the world is brought to life with atmospheric descriptions and vivid dialogues, delivering an immersive and unforgettable adventure. The game seamlessly merges classic RPG elements with innovative features, providing players with a unique and customizable gameplay experience. Building upon a classless system, it offers an extensive range of character development options, allowing players to shape their abilities and skills to suit their playstyle. The inclusion of all-new role-playing elements adds depth and complexity to the game's mechanics, intriguing moral choices, and immersive narrative arcs. The Moral Compass introduces a groundbreaking morality system that goes beyond traditional notions of good and evil. Instead, it focuses on a character's philosophical leaning, allowing players to shape their protagonist's world view in unique and nuanced ways. For example, a character who leans towards utilitarianism may prioritize the greater good, making decisions based on the overall benefit to society, even if it means sacrificing individual lives. With every tough decision that is made, the characters Moral Compass can shift, potentially making them more broad or narrow-minded or even able to change their morality entirely as the journey progresses. The system allows players to create a protagonist with a unique moral identity that influences their journey and relationships, but also is influenced by every choice they make. Roam the vast Outback, explore decaying urban centers, and navigate treacherous desert regions as you uncover the secrets of this hauntingly beautiful and dangerous land. Survive, fight, and forge alliances in a unique setting that captures the essence of Western Australia's diverse people and landscapes and brings a fresh twist to the post-apocalyptic genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly feel bad about giving this game a bad review, because the developers are reacting very reasonable to the feedback they are receiving and it's clear they worked hard on certain aspects of the game. I can tell love was put into this project. However, there are a lot of issues with the game that ranging from annoying, to buggy to just not compelling game design, and I don't think this package will be able to overcome them all. I'll pull some examples together from each bucket.Some things I found annoying;'c' the perennial hotkey for character sheet in the CRPG genre, opens up the moral "C"ompas. Unlike the character sheet, which I need to look at to level up my character, I don't have any active need to look at the moral compass, ever, since it shows up in every single dialog and the impact of a dialog choice on what I say is so clearly outlined, that it encourages min-maxing morality instead of chatting up the locals. When you have more than one party member selected and you want to talk to someone or interact with something everyone shows up and then adjusts to the proper formation of facing the person/thing in a flying v before the interaction occurs. It feels like madness.It feels, relatively speaking to other similar games, that I'm running slowly relative to the map size, it also feels like vision range is a bit short. I see my character at a full run, but it takes longer that I'd like to get to location and I have to make a lot of passes back and forth to see everything, this combined with the parties flying wedge shuffle (and general lack of interaction opportunities) make exploring feel tedious. Buggy:Got the same dialog option multiple times when talking to an NPC, selecting one immediately ended the conversation, then had to reopen the dialog and select another option because the game didn't flag as me being complete with the dialog tree, which was a prerequisite for the main quest (this was the older gentleman NPC who is the mayor, and whose name I can't check right now, and I think it occurred while leaving the crossroads town). This was my mistake based on how the UI handles levels. Addressed by Draug in comments. I'm not sure what RNG system is in use, and I'd love to check and see if what the die rolls were doing but it took me between 24 and 30 shots to score 4 hits (to kill two training dummies) with a 40% probability. The expected value was 10 shots, the hit rate was 16.7% and the odds of getting 14 extra misses at 40% chance of hitting would win you the lotto. This was the only combat I experienced in my playtime to date, and I'v finished five, what I would call major zones. Design issues:Skills and traits feel like they barely matter, you get a very small pool of cheat points, I'm pretty sure checks are based on raw skill score, your cheat points can be used once per level, so they should be very precious and impactful, but I only had one opportunity to spend them, I went with it and spent virtually my entire pool, and I made a football throw check that appears to have done nothing. I've never seen evidence of another skill check being performed.There's no tension in this game. No fights, no checks, no time pressure when events that seem like they should be time sensitive occur, no dynamism in NPC interactions, escalating stakes or difficult conflicts, if you don't start problems, things seem to go off pretty much without a hitch. I won't say there's no choice and consequence, it's more like even when things are going sideways in the plot pretty much everything is under control, does it matter how much I explore the site between the first two towns (spoiler avoidance), I think it doesn't to be honest, seems like you can take off any time and nothing I learned seemed to help me later. As a showcase for Australian culture it's fine, but as a game that sucks. Because of the above points, it doesn't matter where you put your skill points. I'm okay with having multiple solutions to problems, and locked content is fine, the first place that choices should matter in a free form CRPG is your character sheet, but with limited opportunities to fight, use skills or otherwise meaningfully showcase your character choices, it feels empty. Finally the world itself feels bare bones, the majority of npc's have one line to say and won't open a dialog box, The interactions between NPC's feel all deterministic and pre-scripted most of the people who will actually talk to you early are vendors. You really don't have any way to make money early game, nor as far as I can tell, much use for any of these items, so it's got this very 'why can I only buy from everyone I meet and who for plot reasons won't ever be able to return to' type of feeling. On the plus side, the game has a very nice look, it's very fleshed out in some odd ways like item variety the voice work so far feels solid, each location has a uniqueness, which is unfortunately overshadowed by the lack of ways to engage, and so far it feels very Australian,  with the lingo, the camels, the kangaroos and the environment. I'll probably keep pushing through it as a cultural experience, more than a game, but it's unfortunately kind of boring from game-play and participatory experience perspective, which is sad because they put in the legwork a high fidelity game with at least serviceable underpinnings, which is the hard part of game development and kind of missed the mark on the pacing, content and execution, which feels like the less demanding part of the equation.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of reviewers lamenting the lack of a neutral option ofr giving a review on Steam, and with this game, I finally understand why.Only this time, it is less of a neutral review, more of a "let someone else buy it and support the devs" kind of deal.Onto the game itself: If you are reading this and are at least somewhat like me, you probably read the description and WANT to like this game. You WANT the morality system to be good. You WANT the setting to entertain you. YOU WANT to believe that it sounds promising. But the game will leave you wanting.The best description of the first few hours are best compared to a TTRPG game with a bad DM. A DM who has a story to tell, concepts to play with, but treats their players more as a passive audience, rather than participants. It does not care how you want the pacing to be done. It does not care what options you want to try. It does not care whether you are having fun or not.To give an example: the first 5 hours of the game are a linear series of fetch quests with one (1!) scripted fight, with no choice of where to go, and with very limited variability that does not tie into the actual predetermined outcome of the events. Five hours of walking around, talking to NPCs whose names start to blend together, and picking your preferred morality choices in dialogues. The morality system is in itself a very questionable gimmick. While marketed as genre-redefining, it... just isn't. It reads like a first year phillosophy student infatuation rather than serious exploration of possible topics. It does not ask you questions - it asks you to choose from four basic answers:'I value personal sacrifices if they are productive''I value sacrifices because I think that they are neat''I value opportunism as it severs the interests of me or my group''I value opportunism because screw everyone else'The quotes of classic philosophers on load screens don't help either. If your morality system revolves around aphorisms that are 500 years behind current ethics discourse (at best), and it plays as an online personality quiz, it is a first draft, not a genre-redefining characteristic. My fall-off point was after the first major quest in a settlement where you are roped in to help one of two candidates win an election for local governor. This is a classic concept for RPGs - and I did not think it could be messed up, but alas. It is a perfect illustration for this game: your actions during the quest do not matter. At the end of it, you watch a cutscene that erases the impact of your actions, some characters act out a scene while you stand by and do nothing, and the story goes onward without even acknowledging that you may have tried to achieve a different outcome.The DM wants to tell a story. Shut up and observe in awe.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a rare thing, to get a proper cRPG these days. Rarer still, to have one set in my own country. To see the bush, native wildlife or to hear the Aussie accent, instead of the same old Americans. It's got nothing to do with patriotism, but the idea of a role-playing game set in Australia could have been something really special.I love role-playing games, with everything ranging from the Infinity Engine to , and it's clear the devs feel the same. The original  has long been my favourite (and peak) of the series, so from the moment I came across the booth at PAX Aus 2019, I really,  wanted this game to succeed. Unfortunately, I can't say that it has. This game does a lot right, but in aiming for the sun,  comes up short. And that's a real shame.To understand why, we first need to look at what kind of game this even is. One of the first big missteps is a result of that influence I mentioned earlier.  this is not, and if you're coming into  expecting that, you're obviously going to be disappointed. Of course, that's not a bad thing, but now that I've played it and got a proper feel for the game, it's not like any of its major influences. It's not an existential character drama like , it's not mechanically deep like  and it doesn't have the strong worldbuilding of the Forgotten Realms.If anything, I'd describe it as a spin on  with the same kind of disposable characters, laborious combat, quests only there to justify gameplay and lacking the depth and "soul" of the greats. If that wasn't bad enough,  makes the baffling decision to frontload the first part of the game with a long,  sequence of heavily scripted quests that awkwardly pulls the player from one location to the next before the world has had any chance to breathe. Even now, writing this review, I barely remember any of the characters' names or who they are beyond the surface level. The central morality system that was meant to be a game-changer is just... the same alignment chart we've seen a million times before. Worse than that, I don't have any reason to care. Is it truly Machiavellian when the fate of a NPC that ran onscreen 30 seconds ago is now in my hands? And sure, it's not fair to blame  when the issue of meaningful nuance has been plaguing RPGs for decades, but the compass was  as revolutionary. All the quests I've encountered so far have been pretty straightforward, dialogue can have its moments with personalities shining through, and then they just... end. The writing is fine, but that's a whole other problem because it rarely stands out. It also leans heavily on lingo to the point it feels over the top. I mean, I'm Australian and no one actually talks like that. Couldn't you have dialled it down just a bit and focused on being genuine and authentic? Because it detracts from those little moments of Australiana that do hit home.On a better note, the art direction is beautiful. The iron red sands of the outback, rusty shacks nestled between Eucalyptus trees, roos hopping along through shrubs. The whole world has this worn, cosy feeling to it and textures use a paint brush style that adds to that feeling. I also really like the soundtrack, with some of the music reminding me of Nick Cave and Warren Ellis' work on  and . is very much an indie game. Before you start applauding my ability to state the obvious, that's the best way to sum things up. Drop Bear Bytes did a good job with what they had, the team genuinely deserves respect for what they've pulled off, but this is an ambitious game that was clearly made on a tight budget. Anyone who's played an RPG before knows they tend to come with their fair share of jank, but  goes beyond that. It lacks major quality of life features and feels unfinished.Combat is really rough. It has fundamental design issues that I don't understand how they got through playtesting, such as being unable to click on enemies that are either behind or too close to party members as a result of the fixed isometric camera. Or having to wait for the whole party to line up every single time you interact with something. There are no shortcuts either: no way to end turn, no alternative to clicking the skill and item wheel, no way to speed up how slow each character is... even the cover system is a bit iffy. Crouching down behind something with a shield indicating full cover doesn't seem to do anything when a party member is hit anyway.And good luck, because there are no tooltips or combat log. I can't rebind any of the controls and I can't turn off subtitles in cutscenes either. While the visuals are great, the UI has that cheap Unity feel.Maybe I'm missing something, but I can't split the stacks of items either, which makes trading difficult. I don't want 5 Lamingtons, just 1... but I guess I have to buy them all. Dialogue is functional, although it can lock up a bit when going from the trade screen back to previous lines.Even if this all worked perfectly though, it still doesn't change the fact that the character progression, combat, economy... it's all as shallow as the random, pseudo-intellectual philosophy quotes. I've been picking up items the whole way through, radio parts and then a working radio, rope - which if you know, you know - and I've got tonnes of water and food in the party inventory. Some books, batteries, crafting ingredients and other stuff. But what's it all for? Why am I investing in combat skills that sound nice, but I don't ever feel the need to use them? This is meant to be a long game and yet my character is already over 100 with the ranged weapon skill and there's no tangible difference anyway. Builds don't seem to matter, party composition doesn't matter and loot is completely unremarkable, if not useless. Combat is a chore with very basic encounter design.To be fair, there  been lasting choices, such as a character living or dying, and the player backstory feature seems to offer a substantial change for how things kick off, although I haven't played the others to see how it goes. When it comes down to it though, this is meant to be a narrative-driven game but lacks anything to really engage the player. Nothing matters, so what's even the point of continuing?I hate to do this. If it's not already clear, I really did want the best for this game and the dev team. Make no mistake, there are glimpses of that in the time I've spent with  but frankly, I don't have it in me to continue. Perhaps I'm way off the mark with this, but my suspicion is that something went very wrong behind the scenes. If you've been following this game for a while, you may remember that it was set to release late last year when, just a few days before release,  went silent and changed to 'Coming Soon'. This doesn't happen out of the blue. Whether it's publisher interference, contractual issues or running out of money, it's clear that development hasn't been easy as the game's been pushed back again and again, year after year, and changed hands several times. That being said, it still doesn't excuse the shortcomings of the final product. We can only judge what's in front of us on its own merit and unfortunately,  comes up short.You may very well enjoy the game, provided you're willing to look past its many flaws and lack of depth. The setting is unique, if nothing else, and I appreciate what the game tried to do. But this ain't it. The resurgence of classic RPGs has seen plenty of hits, but even more misses as indies claim influence but fail to live up to expectations. Beyond the art style, for every part of , you can find better elsewhere.
