_childDocuments_.review: This game has greatly improved since launch and is now genuinely fun to play. As of June 2024 I had minor quest progression, graphics and game-play glitches, but because the game maintains several rolling auto-saves it was always easy to reload before these glitches.I really liked the game's writing, world building, visual style, sound design, and use of over-the-top characters and situations to examine 'tricky ideas'. The 'Punt' system (a pool of one-off skill check % boosts that refreshes when you level up) is fun, I just wish it also let you boost skill ranks to unlock dialog checks (in a perfect world doing this would trigger some Australian 'she'll be right' flavour text). The combat is functional but not super mechanically deep, so manage your expectations. The stats and systems are crunchy in the way a CRPG should be, although some skills don't really seem to do much until you're punished for not having them (Throw, Tinker, etc.). The moral compass system (perks and penalties that unlock based on your in-game morality) is genuinely great (more games should unlock friendly fire as a perk if your character is a jerk!) and I'd love to see it expanded if there's ever a sequel or expansion.It's not perfect, but I enjoyed this game. My heart goes out to the Devs who, from what I can see in these forums and based on the recent major patch, have really leaned into the honest and direct feedback that's been provided here and elsewhere. You can see how much love they have for the game. I wish it had launched in its current state. If you liked CRPGs like Planescape: Torment, Tyranny, Tides of Numenera or Colony Ship you should give this game a go.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not only the roads that are broken in this game.Pretty much every mechanic is not well implemented. Combat is awful and there is no reason why sometimes you can't target an enemy. You play behind scenery and you only have outlines of dead enemies on top of the ones still active. You can't rotate the map to see what's going on, sometimes you get thrown into a fight just because you enter a new location. What a mess.You could think the story would save this but no, it's very boring. The Morality system is genius but once again not well implemented and the story will take you through, no matter what choice you make, because you have to go there to make the story progress. The only difference is the type of answer you can give but overall, the choices don't have the impact they should.You can't make any change to your crew unless you equip them and get out of Merredin. But if you want to move equipment between to character you have to equip them. If you don't remember what they have there is no way to look at their gear. Because it cost 1 ap to switch weapon, you waste a turn with some of your character at the beginning of a fight because they spawn to close to an enemy with the wrong weapon.Enemies only seem to have one level of difficulty so they are very tough at the beginning, but after level 12 they become super weak. Keeping track of what quest is what is the biggest problem here. you end up with 20 quest open just because you talk to NPC. sometimes the game does not track what you have complete so I have mission with checkmarks saying I have completed all the step but they remain active. hitboxes of object on the ground like cadavers doesn't always work, same for point of interest sometimes you click and nothing shows up.Voice acting is terrible. and inconsistent as some line are read and some aren't for the same main character.The whole thing is super clunky and gets more frustrating as you play. edit :THANK YOU TO THE DEV FOR THE RESPONSE AND I WILL PROBABLY CHECK THE GAME AT A LATER TIME TO SEE HOW IT HAS IMPROVED. Good Luck.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the setting, I love the atmosphere but the gameplay is just so clunky and bad. The combat system is atrocious. There is no hex-grid, you can't view the battlefield from a different angle or even tactical overview. Enemies everywhere are giga-op in the beginning, like I had to reload fights multiple times to hope for good rng on my hits and bad rng on the bad guy's hits. I really dislike the whole magic thing, that feels so tacky.From the description and the whole story up to that town it feels very athmospheric and immersive, however it all goes down the drain quickly. Once you are able to free roam and do quests, you will quickly realize that there is no real choice. If you don't do the quests in a pre-determined order you will simply fail. I had hoped for a better game as the setting and especially the little comic sequences are really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool. However the combat is so bad I can't bring myself to play further.

_childDocuments_.review: It's during moments like these that I wish Steam's review system wasn't so binary. While I try to stay detached from the games I'm to review, one or two slip by this self-imposed rule. I won't deny that my anticipation for Broken Roads has affected my opinion of the finished product in one way or another. The idea of Broken Roads propagated by the mainstream press is a far cry from the game I played to completion. The game's witty Aussie charm and gorgeous visuals are let down by its underwhelming narrative, static game world, and barebones combat mechanics. But, if you're a newcomer to CRPGs, then Broken Roads may satiate your urge. Even then, my suggestion is to wait for the developers to clean up the remaining bugs.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh Boy, i would love to reccommend the game, you can see the love poured into it. unfortuneately at this stats its simply no fun. i finished the game after about 11 hours and exploring everything, being max lvl. the game feels short, the story is okay but underwhelming for what i expected. combat is boring and very easy after a certain point, characters feel bland, there is barely any interaction. the morale compass and choices sound nice on paper, in reality they dont really matter. same goes for skills, there is a handful of skillchecks in the game, not enough to warrant the amount of skills, really. i encountered two bugs, where i couldnt finished quests. once questgiver simply dissapeared, never to be seen again and another didnt have the option to give them any money, like the quest said i should. the bog bad boss didnt survive the first round of combat, which is underwhelming. i hope the upcoming patches can fix some of these issues. the setting is awesome and interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is grossly overpriced for what it is.I was excited for Broken Roads when the demo hit early access, and it left me wanting to know more about the characters and story in the post apocalyptic land down under.  Sadly, the 'more' part is lacking and tells a barely coherent story after it picks up where the demo left off.Broken Roads starts off very strong with a colorful cast of characters and does a great job in its initial world building of a hard life in an unforgiving land of hostility and mistrust.  Kill or be killed, eat or be eaten, cooperation only when you stand to gain something of value in return, mercy and compassion in small doses when it costs you nothing to simply be 'nice'.  The main story also starts off strong and I found myself wanting to know more about the handful of rugged men and women of the Scouts who treat each other like family in every sense of the word.All of that starts to fall apart when you arrive at Merredin.The best description I can give without littering this review with spoilers would be the story and direction of the narrative felt like a table-top roleplay session.  One where the DM had planned out the first hour of play, then started making ♥♥♥♥ up on the fly past that.  So many things, like the election debate and the events that follow behind that, are both clumsy and disjointed in its delivery.  The cinematic and voice narration that serves to advance the story during this event may as well have been speaking in a language I didn't fully understand.  It throws many, many names and emotional responses at you like a room full of people all talking at the time, about the same thing, but almost none of it meshes together in a meaningful way.  The who, the what, and the why I should even care was a serious question at this point, and I found myself struggling to find an answer.Combat.  I'm not going to bash it for its lack of depth and complexity.  Does it need to be complex?  No, not really.  Should it at least be fun?  Absolutely!  Is the combat in this game fun?  Absolutely not.  It serves its purpose in the most basic of ways.  No more, no less.I gave serious consideration to starting over just to see if maybe I simply missed things the first time around, but to be perfectly honest, I don't really have a desire to do that or continue my current save.  I can't recommend this game to anyone.  Not in it's current form.

_childDocuments_.review: The wasteland is as classic a setting as you can pick for one of these things and I am normally down for that. I love games where you have to gather your party before venturing forth, and it’s clear Broken Road’s dev team did too. This is a traditional as hell CRPG with isometric exploration, turn based party combat, and really masturbatory philosophical inquiries—the game onboards you with a little ethics quiz that places you on a literal moral compass.All of that is cool, all of that I want, but Broken Roads just has an execution problem. Despite a feature list and named store page inspirations that suit my tastes, this one has not resonated with me.I’ve spent about nine hours begging for it to come alive and ended up landing on a reinstall of Wasteland 2 to scratch those itches instead.Because Broken Roads isn’t terrible, it’s just a little boring. I know it sounds stupid to call one of these things “slow”, deliberate pace is practically a core genre tenant, but Broken Roads takes forever to get to the point.I was three hours in before I got my first non tutorial combat encounter, and by then I had maxed out my sharpshooter stat from all the story quest experience that I didn’t even get the satisfaction of feeling that progression, and was nearly a god by the time raiders became part of the equation.The first two of four acts have you completely on a leash, following highly scripted sequences and teleporting between towns that need your help or need your subjugation depending on your disposition. You’re basically a passenger until the game finally eases up the reins in act three and gives you a map and some broader objectives to pursue as opposed to just clicking around town and playing dialogue tree Simon says.Let’s start with some of the good, though. Broken Roads’ wasteland setting isn’t as generic as the screenshots suggest, thanks to an infusion of Australian culture and even mythology. You’ll spend time meeting with aboriginal tribes, with a strong enough commitment to authenticity that it uses those CRPG dialogue mouseover tooltips for Aussie slang and locations instead of fantasy lore.That is awesome, and the fact it was made by a dev team from home turf makes Broken Roads’ location feel like more of a cultural export than it does a classic video-game setting. You guys gotta start calling me a ‘legend in my own lunchbox’ if I get too self aggrandizing.It’s also a pretty game. Despite animations that can’t always keep up with the intensity of combat and key story moments, the actual art style itself is beautiful. It ties everything together into a smeary water-color look that’s easy on the eyes.Thematically it constantly reinforces themes of authority and community: what each of those are and how they should be used when the ‘wasteland’ has set everything back to zero. It’s that community theme where Broken Roads starts to get a little tired, though: it beats that drum so hard but doesn’t really tie any interesting gameplay systems to it.Almost every single town I visited followed the same format. Meet with the town elder, learn their problems, determine if you want to help or undermine their presence at the top, and most importantly do their quest that asks you to talk to every single other person in town to introduce yourself.It gets real old, real fast, and I think part of the problem is that this ethics pie chart was probably supposed to be commanding more of my attention than it actually did. “The Moral Compass” shifts and swings depending on the dialogue options you choose. Most of the non investigation dialogue choices fall under Utilitarian, Humanist, Machiavellian, or Nihilistic, but for all intents and purposes that seldom changes how the actual mechanics of CRPG dialogue play out.You get a tree of options to pick, some are tied to your stats and background and now some are also tied to your morality. Ok.It’s cool but not, uh, ‘genre redefining’ like its store page and some fluffier previews made it look. It does end up tying some combat boons and passive traits to your placement on that pie which is neat, but caring about those would also demand caring about the combat—which is one of Broken Roads’ least interesting components.You only directly level up your character and not your party members, which is why I assume Broken Roads is lenient about equipment. From what I can tell there’s no stat prerequisites for nearly anything; there was nothing stopping me from equipping every single party member with a sniper rifle, then literally just clicking on every single opponent in every single combat encounter right from their starting location.If ammo management and conservation or stat penalties for improper equipment were on the table I may have been forced to pivot or make use of alternative strategies, but if there is anything in Broken Roads that punishes this behavior I didn’t come across it in my time spent. Interesting encounter design just wasn’t a major design priority, most of your fights will be the randomly generated kind you get while exploring the overworld. I ended up just not engaging with them because they were strategically unsatisfying and, again, as far as I can tell, there’s no punishment for just hitting the flee button every single time before combat starts (aside from the opportunity cost of not looting and getting that experience, I guess).The whole thing feels underproduced, and maybe a little too vanilla to make tolerating that underproduction worthwhile. You know how CRPGs will frequently delegate intense scenes to artwork instead of animations as a budget technique?Broken Roads does that too, but it frequently will use a singular, still image for minutes at a time with nothing but voiceover. It doesn’t even have the decency to pan or zoom on the image, the game literally asks you to just look at a .jpg for like 150 seconds on what’s supposed to be dramatic scenes.The overworld map is just a triangle making its way to still images representing the different locations, and it doesn’t really do enough to abstract this with geography or danger or visual flourish. It just feels like a point of interest menu with extra steps, though points of interest may be too generous as well. Half the time you come across one and zone in there’s really nothing of note happening there.There’s little challenge, depth, or reward, and depending on which act I was in it felt like I was either being linearly shepherded through tasks with no agency or aimlessly walking around doing nothing; and without interesting character building opportunities or combat, I haven’t felt too bad about walking away from this one.The reason to play Broken Roads is for its setting and its focus on sharing Australian and Aboriginal culture, and its occasionally provocative ethical questions. But the game stringing those concepts together tries so hard to be traditional that it’s just kind of bland, and fails to give me a reason to not just replay one of its muses. It’s a competent budget recreation of the CRPGs that inspired it, but lacks their depth of systems or satisfying stat-driven teambuilding. I hope the people who may resonate with Broken Roads do find it. For me, I don’t think I’ll be sticking my beak in it for any longer.

_childDocuments_.review: This is barely a game, and I don't really think it wants to be.Let's get the few positive things out of the way: The atmosphere and graphical style is great, and the uniqueness of the setting elevates the game a lot, but it is not enough to carry it on its own.Also the developers are nice and didn't try to pin the unsuccessful launch at the customers.That's it.Everything else is either lacklustre or plain bad. The story is barely functional, and relies on nonsensical random plot twists to invalidate player decisions, freeing the developers from having to actually acknowledge the consequences of said decisions. Player agency is at a minimum anyway, oftentimes the game will directly deny you logical actions and force you to a certainAt one point I was kidnapped (along with all the party NPCs who weren't with me at the time) and teleported OFF SCREEN to the next story location after telling an NPC no to a quest offer. It was so jarring that for a while I thought it was a bug, but no. That's how this game rolls.And it's not just the big things. Your character doesn't matter. Ever. The story decisions are either made by NPCs or are quickly made completely irrelevant by some random plot twist. Your character's skills and trait never come into play. (in 5 hours of playtime, I have seen a singular skill check, which was to throw back a football to some kids). There are no clever mechanics or little side quests to interact with the world or play around with the game's systems because there aren't any. There are only fetch quests: go to A, bring back B.Writing could maybe save it, but while it is competent and even good at times it always fails to involve you. NPCs can talk about their relationsships to each other or tell you about themselves but there is never a conversation to be had. "Tell me about X" is all you can do to interact in this game, and there is never a chance to REACT anything. In the aforementioned kidnapping incident there wasn't even an option to go 'Hey guys, we have just been all kidnapped randomly off screen from various parts of the city and we apparently never even put up a fight, that's crazy, huh?', because your character doesn't really exist in this story.As for the 'groundbreaking' morality wheel, it is almost laughably simplistic. You get 4 moralities with fancy names, and your character can have access to two of them at once. This essentially means locking away half of the dialogue options for no real reason. If you are a 'nihilist' than you can never make a 'humanist' choice, you know just like in real life there never was a person who occasionally made a choice that goes against their established pattern. That might be interesting and we can't have that.It also makes your dialogue choices amount to nothing, since dialogue is scarce in the game, and the changes you make to your established 'morality' are minimal, so you are pretty much stuck with what you picked at the beginning and that's that.The worst part though is how smug the game is about it, even bombarding you with fancy quotes from famous philosophers in its loading screen, like a collage student who just sat through his first philosophy 101 lecture and thinks that he is a wise sage now.There is also combat. It works, technically, but you always get the impression that the game doesn't really want it to be there, kind of like it doesn't really want you to be there. You are just in the way of its amazing story with your pesky guns and decision making.As I said in the beginning, the devs have been nice about criticism and there has been many promises about sticking with the game and fixing it. While that is admirable, I really don't think there is fixing this one. Just take the loss and learn from the experience. That's what I am planning to do with my wasted time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely review games.  Mostly because I do not consider myself a literary talent.  However, in this case I felt compelled to write one.I've been playing cRPG's since 1992.  I started with Ultima Underworld and realized that I was hooked.  New worlds opened up to me and allowed me to create some assemblance of myself in a game and send it out to  do great things.  I've been playing them ever since.Now this takes me to "Broken Roads".  I really enjoyed this game.  Took me about 39 hours to complete it.  I wasn't sure what I was getting into when I first started, but soon I was swept up into it's world building, characters and heart-rending events.Some of the high points for me were as follows:* Loved the music!  Total chill vibe that made me think of the outback.* Loved the fact that you weren't superhuman and only you could be the savior of the universe fighting against some world ending organization or being.  You were just a person caught up on the conflict of growing up in the wasteland and you have to figure out how to make your way across the land solving quests.  How you do that is up to you and what path you take can lead you to different ending at times.* And the biggest thing for me was something I didn't expect and loudly exclaimed "NO WAY" when it happened.  MAGIC  some people.  (That's all I'll say about that)* Enjoyed the turn-based combat.  The leveling was straight forward and not overly complicated.Now all this being said, the game is not perfect.  There are some quests that need better explanations and I would love it if you could use your companions for statistics checks.  (Example: My tinker skill is 10 but my companion is 70.  Having them step in and use their expertise would be cool)  There are some other small issues as well, but the devs are hard at work putting in patches and QOL fixes.I will absolutely play this game again and I give HUGE props to this small indie company who I believe could be a huge hit in the future.  There are some moments of brilliance in this game and I expect it to flourish as they continue to make improvements.  I'm looking forward to their next game as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Walked out of the Flaming Galah pub and clicked on a random NPC in high-vis, who threw his arms up in response and yelled, "You wanna fxxking go?" Haha sadly 10/10 spot on.As an Aussie and RPG lover I was super stoked to learn about this game and played the demo. Incidentally, I got distracted (looking at you, Kenshi) and didn't pick it up at launch. When I did come back to check it out, it was getting smashed by negative reviews. I grabbed it anyway because there was no way I wasn't playing it!It's not Fallout. It's not Wasteland. It's not Atom. It wasn't hard. It wasn't long. It's not perfect. There were things that bugged me. A lot of skills didn't seem important. But I had good old casual fun with it, though I'm kinda biased since the game spoke to me. What a breath of fresh air to hear my accent in a game, to see my slang, to have places I know or have been to mentioned. I laughed out loud when Dead Ringer gave his slant on the State of Origin. (A side note, )The art was beautiful throughout. My favourite locations were the Lake (name escapes me) and Koorda Underground - very pretty artwork. This game was made with a lot of love and heart with little details like DJ's satchel and Jess's hat. The critters were gorgeous! I'm not Indigenous but the Koorda quests were probably my favourites - helping people because they're family. The cultural aspect was lovely and really highlighted Indigenous connection to people and country. DJ seemed to be the most fleshed out party member, maybe the only one.I didn't complete all of the quests. Some were minor and I just didn't know how to (couldn't seem to find a comic book!). Some were listed as mains but seemed like they were just on repeat (find more books!). Some I failed because I didn't talk people round, or progressed the proper main quest line before completing. I reached level 20 without issue despite this. Combat was pretty easy. I did end up being a one-trick pony though with all my team equipped with sniper rifles and my main using hydroheals. I don't think I ever used any medpacks. Raids were smooshed as they tried to close in on my team. Poor Big Baddie didn't stand a chance. I felt like there was going to be more content with a threat that is mentioned, but then I got the epilogue slides so yeah, nah :)I imagine most Aussies will get a bit of a kick out of this game. It's not perfect but I reckon it doesn't deserve to drown in the wave of negativity that smashed it. Thanks for the game :)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review in progress that I will update once I finish the game or at least advance some more.Game has strong alignment-based reactivity. Different alignments solve quests in different ways and the behaviour of NPCs changes based on your alignment with NPCs reacting differently to player characters of different alignments.Reactivity based on origins. For example: some quests are offered only to specific origins and your origin is quite often mentioned in dialogue.Multisolution quests are present, especially the big important ones. Skillchecks seem to come into play quite often as well, offering different quest/encounter resolutions.Game reminds of Age of Decadence far more than it does of Fallout or Wasteland, except the difficulty is not on the level of AoD.This is the kind of game that has to be played multiple times to experience all the content. Judging the game's length on the basis of a single playthrough is either dishonest or completely ignorant since all good RPGs with actual Choice&Consequence and roleplaying depth work this way.So far, I have absolutely nothing to complain about. The only thing that might be a problem to some people is that the early game isn't really rich in combat encounters, but that's not the focus of any real RPG. I do hope that as the game opens up, quest solutions via violence will become more frequent, but we'll see.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No, but it is a post-apocalyptic, turn-based role-playing game with tough moral decisions, mutated enemies, different party members with their own will, all in isometric graphics and with an exciting story. There can never be enough good role-playing games, especially when they are obviously inspired by my all-time favorite Wasteland (or the much more modern Fallout). It's set in Western Australia, the world has been destroyed after a nuclear war a few years ago and the law of the jungle largely rules again. Human civilization consists of the survivors of the apocalypse, who have retreated to small settlements and built a life using the remnants of our current technology, while strange creatures and (mostly) vicious humans roam outside the settlements. Resources are scarce, hunger and epidemics are the order of the day. Your friends are slaughtered soon after the game begins, and it's up to you to find a new home for the survivors and perhaps exact a little revenge. Mad Max sends its regards.The first mission immediately reminds me of Fallout - we have to escort a technician to another settlement to repair the radio. We then have to escort someone else back from the settlement through the dangerous wilderness. Bandits and other unfriendly encounters are to be expected. During the conversations, we often have the opportunity to choose our answer from several options. We can read the dialog already spoken at any time during the conversations. Which brings us to reading - Broken Roads is a narrative role-playing game, without reading it makes little sense. You shouldn't expect an epic like in Planescape: Torment, but there are some texts to read.Your party consists of up to five characters, which you move through the environment in real time with a simple mouse click. During battles, the game switches to turn-based control. Outside of combat, you can access your inventory, an overview of your heroes' stats, the quest log or the map at any time. Closely examining your surroundings pays off, as you will always receive experience points for looking at various hotspots.The world is reminiscent of games like Wasteland 2, with lovingly designed locations such as a commune full of philosophers in a grain silo, a merchant in a cave system or a settlement with anti-social scientists. Many of these new communities have a completely different moral system to our (western) world today. The dialog is one of the strengths of the game, almost every character has something to say (briefly), even the unfriendly encounters are really well written. This is also where the morality system comes into play, as you often have the choice between different world views. Once you choose one of these viewpoints, your moral compass needle is driven deeper into that perspective, offering more dialog options from that school of thought. However, if you make a decision that runs counter to your current philosophy, it leads to a more dramatic departure from it.While the conversations are quite well done, the turn-based combat system is comparatively primitive. There is a lack of weapon, enemy or ability variety to create truly interesting tactical scenarios. Each character has a certain number of action points in which they can move, fight or perform another action. The screen can be zoomed continuously. Ultra widescreen (21:9) resolutions are supported without any problems. Incidentally, you can save at any time outside of battles; cloud saves are created.A relatively short, philosophical role-playing game in which you and your small group travel through a post-apocalyptic Australia. Lots of conversations, lots of small quests, some primitive turn-based battles, a little character development, hand-drawn graphics, difficult moral decisions. Kangaroos, camels, scorpions, traders, bandits... basically everything a good role-playing game needs. But we definitely don't have a new cult classic here.

Most gamers should still appreciate the nice isometric visual style, although this only takes the game so far. Sadly, many parts needed significant tuning and better integration. _childDocuments_.review: I want to start by up front saying I think the game got a ludicrous and inordinate amount of flack for a rough launch. I did wait to buy it until it appeared that some stuff had been cleaned up, but even viewing it from a distance it was pretty obvious that there was something of value here, even as troubled as the launch was. I still feel that way after playing it, and you should play it. It scratches the old-school Fallout itch. Is it ATOM RPG? No, but I see a lot of similarities to Dead State, another game in this genre that had a troubled launch but brought some needed innovations. I'm bummed that we almost certainly won't get to explore this world in DLC or sequels. It's a good game.A lot of stuff that people are still complaining about are just part of what this kind of game is, like quests that make you actually figure out some stuff yourself instead of giving you a Pip-Boy that, as an insane old Brotherhood of Steel renegade once noted, "tells you what to do and where to go." Some of the other complaints are just kind of baffling--what did you expect from a game set in Australia if not characters who talk like Australians? The only minor quibble I have there is that maybe a few more terms could use explainer tooltips--I do not know who Joe Bloggs is or why he is significant, even though context clues tell me most of what I need to know--but that's minor. It's a good game!It's not a perfect game. And since the devs appear to be responsive to reviews that give constructive feedback, here's my two cents: the problem is combat. The game feels like it's stuck on super-easy mode. Other than one early-game fight which I could easily have avoided but chose to pick anyway, it feels like all the mechanics are turned off or something.1) I'm blasting things at point-blank range with a sniper rifle, with 100% hit chance. This militates away from using anything but sniper rifles, because there's functionally no minimum range if you're putting a decent amount of skill points into Shooting.2) Every gun appears to have the same AP cost, which means there's no reason to carry a sidearm. The reason sidearms exist in any context is the old adage that it's usually faster to pull your sidearm than to reload. But that's not true here. It is literally exactly as fast to reload your cumbersome bolt-action sniper rifle as it is to reload your pistol, and sometimes faster depending on your build.3) The game claims that it's possible to accidentally hit a party member, and indeed my character is unable to take shots that theoretically could do so due to a morality perk, but I have not seen it happen once, despite a lot of chances. I can't even make it happen on purpose when I try to test out whether it's possible.All of this adds up to what I think is a cardinal mistake in combat design: the obvious, clear, definitive best-in-slot item. That's maybe less egregious when it's a super-rare one-of-a-kind rare drop, but this isn't that kind of game. I'm swimming in sniper rifles, and the scrap to upgrade them. The incentive is to just take out a party of five people with sniper rifles and AP-boosting gear. Melee is inherently gimped by the fact that you have to actually close on your opponent, which arguably makes you want to have *worse* initiative so you can actually attack on the first turn; that would be interesting if it felt like an intentional design choice, but it doesn't. Every gun that isn't a sniper rifle also feels pointless as soon as you have the dollars and scrap to upgrade a set of them to the max.This is really glaring in a game where combat features so heavily. This *isn't* Disco Elysium. It's not Planescape Torment either. It's a Fallout game made by people who also liked Disco Elysium and Planescape Torment, and I mean that in a complimentary way. But the , which sets a certain kind of expectation for what this world is. Everything about the story, the party members, the NPCs, and the world at large tells me that this is a dangerous wasteland full of nightmarish threats and mass-murdering raider gangs, but in the actual combat it's not uncommon for me to wipe out an entire gang before they even got to take a turn.There are other concerns--companion reactivity to player decisions, to the world, and really to anything is strangely nonexistent, given that my party members clearly have opinions about me--but they're very forgivable in what I wish was the first game of a series. The real problem is the combat.

_childDocuments_.review: *** Update Below ***I was looking for a great game to stream this summer and am glad I chose this one. While it for sure had a rocky start, the team has been diligent at getting things back on course. The game has interesting and likeable (and interesting and punchable) characters. The combat system is easy to understand. Levelling is straightforward. The morality system and skills attached to it are a fascinating twist on things. If you enjoy games like Pillars of Eternity, Tyranny, Disco Elysium or ATOM - this will likely tickle your interest.*** Update ***The game took me roughly 25 hours to beat. And I for sure didn't do everything. Could you speed run it, for sure - but anyone who is looking to blast through parts of a game can do so. There was lots to read, consider, and the ending I got (Which is not what I'd call a 'GOOD' end) really made me look back and consider the actions I had taken. It was lots of fun, the story and the world they built was interesting. Yes - there are a few kinks in the game, but even as I was playing I saw that the team was working on getting things sorted. I will say, my attempts to please everyone, to have my cake and eat it too, only left me with friendless and with no cake. Excellent game, team. I look forward to the updates and to revisit it. And maybe be less of a jackarse.

_childDocuments_.review: Regardless of other negative reviews; I bought this game because one of my favorite youTubers recommended it. I knew that it was short for the price, but was expecting to play it multiple times on different paths so it would be worth it. Unfortunately, the story just wasn't that interesting for me. The companions were not unique enough to hold my attention. The quests were a bit too much go to A then B then back to A and finish the quest. Then, on top of that, the combat was awful. The character creation is excellent, in theory. I really enjoy the way the stats are layed out and what they effect for combat. Maybe I'm just that good at optimizing, but it sure felt like what I did with my stats didn't matter for combat becaus the combat was just that easy. Click on stuff and it dies. Cool beans.TLDR the game is too short, doesn't have unique enough companions, and doesn't have great combat. There are other excellent indie RPGs I've played in the last year (Colony Ship sticks out if you're looking for something new). These days, to hold my interest, an RPG has to be better then another playthrough of one of my other cRPGs that I've already played 3+ times (such as WOTR, Wasteland2 or bg3) which Broken Roads failed to do. I do not expect a full indie release to be better games in anyway, but I do expect them to hold my interest for at least the first run.

_childDocuments_.review: That's it, I am done with this failure of a game. And I had such high hopes for it, I do so enjoy my turn-based cRPGs, and this one looked promising - we might have way too many post-apocalyptic RPGs available, but this one looked original because of Australian elements (I mean, who wouldn't enjoy kangaroos sauntering around you, right?). Can't comment on fighting system, I literally had one tiny encounter in 5,5 hours (I would still mention that difficulty levels are a must, our skills and preferences differ vastly, and offering only some midrange version alienates both casual and hardcore gamers). What I can comment on, however, is writing. It's so boring, so bland. I haven't seen even a single memorable character, had an interesting dialogue or completed a noteworthy quest. When a certain incident with some kind of strange energy happened, I was probably supposed to recognise the perpetrator, but I couldn't, he was yet another faceless person to me. By now, I'm tired of waiting for this world to suddenly become alive and immersive (and the fact that music is extremely generic isn't helping).Oh, and it's buggy. I got teleported to another part of a town for scripted dialogues two times in a row, talked to an NPC who was pretty far from me (I guess, we were screaming really loudly), had a quest added to my journal without talking to a questgiver, passed through a solid fence and was finally hardlocked after obviously choosing a wrong answer in an extremely important discussion about some national dish (ok, I admit, the latter was almost amusing) — all this within about 15 minutes. After closing the game via task manager I realised that I had absolutely no wish to run it again.

_childDocuments_.review: Broken Roads is a video game with an interesting moral compass mechanic that devs call "genre-redefining". As a person working in a field of normative ethics, I was very excited to see how this moral compass works. Unfortunately, this good idea seems to be poorly impelemented. Let's start with a questionable choice of the four moral philosophies: humanism, utilitarianism, Machiavellism and nihilism. These concepts are simply incompatible with each other. According to devs: humanist cares about everyone, utilitarist cares about the majority, Machiavellian cares about his gang and nihilist cares only about himself. This seems very inadequate. Questions at the beginning of the game, that are supposed to set the moral compass, are also unfortunate. Well, maybe not the questions themselves, but answers and affiliated with them moral classes. I proposed corrected version of this moral compass, but apparently devs were not interested. Maybe I'm overreacting, maybe it's just a professional bias, but it kinda breaks the immersion for me. I'm just concerned that this feature might spread incorrect understanding of normative ethics. It's important to me, but if you don't care about it, enjoy the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Broken Roads

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually review this early in my first playthrough, but I'm seeing a lot of undue negativity that I feel gives the wrong impression about the game. There is a lot to love in Broken Roads: The setting while not revolutionary is refreshing and fun to explore, the dialogue is well written, exploration is rewarded and there is plenty to find, and I cannot express myself yet on the story but what I have seen so far is promising, if maybe a little disjointed.Combat is a bit disappointing, but I really do not play CRPGs for the combat, and what we have is still functional and competently put together, if a bit uninspired; though I feel the bigger issue lies in encounter design rather than the combat system itself.Ultimately, Broken Roads feels like the first venture of a green team in CRPG development, with the game showing off some  issues that would be obvious to a more experienced dev, and due to the relatively ambitious project they are more glaring than usual. Still, there is a good game here, maybe not excellent but more than worth the thirty dollars and the 10-20 or so hours it takes to fully experience it.
_childDocuments_.name: Broken Roads

_childDocuments_.review: While Broken roads had a few interesting concepts that make it stand out, it doesn't usesthem to their full potential. The morality system which is split between utilitarian,machiavellian,nihilist and Humanist and while it is a refreshing break from the simple Good/evil binary it doesn't have a major effect on much in the game beyond dialogue options and it still falls into same pit that the good/evil binary does. I wanted to be a nihilist with a streak of humanism but there wasn't any room for that in the game. Further, the instances where morality would be involved were sparse. For something that is the character customization it should have an impact on every aspect of the game.The combat is nothing to phone home about like every other aspect of the game its underdeveloped. It was a struggle at first but after a few level ups and half decent gear its a cake walk. Cover isn't even necessary. There's also a weapon crafting/mod system but all that amounts to is getting a bigger number. Any weapon you can craft you can rip out of the hands of a dead raider as well making it kinda pointless. It wouldn't have been hard to add unique weapons to the game either.The world is empty  threes a handful of settlements that have a few quests and the rest of the locations are just raider shooting galleries or nothing. There's this huge map and all this space and nothing there. One can only initiate combat through dialogue  which is stupid.The story, like every other part of the game is a mess. It starts of strong but falls off hard near the end. There  were only two places that felt like they got a lot of attention and they both are forgotten by the endgame. The endgame city doesn't have anything to do in it but the final quest. Construction materials are found everywhere and I was thinking maybe I oughta collect this junk and rebuild the mc's home which was burnt down but that was forgotten about after the first act. The philosophical discussions with different characters in the were interesting but jarring and could have been implemented in a more seamless way instead of getting a philosophy 101 lesson. The ending was a major let down. With the heavy influence of philosophy I excepted there to be an option to have some sort of debate with the bbeg about philosophy and potentially talk him down but there didn't seem to be an option to do that so I lit his ass on fire and shot him twice in the head. How fun. The tried and true slide show only went over a few actions I did. Also in spite of what you do the endgame city falls into ruin and nothing really changes so pretty much everything was pointless.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - this game is JANKY AF. the mechanics are awful, and the storyline is insipid. You will feel minimal agency playing this game but be fully cognisant that your time is being wasted via meaningless character upgrades (scale of 1-100 for 12 different attributes - really?!) and "moral compass dialogues" that have literally no impact on the outcome of this point-and-click game.I tried very hard to like this game and will keep playing given how much money I spent on it. The narrative is awful and the dialogue is shallow in terms of depth, but what is most underwhelming about the game is the actual mechanics itself. There are no actual quests or side-quests beyond following a linear story-line. The "moral compass" responses seem to have no differentiation, and the side-quests are just a meandering "go talk to Person X for Person Y" which you fulfil just by clicking randomly on the map until you find Person X. Then you click on some random dialogue bits, which completes the quest, before you return to Person Y.  This isn't really an RPG...it's basically just a point and click game masqueraded with a bunch of pointless RPG-like game features.

I liked the characters enough, but maybe a little more discussion options and interactions with them separately as the game went on to let us know how they were feeling - like they'd approach you in town between outings separately to say "Hey I didn't appreciate that choice you made" or something similar.The combat was absent for a good while at the start of the game, and I actually didn't mind this so much, but I can see it's a sore point for some. _childDocuments_.review: I've been interested in the philosophical RPG concept and the moral compass ever since I first heard about those. It's great that the game allows for behaving in morally gray areas. Killing a man who is about to die or trying to help him even though he wouldn't survive? Which one is more humane? Most of the quests are well-written and fun. I really enjoyed playing all the story. And I investigated other options by saving and loading the game. The choices you make really change the whole story. Starting from what you choose as your origin! Initially, I couldn't finish the game because there was a bug in the main quest. When I reported it, they published a hot fix in 24 hours and I was able to finish the game! So, yeah, there are some bugs in the game (it's an indie title!) but I can still recommend Broken Roads for sure. Especially if you love narrative games. Developers are still working hard to improve the game, even hiring new people to repair this gem. I think they deserve much better than what the game received from the players when they first launched it. With each update, Broken Roads gets more enjoyable and polished. You just need to report the bugs properly and be fair. I'm confident that playing this game will be a beautiful experience for RPG enthusiasts.  I have to emphasize this again: It's a shame that Broken Roads has fallen victim to bugs and got such negative reviews because they've really created a beautiful story, an amazing art style, cool soundtracks and an engaging world. You can feel that they really loved this game while developing it. I wish they had polished the game a bit more before releasing it...

_childDocuments_.review: It's got a lot of bugs at the moment that range from minor annoyance (exiting a building and triggering a cutscene, but the character has to walk all the way across town to speak to you) to major problems (clicking on  a body to loot not registering if there are two bodies close together, or only registering one body and refusing the second), and the morality system seems half-baked. I'm also having a hard time liking any of the characters, but I've been told Australians are "just like that" so I can't tell if it's from writing or a culture clash. I REALLY want to like this game - post apocalyptic australian rpg? That's everything young me wanted after Mad Max. I like the art, I think the voice acting ranges from okay to great, and, like I said, post-apocalypse Outback is just so NEAT! But the combat isn't fun, the fact that there's no ammo economy feels lazy and kinda' cheap, and the story triggers important events in ways that feel like they needed narrative cues. That last one, however, is more of a caveat to players - try to do the main quest stuff asap, and reaaaally pay attention. I'll check back in a little bit, but I'd say wait for a discount. A decent discount, at that.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve never posted a review on Steam before (so please bear with me), but I’ve felt compelled to do so for this title in particular, because the seething experience that a decent chunk of reviewers seem to have had just doesn’t reflect my own, enough that I felt like I should say something about it, at least. For someone keen on cRPGs old and new, someone looking for an original and unique game world grounded in an unfamiliar, real-world setting, or just someone interested in a different take on the classic cRPG experience, I think this is for you. For someone wanting Wasteland Elysium or Baldur’s Gate 3 with guns and nukes… probably not for you. I’ve only properly gotten into cRPGs following the recent explosion of Baldur’s Gate 3. I’ve always found the systems, mechanics, and gameplay of the genre very tedious to get into, and I understand that that’s a me thing. It was only on my third restart of BG3 that something in my mind clicked, and I’ve returned to many different cRPGs I’ve purchased before, experiencing those worlds with a newfound excitement and engagement now that the third-person, souls-like jelly in my skull has become a little more enlightened. I’ve had my eye on Broken Roads for a brief while now following my recent foray into other cRPGs, and I’ve always found the setting of Australia – particularly the desolate expanse of the Outback, an incredibly fascinating and mystical one. So, with newfound excitement and intrigue in hand, I decided to give it a go. I’ll get some valid criticisms out of the way from the jump a.k.a. … - The combat isn’t great and can be frustrating at times, though it’s definitely serviceable. The RNG is not in your favor here.- The UI has a few bugs when it comes to targeting enemies during combat due to foreground objects covering them.- Same goes for exploration with a few interactable Points of Interest/Lootable icons that just don’t activate when prompted.- The first few primary quests I’ve experienced have quite linear conclusions, with various branches/paths converging on a singular outcome.- Some dialogue prompts are just plain bugged out and forced me to reload a quick save/manual save in order to rectify the problem, though this was a rare occurrence. - The writing doesn’t really delve much (or hasn’t so far at least) into some aspects of the lore and history of this world, which is a shame, because the aspects that are fleshed out are really interesting and engaging. And that’s it. Those are the biggest problems. At least in my opinion. And from what I’ve seen in the dev responses on some of these reviews, as well as those on YouTube, the team is already working on hammering out some patches to rectify a bunch of these issues. I can understand – though obviously don’t agree – why some players have given this a thumbs down. What I can’t comprehend are some of the wildly hot takes completely trashing the game. I mean, I feel like I’m having a completely separate experience to the hellish slog they seem to have endured. Which brings me to... Almost everyone else has said it, and I’ll say it too: the art and presentation of the game is beautiful. I’m a sucker for that painterly, 3D style, and this title definitely doesn’t disappoint in that regard. - The moral compass system is really intriguing and relevant throughout all of what I’ve played so far. I agree with what some others have said in that it’s by no means genre-defining, but I acknowledge its addition to the overall experience of the game, and I think it heightens interactions with various NPCs and main characters as a result of its inclusion and implementation. - Something I haven’t seen many mention is that you also unlock exclusive skills for your character depending on your moral stance, including how that stance might shift as you progress through the story. - I also enjoy how the moral compass system opens the door into a wider conversation regarding philosophy/philosophical paradigms. Sure, it’s not a front row seat to a three-year undergrad philosophy course, but it’s more than enough to prompt a further exploration of those topics internally, and I think I’d rather enjoy the chosen approach of sipping on such heavy topics than to be drowned in a vortex of dense philosophical discourse. - The writing here works best through the characters the story presents. They’re grounded and believable, with enough individual flair to make them stand out. That carries through in the dialogue and their responses to the player character. I never felt like hearing or reading the dialogue was cringe or a chore by any measure. In fact, it’s been one of the strongest driving forces of the experience for me. - Furthermore, towards writing: I took it upon myself to try and start a different origin and make some different choices to see just how firmly the Bad DM/Railroad analogy that others have expressed holds up to scrutiny when tested, and I have to say – to some extent that is true. But only just. At least with the primary quest you need to complete before the world opens up. I will say however, that my experiences playing a Gun for Hire and a Surveyor differed greatly in how I was lead to that point of the story, as well as subsequent quests/choices past that. - The sound design is solid as well. The almost dazed, oneiric tracks that keep you company through your travels really echo the strange, lonesome, desolate nature of the setting, with the combat tracks taking on an almost primal, rhythmic bent that introduces enough tension into encounters to perk your ears up, so to speak. This isn’t the next greatest cRPG of all time. But what it is, is a really solid, enjoyable role-playing experience with great characters, and an engaging narrative. I’ve found myself thinking about playing this when I’m at work, returning to the dust and grit of the post-apocalyptic Australian wasteland to uncover its secrets and mysteries. A game doesn’t induce that feeling within me all that often, but when it does, I’ve got to acknowledge that there’s something .This is the kind of Indie project I enjoy supporting, because there’s a passion behind this. Plenty of it. Beyond what’s in the game itself, I’ve seen that clearly in the responses the devs have posted to all kinds of reviews: great, good, bad, and glaringly bad. And for a debut game from a really small Indie studio, I’ve seen way, way worse do better, and I don’t think that’s particularly fair in this regard. I also don’t think it’s particularly fair to compare this to BG3 or Disco Elysium – especially since BG3 was in development for nearly a decade including its early access period and Disco Elysium only bloomed with twice as much time in the creative oven. For a development window of 5 years, with what I’m sure was much less budget, I believe the devs have hit the mark and made a thing that stands on its own really. Lastly, I believe this title is worth its asking price, and in my opinion – which I understand is just one in a  ocean of voices – if you have the funds to spare and you’re keen on a solid cRPG experience with a novel setting and really engaging characters and writing, I’d for sure give this a go. Other than that, thanks for taking the time to read this review and Happy travels. And watch out for the Combat Wombats.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been following the progress of this game for a bit, and I even went out of my way to meet the devs when they were at PAX Melbourne, Very friendly and really passionate about the gameAnyway, let's talk about the game. Being Australian this has a special spot for me as we don’t often get to see this great country of our represented in games. The hand-drawn art captures the Outback feel perfectly, reminding me of my trip across the Nullabour when I was a young fulla, and the music sets the mood just right.It's not your typical RPG, though. Its got a simple OG Fallout fell but with an Auzzie twist. The storytelling is immersive, and the choices you make help immerse in the story. Plus, they throw in some  Auzzie slang (with translations), which adds to the charm.Combat's turn-based, which I'm a fan of. Keeps things interesting without being too complicated.And the devs are really responsive in their Discord! It's awesome to see them so engaged with the community.Sure, it takes a bit to get going, but trust me, it's worth the wait. Once you're in, you'll be hooked.Overall it might not be everyone's cup of tea, but if you're into exploring rich worlds and making tough choices, give it a shot and you'll see the effort that has been put in.

_childDocuments_.review: Broken Roads does feel more like a point-and-click adventure with RPG mechanics instead of full-fledged RPG. I did enjoy playing through the story and helping shape events, but I wasn't particularly invested in the character I was playing, or in their relationships with other characters. If you walk in with those expectations it's a pretty good (if a little clunky) time. The world, while on the smallish side, did feel more dynamic than I was expecting. I was happy to see the consequences of my actions outside of the quests themselves, and the world felt more lived-in than most RPGs. That said, there were plenty of times where quests wouldn't telegraph their intentions well enough or be outright buggy. It was also pretty perplexing when (no spoilers) most of my companions left at the end, where the situation didn't really line up with their reasoning. But the ending itself did line up nicely with my actions, which was satisfying.Everything else was nice to serviceable. Nothing super broken. A few patches should clear up minor irritations and tighten up the quests and systems. Took about 13 hours for my first play-through. I'm curious enough afterwards to go back and try some things out for a second play-through.

_childDocuments_.review: So I am at odds with this game. On one hand, I love the dialogue, setting and the moral choice system had me legitimately struggling to make decision. On the other hand, this game has some serious mechanical issues and kind of falls down in the last hour.Pros:-Dialogue and description are well written, they feel very Australian and some of them had me audibly laughing;-The art style is gorgeous and tonally fits the setting, same with music and sound effects; and-The moral choices through out the game were tough, and had me stumped at several points as I struggled to pick which option.Cons-The game is still pretty buggy, most of the steam achievements didn’t unlock for me, multiple side stories became bugged and became impossible to complete as well as a couple of soft crashes. Though nothing unmanageable, hopefully this will be fixed over time;-The game lacks allot of quality-of-life fixes. The frequency of autosaves, auto collecting all items after a combat, and the quest tracking seems a bit unreliable;-The end game falls down a bit both in combat and the story. The combat becomes painfully easy if you are completing the side quests and the ending sequence was very average narratively; -I wish I knew more about the party members, I spent the entire game with the same 4 party members and honestly could not tell you anything about them aside from their occupation; and-This game also needs more voice lines, the impact of allot of the narrative beats would be greatly improved by the characters speaking rather then just reading the text. While the narrator is good, it really feels like the characters should be reading their own lines in cutscenes.Overall I think Broken Roads is worth your time, probably not worth its day one price, but I can certainly see myself replaying it after a couple of patches.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I would rate this as a not quite complete Fallout 1/2 style CRPG with some interesting ideas that don't quite work and some inherent design flaws that are baked into the game.Positives-I enjoyed the writing in the game overall with only one real exception and it felt like it did a good job of selling a distinctly Australian vibe as well as some more original post apocalyptic ideas. -I also liked the effort to incorporate a karma meter into the game that tackled different philosophical concepts that weren't just rote light side or dark side choices.-The art and environmental work is great and feels like it had a lot of love put into it and since those are the graphics your going to be staring at for 90% of a CRPG that seems like the most important bit of the graphics to call out. The character models are good as well but again your rarely going to get too close of a look at those in a CRPG.-The game does a good job of providing interesting moral choices throughout the game and beneficially they're aren't all connected to the karma meter system so you can end up playing someone unethical with one of the 'nicer' philosophical views. While you will usually be asked to justify your actions generally almost all of the philosophical views have some sort of rationalization for your actions which is sort of good and sort of bad as I detail below.Meh's-The aboriginal community's writing in Koorda doesn't feel quite as strong as the rest of the game. I don't mean that in the sense that it's offensive at least as far as I can tell just that it feels like the writers weren't fully comfortable with writing a bunch of aboriginal characters and so they come across as being unfortunately rather bland and generically friendly. The rest of the game is pretty good at showing characters as being normal in the lazy, irritated or tired way and the aboriginals just come across as a bit perfect in a boring way in comparison. -The karma meter doesn't feel like it has a ton of effect in game. Sometimes it seems to give you unique dialogue options but aside from a few rare instances it almost always seemed like all of the philosophies were represented in persuasion dialogues or reactions. Which sadly means it just comes out feeling like fluff which is a shame because it seems like a really cool idea that doesn't quite get utilized to it's full potential. I feel like it ultimately would have been better to have just done a Neverwinter Nights 2 or King Arthur: A Knights Tale style morality cross but I always appreciate dev's trying to use a karma meter in a game.Negatives-The combat feels never really manages to be super interesting and the game feels somewhat indecisive as to whether it wants to be a Disco Elysium style narrative first game or a Pillars of Eternity style CRPG with a high concept story. -The quest logic as of 6/1/2024 is a bit messed up and the sign posting could definitely be better as far as where to go and what to do. This seems to be a pretty consistent problem for indie CRPG's although the devs are actively working to patch it.-Your companions are also sadly underdeveloped being more in line with BG1 companions just following you around silently without much to add outside of fighting in combat.-The main story is a bit messy as well in a few different ways. Why exactly your character is running around doing what they're doing never felt like it was super firmly established to me. Your character seems like they're working towards getting the town Brookton rebuilt but by the time you've done everything asked of you by the people who can help the game pushes you along to the settlement that the antagonists are from but doesn't really establish why you need to go there aside from just checking it out. The main villain manages to be pretty one note being more or less an egoist that wants to rule over a city in a bottle and lacking much in the way of interesting beliefs beyond that.TLDR - The game is interesting with good points and bad, grab it after a few patches and give it a whirl and you'll definitely get a unique experience but nothing life changing.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a bit confused by the reviews for this game. It is easy to play - a familiar isometric, good pathfinding, easy to understand (but not easy) combat. The moral compass works really well - you can just stick to your chosen morality which assists with some choices. The story is compelling, while not being as deep as some AAA titles - I'd say the story is as deep as Starfield (not a high bar) but not BG3. - I choose to play some indie games and accept there will be limitations.Overall I'm happy with my purchase and will be putting more hours into Broken Roads.

_childDocuments_.review: I felt the need to write a "first impression" review here since there's a lot of weird negative reviews (someone really complaining that [C] is not the button to open a character sheet? Really...? I mean: really....??)I'm certainly just at the beginning but I am hooked for a day now without having the feel to stop anytime soon. If the game suddenly derails and becomes a mess, I will surely change my review but as it is right now, it is a thumbs up.The setting. Picking Australia, with all it's slang, is sure something refreshingly new compared to the good ol' USA or some Easten European state. (thank you for handing out a dictionary for Aussie slang, too.)The artstyle and the music are amazing. Especially the music. The assets have this certain "painted" style one might know from Disco Elysium, for eg, yet different. But similar. The music however - I need to point it out again - carries hard.In fashion of true RPGs, you have plenty of dialogue choices to make, that also get fluffed up with this whole morale compass system. In true RPG fashion, there's also a lot to read.It's not fully voices, but the VA is decent. One who's kind of not on point is the narrator though. No clue what she was trying to do here while voice acting.You can pet the cat. It will meow.You can seduce vendors and make them question their sexuality.Edit:I've finished the game now (leaving some Side Quest unresolved though) and have to say that the ending felt quite underwhelming and anti-climatic and the endboss fight was a joke. Yet the thumb remains up, because I enjoyed the journey and also because the devs are working hard to get rid of the flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not someone that leaves many reviews, but I thought this game deserved another review and maybe a different view on it.The game starts a little slow and it’s a bit linear at the beginning as it tries to get you into the story and characters. The voice acting is great and the dialog is also well thought of and very Australian if maybe over the top which I think is very intentional. I like to take my time with these types of games and to search all the areas and find any hidden gems and there is enough to keep you going with this process. This game doesn’t have treasure hidden around every corner and every container, so you have to work for it a little more to find things and I think that does make it a bit more realistic compared to many other games of this type that have treasure hidden everywhere for instant gratification. It takes a bit of time, but once you further into the game then it opens up the map and allows you to travel anywhere you like, similar to how the map works in Wasteland 2 and other games. This is really where the game gets better for me. The turn-based fighting is good enough, it’s not the best and there are few glitches on how the attacks work, how to target overlapping people, but once you know some of the quirks on the fighting system then you can work around them and for the most part it gets the job done. For me its just part of the charm of the game. It’s not a clone of another games fighting interface, it does things in its own way. Could it be better, yes it could. The developers know there are some issues and they working to fix this on the future patches which is great as that’s what you want when a new game gets launched. I haven’t run into any glitches that have caused a crash, or stopped me from completing a quest or any fights. If something does go wrong, you can always load an auto-save which happens regularly anyway. The morality system is a bit different to other games where it will focus responses on which way you aligning and how your responses are going, however it feels like quite a broad overlap on alignment. So, if you plan on only being evil it will focus on those options, but still give you room to have some friendlier responses. I haven’t played in different ways to say how much it really affects the game and all the responses.The graphics and art are amazing throughout the game and really give you the Australian vibe especially with the wildlife running around, the red sands and rusty tin shed towns and buildings. They have done a great job in getting that atmosphere right and using proper town names etc. I think people often forget that this is a small Indie game developer who have never made a game like this before.  Unfortunately it’s being compared to games like Disco Elysium, Divinity 2 and Wasteland 2 from big developers with big budgets. I came into this game not setting any expectation from it and maybe that’s why I am enjoying the game more than others. Often games get hyped up before launch and then they receive negative feedback when it doesn’t hit those high expectations even if the game is actually solid and still fun to play. Update:I have enjoyed completing the game and I will re-play it once some more updates are in and then maybe focus on some of the achievements. Any game I can get 60 hrs out of and look at playing again down the track is worth it for me.

_childDocuments_.review: To be perfectly honest, it might not have been for me. I probably lack a certain cultural context to fully appreciate this game and setting in particular. It's definitely something new setting-wise. However, if you're not a native speaker of English or very familiar with the language, it's a bit frustrating to pick up the Australian terms and lingo. There are some high-lighted words to help you out. It get's really frustrating when you get into the Aboriginal terms when you visit their village, as you get introduced to an entirely new language. It's a fine gesture to include it, but I was already struggling with Australian English. By the second time I was in Koorda doing their quests my eyes just glazed over all of it and it became frustrating and tedious to parse through it. It was too much for me. Not everyone will have a problem with that of course. I was frankly also very irritated by a majority of the characters. The setting is very rural, and the game portrays that particular mentality very well—the people are mostly coarse, rude, aggressive alcoholics, or self-righteous inflexible traditionalists. Yeah, nah. It reminded me of a part of my extended family, the part I generally avoid like the plague. So, if you have a similar issues or dislike being reminded of such relatives, be warned.Mechanically the game feels a bit obsolete. Most quests are unclear and vague on what you have to do or where you have to go, so there's a lot of clicking around to find the exact solution or progress point. The combat mechanics are decent enough. The dialogue trees are rather rudimentary and they mostly get the job done. What I actively hated is the game taking away control from me and skipping me two or three autosaves forward, e.g. you finish a simple quest and get teleported to a new location immediately, with no way of saving beforehand. And you can't just reload while you're in a forced dialogue. Mate, just let me reload if I feel like it. It was especially egregious in Kalgoorlie specifically when you get Bitey the sheep and the game immediately teleports you to Merredin, a completely different town. Can I get a warning before you decide for me where I'll be playing? I didn't want to go to Merredin, and it's either reload (and hope you have a convenient autosave or quick save handy otherwise it's progress lost), or trek back to Kalgoorlie. Both options waste your time.Again, I might not be the target audience. The setting was new for me, and at least it's fun to try and experience new things, but I didn't have a particularly good time in West Aus, the mechanics seemed a bit obsolete, and there were many annoyances. Nothing in particular was broken or unplayable. I hope others will have more fun with it than I did.

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased the game during the Autumn Sale.  The game has some unique aspects.Unlike the video on the store page, the game is mostly a narrative RPG.   The setting is Australian Outback hundreds of years after an all-out nuclear war.  It is small party, top down, turn based combat.  But much of the game is completing quests.  The intro video does not really capture what the game is like.  The text description is quite accurate. There is combat, but it is not very difficult most of the time.   The random encounters mostly serve to refill inventory to sell.The most distinctive thing is how four major moral perspectives are integrated into the game.  A major quest is collecting old books of moral philosophy.  I've never seen that in an RPG.  The books selected by the developers were well chosen.The pluses of the game are the location, the voice acting, and how the "magic" system is integrated into Australian folklore.  The minuses of the game is the simple and easy combat system, quests that are mostly mundane (like many RPGs), and a few of the quests are a little flakey.  But the developers continue to read the discussion thread and address problems so the game should continue to improve.  It is interesting and playable at this point in the game development.If you are looking for a lightish, mostly narrative RPG with a unique setting that comes to life, this is a good game for you.  If you are looking for a combat challenging game requiring considerable tactical thought - you will probably not enjoy the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying the game so far. On the surface, there's a beautiful handpainted look that ties the 2D and 3D assets together. The world feels very grounded and it lets the charm of the setting come through.The story is a slow burn at the start, which I really like. It lets you immerse yourself in the world and feel like you're one mundane part of it. I like that the characters feel like very ordinary humans, just trying to get by. Your character fits in easily, and your origin story does have an impact on some dialogues.It's a story heavy game, but the dialogue and writing is snappy and well paced. When you ask a simple question, you don't get bombarded with huge backstories, which makes the large amount of dialogue easy to engage with. The morality system is interesting on the surface, but probably a bit mis-named. I can tell some people will get hung up on pedantics about whether something is actually humanist or utilitarian, but the system for what it is gives you different ways to approach a situation, and adds a lot of replayability. You kind of choose a path at the start, and options that conflict with your starting position aren't available, so if you want to change alignment so to speak, you have to do it very slowly over the game, or replay from a different alignment.The combat is serviceable. It doesn't feel like combat is the main focus of a game, so I'm happy for it to be on the more simplistic side. If you want very deep, tactical combat, you won't find it here.Overall, this is a nice little CRPG. It's not a massive world changing epic, it's simple, immersive, and has a unique charm I admire. It has more interesting things going for it than it has things that detract from the experience, and I'm looking forward to where the game is going.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I recommend this for fans of old school RPGs. Good:Handpainted graphics style is beautiful.  I admired it all throughout the game. It's the best thing about this game IMO. And it is consistently great. The visual artists deserve kudos for elevating this game compared to where it would have been without their work. I wouldn't have finished it.The Australian setting is used well, especially the language, customs, and culture.  I found it refreshingly new in terms of game personality. The writing is pretty good.  It's a little undergrad level philosophy with lots of explaining but it tries at least. It's pretty clever and funny sometimes.The NPCs have some personality which is nice.I didn't find it buggy. I waited for the May patch.Took me 20hrs not 10hrs like early reviews stated.The team is supporting the game well after launch w/ regard to patches and communicationthe music is pretty good and to my ears fits the game Meh:The price is on the high side considering it's level of polish, production values, depth, and level of creativity and innovation.  I'm thinking $20-25 is more like it.Voice acting especially the narration is so-so. And it's very inconsistently applied even within  the space of a single conversation. Controller support is there but some of the menu navigation is a bit cludgy. Have trouble navigating different sub menus/screens.The morality meter didn't feel well integrated into the game in a way that I could recognize. For me it felt more like a marketing gimmick.Bad:Combat, boring. And you become overpoweringly strong by mid game able to defeat everyone.  No difficulty settings so you can't make it harder. My 3 snipers 2 shotted most enemies so nearly the entire enemy squad was dead in a single turn. Even the end boss was easy to kill.Some of the story flow based on choices can seem abrupt,  with me wondering why X happened based on my choice. The game could flow better in that regard especially late game important decision points.Not many interesting random encounters,  just basic trading or combat. I feel no incentive to replay the game b/c the gameplay lacks the depth and creativity to make me want to do it all again.Overall:Wait for it to go on sale, but it is worth playing.
