_childDocuments_.review: This rough gem of a passion project is going to appeal to classic RPG fans that love a solid traditional long read adventure. It is reminiscent of games like  Baulders Gate and Fallout 2, where the writing is the guiding light and dialog options reign supreme. It emplores you to take your time and enjoy the authenticity of its execution. Unfortunately, for all of its fantastic art style, epic music score and writing, the combat side of the game is obviously lack luster and leaves you wanting a bit more as far as tactical gameplay and AI are concerned. This game bleeds Australia and they have done such a creative job producing an atmosphere that really grabs a hold of you without ever feeling like it's too rich or corny. It even includes a "slang translator" that helps you understand the nomenclature and I must say, it's fair dinkum!The morality system is introduced as a core mechanic but I felt like it was slightly underutilized and doesn't really have as much control over the way everything plays out as I hoped it would. I feel like it would have more of an impact if it directly influenced aspects of the game such as character class or relationships between important NPCs and the main character. There is a skeleton of an amazing game here and although it has many flaws, the devs seem to have been working hard as the most recent patch seems to have made significant fixes and changes.I would at the very least wishlist this one and keep checking in on its development as this could very well be a sleeper hit or future cult classic.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this one. Its one of the few games I bought at release, because I wanted to support the concept and the developers.Unfortunately its an interesting and unique Australian RPG setting, disappointingly executed. Dialogue is well written enough, with plenty of Australiana flavour, but the leanings towards philosophical theory in the final chapter, while educational, is rather dry. Voice-overs are sporadic in their use, and are of varying quality. The story seems disjointed and rushed. Quests often feel ambiguous as to whether they can be progressed or not. Characters are uninteresting and underdeveloped, while the companions don't get to show much personality, and don't seem to have any personal quests. After going through their dialogue trees once, there is not much more from them, save for very occasional interjections during quests. The morality system feels underutilised, and skill checks feel few and far between. Combat is rather bland, and feels unbalanced, particularly towards the end game where my combat skills were already maxed, and I had a few more level ups banked (the final boss died before it could have a turn). Magic seems unnecessary. It's mostly random encounters, which I ran away from anyway, as they didn't offer much reward.The backgrounds and character models are quite attractive in my opinion, and I enjoyed the music (although it was somewhat limited).There were occasional bugs - unable to back out from a menu once during combat, NPCs disappearing when re-loading a save file, duplicate characters appearing.I appreciate the dev's stated commitment to improving the game. However, considering the 5 month delay to get it to its release state, I am not certain they will be able to remedy the fundamental issues with the game, such as the disjointed story, and lack of skill checks etc. Yeah, nah.

_childDocuments_.review: I love games like this. I love this game more since it takes place in an area I lived for 11 years. I love it even more because it makes me want to break out my philosophical texts and have another read through. The game still has some bugs, yes, but I also the devs hard at work bringing out updates and hotfixes, and honestly that kind of devotion to their game means more to me than an instant perfect product. The game is graphically beautiful and I've gotten a lot of joy from the landscapes depicted and the corresponding wildlife. I laugh every time there is a "translation" in the dialogue for those are unfamiliar with Aussie slang and the first time I realised there were drop bears in the game. The story is brutal. When I play choice based games I really do want to make the "right" choice at all points and help as many people as I can and I'm just not sure how much that is possible in this world. It absolutely pulled me out of my comfort zone, but in the best possible way.Special shoutout here to the music. The main menu digeridoo music... I could listen to it all day. Some of the SFX sounds are a little much, but that's what volume adjustors are for.In any case, I'm sticking around for more. By all means, wait for a few more updates, but I've loved every minute in this game so far. Even the brutal ones.

_childDocuments_.review: ---UPDATE---This is an update to my first review, and a change in my judgment of the game. I played about 10 hours of the second patch (May 2024), and i must say that many of the issues i found in the game at launch are solved. Avoid for now.The game characters have nonsensical reactions to event in game and to what happens and what you do.Probably bugs in the action/reactions scripts, or just bad writing, but just to make ONE example, a very important NPC gets hanged, his friends do not react, nobody seems to talk about the event, you can't even speak about it to the governor of the place that did the hanging.This is just one example, the one that was the proverbial last drop for me that drove me to uninstall the game, but there were many other similar instances in my playthrough.Note when i published this review, and wait to check if there are patches or other things because right now the experience is frustrating at best, and i am truly angry at myself, because i started playing despite the bad reviews to have an open mind, and because i have a soft spot for everything that comes from australia.But this game... it's bad. _childDocuments_.review: Should you play this? nah,yeah it's worth a squiz i reckon. I'm off for a smoko.TLDR: GOOD GAME, GREAT IDEAS, MIXED EXECUTION (definitely more good than bad).(OLD REVIEW BEFORE MAY PATCH)I want to LOVE this game and i was actually having a good time for like 2 hours. The game has some UI and system shortcomings like not being able to individually select party members but its clear the devs put lots of effort into the world and as far as combat goes i would say its really good, streamlined and modernised turn based combat. Much like wasteland 3. After 2 hours i'm yet to see the open world in this open world RPG and the freedom i'm given is very much in the speech options which isn't necessarily a bad thing. I'd recommend playing this but after the roadmap the devs released a few days ago i would say wait until mid may before playing this. In some ways i think this game should've been released as early access. It's a real shame because i want to keep playing but seeing what will be changed soon i think it's best to wait and start a new play through. Most of the blaring problems with the game (Lack of VO, lack of open ended quests/levels, etc) will apparently be fixed in the coming weeks so do play this but NOT RIGHT NOWREVIEW POST MAY PATCH. SPOILERS!!!!!!!It's clear the devs want to improve this game and the improvements are greatly appreciated. Much of my original criticisms are either gone or at the very least lessened, with a more open open world and quests with a variety of options and solutions, even if some quests don't work half the time. For the most part this is not a problem, however i would say that better communication between the player and how the quests will change based on your choices would make this issue much less annoying. For example, when collecting the ripper's bounty, the only way to collect on the bounty truthfully is by killing both the ripper and his wife. However, in my first run, i chose to spare his wife, thinking I only needed him dead to complete it. After I realised this wasn't the case, i couldn't go back and kill her and i had to restart that part of the quest. This may seem small but similarly some quests, notably in lake deborah, koorda and merridin will not progress even if every criteria and step is completed, meaning you waste a couple of hours only to get nothing in return. Overall, most of the quests work fine and honestly are quite memorable whether it's influencing a local election or infiltrating a local rebel cell. Even the fetch quests can be kind of interesting. I mean fetch quests are fetch quests there's not much you can do to make them more fun and while they are abundant in this game, they don't feel entirely forced or superficial. The purpose makes sense and the dialogue is usually pretty funny. XP bar goes up = neuron activation. Every character felt unique and were always entertaining to interact with, even if most were just quest vendors, exposition dumps, or merchants but isn't that the same for most RPGs?The companions were great fun and will keep you entertained from merridin to kalgoorlie. The party banter and different personalities are always fun to see. The only character who I think could've been improved is the main villain. You meet him near the end and he has very little to say and sometimes appears good and sometimes evil. Fortunately this isn't that big of a problem as the environment and other characters help to tell the story and give information that will inform your opinion of the villain's beliefs and intentions. I quite like this as it encourages exploration and feels a lot less like an exposition dump.My biggest complaint other than bug fixes, quest issues and just general stuff, is the combat. I  love the combat overall, but to make it even better I would allow an option to engage in combat manually, allowing you to get the jump on the enemies. Additionally, the ability to individually move party members before combat starts to get good positions, heal, etc. It's a minor change but i thought it would give more strategy to encounters. Similarly, the way skill checks work is by only checking the skill requirement against the player character, instead of checking each party member. This essentially makes companions interchangeable and just faceless soldiers used in combat. Ultimately, this makes the party seem less interesting and encourages making every character good at combat but nothing else and making the player character good at things like vigilance, biology, tinkering.I hope this review doesn't come off as cynical and negative. It's just i can see the passion and love that went into making this game and it's frustrating to see how close this game is to being great rather than good. The 'cyclopeida is a really cool idea and the game seemingly does a great job respecting the cultures and groups they use (i'm not an expert obviously). I love the writing and locations i just think some of the games systems need a little tweaking here and there. Regardless this game offers a unique and fun spin on a pretty well-trodden genre and has all the best intentions and love a great game needs. I hope this game gets more content with a sequel, DLC or even a version which the devs deem as the definitive version.

_childDocuments_.review: This Austrialian masterpiece starts you in the Outback and instead of going the obvious Mad-Maxy road of greasy, spiked and obscenely pimped and decorated muscle car apocalypse most of the old fogeys craved the devs offers us camels and “Broken Roads” subverting expecations on the get go. Like every piece of art, it should evoke an emotional response.And the chosen setting is highly interesting with a lot of players wanting to celebrate this as an indie gem with a strong auteur soul evoking feelings among its myriad player base.Let’s cut the crap with all those fancy sounding words: People gave this a bad review because there wasn’t enough combat and I was a fool for believing these idiots. I created the most incompetent bushwacking, dingo chasing, combatant for this game. A Trader with high intelligence and Charisma and zero combat skills. In the tutorial area I rush to the (Optional) combat training area and get immediately chastised that I have to come back later and finish the tutorial quest. Deprived of the enjoyment of getting explained how his shotgun works he shuffles along the tutorial mission only to be ambushed by two crazy looking weirdos, with one of them wearing barely anything but a potato Sack on their head (your run of the mill Australians apparently). Here I am, having to kill two idiots with a character that is intelligent enough to engineer a smart combat drone with homing missiles just with some scraps, a piece of sand paper and camel poop, and charismatic enough to sell it your grandmother but unable to figure out how a bloody shotgun works.He has 5 Action points, shooting his shotgun costs 3 points. Reloading costs one Point. He is never going to shoot twice; he always has an extra action point he can only use as movement. He has a 60% hit chance on point blank hitting the naked potato-sack wearing dude in front of him and he might may take aim for 5 Action points total for a steady shot (with a shotgun) to get his point blank hit chance up to 63%. The unbridled disappointment continues: If his shotgun hits, the “shot-gun to the face” damage takes away between 40-70% of the health of the crazy dude. Meaning he has at least to hit that dude twice to stop him, if he is unlucky that fella needs 3 shotgun volleys to be put down.In the meantime, the mate of the potato-sack wearing psycho bravely continues to shot at my character with her pistol, missing almost as much. So after 15 reloads (you can’t save during combat) I had up to 25 turns of combat where the two kept missing shot after shot after shot.Seemingly your character can’t be killed in the tutorial mission, so the enemies just opt to miss all the time once his health drops to 1 hp or something. This would have been hilarious if it wasn’t the most unsatisfying combat encounter of my decade. There is too much of it.I had so much combat in this game I never want to experience it again, ever!And if the devs give us the options to create an incompetent fighter they should at least have some path to avoid this crap. And I haven’t even begun to describe the moral choices of this game which seem off to me as well. In the almost 90 minutes I spent in the game most of my dialogue choices didn’t feel appropriate, even the ones that were unavailable because of my character’s world view, but that just my personal preference, or me being distraught by the harrowing combat experience.Well, a piece of art should evoke an emotional response. This masterpiece made me feel miserable and angry, and led me question my life choices that led to this point. I’m strongly considering a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, the trailer makes it look like a Fallout 2 sorta game.  It is vaguely like that, UI is pretty janky, next to zero voice overs in the first 40 mins or so, so you're reading most of it.  Dialogue is pretty simplistic but plays out using a moral compass system that is a bit strange.WASD movement, no camera controls other than some basic zoom in/out.  Tab to highlight actionable items.  Click a bucket, click a shovel, click some sheep poop, congrats, you've completed your first quest.   Combat is more like Wasteland 2.  A bit janky, but ok.  2 action turn based combat.  1 action allows you to move, the other to act (or save both for some double actions)Standard inventory of post apoc junk.  Equip an old rifle, shoot at the guy with 74% chance to hit, etc, repeat.I might get better.  I really wasn't hooked during the first intro missions at all.  There was some bugs with chat choices leading to the wrong outcomes or inescapable loops.  I figured if there was bugs that early in the game, its going to get worse fast.  Anyway, this one isnt for me. _childDocuments_.review: Overall, recommended for people who like the setting and don't mind replaying since screw ups / bugs abound!In a word - fantastic. Going for a sort of Arcane Punk meets Waylander vibe, overlaid with a strong Aussie flavour, it really nails the vibe of a post-apocalyptic Australia. As an Australian I really loved seeing my slang and culture in a game - so top marks here.Kinda meh. Depending on your background, you have a somewhat plausible reason for getting involved in events - but all of the backgrounds equally give you a reason why you would just walk away. The big bad in the game has a great name (funny and makes sense if you are Aussie) but having most of your party walk away from the fight seems odd. Maybe it depends on quests (see below), or maybe I did something wrong, but felt discordant. - by mid game I was steamrolling everything in 1-2 rounds. No difficulty setting, so intended? Anyone who has played these sort of games before knows that winning = action economy, so pump Int and Agi, have a squillion actions and only go into round 2 when there are more than 8 enemies. - I had 4 quests bug on me, so couldn't finish. A couple of side quests that were meh and 1 that seemed to have no way to complete. Overall I did attempt every quest I could find, explored the whole map, spent a long time faffing around with vendors etc - and still completed in about 13 hours. So those critical of the quoted 25 hour play time are being fair. Maybe it is meant to include a 2nd playthrough? - This was an interesting concept. There is even a character (if you do her quests) who actually explains how you can be a nihilistic humanist etc. Guessing someone on the Dev team did Philosophy at Uni! The only thing I didn't like is that sometimes you literally CANNOT pick a bunch of the dialog responses depending on your morality. This reduces player agency in a non logical way (maybe my nihilist is utilitarian in the right scenario). - Cool though makes an already overpowered stat, even more overpowered (Int). Also since 2 of your companions are pyros, basically makes that tree worthless and creates a feel bad moment if you pick it.

_childDocuments_.review: I created my character as a hired gun. I wanted to play the game as the guy who solves his problems with a gun most of the time.  Increased all related attributes with every level up. And as of writing this review I'm 2,5hrs into the game, reached level 5, completed chapter 1 and you know what? I haven't fired a single bullet yet. Not even 1. All I did was to go there, get this, talk to that guy, move on.  I mean, making a game without combat is perfectly fine of course, but then why do you have all those combat related attributes if there won't be any combat? On the positive side, I must say that the art is gorgeous. I don't regret buying the game, as I see there is potential here. Hopefully future patches will change things. But as of now, it's a 5/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: So this game is incredibly boring, shallow and misleading. Its setting is more akin to a really bad g rated burning man festival walking simulator than a post apocalypse where your choices matter, Empty locations card board cutout reused enemies and the most boring fetch quests comprise the majority of the game experience you will encounter. Combat was clearly an afterthought due to character stat customization and strategy playing zero part in your success or loss due to most battles simply consisting of your team hitting the enemy mob over the head repeatedly with a generic weapon. No mutant animals, people or anything really unique or interesting in this setting aside from the "Magic" twist they put into the game that falls flat and is never explained at all. The philosophical paths you take really don't grant any interesting bonuses to your character nor do they give you any unique choices with meaningful consequences throughout the game play experience. The character animations are very minimal and repetitive and the whole time you play it will seem that your team is moving underwater while traversing the desolate and content barren locations. There are several locations in the game that have no interactive characters and nothing to do at all in them whatsoever aside from picking up loot that doesn't seem to have any purpose in the game. This was the only RPG that I have ever played where you don't get to initially fight against or see the main antagonistic faction in action upon their introduction but only get to see a weird pseudo battle from a far instead. In summation the game is not worth your money and you're better off playing Tyranny, Dragon age Origins,Pillars of eternity or Alpha Protocol until the devs make some major changes.To the Devs: Mates, please add some majorly mutated animals, weird deranged humans and some fearsome foes. All of the raiders and villains in this game were less scary than middle school hall monitors. Its the post apocalypse, let your imagination run wild. Also add more unique and interesting weapons and add some more musical tracks for your combat encounters that are more exciting and less chill.

_childDocuments_.review: It's enjoyable for what it is, and I'm keen to try different character backgrounds on subsequent runs once the bugs have been ironed out.I adore the Australiana setting, the artwork is gorgeous, the characters are quirky, overall I loved traversing this world and will stay seated for whatever the devs put out next. The game has a lot of potential that's unfortunately bogged down by spreading itself thin over too many concepts it doesn't particularly excel at.Like magic, I'm still not sure what I'm supposed to do with it by the end of the game. I had the sense you can use it in combat? But weapons fighting takes precedence in combat UI and skill tree anyway that I had no incentive to invest in magic. It could've been compelling for magic to be this mysterious power we had no access to throughout the game, only for it to handicap us in the final encounter for example. Just my two cents! I like the combat mechanics but it could do with a bit more polish, so more time refining melee/ranged combat and less on tacking magic on wouldn't hurt.Re: quests, I enjoyed them. There are some great ideas here. I particularly love the ones that effect outcomes of other quests like  or . I just wish they tied together better. Quest decisions could have had an impact on morality which would make the morality system more prominent.There were many bugs caused by quests not closing properly, e.g. completing Quest A wiped a character off the map, so I couldn't complete Quest B where I had to give them some items. No indication in the journal either as to where they'd gone so I scoured every location hoping the character had moved somewhere. No dice. Could've been prevented if the journal had just told me I failed Quest B for reasons.Progressing too far into a quest should lock you out of related ones, or you should be warned of time sensitive ones so you can prioritise accordingly. After the  It was a mess, but nothing a few patches can't fix.A lot of the quests also involve finding the right people to talk to, or finding a container/vendor with the right items. This would've been fine had the hints been more obvious but as it is, there isn't much variety between characters to make their roles or wares memorable, containers blend in with the scenery so you have to painstakingly move your cursor over every inch of every map to find one, it just leads to a lot of time spent going through every location interacting with characters and containers who may not have much to offer in the hopes you'll find The One. I gave up on a bunch of quests in the end because I felt I've tried every person/object/location under the sun with no leads forthcoming. It doesn't lend to very creative problem solving.But hey, I would've loved the exploration more had it not been done under the pretense of these arduous quests. Overall I'd play Broken Roads again once the kinks are ironed out, especially now that I know where most things are and in what order quests should be done.

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a couple of hours to really get into Broken Roads but once I got my head around the avalanche of characters you meet in the first hour I found myself getting drawn into the story. This is a quite story-heavy game but fortunately it's shaping up to be a good story... something mysterious is brewing (no spoilers!) and I need to know what it is. The gameplay itself is a bit rough around the edges, it doesn't have the polish of a big budget game. For example gathering companions to go on a mission out in the world is janky because you just pick them by name with no information about them, not even a portrait. For the first few missions I had no idea who any of them were because I couldn't remember their names from the menagerie of characters I'd just been introduced to. Then the combat with those characters is just reactive and not strategic because I have a bunch of random characters that I couldn't distinguish between. I'd rather have less combat. This stuff detracts from Broken Roads and gets in the way of enjoying the story, but I can cope with it.Where Broken Roads shines is its atmosphere. They have built a world that feels legitimately post-apocalyptic Aussie, and I love how much it leans in to its Australianess. The art and music in the game are excellent. It feels like real place and it has character. It's this world and story they've created for it which is drawing me back in despite the shortcomings of the game itself.

_childDocuments_.review: Broken Roads is a cult classic in the making. It hearkens to the best parts of games like Fallout 2, and many other CRPGs of the '90s, and it fits right in alongside classic Fallout and the Wasteland games. It’s flawed in some areas, with bugs in spots, but it offers tremendous role-playing and storytelling that make it more than worth your time to spend upwards of thirty or more hours in post-apocalyptic Australia. _childDocuments_.review: Broken Roads is an ode to the cRPGs of old, but it’s also a step forward for the genre, showing that the ‘90s approach still has a place today. _childDocuments_.review: I originally gave this a very poor review and was sort of sarcastic with my approach.  This revised review will attempt to go into more detail.  I also re-purchased it to give the game a fair chance. This is a CRPG for one, not a TRPG. So forget about tactical gameplay.  Combat consists of clicking on an enemy and just shooting them.  There are additional special attacks but they don't compare to just shooting your gun twice a turn.  Make sure each character has 6 action points and each combat encounter will be a cinch. Execution of gameplay is amateur.  Several examples....first 10 minutes of the game as the barter crew profession, and the first quest is to talk to a guy, to then talk to another guy, to do a combat encounter, to then go back to that 2nd guy, to then go back to the 1st guy, to then turn in the quest item.  This is the first major quest in the first 10 minutes of the game.  Very poor mission for this early.  It's tedious.  2nd example is leaving Merriden and forming your party, it's just a bunch of names on a list you have to click.  Each one at a time.  Did you forget who hat person is? Too bad.3rd example is getting magic powers after chapter 1.  So you completed chapter one and you assume you have to leave town to progress the story.  Well, they give you magic at this time.  You can put skill points into magic skiills.  So, you leave town and get into a combat encounter...lo and behold, no magic abilities.  Hmmm.  Turns out, you had to go back to Merriden to trigger a cutscene that will then give you those magic abilities.  VERY poor execution here. Bugs.  There are a plethora of them.  One in particular where you can't complete a side quest if you did the main quest a certain way. It'll break the quest and it cant be completed. This has been reported by several people. Sound design.  Rather than play melancholic music tracks reminiscent of a post apocalypse, most of the music is up beat, with a twang of the guitar playing constantly.  Not my cup of tea. I prefer the music from Fallout 1 nearly 30 years ago.  Narration.  Poor.  The narrator sounds like they grabbed their next door neighbor for an afternoon and paid her in cookies and milk. Very poor narration.  She sounds like she's reading the script in real time as she's speaking, with too much inflection and deflection in her voice to make the narration sound presentable, but it just comes off as amateur. On top of that, the sound quality of the narration is poor. You can hear cracks and pops as she speaks into the mic. The developers were funded by a grant from the Australian gov't and it shows.  There is no heart in this game whatsoever. I still play from time to time to see where exactly they went wrong.  Clearly, this was an amateur endevour by amateur developers.  The budget is shoe string and you can tell.  It's a shame that this was so poorly executed.
_childDocuments_.name: Broken Roads

_childDocuments_.review:
Born of a love for traditional computer role-playing, Broken Roads provides a rich, engaging narrative in which players make their way across a desolated future Australia.

Blending together traditional and all-new role-playing elements on top of a classless system offering nearly unlimited character development options, Broken Roads presents players with an original morality system: the Moral Compass. This novel design sees dialogue options and questing decisions influence, and be influenced by, a character's philosophical leaning.

name: John Wick Hex
detailed_description: John Wick Hex is a fast-paced, action-oriented strategy game that makes you think and strike like John Wick, the professional hitman of the critically acclaimed film franchise. Created in close cooperation with the creative teams behind the films, John Wick Hex is fight-choreographed chess brought to life as a video game, capturing the series’ signature gun fu style while expanding its story universe. Players must make quick decisions and choose every action and attack they make, all the while considering their immediate cost and consequences. Featuring a unique blend of strategic momentum-based combat, John Wick Hex captures the feel of the unique tactical combat from the films and blurs the line between the strategy and action video game genres. Perform well and progress in the main story mode (which features an original story created for the game) to unlock new weapons, suit options and locations. Each weapon changes up the tactics you’ll use and the manner in which you’ll play. Ammo is finite and realistically simulated, so time your reloads and make the most of weapons you scavenge on the job. Experience an original new story set prior to the events of the films which sees John on a desperate mission to rescue Winston and Charon from a dangerous new adversary seeking his birthright. This story is brought to life by the world class voice talents of Ian McShane and Lance Reddick, reprising their iconic roles from the films, and voice acting legend Troy Baker, joining the stellar cast as the game's eponymous villain 'Hex'. John Wick Hex compliments the style of the films with a unique graphic noir art design and an original score by renowned composer Austin Wintory. Please Note: PC version does not support controllers

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, and for the on sale price it is not bad, but I can't say it's good. The animation is basic, the idea while displayed amazingly in the trailers is rudimentary and bland in actual play. Wick's move list is extremely basic and any displays of his "Gunkata" are purely coincidental. In the movies, he is a close quarters combat god basically, the closer he is to his opponents the more dangerous he is. In this game it is pretty much the opposite, the more surrounded he is the less powerful he is. None of his moves combo into each other and the timeline bar feels incredibly slow. The biggest disappointment for me was the lack of thought in the movement. You use your "takedown" move to put a guy on the ground and if you decide to punch him, the animation snaps to a prerendered movement, automatically lifting the opponent onto his feet to get punched by one of the 3(?) animations. Why couldn't he simply punch him on the ground? Do two strike attacks in a row and he puts his weapon on his back to attack, then does it again. The ability to chain moves would have been awesome. The potential could have been so much higher especially due to the semi turned based quality of it. His push move which basically allows him to push his opponent in a single direction does not allow you to shoot the opponent at the same time, if you push the enemy into another group of enemies or use that body for cover as you push close to them, they instead shoot right through their friend and into you. It's like they didn't even watch the movie for reference. I hope that the developers have more plans for this game because as it is, it is severely lacking and disappointing. If you get it on sale, it's not horrible. But you will constantly be thinking about how this must be early Wick, before he learned how to be the badass we see in the movies
_childDocuments_.name: John Wick Hex

_childDocuments_.review: Positives+ definitely feels John-Wick-like, moving between multiple targets, throwing guns at enemies to buy time+ interesting strategic choices around Time Units consumed+ Short individual level length lends to replays and improving on own performances+ Ian McShane! (and Lance Reddick i.e. a couple of "proper" movie voices for the cut scenes)+ Visually stylish+ Inexpensive+ The chance to watch a realtime playthrough of the action is a nice touchNegatives- Feels unpolished. Character animation quality and design is very basic and the limited camera control offers little enjoyment of some nice looking locations.- The basic strategy is solid and interesting, but it's all about either position, shoot or melee. There's little variety in the weapons apart from dmg/time, so the cycle of dodge, shoot punch, over and over lacks longevity. It could really use more environmental improvisation, which is the heart of John Wick and something of which SuperHOT demonstrated the possibilities- In fact while this is turn-based, the closest comparison to it IS SuperHOT.- Once again, Hex-based movement in man-made/interior locations just doesn't work as well as a grid, but this is a classic tabletop problem.Would like to see> Improved animation, both in fluidity and variety> More John Wick style multi-kills using environments, combos or enemies as shields> A proper director's cam for the realtime playback would be a wonderful toy

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game and it was enjoyable for a while, but in the end for me just misses the mark. It makes me sad because this game has so much potential but limited move options mixed with some poor designs and unnecessary RNG made the game more frustrating than fun.I like the way all actions happen on a time scale and you can see what your enemies are about to do. Developers nailed this 100%. The move list isn't bad and most have their place, but to really feel like John Wick there should have been more. In the movies John is constantly grappling one enemy while shooting another. This mechanic is missing. You can't shield yourself from gunfire with another enemy. This makes the push option largely useless. I would have liked to see a push and shoot option where John can either shoot the enemy being pushed or another enemy while being shielded. There should have been a disarm move as well (or even further - disarm and keep weapon or disarm and discard weapon). We should have been able to chain moves together like a Roll into a Takedown or a Takedown into a Strike instead of John taking down a target, then selecting strike on the next and the target magically gets off the floor for John to do pre-rendered stance strike animation. This is just laziness by the devs. As another reviewer wrote: In the movies, the closer John gets, the more deadly he becomes. Sadly, this game is the exact opposite and the limited moves make it this way.I would have loved to have been able to pick up magazines or better yet, be able to carry 2 weapons and swap if needed. Why are Johns only options while crouching shoot and a dodge roll? I have to stand up before a melee attack or even worse before picking up another weapon OFF THE GROUND... ridiculous.In a game where ammo is so valuable, why are guards constantly dropping weapons that have not been fired at less than max capacity? If I start up a section and shoot the first guard. His gun may drop with 10 rounds or it may drop with 7. This RNG difference can make or break a run and it's completely unnecessary. If I opt to shoot an enemy with low health with a machine pistol or SMG, and John kills him/her with the first round, why does John insist on wasting another 4-5 rounds? I could understand 1 or maybe 2, but 3, 4, or 5 is an unnecessary waste especially when other guns do not behave like this. Why are so many unarmed thugs so willing to just stroll right up to an armed John Wick?I don't agree with the unlimited (or seemingly unlimited) enemy spawn either. I can see why this was a design choice, but I didn't care for it. As many others have stated, the animations are just limited and not very satisfying to watch. This is not a game breaker for me but a lot more work could have gone into the animations. I also would have enjoyed partial stealth mechanics (thinking of start of club scene from first John Wick movie). If you like John Wick and strategy games, this may be worth $10 to you. I got what I paid for and I don't regret the purchase however I don't want to recommend it to others. I enjoyed the start, but as the game progressed it became more frustrating than fun where this had the potential to be a 10/10 gem with a little more time and thought from development/publishers.

_childDocuments_.review: This game definitely has some interest aspects and fun mechanics, excellent voice acting (as usual) from Ian McShane and Lance Reddick, neat levels, cool colour scheme, and combat potential.This game has potential, it could be a fantastic and interesting turn based strategy game set in the John Wick universe. However, it falls apart for me at the combat.You play as John ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Wick, not a ♥♥♥♥♥-up opossum with an AK-47, it should not be a coin toss whether or not I hit a stationary target at 15m with a Carbine. The hit chances are the most obnoxious and frustrating part of the game, 70/80/90% almost guarantee a miss and with preset firing, it's a pain in the ass. You cannot fire just 2 shots with ANY of the automatic weapons, they all fire 4-5 shots regardless if the target only needs 2 to die just to waste your ammo.The combat in general feels clunky, the animations look decent enough but I can see how they are a major letdown from the films. John Wick in this timeline knows only 3 different ways to deliver a standing strike and needs a full second or longer to watch a target from ADS before actually shooting even if they are literally standing in front of him. Takedowns are fairly fluid, even if the character models warp through each other, but again there's no variety.You can't shoot from cover, throw stuff around corners, use your environment, or dive into a roll.The game is rather difficult, but before that, it's obnoxious. It's the clunky combat and unpolished feel of the gunplay that lets the game utter the final phrase of WIck's past enemies, "Be seeing you John."

_childDocuments_.review: It's good that it was a short game. The system was pretty interesting, but not deep or fun enough to play for more than ~6 hours. Those 6 hours were pretty good, but the game felt like it was already stretching its systems.The few moves available at the beginning of the game are the only moves you ever have. The only progression in the gameplay is the addition of new enemies and the new guns they drop. For a 6-hour game, that's mostly fine, but the moveset felt pretty limited, so it was disappointing to not get anything more.I didn't feel like the murder monster I was supposed to be. There are no moves that affect more than one enemy at a time. Avoiding the AI was usually more about tricking it than anything else. There were a few instances where I ducked behind low cover, causing the enemies to lose sight of me and start a 'move' command. I would instantly pop back up, shoot one while it was still moving, then duck again, waiting for them to start another 'move' command, then repeat. It was effective, but it didn't feel John-Wick-y. An area-of-effect tool, zone control mechanic, or even allowing the enemies' bullets to hurt other enemies could have made positioning much more interesting. Instead, it was mostly running in and out of cover, forcing the AI into long 'move' commands.Most significant, however, was the lack of ways to quickly interact with enemies. This is tough criticism to make because the game is all about effectively sequencing your actions and laying out plans for how to use your time. Still, I feel like such a turtle the whole game. It was common, when facing multiple enemies, for my best option to be 'walk away and hope they miss'. The only evasive maneuver requires that you crouch first, and it takes a full half-second to reach a crouching position. There's a big gap between the unstoppable bogeyman John Wick is supposed to be and needing a full half-second to go from standing to crouching. Because all actions took a long time and they could only affect one enemy, facing a group of three or more enemies head-on was often suicidal. There wasn't any gameplay reward for taking on challenges like facing a group head-on, and the tools to do so weren't really there either. It meant there was a lot of 'running backwards to cover'. Again, not necessarily a problem, but it wasn't very fun.It was a good 6 hours, but I was hoping for some more wild John Wick moments. Instead, too often, the best thing for the bogeyman to do was 'run away'.

_childDocuments_.review: John Wick Hex is a isometric real time strategy game where you control the infamous assassin as he shoots and fights his way across multiple stages. It’s incredibly unforgiving, punishing you for the slightest mistakes, but really well thought out and well worth playing.Set before the movie series, Hex kidnaps both Winston and Charon, and the high table send John to kill Hex and recover them. The background is explained in between and during missions (comic book style), and as you finish missions Hex slowly explains his motives and how John threw a wrench into them, and why it’s personal. John has to proceed through different underbosses that are aligned with Hex, chasing clues as he hones in on his location.Gameplay is all about resource management (focus, ammo and bandages), and the fog of war (line of sight) the enemies have to you. It’s very unforgiving and punishes you for mistakes that could have been made in the planning stage (where you can drop additional resources into missions), or from failing to dodge or managing fights better. Since everything carries over between missions (until you finish an area) starting a new stage on low health, focus or an empty gun can be fatal. It takes a little while to get used to it, but once it clicks together you realise they have done a masterful job of setting up an action sequence (with you as the director), the replays can be fun watch (depending on your ability). As John you have a wide range of actions you can take, with everything displayed as how long it will take in a timeline (your quicker than most enemies). You move via a hex grid pattern, and can perform actions or chance stance to increase your aim or roll out of danger. You can melee enemies when close enough, striking them, or at the cost of focus either push them out of the way, or performing a takedown (which is usually fatal to everyone except the toughest enemies). If timed right you can parry enemies (which stuns them), which can give you the required time to escape, take an emery down or engage someone else. You start each area with your trusty custom gun, but usually end up having to switch to any of the cast off weapons by dispatched enemies fairly quickly. Each weapon has a different damage output and firing times, and i found it handier to have the quick firing weapons rather than the stronger guns that take ages to fire (and leave you open to getting shot). You do tend to get mobbed frequently, and being careless ends up being a death sentence. The underbosses throw a challenge into the game, as they usually have underlings with them, and recover their focus if you wear them down. It can make those missions a cat and mouse, as you take out the chaff, then go for the kill.The games stage design is quite good, and built around line of sight and testing your ability to manage Wick and the enemies. There are plenty of pillars and areas you can duck or hide behind or bottleneck your next victim, and enemies seem to be keyed to spawn at set points (though the enemy that spawns seems to be randomised). Using the stages layout is the only way you can progress. There are plenty of different locals, from inside buildings, warehouses, tunnels, parks, and large outsides to progress through. Enemies are carbon copies of each other (every “type” of enemy will be the same), but it easily helps with threat detection and you don’t need to click on every enemy to see their stats. Usually the melee enemies can be left until last, as its also more prudent to take out the gun welding enemies first (if you aren’t going to hide and make them come to you) in most cases.The voice acting uses the same actors from the movie (excellent), and Troy Baker (Hex) never seems to do a bad job. The game has a really decent soundtrack, which to me seems like a mix of something western (duelling pistol vibe with the guitars), with a heavy mix of techno and bass. Some of the guns don’t sound as grunty as I think they should, but that could be because of the pumping soundtrack. Getting 100% Achievements will require a fairly good understanding of enemies and how the game mechanics work (and a hefty dose of luck), as you need to complete each stage with the best rating and on the hardest difficulty. Finishing the game on the normal setting was difficult enough.For more reviews please visit

_childDocuments_.review: The best aspect of John Wick Hex, as it should be, is its gameplay. At its core, the stop/start strategy style of the game really puts you in John Wick's mind as you navigate all the different choices you have. You move along dots on the map slowly inching your way through the level, revealing the environment with each careful step. Along the way you encounter various enemy types that require different ways to take them down. You have choices between melee and range attacks, both of which you need to alternate depending on the situation, and all of your choices need to be measured in accordance to the Timeframe System. There are enough combat options to keep it difficult and varied, but it could use a few more to really flesh out John Wick's character and compliment the combat prowess he possesses in the film trilogy. It's easy to grasp, but difficult to master and nonetheless I give it: While the art style is really nice and unique, the one thing holding this game back almost entirely is its animations. They're very janky and sometimes almost comical. I think this area could've used a whole lot more polish before they published the game. Enemies who don't even use guns have their hands fixed in a gun holding position, as does Wick when he's not even holding a gun. There isn't much variety in terms of strikes and takedowns, although they do look cool sometimes. At the end of each level there is a real time replay of everything you did in a level and those are satisfying to watch so they almost make up for the janky animations contained in them. This would be a 4/10 because of the animation glitching, clipping, and lack of attention to detail, but the replay feature bumps the graphics department to: The music is pretty cool. It's close to what they have in the movies, being a bit electronic with subtle hints of rock in it. It ramps up at the right times, especially during those replays that show everything you did in real time. Unfortunately the sound effects are either weak or non-existent for some animations like throwing your gun at someone and parrying their attacks. Melee sound effects are also mistimed during the replays. This makes the replays a little less epic, especially when enemies don't SELL the hit from being parried.The music makes up for the otherwise weak and nearly non-existent sound effects giving it: Another weak aspect of this game is its User Interface. A lot of the boxes and text are way too small, which are fine for me to read, but for people with vision impairments it might be tough to navigate. There is no reason for everything to be so small, and it's a shame that there's no alternate controller options where you can snap between decisions. Instead you have to use your right joystick to act like a mouse in a system that could have easily used a snap on function. Hell there isn't even any KEY BINDINGS for certain actions to speed up your decision making. Everything you need to do needs to be clicked on manually on a small button on screen somewhere.For a game with this amount of complexity a better UI could have easily made the game itself way more fun than it already is, landing the UI score to be: Despite my grievances with the UI, animations, and sound effects, John Wick Hex is still a really good game thanks to its gameplay mechanics. It's unique and I haven't experienced anything like this yet so I love it. The blend between turn based strategy and somewhat real time reaction keeps you on your toes as if you were the Baba Yaga yourself. Being a huge John Wick fan and a fan of strategy games, I'm willing to look past its MANY faults and focus on the core experience the developers intended. I give this game an overall score of: To warrant a higher score if they ever make a sequel to this or patch it up: I'd give it a 7/10 if they fix the janky animations and mistimed sound effects, 8/10 if they fixed the nearly inaccessible UI, and 9 or even 10/10 if they gave us even more action options, like the ability to roll from a standing position, to leap over obstacles, or use enemies as human shields. Definite recommend if you want something very unique and to the point, and only if you're willing to look past some janky animations and inconsistent sound design.

_childDocuments_.review: Now I see why they put this initially as an exclusive on Epic Games, you don't have user reviews on there to show how bad the game is. The low amount of purchases on Steam (only 80 reviews!) and the low rating among the only 80 user reviews should have warned me it was a bad game.But being the fan of the movies I am I just had to buy it when a sale finally popped up. But the game is just really ♥♥♥♥, the animations are crap and do not flow between moves, the movement and combat feels very stiff and utterly opposite of how we see John Wick in the movies. The gunplay is bad, the combat is bad and the movement design is bad. No idea why a "focus" mechanic was needed it just feels unnecessary and ruins the flow of the combat, the limited ammo and health was already plenty to make the game challenging, limiting combat with "focus" bar is just silly.It also makes no sense you can't do all moves from crouch, I thought hey let me wait for this enemy to pass so I'll crouch and then take him down from cover, well guess what all you can do from crouch is shoot/throw your gun and roll. You can't slow walk, you can't do takedowns from cover and you can't even "refocus" from cover.I alt-f4'd the game when I saw how bad the animations were, I did a takedown on an enemy, that put them in a crouched stun position then I did a strike and you see the character models just teleport to the new position needed for the strike animation.This game is a mess and not fun, not challenging in the right ways and just poorly thought out mechanic wise.The biggest 'crime' of this game is that it utterly does not understand the movies, surely the devs played their own game right and saw right away that the gameplay just has 0 in common with the movies. The only thing this has in common with the movies is the characters and story. But gameplay has nothing to do with the movies and they literally should be ashamed to call this game "John Wick". As a result I think this game probably would have been more successful without the John Wick licence as at least then players wouldn't be buying it thinking they would get something resembling John Wick in gameplay. It could have been "Dave Hex Combat" or something and probably would have been more successful.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit on the fence with this one and the "Mixed" rating on Steam feels like what the rating should be. For the most part, a lot of the reviews are "bUt I dOn'T lIkE tUrN bAsEd GaMeS!" Then this wasn't for you in the first place. Do people actually just buy games because of an IP without actually doing any research? Don't answer that...Anyway, John Wick Hex is certainly a very interesting idea. I'd rather play a clunky game that feels new than a polished game that just does the same things as everybody else. The first hour or two are actually pretty fun as you learn the mechanics, figure out how the AI reacts, learn the counters, and start to feel like John Wick clearing out a building by himself.The main problem is the difficulty ramp as the game progresses. The game doesn't really offer much in terms of upgrades. Each level is split within 5-6 mini stages. You can only upgrade going into a level, not between mini stages. In fact, what you complete a mini stage with is what you start the next mini stage with. This makes the game feel incredibly punishing. Once you start getting to around the midway point of the game, you'll find yourself restarting the first mini stage whenever you take any damage because you only get 2 bandages for the whole level and can't waste that resource early. Problem is restarting a stage because you take damage feels really tedious so then you start eating the damage and you end up in the later stages with no resources going up against the toughest enemies.Beyond that frustrating aspect making the game feel really tedious, the upgrades they offer are really passive abilities. Things like "push requires one less focus." None of the abilities really help you take down enemies. Then you add on to the fact that they throw so many enemies at you. There will be sections where you just don't stand a chance. You'll die and it won't feel like you made a tactical error, you just leave feeling "What did the game expect me to do here?" Guards will infinitely spawn from doors, sometimes you get surrounded, and there's just nothing you can do except die and restart. That's where the game lost me. The first half of the game was interesting and fun. Once I hit the midway point, the game immediately became a tedious chore.In all honesty, I would recommend playing this if you can get it for cheap just for the first 2-3 levels because it is a unique game and pretty interesting. But once you start getting to the point where the game just becomes unfair, call it quits. I did enjoy my short time with it but I really can't be bothered to continue from here.

_childDocuments_.review: In short:John Wick Hex is a ttrpg-like game that runs on a grid system where John Wick can take a number of actions like shoot a bad guy, or move to the next grid point, just like taking a turn in an rpg, with each action taking a cost to perform, such as needing ammo to shoot or focus to do melee takedowns. In John Wick Hex, all your turns affect the world in real time, so say, if you decide to walk to the next grid point one point away, John will take 0.3 seconds in real time to do so. All actions in the game are reflected on a timeline on the HUD where you can then seen both yours and the enemy ai's actions and how long they will take in real time to complete each action. For example, John tries to shoot one of 2 armed enemies with a pistol. Both enemies see John and take aim. John takes 0.9 seconds to start shooting and manages to kill the first thug but the second thug takes 1.2 seconds to aim and shoot. The game will then pause after John kills the first thug and now you can make a number of actions to 'take your turn'. However, once you've made your choice of action, John now has 0.3 seconds to take that action before another thug shoots him. Say John chooses to shoot the other thug, which is an action that takes 0.9 seconds. The game will then play out the action in real time where John takes the bullet from the enemy 0.3 seconds later like a man unflinching and 0.6 seconds later, he guns the thug down for ruining his new bullet proof suit. The levels usually consist of either John having to make his way through a hallway of thugs to reah the exit, or John having to make his way through a hallway of thugs to kill a boss. While this may sound repetitive, the moment to moment fights that occur and the time it takes for you to plan out your fights is usually a blast and if fun enough to carry you through the level. The best thing is that after absolutely annihilating the hallway of thugs, you get a replay button when you finish the level to watch in REAL TIME how your John Wick tore all those pitiful thugs to shreds. Ignoring the un-synchronized melee sounds and weirdly placed soundtracks on some levels, this one button makes you feel like you're watching a scene from the movies, this time, you where behind the wheel of the murder machine himself. Personally, this is definitely a fun game worth your time. The ability to watch replays of how you polished off some 10 guys in a packed room is really satisfying to see. In addition, on operation mode, having infinite amount of time to plan your next move allows for some trilling combat puzzles that are a blast to play through.However, small things like timeline issues (such as interruption bugs), movement bugs and some really badly balanced maps (aka alps -4, the forest of frustration) can hinder enjoyment of the game.Overall, a solid game, that with a little more polish on its presentation and balancing, can definitely make for a fun weekend experience.While I do have grippes about how some of the game and bugs play out, I do feel this is a game definitely worth a weekend spent to play it. Recommendation: Buy on Discount if interestedAnd Chinatown is clearly the best map in the game. Any other opinion is clearly wrong ;P

_childDocuments_.review: John Wick Hex is not a bad game by any means. It's more clunky and repetitive than it is "bad", but that's why I can't really recommend it.Setting the John Wick IP aside, which led me to this game, the main gameplay mechanic is pretty interesting. It's more "cinematic" that it is a turn-based game, as you (and your enemies) program your actions on a timeline not that dissimilar to video editing softwares. In a sense, you direct the action in order to make it as smooth as possible, which is pretty intriguing and exhilarating ... for the first couple of hours.The main problem of the game is that it feels like a prototype : It lacks variety in the gameplay, and its simplistic art style fails to hold up on the long run, especially with the lack of diversity and rigidity of the animation ; The "replay" animations at the end of each level are interesting at first, but end up underlining this lack of diversity and variety, as they all look the same, and undercooked.So, if you're looking for an interesting take on "turn-based" action, John Wick Hex might interest you, otherwise, chances are it won't be your cup of tea if you came looking for "The John Wick Experience".

_childDocuments_.review: John Wick Hex is a turn based combat game based on the action films starring Keanu Reaves. Gameplay is very similar to Superhot, but with an overhead camera perspective.Time only moves when you move, and every action you take costs a specific amount of time to activate. You can see what actions nearby enemies are about to perform, and how long they’ll take, so you can plan your moves accordingly.John’s actions include melee attack, shoot gun, reload, throw/pick up weapon, crouch/stand up, dodge roll and use bandage to heal.Melee attacks can stun lock enemies (including bosses, making them quite easy to beat), but often you’ll be surrounded by multiple enemies, many armed with guns, so you need to keep moving to avoid their bullets, and use scenery to block their line of sight.There are a variety of guns including pistol, revolver, uzi, sub machine gun, assault rifle and shotgun. Unlike most games, the pistol is actually the best weapon because it fires much faster than other guns, and when you hit an enemy it cancels their attack. When an enemy is going to shoot first, its better to just dodge out of the way, or throw your weapon at them to stun them. Most weapons don’t have extra ammo to reload, so you’ll change weapons often.After completing a level, you can view a replay which shows all actions taken in real time. Sometimes this can look cool, when you put together a string of moves like shooting one guy, throw weapon at another, crouch, dodge roll to where the first guy dropped his gun, pick it up and shoot the second guy. But when you move around the level you often have to zig zag between tiles, which looks stiff and robotic in the replays.The control interface isn’t great, because you can’t move the camera by moving the mouse pointer to the edge of the screen, which feels wrong. You can only move the camera with WASD, and you can’t even rebind those keys (personally I prefer arrows).Finally, I can’t post this review without mentioning the penultimate level, which is one of the worst difficulty spikes I’ve encountered in a game for a while, and caused me to finish the game in a negative mood. While previously I might have died once or twice on a level, this one took me probably close to 20 attempts. To complete a level you have to reach an exit marker, which is locked if there are enemies nearby. Usually it isn’t a problem to kill a couple more guys. However, on this level there seems to be infinitely respawning enemies, and there are 3-4 spawn points very close to the exit. The exit is actually also an enemy spawn point, and I’m sure you can see how that might be a problem.On each attempt I would kill 20-30 enemies (after a while I actually started counting them), with 4 enemies active at a time, but every time I killed one another would spawn, keeping the exit locked. Eventually I’d run out of focus which is required to dodge, get surrounded by gun wielding enemies, and die. It didn’t help that on 3 occasions, the game actually bugged out, I couldn’t interact with anything, couldn’t move, couldn’t shoot, couldn’t do anything except exit to the menu and restart the level. I was literally in “one more go and then I’m done” territory when I guess I got a piece of luck in the spawn patterns and found a moment where the exit was unlocked.Overall John Wick Hex is a good idea that is fun when it works, but is also let down by some design flaws. Pick it up on a deep sale if you’re a big John Wick fan.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting concept and has some promise but the gameplay as it is is just not fun in the later missions. The sheer number of enemies the player has to kill combined with the 'very' limited set of possible moves you can do and the timing for everything being on par with- or worse than what hostiles can do just makes this extremely repetitive and frustrating.How many times in those movies do we see John Wick holding a guy he just tackled down while shooting other assailants until he's got the free time to finish him off, for example?Why, when we spend our very limited ressources to make a deaddrop in the mission somewhere, like a gun, some bandages or whatnot, do we not get those things marked when we're actually there? Add to that that these things don't actually always seem to work in the first place. I've scoured a particular map I had bought a dead drop gun for for an hour and couldn't find it anywhere so... slow applause please.Soundtrack is okay but a bit bland in places, story seems a bit unimaginative, visuals are okay for the most part, tho of course a bit simplistic.Animations are... somewhat crude which of course enforces huge limitations on the players freedom of movement. Why can't we do a dodge-roll while standing up? Why can't john wick vault over a table or drop to a prone position or anything? Too simplistic in gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: John Wick Hex is a strategy game based on the popular John Wick movie franchise. The game puts the player in the role of the protagonist, John Wick, as he travels around the world carrying out secret missions against a variety of criminal organizations.The game makes excellent use of the John Wick setting, combining tactical combat and RPG elements with a movie-like presentation. Combat places the player in turn-based command of John and his allies, allowing the player to choose between various tactical options to complete their missions. The use of time as a resource allows for interesting decisions and keeps the action fast-paced and intense. The game also features a fantastic art style, capturing the look and feel of the John Wick movies perfectly.Overall, John Wick Hex is a brilliant game that succeeds in capturing the essence of its source material. The combat is robust and satisfying, while the overall presentation is top notch. From the great soundtrack to the movie-accurate art style, this is a game that any fan of John Wick should not miss.

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique take on John Wick license .Instead of having the usual action-movie based third person shooter max-payne clone game , Bithell Games (the dev) takes a different approach with the time-based tactics design, allowing you to take a role in the decision making process inside John Wick's mind. .  You will be fighting hordes of enemies with limited resources, you have to rely on blind spots and advantageous melee tactics to advance through enemies.Bear in mind that this isn't a turn-based game as some might think ,you can imagine as a hotline miami game with mandatory pauses to allow you to take the right decision during gameplay.It is also worth mentioning that the game features an original non-cannon story ,with a writing tone similar to the movies ,it also features support characters from the movies (with their original VA).For that,  ,especially for John Wick fans ,though bear in mind that the game is quite short (6h on average).

_childDocuments_.review: I started playing this game because I watched John Wick 4 last week and had an itch. I don’t think I’ve ever played a game quite like this and I think if you’re interested in trying out games with novel mechanics, this one is worth looking at.Time to beat:There are about 7 levels in the game with 5+ stages per level. Stages are like tiny areas to traverse and completing one is a checkpoint. It can take 5-10 minutes to complete a stage and I spent 6 hours playing the game before I reached the end. If the stages were padded out more,I would have been fatigued. I respect games when they have a limited scope and execute it well (enough), so the game time worked for me. If you want something with more meat, this isn’t that. Combat: Every action you make takes up a certain amount of time that’s shown in the progress bar at the top of your screen. Enemy character actions are shown as a progress bar below your bar, so it can be trivial in the 1 v 1 to figure out what option you need to ‘win’ an interaction by comparing bars and choosing the faster option. The game becomes more difficult by introducing multiple enemies, where your decisions aren't as straightforward, In addition, the game makes use of fog of war, so you can’t see around corners (neither can your enemies). You can hear doors opening, so you know if enemy just spawned behind you and you can take that into account as you are making decisions.I feel like it might be easier to help explain the fun of the gameplay loop with a hypothetical. For example, the melee takedown is a great option that does good damage, stuns an enemy, and allows you to reposition slightly. It can also be easy to over-commit to a takedown on an enemy. If you take too long, the enemies outside of the fog of war will enter in your sight line. As you are finishing your takedown animation, those enemies are nearly done readying their firearm and about to fire and you will have to eat the damage. Even if you're faster than the enemies in front of you, you can't compare your time bar with an enemy outside the fog of war. Sometimes you can lose just by moving into the wrong position and you won’t know it until you play out the options.Flaws:-	Bosses are easy to stun lock with takedown; takedown only costs focus; focus is a resource that’s easy to maintain-	Brawlers and groups of brawlers were not threatening without gunmen because they would not attack when John is in a takedown or strike animation (they are threatening with gunmen because you don’t have time to deal with them anymore)-	No traps and obstacles to prevent camping-	Lack of better tools to diversify strategy (camping is fine unless it’s basically all you’re doing)-	When there a bunch of guns on the ground, it can be difficult to click on an enemy vs clicking on the pickup gun button (which will kill you)-	Playback feature was jankyEverything else:I enjoyed the comic book/graphic novel aesthetic; the menus were clean; the script was corny and the voice acting was great; and the music was appropriate for a game of this genre and escalated at the right moments.Conclusion:This game has flaws, but there’s something here that’s worth looking at that other games don’t do. Also, I’m kind of impressed that a game like this is attached to a well-known IP like John Wick. I hope more people/developers look at the gameplay in this title because I'd like more games like this to be made and refined.

_childDocuments_.review: The game captures the essence of John Wick's fight style perfectly. Every move you make must be calculated, just like planning an attack on the Autobots. The graphic style, inspired by comic books, looks like something out of the minds of the Constructicons. The game's soundtrack is a masterpiece, just like Soundwave's tapes.Well, what can I say? This game is for humans, after all. As a Decepticon, I find it a bit too simplistic, like fighting against the Dinobots - fun, but not a real challenge. The game doesn't have the same level of violence that I'm used to, but what can you expect from a game made by humans?Final Verdict:Overall, John Wick Hex is a game worth playing, even for a Decepticon like me. It's not as thrilling as flying in a Seeker squadron or piloting Metroplex, but it's a decent game for humans. If you like action games that require strategy and planning, you might enjoy this one. Just don't expect to be as powerful as a Decepticon, or as smart as me.

_childDocuments_.review: (don't mind the hours played on ps4)John Wick... the hitman we all love.This obviously isn't the best way to represent the killing masterpiece. Good choice for a strategy game tho.There are 2 mods to play, operator and expedited. Of course, you can play in the advanced mode (expedited) to keep the game smooth but it will be harder and you will have a bigger chance to die. If you are going to play no matter what, try both mods to see which fits you, and then continue the game for a better experience. I played operator because you only have 5 seconds to decide in the other mod.The graphics and colors fit the game perfectly and the sound effects are all fine. Also, the story is represented well. For the mechanics and gameplay, I can't say that. There are some cons like you can't take cover and even when you get behind anything to cover yourself from an enemy, you can't do anything. The takedowns and strikes could be better. Camera angles aren't always the way you want them to be. You can't adjust keybindings. Some of the shooting odds are way off the edge etc.I think it would be better if it was something fast like My Friend Pedro. I personally love John Wick but I didn't enjoy the game. It's not good enough to spend time for a 2020 game. If you want to try anyways, wait for the %70 discount.Thank you for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: Highly enjoyable with some expected AA industry jank.What we have here is something of a SuperHOT-esque turn based tactical game with time management. Every action has a set amount of seconds that it takes and mercifully, it gives you all of the enemies time bars at the top so you know when your shots will land before theirs does. If it won't, then you have to act accordingly. In my three hours of game time (which is just the first two levels in completion), I can count several times where merely crouching had me dodge a bullet because I wouldn't be able to get a shot off. So there's a second by second decision making but you don't have to make these decisions hastily - unless you play the higher difficult that only gives you five seconds to make decisions once the game pauses (typically when a new enemy enters John's visual range).It's a lot of fun but I had some moments of frustration. The game seems pretty stingy with healing items, I couldn't find any on-map bandages on the second level at all, whatsoever. I was stuck with the one I brought in the game with me. While the first tutorial level put one in your path, there's a chance the game is hiding them behind nooks and crannies for you to explore for them.I assume this means the game is just forcing you to pick your battles carefully. Indeed it took me an entire thirty minutes to defeat the second boss level, "Osborn," a brutal gauntlet of constantly respawning enemies. When I finally beat it and watched the reply, I was forced into the hole the level spawns you in while I killed, shot, and melee'd six or seven enemies before I found an opening to actually leave. Again, this seems like a mechanic to force you to move but there's far too many scenarios where I'm actually forced to bunker down, otherwise I'll just be shot to death. At one point I was stuck in a melee with four guys and there was nothing I could do.Ammunition, gear, and health persist throughout an entire level so there's a decent chance you may be forced to restart the entire thing over just to start at full. It took me another 30 minutes to escape the last two segments of the Osborn level because I was at a permanent 3 health that I had no way to recover so it was a ton of trial and error.That really is the name of the game, here. Trial and error. People say this is a 3-5 hour game but I'm three in and only two levels to my name. It was satisfying to be able to do the final segment of level two with just one health but it was a lot of waiting around corners for enemies to wander towards me.The coolest idea behind this game is the replay function. I never actually played SuperHOT so I don't know if they do a real-time replay at the end of their levels but Hex will replay your actions in real time after you beat every segment. It's a lot of fun to see and I hope games in the future develop this tech, because there is some jank to it. Through the reply there will often be half-second pauses before John and the enemies actually act so it doesn't capture the same flow that the movies do. It's basically copying your every move so with some time in the oven, I imagine this could be smoothed out.It's a fun game though and I recommend it, especially on the recent sale.
_childDocuments_.name: John Wick Hex

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of John Wick since the first movie, I was really pleased to see this game's concept: a tactical strategy shooter on the lines of the wonderful X-Com games.This is how John Wick fights: evaluate the situation, plan, execute, look at the results, start again. The RNG doesn't bother me: in the movies JW both has a almost supernatural awareness of his surrounding and gets his nose smashed by the first random bozo lurking behind a column. It is a fight between tactical logic and chaos.You control only John Wick, a one-man army superior in skill and physical moves to anyone else in the world. Problem is: you are alone. The scenarios ("Chapters" in the game") ask you to go from point A to point B.  Between them you have a horde of enemies, some part of the scenario, some RNG. Good luck.John can do everything you see in the movies: firing (of course); take down close enemies; throw at them his empty gun (!); crouch and roll (your aim is better but you spend precious "focus point"); pick the fallen enemies' guns; and even just wait. There is a deep satisfaction in crouching behind a cover, roll away and then just behind a enemy, take him down, take his gun and immediately kill a second enemy that blundered on the scene.The overall plot is a prequel to the first movie. Having the voice of the original actors (Ian McShane and the late Lance Reddick) narrating the story is a welcome touch. Also welcome is the ubiquitous Troy Baker, playing the mysterious bad guy who puts things in motion.The visuals are both spare and neon-drenched, like in the movies. While the action may seem repetitive, the variety of maps and enemies keeps things fresh. At the core of the game we have John Wick planning his next movie with chess-like precision only to have to desperately improvise three seconds in. This keeps thing tense, and mastering John is the key to survival.A final nice touch is the possibility, once you complete a level, to rewatch the action in a movie-like summary. It is not perfect, but it is a great proof of how this game recreates the "John Wick" experience.I read in the comments that there are better games. Good! But "John Wick Hex" is spare, linear and to the point. I played it twice and is was a blast both times. My mark is 8/10.
