_childDocuments_.review: "Sons of Valhalla" welcomes players into a pixel art world inspired by Norse mythology, offering a gameplay experience reminiscent of the Kingdom series. Despite its brevity, the game maintains engagement by introducing new challenges with each level, ensuring a dynamic experience for players. However, its most notable feature lies in its rune system. These runes allow players to customize character stats, providing flexibility to tailor gameplay to individual preferences.The risk of losing a rune upon death adds tension to encounters, amplifying the importance of decision-making throughout the game. One area for potential improvement is the management of runes; players currently face limitations in experimentation due to the need to choose between keeping or discarding runes upon discovery. It would be great to see a future update implementing a system to store runes for later use. This could enhance the player experience, enabling greater experimentation of different play styles. In terms of combat, "Sons of Valhalla" offers a straightforward experience that often revolves around repetitive button-mashing, lacking depth in its mechanics. Swapping between ranged weapons mid-combat feels cumbersome and interrupts the flow of gameplay. However, where combat truly shines is in the game's unique boss encounters.Overall, "Sons of Valhalla" delivers an engaging journey through its pixelated landscapes, offering players a unique blend of strategy, combat, and customization within a charming Norse-inspired setting.

_childDocuments_.review: Sons of Valhalla? A Viking Saga of Conquest and Repetition! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)"Embark on a pixel-art journey of vengeance and discovery, but be wary of the monotony that may lay ahead."Sons of Valhalla positions itself ambitiously in the gaming landscape, merging side-scrolling combat with base-building mechanics against the rich backdrop of the Viking Age. Players step into the boots of Thorald Olavson, vowing revenge against a treacherous Jarl in a narrative that promises raids, conquest, and personal combat. The game's pixel art breathes life into this era, inviting players to build, besiege, and battle across a meticulously crafted England.The core gameplay mechanics offer a blend of strategic base-building and direct combat, urging players to manage resources, recruit diverse units, and lead assaults. The game attempts to strike a balance between offensive maneuvers and defensive strategies, presenting a tug-of-war dynamic that's enriched by the inclusion of unique units like combat blacksmiths and shieldmaidens. The addition of siege engines and runes introduces layers of tactical depth, promising a saga filled with epic battles and strategic conquests.Despite its grand vision, Sons of Valhalla faces criticism that cannot be overlooked. Players have pointed out a sense of repetitiveness that seeps into the gameplay after the initial hours, highlighting a lack of complexity in base-building and resource management that falls short of expectations. The promise of variety and tactical depth is often shadowed by the game's execution, which seems to funnel players into a cycle of similar missions and underwhelming unit mechanics, detracting from the strategic gameplay it aims to deliver.Critiques also touch on the game's story, labeling it as overly simplistic and short-lived. The game’s pixel art and boss fights receive praise for their design and entertainment value, yet this isn't enough to overshadow the game's perceived shortcomings. Comparisons to Kingdom: Two Crowns suggest that while Sons of Valhalla borrows elements from successful titles, it struggles to carve out a unique identity that fully capitalizes on its offensive gameplay shift.However, it's not without its merits. The game’s focus on direct combat and the ability to lead assaults offers a refreshing twist, and the strategic use of runes adds a layer of depth to both economy and combat. These features, coupled with engaging boss fights and satisfying archery mechanics, provide glimpses into the game’s potential to deliver a fulfilling Viking Age experience.Sons of Valhalla sails into the gaming seas with a banner of ambition, aiming to merge the thrill of Viking raids with the satisfaction of base-building and strategic combat. Its beautiful pixel art and the premise of a revenge-driven saga initially captivate, offering a journey of conquest and exploration. Yet, the voyage is marred by repetitiveness and a lack of depth that leaves players yearning for more.For those drawn to the lore of the Viking Age and the allure of pixel art, there's enjoyment to be found in the raids and the occasional strategic decision. However, players seeking a complex base-building experience or a deeply engaging story may find the game lacking. Sons of Valhalla is a tale of what could have been, a game with the potential that, with further development and refinement, might one day fully unleash the saga it seeks to tell.Interested in discovering great Steam games? _childDocuments_.review: I backed this game on Kickstarter. The devs have released regular posts with updates and overall the process was good. I've been eagerly following and awaiting this release.It's a fun little game. It's like Kingdom with combat. Nice pixel art. Not much content at the moment. The campaign start to finish took me 7 hours. The campaign levels are very repetitive. Enemies all spawn from the right side of the map. You fight your way through some random camps and eventually enter a boss arena. There is some nice variation with the different enemy types in the different camps and mini-bosses. Also the rune system works very well and adds a lot of depth to the gameplay.My main criticism is there is very little replayability. I have no desire to revisit the campaign in it's current state. Kingdom New Lands and Two Crowns (+Norselands DLC) kept me occupied for nearly 100 hours and the levels didn't feel repetitive in the same way as SoV. The endless mode may present some replayability. I haven't tried it yet.The only bug I experienced was when trying to dodge roll while in the middle of charging an arrow. My character got locked in the slower movement of the arrow charge animation even though I wasn't charging the arrow anymore. I managed to get out of it by dodge rolling again.It's a SOLID foundation and the little that is there is fun. Still I fully recommend this game as I believe the devs will fill it out with content and possibly some DLCs down the road.

_childDocuments_.review: Scratches a certain kind of itch for me.  I definitely give it a thumbs up, but I also get why some other folks have complaints.  So read on if you want to hear my take on those specific issues.  Am about 3/5 through the game, and enjoying myself enough to keep playing more in the future.First up, is this action or strategy?  ...Yes.  It's definitely a bit of both.  I've always liked mashups of this sort, going all the way back to Actraiser.  The strategy and upgrade tree is not especially deep, but I could see where future content could go with it.  As it stands, it reminds me a bit of Terra Nil, where it reminds me of the main genre it orbits, without being as intricate or taxing as the main genre.The key thing is that both Terra Nil and Sons of Valhalla are a breath of fresh air, and do what they set out to really well.  They also both happen to be gorgeous.  But at the same time, they're both going to invite some criticism from fans of their primary genre who wanted a rabbit hole of complexity.  So it depends on what you are personally looking for.The controls are something I've seen some people say are stiff, but I really think that's not accurate.  It's not fluid like Dead Cells or Devil May Cry, but it's also clearly not trying to be.  In games like that, I find that my ability to interrupt animations and to spam buttons actually makes me play less tactically.  Part of the charm of a lot of the Soulslike games (which is this NOT!) are that they have kind of plodding movement, and you're committed to a choice once you make it, for a second or so.  This cuts down on button spamming, and makes people actually plan and time their attacks.  But if you DO try to button spam, you're going to wind up feeling like it's ignoring half your inputs (in this and the other games I mentioned), which will make it Feel Bad.  If you just slow down and actually input the attacks and moves you want to make, it feels great.  I really prefer this style of combat in general these days, as I tend to otherwise panic and spam.I've seen a number of reviews comment on this game being grindy, but I suspect that is kind of a matter of planning.  If you invest very heavily in resource production buildings and upgrading them, and are good at combat, and only sometimes use your soldiers, then you're going to be swimming in resources by the time you get partway across a map.  It feels like a pretty nice tug of war, where I'm only slightly ahead of things, and occasionally losing ground.If someone were to not do many resource building upgrades, or not heavily invest in building those in general, then I can imagine there would be long periods of waiting around.  I have not actually tried this myself, but it seems like a "mind the gap" situation from what I have played.The other thing is the actual weapons and attacks themselves.  If you use the basic attack, which is the thing that hits fastest... it does like no damage.  If you hold the attack button and charge up a "double attack," then it feels like it does a lot more than double damage.  This actually slows down the combat even more, in an interesting way.  You have to plot your spot to plant your viking butt in the middle of a group of enemies, aimed so that when the double attack is charge, you can do maximum damage to the most enemies and knock them over.  It adds some positioning and spatial/time thinking that is one of my favorite things about the game.But for someone ignoring the double attack and just using regular attacks, I would imagine it would feel, frankly, pretty awful.  I bet you have to hit enemies like a hundred times to get them dead, and it's not much area of effect, and so on.  Don't do that.  The game suggests you don't do that, but it doesn't enforce it.  I almost wish the basic attack didn't exist, because it just gives the wrong idea entirely.  I am reminded of Gunpoint in terms of how I actually play this game, where each attack is methodical and has a lot of oomph behind it.  If you don't use the double attack, then it won't be like that at all.Then there are the ranged weapons.  The basic arrow is so weak that it's not very useful for much of anything except picking off archers who are very high.  This is useful, but just niche.  If you have your own archers with you, you can ignore it.  But if you get a certain rune, there's a charged version of the basic arrow that has no arc and pierces through all enemies in a line.  That one does way more damage, and is really useful.  The fire pots are both fun and funny and really useful, get those quick.  I feel like the oil pots and fire arrows are kind of redundant, but maybe I'm lacking imagination.  The javelins are quite good for hard targets that you need to stay back from a bit.  Unlike what some have suggested, they are not an instant-win solution.  I feel like the core quad of double-attack, charged arrow, fire pot, and javelin makes for a really interesting moveset, and that's something that expands through the first three or four levels.For my actual soliders, I pretty much just build them when I need them to defend, or when I run into a wall where I need them to attack.  A single battering ram or catapult along with a horde of other mixed soldiers provides a lot of outgoing damage and cover, and it feels good to be in the mix of them.  Having some shamans around to heal makes your own gates stay up more when you're not there, so you don't have to babysit.I sat down to just play a bit of this game the first night, and wound up getting thoroughly hooked through way more content than I intended to.  My second night with it, I just wanted to play a tad more, and I wound up getting hooked through like twice as much as I planned.  This rarely happens for me, so I really feel that's high praise.Given the nature of just how fun this is, but the fact that it might only be about 10 hours long, I can see how some folks would be frustrated wanting more.  I also think that the opportunities to "do it wrong" in terms of how you play, and then have a bad time, are higher than ideal.  If you're running around just regular-attacking everything and using regular arrows, and have not maxed out your production buildings, it must indeed be a grind fest.  If you focus on the things I've been mentioning all review, then there's not a grind, and you're in for a good time.  It's one of those rare cases where I wished a game gave players a bit less freedom (to shoot themselves in the foot).I've been playing on Steam Deck, and have not seen any bugs.  However, there is like 20 seconds of pure black screen when you launch the game, no throbber or anything, so it can seem like the game isn't properly starting when you launch it.  Just as a heads up.TLDR, based on how I've been playing the game, I haven't had any real complaints other than the black screen wait on startup.  But I can see traps that other players with different styles might fall into.  It's a quite good game, and worth it if you understand what you're in for when you actually start it.  If I had a magic wand, in the future I would love to see things like more runes, more levels, a cash in with runes I have no room to equip into something else, and so on.  I could see this as being something I come back to either every 4-5 years just for the fun and flow of the combat in its current state, or more frequently if the other elements are added.

_childDocuments_.review: You are a viking on a journey to find your beloved Raya, lay siege to England in search of her.If you're a fan of Kingdom: Two crowns, it is not too dissimilar in terms of building and resource management (though its a bit more complex than that, various resources such as money, wood and food are needed), aside from some minor things such as there are points you can build as opposed to gradually expanding. As well as a variety of different types of troops you can recruit: Various melee troops, healers, siege weapons to break through walls more easily, You can even join in on fighting as well! There is a sort of rogue-like mechanic that is explained before you even begin the game proper of - if you die - you will lose one of your Runes (A power up for various things such as buffing troops, your walls/camps, and even yourself).The campaign is good, my only real complaint about it is that the voice acting for the two "protagonists" seem to be very inexperienced compared to the rest of the cast. This becomes obvious with every boss dialogue, or they are at least new to VAing compared to the rest, which sometimes broke my immersion.There is another two modes called "Raya's Escape" and "Horde Mode", the first is, in essence, Raya escaping in a canon manner to the main campaign's narrative, though it is incredibly brief and quite easy to beat. If anything I wish there was more complexity and it was longer, though I understand why its so brief due to the canon of the story. Throwing waterskins to put out lightsources so you can hide more easily in the shadows and pots you can throw to gain the attention of guards elsewhere is good, but again, it feels too short-winded and I feel it could've just been put into the main campaign as a sort of "break" from going full on Viking mode instead of a new mode, unless the devs intend to expand and add more levels to it somehow, even if it means getting canonically caught trying to escape elsewhere anyways.Depending on your difficulty, (I started on normal first), bosses are initially quite tough, especially if you don't pay attention to their move sets, though once you've gotten powerful enough yourself, they become relatively easy, I even beat the final boss of the game first try on normal difficulty, though plan to replay the game on the hardest difficulty (Which unless I'm wrong, you don't get an achievement for. I'd ask the Devs to add this for "bragging rights" in the future and something to encourage people to replay the game on higher difficulty for replay value).Finally, Horde mode is pretty fun, you have only one camp for a total of 6 building spots, meaning you need to pick and choose your units carefully, as well as how you'll get resources to build their respective training points, their upgrades and the price to purchase them. Complete each wave and you'll get a choice of three runes, then repeat.Overall, it is quite short, but it is a good game nonetheless. It just needs a few tweaks here and there, which as of writing a lot of patches are being released, so some of the non-mentioned issues will be fixed hopefully.In summary, a good game that is a little short, though could easily be made longer with incentives to try different difficulties. Though this post may age like milk in a few months or a bit longer.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I've been waiting for Sons Of Valhala for so long and I got really excited on release day.BUT, I've been so disappointed buy the gameplay loops. The runes you attach have no palpable impact on the game feel : Your hero feels the same even if you equip all purple runes. The back and forth restock loop (for health and stamina) is a very annoying emergent gameplay. It makes the game easy and less exciting as it should be. Also, the fact that I spammed double attack for the past 3 hours means that the character needs more attack variety.I'm a big fan of Kingdom series. Of course, I was expecting something different, and it is actually the case, which is good. But it's bland and without any depht. detailed_description: Discover the legacy and embark on the journey to Amerzone. Wishlist now! Reviews Deluxe Edition The Deluxe Edition of Syberia: The World Before contains : The Soundtrack A short version of the Syberia : The World Before – Prologue script by Benoît Sokal and Lucas Lagravette The Game Fan Kit : 3 wallpapers, 3 avatars and 3 original storyboards by Benoît Sokal About the Game Unravel the intertwined fates of Kate Walker, a New-York attorney whose life was turned around by the call to adventure , and Dana Roze, a young and promising pianist in Vaghen whose career is threatened by the shadow of the Second World War A tale like no other! Embark on a magical journey through the enchanting cities of eastern Europe, both in 1937 and 2004 . Accompanied by the music of Inon Zur and the Budapest Film Symphony , piece together the puzzles that will disentangle the mysteries of two lives entwined together Carve your path across an unprecedented adventure using your wits , repair broken instruments, open tricky locks, find elaborate ways to activate mechanisms from the past , but above all watch closely your surroundings for clues The Budapest Film Symphony, led by the internationally acclaimed composer Inon Zur (Prince of Persia, Dragon Age, Fallout…) created a sublime score , and interpreted meaningful themes for the characters and locations throughout the game Syberia: The World Before is the culminating point of the late Benoit Sokal’s steampunk and wonderous universe . After the first 2 Syberia game’s in the early 2000’s, now considered Point and Click classics , and the 3rd installment of the series in 2017, Syberia is back in all its glory, with a brand new story that can be played independently and modern graphics

_childDocuments_.review: The game is harmless but enjoyable, I liked the story. Graphics were good and puzzles doable.Kate walker however  was thoroughly unlikeable for me. In the first three games she was a naive young woman bullied by her boss and her fiance but trying to get the job she was sent to do done. That changed to trying to help a dying old man. Fair enough. In this game she is overbearing, pushy, selfish, with no regard for other people's privacy or property. As for the fiance who dumped her for her best friend? He dodged a bullet because it turns out Kate is gay.They should have changed the protaganist's name because this woman is NOT Kate Walker.

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe the story would get better over time... but the gameplay is just way too anoying and slow. You need to write a letter, find something to write it with... hunt through random droors/boxes/etc... find a pencil... go to write, but get told then that it's not good enough to write a proper letter with... hunt for a quality pen! Or after an incident you're told you can't leave, not safe... you talk to your parents... they tell you to give them some space/time, you go to leave to your own room, and you're character says you can't leave till you talk with your parents.Simply put, prepare for the cases of having to find and do some contrived thing to get your character to willingly progress from an area, but your character, or those around them they listen to, despite being steadfast in not doing anything except one singular thing at that point in time... will rarely tell you or inform you in any way as to exactly what that thing is they want/are thinking. For some people with tons of time to spare, ok, click on everything twenty times, slowly walking around looking like zombies (the walk animations are pretty stiff and jerky looking), but if you want a game that respects your time and doesn't frusterate you, go play something else. If you just want a story, go read a book or watch a movie, it'll save you tons of time and probably be far more enjoyable than this was at least at the begining. Wich after such frusterating cases of it not letting me progress, but not telling me what to do, I just quick figure if that's how this games going to be I'd best stop early.So avoid if you value your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Kind of "meh" to be honest.  I will likely keep playing because I am past the refund window but I cannot say that it is worth the price of admission.  I recall the previous games being more challenging, then again, I was a child  There's not much in the way of choices, the only consequence to not rooting out every clickable is missing out on background, which is not very interesting.  The character is not that compelling, though, maybe that is just a matter of perspective.  The nat-soc party references are heavy-handed, in my opinion, and I grew up being with WWII stuff since it was a bigger deal in Eastern Europe.  I get that we have somewhat of a nazi thing going on in the states but I am not sure what if anything the references do aside from possibly alienating the nazi gamers, who I understand are plentiful.  Anyway, the story is OK, the puzzles are too easy.  So, like I said, "meh".

_childDocuments_.review: The music is superb. The story is amazing. I love history and love the sort of mystical adventures of the previous Syberia games and this one has all of it, and then some. _childDocuments_.review: The good- Sate of art visuals. Fantastic chromatic palette. Great, atmospheric lighting. Models and textures with tons of details.- Gorgeous world with lots of different areas and awesome vintage, melancholic atmosphere. It combines magically old and modern elements. Vaghen's is so beautiful with its art deco buildings along with all those touches of automatons.- Fantastic story with a lot of agony, twists and some genuine emotional moments, especially if you have played the previous games of the series. It's interesting that it takes you forth and back in time so you can play characters from various timelines.- Amazing, unforgettable characters with strong personalities and deep backstories. You'll fall in love with all of the protagonists.- Awesome music that fits perfectly the world's vintage vibes and enhances even more the atmosphere.- Great direction and photography. Nice framing, cameras' movement, editing, pacing and fantastic cut scenes. Everything is top notch. It feels like a movie.- Very natural and emotional voice acting performances.- It adds in the series puzzles that you have to closely examine mechanisms from all sides, find the right buttons and sequence of actions in order to make them work. This looks a lot like "The Room" games, although the puzzles here are easier and less complex. This concept fits perfectly with the Hans Vorarlberg's automatons world.- Realistic, rich environmental sound design that makes its world feel even more immersive.- Well designed journals with a lot of nice details surrounding the text.- No annoying pixel hunting. All the interactive points get revealed when you move the cursor near them.- By putting you in the middle of WWII it helps you taste the political situation of the era and feel how pogroms and fascism affected people's lives. I would prefer to use real names and countries though.The bad- It's much different than the rest of the series and most traditional point and click adventure games. Here, interactivity is limited in few objects and screens per chapter. It never really opens up, it doesn't encourage exploration and you don't collect so many objects in your inventory in order to creatively use them in a future puzzle. It's much more linear and looks more like an interactive movie.- Puzzles are easy and limited in solo functioned mechanisms here and there. Items in your inventory cannot get combined each other and every solution feels pretty straight forward. I expected something more imaginative.- Controlling your character with a mouse inside a fully 3d world with these angles of view can be annoying. Some objects constantly prevent you of clicking at the desired position while sometimes you don't know where to go because of facing the camera. Rotating the camera doesn't work as desired either.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a real Syberia fan. This story has been with me since the very first of the saga. I got to say that Syberia: TWB is a step forward since Syberia 3. It brought back the Syberia atmosphere that Syberia 3 lacks. And it made a good balance between a mouse and a gamepad in this genre. However, the story is a little too short and slow-paced. I'm also disappointed Automatons are everywhere, but I couldn't see Hans in the story.The music is excellent. That makes me can't wait to play the theme on my piano.The ending is a bit sad and disappointed because I was hoping to see the story end, but unfortunately, it has an open ending leaving many things to be told.There were two or three little bugs I've encountered, I had to close and restart the game to get it working, but the good thing is no game progress was ever lost.Still, Syberia 1 & 2 are my favorites of all time, and I think TWB is a must-have if you are a fan of Syberia.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a few hours in to the game at the time of this review.I'm not too sure exactly where the plot's going just yet, but the game has that same slow burn feeling that I enjoyed about the first Syberia game, and a deepening mystery that is shaping up to be great.  The art and animation are next-level, and the score is the best score of the year so far in any game I've played.On the negative side, I am experiencing some minor slowdowns and dropped frames on a few of the animations.  Also, I went back to replay a section, and I noticed that there's no way to speed up or skip scenes or dialogue in any way.If you enjoyed Syberia 3 (I liked it quite a bit!),  you are certainly going to enjoy this game.  Already, there have been some scenes that have validated the price of admission for me - the piano scene at the top of the game is phenomenal, and I am loving the beautiful historical town/mountain area I am currently in.If you hated Syberia 3, I'm not sure The World Before is going to be enough to win you over.  I suppose it would depend on the reason you didn't like it so much... but I think you should approach this game with an open mind, and give it a shot.  I also think that a series newcomer could jump in and play this game, as well - especially if the more challenging classic-style puzzles of the earlier entries weren't your thing, as The World Before is designed to be more accessible, with a stronger focus on story.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: After almost 20 years I still have vivid memories of first Syberia games with their puzzles with automats. So it was my nostalgia, which made me buy this.Overall I enjoyed the game as it was set in beautiful scenery with bittersweet story. Music had the same atmosphere so familiar from previous games. It felt rather lovely to be in the world of Syberia again.But I really missed the puzzles, they were sparse and trivial. Although I agree with the argument that this a narrative driven game, it still felt that point 'n click aspect was like an afterthought. I'm let down in this regard, so I do not give a full, excited endorsement to the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful, heartfelt journey and a proper sendoff to Benoît Sokal who sadly passed in 2021. The game is a massive improvement to Syberia 3 in every sense, and really shows off what the Unity engine is capable of. There's a distinct push for giving the story priority in this entry, but I kind of liked this shift. The puzzles are still there and you'll find secondary objectives, but they're both effective tools to keep the story moving forward this time - more so than the earlier games. Also, you can jump into this without playing those. There's a nice optional recap in the menu, available from the start.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: *Review updated after finishing the game*The original Syberia and its sequel have been some of the most memorable games for me for decades (the 3rd one was a bit of a disappointment) - and I’m really glad to see that this game once again evokes that same wonderful atmosphere and immersion as the original.The story is, I think, not quite as good/gripping as the first Syberia, and especially at first seems to verge a little bit on cliche here and there - but it’s told with lots of care and the atmosphere just pulls you in completely. Long before the halfway point, it almost becomes impossible to stop. The graphics are absolutely stunning throughout, as is the cinematography (my laptop has settings on Ultra and I’m just going ‘Oh wow!’ all the time). The music is amazing and really adds to the whole package.I loved my playthrough, and found the ending fitting and also moving (but no spoilers!) I do regret a little that there are so few puzzles - the ones we do get are quite easy to solve. The original two games were nicely challenging puzzlers, while this one is really much more of an interactive narrative. It succeeds in that very well, though (especially the time-shifts work very well), so it’s just a different approach. I personally enjoyed the puzzle challenges, but still really enjoyed this game for its different approach.Overall, this is a truly beautiful game, full of atmospheric immersion, and definitely a tribute to the Syberia franchise and the late Benoit Sokal. Definitely recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game. It's a slow-paced adventure game, with focuses more on the story rather than the gameplay (there are puzzles, don't worry). If you enjoy stories about love/death/family in exotic and atmospheric locations including mechanical devices, in a era resembling WW1, then you'll probably like this game. Take your time, enjoy the dialogues, scenery and (sometimes long) cutscenes, and let the game take you to a new journey. Mouse controls are good too (not like the previous Syberia which I stopped playing because of the controls).

_childDocuments_.review: I have never played Syberia's previous games despite knowing about them and being an adventure fan. It is hard to say why I never did, but probably because I considered them "slow" when I was younger. It is not necessary to have played the previous games, thankfully, but it did mean that it took me about an hour to really get into Kate Walker as a protagonist, while Dana Roze was immediately appealing. Syberia - The World Before is also a "slow game", although neither of those words a perfect descriptions of the experience. The world of Syberia wants to be discovered and marveled at and thankfully there is a lot to marvel at. The graphics are simply beautiful and the parallel universe version of Europe with Automatons is generally a joy to look at and listen to. Really, really well done presentation.As for the "game" part, well, there is interaction at least. But when the player is not trusted in guiding a tiny rodent automation from point A to B without locking any other input other than the "up arrow/button", I get the feeling that the designers wanted to create a gorgeous, but non-interactive movie experience instead. Regardless of whether your input of choice is keyboard and mouse or gamepad (as for me), the gameplay portion is always clunky with some invisible walls, Kate/Dana getting stuck at dust specks or the camera POV changing and the character awkwardly changing directions mid-walk. The balance of designers to programmers seemingly was heavily shifted towards the former with this one.But enough lamentation, as I did nevertheless greatly enjoy the game for its engrossing story (even if the real-world counterparts of the dark side of history hit hard at times) and mostly sympathetic characters (aside from  who lived  as a spoiled brat; and the quasi-Nazis, obviously). The story reveals were telegraphed, red-herring'ed and then deus ex machina'd again, but that did not distract from its appealing nature. The game was about Dana more than Kate and Dana's story was simple, but also touching, human and interesting. I enjoyed Kate's sections as well, but Dana's were just a bit more interesting to the story overall.If they make another one, I am very much inclined to play (and hopefully enjoy) that one as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: This game is wonderful. It brings back memories for the first three games. I read the forums on the "lesbian" aspect presented, I didn't see it that way, I saw it as an unconditional love (like what we have for friends or family), so take that as you interpret it. I loved every bit of this game. The puzzles, the story line, the new introduction of something not just on Hans Voralberg (likely misspelled) and his creations, but involving Kate's life, her own identity and who she is as a person. I loved seeing her story connect in this way, we only know a little bit on her throughout the other games. Here we get to see her become so completely changed with what her life is and her identity of who she is, what she is now living for and a full circle for her character development. I actually teared up, and paused the game to have some happy cries throughout the game just from the way this hit my memory and the intensity of the story's plot. I recommend this game for anyone who has already played the other games, and who are interested in a wonderful story and plot to follow. Gameplay is a point and click, you can use keyboard for parts, but it is a calm game play with a perfection of decisions.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is yet another masterpiece of a brilliant series.The menu provides a video with the background story of the previous games, but I really recommend playing all of them. The first two games will enchant you, the third game is strongly debated, but it's good in my opinion too (despite clunkiness).So. The story in the first game begins with the selling contract of a well established quality automaton factory in the french alps, background family drama and a further journey of our lawyer Kate Walker. This game, too, has a strong focus on automatons and fine machinery. The beginning picks Kate up at the Siberian "salt mine", where she is held captive and parallely shows us the story of a young woman from the 1930s. Along Kates journey we get Oscar back and their humor & friendship is still perfect.All in all "Syberia: The World Before" is a magnificent game, with puzzles and exploration as in the previous games. It supports five audio languages (well performed) and 12 subtitle languages. The graphics are stunning, the soundtrack and the story are beautiful.If you loved the previous Syberia games, you will love this one. If you love automaton mechanisms, puzzles and atmosphere, you will love it too.

_childDocuments_.review: This is truly an amazing game Tragic, but rich, where the destinies and notes of the Wagen anthem are unusually intertwined with unique and original characters and incredible events.Yes, the plot rules the show here. This is the story you want to hear to the end. You sincerely empathize with these characters, you believe these feelings, you understand their actions and behavior. And the main one - the Path. You'll understand what I mean.Of course, a monumental work by B. Sokal.The remaining components of the game honorably stand up to the standard of quality - incredibly beautiful landscapes, a unique graphic style, the way the novel is told, organic puzzles and mechanisms, the absence of annoying characters (even Oscar behaves moderately and gently, fitting perfectly into the plot), and, of course, the music from maestro Inno Zur, as the leitmotif of this story.In loving memory of Benoit Sokal. To the Creator who 'invented' an amazing world.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who binge-played all previous game in the past few months, I can assure you STWB is a perfect ending for the franchise, and probably their best work.   This game gets under the surface of Kate's character and give you a deeper, more intimate view on her psyche. The story takes you on a journey that can seem pretty far from the first three, but which still deeply feels like a Syberia game.  The OST is incredible, the game is beautiful and the town you navigate in is charming.   The only thing I disliked is the autosave system : you can't reaccess past scenes, so if you're going for an all achievement run like I did, I'd advise you to backup your save regularly.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game on so many levels. It has the look and feel of the original game. When the first Syberia was released, the graphics were good compared the many other games of the time. This game is like sweet eye candy with the many colors, variety of textures and mechanical designs employed throughout.Kate is a thoughtful but flawed character written so well is this chapter, I easily connected with her feelings and dilemmas. Oscar sounded a bit like C3PO, but I truly like his role in this story, as the cute little automaton instead of the android-like robotic sidekick.The Hint system was helpful, although the puzzles were not impossibly difficult to solve. The puzzles fell into line with the story which I thought was appropriate.The story starts off slow, setting the stage, but then evolves into a heart warming saga with compelling plot twists and turns, spanning two generations. After playing for 10 hours I truly didn't want this game to end, while simultaneously dying to know how it would end. I enjoyed it that much. I'm so sorry for the passing Benoit Sokal. The dedication of this game to him warmed my heart. The creators and designers made a wonderful game to remember him by. I will replay this game again, only more slowly, fully exploring the immersive world they created here. I highly recommend this game, which is much more than a game. Its an experience and a well designed one at that.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, this game perfected everything the Syberia franchise stands for: the story, the art style and the machine tinkering puzzles. _childDocuments_.review: Syberia the world before is a fantastic game! A masterpiece in story telling, characters, landscapes and music. The story in STWB is a simple personal story of a woman seeking another person, there are no big stakes, or "save the world" plot. Just life. The life of the characters, that can unfolds while Kate Walker continues her journey. It is so interesting to experience a game about simple people, living extraordinary life. It reminds the gamer that life itself can be an adventure, you don't need to be Kratos, or Drake, or Lara. Life has mosters, villains and heros. I really hope Microids make a sequel, since there is so much more potential! Beautiful game, really enjoyed it, nice puzzles. I experienced no bugs.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: The writers of Syberia have outdone themselves with this game. They create these beautiful, intricately-woven and connected stories filled with heart. The environments they create are beautiful, sometimes haunting, ambient and immersive. A fantastic series for true adventure-lovers and this last chapter really outshone them all.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic game that show a great evolution of the adventure genre. The story is captivating and well written, even if the beats are expected they still hit emotionally hard. The story is supported by outstanding voice actors that help suspend disbelief in the alternate reality world created. Speaking of the world, the world building and design is evocative - I spent ages just looking at the city of Vaughan. The puzzles and gameplay were modern and mostly well-executed (I encountered some bugs that marred an otherwise highly-polished game). No puzzle was overly confusing or obtuse. Overall, an outstanding game that makes me positive of the adventure genre and hoping for Syberia 5!
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very inspiring story of a woman who knew she had a past in near Switzerland and finds out she looked like a talented woman there. It goes all the way back to world war and traces her past. You go on all sorts of adventures from the beginning fighting soviets captured and off to her quest. It was so neat and made put your thinking cap on to figure out the puzzles to fix things or get clues to her past. She interacts with Oscar who's like her best friend like a pet dog who can speak. Sadly at the end you found out the person responsible for this wonderful game is no longer with us, so I guess the quest of Kate Walker ends without knowing she ever met her real grandmother, but I'm guessing she does. I wish this company made more of this quality and amazing inspirational game.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: I played previous games in my childhood and many times after. They have their quirks and cranks, over-the-top kitch moments, and some fairytale silliness. Ochi chornye, snow ostriches, and whatnot.  But they always abided the same spirit: a story of genius and creativity, a lesson of following a dream to the end and beyond. The fourth and final game should have been the brightest peak of this route... or at least a gracious and respectful wrapping to it.But it is not. And it is way worse than just "not enough" or "not quite so". "The World Before" atrociously betrayed the memory of Benoît Sokal and the whole world of Syberia. In every possible way except most of graphics and music. Inon Zur did an amazing job unlike the writers, his music tells another, much better story. Vaghen is pretty and clean (I recognize dreams of fellow parisians), but it. is. the.  explorable location in the game about distant voyages. Slow pacing cinematic gameplay is not bad, fresh even (though dear Oscar is badly revived and horribly misused), but again - what story does it serve?Syberia was about a genius inventor and the dream of his life. And, of course, about Kate, walking this path with him and learning how to chase her own destiny independently instead of being a soulless "automaton" of society (shown through new york job and relations). She learns how to be alive, just as Hans animates his creations. In this regard, it somewhat reminds the story of Pinocchio, enriched by the artistic and musical talent of creators.And "prequel"... is about nazis, bigfoots and piano player. It starts in a labor camp and ends in ruins of logic and emotions. The excruciating birth of Kate's destiny during three games and her countless adventures and trials all result in her leading to the cold and wild "Tibetan" forest to meet an 85-year-old woman slowly dying in the company of semi-intelligent hairy yetis. The only connection is that she is her grandmother who all her life didn't even know that she has a daughter. Thus, Kate either buries her and stays there, possibly mating with yeti, or just returns home - herself dead inside, completely ruined and without any purpose at all. These are the only possible conclusions because a forest full of yeti-cities and "unexpected" Voralberg inventions (like the "new train") would be even worse.Who and how could have decided that the best scenario for an ultimate Syberia is a game not about Kate, not about Voralbergs, not about automatons, but a completely unrelated person the only traits of whom being that she is Jewish and, like, plays piano really well? How come the final of the series about creativity and visionary minds tells a grim and most mundane story about WWII, with deaths and losses on every step, full of soap-opera style "romantic" plots and the same soap-taste characters? Instead of becoming a human boy, Pinocchio decides to burn himself in the fireplace because Geppetto's  had an affair with a Fox, and wise Cricket became her drug dealer. What?I have a strong suspicion that the script was originally written for completely another game (or movie) - a story about fascists and "pogroms", Jewish refugees, and some distant nation instead of yetis. The evidence for this is the seams between this story and Syberia - they are very visible, rough, and plain insulting. First is "Katyusha": to push Kate Walker into WWII drama, her sudden lesbian friend from a Russian gulag finds a portrait of some girl resembling her. And instantly dies. Thus, Kate "just has to" search for this girl instead of, you know, returning to Aralbad for papers? Finishing her duty in Valadilene? Raising youkis in Komkolzgrad? Pretty anything would be better. Then Kate abruptly moves to some new town, skipping at once all "unimportant" Syberia part and remains pretty non-existent until the very end, being a mere listener for someone else's story. Katyusha, by the way, does not even appear in "dream" form (that she does before) when said girl is finally found. And here the second "seam", even more protruding: Walker founds she has a grandmother (not Voralberg at all, just some unrelated piano player) and returns to America... but wait, it is a Syberia game! Suddenly the train-ex-machina appears, built by  and existing because of , but looking the same as That Train, you know, for fans' sake.This game ruins Syberia moral, Syberia spirit and even Syberia atmosphere. It destroys Kate's character and her whole arc. The grand finale could not care less about Syberia. What remains, reminds of the city after the Brown Shadow invasion: deserted, wasted, desecrated without all and any respect to the origins. Playing classic games, I will instead think of smoking bigfoot and his human girlfriend that sold her friends to nazis because of contrived jealousy. , eh?

_childDocuments_.review: I am grateful to have been gifted this journey—a beautiful, moving journey I will remember for the rest of my life. Elegantly, Syberia blends history with mystique, setting the reality of World War II within a fantastic, clockpunk version of Europe. Everything is mechanised and wonderfully Art Nouveau—plant motifs set in metalwork bring about a dream-like world. Combined with emotive, instrumental soundtrack by Inon Zur, it is easy to feel as if soaring above the clouds. Unfettered.Great taste in artistry goes hand in hand with mature writing. Syberia’s story is fraught with touching, human moments. There is an omnipresent sense of wonder and gratitude for everything which makes life nicer. It is optimism as it ought to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: The story by Lucas Lagravette will break your heart and move you to tears, and at the same time it’s not too gloomy or banal. There’s also a lot of space for charming humor. Music by Inon Zur is already a hallmark of the "Syberia" series, and in the fourth part it’s at a very high level - I recommend playing with headphones! The new "Syberia" changes the approach to the story. The way of storytelling is more modern here, we move from scene to scene, which gives the game dynamics (this is the first "Syberia", which could be easily transformed into a novel - and I would love to see it). Kate gains a lot of psychological depth and  for me. But you should pay attention to all characters - starting with Dana Roze, of course. They’re all well written, so you can care about their fate - even when it comes to side characters (Rector Mahler, you’re my idol).You can find critical voices regarding the change of historical events, shown in the game - a new country appears between Germany and Switzerland, the Nazis are called “The Brown Shadow” here. I don't consider it a problem. Just look - this way  The war was an excuse to show the tragic fate of the individual, and setting the plot in a fictional country allowed to create this sleepy, addictive atmosphere “Syberia” is known from. I also have to mention the end.  I just couldn't imagine a better ending. I’ve been a fan of this series since I was 6 years old. I spent my whole life with it. Kate's journey is the biggest metaphor and the greatest desire for me. And so  I have a great hope that soon we’ll see part 5, because Benoit Sokal's team proved that they perfectly understand the world of "Syberia" and they’re can create
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: Different from the previous games but personally the change was needed, we saw what happend with the 3rd game. The story was really touching, i like how the main focus changed to Kate and her story, not the myth of Syberia anymore, and the connection with WW2 made it easy to connect with the characters, comparing with what happend in real life.I only have two complain: - lack of puzzle, even if the little that where present where good in my opinion (the plaza one was the best imho)- too many cutscene, more interaction with the characters would have been better than sitting there listening for hours to dialogsOverall a really cute game, better than the previous one, but not at the level of the first.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm conflicted. The story is so good! If you like visual novels, you'll love the story. But the gameplay is so bad, so un-fun, that it actually interferes with the experience. I would have preferred to just click "next" through the whole story and watch all those beautiful scenes, over what I ended up having to do: walk around endlessly in cramped spaces with bad controls, trying to find the exact spot I had to stand to be able to click on a tiny hotspot (often these are presented as white dots against a white or hazy background) so I could read something barely relevant to the plot. Or worse, solve a puzzle so easy it doesn't even count as a "puzzle," just a confusing series of slow motions I had to make in order to open or move some inane item. The gameplay was infuriating and made the game take much, much longer than it should have. I played all the way through to the end, and that's a testament to the wonderful writing and beautiful art design of this game. I wish they had invested as much in user experience as they did in creating an inspiring story.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: It's a walking simulator, not a single hint about great predecessors. Puzzles are supper dumb, like move this left and another thing right. All gameplay, and this is not an exaggeration, all game play is based on:  find an active circle with your mouse, click it and watch time wasting scene. So basically, it’s a walking simulator with point and click mechanics. In addition, cut scenes and dialogues can’t be skipped, and that’s understandable, cos the game doesn’t have content at all, so all you have to do is watch dull cutscenes and listen to same quality dialogues. So as walking simulator I give this game 10/10, as a Syberia franchise 2/10. Huge disappointment.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: First thing first, I must clarify that it would be hard to view this game as a sequel of the Syberia franchise.. It doesn't own the hardcore puzzles like other episodes. All puzzles are quite simple, and that makes it a walking-sim and visual novel. The tone of the game has been changed fundamentally, previous Syberia games feel like either sci-fi or fantasy, the world is totally based on imagination. But this one is a work of realism, its genesis is based on the real history, it is still a fiction, but we can recognize many elements that are from our world, such as Starbucks. The World Before owns a splendid story, it would be our first time to get into Kate Walker's life , to understand her past, her family, and her friends. In other words, Kate is alive in this episode, she finally owns a full soul and personality. the other MC Dana, is also well imaged, and players will be touched deeply by their fate.you will follow two girls' adventure that cross 70 years to reveal a compelling story happens in a crucial moment in the history, plus with the beautiful music,The World Before presents us a different level of storytelling compared with it's predecessors.  The double story lines provide a unique and creative interaction between the MCs, in other words, Kate can reenact what Dana did through props like her paints, diaries, photos and historical documents. Such a interaction that beyond time is essential for players to solve all kinds of puzzles in this game. So, if you are a story lover like me, if you want an emotional  journey, this will be your game. But if you take the hardcore puzzles as the essential, you would be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished game. Great story, acting, sound, set pieces. Can tell the devs wanted to make up for the awful last syberia game. _childDocuments_.review: A great addition to the series.I applaud the story telling along every step a long the way in Kate Walkers Journey to discover the truth about herself, Dana Rose and the bonds of family.As we toggle to and fro between the two characters we get an up close and personal introduction of each character. There is a lot of beautiful scenery, ample lighting and site seeing.(((((( SPOILER ALERT )))))))The only one problem after all that emotional roller coaster is, at the very end we turn into a liar as we are left with no choice not to return to New York. _childDocuments_.review: Well this was a ride, I think I went through every single emotion known to human existence. In short, the game is beautifully created, the art work stunning, the story telling for the most part was on point though it did get a little flat in some places,  I do feel this is subjective however and down to the individual.  If you're not into politics/war then you might get a bit meh about it.The game play is straightforward with only a couple of annoyances, moving around at times was a little clunky but it was minor and only on occasion. Objectives and puzzles to clear were not too taxing on the brain so all in all the whole experience  ran smoothly and enjoyably.  It took me around 17 hours to play, purely because I like to take my time looking around and appreciating all the work that's put into creating such amazing graphics, and it was well worth that time.  10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Syberia: The World Before

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't really an easy game to review for me. Part of me wanted to love it, and there's definitely some great stuff in here; however, I did also feel that some stuff wasn't done exactly right, and part of it was a little bit annoying. The story is quite nice (albeit a bit cliched and quite predictable), but while I was playing it, I found myself thinking how it would make a better movie, many times over. I think there are a few reasons for that. - For starters, the game isn't what you would expect from playing the other games; it's more realistic, much less fantastical (in contrast to the others), and yet it still has some stuff that makes zero logical sense (with the biggest one probably being the actual reason that kick-starts the whole adventure, right after the prologue). It's way less Syberia-esque, and still it's full of references to the previous games, characters and locations. The tone of the story is way darker and more mature (including dead bodies, murder, and general war-related violence), and yet it has some stuff that would only appear believable to children. It is kind of an odd (and a bit of a contradictory) mix. And in spite of all that, it's still really enjoyable. I can't say I had a bad time playing it. I think it definitely stands out among most adventure games, so any fan of this genre should totally check this out. But the reason behind it definitely isn't found on the gameplay: - Puzzle-wise, most puzzles are very much on the easy side, and while they aren't your typical adventure game kind of puzzles, they still feel very much like a chore, quite a few times. The characters are still very hard to maneuver, even with the recent patch that supposedly tackled that issue (admittedly, I think it has improved, but it was still a pain). I think it has improved on that from Syberia 3 (not really an accomplishment xD), but they did remove the possibility of using the arrows to move them, and I think that may have helped, paradoxically. I'd suggest trying a controller out; I've played with mouse and keyboard, and it could get quite annoying xD. Another aspect that would have made a big difference is the ability to skip cut-scenes, dialogs, and interactions. For example, if you hit a hot-spot once, sometimes you'll see a close-up of several things on the scene, or hear comments from your character; now, if you hit it again, it repeats the exact same thing; this wouldn't be a problem if the sequence lasted 1 or 2 seconds, but it can take up to 10 to regain control of the character and be able to move on. You'll learn not to try hot-spots more than once, but on this day and age, I think it's surprising a skipping mechanic isn't implemented. Another thing is the save-system; It's not an usual pet-peeve of mine, and it wasn't awful here, especially once you got the hang of it, but having manual saves available would have also been nice. In any case, most of the time (with the exception of when you get stuck on a puzzle) will be spent watching various cut-scenes. And this is actually a good thing:- The art, the scenery, the voice acting and sound design, they are all amazing, gorgeous and fantastic. Animations are quite nice too. However, since much of the game is spent just sitting and watching, I kept finding a hard time not comparing it to some modern animated films. In that respect:- All these things combined are what lead me to believe that gameplay gets a little bit in the way of the story, and that it may have actually worked better as a movie or mini-series, rather than as a game. Somehow I feel that there were some missed opportunities to make the player more actively involved (maybe making more decisions for example), and thus exploit the "game" aspect a lot more. With that in mind, I do think this game would probably make a hell of a good watch on youtube for people wanting to see it xD.- However, even when not everything here is perfect, it's hard not to recommend such a well-crafted game; the love is there, the art is amazing, and it is definitely a great addition to the franchise. If there's a sequel, I'll definitely be there to check it out in the future (and I hope there will be). P.S.: pay no attention to my playtime, it should be around 15 hours. I'm having a very weird issue with Steam (it may be related to Unity, because it started while I was playing a game before this one, but that was also made in Unity), where my connection died every time I started playing this (a few minutes later). So basically, it failed to register my playtime correctly.

_childDocuments_.review: My score for this game: 10 out of 10.The whole series are so heart-piercingly beautiful, it's unbeliveable somebody tried to make something so subtle and refined nowadays.The style reminds of dynosaurs (or hairy mammoths?) which are extinct.The last journey of Kate is clearly an allusion to the life of not-very stable young woman.Strange charming tiny towns in the middle of Europe are obviously dreams of safe places which are always so elusive.Constant stream of mechanical puzzles thrown in the way are reflections of incessant struggles everyone has to overcome in her life.Talking to Oscar, her own mechanical companion, is a clear sign of mental troubles.Lastly, everything around, gradually deteriorating and decaying, is a very convincing image of the life itself.I love this hardcore level of depression, guilt and sliding to madness, because we all have this in us.This game itself is the last survivor of those barren frozen lands, there will be nothing like this anymore.Thank you, Benoit Sokal.

_childDocuments_.review: The worst part of engaging with postmodernist fiction is that you end up seeing the same thing over and over because of the author's need to convey an idea, feeling like they didn't get it exactly right and restarting again.Starting The World Before after Syberia 3 you'd be forgiven for thinking that Microids learned on their mistakes. The main character underwent a radical change of appearance and is fostering a relationship with an actual non-mechanical human person that is able to reciprocate. She is suffering unfairly albeit predictably the realistic consequences of her actions. Growth of characterisation? In a Benoit Sokal game? Nevermind, it's just a pretext to kickstart another wild goose chase. Can I go back to the cool Kate Walker that has a punk girlfriend? But no, it will be all over soon, we will be back to default looks, default behaviours, default (by now) Syberia experience. Kate Walker isn't allowed to stop for a second and reflect on her selfdestructive tendencies - a thing the game's writing highlights, but doesn't elaborate on. Lampshading cannot replace character development or storywriting.The parallel plot is probably the better thing to happen to the franchise, but even then it's uninspiring. Every once in a while you would think "I can see where this is going and it would be pretty cool if they subverted the expectation here, went somewhere else instead" and suddenly they do and it feels refreshing. Then it's all messed up when they reveal that the original guess was the correct one anyway, we come back on track. The game attempts to bring up serious adult subjects, but doesn't commit in favour of magic realism. Good job pretending to make bold statements, but instead doing a by-the-numbers story.The game controls extremely sluggishly. The movement is glacial and you will be terrified of exploration for fear of loss of time. You still need to align the character perfectly, you will still get stuck. The camera is still semi-fixed and the logic of where it is pointing bends itself to no one. Silent Hill came out 23 years before this game, why is this still happening? It's not cinematic, people have enough controls for both movement of character and camera, we don't need to hide ugly skyboxes and lack thereof nowadays. Maybe I want to look at things. The game is actually pretty when it doesn't lag or stutter. The voice acting is better than before, actually mixed correctly, but there are obvious gaps in directing, you will hear the same person switching back and forth between "sanatorium" and "sanitarium" within the same dialog and different actors cannot agree on how they pronounce names. The accents are terrible. The delivery is competent, but obviously everyone is bringing different energies into a conversation.All the adventure game tinkering devolved into following a straight path and occasionally solving something akin to puzzle boxes from The Room franchise (but not nearly as complex). If you are stuck on something it's because you cannot do it right now, not because you cannot figure it out.The story ends in a sequel hook as if the writers have anything left to say, but Kate Walker really is doomed to send elderlies to the mammoths, get in trouble with authorities, help defenceless caricatures while astounding locals with her behaviour in an endless cycle, and talking to an automaton that isn't a real character, but a surrogate for the conversations inside her head. And the cowards can't even give us the cool haircut with blue dye for more than 15 minutes.

_childDocuments_.review: What a wonderful story! Absolutely recommend this game.Syberia The World Before is the 4th game in the Syberia series. It is a point and click game but can be played entirely with a controller. The story follows the events of the 3rd game. While a recap is provided in the main menu, i highly encourage you to play Syberia and Syberia 2 in order to experience first hand the journey of Kate Walker. Visually the game is beautiful, with great looking characters and places. The music and voice acting are great and truly convey the emotion the characters are feeling. The narative itself is excellent with great dialogue and a very fullfilling story.The gameplay is that of a point and click game, where puzzles need to be solved in order to progress the story. The puzzles themselves are all based in logic, and therefore there are no crazy combinations that would require you to consult a walkthrough, which is a very welcome change in my opinion.All in all i greatly enjoyed my time with Syberia - The World Before and look forward to the continuation of the story with the next game.P.S: Bravo to everyone involved with the game! RIP mr Benoit Sokal.

_childDocuments_.review: What an incredible return for my favorite adventure series! Such beautiful presentation, story, music, and gameplay. It's just amazing how the whole game turned out. This is such a glorious return for Syberia.But to give an idea on what the experience is. Kate Walker returns as the lead again in pursuit of another mystery of the old world. But this time the crux of the journey is more personal for her. The gameplay improves what Syberia 3 started. A point-and-click game that works well with a controller. But here the controls doesn't deter from the mouse and keyboard experience like how it did in Syberia 3, in my opinion. Puzzles are logical and are easy enough to handle if you can grasp the logic the game world establishes all throughout the game world.Next up I suppose is the outstanding presentation. This game is definitely a looker. I'd also say that it's a hallmark of the Unity engine's graphics capability. I hope you can run the game at ultra graphics preset. But the game uses the graphics tech well with incredible "cinematography". Clever camera shots, well acted & written scenes, and beautiful music all work in tandem to play out this emotional story. Also, shoutout to Inon Zur and the rest of the music team. This soundtrack is a dream. I'm also just astounded at how great this game's story is.Delving into why the story is astounding would just ruin it with spoilers. But again I'm astounded at how they manage to evolve Kate Walker and Syberia's story and world from the previous games into this game. At first it was weird to turn it into a personal story. But the more the game played it out the more I realized how clever and how well they used the previous games with this new story.I've been very vague and somewhat flowery with the language in this review. But the game has genuinely pulled at my heartstrings and left me glad that I experienced this game, like how I wish adventures would do so. This game will stay with me for a long time, I think. And I think this game has a set a high bar for me when it comes to adventure games now. I dare say this might even be my favorite game of the year for 2022.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a beautiful adventure game. I didn't finish it.This is a part of an old franchise but it feels very detached from it. From what I've seen the plot is not connected to the first three games, though the heroine is the same. Initially, it looks like a modern walking simulator, but there are some actual puzzles there. Most importantly there are beautiful environments, mainly old European city landscapes and insane clockwork contraptions. On the other hand, characters look like they're from a different graphical era. Maybe it's an unfortunate attempt at stylization, but any time a character emotes on the screen it took me out of the experience.Another thing that took me out of the experience is the story. It didn't grab me and there are some questionable things in it. MC motivation is alien to me, and the background story is just strange. Apparently this is alternate history, but only in parts. USSR fought WW2 against German fascists, and these German fascists hated a certain ethnicity. Only the party is not the one you think of, they have a different symbol, and the ethnicity is a fantasy ethnicity in addition to the game happening in a fictional European Country, but at the same time, a lot of real countries and people active in WW2 are mentioned. It's bizarre! But not in an entertaining way, it's just confusing.The puzzles are simple and boring, the cutscenes are long and aren't as fascinating as they should be to make me care. The music and the environment were great, but they weren't good enough to make me finish the game.
